# DEDICATION,

### TO THE

## God-fearing, Zealous, and Truth-loving Practitioners of Godliness.

->*Pious Practitioners,*<-

<margin>* Andrade, Book 2, *Defense of the Council of Trent*; Peter Canisius, *Manual*, Chapter 22.</margin><note>These references are to prominent Counter-Reformation Catholic theologians, Diogo de Paiva de Andrade and Peter Canisius, whom the author intends to refute regarding the authority of the Bible.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'O' featuring a bird (possibly a pelican or phoenix) in a central circular frame, surrounded by dense floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc> Among all the testimonies that the Men of God give regarding the **Holy Scripture**, by no means the least, but indeed one of the foremost, is *Paul's* testimony in *2 Timothy 3, verse 16*, saying: *All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.* In these words, the Apostle first provides a declaration of from whom the Scripture originates: from God. This speaks plainly against many of the <term>Papist teachers</term><note>A common 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholic theologians, used here in a polemical context to distinguish Reformed theology from Catholic tradition.</note>, * who write that there is nothing "Divine" within the Books of Scripture themselves that could make us believe their content, but rather that the Church alone possesses that power. That the value of the Scripture is to be judged according to the opinion of the Church is proven false by the Apostle when he says, *All Scripture is given by inspiration of God*, agreeing with the Apostle Peter in *2 Peter 1: 20, 21*: *Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the Scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.* This, the **Reformed Christians** hold as a foundation of their faith. 

But *Paul* goes even further in the previously mentioned words and shows for what purpose the Scripture is useful: Namely, for *Doctrine*, because within it are contained all those points of teaching which are necessary for our life and <term>Blessedness</term><note>Original Dutch: "Geluksaligheydt." A term combining happiness, prosperity, and eternal salvation.</note>; a teaching concerning God and His Service; teachings without which we remain unlearned. Indeed, without the knowledge of the same, no one shall enter into life: (*John 17:3*) for, *This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.* Besides this, the Scripture serves for *Reproof* of all those who contradict its truth and set themselves against it; for *Correction*, that is, for the conversion and faith of those who have wandered from the right way of truth and life; for no one, wandering from the Truth, can be set right and shown the path of salvation except from and according to the Scripture, which many passages and examples therein sufficiently demonstrate to us. Finally, the Scripture serves for *instruction in righteousness*, which...

He outlines the fourfold utility of the Bible—doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction—as essential for the "practitioner of godliness."</summary>

That the value of the Scripture is to be judged according to the opinion of the Church; the Apostle proves the contrary when he says, *All Scripture is given by inspiration of God*, agreeing with the Apostle Peter, *2 Peter 1:20-21.* *Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the Scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.* The Reformed Christians <note>The "Gereformeerde Christenen" refers to followers of the Dutch Reformed Church, the state-supported Protestant denomination in the Netherlands at this time.</note> hold this as a foundation of their faith: but *Paul* goes yet further in the previously mentioned words, and shows to what purpose the Scripture is useful: Namely, for *Doctrine*, for therein are contained all those points of Teaching which are necessary for us for life and Blessedness; a Doctrine concerning God and His Service; Teachings without which we are not truly taught. Indeed, without the knowledge of the same no one shall enter into life: (*John 17:3*) for, *This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.* In addition to this, the Scripture serves for *Reproof*, of all those who speak against its truth and set themselves against it; For *Correction*, that is, for the conversion and faith of those who have wandered from the right way of truth and life; for, no one, wandering from the Truth, can be brought back to the right, and shown the path of salvation, except from and according to the Scripture, which points this out to us sufficiently in many places and examples; Finally, the Scripture serves for *instruction which is in Righteousness*,

> *Put to death therefore your members which are upon the earth: namely fornication, uncleanness, shameful passions, evil desire, and greed, which is Idolatry. For which things' sake the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience: In which you also once walked, when you lived in them. To this end the *Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists*, and other Men of God, as well as so many *Ancient Teachers* <note>The author refers here to the "Church Fathers," the influential theologians of the early Christian centuries.</note> in the early Church, have used the Scripture; their teachings to the ignorant, their refutations of those in error, their exhortations to conversion and faith, and their instructions in the way of Godliness sufficiently prove this—to lead men away from a wicked and scandalous life, and to make them walk after the example of Christ, in true Godliness and Holiness of life. And since the human race is so corrupted in its nature that it repeatedly steps aside from the path it must travel, the *Prophets, Apostles, Evangelists*, and other Men of God have urged these teachings for refutation, correction, and instruction, often and many times over; it is unnecessary to light a candle for this purpose, since the Sun shines so clearly. <note>This is a common 17th-century idiom meaning that the point is so obvious it requires no further proof.</note>

This current Age is no less fruitful in such Men who use the Scripture (as being inspired by God) for Teaching, Refutation, Correction, and for Instruction which is in righteousness, both in their public Sermons and published Writings. Although I do not condemn that manner of Preaching in which this is absent, nevertheless (saving the honor and reputation of so many learned and zealous Men) that is more an Oration than a Sermon, following the rules of **Rhetoric** <note>The art of persuasive speaking or fine oratory.</note> more than the **Scripture**, which desires that we shall teach, and make use of that Teaching—either for the refutation of those <term>wandering spirits</term><note>A term for heretics or those who have strayed from orthodox doctrine.</note> and errors which oppose our points of doctrine, or for correction and instruction in righteousness—presenting to men Faith, Conversion, and the renewal of Life: what these are, from whence they come, how they are received, their effects, the means to attain them, and the signs by which they may be known. In short, applying everything toward practice. This manner of Preaching is not new, first discovered or practiced a short time ago in *England* <note>The author is likely referring to the influential "Puritan" or "Practical Divinity" movement in England, which emphasized heart-felt piety and moral living, and was being adopted by Dutch Reformed ministers during the "Nadere Reformatie" (Further Reformation).</note> and blown over to us from that region by a powerful wind; no, this is the very aim of the Scripture, and for that purpose the holy Men of God used it, as was shown above. The same rule has also been followed by the highly learned <term>W. Teellinck</term> <note>Willem Teellinck (1579–1629) was a central figure in the "Dutch Second Reformation," a movement focused on personal piety.</note> and <term>G. Udemans</term> <note>Godefridus Udemans (1581–1649), another influential Dutch minister known for his writings on Christian ethics and trade.</note>, along with many others; and so many zealous men, experienced in the **Practice of Godliness**, still maintain this daily (both within this distinguished City and outside of it, and in many other places) in their public Sermons and Writings.

It is indeed true that among all **Theologians**, the English excel in this: working out their Sermons in a singular manner (concerning the exercise of Godliness). Yet even so, if they had never come to our soil, the intellect of the Dutch is also powerful and clever enough to give such Sermons and Writings to their fellow countrymen. They do not need to ship over to *England* to learn the Practice of Godliness there; their own brains (if only exercised) are capable enough (with God’s blessing) to practice this themselves. 

Yet, as so many English Divines daily speak **Dutch** <note>original: "Neder-duytsch," referring to the translations of English works into the Dutch language.</note> (I know not for what reasons) and are urged upon the Netherlanders, it seemed good to some people a few years ago to translate something by the highly learned **Mr. Christopher Love**, whether out of love for the Person, or because of his untimely Death, or because of his Honey-sweet discourses, etc. Scarcely were these writings off the Printing-presses before they were in everyone’s hands, read with great pleasure by many, and even found a place in the Study-chambers of some Scholars. This has encouraged the Translators more and more, so that finally everything that has been preached, or at least written, by this learned Man (as far as we can find) has finally been bound together into one small volume, and is now offered to the World. It is presented with the hope that it shall be received with no less zeal, desire, and passion than some previously printed pieces were accepted; the more so, as this Work contains (besides the previous 6 or 7 treatises, which were by no means the least) tracts that have never "spoken Dutch" before, and are more conveniently contained in one Book than divided into so many separate pieces.

What honor the Author has earned with these writings of his, or the Translators in their translating, or he who has thus joined them together, we leave for everyone to judge. In our opinion, this highly learned Man may well have as great a name among the Netherlanders as other English Writers (since the Dutchman indeed craves this spiritual food). For to see so many writings from a young Divine—a Man of thirty-five years, born in **Wales*** <note>original: "Wallis"</note> (an un-noble place, and of common Parents), who for fourteen years never heard a single Sermon, but in his fifteenth year was wonderfully converted by God, and who had to leave the world through an untimely death—this man, I say, deserves a place among us as much as anyone else; the more so, as there are contained here in this Work so many fundamental...

This rule has also been followed by the highly learned *W. Telingh* and *G. Udemans* <note>Willem Teellinck (1579–1629) and Godefridus Udemans (1581–1649) were founding fathers of the *Nadere Reformatie*, a Dutch movement similar to English Puritanism that emphasized personal piety.</note>, along with many others; and so many zealous men, practiced in the application of **Godliness**, still maintain it daily in their public sermons and writings (both within this distinguished city and outside it, and in many other places).

It is indeed true that among all *Theologians*, the English excel in this, working out their sermons in a singular manner (regarding the exercise of Godliness); however, even if they had never come to our soil, the intellect of the Dutch is also powerful and clever enough to provide such sermons and writings to their fellow countrymen. They do not need to ship over to *England* to learn the Practice of Godliness there; their own brains (if only exercised) are capable enough (with God’s blessing) to practice this themselves. Yet, since daily (I know not for what reasons) so many English divines speak Dutch <note>original: "Nederduytsch" (literally Low-German, the term then used for the Dutch language).</note> and are urged upon the Dutch people, some thought it good several years ago to translate something from the highly learned *Mr. Christopher Love*—either out of love for the person, or because of his untimely death, or because of his honey-sweet words, etc. Scarcely were these writings off the printing presses when they were in every man’s hands, read with great pleasure by many, and even found a place in the studies of some scholars. This has encouraged the translators more and more, so that finally everything preached—or rather written—by this learned man (as much as we can find) has finally been bound together in a small volume, and is now dedicated to the world. We hope it will be received with no less zeal, desire, and passion than the previously printed pieces were accepted; especially since this work contains, alongside the preceding six or seven (by no means the least significant) treatises, those that have never spoken Dutch <note>Meaning they have never before been translated into the Dutch language.</note> and are more conveniently contained in one book than divided into so many parts.

For, if you wish to speak of and have knowledge of a failing and **Sick Land**, when, how, and through what a Nation is weakened; as well as who can heal the same, how, and by what means this happens, read the first Sermon, delivered at *Uxbridge*, under the name of *England’s Sickness*. If you wish to go to God in holy Meditation and Godly Resolutions, see his *Devout Meditations*. If you wish to have knowledge of **Flesh and Spirit**, their conflict and operation, how you shall distinguish the movements of the Flesh and the Devil from the movements of the Spirit and Heaven, as well as how you shall Walk Blessed through the Spirit, read the *Conflict between Flesh and Spirit*. If you wish to show a Christian his duties, what he must do and leave undone, follow or shun, the following Treatise shall instruct you. All Christians, if you wish to know your conduct, how it must occur with fervor, diligence, and **holy violence** <note>A common 17th-century term for intense spiritual zeal, based on the biblical idea of "taking the kingdom of heaven by force."</note>, see the *Zealous Christian*. If you wish to speak of the Glory of Believers in the other World, of their honor and perfect happiness, with God, Angels, and Saints in Heaven, search through the *Glory of Heaven*; and on the other hand, if you wish to terrify the Godless by God’s absolute power over men, by the cruelty of the Devil, the pain and sorrow of Hell, behold the *Terrors of Hell*. If you wish to know how God chooses and calls man, the assurance of both, the signs and means to reach it; as well as the excellent comforts contained herein, seek, read, and ruminate upon, *On the Assurance of our Calling and Election*. Likewise, if you wish to speak of the Heavenly Creatures, the **Angels**, their operations in Heaven and duties upon the Earth, *The Ministry of Angels* shall inform you of this. If each of you wishes to know your conduct and manner of life, what is permitted or forbidden to you in trade, in buying and selling, turn to *A Christian's Instruction*. If you wish to know God’s Justice, whether He may rightfully punish children for the crimes of their forefathers without violating His Majesty, read the *Sinners’ Last Will* <note>original: "Sondaren Testament."</note>. Furthermore, if you wish to learn how to properly care for your heart, that precious **Jewel** in you, how you shall preserve it and not let it be stolen from you by the Devil, World, or flesh, examine *A Christian's Preservation*. If you wish to know that glorious attribute of **God’s Omnipresence**, how His All-seeing eye goes through the whole World, beholding the good and the evil, see the Treatise written on that subject. If you wish to know what sin is, the evil it works, and how it must be confessed, and what an upright confession is; and moreover, how and on

The author refers to specific sermons in this collection based on these verses.</note> And so on; all the Treatises shall give us Heavenly and excellent instructions and teachings on how we shall walk through this **Wilderness of the World**, and work out our Salvation in fear and trembling.

Therefore, Honorable and God-fearing zealots in the **Practice of Godliness** <term>Practice of Godliness: A 17th-century term for "living out" one's faith through specific spiritual disciplines and moral conduct.</term>, take up this Work; you shall never regret having read such a learned **Practitioner** <note>original: "Practizijn" — here referring to a spiritual doctor or a theologian who focuses on the practical application of faith.</note>; his style is not high-flown, but simple, sweet-flowing, and clear, in the manner of the Saints; formerly this Writer was a stranger to you, but through translation he has become your fellow countryman; house him not only in your brain, or bosom, but make room for him in a hall in your heart; he shall be a pleasant, instructive, and very profitable guest to you; and shall teach you from God’s word as much as is necessary for life, the exercise of Godliness, and Heavenly Glory: what more shall I say; one more word, and then I finish.

Many shall think, what does such a Writer concern us, who for his seditious Preaching and imprudent outbursts from the Pulpit was beheaded on **Tower Hill** <note>Christopher Love (1618–1651) was a prominent Presbyterian minister executed for his involvement in a plot to restore Charles II to the throne during the English Commonwealth.</note> by order of Parliament. Zealous Christians, I do not wish to excuse him, nor to examine his Sentence, whether it was justly carried out against him or not; I leave this for God to Judge, knowing the lesson of Christ, *Matthew 7:1: And judge not, that ye be not judged.* I shall only say this, if one may believe his dying mouth (which indeed ought to be done), he was innocent; moreover, his Writings must not displease us for that reason, but rather be more acceptable; for have not so many Holy Men perished by an untimely death? Of whom the Apostle counts a whole Register, *Hebrews 11:37. Some were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, put to death by the sword, and others again by something else, of which the **Books of Martyrs** are full;* <note>The author likely refers to John Foxe’s famous "Actes and Monuments," popularly known as the Book of Martyrs.</note> shall one therefore reject their Writings? O no, one should sooner investigate them, to know their deeds and walk of life.

Finally, these Treatises are arranged in the order that seemed best to us, and are all the Author’s own Writings, bearing the usual signature; only some doubt the **Practical Divinity** <note>original: "Werkige Godts-geleertheyt"</note>, whether it is a work of such a sharp brain and excellent understanding; for this reason One (who should not have) dared to criticize it so boldly, to make such flimsy and unsalted <note>A Dutch idiom meaning "tasteless" or "poorly reasoned."</note> notes upon it, which an apprentice might notice with half an eye; it is true that there are errors in it, as also in this great Work, not all things are to be taken as good, but let the wise judge for themselves; every Saint has his failings; he is well off who has the fewest; as for us, seeing that the World is already taken with this **Practical Divi-**

### Genesis chapter 6, verse 3.
->Then the Lord said, my Spirit shall not strive with man forever, because he is also flesh: yet his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.<-

---

<margin>The 1st Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry within London, October 27, 1650.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' containing a religious scene with figures, captioned "MATTHEW: II." below the illustration.</image-desc>
This chapter contains two parts within itself; first, God's intention to cause the world to perish by the Flood. Second, the providence of God in preserving Noah and his entire household during this general judgment through the preparation of an Ark.

Our text falls under the first main point, namely, the intention to destroy the world by a flood. Regarding this judgment, the breeding cause is stated here: when men began to multiply on the face of the earth (and that because, following the example of Lamech, they took many wives at once), they also grew in sins; and therefore the Lord God wished to diminish the number of those in the world, in order to thus decrease the sins of the world. The specific sin for which God wished to destroy the world is expressed here in the second verse, where it says that the Sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and they took for themselves wives from all whom they chose. By the "Sons of God" mentioned here, the <term>angels</term> <note>While some early traditions suggested these were fallen angels, Love follows the standard Protestant interpretation of the time.</note> cannot be understood, as <term>Tertullian</term> <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage.</note> and some others among the Church Fathers believed (although they are also called by this name in other places), for Christ, speaking of the angels, says that the angels of God neither take in marriage nor are given in marriage.

<margin>Job 1:6, Job 38:7.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 22:30.</margin>
<margin>Question.</margin>
You will ask, but who then should be understood here in this place by the "Sons of God"?
<margin>Answer.</margin>
The answer is that good interpreters believe the descendants of the godly <term>Seth</term> <note>The third son of Adam and Eve, whose lineage was considered the faithful line.</note> are understood by this, who, because they maintained the correct worship of God among them, were called Sons of God; and these Sons of God saw the daughters of men—that is, the descendants of the <term>unrighteous Cain</term> <note>The first son of Adam, who murdered his brother Abel; his lineage was associated with worldliness and sin.</note>—and they married into the

<column-break/>

descendants of the evil Cain, and thus religion began to decline through these marriages and mixings of the evil <term>Cainites</term> <note>The descendants of Cain.</note> with those who confessed the true worship of God; and wickedness began to multiply in the world, which is why the Lord God intended to destroy the world.

In this entire verse, you have three parts.
1. The general judgment and the sorrowful punishment which is threatened: *Then the Lord said, my Spirit shall not strive with man forever.*
2. The reason which is given for this: *because he is also flesh.*
3. A softening and postponement of this punishment: *yet his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.*

Here, the following difficulties must be explained and cleared away.
1. What is understood by this: *my Spirit shall not strive with man forever.*
2. What is expressed by the added reason: *because he is also flesh.* Someone might think that this reason proves the opposite of what is said here—namely, that God would overlook man's faults for that reason. Nevertheless, it is a reason for punishment here, even though in other places it is a reason for mercy.
3. What is made known by these words: *yet his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.*

<margin>Question.</margin>
The first question is: what is understood by this? *My Spirit shall not,* etc.
<margin>Answer.</margin>
I answer that some understand the "Spirit" to be the soul of man, as it is also taken in the common Latin translation <note>original: "ghemeyne Latijnsche oversetting," referring to the Vulgate, the 4th-century Latin version of the Bible.</note>, and that it is called "my Spirit" because God had breathed the soul into man: so the meaning would be "my Spirit," that is, the soul of man, shall not remain in man forever, but he shall die. But our best interpreters reject that explanation. And most of them (not to trouble your head with other opinions

->Presented in 27 Sermons by<-

### Mr. CHRISTOPHER LOVE.

->Genesis chapter 6, verse 3.<-

> Then the Lord said, My Spirit shall not strive with man forever, 
> since he is also flesh: yet his days shall be

<margin>
The 1st Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry <note>A historic Anglican church in the City of London, where Christopher Love served as minister.</note> within London on October 27, 1650.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'D' depicting a man with an axe cutting down a tree, illustrating Matthew 3:10. Small text at bottom reads: MATTH. III.</image-desc>

This Chapter contains two parts within itself; first, God's intention to destroy the world by the Flood. Second, God's providence in preserving Noah and his entire household during this general judgment, through the preparation of an Ark.

Our text falls under the first main point, namely, the intention to destroy the world by a flood. Concerning this judgment, the burgeoning cause is stated here: When men began to multiply on the earth (and following this, Lamech took many wives at once), they also grew in sins; and therefore the Lord God wanted to reduce the number of those in the world, to thus cause the sins of the world to decrease. The particular sin for which God wanted to destroy the world is expressed here in the second verse, where it says that the Sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, and they took for themselves wives from all whom they had chosen. By the "Sons of God" spoken of here, the angels cannot be understood, as Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD.</note> and some others among the Church Fathers have thought (although in

<margin>
Job 1:6.
Job 38:7.
Matthew 22:30.
</margin>

other places they are also called by this name) for Christ, speaking of the angels, says that the angels of God neither take in marriage nor are given in marriage.

<margin>Question.</margin>
You will ask, but who then should be understood here in this place as the Sons of God?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
It serves as an answer that good interpreters believe the descendants of the godly Seth are understood by this; who, because they held the right worship of God among them, were called Sons of God; and these Sons of God saw the daughters of men—that is, the descendants of the pious Seth married with the

<column-break/>

descendants of the wicked Cain; and thus religion <note>original: "Godts-dienst," literally God-service or worship.</note> began to decline through these marriages and mixings of the evil Cainites with those who confessed the true religion, and wickedness began to multiply in the world, which is why the Lord God intended to destroy the world.

In the entire verse, you have three parts:
1. The general judgment and the sorrowful punishment which is threatened: *Then the Lord said, My Spirit shall not strive with man forever.*
2. The reason given for this: *since he is also flesh.*
3. A softening and postponement of this punishment: *yet his days shall be a hundred and twenty years.*

Here, the following difficulties must be explained and removed:
1. What is understood by this: *My Spirit shall not strive with man forever.*
2. What is expressed by the added reason: *since he is also flesh*; someone might think that this reason proves the opposite of what is said here—namely, that God would overlook man's actions for that reason. Yet here it is a reason for punishment, though in other places it is a reason for mercy.
3. What is made known by these words: *yet his days shall be a hundred and twenty years.*

<margin>Question.</margin>
The first question is: what is understood by this; *My Spirit shall not, etc.*

<margin>Answer.</margin>

But our best interpreters reject that explanation. And most of them (not to trouble your head with other opinions)...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Genesis 6:3, focusing on the theological interpretation of God "striving" with man and the chronological difficulty regarding the 120-year warning before the Great Flood.</meta>

# The Withdrawal

<margin>
Mercer. <note>Jean Mercier (d. 1570), a French Hebraist and theologian.</note>
Musculus. <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a prominent Reformed theologian.</note>
Rivet. <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a French Huguenot theologian.</note>
</margin>
On this text, scholars such as Mercer, Musculus, Rivet, and others explain it thus: *My Spirit shall not strive with man forever.* By "Spirit," we are not to understand the spirit of man, but the Spirit of God—the third person in the blessed Trinity. And when He says that His Spirit shall not strive with man, it must be understood as the workings and influences of that same Spirit; that the Spirit will no longer accompany the ministry of Noah (who was a 
<margin>
2 Pet. 2:5
</margin>
preacher of righteousness) and of the Patriarchs. It is as if He said: "I shall now withdraw my Spirit from the established means of worship; He shall not strive with man forever." It is exactly as if He had explained Himself with more words: "I see indeed that
<margin>
1 Pet. 3:19, 23 <note>The original cites 1 Peter 2, but the context of spirits in prison refers to 1 Peter 3.</note>
</margin>
although my servant Noah testifies and preaches against the increase of the world’s godlessness, yet it is all in vain. I am now weary of their rebellious stubbornness, and therefore I have finally resolved to destroy them entirely. I will no longer bear with them nor tolerate them. *My Spirit shall not strive with man forever,* etc."

<margin>
2nd Question.
</margin>
The second question is: what power is there in this reasoning, *since he is also flesh?* Someone might think that this is no reason for such a sorrowful judgment; God remembers that we are but flesh, so why would He then act so severely?

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
To answer this, one must know that by the "flesh" spoken of here, we must not understand the natural substance of the human body, but rather man’s corrupt nature <note>Theologians often used "flesh" to refer to the sinful inclination or "Original Sin" inherited from Adam.</note>. "I shall withdraw my Spirit from you"—and why? Because you have entirely surrendered yourselves to the lusts and promptings of the flesh. You are fleshly men and follow the desires of the flesh, and therefore my Spirit shall not strive with you.

<margin>
3rd Question.
</margin>
The third question is: what is the meaning of these words, *yet his days shall be a hundred and twenty years?* What must be understood by this?

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
In response, it cannot be taken (as Tostatus <note>Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish bishop and biblical commentator.</note> and others believe) to mean the span of a human life—as if man, because of his wickedness, would now have a shorter life. For after the flood, men lived longer than a hundred and twenty years. Shem lived 600 years; Arphaxad 425 years; Serug 230; Abraham 175; and Isaac 180. This is the true meaning: although I will turn my Spirit away from the established means of worship, nevertheless his days shall be one hundred and twenty years. That is, another hundred and twenty years shall pass before the flood comes upon them.

<margin>
Objection.
</margin>
But here lies an objection: how can it be said that there would be a hundred and twenty years before the flood would come, when at the time these words were spoken, Noah was five hundred years old, and the flood came when he was six hundred years old? There would then be twenty years less than God had promised.

This is a very tangled knot, and interpreters take great pains to untie it and to uphold God's faithfulness in this: *let God be true, and every man a liar.* Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> answers that indeed
<margin>
Jerome.
</margin>

<column-break/>

God truly promised a hundred and twenty years, but that the wickedness of men grew so much between the making of that promise and its fulfillment—and provoked God to such anger—that He retracted twenty years from the promise. So also says Musculus,
<margin>
Musculus.
</margin>
who adds that when God makes a promise, He reserves the conditions for Himself. For just as God may not bring about a judgment which He threatens against a people if they heartily repent—as we have an example of this in the Ninevites <note>Referring to the Book of Jonah, where God spared Nineveh after the city repented.</note>—so He is also not bound to give the promised grace in the case of unwilling, stubborn, and incorrigible wickedness. We see this in the household of Eli. "I had clearly said" (said God to Eli) "your house and your father's house should walk before my face forever: but now the Lord says, far be it from
<margin>
1 Sam. 2:30.
</margin>
me," etc.

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
But the best and correct answer to this is: namely, that this promise was not made to Noah when he was five hundred years old, but when he was four hundred and eighty years old. For although it was said in the last verse of the fifth chapter that Noah was five hundred years old, it is nonetheless not said there that he was that old when this promise was made. This is the explanation of Rivet, Mercer, and others.

<margin>
Objection.
</margin>
There is one difficulty in this answer: one might say that this promise was made *after* Noah was said to be five hundred years old.

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
To which I answer that it is customary in the Scriptures not to maintain a strict chronological order in the telling of histories, so that some things which happened later are presented first, and those that happened earlier are
<margin>
Gen. 2:21-22.
</margin>
placed later. For example: we read of the creation of the Woman after the seventh day. Moses did not wish to maintain a precise order, but placed things that happened before at the end. Likewise, you have another example of a matter that is stated before it occurred. We read of Terah in Genesis 11:32 <note>Original text cites 11:23, likely a typo for 11:32.</note> that he was two hundred and five years old and he died; yet it is only ten chapters later that mention is first made of the birth of Isaac, even though Terah lived for about thirty-five years after Isaac's birth. I only bring this up to show how this answer is consistent with other passages of Scripture. To this may also be applied what the wise Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential French Reformer.</note> says to remove these doubts: that although Noah is said to be six hundred years old when he was only five hundred and eighty years old, nevertheless because he was within twenty years of being six hundred, the Holy Spirit says Noah was six hundred years old—thus expressing the time of his life by a whole or round number. And thus the difficulties are now explained.

*My Spirit shall not strive with man forever, etc.* One can observe from that entire chapter that when God threatens the judgment of a Great Flood <note>Original: "Zunt-vloet" (Sondvloed/Deluge).</note>, He wishes to send an even worse judgment beforehand; from which one can conclude that God's withdrawal of the established means of worship—or the withdrawal of the power of His Spirit from those means—is a worse punishment than any physical chastisement. I recount this...

<summary>This page analyzes the theological meaning of God's "Spirit" striving with man, identifying it as the Holy Spirit's influence through preaching. It also addresses the chronological discrepancy between the 120-year warning and Noah's age, concluding that the withdrawal of God's Spirit is a more severe judgment than the Flood itself.</summary>

# Of God's Spirit

->A 2<-
<meta>catchword: There</meta>

this in the preface / so that when you hear me discuss the weight of this judgment / you may perceive it as a very sorrowful and heavy matter.

Before I proceed further to the Doctrine / I shall distinguish between a twofold withdrawal of the Spirit of God. When the Scripture says, *My Spirit shall not strive with man forever*, it contains two things.

1. My Spirit shall not strive forever in the ministry of the word through powerful operation.
2. My Spirit shall not strive forever through inner movements and rebukes of the conscience.

I shall deal with both of these ways here.

### The first Doctrine is this:

<margin>1st Doctrine.</margin>
That it is a completely sorrowful and lamentable judgment when God withholds and withdraws the workings of His Spirit from the outward ministry of His word. I could likewise have noted from the word that the work of conversion is a heavy work / and that it is not easy to convince a man. But I shall follow the Doctrine / which I have proposed / and in the opening of the same I shall handle two things.

1. I shall show that it is a sorrowful judgment / when the Spirit of God is withdrawn or withheld from the ministry of the word.
2. I shall give the reasons / why God sends this judgment upon any part of the world.

1. For proof of the first / I shall only pose this one point / it appears that it is such a great judgment / because / when the Spirit is withheld from the means of worship / there can be no power in them to convert a soul. A sword in the hand of a living man can pierce and wound / but a painted sword in a painted man's hand can do nothing at all : So also the word of God preached without the Spirit of God / can do no more than a sword in the hand of a Saint George on horseback. <note>The author refers to common artistic depictions of St. George; he means the image is static and lacks life-giving power.</note> It may please the imagination somewhat and tickle the ear / but it never pierces through to the heart / the

<margin>2 Cor. 3 v. 3.</margin>
Spirit of God must work upon the heart. *You are a letter of Christ;* (says the Apostle) *written not with ink, but by the Spirit of the living God.*

<margin>1 Cor. 2 v. 4.</margin>
And as the same Apostle speaks / *my preaching was not with enticing words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power.* The mighty power of God must work upon the heart. The ministry of the word is like the Pool of Bethesda. There was no inherent power in the water to make one healthy / but the

<margin>John 5 v. 4.</margin>
text says / *when the Angel stirred the water, whoever then stepped in first, was made well, from whatever disease he was afflicted:* The ordained means are like this Pool-water. In the bare preaching and hearing / there is no natural power / but the Spirit of God must move those waters / otherwise they have no operation. The let-

<margin>2 Cor. 3 v. 6.</margin>
ter kills, but the Spirit gives life, which words must not be taken in the sense of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253), an early Christian scholar known for allegorical interpretations of Scripture.</note> / namely / by the letter / the literal sense / and by the Spirit / the allegorical or figurative sense; nor is by the letter understood the Old Testament / and by the Spirit the New Testament; as the Anti-

<column-break/>

nomians <note>A group that believes Christians are released by grace from the obligation of observing the moral law.</note> or Law-despisers say / but the meaning of the words is this / the letter, that is the word of God / as much as it is written without the Spirit of God / kills, and leaves a man in his deadly state; but the Spirit gives life, that is / the Spirit supporting the ministry of the word / makes the same powerful to bring about spiritual life. Thus it is manifest that it is a sorrowful judgment / when the Spirit is withheld from the ordained means of God / because those means without the Spirit can bring no benefit at all.

### 2. Now what reason is there / that God sends this sorrowful judgment upon any people?

In answer I shall pose some general / and some particular reasons.

First in general / this is the reason / why God withholds and withdraws the workings of His Spirit in His ordained means of worship; because men do the Spirit of God wrong; If man grieves the Spirit / and quenches His movements / then it is also right for God to withhold the workings of the same. The Scripture makes mention of a threefold wrong / which one does to the Spirit of God / for any one or all of which God the Lord may come to withdraw His Spirit.

<margin>The Spirit of God is a delicate matter; he treats us just as he is treated. Tertullian. <note>original: "Res delicatula est Spiritus Dei ita nos tractat sicut tractatur." Tertullian was an early Christian author from Carthage.</note></margin>
<margin>1 Thess. 5 v. 19.</margin>
1. There is a quenching of the Spirit. *Do not quench the Spirit.* One quenches the Spirit / when one does not heed and neglects the movements of the Spirit in our hearts. Take good heed then / that you do not omit any good duties / nor neglect the movements of the Spirit / for how do you know / that the Lord might not come to withdraw His Spirit. The wind might stop blowing / if we did not keep our sails ready / when it blows.

<margin>Eph. 4:30.</margin>
2. Another wrong / which is of a worse nature / is the grieving of the Spirit. *Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you are sealed until the day of redemption.* One grieves the Holy Spirit / whenever one does some sinful deed / for which the Holy Spirit rebukes us / and we nonetheless wish to proceed in committing the same; when one listens more to the movements of sin / than to the movements of the Spirit / more to the deceits of Satan / than to the movements of the Spirit / this grieves the Spirit exceedingly : just as it would grieve a friend / if one rejected his counsel / and rather followed the counsel of an enemy.

<margin>Isa. 63 v. 10.</margin>
3. Another wrong / which one does to the Spirit / is to cause the Spirit pain <note>The Dutch "smerten" is often translated as "vexing" in English Bibles (KJV: "but they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit").</note> / *They have become rebellious, and they have caused his Holy Spirit pain.* And this is a high degree: for then a man can be said to cause the Spirit pain / when he quenches and grieves the Spirit / and that through many repeatedly performed evil works. A man is grieved / when his friend shows him some discourtesy / but whenever he proceeds in doing him more evil / then there arises in him a torment and pain. So it is also with the Spirit of God / when we pay no heed to the movements of the same / and notwithstanding His warnings we nonetheless want to involve ourselves in committing sin / then we do not only grieve the Spirit / but also cause Him pain / and so says the Prophet: *They have become rebellious, and have caused his Holy Spirit pain.*

<margin>Isa. 63 v. 10.</margin>

# The Withdrawal

<margin>Acts 7 v. 51.</margin>
4. After that, the wrong done to the Spirit is expressed by **resisting the Spirit**. *You always resist the Holy Spirit.* And this is an even higher step than any of the previous ones. And it happens when a person knows that these or those movements are from the Spirit, and yet willfully and stubbornly resists His persuasions and movements.

<margin>Acts 5 v. 9</margin>
5. Furthermore, the Scripture describes it as **tempting the Spirit**. <note>original: "versoecken"</note> *How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?* Calvin explains this passage thus, saying that their tempting of the Spirit consisted in this: that Ananias and Sapphira, having sold a possession, brought a portion of the price and laid it at the feet of the Apostles, but kept back the rest, wanting to carry it out so secretly to test whether the Holy Spirit was also an all-knowing God, capable of punishing that hidden sin. Now, this was a higher sort of wickedness, and a great presumption against God’s providence, to test the omniscience of the Spirit of God.

<margin>Heb. 10 v. 29.</margin>
<margin>Matt. 12 v. 31.</margin>
6. And finally, another wrong is made known in the Scripture, by **doing despite to the Spirit of grace**; <note>The Dutch "smaetheyt" implies an insult or contemptuous treatment.</note> and this is the highest of all the greatest wrongs that a Devil in Hell or a man on earth can do against the Spirit: this is the sin against the Holy Spirit which shall not be forgiven to men. But in what does this "despite" consist? I answer that it does not consist in the neglect of good movements, for even the godly can fall, and sometimes do fall into these negligences: that one does not listen to the warning of a friend is not doing him "despite." Therefore, no despite can be done to the Holy Spirit unless the following things come together.

<margin>Heb. 10 v. 26.</margin>
1. That one commits the sin not only out of an unavoidable weakness, but out of **willfulness**; so it is written, *if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sin.*

2. It is a sin which is committed not out of ignorance, but with **knowledge**.

3. That sin is committed not only willfully and with knowledge—for even the reborn sin partly with their will—but also out of **malice and hatred** of the Spirit of God, which is the true distinguishing mark; and this the theologians attribute to the Pharisees, who knew and were convinced by the miracles which Christ did that He was indeed the Son of God; and although they knew this and were persuaded of it, they nevertheless wanted to put Him to death out of surrendered malice and ill-will against the Divinity of Christ. So, to gather everything together, the general reason why God will not let His Spirit strive with men is this: because they do such wrong to the Spirit of God. The specific reasons can be these:

<margin>1 Thess. 5 v. 19, 20.</margin>
1. A **contempt for the ministry of the word**. I shall not say now, a contempt for the Ministers themselves—although this is an evil which God also will punish—but in truth, a contempt for the ministry and for the institution of preaching can provoke God to withdraw the workings of His Spirit; if

<column-break/>

you despise prophecies, you also quench the Spirit, and then the Spirit shall not work upon you as He otherwise would have done. God will not accompany His word with power in those who despise or reject the ministry of the same.

<margin>1 Sam. 4 v. 2, 3.</margin>
2. Another reason is because people are **too much attached to the hearing** of the preached word: people come to hear the preached word in the strength of their own Spirit, and therefore God does not want to give them the workings of His Spirit; when one trusts and clings to those externally instituted means, it is just for God not to give the benefit of them. Just as the Israelites, having suffered defeat against the Philistines in which they lost about 4,000 men, thought the reason was that they did not have the Ark of God with them; but when they had the Ark with them, it is said that on the second day 30,000 of Israel's infantry fell. Thus God punished their sinful trust in the outward sign of His presence, and therefore they had less success when they had the Ark with them than when they did not have it. God then withholds the workings of His Spirit from the instituted means because people sinfully remain attached to them, and do not pray to God the institutor himself for the blessings of His Spirit. We must view the institutions as means, and the Spirit of God as the worker of grace. The instituted means can do us no good without the Spirit, and the Spirit usually will do us no good without those means. Therefore, we must not despise the instituted means, nor must we stop at them, so that the Spirit of God does not depart from us.

<margin>Mark 4 v. 24.</margin>
3. God also withholds His Spirit from the word because people **abstain from preparation** to hear the word. *With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you,* it is said regarding the hearing of the word; if you measure to God in a holy contemplation to prepare yourself for hearing, so shall God also through His Spirit mete out a blessing to you in the hearing.

<margin>Isa. 5 v. 5.</margin>
4. Another cause can be a **general fruitlessness** under fruitful means. When people sit (as it were) under the drippings of Heaven and yet bear no fruit, God is thereby provoked to do what He did to His vineyard: namely, to take away that hedge and let the beasts of the field destroy it, as well as letting no rain fall upon it.

5. Finally, this is the cause: when the people who have the ministry of the word among them **increase in sins**. And so it stood with the Old World, which enjoyed the ministry of Noah, Methuselah, and other Saints, and yet their wickedness grew exceedingly great, which greatly provoked God and moved Him to withdraw His Spirit, so that He would strive with man no longer.

# Of God’s Spirit

### Genesis 6:3

->Then the Lord said: My Spirit shall not strive / forever with man, etc.<-

<margin>
2nd Sermon at
St. Lawrence
Jewry within
London on
Nov. 2,
1650.
</margin>

After I have opened and explained these words and shown that it is a heavy and sorrowful judgment of God when He withholds and withdraws the workings and influences of His Spirit from the ministry of the Word, as also having set down the reasons for it, I now proceed to the application of the same, and that to two kinds of people.

First, to those who find within themselves the strivings and workings of the Spirit in the ministry of the Word.

Secondly, to those from whom the Spirit is withdrawn from the ministry that occurs among them.

<margin>1st Application.</margin>
Those who are persuaded that they find the Spirit of God working on their hearts in the ministry of the Word must pay heed to these following six warnings and propositions.

<margin>1st Proposition.</margin>
Ensure that you are certain that you do not err by mistaking moral persuasions <note>The author distinguishes between "moral persuasion"—an intellectual or emotional agreement with logic—and "special working," which is a supernatural change of heart.</note> for a special working of the Spirit in you. Whenever human reason is convinced by the strong proofs of Scripture, then there is a moral persuasion; and thus the Word of God can bring a person quite far, and yet there is only a common working of the Spirit. Reason can be convinced and the affections can be greatly stirred, where nevertheless the powerful working of the Spirit is absent; there can be sproutings of joy, as in the listeners of John the Baptist, who rejoiced in him for a time; or the hangings of fear, as in the time of Felix; or times of sorrow, as in Esau and Ahab. See, moral persuasions are very similar to the workings of the Spirit, and so that you do not take the one for the other, I shall set down these three distinctions.

<margin>Psalm 51:6.</margin>
1. Moral persuasions extend only to the outward man, but the workings of the Spirit go through to the inward man, to the heart and to the innermost parts. "Behold, you desire truth (says David) in the inward parts: and in the hidden part you shall make me to know wisdom."

2. Moral persuasions only make a person shun sin more out of fear of punishment than out of love for holiness, or hatred of sin with regard for God; whereas, on the contrary, the workings of the Spirit change the heart, and therein stir up and cause a love for holiness and a greater hatred against sin than fear of punishment—namely, because of the contrariety of sin against God's goodness, holiness, and supremacy.

3. Moral persuasions only show themselves in actual sins <note>Referring to specific outward acts of sin.</note>, but the working of the Spirit weakens even the inherent readiness <note>original: "haetvaerdighepdt," referring to a habitual inclination or disposition toward evil.</note> to sin. And from this appears the strength and power of the workings of the Spirit: that they change and restrain the habit and inclination toward evil.

<margin>2nd Proposition.</margin>
You who have found the Spirit of God working on your hearts in the ministry of the Word: give God alone the glory and honor

<column-break/>

thereof—not to the means, nor to yourselves in the use of those means; do not attribute it to the Minister either, nor even to the ministry, but to God alone. <margin>2 Cor. 3:3.</margin> "You are our letter (says the Apostle) written not with ink, but by the Spirit of the living God." He compares the people to the paper, the ministry to the ink, and the Minister to the pen—but the Spirit of God must do the writing therewith. The ministry becomes powerful through the working of the Spirit. <margin>2 Cor. 10:4.</margin> "The weapons of our warfare are powerful through God for the pulling down of strongholds." I do not say *we* are powerful, but the Gospel is powerful; and that not in itself, but it is powerful through the workings of the Spirit of God. <margin>1 Cor. 15:10.</margin> And so also says the Apostle: "I have labored more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me." The Ministers of the Word must say with Peter: <margin>Acts 3:12.</margin> "Why do you look so intently at us, as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?" No, but the name of Jesus Christ has made this man strong. Give then the glory not to the Minister, nor to your own self; for you did not convert yourself—you did not give yourself your first being in nature, much less in that grace. It is only God's grace, and not man. <margin>Luke 19:16, 18.</margin> "Your pound (said that servant in the parable) has gained ten pounds, and your pound has gained five pounds"—not my labor, but *your* pound.

Say then to God for all the good which you have received through the established means of divine service: Your Spirit has been the worker thereof; to You belongs all the honor. <margin>Psalm 115:1.</margin> "Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto Your Name give glory."

<margin>3rd Proposition:</margin>
You who have found the workings of the Spirit in the ministry of the Word: see to it that you are thankful for it. Observe indeed that the Spirit now works more clearly and powerfully under the Gospel than He ever did under the Law. And this is a very comforting proposition. The Spirit of God works more clearly and powerfully.

First, He works more clearly now, for in the latter times the Spirit speaks expressly. <margin>1 Tim. 4:1; 2 Pet. 1:21.</margin> And the holy men of God, being moved by the Spirit of God, wrote it. The closer Christ's becoming flesh was, the more clearly the matters of the Covenant of Grace became known. <margin>Luke 1:1.</margin> And so says the Holy Evangelist Luke, writing to Theophilus: "Most excellent Theophilus, the things which we relate have complete certainty among us." Because these things were first presented obscurely, they were believed with difficulty; and therefore you read <margin>Eph. 3:5.</margin> that "in other ages the mystery of Christ was not made known to the sons of men, as it is now revealed to us by His Spirit." It was a mystery which was hidden from the foundation of the world; not indeed entirely hidden in comparison to the revelation now occurred, but it was not so clearly revealed by the Spirit. <margin>note: "πολυμερῶς" (polymeros) - meaning 'in many parts' or 'at various times'.</margin> To this one must note that the Spirit in the Old Testament made these things known in stages, now and then a little, but the full revelation of the glory of Christ was reserved until the time that Christ came in the flesh. <margin>Heb. 1:1.</margin> Just as at first in the time of Adam, it was only known to the world that the Savior of the human race should be born of a woman. And thereafter in the time...

# The Unfolding

<margin>
Gen. 12 v. 3.
Gen. 49 v. 10.
Isa. 7 v. 14.

</margin>
In the time of Abraham, it was further revealed that Christ, who would save the world, should come forth from the loins of Abraham. But thirdly, although it was known that He would be the seed of the Woman and the seed of Abraham, it was nonetheless not yet revealed from which tribe He would be born; but this was declared to Jacob, namely, from the tribe of Judah. Again, in all this time it was not made known how He would be born, and therefore it was said in the time of Isaiah: *A Virgin shall become pregnant, and she shall bear a Son.* But the place where He would be born was not revealed until the times of the Prophet Micah, when it was said: *And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, though you are small among the thousands of Judah, out of you shall come forth to Me one who will be a ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity.* Also, the time of His coming was not known until it was revealed to Daniel.

<margin>
Heb. 1 v. 1.
</margin>
Thus you see now how true it is what the Apostle says: *that God in former times, at many times and in many ways, revealed Himself to the children of men.* <note>Original: "Godt voortijdts veelmael en op velerley wijse aen de kinderen der menschen sich geopenbaert heeft." This refers to the concept of "Progressive Revelation," where God reveals his plan in stages over centuries.</note> So that we have great reason here to thank God that we were not born in those ancient days but in these, in which the Spirit of God reveals the mysteries of religion openly and clearly.

<margin>
Matt. 11 v. 12.
</margin>
Secondly, just as the Spirit in these days of the Gospel makes Himself known more openly and clearly, so He also works with greater power upon the inclinations of men. Therefore it is said *that from the days of John the Baptist until now, the Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.* That is, the Spirit, through His powerful operation, makes men more vehement and fiery to obtain Heaven than they were previously under the Law. There is now a more glorious revelation of the Spirit in His workings; and for this reason, one reads of that promise regarding the abundance of Gospel grace in the Prophet Isaiah: *that the light of the Moon shall be as the light of the Sun, and the light of the Sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days.* There is a full revelation of the Spirit in the days of the Gospel; and therefore one reads that when Ezekiel describes the Holy City in his prophecies, and John portrays the New Jerusalem in his Revelation, John describes his City much more gloriously and broadly than Ezekiel did his. This is to make known (say the interpreters) that God now reveals more through His Spirit than He did in previous times.

<margin>
Isa. 30 v. 26.
4th Proposition.
Acts 8 v. 28, 29.
</margin>
You who have found the Spirit of God powerful in the ministry of the Word, consider that the Spirit does not work upon man without means, but through means, and that is to place a dignity upon the ministry of the Word. <note>The "means" or "instruments" refer to the physical preaching and reading of the Bible, which the author argues are necessary tools for the Holy Spirit.</note> The Spirit does not wish to teach men without any means, but sends them to an outward ministry, which gives a greater dignity to that service. I shall give you famous examples or models of this, in which the Spirit does not want to teach without means, but wants the outward ministry to be used. One of these you have in the Moor, the Eunuch, who was reading the Prophet Isaiah on his chariot; and the Spirit, noticing that he did not understand what he was reading, commanded Phi-

<column-break/>

-lip to go to him and join his chariot, in order to explain what he was reading. The Spirit did not want to do that Himself immediately, but commanded Philip to go to him. The interpreters note from this how great a dignity the Spirit of God places in the ministry of the Word, in that God—in those days when visions and revelations were still in use—nevertheless established the ministry of the Word.

<margin>
Acts 9 v. 4 etc.
</margin>
We have another example in the conversion of Paul. When he saw that vision and heard the voice crying out, *Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?* and he cried out, *Lord, what will You have me do?* Christ did not want to tell him that without means, but said: *go to Damascus, there you shall come to Ananias, who will tell you what you must do.* Christ did not want to teach Paul without a mediator, but sent him to Ananias, to place greater dignity upon the Gospel ministry. Therefore, whoever wishes to wait for the Spirit must use the established means of worship, just as those who wanted to be healed had to step into the pool of water when the Angel stirred it. You have a third example in Cornelius the Centurion; when he saw the Angel and became very afraid, saying, *What is it, Lord?* the Lord commanded him to send for Peter, who would tell him what he had to do. Thus the Lord God honors the ministry of the Word.

<margin>
Acts 10 v. 3 etc.
</margin>
I recount this preferably to show you the vanity of the Spirit-drivers <note>Original: "Geest-drijvers." This refers to radical religious groups (often called Enthusiasts) who claimed they received direct, private revelations from God and therefore did not need the Bible or trained ministers.</note> who want to abolish the ministry and put the immediate teaching of the Spirit in its place. But here we see the great dignity which the Spirit places in the ministry of a poor, weak, and brittle human being, in that He does not want to teach men immediately, but sends them to the ministry of the Gospel.

<margin>
5th Proposition.
Isa. 8 v. 20.
</margin>
Although the Spirit occasionally works without the Word (being fully sovereign in His operations), He has nonetheless never worked upon anyone's heart *against* the Word. *To the Law and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.* I recount this proposition to condemn those idle impulses of the Spirit which men claim nowadays. Let such people remember that it is not from God, but an instigation of the Devil, to maintain a driving of the Spirit which is contrary to the Word of God. And yet, many have abandoned the bright lamps of God's Word to follow the will-o'-the-wisp <note>Original: "dwael-licht" or "Ignis fatuus." A light that misleads travelers, used here as a metaphor for false spiritual inspiration.</note> of their own imagination.

<margin>
Ignis fatuus.
6th Proposition.
</margin>
You who have found the powerful operation of the Spirit in the ministry of the Word: Praise and thank your God that He has not let you use a bare, empty, and powerless ministry. The Word, in so far as it is in our mouths without the operations of the Spirit, is but a poor, weak, and empty thing, through which men are often accidentally perverted and hardened. But you who have found the Spirit, empowering the Word in the ministry of the same: Bless God, who has placed such a rich treasure in earthen vessels. What the Apostle says to those of Corinth has come to your benefit. *Our preaching* (he says) *was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power.* Thank God that He has placed such power in the ministry of the Word for the benefit of your souls. This is now the first use...

<meta>This page continues the previous discussion on the Holy Spirit's role in the "ministry of the word" (preaching). While the previous page likely concluded a section on those experiencing the Spirit's power, this page shifts to a warning for those who feel the Spirit has abandoned their religious life.</meta>

### Of God’s Spirit.

...help for those who have preserved the ministry of the word, accompanied by the power of the Spirit.

<margin>2. Application.</margin>
Secondly, this shall serve for those from whom the powerful working of the Spirit is withdrawn from the ministry they enjoy.

To these I wish to make seven things known.

<margin>I.</margin>
First, that God is a voluntary cause, not bound to the outward service, but he is free to work how, when, and in what manner it pleases him. The wind blows <margin>John 3:8.</margin> wherever it wishes, so is everyone who is born of the Spirit. By the wind, the Spirit is understood; there is a sovereignty and freedom in the Spirit of God to work when it pleases him or to withhold the working from whom he will. And therefore <margin>Ps. 51:14.</margin> God's Spirit is called a free Spirit <note>Original: "vrymoedigen Geest," often translated as a "willing" or "generous" spirit in English Bibles.</note>. <margin>James 1:18.</margin> By his own will, by his own will, he gave us birth through the word of truth.

<margin>II.</margin>
Second, notice that when God withholds his Spirit from the outward preaching, it is not simply an act of his sovereignty, but also a work of his justice, for the sake of your sins, with which you have angered him. Through your sins, you provoke God to withhold the power of his Spirit from his institutions, and therefore you are hardened, and receive no benefit through them. You do some wrong to the Spirit, of which I have spoken before; namely, either you have quenched the Spirit, or grieved him, or resisted him, or done him violence, or tempted him, or finally, you have treated him with contempt. Therefore, do not lay the blame on the Lord, but judge yourselves. Sin was the cause why God withdrew his Spirit, so that it would not strive with the people of the old world; it was their disobedience, just as the Apostle Peter <margin>1 Pet. 3:19-20.</margin> says: *Christ went through his Spirit and preached to the spirits who are in prison, who formerly were disobedient, when the patience of God waited once in the days of Noah.* Their disobedience caused God to withdraw the power of his Spirit. If, then, the Spirit does not work upon you, think no evil of God, but blame yourself; he was provoked to it. Thus God departed from the people of Israel for their sins' sake. <margin>Ps. 81:11-12.</margin> *But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not want me. So I gave them over to the stubbornness of their hearts, that they walked in their own counsels.* The Spirit is compared in Scripture to a Dove. Now, a Dove will always stay in the house where it was raised, unless the dove-house, being full of stench, is not cleaned. The Spirit of God can aptly be compared to a dove in this; keep your hearts pure, and the Spirit will remain with you; but keep them stinking and the Spirit will soon leave you. Sin is then the cause why the Spirit withdraws from the established means of worship, and people are left to themselves; and God does this as a work of his justice, punishing sin.

Third, if God withholds his Spirit from the preaching of the word, the fault must be attributed to yourself and not the word. Many complain (like the lady in Seneca's writings) that the place is dark, when they themselves are blind

<column-break/>

and the place lacks no light, but they lack eyes. Commonly, if people do not profit from hearing the word, it is blamed on the minister who preaches the word: And truly, we Ministers have our faults as well as others; if we do not preach clearly and with proper order, then it is a fault in us; nevertheless, I say, if the seed does not grow, the fault is not in the Farmer, nor in the influences of the Heavens, but in the unfitness of the Land. Now, so that you may know where the blame lies, note this:

1. If a Minister speaks clearly and without partiality or evil passions, and you still receive no good through him, then it is your own fault and not his. It was the fault of the Herodians and not of Christ that they had no benefit from Christ's preaching, for they themselves gave this testimony of Christ: <margin>Matt. 22:16.</margin> *Master, we know that you are true, and teach the way of God in truth.*

2. If others profit through his service and you do not, it is a sign that it is not his fault, but yours. If at a feast others are fed and you hunger, it is a fault not of the food, but of your stomach.

3. In case you received some good through a Minister in high times <note>Likely referring to religious festivals or periods of spiritual revival.</note>, and now do not; if previously your affections were stirred, your longing increased, and your love kindled, and you now feel no such working in you, then it is your own fault. It was the fault of John the Baptist's listeners, and not of John's teaching, that they rejoiced only for a time. So it was also the fault of those in Galatia that they did not profit through Paul's service as before. <margin>Gal. 4:15.</margin> This is not due to the seed, but to the badness of the earth in which it is thrown. If you do not profit through the word which you hear, you must blame your own evil heart, not the word, nor the dispenser of the word.

Fourth, although the word of God, considered purely in itself, must be attributed great dignity and excellence, yet there is no power in it to convert a soul without the cooperation of the Spirit. Just as in the pool of Bethesda, <margin>John 5:4.</margin> the water did not make one healthy, nor the stepping into the water, but the stirring of the Angel. So also the word does not heal when being alone, nor does the hearing of it, but the Spirit; the letter kills (says the Apostle) but <margin>2 Cor. 3:6.</margin> the Spirit gives life; the letter, that is the word without the Spirit: the Spirit alone can give life. The Spirit usually will not convert without the word, and the word cannot convert without the Spirit. *I create the <margin>Isa. 57:19.</margin> fruit of the lips; Peace, peace.* By the "fruit of the lips," the Prophet understands the Gospel ministry: yet God does not say "I create peace through the fruits of the lips" <note>The author is emphasizing that God (the Spirit) is the active creator of the peace, while the lips are merely the instrument.</note>. The cooperation of the Spirit with the word makes the word powerful, and therefore the Gospel is called the ministry of the Spirit. <margin>2 Cor. 3:8.</margin>

Fifth, it is a heavier judgment when the Spirit is withdrawn from the word than when the word itself is withdrawn; the reason is that the Spirit can convert a person without the word, but

<margin>3rd Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry within London on Nov. 3, 1650.</margin> <note>Original: "Laurence Iurience." This refers to St. Lawrence Jewry, a prominent Anglican church in the City of London known for its influential sermons.</note>
After I have shown that it is a sorrowful judgment when the Spirit is withheld somewhere from the preaching of the word, and have presented various warnings and propositions regarding this judgment, I now proceed to answer an objection.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
*Someone might say: it is true, this is a very sorrowful judgment, but what proof does one have, or by what can one recognize that this judgment is present?*

<margin>Answer.</margin>
To this I answer that one must know that this is a very dark matter and cannot easily be explained; therefore, many of the specific answers I shall give will be more like probable conjectures than infallible proofs. Many things make me fear that the saving work of the Spirit is partly being withheld from the ministry of the Word.

<margin>1st Proof.</margin>
1. And first, we have reason to fear that the Spirit is partly withdrawn from the ministry of the Word among us because fewer are now converted through the preaching of the Word than in former times. Since the Spirit now ceases to support the ministry of the Word with a great number of converts, it is proof that the Spirit is partly withdrawn. When the Disciples first preached the Gospel, Satan fell before the word like lightning.
<margin>Acts 2:41.</margin>
Through the preaching of Peter <note>Original: "Predicati Petri."</note>, three thousand were converted on one day; and now it happens that we preach three thousand times and barely convert one. Many nations were brought in and converted in the morning of the Gospel, according to that Evangelical promise:
<margin>Psalm 110:3.</margin>
*From the womb of the morning you have the dew of your youth;* that is, many peoples shall be converted through the first preaching of the Gospel, which would be spread over the earth like the morning dew. But in this our time in which we live, the number of converts is far fewer; and not only fewer in respect to that former time, but also in our own era. What a great number of young people were brought in within these few years through the preaching of the Word? But how the work of conversion stands still now! The Ministers used to fish as if with nets, and many were brought to the knowledge of Christ; but now we fish as if with a hook—now one comes in, and then another. This can be a probable demonstration that the Spirit of God is partly withdrawn from the ministry of the word.

<margin>2nd Proof.</margin>
2. Another provable conjecture is this: when people who live under the ministry of the Word do not become better but worse and worse. For the fact that they enjoy the preaching of the Word for many years and yet become blinder, duller, more perverse, and more godless, indicates that the Spirit of God is certainly withheld from them, and that their destruction is near.

<margin>Heb. 6:7, 8.</margin>
*For the earth, upon which the rain often falls and yet is unfruitful, is near to cursing, whose end is to be burned.*

<margin>3. Proof.</margin>
3. There is reason to fear that the Spirit is being withdrawn from God’s service, because more are perverted by error than are converted by the truth; especially in these recent years, from the time that spirits of error have had freedom and permission. What a multitude has been perverted and led astray by the errors of the godless: this is a proof of a hardness of heart sent by God as a righteous judgment upon the Land. We have fallen into those times
<margin>2 Peter 2:1, 2</margin>
of which the Apostle Peter speaks: in which there shall be false teachers, who shall secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many shall follow their destructive ways. How many in these days are turned away, following the destructions of false teachers, which is surely a proof that the Spirit is being withheld from the ministry.

<margin>4. Proof.</margin>
4. This can also be a reason why the word has so little power over the hearts of men; because the word of truth is so corrupted with error. Just as seed will never grow in a field where there are many weeds, so also God’s word will bear no fruit in a Church where many errors have arisen. The arrival of damnable heresies holds back the working of God’s Spirit in the hearts of men. Of
<margin>Matt. 7:29.</margin>

<margin>Mark 7:13.</margin>
Gospel of Mark: you make (he says) God’s word powerless through your traditions, which you have established. It had no power over the consciences of their followers; their erroneous traditions made the word of God powerless, just as in these our days these erroneous opinions do—how they strip the word of God of its glory and brilliance! And how they hinder the working of the Spirit? Is this not what many say: how shall we believe the preachers? If we go to one assembly, we shall hear one thing preached; if we go to another, we shall hear the same thing contradicted. How this makes the people stumble, and how greatly it hinders the working of the Spirit upon them! The Apostle Paul, when he speaks
<margin>2 Cor. 4:2. <note>original Greek: "δολῶντες τὸν λόγον" (dolontes ton logon), meaning "handling the word deceitfully."</note></margin>

do to their wine. But we make ourselves (he says) through the revelation of the truth acceptable to every man's conscience in the presence of God.

<margin>5. Proof.</margin>
5. Another reason why God holds back the working of his Spirit can be this: because people forsake the calling of the preaching office. God will not allow preaching to be powerful for those who despise it. Many people despise not only the preachers, but also their service itself; they reject the calling, and would gladly do away with the office altogether, and therefore it is just in God’s eyes that those who do not believe in the office of preaching shall

<column-break/>

not find the power of the Spirit therein. This is why the Apostle Paul says to those of Thessalonica: Our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much assurance: as 
<margin>1 Thess. 1:5.</margin>
you know what kind of men we were among you for your sake. It is noteworthy regarding John the Baptist that the reason why he had such influence over the people, so that all Judea and the entire surrounding country went out to him, was this: because they held him 
<margin>Matt. 3:5; 25:26.</margin>
to be a Prophet. The people believed that his office was from God; they all believed that the

<margin>Matt. 21:25, 26.</margin>

<margin>6. Proof.</margin>
