<margin>Jer. 23:21.</margin>
miah, where the Lord says that he did not send those prophets; yet they ran; and he did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. But what benefit shall they bring to the people to whom they have prophesied? Of that it says in the 32nd verse: therefore they shall not profit this people at all, says the Lord. Such shall be the fruit of the preaching of those who take up the office without a calling.

<margin>7. Proof.</margin>
7. The final reason why the Spirit of God does not support the ministry of the Word as well now as in former times can be this: because the judgment of the sword <note>A common 17th-century term for war or military conflict.</note> is over the Land. You might perhaps think this is a strange reason, but it can be shown thus. Other judgments, such as physical sickness, pestilence, famine, or the like, go together with the word and bring the preached word to the hearts of men; but the sword is a judgment which makes men wild and beastly, one against the other, whereas in other judgments men look to the hand of God. How many were converted before these Wars: but since the sword came among us, how cruel has one neighbor become toward another? How has that loveliness and friendliness (for which the inhabitants of England are so praised) changed into wild rudeness? This concludes our first part, in which we have plainly shown you how great a spiritual judgment it is when the Spirit is withdrawn from public service, and have also explained the proofs and causes of such a judgment.

<margin>Second Part.</margin>
Now I come to the second part, to show you that it is a lamentable judgment when the Spirit is withheld from the inward movements of the consciences of men in their ordinary walk of life. In handling this, I shall follow this order. The Spirit of God can be withheld from men in their inward movements of the conscience in two ways.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Holy Spirit’s withdrawal as a divine judgment. # The Withdrawal

§ 1. In respect to sin.
§ 2. In respect to bounden duty.
1. In respect to sin, the Spirit can be withheld in two ways.
1. **Before** the commission of sin, so that He neither deters nor advises you against it.
2. **After** the commission of the same, so that He neither rebukes nor convicts you of it.

I. First, I shall show you how it proves to be a misery when the Spirit is withheld from someone, both before and after committing sin.
II. Secondly, for what reason the Spirit of God is withheld in these two ways.
III. Thirdly, how far a child of God <note>A "child of God" refers to a believer or a person considered part of the elect in 17th-century theology.</note> can be thus forsaken by the Spirit.

<margin>First question answered.</margin> First, that it is a heavy judgment when the Spirit is withheld from someone before the commission of sin can be proven as follows.

I. First, because if the Spirit does not advise you against it, you will be ready and prepared to give yourself over to every sin to which you are tempted. People who are enticed to sin, without the opposing warnings of the Spirit of God, are like a city <margin>Prov. 4:23.</margin> whose walls are broken down and lie open to every kind of enemy attack. The warnings of the Spirit are like Forts and strong Ramparts to protect a person's heart. When the Devil, through his workings, suggests sin, the Spirit comes through His movements to lovely advise against it, saying: "Oh, do not break God’s Law; do not damage or wound your own conscience." Through these warnings, the heart is sanctified; but when these depart, how easily a person is given over to evil. Of <margin>Acts 16:7.</margin> Paul and Timothy it is written that they attempted to travel to Bithynia, but the Spirit did not permit them. So it can also be said of many people in respect to sin: he attempted, through the corruption of his heart, to commit this or that sin, but the Spirit did not permit him. Just as a godly person cannot do all the good he would wish to do because of the "flesh" <note>The "flesh" refers to the human inclination toward sin.</note>, so he shall also, at times, not do all the evil he would wish to do because of the Spirit. When the wind blows with a strong breeze, then the ship can sail against the current, which otherwise would drift back with the stream; so it is also with the breathings of the Spirit—they help a person overcome the currents of both temptation and corruption. But if the Spirit is withdrawn, how inclined a person shall be to commit sin!

Secondly, if the Spirit leaves you, you will not only be capable and ready to consent to sinful temptations, but you will also quickly commit the sin. We read of that senseless youth who, being delayed by the flattery and sweet talk of a <margin>Proverbs 7:22.</margin> Harlot, is said to follow her immediately. Once one is tempted to sin, and the Spirit does not advise against it, one is as quickly overtaken as Gunpowder becomes fire. So powerful are temptations upon a corrupt heart if the warnings of God’s Spirit do not protect and preserve it.

But this is not yet all; a person shall

<column-break/>

not only be capable of falling, and fall quickly, but—which is a even greater evil—he shall be raging after his lusts, burning in sin, and poisoned with evil. This the Holy Spirit makes known to us, speaking of the Heathens who did not have the Spirit of God, saying that they became "past feeling"; that <margin>Ephe. 4:19.</margin> they—they were without the workings of the life-giving Spirit. But what follows? They have (it says) given themselves over to lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness <margin>to work all uncleanness with greediness <note>original: "εἰς πᾶσαν ἀκαθαρσίαν ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ"</note></margin> greedily; that is, they sinned and thought they could never sin enough. Just as a covetous man, who greedily hungers for gain, thinks he can never have enough, so these think they can never be satisfied in their whorish lusts. Note here a particular progression <note>The author uses the word "trapklimmingh," meaning a step-by-step ladder or escalation of behavior.</note> in this sin:

1. They have become **past feeling**. Now, what follows? It does not say they were thoughtlessly carried away to sin, but they *gave themselves over* to sin. When the Spirit is in a man, he is never carried to it without a struggle; but let the movements of the Spirit once be withdrawn, and he will give himself over to the Devil.

2. When the Spirit is withdrawn, they do not only give themselves, but they give themselves over to **lasciviousness**; that is, they give themselves not partially, but entirely over to sin.

3. It says "they gave themselves over," and <margin>1 Kings 21:25.</margin> this was worse than the act of Ahab, who had *sold* himself to do evil. Now, for a man to sell himself to the Devil is a great evil, but whenever someone *gives* himself over to him, this wickedness is much greater.

4. They did not only give themselves over to sinful thoughts, but as the text says, they gave themselves over to **work uncleanness**; they did not remain satisfied with the contemplation or internal viewing of wickedness, but they were also workers of unrighteousness and made it their trade.

5. It is said that they gave themselves over to work **all uncleanness**; not only some, but all sins—and that **greedily**, which serves my purpose. Where will that man not run who is driven by an evil spirit?

If the Spirit of God does not oppose the Devil's movements with contrary movements, then that poor soul will bring his own soul with great violence to damnation, and will not stand still before he comes to Hell, unless the Spirit of God breaks his course and says to him: "This is the way, walk in it." But when the Spirit is withheld, then every man turns about in his course, like an unruly horse running violently into battle when it is not restrained and checked by the bit and bridle, Psalm 32: v. 9. Such is also the man who does not have the warnings and restraints of his conscience and the advice of the Spirit.

<margin>III.</margin> Thirdly, a man being forsaken by God's Spirit, whenever he is tempted to sin, shall not only fall into it readily, quickly, and violently, but—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Holy Spirit's withdrawal as a divine judgment. Having previously established that the Spirit can be withheld before one commits a sin (removing preventative grace), the author now explores the consequences of the Spirit being withheld after a sin is committed, and begins to list the reasons why God might execute such a judgment.</meta>

### Of God’s Spirit.

<margin>2 Thess. 2:12.</margin>
...but also with a delight <note>Original: "wel behagen." In this context, it refers to finding satisfaction or pleasure in wrongdoing.</note>; and this is the worst of all. Thus we read of those who did not believe the truth, that they took delight in unrighteousness; they did not merely commit the sin, but they even devised it with pleasure.

And so I have now clearly shown that it is a sorrowful judgment when the Spirit is withheld before the commission of sin.

<margin>Second question answered.</margin>
That it is also a great judgment when God’s Spirit is withheld from a person **after** the commission of sin can be shown as follows:

<margin>1 John 16:8.</margin> <note>The author likely refers to John 16:8, where the Spirit "will convict the world of sin."</note>
I. Because otherwise you shall not be convicted of the evil you have done; the Spirit convicts the world of sin, and there is no powerful conviction except for the conviction of the Spirit.

<margin>II. Jer. 8:6.</margin>
II. You shall never have remorse for sin if the Spirit does not rebuke and convict you of it after its commission; for the conviction of the Spirit precedes remorse. Therefore the Prophet says: *there is no one who has remorse over his wickedness, saying, "what have I done?"* A person must first be convicted that what he has done is evil before he can feel remorse for it. We have a proverb among us: *what the eye does not see, the heart does not rue* <note>Equivalent to "out of sight, out of mind," but here meaning if the soul doesn't "see" the sin, it won't feel pain over it.</note>; so too, if the eye of the soul does not see the sin, the heart shall never be troubled because of it.

<margin>III. 1 Cor. 6:11.</margin>
III. Your nature shall never be sanctified and cleansed from the filth of sin unless the Spirit works upon you after you have fallen into sin. Sanctification is a work of God’s Spirit; therefore the Apostle Paul says, speaking to those of Corinth regarding godless and unregenerate men: *and such were some of you; but you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.*

<margin>Ephes. 2:22.</margin>
Thus believers are said to be a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. From this you may observe the distinct works of the Trinity <term>Trinity</term> <note>Original: "Op-eenigheydt." A literal translation would be "Up-oneness," a 17th-century Dutch term for the Triune nature of God.</note> in the heart of a believer. God the Father chooses this House; God the Son buys it; and God the Holy Spirit cleanses it and tidies it up; otherwise, it would be a stinking and dark dungeon. Your spirit can never be a fit house for God to dwell in unless God’s Spirit cleanses you with the broom of sanctifying grace.

<margin>Rom. 8:13.</margin>
Without the Spirit, you can never subdue the power of sin. Therefore the Apostle says: *if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if through the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.*

Because of the Spirit, we kill sin; so you see then what a misery it is to lack the Spirit in both His deterrents and His convictions, both before and after the commission of sin.

<margin>The third Question.</margin>
But why does God withhold His Spirit, so that He neither advises men against sin when they are tempted to it, nor convicts them of sin after they have committed it?

<margin>Answered.</margin>
I answer: in general, you must know that God does not do this as an act of absolute sovereignty <note>Meaning God isn't just being arbitrary or showing off His power.</note>, but as an act of justice. You wrong the Spirit, and therefore God withholds the Spirit. In particular, five reasons can be established

<column-break/>

as a foundation for why God withholds His Spirit from striving with men.

<margin>I. Psal. 81:11, 12.</margin>
First, because in times past you have refused to listen to the many movements and persuasions of God’s Spirit. The Spirit has told you that if you walk in such evil ways, the end of them shall be death. How often has He suggested to you that if you go in these or those paths, you shall be lost for eternity? And yet you have gone on to sin and would not hear the Spirit. Thus God complains of His people through the Psalmist: *My people did not hear my voice, and Israel would have none of me; so I gave them up to the stubbornness of their own hearts, to walk in their own counsels,* as if He were saying: they would not hear me, and therefore my Spirit shall no longer advise them. I shall leave them to themselves and let them walk in their own ways.

<margin>II. Isa. 63:10.</margin>
Secondly, because you perhaps put sinful passions, which come from the flesh, in the place of the movements of the Spirit; and the Spirit will not endure this wrong—as when men say that their hellish rage is a heavenly zeal of the spirit, that their errors are teachings of the Spirit (who is nevertheless the Spirit of truth), and that the Devil’s deceptions are divine inspirations. This is no less an indignity than if a subject presented his illegitimate child at the gate of his Prince. And some believe this is what is meant by *grieving the Spirit*, of which we read in the Prophet Isaiah. And this can be another reason why the Lord comes to withhold His Spirit.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, because men much more easily follow the suggestions of the evil spirit than the movements of the good Spirit. Your friend will not want to come to your house if you give his enemy a good welcome. You insult the Spirit of God to the highest degree when the Devil easily overcomes you, and when you sin without any temptation, or at least upon a very small temptation. This is also the reason why such a severe judgment is attached to the third commandment: that God will not hold him guiltless who uses His name in vain; because the temptation to the sin of swearing is less than to any other sin in the world. Other sins correspond more to flesh and blood, but one has the least temptation to swearing and cursing. The curser serves the Devil for nothing; he has neither profit nor pleasure from his sin, and therefore God ties such a hard punishment to it. If you run to sin upon a light temptation, and will not listen to God’s Spirit upon an earnest movement, then you provoke God to withhold the strivings of His Spirit from you.

<margin>IV. Prov. 16:10.</margin> <note>The text describes Prov. 16:30: "He shuts his eyes to devise perverse things."</note>
Fourthly, because in the past you have meditated and deliberated how you would commit sin; therefore the Spirit withdraws Himself from you in the time to come. Many commit sin with deliberation, reflection, and meditation; and he who commits sin with intent and deliberation insults God’s Spirit greatly. Of the wicked man it is said that *he shuts his eyes to devise perversity*. The closing of the eyes is the posture of one who ponders, meditates, and deliberates. Just as it is with a friend, if...

# The Withdrawal

If you happen to give someone a blow by accident, although he may be somewhat angry at first, nevertheless, when he considers that it was against your will, he will soon be satisfied. But if he sees that you are deliberating and intending to kill him, he will be moved by that never to come into your company again. So it is also with God's Spirit: when He sees you fall into sin thoughtlessly and unexpectedly, He will not withdraw Himself from you for that reason; but when He sees that you are, as it were, laying snares, and that you are deliberating and considering how you shall commit the sin, that provokes Him to depart from us for a long time, if not forever. Such premeditated sins are, in a special way, directly against God. In this regard, it is worth noting what we read of David, that <margin>1 Kings 15:5.</margin> he had done what was right in the eyes of the Lord all the days of his life, except only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Why does the text not rather say that he was perfect, or did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, except only in the matter of Bathsheba, for that was the filthiest sin? This reason is given here: namely, the Spirit of God says that he was a perfect man except only in the matter of Uriah, and not in the matter of Bathsheba, because the latter happened suddenly and thoughtlessly; he was caught off guard in haste by a temptation. But the matter of Uriah happened more with deliberation, reflection, and consideration; for first, he summons him home to cover his filthy deed, then he makes him drunk, and finally, he has him deliver a letter to Joab containing the plot for his own death, so that the sin was committed with such intent that God's Spirit gives him a "brand-mark" <note>A permanent mark of shame or a stigma.</note> for it. Guard yourself, then, against deliberated sins. I do not judge every one of you; whether he stands or falls, he shall be judged by God; but this I say, that it is a sin which especially angers the Spirit of God. It is the saying of a certain theologian,

,, and it is true: that a deliberated
,, will to sin, without the deed, is more
,, sinful than the actual sin without a
,, deliberating will; and so in the case of Peter,
,, that person does more evil who intends to
,, deny Christ, even though he never does it,
,, than Peter, who actually denied Christ
,, and had never intended to do so. Therefore,
,, pay attention to your intentions and reflections.
,, If you sin with premeditation, well, this is the
,, next step to the sins of those against whom
,, the Prophet prays: Lord, be gracious to those
,, who sin out of wickedness.

Fifthly, the Spirit of God is withdrawn when people misuse the Holy Spirit as a cover for wicked lusts, just as the hypocrites do, who speak much of the Spirit only to commit sin and to enjoy their lusts with greater unconcern. So Simon the <margin>a pretext for greed. <note>Original Greek: "πρόφασις πλεονεξίας"</note></margin> Sorcerer <note>Also known as Simon Magus, who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit in the Book of Acts.</note> desired the uncommon gifts of the Spirit so that he might appear holy and enrich himself; this was but a cover for greed, as the Apostle speaks in 1 Thessalonians 2:5. Many grieve and provoke the Spirit to depart from them when they do not serve God themselves, but rather serve themselves under the appearance of religious service.

### Genesis 6, verse 3.

> Then the Lord said: My Spirit shall not strive with man forever, etc.

<margin>The 4th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry within London, November 10, 1650. The third question.</margin> I now proceed to answer another question or case of conscience, which is very profitable, and it is this:

-> How far the Spirit of God can be withheld and withdrawn, <-

even from a godly person, both before and after the commission of sins?

First, I shall show you how far God's Spirit can be withheld before the sin, and secondly, how far after the commission of the sin.

<margin>I.</margin> In a particular respect, God's Spirit can be said to be withdrawn from a godly person before the commission of sin:

First, such that He will not enlighten you and make known to you that it is a sin to which you are being tempted. So we read of the Patriarchs or ancient fathers, many of whom married multiple wives at the same time. God's Spirit was so withheld from them in those dark times of the world that He did not enlighten them—even up to the day of their death (as far as we can read)—that having several wives at once was a sin, and therefore they lived and died in it.

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, although you are so enlightened that you know that what you are being tempted to do is sin, nevertheless, you can be so abandoned by the Spirit that you can be carried away by the violent turbulence of your lusts and the power of temptation to commit the sin, as we find in David. David could not have been unaware that adultery was a sin; and yet when God's Spirit left him, the strength of his lust and the intensity of the temptation were such that he was led astray to commit it.

<margin>III.</margin> Thirdly, a godly person can be so far abandoned by the Spirit that when he is tempted to sin, he rather takes counsel with "flesh and blood" <note>A biblical idiom for human nature or worldly wisdom as opposed to divine guidance.</note> than with God's Spirit, as to whether he shall indeed commit the sin or not. And so a godly person, when his life, freedom, and status depend on it, often chooses his own preservation rather than internal peace; and this is very far gone, yet it was so with David in the matter of Uriah.

<margin>2 Samuel 11. IV.</margin> Fourthly, the godly can be so abandoned that they deliberate and consider how they shall commit a sin before they do it. Theologians commonly establish this as a distinction between the godly and the ungodly: that the latter sin with premeditation and the former do not. But there are examples in Scripture which show that even the godly sometimes deliberate and consider how they shall commit the sin. Now this is, as the theologians show, to be at the threshold of Hell, so that there is little between them and damnation. It is true, David's sin of adultery was not so premeditated beforehand as was the killing of Uriah; for here he deliberated on the means by which, the time when, the manner how, and the instrument with which Uriah should be killed. Now this was a very deliberate sin, yet a godly person can be abandoned that far. Therefore, how great a cause they have to bless God,

# Concerning God’s Spirit.
B

and to glorify and magnify His voluntary grace / to those who come so near to Hell / and yet do not fall into it. Your clothes may smell of the fires of Hell / and yet it may be that you are never set ablaze. Premeditated sins <note>original: "Voorbesmette sonden"; literally "pre-contaminated" or habitual sins that prepare the way for worse</note> are the path to the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit / which occurs through a loss of hope / therefore guard yourself against such sins.

<margin>V.</margin>
Fifthly / God’s Spirit can leave you / even if you are a godly person / so far that you fall into those sins / which are contrary to those very graces / in which you are most outstanding. It is not such a great thing if a chaste person merely fails to avoid sins / that are not so contrary to his natural disposition. But that a chaste person is so far forsaken by God / that he falls into Adultery / and that a gentle-minded person falls into irrational passions / that is a great evil. I will present to you several examples of the godly / who were thus forsaken by God’s Spirit.

<margin>Gen. 12:11, 12.</margin>
We find in Scripture concerning Abraham / that he was called the Father of the faithful; how extensively the Apostle praises Abraham’s faith: yet God forsook him so much / that he fell into unbelief and mistrust of God / by denying his own Wife <note>Referring to Abraham claiming Sarah was his sister out of fear</note> / which was very contrary to that grace / in which he was so outstanding. <margin>Gen. 9:21.</margin>

<margin>Num. 12:3.</margin>

<margin>Second part of the question.</margin>
<margin>1. Answer.</margin>
Now let us go and see / how far God’s Spirit can leave a believer after the committing of sin.

It may be / that the Spirit does not convict you / that what you have done is sin / after you have committed it / and so it was with the Patriarchs in the early times of the world / who married many wives at once / which nevertheless was against the first institution of Marriage / which was between one man and one woman; now God’s Spirit was withheld from them so far / that after they fell into that sin / they were not convicted of it / and therefore they lived and died in it.

<margin>2. Answer.</margin>
The Spirit can be so far from convicting a believer of a sin / and so far withdrawn from him / that after he has sinned / he goes on to defend the sin he has committed / to justify it. Thus Jonah sinned by not being obedient to God’s command to go to Nineveh / and when God came to spare Nineveh / Jonah became very angry; when God came to him to reason with him / asking whether his anger was rightly kindled, he answered / "yes, indeed my anger is rightly kindled even unto death." Here was a good man so darkened in mind / that he wanted to justify his own evil passions before God’s face. So Israel under the name of Ephraim wanted to defend her own wickedness.

<margin>Hos. 12:7, 8.</margin>
"In the Merchant’s hand" (says the Prophet) "is a deceitful balance, he loves to oppress." Yet Ephraim says, "nevertheless I have become rich, I have gained great wealth, in all my labors they shall find no iniquity in me, that were sin." And yet God accuses her of using a deceitful balance.

<margin>3. Answer.</margin>
A godly person can lie under a sin for a long time / yes, for many years / and God’s Spirit may work no gnawing of conscience in him / regarding the sin he has committed / and this is very sad. Thus David was deprived of the Spirit / for he committed Adultery with Bathsheba, and until the child was born / and the Prophet Nathan came to him / we do not read that he was in any way troubled because of his sin; the Spirit worked in him no gnawing of conscience / which must have been nine months / according to the term of women. And what is more / we read of the Brothers of Joseph, that they threw him into the pit / and sold him to the Ishmaelites / and although they acted so unnaturally with their Brother / yet Scripture relates / that they were first troubled after twenty-one years...

<margin>4th Answer.</margin>
**God’s Spirit** can be so far withdrawn from a godly person / after they have committed a sin / that they would rather commit even more sins to hide that first sin / than to have repentance for it; and this is a great step toward Hell. Nevertheless, we see this in **David**; for after he had fallen into Adultery / he did not awaken his conscience to have repentance for this sin of his / but set his mind to work to cover his sin; and to that end, he summoned **Uriah** home / so that he might lie with his wife / and thus David might cover his own sinful deed; and he even made him drunk. When he could not bring him to do this through all these means / then he plotted over his death / and made Uriah the messenger of his own death. **Peter** was indeed godly / yet he committed many sins to excuse one; indeed, he was quicker to commit many sins than to have repentance over one / namely / when he denied **Christ**. First, he denied him / after that, he denied him with an oath / and thirdly, he denied him with a curse; now, whether he cursed **Christ** / or himself / or both / is uncertain. Thus he began many sins to excuse one / which is a high degree of sin / and yet a godly person can go that far.

<margin>5th Answer.</margin>
A godly person / after having committed a sin / can be so far without strength to kill that sin / that they even fall into it a second time / and often. We have many examples of this in the Scripture. **Abraham** fell twice into the sin of lying / by denying his own wife.
<margin>Gen. 12:13, Gen. 20:2, Gen. 42:15, 16.</margin>
So **Joseph** fell twice into the sin of swearing. **Solomon** sinned against the Lord / after He had appeared to him twice. And
<margin>1 Kings 11:9</margin>
so also the children of **Israel** fell ten times one after another into the sin of murmuring against God. Thus **Jehoshaphat** sinned twice by making a sinful alliance with godless kings. I do not recount all of this
<margin>Num. 14:22, 1 Kings 22:45, 2 Chron. 18:2.</margin>
to lay cushions for anyone <note>A metaphor for providing excuses or comfort in sin.</note> / to continue in the way of sin / but only for the relief of troubled consciences. It can happen that far / that God’s Spirit leaves a believer / both before and after the committing of a sin.

Before I come to the treatment of the restraints of God’s Spirit / in respect to that which is good / I shall give the usefulness of what has now been said. If God’s Spirit then leaves you so far / I conclude from that firstly:

<margin>1st Use.</margin>
**That you must not blame God** / as a work of His sovereignty / but as a work of justice. God is provoked to do this. Why does God’s Spirit say to you / just as the Lord says to **Ephraim**:
<margin>Hos. 4:17.</margin>
"**Ephraim** is joined to idols, let him alone." Why does God’s Spirit leave you? You have done one or another wrong against the Spirit / you have either quenched the stirrings of the Spirit / or grieved the Spirit / or caused Him pain / or resisted Him in His workings / and therefore you no longer hear the warnings of the Spirit in your heart.

<column-break/>

<margin>2nd Use.</margin>
Secondly / **do not judge a person when you see them fall into sin** / do not be hard against them: if **God’s Spirit** were withdrawn from you / you would sin a thousand times more than that person. The Scripture commands / that you should restore those who are overtaken by any trespass with the Spirit of gentleness: looking to yourself / so that you are not tempted. If you see a person sinning / do not judge him; look to yourself / for if the Devil came to tempt you to a worse sin / and the Spirit were withdrawn from you / then you would sin worse than that person has sinned.
<margin>You today, I tomorrow. <note>original Latin: "Tu hodie, ego cras." A traditional reflection on human frailty attributed here to St. Augustine.</note></margin>

<margin>3rd Use.</margin>
Thirdly / **how great a cause you have then to thank God** / that He lets His Spirit strive with you and not with other people. First / praise God / that His Spirit was given to you. And the word is the Spirit / the voice behind you / saying: "This is the way, walk in it"; and through this means you are protected from many temptations / and freed from many evils. If only a tempting Devil and your corrupt heart came upon you / and God’s Spirit were withdrawn from you / into how great a sin would you run? Even a godly person would, in such a case, give themselves violently to evil / like a horse runs violently into battle / if the Spirit did not restrain them from sin. Secondly / thank God for other people / that He binds and bridles the spirit of men through the common restraining power of the Spirit. If it were not so / no one could live peacefully in this world; all human society would be undone; one would be enraged and raging against another: we would kill and murder everyone who angered us / deceive those who dealt with us / lie against those who came to speak with us / indeed, we would commit all sins. In this last and evil age of the world, much evil is done / but much more godlessness would occur / if the Spirit did not lay a bit and bridle in the consciences of men.
<margin>Man is a wolf to man. <note>original Latin: "Homo homini Lupus." A proverb suggesting that humans left to their own devices are predatory toward one another.</note></margin>

<margin>IV.</margin>

Perhaps you have sinned unknowingly / hastily / vehemently, and with premeditation: all the more that the Spirit was withheld from you before the sinning, pray that He strives with you all the more afterward / and that in these three ways.

1. That He works in you a clearer conviction of the sin / that He shows it to you / not in general / but in particular / clothed with all its shameful and aggravating circumstances / to convict you for your salvation / so that a sort of compensation might occur / for the Spirit having been withheld from you before.

2. That He humbles you more deeply; however much the Spirit was withheld from you before the sinning, desire that He casts you down all the more after the sinning. This was prefigured under the Law; he who merely touched an unclean thing was unclean until evening, but the person who had carried uncleanness upon himself / had to cast off all his clothes. So also / if you have only touched a sin / then you must humble yourself / but if you have fallen into a sin / of which the Spirit did not convict you / then you must...

> Then the Lord said: My Spirit shall not strive with man forever, &c.

<margin>5th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry in London, November 17, 1650.</margin>
<note>St. Lawrence Jewry is a historic church in the City of London where many prominent Puritan and Anglican divines preached.</note>
Now I go forward to treat of the withholdings of the Spirit in respect or regard to what is good, so that no holy motions are awakened in the heart toward one’s bounden duty. But before I come to speak of that in particular, I shall set forth a fourfold distinction of the motions of the Spirit toward the good.

<margin>John 14:26</margin>
1. There are **awakening acts** of the Spirit, through which holy affections rise up in the heart, and the coals of inclination and grace are fanned into flame within the same; and this is that which was promised by Christ, that the Holy Spirit shall *bring all things to remembrance*.

<margin>Rom. 8:26. <note>original Greek: συναντιλαμβανεται - "to take hold of together with"</note></margin>
2. There is a **helpful act** of the Spirit, for which reason the Spirit is said in Scripture to *come to the aid of our infirmities*. We read not only of an intercession of the Spirit, through which we are accepted by God, but also of an intercession through which the Spirit stands by us and helps us. Just as a tree, although it has a seed-like power within itself, nonetheless bears no fruit without the helping influence of the Heavens, so also God’s Spirit helps us in our working.
<margin>Ps. 51:13. Eph. 2:19, 22. Col. 2:8.</margin>

3. There is also a **strengthening act** of the Spirit, for God’s Spirit does not only come to the aid of the souls of men, but also brings them to strength and the growth of grace. Therefore we read of the *supplies of the Spirit*, that is, further steps and measures of the Spirit.
<margin>Phil. 1:19. <note>original Greek: Επιχορηγια τῦ πνευματος - "The supply of the Spirit"</note> Rom. 9:1. 2 Cor. 1:12.</margin>

4. There is a **comforting and witnessing act** of the Spirit, when God’s Spirit supports and confirms the testimony of your conscience to make known the uprightness of your heart. So you read of Paul, that his conscience bore him witness

<column-break/>

through the Holy Spirit. God’s Spirit testified with his spirit to the truth and uprightness of his heart. Now, although I could treat of all these particular things and show what a sorrowful judgment it is when the Spirit is withheld in these respects, I shall nonetheless speak only of the first, and show how sorrowful a judgment it is when the Spirit is withheld in His awakening acts, so that He does not cause holy motions toward the good to rise up in the heart.

In treating this, I shall follow this course:

First, I shall show you wherein it appears to be a judgment when the Spirit is withheld in respect of holy motions toward the good.

Secondly, when the Spirit favors us with such motions, how we shall be able to distinguish them from the motions toward the good which the Devil might come to awaken in us.

Firstly, these three miseries come upon the one from whom the Spirit is withheld in His motions toward the good.

<margin>Phil. 2:13.</margin>
1. There shall be in your heart an **emptiness and lack of holy thoughts**. God’s Spirit is like the balance wheel <note>original: "onrust" - the internal mechanism that keeps a clock moving</note> in a clock; if that stands still, then everything stands still; so too, if God’s Spirit is still within you, then none of your affections, which are the motions of your soul, can ascend upward. *It is God who works in us, both to will and to work according to His good pleasure.* You cannot even have the will for that which is truly good if God’s Spirit is withheld. In that state, the human heart is like that house of which it is said in the parable, that when the Devil came to possess it, he found it *empty, swept, and put in order*; empty,
<margin>Matt. 12:44.</margin>
namely, of any holy thoughts and lovely motions; and put in order—not with the graces of God’s Spirit, but with the decorations of the Devil. If you wish to know what sort of decorations these are, then read *Matthew 15:19-20*. Your heart shall then be empty of all good motions when God withdraws His Spirit.
<margin>Matt. 15:19-20.</margin>

<margin>II.</margin>
2. Your heart shall be **filled and tormented by the Devil** with evil motions. For a person’s heart cannot lie idle and empty for long; if it is not filled with the motions of the Spirit, it will be filled with the incitements of the Devil. If the heart is not Christ’s garden, then it shall become the Devil’s nursery; if it is not Christ’s armory, it shall become the Devil’s workshop; if it is not the temple of the Holy Spirit, it shall be the chapel of the Devil. Now this makes the misery all the greater: when evil motions torment and fill the heart, the Scripture expresses this by saying that the Devil *fills the heart*. If the winds of the Holy Spirit do not fill the sails of your heart to drive you forward toward Heaven, then the incitements and stirrings of Satan shall help drive you toward Hell. And it is worth noting that, just as the Scripture speaks of the *indwelling of the Spirit*, namely through His motions in the hearts of the godly—as we say, "the Sun is in the house" when only its rays are in there—likewise, when evil motions fill our hearts, the Scripture says that the Devil is in there; and so the Apostle Peter speaks to Ananias: *why has Satan filled your heart?* This must
<margin>Eph. 5:18. 1 John 4:13.</margin>
<margin>Acts 5:3</margin>

# The Withdrawal

must not be understood as a physical possession; rather, the meaning is that the Devil placed that greedy impulse in his heart. The Devil was within the impulse that was in the heart: therefore, people should pay close attention to evil impulses, for those have the Devil within them. When Judas had an impulse to betray Christ, it is said: *And Satan entered into Judas*; the Devil came into him through that evil impulse, for immediately afterward he went away and spoke with the Chief Priests, and reached an agreement with them regarding the betrayal of Christ. And "he who has boarded a ship with the devil must cross with him," <note>original: "die met de duyvel gescheept is, moet er me over"—an old Dutch proverb meaning that once one starts down a path of sin, they are compelled to see it through to the end.</note> as the proverb says. How great a misery is this then? If God's Spirit is withheld in your good impulses, then the Devil will possess your heart through evil impulses.

3. If the Spirit is withdrawn in her <note>In 17th-century Dutch, the Spirit (Geest) was often referred to with feminine pronouns.</note> awakening acts, so she shall also be withheld in her supporting and helping acts; and this is a further misery: if you are never moved to do good, then she will never support you in it. It is true, there can at times be impulses toward the good in the heart which are not further supported by the Spirit. The intent which many take up to be reformed is a common work of the Spirit, which often is not put into practice through any further assistance of the Spirit, just as there are sometimes convictions without conversion. But this is certain: that where the Spirit does not move toward the good, no assistance will be given to perform it. Water cannot rise higher than the source from which it flows. If your impulses are merely natural, then there will be no more assistance than that which comes from nature. We can recognize the misery of the Spirit’s withdrawal in her working and helping power from these following specific signs:

Namely, 1. When the Spirit is thus withdrawn, the soul is not so willing to do good, nor is it so set with pleasant delight and pleasure upon holy duties, but does them rather as if being forced, and with as little desire as a child has to go to school, or a thief to his hanging, as they say.

2. One then performs the required duties not so often as before—what one first did seven times a day with David, or three times a day with Daniel, now happens not even seven times in a month, or three times in a week.

3. It also happens without such great zeal, nor with such hot and active affections as before; but people are then lazy, lukewarm, listless, and dead in all holy exercises.

4. Likewise, there is no such constancy in holy impulses; rather, they are quickly passing and drifting away, not remaining firmly fixed upon the heart.

<margin>Question.</margin>
But how shall a person know the distinction between the awakening of the Spirit in the heart toward the good, and the impulses of the Devil to do good?

This case is of great use in the practice of godliness, because it can happen—yes, it often happens—that the Devil comes to move a person toward the good. The Devil sometimes appears in this case as an Angel of light: therefore, to answer the question, I shall present several marks.

<column-break/>

<margin>Answer. 1st Mark.</margin>
First of all, if you have an impulse to do good outside of your <term>office and calling</term><note>The concept of "calling" (beroep) was central to Reformation thought, meaning the specific social or professional role God assigned to an individual.</note>, then this impulse is from the Devil and not from God. You have an example of this in Saul: when the Philistines came down against him, and—see—he said, *I have not earnestly prayed before the face of the Lord: so I forced myself, and offered a burnt offering.* The thing he did was indeed good—namely, offering a burnt offering and praying—but that was not Saul's office or calling <note>Saul was a king, not a priest; only priests were authorized to offer sacrifices.</note>; and therefore, although it was a good thing, the impulse toward it nevertheless came from the Devil. As we also read, the Lord was highly displeased by this deed of his, and Samuel rebuked him for it in verse 13, saying, *You have done foolishly, you have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God.* <margin>1 Sam. 13:12.</margin> So you read of Uzziah, that he did not want to leave off Divine service, but wanted to burn incense to the Lord himself; yet before he had done it, he was plagued with Leprosy. It was a good thing to make an offering, but it was not good in Uzziah, who was not called to it. <margin>2 Chron. 26:18.</margin> And just as this is true in Divine matters, so it is also in civil affairs; suppose a private person does the work of a Sovereign, where it is not his calling; this comes not from God, but from the Devil. Absalom undertakes to do justice for the people, but how? He was merely a usurper of the Royal Office, and just as he had no right to the Royal power, so he also had no calling to publicly administer justice. For when private individuals, pretending their own special gifts, take upon themselves public service, it cannot come from God's Spirit: for the Spirit keeps everyone within his bounds. Therefore the Apostle says, *Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called with God.* <margin>1 Cor. 7:20, 24.</margin> The Spirit makes people do good within their own office and calling; the Devil does not do this. When the fire lies on the hearth, that is good, and it was placed there by your servants; but when it lies on the roof or the attic of the house, that was done by an enemy. So too, impulses toward the good within your office and calling come from God’s Spirit, but impulses toward any good outside of your calling are given by the Devil.

<margin>2nd Mark.</margin>
Secondly, it may be that the Devil moves you toward good, but perhaps to hinder some greater good. It is very noteworthy when our Savior began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day. <margin>Matt. 16:21, 22, 23.</margin> That Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, *Lord, be merciful to yourself, this shall not happen to you.* Now, this came from the Devil, to hinder the work of man’s salvation; therefore Christ says, *Get behind me, Satan, you are an offense to me: for you do not mind the things that are of God, but those that are of men.* These words have a special emphasis in them: truly the <term>Papists</term><note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics, used here to contrast Protestant theology with the doctrine of Papal authority.</note>, who claim an apostolic succession from Peter, would excuse Peter in this impulse, yes, even hold this for a Godly impulse; but the Reformed Christians all agree here that Peter's impulse was naturally good, for he

# Of God's Spirit.

<margin>2 Corinthians 3:7</margin> <note>The text likely intends 2 Corinthians 2:7, which discusses forgiving a repentant person so they are not "swallowed up by overmuch sorrow."</note> ...is human; nonetheless, much sin is mixed within it. The Devil has a two-fold purpose in moving the young convert toward the good: namely, either to make them more quickly weary of God’s service, or else to make the godless think that religion is very difficult. I do not say this to quench or stifle anyone's good impulses. I know well that where one person does too much, ten thousand do too little. But we must see to it that we, like the Church of Corinth, are not too severe. For just as they had nearly swallowed up the excluded person through excessive punishment and overflowing sadness, so also will excessive narrowness and severity discourage people and draw them away from the ways of Christ.

<margin>11th Mark.</margin> Eleventhly, those impulses come from the Devil in the event that one is moved toward those things which serve only as an introduction or a preparation for duties, rather than being the duties of religion themselves. This is a great craftiness of the Devil; if he can keep men in the <term>forecourt</term> <note>The outer area of the Temple; here a metaphor for the preparation for worship rather than the worship itself.</note>, they shall never enter the church. For example, reflection is a preparatory duty for prayer, contemplation for hearing the Word, and self-examination for receiving the Lord’s Supper. Now, if the Devil can keep you busy in that preparation for so long that you can take no time for the principal duties themselves, then the Devil has achieved his purpose. <margin>A Parable.</margin> Christians are often very imprudent in this; it is much as if someone who was assigned to play a sweet-sounding tune for a company for one hour spent all his time tuning his instrument to the right pitch. So it is with many Christians. No; preparation for holy duties must only serve us for advancement in the same. He who is busy in preparation for so long that he neglects the duties themselves, removes the very purpose of the preparation. I know well that there are some who never prepare themselves for duties; and then there are others who, through the craftiness of the Devil, deprive themselves of much time in their preparations which they ought to have spent in the principal duties themselves.

<margin>1 Peter 1:13</margin> But the Spirit of God girds up the loins of our understanding so that he makes us ready to carry out our required duties with haste.

<margin>12th Mark.</margin> Twelfthly, the impulses toward the good come from the Devil when one is moved to use the same as a <term>cloak</term> <note>A "deckmantel" or covering used to hide one's true, often wicked, intentions.</note>, in order to commit godlessness with less suspicion and greater boldness. So it was with Absalom, for it was good that he wished to do justice to all the people, and that when they came to his Father for judgment, he spoke to them kindly and kissed them: but this was only as a cover, so that they should have no suspicion that he was taking over his Father’s Kingdom. In like manner, the Scribes and Pharisees devoured widows' houses, and as a cover they made long prayers. To make long prayers was indeed good, but to do so with such a high-handed purpose was highly abominable; so that if anyone's impulses toward good have this purpose—to sin with more freedom and less reflection—then they come from the Devil and not from God. The Devil does not care

<column-break/>

how godly you appear, as long as you are in fact evil and sinful.

<margin>Utility.</margin> Oh, do not conclude then that you are in a <term>state of grace</term> <note>The condition of being under God's favor and destined for salvation.</note> because good impulses sometimes enter your heart; for you may well have good impulses and meanwhile still be an evil person; not every flicker is a fire from the Sanctuary. Remember then, that you may well have a thousand good impulses, and nonetheless travel to Hell. It was a good impulse in Balaam, <margin>Numbers 23:10</margin> when he said, *let my soul die the death of the righteous*, yet he was one <margin>2 Peter 2:15</margin> who loved the wages of unrighteousness. Although I do not wish to discourage anyone in their good impulses, I say nonetheless that you may well have them while they proceed from the Devil rather than from God’s Spirit. Therefore, take close heed of your ways and your impulses toward the good, and see whether they come from the <term>strivings</term> <note>The internal struggle or "wrestling" where the Holy Spirit convicts a person of sin.</note> of God’s Spirit with you, or from the stirrings of the evil spirit which is against you.

### Genesis 6:3.

> Then the Lord said: My Spirit shall not strive with man forever, etc.

***

<margin>6th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry in London, November 24, 1650.</margin><margin>The third question.</margin> NOW I proceed to a third question, which is this: for what reason does God the Lord withdraw from the souls of men, or withhold the strivings of His Spirit?

I shall set forth four reasons for this as causes of this judgment.

<margin>1st Answer.</margin> First, because you quench the impulses of God's Spirit; therefore He withdraws the movements of the Spirit. God's Spirit is a tender thing; one must not wrong or misuse it, otherwise it will deal with us just as we deal with it. Your act is a sinful act, but what God does is a work of righteousness. <margin>The Spirit of God is a delicate matter; he treats us as he is treated. — Tertullian.</margin> <note>Original Latin: "Res delicatulo, est Spiritus Dei, ita nos tractat sicut tractatur."</note> Because Israel would not listen, therefore God gave them over to the stubbornness of their own hearts. So it was with the Bride in the Song of Solomon. <margin>Psalm 81:12, 13.</margin> Christ came knocking at the door, saying, *Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one; for my head is filled with dew, my locks with the drops of the night.*

<margin>Song of Solomon 5:2, 3, 6.</margin> But she said, *I have taken off my robe, how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?* Thus she turned Christ away, and upon this Christ withdrew himself; and then she sought him with sorrow, but could not find him. *I opened* (she says) *to my Beloved, but my Beloved had turned away, he was gone: my soul failed when he spoke, I sought him, but I could not find him, I called him, but he gave me no answer.* Because we reject Christ and quench the impulses of His blessed Spirit, therefore He rightfully departs from us.

Spiritual desertions are of three kinds:

1. Either the warning desertions, to prevent sin, as Paul was buffeted <margin>2 Corinthians 12:7</margin> so that he would not exalt himself.

2. Or testing desertions, to test and exercise grace. In this way Holy Job was deserted.

3. Or punishing desertions, as a chastisement for spiritual sloth; and so in the...

# The Withdrawal

...the example of the Bride, as we have just discussed.

</margin>
II. Secondly, because humans are more ready to accept the evil impulses toward sin than the impulses of the Spirit toward the good. Just as a friend, seeing that his old acquaintance would rather listen to the requests of an enemy than to him, is stirred to break off that inner friendship; so too the Spirit of God—who has been your oldest and best friend—seeing that you would rather give ear to the whisperings of the evil spirit than to His movements, is prompted to depart from you. Here I can apply the history of Rehoboam. When the dignified and wise elders of the children of Israel saw that the reckless king had rejected their counsel and clung to the immature and hasty judgment of a group of loose young men, they abandoned him, and ten of the twelve tribes fell away from him. Even so, the Holy Spirit abandons those who abandon His movements and His soul-saving instructions. <note>Rehoboam was the son of Solomon whose harshness led to the split of the Kingdom of Israel.</note>

III. Thirdly, because people have misused the movements and workings of the Spirit for evil and sinful ends, such as for the applause of the people, for vain glory, for some hidden advantage, or as a cloak to hide some secret lusts. When such evil use is made of the Spirit's workings to excuse one's desires, God's Spirit is prompted and moved to abandon those people who put spiritual gifts up for sale for evil uses. What is this but someone lighting their lantern at the lamp of the Sanctuary <note>The "Sanctuary" refers to the Tabernacle or Temple.</note> in order to go out and steal? This was the sin of Simon the Sorcerer, who wanted to buy the gift of the Spirit with money, to misuse it for a high end. This grieves the Spirit of God greatly.

<margin>
Acts 8:19
</margin>
IV. Fourthly, because people take those sinful inclinations which come from the flesh and attribute them to the Spirit; namely, when they count and regard their own hellish rage as the heavenly fire of the Spirit, Satan's deceptions as the Spirit's movements, a loose and unbridled life as the spiritual freedom of Christians, wandering opinions as the teachings of the Spirit, and a prideful peace as the testimony of the Spirit. This is as if an adulterous beggar laid his bastard child at the King's door; and it provokes God's Spirit to abandon such people and withdraw His movements from them.

<margin>
Ten marks and signs of the withdrawal of the Spirit.
</margin>
Now I proceed to the signs or tokens of the withdrawal of the Spirit. Note that when I speak of the withdrawal of the Spirit, I do not mean a total withdrawal, but a partial one—that is, certain degrees of the same. I shall present ten signs; if you find any of these in yourself, you may be fit to pass a righteous judgment upon yourself.

I. First, if the Spirit is withdrawn from you, you will not set your heart as willingly to do good as you did in former times. Your soul first ran quickly along the good path, but now that the wheels of your soul's wagon have been taken away, you go

<column-break/>

onward with sorrow. It is not the wagon of Amminadab—that is, of "my willing people." <note>original: "Amminadab" — a name from Song of Solomon 6:12, often interpreted in this period as meaning "a willing people" (Am = people, Nadav = willing).</note> God's people in the days of the Gospel are described as a willing people: *Your people shall be very willing in the day of your power* <note>original: "U volck sal seer ghewilligh zijn op den dagh uwer heyr-kracht"</note>; "a people of willingness" it says in the original text <note>original: "עַמְּךָ נְדָבֹת" (Ammecha nedavot)</note>. But a person from whom the Spirit is withdrawn is driven to do good not so much out of delight as out of compulsion; he comes as reluctantly to those duties as a thief to hanging (as is seen) or a child going to school, who does everything commanded of him with much resistance and hesitation, and not with willingness. He is pulled rather than led to his bounden duty, and is forced to do good by a fearful dread of Hell and some hope of Heaven, or perhaps to quiet the barking and gnawing of a natural conscience. When the Spirit is withdrawn from you, you do not do your duty as willingly as before. That is one.

II. Secondly, you do not do good with as much preparation as you were accustomed to. Formerly, you could do as Abraham did, who left his donkey and his servants in the valley; you could shake off all obstacles that might hinder or turn you away. When you were to pray, you used reflection; when you were to hear God's word, you prepared yourself; when you were to receive the Supper, you examined yourself. But now that God's Spirit is withdrawn from you, you lay aside those preparatory duties which are so helpful in those services through which we have communion with God. The soul used to adorn herself like a Bride when she goes to the King to enjoy communion with the great God; but since she has now become careless in that preparation, it is a sign that the Spirit is withdrawn.

III. Third, you no longer have such great delight of heart in holy duties as before. That duty which you previously did for pleasure is now like a task that must be finished; at first it tasted to you as sweet as honey, now you find no more taste in it than in the white of an egg. <note>Reference to Job 6:6.</note> There was a time when you could say with the Psalmist: *I rejoiced in those who said to me: let us go into the House of the Lord*, and you held God's service so high that you could say with David that *one day in the courts was better than a thousand elsewhere.* But alas! where is this delight now? Now the bounden duty is like a burden, and not a source of joy.

<margin>
IV. This grieves the Spirit, when we, as it were, stifle and extinguish its most holy movements toward holy duties.
</margin>
IV. Fourthly, it is a proof that the Spirit is partially withdrawn when you do not perform those duties as often as before. You could first pray seven times a day with David, or three times a day with Daniel, but now not three times a week. How the frequency of your duties has decreased! I would have everyone in such a state notice:

1. You have no fewer enemies now than before; why then should you attend to your duties less? The alertness of the enemy is kindled by our inattention and carelessness.

2. You also have no fewer temptations now; and why then should you not pray often to be delivered from them?

3. You have no fewer sins now than before—indeed, perhaps more—so why then would you now pray less for forgiveness? He who sins often must also pray often for forgiveness.

4. You have no less need for grace now than before—indeed, perhaps more—why then are you not as diligent in praying to God for grace? If you do not perform your holy duties as often now as before, it is a clear proof that the Spirit has partially withdrawn from you.

<margin>V.</margin>
Fifthly: if you do not have that fervor and holy devotion that you had before, it is a bad sign that you have greatly decreased in grace. This is set as a warning sign regarding the decline of the <margin>Revelation 2:4</margin> Church of Ephesus; *But I have this against you, that you have left your first love.* It does not say you have *lost* it, but that you have *left* your first love; grace can indeed be left behind, but not entirely lost. That first delight you had in the ways of God, you have abandoned; you have diminished in these affections. <margin>Jerome says: "Do you think so? Did Jonah pray like this in the depths, or Daniel among the wolves <note>original: "Leones" (lions), though the Dutch text says wolves.</note>, or the thief on the cross pray so fervently?" Augustine says: "Many pray fervently at the novelty of their conversion, afterwards coldly, then languidly, then negligently." 2 Timothy 1:6. <unclear>divi curreper.</unclear></margin> Jerome rebukes the negligent in prayer thus: "What do you think," he says, "did Jonah pray like that in the sea, or Daniel among the wolves, or a thief on the cross, as you do?" Many are so far abandoned by the Spirit that they have come to the state of which Augustine complained in his time: namely, that many at the beginning of their conversion pray with feeling and with fervor, but after the passage of time they pray coldly, faintly, and negligibly; they lost those affections which they first had. They must stir up the fire <note>referring to 2 Timothy 1:6, "stir up the gift of God"</note> which lay hidden under the ashes.

Sixthly: this is also a sign of the withdrawal of the Spirit: when someone performs a duty with less spirituality and haste than before. Distractions break in, and wandering thoughts go out; holy stirrings diminish and pass by. When such things no longer find a permanent home in the heart as they did before, it is a sign that the Spirit is partially departing from you. For where God's Spirit is, there he strengthens the heart and makes it firm in holy movements. Therefore David prays, *let the free spirit uphold me.* <note>Psalm 51:12.</note> When there is much fickleness and instability in the heart, it is a sign that the Spirit is partially leaving that soul.

<margin>VII.</margin>
Seventhly: if in the practice of religion, you do not bring forth as much fruit as in former times. Formerly, religious duties made an impression on your heart like a signet ring on soft wax, but now they do no more than a seal upon a marble stone. Formerly, the spiritual means of religion fell upon you like rain upon the valleys, but now they are to you like water poured out upon a rocky cliff. Many people perform religious duties without profit and are like the Cypress tree, of which it is said that it is very good for the scent and the sight, but nevertheless unfruitful. Many Christians are like this tree; they grow in God's garden and are good in the sight of others, but they bring forth no fruit. If you are not a fruitful tree in the Garden of Grace, it is proof that the Spirit of Grace is being withheld from you.

<column-break/>

<margin>VIII.</margin>
Eighthly: when your religious duties are not as spiritual as in former times, it is proof that the Spirit is partially leaving you. And this is evident in two respects:
1. When less grace is exercised.
2. When more sins are committed in the carrying out of the duties.

1. If there is less grace exercised in the duties—as if there is less affection, less purity, less delight, less love, less joy, and fewer heavenly reflections than were found in previous years—it is a sign that the Spirit has partially departed from you.

2. If in the performance of your worship you commit more sins than before—such as if there is more spiritual pride, more fleshly confidence, more seeking of self-profit, more wandering thoughts, more irreverence toward God, more hardness of heart, and more weariness of your soul in holy exercises—this shows in you an abundance of sin, and it is proof of the withdrawal of the Spirit. I appeal to your own conscience: judge for yourself whether some or all of these conditions are found in you. And whether this is not particularly there: namely, that you do not perform your religious duties as spiritually as before; that you have practiced more sin and less grace therein. This can be explained through a parable. One never sees a crow <note>original: "Kraep"</note> picking at a living person, but if he is dead and lies in a pit, how all kinds of predatory birds will attack him! One never sees worms crawling on a living person, but let him once be dead and his soul separated from him, how quickly the vermin will eat his dead body. I bring this parable only to this end: that what the soul is to the body, the same is the Spirit of God to the soul. Just as while the soul is united with the body, no crow or bird of prey will touch it, so also while God’s Spirit makes you alive, no foul desires will seize you. But if once God’s Spirit, which is the life of your soul, is withdrawn, then great multitudes of evil desires will attack your heart in all those duties which you perform for your God. Your heart will be a nest of unclean birds, a hiding place for demons, if God’s Spirit is but once withdrawn.

<margin>IX.</margin>
Ninthly: from this you may also know if the Spirit is withdrawn from you: if you do not perform your religious duties as carefully and diligently as you did in the past, but carry them out with greater negligence—with "folded arms," as they say. When God’s Spirit is withdrawn from a soul, then that soul becomes careless in good duties in two respects. 1. You will be careless in the *manner* in which you do them, and never take care how you shall make your spirit fit for the performance thereof. And then secondly: you will no longer take care for the *end* of the duties: namely, that your soul may be bettered thereby and you be made more fit to enjoy your God.

<margin>X.</margin>

# The Withdrawal

...duties, and does not receive from them as much exercise and influence as in former times; I mean to say that in such a case, good duties do not have such an influence toward the improvement of our conduct. God did not institute your duties for their own sake, so that you should rest in them, but for other ends, for the benefit of your life and conversation; therefore the Apostle says, if 
<margin>Galatians 5:25.</margin> 
we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. These duties, in which the Spirit assists us, must have an influence upon our lives: therefore, you who persevere in holy duties without them having an influence upon your heart, you may indeed be a great hearer of God’s word, but you do not live godlily; you are a great professor of religion <note>original: "belijder van den Godts-dienst," meaning one who publicly declares their faith.</note>, but your works do not agree with your profession; this is a proof that your duties have no saving influence upon your life. You may well pray, but you do not live well; you are a good man on your knees, but an evil man in your dealings; this is a sign that God’s Spirit is withdrawn from you. Now attend to your hearts, and test them in all these particular things, and see whether God’s Spirit has departed from you or not.

<margin>Use for comfort.</margin>
So that no troubled conscience might be in any way discouraged by what I have said, I shall here present words of comfort for such persons.

<margin>I.</margin>
First, consider that although the life-giving workings of the Spirit can be withdrawn from a godly person, nevertheless the gracious presence of the Spirit cannot be withdrawn. Therefore, O believing soul, do not despair, nor lose heart; the Spirit is for you like the Sun behind a cloud; it is always in the firmament, so also the Spirit is in your heart; and although it is under a cloud regarding its influences, yet it is continually with you regarding its presence. A believer can indeed have within himself true and actual grace, even though he does not have the comfort of it.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, observe that you can <note>The text likely intended "discern" or "recognize"</note> God, who says that these signs and occurrences [show] the withdrawal and departure of the Spirit from you; and remember that God never allows the motions and workings of the Spirit to be equally great forever and continually. No; it is with your soul in this case as it is with natural things: in the Sea there is the ebb and flow; in the seasons of the year there is the Winter as well as the Summer, and the Autumn as well as the Spring. As it is with the times and seasons in natural things, so it is also in spiritual things. God’s Spirit is not continually in man in the same measure, but there is an ebb and flow in it. In this, our heart is like the sky: sometimes it is bright and clear, sometimes overcast. The Sun is indeed always in the firmament, but it does not always give the same heat and influence upon the earth. So it is also with the Spirit of God in the hearts of His children: it does not always have the same influence upon the heart. There can be a time in which you are in your Winter, in which your graces have no color and no greenness; nevertheless, the Spirit is always in you, and will let you flourish in the Springtime. The tree can indeed have life in the root when, during the wintertime, it has neither leaves, nor blossom, nor fruit. The life of a child of God can well be hidden in Christ, the root of all spiritual life, although it is occasionally touched by the winter-frost, both in respect to the growth, exercise, and comfort of grace.

<column-break/>

<margin>III. Jesus Christ is not only a faithful, but also a merciful High Priest, Hebrews 2:17.</margin>
Thirdly, remember that Jesus Christ well knows that you cannot fulfill your religious duties without weakness during the whole time of your life; and therefore He has His perfect righteousness to cover the imperfection of the duties, and this must strengthen the hearts of poor Christians to the highest degree. It is a worthy observation of a learned man regarding <margin>Song of Solomon 2:6.</margin> <note>The margin says 2:6, but the quote is traditionally from Song of Solomon 3:6.</note> where it is written: *Who is she that comes up out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense.* By her who came up out of the wilderness, the Bride of Christ is understood. Note two things here: first, she comes up out of the wilderness; so then the Church can indeed be an oppressed and distressed church, even though she is a true and religious church. It refers to the great trials with which God exercised His people when He led them through the wilderness of Canaan.

Secondly, she is said to come up out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke. Now what is understood by this? A certain theologian gives this meaning: God’s people can indeed have "smoky" duties, having become black through many of their weaknesses; they can indeed be pillars of smoke and have much soot upon them. But what is now your comfort? Although it is said that the Bride came up as a pillar of smoke, yet she was perfumed with myrrh and frankincense; that is, she had the righteousness of Jesus Christ to perfume her duties; He perfumes my duties with the Myrrh of His own righteousness. And when the prayers of the Saints, which are compared to incense, <margin>Psalm 141:2.</margin> are offered up by Christ, then they go up to Heaven as a very sweet and lovely offering, much more acceptable than the costly smoke of the most precious resins of Arabia. Oh, let your heart then be supported; you are indeed black because of your weaknesses, but there is a scent which can make all your duties sweet.

Therefore it is written that an Angel came and <margin>Revelation 8:3 and 4.</margin> stood at the Altar, having a golden censer: and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all Saints upon the golden Altar which is before the throne. This does not support the opinion of the Papists <note>original: "Papgesinde," a derogatory term for Roman Catholics common in the 17th century.</note>, as if we must use the mediation of angels; but by the Angel is not understood here a created Angel of the Lord, but the Angel of the Covenant, the Lord: and what was His office? He had much incense, which He offered with the prayers of the Saints. All the people of God seek to cover their imperfect duties in the righteousness of Jesus Christ, and then it is said that the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the Saints, went up from the hand of the Angel before God; that is, the righteousness of Jesus Christ is offered to the Lord with the prayers of the Saints, whereby they are made acceptable.

Fourthly and finally, this can be your comfort: although you cannot perform your divine service without weakness, nevertheless you do so without known hypocrisy; although you sin in the manner of your doing, yet you do not wish...

I now proceed to some further use and application of this matter, which I shall do by presenting certain particular consequences, directions, or propositions concerning the withdrawals of God’s Spirit.

<margin>concerning /</margin>
First, then, be convinced that you have such a high need for the motions of the Spirit to be constantly granted to you, and this on four grounds.

<margin>proposition.</margin>
1. If you consider the weakness and inability of your nature, both regarding holy motions and holy workings. A human being is not only too weak to do good, but also to bring forth any good motion. Therefore the <margin>Philippians 2:13; 2 Corinthians 3:5.</margin> Apostle says: *It is God who works in you, both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.* Even the longing of the soul for what is good is something above nature and must come from God; therefore the same Apostle says, *Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is of God.* The lower heavens or orbital spheres move only when they are driven and moved by the uppermost. A mole could as easily move the earth from its center, or a fly drink up all the water of the sea, as you could of yourself bring forth any good motion or ability to do good; all our help must come down from the <margin>Romans 8:13.</margin> Spirit of God; and therefore Paul says: *If you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.* Therefore, your weakness shall make you see how you have need of the Spirit.

2. Consider not only the weakness, but also the resistance which is in you against the good. And therefore the Scripture speaks not only of grieving the Spirit and quenching it, but also of resisting the same, Acts 7:51. <note>The OCR reads "5. 51," but the reference to resisting the Spirit is Acts 7:51.</note> Furthermore, these manners <margin>Song of Solomon 1:4; John 6:44.</margin> of speaking in the Scripture—*Draw me and we will run after you*; *No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him*—indicate not only a weakness, but also an unwillingness to come, and a hesitating of our hearts to subject ourselves to the Law of holiness, until <margin>Psalm 110:3.</margin> the time that God makes us a willing people in the day of His power. <note>The original Dutch "heyrkracht" refers to God's "army-power" or "mighty power."</note>

3. That strong resistance of nature against holy motions must convince you that you have the highest need of the Spirit. Although grace is of an active nature, nevertheless there is a disorder in the subject <note>The "subject" here refers to the human person in whom grace resides.</note>; therefore the grace of the Spirit must be moved to action. Fire, as you know, is indeed of an active nature and fit for burning; but if it is placed upon green or wet wood, then the greenness will resist the power of the flame. And so is grace in our nature; it is like fire placed on green wood; it must be blown upon a little before it will burn. Therefore the Apostle sighed these words to Timothy: *stir up* (he says) *the gift <margin>2 Timothy 1:6.</margin> of God which is in you,* blow upon the coals; there is great resistance in our hearts against the Spirit of God.

4. Reflect on the abundance of evil motions which will break into your heart if the motions of the Spirit are withdrawn from you; and then you shall see how greatly you need the Spirit's motions. Your heart will be a hiding place for the Devil and evil lusts if the Spirit be absent. Just as smoke rises up from the chimney, so shall corruption rise up from your heart. Just as a fanned fire throws up sparks, so shall evil motions come into your heart when corruption is Kindled by temptation. You are unwilling and resistant toward the good. The Spirit must awaken you; to this end you have a passage in the Prophet Isaiah: *He awakens <margin>Isaiah 50:4.</margin> me* (he says) *every morning.* You have need to be awakened by God’s Spirit day by day because of your daily indisposition. From this you can see how you need the Spirit of God.

Secondly, it is not enough that you <margin>2nd Proposition.</margin> are convinced of the necessity of the Spirit's motions, but you must also be convinced that you fall back into such a bottomless depth of misery if the motions of the Spirit are withheld: which shall appear through these three considerations.

1. It is considered a great misery in Scripture if even the common workings and gifts of the Spirit are withheld; and therefore you read how pitifully Saul complained <margin>1 Samuel 28:15.</margin> because the Spirit had departed from him, which was only in the common gifts. So also of Samson it is said that he did <margin>Judges 16:20.</margin> not know that the Spirit had departed from him, namely the Spirit of strength. If this is now a lamentable matter when the Spirit is withdrawn in its common gifts, shall it not then be reckoned as a sorrowful misery when the Spirit is withdrawn in its saving, comforting, and sanctifying workings?

2. Because while the Spirit is withdrawn, you are constantly in danger of loss. This can be better explained with this parable. Suppose a great merchant has a ship at sea, richly laden, which is close to the harbor, but because of a great calm or storming winds, is not able to enter. Now as long as the ship is not in, the merchant is also in constant danger of loss. Apply this to the spiritual: this ship is your soul, the cargo is grace, and the harbor is Heaven; the cool winds are the motions of the Spirit, the rising storm-winds are temptations: now if the motions of the Spirit do not help you, you shall not be able to enter the harbor. From this you can see your misery, being without the motions of God's Spirit.

3. Because, if good motions ->not<- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "not" on the next page.</note>
