# Of God's Spirit.

...to obtain that humble and penitent disposition of the heart, which must be present in a forsaken soul—judging that he is rejected and forsaken by God because of his sin—but sometimes these [withdrawals] are warnings, and sometimes they are trials.

<margin>6th Proposition.</margin>
Sixthly, be more diligent in causing the Spirit to return when He has been withdrawn, than in constantly casting your eyes upon your misery during the Spirit's absence. Many Christians have the fault of being quietly content with fruitless and sorrowful lamentations over their loss, but are not industrious in considering how to regain what they have lost. It was not enough for Joshua to lie down on his face because of the transgression at Ai <note>Joshua 7:10–11; after a defeat, Joshua mourned, but God commanded him to get up and deal with the sin in the camp.</note> (Joshua 7, v. 10, 11), but he had to stand up, clear up the matter, and strive to bring the covenant-breaking to light. There are some professors of religion who think to excuse their vanity and spiritual negligence with weeping and complaining. You have lost the Spirit; do not stand still and gaze at your loss, but reflect on what you must do to get the Spirit back. To this end, follow these three rules:

1. Cleanse your conscience of the maintenance of any known sin; make your heart pure and fit for Christ, and then His Spirit will come to you. Let your heart be like <margin>Luke 22:12.</margin> the guest chamber in which Christ came to eat the Passover; it was an upper room, a furnished room, and a clean room. See to it that your heart is prepared and cleansed with the broom of sanctifying grace, away from the persistence of sin, and this will be a means for you to recover the Spirit.

<margin>James 5:13.</margin>
2. Go to God in prayer, which is a general remedy for all kinds of spiritual disorders. *Is any among you afflicted, let him pray,* says the Apostle James. Though the difficulty be ever so great, prayer will be a means to deliver you. Prayer is appointed by God as a means to obtain God's Spirit (Luke 11, verse 13), and also speedily, because it is God's institution.

3. Do not only pray, but also bewail your state in prayer; spread your complaints before the Lord and say: "Lord, how is my heart now like a birdcage for unclean birds <note>original: "vogel-kooy voor onreyne ghebogelt" — a reference to Revelation 18:2, describing a fallen state.</note>, a hiding place for sin and the Devil!" For this my heart is now most fit. How are those strong and blossoming graces, which I once had, now withered like the grass on the rooftop? I, who was once embraced with an everlasting arm, am now forsaken by the Spirit. I was formerly a blessed field, and like the Cedars of Lebanon, shooting forth my roots and delightful branches. But now I am like a wild tree of a forest, which brings forth nothing. <margin>2 Samuel 1, verse 21.</margin> Formerly I was like a fruitful branch of the vine of Christ, but now I am like the mountains of Gilboa, upon which neither water nor dew falls. Bewail yourself thus in the presence of the Lord, and perhaps when He sees you with tears in your eyes and your prayers in your hand, He will return to you; though He has forsaken you, yet He has not forgotten you; though He has cast you down, yet He will not reject you forever (He will not cast off His people) if you do not forsake Him: labor then through

<column-break/>

prayers and tears, to regain what you have lost through the fall.

<margin>7th Proposition.</margin>
Seventhly, consider it a sadder and heavier judgment that the sanctified and sanctifying motions of the Spirit are withdrawn, than that the comfort of the Spirit is withheld. This is a fault among many Christians, especially among those who are troubled in their conscience: all their complaints are about the lack of assurance and comfort, saying, "I do not know whether Christ is mine or not," etc. All their concern and sorrow turns on this pivot. Therefore it is much to be feared that self-love, rather than love for Christ, is the foundation of many such complaints that people make, saying they are forsaken. Yet it is a sadder judgment if you lack the awakening motions of the Spirit <note>The inner promptings to do good or feel conviction.</note> than if you happen to miss the testimony and consolations of the Spirit. It is sadder that the lovely motions of the Spirit are withheld, than that the comforts of the Spirit were withdrawn.

<margin>8th Proposition.</margin>
Eighthly, the common gifts of the Spirit can sometimes be given, while the saving gifts of the Spirit are withheld. So it stood with many in the Church of <margin>1 Corinthians 1:7.</margin> Corinth. The Apostle says of them that <margin>1 Corinthians 3:3.</margin> they lacked no gift, but as far as grace is concerned, he says of them that they were carnal and walked as men.

<margin>9th Proposition.</margin>
Ninthly, note this: that it can happen that the motions and workings of the Spirit are truly withdrawn from a person, who in his own imagination thinks that he fully enjoys them. In this, it can go with a man just as it did with Samson; he was told that the Philistines were upon him, and <margin>Judges 16, verse 20.</margin> he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times, and shake myself free." For he did not know that the Lord had departed from him; he did not know that his strength was gone. Thus you may sometimes be forsaken by the Spirit and not know it. The reason for this is, partly because the Spirit departs from you in degrees (one cannot discern a person's growth because he increases gradually; as it is with your natural growth, so it is with your spiritual decline), and partly because the heart is very deceitful, careless, and negligent in examining and testing how it stands with your soul. Therefore, let this be in your thoughts: that the motions of the Spirit may well be withdrawn from you, even when in your opinion you are certain that you possess them.

<margin>Application of this Doctrine through consolation.</margin>
I shall conclude this matter with a few words of comfort, so that no one may by chance become troubled or discouraged by what I have said concerning the withdrawal of God's Spirit.

<margin>1st Use.</margin>
O you Christian soul, who complain that the Spirit is withdrawn from you, remember that although the Spirit is withdrawn from you, it is not a total but a partial withdrawal; it is only in some things, and not in all: in some motions and help, not in others. The Spirit is never entirely withdrawn from the godly. The Spirit is nonetheless present, even though comfort and assurance are not there.

<margin>2nd Use.</margin>
<margin>It is with the soul here as it is with herbs in the winter.</margin>
Let this be your comfort: that the Spirit departs from you only for a time, and not forever. Only for a short moment is the Spirit away from you (Isaiah 54:8). In a lit-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Holy Spirit's withdrawal. The previous page offered rules for reclaiming the Spirit through a clean conscience and spiritual diligence. Here, the author distinguishes between the actual absence of the Spirit and a believer's mere perception of its absence, before transitioning into a new sermon on walking by the Spirit to overcome worldly desires.</meta>

# The Withdrawal

<margin>And in the trees, all the sap is not gone, but it has moved backward into the root.</margin>
...in a small moment of wrath I have hidden my face from you for a moment. It is but a small wrath, and for a short while. What Christ said of himself to his Disciples—"I shall go away, but I shall come again to you"—may also be said of the Spirit. Although He is sometimes withdrawn, nevertheless within a short time He shall return.

<margin>3rd Application.</margin>
You say that the Spirit is withdrawn, but it is perhaps only a perceived and not an actual withdrawal. What I mean to say is this: perhaps you think it to be so, when in reality it is not. For among all people, the God-fearing are the most ready to have suspicion regarding their own hearts or their own state. You may well have—just like Benjamin—a silver cup in the mouth of your sack <note>A reference to Genesis 44:2, where Joseph hides a cup in his brother Benjamin’s bag to test him; the cup represents a hidden blessing or sign of love that the owner is unaware of.</note>, a token of Joseph’s love, without you knowing it. From your belly may flow a fountain of living water, and you may be ignorant of it. Just like Hagar, when she thought she would die of thirst, had a spring of water right by her. Therefore, that withdrawal is perhaps not actual, but only in your feelings. It is with the soul in respect to the Spirit of Christ just as it was with Mary Magdalene, who, when she spoke with Christ, did not know it, but asked Christ where He had laid Him. *John* 20, verse 15.

<margin>Gen. 44:2.</margin>
<margin>4th Application.</margin>
Consider that Christ perhaps withdraws not out of hatred, but to test you, to see if you will follow Him. Just as a mother will occasionally run into a corner and hide herself from her child; not to make her child despair, but to test its love, to see whether it will seek her or not. So also may Jesus Christ sometimes come to leave you, and withdraw His Spirit, to see whether you will also fervently follow Him, and deem the movements of His Spirit worthy enough to strive after. And thus I have briefly explained to you the withdrawals of the Spirit of Christ, from the established means of religion, and from our souls. I have shown you both the cause and the remedy of this miserable state. The Lord give you understanding in all things.

### Galatians 5, verse 16.

> And I say, walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.

<margin>8th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry <note>A prominent historic church in the City of London, rebuilt by Christopher Wren after the Great Fire.</note> within London, December 1, 1650.</margin>
My intention—after having recently spoken of the misery of those from whom the movements of God’s Spirit are withdrawn—is now to treat the happiness of others, who walk according to the movements and guidance of the Spirit, based on these words: "Walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh."

Which words are an Apostolic lesson or warning, and stand entirely on their own; therefore, I shall treat them without regard to what goes before or follows after. The method which I shall maintain herein shall be as follows:

First, I shall explain the words; thereafter, divide them into parts; thirdly, draw some observations from them; and lastly, I shall make an application of it all.

<column-break/>

### Four things must first be explained.

1. What is understood by "the Spirit"?
2. What is signified by "walking by the Spirit"?
3. What is it "not to fulfill the lust of the flesh"?
4. How can it be said that man shall "not fulfill the lust of the flesh"?

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
### What is understood by the Spirit?

<margin>1st Answer.</margin>
In general, it signifies the entire Divine Being, distinguished in three persons. "God is a Spirit," *John* 4:24; that is, a Spiritual Being. 2 *Cor.* 3:17.

<margin>2nd Answer.</margin>
In particular, it signifies the third person of the blessed Trinity, 1 *John* 5:6.

<margin>3rd Answer.</margin>
By "the Spirit" are also understood the gifts of the Spirit, *Luke* 1:15.

<margin>2nd Question.</margin>
### Now, what is understood by walking by the Spirit?

<margin>Gal. 3:5.</margin>
<margin>Gal. 5:11.</margin>
<margin>Gal. 5:25.</margin>
To answer this, something must first be laid out that serves to explain these words. First, mention is made of "receiving the Spirit"; secondly, of "living in the Spirit"; thirdly, of "being led by the Spirit"; and fourthly, of "walking in or by the Spirit," as in the words of my text. By "receiving the Spirit" and "living therein," the first implantation or working of God’s Spirit upon us in our rebirth <note>The term used is "weder-geboorte," meaning regeneration or being "born again."</note> is made known to us. And by the other two ways of speaking—namely, being "led by the Spirit" and "walking"—which signify one and the same thing, is presented the further working of the Spirit upon the soul in the work of sanctification. So, whoever wishes to walk by the Spirit must follow the movements and instructions of the Spirit. Therefore, if you wish to walk by the Spirit, you must not follow the impulse of your own spirit. Many nowadays are stuck in that fault: that instead of being led by God’s Spirit (of which they nevertheless boast), they follow the promptings of their own spirits. Of such people the learned Melanchthon <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a German reformer and collaborator with Martin Luther.</note> says that they regard their own dreams as being as regular as God’s Word, thinking that it all comes from God’s Spirit. Yet it is so far from that, that they would call out the lusts of the flesh; on the contrary, they caress and follow them. The meaning then of these words is to walk according to the leading of the Spirit. This same thing is expressed in other words: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit" <note>original Latin/German/Dutch context: Romans 8:1</note>; that is, if we follow the movements and instructions of God’s Spirit, we can be said to walk by the Spirit.

<margin><note>original: "Quicquid somniant fanatici volunt esse Spiritum Sanctum."</note> Whatever fanatics dream, they want it to be the Holy Spirit. —Melanchthon.</margin>
<margin>Rom. 8:1.</margin>
<margin>3rd Question.</margin>
<margin>Answer.</margin>
### But what benefit shall spring from this?
"You shall not here fulfill the lust of the flesh." Before I come to answer this, I must warn you of this: namely, that the Apostle does not say, "you shall not then *have* the lust of the flesh." For, as you know, he who most follows the movements and guidance of the Spirit in his practice also finds within himself the workings of corrupt nature. As long as you have this natural body, you shall also have in you this lust of the flesh; but the Apostle says, "You shall not *fulfill* the lust of the flesh."

<summary>This page discusses the difference between the actual and perceived withdrawal of the Holy Spirit and begins a sermon on Galatians 5:16. It emphasizes that while believers may always feel the "lust of the flesh," walking by the Spirit prevents them from acting upon those desires.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual state of a soul from which the Holy Spirit has withdrawn. The previous page established that a heart empty of the Spirit becomes a dwelling for evil, and that humans are naturally more inclined to sin than to holiness. This page offers practical advice on how to recover the Spirit’s presence.</meta>

### concerning God's Spirit.

...to obtain that humble and penitent disposition of the heart, which must exist in a forsaken soul; to judge that he, for his sin's sake, is rejected and forsaken by God—though God is sometimes warning him, and sometimes testing him.

<margin>6th Proposition.</margin>
Sixthly, be more diligent in making the Spirit return when He has withdrawn, than in constantly casting your eyes upon your misery during the Spirit's absence. Many Christians have this fault: they are quietly satisfied with fruitless and mournful lamentations over their loss, but are not industrious in practicing those things that might regain what they have lost. It was not enough for Joshua to lie down on his face because of the transgression at Ai <note>Joshua 7:10–11 describes Joshua mourning a defeat until God tells him to get up and deal with the sin in the camp.</note>, but he had to stand up, find out the cause, and seek to bring the breach of the covenant to light. There are some professors of religion who think to excuse their vanity and spiritual negligence with sighs and complaints. You have lost the Spirit; then do not stand still and stare at your loss, but consider what you must do to get the Spirit back. To this end, follow these three rules:

1. Purify your conscience from the maintenance of any known sin; make your heart pure and fit for Christ, and then His Spirit will come to you. Let your heart be like that guest chamber where Christ came to eat the Passover; it was an upper room, a furnished room, and a clean room <margin>Luke 22:12.</margin>. Ensure that your heart is prepared and purified with the broom of sanctifying grace, away from the persistence of sin, and this will be a means for you to recover the Spirit.

2. Go to God in prayer, which is a general remedy for all kinds of spiritual disorders. *Is any among you suffering? Let him pray,* says the Apostle James <margin>James 5:13.</margin>. Let the difficulty be ever so great, prayer shall be a means to deliver you. Prayer is established by God as a means to obtain God's Spirit <margin>Luke 11:13.</margin>, and also quickly so, because it is God's own institution.

3. Do not only pray, but also bewail your state while praying: spread your complaints out before the Lord and say: "Lord, how is my heart now like a bird-cage for unclean birds? <note>A reference to Revelation 18:2, symbolizing a soul filled with impure thoughts.</note> A hiding place for sin and the Devil? For this my heart is now most fit. How are those strong and flourishing graces, which I once had, now withered, like the grass upon the housetop? I, who was once embraced by an eternal arm, am now forsaken by the Spirit. I was formerly a blessed field, and like the cedars of Lebanon, shooting forth my roots and delightful branches. But now I am like a wild tree of a forest, which brings forth nothing at all. Formerly I was like a fruitful branch of the Vine of Christ, but now I am like the mountains of Gilboa, upon which neither rain nor dew falls." <margin>2 Samuel 1:21.</margin> Mourn for yourself in this way in the presence of the Lord, and perhaps when He sees you with tears in your eyes and your prayers in your hand, He will return to you. Though He has forsaken you, He has not forgotten you; though He has cast you down, He will not reject you forever (He will not cast off His people) if you do not forsake Him. Labor then through

<column-break/>

prayers and tears to regain that which you have lost through the fall.

<margin>7th Proposition.</margin>
Seventhly, consider it a sadder and heavier judgment that the hallowed and sanctifying movements of the Spirit are withdrawn, than that the comfort of the Spirit is withheld. This is a fault among many Christians, especially among those who are troubled in their conscience: all their complaints are about the lack of assurance and comfort—"I do not know if Christ is mine or not," etc. All their concern and sadness turn upon this pivot. Therefore, it is much to be feared that self-love, rather than love for Christ, is the foundation of many such complaints made by those saying they are forsaken. Yet it is a sadder judgment if you lack the awakening movements of the Spirit than if you miss the witness and consolations of the Spirit. It is more sorrowful for the lovely stirrings of the Spirit to be withheld than for the comforts of the Spirit to be withdrawn.

<margin>8th Proposition.</margin>
Eighthly, the common gifts of the Spirit <note>The author distinguishes between "common gifts" (like talent or intellectual knowledge) and "saving gifts" (internal holiness).</note> can sometimes be given even where the saving gifts of the Spirit are withheld. Such was the case with many in the Church of Corinth. The Apostle says of them that they lacked no gift, but as for grace, he says of them that they were carnal and walked as men <margin>1 Corinthians 1:7; 1 Corinthians 3:3.</margin>.

<margin>9th Proposition.</margin>
Ninthly, note this: it can happen that the movements and workings of the Spirit are truly withdrawn from a person who, in his own imagination, thinks he enjoys them fully. In this, it can go with a man as it did with Samson; it was said to him that the Philistines were upon him, and he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." For he did not know that the Lord had departed from him; he did not know that his strength was gone <margin>Judges 16:20.</margin>. Thus, you can sometimes be forsaken by the Spirit and not know it. The reason for this is, partly, because the Spirit departs from you by degrees (one cannot discern a man's growth because he increases gradually; now, just as it is with your natural growth, so it is with your spiritual decline). On the other hand, the heart is very deceitful, careless, and negligent in examining and testing how it stands with your soul. Therefore, let this be in your thoughts: that the movements of the Spirit may well be withdrawn from you, even when you are, in your own opinion, assured that you possess them.

I shall conclude this matter with a few words of comfort, so that no one might happen to become troubled and faint-hearted through what I have said regarding the withdrawals of God's Spirit.
<margin>Application of the Doctrine through comfort.</margin>

<margin>1st Use.</margin>
O you Christian soul, who complains that the Spirit has withdrawn from you, remember that although the Spirit is withdrawn, it is not a total but a partial withdrawal; it is only in some things, and not in all. In some movements and helps, but not in others. The Spirit is never entirely withdrawn from the godly. The Spirit is nonetheless present, even though comfort and assurance may not be there.

<margin>2nd Use.</margin>
<margin>It goes here with the soul as in winter with the herbs.</margin>
Let this be your comfort: that the Spirit departs from you only for a time, and not forever. For only a small moment is the Spirit away from you <margin>Isaiah 54:8.</margin>. In a...

->by the Spirit.<-

flesh. Now, by the **desires of the flesh**, you must not understand in a restricted sense only the sin of wantonness or impurity—which in other places is rightly also called the lust of the flesh—but you must take it in a broad and general sense for all those corrupt and unregulated inclinations toward sin which exist in the nature of man. When the Apostle says, then, that you shall not **fulfill** these desires, his meaning is not that you shall never sin at all, but that you shall not commit sin with such strong and full consent, nor with such deliberate intent as unregenerate men do, who do not possess God's Spirit.

<margin>4th Question.</margin>
But how can this be true: that if we walk by the Spirit, we shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh, when experience nevertheless teaches us that however precisely and carefully a man may walk, and however spiritual he may be, he will still find himself inclined toward the desires of the flesh, and will practice them, and that corruption which lies hidden in his nature will break out in his life?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
I have two things to answer to this. First: although a man walking by the Spirit will indeed still have the desires of the flesh, it is nonetheless true that a godly person walking thus shall not **fulfill** the lust of the flesh, and the reason is this: There is a distinction between the **working** and the **fulfilling** of the desires of the flesh. When a godly man sins, he indeed "works" the desire of the flesh, but he does not "fulfill" it, because he does not commit the sin with such full agreement, nor with such deliberate and complete action of his will as the godless do. Sin carries away the godless with greater violence and power, and with a more premeditated action of the will. In this way, some interpreters resolve this difficulty.

<margin>Musculus on this passage.</margin> <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563) was an influential Protestant reformer and theologian.</note>
Secondly, others answer it this way: *Walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh*; that is (they say), *to that extent* <note>original Latin: "eatenus"</note>—while you accept the stirrings of the Spirit, the stirrings of sin shall not overpower you. Insofar as you follow and listen to the good stirrings of the Spirit, you shall not be overcome by the sinful stirrings of your corrupt nature or of the Devil. *You shall not fulfill the desire of the flesh*—so it stands in the original text—not "desires" [plural], which is why it is translated in the singular. From this, the meticulous scholars show that many sins are contained within that one innate sin; indeed, that all the sins of the world are (so to speak) in the belly of original sin.

There are three parts to this entire verse:
1. The commanded duty: *Walk by the Spirit.*
2. The connected benefit: *You shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.*
3. The certainty of receiving that benefit: *I say, etc.*

I shall draw two teachings from these words.

<margin>1st Doctrine.</margin>
1. That believers must have a special diligence to walk according to the guidance and the stirrings of God’s Spirit.

<column-break/>

<margin>2nd Doctrine.</margin>
2. That those who walk according to the stirrings and the guidance of God’s Spirit shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.

In explaining the first Doctrine, I shall answer several questions.

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
Why must a believer walk according to the guidance of God’s Spirit? And what are the reasons for this?

<margin>1st Reason.</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 30:21.</margin>
1. Because it is a large part of the Spirit’s office—following converting grace—to awaken the heart and move it toward greater grace, and to lead the person on the path upon which he must walk. This is expressed thus by the Prophet Isaiah: *And your ears shall hear the word of one behind you, saying, "This is the way, walk in it," when you would turn to the right hand or to the left.* What the Star was for the Wise Men from the East <margin>Matt. 2:9.</margin>, and the pillar of fire for the people of Israel when they traveled through the Wilderness: that is also what the Spirit is for the Believer, leading and guiding them on the eternal way. If you then do not walk according to the stirrings and guidance of the Spirit, you hinder the office of the Spirit as much as is in you.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>
<margin>Job 1:7.</margin>
<margin>1 Pet. 5:8.</margin>
2. It is your bounden duty to walk according to the guidance of God’s Spirit because the Devil is always trying to suggest evil stirrings to you; he roams about the earth and walks through it, not to do good but to do evil; he goes about seeking whom he may devour. And not only the Devil, but also your own spirit is a false spirit, luring you and provoking you to sin: just as a glowing oven throws out sparks, and the chimney throws out smoke, so your spirit gives off sinful stirrings.

There are also many wandering spirits; *many false Prophets have gone out into the world,* 1 John 4:1. Many deceivers and evil Teachers have gone out into the world. *And do not believe every spirit,* says St. John, *for many false prophets have gone out into the world.* Such people who pretend that they have the Spirit and are Teachers of the truth, but in reality offer nothing but error. If there is a tempting Devil outside of us, and an evil unbelieving heart within us, as well as deceiving Teachers around us in the world, how well then ought we to treasure and follow the stirrings and the guidance of God’s Spirit.

<margin>3rd Reason.</margin>
<margin>2 Thess. 2:2.</margin>
3. Because the deceptions and spiritual delusions of false Teachers are presented and adorned in such a way that they seem just like the stirrings of the Spirit. For this reason, the Apostle warned those of Thessalonica: *that you be not soon shaken in mind, nor by Spirit, nor by word, nor by letter, as if from us, as that the day of Christ were at hand.* If anyone now asks what is understood here by these words: *that you be not soon shaken in mind by any false spirit?* Learned interpreters answer that by "Spirit" is understood revelations, inspirations, and whisperings which are claimed to come from the Spirit of Christ. It was a horrible blasphemy in that godless deceiver Mahomet <note>A common 17th-century Western European spelling for Muhammad. The author here reflects the typical religious polemics of the era, viewing other faiths through a lens of "deception."</note> that he claimed the fits which came over him through his falling sickness were raptures of the Spirit of God; and that the Dove, which he had taught to come to him and eat out of his ear, was the Holy Spirit which [taught] him...

<margin>Scultetus on this passage.</margin> <note>Abraham Scultetus (1566–1624), a German professor of theology and a frequent commentator on the Epistles.</note>

# The Withdrawal

<margin>...and in the trees, all the sap is not gone, but it has retreated into the root.</margin>
...in a little wrath I have hidden my face from you for a moment. <note>A reference to Isaiah 54:8.</note> It is but a small wrath and for a small while; that which Christ said of himself to his disciples, "I shall go away, but I shall come again to you," may also be said of the Spirit; although He is sometimes withdrawn, nevertheless within a short time He shall return.

<margin>3. Use.</margin>
You say that the Spirit is withdrawn, but perhaps it is only a perceived withdrawal and not an actual one. I mean to say: perhaps you think it to be so, when in truth it is not: for among all people, the godly are the most ready to have suspicion of their own hearts or their own state. <margin>Genesis 44:2.</margin> You may well, like Benjamin, have a silver cup in the mouth of your sack—a token of Joseph’s love—without you knowing it. From your belly may flow a fountain of living water, and you may be unaware of it. Just like Hagar, when she thought she would die of thirst, had a spring of water near her. Therefore, perhaps that withdrawal is not actual, but only in your feeling. It is with the soul in respect to the Spirit of Christ as it was with Mary Magdalene, who, when she spoke with Christ, did not know it, but asked Christ where he had laid him. John 20 verse 15.

<margin>4. Use.</margin>
Consider that Christ perhaps withdraws not out of hatred, but to test you, to see if you will follow him. Just as a mother will sometimes run into a corner and hide herself from her child, not to make her child despair, but to test its love, to see whether it will seek after her or not. So also may Jesus Christ sometimes come to leave you, and withdraw his Spirit, to see if you will also eagerly follow him, and deem the stirrings of his Spirit worthy to be pursued. And thus I have briefly explained to you the withdrawals of the Spirit of Christ from the instituted means of worship and from our souls. I have shown you both the cause and the remedy for this miserable state. May the Lord give you understanding in all things.

### Galatians 5 verse 16.

> And I say, walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.

<margin>8. Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry <note>original: "Laurence Jurii." This refers to the historic church of St. Lawrence Jewry in the City of London.</note> within London, December 1, 1650.</margin>
My intention is, after having recently spoken of the misery of those from whom the stirrings of God’s Spirit are withdrawn, now to treat of the happiness of others, who walk according to the stirrings and guidance of the Spirit, and that from these words: *Walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh.*

Which words are an Apostolic lesson or warning, and stand entirely on their own; therefore I shall treat them without reference to what goes before or follows after. The method which I shall maintain herein shall be as follows:

First, I shall explain the words; thereafter, divide the same; thirdly, draw some observations therefrom; and lastly, I shall make an application of everything.

<column-break/>

Four things must first be explained.
1. What is understood by "the Spirit"?
2. What is signified by "walking by the Spirit"?
3. What it is "not to fulfill the lust of the flesh"?
4. How it can be said that a person shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh?

<margin>1. Question.</margin>
### What is understood by "the Spirit"?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin>
In general, it signifies the entire Divine Essence, distinguished into three persons. God is a Spirit. John 4:24. That is, a Spiritual Being. 2 Corinthians 3:17.

<margin>2. Answer.</margin>
In particular, it signifies the third person of the blessed Trinity. 1 John 5:6.

<margin>3. Answer.</margin>
By "the Spirit" are also understood the gifts of the Spirit. Luke 1:15.

<margin>2. Question.</margin>
### Now, what is understood by "walking by the Spirit"?

<margin>Galatians 3:5. Galatians 5:11. Galatians 5:25.</margin>
To answer this, something must be explained beforehand which serves to clarify these words. First, mention is made of *receiving* the Spirit; secondly, of *living* in the Spirit; thirdly, of *being led* by the Spirit; and fourthly, of *walking* in or by the Spirit, as in the words of my text. By "receiving the Spirit" and "living therein" is made known to us the first implantation or working of God’s Spirit upon us in our <term>rebirth</term> <note>original: "weder-gheboorte" (regeneration).</note>. And by the other two ways of speaking—namely, "being led by the Spirit" and "walking"—which signify one and the same thing, is presented the further working of the Spirit upon the soul in the work of <term>sanctification</term> <note>original: "hepligmakinge."</note>, so that he who wishes to walk by the Spirit must follow the stirrings and instructions of the Spirit. Therefore, if you wish to walk by the Spirit, you must not follow the impulses of your own spirit. Many nowadays are stuck in that fault, that instead of being led by God’s Spirit, which they nonetheless boast of, they follow the promptings of their own spirits. Of such people the learned Melanchthon <note>Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560), a key German Reformer.</note> says, <margin>Whatever fanatics dream, they want it to be the Holy Spirit. <note>original Latin: "Quicquid somniant fanatici volunt esse Spiritum Sanctum."</note></margin> that they regard their own dreams as being as regular as God's Word, thinking that it all comes from God’s Spirit; and thereby they are so far from subduing the lusts of the flesh that, on the contrary, they cherish and follow them. The sense of these words is to walk according to the guidance of the Spirit. This same thing is expressed in other words: <margin>Romans 8:1.</margin> There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit; that is, if we follow the stirrings and instructions of God’s Spirit, we can be said to walk by the Spirit.

<margin>3. Question.</margin>
### But what sort of benefit shall spring from this?

You shall not here fulfill the lust of the flesh. <margin>Answer.</margin> Before I come to answer this, I must warn you of this: namely, that the Apostle does not say, "you shall then not *have* the lust of the flesh." For, as you know, he who most follows the stirrings and guidance of the Spirit in his practice also finds within himself the workings of corrupt nature. As long as you have this natural body, you shall also have in you this lust of the flesh; but the Apostle says, "You shall not *fulfill* the lust of the flesh."

of the flesh. **Now**, by the "lusts of the flesh," you must not understand in a narrow sense the sin of wantonness or impurity—which in other places is rightly called the lust of the flesh—but you must take it in a broad and general sense for all those corrupt and disordered inclinations toward sin which exist in human nature. When the Apostle says, then, that "you shall not fulfill these lusts," the meaning is not that you shall never sin, but that you shall not commit sin with such strong and full consent, nor with such intent as <term>unregenerate</term> <note>Those who have not experienced a spiritual rebirth or conversion.</note> people do, who do not have God’s Spirit.

<margin>4th Question.</margin>
**But** how can it be true that if we walk by the Spirit, we shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh, when experience teaches us that even if a person walks ever so precisely and carefully, and is spiritual, they will still incline toward the lusts of the flesh and practice them? When a godly person sins, they may "work" the lust of the flesh, but they do not "fulfill" it, because they do not commit the sin with such full agreement, nor with such deliberate and complete action of the will as the godless do. Sin carries away the godless with greater violence and power, and with a premeditated action of the will. In this way, some interpreters resolve this difficulty.

<margin>+ Musculus on this passage. <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563) was a prominent German Reformed theologian.</note></margin>

As long as you follow and listen to the good movements of the Spirit, you shall not be conquered by the sinful movements of your corrupt nature or of the Devil. 1. The commanded duty: "Walk by the Spirit."
2. The attached benefit: "You shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh."
3. The certainty of receiving that benefit: "I say," etc.

<margin>1st Doctrine.</margin>
1. That believers must have a special reliance to walk according to the guidance and movements of God’s Spirit.

<column-break/>

**In** explaining the first doctrine, I shall answer several questions.

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
Why must a believer walk according to the guidance of God’s Spirit? And what are the reasons for this?

<margin>1st Reason. Isaiah 30:21. Matt. 2:9.</margin>
1. **Because** it is a great part of the Spirit’s office—after converting grace—to awaken the heart and move it toward greater grace, and to guide the person on the path they must walk. 4. We ought to walk according to the promptings of the Spirit, because by so doing, we shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh. And this reason lies here in the text, which I shall not handle nor touch upon here, as it will be properly spoken of in the Second Doctrine.

<margin>1. Question.</margin>
How can one distinguish the promptings of the Spirit from the natural movements of our own conscience?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
For the explanation of this point, I shall set down five marks or special distinctions, by which we may know the one from the other.

<margin>1. Mark. Rom. 8:26. 2 Tim. 1:7.</margin>
1. When the Spirit moves a person toward the good, He not only stirs him toward it, but He also helps him in doing it. Therefore the Spirit is said to come to the aid of our weaknesses, and to pray for us with unspeakable groanings. God’s Spirit is a Spirit of power, to make us strong in our good duties. Just as the Spirit awakens someone to what is good, so He also helps them in it. But although the natural movements of the Conscience may bring a person to do some good, nonetheless it can <margin>I see the better things and approve them, yet I follow the worse. <note>Original Latin: *Video meliora proboque, deteriora sequor.* A famous quote from the poet Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, often used in theology to describe the human struggle between knowing what is right and actually doing it.</note></margin> give him no power to work the same out; it leaves him like Ovid's Medea, who indeed saw the good, but would not do it. Natural promptings deal with the soul just as Pharaoh did with the Israelites, whom he commanded to make bricks, but gave them no tools for it. So also the natural Conscience moves one to a required duty, but it brings no power at all to him to do it. Therefore we read <margin>Rom. 8:7.</margin> that the law was powerless through the flesh—powerless, that is, to be justified by it, because Man has no power to fulfill it.

<margin>2. Mark. Through love of virtue, not fear of punishment. <note>Original Latin: *Virtutis amoris non formidine poenam.*</note> 2 Tim. 1:7. Rom. 8:14, 15. One is led by the Spirit, not dragged. <note>Original Latin: *Ducitur à spiritu non trahitur.*</note></margin>
2. The Spirit moves a person to do good, more because of the loveliness and beauty that is in holiness, than out of fear of the pains of Hell. For this reason we read that God has not given us the Spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind <note>The Dutch *ghematigtheyt* refers to self-control or a sound, sober mind.</note>. We do not do good simply out of fear, but out of love for God and holiness. So also says the Apostle Paul: "For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God: for you have not received the Spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as children, by which we cry, Abba, Father." God’s Spirit makes one do good, like a child out of love for his Father, and not out of fear. This is the work of God’s Spirit. But the movements of the natural conscience toward the good do not proceed from any excellence which he sees in the good that he does, but only out of fear of punishment; he sees damnation before his eyes if he does otherwise.

<margin>3. Mark.</margin>
3. God’s Spirit moves a person not only to do that which is good in itself, but also to take close heed of the end [the goal] /

<column-break/>

for which he does such things, so that he may have a good intention; and therefore the Apostle says that <margin>2 Tim. 1:7.</margin> God has given us the Spirit of a sound mind; that is, the Spirit not only brings a person to the performance of good duties, but also ensures that he has an upright intention in doing the same. But the natural Conscience goes no further than the duty, so long as it is merely accomplished, however unbecomingly or imperfectly. Just like the Harlot of whom Solomon speaks, who <margin>Proverbs 7:14.</margin> had offered peace offerings and paid her vows, but for an abominable and evil end: so that she might play the Harlot all the more shamelessly. First she played the hypocrite, then the Harlot.

<margin>4. Mark.</margin>
4. God’s Spirit, moving a person toward the good, also sets for him a measure in the way of doing the same. The duty must be done with a strong inclination, with love, faith, fervor, and a settled mind; but the natural Conscience, though awakening someone to some religious duty, cares no further, provided it be merely done, however it might be done; it may move someone to pray or to hear God’s Word, but never makes one take heed of the manner in which those duties are performed.

<margin>5. Mark.</margin>
5. God’s Spirit moves a person so powerfully that he continues in doing good, notwithstanding the difficulty and the danger, which shall not hinder him from completing the same. The movements of the Spirit are like new Wine in a wine-vat; which, having no opening or air, threatens to burst into pieces; holy movements break out into holy actions. The godless are like those who are sick until they have worked out their wickedness; they cannot satisfy nor quiet themselves until they have acted sinfully. But those who have natural movements toward the good do not go further, but stand still there, and never bring any perfect good work to fruition. Balaam had a good impulse; "Oh," (he said) "let my <margin>Num. 23:10.</margin> soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like his." What a heavenly, surging prayer this was: it was indeed a very good wish, but nonetheless a lazy wish. He wished to die the death of the righteous, but he did not want to live the life of the righteous. He would not put into practice that which he had. Natural movements freeze (so to speak) between their lips; they only long and wish, but never come to the working out of their duties. Difficulties discourage a person, so that he does not follow through on his good intentions <margin>Proverbs 20:4.</margin> with a constant action; "the sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold."

<margin>3. Question.</margin>
Yet how should one be able to distinguish the movements of the Spirit from the deceptions of Satan? The promptings of the Devil are like the movements of the Spirit, and there have been at all times people who have taken their own deceptive imaginations for the movements of the Spirit: therefore, to distinguish the one from the other, one must know:

<margin>1. Distinction.</margin>
1. That the movements of God’s Spirit are always in agreement with the written Word. The written words and the movements of the Spirit fit together perfectly. Solomon joins them both together: <margin>Proverbs 1:24.</margin> "Behold, I will pour out my Spirit abundantly unto you..."

<summary>This page outlines five practical marks to distinguish the Holy Spirit's influence from natural conscience, emphasizing that the Spirit provides both the desire and the power to perform duties out of love rather than fear. It also begins a discussion on how to differentiate divine promptings from the deceptions of the Devil by checking them against Scripture.</summary>

<margin>Isa. 59:21.</margin> pour out; I shall make my words known to you. So also the Prophet Isaiah: My Spirit which is upon you, and my words which I have laid in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, etc. The promptings of God's Spirit are always consistent with the
<margin>Isa. 8:20.</margin> Word of God. To the Law and to the testimony: If they do not speak according to this word, it shall be that they shall have no dawn <note>Original: *dageraet*. This refers to the light of truth or spiritual enlightenment; those who contradict Scripture are in total darkness.</note>. All other promptings that conflict with the Word are deceptions of the evil spirit.

<margin>2. Distinction.</margin> 2. The promptings of God's Spirit in men are not for the purpose of foretelling future things, but are holy promptings urging one toward holy duties. Therefore, those are Devilish deceptions of the Papists <note>Original: *Paus-geſinden* (Pope-inclined), a common 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics.</note>, who boast of a prophetic spirit and of foretelling future things, as well as those Star-gazers and fortune-tellers who pretend to predict future occurrences, saying: this season <note>Original: *gety*, meaning a tide or time/season.</note> shall have the upper hand this month, and that season another month. All of this does not come from God's Spirit; which, according to the rule of Scripture, is firmly established once and for all, pointing us to the Word as the rule of our obedience.

3. The promptings of the Spirit, wherever they may be, produce grace and suppress sin: they work grace, and therein one reads of the helpful, active, and fulfilling work of the Spirit. Those promptings are then from the Devil which arouse sin and nourish damnation. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if through the Spirit you kill the workings of the flesh, you shall live. The promptings of God's Spirit are holy, awakening grace and suppressing sin. And
<margin>Mic. 2:11</margin> therefore it is written: If there is someone who walks with the Spirit and lies falsely, that is, if someone boasts of revelations from God's Spirit and yet prophesies of wine and strong drink—meaning that through his teaching he makes drunkenness or any other sin appear greater <note>That is, he encourages or excuses the sin through his "revelations."</note>—that man lies, and is not sent by the Holy Spirit, but by the Devil.

I proceed now to the examination of a fourth question, which is this: how may one distinguish those common promptings of the Spirit in the godless from the saving promptings of the Spirit in the reborn?

The reason why I shall handle this question is because the Scripture says that the godless can also become partakers of the Holy Spirit. To answer the question then, we must know that there are two kinds of distinctions between partaking of the Spirit in the godless and in the godly.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A vertical curly bracket groups the following two items:</image-desc>
1. In the degree.
2. In the manner of partaking in the Spirit.

<margin>1. Distinction.</margin> 1. In the degree; a reprobate <note>Original: *verworpening*, referring to those not predestined for salvation in the author's Reformed theology.</note> may well be a sharer in the promptings of the Spirit; however, he does not have the Spirit in such a degree as a reborn person has.
<margin>Forbes.</margin> Forbes <note>Likely referring to Patrick Forbes or John Forbes of Corse, prominent Scottish theologians whose works were well-known in the Netherlands.</note>, in his learned Treatise concerning this question, uses this comparison. The "Godless (he says) have a share in the Spirit,
<margin>To taste with only the tips of the lips. <note>Original Latin: *Summis tantum labris gustare*, a classical idiom for experiencing something superficially.</note></margin> "just as cooks have a share in the food: they "prepare the meal and taste just as much of it "as their palate can catch a good scent of, but "they do not take so much of it that it "can strengthen them for a meal which "can delight and nourish their nature. But "the reborn are like the invited guests, "who not only taste the prepared food "but also make their meal of it. The "godless have only a small taste of it, and
<margin>Heb. 6:4.</margin> therefore the Apostle says of them that they have tasted the Heavenly gift. They are just like those people who, passing by an apothecary's shop, happen to smell the sweet scent of his jars; but the sick person alone enjoys the benefit of his restoratives. So it is also with the Godless; God gives them all a taste of His Spirit, but they do not have so much that it can benefit their soul. The Godly alone have those saving communications of grace. Just as there were many among the Israelites who had a taste of the fruits of the Land of Canaan, yet who were never saved: so also some can taste the Heavenly gifts who will never enter into Heaven.

<margin>2. Distinction.</margin> 2. Just as there is a distinction in the degree of receiving the Spirit, so there is also a distinction in the manner.

Firstly, in a reprobate person, the promptings of the Spirit are not long-lasting, but pass by easily and vanish like a shadow. And therefore the Lord God says through the Prophet Hosea, speaking to Ephraim: Your faithfulness is like a morning
<margin>Hos. 6:4.</margin> cloud, and like a dry dew that passes away. The Sun chases away the clouds and dries up the dew; so also the promptings of the Spirit in the reprobate quickly vanish and go away. But the promptings of the Spirit in the Godly are like a permanent resident: they dwell with him; therefore our Savior says, If my
<margin>John 15:7.</margin> words remain in you, whatever you wish, you shall desire, and it shall be done for you. Christ’s words in the Godless are passing through like traveling guests, but in the Godly they remain and rest firmly upon a religious person all the time of his life; he always has a conscience void of offense (Acts 24:16). My soul is broken because of the longing for your judgments at all times, says David in Psalm 119:20. And, that I might dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Psalm 27:4). The promptings of God's Spirit are not in the Godly by fits and starts <note>Original: *met haſten en ſtooten* (with haste and bumps/pushes).</note>, but they remain and endure always.

The wicked have a hundred promptings from Satan toward evil for every one prompting from God’s Spirit toward good, and these are as rare as a swallow in the winter. As long as a wicked man has evil thoughts, he is in his own element; and he does this as naturally and as often as he draws his breath. But good promptings are like strangers in his heart.

<margin>III. Num. 23:12.</margin>
Thirdly, the promptings of the Spirit in the wicked are not willing, but forced and pressured. They are not in them like water flowing from a fountain, but like water rising out of a distilling kettle, being driven upward by the fire that lies beneath it. The promptings of the Spirit in the wicked can be squeezed out on two grounds. First, by the natural conscience, which tells them they must not be such "painted devils" that they never have any good promptings at all. Balaam <note>A biblical figure who was hired to curse Israel but was compelled by God to bless them instead.</note> truly desired to curse the people of Israel, but his natural conscience forced him to bless them. And he said: "Must I not take heed to speak that which the Lord hath put in my mouth?" Or secondly, it can come from the sensation of outward judgments; this may be the cause why they accept good thoughts.
<margin>Proverbs 1:27, 28.</margin>
When your fear comes like a devastation, and your destruction comes as a whirlwind, then they shall call upon me. There must be a whirlwind of fear that drives them to call upon the name of the Lord, which agrees with what the Prophet
<margin>Hosea 5:15.</margin>

<margin>Deut. 5:27.</margin>
to Moses: "Go thou near, and hear all that the Lord our God shall say: and speak thou unto us... and we will hear it, and do it."

<margin>IV. Proverbs 16:30.</margin>
Fourthly, the promptings of the Spirit in the reprobate <note>Those considered rejected by God or destined for damnation.</note> are accidental, and not forethought or considered; such as fall in suddenly without preparation or meditation. These promptings tumble into their hearts they know not how. The wicked person takes counsel over evil thoughts; therefore the Wise Man says: "He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things." The closing of the eyes is the posture of one who puts his intellect to work. Thus the wicked consider how they shall put a villainous device to work, and so they set their senses upon evil. To this end, the Apostle Paul says that God shall
<margin>1 Corinth. 4:5. <note>Original Greek: φανερώσει τὰς βουλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν, meaning "will reveal the counsels of the hearts."</note></margin>
reveal the counsels of the hearts. Thoughts of sin, when considered, are called "counsels of the heart," and those God will lay open. The wicked are said to make plots against the righteous; but they do not strive for good thoughts. When those come, they fall in by chance, and also vanish without further reflection.

<margin>V.</margin>
Fifthly; the good promptings in the wicked are only partial and not general. Just as they do not move toward the good at all times, so they do not move toward *all* good. They only have promptings to do some outward good so that people might speak of their names with praise; but they do not extend to all heartfelt promptings for good, nor do they aim to kill strong lusts or to bring sin under subjection; whereas

<column-break/>

<margin>Heb. 13:18.</margin>
nevertheless, the promptings of the Spirit toward good in the godly are general, as much toward one good as another. "We trust," says the Apostle Paul, "that we have a good conscience, in all things willing to live hon-
<margin>Acts 24:16.</margin>
estly." And as the same Apostle says in another place: "Herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward
<margin><note>Original Latin: Universali-tas objecti & subjecti, meaning "Universality of the object and the subject."</note></margin>
God, and toward men." The promptings of God's Spirit upon the hearts of the godly have a universality, through which their whole heart is moved toward all good, and at all times.

<margin>VI. 2 Cor. 1:17, Psal. 119:2, Dan. 1:8.</margin>
Sixthly, the promptings of the Spirit upon the wicked are fruitless promptings, which have no powerful influence upon their lives. The heart of a fool (says one) is like a wagon wheel, and his thoughts are like the axle thereof; it goes around like the wheel all day long, and yet throughout it remains in its place. So it may sometimes happen that the wicked have good thoughts and good promptings, but these have no influence upon their lives; they are fruitless stirrings. But the promptings toward good in the godly have their exercise and operation, and their holy intentions are joined with prayer.

<margin>VII. A Similitude.</margin>
Seventhly, the promptings of God's Spirit in the reprobate are indeed toward the good which is done in public, but not that which is done in secret. They will do good so that their names may be praised. The winds of vain praise may cause the sails of their hearts to swell and fill them with good promptings. The wicked may well be compared to a Nightingale, of whom it is said that if she perceives someone listening to her, she will sing all the sweeter. So it is with the wicked; they are better before men than before God, better in the Church than in their inner chamber. It is told of a certain Monk who could fast for several days in a Cloister, but not even half a day in the desert; and being asked for the reason, he gave this answer: "When I fast in the Cloister, then I feed myself with the vain honor and praise of men, but I cannot do so in the wilderness." It is the same with outward professors <note>Those who "profess" faith outwardly but may lack inward sincerity.</note>; their promptings bring them to outward and visible good, but not to inward and hidden duties—namely, to test their hearts, to keep watch over them, and to preserve fellowship with God in secret. If you fall short in this, then you also do not have the powerful and saving prompting of the Spirit.

I shall make a twofold use of this: first for humiliation, second for instruction.

<margin>1. Use for Humiliation. I.</margin>
Is this a required duty of God's people, that they walk according to the guidance and the promptings of God's Spirit?
<margin>John 3:8.</margin>
1. Well then, humble yourselves, because you take so little heed of and notice the promptings of the Spirit so little. The Spirit is compared to the wind: "The wind bloweth where it listeth." But who is there who always pays close attention to the wind? How often do people walk across the streets and yet do not notice the wind, or which way it blows? So it is also with the Spirit; the Spirit often comes to us gently, but we do not pay attention to it. That which Job says
<margin>Job 9:11. <note>The OCR says 9:18, but the quote "He passeth by me" matches Job 9:11.</note></margin>
of the Lord: "Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not..."

<summary>This page distinguishes true spiritual promptings from the false or superficial impulses of the "wicked." The author argues that while the ungodly may feel occasional "forced" urges to do good for public praise, the truly godly experience a universal, constant, and inward transformation driven by the Holy Spirit.</summary>

and I shall not see him; we may say the same of God’s Spirit: He was with me, but I did not notice it. Thus our Savior speaks of the world, that it cannot receive the Spirit of <margin>John 14:17.</margin> Truth: for it sees Him not, nor knows Him. Not that they could see the Spirit with a physical eye, for the Spirit is not a physical being; but they neither see nor know Him, that is, they do not see His movements, nor do they have any experiential knowledge of the workings of the Spirit. Natural men <note>The "natural man" refers to someone living according to human nature without the influence of divine grace.</note> carry no knowledge of their own spirit; much less would they know the movements of God’s Spirit. Just as we cannot see the Sun except by its own light, so we cannot perceive the Spirit without the Spirit. Many people in this world are like that master of the feast, of whom it is said that when Christ had changed the water <margin>John 2:9.</margin> into wine, he did not know from where the wine came. This passage of Scripture can thus be applied here: there are many people whose "water" the Spirit would indeed change into "wine"—that is, change their corrupt movements into holy and lovely movements—yet they do not know it, and do not wish to see it.

<margin>II.</margin>
2. If you are not guilty of that—namely, of neglecting the movements of the Spirit—yet humble yourself because of the weakness of the flesh, so that you cannot always accept the movements of the Spirit, even when you come to know them. We read <margin>John 14:17.</margin> in John, chapter 14, where Christ speaks of the sending of the Spirit, that the world cannot receive Him. He does not say, the world *does not* receive Him, but the world *cannot* receive Him, to point out the weakness <margin>Rollocus.</margin> <note>Likely referring to Robert Rollock (1555–1599), a Scottish theologian and commentator popular in Reformed circles.</note> of the flesh, so that men cannot accept the holy movements. Rollocus, on this passage, compares the heart of a natural man to wet wood, which cannot easily be set on fire. The natural man does not understand the <margin>1 Corinthians 2:14.</margin> things that are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. And the mind of the flesh is enmity against God: for it does not subject itself to the Law <margin>Romans 8:7.</margin> of God, for it cannot. There is not only a single omission of the act, but also an incapacity in the soul. This is our weakness: that in the flesh we cannot embrace and accept those movements of the Spirit, even though we know them.

<margin>III.</margin>
3. Humble yourself, because you cannot bring those movements, which you know, into holy practice and exercise. Many people do accept the movements of the Spirit, but they do not work out those lovely movements; the Spirit moves them to pray better, to hear God’s word better, and to lead a holier life; and yet they generally remain as they were: and although they may occasionally intend to live better, yet how quickly those intentions are forgotten! Such people may complain with Job in this case: My thoughts (intentions) are plucked out, the <margin>Job 17:11.</margin> possessions of my heart. Without doubt these were good thoughts, as if he said, I intended to live so and so, had God made my way prosperous: but now my thoughts are plucked out and broken off, and I am deceived in my own thoughts. Many of us may well make this complaint;

<column-break/>

that our intentions are disappointed. The Spirit has awakened many good movements in our hearts, and yet we could not bring those holy movements into practice and action. But a time shall come when every child of God shall take up a good intention and purpose, and put it into work, and that he shall say with David, *I will confess my sins,* and do the same, Psalm 32, v. 2, 3, 5.

<margin>IV.</margin>
4. Humble yourself because of that corrupt aptitude of your nature to embrace and accept all sinful movements. How unlike we are to our Savior: the Tempter came to Him, but he had nothing <margin>John 14:30.</margin> in Him; he found nothing upon which he could apply his temptation. But when the Tempter comes to you, he finds something in you; he finds in you a nature which is disposed and fit to enclose the temptation within it, which he suggests to you. Christ’s nature was a crystalline glass filled with pure water; though the Devil shook the glass, it remained entirely clear throughout; but when the Devil comes to us, he finds us like a puddle of water, and if he but barely touches that puddle, how quickly the filth comes to the top! A dunghill may have its herbs, and flowers may grow upon it; but if you happen to touch it and dig into it, how quickly shall the stench of the dunghill take away the pleasantness of the flowers? Although our natures do not seem as evil as they truly are, nevertheless when the Devil merely touches them, it shall appear what we are. A heart may be compared to a tinderbox <note>original: "vyerſlaghdoos"</note>, the corruption of nature to the tinder in that box. Now let the Devil but strike the flint against the steel—that is, fit a temptation to our corruption—and how quickly we shall give off fire. Christ’s nature was like iron, which cannot be ignited by any sparks; but the Devil tempts us, and our natures are like the tinder in the temptation. What great reason we have then to humble ourselves and greatly abase ourselves when we remember that we are so inclined and fit to follow the Devil’s suggestions.

5. Be humbled because of that aversion and turning away of our nature from the movements of the Spirit. Our natures were, in the state of innocence, like the rivers of Egypt before they were turned into blood; then they were the proper element in which the fish lived: but once they were changed into blood, all the fish died. In the state of innocence, your nature was the proper element in which the movements of God’s Spirit were; but when your nature was changed into blood through the Fall, then the movements of God’s Spirit went away. The words following my text indicate the contrariety of <margin>Galatians 5:17.</margin> our natures: *the flesh lusteth against the Spirit.* Yet "the Spirit" is not understood as the born-again part of man, but the movements of God’s Spirit. The corrupt nature wars against God’s Spirit in His movements and workings. The enmity of man’s nature against God’s Spirit is expressed in three ways in the Scripture, namely:
1. To grieve the Spirit. <margin>Isaiah 63:10. Acts 7:51.</margin>
2. To resist the Spirit; and

3. **To do insult to the Spirit of grace.**
By all these manners of speaking is meant the high degree of enmity, and that human nature bears a deadly hostility against the movements of the Spirit.

<margin>2. Use for instruction.</margin>
Now, for your instruction, I shall reveal various consequences which can be drawn from this doctrine, and these shall be of two kinds. First, I shall propose some general propositions; secondly, some particular directions concerning the movements of the Spirit.

<margin>1st Proposition.</margin>
First, the movements of the Spirit are entirely voluntary; the Spirit gives them to whom and in what measure it pleases him. The wind blows <margin>John 3:8.</margin> where it wishes: that is, the movements of the Spirit are distributed according to God’s free good pleasure. God's Spirit is called a voluntary <margin>Psalm 51:14</margin> <note>original: "vrywillighen," often translated as "free" or "willing" in English Bibles.</note> Spirit. It is a Holy Spirit when you look at its workings; but a voluntary Spirit when you look at the foundation of the working. And therefore the Apostle <margin>James 5:16 <note>The text cites James 5:16, but the quote "Of his own will he brought us forth..." is actually James 1:18.</note></margin> James says: Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth. God's Spirit is a voluntary worker.

<margin>2nd Proposition.</margin>
Secondly, no one enjoys the movements of the Spirit equally at all times. Just as the Sun, although it is always in the firmament, nonetheless does not always have the same influence; so too the same Spirit is not constantly in the hearts in the same measure. Just as it is with the wind—sometimes it is still, at other times it is stormy—so it goes with the Spirit in the hearts of the godly; they do not always have it in the same measure.

<margin>3rd Proposition.</margin>
Thirdly, men walk more after the movements of the evil spirit than of the good Spirit. Theologians generally conclude this from the 19th and 20th verses following <margin>Galat. 5:19, 22.</margin> my text, where it is said that the works of the flesh are manifest, and there he provides a list <note>original: "naemtafel," literally a name-table or catalogue.</note> of them. But when he comes to speak of the works of the Spirit, he does not give them that name, but calls them the fruits of the Spirit, to make known to us that men walk more after the flesh than after the Spirit. So also speaks the <margin>Ephes. 2:2.</margin> Apostle of men who walk according to the course of this world, and according to the spirit that works in the children of disobedience, not according to the movements and promptings of God's Holy Spirit.

<margin>4th Proposition.</margin>
Fourthly, there is more fruit and profit to be found in walking after the movements of God’s Spirit than after the sinful movements of the evil spirit. And I gather this from the change in the manner of speaking; when the Apostle makes a list of the works <margin>Galat. 5:19, 22.</margin> of the flesh and of the Spirit, he says, the works of the flesh are manifest, but the fruit of the Spirit is, etc. To give us to understand that there is neither fruit nor profit in sin; and therefore the Apostle says in another place: What <margin>Rom. 6:21.</margin> fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed? for the end of those things is death. Sin brings forth no fruit but sorrow and shame: sin is a work of the flesh, and a slavery to the Devil. Sin is a work, and a work of the flesh, and there is no profit in it; but in the Spirit there is fruit; if you then 

<column-break/>

accept the movements of God's Spirit, then fruit and profit shall come to you from it. He who sows to his own <margin>Gal. 6:8.</margin> flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption: but he who sows to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting. There is no profit in following the flesh, but indeed in walking in the Spirit. Luther has an apt explanation regarding what Paul says in <margin>Rom. 11: verse 13. <note>The text cites Rom 11:13, but the quote "armor of light" is actually Romans 13:12.</note></margin> Let us cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light. Sin is called a work of darkness, and if one wished to look at the contrast, grace should be called a work of light; but it is not called so, but rather the armor of light: Why is such an unequal contrast made here? Luther gives this reason: sin is called a work of darkness, and not armor, to signify that there is no power in it against the wrath of God; but grace is called the armor of light because, just as armor is for decoration and protection, so grace adorns the soul and preserves it from the coming wrath. I shall conclude this part with what the Apostle Paul says: the minding of the flesh <margin>Rom. 8:6.</margin> is death, but the minding of the Spirit is life and peace. There is peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come; he who walks according to the guidance of the Spirit has profit here, and hereafter eternal life and salvation.

<margin>10th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry in London, December 8, 1650. 1st Rule.</margin>
**I** proceed to the particular directions concerning the movements of God’s Spirit.
First, when God’s Spirit gives you holy movements in your hearts, do not let them lie still until you have put them into practice; holy movements must be followed by holy intentions, which should then be followed by holy actions. Many Christians have this fault: they let the good movements die away in their bosom, and they then come too late and at an inconvenient time. That which we read of Daniel must serve for our imitation. He purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the King’s meat, nor with the wine which he drank: <margin>Dan. 1:8.</margin> therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. He did not rest on the mere movement and intent, but he pursued it and did his utmost to carry out his purpose. But as for us, how might we rightly (as I said before) complain with Job, "My thoughts are snatched away (my <margin>Iob 17:11.</margin> purposes), the possessions of my heart." Holy movements must then be followed by holy intentions and fulfilled with holy actions.

<margin>2nd Rule.</margin>
Secondly, when God the Lord grants you the movement of His Spirit, do not think that you possess the Essence and the Person of the Spirit, which is a blasphemous error of the Familists <note>The Familists (Family of Love) were a mystical religious sect that some accused of believing they could become "godded with God" or achieve a state of perfection where they were one with the divine essence.</note>, because they make no distinction between the movements and the
