the Person of the Spirit. This is their view: that a believer does not only possess the grace of the Spirit, but also the Person of the Spirit, which is nothing other than changing humanity into divinity. Allow me to explain this through a comparison. We commonly say that the Sun, which is in the firmament, "stands" in such a house or such a window; by this, we do not mean to suggest that the physical body of the Sun is there, but only that the light, the warmth, and the influence <note>original: "inbloepinge," referring to the inflowing radiation or effect of the sun.</note> of the Sun are there. So also, although the Scripture tells us that the Holy Spirit dwells in us, the meaning is not as if the Person of the Holy Spirit were [physically] in us, but only that his movements and the gifts of grace are there. And therefore, in both those ways of speaking—"You are the Temple of the Holy Spirit," and "the Holy Spirit dwells in you"—there is, as Paræus <note>David Pareus (1548–1622) was a prominent German Reformed Protestant theologian.</note> says, a metaphor or a figure of speech.
<margin>1 Cor. 3:16 The Spirit of God dwells in us, because he rules, governs, and sanctifies. Paræus. <note>original Latin: "Spiritus Dei habitat in nobis, quia regit, gubernat, & sanctificat."</note></margin>

<margin>3rd Rule.</margin>
Thirdly, take great care that you do not mistake the deceptions of Satan for the movements of the Spirit. Above, I have pointed out the identifying marks by which you can distinguish the movements of the Spirit from the Devil’s inspirations and delusions. I shall now only state this, which is an infallible rule: all movements which do not harmonize with the written Word come from the Devil and not from God. I have given you two passages of Scripture in which the Spirit and the Word are joined together. See to it then, that all your movements agree with the written Word.
<margin>Prov. 1:23. Isa. 59:21.</margin>

<margin>4th Rule.</margin>
Fourthly, do not believe everyone who says that he is driven by the Spirit. There are many puffed-up teachers nowadays (who in truth are masters of error, yet wish to be regarded as students of truth) who say they have the inspirations of the Spirit, while they have nothing less.
<margin>1 John 4:1. 2 Thess. 2:2.</margin>
But as the Apostle John says, *do not believe every spirit*—that is, every deceived teacher—*but test the spirits whether they are of God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.* They are called "spirits" because they claim with such boldness to possess the Spirit.

<margin>question.</margin>
But so that you may recognize such people, I shall handle this question: namely, by what can one distinguish those people who pretend to have the Spirit when they do not?

<margin>1st Answer.</margin>
Such people, who only pretend to have the Spirit, are always grand and boastful regarding the gifts of the Spirit: their internal opinion of "having the Spirit" awakens a high degree of pride in their hearts. This is certain and fixed: those who are truly driven by the Spirit are always humble. Such was the case with Paul: *I give my opinion* (he says) *and I think also that I have the Spirit of God.* Paul knew well that he had the Spirit; nevertheless, he wished to speak in humility, not boasting as many did. And so at another time he said, *I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago (whether it happened in the body, I do not know, or out of the body, I do not know: God knows) that such a one was caught up into the third Heaven, and heard unspeakable words, which a man*
<margin>1 Corinth. 7:40.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinth. 12:2, 3, 4.</margin>

<column-break/>

is not permitted to speak. Who was that man? None other than himself; his humble modesty made him speak in the third person. Therefore, it is proof that those who so brag of the Spirit, and are defiant and proud of it, do not in fact have the Spirit of Christ, which is a Spirit of gentleness and humility. Those who exalt the Spirit so much that they come to despise the established means of worship and the office of preaching do not have God’s Spirit. In the time of the New Testament, when divine visions and inspirations were still in fashion, the Spirit nevertheless did not wish to teach people directly, but pointed them to the outward service. We have a famous example of this (as I have noted above) in the Ethiopian <note>original: "Moorman," literally "Moorish man."</note>, the Chamberlain, who was reading the prophet Isaiah on his wagon; the Spirit did not wish to explain the meaning of it to him, but commanded Philip to go to him and clarify it. So also, when Christ revealed himself to Paul, he did not wish to teach him himself and without means, but commanded him to go to Damascus, and there it would be told to him what he must do. We have a similar example in Cornelius; the Spirit did not wish to teach him directly, but charged him to send for Peter; he would tell him what he must do. From these examples, we see how the Lord God has honored the service of the Word. And therefore those who praise the Spirit highly and mock the service of the Word, as if waiting for the direct teaching of the Spirit, undoubtedly do not have God’s Spirit.
<margin>2nd Answer.</margin>
<margin>Acts 8:27, 28, 29.</margin>
<margin>Acts 9:6</margin>
<margin>Acts 10:5, 6.</margin>

<margin>3rd Answer.</margin>
Those who say they have the Spirit, and yet boast and brag more of the workings of the Spirit in the revelation of future things than in present movements toward holy duties, are deceived by the deceptions of Satan. There are many today who take it upon themselves to predict future occurrences: but this can be nothing other than a deception of the Devil, because the gifts of the Spirit to predict future things have now ceased, and they are no longer in the Church. I do not deny that the Devil can indeed come to predict some future outcome through a special revelation of God, but I am also certain that your Star-gazers <note>term: Star-gazers <gloss>astrologers</gloss></note> cannot do the same through the help of the stars. Thus the Devil appeared to Saul in the form of Samuel, and said, *Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me: also the Lord shall give the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.* Well, how did the Devil come to know this? Only through a special revelation of God, because the Lord permitted it for the delusion of the godless Saul. Or otherwise, the Devil can know future things through the great knowledge he has of the prophecies of Scripture; the Devil can well understand those prophecies which are dark to us: therefore one reads in the histories that the Devil predicted the outcomes of wars. Thus the Devil predicted to Alexander at the oracle <note>original: "waeghbaeck," likely referring to the tripod or the prophetic beacon/seat at the Oracle of Delphi.</note> in Delphi that both the Chaldean and Greek monarchies would be brought under his command. This the Devil predicted to him. So
<margin>1 Sam. 28:19.</margin>

<header>On Walking [in the Spirit]</header>

that if people take it upon themselves to predict future, accidental things peremptorily and absolutely, then I may openly tell you that it comes from the Devil and not from God.

<margin>2nd Rule.</margin>
Another direction regarding the movements of the Spirit is this: Record all the helpful means through which you may obtain the movements of the Spirit. There are three which I would like to point out and recommend to you for this time.

1. Often conduct holy conversations and discourse with good company, associating with those who possess the Spirit regarding spiritual matters; this is a special means for you to gain the movements of the Spirit. What Christ did while here on earth, he will yet do through his Holy Spirit. We read that when the two disciples went to Emmaus, reasoning and talking together, <margin>Luke 24:14.</margin> Jesus drew near and went with them. Christ will then draw near through the movements of his Spirit to those who speak and conduct discourse on holy matters.

2. Give proper and close attention to the established means of worship <note>The "means of grace," such as preaching, sacraments, and prayer.</note>, for those are the "Bath-water" <note>A reference to the Pool of Bethesda (John 5), believed to have healing powers when stirred by an angel.</note> which the Angel wishes to stir at certain times. It is a noteworthy passage which one reads in the <margin>Isaiah 30:20, 21.</margin> Prophet Isaiah, where the Lord says that your Teachers shall no longer fly away as if with wings, but your eyes shall see your Teachers, and your ears shall hear the Word of the one who is behind you, saying, "this is the way, walk in it." Note the joining of the words: you shall see your Teachers, and while seeing, you shall hear the word or a voice—namely, of the Spirit. The established means carry the movements of the Spirit to us. And to this I may apply what we read in the Prophet Zechariah <margin>Zech. 4:7, 12.</margin> where it says that the two branches of the Olive trees poured the golden Oil from themselves through two golden pipes, which thus ran into the candlestick. This candlestick is the Church; the Oil represents the movements of God's Spirit; and these movements run through the established means of worship—these are those golden pipes which convey the movements of the Spirit into our hearts. It is with the movements of the Spirit and the holy institutions just as it is with the blood and the spirits <note>In older medical theory, "spirits" were vital fluids or energies carried by the blood.</note> and the veins and arteries; for just as those convey the blood and spirits to every part, so also do the established means conduct the graces and comforts of the Spirit to every believing member of Christ. Be constant in hearing the Word and in Prayer. This shall be a means for you to obtain the Spirit. Christ makes this an encouragement and <margin>Luke 11:13.</margin> a motive for prayer: "If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more (he says) shall the Heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him." Go then to God in prayer, and that shall be a means to bring the Spirit into your heart.

3. Be often alone in holy meditation. Christ could tell you that he was alone, <margin>John 16:32.</margin> and yet (he said) "I am not alone, for the Father is with me." So also, if you are alone in contemplation, you shall not be alone, because the Spirit shall be with you in its holy movements. Just as it

<meta>catchword: Just as it</meta>

<column-break/>

is written of Isaac, that when he went out to meditate and to pray, he saw Rebecca, <margin>Gen. 24:63, 64.</margin> for whom he had prayed so long; so I may say to you: be often in contemplation, and the Spirit, for which you have prayed, shall be given to you. Just as Elijah, being on <margin>1 Kings 19:12.</margin> the mountain, noticed that the Lord was in the whistling of a gentle silence <note>Often translated as "a still small voice."</note>, so too the soul shall find that although the Spirit is not in the strong wind of stormy passions, he will nevertheless be in the quiet voice of holy meditation.

<margin>6th Rule.</margin>
Sixthly, long more for the holy movements of the Spirit than for the uplifting comforts of the Spirit; and the reason is this: because you have more need of the movements than the comforts of the Spirit. You can well get to Heaven without comfort, but not without grace. Although it is an uplifting work of the Spirit to make my life comfortable, it is nonetheless a holy work of the Spirit to make my soul fit to be saved. The sealing work of the Spirit, through which I cry, "Abba, Father," gives comfort; but the sanctifying work of the Spirit, through which I kill the works of the flesh, <margin>Rom. 8:13, 14, 15.</margin> is the foundation and bedrock of that comfort.

<margin>7th Reason.</margin>
And finally, see to it that you do not mistake the moral persuasion of your conscience for the movements of the Spirit. This is a very profitable rule. People are accustomed, when they have a good impulse, to attribute it to the Spirit, yet one can have a thousand good impulses in one's heart which arise only from a moral persuasion. A castaway <note>original: "verworpe-lingh," referring to one not among the elect.</note> can go quite far through nature alone. How do we read of flames of joy in Herod? He heard John the Baptist gladly. Of feelings of fear and terror in Felix? And of torment and sorrow in Judas? And yet all these came from the strength of moral persuasion or conviction, and they were not the soul-saving workings of the Spirit.

So that you are not deceived regarding moral persuasion, I shall give a fourfold distinction between it and the workings of the Spirit.

1. Moral persuasion may move a person to do good, but it never changes the inclinations. And therefore one reads of those who <margin>2 Thess. 2:10.</margin> did not receive the love of the truth; by which it is suggested that people sometimes accept the truth through the strong movement of the same, and yet not out of love for it. This is why it says one must practice the truth <margin>Eph. 4:15.</margin> in love; whatever you do, you must do in love. Now, moral persuasions may move you to do some good, but they do not awaken your inclinations in love toward what you do.

2. Moral persuasion pushes a person to do good, but never gives him the strength to do that good. Moral persuasion may give a person the eye to see what must be done; but the Spirit <margin>Rom. 8:26.</margin> gives not only the eye, but also the hand, and helps us to work out that good to which he persuades the person.

3. Moral persuasion moves people to do good more out of hope for reward

4. <margin>Use of comfort.</margin>
<margin>Acts 2:17</margin>
Let this serve for our comfort. In the last days, the Spirit speaks expressly: previously they saw everything, but obscurely; but now we see face to face—that is, much more clearly. Thank God for this; it is a general comfort that more of God's Spirit is preserved under the New Testament than was distributed under the Old.

In particular, I shall propose six words of comfort for those who walk according to the guidance and movements of God's Spirit.

<margin>I.</margin>
<margin>John 16:13.</margin>
First, God's Spirit shall be a sure Guide to you, and shall reveal all truth to you and lead you therein. So says our Savior: *He will lead you into all truth,* that is, all truth which is necessary for salvation. You have a similar passage by the same Evangelist, where it stands: *The Spirit shall teach you all things,* that is, all things necessary to be known for an Elect person to be saved. The Spirit of God reveals to His people the mysteries of salvation; and therefore one reads: *Things which the eye has not seen, and the ear has not heard, and have not entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him.* But God has revealed it to us by His Spirit. The Spirit makes known to us Gospel truths and reveals to us Gospel mysteries. The spiritual person discerns all things, but he himself is discerned by no one. He has the Spirit of God, by which he is powerful enough to discern the true Doctrine from the false (says the Apostle) and is discerned by no one—that is, he is so assured of the truth of his Doctrine that other men cannot mislead him.

# On Walking

<margin>Psalm 36:5</margin>
of hearts; all the deliberate thoughts and intentions to sin which have been in your heart, God will make manifest, and He will judge you, even for the secret counsels of the heart. The Psalmist David says that a wicked man devises injustice upon his bed and sets himself on a path that is not good. **He devises injustice**; there is his deliberation, and he sets himself on a path that is not good; that is a more severe expression of it. A godly person may be led astray by the Devil and his own heart, but the ungodly set themselves upon the path of sin.

<margin>Galatians 6:1. <note>original Greek: "εαν προληφθη", meaning "if he be overtaken."</note> <note>original Latin: "id præoccupatus sit à carne & Satana & incautus incidit in infidias Beza", meaning "that is, he is preoccupied by the flesh and Satan and incautiously falls into snares, according to Beza."</note></margin>
A godly person may be overtaken by some sin, as the Apostle says, which indicates that he is moving away from sin; but an ungodly person does not move away from sin, but rather sets himself upon a path that is not good. I acknowledge indeed, as the theologians here unanimously teach, that truly in some sense an intention and deliberation to sin can exist in a godly person; nonetheless, there is a great difference here between the godly and the ungodly. There is a difference between deliberating over the *act* of sin and a counsel to find an *opportunity* for how one shall commit the sin. A godly person may reflect on the sinful act, but not on how he might find the opportunity to become wicked. In David, there was a weighing and deliberation when he committed adultery, but he did not deliberate to find the opportunity; he did not go onto the roof of his house thinking to himself that he would see a woman there to lust after her. But when he was there, the Devil showed him an opportunity, and once that opportunity was found, then he began to deliberate how he might commit that foul sin. The same can be said of his counsel regarding the death of Uriah, for although he did that with premeditation, he was nonetheless driven to it by the violence of the temptation which then tormented him. But the ungodly deliberate on how they shall find opportunities for sin; they are their own devils; by reflecting on how they shall do injustice, they stir up the devils to tempt them.

<margin>7th Distinction.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 5:8.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 8:6.</margin>
Seventh, the godly do not fulfill the lusts of the flesh as vehemently, nor with such strong intent as the ungodly do, who are so violently set upon their desires. The adulterous thoughts of the ungodly are compared to the neighing of well-fed stallions—which is a strong longing—and to a headstrong horse in battle. The ungodly pursue their lusts as fiercely as a horse raging in the fray. One reads in Exodus in the 32nd chapter that the people "lay in evil," <note>likely referring to being "set on mischief" or "broken loose" in the Golden Calf incident</note> by which their vehemence in doing evil is made known. How Ammon raged until he fulfilled his desires; so much so that he became sick because of it. How sick Ahab became because of Naboth’s vineyard; so intensely were they inclined toward their lusts. But the righteous, although they sin, nonetheless do not commit sin with such a strong desire; and therefore the Apostle makes this distinction between the godly and the ungodly: the ungodly commit all uncleanness, and that with greediness. Regarding the ungodly, it is said that their heart walks after abominations and horrors.
<margin>2 Samuel 13:2.</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 21:4.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 4:19. <note>original Greek: "εν πλεωνεξια", meaning "with greediness" or "covetousness."</note></margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 11:21.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>8th Distinction.</margin>
Eighth, the godly do not sin with such a firm purpose as the ungodly do; the ungodly stand so firmly upon their desires that they cannot be pulled away from them. When God commanded the people to leave their idolatry, they said, "It is hopeless; no; for I have loved strangers, and them will I follow." As if they said: we have done evil, and we want to continue doing evil. So also at another time when they had burned incense to the Queen of Heaven, and the Lord had commanded them to leave their idolatry and threatened to punish them, they said nonetheless: regarding the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you. This stood firm with them: to follow their ungodly ways. An ungodly person sets his heart so much on sin that it deprives him of his sleep. They do not sleep unless they have done some evil; and their sleep is taken away unless they have made someone stumble. But the godly do not sin with such a firm purpose. It may be that they have a purpose to do sin, which they also know to be sin, but through a little good counsel they are pulled away from it. It is noteworthy what one reads of David. His purpose was to kill Nabal and his entire household—truly a bloody purpose. He had bound himself with an oath and had now gone up to carry out this bloody resolve; but at last Abigail meets him; and how quickly he is brought from this purpose by her good counsel! *Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me. And blessed be your advice, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from coming to shed blood.* The godly do not have such a firm purpose to commit wickedness; but a little good counsel will bring them away from it, and they will bless and thank God for such preventative counsel and for the one who gives it to them.
<margin>Jeremiah 2:25.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 44:16.</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 4:16.</margin>
<margin>1 Samuel 25:32, 33.</margin>

<margin>9th Distinction.</margin>
<margin><note>original Latin: "Nil gravitate in suo centro", meaning "Nothing is heavy in its own center."</note></margin>
Ninth, they do not sin with such satisfaction and tranquility as the ungodly. See, the ungodly sin with satisfaction because, when they sin, they are in their own element. Now, just as the natural philosophers say of the elements—that they are not heavy in their own places, just as the earth is not heavy in its own place—so also with the ungodly; they wallow like a sow in the mire; they have pleasure in being there. But how troublesome it is for a little sheep to be in the mire! Its pleasure is to be in the green pastures. The ungodly not only walk and stand in sin, but also sit down in it, which indicates their satisfaction therein. But it is not so with the godly; there is such a distinction between sin in a good man and a bad man as there is between poison in a human and in a toad. The poison is pleasant to the toad, for it agrees with its nature; but on the contrary, how harmful and troublesome is that same thing to a human. So also sin differs in the godly and the ungodly. Sin pleases the ungodly because it is natural to him; but in the godly, sin is like poison in a human body—it pains and torments him.
<margin>Psalm 1:1.</margin>

<margin>10th Distinction.</margin>
Tenth, a godly person does not make such a habit of sinning as the...

Now gather all these specific things together, and you shall see the truth of the text: That if you walk by the Spirit, you shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh; that is, you shall not sin in that manner and measure as the ungodly sin.

<margin>1st Utility.</margin>
Well then, you who have the Spirit of God, thank God that you have such a preservative or preventative means to keep you 

<column-break/>

from sinning in the way that the ungodly sin. What else is the reason that the ungodly sin so, if not because they do not have the Spirit of God? Do you have the same sinful stirrings and inclinations which the greatest of them have? The horrible works of other men are nothing other than explanations of what is in your own heart. You have reason to praise God, because otherwise you would commit more sins than you do; and the sins which you do commit, you would do in a more evil way, and with greater willingness, intensity, and wantonness; thank God then in this respect for His Holy Spirit.

Notice from this the happiness of a God-fearing person, and the misery of an ungodly person. This is the happiness of one who fears God: that he has the Spirit to restrain him from sinning as other men sin. And the Scripture speaks in this respect of a godly person as if he had no sin at all. *Whosoever is born of God* 
<margin>1 John 3:9. <note>original Latin: "Non homines sed monstra hominum sunt pelagiani, Cathari, Celestiani, Donatistæ, Anabaptistæ, Libertini ; qui ex hoc loco perfectionem illam somniant, à qua absunt ipsi omnium hominum longissimè, Beza." (Translation: "The Pelagians, Cathars, Celestinians, Donatists, Anabaptists, and Libertines are not men but monsters of men; they dream of a perfection from this passage, from which they themselves are the furthest of all men." — Theodore Beza)</note></margin>
(says the Apostle) *doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.* This must not be taken in an absolute sense, as if they had no sin, but in comparison; they cannot sin in the way the ungodly do. *I write these things to you* (says the same Apostle) *that ye sin not.* And just as it is written of Job, that in all this he sinned not. These manners of speaking (as I have said) must not be taken absolutely, but relatively or in comparison; that is, not that the godly do not sin at all, but that they do not sin in the way that the ungodly do. *Thou shalt visit thy habitation, and shalt not sin* <note>Often translated as "not find anything amiss."</note>, 
<margin>Job 5:24.</margin>
says Job. What an honor is this then for the God-fearing, that because they do not sin like the ungodly, the Scripture therefore speaks of them as if they did no sin at all. But further, behold the misery of the ungodly; in what a sorrowful case are they, who do not have the Spirit of God to restrain their sinful nature from sin? What slaves of sin are they! What vassals or subjects are they to their own lusts! When the devil from without and their own lusts from within tempt them, they do not have God's Spirit to restrain them. The ungodly sin in such a way that the righteous cannot sin. And therefore the Lord God says, *They have corrupted themselves, they are not his children; their spot is a blemish.* <note>Deuteronomy 32:5.</note> I confess, it is true, there may be something of these specifically mentioned things in your practice and life; you may have had some willingness, some delight, and some deliberation in sinning: but do not therefore cast away courage, as long as you do not give your heart over entirely, and if there is not in you such a strong drive of the will toward sin as is found in the ungodly.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the "walking in the Spirit," transitioning into a specific exposition of Galatians 5:17. It marks the beginning of the 12th sermon in this series, delivered in London in 1650.</meta>

# Conflict between

### Galatians 5 verse 17.

> For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.

<margin>12th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry within London on the 15th of December, 1650. <note>St. Lawrence Jewry is a historic church in the City of London, where many influential Puritan sermons were delivered.</note></margin>
After I have dealt with the preceding verse in several sermons regarding walking by the Spirit, I now proceed to the treatment of this verse, which contains within itself the conflict between the flesh and the Spirit.

At this time, I shall only explain the first part of the text, and thereafter I shall address the others in order.

The first attack in this spiritual battle is made by the flesh: *the flesh lusts against the Spirit.*

To open this, I shall explain two things.
1. What is understood by "the flesh"?
2. What is signified by "the Spirit"? And then, what is meant by the "lusting" of the flesh against the Spirit?

<margin>1st Question answered.</margin>
By "the flesh," the corruption of human nature, caused by original sin, must be understood; this corruption can be considered either as a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "heblijckheydt," meaning an ingrained disposition or state of being</note> or as an operation. If one considers the flesh as a habit, then it points to that first root and original lack of inclination toward the good in human nature.

But if it is taken as an operation, then it signifies our corrupt movements against grace, and so I take it in this place; *the flesh lusts against the Spirit*, that is, when the Spirit of God, through divine knockings, strikes upon the heart in holy movements, then there is a resistance of the flesh against these movements, by suppressing them and bringing the heart toward evil.

The corruption of nature may be called "flesh" for these reasons:

<margin>I.</margin>
First, because the soul was infected with corruption immediately upon its union and joining with the body. It is indeed true that there is a dispute among theologians as to when the soul receives corruption, since it is infused through creation and is therefore pure. But almost all authors agree on this: that immediately upon the union of the soul with the body, it is said to have corruption for this reason; and by its nature it is called "flesh" because man is naturally corrupt as soon as soul and body are coupled together.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, the corrupt nature is called "flesh" because this corruption of nature stays with us as long as we carry "flesh and blood" about with us here; as long as one has flesh here, one shall also have sin. The "body of death" <note>A biblical term from Romans 7 for the sinful nature.</note> can only be brought to nothing through the death of the body, and therefore corruption may be called flesh.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, because the movements of the cor-

<column-break/>

<margin>Ephesians 5:29.</margin>
rupt nature are as dear to a man by nature as his own flesh. *No man ever yet hated his own flesh.* And this is the reason, <margin>Matthew 5:29, 30.</margin> why the Scripture calls that corruption a "right hand" and a "right eye"; namely, because the corruption of nature is closely united with the man.

<margin>2nd Question. Answer.</margin>
What is understood here by "the Spirit"? Some believe that by "the Spirit" is signified the soul of a born-again man; but this does not seem to fit well, because the objective of this passage implies something else, although that may also be included. Therefore, by "the Spirit" must be understood the holy movements and operations of God's Spirit, and it is against these that the flesh is said to lust. That this <margin>Galatians 3:2, 14. Galatians 4:6, 29. Galatians 5:5, 16, 17, 18, 22, 25.</margin> must be understood in this way is obvious, because the word "Spirit" is taken in this sense in the preceding verse, and also in the verse which follows my text: so that by "the Spirit" I understand the movements and operations of God's Spirit in the soul. And in this sense, the word "Spirit" is taken in many places of this epistle.

<margin>3rd Question. Answer.</margin>
What is understood by "lusting" or "desiring"? When it says, *lusting against the Spirit*, one may note that it does not say "working" against the Spirit: although sin is of an active nature, it is nonetheless not always working, but it is always lusting; there is an opposing inclination and posture in nature against the work of God's Spirit upon the heart. In these words, one must pay attention to three parts.

1. A two-fold fight: *The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.*

2. A two-fold cause: *These are contrary the one to the other*; the flesh stands against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.

3. Here is a two-fold result: *So that you do not do the things that you would*; the flesh lusts against the Spirit, so that you cannot do the good that you would, and the Spirit against the flesh, so that you cannot do the <insert>evil</insert> that you would. <note>The Dutch text repeats "the good" (het goet) here, but the theological context suggests the Spirit prevents the believer from doing the evil they might otherwise intend.</note>

Before I come to the Doctrine, I shall set forth a few specific things beforehand which must be taken into account.

<margin>I. Ecclesiastes 7:29.</margin>
First, this battle between the flesh and the Spirit was not found in the state of innocence; then there was a harmony between the movements of God's Spirit and all the powers and faculties of both soul and body; *God made man upright.*

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, this battle shall not be found in the state of glory: for then you shall be nothing but Spirit, and no corrupt flesh, for the flesh shall then be entirely annihilated.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, this opposition is not found in tender childhood: it is indeed true that there is a corrupt nature in young children, and there are sinful movements in children, but there is not that actual opposition, because they can exercise neither grace nor sin.

<margin>IV.</margin>
Fourthly, this battle is not found in the state of nature, which is unregenerate: as long as a man is entirely unregenerate, he has no saving movements in him, and there can be no opposition except where two stand against each other.

<summary>This page introduces an exposition of Galatians 5:17, defining "flesh" as the corruption of human nature and "Spirit" as the holy operations of God. It outlines the spiritual warfare that exists only in the regenerate believer, excluding those in states of innocence, glory, infancy, or total unregeneration.</summary>
<keywords>flesh and spirit, Galatians 5:17, original sin, St. Lawrence Jewry, spiritual warfare, regeneration, corruption of nature</keywords>

<margin>V.</margin>
Fifthly, this struggle shall last the entire duration of this life. No end can come to it before this life ends; you shall not be delivered from the stirrings of sin before you lay down the body of the flesh.

<margin>VI.</margin>
Sixthly, this battle between the Flesh and the Spirit exists even in the holiest people there are: and those who have the most grace feel the fight of the flesh against the Spirit the most.

<margin>VII.</margin>
Seventhly, even the reborn <note>original: "wederboorne," referring to the regenerate or those spiritually "born again"</note> themselves often cling more to the stirrings of the flesh than to the stirrings of the Spirit; they sin more often than they are obedient; they embrace sinful stirrings more than they accept Divine stirrings. Some conclude this from the Apostle’s change in speech when he says, The works of the <margin>Gal. 5:19.</margin> flesh are manifest, but he does not speak so of the fruits of the Spirit; indicating that men are more prone to conspire with the flesh than with the Spirit.

<margin>VIII.</margin>
Eighthly, these stirrings of the corrupt nature do not only hold their place in the lower part of man—namely the desiring faculty, inciting to gluttony and evil lusts, and the faculty inciting to hatred and wrath—but they are also in the upper part (though the Papists <note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics</note> would have us believe otherwise); the noblest and most rational faculties of man have become corrupt; you have become vain in your reasoning, and vain in your imagination, your understanding is darkened, your will rebellious, your affections disordered; your highest faculties are contaminated. Having established these particular points, I now proceed to the Doctrine, which is this:

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
## Doctrine.

> That the movements or inclinations in our nature toward sin always struggle or war against the movements of God’s Spirit, which urge us toward the good.

I shall not dwell long on proving this point; it stands clearly in God’s Word; every person has experience of it; therefore, in handling this, I shall answer several questions, and thereafter I shall give you the practical application.

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
### 1st Question.
In what does this struggle between the flesh and the Spirit consist?

<margin>1st Answer.</margin>
### 1st Answer.
<margin>Rom. 7:5.</margin>
First, in the stirring up of movements toward sin in the heart, just as the Spirit begins to loathe sin. Thus speaks the Apostle Paul in the name of the reborn: *When we were in the flesh, the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work by chance <note>modern translations often use "effectively" or "at work"</note> in our members to bring forth fruit unto death.* Among these are not only the stirrings of the corrupt nature in the unregenerate, being in conflict <margin>Jas. 1:14.</margin> with God’s Spirit, but also in the reborn man. *Every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed,* that is, by original sin: so also Paul speaks of himself as <margin>Rom. 7:23.</margin> reborn. *I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.* The Apostle calls sin a "law" because it had power over him and took him captive; the law of his members fought against the law of his mind by enticing him to sin.

<margin>2nd Answer.</margin>
### 2nd Answer.
Secondly, in the extinguishing and suffocating of the good stirrings of the Spirit, which

<column-break/>

urges us toward the good; the office of the Spirit is not only to witness to us of the gifts of grace given to us, and to make us see our profit and good in Christ; but also to work and cause holy movements to arise in the heart. Now the flesh does its utmost to extinguish all these good movements: for this reason Paul complains of himself, *That the good that he would, he did not,* <margin>Rom. 7:19.</margin> *and the evil which he would not, that he did;* and this proceeded from that corruption of nature, of which he so complains in that entire chapter; and herein consists the opposition which exists between the flesh and the Spirit.

<margin>3rd Answer.</margin>
### 3rd Answer.
Thirdly, in resisting and hindering you <margin>Rom. 7:18.</margin> when you are busy in any good duties; if the flesh cannot get the upper hand in drawing you away from the duties, it will labor to bring you to doing them poorly, and herein consists its great sinfulness. *To will is present with me* (says Paul) *but how to perform that which is good I find not;* as if he said, I always carry an evil nature within me, which stops, hinders, and weakens me, so that I cannot do the good that I would; herein consists the fight between the flesh and the Spirit.

<margin>2nd Question.</margin>
### 2nd Question.
In what manner does the flesh set itself against the Spirit and incite to sin? The Spirit warns against sin, and the flesh entices to sin. Now what path does the flesh take to entice us to sin, and thereby to struggle against the Spirit?

<margin>1st Answer.</margin>
### 1st Answer.
In general, I answer that the way and manner which the flesh maintains in setting itself against the Spirit is very wicked and cunning. For this reason Paul says: *Sin, taking occasion* <margin>Rom. 7:16.</margin> <note>Likely a typo for Rom. 7:11</note> *by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me;* by "sin" he understands not actual sin, but original sin; the sin of nature is very cunning in deceiving, as shall appear.

<margin>Eph. 4:22.</margin>
1. By the names which the Scripture gives to the sin of nature; they are called "lusts of deceit." That sin is very deceiving, according to the admonition <margin>Heb. 3:13.</margin> of the Apostle: *Exhort one another daily, while it is called "Today"; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.*

<margin>Rom. 7:11.</margin>
2. The deceitfulness of this sin of nature appears from the experience of God’s people. *Sin, taking occasion* (says Paul) *by the commandment, deceived me and by it slew me.*

<margin>Jer. 17:9.</margin>
3. Because this sin of nature makes the heart <margin><term>Whatever makes a thing [to be] such, is itself more such.</term> <note>original Latin: "quidquid efficit tale est magis tale," a logical principle meaning that the cause of a quality must possess that quality even more intensely.</note></margin> more cunning than anything, even deadly; the heart is deceitful, and it is cunning in that.

<margin>2nd Answer.</margin>
### 2nd Answer.
In particular, there are seven ways in which the corrupt nature entices men to sin.

<margin>1.</margin>
First, by dressing up the sin with the color and appearance of virtue; just as a loose woman sometimes puts on a modest garment so that she might not be suspected: so also the heart often adorns sin, so that it may deceive you all the more quickly. Just as it commonly goes, that the fair face of the virtues is often smeared with much filthiness through the corruption of our hearts, so that tenderness of conscience is called "unnecessary scrupulosity" and "anxiety," and zeal is called "rashness"—

<summary>This page discusses the lifelong and pervasive nature of the conflict between the "flesh" (human corruption) and the "Spirit," noting that even the intellect is tainted. It outlines how the flesh actively suffocates good impulses and uses cunning to disguise sinful behavior as virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 41 regarding the "struggle between the Flesh and the Spirit," specifically focusing on the deceptive tactics the "flesh" (our corrupt human nature) uses to lead a person into sin.</meta>

<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>Struggle between</header>

<column-break/>

...holiness, or a holy walk, as a needless and narrow scrupulosity; patience in enduring some suffering, as faint-heartedness and dejection of the Spirit. <note>The author is describing how the "flesh" mislabels virtues to make them seem like weaknesses.</note> Likewise, on the contrary, your corrupt heart will paint foul sin with the ornament of virtues. Thus many give the foul sin of greed the name of the virtue of temperance and frugality; the proud call it neatness; drunkenness is called good company; squandering is called generosity; and the world applies such a polish to the foul face of sin.

And as it goes in practice and daily walk, so it is also with various opinions. How are those old heresies (which one can find in Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian known as the "Father of Church History."</note> and other authors) now decked out with the honorable name of "new lights"? How do the deceptions of Satan receive the name of "movements of the Spirit"? And a loose and unrestrained life, the name of "Christian liberty"? This decking out of sins with the paint of apparent virtues comes from our corrupt natures, and is a path upon which the flesh entices man to sin.

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, by making you believe that some sins are such that there is no fear of you ever committing them. In this regard, the Devil has a great advantage over men. Our own hearts sometimes tell us that some sins are so small, and so contrary to our natural disposition, and that we have such a great measure of grace, that we shall certainly never commit them. Thus it was with the godless Hazael, when the Prophet told him what evil he would do to the children of Israel; that <margin>2 Kings 8:12, 13.</margin> he would set their strongholds on fire, and kill their young men with the sword, dash their young children to pieces, and rip open their pregnant women; Hazael could not believe this, but said, "What is your servant, <margin>Matthew 26:33.</margin> who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" So also was Peter deceived by his heart. "Even if they all stumble because of you" (he said), "I will never stumble." But how did his heart deceive him? Thus even a God-fearing man can be beguiled by his own heart. Men do not want to believe that their hearts are as proud as they truly are; and once the heart is brought to this thought—that there are some sins which it will not commit—a person becomes through that means careless and unconcerned, and is thereby more easily drawn into it. Thus David made a <margin>1 Samuel 24:5, 6.</margin> conscience of smaller things, for his heart struck him because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe; but he did not think that he would later fall into those coarse and offensive sins of Adultery and Murder; and so his heart became careless and deceived him.

<margin>III.</margin> Thirdly, the flesh entices a man to sin by promising him pleasure and delight in the commission of the sin; but it conceals the harmful evil that follows, and <margin>James 1:14.</margin> how are thousands deceived by this? "Each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desires." We are lured <note>original: "ghesept," a term related to baiting a trap or hook.</note> by being enticed by our desires; the word has a very powerful emphasis, and is a metaphor taken from fishermen, who show the fish the bait but not the hook; and just as the

<column-break/>

fisherman deals with the fish, so also the Devil and your corrupt nature work with you; they will show you the pleasure, but not the danger of the sin; the bait, but not the hook; as the Apostle Peter speaks, "enticing unstable souls." Your own heart deceives you. Just as the Devil, before <margin>Genesis 3:2.</margin> Adam had a sinful nature, used this craftiness against him, so now your own heart uses it against you. "If you eat of this fruit" (said the Devil), "your eyes shall be opened; and you shall be like God, knowing good and evil." The Devil hid the hook; he did not show her that they would be driven out of Paradise, but he kept their danger hidden, and thus deceived her. Now your own corrupt heart fights against you with the same tactic. "The way <margin>Proverbs 12:26 and 11:18.</margin> of the wicked causes them to stray," says Solomon. The wicked man performs a deceptive work: but for him who sows righteousness, there is a sure reward. The work of the wicked gives him a <margin>Coals instead of treasure. <note>original Latin: "Pro thesauro carbones." An ancient proverb meaning something that seems valuable turns out to be worthless.</note> IV.</margin> sham reward, but it is only the godly person whose reward is sure.

Fourthly, by persuading you to keep small sins at hand, with the promise that if you only indulge in these, you will never come to commit the greater ones. This is a great deceitfulness of the heart by which thousands have fallen; for small sins are actually an entrance to greater sins. A small thief, being placed inside a house, can open the doors so that larger and stronger thieves may enter. I have read a story of a youth who was tempted by the Devil and his own heart to three sins: namely, to murder his Father, to dishonor his Mother, and to get drunk. The first two sins he did not want to do, because he had a natural horror of them; but he thought, "I will indulge in the last one, because that sin is the smallest," which was nonetheless enough to do the others; for while drunk, he killed his Father and dishonored his own Mother. Guard yourself well then from this deceit of sin. Your heart will not advise you to all sins at once, but it will seek to draw you there by steps, from smaller to greater sins, until you become abominable therein. "See" (says the Apostle James), "how great a forest a little fire <margin>James 3:5.</margin> kindles!" Small permitted sins may be the occasion to bring forth very great sins. Therefore, take care that you are not deceived by the corrupt advice of nature.

<margin>V.</margin> Fifthly, the flesh will tempt you to sin on this ground: because it is only a small sin, just as Lot said of Zoar, "Is it not a little one?" But notice that this is pure craftiness of sin to destroy you: for although one sin is less than another in respect to the act, they are nonetheless all equal in respect to the Object against whom the sin is committed. God is not small, against whom one sins, so there can be no small sin; sin must be measured by the Object, and not by the act itself. If one gives a lowly person a blow, it is reckoned as nothing; but if the same is done to a person of dignity, how poorly is that taken? Therefore, if your heart says to you, "that is only a small sin," then say, "the God against whom I sin is no small God," and the merit where...
<meta>catchword: high</meta>

...for the forgiveness obtained for that sin is no small merit; and hell, being prepared for the punishment of even a small sin, is no small pain; therefore, take heed of your heart in this regard.

<margin>VI.</margin>
<margin>Gen. 19:32.</margin>
Sixthly, your heart may come to entice you to sin under this pretext: that some good may follow the commission of that sin. How many are caught in that snare? By this, the daughters of Lot were ensnared, so that they lay with their own father under the cover that they might preserve the lineage of their father. They saw that there would be no descendants from their father, and thought that the Church of God would thus die out; this was their aim, and therefore, to preserve some seed, they chose to give themselves to sin. This is expressly against the Scripture, which forbids doing evil so that good may come <note>A reference to Romans 3:8, a common theological argument against "situational ethics."</note>: will you speak unrighteously for God? And will you speak deceitfully for Him? And if we may do evil under the pretext of good, then by the same rule the treachery of Judas could be excused, because such great good came through Christ's death. But further, if you commit sin so that good may come of it, you are using a means that prevents you from obtaining the beloved good. It is worth noting the case of Saul, who, pursuing the Philistines, had given a cruel and sharp command to the people and swore an oath that they should not take a bite of food until evening, so that he might avenge himself on his enemies. Saul's pretext was good, but because he used an unlawful means, the people became faint and succumbed for lack of food, whereas they otherwise would have obtained a much more glorious victory. When men use sinful means to obtain good, it is only just in God's sight to let them be deprived of the good they desire.

<margin>Job 13:8.</margin>
<margin>Rom. 3:8.</margin>
<margin>1 Sam. 14:24.</margin>
<margin>VII.</margin>
Seventhly and lastly, your corrupt heart will tell you that although you may not boldly commit sin, you may nevertheless occasionally be present at the *occasions of sin* <note>The "occasions of sin" refers to people, places, or things that typically lead one into temptation.</note> without becoming defiled. Thus Peter was deceived by his heart; he wanted to go into the High Priest's hall, where there was an opportunity to sin, thinking that he would not fall into it there. So also the Israelites wanted to marry foreign women, which was an opportunity through which they finally fell into the service of foreign gods. Guard yourself, then, against the opportunity for sinning. Solomon has a good saying: *Can a man walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched?* <note>original: "sal jemant op koolen gaen, dat zijn voeten niet en bernen?" from Proverbs 6:28.</note> His meaning is that no one can keep company with a harlot and still remain chaste. Seeking opportunities to sin leads to the commission of sin; you should not venture onto ice or slippery places because there is an opportunity to fall; if you desire to be delivered from the one, do not be bold in the other.

<margin>Prov. 6:28.</margin>
<margin>1. Utility.</margin>
Well then, you who carry flesh and blood and sinful natures with you, and experience the struggle of the flesh against the Spirit, consider within yourselves why the flesh fights against you; it is for nothing less than your immortal souls, as the Apostle Peter says: *I beseech you* (he says) *as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.*

<margin>1 Pet. 2:11.</margin>

<column-break/>

The flesh seeks to bring the soul to damnation. It is in this struggle as Caesar said of the battle he fought with the children and allies of Pompey: namely, that in other battles he was accustomed to fight for glory and majesty, but then he was forced to fight for his own life. Remember that your precious soul is in danger in this struggle. Therefore, I pray you, set yourself with God's Spirit against the flesh, and not with the flesh against the Spirit.

<margin>2. Utility.</margin>
When you are overtaken by sin, give the blame to no one but your own heart—not to God, nor to the Devil.

<margin>Eccles. 7:29.</margin>
1. Not God, for He made man upright; He gave man a pure and undefiled soul, but they have sought out many inventions <note>original: "vonden," meaning schemes or contrivances.</note>; therefore, blame yourself. *Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God; for every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.*

<margin>James 1:13.</margin>
2. Do not lay the blame on the Devil. Men are naturally inclined, when they fall into sin, to cast the blame away from their own evil natures and lay it entirely on the Devil. But if one looks at the Scripture, one will never find that a God-fearing person laid the blame on the Devil after they had sinned. It is true, Adam and Eve did this, but there was a different reason for that, because they had no sinful nature to tempt them; but after they had fallen, their sinful nature tempted them, and not the Devil. It is written of David that Satan stood up and provoked him to number Israel, but David himself did not speak so, but said: *I have sinned greatly, and have acted very foolishly.* David accused his own heart, and the reason is that a man's heart rouses him to sin much more powerfully than the Devil does. Alas! What could the Devil do if we had no sinful inclination within? When the Devil came to Christ to tempt Him, he found nothing in Him, and therefore he could not overcome Him: *The prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me,* said Christ. But it is quite different with us; temptations join together with our corruptions and fit each other perfectly. When the Devil comes to you, your heart is like flax near the fire, or like gunpowder (Buskruyt) which, having a spark of fire in itself, quickly blows up. Lay the blame then not on the Devil, but on your own heart; neither the Devil nor the world could do you any harm were it not for your own heart, which harbors like a false traitor in your breast and draws the soul into the snares and temptations of the Devil.

<margin>1 Chron. 21:1.</margin>
<margin>verse 8.</margin>
<margin>John 14:30.</margin>

# The Struggle Between

<margin>1. The nature of the flesh. Romans 6:12</margin>
First, the <term>flesh<note>In this context, "the flesh" (Dutch: *het vleesch*) refers to the fallen, corrupt human nature that resists God, rather than the physical body itself.</note></term> is a mighty enemy against the Spirit; it is not a weak but a strong enemy. Therefore, the Apostle says that sin should not reign in your mortal body. In the <term>unregenerate<note>Those who have not yet experienced a spiritual rebirth or "born again" conversion.</note></term>, the flesh is like a mighty absolute monarch who rules without any contradiction; indeed, the flesh binds them like a law. And in those who are <term>born again<note>Those who have undergone a spiritual transformation through faith.</note></term>, sin is like a violent tyrant who occupies a large part of a believer's soul. Paul
<margin>Romans 7:14</margin>
complains that he was "sold under sin," for although after his rebirth he did not sell himself to work wickedness, he was nonetheless taken prisoner by the flesh, as if by a mighty and strong enemy. Just as victors sell their prisoners, so too was Paul sold. Theologians commonly compare our corrupt nature to the great Goliath, and grace to the little David. Goliath is indeed stronger, but David gains the victory; although corruption may be powerful, grace shall nonetheless obtain the victory in the end.

The power of the flesh can be seen from these proofs:

<margin>1 Corinthians 10:4; Romans 7:23.</margin>
1. From the names given to our corrupt nature in Scripture: it is called a "stronghold"; one might easily overcome an ordinary dwelling, but it is difficult to attack a stronghold. It is called the "law of sin," because it has such power over the soul as the law has over the subjects of a kingdom; it is said to "reign," because it has the power that a prince has over his people.

2. That it is powerful is evident from the great strength that must be employed to bring this enemy down. The power of the Almighty God is required to overpower these corrupt movements, and therefore the Apostle says "the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds." The weapons must be sharpened with the power of the Godhead to cast down these strongholds.

<margin>Ephesians 2:2.</margin>
3. Corrupt nature is strong because it is aided by a strong spirit, the Devil: he stirs you up to sin, and it is from this that the corruption of your heart is so strong. The sea is moved by itself, being a fluid body; but when a fierce storm arises, then it tosses and foams terribly. So it goes with corrupt nature; if there were no Devil, you would be a devil to yourself and would commit sin; but when a Devil also comes to stir that sea of your corrupt nature, how it rages and swells then! He is the "prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the children of disobedience."

<margin>Romans 7:14</margin>
4. That the flesh is powerful is known from this: that it often overcomes the Spirit. The Apostle says that the flesh has the upper hand over the Spirit not only in the godless, but also sometimes in the reborn. "The law is spiritual," he says, "but I am carnal, sold under sin." He speaks of himself as one born again; he does not say that he sold himself, which was a characteristic of the godless King Ahab, but his corrupt nature led him away captive to sin, just as a victor leads his prisoner away.

5. The flesh is a strong enemy because

<column-break/>

the flesh exists in greater measure in the reborn than the Spirit does: you have more sin in you than grace or gifts; more of the corrupt nature than of the renewed nature. In the best of God’s children, there is more ignorance than knowledge, more pride than humility, and generally more sin than obedience.
<margin>Galatians 5:19.</margin>
This can be gathered from the list of the "works of the flesh" and the "fruits of the Spirit."
<margin>Hebrews 12:2.</margin>
There, seventeen sins are listed as fruits of the flesh, and only nine virtues as fruits of the Spirit, to show that there is more of the old nature in your heart than the new, more of the "old leaven" than of the "new lump," more dross than gold. God allows this to keep His children in humility and in a constant dependence and watchfulness upon Him. The souls of the righteous are never made perfect until they enter Heaven; and in the meantime, the wonderful power of Christ is shown in keeping a tiny spark of grace alive in the midst of a sea of corruption.

<margin>2. Nature. Romans 8:7.</margin>
Secondly, just as the flesh is powerful, so it is also a malicious enemy against the Spirit. "The carnal mind is enmity against God," and this very malice against the Spirit is evident in two ways.

<margin>Romans 7:18. <note>original: "Carne carendo" (Lacking in the flesh)</note></margin>
1. It does not allow any good to be in it. "I know that in me (that is, in my flesh) dwells no good thing," says the Apostle. Although there may be some good in the person, there is nonetheless no good in the flesh—that is, in his corrupt nature.

<margin>Romans 7:11</margin>
2. The flesh is satisfied with nothing less than the death of the creature in which it dwells; now this is indeed a very terrible enemy. It not only kills the movements of the Spirit but is also malicious toward the person themselves. 
<margin>Romans 8:13.</margin>
Therefore, the Apostle Paul says, "sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me." And again, "if you live according to the flesh, you shall die." It is only satisfied with the death and eternal damnation of the soul; this shows that the malice of the flesh is truly great.

<margin>3. Nature.</margin>
Thirdly, corrupt nature is a universal enemy against the Spirit, and its universality is evident in three respects.

<margin><note>original: "Anima est tota in toto corpore & tota in qualiber parte" (The soul is whole in the whole body and whole in every part)</note></margin>
1. The flesh possesses the whole person, all the parts of your body, and all the faculties of your soul. The flesh is in the soul just as the soul is in the body. Now the philosophers say that the soul is "whole in the whole body and whole in every part of the body"; even so, corruption and sin are in the whole soul. The entire corruption of nature is in the whole person and in every part thereof: in your body, eyes, ears, hands, in and throughout all the parts; not only in the desiring and the anger-prone parts, but also in the higher parts, such as the will, the understanding, and the reason; it is universal in every part of the person.

<margin><note>original: "Primus homo fuit omnis homo" (The first man was every man)</note> Romans 7:8. <note>original: "Primum peccatum fuit omne peccatum" (The first sin was every sin)</note></margin>
2. It contains within itself the power of all sin. There is nothing that encompasses all evil in its power except corrupt nature. Just as we may say of the first man that he *was* all men, so we can also say of the first sin that it contains all sin—that is, the power of all sin. "Sin, taking occasion by the commandment," says the Apostle, "wrought in me all manner of concupiscence." Corrupt nature is a tendency toward all the daily evil in the world. This can be explained...

It argues that even in the "born again," the corrupt nature remains a formidable force that can only be countered by divine power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the numbered list of the characteristics of "the flesh" (the fallen human nature) as an enemy of the Spirit, exploring its insatiable, tireless, and internal nature before concluding with reasons for gratitude for God's grace.</meta>

<page-num>45</page-num>
# Flesh and Spirit.

...are shown through the example of an egg. An egg has within itself, in potential and in fact, all the parts of a <term>fowl<note>Dutch: *Hoen*; referring to a chicken or hen.</note></term>; it only lacks the warmth of the hen to brood and bring it forth. In the same way, our corrupt flesh has within itself all sin; and just as the hen brings forth the chick, so the Devil broods upon and brings forth sin.

3. It sets itself against all the grace of God's Spirit. Other sins—take whichever sin you wish—only stand against a specific, opposing grace. Particular sins have only a particular opposition: for example, the sin of pride sets itself against humility; greed against mercy; drunkenness against sobriety; injustice against justice; anger against gentleness; hate against love; and so it is with all other sins. They have only a particular opposition against particular gifts of grace; but your flesh sets itself generally against all grace.

<margin>4th Characteristic.</margin>
Fourthly, the flesh is an insatiable enemy, and that in two respects.

1. In respect to sin: because if we give ourselves over to sinful movements today, our corrupt nature will not be satisfied with that; if you commit sin today, you must also do it tomorrow—indeed, all your days. Corrupt nature is like those four things of which <term>Solomon<note>The traditional author of the Book of Proverbs.</note></term> says they are never satisfied; and as he speaks elsewhere: <term>Hell and destruction are never full<note>original: *De helle ende het verderf en worden niet versadight*</note></term>: so the eyes of man are never satisfied, which refers to the corrupt nature in the eye. Sinful desire in the heart ensures that an adulterous eye is never satisfied.
<margin>Proverbs 30:16.</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 27:20.</margin>

2. In respect to punishment as well as sin: suppose that sin brings sickness upon your body, or poverty upon your estate, yet you will still not leave your sin; the flesh loves even the defilement of your soul.

<margin>5th Characteristic.</margin>
Fifthly, the flesh is an indefatigable enemy against the Spirit. If the flesh had all the aforementioned qualities except this one, there might still be hope that it would eventually become weary and exhausted. But this is the nature of corruption: it is hostile toward the Spirit without becoming tired. Things that work by nature do not grow weary of working; fire is never tired of burning, nor water of ebbing and flowing, because those creatures are natural; the Sun is never weary of running its course because that movement is natural to it. Sin is natural to you, in which you were born and raised, and therefore it works without becoming weary. This war between flesh and Spirit is without any truce.

<margin>6th Characteristic.</margin>
Sixthly, corrupt nature is an internal enemy and lives not only beside us, but also in us; and therefore Paul says: *I do not do it myself, but the sin that dwells in me.* An enemy that attacks the city from the outside cannot do much damage if the walls are strong and well-manned; but if there are traitors within as well as attackers without, then that city shall be in danger. Remember that you do not only have the Devil on the outside, but also the corrupt nature within, which always seeks to betray you. There is more danger to be expected from one little thief who is inside than from all the robbers who are outside. Corrupt nature is that little thief who will always seek to betray you to the Devil.

<column-break/>

<margin>7th Characteristic.</margin>
Seventhly, this corruption of nature is a constant enemy against the Spirit. There is nothing which is working without ceasing except for corrupt nature. The eye does not always see; the sea does not always flow; the sun does not always shine; but corrupt nature is always active. The Spirit will no sooner send up a good impulse than the flesh will immediately try to send it back and extinguish it. The Devil does not always tempt, and the world does not always trouble us, but the flesh resists the Spirit throughout.

<margin>8th Characteristic.</margin>
<margin>*James 1:14*</margin>
Eighthly, the flesh is a cunning enemy against the Spirit, and works more through enticement than through force. *Every man is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust and enticed.* This is a metaphor taken from fishermen, who show the bait but hide the hook. It works, then, craftily and cunningly.

<margin>9th Characteristic.</margin>
<margin>*1 Thess. 4:5*</margin>
Ninthly, it is a fierce enemy against the Spirit. The Apostle, exhorting those of Thessalonica to sanctification and honor, forbids them to walk in the evil movement of lust, as the Gentiles do who do not know God; or in the "passions of lust," as it says in the <term>original text<note>Referring to the Greek text of the New Testament.</note></term>. Corrupt nature holds a person very fiercely; therefore it is called a "burning in lust"; and what is fiercer and more violent than a burning fire? Corrupt nature sets the soul on fire; it is also compared to a horse running headlong into battle; it is called a "pulling along of sin with cart-ropes" to indicate the intensity of a sinner; corruption, then, is fierce and powerful.
<margin>*Romans 1:27*</margin>

<margin>10th Characteristic.</margin>
Tenthly, it is an equally great enemy in all people; not more in one and less in another, but in all precisely the same. We are all troubled by it to the same degree, and the reason is that all people were equally in <term>Adam<note>The biblical first man; in theology, his "original sin" is inherited by all humanity.</note></term>; otherwise, some would have been more guilty of Adam's sin than others, which is impossible. We are all children of Adam, and therefore we are all equally defiled. But it is certain that *actual* corruption breaks out more in some than in others: some are more worldly, more unrestrained, and more possessed by cravings than others, because in some there are stronger natural inclinations and more powerful corruptions toward certain sins than in others. And therefore you, who are <term>born again<note>Those who have undergone a spiritual transformation.</note></term>, have as much cause to weep for a corrupt and sinful nature as any Devil in hell has. And these are the properties and characteristics of that enemy which wages war against the soul.

<margin>1st Utility.</margin>
Let our observations then serve to stir you to gratitude: that notwithstanding corrupt nature having all these qualities—namely, that it is so powerful, so high-acting, so general, so insatiable, so tireless, internal, cunning, and such a fierce enemy—nevertheless, <term>converting grace<note>The divine influence that turns a person toward faith.</note></term> could not be hindered by it. Thank God that His converting grace has overcome this enemy and has brought it under, despite all its strength, wickedness, and craftiness.

2. Thank God for <term>strengthening grace<note>The ongoing divine support that helps a believer persevere.</note></term>. This is one of the wonders of the world: that a child of God has so much corruption within themselves, and yet that corruption does not come to destroy and nullify grace.

<summary>This page concludes a ten-point list describing the corrupt nature of "the flesh," characterizing it as a tireless, internal, and insatiable enemy that inherited its power from Adam. It ends by encouraging believers to be grateful that God's grace is powerful enough to overcome such a formidable internal foe.</summary>

-> # The Battle Between <-

...to do. The wonder is evident here: Adam, who had no sinful nature—since he was only a changeable creature—being left to the freedom of his own will, nevertheless fell when tempted by the Devil. And the Angels in Heaven, who had no evil nature within nor a tempting Devil without, fell just the same. But you, who have both—a tempting Devil without and a corrupt nature within—you shall nevertheless not fall away. Oh, thank the Lord God for that! This comes from the fact that you have been accepted into an **unchangeable covenant**, because you have been chosen by an **unchangeable decree**, and are preserved by an **unchangeable God**. Therefore, being once in the covenant of grace, you are always preserved within it. Praise God for this, His unchangeable grace shown to your poor soul, by which you are preserved unto
<margin>1 Peter 1:5; Jude 1:14 <note>original: "1. Petr. 1. 5. Jude v. 14."</note></margin>
salvation, and by which God’s people are kept from stumbling.

<margin>Second Use.</margin>
Let this also serve to awaken **carefulness** against the movements of sin and our corrupt natures. If the flesh has all these qualities, do you not have reason to keep a close watch and oversight over your hearts? There is this reason why you must be so diligent: because your corrupt nature has a manifold advantage over the gifts of grace.

First, it has been in you **longer** than grace. Therefore it is written in the first place: *the flesh lusts against the Spirit*, which is already far ahead of you. Just as you can see in matters of war: whenever a battle is fought, that army which first takes the field will also choose the most advantageous position for its own benefit. Your corrupt nature, which wages war with the Spirit, was first in the field and thus has both the ground and the wind with it. You are born a sinner with an evil nature, but not with a divine nature; therefore the flesh, in this struggle, begins the fight first. Keep watch, then, against the flesh, which has this advantage against you.

<margin>* 1.</margin>
Secondly, the flesh has the advantage not only of time, but also of **number**. There is now more of the flesh than of the Spirit; more types of sin than of grace. In the best garden there are more weeds than flowers, and in the best soul there are more corruptions than graces.

I may appeal to your own experience, whether you have ever performed as many virtues as sins. In this chapter where my text is found, mention is made in the <term>list of names<note>Referring to the list of "works of the flesh" vs "fruits of the Spirit" in Galatians 5:19-23.</note></term> of seventeen sins, and only of nine gifts of grace, to show that the flesh is more prevalent in us than the Spirit. There are swarms of desires and <insert>base</insert> thoughts, but alas; how few good thoughts and holy movements of God's Spirit are in the best of us.

<margin>* 2.</margin>
Thirdly, the flesh has much of an advantage in respect to **disposition**. Corruption is more in agreement with your nature than grace is; grace is above nature, but sin is in and with nature. The way of grace is up the mountain; the way to Heaven is against both wind and tide. It is not so with corruption, for that has both with it. Therefore, keep watch over your hearts based on this observation.

<margin>Third Use.</margin>
Burst also into thanksgiving to God, that

<column-break/>

while your corrupt nature has so many evil qualities, He nevertheless does not allow more wickednesses to be committed. It is a grace that from such an evil root no more poisonous fruits come forth. If God let the Devil have his way in your own heart and gave you over to your own inclinations, there would be no sin committed by anyone that you would not also commit; you would be a **devil incarnate** <note>original: *gevleyschden Duyvel*, literally "fleshed devil".</note>. Thank God, then, that your works do not fully match your inner state, and that your life is not as evil as your heart.

2. Thank God for other people; it is a wonder that evil men, having no new nature to resist the old nature, do no more evil in the world. God bridles and curbs their evil natures. If God did not bridle the wantonness of the godless, the world would have long ago been overwhelmed in confusion by the disorder of their evil works.

<margin>Fourth Use.</margin>
If it is so that corrupt nature has all these qualities, then **humble yourself** in the feeling of your corrupt nature. Notwithstanding that you may be endowed with many noble gifts and graces, yet be humble because, although you have a divine nature, you also have a corrupt nature which always sets itself against it. It is like the **Peacock**: although she has the finest feathers of all the birds on earth, she nevertheless has foul feet. And like the **Swan**, which has the whitest wings <note>The Dutch text says "feet" (*voeten*) twice, likely a printer's error for "wings" (*vleugelen*) in the swan comparison.</note>. So also, you who are white and blameless in your life, remember nevertheless that you have a black skin and foul feet—that is, sinful inclinations and evil movements which arise from a corrupt nature.

These following considerations may move us to remember and be careful against our corrupt nature:

1. It is a sorrowful consideration, which can stir us to humility and care, that you have as much evil in your heart as the most wicked person living on earth.

2. It is very **old** in us; it was in us before we were born. Before you were in the world, sin was in your nature; for as soon as you had life, you also had sin.

<margin>Leviticus 11:35 and 15:12 <note>original: "Lev. 11. 35 en 15. 12."</note></margin>
3. This corruption of nature shall be with you as long as we live in this world. Our bodies are compared to **earthen vessels**, and the Scripture says of the uncleanness of an earthen vessel that if anything unclean were placed in it, no matter how much it was washed and scrubbed, the vessel would not become clean thereby, but it must be broken. So it stands with you; the vessel of your body must be broken before your corruption can be fully taken away.

<margin>Hebrews 12:1 <note>original: "Hebr. 12. 1."</note></margin>
4. This corruption **surrounds us easily**. The movements of sin in your nature are like sparks of fire in a heap of flax; they move your nature to easily do evil. Therefore, be persuaded by this to carry a close and diligent care over your own heart.

<margin>Galatians <note>original: "Galat."</note></margin>
