## Struggle between the Flesh and the Spirit, Part IV

The tree sleeps. <note>This refers to a common medieval and early modern belief that elephants slept leaning against trees because they supposedly lacked joints in their legs. If the tree were cut, the elephant would fall and be unable to get up.</note> Now it is told that if an elephant has fallen to the earth and is helped up by someone, it follows its benefactor (just as that grateful lion followed Andronicus <note>Likely a reference to the classical tale of Androcles and the Lion; the author uses "Andronicus."</note>) wherever he may go. So it is also with us; we were fallen, and we could be lifted up by no one other than through Christ’s help. How then ought we to be drawn up with holy gratitude to God, who for this purpose allowed us to fall, so that we might thereby learn to be grateful for the help of Jesus Christ, and for the hope that we have in that help?

<margin>4th Reason.</margin>
Fourthly, God allows corruption to remain in nature to test His people, to see which side they will choose in this struggle. Here, two great armies are drawn up, one against the other, and God the Lord leaves the flesh in you to test you: which side will you cling to? Will you hold with the stronger side and worship the "rising sun"? <note>A metaphor for siding with whoever appears to be winning or holds temporal power.</note> That is, will you conspire with the flesh? For the flesh usually has the upper hand, though surely the final outcome and victory shall belong to the Spirit. Now, if you wish to fight against the flesh and set yourself with the Spirit against the impulses of sin, God will test you in this. Just as the Canaanites and Jebusites were left in the Land to test the Israelites—to see if they would cling to the true religion—so God also leaves corruption in us to test the truth of our grace.

<margin>5th Reason.</margin>
Fifthly, God the Lord allows the impulses toward sin to remain in the hearts of His own people so that He might use those very impulses to keep men from actually sinning; and this is a mystical or hidden observation. Our God arranges it so that we keep the closest watch against those sins to which we are most tempted. It may be that someone, being suddenly tempted, happens to overstep. But God, in His wisdom, notices that a person who is frequently wounded by the inner stirrings of sin uses these stirrings to prevent the sinful act itself. If David had frequently felt the stirrings toward those great and abominable sins of adultery and murder, he might have had time to reflect and prevent the committing of them. Likewise Peter regarding the denial of Christ. But both of these servants of God were suddenly overtaken. And these are the reasons why God leaves our rebirth <term>rebirth: the process of spiritual regeneration</term> so imperfect.

<margin>5th Question.</margin>
This fifth question is this: what rules must one follow so that the stirrings of the flesh toward sin do not gain the upper hand against the Spirit?

<margin>First Rule.</margin>
First, if you do not want the flesh to overcome you in its sinful stirrings, then resist them while they are still merely impulses, before they break forth into actions. Kill the basilisk <note>A mythical reptile said to kill with its breath or gaze; here used as a metaphor for sin.</note> while it is still in the egg; trample out the sin, which is the fire of Hell, while it is still but a spark—namely, in its suggestion and impulse. Just as we say it is easier to keep an enemy out than to cast him out once he has been let in, so it is also easier to keep sins out than to cast them out. Sin in its impulse is...

<column-break/>

...like an enemy in the suburbs, who has not yet been let into the city. And if you do not want to follow these impulses, then stand against them while they are still such; extinguish them while they are merely stirrings. If one pays attention to a sickness in time, before the "evil humors" <note>An old medical theory that health was governed by four bodily fluids; "bad humors" caused disease.</note> have gathered together, one can easily cure it. Deal with your sins just as Pharaoh gave orders regarding the children of the Israelites: he would not wait until the children had grown up to their full years, but commanded the midwives to kill them as soon as they were born. This was a cruel act in him, but do so with your sins, and it shall be a merciful act for your soul. That which Pharaoh did in horrible cruelty, you must do in good prudence against your sins: kill them when they are first born. And there are three pressing reasons why you must do so.

<margin>Resist the beginnings; the medicine is prepared too late when the evils have grown strong through long delays. <note>original: "Principiis obsta, sero Medicina paratur; tum mala per longas invaluere moras." — A famous quote from Ovid's *Remedia Amoris*.</note></margin>

1. Because if you resist the impulses while they are merely impulses, you shall be assured that the suggestions and incitements of the devil will not pursue you alongside the stirrings of the flesh. Just take this test: if you have an impulse toward sin in your nature and you consent to it, then the devil will join himself to your corruption to bring you to that sin again. The devil does not know the stirrings toward sin that are in your heart; but when you follow such stirrings—for instance, if you are tempted to lust and you give yourself over to it—then the devil knows by this what impulse was in your heart and how you loved that sin. And so he will be ready to tempt you to commit that sin again. Resist the impulses, then, while they are what they are, and by this means, you shall prevent the devil from adding his incitements to the sinful stirrings of your heart.

2. If you do not resist the impulses while they are impulses, there will be a more eager and violent inclination toward sin in your nature than there was before. Working out a sin is not a way to make a sinful impulse stop or to suppress it, but rather to make it grow. It is like oil thrown into a fire to make it burn all the more. The means, then, to extinguish sinful impulses is to resist them while they are such. In philosophy, it is said that actions strengthen habits. If someone has a habit (the Latin-speakers call it a *habitus*) of some virtue, if he practices that virtue, he makes the habit all the stronger. So it is also with sin: working out a sin creates a greater inclination toward it. Therefore, it is necessary that you bring the impulses of sin under control, so that they do not lead you further into sinful actions. For whenever sinful suggestions come together with sinful inclinations, the inclination brings forth consent, and consent brings forth the action, and the action brings forth persistence in sin. Thereafter comes delight, then carelessness, and finally a mocking contempt for all reproof and means of improvement.

<margin>Habit is acquired by actions; actions perfect the habit. <note>original: "Habitus acquiritur actibus: actum consummant habitum."</note></margin>

3. If you do not bring sin under control in its early impulses, it will be much harder for you to suppress the corruption. If a house is on fire, and you can...

# Flesh and Spirit.

If one keeps the fire inside, there is no danger of a great conflagration; but if it breaks out into the open air and the wind catches it, then it will burn exceedingly. So it will be with you regarding your sin: if you do not suppress it when it first stirs, it will be difficult for you to submerge it afterward. Take medicine to prevent sickness; the well-being of body and soul is more easily maintained in good order than restored. An ignored ulcer grows into a cancer as one part after another is corrupted, until there is no health left in the flesh.

<margin>Proverbs 5:8.</margin>
Secondly, remove all external opportunities <note>The author uses "gelegentheden," referring to the "occasions of sin"—external circumstances that make sinning easier.</note> for that sin toward which you feel an impulse to commit, whatever kind of sin it may be. Suppose it is pride: then do not wear those clothes which might give you an opportunity for pride. If it is drunkenness, keep yourself from evil company. If it is impurity, do not approach the door of the harlot; carefully shun the opportunities for sin. In this,
<margin>Genesis 39:10.</margin>
one must follow the example of Joseph. It is written of him that when his master’s wife spoke to him day after day, he did not listen to her, to lie by her or to be with her; he stayed out of her sight as much as he could. And this is the counsel
<margin>Exodus 23:7.</margin>
and the command of the Lord: stay far from false matters. The opportunities for sin are like the stimulators of a corrupted nature; otherwise, what would be the reason that a person not thinking of sin, when presented with an opportunity, would feel an impulse to commit it? Therefore, do not be bold in venturing into the opportunities for sin, and when you are moved toward any sin, shun all outward occasions for it. A certain theologian compares people who dare to venture into the opportunities for sin to those who pray to God that they may not be burned, and yet insist on sticking their fingers into the candle. You who pray against the stirrings of sin, take care also that 
<margin>1 Thessalonians 5:22; Jude verse 2.</margin>
you abstain from the opportunities for sin. The children of God must abstain from every appearance of evil, and hate even the garment spotted by the
<margin>Numbers 6:3, 4.</margin>
flesh. The Nazirites <note>A group in ancient Israel consecrated to God who took specific vows of abstinence.</note> had not only to separate themselves from wine, but were not even allowed to touch the skins of the grapes.

<margin>3rd Rule.</margin>
Thirdly, work to disarm the flesh. Just as the godly have their weapons, which are listed by name in the sixth chapter of the Letter to the Ephesians, so also the flesh has armor to make itself strong. It is armed with power—strive then to conquer it; it is armed with cunning and with manifold temptations to sin. Work well to disarm the flesh of all its pretenses and crafty tricks.
<margin>1 Samuel 13:19.</margin>
In this case, you must deal with sin just as the Philistines dealt with the Israelites. Fearing that the Israelites would take up war against them, the Philistines used this craftiness: they would not allow any iron weapons to be found among them, nor even a blacksmith to be in Israel to make those weapons. Do as the Philistines did: dis-

<column-break/>

arm sin; take away every opportunity which the corrupt nature might have to
<margin>Jeremiah 35:9.</margin>
work transgression in you. You must do as the Rechabites <note>A biblical family known for their strict obedience to their ancestor’s command to never drink wine.</note> did, who were commanded to drink no wine; they would not break this command for any enticement or temptation. Disarm sin by taking away its opportunities.

<margin>4th Rule.</margin>
Fourthly, resist the evil impulses rather than arguing with them. It is the folly of many that they wish to argue with the temptations of sin, yet there has never been anyone who took counsel with "flesh and blood" <note>A biblical idiom for human nature or worldly wisdom as opposed to divine revelation.</note> who was not eventually overcome by it. Regard the flesh as your enemy, but never as your advisor. The flesh is a great "thinker"—it has such cunning entanglements and crafty tricks to lead a person into sin. Therefore, do not argue with it, otherwise you will argue with the flesh just as our first ancestors did with the devil, who, after they had argued, fell into eating the forbidden fruit. The flesh will tell you, "this is a profitable sin for you," or "the other is notable and pleasant." Therefore, beware of sin and resist the flesh rather than arguing with it.

<margin>Fifth Rule.</margin>
Fifthly, devote yourself often to the mortification <note>original: "doodinghen," meaning to put to death or deaden the power of sinful desires.</note> of the "old man" <note>A theological term for the unregenerate, sinful human nature.</note> and to the exercise of those duties which serve that end; this will be a special means to preserve you. I will point out those duties to you for that purpose: namely, spiritual alertness, prayer, and fasting. Two of these duties were prescribed together by our Savior: "Watch and
<margin>Matthew 26:41.</margin>
pray," He says, "so that you do not fall into temptation." The flesh will always assault you, and so will the devil. Because of your flesh, we have need to constantly watch and pray. The war between the flesh and the spirit is an irreconcilable war, 
an implacable war. <note>original Greek: "polemos aspondos," literally a war without a truce.</note> Always be watching
<margin>Latin: "I had asked for chastity before (O God) and had said give me chastity and continence but not yet. For I feared lest you might quickly hear me and quickly heal me from the disease of lust, which I preferred to be satisfied than extinguished." Augustine's Confessions, Book 8, chapter 7.</margin>
against the opportunities for sin. Watch over the outward senses of your body and over the inward powers of your understanding; be much in prayer so that the sinful impulses may be suppressed and brought under. And do not pray as Augustine did, who confessed that before his conversion, he prayed by the light of his natural conscience against wantonness and impurity and the sins of his youth, but feared that God would actually hear his prayer; do not you pray so. Also add fasting to the duty of prayer, which Paul had as a habit. "I discipline my body," he says, "and bring it into subjection," namely, the corrupt nature. By "the body," one should not understand the physical body—like those who cause their bodies pain and torment through weeping, fasting, and gestures—but the "body of death" and the sinful workings of the corrupt nature, which he subdued through fasting, prayer, and alertness. A little care cannot accomplish this; we
<margin>1 Corinthians 9:27.</margin>
must be as alert as the wrestlers and fencers, who are very ready to throw their enemy down before them.

# The Battle Between

what Christ said to the Devil, that you must say to the Devil and your flesh: "It is written," He said. Position yourself with the written Word against the Devil and your own heart. Be so well-versed in God's Word that no temptation can come before you for which you cannot bring proof-arguments from the Word against it. We ought to use the sword of the Spirit—which is the Word of God—very diligently, and thrust it into the entrails of the sinful flesh. And if you enter this path in this matter, you would be less tormented by a tempting Devil and a corrupt heart than you are now.

<margin>Utility for consolation.</margin>
The use which I shall make of what you have heard shall be for the comfort of faint-hearted consciences. It seems to me I hear many godly people saying: "O woe is me, I have a felt experience in my own soul that my heart has all those evil qualities which you have named, and my soul also gives me witness that I use the means which you prescribe: I shun all opportunity for sin, I watch and pray against sin, and yet, God knows, I cannot subdue that filthy heart." To those who make this complaint in the uprightness of their heart and the feeling of their sins, I have words of consolation to speak here.

1. You must never expect a holy eradication <note>The author uses "uytroepinge," literally a rooting out or total elimination.</note> of the corruption of your nature; no, as long as you live here, you shall only have a partial suppression. The corrupt nature will be in you; yet, just as it is said of those beasts by the Prophet
<margin>Daniel 7:12.</margin>
Daniel: "Their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time." So also the dominion of sin is taken away—sin shall not rule over you—but the life of sin remains; the body of death shall live in us as long as we live in the body. The corrupt nature will live in you, although it shall not reign in you, just like that tree
<margin>Daniel 4:24, 27.</margin>
of which it stands in Daniel, whose branches were chopped off, and yet the stump remained in the earth. It may be that you prune away the actual evil, but remember that the root will remain; just as one sees in the ground-ivy <note>original: "aert-veyle." A common 17th-century metaphor where sin is compared to ivy on a stone wall; the ivy's roots are so deep that the wall must be demolished to truly remove it.</note> which grows on a wall, that it cannot be uprooted until the wall is thrown down; so also sin (which is like ivy in the wall) cannot be cast out of your nature until your body is cast down. We indeed have a promise for the children of God that sin shall not have dominion in them, but nowhere is it written that sin shall not be in them as long as they have their being.

2. There is a great difference between the corrupt movements of your nature to pursue sin, and the fulfilling of the lusts of the flesh. I know well that there is none among us all who does not in some things accept the movements of the flesh, but not all fulfill the lusts of the flesh. It may be that you follow the movement to which your sinful heart stirs you, and yet do not fulfill the movements of sin. The Scripture gives us this distinction: "And make
<margin>Romans 13:14.</margin>
no provision for the flesh, to fulfill its lusts." The godly may come to commit the lusts of the

<column-break/>

flesh, but they do not pursue them <note>The author distinguishes between falling into a sin and "making provision" or planning for it.</note>; you do not provide for sin like a man provides for his household, which he wishes to keep alive; you do not provide the flesh with food. Therefore support your heart with comfort: although sin be in you, you shall nonetheless not perish because of it.

3. You who have employed all means and yet find that the flesh overwhelms the Spirit, notice that strong and powerful movements toward sin do not always indicate the strength of sin, but rather the weakness of the same, and that sin is decreasing rather than being in its full strength. It is observed that things that are dying also struggle and wrestle with great strength; a bird, a weak creature—if you pull off its head, with what strength will it sprawl? This is no sign that the bird is gaining strength, but that its strength is passing away. So it may be with you; you have strong movements toward sin, but sin may now be playing its last game. The lusts are said in Scripture to be crucified; now it is with crucified sin as it was with the godless and impenitent thief—he was bound and nailed by hands and feet, and yet he raved and raged; so it is also when lust dies: it raves and rages all the more. This is also seen when one takes medicine; at first, it will make the person sicker than the sickness itself did, not because the person is then worse off, but only because the medicine spreads itself through his whole body. So it may be with you; when sins wrestle with you, God gives you a medicine, and though it be strong, God will nonetheless make it serve in the end for the purging out of evil humors <note>In 17th-century medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament.</note> from your soul.

4. If the corrupt movements in your soul are strong, then bend the strength of your heart in prayer to God for the countering of these corruptions. If a maiden who was being raped did not cry out, she was
<margin>Deuteronomy 22:24, 27.</margin>
considered by the Law to be guilty and consenting. The more the Devil and your corruptions tempt you, the more earnestly you must pray to God and cry for help. Complain about those manifold assaults which the corrupt nature and the Devil make upon you; and by fleeing to God for help and assistance, your soul shall never perish because of your misdeeds.

<margin>15th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry in London, December 29, 1650. 6th Question.</margin>
Now I proceed to the last question, which is this: How can one discern when the movements toward sin come from the flesh, or when they come from the Devil alone, and are thus entirely devilish? Before I answer this question, I shall first show what use it has; secondly, I shall set forth some propositions regarding it; and then I shall handle the question itself. 

This question has a threefold use.

->**Flesh and Spirit.**<-

E 2

1. It is necessary that one understands these things, because when the unregenerate <note>Those who have not experienced a spiritual rebirth or conversion.</note> are tempted to sin, they lay all the guilt upon the Devil, and none upon their own heart. These people, placing all their sins on the Devil's account <note>The original uses "sterf-stock," referring to a tally stick used for debts; here it means a scapegoat for one's own faults.</note>, do not <margin>Gen. 3:13.</margin> give the Devil his due. So Eve laid the guilt on the Serpent: "The Serpent deceived me, and I ate." But David was of another mind; for when he was tempted and stirred up to sin by numbering the people, and <margin>2 Sam. 24:17.</margin> that through Satan, he nonetheless confessed: "Behold, I, even I have sinned, and I, I have acted wickedly." It is in the nature of men, when they are tempted to sin and commit it, to blame the Devil for it; therefore it is highly necessary to know what the distinction is. For one must not do the Devil an injustice, but as the English say, "give the Devil his due": for sometimes he is merely a bystander and does not work in our sins.

2. The untangling of this question is necessary because the reborn (especially those who are troubled in their conscience) often attribute those sins to themselves which ought rightly to be laid upon the Devil; such as when the Devil gives them blasphemous thoughts against which human nature rebels; nonetheless, they want to take the blame themselves. Therefore, just as the ungodly on one side falsely force their sin upon the Devil, so also the godly on the other side wrongly accuse themselves.

3. Because, if the impulses to sin truly come only from the Devil, then they are indeed our misery, but not our sins, provided we do not accept and consent to them. The Devil lays his bait at our doors, and many times he would like to break into the soul like a thief, but through faith he is resisted; and if the impulses to sin are merely *in* us <note>Meaning they are external suggestions rather than internal desires.</note>, then they are not our sins. This is only to be tempted to sin, but to follow the temptation, that is sin. But the evil impulses coming from the corrupt nature—even though you do not consent to them—those first movements of the heart toward sin are sinful in their essence, because they come from an evil nature which is within; evil movements rising out of evil hearts are fruits which come from an evil root, and therefore we must weep over them. For these reasons, it is necessary to answer this question; but before I come to that, remember these warnings:

1. That whether the temptations come from the Devil or from the corrupt nature, you must nonetheless be certain that they are both sinful, and therefore both must be rejected.

2. That we must not be so much concerned with distinguishing these impulses as with resisting them; for if someone is more precise in making the distinction than diligent in resisting them, it is merely curiosity and not sincerity.

3. There is a perceptible distinction between the impulses to sin which come from the Devil and those which come from the corrupt nature, and yet it is difficult to show wherein the precise

<column-break/>

part of the distinction lies. This is the reason which a certain modern theologian gives: because the Scriptures attribute those temptations, which are said in Scripture to come from the Devil, to the hearts of men. Thus, in the fifth chapter of Acts, at the third verse, the lie of Ananias is laid upon the Devil, and at the fifth verse, upon the man himself.

But to answer the question: these are the Signs from which you can distinguish the impulses to sin coming from the flesh from the impulses which come from the Devil.

<margin>1st Sign</margin> Firstly, the impulses of Satan toward sin are commonly contrary to the light of nature; they are unnatural sins against which even the light of nature struggles. Therefore, theologians teach that the temptation to blaspheme God and to destroy oneself comes from Satan, because they are unnatural. These impulses do not arise primarily from the flesh, but from the Devil, because they are contrary to nature, and therefore they do not come from nature. Temptations to unnatural wickedness are from Satan; their horribleness shows from whence they come. For to think evil of God is entirely devilish, because it is against the light of nature to have even any slight or unseemly thoughts <margin>Job 1:16</margin> of God. It is a good observation concerning what is written of Job, that "the fire of God fell from heaven" and ignited among Job's sheep. Why did the Devil not rob him of his sheep in the same way as he had taken his other cattle—namely, through the Chaldeans and Sabeans, who took them away? This reason is given: the Devil did not know how he might bring Job to blaspheme God, and therefore he caused a fire to come from heaven to consume his sheep, so that Job would behold it as coming immediately from God, and so blaspheme Him. Therefore, the primary instrument of such temptations which stir up God's people to blasphemy is Satan. Nevertheless, there is in the nature of man the seed of blasphemy just as of all other sins; there is in human nature a susceptibility and a fit disposition for the blasphemous temptations of the Devil. Nonetheless, the first suggestion of them usually comes from the Devil; therefore one reads that when Judas went to betray Christ, it says that <margin>Luke 22:3.</margin> the Devil entered into him. The impulse came from the Devil because it was an unnatural sin. For that a servant should betray a Master, and a good Master, is reckoned an unnatural sin; and therefore it is laid upon the Devil. Although Judas was guilty because he accepted this temptation, the Scripture nonetheless attributes it to the Devil as being the first mover to that unnatural sin. Even so, the seeds of unnatural sins are in human nature. And so the Apostle lays the unnatural sins of the Heathen upon the <margin>Rom. 1:24.</margin> lusts of their own hearts.

<margin>2nd Sign.</margin> Secondly, the impulses of the Devil are commonly toward gross sins which have no place in the inclinations and passions of the heart. The reason is this: because although the seed of gross sins is in nature,

# Struggle between

nevertheless, men are by nature more inclined toward spiritual and inward sins: nature gives man inward sins, and the Devil gives gross and outward sins. And this is the great misery of man: that the Devil does not tempt him to those sins to which his corrupt nature already tempts him. <margin>Acts 5, verse 3.</margin> The lie of Ananias is blamed on the Devil: "Why has Satan filled your heart?" <margin>Matthew 5:37.</margin> And so sinful swearing is attributed to the Devil, as being a great sin. It is the mark of the Devil to drive men toward great, outward sins; but corrupt nature always entices one to those sins which most correspond with your own corrupt inclinations, such as self-love, vain glory, worldly desires, spiritual pride <note>The original "geestelijcke hovaerdye" refers to a sense of moral superiority or pride in one's religious standing.</note>, fleshly confidence, evil intent, idle thoughts, and the like. These are swarms of inward desires which proceed from your corrupt nature, and toward these your nature inclines.

<margin>3rd Sign.</margin>
Thirdly: the temptations of Satan are commonly accompanied by much terror and fear when they are suggested. When a temptation attacks someone so strongly that it makes them tremble and a great terror comes over them, it is proof that it comes from the Devil. The reason is this: because nature only stirs one toward those sins which are most pleasant to nature. Nature does not cause a "fire" <note>An internal agitation or burning distress.</note> in the conscience.

<margin>4th Sign.</margin>
Fourthly: Satan's temptations usually arrive when a suitable object and opportunity to commit a sin is present. Just as when someone is troubled in their mind and sees water, the Devil tempts them to drown themselves; or when he sees a knife lying there, he tempts him to take his own life. Or when someone sees an object of beauty before them, they are then tempted toward impurity—see, such temptations commonly come from the Devil. It is true, the Devil can disturb the imagination even when no object is present, but that happens seldom. We also have examples in Scripture of those who, when the opportunities for sin arose, were tempted toward them. <margin>Genesis 3:6.</margin> Eve, when she saw that the tree was good for food and that it was a delight to the eyes—there was the object, and from that came the Devil's temptation; she took of its fruit and ate. And thus it was with David; <margin>2 Samuel 11, verse 2.</margin> when he fell into the sin of impurity; when he walked upon the roof of his house, he thought of nothing less than becoming unclean; but being on the roof and seeing Bathsheba naked, the Devil tempted him to it, and then his nature conspired with the temptation, as the opportunity had already presented itself. However, it is commonly the movements of corrupt nature when no opportunity is present. Therefore, if someone has worldly and covetous thoughts while in their bed, when no opportunity is given, then this comes from the corruption of their own heart. And such are also all those speculations and contemplations of the mind regarding evil; they come solely from your own heart. And I must tell you this: that although the Devil may be the first in the opportunities and temptations to sin, nevertheless, if you afterwards consent to the opportunity or temptation,

<column-break/>

then you must lay the guilt more upon your own heart than upon the Devil.

<margin>5th Sign.</margin>
Fifthly: movements toward sin that come from Satan usually overtake a person in a moment; before that point in time that such movements were suggested, it was never even thought of. Such movements come from the Devil; they break out suddenly (as Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch.</note> says) like lightning into a house. So we read in Luke 22:31 regarding Peter: "Simon, Simon," (says Christ) "Satan has greatly desired to sift you." What is meant by this? Nothing other than that temptation with which the Devil tempted Peter to deny his Lord and Master. It is indeed true that Peter's heart was also to blame, for he had the seed of that sin within him; nonetheless, Scripture lays it upon the Devil as being the first tempter, because Peter had not even thought of such a thing a moment before. But when he came to warm himself in the Hall of the High Priest, <margin>Luke 22:55.</margin> the Devil tempted him to it, and then Peter was overtaken by it. So, those temptations which fall into someone's mind without them having thought of them beforehand have their origin from the Devil; but movements toward sin which come from corrupt nature are more deliberate and lasting. They also do not arrive with such violence as the temptations of the Devil; and the reason is because they agree more with one's nature, and thus cause less agitation in the minds of men.

<margin>First Use.</margin>
This must first serve us as a warning. You must know that, although there are these distinctions between the movements toward sin that proceed from the Devil and from corrupt nature, nevertheless no sin is committed in the world which could not happen even if there were no Devil to tempt, and even if he stood by merely as a spectator. In the human heart is the seed of all sin; and therefore our Savior says: <margin>Matthew 15:19.</margin> "Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies." Our Savior speaks of these in the plural number to show that there are all kinds of sins in the human heart, and all sins in all their degrees. If God but once left nature to itself, how quickly would you run into all kinds of evil.

<margin>2nd Warning.</margin>
Know also, that in all evil works there is commonly a concurrence <term>concurrence|a coming together or cooperation</term> between Satan and the flesh. For instance, suppose the flesh begins to tempt; the Devil then helps that temptation. And if the Devil tempts, the flesh springs upon the temptation and consents to it. So that, although there is a distinction between the temptations, there is nonetheless commonly a working-together of the flesh and the Devil; so that if corrupt nature begins, the Devil will help the attack, and if the Devil begins, corrupt nature will join in and fulfill it. Corruption is the tide, and temptation is the wind, to make the stream of the sinful course run all the more strongly.

<margin>3rd Warning.</margin>
Although it may be true that, having examined yourself, you may find that many movements toward sin, such as unnatural...

# The Conflict Between #

<margin>Fourth application.</margin>
Finally / you who are <term>reborn<note>original: "weder-gebooren." In 17th-century theology, this refers to the spiritual rebirth or "regeneration" of a believer.</note></term> / remember that you carry flesh and blood within you / you have the flesh desiring against the Spirit / there is a contradiction in your spirit against God’s Holy Spirit: go then and bewail that opposition and the ugliness of your heart / and say like Rebecca, when she had two children in her womb / who struggled against each other / *Why am I thus?* You have an Esau and a Jacob within you / namely nature and grace / evil impulses wrestling against good impulses; go to God the Lord / and say / *why am I thus?* and with Paul; *O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?*

->Galatians 5, verse 17.<-

> For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary to one another; so that you do not do the things that you would.

<margin>16th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry <note>original: "Laurentii Jurii." A prominent Anglican church in the City of London.</note> within London, December 29, 1650.</margin>
I proceed now to the second part of the Conflict / namely the desire of the Spirit against the flesh; the flesh made the first attack / because there was flesh in us before there was Spirit / but the Spirit takes up the War / and just as the flesh desires against the Spirit / so the Spirit desires against the flesh.

<margin>Ephesians 6:12 explained.</margin>
Before I draw the Doctrine from this / I shall open a passage of Scripture to you / which here seems to speak to the contrary / and it is Ephesians 6, verse 12, where it stands / *That we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.* This passage can be brought into agreement with our text in two ways.

Firstly / when the Apostle says / *we wrestle not against flesh and blood / but against principalities and powers* / the words can be understood / not simply and absolutely / but in comparison; and if you take "flesh and blood" there to mean corrupt nature / this shall be the meaning / that we do not only have the conflict against flesh and blood / that is / the corrupt nature within us / but we also have the Devil without us / against whom we must be stirred up. But a better reconciliation of that passage with our Text is this. It says in the Text / that we wage war against the flesh: now although the same word is used in both places / it is nevertheless in a different sense / and so that you might know how it is taken in both places / note these three meanings of the word.

1. "Flesh and blood" is sometimes taken for the corrupt nature / and so must be understood what Christ says / *flesh and blood has not revealed this unto you.*
<margin>Matthew 16:17.</margin>

2. "Flesh and blood" is taken for the natural body of man / as in 1 Corinthians 15, verse 50. *Flesh and blood cannot inherit the Kingdom of God*, that is / as we now live in the world / for as much as our bodies are now natural / corruptible, and mortal / so they cannot receive the glory and blessedness of Heaven.

3. "Flesh and blood" is in the Scripture

<column-break/>

taken for godless men / as in Ephesians 6, verse 12. *We wrestle not against flesh and blood*, that is / not so much against the godless / as against the Devil / the ruler of the darkness of this world / and thus you have the reconciliation of these passages. The Spirit desires against the flesh / that is / the movements and workings of God’s Spirit set themselves against the movements toward sin of the corrupt nature. Take then from this the following Doctrine.
<margin>
Isaiah 56:3.
16:23.
Jeremiah 25:31.
Zechariah 2:13.
</margin>

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That the movements and workings of God’s Spirit in the reborn, wage War and conflict against the movements of sin, which come from the corrupt nature.

In handling this Doctrine / I shall do these four things.
1. I shall show you what the nature of this conflict is.
2. In what it consists.
3. How you might distinguish this conflict / which the Spirit has against the movements of sin / from that conflict against sin / which can be found in someone's natural Conscience.
4. I shall give you the rules regarding this conflict.

->What is this conflict?<-

I answer first by way of narrowing it down; There are four kinds of conflict against sin / which are not the conflict of the Spirit.

Firstly / there can be a conflict of one sin against another sin / one corruption may fight against another / and a lesser sin can often be overcome by a greater / and this is frequently found in natural men: as for example / pride and greed; a proud man must have something / wherewith he shall feed his pride / and because he is proud he must be in fine company / and go dressed handsomely and expensively; but greed, being a contrary fault / shall perhaps set itself against the pride / and rebuke it. So shall the irregular love of the world say to a spendthrift / who wastes his days in gambling and playing / that he gives out too much money; so can one corruption fight against the other / and it shall not therefore be the conflict of the Spirit against sin.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly / there can be a conflict against sin in the natural inclinations / in which nature seeks the preservation of itself. ## Galatians 5, verse 17.

> For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other; so that you do not do the things that you would.

<margin>16th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry in London, December 29, 1650. <note>original: "Laurentii Jurii." This refers to the historic church of St. Lawrence Jewry, known for its influential lectures during the Puritan era.</note></margin>
I proceed now to the second part of the Struggle: namely, the desiring of the Spirit against the flesh. The flesh made the first attack, because in us there was flesh before there was Spirit; but the Spirit takes up the War, and just as the flesh desires against the Spirit, so the Spirit desires against the flesh. 
Before I draw the Doctrine from this, I shall open to you a passage of Scripture which seems to contradict this, which is Ephesians 6:12, where it says: 
<margin>Eph. 6:12 explained.</margin>
That we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. This passage can be reconciled with our text in two ways. 
First, when the Apostle says, "we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers," the words can be understood not simply and absolutely, but in comparison. And if you take "flesh and blood" there to mean the corrupt nature, the meaning will be that we do not *only* struggle against flesh and blood—that is, the corrupt nature within us—but we also have the Devil outside of us, against whom we must be stirred up. 
But a better reconciliation of that passage with the Text is this: The Text says that we wage war against the flesh; now, although the same word is used in both places, it is nonetheless used in a different sense. And so that you might know how it is taken in both places, notice these three meanings of the word: 
1. "Flesh and blood" is sometimes taken for the corrupt nature, and so it must be understood when Christ says, "flesh and blood
<margin>Matt. 16:17.</margin>
has not revealed this to you." 
2. "Flesh and blood" is taken for the natural body of man, as in 1 Corinthians 15:50: "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the Kingdom of God," that is, as we now live in the world, because our bodies are now natural, corruptible, and mortal, they cannot receive the glory and blessedness of Heaven. 
3. "Flesh and blood" is taken in Scripture for 

<column-break/>

godless people, as in Ephesians 6:12. 
<margin>Isa. 56:3, 16:23; Jer. 25:31; Zech. 2:13.</margin>
"We wrestle not against flesh and blood," that is, not so much against godless men as against the Devil, the ruler of the darkness of this world; and thus you have the reconciliation of these passages. The Spirit desires against the flesh—that is, the movements and workings of God’s Spirit set themselves against the movements toward sin of the corrupt nature. Take then from this the following Doctrine. 

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That the movements and workings of God’s Spirit in the reborn wage war and struggle against the movements of sin which come from the corrupt nature. 
In handling this Doctrine, I shall do these four things: 
1. I shall show you what the nature of this struggle is. 
2. Wherein it consists. 
3. How you might distinguish this struggle, which the Spirit has against the movements of sin, from that struggle against sin which can be found in someone's natural Conscience. 
4. I shall give you the rules concerning this struggle. 

### What is this struggle?

I answer first by way of distinction; there are three kinds of struggle against sin which are *not* the struggle of the Spirit. 
First, there can be a struggle of one sin against another sin; one corruption may fight against another, and a smaller sin may at that time be overcome by a greater one; and this is often found in natural men. As for example: pride and greed. A proud person must have something with which to feed his pride, and because he is proud, he must be in fine company and go about in handsome and costly clothing; but greed, being an opposing fault, will perhaps set itself against the pride and rebuke it. So will the unregulated love of the world say to a drunkard, who spends his days in carousing and gaming, that he spends too much money. Thus one corruption can struggle against the other, and it will not therefore be the struggle of the Spirit against sin. 

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, there can be a struggle against sin in the natural inclinations, in which nature seeks the preservation of itself. Just as one sees in the irrational creatures, whom fear often holds back from that which their natural desire would otherwise reach for. A wolf would very much like to tear the sheep apart, but fear of the Shepherd restrains him. Such a struggle exists between anger and fear. Someone being disturbed is urged on by wrath to take revenge on the one with whom he is angry; but another passion (fear) says to him: "If you come to kill this man at whom you are angry, the Judges will lay their hands on you." This does not come entirely from the Spirit. 

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, there is a struggle which proceeds from a person’s natural disposition; some have such an excellent and courageous heart that they naturally struggle against certain faults. As Luther says of himself, that he was never tempted toward the sin of greed, because he had such a generou- <note>The word is cut off, continuing on the next page as "generous."</note>

### IV.
Fourthly, there is a struggle that arises from the light of reason and the natural conscience, which restrains and rebukes a person because of sin. The pagans, through the light of natural conscience, were able to see and reject sin; they considered it a vile thing for one to give themselves over to wicked and beastly desires. <margin>2. Question.</margin>
The second question is: in what does the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh consist?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
This struggle of the Spirit against the flesh has a twofold aspect: first, regarding sin, to prevent it; and second, regarding the good, to incite the soul toward it.

In relation to sin, the Spirit does these five things:
<margin>John 16 verse 8. Romans 7:7.</margin>
1. He enlightens a person and reveals to him sin that he never saw before. So says Paul: "I would not have known lust to be sin if the Law did not say, 'You shall not covet.'" God's Spirit revealed sin to Paul through the Law, and to discover a fire is the first step in opposing it.
2. The Spirit not only reveals sin but also resists the motions of sin that come from corrupt nature; the Spirit "desires against the flesh," that is, it sets itself against the workings of corrupt nature, as it says in our text.
3. The Spirit sets the conscience in motion, so that it rouses and rebukes the person for entertaining evil impulses and making his body a lodging-place for sin. "The Spirit convicts the world of sin."
<margin>John 16 verse 8.</margin>
4. The Spirit sanctifies the nature of man and washes him from the filthiness of sin. 1 Corinthians 6:11. Therefore the Spirit of Christ is called *the Holy Spirit* <note>original Greek: "αγιον πνευμα" (hagion pneuma)</note>: because the Spirit makes the hearts of God's people holy. The Spirit is not only Holy in Himself but is also the Author and worker of holiness in the hearts of believers.
<margin>Romans 8 verse 13.</margin>
5. The Spirit of God suppresses the motions of sin: He not only resists but also helps the person to kill the impulses of sin. "If you through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live," says the Apostle. And you have a promise regarding this in the verse preceding my text: that if you walk by the Spirit,

<column-break/>

you shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh. It does not say you shall not *do* the lusts, but you shall not *fulfill* them; they shall not have such supremacy over you as they do over the godless. Thus you see how the Spirit sets itself against the flesh regarding sin.

In relation to the good, the Spirit opposes the flesh in several ways:
1. By pointing out and revealing to the person that which is good. So the Lord promised through the Prophet: "Your ears shall hear the word of him who is behind you, saying: 'This is the way, walk in it.'" The Spirit reveals to man his way, his work, and his duty.
<margin>Isaiah 30:21.</margin>
2. Not only so, but the Spirit also stirs up holy motions and holy intentions, so that you might perform that duty. It not only shows you the way but also compels you to walk in it.
3. The Spirit helps a person in doing good when the flesh hinders it. "We do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself prays for us," and comes to the aid of our infirmities.
<margin>Romans 8:26. *Helps together* <note>original Greek: "συναντιλαμβάνεται" (synantilambanetai), meaning to take hold of a burden together with someone.</note></margin>
4. The Spirit deals out more and more grace to His people, by which they may be made capable of doing good: He gives a continual supply of help, and therefore one reads of "the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ." Thus you see in what the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh consists, both regarding sin and regarding the good.
<margin>Philippians 1:19.</margin>

There is a difference: 1. In the manner of this struggle. 2. In the extent of it. 3. In regard to the causes and principles from which this struggle arises. 4. In the duration. And 5. in regard to the outcome and the end of this struggle.

...the committing of sin is voluntary, but the opposition to it is forced. Conscience in an ungodly person is like the light of a candle to a thief; it shines constantly in his face while he is busy stealing. But in the godly, it is exactly the opposite: the committing of sin is against their will, as in Romans 7:19 <note>original: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do."</note>. The fight within them is a voluntary fight; they rejoice when the Spirit performs its office, and when grace in the renewed part of the soul suppresses the corruption of their hearts. The ungodly are said to be "willingly ignorant," but the Apostle says that the godly "desire to live honestly in all things."

<margin>Hebrews 13:18.</margin>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:4</margin>
Truly, an ungodly person does not fight gladly against corruption; his heart would rather be in the house of mirth, as the Wise Man says <note>Ecclesiastes 7:4 notes that "the heart of fools is in the house of mirth."</note>. He does not like his conscience to come and disturb him; he would gladly strangle his conscience, for he is unwilling to fight against the flesh. But a godly person is very willing; therefore we read that they sigh to be unburdened (for sin is the greatest burden); they lie under sin as under a heavy load and wish to lay it down.
<margin>2 Corinthians 5:4.</margin>

### II.

2. The struggle that exists in the ungodly is but a struggle in jest, like children playing together who want to wrestle and fight only out of sport, and not to do each other any harm; or like fencers who make many feints <note>original: "babbaden," likely referring to the flashy but harmless movements of stage-fencers.</note> and wish to give each other some clever blows, but have no intention of killing. It is not like a soldier who comes into the field with the intent to kill his enemy. But so it is with the reborn; in their struggle, they earnestly seek to kill sin, as the Apostle Paul says: "I do not fight as one beating the air, but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection." The words <term>I buffet my body</term> <note>original Greek: "ὑποπιάζω μου τὸ σῶμα" (hypopiazo mou to soma)</note> have a special emphasis; it is a metaphor taken from wrestlers who fought for their lives. The word actually means to beat someone black and blue, and to do them all the harm one can. Therefore Paul says: "I do not beat the air, but I earnestly strike down my body." "Those who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh," says the same Apostle; we also have a promise for the same: "that if you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live."

<margin>1 Corinthians 9:26, 27.</margin>
<margin>pummel/buffet: boxers are said to do this when they beat an opponent with fists or weighted gloves. <note>original Latin: "ὑποπιάζω, dicuntur pugiles, cum pugnis aut cæstibus Antagonistam obtundunt Paræus."</note></margin>
<margin>Galatians 5:24. <note>The text incorrectly cites 5:20.</note></margin>
<margin>Romans 8:13</margin>

### III.

3. The struggle coming from the natural conscience is a disorderly struggle, just like people fighting in a riot. But the reborn fight against sin like people in a military host <note>An organized army.</note>. The disorderliness of the fight of the unregenerate is evident in this: it is divided between different powers. An ungodly person has the will and the desire to commit this or that sin, for there is no reborn part in their will; but there may well be something in the understanding—and there often is—and therefore, although the ungodly would gladly practice one or another wickedness, their understanding nevertheless tells them that sin will not only bring them to shame here, but also damn them hereafter. Thus, the fight in the ungodly takes place between different faculties or powers, and is therefore disorderly. But the fight in the re-
<margin>I see the better things and approve them, but I follow the worse. <note>original Latin: "Video meliora, proboque, deteriora sequor." A famous quote by the poet Ovid, though attributed here to Seneca’s "Medea."</note></margin>

<column-break/>

-born is an orderly fight within the same power; not the will against the understanding, or the understanding against the will, but the will against the will, and the understanding against the understanding, and the affections against the affections—their renewed part wars against the unrenewed part. So also the memory, as far as it is converted, labors to remember holy truths and to thrust out the retention of evil. The reborn part sets itself against the unregenerate part; in the passions, the war is within the same faculty: the love they bear toward God and divine things wars against self-love, love of the world, and love of sin. These are the distinctions between the struggle of the reborn and the unregenerate against sin, regarding the manner of the struggle.

<margin>The second distinction. I.</margin>
Secondly, there is a distinction in respect to the extent of this struggle, and that in these three particular things:

1. The struggle of the natural conscience against sin reaches only to the sins of civil life—to outward sins—and not to the sins of nature, the inward sins. The reason is this: the natural conscience does not know that natural corruption is sin. Now, if nature has no eye to detect the sin, it shall also have no hand to fight against it. Paul, as long as he was unregenerate, did not know that lust was sin. Therefore, the natural conscience does not know original sin. We read of ungodly men in whom natural conscience went so far that it gnawed and rebuked them because of outward sins, like Cain because of his murder, Ahab because of his idolatry, Saul because of his cruelty, and Judas because of his treachery. But nature does not fight against nature; it may come to fight against the branch, but not against the root. But it is different with the conscience that is enlightened by God’s Spirit: it fights against the inward motions and workings of sin. Once Paul was converted, he complained of a "law of sin" that was in his members, and of a "body of death," and therefore he cries out: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from it?" The natural conscience may strike someone because of the sins of this life, but only a renewed conscience will rebuke a man for the sins of nature.
<margin>Romans 7:7.</margin>
<margin>Romans 7.</margin>

### II.

2. Just as the natural conscience does not reach to the sin of nature, so it does not reach to the nature of sin. This is my meaning: the natural conscience never struggles against the nature of sin, but only against the punishment of sin. It does not rebuke man for sin under this consideration—that it is against a holy God and a holy and pure Law—but the natural conscience only opposes the punishment of sin, and not the nature of sin. It is not because sin defiles the soul, but because sin destroys the soul; not because sin erases the image of God, but because sin causes men not to see the face of God; not because God hates sin, but because God punishes sin. But the reborn...

# Struggle between [Flesh and Spirit]

<margin>
Numbers 6:3, 4.
</margin>
The Nazarites <note>A group of Israelites consecrated to God who took specific vows of abstinence.</note>, who were permitted to drink no wine, were also forbidden to eat anything that was made from the grapevine; they were not allowed to eat the seeds or the skins of the grapes, so that no opportunity for sin would be given to them. And the Wise Man, showing the wickedness of adultery, <margin>Proverbs 5:5, 8.</margin> warns us not to approach the door of her house. It is not a sin to approach someone’s door; but because being at the door of a harlot may give opportunity, and stir up impure thoughts and lustful desires, we are therefore commanded not to approach her door. It is noteworthy that God did not want to be called *Baali*, but *Ishi*: there was <margin>Hosea 2:15.</margin> nothing evil in the word *Baali*, for according to common usage it means "My Husband," just as <margin>Isaiah 54:5.</margin> Isaiah 54:5 says, "Your maker is your husband," where the <margin>Baal: Lord or husband. <note>original Hebrew: בעל</note></margin> Hebrew says, "your *Baal*," that is, your Lord or husband. But this was forbidden so that the name of an idol, being common among them (for they commonly called their idols *Baalim*), would not entice them toward idolatry.

To this end, theologians commonly cite the passage in Deuteronomy 25:13, where it says: "You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, a large and a small." You might think that having two weights in a bag is no sin; you might say, "Though I have them in my house, I neither buy nor sell with them," and you might say, "They are only in my bag, and not on my scales." No; but God says: you shall not have them in your bag, so that the evil may not be a temptation to you to move them from your bag onto your scales.

<margin>
Leviticus 11:7, 8.
Isaiah 65:4.
</margin>
Likewise, the Israelites were forbidden to eat the meat of swine. Nevertheless, we read that the Lord accused the Israelites of two things: "They eat swine’s flesh," He says, "and the broth of abominable things is in their vessels." God had only forbidden the eating of swine’s flesh, and yet here He also rejects the broth. And why? It is because consuming the broth could be a temptation for them to also eat the meat. Therefore, take good care that you give no opportunity to the flesh, so that you are not ensnared by it.

<margin>Augustine, Confessions, Book 6, Chapter 8.</margin>
Augustine recounts an example of this. A certain Alypius was pulled by the rude and troublesome persistence of his friends to be present at the gladiatorial games <note>original: Scherm-speelen</note> of the Romans. But he resolved to keep his eyes closed the entire time, so that, although present in body, he would be absent in heart. But when a great shout went up at the fall of one of the fighters, he opened his eyes, and thus became an eager observer of that bloody and barbaric spectacle. Therefore, beware of placing yourself in situations of sin.

<margin>3rd Rule.</margin>
Thirdly, if you do not want the flesh to rule over the Spirit, then do not keep your thoughts and contemplations busy with sin. To frequently imagine and behold sin weakens the movements and workings of the Spirit, and it strengthens the movements of sin in your heart. The Prophet Ezekiel speaks of this in his 23rd chapter, verse 19: "She multiplied her harlotries, remembering the days of her youth."

<column-break/>

Bodily impurity is caused by beholding sin in the brain, and it is the way to harden the heart against the movements of the Spirit.

<margin>
4th Rule.
Resist the beginnings, etc. <note>original Latin: "Principijs obsta"</note>
</margin>
Fourthly, if you want the Spirit to have the upper hand, then resist and fight against your desires in good time; do not wait too long before you begin to fight. People often delay so long before they begin that they are already conquered before they come to the fight. Be ready then to oppose sin at its birth; do as Pharaoh did, who did not let the children of the Hebrews reach their full years, but killed them as soon as they were born. Deal thus with your sins.

<margin>
5th Rule.
That which is within prohibits that which is foreign. <note>original Latin: "Intus existens prohibet alienum"</note>
</margin>
Fifthly, cherish and maintain the movements of the Spirit; as often as you find them warning you against sin, let the movements of the Spirit remain within you, and they will keep the movements of the flesh outside.

<margin>
6th Rule.
Those who have deliberately defected... a war without a truce. <note>original: "Qui deliberate desciverunt πόλεμ. δοκός." The Greek refers to a "polemos aspondos," a war where no treaty is possible.</note>
</margin>
Sixthly, enter into no treaty with sin; for if you speak of a covenant with sin, then you have reason to doubt the victory. The flesh is a deadly enemy, and you must either kill or be killed. No peace agreement can be made between the flesh and the Spirit; this war is of such a nature that neither a peace treaty nor a ceasefire is to be expected in all the time of your life.

<margin>Galatians 1:16 compared with Acts 26:19.</margin>
It is a notable observation if you compare Galatians 1:16 with Acts 26:19. In the letter to the Galatians, we read the history of Paul’s conversion, and he says: "I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood," that is, with my corrupt nature, regarding what perils I might encounter or what danger I would have to endure. And in the Acts, where Paul recounts the same history to King Agrippa, he says: "I was not disobedient to that heavenly vision." To give us to understand—says a learned man—that debating and consulting with flesh and blood is a sort of disobedience to the heavenly vision. Even if you do not grant the flesh its will, it is nonetheless a sort of disobedience to consult with the flesh; and therefore, never enter into peace negotiations with your sin.

<margin>7th Rule.</margin>
Seventhly, resist sin universally, that is, every sin without exception, and do so in sincerity. If you hate the garment that is spotted by the flesh, then you shall also hate the flesh. Herod did much, but he did not leave his Herodias <note>Referring to King Herod's refusal to give up his unlawful wife, which led to the execution of John the Baptist.</note>.

# Flesh and Spirit.

<margin>Opposites can exist in a single subject when they are in a lower degree. <note>original Latin: "contraria possunt in subjecto gradu ffo [inferiori]."</note></margin>
...this conclusion: that contrary things can be bound together within the same subject. It is true that conflicting things cannot exist in the same subject in their most intense and highest degree, but they certainly can in a lesser and lower degree; and so it is here. The Apostle speaks of the **flesh** and the **spirit** in the same <term>reborn person<note>A "reborn" or "regenerate" person is a theological term for someone who has undergone a spiritual renewal through faith.</note></term>, and of their opposition to one another—not in the highest degree, but in a lower one. In the highest degree, they cannot coexist, because in Heaven there is perfect grace without sin, and in Hell there is nothing but sin without grace. But on earth, we are partly sinful and partly graced; therefore, these two opposites can very well coexist in a lesser degree within a person who has been born again. These two stand against one another; it is impossible to imagine a more bitter contrast or a more direct opposition in the world than that between the flesh and the spirit. There is no greater conflict between light and darkness, Heaven and Hell, fire and water, than between flesh and spirit. <term>Direct opposition<note>The original Dutch "Rechtstrijdicheyt" implies a fundamental, legal, or natural contrariety that cannot be settled.</note></term> is more than mere enmity, for enemies can be reconciled, but direct opposites never. Certainly, one opposite may cast out the other, but it can never be reconciled with it; water may extinguish fire, but it cannot be united with it; and light may drive away the darkness, but they can have no fellowship with one another. The opposition of the flesh against the spirit consists in this: that all the good which the spirit desires, the flesh does not desire; and to whatever evil the flesh incites, the spirit warns against. This is the opposition and the cause of the struggle within the reborn.

<margin>General Doctrine.</margin>
The Doctrine is this: That there is a two-sided and irreconcilable opposition between the flesh and the spirit—between nature and the gifts of grace—in the hearts of reborn men.

I call it a "two-sided" or mutual opposition because it is not a conflict from just one side; rather, the flesh stands against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. Furthermore, I call it an "irreconcilable" opposition because, although enemies may be reconciled, opposites can never come to an agreement.

In handling this chapter, I shall first prove the truth of this, and then I shall conclude with an application for the practice of <term>Godliness<note>Original: "Godtsalicheyt," referring to a life lived in devotion and piety.</note></term>.

<margin>1st Proof.</margin>
And first, this opposition is evident from the conflicting names given in the Scripture to the flesh and to the spirit. Thus, here in the text, corruption is called **flesh**, and grace is called **spirit**; corruption is called **darkness**, and grace is called **light** (Romans 13:12). One is called a **law of death**, but grace is called the **Law of the spirit of life** (Romans 8:2). Corruption is called the **defilement of the flesh** (2 Corinthians 7:1), but grace is the **purity of the spirit** (1 Timothy 4:12). So, by these conflicting names given to the flesh and Spirit, the opposition of both is made known.

<margin>2nd Proof.</margin>
Secondly, they are contrary in their cause and origin; for first, corruption is called the work of the devil;

<column-break/>

"and for this purpose the Son of God was revealed, that He might destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8). But grace is called the **work of God** (Philippians 1:6). Furthermore, corruption is called the **desire of the devil** (John 8:44), but grace is called the **fruit of the spirit** (Galatians 5:22). So they have a contrary origin. <margin>John 3:6.</margin> "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the spirit is spirit."

<margin>3rd Proof.</margin>
Thirdly, they have contrary workings: the flesh is said to desire against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. Because of this, sinning is called "walking in opposition to God" in the Scripture. <margin>Leviticus 26:21. <note>The source text cites chapter 28, but Leviticus has only 27 chapters; the author refers to the "walking contrary" passage in chapter 26.</note></margin> Sin causes a person to go against God, but the spirit draws a person to walk in God's ways. Sin is that *Delilah* who never leaves a person alone, but presses him and bothers him to follow the temptations toward sin.

<margin>4th Proof.</margin>
Fourthly, they are different in their end and outcome; the aim of the flesh is to bring the soul to damnation, but the movements and workings of the spirit are to keep the soul. We are commanded to abstain from fleshly lusts which wage war against the soul; the Apostle tells us that if we live according to the flesh, we shall <margin>Romans 8:13.</margin> die; but if we, through the spirit, put to death the deeds of the body, we shall live. Sin tends toward death, but grace toward eternal life. And therefore the same Apostle says: "the law of the spirit of life in <margin>Romans 8:2.</margin> Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and of death." Through these proofs, it appears most clearly that the flesh and the spirit stand against one another.

<margin>First Use.</margin>
This Doctrine serves, first, for our instruction. If these two stand so against each other, then let us—considering the opposition of the flesh against the spirit—learn these three things from it.

<margin>1.</margin>
1. Learn to marvel at the free grace and kindness of God, that notwithstanding this opposition of the flesh against the Spirit within you, God is nevertheless not provoked to anger and wrath by it, but rather to mercy and grace. Herein God's great love for His people is shown. God does to us as we would do to a person who has taken poison: namely, have compassion for him; even though we hate a toad, which has poison within itself. When God sees sin in His people, which torments them like poison in the body, even though they have such sinful natures that oppose grace so much, this nevertheless does not provoke wrath in God, but favor and compassion. It is worthy of note that some compare these two Scripture passages together: Genesis 6:5, 7 with Genesis 8:21. <margin>Genesis 6:5, 7: compared with Genesis 8 verse 21.</margin> In the same chapter of Genesis, it is written that the Lord saw that the <term>imagination<note>The Dutch "gedichtsel" refers to the intent, fabrications, or inner thoughts of the heart.</note></term> of man's heart was evil, and only evil, every day; and therefore God says, "I will destroy man from the face of the earth." There, God is provoked to wrath by their corrupt nature and its workings. But compare that passage with Chapter 8, verse 21, where you read that God will no longer curse the ground for man's sake, because the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth. This is a strange reason; someone might think that...

that therefore the opposition should occur; and yet God does not bring a curse upon the earth, but even adds a promise to it: as if he said; although I might destroy man, just as I did in the **Great Flood** <note>original: "Sond-vloet"</note>, I shall nevertheless not do it, even though the thoughts of his heart are evil every day; no, though his heart be so wicked, I will not destroy him. <margin>II.</margin>

Learn to marvel at the grace and mercy of God, that although there is such a contradiction in our nature against the Spirit, the Spirit nevertheless works converting grace irresistibly; that the Spirit overcomes man and throws down the "strongholds of nature" <margin>2 Corinthians 10:4.</margin> so that God's Spirit brings forth other contrary things out of these conflicting things <margin>2 Corinthians 4:6.</margin>; for so God does, commanding that the light should shine out of the darkness. Marvel that this spark of fire is not extinguished by this flood of corruption; that this opposition in your heart against grace does not come to destroy grace. If you are once in the state of grace, you shall always be in it; and therefore let this increase our wonder: Adam had perfect grace, yet no perseverance; but you have imperfect grace, and yet you are set so firmly in it that you shall not fall away.

<margin>Second use.</margin>
Secondly, this also serves for **humiliation**: and certainly all these teachings on the corruption of nature tend primarily to the humbling of that proud heart of man, who is degenerate and fallen from such a glorious state. Humble yourself, O man! although you have a principle of grace within you, there is nevertheless something in you which carries on an opposition against grace; you have an enemy within you against that seed of grace. *The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, and these are contrary to one another.* I speak now not only to the unregenerate, but also to the reborn: there are seven considerations which can move you to humility.

<margin>First motive for comfort.</margin>
First, observe that the flesh (and consequently also this opposition against grace) was in you earlier than grace: for it was in you before the Spirit of grace was in you. Theologians make the struggling of **Esau and Jacob** in the womb of Rebecca a <term>Symbol<note>In this context, an allegory or type representing a spiritual reality.</note></term> of corruption and grace in a reborn person; they jostled together in her womb; and it is noted that Esau, the evil son, was born first, and Jacob, the good son,

<column-break/>

last: by this is portrayed nature and grace, which struggle in the heart of a reborn person; but remember that sin is the elder of the two; you have the flesh earlier than the Spirit: nature is the elder brother. Indeed, as soon as there was a union between the soul and the body, sin was in the soul; and not only did you have sin before you could work grace, but even before you could use reason. This brings to mind what **Augustine** relates in his *Confessions* regarding a small child, who saw another child sucking his mother's breasts; and (he says) before the child could speak, I saw a jealous nature in it, for the <margin>I have seen and experienced a jealous child, not yet speaking, who grew pale with a bitter look toward his foster-brother. <note>original Latin: "Vidi ego, & expertus sum Zelantem, parvulum, nondum loquentem, pallidus amaro aspectu collactaneum. Aug. lib. 1. Conf. c. 7."</note></margin> child turned pale, looking bitterly at the other sucking his mother's breasts; and this (he says) made me think of my **original sin**. And truly, this is a great advantage for the flesh, that the flesh is in man first; just as, if two armies are to fight a set battle, the army that takes the field first has much advantage over the other which comes to the field last. Likewise, the flesh has the "sun and wind" against us; it has much advantage in this respect, that it is in you first; therefore, humble yourself.

<margin>Second motive.</margin>
Secondly, humble yourself upon this consideration: that the flesh, and the opposition of the <margin>Galatians 5:19, 20</margin> flesh against grace in your nature, is more abundant in you than the gifts of grace. It is not only earlier, but also in greater abundance; although a Christian has the Spirit, every reborn person nonetheless has more of the flesh; you have now only received the "first fruits" of the Spirit, but you have the entire harvest of sin and original corruption. In a reborn person, there are more swarms of lusts and unholy thoughts than there are divine thoughts; just as in every hedge there are more thorns than fruitful trees, so there are also in a spiritual man's heart more thorns of corruption than fruitful trees of grace. <margin>Third motive.</margin> And just as in every field there are more thistles and weeds than lilies and roses, so there is in every heart more of the corrupt nature than of true grace. Sin grows of itself out of nature, but grace comes only through God's cultivation. Corruption is natural, but grace is supernatural. <margin>Romans 6:19.</margin> To this end, what the Apostle says is noteworthy, exhorting us: *As you have yielded your members to be servants to uncleanness, and to iniquity unto iniquity, so now yield your members to be servants to righteousness <margin>Fourth motive.</margin> unto holiness.* Theologians note here that the Apostle, speaking of sin, expresses that servitude in three ways—namely, that our members have been servants to "uncleanness," and to "iniquity," "unto iniquity"—but when he speaks of grace and holiness, he only mentions two: namely "righteousness" and "holiness." This is to signify that there is a greater abundance of sin in you than gifts of grace. Search every faculty of a believer, and you shall find more sin than virtue therein. First, behold the understanding, and you shall find that there is more ignorance than knowledge in it; <margin>I only know this, that I know nothing. <note>original Latin: "Hoc tantum scio, me nihil scire." Attributed to Saint Jerome.</note></margin> and so **Jerome** confesses of himself, that he was ignorant of more truths than he knew. In the memory, there is more forgetfulness of good than
