->### Flesh and Spirit.<-

F 2

retention: you forget more good than you remember; the best person who lives does not retain as much from a sermon as they actually forget. And therefore the Apostle gives us this lesson: **That we must hold all the more to that which has been heard by us, so that we do not (like broken and leaking vessels) at any time flow away.** <note>Hebrews 2:1</note> For in the original text it says, *lest at any time we should drift away* <note>original Greek: "μὴ ποτὲ παρερρυῶμεν"</note>, which is a metaphor or borrowed speech taken from leaking vessels. Likewise, in the imagination, there are more sinful and impure thoughts than godly and holy contemplations. In the affections, there is more love for earthly things than for heavenly things: you are more grieved over oppression than over sin, more over the evil of punishment than the evil of the sin itself. If you examine all people well, you shall find more corruption of nature in them than holiness and gifts of grace; the Apostle points this out in that list of the works of the flesh and the fruits of the Spirit: where he lists seventeen sins and only nine gifts of grace. <note>Referencing Galatians 5:19-23.</note> Corruption is like the great **Goliath**, and grace like the little **David**: nevertheless, although corruption may be stronger and more abundant in us than grace, we shall in the end obtain the victory; though Goliath be stronger than David, all the <term>regenerate<note>Those who have experienced spiritual rebirth.</note></term> shall nevertheless, like David, have a good outcome and victory in the end.

<margin>Consider.</margin>
Thirdly, so that you might humble yourself, observe that this opposition of nature against grace works within you with great difficulty: if this opposition only showed itself now and then on some unusual occasion, it would not be so much; but this corruption works without becoming weary against grace. The gifts of grace and good motions are supernatural, and therefore they are sometimes difficult and wearisome to us, who are flesh and blood: but the corrupt motions toward sin are natural to man. Now those things which work out of nature also work tirelessly: Just as the Sea is never weary of flowing, nor the Sun of running its course, and just as fire is never weary of burning, so also is the corrupt nature never weary of fighting against the Holy Spirit. Our whole course and way to Heaven is uphill, and against the tide and the wind of corruptions and temptations.

<margin>Consider.</margin>
Fourthly, humble yourself on this ground: that this conflict of nature against grace shall be continuous, even until your dying day. It would be something if this opposition only came sometimes, and that then nature grew weary, or otherwise if it ceased at a certain age of a person's life; but this corruption will oppose the gifts of grace as long as you live. You may save yourself from <term>actual sin<note>Specific sinful acts, as opposed to the underlying sinful nature.</note></term>, but you can never rid your heart of this habitual corrupt nature. It is a notable saying of **Cyprian** <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage, a 3rd-century bishop and martyr.</note>: *It is more,* (he says) *to take away one sin than many sins;* by this he means that it is harder to take away this one sin of nature than many actual sins; for it may be that you are not moved now by those sins which you practiced a year ago, and that the sins which plague you now will not plague you hereafter: but the sin of your nature has troubled you last year and this year; and

<column-break/>

shall do so all the days of your life.
Just as ivy stretches so deep into the joints and the inside of a wall that, even though you prune the branches, you cannot uproot it unless you tear the wall down: so it is also with us; the root of our sins cannot be pulled out until God overthrows this wall, our body.

<margin>Leviticus 14:41, 45.</margin>
This was prefigured under the **Levitical Law**; the house which was infected with a "fretting leprosy" could not be made clean by scraping and throwing out the dust, and therefore God commanded that the house should be broken down and carried out of the City. The corruption of our nature is like that leprosy, which cannot be healed except by the breaking down of the wall of the house: so also nothing else can completely destroy and root out the "body of death" than the death of the body. This leprous house is an image of your impure body, and the scraping of the same is a symbol of your utmost endeavors to cleanse your heart from sin; and yet, through all this, the house could not be entirely cleansed until it was cast down; so also your body cannot be fully purified and sin rooted out until it be broken down and cast into the dust.

<margin>Luke 23:39</margin>
Keep in mind that a learned writer makes the unrepentant thief on the cross a symbol of the sin of our natures; when he was nailed to the cross and (as they say) his hands and feet were bound, he had only one member free, namely his tongue, and with that he began to rail against **Jesus Christ**; even so (says that Author) are our natures; when someone lies on their deathbed and can move neither hands nor feet, even then he has a nature set on fire by the flames of Hell, with which he sins against God. Oh, let this greatly humble us in the sight of God.

<margin>Fifth motive.</margin>
Fifthly, observe that although this opposition of your nature against grace is contrary to grace, it nevertheless corresponds very well with your nature. The corrupt nature will come to tempt people to those sins which are most pleasant to flesh and blood.

<margin>Matthew 4:1, 3.</margin>
The **Devil** spoke thus when He tempted Christ in the Wilderness while He was hungry: *command that these stones become bread*; this temptation suited the state of Christ very well: for he had fasted forty days and forty nights and was hungry; the devil fitted his temptation to that; and if the devil does so, how much more then will our natures fit the temptations to our state? Because a person's own heart knows better than the devil what corresponds with our inclinations. The devil (it is true) knows a person's inclination from their actions, and otherwise he cannot know it: But our natures are so corrupt that they will propose temptations which are most pleasing to flesh and blood, and will entice us to those sins to which we are most prone by habit or by natural inclination. And of this the Apostle **James** speaks, as I have noted above;

<margin>James 1:14. *drawn away and enticed* <note>original Greek: "ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος"</note>.</margin>
when he says, **That every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust and enticed.** It is a metaphor taken from fishermen, who [use] their bait...

Humble yourself then in this regard, because sin corresponds so closely with your corrupt nature.

<margin>
The sixth motive.
</margin>

Sixthly, humble yourself also for this: that your corrupt nature will carry you away to the committing of such sins of which you believed in your heart that you would never fall into them. You have an outstanding example of this in Hazael, to whom the Prophet Elisha foretold what evil he would do to the children of Israel; namely,

<margin>
2 Kings 8:12, 13.
</margin>

that he would set their strongholds on fire, and slay their young men with the sword, and dash their young children to pieces, and rip up their pregnant women; then he said: "But what is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" He could not believe it, and yet he did it—and even more so than the Prophet had told him. Here then is reason to humble oneself: there is such an evil seed in your nature which will stir you up to sin in ways you cannot imagine being there. Why else would Christ

<margin>
Luke 11:34. <note>The author likely intended Luke 21:34, which matches the quote provided.</note>

exhort his Disciples to take heed to themselves, lest at any time their hearts be weighed down with carousing and drunkenness, and the cares of this life? Dear heart, what danger was there that the poor Disciples would be overtaken by these sins? Yet nevertheless, Christ knew that they had to guard themselves against them; although they were excellent Disciples of Christ, they nonetheless had the seed of these evil sins in their natures. It is an observation

<margin>
Capel on Temptation. <note>Refers to Richard Capel (1586–1656), an English Puritan author of "Tentations: Their Nature, Danger, Cure."</note>
</margin>

of Master Capel, that a godly person will be tempted at one time or another before their death by the Devil or their own heart to break every commandment of the Law, and to doubt every article of the Faith; and therefore do not think that you are of such a well-disposed mind that you will never fall into error. And you who live holily, be not too confident nor too careless, thinking that you will never fall as this or that person has fallen. Remember that you indeed have just as evil a nature, and if God permitted the Devil, your own heart, and your inclinations to work together, you would fall into as evil a sin as anyone in the world has ever committed. There is such opposition in your nature against the gifts of grace that the sins of the world would seem light by comparison. Augustine had a fine saying when he saw someone fall into sin: *You today; I tomorrow.* <note>original Latin: "Tu hodie; ego cras"</note> You fall today, and I may fall tomorrow, if God does not help me.

<margin>
Seventh motive.
</margin>

Seventhly and lastly: Observe that this contrariety is a universal opposition. It would be somewhat excusable if there were only opposition against some and not all gifts of grace; or it would still be a little tolerable if there were only opposition in some parts and not in all. But since this opposition is present in every respect, how lamentable and intolerable this is: although you are godly, you nevertheless have this in common with the godless—that your entire body and soul are defiled. There is indeed a gift of grace

<column-break/>

in every part of your soul, but there is also sin likewise: there is ignorance in your understanding, forgetfulness in your memory, stubbornness in your will, disorder in your passions, hardness of your heart, and a lack of attentiveness in your conscience. It is nonetheless true that although every faculty may be defiled, every part of the godly person is nevertheless <term>regenerate<note>Spiritually reborn through divine grace.</note></term>. Corruption is in the soul just as the soul is in the body: the whole soul is in the whole body, and the whole soul is in every part of the body; so it is with original corruption: it is entirely in every person, and entirely in every part of a person. A certain writer notes that corruption is more in the soul than the soul is in the body: for although the whole soul is in the whole body and in every part thereof, it is nonetheless not in the same manner in every part of the body as it is in the whole body. It is in a more excellent way in the whole than in a part. But corrupt nature is more in the person than the soul is in the body; for although the soul is in the body, it nonetheless has specific uses in the members of the body: it is in the eye to see and not to work, and in the hand to work and not to see; it is in the ear to hear and not to walk, and in the foot to walk and not to hear. But sin is in the soul not for specific workings, but it is in every person and in every part of a person, stirring and enticing to every kind of evil. This is the universality of that corruption which is found in human nature, for which we have great reason to humble ourselves.

Having now explained the enmity and opposition that exists between the flesh and the Spirit, I shall answer two cases of conscience which pertain to this doctrine, and they are these:
1. If the flesh wages such a battle against grace, for what reasons does God allow such conflicting principles to remain in the hearts of the regenerate?
2. If there is such an opposition which can never be reconciled, to what end must a person struggle against the flesh?
Why does God allow there to be such opposition against grace even in the regenerate?

<margin>
Answered.
I.
</margin>

To this I answer these four things.
First: God does it for the clearer manifestation of His grace. God would have shown His goodness if man had never fallen, but having fallen, God shows him His grace. The end of our redemption is that God's grace and mercy should reign. And you can see a manifest sign here: namely, that God works grace in you, even though you have such opposition against it in your heart.

Though grace does not cast it out entirely, and though grace is fought against, it shall never be overthrown. Grace shall at last be the victor, even though it must fight continually while we are here in this life.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, it pleases God to leave such opposition against grace in the hearts of the reborn <note>original: "wedergeboornen," referring to those who have undergone a spiritual conversion</note>, so that they might esteem Jesus Christ all the more highly. If you had no principle within you that fought against grace, you would only wonder at God as a Creator; but having sin within you now, you come to see how greatly you have need of a Mediator. Adam had no need of a Savior in the state of innocence, but since you have now fallen through sin and have a root of enmity in your nature, that enmity cannot be taken away except through the power of a Savior who works sanctification in you. Only a Savior can free you from the guilt of this enmity, namely Jesus Christ; as the Apostle speaks: *I thank God through Jesus Christ, who has delivered me from the body of death.* <note>The author is quoting Romans 7:24–25.</note> He has delivered you from this guilt and enmity.
<margin>Romans 7:25.</margin>

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, the Lord leaves this corruption of nature in the hearts of His people in order to stir up a greater measure of deep humility <note>original: "berootmoedigingh"</note> within them. The duty of humility would have no place in us if God had not left the remnants of original sin in the hearts of the elect. Truly, you would have taken your delight in God for all eternity, but you would not have had this foundation of humility if sin had been completely rooted out. Thus it stood with Paul, an eminent Apostle; *to him was given a sharp thorn in the flesh, namely a messenger of Satan, to buffet him with fists, so that he should not exalt himself.* <note>Referencing 2 Corinthians 12:7.</note> Various interpretations are given for these words: Some insist that this "thorn in the flesh" refers to Hymenaeus and Alexander <note>Early Christians mentioned in 1 Timothy 1:20 who were said to have abandoned the faith</note>, who troubled Paul so much, but this is without any foundation. Others think that it was some sharp physical illness, but that would be difficult to prove. Others understand it as a particular sin of impurity, but that cannot be granted, because Paul had the gift of continence and wished that everyone was as he himself was in that regard. But the most learned and excellent interpreters say that it refers to the sin of nature <note>original sin or innate human frailty</note>, and that it is called a "messenger of Satan" because the Devil joins himself to human nature and stirs up the corruption of the human heart. Now, why was this thorn in the flesh left in Paul? Was it not to humble him, and so that he should not exalt himself? Thus the Lord allowed *fiery scorpions to arise in the Wilderness* to humble the Israelites. And so the Lord allows corruption to remain in you to humble you, so that you should not be puffed up in yourself, but when you perceive the corrupt workings
<margin>2 Corinthians 12:7</margin>
<margin>Hymenaeus Alexander</margin>
<margin>Ambrose, Cyprian <note>References to the early Church Fathers St. Ambrose and St. Cyprian.</note></margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 8:16.</margin>

<column-break/>

of your nature, you might then be all the more lowly and base in your own eyes.

<margin>IV.</margin>
Fourthly, the Lord God leaves this corrupt nature in you for the exercise of your grace. For the gifts of grace are never more challenged than when they are fought against; through this, God wishes to prove the truth of your grace and the sincerity of your heart—whether you will side with the Spirit or with the flesh. Just so, God left the Canaanites remaining in the land to test the Israelites, to see if they would conspire with them. Thus a principle of conflict against grace is left in us to test us, whether we will join ourselves to the flesh or whether we will follow the movements and counsels of God's Spirit.

<margin>Second case.</margin>
The other question is: To what end shall a person fight against the corruption of his heart, seeing as we shall carry this corruption with us even into our graves? We have heard that contrary things can never be brought into agreement; why then should one struggle against corruption if there is to be no end to the fight?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
I shall bring forward three reasons from which it will clearly appear that although it is true that you cannot cast out this opposition against grace in your hearts, you nonetheless have weighty reasons to fight against it continually.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
First, if you do not fight against the corruption of nature, it will break out into your life with greater rage and violence. Currently, you have an impure nature, but if you do not oppose it, you will have a godless life; if you leave your nature undisturbed, it will soon be like uncultivated land which is overgrown with thistles and thorns. *Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies.* <note>Quoting Matthew 15:19.</note> If we do not extinguish the evil thoughts in the heart, they will (as you see) break out into the evil and disorderly practices of life. So, although you cannot cast out the original corruption through this effort, nevertheless, if you do not turn against it, you will have it not only in your heart but also visibly in your life.
<margin>Matthew 15:19.</margin>

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Secondly, while you cannot indeed cast out and root out this opposition of nature, you can certainly suppress and weaken it. You can deal with it just as Joshua dealt with the Gibeonites: he let them live, but he made them hewers of wood and drawers of water <note>Joshua 9:21; meaning they were kept alive but forced into servitude</note>. And just as the Israelites dealt with the Canaanites: they did not cast them out, but they bound them to pay tribute. Likewise, although you cannot expel the corruption of nature, you can nonetheless suppress it, and the more you fight against your corrupt heart, the more you shall bring it into subjection. There is a notable Law which God gave to the Jews regarding a house infected with leprosy <note>original: "Melaetsheyt"</note>; God commands the people to do this: if the house were leprous, they should scrape all the stones within the house, and if it could not be made clean by that, they should then break the house down. Your nature is this leprous house: leprosy has defiled your nature, and God commands you to do thus to your nature
<margin>Leviticus 14:41, 45.</margin>

<summary>This page explains that God allows spiritual conflict to remain in believers to foster humility, dependency on Christ, and the exercise of faith. It argues that while internal corruption cannot be fully removed until death, it must be actively suppressed to prevent it from manifesting as outward sin.</summary>

# The Battle Between

...nature, just as the Jews were required to do to their houses—they had to scrape off every stone <note>This refers to the laws in Leviticus 14:40–45, where a house infected with "leprosy" or mold had to be scraped or even demolished to be purified. The author uses this as a metaphor for the human heart.</note>. Likewise, strive to cleanse your heart; purify it with the broom of sanctification. Even if all your efforts seem to fail, your "house" will finally be clean when it is cast down by death. But as long as you live in this world, fight against the workings of your corrupt nature; and although you cannot cast it out entirely, you can nevertheless bring it into subjection. Even though our gifts of grace will never be so strong in this life that they could completely cast out our corruption, nonetheless, if you maintain this struggle with all your might, you will bring your corruption under such control that it will never extinguish grace.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Thirdly, you must know this: failing to struggle against your corrupt nature is proof that there is no grace within you. There is no conflict within a single thing; conflict must always be between two things that stand against each other. Just as corrupt nature stands against grace, so grace also stands against corrupt nature. Therefore, if you are peaceful and still, and do not fight against corruption, it is a clear sign that there is no grace in you <note>The author argues that the very feeling of an internal struggle is a positive sign of spiritual life; without grace, there would be no "second side" to fight the "flesh."</note>.

---

<margin>Rules concerning this conflict</margin>
<margin>I. Deliver me, O Lord, from myself. Augustine. <note>original: "Libera me Domine a me ipso."</note></margin>
Now, let this opposition within your heart against grace cause us to remain ever-watchful and to keep a zealous guard over our hearts. You do not know how far the corruption of your heart might carry you before you die. Do not think with certainty, "I shall not fall into that sin." Do not be so reckless, for you possess a nature that can tempt you to the worst sins ever committed on earth. I have shared with you an observation by Master Capel <note>Richard Capel (1581–1656) was a prominent Puritan physician and minister known for his treatise "Tentations," which analyzed the psychological and spiritual nature of temptation.</note>: that before death, a Christian may well be tempted to break every Commandment of the Law and to doubt every article of Faith. You possess a contrariety against all grace, and therefore a leaning toward every sin. Keep, then, a vigilant eye upon yourself. Peter did not hold himself in enough suspicion when he said to Christ: *Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.* Yea, he said, *Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee.* And yet Peter did both: he was offended by Him, and he denied Him—and that with a curse and an oath. Had Peter known his own heart, he would never have spoken so. The godly often do not know where the corruption of their natures might lead them. Perhaps you are a holy and graced Christian, walking blamelessly in your community; but consider that if God were to let your nature loose, you would soon be snatched away by a violent greed for sin.

<margin>Matthew 26:33, 35.</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 8:13.</margin>
Hazael, as I have indicated above, did not think this wickedness was in his heart, of which the Prophet forewarned him; therefore he said: *But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?* <note>Hazael was an official in Syria who was horrified when the prophet Elisha predicted he would commit atrocities, yet he later did exactly those things (2 Kings 8:13).</note> Even Christ Himself warns His disciples to take heed that their hearts be not at any time burdened with surfeiting <note>original: "brafferye," meaning gluttony or excessive indulgence</note>, and drunkenness, and the cares of this life. A strange warning (one might think) for such men as they were; indeed, a fruitless warning for such godly people. The disciples were

<margin>Luke 21:34.</margin>

<column-break/>

at that time not even hungry, so how could they be guilty of gluttony? They had no place where they could lay their heads; would they then be overcome by drunkenness? And they did not possess the things of this life; would they then be anxious over them? This seems very strange, yet Christ knew that the seed of sin was in their natures, just as it is in ours. Therefore, we ought to keep a reflective eye upon our own hearts. Just as in the first creation all creatures were seeded within the first lump of matter, and only the movement of the Spirit was needed to bring them forth; so too is the seed of all evil within our natures, lacking only the opportunity and the temptation to bring that evil to light.

<margin>Proverbs 7:2.</margin>
<margin>Second Rule.</margin>
Second, remember that however great the opposition against grace in your heart may be, you must not lose courage. Although you now notice that corruption in your nature more than you ever did in your past life, do not be discouraged. There are many godly souls in this same situation who never saw more corruption and violence than they do now. They thought sin was dead, but now they see that it lives; they thought its power was weakened, but now they see it is even sharper. Such people must nevertheless keep heart, and for these reasons:

1. Because this perhaps does not stem from an actual growth of sin in your nature, but from a clearer discovery of sin. It is not that the object has multiplied or grown, but that your sight has been made clearer. A godly person sees more corruption in his nature than he ever did before—not because there is more corruption now than there truly was before, but because God has given him a clearer insight into his own heart. I could explain this through this parable: On a dark day, you see no dust-motes or tiny specks moving up and down in your room; but if the bright rays of the Sun shine in, you see a multitude of dust-motes flying. Now, the dust was there before, but you did not see it because the Sun did not reveal it to you. So it is with people; before their conversion, they have an abundance of desires in their hearts, but they do not see them because the Sun of Righteousness has not shone upon them.

<margin>Romans 7:13.</margin>
You have a remarkable passage in Paul, Romans 7:13: *Sin has become death to me, that it might be revealed as sin, working death in me through that which is good.* Sin was indeed sin before, but it was not revealed to be sin until he was converted. And now he says: I see the workings of my corrupt nature; while I was a Pharisee, I neither saw nor knew that I was as ugly and sinful as I now realize I am. Thus, when the light breaks into the soul, those sins reveal themselves which lay hidden; and those which at first seemed only like splinters now appear as beams, and those which seemed as small as gnats now reveal themselves to be as large as camels.

<margin>Third Rule.</margin>
<margin>Romans 8:7.</margin>
2. This can come from a more tender sincerity in your conscience, which you did not have in times past. Before, your conscience was hardened, calloused, and unfeeling, fighting against the sensation of sin; but now God has melted it and made it soft.

<margin>Fourth Rule.</margin>

nature; just as the Jews were required to do to their houses, they had to scrape off all the stones <note>This refers to the laws in Leviticus 14 regarding a "leprosy" or mold in a house, where infected stones had to be scraped or removed to purify the home.</note>; so also seek to purify your heart, cleanse it with the **broom of sanctification**, and if all of this cannot help, yet your house shall be pure when it is cast down through death. But as long as you live here in the world, fight against the workings of your corrupt nature; and although you cannot cast it out, you can nevertheless subdue it. Although our gifts of grace in this life will never be so strong that they could cast out our corruption, nonetheless, if you maintain this struggle with all your strength, you shall so subdue your corruption that it will never extinguish grace.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Thirdly, you must know this: that to not fight with your corrupt nature is proof that there is no grace in you. There is no conflict within one thing, but it must always be between two, these standing against one another: just as the corrupt nature stands against grace, so grace also stands against the corrupt nature: therefore, if you are at rest and still, and do not fight against corruption, it is a clear proof that there is [no] <note>The Dutch text says "datter genade in u is" (that there is grace in you), but the context of the argument "not fighting proves no grace" suggests a missing negative or a rhetorical point about the absence of conflict implying the absence of the opposing force of grace.</note> grace in you.

<margin>
Rules regarding this conflict
I.
**Deliver me, O Lord, from myself.** Augustine. <note>original: "Libera me Domine à me ipſo."</note>
</margin>
Well, let this resistance which is in your heart against grace make us watchful in all things, and let us watch over our hearts; you do not know how far the corruption of your heart can carry you away before you die, and do not think with certainty "I shall not fall into that sin"; do not be careless, for you have in you a nature which can come to tempt you to the stiffest sin that has ever happened on earth. I have recounted to you a remark by **Master Capel** <note>Likely Richard Capel (1581–1656), a prominent Puritan minister known for his writings on temptation.</note>, that a Christian may well be tempted before his death to break every Commandment of the Law and to doubt every article of the Faith; you have in you a contradiction against all grace, and therefore an inclination toward all sin. Keep then a watchful eye over yourself. Peter did not hold 

<margin>Matthew 26: 33, 35.</margin>
himself suspect enough when he said to Christ: *Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended*: yes (he said) *though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee*: and yet Peter did both; he was offended by him, and he denied him, and that with a curse and an oath. Had Peter known his own heart, he would never have spoken so. The godly often do not know to what end the corruption of their natures might carry them. Perhaps you are a Holy and graced Christian, and you walk blamelessly in the place where you live; but consider, that if God once let your nature loose, you would soon be snatched away to sin with a violent greed. **Hazael**, as I have pointed out above, did not think that this wickedness was in his heart, of which the Prophet foretold 

<margin>2 Kings 8: 13.</margin>
him, and therefore he says: *But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?* Yes, Christ himself warns his

<margin>Luke 21: 34.</margin>
Disciples that they should take heed to themselves, *lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life.* A strange admonition (someone might think) for such as they were; yes, a fruitless warning for such godly people; the Disciples we-

<column-break/>

re at that time not even hungry, and should they then become guilty of surfeiting? They had no place where they could lay down their head, and should they be overtaken with drunkenness? And they did not have the things of this life, should they then be careful <note>In the older sense of being full of "cares" or anxieties.</note> over them? This seems very strange, yet Christ knew that the seed of sins was in their nature, just as we also have it; therefore we ought to have a reflective eye over our own heart. Just as in the first creation all the creatures were seed-like in the first lump, and only the movement of the Spirit was needed to bring them forth: so in our natures is the seed of all evil, and there only lacks the opportunity and the temptation to bring that to light.

<margin>Second Rule.</margin>
Secondly, remember that however great the resistance in your heart against grace may be, you must nevertheless not let your courage sink; although you notice that corruption more in your nature now than you ever did in the past time of your life, do not be discouraged for that reason; there are so many Godly souls in this condition, who never saw more corruption and violence than now; they thought that sin was dead, but now they see that it lives; they thought that its power was weakened, but now they see that it is more sharpened. Such people must nevertheless take heart, and that for these reasons.

1. Because this perhaps does not come from an increase of sin in your nature, but from a clearer discovery of sins; not because the object is multiplied and enlarged, but because your sight is made clearer: a Godly person sees more corruption in his nature than he ever saw before; not because there is now more corruption in it than there truly was before, but because God has given him a clearer insight into his own heart. I could explain this through this comparison. On a dark day you see no dust motes or specks moving up and down in your room; but if the bright rays of the Sun shine therein, then you see a multitude of dust motes flying; now the dust was there before also, but you did not see it because the Sun did not show it to you; so it is also with men; before their conversion they have an abundance of lusts in their hearts, but they do not see them, because the **Sun of Righteousness** has not shone upon them. You have a notable passage in Paul, Romans 7:13. *Sin became death to me, so that it might be revealed to be sin, working death in me through that which is good:* sin was indeed sin before, but once he was converted, he now says, I see the workings of my corrupt nature: while I was a Pharisee, I neither saw nor knew that I was so ugly and sinful as I now indeed do. So that, when the light breaks into the soul, those sins show themselves which lay hidden, and those which at first seemed only like splinters, now show themselves as beams; and those which seemed as small as gnats, reveal themselves now as thick as camels <note>Alluding to Christ's metaphors in Matthew 7:3 (motes and beams) and Matthew 23:24 (straining gnats and swallowing camels).</note>.

2. This can also come from a tenderer sincerity in your conscience, which you did not have in past times: previously your conscience was hardened, desensitized, and unfeeling, fighting against the feeling of sin; but now God has melted and made it soft;

<meta>This page continues the sermon on the spiritual struggle between the flesh and the Spirit, moving from the description of the conflict to its practical consequences in the life of a believer.</meta>

### Galatians 5, verse 17.

> For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary to one another; so that you do not do the things that you would.

<margin>20th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry in London, January 19, 1650.</margin> <note>St. Lawrence Jewry is a historic church in the City of London, known for hosting important sermon series during the Commonwealth period.</note>
Now I shall proceed to the twofold consequence of this twofold struggle, in which there is also a twofold relationship: the flesh lusts against the Spirit, so that you do not do the good which you would; and the Spirit lusts against the flesh, so that you do not do the evil which you would. The words do not have much difficulty in themselves, and therefore I shall not say much to explain them. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Western Christianity.</note> understands these words thus: "so that you do not do the things that you would," meaning you cannot do the good which you would. But Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), an influential Reformed theologian.</note> understands it as both taken together: you do not do what you would. As if he said: the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and so you cannot do the good which you would; and the Spirit lusts against the flesh, so that you cannot do the evil which you would. The Doctrine which flows from the first part of the consequence—namely, the flesh lusts against the Spirit, so that you cannot do the good which you would—is this:

->Doctrine.<-

That the corruption of the flesh, even in the reborn, often turns them away from and disturbs them in their holy duties.

<margin>Romans 7:18, 22.</margin>
To confirm this, you have not only the testimony of the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> that it was so with other men, but also his own experience; for thus he complains of himself: "the will is present with me, but how to perform that which is good I find not. When I would do good, then I find that evil is present with me."

I shall divide this Doctrine into two parts and show that this corruption of nature, in respect to doing good, has a twofold evil consequence or effect.

First, it prevents a person from doing good. Secondly, it hinders a person while doing good.

I shall now stand upon these particular things and shall begin with the first: That corrupt nature prevents a person from doing good.

To explain this, there is an apt symbol in the history described of Tamar, who had twins in her womb, Perez and Zerah. Now it says there that Zerah first put out his hand, and the midwife bound a scarlet thread around his hand; but Perez struggled with Zerah and so came out first. Theologians apply this history here: that a godly person may, like Zerah, begin to do a duty, but corrupt nature, like Perez, prevents the birth of Zerah; corrupt nature prevents the reborn from doing good.

Now I shall point out to you what those crafty tricks of human nature are which prevent one from doing good. There are fifteen such subtle acts which corrupt nature uses to that end.

<margin>The first cunning of the flesh.</margin>
First, the flesh prevents a person from

<column-break/>

doing good by making him believe that he is above the use of religious duties: this suggestion comes from a proud, fantastical nature. These duties (say the foolish <term>Familists</term> <note>The "Family of Love," a radical sect that believed spiritual perfection made outward church laws and ceremonies unnecessary.</note>) are but fleshly forms, and for the lowest order of Christians only, but not for those who have grown to a high stature and possess higher gifts. Corruption often uses this argument for neglecting the use of duties, and we see that this already happened in the days of the Apostles, as the Apostle Paul indicates when he says,

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:11, 12.</margin>
"There are contentions among you, in that every one of you says, I am of Paul; and I, of Apollos; and I, of Cephas; and I, of Christ." Here the Apostle does not only accuse those who exalted one Apostle above the other, but he also rejects a fourth sort of people, who said they were "of Christ." And why does the Apostle reject such as these? See, this is the meaning: The Apostle condemns <term>Enthusiasm</term> <note>original: "Geest-dryvery." In the 17th century, this referred to "fanaticism"—the belief that one receives direct revelations from God that bypass the Bible or organized church duties.</note>. These people went so far, rather than exalting Paul or any other of the Apostles, as to say they were entirely "of Christ"—that is, they claimed to be full of revelations and divine inspirations according to their own boasting. Now the Apostle rejects those who so exalt Christ that they reject ordinary service. And to give you an antidote against this poison of corrupt nature, I shall set down these three particular things.

<margin>Remedies against this. 1.</margin>
First, that the Word makes a promise that in the most glorious times of the church, duties and instituted religious services would be customary among believers. For so John says,

<margin>Revelation 11:15 compared with verse 19.</margin>
Revelation 11:15: "The seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever." And in the nineteenth verse it follows: "The temple of God was opened in heaven, and there was seen in his temple the ark of his testament." That is, there would be Gospel-instituted duties in the purest times of God's church, after the Antichrist would be destroyed; nevertheless, there would then be a Temple, and therein the Ark of God's Covenant, namely, Gospel-instituted duties.

<margin>2.</margin>
Secondly, the Scripture says that the strongest Christians must practice the duties of religion, and so the Apostle

<margin>Romans 15:14, 15.</margin>
Paul says to the Romans, that he was persuaded of them, that they themselves were full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another; but (says he) "I have written the more boldly unto you, as putting you in mind." As if he said: although you are full of knowledge and goodness, nevertheless I must put you in mind of your duty. The strong are also necessitated to exercise themselves in duties and instituted services: 1. To strengthen their judgment in the knowledge and the faith of the truth (1 John 2:21): "I have not written unto you because you know not the truth, but because you know it." 2. To strengthen their memories in the remembrance of the truth (Jude verse 5): "I will therefore put you in remembrance, though you once knew this." 3. To stir up their affections all the more toward the love of the truth (2 Peter 1:12): "Wherefore I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things, though you know them, and..."

# Flesh and Spirit.

and are strengthened in the present truth.

<margin>III.</margin>Thirdly, you must be busy in the practice of your duties until the time you enter Heaven. We read of the Israelites that the Lord God sent them Manna from Heaven as long as they were in the wilderness, but once they entered Canaan, those provisions ceased. Likewise, while you are in the wilderness of this world, you must be fed with the Manna of established religious duties <note>The author uses "duties" to refer to spiritual disciplines like prayer, reading Scripture, and attending church.</note>; but when you come into Heaven, then, and not until then, shall they cease. Only the Heavenly Jerusalem had no Temple (Revelation 21:22, 23). Therefore, more blameworthy is the ingratitude of those who make no other use of their long life under the established worship of God than to proudly pretend that they are above the same.

<margin>Second craftiness.</margin>Another craftiness of our corrupt nature is the pretending of pressing and unusual affairs and opportunities in the world, and these make some a hindrance to their duty. They will tell you that their circumstances are necessary, and that they have barely enough time to follow their trials; therefore they hope that God will excuse them, even though they do not practice religious duties as often as other people. Such were those who were invited to the Great Banquet mentioned in the Gospel of Luke, who with one accord began to excuse themselves: one had bought a field and therefore must necessarily go out and see it. Another had bought five yoke of oxen and was going to test them; and another had married a wife and therefore could not come. Such pretenses as these are found in our corrupt nature, so that worldly callings may serve as an excuse for why they do not observe religious duties. To remove this from your understanding, I shall place these four specific things before you.
<margin>Luke 14:18, 20.</margin>

<margin>Remedies against. I.</margin>First, that God has never ordained that our particular calling—insofar as we are human beings—should hinder our general calling—insofar as we are Christians—or that civil duties should push out divine ones. A wise arrangement of God's providence in our worldly affairs will give you time enough to practice religion; a holy foresight and providence will "redeem the time" for praying, hearing God's word, and so on.

<margin>II.</margin>Secondly, observe that this is the right way to obtain God's blessing over our outward calling: namely, to be very busy in religious duties. A man who had only two acres of land once said this when he saw a rich Lord's land: the poor man’s field was fruitful, and the Lord’s was barren. When the Lord came to him and asked the reason, "Oh Lord," he said, "I have watered my little field every morning with prayers and tears." This is the way to be blessed in the world; give to God what is His, and He will give you what is yours. "Seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you."
<margin>Matthew 6:33. Luke 12:31.</margin>

Thirdly, you say you must [take care of] your calling

<column-break/>

and so you neglect your duty which you owe to God. Well, take note: God will be provoked thereby to ruin your outward trade and make it wither; for it is in vain, without God's blessing, to rise early, to stay up late, and to eat the bread of sorrows, as the Psalmist speaks. God often curses your outward state because you refuse Him your religious duties.
<margin>Psalm 127:2.</margin>

<margin>IV.</margin>Fourthly and finally, God was angry with Moses for the neglect of his duty, as well as with the Israelites, even though they had more pressing concerns to argue with than all of you. Although Moses was on a journey—and one might think that was surely a good excuse for him, that he did not circumcise his son—nevertheless God had such great displeasure in this neglect that He met him at his inn and sought to kill him. God would not excuse the neglect of His instituted duty, even though the necessity of the journey might have been an excuse for Moses. So too was God disturbed with the children of Israel because, while they were in the wilderness, they had neglected this institution of circumcision; and yet they might have excused themselves because they moved from place to place and set up their tents now here, now there. Although this pretense might seem quite fine, nevertheless God was not satisfied with it; from which we can learn that neither our worldly trade nor necessary concerns in the world can excuse us from practicing our religion.
<margin>Exodus 4:24.</margin>
<margin>Joshua 5:5, 6.</margin>

<margin>The third cunning.</margin>Another craftiness of corrupt nature is this: that a person will intend and promise to observe religious duties, but not until this, his present state in which he is, has changed. A person sitting down will say: "If I were in another state, then God would have more service and duty from me than He has now; but in this my state, I have neither time nor opportunity." This is a very loose trick with which your corrupt hearts seek to draw you away from your duties. Suppose you are a young servant; then your heart will suggest this to you: "If only you were a Master, oh, how many hours would you then spend in the service of God!" If you are a poor person, you say: "Oh, if I were rich, how generous would I be?" If you are in a position of service, you say: "What good would I do if I were a person of Authority!" This was the vain thought of Absalom. But remember this: if your state were changed and your heart remained unchanged, you would nonetheless remain the same throughout, even if your state were changed. And to you who are thus deceived or being deceived by your treacherous hearts, I wish to bring these specific things to mind.
<margin><note>original: "Semper incipio vivere" — "I am always beginning to live." This is a quote from Seneca regarding those who constantly postpone their spiritual life.</note></margin>

<margin>Remedies against this. I.</margin>First, you must know that it is pure deceit of the heart to think that if your state were changed, you would be a changed person. This is evident because if you are not pious in your present state, you cannot be pious in any state if your heart remains the same. The reason is that your evil heart makes you ungodly in your present state, and if that stays with you, so you shall also be evil in another state. If you are a bad servant, so you shall [be a bad master].
<margin><note>original: "Cœlum non animum mutat" — "He changes the sky but not his soul." This Horace quote suggests that moving or changing circumstances doesn't change one's character.</note></margin>

The author uses biblical examples like Moses and the Israelites to argue that spiritual obligations must always take priority over earthly concerns.</summary>

# The Struggle Between
## The Flesh and the Spirit

you will also be a bad Master; and if you are a bad child, you will also be a bad Father: If you are not pious in an unmarried state, you will also not be pious in a married state, unless your heart is changed; and if not, your life will also not be changed.

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, consider this within yourself: that perhaps every other state of life for which you long with admiration has more snares, hindrances, and inconveniences than the present state about which you complain. Now you are young and you complain that you have no time to pray; well, what would you do if you had the burden of an entire household upon you? A public station has more distractions and obstacles than any private station; therefore, do not deceive yourself.
<margin>1 Corinthians 7:34</margin>

<margin>The fourth craftiness.</margin> A fourth craftiness of our corrupt nature, used to keep a person from their duties, is to place an ugly mask upon the beautiful face of religious duties. Just as the flesh—in order to lead a person into sin—knows how to smear and paint sin so that it appears as the beautiful face of virtue; so too the heart, on the other side, to keep a person from duty, will attack the beautiful face of godliness with fleshly prejudices. Just as Judas took great offense at that excellent and memorable work of Mary in that respectful generosity she showed to Christ in breaking the jar of ointment—indeed, he considered it an excessive waste—so also your corrupt heart will suggest to you that zeal for God is nothing but recklessness and indiscretion; that sanctification <note>In this context, the process of becoming holy through spiritual discipline.</note> is nothing but melancholy of the mind; that patience (namely, not repaying evil with evil) is merely an ugly moderation; that walking with God is just a sort of monk’s life; that a conscientious care to keep the Sabbath holy is "Jewishness"; and that having a tender conscience is nothing other than a needless anxiety. By these means, people who allow their hearts to argue in such a fleshly way are turned away from all that is good; therefore, if you wish to prevent this deception, try to see the innate luster and beauty of holiness, and the ugliness of sin.
<margin>Matthew 26:1 <note>Likely referring to the story of Mary anointing Jesus in Matthew 26:7-13.</note></margin>

Another work by which the heart of man deceives him is to do some smaller good, and thereby prevent the practice of a greater good: and thus the Devil and a person's own heart often lead him astray. It is an observation of Master Greenham <note>Richard Greenham (c. 1535–1594), a prominent English Puritan clergyman known for his practical divinity.</note> that in many households, every small and trivial thing comes to hinder Prayer; and this is the nature of the human heart: to make every minor matter into a turning away from duties and the exercises of religion. So it was with the Pharisees; they tithed mint, dill, and cumin, and thus they neglected justice and the weightiest things of the Law. Many people will satisfy themselves with reading a chapter at home, and will thus neglect the preaching of the Word and common Prayer; this is purely the hollow deception of a person's own heart, just like the ancient heretics called <term>Euchites</term> <note>A 4th-century sect also known as Messalians, who believed that only constant prayer was necessary for salvation, neglecting all other sacraments and duties.</note>, who were so busy in Prayer that they neglected all other religious service.
<margin>Matthew 23:23</margin>

<margin>Remedy against this.</margin> To those who use one duty to 

<column-break/>

cast out another, I wish to say: they should remember that duties do not struggle against one another, but that one stands under the other, and thus they help each other. I may say of the duties of religion what the Scripture says of the Lamps of the Sanctuary, which were made so that one Lamp would light the other; so also are the duties of God ordained so that one helps the other. Prayer makes one fit to hear God's word, and hearing makes a person fit for meditation, and meditation for Prayer, and so with all other duties. Therefore, those who allow one duty to hinder another make those things struggle against each other which the Lord God has joined together.

<margin>The sixth craftiness.</margin> Another cunning trick which the flesh uses is this: if it cannot persuade people to neglect religious duty entirely, it will nonetheless cause them to diminish in it. Perhaps your corrupt heart cannot move you to reject Prayer and the hearing of the Word so completely that you would never practice those services; nonetheless, it will seek to gain much from you by making you pray and hear God's Word more seldom than you did at first. Just as it is a deception of the heart to bring us from small sins to great ones, so it is also the craftiness of the flesh to bring us from "seldom" to "never" performing our duties. And to give you an antidote against this poison of nature, I shall present these following considerations.

<margin>Remedies against this. 1.</margin> Firstly, it is the craftiness of your heart that it does not make you throw away all duties at once, but makes you diminish gradually and by degrees (Revelation 2:4). The Church of Ephesus diminished by degrees; it first left its "first love," and after that its "first works." The reason is because your heart and the devil know that diminishments, when they happen by degrees, are less felt; whereas a total neglect is immediately opposed by a <term>natural conscience</term> <note>The inherent human sense of right and wrong, even without divine grace.</note>. You must pray sometimes and hear God's word, otherwise your conscience would gnaw at you; but a decline by degrees is not so easily felt or noticed. Therefore, the devil and your own heart will let you pray and hear, but not as often as you did before; in this snare many of God's people have been caught.

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, consider that the soul is in as great a danger through a gradual decline in religious service as through total omissions. A leaking hole in a ship, even if it is small, will in the end as surely and with greater danger cause the ship to perish as a violent storm, because it does so without being felt or noticed. Long-lasting "consumptions" <note>An old term for wasting diseases like tuberculosis.</note> bring people as surely to death as violent and burning fevers; it is true, a pestilential fever can kill a person within three days, but a consumption will bring him just as certainly to his grave.

<margin>The seventh craftiness.</margin> But seventhly, corrupt nature will suggest to you that you may well neglect religious duties because of the unchangeable decree of God. Corrupt nature will tell you that if you are ordained to salvation, all your praying and hearing will not save you; and if you are ordained to [the] salva-

<margin>The eighth <br/> craftiness <br/> of the flesh</margin>
Eighthly / you will say this / through the prompting of a self-deceiving heart: I am unfit to do any good; this is the saying of many / if I were fit / then I would pray more / if I could restrain myself more / I would go to Church more; but because of my unfitness I am turned away from religious duties. This is the argument of nature. It serves as an answer:

<margin>I. <br/> Remedies <br/> against this.</margin>
First / that your powerlessness cannot nullify your obligation to the moral Law. Although you are unfit to carry out the duties; that does not release you from your required duty; you are bound to do that duty / although you cannot do it well. Have you lost the ability to obey? Look here / God has lost no sovereignty to command: natural powerlessness does not excuse voluntary neglect.

<column-break/>

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly / suppose / you are truly unfit to carry out the duty; nonetheless think that your fitness herein depends on God's promise / and not on your own strength: you are unfit; well, God is fit. You are under the promise / so take up the duties / and God has promised the assistance of His Spirit.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly / notice that there is less evil in the performance of a duty / even if you happen to sin in the manner of doing it / than in a holy omission; that man sins less / who in praying does not pray well / than he who does not pray at all. Certainly, defects in the duty partially violate God’s command / but a total neglect breaks the entire command: the duty is essential / but the deficiency is accidental. <note>In 17th-century logic, "essential" refers to the core requirement, while "accidental" refers to a flaw or quality that is secondary to the act itself.</note>

als. Although you are unfit to perform the duties; that does not release you from your beholden duty; you are bound to do that duty / although you cannot do it well. Have you lost the fitness to obey? Well look to it / God has lost no sovereignty to command: natural impotence does not excuse voluntary neglect.

<margin>
II.
</margin>
Secondly / granted / you are truly unfit to perform the duty; yet think that your fitness herein depends on God's promise / and not on your own strength: you are unfit; well God is fit. You are under the promise / well then take the duties in hand / and God has promised the assistance of his Spirit.

<margin>
III.
</margin>
Thirdly / notice that there is less evil in the performance of a duty / although you happen to sin in the manner of doing it / than in a holy omission; that man sins less / who praying does not pray well / than he who does not pray at all. Certainly defects in the duty partially dissolve God's command / but a total voluntary neglect breaks the entire command: the duty is essential / but the failing is incidental.

# Flesh and Spirit.

<margin>1:6.</margin> Fifthly, remember that the Scripture says that those who sinned the least were also the most devoted to God's service. Of Zechariah <note>original: "Zacharias"</note> it is written that he walked in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless, and yet <margin>Luke 1:10, 2.</margin> the Scripture praises him because he was frequently in the Temple. And of Cornelius the Scripture says that he was a godly man who feared God with all his house, who gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God continually; although he was a godly and holy man, yet he prayed to God continually; he was diligent in serving God, although he did not sin greatly. So <margin>Luke 2:37</margin> it is written of Anna, that she served God night and day. And of the early Church it is written that they persevered in the doctrine of the Apostles, etc. <term>proskarterountes</term> <note>original: "προσκαρτεροντες" — meaning to continue steadfastly or attend constantly.</note>, &c.

<margin>The twelfth wile.</margin> Furthermore, the flesh will tell you that many who were at first very religious have since abandoned it; and you will say, "Why should I not do the same? I see indeed that those who were at first so eager to hear sermons now do not hear them; those who at first prayed so often now never pray; those who at first served God greatly now do not do so." This is a proof known to man's evil heart; I shall answer this with three points.

<margin>Remedies against it. I.</margin> Firstly, it is true, and all the more lamentable, that many were formerly very religious who later abandoned it; but nevertheless, take care that you do not fall into the same sin and perdition. The Scripture brands and accuses such people heavily. You have two texts for this; one is in Hosea 4 verse 10, where the Lord God complains that they had neglected to take heed of the Lord; they once sought God and took heed of His ways, but <margin>Psalm 36:4</margin> now they had neglected that. You have another place in the Psalms; "They have ceased," (he says) "to be wise and to do good"; they formerly did much good, but now they have ceased from it. The Scripture brands such people as godless apostates.

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, notice that in other matters you would consider this an absurd argument; what you think is reasonable in spiritual things, you would think unreasonable in worldly ones. If someone said to you that other people have stopped doing business and have gone bankrupt, and that you therefore ought to do the same, you would consider that very unreasonable; and you would say, although other people have been foolish and thrown themselves out of their station, yet that is no example for you to follow.

<margin>III.</margin> Thirdly, know that whoever was once very religious and has now abandoned it will later (if they are children of God) be brought by God back to true sorrow and repentance; God will show them their folly to their shame. You have an example of this in the second chapter of <term>Hosea verse 7</term> <note>The text cites "verse 6," but the quote is from Hosea 2:7.</note>. The Church there fell away from God; but, she said, "I will go and return to my first husband: for then it was better with me than now." When I served God and walked in His ways, from which I have now wandered, it was better for me then; therefore I will return. Thus will all those speak who have stopped

<column-break/>

serving God, if they belong to God.

<margin>The thirteenth wile.</margin> Some suggest this: that they abstain from certain religious duties because they wish to prevent more evil thereby; and this is a crafty entanglement of the flesh. And just as people are enticed on one hand by their evil hearts to commit sin so that good might come of it, so on the other hand their hearts would gladly make them believe they should neglect their duties so that no evil comes of it. These are two deceptions of corrupt nature, of which the Catholics <note>original: "Paunsgensinden" — literally 'those of the Pope's party.'</note> are guilty, for they withhold the Bible from the common people under this pretext: so that the people do not fall into error and sin. Concerning this, <margin>There are some men who, when they have heard that they ought to be humble, do not want to learn anything, thinking that if they have learned anything, they will become proud. Augustine on Psalm 130.</margin> Augustine makes mention of some who did not want to hear God's word, nor gain knowledge, with the pretext that some have become proud because of their gifts and knowledge. Regarding this deception, I will say three things.

<margin>Remedies against it. I.</margin> Firstly, it is a good rule of the Scholastic teachers <note>original: "School-leeraers" — referring to medieval university theologians.</note> that one must not neglect what is good in itself and necessary to avoid sin, even though it may incidentally <note>translated from a concept of "per accidens."</note> involve a sin. If someone did not want to hear God's word so that they would not be distracted, or did not want to pray so that they would not have a wandering of thoughts, they would thus practice no religion at all. Now, hearing and praying is good in itself; but that you were distracted in hearing, or that your senses wandered in prayer, this is an accident; therefore you must not neglect those duties which are good in themselves on the pretext that you would become guilty of some lesser evil.

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, those people who reason thus—that they do not want to practice religion because they sin in doing so—could by the same logic also say that they do not want to attend to their profession in the world because they sin in it. Therefore, although this argument has some appearance of truth, and many doubting Christians are ensnared by it, you would thereby be drawn away not only from religious duties but also from civil duties.

<margin>III.</margin> Thirdly, know that by using this cover to avoid evil, you run into a greater evil; the reason is that voluntary neglect and holy omissions are heavier than spiritual defects committed while performing religious duties. It is a smaller sin to be distracted in prayer than not to pray at all. This is then but a lazy argument of corrupt nature to make us neglect our religious duties.

<margin>The fourteenth wile.</margin> Another argument is taken from the inability to fulfill our duties. The flesh will tell you that if you could perform your worship better, you would also have the desire to do it often; but alas, you are not capable of performing the duties. When you come to hear God's Word, you have no faith to receive it, and no memory to gather it up like a treasure. When you come to pray, you have no well-disposed mind, nor proper impressions; and for this reason the flesh pleads thus, that the <meta>onbe-</meta> <note>Translator's note: 'onbe-' is the start of 'onbequaemheyt' (inability), the catchword for the next page.</note>

Firstly, that many Christians who plead their unfitness often neglect the duty more out of a dislike for it than out of actual inability. Seneca says very well to this end in one of his Letters: people (he says) pretend that they cannot do good, but the true cause is that they will not do it. <note>original: "Nolle in cauſſa est cum non poſſe prætenditur" — Unwillingness is the cause when inability is the pretense. Seneca, Epistle 116.</note> It is not then an inability in nature, but an opposition in the heart, why they do not observe their duties. It is noteworthy that where the Apostle speaks of an inability for the service of God, he also mentions the enmity of a natural person's heart against the same. The mind of the flesh (he says) is enmity against God, for it does not subject itself to the Law of God; for it cannot. <note>original: "Het bedencken des vleeschs" — often translated as the "carnal mind" or "mindset of the flesh." Secondly, Christians are by nature inclined to use their unfitness as a reason for their neglect of God’s service when the danger associated with it keeps them back more than the unfitness itself. You have a notable example of this in Moses, who was a pious man. The whole history is briefly recorded in the fourth chapter of Exodus. God commands Moses to go to Egypt and to take the care of His people upon himself; but what does Moses say? "O Lord," he says, "will You send me to lead this people? Oh, I am not fit; I am not a man of eloquent speech, neither yesterday nor since You have spoken to Your servant: for I am slow of speech and slow of tongue." This pretense had some appearance of truth, and therefore he said in the thirteenth verse, "O Lord, please send by the hand of whomever else You will send." But was the unfitness of Moses the true cause why he did not want to go? Not at all; therefore, in the nineteenth verse, the real reason is revealed: "Return," said the Lord, "to Egypt, for all the men are dead who sought your life." There God points out the cause with His finger. Moses had previously killed an Egyptian, and they had searched closely for him. And when God commands Moses to return to Egypt, he was terrified. But Moses did not say this to God; instead, he pleaded his unfitness. Then the Lord told him that the men were dead who sought his life; and then, it says there, Moses took his wife and his sons and returned to the land of Egypt.

Thirdly, know that there are two kinds of fruit that follow godliness: first, a true and actual fruit, and second, a felt fruit. Sometimes the fruit is felt, and a person's affections are stirred, and their desires are brought under control; but although the fruit is not always felt, it is nevertheless always actual. A godly person obtains an actual good through the religious duties he performs; whatever good each person shall have done, that same thing he shall receive from the Lord, whether he be a slave or free. No one shall open the doors of God's house in vain. The wicked Ahab performed only a temporary service for God, and God also gave him a temporary reward. There is, then, always a true reward that accompanies the performance of our religious duties. And thus I have presented the wiles and deceptions of the flesh, through which it seeks to draw people away from the service of God, and I have also answered them all together, so that you may not be deceived by its craftiness.

The utility of all this will be for those people who feel in their consciences that they have been deceived by some of these wiles of their corrupt nature, such that they have neglected good duties. I would like to bring these five considerations to their minds.

It is noteworthy that the sentence which will be spoken on the Last Day by the Judge of the whole world makes mention not so much of actual sins as of the neglect of good duties for which people shall be condemned. "Depart from me, you cursed," Christ will say; "for I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me nothing to drink. I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me." In these words, they are condemned solely because of their omissions in their required duty. Perhaps you do not die a drunkard, nor an adulterer, nor a swearer, nor a deceiver; but if you die being negligent in religious duties, I tell it to you: the accusation will be bound against you. It is also noted of that servant who had received only one talent, that Christ commands that he should be cast into the outer darkness; why then? He did not misuse his Master's talent, but because he [did not use] the same...

<meta>This page continues the argument that spiritual unfitness is no excuse for neglecting one's duties to God. It moves from general warnings to specific examples of how God punishes "sins of omission"—the failure to do good—as severely as "sins of commission"—the active doing of evil.</meta>

# Flesh and Spirit.

did not apply himself; therefore the sentence went against him. For this reason, remember this, you who neglect good duties; you shall not be lost for the squandering or the evil use of your time, but because you <margin>Matt. 3:10.</margin> did not use it well. The tree is threatened with being hewn down, not because it brought forth evil fruit, but because it brought forth no good fruit. <note>The author uses the parable of the barren fig tree to argue that being "neutral" or "doing nothing" is a spiritual failure.</note>

<margin>II.</margin> Secondly, consider that the Scripture particularly marks those who persistently neglect the duties of religion. <margin>Ps. 36:4.</margin> They cease to understand how to do good, says the Psalmist; and they have neglected to take the Lord into account, says the Prophet <margin>Hos. 4:10.</margin> Hosea. But above all, consider that heavy curse of the Prophet Jeremiah: "Pour <margin>Jer. 10:25.</margin> out thy fury upon the heathen," he says, "that know thee not, and upon the families that call not on thy name." And to this end, it is very remarkable what is written of the Ammonites and Moabites in Deuteronomy 23, where they <margin>Deut. 23:3, 4.</margin> were excluded from the congregation of the Lord even unto the tenth generation because of their neglect—namely, because they did not meet the Israelites on the way with bread and with water when they came out of Egypt.

<margin>III.</margin> Thirdly, consider that the neglect of religion renders people unfit for it when they eventually wish to begin or persevere in it. Keys that are used remain shiny, but if they are laid down somewhere, how quickly they rust? So it is with your heart; you shall gather rust if you lay aside your duties. Fire is extinguished not only by water, but also <margin>Prov. 26:20.</margin> by the withdrawal of wood. Where there is no wood, the fire goes out; and therefore remember that if you lay no wood upon your duties <note>A metaphor for putting effort or "fuel" into spiritual practices like prayer or study.</note>, the heat of your affection will soon go out. The longer we let our religion stand still, the less fit we shall be for it: just like a schoolboy, if he lets his studies stand still, he shall be all the more unfit for those exercises.

<margin>IV.</margin> Fourthly, God has more displeasure in sinful and [neglect of] holy omissions of good, than He has in many committed sins. There is a remarkable passage concerning Moses in Exodus 4:24. God was angrier at Moses because of a sin of omission than for any actual sin which he had committed. It says there: "The Lord met him in the inn, and sought to kill him"; what was the cause? Behold, it was only because he had neglected to circumcise his son when he was eight days old; this provoked God so quickly to anger that He sought to kill Moses: yet Moses could have brought forward more plausible excuses for his neglect than we can do for many religious duties which we overlook. I say this to show you the danger of the sin of omission. <note>A "sin of omission" is failing to do what God commands, while a "sin of commission" is doing what God forbids.</note>

<margin>V.</margin> Fifthly and lastly, consider that you do not accept such proof as valid in other matters. If your servants dealt with you in this way—that when you command them to do this or that work, or to perform such service, and you demand an account from them—would you then accept such an excuse if they said they did not steal your goods from your shops, nor your money from your chests, and that they do you no wrong? Would you

<column-break/>

accept those excuses? Certainly not. Well, I pray you, you are all servants of the God of Heaven; He is your Master; and though you say thus: "Lord, I am no gross sinner, I have not dishonored Your name as others have, and I am no blasphemer of Your name," yet God shall nonetheless settle accounts with you because you have not called upon His name. Therefore, beware of the neglect of good duties, and of all those hidden entanglements of the flesh which lead to these sins and make excuses for them.

### Galatians 5, verse 17.

> For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.

<margin>22nd Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry in London, January 26, 1650.</margin> <note>St. Lawrence Jewry is a historic church in London; 1650 places this during the English Commonwealth period.</note> After I have shown above by what means and ways the flesh seeks to draw people away from religious duties, I shall now also show you how the same seeks to hinder and disturb people in the performance of those duties. This subject is very useful in the exercise of godliness, and there are many cases of conscience <note>Technical term for specific moral dilemmas or spiritual struggles.</note> which can be properly handled here. But before I propose the questions which I intend to treat, I shall set before you these ten propositions or theses regarding the hindrances of the flesh in the good duties of the godly.

<margin>The first proposition.</margin> The first is this: that the corruption of the flesh is more powerful in disturbing the godly in holy duties than in leading them away from the same. Certainly, corrupt nature overcomes the unregenerate <note>Those who have not experienced a spiritual rebirth.</note> in drawing them away from religion, but the opposite is true in the regenerate. The godly are not so much subject to being drawn away from holy duties as they are to being disturbed within them; the neglect of duties can be recognized as evil even by a natural conscience, and therefore the godly are not often overcome in that way; but of the hindrances *within* the duties, the natural conscience does not have such knowledge.

<margin>The second proposition.</margin> The second is that a God-fearing person is more disturbed in his religion by his own heart than by the Devil or the world, or anything else outside of him. We often blame our vocation, and the Devil—that he goes about us and is busy ensnaring us—when we have more reason to blame our own evil heart. Just as it is characteristic of the godly, when they sin, to blame <margin>2 Sam. 24:10.</margin> their corrupt nature and not the Devil, as David did; so it is also when the godly are disturbed in their religion, that they blame neither the Devil nor the world <margin>Rom. 7:18.</margin> so much as their own hearts. As the Apostle Paul says of himself: "To will is present with me; but how to perform <margin>v. 20.</margin> that which is good I find not"; that is, I do not find that fitness to be very attentive in religion: but whom does he blame? Not the Devil nor the world, <margin>Rom. 7:25.</margin> but it is the sin that dwells in me. And in verse 25 he says, "With the mind I myself serve [the law of God...]"
