# The Struggle between <note>The header is incomplete in the original; based on context, it refers to the struggle between the Flesh and the Spirit.</note>

unfitness for duty should pull a man away from duty. Many Christians whose consciences are troubled are overcome by this. Here is the answer.

<margin>Remedies against this.</margin>
Firstly: many Christians who plead their own unfitness often neglect their duty more out of an aversion to it than out of actual inability. Seneca says very well to this end in one of his books: men (he says) pretend that they cannot do what is good, but the true cause is that they do not want to do it. It is an aversion in the heart that prevents them from performing their duties. It is noteworthy that where the Apostle speaks of an unfitness for the service of God, he also mentions the enmity of a natural man’s heart against the same. The carnal mind (he says) is enmity against God, for it does not subject itself to the Law of God; indeed, it cannot. So those who plead their unfitness have reason to examine their hearts, to see if their neglect of God’s service does not stem more from a perversity of the mind than from an inability in their capacity.

<margin><note>original Latin: "Nolle in causa est cum non posse praetenditur."</note> Unwillingness is the cause when inability is the pretext. Seneca Epistle 116.</margin>
<margin>Romans 8:7.</margin>
<margin>Exodus 4:10, 13, 19, 20.</margin>
Secondly: Christians are naturally inclined to use their unfitness as a reason for their neglect of God’s service when the danger associated with it keeps them back, rather than the unfitness itself. You have a remarkable example of this in Moses, who was a pious man. The whole history is set out at length in the fourth chapter of Exodus. God commands Moses to go to Egypt and take the care of His people upon himself: but what does Moses say? "O Lord," he says, "will You send me to lead this people? Oh, I am not fit, I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor since You have spoken to Your servant: for I am slow of speech and slow of tongue." This pretext had some appearance of truth, and therefore he said in the thirteenth verse: "O Lord, please send by the hand of whomever else You will send." But was the unfitness of Moses the true cause why he did not want to go? Not at all; therefore in the nineteenth verse the real reason is revealed. "Return," said the Lord, "to Egypt, for all the men are dead who sought your life." There God points out the cause with His finger. Moses had previously killed an Egyptian, and they had sought him out; and when God commanded Moses to return to Egypt, he was terrified. But Moses did not say this to God; instead, he pleaded his unfitness. Then the Lord told him that the men were dead who sought his life; and then, it says there, Moses took his wife and his sons and returned to the land of Egypt.

<margin>The fifteenth trick of the flesh.</margin>
The last deception is taken from the fruitlessness of serving God; see, the flesh will approach you thus: "Why do you need to walk in a godly way? You have prayed many times and heard many sermons, and you have not become a hair better for it." Here is the answer.

<margin>Remedies against this. I.</margin>
Firstly: you owe God your service simply because you are His creature, even if He never gave you any fruit from His service.

<column-break/>

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly: the service of God is its own fruit; and also the performing of our duties is a reward in itself. Even if God never brought you to Heaven, you already have a reward in part because God allows you to serve Him here. You have your fruit unto holiness, as the Apostle says, and the end is everlasting life. Holiness and godliness are the very path of our service.

<margin>Romans 6:22.</margin>
<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly: know that two kinds of fruit follow godliness: first, a true and actual fruit, and second, a felt fruit. Sometimes the fruit is sensible, and a person's affections are stirred, and his desires are subdued; but even though the fruit is not always felt, it is nonetheless always actual. A godly person obtains an actual good through the religious duties he performs; whatever good anyone does, he shall receive the same from the Lord, whether he be a slave or free. No one shall open the doors of God’s house in vain. The wicked Ahab performed only a temporary service to God, and God gave him a temporary reward. There is, therefore, always a true reward that accompanies the performance of our religious duties. And thus I have presented the promises and deceptions of the flesh, by which it seeks to draw men away from the service of God, and I have answered them all, so that you might not be deceived by that same craftiness.

<margin>Ephesians 6:8.</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 21:29.</margin>
<margin>The Utility.</margin>
The usefulness of all this will be for those people who feel in their consciences that they have been deceived by some of these tricks of corrupt nature, such that they have neglected good duties. I would like to bring these five considerations to their minds.

<margin>I.</margin>
First: that a man can go to Hell just as much for the neglect of good duties as for the actual committing of sins. The natural conscience will tell a man that gross sinners shall not inherit the Kingdom of God; but the Scripture will also tell you that men shall go to Hell for the omission of good. It is noteworthy that the sentence which shall be spoken on the last day by the Judge of the whole world does not mention actual sins as much as the neglect of good duties, for which men shall be condemned.
<margin>Matthew 25:41, 42, 43.</margin>
> "Depart from me, you cursed," Christ shall say; "For I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat: I was thirsty, and you gave me nothing to drink. I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me."

They are condemned solely because of their omissions in their required duty. Perhaps you do not die a drunkard, nor an adulterer, nor a blasphemer, nor a deceiver; but if you die being negligent in religious duties, I tell you, the accusation will be found against you. He did not squander his Master’s talent, but because he <insert>did not use</insert> it... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as it continues on the next page.</note>

Look, it was only because he had neglected to circumcise his son when he was eight days old; this provoked God so much to anger that he sought to kill Moses. Yet Moses could have brought forward more plausible excuses for his neglect than we can do for many religious duties which we overlook. I say this to show you the danger of the sin of omission.

<margin>V.</margin> Fifthly and finally, consider that you would not accept such a defense as valid in other matters. ### Conflict Between ###
<meta>catchword: heart</meta>

...the Law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin. The flesh has the force of a Law, through which we come to sin even in the service of God; and therefore, O man, do not accuse the devil, nor the World, but your own heart.

<margin>The third proposition.</margin>
The third is that the corruption of the flesh, which disturbs us in God's service, is manifest and powerful, both in secret and public duties. Your heart will attack you vehemently when you are alone between God and your soul, and also when you are in the general assembly; your own experience will confirm the truth of this: what wandering and distracted thoughts do you find within you whenever you are in your private room? Indeed, how difficult it is even in public duties to bind one's thoughts, to fix one's mind, and to restrain one’s devotion.

<margin>The fourth proposition.</margin>
The fourth is that a man's heart and corrupt nature are more apt to disturb him in unusual duties than in common and ordinary ones. Therefore, a man shall find more evil thoughts within himself on a solemn Fast-day than on an ordinary day. Have you ever set yourself to a special and solemn visitation and meditation? If so, then you have also found your heart more unsettled in those duties than in hearing God's Word or in praying: and the reason is because those solemn duties help most of all toward the Christian’s growth in grace; and therefore, nature will be at its most unceremonious <note>The original Dutch *aldersonbermoepelykst* implies being relentless or acting without restraint.</note> in those religious duties to move and disturb you. The Devil will also not fail to stir your heart to hinder you in those services by which his Kingdom suffers the greatest damage.

<margin>The fifth proposition.</margin>
The fifth proposition is this: that the less people prepare their hearts for God's service, the more they shall be disturbed therein by their corrupt nature. Greenham <note>Richard Greenham (c. 1535–1594) was a prominent Puritan clergyman known for his works on practical divinity and the "cure of souls."</note> also accounts for this in his observations. "What is the reason," he asks, "that Christians can never pray without distractions, nor hear God's Word without wandering thoughts? O man!" he says, "believe me, who has experienced it: if you prepared yourself more for God's service, you would be less distracted in it." A medicine for the body does little good if it is taken on a full stomach and if the body is not prepared; so it is with duties and established services of God: they will do you little good unless you first prepare yourself for them.

<margin>The sixth proposition.</margin>
The sixth is that the flesh disturbs us more in those duties that others perform than those we do ourselves. A Minister, when he delivers a Sermon, has fewer flying thoughts while preaching than he would have if he were a listener; the reason is because at such a time his understanding is busy thinking on those things which he must present to his hearers. Likewise, if any of you were praying in a company, you would not be so distracted therein, because the people's praise and the respect you bear the company before whom you pray so bind your thoughts that they do not wander, so that you do not come to shame in that duty; but if you prayed together with others, you would be more careless and more distracted.

<column-break/>

Therefore, you to whom it is not given to preach or pray in public, watch your heart well, for the flesh will more easily disturb you in those duties in which you join with others than in those which you would perform yourself.

<margin>The seventh proposition.</margin>
<margin><note>original Latin: "Ferventior esse solet, qui rem primum aggreditur. Plurimi novitate conversionis ferventior orant, postea languidi. postea negligentior. Aug."</note> He who first undertakes a thing is usually more fervent. Most pray more fervently in the novelty of conversion; afterward they become languid, afterward more negligent. — Augustine</margin>
The seventh is that the corruption of the flesh in the holy may sometimes be more vehement after one has been busy in God's service for a long time than it seemed to be at your first conversion. It may be that someone in their first conversion can pray without being distracted, but that their love, their joy and delight—indeed, their whole soul—is caught up in the service: but after the passage of time, after some duration and perseverance in the ways of God's service, it can happen that he begins to grow faint, and performs all his duties only outwardly, cursorily, and out of habit. Augustine also noted this, saying that many pray with feeling and zeal in their first conversion, but thereafter in a briefness and deadness, losing that liveliness and warmth of affection which they maintained within themselves at their first conversion.

<margin>The eighth proposition.</margin>
The eighth proposition is: that in all the time of our lives, we do not perform one service to God which does not have upon it some corruption of the flesh; although the service in itself is good, something evil nevertheless clings to it, insofar as it comes from you. Praying is good, and hearing God's Word is good, but insofar as these services of God pass through the heart of your unrefined soul, they become unclean—even so much so that God could rightfully accuse even the reborn of their sin in their holy duties.
<margin>Romans 7:21.</margin>
"When I want to do good," says Paul, "I find that evil is present with me." It is true, the natural movements of the flesh may be trimmed away, but some sinfulness always clings to your service of God. Worthy of observation is this ceremonial or ecclesiastical Law of which we read in Exodus 28: namely, that Aaron should have a plate of pure gold upon his forehead when he entered into the Holy of Holies, so that he might bear the iniquity of the holy things <note>The "iniquity of the holy things" refers to the idea that even our best religious acts are tainted by human imperfection and need atonement.</note> of the children of Israel. This means (says a theologian) that Jesus Christ, our forerunner, has entered into the Holy of Holies, and through his intercession and sitting at the right hand of his Father, has that plate of pure gold upon his forehead, where he bears not only the iniquity of our lives but also of our holy things; and if it were not so, and if no duplicity clung to our unholy duties, so that we could perform some pure service of God without any clinging corruption, you still could not stand before God in the best prayer you ever made, or in the best service you ever performed. We have need of a Christ as a Mediator, not only for our sins, but also for our service to God.

<margin>The ninth proposition.</margin>
The ninth is this: that it is the most difficult thing in the world to bind the heart so firmly to any service of God that the flesh does not come to disturb you. Just as Eliphaz reasoned with Job, so may everyone do with his own heart: Why does your heart carry you away? 
<margin>Job 15:12, 13.</margin>

### The tenth proposition. ###

<margin>
Exodus 27:4–5
</margin>
The last proposition is that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses your holy duties from that clinging guilt and filth. God knows that you are but humans and not <term>Angels</term> <note>meaning perfect, sinless beings</note> when you come to serve Him. You are imperfect here, and therefore He does not expect a perfect service from you. Therefore, here is your comfort: that your failings in God’s service shall never condemn you, provided you are <term>reborn</term> <note>Dutch: *weder-geboren*; referring to the spiritual rebirth or regeneration in Christian theology</note>. You may often be hindered in your service to God, but those disturbances will not lead you to damnation, because Jesus Christ wipes away the stains from your religious duties. We read in the <term>Ceremonial Law</term> <note>The laws given to Israel regarding rituals and sacrifices</note> that the Altar of the burnt offering had a grate made of bronze network, so that the dust and the ash would fall through it and thus be carried away. This is an example of the intercession of Jesus Christ: for although you may have great emotion and fire in your services and offerings to God, there is nonetheless much "ash" of corruption mixed in. Just as that grate was made to remove the ash, so also is Christ the <term>Mediator</term>, who desires to carry away all our failings in God's service. And this ought to give courage to the children of God, so that even though they are weak in their worship, they do not come to neglect it. Are you eager 
to hear God's Word? Then do not stop hearing it; and though you are frequently distracted in prayer, do not neglect the Prayer; for it is the office of Jesus Christ to bear the iniquity of our holy things. These are the propositions and conclusions which I wanted to set forth before I came to the handling of the following point of doctrine, namely:

<margin>
Doctrine.
</margin>
**That corrupt nature, even in the reborn, has such power that it often disturbs and hinders them in the performance of holy services.**

In handling this Doctrine, I shall discuss these distinct things:

1. I shall confirm the truth of this Doctrine.
2. I shall show you in what way the <term>flesh</term> <note>the "vleesch" or fallen human nature</note> comes to hinder us in God's service.
3. In what things the disturbances and hindrances of the flesh most clearly appear.

<margin>
The first question.

Romans 7:18.
<note>Reference printed as Rom. 7. 11.</note>

<note>original Greek: "το γαρ θελειν παρακειται μοι το δε κατεργαζεσθαι το καλον ουχ ευρισκω"</note>
For to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
</margin>
But first, as proof of this Doctrine, you have not only Paul’s testimony, but also his own experience: *The will is indeed with me, but to do the good, that I find not*; that is, I do not find how I shall work it out, or how I shall bring a service of God from the beginning to the end. In the original text, the same word is used as in Phi-

<column-break/>

lippians 2:12, where we are commanded to *work out* our salvation with fear and trembling. Now, just as he complains of himself and gives you his own experience, so we may all join our experience with his and say that we "do not find" how to do the good. Just as rust clings to iron, so the flesh clings to all our services to God. In general, does our own heart not tell us that there is a great deal of worldliness in it? And are there not many vain and untimely thoughts in the duties we perform for God? And that not only in common duties, but also in private ones? In **Prayer**, how the flesh disturbs us through vain and unfit thoughts and evil motives! How it kills our affections, how it damns our zeal, and how it distresses our hearts! In **hearing God’s Word**, how the flesh throws prejudices and misunderstandings, unbelief and forgetfulness into us! In **Meditations**, how it causes our hearts to go up and down unsteadily, so that we cannot bring our meditations to a complete end? In **Conversations**, how the flesh mixes our rebukes with vain glory? When you come to the **Lord’s Supper**, how the flesh then prevents you from showing sincere sorrow, prevents your love from being kindled, and prevents your joy in Christ from being awakened? Well, what great reason you have to complain, just as Augustine did when he saw a shepherd tie a stone to the leg of a bird; and as the bird tried to fly upward, it was constantly pulled back down by the stone. So he said, "It is exactly like that with my soul; I would gladly fly on high through holy Meditations, but there is a stone tied to my leg—namely, a corrupt nature—by which I am continually thrust down."

<margin>
2nd Question.
</margin>
### The second Question is: in what way the flesh hinders us in holy duties? ###

<margin>
1st Answer.
</margin>
I shall limit my Answer to these two particular ways which the flesh is accustomed to take in thus hindering us:

1. By advising people that they should decrease and diminish their services to God.
2. By throwing in vain and untimely thoughts.

I say first, by seeking to make people decline in their worship; and thus nature can bring you to the omission of God's service, or at least to making less of a task of God's service than you did before—namely, to pray and hear God's word more rarely. Herein lies a great craftiness of your corrupt heart: that it seeks to make you believe that you do not need to be so zealous, because even smaller actions make the readiness to act weaken and slacken. Certainly, faint and cold praying will in time bring you to not praying at all. To all those who are thus ensnared by the flesh, so that they decline in God's service, I have these three things to say:

<margin>
Remedies 1.
</margin>
First, you have no less need to practice prayer and God's service now than in former times; why then should you serve God less? You have no fewer temptations from the Devil now...

<summary>This page discusses the inherent difficulty of maintaining a focused heart during worship due to "the flesh," using analogies like the bronze grate of the altar and a bird weighted by a stone. # The Battle Between #

...no less corruption in your soul, no fewer spiritual defects, and no less impurity in the church than before; therefore, do not let your nature gain the upper hand, lest it cause you to decline in your **Worship**.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, just as it is a deceit of the heart regarding sin to lead you from small sins to great ones, so it is a deceit of nature regarding virtue to lead you from little **Worship** to no **Worship** at all.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, gradual diminishment and decline in **Worship** can be just as dangerous for your soul as holy omissions; and you can just as easily go to Hell for the first as for the second, although holy neglect provokes God to more anger. Although someone is in greater danger of death who suffers from a <term>fever</term> <note>literally "the shakes" or "ague"</note> than one who suffers from a slow <term>consumption</term> <note>a wasting disease like tuberculosis</note>, nevertheless, the one will bring him to death just as surely as the other. Those people who cast off **Worship** entirely die of a burning fever; but you who decline in **Worship** may come to die of a long-lasting consumption. You may waste away more and more until you are nothing but a skeleton in your **Worship**, so that in your Spirit you have neither the desire nor the strength for the exercises of sanctification.

<margin>Second answer.</margin>
Secondly, and most importantly, I say that the flesh hinders us in **Worship** by throwing in idle and useless thoughts while you are busy in your service to God. These intruded thoughts are of two kinds: namely, either good and permissible in themselves, or evil and impermissible.

<margin>I.</margin>
First, the flesh will throw in thoughts which, considered in themselves, are lawful, but are merely ill-timed. I may say of these, just as the <margin>Leviticus 26:4 compared with Proverbs 26:1.</margin> Scripture speaks of rain—that rain at a proper time is a blessing, but rain during the Harvest is a curse—so too are good thoughts a blessing in their time. But if <margin><note>original Latin: "Quamvis non fit cogitatio mali, est tamen cogitatio mala."</note> Even if it is not a thought of evil, it is still an evil thought.</margin> good thoughts come into you to distract you and draw you away from any good work in which you are engaged, then they are sinful. If you are hearing a Sermon and you think of praying, or if you are in Prayer and you then think of the Sermon, those thoughts are ill-timed and therefore sinful. Just as in printing, no matter how beautiful the letters are, if they stand in the wrong place, they make no sense. Likewise, that impulse was good in Luke 12:13, *Master, tell my Brother to divide the inheritance with me*, yet it was entirely ill-timed because it was proposed while Christ was preaching.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, the flesh will sometimes throw in thoughts which are sinful in themselves; and thus the Prophet complains of the Israelites: <margin>Ezekiel 33:31</margin> *They come to you as people used to come, and sit before your face as my people, and hear your words, but they do not do them: for they make lovely songs with their mouths, but their heart walks after their greed.* Even in their **Worship**, they had sinful thoughts of how they might fulfill their greedy desires.

---

<margin>3rd Question.</margin>
The third Question is: wherein is the strength of the flesh most evident in disturbing us in holy services?
I shall answer this Question in two ways.
1. That the flesh seeks to disturb people in the *manner* of practicing their **Worship**.

<column-break/>

2. In their *aim* or purpose for why they practice it.

---

These are two of the primary assaults of the flesh in this regard.

<margin>1st Answer.</margin>
First, the flesh disturbs a person primarily in the *manner* in which he performs his **Worship**; and that in these various ways.

<margin>First ambush.</margin>
Firstly, the flesh ensures that a person performs their **Worship** with weariness and without cheerfulness. Solomon says that much reading is a weariness of the flesh; and if <margin>Ecclesiastes 12:12.</margin> reading is so, how much more are religious exercises? When the mind is drawn toward them, the devil and man’s own nature stand ready to hinder and disturb us therein. Human nature, in particular, is quickly exhausted; this is why you are so strongly exhorted <margin>Galatians 6:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:13.</margin> not to grow weary in doing good. And what is the reason for this other than that the corruption of man's <margin>Malachi 1:13.</margin> heart constantly seeks to make him weary? Everything that nature performs, it performs tirelessly; therefore the Sun is not weary of shining, nor the fire of burning, nor the Sea of ebbing and flowing, because these are natural movements. It is natural for a man to commit sin, and therefore the Scripture says that people do not tire of committing unrighteousness; but to practice holiness and grace in any **Worship** is not only above, but also against nature. This is why in Scripture, Hell is compared to a pit and Heaven to a mountain. Now, as one knows, it is easy even for a child who can barely walk to tumble into a pit, but it is difficult to climb a mountain. You can very easily fall into the bottomless pit, but the way to Heaven is up the mountain and difficult to ascend; and therefore it is written in the Prophet Isaiah that the mountain <margin>Isaiah 2:2.</margin> of the Lord’s House shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; namely, because the practices of **Worship** are against nature and go, as it were, against wind and stream.

Now it comes to mind that a <term>Theologian</term> <note>literally "God-learned one"</note> explains the corruption of man's heart, which hinders him in **Worship**, through a parable taken from a bird in the egg. As long as the bird is in the shell, it cannot move; but as soon as it has pecked its way out and the shell is broken, it has a lively movement. So it is with a person engaged in **Worship**; while he is troubled by flesh and blood, he is like a bird in the shell who cannot move himself. But if the shell is broken for someone—that is, if corruption is brought under subjection and grace gains the upper hand—then he is like a bird out of the shell and can move and act livelily in the holy services of God.

<margin>Zechariah 5:9.</margin>
The Prophet Zechariah speaks of those who had the wind in their wings: to indicate (as the commentators explain that passage) the speed and haste which those **Reformers** used. But we, on our way to Heaven, have neither wings nor the wind; rather, we go against wind and against tide, and yet we would gladly run without ceasing the race <margin>Hebrews 12:1.</margin> that is set before us, by which we are then easily tired, especially when it is up the Mountain.

-># Flesh and Spirit. <-

<margin>Hebrews 12:1</margin>
In this, then, is revealed the corruption of your hearts: that it causes you to perform your **Worship** with retraction <note>original: "herroepinge" - suggesting a heart that pulls back or is not fully committed</note>. This corruption is like a block intended to hinder us; and therefore the Apostle commands us to *lay aside every weight and the sin that so easily ensnares us.* Corrupt nature is a burden; and you know that if someone runs a race with a weight upon his shoulders, he is quickly exhausted.

<margin>The second defeat.</margin>
Secondly, corrupt nature causes you to perform your **Worship** with wandering thoughts. Just as in the sea one wave follows another, and as in the sky clouds follow the rain, so also in the heart one useless thought follows another. The corruption of man's heart makes him vain in his thoughts. O man, while you are in God's house, the devil is in your heart as if in his workshop, creating vain contemplations and thoughts in your mind, by which you are turned away from God. You have a notable illustration of this if you compare two scriptural texts together, both of which are the words of Solomon. <margin>Ecclesiastes 2:14</margin> In Ecclesiastes 2:14 it is written: *The wise man’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.* Yet, if one considers the natural position and placement of the eye, the eye of a fool is just as much in his head as that of a wise man. What then is Solomon’s meaning when he says that the wise man’s eyes are in his head? He means to say this: that the wise man’s eyes are fixed and unmoved upon a certain matter, not wandering everywhere. But how is it with the eyes of a fool? Solomon says in <margin>Proverbs 17</margin> Proverbs <note>original: "By-vuck" - an archaic Dutch term for the Book of Proverbs</note> 17:24: *The eyes of a fool are at the ends of the earth.* That is to say, he has a wandering heart, which is by no means fixed upon **Worship**. Solomon gives this lesson in <margin>Proverbs 4:25</margin> Proverbs 4:25: *Let your eyes look straight ahead, and let your eyelids look right before you.* That is, the thoughts of your heart must not be turned aside, neither to the right nor to the left. But herein is the misery of a God-fearing person: that the flesh often makes him serve God with wandering and straying thoughts. As Augustine complains: *My heart has gone from me, and I cannot overtake it, and even when I have overtaken it, I still cannot hold it fast.* You know how slippery an eel is; the harder you grip it, the more easily it slips from your hands. So it is with your heart; you may try to hold it fast, but it will slip away from you, do what you can. And from where does this come, if not from the wickedness of your nature?

<margin>The third ambush.</margin>
Thirdly, the flesh causes you to perform your **Worship** by trusting in it; that is, you rest upon the act itself. If the devil cannot stop you by throwing in distracting thoughts, he will seek to hinder you by throwing in thoughts of vain confidence. Against this evil you must stand on guard. *We are those* (says the Apostle to the Philippians <margin>Philippians 3:3</margin>) *who serve God in the Spirit, and glory in Christ Jesus, and put no confidence in the flesh.* That is, we do not remain attached to our own performances of service. *And do not trust in false words* (says the <margin>Jeremiah 7:4</margin> Prophet) *saying, "The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord."* This was the cunning of the devil: when he could not make the people despise the Temple, he did his best to bring them to the other extreme—namely, to trust in the Temple

<column-break/>

and the service performed therein; and therefore God calls those "false, lying words." Scripture recounts a battle fought by the Philistines against Israel, in which <margin>1 Samuel 4:2</margin> about four thousand men of the Israelites fell. When they had suffered this defeat, the survivors went to investigate the reason why the hand of the Lord had been against them; and they concluded it was because the Ark of God was not with them. "Well, let us" (they said) "take the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord from Shiloh to us; and let it come into the midst of us, that it may save us from the hand of our enemies." So they did, but when they had brought the Ark to them, it is written that they lost <margin>1 Samuel 4:10</margin> thirty thousand foot-soldiers in the second battle. What was the reason they had even less success when they had the Ark with them than before? The reason was because they placed their trust in the Ark, which was merely an external sign and testimony of God's presence. Therefore, God wanted to punish their fleshly trust, for this is the cunning of the devil: if he cannot pull you away from **Worship**, he will then try to make you trust in it.

*For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you would.*

<margin>23rd Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry in London on February 2, 1650. The fourth ambush.</margin> <note>St. Lawrence Jewry is a prominent church in the City of London, rebuilt by Christopher Wren after the Great Fire.</note>
In the last sermon, I showed you the ways through which the Devil and your own heart try to pull you away and hinder you in **Worship**. Now I shall add some others to them; and the fourth is this:

The flesh will do its best to make you perform your **Worship** with distrust. Faith is that shield with which we resist the devil, and Scripture commands us <margin>Ephesians 6:16</margin> *above all, to take up the shield of faith, with which we shall be able to quench all the fiery arrows of the wicked one.* Corrupt nature seeks above all to weaken your faith. <margin>Luke 24:25</margin> *O foolish and slow of heart to believe!* says our Savior. See, Christ lays the blame on your hearts; while your flesh is busy making you slow of heart to believe and to trust in Jesus Christ. <margin>Hebrews 11:6</margin> *He who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him.* Without faith, you can perform no service in which God would take pleasure; and therefore this is one of the primary designs of the devil: to rob you of your faith. Christ said to Peter that Satan had desired to sift him like wheat, but (He says) <margin>Luke 22:31, 32</margin> *I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.* Satan singled out Peter's faith above all his other gifts of grace, and therefore the care of Christ revealed itself most of all in preserving Peter's faith from failing. And just as the devil acts here, so also our heart is busy within us to rob us of our faith, but Christ has prayed for us; and true faith shall never fail.

Fifthly, this is also a plot of the flesh: that it makes you perform **Worship**...

<margin>*He does nothing unless commanded.* <note>original Latin: "Nil nisi jussus agit."</note></margin>
performing [worship] with compulsion and not voluntarily; the flesh puts a person in such a posture that he is rather pushed than led to **Divine Service**: he is driven there, like a child to school, or a bear to the stake—that is, with much opposition. In contrast, he leaves Divine Service like a bird leaves a snare—that is, with much delight.

<margin>The sixth ambush.</margin>
Sixthly, the flesh will cause you to perform your **Divine Service** unfaithfully, without delight of heart. And this is a great craftiness of the flesh: even if it cannot make you stop serving God, it will nevertheless ensure that you never have joy or pleasure in that service. Thus, I have shown you what the disruptions and obstacles of the flesh are regarding the *manner* of our Divine Services.

But secondly, the flesh hinders and disturbs a man also in the **end and aim** <note>The "end" refers to the ultimate goal or motivation for an action.</note> for why one performs Divine Service. Therefore, I shall show you here which evil ends the flesh casts into us when we serve God; for if the flesh cannot hinder you in the *manner*, it will do so in the *goal*. I shall then, I say, briefly review and consider how the flesh comes to hinder a man in his service regarding the end. There are certainly such evil ends which the flesh casts in whenever you are busy in Divine Service.

<margin>The first evil intention.</margin>
Firstly, the flesh will make you perform your good duties more out of **vain glory** <term>vain glory: seeking honor or praise from other people rather than from God</term> than for the glory of God. It is noteworthy what you read in Galatians 5, verse 26. The Apostle concludes that chapter with this warning: *let us not be seekers of vain glory*; after he had shown them what the fruits of the Spirit were and had exhorted them to walk by the Spirit, he then gives them this advice: that they should not be seekers of vain glory, indicating that there is such an inclination in man's nature to make him ambitious even in doing good. The Apostle James also expresses this when he says: *Do you think the Scripture says in vain, the Spirit that dwells in us lusts to envy?* Envy is a fruit of vain glory, for it is a desire that another's abilities might be covered so that ours might shine all the more clearly. And for this reason, some among the Philippians were said to preach Christ out of envy—that is, they gladly displayed their gifts to obtain the people's praise and thus to be placed above Paul. It was only their vain ambition which made them strive to surpass Paul: they did not seek Christ's honor, but their own; not the things of Christ, but their own.

<margin>Philippians 1:15</margin>
<margin>The second evil intention.</margin>
Secondly, the flesh will make you perform **Divine Service** more for outward and worldly profit than for any inward and saving benefit. Thus God complains of His people, that they gathered for *Grain and New Wine*; they did not cry to God for grace, but for grain and wine; they served God for their worldly profit. So also the Lord God speaks through the same Prophet concerning Ephraim, saying: *Ephraim is a heifer, that loves to thresh.* Ephraim loved the Divine Service that could bring in profit and advantage. The flesh never looks in the Divine

<margin>Hosea 7:14</margin>
<margin>Hosea 10:11</margin>

<column-break/>

Service toward spiritual good, nor does it strive for the fellowship of Christ to obtain a **mortification** <term>mortification: the spiritual practice of "killing off" sinful desires or the power of the corrupt nature</term> of corruption, and an awakening of holy affections, with progress in the way of grace and holy experience.

<margin>The third evil intention.</margin>
Thirdly, the flesh will make you serve God more to quiet your **Conscience** than to purify it; just as a thief throws food to a dog only to stop its barking, so that those in the house might not wake up; so do men deal with their consciences. They perform Divine Service because their consciences, like barking dogs, rebuke and accuse them, and therefore they will serve God to still the cry of the conscience, which would otherwise attack them very harshly—just as the sailors in the book of the Prophet Jonah called to their god only because the peril of death awakened their natural conscience.

<margin>Jonah 1:5</margin>
<margin>The fourth evil intention.</margin>
Fourthly, the flesh will let men serve God more out of fear of the threats for the neglect of Divine Service than out of love for the Command which ordains the service. The flesh never delights in the commands of God, but all its fear is for the terrible threats of God’s Law. If there were nothing in the Scripture but promises and commands, then a godless man would do nothing at all and yet still be confident; but because threats are also woven in, therefore the godless also take up Divine Service and duties. It is written of the righteous that he *fears the commandment*, but a godless man never fears the command; he may fear the punishment and the threats, but only a godly man dares not neglect Divine Service because God commands it.

<margin>Proverbs 13:13</margin>
<margin>The fifth evil intention. *Love of reward, or mercenary love.* <note>original Latin: "Mercedis amor, vel amor mercenarius."</note></margin>
Fifthly, the flesh will cause the performance of **Divine Service** to be undertaken more out of hope for the eternal reward than out of any inward and spiritual excellence which the soul sees in the service. Now, although God will allow us to have a love for the reward, nevertheless He does not want us to look only or mostly upon that.

<margin>The sixth evil intention.</margin>
Sixthly, corrupt nature will make men serve God more to avert outward judgments upon the body than inward ones upon the soul. Thus the heathen sailors cried to their gods when they were in a storm and thought they would perish, so that the storm might cease and they might reach land safely; everyone fell to praying. But this is only a slavish and fleshly aim of Divine Service: that one performs it more to escape judgments upon the body than upon the soul. And so it was with the Egyptians; when the Lord God struck their firstborn, Pharaoh and the Egyptians cried to the children of Israel: *Rise up, get out from among us, you and your sheep and your cattle, and go, serve the Lord your God.* And they urged them strongly, for they said, "We are all dead men." Pharaoh did not want to let them go before, but when their departure could serve for his preservation, he then commanded them to go out. It is in the nature of all men to perform Divine Service more to escape outward than inward afflictions and judgments. To this effect says

<margin>Jonah 1:5</margin>
<margin>Exodus 12:31, 32, 33.</margin>

# 81 Flesh and Spirit.

<margin>
Jeremiah 22:23.
</margin>
the Prophet Jeremiah says: *O you who dwell in Lebanon, and nest in the Cedars, how favored will you be when pains come upon you, the woe as of a woman in labor.* <note>original: "O ghy die in den Libanon woont... hoe begenadight sult ghy zijn..."</note> It is the external and not the internal parts that bring the godless to **Divine Service**.

<margin>
Hebrews 2.
</margin>
Seventhly, the flesh will allow people to serve God so that they may sin with greater freedom and less suspicion. The Apostle had to defend himself against this very thing—namely, that he did not preach the Gospel as a cloak for sin. This is a natural human tendency; just as the harlot wanted to cover her wickedness with her thank-offerings, so many godless people want to cover their sins with a veneer of **Godliness**. Our Savior condemned the Scribes and Pharisees for this, for they *devoured widows' houses* under the pretense of long prayers. They did not do wrong in the act of praying itself, nor in the length of the prayer—for long prayer is no sin—but they failed in the *purpose* of their prayers. They prayed long so that they might devour widows' houses; they made a profession of Divine Service to be esteemed as righteous by the people and worthy of being entrusted with things, so that they might get the estates and money of widows into their hands and thereby deceive them. For I consider this to be the particular meaning of that passage. Thus, I have brought to an end the confirmation and explanation of this Doctrine.

<margin>
The use for instruction.
</margin>
This Doctrine shall serve first for instruction, and secondly for comfort. First, there are eight consequences serving the general main point, which I shall draw out for instruction regarding the hindrances of the flesh in the service of the **reborn** <term>reborn: those who have undergone a spiritual renewal through grace</term>.

First, see here the great misery of the **unregenerate** <term>unregenerate: those still in their natural state of sin, not yet spiritually "born again"</term>. If the flesh so hinders the Godly—who nevertheless possess the gifts of grace—how much more does the flesh render powerless the godless, who have no grace at all. People who are in their natural state are in a dead state; they are dead people who can work no good. They are "powerless," as the Apostle speaks; he compares a man to someone who has fallen into mud and slime and has no strength to help himself. Or it is a metaphor taken from a dead body, which is entirely unable to help or move itself; and therefore the Apostle uses this word, *body of death* <note>original Greek: "σῶμα θανάτου"</note>—a dead, weak, or powerless body.

The Scripture describes the natural man in four ways:

<margin>
Genesis 6:5.
</margin>
1. That he has lost his powers; therefore you can perform no good work. The imagination of man's heart is only evil every day; the heart of man is evil; there is no good in it, and it is *only* evil, and it is *always* and without ceasing evil—it is evil every day. This is man’s natural state. *The mind of the flesh does not subject itself to the Law of God, for it cannot.* <note>Romans 8:7</note> There you have the weakness of man’s nature.

<margin>
Romans 8:7.
</margin>
2. You have no power to have any good movement; you cannot only perform no good actions, but you cannot even have good thoughts. The Apostle Paul confirms this, saying: *Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to*

<margin>
2 Corinthians 3:5.
</margin>

<column-break/>

*think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God.*

3. A natural man is not able to speak a good word; he can do nothing good, nor think, nor speak. Christ, rebuking the Pharisees, said to them: *You brood of vipers, how can you speak good things, being evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.*

<margin>
Matthew 12:34.
</margin>

4. <note>The original text repeats "3" in error; this is the fourth point.</note> A natural man cannot understand that which is good for salvation. *He does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.* If a God-fearing person is not able to perform good duties well, how much less an unregenerate person.

<margin>
1 Corinthians 2:14.
</margin>

But you will say: Do the godless not also hear God's Word? Do they not pray? Do they not give alms and perform many other services? Are these not good works? How then is a man powerless to do good?

<margin>
First objection.
</margin>

I answer that good works can be viewed in two ways: either **piously** or **materially** <note>original Latin: "formaliter aut materialiter"</note>. Certainly, a godless man can do that which is "materially"—that is, in itself—good. Thus, hearing God's Word, praying, and giving alms are good when considered in themselves. He can do what is outwardly good, but to do good "piously"—that is, with all the requirements and coinciding circumstances required for a good work—that is not in the power of any godless man in the world.

<margin>
Answer.

Formally or materially.
</margin>

Many circumstances must come together for a work to be good.

Among others is this: that he who does the work must be in Christ. The very same work for which an evil man will go to Hell shall be for a God-fearing man—if he does it—a way to Heaven. So the person who does the good must have a right standing in Christ; we must acknowledge every good thing which is in us through Jesus Christ, as the Apostle speaks. Therefore, although the godless can do what is morally good, they still cannot perform any work which is **Divinely good**.

<margin>
What is required for a good work.

"He does not say 'you can do nothing difficult,' but He says 'you can do nothing.'" - Augustine. <note>original Latin: "Non dicit nihil difficis potest sed nicit nihil potest perficere sed nil potest facere Aug." A reference to John 15:5.</note>

Second objection.
</margin>

But if the godless cannot do good works, but rather sin in the doing of them, for what purpose should they perform any Divine Service? They sin if they do not pray, and they sin when they do pray; why then should they perform any of these duties?

To this, the answer is that these objections truly correspond with "flesh and blood"; and Job presents them in the person of a godless man: *I shall be godless,* he says, *why then should I labor in vain?* As if he said: If I sin when I pray or hear God’s Word, why then do I work for nothing? And to answer this objection, I say:

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>

Firstly, although a godless man sins in Divine Service, he must nevertheless perform it; he is obligated to it, though not for the purpose of sinning in it. That which is good in itself must not be omitted, even though some accidental evil follows it. It is good in itself that a man hears God's Word, prays, and performs other religious duties, but it happens...

<summary>This page argues that while the unregenerate can perform "materially" good deeds like prayer or almsgiving, they lack the spiritual capacity to perform "piously" good works acceptable to God. It highlights the "body of death" and the total inability of fallen human nature to please God without being in Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the "flesh" (fallen human nature) and its inability to perform spiritual duties. # 82 Struggle Between

<margin>
II.
</margin>
it happens only by chance that someone sins within it; for if this reasoning were valid, then for the same reason the Sun would have to stop shining because it heats some bodies too much and brings on a fever, or because it dries out the earth too much.

Secondly, one sins less in the performance of **Divine Service**, even if one happens to sin while doing it, than if one neglected it entirely.

<margin>
Third objection.
</margin>
But you will say: if a godless person is thus unfit and powerless to perform **Divine Service** well, what purpose do God’s Commandments serve? This is an objection of the <term>Pelagians</term> <note>Followers of the 5th-century monk Pelagius, who believed humans could achieve goodness through their own efforts without needing prior divine grace. Here, the author uses it to label his theological opponents.</note>. Does God not mock man, they say, when He commands godless people to worship Him and turn to Him, even though they are as powerless to perform these duties as they are to move the world from its place?

<margin>
Answer.
1.
</margin>
To this I answer that although the godless are so powerless, God nevertheless has great reason to command such things.

First, to let them see what they once were; for in the state of innocence <note>The theological state of humanity before the Fall of Adam.</note> they were completely capable of doing the will of God.

<margin>
II.
God commands not what we can do, but what we ought to do. <note>original: "Deus jubet non quod possumus sed quod debemus."</note>
</margin>
Secondly, although God commands people to do what they cannot, this is nonetheless useful to humble them, so that they may thereby acknowledge their own powerlessness.

<margin>
III.
The Word of God is not only declarative but also effective. <note>original: "Verbum Dei non est declarativum modo sed effectivum."</note>
</margin>
Thirdly, although God commands people to do what they cannot achieve themselves, God the Lord nevertheless gives His own power at one time or another, through His command, to all the elect; even if they are unregenerate, He makes His command powerful in their souls. With God's command, a Divine power went to the dead Lazarus, by which he rose from the grave; God, who commands the godless to repent, can also pour a power into his heart to make him repent. Thus, there is great reason and usefulness in God’s commandments, even though natural men cannot obey them.

<margin>
Second consequence.
Under the praise of grace lie the enemies of grace (Augustine). Not a free will, but a captive will. Not free, but set free. <note>original: "Sub laudibus gratiæ latent inimici gratiæ... Non liberum sed servum arbitrium. Non liberum sed liberatum."</note>
Judges 16:19, 20.
</margin>
Secondly, if the flesh is so powerless toward the good, then the folly of the teachings of the Pelagians, <term>Papists</term> <note>A 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics.</note>, and <term>Arminians</term> <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius who argued that human free will cooperates with God’s grace, a view the author here rejects as exalting "nature" over "grace."</note> becomes clear, for they exalt the power and strength of nature and the free will of man toward supernatural good. Scripture clearly refutes them, for the flesh itself hinders the free will <note>original: "vryame so see" — likely a transcription error for "vrye-wil" or "vrye-macht."</note> so much that they cannot do the good they wish to do. Oh! How great the enemies of God’s grace are these who exalt the power of nature beyond its bounds, and that under the pretext of making God’s grace greater. It is true, man has not lost the *capacity* [for will], but he has lost the *good quality* of it; he has lost the uprightness of his will. I may say of them that their error comes from the same ground by which Samson was deceived; when his wife had shorn off his locks of hair, he awoke from his sleep and said: *I will go out as at other times,* but he did not know that the Lord had departed from him. So may I also say of these people: they would like to rouse themselves as at other times, but their locks have been cut off—through their fall in Adam, that in which their strength lay has been shorn away. If they would only reflect more on the fall of man, they would not exalt the power of nature with such great admiration.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Third consequence.
1 Samuel 12:27, 28.
1 Corinthians 15:10.
Galatians 2:20.
Luke 19:16.
Philippians 1:6.
</margin>
Thirdly, I conclude from this that it is the duty of every Christian to praise and thank God for all these saving abilities which anyone has toward the good. If you have the strength to do any good, it is God's grace. Do as Joab did for David; when Joab had captured the royal city, he sent messengers to David so that David would have the honor of the victory; Joab had indeed done the work, but he still wanted to give David the honor. Do the same for Jesus Christ. If you have performed your duty well, do not say, "I have done so and so," but "Christ has worked that in me," just as the Apostle speaks: *I labored more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.* Likewise, in another place he says, *I live; yet not I, but Christ lives in me.* He wanted to attribute nothing to himself. It is God's grace by which we do any good; the servant in the parable acknowledged this: *Lord,* he said, *your pound has gained ten pounds.* He did not say "my labor" or "my management," but "your pound." Give God the honor, then, for all the good you do; exalt the free grace of God for the beginning, the progress, and the completion of any good work. *He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.*

<margin>
Hebrews 1:12.
Philippians 2:13.
Ezekiel 34:16.
Romans 8:14.
1 Peter 5:10, 11.
</margin>
And He who is the Author will also be the Finisher of your faith. God's grace gives us strength to do any good; *it is God who works in you, both to will and to work according to His good pleasure.* The entire chain of our salvation must be attributed to God's grace. If you are called and confirmed in grace, then marvel at grace and not at nature. We would faint if the Spirit of God did not lead and uphold us. The Apostle Peter sets this before our eyes very strikingly: *The God of all grace, who has called us to His eternal glory; after you have suffered a little while, may He Himself perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you. To Him be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.*

<margin>
Fourth consequence.
Romans 7:24, 25.
Exodus 38:8.
Genesis 25:23.
</margin>
Fourthly, does the flesh make you unfit to do good? Oh, then strive to have a vision and to sharpen your awareness of the obstacles and disturbances you have sensed from the flesh. Thus Paul cried out, *O wretched man that I am!* In Exodus, it is written of a washing basin in which the people's offerings had to be washed, that its base was made with mirrors; so that, as some say, when they came to offer their sacrifices, everyone would look at their face in it to see what stains might be upon them. So also, when you come to **Divine Service**, see, here are the mirrors of the flesh to hinder you, and be humbled. It is written of the Bride, *Return, return, O Shulammite, that we may look upon you.* Then it is asked, *What will you see in the Shulammite?* and the answer is, *As it were the company of two armies* <note>original: "reye van twee heyren" — likely referring to the internal struggle between the old nature and the new.</note>, indicating this conflict. And just as Rebecca said, when the children struggled together in her womb, *Lord, why am I thus?* you should say the same if you have an Esau and a Jacob within—the flesh against the Spirit. Complain to God, saying: *Lord, why am I thus? Why does the flesh trouble and disturb me in all my worship?*

# Flesh and Spirit.
## 83

<margin>
14. Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry <note>A historic parish church in the City of London, rebuilt by Christopher Wren after the Great Fire.</note> within London on February 2, 1650.
</margin>

### Galatians 5:17.

> For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary to one another; so that you do not do the things that you would.

---

I now proceed to draw some other consequences, very useful for practice, from this doctrine: that the flesh often hinders and disturbs even the godly themselves, so that they do not do the things they wish; and the fifth in order is this:

How greatly then even the best of God's children need the mediation and intercession of Jesus Christ, whenever they offer any Divine Service to God; for if we came to God without Christ, with these defilements and disturbances of the flesh in our worship, God might say to us, just as Elisha said to the King of Israel: <margin>2 Kings 3:14</margin> "Truly, were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat the King of Judah, I would not look at you nor see you."

So might God the Father say to each of us: "Truly, if I did not regard Jesus Christ, I would not accept you nor look upon you in any Divine Service which you perform." And just as Joseph said to his brothers, *Unless you bring Benjamin with you, you shall not see my face again*, so also unless you bring the Lord Jesus Christ with you, you will not be able to see God's friendly face. One reads in <margin>Exod. 28:36.</margin> Exodus that Aaron the Priest of the Lord had to have a plate of pure gold on his forehead, in which was engraved: "Holiness to the Lord," to indicate that when you come to perform any Divine Service, you also then need the Mediatorship of Jesus Christ, who through His intercessions bears the iniquities of our holy things. Although you have the assistance of the Spirit in the carrying out of the Divine Service, you nevertheless need the mediation of Christ <margin>Rom. 8:26, 34.</margin> for your acceptance; and therefore one reads not only of the intercession of Christ, but also of the intercession of the Spirit; *The Spirit prays in us, and Christ prays for us.*

<margin>Sixth consequence.</margin>
Sixthly, if the flesh so disturbs you in Divine Service, how greatly must you then keep watch over your heart when you are busy in that service: how much must you then strengthen yourself against the manifold attacks and disturbances of the flesh? Those who live by the seaside are forced for their preservation to build great hills and dikes, so that the sea does not wash them away; whereas for those who live in inland cities, small ditches are enough. Corrupt nature is a Sea, and one must build entire hills and dikes in one's heart, otherwise corrupt nature will send up a flood of vain and untimely thoughts. It is well noted by Ainsworth <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622), a prominent English Nonconformist theologian and scholar.</note> on Numbers 4:23, where it says that all of the sons of Gershon, from thirty to fifty years old, should come in to perform the service in the tent of meeting. The word which means "to perform service" also means "to fight a battle," and so Ainsworth translates it. And why does the Scripture speak thus? Only to

<column-break/>

make it known that when you perform any Divine Service, you must also then fight a spiritual battle. One reads in 1 Peter 4:7 of watching unto prayer, and in Colossians 4:2 of watching in prayer; you must not only watch *unto* prayer—that is, before you pray—but also *in* prayer, while you pray. There are also other disturbances besides these of the flesh, against which you must watch. First, from the world; now this is the Apostle's desire, that we should be without care <margin>1 Cor. 7:32, 33.</margin> and cling to the Lord without being pulled hither and thither. Worldly cares are an obstacle to holy duties; therefore we must watch against them. Secondly, we are also hindered by our natural weaknesses; we must also watch against those. And so I understand with Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian.</note> what Christ said in Matthew 26:41: "The spirit is indeed willing, but the flesh is weak." By "the flesh" here, one must not understand corrupt nature, but bodily weakness. Thirdly, besides the world and natural frailty, the devil also works many obstacles and hindrances <margin>Gen. 15:11.</margin> in us; and in this case you must do as Abraham did, who when the birds came down upon his sacrifices, drove them away. Deodatus <note>Jean Diodati (1576–1649), a Genevan Protestant theologian of Italian descent.</note> says that the coming of the birds upon Abraham's sacrifice aptly illustrates how the devil distracts an elect person when he is busy in any holy work. Do then as Abraham did: when these birds—as the devil is compared to them in Matthew 13:4—these foul and unholy spirits come to disturb you in Divine Service, then drive them away along with all those untimely and vain thoughts which the devil throws into you. In the first chapter of Job one reads that on a certain day the children of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and that Satan also came in the midst of them. By "the children of God" <margin>Job 1:6.</margin> the Angels cannot be understood here, for otherwise it would follow that the devils can also be in Heaven where the good Angels are; therefore by this the children of Job are understood, just as the descendants of Seth are also called <margin>Gen. 6:2. See Zech. 3:1.</margin> the "sons of God" in Genesis 6 who saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful. Now what serves my purpose is that Job's children, on a day, presented themselves before the Lord, which is, according to the commentators, on the Sabbath day. When they presented themselves before the Lord on this day, it says that Satan also came among them, and doubtless not with a good intention, but <margin>The most celebrated feast of the Sabbath, according to Pineda. <note>original: "Celeberrimus Sabathi festum Pined." Sebastian de Pineda was a Spanish Jesuit commentator.</note></margin> as much as he could, to hinder and disturb them in these religious works. Since you then have not only your own heart, the world, and natural weaknesses, but also the devil to hinder and draw you away, how great a reason you have to watch over yourself to your utmost ability.

<margin>Seventh consequence.</margin>
Seventhly, if the flesh thus disturbs you in Divine Service, then place no confidence in your most holy service-performances: would you dare to fix the weight of your soul upon such a weak foundation? If your Divine Services are mixed and defiled with so much evil, how could you then dare to trust in them? Job says, *though I were righteous, yet I would not answer you* <margin>Job 9:15, 28.</margin> and again, *I am afraid of all my sorrows: I know that you will not hold me innocent.*

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of Christ's mediation because human "flesh" corrupts even the best efforts at worship. It exhorts the believer to maintain extreme spiritual vigilance against the distractions of the world, physical weakness, and the devil during prayer.</summary>

# Conflict between Flesh and Spirit

<margin>verse 30.</margin> maintain. In the common Latin translation <note>The Vulgate</note> it says: "I was afraid of all my good works"; further he says: "If I wash myself with snow-water, and cleanse my hands <margin>verse 31.</margin> with soap; yet You will plunge me into the ditch, and my own clothes shall abhor me." <note>A paraphrase of Job 9:28–31.</note> Even if I conduct myself ever so well in Your service, You would still find much evil bound within me. If, then, your best services are mingled with sin, then trust alone in Christ for salvation. To apply this conclusion more powerfully to you, I shall present three pressing considerations.

1. In your acts of Divine Service, there are more workings of sin, which come from the flesh, than of virtue, which come from the Spirit; would you then dare to place your trust in them? They contain more sin than virtue, and more wandering thoughts than holy ones. You forget more of a sermon than you remember of it, and the sin of your nature throws in more distracting thoughts than the Spirit of God provides holy thoughts. Your virtues are like the filings of gold, but your sins are like heaps of dust. How then could you dare to rest upon your acts of Divine Service, expecting life and salvation through them?

2. Consider that a single circumstance is enough to make your service evil, but many combined circumstances cannot make it good. Take your prayer: one circumstance in your prayer can make it sinful. Even if the manner of praying is good, if you still have no good end <note>The "end" refers to the goal or motivation.</note>; or if the end is indeed good, but the origin is evil, then it is of no worth. It is a rule in ethics that the circumstances must be weighed more than <margin>In moral matters, the circumstance is of more weight than the substance of the action.</margin> the work itself; and so it is also in theology. A single circumstance can make a service flawed, but many concurring circumstances cannot make it good.

3. Consider that you are guilty of many past sins, and your present acts of Divine Service can make no restitution for those past sins. Take the example of a tenant: if he pays his current rent properly, this will still not be a restitution for his past debt if he is ten or twenty years behind. So it is also with you; you owe much to God and are in arrears for the time past. Even if there were some merit in your good works—as some claim there is—nevertheless, these present works could not provide atonement for past sins. Therefore, do not trust in your religious performances.

<margin>Last consequence.</margin> Eighthly, if the flesh so hinders us in the service of God, we can observe here the evil nature of sin, the hideous quality of original corruption. One can never dwell upon this doctrine too long; therefore, I pray you, go and rightly behold the evil quality of original sin. I could explain it by this example: if you have a bottle full of water, a little gall will make it more bitter than a great deal of honey will sweeten it. Behold also the hideous nature of sin, how it uglily infects you and your works. We read of a Law in Numbers 19:22: "Whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean." This was said of

<column-break/>

ceremonial uncleanness, but it is also true in spiritual matters. You are unclean, and everything you touch becomes unclean; you defile all your acts of Divine Service. There is a <margin>Haggai 2:12.</margin> very useful passage in the Prophet Haggai, in his second chapter. There was a case of conscience which the people had to ask the Priests of the Law. The question was this: "Behold, if <margin>verse 13.</margin> someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment, and with the fold he touches bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or <margin>verse 14.</margin> any food, shall it become holy?" And the Priests said, "No." Then Haggai said: "If someone who is unclean by a dead body touches any of these things, shall it become unclean?" And the Priests answered and said, "It shall be unclean." Here you may note that holy things could not make common things pure and holy; but if an unclean person merely touched the holy things, they became unclean. Now if you wish to know the meaning of this, the Prophet explains it in the following verse: Then <margin>verse 15.</margin> Haggai answered and said, "So is this people, and so is this nation before my face, says the Lord, and so is every work of their hands; and what they offer there is unclean." That is, all their offerings and acts of worship are unclean. According to the manner of speaking in the Gospel, the meaning is this: if someone is in the state of nature <note>The state of being unregenerate or not yet "born again" in the Spirit.</note>, then all his offerings—that is, all his acts of Divine Service— <margin>Titus 1:15.</margin> are unclean for him. For to the defiled, nothing is pure.

<margin>Second utility: for comfort.</margin> The second use of this doctrine shall be for comfort. I shall give eight comforts to those who fear God and are sensitive to the disturbances and hindrances of the flesh in their acts of Divine Service.

<margin>1.</margin> First, know this for your comfort: just as you have the flesh to hinder you, you also have the Spirit to help you in your service. The Spirit shall come to the aid <margin>Romans 8:26.</margin> of your weaknesses, and pray for you with groanings that cannot be expressed. The flesh hardens your heart and kills your spirit, but God's Spirit makes your heart soft and your spirit lively, so as to pray with sighs. And although <margin>1 John 4:4.</margin> the Devil is busy in tempting you, yet He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world, as John says.

<margin>2.</margin> Secondly, consider that a longing to do those duties which you cannot do is reckoned by God as the doing itself. It is worthy of note <margin>Neh. 1:11 compared with Neh. 5:15.</margin> what is written of Nehemiah, if one compares two scripture passages together. The first is Nehemiah 1:11, where he prays, "O Lord, let Your ear be attentive to the prayer of Your servant, who desires (or longs) to fear Your Name." And in Nehemiah 5:15, Nehemiah says, "I did not burden the people like the previous governors, because of the fear of God." So the desire of Nehemiah to fear the Lord is reckoned by God as the fear of God itself. A longing for <margin>2 Cor. 8:12. See Matt. 5:5, John 7:37, Psalm 10:17, Ps. 145:19, Exo. 14:15, 1 Kings 8:17.</margin> any grace is as much to God as having that grace. God will take the will for the deed; if there is a willing mind, a person is accepted according to what he has, not according to what he does not have. See then what a good God you serve, who is willing to take the intention for the effect, and the intent for the fulfillment, just as...

It is noteworthy what is written of Nehemiah, if one compares two Scripture passages together: the first is Nehemiah 1:11, where he prays, *O <margin>Neh. 1:11 compared with Neh. 5:15.</margin> Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, who desires (or longs) to fear your Name.* And in Nehemiah 5:15, Nehemiah says, *I did not burden the people, as the previous governors did, because of the fear of God.* So Nehemiah's desire <margin>2 Cor. 8:12. see Matt. 5:5. John 7:37. Ps. 10:17. Ps. 145:19. Exo. 14:15. 1 Kings 8:17.</margin> to fear the Lord is recognized by God as the fear of God itself: a longing for any grace is, with God, as much as having it. God will take the will for the deed: *If there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.* See then what a good God you serve, who is willing to take the intention for the effect, and the intent for the fulfillment, just as...

## 85

as can clearly be seen through many testimonies of the Scriptures.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly: feeling a lack of grace or a lack of fitness to perform any Divine Service <note>The Dutch term "Godts-dienst" refers to acts of worship, prayer, or religious duty.</note>, and being grieved by it, is reckoned by God as if that lack were already filled. You say you cannot weep, but you would very gladly weep over your sins: well, the feeling of a lack of some virtue is accepted by God as the having of that virtue. And this, in the judgment of some, is the meaning of that passage, <margin>Rom. 8:26.</margin> We do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit itself prays for us with unspeakable groanings. That is, the Spirit helps us to be grieved because we cannot pray, nor have repentance, nor serve God better; and herein consists the help of the Spirit. And this, God will accept.

<margin>IV.</margin>
Fourthly: remember this, that God accepts the sincerity of the heart, even where there is no perfection of grace. You live under a covenant of grace, in which God accepts sincerity for perfection, and looks rather upon the truth of grace than the strength of the spiritual gifts. You complain that you cannot pray; perhaps you lack the gift of Prayer and you are of a slow tongue, but you nonetheless have a true longing, and the ornament of a meek Spirit, and a pure heart. God loves the truth of grace more than the strength of gifts: you can notice that in what one reads of Moses and Aaron, <margin>Exod. 4:14.</margin> I know, said God to Moses, that Aaron your brother can speak very well. Now Moses was not well-spoken; he was heavy of speech and heavy of tongue; nevertheless, when Moses and Aaron were to be used for that great work of Prayer, when Joshua fought against Amalek, God did not choose the eloquent Aaron, but the stammering Moses to offer the Prayer. Moses could pray better than Aaron, although Aaron had better gifts <note>In this context, "gifts" refers to natural talents like oratory or eloquence.</note>.

Fifthly: consider that you perhaps complain of the distractions of the flesh, as if they hindered you in Divine Service, when it is only the weakness of your natural body. Thus the godly often lay their unfitness for duties upon their own hearts, when it arises only from an indisposed and weak body. One must know this: that sometimes the body makes a person unfit for Divine Service, but that inability is without sin, though not without misery. So it was with Paul, <margin>Gal. 4:13.</margin> for he speaks thus to the Galatians: You know that through weakness of the flesh I preached the Gospel to you the first time: And my temptation, which was in my flesh, you never despised nor loathed: but you received me as an Angel of God, even as Christ Jesus. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the church father known for translating the Bible into Latin.</note> understands these words as a physical weakness, preventing Paul from speaking, and yet it says that the Galatians bore with him and did not reject him while he was under this physical weakness. So also Paul says to the Thessalonians, that he wanted to come to them once and again, but Satan hindered him. Some think that this hindrance was persecution; others that it was a storm at sea; but most judge that it was some physical illness, through which the

<column-break/>

Devil hindered him. So, if you have a sick and painful body, and through it cannot work out your duty well, then this is indeed your misery, but not your sin; therefore, in such a case, do not lay the blame on your heart. For in this matter it is with a person as it is with a strong and healthy man riding upon a poor, tired horse. Likewise, although the soul may be active and powerful, it is nonetheless sometimes forced to keep still with a weak, sick, and tired body.

<margin>VI.</margin>
Sixthly: remember this, that God accepts in the performance of service all that is His, and covers all that is yours. The water which is salty in the sea is sweet in the river: the service that comes from you is salty and brackish, but coming through the river of Christ's blood, it loses its unpalatable taste. And what a great concession this is in God: to cover what is yours, and to accept what is His own. It is a rule in Philosophy that the naming of a thing is always taken from the greatest part. <margin>The naming follows the greater part.</margin> <note>original: "Denominatio sequitur majorem partem."</note> God names a person by his best part; he sins in Prayer, and he works good in Prayer. Just as when water is mixed with wine, so that by that mixing the wine becomes much poorer, nevertheless because the wine gives a scent and the color of the wine is still retained, it is altogether called wine. In the same way, although there is a mixture of sin and virtue in your heart during your Divine Service, nonetheless the whole shall be called a virtuous work.

<margin>VII.</margin>
Seventhly: although the flesh hinders you in the performance of Divine Service, there is nonetheless a full distinction between a godly and an ungodly person, even in this case, although distractions are found in the one as well as the other. First: the ungodly are pulled away by the flesh, but they do not have the Spirit as the pious do to stand against the corruption.

Secondly: the ungodly have no renewed principles of grace in their hearts to resist the corruptions of the flesh, as the godly have. The born-again cannot sin <margin>1 John 3:9</margin> <note>The text cites 1 John 3:15, but the context of "seed of grace" refers to 1 John 3:9.</note> (namely, in the way the ungodly do) because the seed of grace remains in them.

Thirdly: the ungodly do not distinguish so clearly, nor weep so feelingly over the distractions of the flesh, as the godly do.

Fourthly: the ungodly shall never be released from the evil workings of the flesh, neither in this world nor in the world to come. Sin shall hinder their Divine Service in this life, and in the future life cut it off entirely. But the godly, being tormented here by the flesh, shall nonetheless be freed from it at some time. And thus I have finished the first part of the twofold consequence.
