# Struggle between
## 86

### Galatians 5:17

> For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary to one another; so that you do not do the things that you would.

<margin>
25th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry <note>original: "Laurentii Jurij"; this is the church of St. Lawrence Jewry in London, where many famous Puritan sermons were delivered.</note> within London on February 19, 1650. The Doctrine.
</margin>

I shall now proceed to the second consideration of these words; which is the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh, so that people cannot do the evil which they would wish to do.

**The Doctrine is this:**
That God’s Spirit often preserves the reborn, so that they do not come to do the evil which they would otherwise want to do.

In handling this Doctrine, I shall open these three particular things.
1. I shall show you how the Spirit preserves a person from doing the evil which they wanted.
2. In what this work of the Spirit consists.
3. How one might know the difference between the *restraining grace* of the Spirit, which keeps the godless from sin, and the *renewing grace* of the Spirit, which preserves the reborn from evil.

<margin>
First question answered.
</margin>

### 1.

The first question: how does the Spirit hinder a person from doing the evil which they would otherwise do? To this I answer with these five points.

<margin>
I.
</margin>
First, the Spirit restrains a person from doing evil by enlightening their judgment, and making them see the evil of sin in its nature, and the danger of sin in its outcome. Thus one reads in Job 36:9, *He shows them their work, and their transgressions, that they have exceeded.* Here is the enlightenment of their understanding, and then follows in the tenth verse, *He opens also their ear to discipline, and commands that they return from iniquity,* and in the twelfth verse, *if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge.* The sin of nature is described as a state of ignorance, to make it known that a person without the Spirit is blind and cannot see the evil which they commit; the Spirit then enlightens a person, and for this reason one reads that the Apostle Paul was sent to open the eyes of men, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God; indicating that there must first be an opening of the eyes and an enlightenment of the understanding before there can be a departure from sins.

<margin>
Acts 26:18.
See 2 Kings 6:15, 16.
</margin>

<margin>
II.
</margin>
Second, the Spirit keeps a person from sin by awakening the Conscience, in restraining and rebuking a person regarding sin when they are tempted by it. The Conscience is God’s Officer <note>The original Dutch "Amptman" refers to a local official or bailiff; the author is using a legal metaphor.</note> and man’s Overseer: and were it not that the natural conscience prevented it, a godless person would commit every imaginable evil; every godless person would do all those sins for which they had the opportunity. Now, just as committed sin wounds the conscience, so also the Conscience gnaws because of sins before they are committed. The Conscience is like an iron gate and a metal wall, to restrain you from much evil

<column-break/>

into which you would otherwise run. And therefore Joseph took counsel with his Conscience, *How then can I do this great wickedness?* And this restrained him from committing folly with his Master's Wife.

<margin>
III.
</margin>
Third, the Spirit also keeps a person from sin by instilling a principle and root of grace and holiness, fighting against that root of sin which is in human nature. And so says the Apostle John, that whoever is born of God does not commit sin: for God’s seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. He who is born of God has a renewing nature and a new principle in him, which is contrary to the sin of his nature.

<margin>
1 John 3:9.
1 John 5:18.
</margin>

<margin>
IV.
</margin>
Fourth, the Spirit restrains a person from evil by bringing to their memory certain specific passages of Scripture against that sin to which they are tempted. For this reason David says that he had hidden the word of the Lord in his heart, so that he might not sin against Him. Through this means, the Spirit strengthens the heart against sin, as is often testified in the Scripture. Solomon gives this advice to his son: *My son,* he says, *keep my words, and lay up my commandments with you... that they may keep you from the strange woman.* So also says David, *by the word of your lips I have kept me from the paths of the destroyer.* Augustine recounts of himself <note>original: "Augustin. Conf. lib. 8. cap. 18." Referring to the famous conversion scene in the *Confessions*.</note> that when he was inclined toward immorality, God laid this Scripture passage before his eyes, Romans 13:13-14: *Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to fulfill the lusts thereof:* and by this means it pleased God to draw him away from his wantonness and immorality.

<margin>
Psalm 119:11.
Proverbs 7:1, 5.
Psalm 17:4.
Augustine's Confessions, book 8, ch. 18.
</margin>

<margin>
V.
</margin>
Fifth, the Spirit restrains a person from doing the evil they would want by putting into the heart a reverence and fear for the presence of God when they are tempted toward evil. *Fear the Lord, and depart from evil.* The Wise Man joins those two together to show that the fear of God being in the heart preserves a person from evil. So Solomon says in a similar passage that through the fear of the Lord one departs from evil. The awe-inspiring fear of the great God is a good preservative and protective means against sin.

<margin>
Proverbs 1:7.
Proverbs 16:6.
Proverbs 14:16.
</margin>

---

### 2nd Question.

The second question: In what does this work of the Spirit in preserving a person from sin consist? The answer is that it generally consists of three things.

1. In respect to the types of sin.
2. In respect to the time and place in which the sin would otherwise be committed.
3. In respect to the manner of sinning. Firstly, in respect to the types of sin, thus the Spirit preserves a reborn person so that they do not come to commit the sin against the Holy Spirit; although the seed of that sin is in the godly as well as in the ungodly. This the Apostle John proves fully in 1 John 5:18. After he had said that there was a sin unto death, for which he did not say that one should pray, he then says in the eighteenth verse: *We know that whoever is born of God does not sin...*

<margin>
2nd Question.
Answer.
1 John 5:18.
</margin>

# Flesh and Spirit
## 87
### H 2

...he who is born of God keeps himself, and the evil one does not seize him. That is: a godly person shall not be overcome so as to commit this sin unto death <note>The "sin unto death" is a biblical concept from 1 John 5:16, usually interpreted by Puritans as the unpardonable sin against the Holy Spirit.</note>; the grace that is in the heart shall preserve a person, so that the evil one shall not seize him.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
Secondly, God’s Spirit preserves a person so that they shall not commit a sin at the time and place where they might have wanted to. Thus the Spirit preserved David; for in a heated mood he intended to kill Nabal and his entire household, but Abigail meeting David, David’s hot spirit was soon cooled by sweet persuasions; and in this the work of God’s Spirit was wonderfully revealed, for although David decided at such a time and in such a place to do thus and so, nevertheless the all-ruling hand of God’s Spirit held him back.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
Thirdly, and principally, the Spirit preserves a person from sin in respect to the *manner* in which someone does evil. A reborn person shall not sin in the same way they did before they were converted. I have shown you above how the Spirit preserves a person from the accomplishment of sin. Now I shall show you how God's Spirit preserves a <term>reborn soul</term><note>A person who has undergone a spiritual "new birth" or conversion.</note> from sinning in the same manner as they sinned before. I shall bring forward seven particular distinctions for this purpose.

<margin>
1.
1 Tim. 1:13.
1 Pet. 1:14.
</margin>
First, a reborn person shall not sin as **ignorantly** as they did at first. Paul says of himself that God had shown him mercy during his unconverted state because he had sinned ignorantly; but once someone is converted, their eyes are opened, and they shall not sin so ignorantly. To this end serves the exhortation of the Apostle: *As obedient children, do not be conformed to the lusts which were formerly in your ignorance.*

<margin>
Prov. 4:19.
Eph. 2:35.
</margin>
Before conversion, a person walks in the darkness, and as the Wise Man speaks, *he does not know what he shall stumble over.* An unconverted life is a dark life; a person sins and he does not know it. But after conversion, God places a light in the soul, through which he can see the foul nature of sin.

<margin>
2.
Eph. 4:17, 18, 19.
Gal. 5:17.
</margin>
Secondly, you can no longer sin as **insensitively** as before. Before conversion, sin did not upset your conscience any more than sand in the fingers of your glove; but now it is like gravel penetrating your entrails. First you were unfeeling, and as the Apostle speaks, you had your conscience <note>The Dutch text says "toegheschroept," meaning seared or cauterized.</note> seared as with a branding iron; now, seared flesh is unfeeling, but raw and torn flesh is tender. In former times your conscience had no feeling of sin, but if you commit sin now, it is to you as if a sword were pricked into raw flesh. Before conversion, the Law was cast behind the back, but now it is always set before one's eyes; before, you had no feeling of sin, but now it is to you like a dagger in the heart.

<margin>3.</margin>
Thirdly, you can no longer sin as **quietly and well-satisfied** as in former times. Before, you wallowed in sin like a sow in the mire; but now you lie like a little sheep in the mire, wishing with great longing to be in the green pastures. I have said above that the corruption in a God-fearing person was like poison in a person's body, which is very distressing and painful to them; but that sin

<column-break/>

in the godless was like poison in a toad, which agrees with its nature. Before your conversion, you were as well-satisfied with your sin and corruption as a toad, which by nature has poison within itself; but conversion makes sin as loathsome to you as if poison were in your entrails. Sin is for a godless person like

<margin>
Prov. 10:23.
2 Thess. 2:12.
</margin>
**sport and a pastime**, but for the godly it is sorrow and a burden.

<margin>
IV.
Jer. 8:6.
</margin>
Fourthly, you do not desire sin as **boldly** as before. In former times you ran headlong into sin like a horse into battle; the fear of God was not impressed upon your mind; awe for God did not hold you back from sin. But when God has converted a person, they sin with more fear of heart than before. and it is remarkable that when the Holy Scripture speaks of a reborn person, it speaks of them not just as avoiding sin, but as **fearing** it. A godly person does not only shun light-minded swearing, but they *fear the oath.* And for this

<margin>
Eccl. 9:2.
Prov. 13:13.
</margin>
reason they are also said to *fear the commandment.* A godless person may fear the threats and punishments, but only a God-fearing person fears the commandment, and they do not want to sin for the reason that it is against a holy Law.

<margin>
V.
Jude v. 15.
</margin>
Fifthly, you shall not sin as **willfully** as you did before. The Scripture says that the Lord shall punish all the godless because of all their godless works, which they have done godlessly. See, the Scripture speaks not only of godless people and godless works, but of doing godless works *godlessly*—that is, in a very godless manner, in a very willful and evil manner. But you cannot sin in this way

<margin>Heb. 10:29</margin>
after your conversion. We read of some who treat the Spirit of grace with contempt; but a godly person shall never sin so. It may be that the stirrings of the Spirit are quenched, and the Spirit is grieved, but they shall never treat the Spirit with

<margin>Ps. 59:6.</margin>
contempt. A godly person shall never sin out of willful malice.

<margin>VI.</margin>
Sixthly, you cannot do evil as **willingly** as before: for before your conversion you ran headlong into sin with your full will, but now you go and give yourself to sin with much unwillingness. This change is wrought in you by converting grace: before, you sinned with your whole will, but now one part of the will stands against the

<margin>Rom. 7:25</margin>
other, and therefore the Apostle says: *I myself serve the Law of God with the mind, but with the flesh the law of sin.* Whereas the whole person was given over to the bondage of sin before conversion. Although a child of God still sins after being converted, it is nonetheless by a surprise—just as Peter denied Christ in a moment of haste—but a godless person sins with premeditation, just as Judas betrayed Christ.

<margin>VII.</margin>
Seventhly, you shall not sin as **shamelessly** as before conversion: for then people sinned and were not ashamed, as the prophet Jeremiah speaks, but now they fear and blush.

<margin>
Jer. 6:15.
3rd Question.
</margin>

# The Battle Between
## 88

...to be restrained from evil—is this common to the ungodly as well as the godly? I shall not treat that question now, but shall save it for the next <term>Sermon</term><note>The original Dutch 'Predicatie' refers to a formal religious discourse or sermon.</note>. I shall only conclude this Sermon with some applications of what you have heard.

<margin>Utility.</margin>
If the Spirit restrains the <term>reborn</term><note>Those who have undergone a spiritual conversion or 'new birth.'</note> so that they do not do the evil they intended, then take note of the following:

<margin>I.</margin>
First, the great misery of those in whom the Spirit does not perform this great and good work; see how great the <term>servitude</term><note>The text uses 'dienst-knechten,' literally 'service-servants' or bondslaves, highlighting the lack of freedom in sin.</note> to sin is for those who do not have the Spirit, and how they lie open to every attack of the devil. The movements and warnings of the Spirit are like a **Bulwark** and a **Fortification** to guard the heart against sin. The Spirit is like a sluice gate in a canal; if it is lowered, it keeps the water within its bounds, but if it is raised, there will soon be a great flood of water.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, if you wish to have the Spirit to preserve you from evil, you must also strive to preserve yourself; the preservation of the Spirit does not exclude the holy care of man to preserve himself. David put this into practice; he guarded himself against his own iniquity. He did not want to make God’s care in preserving him an opportunity to be lazy himself. Remember and take this as a rule: that if you do not seek to keep yourself from the opportunities for sin, the Spirit will also never preserve you from sinning. Therefore we read that he who is born of God keeps himself, and the evil one does not touch him; so also says **Jude**: *Keep yourselves in the love of God.*
<margin>
Psa. 18:24
1 John 5:18
Jude v. 21
</margin>

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, what great reason the reborn have to thank God, both in respect to themselves and in respect to the ungodly.

1. In respect to themselves: for to what evil would the flesh not have pulled you, had you not had the opposing workings of the Spirit? I appeal to your own conscience: how many times have you intended to commit wickedness—indeed, how far have you gone in it? So far that you even deliberated on the time, the place, and the manner in which you would carry out the evil; yet, God restrained you from that intention, so that you could not do the evil that you willed. What reason you have then to thank God, not only for an infused grace, but also for a <term>prevenient grace</term><note>From the Latin 'gratia praeveniens,' meaning grace that 'comes before' or precedes human action to restrain it or prepare the heart.</note> by which you were held back from sin. So it was with David: he fully intended to kill Nabal along with his entire household, but the Spirit of God prevented him through the counsel of a poor woman. See then what great reason you have to thank God for preventing grace. To move you further to this, I shall give you some things to consider in two respects:

1. If you consider the universality of that corruption which is in your nature.
2. If you notice the strength of the same.

First, if you reflect on the universality of corruption: it has spread over all men. All children of Adam are infected with that common contagion; they have all sinned in him and deserved punishment, and so they are all subject to the defilement of Adam’s sin.
<margin>Rom. 9:12</margin>

<column-break/>

Secondly, it is universal in respect to the parts of man; there is not one part of man which is not defiled with sin, even in the reborn. Just as in them every part is somewhat sanctified, so is every part also somewhat unsanctified; as grace is in every part, so also is sin.

Thirdly, it is universal in respect to its high-reaching effects: man’s nature is foolish toward all good and inclined toward all evil. The corruption of nature is explained by theologians through comparison to that <term>original mass</term><note>A reference to the 'massa perditionis' or the chaotic matter of the first day of creation, here used as a metaphor for the potential for all sins to exist within human nature.</note> which was created on the first day, in which all the creatures that God created thereafter were present in potential. So it is with the corruption of nature: it has within itself, <term>potentially</term><note>Original: "Virtualiter."</note>, all the sins that occur in the world.

Fourthly, there is a universality in respect to time; this corruption of nature was not only in one age of the world and not in others, but always, as long as the world has stood. It reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam's transgression. Now put all this together—that all men and all parts of men in all times are corrupted, and that this corruption incites one to every sin: consider only this, and you will have great reason to marvel that no more ungodliness occurs in the world.
<margin>Rom. 5:14</margin>

But secondly, consider not only the universality but also the strength of that corruption: if it were but a weak companion, it would not be so much to fear; but there is great strength and power in it, and therefore it is sometimes called a beguiling and a pulling enemy; if it cannot entice you through craftiness, it will pull you with force.

2. We must glorify God's grace in respect to the ungodly, who are enemies of the Church of God. If the **restraining grace** of God’s Spirit did not hold back the ungodly from doing the evil they would wish, one could not live in the world. For every ungodly person would murder anyone who angered him; he would deceive everyone who dealt with him; all human societies would be turned upside down; indeed, God's church would be rooted out from under Heaven, were it not that God bridled men through the common workings of the Spirit. David says that God makes the wrath of man to praise Him, and the remainder of wrath He shall bind up; he speaks of the enemies of God and says that God shall bind up their wrath through the common workings of His Spirit, and it shall be manifest to the praise and glory of God and for the good of His people. You have an excellent example of this in Laban and Jacob. Laban came against Jacob with an evil intent, but God came to him and gave him a command that he should speak with Jacob neither good nor bad. God laid a mighty bridle on Laban's spirit, so that he could not carry out the intended evil. Likewise, you see this in Esau: he pursued his brother Jacob with a deadly hatred—so much so that he resolved to kill him once the days of mourning for his father’s death were over; but Esau changed his **countenance** so much...
<margin>
Psal. 76:10 <note>Original cites 76:11.</note>
Gen. 31:29
Gen. 33:4
</margin>

<margin>II. I</margin>
Secondly, conclude from this how much God’s children must keep their hearts on guard, so that they do not carry themselves into such evils which they thought they would never commit. If you believe the Spirit is withdrawn from you, so that He does not restrain you, what evil would you not commit?

<margin>Galatians 3:9. Abraham, the father of the faithful, not efficiently but as an example. <note>original: "Abrahamus pater fidelium, non-efficienter sed exemplariter"</note> Genesis 12:13, Genesis 20:2, Numbers 12:3, Psalm 106:33, James 3:11.</margin>
There are examples in the Scripture of godly people who fell into those sins in which they thought they would never fall; indeed, those [sins] that most strongly conflicted with the very virtues in which they were most outstanding. Abraham was, in his time, the very strongest in faith, and was therefore called the Father of the Faithful; now, who would have thought that Abraham would fall into unbelief? Yet he did: for, distrusting God’s providence, he told two lies—one to Pharaoh, King of Egypt, and the other to Abimelech, King of Gerar. Likewise Moses, of whom the Scripture says that he was more meek <note>The Dutch "sachtmoedich" refers to gentleness or humility.</note> than all the men who were on the face of the earth; nonetheless, he spoke somewhat unadvisedly with his lips and fell into a coarse, unregulated wrath, which sin most directly opposed the virtue in which he was most outstanding. So also of Job, the Scripture says that he was the most patient man on earth, and yet Job was carried away to the highest degree of impatience, so that 

<margin>Job 3:3.</margin>
he vehemently cursed the day of his birth, and the night in which it was said, "a man child is conceived." I set these examples before you to make you see what great reason you have to thank God that He has kept you from certain sins, and how you must keep your heart on guard if God’s Spirit were but withdrawn from you.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, pray to God that the Spirit may perform His office in your soul, that He might keep you back from doing the evil which you intended. We read of David, that he prayed: Lord, keep your servant back also from presumptuous sins. You must pray that the Spirit will curb and restrain your corruption when you are tempted to sin; because there is no one, however pious, who can stand by their own strength, however great it may be, and thereby shun evil when tempted to it, even if it were ever so hideous. Oh, pray then for prevenient grace <term>Prevenient grace: a theological term for grace that "comes before" human action to lead a person toward God or restrain them from evil.</term>, that God will preserve you through His Spirit, so that you do not do the works of the flesh. Therefore, Christ has taught us to pray, 

<margin>Matthew 6:13.</margin>
Lord, deliver us from the evil [one], namely, him whom we cannot withstand by our own powers.

Secondly, this also serves for the instruction of the unregenerate <note>Those who have not experienced a spiritual "new birth" or inward conversion.</note>, who only have restraining grace to keep them from sin. Such persons must first consider what great reason they have to thank God for this benefit: although they shall go to Hell, they must nonetheless thank God for those restraining graces on earth. For although these do not make you good, they will nonetheless bring it about that you shall be less evil; and though they cannot make you spiritual, they shall nonetheless make you "civilly good" <note>This refers to outward moral behavior and good citizenship, which the author distinguishes from true holiness.</note>. For through restraining grace, a person can obtain these benefits:

<margin>1.</margin>
1. That he does not commit so many or such great sins.
2. That he does not deserve such great punishment.
3. He will give less offense to Religion.
4. He will not provide such a bad example.

<column-break/>

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, you who have restraining grace, be warned that you do not go about boasting of it. The Pharisee had restraining grace, but he used it poorly. "O God," he said, "I thank you that I am not a robber, nor an adulterer, nor even like this tax collector." If God restrains you from 

<margin>Luke 18:11. The Pharisee praised not God, but himself. <note>original: "Non Deum sed se ipsum laudavit Pharizeus"</note></margin>
those sins, do not brag about it; who has made this distinction between you and the others? Is it not God? Well then, do not be proud of it.

<margin>III.</margin>
Thirdly, see to it that you do not take restraining grace for a sign of renewing grace <note>The author distinguishes between being "held back" from sin and being "made new" in heart.</note>; and here I could show you ten ways in which you might be deceived. But of this in the following sermon.

### Flesh and Spirit

<margin><unclear>Solitary. Ames. book 4.</unclear> <note>Likely a reference to the Puritan theologian William Ames.</note>
<unclear>...is duty... Ambrose.</unclear></margin>
...the confession of the same usually follows one’s upbringing; and this can be a reason why people do not commit the evil they intended—because a religious upbringing has a power to hold them back; yet this is not renewing grace.

Secondly, the physical weakness of the body—whether caused by old age or by sickness—can be a means to bind people away from many sins. <margin>Ambrose.</margin> <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), an influential Bishop of Milan.</note> Ambrose calls illnesses the "workshops of virtue." Truly, sickness may well be a prison, but it is no grave for sin; only spiritual mortification is a true slaughter of sin. Sickness merely keeps the sin inside. When people must constantly lie in bed, so that their legs rattle within their skin, they do not have much pleasure or idle time to think about excess. <margin>Genesis 20:6 compared to v. 17.</margin> Thus we see in Abimelech how God kept him from sin through one sickness or another that He sent him; you can notice this by comparing the seventeenth verse of the same chapter: for in verse 6, God says to Abimelech that He had prevented him from sinning against Him. There it only says in general that God prevented him, but verse 17 indicates the *manner* in which God did so. Abimelech would gladly have defiled Abraham’s wife, but God sent him a certain sickness; therefore it says that Abraham prayed to God, and God <margin>Old Latin.</margin> healed Abimelech. Rivet <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a prominent French Huguenot theologian who lived in the Netherlands.</note> says regarding these words that as soon as he took Sarah into his house, God struck him with a heavy sickness, so that he was not capable of committing such folly with her. And he gives this reason: because Isaac was the promised seed; but if Abimelech had lain with Sarah, then perhaps the child would have been regarded not as Abraham’s, but as Abimelech’s child. And therefore God sent him a certain painful sickness, so that he would be powerless to commit that evil.

<margin>2 Kings 8:12.</margin>
Thirdly, the outward insignificance and poverty of a person’s current state also prevents many people from sinning—people who, if they had riches, would greedily work out their wickedness. This was the case with Hazael; while he was a servant, he could not do much evil; his outward state was so lowly that he had no suitable opportunity for it. But when he became King in his master’s place, [Elisha told him]: *Then you shall set the cities on fire, rip open the pregnant women, and dash the young children to pieces.* He never thought he would have been so wicked, but when he became king, he did that and much more. We may well thank God that (as the proverb says) the most aggressive cows have the shortest horns; <note>A Dutch proverb meaning that those with the most ill-will often lack the power or means to carry it out.</note> that is, that the ungodly are sometimes not rich, high-ranking, or of great power. God often arranges it so that people who have a very evil nature do not have the proper opportunity to work it out in their lives.

Fourthly, the terror of a natural conscience can also sometimes keep people from sin. God’s Spirit not only testifies at times with the Spirit of the believers, but He also disturbs the spirit of the ungodly; and although an ungodly person does not leave sin alone out of a desire to obey the Law, he nevertheless does so for reasons arising from the conviction of a natural conscience. For that conscience holds dominion over an ungodly man, so that he shall not do the evil that he wished to. <margin>Romans 2:14.</margin> The Gentiles, says the Apostle, who do not have the Law—namely the written Law—do by nature the things contained in the Law; these, not having the Law, are a law unto themselves. Thus these (though they were Heathens, says the Scripture) were a law unto themselves; that is, they had a conscience which stood in the place of a Law for them.

Fifthly, the fear implanted in people by human laws and strict penal decrees is also a means to restrain people from many sins. When a Divine Law finds no place in the conscience of an ungodly person, a human law will restrain his actions. How many murders would take place if they did not fear losing their necks more than losing their souls? It is a great blessing to have good laws in a land, because they restrain people from committing evil when God’s Law has no power over their consciences. One reads in Scripture that people were wonderfully bound and restrained from ungodliness by this reason alone: for when the favorites of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, came to complain about Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego regarding their God whom they served, it was ordained that the three youths should be thrown into the fiery furnace, and that it should be made seven times hotter than usual. When they were thrown in, it says that they walked in the midst of the fire as if in a delightful place. This convinced the King and his noblemen so much that the King made a law and gave this command: <margin>Daniel 3:29.</margin> *That every people, nation, and language that speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be cut in pieces, and their houses made into dung-heaps.* Here was only a man’s law, which so greatly disturbed and moved the people that, although they previously used to revile the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, they now remained completely silent. I relate this only to show you what great power a human law has to bind the sins of the ungodly.

Sixthly, people can be restrained from sin solely by the presence and the example of the godly among whom they live, who pay attention to their ways. This brings to mind a proverb that was common among the Romans: "Guard yourself, Cato sees you." <note>The Roman statesman Cato the Younger was famous for his strict morality; his name became a shorthand for an ever-present moral witness.</note> Cato was regarded as a good man; therefore, when someone did something wrong, they had this saying: "Guard yourself, Cato sees you." So too one finds in the Scripture concerning Herod, that he <margin>Mark 6:20.</margin> feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and held him in high regard. There is a story in the *Book of Martyrs* <note>Likely referring to the *Martyrs Mirror* or *Foxe's Book of Martyrs*, recording the lives of Christian witnesses.</note> at the beginning of the first book, concerning John the Evangelist (who wrote the Revelation). While he was riding on the path, a band of thieves came upon him; and it so happened that the captain of these thieves was a young man who had lived under John’s ministry. Although John hardly recognized him, he nevertheless knew John well; and it says that when he saw the old man, he ran away, the guilt...

->### Conflict Between<-

<margin>Galatians 4:18. Philippians 1:27. Thus, the presence and example of the pious is often an opportunity to keep others from sin.

<margin>VII. Heroic and noble spirit. <note>original: "Spiritus heroicus, & generosus."</note></margin> **S**eventhly, people can be restrained from sin out of a majesty of spirit and the nobility of man’s natural disposition. Thus Luther writes that before his conversion, while he was still a monk in the Romish Church, he was never inclined toward greed; he was of such a noble spirit that such a sin did not cling to him. So also Paul says that he had the gift of continence by nature. It is also recounted <margin>I would rather there were no Plutarch, etc. <note>original Latin: "Malo nullum fuisse Plutarchum, &c." This refers to a famous sentiment that it is better to be forgotten than to be remembered for bad character.</note></margin> of Plutarch, that he supposedly said, "I would rather there had never been such a man in the world, than that people should say Plutarch is fickle, unjust, or inconsistent." Paul, speaking of the Heathens, says that although they do not have the Law, they nevertheless by nature do the things of the Law—that is, through a more refined nature. This is the reason why some people are so irritable and passionate, while others are not; it does not come from renewing grace, but because some are more noble in spirit than others. Because of this, many evil deeds are left undone, even though the people lack renewing grace <term>renewing grace: the theological concept of a complete inward transformation by the Holy Spirit, as opposed to mere outward restraint.</term>.

<margin>VIII. Out of fear of punishment rather than hatred of evil. <note>original: "Formidine poenae potius quam detestatione mali."</note> Exodus 12:33. Matthew 26:5.</margin> **E**ighthly, the wicked can be restrained from evil out of fear of punishment, whether temporal or eternal. Sometimes they are bound by fear of outward judgments, as it was with the Egyptians; they cried out, "Let the Israelites depart, or we are all dead!" They had to let them go, not because God willed them to go, nor out of love for the Israelites, but out of love for themselves—we are all dead if they do not leave. So we read of the Chief Priests and Pharisees, that they would not kill Christ during the Feast, so that there would be no riot among the people. It was not love for Christ, but for themselves. Similarly, many politicians and "world-wise" men would commit much injustice and godlessness if they did not fear the people.

<margin>Isaiah 33:14.</margin> **N**inthly, the fear of Hell and the wrath of God can lie so heavily upon the soul of a sinner that he will come to leave behind much godlessness, for he fears burning eternally in Hell. To this end, you have a notable passage in the Prophet Isaiah: "The sinners in Zion," he says, "are afraid; fearfulness has seized the hypocrites." Why so? This is the reason: "Who among us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?" The fear of God’s wrath stirred in them a dread of sin.

<margin>Mark 10:17.</margin> **F**inally, the hope of a temporal and eternal reward can also be a cause why people flee from sin. This was the case with that young man who said, "What shall I do that I may inherit eternal

<column-break/>

life?" Christ answered him, <margin>v. 19.</margin> "You know the Commandments: You shall not kill, you shall <margin>v. 20.</margin> not commit adultery, you shall not steal." And he answered, "All these things I have kept from my youth." In his obedience, he looked more to the reward than to the rule. Similarly, Balaam was restrained from committing godlessness by the hope of a blessed end. Through all these aforementioned circumstances, the wicked can be bridled from sin, though they are nonetheless entirely without any true grace.

---

<margin>The first usefulness.</margin>
The usefulness which we can draw from this will first be for those ungodly people who are restrained from sin on any of the aforementioned grounds.

<margin>I. It is beautiful to stand firm in prosperity and in terrifying times. <note>original: "Pulchrum est in secundis, terrif- [terribilibus] que consistere." A quote attributed to Cicero.</note> Cicero. 2. 11.</margin> **F**irstly, through this you shall have less sin from others—or that you would have had yourself—if you had been without this restraining grace; although it does not make you good, you are nonetheless less evil because of it. Even if you are not thereby holy and spiritual people, you are nonetheless good civil citizens.

<margin>II.</margin> **S**econdly, your punishment shall be smaller and lighter than it would have been if God had not given you the bridling grace to restrain you from sin. A Heathen who has restraining grace will be punished less than a Christian who does not have it. A sober Heathen will be punished less than a drunken Christian.

<margin>III.</margin> **T**hirdly, consider that when you leave sin aside, you will not break the peace of your conscience so terribly; for public and gross sins lay the conscience open and fill it with terror and fear. But the less you commit sin, the less your conscience will be disturbed.

<margin>IV.</margin> **F**ourthly, by this you give less offense to Religion than you otherwise would have done. Small sins give Religion only a scratch on the face, but gross sins give her a stab in the heart. Religion receives not nearly as much dishonor from hidden flaws as it does from public evildoers.

<margin>V.</margin> **F**ifthly, you would be able to do more harm through the example of your sins if God abandoned you than you do now. Although you are a wicked person, if God bridles the sin in you, you do not give such a bad example as you otherwise would.

<margin>VI.</margin> **S**ixthly, who knows whether these small beginnings of restraining grace shall be a forerunner of renewing grace? You who are restrained from evil—though you are currently ungodly—what do you know of whether God will change this bridling grace into a renewing grace?

---

<margin>The second usefulness.</margin>
The second usefulness shall be for the comfort of the godly. Surely many pious hearts, through what I have said, might easily develop many fears and doubts, and would say:

<margin>Objection.</margin>
"**F**riend, you have dealt there with the power of God’s Spirit in His common workings, to hinder the wicked from sin through restraining grace; yet we find that not only the godly, but even the ungodly surpass us in this: for a wicked person can bridle those sins which we cannot bridle." This objection might be brought forth by many pious hearts, and to this I shall [answer] here or...

William Ames on Cases of Conscience.

...bring five words of comfort as a response, and this shall conclude everything.

<margin>further. 1.</margin>
First, consider that becoming aware of the unbridled workings of sin in your nature does not prove an increase in sin, but rather an increase in your light and the tenderness of your Conscience. While Paul was yet unknown to himself, he thought he was alive and <margin>Romans 7:9.</margin> imagined he was in a very blessed state before he saw the spirituality of the Law; but when he was converted, and the Commandment came, sin revived and he died—that is, the Law pressing with power upon his Conscience made him see that sin was alive, yet he was then in a converted and blessed state. Just as light breaking into a room reveals what defects and disorder are there, which were neither known nor seen in the dark; so also the Spiritual light, rising in our understanding, reveals our Spiritual failings.

<margin>2.</margin>
Secondly, do not judge yourself to be in an evil state because of a lack of specific restraints against sin; but judge yourself by the powerful revelations of indwelling grace in your usual course of life and manner of acting. It can happen that an impious person can restrain his passions, and you, who are godly, cannot. A traveler may sometimes step onto the wagon-road; but his usual course is taken on the easier footpath: so also, if you fall into sin and miss that restraining grace, it may be that you are walking on the uneven wagon-road, but your ordinary way is the sandy path: for it is <margin>Proverbs 7.</margin> the path of the upright to depart from evil; but now and then you may perhaps lose your way. You must not judge yourself by specific instances of restraint.

<margin>3.</margin>
Thirdly, although you are overtaken by a sin that others, who are worse than you, are not overtaken by, think also that you have more temptations to sin than others; it is true that in some cases the sins of a God-fearing person are heavier than those of a godless person, but in other cases, they are not. The Devil is busier in tempting a godly person to sin than in provoking a godless person to it. When the children of God came together, <margin>Job 2:1, 1:2.</margin> Satan came into their midst. He owes them a grudge; therefore, if they are now and then overwhelmed, they must not judge themselves by those specific acts, but by the constant course of their life.

<margin>v. 1, 6, 7, 11. Basil. <note>Refers to St. Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father.</note></margin>
Fourthly, consider that although you commit a sinful act, yet if sin is not a king or Lord over you, you have nothing to fear. You admit sin like a Usurper <note>original: "Geweldiger"</note>, and not as your own Lord; although you lack the restraint of the Spirit to keep you from evil in some acts, if you are only preserved by God from the reigning power of sin, then take heart; you are in a blessed state.

Fifthly, let this be your comfort: that although you cannot restrain sinful workings now and then, in a short time you shall be a perfect conqueror over all your sins. God shall shortly tread Satan under your feet: now you fight against the Dev-

<column-break/>

-il hand to hand, but then you shall tread him under your feet. Let this be your comfort, you who have the Spirit, desiring against the flesh: your struggle is short, your victory is certain and great, and your reward is the everlasting crown.

### WILLIAM AMES, <note>William Ames (1576–1633) was an English Puritan theologian who spent much of his life in the Netherlands. This text is from his famous work "De Conscientia" (Of Conscience).</note>

->On the<-

### Cases of Conscience:

->In his second Book.<-

#### CHAPTER XI.
#### Of the struggle between the Spirit and the Flesh.

<margin>See above page 254. Question.</margin>
**Q**uestion: How can the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh in the reborn be distinguished from that conflict which is often found in the unregenerate while they sin?

Answer: First, they are distinguished in their causes: for 1. the struggle of the ungodly proceeds either from terror and a slavish fear of punishment, or from a civil disposition <note>Meaning a natural sense of social propriety or "good citizenship" rather than true holiness.</note> which is easily overcome; but the Spiritual struggle arises from a new nature, which of itself does those things which please God, and hatefully and constantly opposes what is contrary. 2. That conflict and counter-struggle found in the ungodly usually only takes place in those grosser crimes which are either condemned by the light of nature, or are held in great horror by all those who are even slightly enlightened: but the Spiritual struggle of the reborn is against all wickedness, even if it is not carried out in any outward act.

<margin>Answer II.</margin>
Secondly, they differ in their objects: for the struggle found in the ungodly is between the testimony of Conscience and the inclination of the will, or between a slight movement of the will toward some moral good and the evil passions which have the upper hand: But that struggle which is unique to the reborn consists in the opposition and striving of a new and supernatural quality or Spiritual life (which has its seat primarily in the will) against the corrupt inclinations, which indeed live together with it, but do not dominate.

<margin>Answer III.</margin>
Thirdly, they differ in their works: for 1. the struggle of natural men can and usually does coexist with the daily and habitual practice of sins: but the struggle of the Spirit always ensures that, although one stumbles in many things, the course and pursuit of life is set and carried out according to God’s will, 1 John 2:9, 10. 2. The struggle of natural men, although it may sometimes be the cause of good being done, nevertheless creates no good principle, good end, nor good manner of acting. But the Spirit struggling against the flesh brings all this with it. 3. The struggle of natural men commonly allows for acts which are evil in their essence:

->**William Ames on the Cases of Conscience.**<-

<margin>further.</margin>
...bring five words of comfort as an answer, and so conclude everything.

<margin>Romans 7:9.</margin>
First, consider that becoming aware of the unbridled workings of sin in your nature does not prove an increase in sin, but rather your increase in light and tenderness of conscience. Paul, while he was unknown <note>meaning: before he knew the true depth of the Law</note>, thought that he lived and was in a very blessed state before he saw the spirituality of the Law; but when he was converted, when the Commandment came, sin became alive again, yet he died. That is, the Law, pressing with power upon his conscience, made him see sin living, and yet he was then in a converted and blessed state. Just as light breaking into a place discovers what defects and disorder are there, which were neither known nor seen in the dark; so also the spiritual light, rising in our understanding, discovers our spiritual defects.

<margin>1.</margin>
Second, do not judge that you are in an evil state because of the lack of specific restraints on sin, but judge yourself by the powerful manifestations of indwelling grace in your usual course of life and manner of doing things. It can happen that an ungodly person can bridle fine passions, and you, who are a "tree of righteousness," cannot do so. A traveler may sometimes walk on the wagon-road; but his habitual course he takes on the easy footpath. So also, if you fall into sin and lack that binding grace, it may be that you are on the uneven wagon-road; but your 
<margin>Also</margin>
ordinary way is the sandy path: for it is the path of the upright to depart from evil; but now and then you might happen to lose your way. You must not judge yourself by particular instances of restraint.

<margin>1.</margin>
Third, although you are overtaken by a sin which others who are worse than you are not overtaken by, think also that you have more temptations to sin than others. It is true that in some cases the sins of a God-fearing person are heavier than those of a godless person, but in some cases, they are not. The Devil is busier tempting a godly person to sin than in provoking a godless person to it. When the children of God came together,
<margin>Job 2:1 / 3:1, 2</margin>
Satan came into the midst of them. He owes them a spite; therefore, if they are now and then surprised, they must not judge themselves by those particular acts, but by the constant course of their lives.

<margin>v.</margin>

# WILLIAM AMES,

#### CHAPTER XI.
#### Of the struggle of the Spirit and the flesh.

<margin>See above, page 254. Question.</margin>
Question: How can the struggle of the Spirit against the flesh in the reborn <term>wedergeboorne</term><note>The "reborn" or "regenerate"—those who have undergone a spiritual conversion.</note> be distinguished from that conflict which is often found in the unregenerate while they are sinning?

Answer: First, they are distinguished in their causes: for (1) the struggle of the godless comes either from terror and slavish fear of punishment, or from a "civic" disposition <note>meaning: social morality or desire for a good reputation</note> which is easily overcome; but the spiritual struggle arises from a new nature, which of itself does those things which please God, and quickly and constantly opposes the contrary. (2) That conflict and opposition found in the godless is usually only present in those grosser villainies which are either condemned by the light of nature, or are held in great horror by all those who are even slightly enlightened; but the spiritual struggle of the reborn is against all wickedness, even if it is never carried out in any outward deed.

<margin>Answer I. 1.</margin>
Second, they differ in their objects <note>the "targets" of the struggle</note>: for the struggle found in the godless is either between the testimony of conscience and the inclination of the will, or between a slight movement of the will toward some moral good and the evil passions which have the upper hand. But that struggle which is unique to the reborn consists in the opposition and strife of a new and supernatural quality or spiritual life—which has its seat primarily in the will—against the corrupt inclinations which dwell together with it, but do not dominate.

<margin>Answer III.</margin>
Third, they differ in their works <note>meaning: the outcomes or actions</note>: for (1) the struggle of natural <note>unconverted</note> men can and usually does exist alongside the daily and habitual practice of sins; but the struggle of the Spirit always ensures that, although one stumbles in many things, the course and pursuit of life is set and carried out according to God’s will (1 John 2:9, 10). (2) The struggle of natural men, although it may sometimes be the cause of good being done, nonetheless creates no good principle, good end, nor good manner of doing. But the Spirit struggling against the flesh brings all of this with it. (3) The struggle of natural men commonly allows for deeds which are evil in their essence: But...

### Conflict between

<margin>Galatians 4:18. Philippians 1:27. Philippians 2:12.</margin>
The accusation of his conscience and the presence of John <note>Likely referring to John the Baptist and Herod</note> pushed him back so much that he fled, not daring to carry out his usual message. To this purpose serves what the Apostle Paul says: *to be zealous in a good thing at all times is good, and not only when I am present with you*; which indicates that while Paul was present, they walked wonderfully well, but when he was absent, they became sluggish. Thus, the presence and the example of the pious is often an opportunity to keep others from sin.

<margin>VII. A heroic and noble spirit. <note>original: "Spiritus heroicus, & generosus"</note></margin>
Seventh: people can be restrained from sin out of a majesty of spirit and the nobility of a person's natural disposition. Thus it seems with Luther, that before his conversion, while he was a monk in the Roman Church, he had never been inclined to greed; he was of such a noble spirit that such a filthy sin did not cling to him. So also Paul says that he had the gift of self-control by nature. It is also recounted <margin>It is said that Plutarch had no equal, etc. <note>original: "Malo nullum fuisse Plutarchum, &c."</note></margin> of Plutarch, that he supposedly said: "I would rather that such a man had never existed in the world, than that people should say Plutarch is light-headed, unjust, or inconsistent." Paul, speaking of the Heathens, says that although they do not have the Law, they nevertheless do by nature things that are of the Law—that is, through a more purified nature. What is the reason that some people are so grumpy and passionate, and others are not? It does not come from renewing grace, but because some are nobler of spirit than others; and through this, many evil works are left undone, even though the people do not possess renewing grace.

<margin>VIII. By fear of punishment rather than detestation of evil. <note>original: "Formidine pœnæ potius quam detestatione mali"</note></margin>
Eighth: the ungodly can be restrained from evil out of fear of punishment, whether temporal or eternal. Sometimes they are bound by fear of outward judgments; and so it was with the Egyptians, <margin>Exodus 12:33.</margin> who cried out, "let the Israelites depart, or we are all dead men"; they had to let them go, not because God willed that they should go, nor out of love for the Israelites, but out of love for themselves; we are all dead if they do not depart from here. <margin>Matthew 26:5.</margin> So we read of the Chief Priests and Pharisees, that they did not want to kill Christ during the Feast, so that there would be no riot among the people. It was not love for Christ, but for themselves. Thus many politicians and worldly-wise men would commit much injustice and godlessness if they did not fear the people.

<margin>IX.</margin>
Ninth: the fear of Hell and the wrath of God can lie so heavily upon the soul of a sinner that he will come to leave off much godlessness, for he fears burning eternally in Hell. <margin>Isaiah 33:14.</margin> To this end, you have a notable passage in the Prophet Isaiah: *The sinners in Zion*, he says, *are afraid; fearfulness has seized the hypocrites.* Why is this? This is the reason: *Who among us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?* The fear of God's wrath awakened in them a terror of sin.

<margin>X.</margin>
Lastly: the hope of a temporal and eternal reward can also be a cause why people come to flee sin. <margin>Mark 10:17.</margin> So it was with that young man, saying, *what shall I do that I may inherit eternal

<column-break/>

life?* Christ answered him, <margin>v. 19.</margin> *You know the commandments: Do not murder, do not <margin>v. 20.</margin> commit adultery, do not steal;* and he answered, *All these things I have kept from my youth.* In his obedience, he looked more to the reward than to the rule. So also Balaam was restrained from committing godlessness by the hope of a blessed end. Through all these aforementioned circumstances, the ungodly can be bridled from sin, though they are nonetheless entirely without any true grace.

<margin>First Utility.</margin>
The utility <note>Meaning: the practical benefit or application</note> which we can draw from this will first be for those ungodly ones who are restrained from sin on any of the aforementioned grounds.

<margin>I. It is a beautiful thing to show restraint in prosperity. <note>original: "Pulchrum est in secundis, temperare" (OCR corrected from "terrifistere") quoting Cicero.</note></margin>
First: through this, you shall have less sin than others, or than you yourself would have had if you had been without restraining grace; although it does not make you good, you are nonetheless less evil because of it; though you are not thereby holy and spiritual people, you are nevertheless good civil people.

<margin>II.</margin>
Second: your punishment shall be smaller and lighter than it would have been if God had not given you restraining grace to keep you from sin. A Heathen who has restraining grace will be punished less than a Christian who does not have it. A sober Heathen will be punished less than a drunken Christian.

<margin>III.</margin>
Third: consider that when you leave off sin, you will not so terribly break the peace of your conscience; for public and gross sins lay the conscience open and fill it with terror and fear; but the less you commit sin, the less your conscience will be disturbed.

<margin>IV.</margin>
Fourth: through this, you give less offense to the godly than you would have otherwise done. Small sins give Religion only a scratch on the face, but gross sins give her a blow to the heart; Religion receives less dishonor from hidden hypocrites than from public evildoers.

Fifth: you could do more evil through the example of your sins if God abandoned you than you do now. Although you are an evil person, nevertheless, if God bridles the sin in you, you do not give as bad an example as you would otherwise do.

<margin>VI.</margin>
Sixth: who knows whether these small beginnings of restraining grace shall be a precursor to renewing grace? You who are restrained from evil, although you are presently ungodly, what do you know whether God will not change this bridling grace into a renewing grace?

<margin>Second Utility.</margin>
The second utility shall be for the comfort of the godly; certainly, many pious hearts might easily stir up many terrors and doubts for themselves through what I have said, and would say:

<margin>Objection.</margin>
"Friend, you have dealt there with the power of God's Spirit in His common workings, to prevent the ungodly from sin through restraining grace; yet we find that not only the godly but even ungodly men surpass us in this: for an ungodly man can bridle those sins which we cannot bridle." This objection might be brought forward by many pious hearts, and to this, I shall offer these four or five...

# T H E  C H R I S T I A N ,

### Presented in several Sermons, upon four Texts of Scripture, by

## Mr. CHRISTOPHER LOVE.

---

->Christ's Prayer, as a support for the Saints.<-

->John 17. verse 15.<-

>I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.

---

<margin>circumstances of time to be noted</margin>

<image-desc>Ornamental initial 'D' containing a woodcut depiction of a bearded man (identified by the inscription as St. Matthew) sitting at a desk and writing in a book. A small winged angel stands behind him. At the bottom of the woodcut frame is the text "MATTH. I."</image-desc>This Chapter encompasses within itself the last and most solemn Prayer (which we find described) that Christ ever performed in the world with and for his Disciples; as he was about to depart from them, he wished to leave them a Prayer, being the best Testament <note>A "testament" here refers to a final will or legacy left to heirs.</note> that he could make for them.

This entire 17th Chapter, from the beginning to the end, contains nothing other than Christ's Prayer to his Father. In which these four things are to be observed:
1. The time when he performed this Prayer.
2. The posture of the body which he used.
3. The manner in which he prayed.
4. The matter for which he prayed.

<margin>Luther.</margin>
The time when he performed this prayer is indicated in two ways.
1. It was immediately after he had delivered a general Sermon, v. 1. Mark from this, that it is lawful and commendable for the Ministers of the Word that they pray after preaching. I say this now all the more readily because in this age there is a generation of people who judge otherwise. <note>Love likely refers to radical religious groups of the mid-17th century who rejected formal or structured ministerial prayers.</note> But this is established here by the practice of Jesus Christ himself; after he had preached, he lifted up his eyes to Heaven and prayed. And it is the saying of Luther, that a good Prayer must follow a good Sermon. Know also in passing, you who attend the ministry of the Gospel, that you must also go to God in Prayer after you have heard his word; when we have preached, you must begin to pray. It is a fine observation of the Holy Greenham. <note>Richard Greenham (c. 1535–1594) was an influential Puritan minister known for his practical piety.</note> I am certain, says <margin>Greenham.</margin> he, that this is a major reason why we 

<column-break/>

produce so little fruit through our preaching: because, although much is preached from the Pulpit, yet little or nothing is prayed in the inner chambers. <note>The "inner chambers" refers to private, individual prayer at home.</note>

<margin>Second circumstance of time.</margin>
The other circumstance of time when Christ performed this stately and heartfelt Prayer is this: it was the day before he was to die; for as soon as he had performed this Prayer, Judas came with a band of soldiers to betray him. Chapter 18. 1, 2, 3. Mark from this the example of Christ;

<margin>Observation.</margin>
That Christians must then have the most holy and fiery affections in their hearts when they are to depart from this world. Jesus Christ prayed well at all times, but he prayed most heartily a little before his death. It is a remarkable passage, Luke 22:44: *And being in an agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat became like drops of blood falling down to the ground.* Jesus Christ, when he was in a great struggle and lay down upon the earth (sweating drops of blood), prayed all the more earnestly or more intensely, straining his affections to the utmost. The <margin><note>original Greek: "ἀγωνία ἐκτενέστερον προσηύχετο" (in agony he prayed more earnestly)</note> Heb. 5:7.</margin> Apostle Paul, speaking of this, says: *Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared.* <note>King James Version phrasing used for clarity.</note> Christ prayed with strong crying, which refers to that earnest Prayer which Christ performed in the Garden, Luke 22:41. As appears from those words, *out of fear*, namely, for that bitter Cup, those unspeakable pains which he endured in his heavy struggle when the entire power of darkness came upon him. Here you see then that Jesus Christ prayed with a very fiery zeal and holy emotion just before he was to die; for the Apostle treats there of Christ's Priesthood, how he offered himself to God for our sins.

<meta>This page continues the sermon by Christopher Love on John 17:15. ### Christ’s Prayer

<margin>The work of Christ must be an example to us.</margin>
Indeed, follow the Lord Jesus here; before you come to die, you must especially have very holy, heavenly, and zealous movements in your hearts. Let Heaven especially possess your soul, just as your soul goes to possess Heaven. O Beloved, in this you must be like the swan, which (according to many) sings her sweetest song just before her death: when you are now about to die, sing with the old Simeon, *Lord, now let your servant depart in peace.* <note>Simeon was an elderly man in the Gospel of Luke who had been promised he would see the Messiah before he died; his prayer is known as the Nunc Dimittis.</note>

<margin>Luke 2:29.</margin>
<margin>The second circumstance of Christ’s countenance.</margin>
The second circumstance to be noted in this Prayer of Christ is the countenance [posture of the face] which he used therein; he lifted up his eyes to Heaven and said, *Father,* etc. It is quite true that gestures are not absolutely necessary in any act of service; it is not entirely necessary to kneel in prayer, yet gestures can help us in prayer. Christ lifted up his eyes to make it known that his heart was also where his eyes looked. Beloved, when you lift your eyes in your prayer toward Heaven, it signifies that your heart is in Heaven. I am certain that it was so with Christ, though it is perhaps different with you. It may be that your eye is toward Heaven in prayer while at the same time your heart is in your shop, or with your bad company, or with your harlots, etc. Remember, O man, to lift your heart as well as your eyes to Heaven; let your heart and eyes both stretch toward the same place. Christ lifted his eyes to Heaven in prayer, and his heart was there also; so it must be with you too.

<margin>Third circumstance: the manner of Christ’s praying.</margin>
<margin>Christ looked to the glory of God.</margin>
The third circumstance in this Prayer of Christ was the manner of praying; and that is expressed in various ways in this chapter.
1. He looked to the glory of God as the final end of that for which he prayed; this must also guide us in our prayers. *Glorify your Son, that your Son may also glorify you.* The aim of Christ's prayer was to glorify his Father; so also must the end of our prayer be to glorify God. Many cry out, "Lord glorify me," where they do not pray with moved hearts, "Lord, let me glorify your name." Christ said, *hallowed be your name,* expressing this pursuit to glorify the name of God; and this was the first petition in Christ’s prayer to show that glorifying God's name must be the first and foremost thing in our prayers.

<margin>Christ prayed to God his Father.</margin>
2. Christ prayed, *O my Father,* to teach you that you must not only pray with a reverent awareness of God, but also with a firm trust in God. Hebrews 11 verse 6: *without faith it is impossible to please God. For he who comes to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.* You must never come to God to seek him with doubt, but you must come with a firm trust, like a child to his Father.

<margin>Christ prays broadly and extensively for his disciples.</margin>
3. Christ prays very extensively for his disciples. I do not say more than that for which Christ prayed for himself; all the rest of the prayer was for his disciples—that God would preserve their unity <note>The original "meenicheyt" likely refers to fellowship or unity here.</note> and truth, and glorify them and all other believers with him in Heaven. Note here the wonderful affection of Jesus Christ toward his Church and people; as he was about to die, he prays more for the preservation of their souls than for his own life. Oh, herein the overflowing love of Jesus Christ is manifest: that while he now expected to die a painful, despised, and cursed death, taking upon himself the wrath of God deserved by our sins, he nevertheless wished to remember his chosen servants, in whose place he stood and for whose sins he died, and that with such an expansion of his heart in prayer.

<column-break/>

<margin>Fourth circumstance: the matter for which Christ prayed.</margin>
The fourth circumstance in this Prayer of Christ is the matter for which he prayed; and this is presented in two ways. Negatively: who those were for whom he did *not* pray. *I pray not for the world,* v. 9. This is an argument against those who plead for universal redemption. If Christ would not waste his breath to pray for them, he certainly would not shed his precious blood to obtain Heaven for them. Thereafter it is stated affirmatively for whom he *did* pray. *I pray for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.* You chosen and born again, for you I pray. These things he requests of his Father for the benefit of his disciples: that God would preserve them, *that they may be one,* v. 11. That God would *sanctify them,* v. 17. That they may come into Heaven and be with Christ, verse 24. And (as in our text): *I pray not that you should take them out of the world, but that you should keep them from the evil.*

<margin>The text explained.</margin>
The words, as you see, are presented in two ways. 1. Negatively: what Christ did *not* pray for his disciples. *I pray not that you should take them out of the world.*

<margin>Question.</margin>
2. With an affirmation: why he did pray. *I pray that you keep them from the evil* of this world. Someone might ask: why did Christ say that he did not pray that his disciples might be taken out of the world?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
Our Lord Christ knew that his end was near, that his hour had come, that he would depart from the world. John 13:1: *Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come that he should depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.* When the disciples heard this, they thought thus to themselves: "Lord, if you will leave this world, how then will it go with us when you are gone? We will be in the world like a ship without a pilot, and like sheep without a shepherd," and therefore they prayed that they might die with Christ. John 11:16: *Then Thomas, called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: let us also go, that we may die with him.* And John 13:37 <note>The source text lists verse 39, but the quote is from verse 37.</note> Peter said to Christ, *Why cannot I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.* All the Apostles were zealous to die for Christ; yet Christ, seeing them so willing to die, says—to restrain their intense emotions—that he would not pray that they should die now; but, says he, "I will pray my Father that when I have gone, and you remain after me in the world, he will then keep you from the evil of the world."

<margin>Reasons why Christ did not pray that his disciples should be taken out of the world.</margin>
You ask me <note>The Dutch "Draeght ghy my" appears to be a transcription error for "Vraeght ghy my" (You ask me).</note> what was the specific reason why Christ would not pray that they should be taken out of the world.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Christ’s prayer in John 17:15: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil." The author is addressing why Christ desires his followers to remain in a world of suffering rather than being taken immediately to heaven.</meta>

->### ...as a support for the Saints.<-

<margin>1. Reason.</margin>
I answer: 1. If the Disciples had died when Christ died, then the people would have thought that they were Christ's partners in achieving our salvation. <note>The author argues that if the apostles had died alongside Jesus, it might have suggested they were co-saviors rather than mere followers.</note>

<margin>Isaiah 63:3.</margin>
For this reason it is written, that Christ has trodden the winepress of his Father’s wrath alone, and that there was no one from the nations with him. <note>original: "de persse van zijns Vaders toorn alleen getreden heeft"</note> Christ wanted to have the glory of our salvation alone. While there were two Thieves—unworthy men—who died with Christ, this was so that the world would see that Christ's death alone earned the salvation of mankind.

<margin>2. Reason.</margin>
A second reason is this: Christ did not desire that his Disciples should be taken out of the world because he had greater work for them to perform. It was as if he said, "The Gospel must be spread and take root through you; you must convert souls; you must gather my elect; therefore, I will not pray to the Father that he take you out of the world, but that he keep you from the evil of the world." Although I do not pray that he keep you from the evil of tribulations and persecutions, which you must suffer in the world for my name's sake, nonetheless I shall pray that he (once I am gone) keeps you from the evil of sin—that you do not fall into sin through the allurements or the contempt of the world, through the wicked temptations of Satan, and through the impulses and inclinations of your own corrupt hearts. I will pray that my Father keeps you from the evil of the times and places in which you live.

From these words, thus explained, I shall draw these five conclusions and teachings.

<margin>First doctrine.</margin>
First, because Christ refuses to pray to his Father to take his Disciples out of the world—those who, out of fear of persecution, wished to die with Christ—take note of this: That it is lawful for no one to wish for death out of the feeling or fear of persecutions and tribulations. This is what we find happened to the salty Jonah <note>The term "soute" (salty/briny) likely refers to Jonah's time in the sea, but also carries the connotation of being stubborn or sharp-tempered.</note> in the 4th Chapter, verse 3: *Now then, Lord, take my soul from me; for it is better for me to die than to live.* This he said with a proud and disturbed mind, having a displeasure because God had spared the Ninevites, thinking that he would be regarded as a false Prophet because of it. Thus the Scripture forbids wishing for death on account of the oppression and contempt in the world, and the reasons for this are these five:

<margin>1st reason why we do not wish for death.</margin>
1. Because your life is a great blessing; and you value it far below its worth when you so hastily wish for death. It is true, there are some who value their life far too highly, and these are those who will not lay down their life for Jesus Christ’s sake, or for the sake of his truth and Church, when they are called to do so. Others estimate their life at too low a price; namely, those who wish to be taken away from this world because of the troubles and oppressions they encounter in the world. This is a sin, for it is a belittling of your life, which is the greatest of all temporal blessings.

<margin>2. Second reason.</margin>
2. Because it is more praiseworthy to pray that God, in his own fit time, will ward off the oppression from us, than to cry out, "Lord, pull us out of the oppression." It is better to pray that God will sanctify our hearts through patience

<column-break/>

and thankfulness to bear that Cross with which it shall please him to exercise us, than that he should deliver us from adversity and persecution by taking us out of the world; for God has ten thousand ways to free us from oppression, besides taking us out of this life; so can he make an end of our tribulations and yet prolong our lives.

<margin>Third rule.</margin>
3. There is more honor to be gained by patiently bearing our burden than by being delivered from it. A Soldier is never renowned for his courage until he has endured the brunt of the Battle. And a Christian never shines in grace until he comes into the fire of tribulations, especially if he suffers in order to give testimony to the truth of Christ. Therefore we must be well-contented, indeed, be rejoiced in our suffering, and not wish for death so as to be delivered from the anxieties of this life.

<margin>Use for reproof.</margin>
Well, if it is so, that it is lawful for no one to wish for death because of any oppression which he has or feels, then many kinds of people stand here to be rebuked; but principally you people who have such troublesome and irritable tempers, such fretful and intemperate souls, that if God only lays some oppression upon you—if he only mixes some cross with your comfort, some gall and Wormwood with your delights—so that perhaps your status is taken away, or you are thrown into prison, and all your worldly comfort is taken from you, immediately you go into a fretful spirit like Jeremiah, cursing your birth-day, and with Jonah wishing for your death. This is sin. It is true, godly men have also erred in this, as in Job 6:8, 9 <note>The OCR says "Ioan. 6" but the context and verse numbers clearly refer to Job.</note>: *Oh that I might have my request; and that God would grant me the thing that I long for! Even that it would please God to destroy me; that he would let loose his hand, and make an end of me.* Here you see a wishing and longing for death, yes, a crying out (as it were) for deliverance; he is an unseemly and earnest seeker of the grave, and this only because the hand of God was heavy upon him. The same distress is expressed in the name of others in Job 3:21: *Who long for death, but it cometh not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures.* There is a sharpness and bitterness in physical death, yet there are some so plagued in the body and oppressed in the spirit that they consider even the bitterness of death to be sweetness: the Gall and Wormwood of oppression makes death as sweet as honey to such people; they long for it as for a honeycomb. And they do not only long for it, but they dig for it, and not in an ordinary way, but they dig as if for a treasure: yes, as if for hidden treasures, which indicates the earnestness of their longing for death. This immoderation also fell upon the heart of the Prophet Elijah. He himself went into the Wilderness a day’s journey, and came and sat under a Juniper-tree: and prayed that his soul might die: and said, *It is enough; now, O Lord, take my soul; for I am not better than my fathers.*

<margin>1 Kings 19:4.</margin>
