threatened to take his life away as well. Perhaps many of you—to whom I speak—have lost your status and your trade, and are now in poverty and disregarded by others, and might therefore easily wish that God would take you out of this world. But know that this is a very sinful state of the spirit: to long for death only to be delivered from the troubles of this life, desiring to lie down in the grave merely to give rest to our bodies and the outward man. If we believe that our life ought not to continue in this world unless we enjoy our outward comforts, rest, plenty, pride, honor, prosperity, and appearances, then we esteem that great blessing of our life far too lightly. At best, it is a weakness, and this is what Christ here rebuked in his Disciples.

Furthermore, since Christ did not wish to pray that his Disciples—who longed for death out of fear of persecution—might be taken out of this world:

<margin>Second Doctrine.</margin>
It is here silently indicated that it is permitted in some cases for a person to long for death, such as:

<margin>When it is permitted to wish for death.</margin>
First, when one wishes for it not because of suffering, but because of sin; when someone desires to shake off the body of the flesh so that he might be released and set free from a body of sin—this is praiseworthy. This was the prayer of Paul; we have, <margin>2 Corinthians 5:8.</margin> as he says, good courage, and are well pleased rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord. To long for death, not because it brings you to your end and lightens your pain, but because it kills your corruption and makes an end of your sins; not as if it were a back door to let your temporal life out, but as a front door to let eternal life in—this is permissible and lawful.

Secondly, it is permissible to long for death in order to obtain a fuller enjoyment of Jesus Christ, as we see in the Apostle Paul: I am hard-pressed <margin>Philippians 1:23</margin> between the two, having a desire to depart and to be with Christ. It is a sin for someone to desire to depart merely to be without a cross <note>The "cross" refers to the burdens and sufferings a Christian must bear in imitation of Jesus.</note>, but it is a virtue to wish to depart in order to enjoy Jesus Christ. O you who say: "I desire to die to enjoy God more perfectly and to live more virtuously"—not because your shroud will wipe away all tears and sighs, but because it will cause all sin and contamination to cease—this is a virtuous desire. We must wish for death not because our comforts are small, but so that our fellowship with Christ may be fulfilled; it must be a door to us, not to let us out of our torments, but to let us into the Heavenly dwellings.

But passing briefly over these things, I proceed to another observation from these words: *I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world*. Why did Christ not want to pray for this? The primary reason was <margin>Third Doctrine.</margin> because he had a greater work for his Disciples to perform in the world. From this, note that our Lord Christ does not desire that any of his servants shall die as long as he still has any work for them in this world. Your days are not only stretched out, and your months are not only with God,

<column-break/>

but he has also determined the work for you which you must do. God says to a Minister of the Word: "You shall preach so many sermons, convert so many souls, and gather so many of my elect"; and when your work is done, then your life shall have an end. You, God-fearing Christian, before you have finished your work, you shall not end your days. This can serve as a great comfort to all who fear God; do not fear death, for Christ does not desire to take you out of the world until you have performed the work for which God sent you into the world.

We shall draw three kinds of usefulness from this: first for instruction, secondly for reproof, and thirdly for comfort.

<margin>The first use: for instruction.</margin>
First, it serves for the instruction of you all.

1. That you do not desire to live any longer than you may finish the work for which God sent you into the world. Do not desire to live to give free rein to your lusts and to do what is good in your own eyes; but do not desire to live longer than you may serve God and do good to others.

2. You who can still do good service in the world are taught here that you are obliged to desire of God that he does not yet take you out of the world. It comes to my mind that <margin>Luther.</margin> Luther notes on this text: That it is the bounden duty of a Minister, especially and more than anyone else, to pray that his life may be prolonged in order to convert more souls to God. And it was the saying of an old Minister as he lay on his deathbed: 
> Lord, if I can still be of service to your people, then let me live longer; I shall not shy away from more labor and trouble if you have more work for me to perform. 
Whoever among you can do service in this world is bound to pray to God that he will lengthen your days, and that you may live to do more good in that place where God has set you.

3. Let me instruct you from this that although you come to endure much evil in the world, nonetheless, if you do much good therein, let your doing of good lead you rather to desire life, than the suffering of evil should awaken in you a desire for death. We must be glad to suffer much evil if only through that suffering we can do much good. When Julius Caesar <margin>Julius Caesar.</margin> said, 
> I have lived long enough, whether I look upon my nature or upon my glory,

> My Lord, although you have lived long enough for yourself, you have not yet lived long enough for your Fatherland. <note>This refers to the dialogue regarding Caesar’s perceived readiness to die versus the needs of the Roman Republic.</note>
Are you a person who does good to your people? <margin>Acts 13:36.</margin> Are you a useful person? Even if you are old, and even if you have the weaknesses of your old age, do not let this make life tedious to you; though you have perhaps lived long enough for yourself, you have nonetheless not lived long enough for others, for the benefit of the Church and the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "Gemeene beste," referring to the public good or the state.</note> in which you live. Take this to heart, seeing that every mother’s son is sent into the world to do something for God. Oh, labor then, so that when your days shall be at an end, your consciences may tell you that you have done that work,

### For the Support of the Saints

you have <note>original: "hebt," continuing from the previous page's sentence about finishing the task</note> for which God sent you into the world. Therefore, King David is praised in **Acts 13:36**, stating that after he had served the counsel of God in his own generation, he fell asleep and was laid with his fathers. He did his work, and then he died.

O beloved, there is nothing in the wide world that will give your souls greater comfort when you come to die (for we must all one day, sooner or later, drink from that cup) than this: namely, that your conscience can tell you, "I have served my God in my life; I have finished my work; and the last work I have to do is to die." When your sight is finally broken and your mouth is closed, and you can take no further refreshment to revive or restore your hidden spirits, then this shall be your restoration: for your conscience will tell you that you have completed the work for which God sent you into the world; and now you have nothing else to do but die and go to heaven. 

There is a remarkable emphasis in what is written in **Job 5:26**: *You shall come to the grave in a full age, like a shock of corn <note>A "shock" is a stack of harvested grain sheaves placed together to dry.</note> comes in in its season.* We know that if someone mowed down a stack of corn while it was still green and had only just sprouted into ears, that corn would not be fit for baking bread. But if he cuts down the corn when it is ripe, then good bread can come from it. Death cuts off the lives of many people while they are still "green in leaf"—unfit and unprepared for death, unripe for heaven and its glory. They are like the grass upon the housetop, which withers before it is cut, or like the seed that fell on stony or thorny ground and never reached maturity. But to the godly, God says: you shall go to the grave when you are ripe for heaven and for God; when you have done your Master’s work, then you shall enter into your Master’s dwellings. You shall come to the grave like a shock of corn in its season. Oh, what great comfort and refreshment of heart this would be for you who have done the work for which God placed you here in the world!

<margin>Utility: Reproof.</margin>
The second utility <term>utility</term><note>In 17th-century preaching, a "utility" or "use" was the practical application of a doctrine to the listener's life.</note> shall be for reproof. If it is true that Christ does not want any of His servants to die before they have finished the work for which they were sent into the world, then this serves to reprove the ungodly of this world, who come to die before they have even begun to do the work for which they entered the world. Are there not many who have lived until their hair is gray and now hasten toward their grave, who have never set their hands to any work for which God sent them into the world? 

Beloved, I shall point you to a sorrowful text of Scripture, and it is worthy of being engraved in gold: **Isaiah 65:20**. *There shall be no more an infant of days, nor an old man who has not fulfilled his days; for the youth shall die being one hundred years old, but the sinner being one hundred years old shall be accursed.* This is the most terrifying text I know in the Old Testament regarding the ungodly, and yet it is comforting for the godly. It is a promise regarding the conversion 

<column-break/>

and the bringing in of the Gentiles. I shall explain the meaning to you: *there shall be no more an infant of days*; that is, a person who has lived many days and many years, yet has no more knowledge of God and has served God no more than a nursing infant. There were many such people living in the time of the Prophets, who were men of many days but children in understanding and knowledge. *There shall be no old man who shall not fulfill his days.* That is, that old man who practices no virtue, who does not serve and glorify God, who does not fulfill the duty of each day, who does not fill his days with righteousness but with sin—this is the man who shall not fulfill his days. 

There are many such old people in the world, whose wrinkled faces and gray hairs suggest they are eighty years old, yet in terms of virtue and knowledge, they have not reached their fourteenth year. Truly, all those among you who are "infants of few days" are rightly to be reproved—that is, those who have done no more service to God and have no more knowledge of God than children. You have lived many days, but they have been only empty days; your hearts are so full of sin that it is no wonder they are so empty of virtue. Is there not many a man and woman who, with shame and sorrow before God, might say to themselves: "Have I not lived forty, fifty, or perhaps sixty years, yet You know, O God, that my days are empty days; in all the time of my life, I have done no good"? 

When godly people die, they are said—according to the common phrasing of Scripture—to die in a "good old age." But an old drunkard, an old adulterer, or an old swearer dying in his old age has a bad, not a good, old age. When you come to die, your conscience will say to you, "I am an old man, but I have not done the work for which God sent me into the world." I once read of an "old disciple" who was ninety years old, and when asked how old he was, he said he was forty-five. They answered, "Your gray hairs show that you are much older." "Well," he said, "if you count the number of my years, I have lived ninety years; but if you count how long I have lived a proper life unto God, then I am only forty-five, for the other half of my life I was a dead man." 

Oh, how many there are in the world who have lived all their days as dead men! There is a passage in **Ecclesiastes 7:17**: *Be not overmuch wicked, neither be you foolish: why should you die before your time?* Some interpreters take it this way: a person walking in drunkenness, excess, and licentiousness shortens, as it were, his days. Others say that whoever lives such a life is dead while he lives, before the time of his death, and when death comes, he is "twice dead." Certainly, no one can die before the time appointed by God. **Job 14:5**: *Since his days are determined, the number of his months is with You, and You have made his limits which he cannot pass.* Now, although you

Perhaps many of you to whom I speak have lost your status and business, and are now in poverty and disregarded by others, and might therefore easily wish that God would take you out of this world. But know that this is a very sinful state of spirit: to long for death only to be delivered from the hardships of this life, or to desire to lie down in the grave merely to give rest to our bodies and the outward man. If we believe that our life ought not to continue in this world unless we enjoy our outward comforts, rest, plenty, high status, honor, prosperity, and friends, then we value that great blessing of our life far too little. At best, it is a weakness, and Christ rebuked this here in His disciples.

Again, since Christ did not wish to pray that His disciples—who longed for death because of persecution—might be taken out of this world:

<margin>**Second Doctrine.** When it is permissible to wish for death.</margin> 
It is here silently indicated that it is permissible in some cases for a person to long for death, such as:

<margin>*2 Cor. 5:8*</margin>
First, when one wishes for it not because of suffering, but because of sin; when someone desires to shake off the body of the flesh so that they might be released and set free from a body of sin, this is praiseworthy. This was the prayer of *Paul*; "we are confident," he says, "and well pleased rather to be absent from the body and to be present with the Lord." To long for death—not because it brings you to an end and lightens your pain, but because it kills your corruption and puts an end to your sins; not as a back door to let out your temporal life, but as a front door to let in eternal life—this is permissible and lawful.

<margin>*Phil. 1:23*</margin>
Secondly, it is permissible to long for death in order to obtain a fuller enjoyment of Jesus Christ, as we see in the Apostle *Paul*: "For I am hard-pressed between the two, having a desire to depart and be with Christ." It is a sin for someone to desire to depart just to be without a cross <note>The "cross" refers to earthly burdens or religious trials.</note>, but it is a virtue to wish to depart in order to enjoy Jesus Christ. O you who say, "I desire to die to enjoy God more perfectly and to live more virtuously"—not because your shroud will wipe away all tears and oppressions, but because it will cause all sins and stains to cease—this is a virtuous desire. We must wish for death, not because our comforts are small, but so that our communion with Christ may be fulfilled; it must be to us a door, not to let us in from our torments, but to let us into the heavenly dwellings.

<margin>**Third Doctrine.**</margin>
But passing over these things briefly, I proceed to another observation from these words: *I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world*. Why did Christ not wish to pray for this? The primary reason was because He had more work for His disciples to perform in the world. From this, note that our Lord Christ does not desire that any of His servants shall die as long as He still has some work for them in this world. Your days are not only stretched out, and your months are not only with God,

<column-break/>

but He has also strictly determined the work which you must do. God says to a minister of the Word: so many sermons shall you speak, so many souls shall you convert, so many of my elect shall you gather; and when your work is done, then shall your life have an end. You, God-fearing Christian, before you have finished your work, you shall not end your days. This can serve as a great comfort to all who fear God; do not fear death, for Christ does not desire to take you out of the world before you have performed the work for which God sent you into the world.

We shall draw three kinds of usefulness from this: first for instruction, second for rebuke, and third for comfort.

<margin>First usefulness for instruction.</margin>
First, it serves for the instruction of you all.

1. That you should not desire to live any longer than you may complete the work for which God sent you into the world. Do not desire to live to give free rein to your lusts and to do what is good in your own eyes; but desire to live no longer than you may serve God and do good to others.

<margin>*Luther.*</margin>
2. You who can still do good service in the world are taught here that you are obligated to ask of God that He does not yet take you out of the world. It comes to my mind that *Luther* notes on this text: That it is the bounden duty of a minister, especially and more than anyone else, to pray that his life may be prolonged, so as to convert more souls to God. And it was the saying of an old preacher as he lay on his deathbed: "Lord, if I can still be of service to your people, let me live longer; I shall not shrink from more labor and trouble if you have more work for me to perform." Whoever among you can do service in this world is bound to pray to God that He will lengthen your days, and that you may live to do more good in that place where God has set you.

<margin>*Julius Caesar. Cicero.*</margin>
3. Let me instruct you from this that although you come to endure much evil in the world, nevertheless, if you do much good in it, let your doing of good stir you to desire life rather than the suffering of evil provoking in you a desire for death. We must be glad to suffer much evil if only through that suffering we can do much good. When *Julius Caesar* said, "I have lived long enough, whether I look at my nature or my honor," *Cicero* replied: "My Lord, although you have lived long enough for yourself, you have not yet lived long enough for your Fatherland." Are you a person who does good to your people? (**Acts 13:36**). Are you a useful person? Even if you are old, and even if you have the weaknesses of your old age, do not let this make life weary to you; although you have perhaps lived long enough for yourself, you have not yet lived long enough for others, for the benefit of the Church and the common good in which you live. Take this to heart, considering every mother's child is sent into the world to do something for God. Oh, labor then, so that when your days come to an end, your consciences may tell you that you have done that work,

->### For the Support of the Saints.<-

O beloved, there is nothing in the wide world which shall give your souls greater comfort when you come to die (for we all must one day, sooner or later, drink from that cup) than this: namely, that your conscience can tell you, "I have served my God in my life; I have finished my work; and the last work I have to do is to die." When once your sight is broken and your mouth is closed, and you can take no heart-strengthening medicine <note>The author refers to physical cordials or restoratives used for the dying</note> to refresh and restore your hidden spirits, then *this* shall be your restoration; for your conscience shall tell you that you have finished the work for which God sent you into the world; and now you have nothing else to do but to die and go to Heaven. There is a remarkable emphasis in what is written in **Job 5:26**: *You shall come to the grave in a full age, as a shock of grain is gathered in its season.* It is known that if someone mows down a <term>shock of grain</term><note>A "shock" (koorn-hoop) is a stack of harvested grain stalks stood upright in a field to dry.</note> while it is still green and has only just sprouted into ears, that grain would not be fit to bake bread from; but if he cuts down a shock of grain when it is ripe, then good bread can come from it. Death cuts off the lives of many people while they are still "green corn," unfit and unprepared for death, unripe for Heaven and its glory; when they are like the grass on the house-tops which withers before it is cut, or like the seed which fell on stony or thorny ground and never reached maturity. But to the pious God says: you shall go to the grave when you are ripe for Heaven and for God; when you have done your Master’s work, then you shall enter your Master’s dwellings; you shall come to the grave like a shock of grain in its season. Oh, how great a comfort and refreshment of the heart this would be for you, who have done the work for which you were placed here in the world by God.

<margin>
Utility of
Reproof.
</margin>
The second utility shall be for **reproof**. If it is so, that Christ does not want any of His servants to die before they have finished the work for which they were sent into the world, then the godless of this world stand here to be reproved, who come to die before they have even begun to do the work for which they came into the world. Are there not many who have lived even unto their grey hairs, and now hasten to their grave, who have never set their hands to any work for which God sent them into the world? Beloved, I shall point you to a somber text of Scripture, and it is worthy of being engraved in gold: **Isaiah 65:20**. *There shall be no more an infant of few days, nor an old man that has not fulfilled his days; for the child shall die a hundred years old; but the sinner being a hundred years old shall be accursed.* This is the most terrifying text for the godless in the Old Testament, and yet it is comforting for the godly. It is a promise of the conversion

<column-break/>

and the bringing in of the Gentiles; I shall explain the meaning to you: *there shall be no more an infant of few days*; that is, a person who, having lived many days and many years, nonetheless has no more knowledge of God, and has served God no more than an infant. There were many such who lived in the time of the Prophets, who were men of many days but children in understanding and knowledge. *There shall be no old man who shall not fulfill his days.* That is: that old man who practices no virtue, who does not serve and glorify God, who does not fulfill the duty of each day, who fills his days with sin and not with righteousness—it is this person who shall not fulfill his days. There are many such old people in the world, whose wrinkled faces and grey hairs indicate that they are indeed eighty years old, and yet in terms of virtue and knowledge, they have not reached their fourteenth year. Well, then, rightly to be reproved are all those among you who are infants of few days; that is, who have done no more service for God and have no more knowledge of God than children; many days have you lived, but they have been only empty days; your hearts are full of sin, so it is no wonder that they are so empty of virtue. Is there not many a man and woman who, with shame and sorrow before God, might say this against themselves: "Have I not lived forty, fifty, yes, perhaps sixty years, yet You know, O God, that my days are empty days; I have done no good in all the time of my life." When godly people die, they are said—in the common manner of speaking in the Scriptures—to die in a "good old age"; but an old drunkard, an old adulterer, or an old swearer, dying in his old age, has a bad and not a good old age. When you come to die, then your conscience shall tell you, "I am an old man, but I have not done the work for which God sent me into the world." I once read of an <note>The "Old Disciple" is a common trope in 17th-century sermons, often referring to Polycarp or similar figures.</note> **Old Disciple** who was ninety years old, and being asked how old he was, said he was forty-five years old. They answered, "Your grey hairs show that you are much older." "Well," said he, "if you count the number of my years, I have lived ninety years; but if you count how long I have lived a devout life unto God, I am only forty-five years old, for during the other time of my life I was a dead man." Oh, how many there are in the world who have lived all their days as dead men!

There stands a passage in **Ecclesiastes 7:17**: *Be not overmuch wicked, neither be you foolish: why should you die before your time?* Some interpreters take it thus: a person walking in drunkenness, excess, and licentiousness shortens, as it were, his days. Others say that whoever lives so is dead while he lives, before the time of his death; and when death comes, he is twice dead. Certainly no one can die before the time appointed by God. **Job 14:5**: *Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with you, and you have appointed his bounds that he cannot pass.* Now although you

Oh, think upon that: even if you cannot die before God’s appointed time, you must ensure you are made ready for death before you have finished the work for which God gave you life. If the Lord Christ prayed that His disciples would not die before they had done their work, how then are those to be blamed of whom—even if they lived until the Day of Judgment—God would have no more service than He has now, and in whom He would see as much sin then as He does now?

<margin>
Third utility for comfort.
</margin>
The final utility is for comfort: if Jesus Christ does not want His people to be taken out of the world before they have finished their work, then know, all you children of God, that as long as God lets you remain here in the world, He still has work for you. Suppose you are thrown into prison; think then that this is a part of your work which you must do for the Lord Christ. Are you a minister of the Gospel, and do you suffer poverty, contempt, or further persecution for righteousness' sake? Think that this is a part of the service which you must do for God. Christ will not take you away when your work is only half-done, but when you have accomplished your work, then you shall go to receive your reward.

<margin>
Bolton.

There comes to my mind a saying of Mr. Bolton <note>Likely Robert Bolton (1572–1631), a famous Puritan preacher known for his works on "walking with God."</note>; as he lay on his deathbed, he said, "O Lord, this is my comfort: that although I have ended my days, I have nonetheless performed my work before I die." Truly, this is comforting for a godly heart, but terrifying for those of you who are godless; you who, when you have ended your days, have not yet begun your work, nor served your God. Oh, this shall one day be a great gnawing of the conscience. Oh, this shall be the worm that shall gnaw you in Hell into eternity: namely, to remember that God gave you your work to do in this world, and granted you time and means for the performance of the same, but you spent your time uselessly, neglected many heavenly opportunities of grace and mercy, and trifled away whole days when you had so much work to do—so that when your days came to an end, you had not yet begun your work. Oh, do not let this guilt lie upon your conscience; do not let this be the worm to gnaw you in Hell: namely, to remember that you lived long in the world, and yet the work for which God sent you into the world, you have not done.

<margin>
The fourth doctrine.
</margin>
Now I proceed to the fourth observation from these words: *I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world.* Note from this: *That no one dies unless God takes them away.* If our life were in our own hands, we would live too long; and if our life were in the hands of our enemies, we would not live a day longer. But now our life is in the hands of God, and therefore we cannot

<column-break/>

die, unless God takes our life away. And this shows that the refuge of a Christian is under divine protection; a godless person cannot thrust you out of the world before your time; God must take you out of the world. It may be that your enemies are envious of you, and that those who hate you wish a thousand deaths upon you; nevertheless, this can be your comfort: you cannot die before God takes you out of the world. According to the way the Scripture speaks, those who die are said to be gathered to their fathers; you shall live just so long until God deems it fit to gather you to Himself, having made you fit for glory. And thus I have finished the first part of the text: *I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world.*

Now I shall show what it is for which Christ prays for His disciples: *But I pray that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.* I do not pray that you should take them out of the world, but that you keep them from falling into sin, from falling away from You entirely to the very end; this is my prayer: that You keep them from the evil of the world. Note from this: *That it can be a great comfort for God's people that they have the prayer of Jesus Christ to keep them from evil while they live in the world.* Although the Lord Christ does not pray for you that you should be taken out of the world, He nonetheless prays for you that you might not come to sin in the same manner and as heavily as the world sins—that you do not follow the temptations of the devil as the world does. This is the primary prayer of Jesus Christ. Now, there are two questions which I shall answer.

<margin>
The fifth doctrine.
</margin>
<margin>
Two questions are resolved. 1. Question.
</margin>
It is true, a dismayed heart may say, I believe that Jesus Christ prayed for His eleven Apostles, that God would keep them in the world from the temptations of the devil and from sin; but does Christ also pray for me, who lives so many hundreds of years later?

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
I answer: our Lord Christ knew well that this objection would arise in the hearts of His children in the following ages; therefore He answers it Himself in **John 17:20**: *Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word.* Christ does not say, "I pray for everyone"; otherwise He would contradict Himself, for He had said in the ninth verse: *I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.* 1. All those whom God the Father has given to Christ, all believers, are included in the prayer of Christ, but not all the world. 2. Again, He does not say, "I pray for all who believe [now]," for then it might be limited to the believers of that time in which Christ lived on earth; but *I pray for those who shall believe*, so that the prayer of Christ to be kept from the evil of the world extends to all believers until the end of the world. 3. # Flesh and Spirit.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
A good observation from Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was a Church Father best known for translating the Bible into Latin.</note>, when he says: Christ does not say, "I pray for all those who have shed their blood for me"; for then only the martyrs would enjoy the benefits through Christ. Nor does Christ say, "I pray for all those who convert souls to me"; for then only the preachers would receive this blessing through Christ. Rather, he says: "I pray for you who believe and shall believe in me." And thus every Christian enjoys a portion and a blessing in the prayer of Jesus Christ.

<margin>2nd Question.</margin>
A second question is this: it is certainly true (some might say) that when Christ was on earth, His prayer had power and utility; but can I imagine that I shall enjoy fruit and utility through that prayer which Christ offered while on earth so long ago?

<margin>
Answer.
The power of Christ endures forever.
Acts 8:60
</margin>
To this I answer that the power of Christ’s prayer remained after the time of Christ, as will appear from this: If the prayer of Stephen was powerful through the conversion of Saul <note>Saul, later known as the Apostle Paul, was present at the stoning of the first martyr, Stephen.</note>, after Stephen was stoned to death with Saul's consent (for Stephen, as he was about to die, prayed that God would not charge them with this sin), shall not the prayer of Christ Himself be powerful after His death?

Secondly, Christ Himself says that His prayer on earth would be for all those who would believe thereafter; so that this prayer of Christ to God the Father, to keep them from the evil one, is as powerful in this generation—and shall be until the end—as it was in the very hour it was offered.

Thirdly, even if it were so that the prayer of Jesus Christ [on earth] was no longer powerful, it still cannot be doubted that Christ’s intercession <term>intercession: the act of praying or petitioning on behalf of another</term> in Heaven is powerful now, for He sits at the right hand of God praying for us. Romans 8:34: *Who is he that condemns? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us.* So also Hebrews 9:24: *Christ is entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us.* And Hebrews 7:25: *Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost (that is, continually and perfectly) that come unto God by him, seeing he ever lives to make intercession for them.* So here is your comfort: even if the power of His earthly prayer did not last until this generation, it is nonetheless undoubtedly true that the power of Christ’s intercession now in Heaven lasts for you until the end of the world. Christ lives forever to pray for you.

<margin>
1st Consequence.
First, from this doctrine:
That we ourselves must pray and not exclude ourselves.
</margin>
Now I shall handle six consequences <note>Or "inferences"—practical applications derived from the teaching.</note> serving the practice of godliness, which this doctrine gives us.

If it is so that Jesus Christ prays for all His people—namely, for His disciples and all believers—that they might be kept from the evil one while they live in the world, then I conclude from this:

First, that we then must ourselves seek God, to keep us from the evil one; the prayer of Jesus Christ for us does not exclude our own praying for ourselves. Christ never intended to pray to His Father to keep us from sin so that we would become careless and never pray that we might be kept from sin ourselves. Although Christ prays that we may be

<column-break/>

kept from evil; yet we must also pray; for so He teaches us in Matthew 6:13: *And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one*; which is the same as what stands here in the text. It is an observation of <margin>Johann Gerhard</margin> Johann Gerhard <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637) was a famous Lutheran theologian known for his "Harmonia Evangelica" (Harmony of the Gospels).</note> in his harmony of the Evangelists. The prayers of Jesus Christ (he says) were not only meritorious, but they were also examples and patterns to teach us what and how we must pray. If Christ prayed that I might be kept from sin and from the evil of the times and places in which I live, should this not teach me to pray that God would preserve me from the temptations and snares that I encounter on the way to Heaven? Christ’s prayer must not exclude your prayers. It says in Luke 22:40: *And when he was at the place, he said unto them, Pray that ye enter not into temptation.* It was not permitted for them to say, "Christ prays for us, therefore why do we need to pray for ourselves?" No, says Christ: "Though I pray for you, yet you pray for yourselves also, that you enter not into temptation." This is the first consequence: Christ’s prayers must not exclude our prayers.

<margin>2nd Consequence.</margin>
Secondly, if this is true—that Christ prays that you be kept from the evil one in the world—let this be a comfort to your hearts, just as it was for Peter in Luke 22:31–32: *And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not.* Perhaps you have not considered this passage nor taken it to heart, but there is much comfort in it; it is said there that Satan desired to sift and tempt Peter, but at that very time the <margin>Christ prays before the Devil tempts.</margin> Lord Jesus was actually praying for Peter. Before the Devil tempts you to accept a temptation, Christ is already praying for you, that you might not be overcome by the temptation. As soon as the Devil merely intends to tempt you, Christ prays for you to prevent the peril. Christ prays not only in the anguish of temptation, when the Devil makes a strong attack on the soul, but before he even comes alongside you, Christ is already praying for you: *Satan desires to sift you, but I have prayed for you.* Oh, think then to yourself: I see the Devil is very busy around my poor soul, tempting and inciting me to commit godlessness; but now watch yourself, and remember that Christ in Heaven prays for you. When the Devil tempts me to give myself to sin, Christ prays that I may not come to do that, through the strength He has given me. Now this can serve wonderfully for comfort: to remember that Christ prays for you, that you are not conquered by the evil of the world.

<margin>
3rd Consequence.
Christ's prayer must crucify sinful impulses in us.
</margin>
Thirdly, this ought to stop and restrain your desires; namely, to remember that Christ prays for you. When the Devil comes to seek you for some sin, then think thus to yourself: "I see now that the Devil is very busy around me, to tempt me to this wickedness; but shall I go directly against my own prayers? Indeed, shall I put the prayer of Jesus Christ to shame?" For just as Christ prayed on earth, so He prays now in Heaven, that I do not come to consent to this temptation; and shall I [disregard] the prayer of my

-># Christ’s Prayer<-

...to bring to nothing my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; when Christ prays to His Father that He might give me strength to withstand temptation, shall I then run so carelessly into temptation?

<margin>4. Consequence: Christ’s prayer must not diminish our own care.</margin>
Fourthly, Christ’s prayer to His Father to preserve you from the evil one must not cause your own care to diminish in preserving yourself from evil. It is a piteous thing when the permission of God the Father and the intercession of Jesus Christ are misused, such as when you become through them presumptuous, bold, and careless in how you must live. Certainly, Christ commands you to pray that you do not enter into temptation. You and I must watch against temptation as if we had no one but ourselves to watch against the devil; we must pray against temptation as if we had no one but ourselves to pray against temptation. Nevertheless, when we have prayed and watched, and have been preserved from the temptations of the devil, we must attribute it solely to the mercy of God and the prayer of Christ, and not at all to ourselves.

<margin>5. Consequence: Our nature is very inclined toward sin.</margin>
Fifthly, Christ prays that you may be preserved from the evil one: learn from this that in our nature there is an inclination to be defiled with the evil of the times and places in which we live. Christ would never have prayed to His Father for us unless there were in our natures and minds a strong tendency to be stained by the evil of the world.

<margin>6. Consequence: No one can by nature preserve themselves. <note>original: "Augustin. tractat. 21. in Johan."</note> Augustine, Tractate 21 on John.</margin>
Sixthly, if Christ prays to His Father that He preserve us from the evil of the world, learn from this that all people are by nature powerless to preserve themselves from it. A devil is a "strong armed man," <note>Referring to Luke 11:21, where Jesus describes a "strong man, fully armed" guarding his palace.</note> and you are a poor, unarmed creature; he is stronger than you, and you could as easily subdue and overcome an army of a hundred thousand men as kill a single desire through your own strength. Augustine notes very well on these words, "without me you can do nothing" <note>John 15:5</note>: that Christ does not say, "without me you can do little," but "without me you can do nothing." You cannot do the least virtuous work without Christ. Oh, behold then the weakness and wickedness of your nature: you can do nothing without Christ; you cannot offer even a small prayer, or overcome the slightest hidden sin <term>verborgentheyt</term> <note>Literally "secrecy" or "hidden thing," here referring to internal or secret sins of the heart.</note> without the Lord Christ. Oh, this must make us see our powerlessness—that Christ was necessitated to pray to His Father for us, that He preserve us, because we cannot preserve ourselves. The mother holds the child fast, and the child holds fast to the mother, but the strength is in the mother. You flee to Christ and hold Him fast—that is well done—but the strength does not lie there. Christ goes to His Father and prays to Him, saying, "Father, preserve such a poor soul, so that when he is tempted, he does not come to a fall." Oh, therein lies your strength: that Christ goes to His Father and prays that you might not at any time come to consent to such a temptation of the devil, or at least that you might not be overcome to the very end, as it was with Peter, who was indeed struck down, but his faith did not fail him.

For further application of this teaching, think then: if Jesus Christ prays to His Father,

<column-break/>

<margin>Five aids to fulfill the Prayer of Christ.</margin>
that He preserve you from the evil one, oh, then I pray you all that you carry yourselves in the world in such a way that you strive to fulfill the prayer of Christ. You ask me, "how shall I do that?" I answer:

Put into practice all those things which God has made your duty to preserve you from the evil one; and take to that end these aids and directions.

<margin>1. Shun arguing with the Devil.</margin>
First, when you are tempted toward any sin, shun all arguing with the devil, all reasoning with flesh and blood <note>A biblical idiom for human nature and its limited, often self-serving perspective.</note> concerning the sweetness and the profit of such a sin; for to argue in this way is the path to hanging your own soul. When the devil comes to tempt you to sin, tell him that you have no idle time to listen to him; you have better work to do and a better rule to walk by; you must listen to the movement of the Spirit, and you can have nothing to do with his suggestions.

<margin>2. Shun all opportunity for sin.</margin>
Secondly, shun all opportunities for sin. If you are inclined toward drunkenness, then do not go near evil company; shun the drinking-benches. If you are inclined toward lustful desires, then shun the company of wicked women; and this is the way to be preserved from evil through God’s grace. It is written of the reckless youth in Proverbs 7:8, that when he was enticed to impurity, he walked in the streets where the harlot lived. First he went to the corner of the street, then to the door of the harlot, and then the devil gained power over him to lead him into the house. If you run boldly and with great danger near to sin, and lay yourself in temptation’s way, then it is no wonder that you are overcome. By thoughtlessly jesting with the opportunities for sin, you tempt the devil to tempt you; and once the devil feels your pulse, he will provide you with a suitable temptation. But if you feared the fire, you would not be burned; if you took care to shun the beginnings and the opportunities for sin, it would be a means to preserve you from evil.

<margin>3. Observe the all-seeing eye of God.</margin>
Thirdly, think that the all-seeing eye of God is upon you, wherever you are and whatever you do, even when you are considering the most hidden way to sin. This observation had great power over Job (Job 31:4): "I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I have given thought to a virgin? Does He not see my ways, and count all my steps?" God sees my heart and my ways, therefore I dare not think, much less carry out, that which is evil. Think that the all-seeing eye of God is upon you, and this is a preventative means to keep you from sin; indeed, this is the way God has ordained to preserve you from the evil of the world. If you sin with the world, you shall perish with the world; if you run with the stream, you shall also drown in the stream; if you do wrong with the godless, you shall be damned with the godless.

<margin>4. Choose suffering rather than sin.</margin>
Fourthly, to preserve you from the evil of the times, think that it is a lesser danger to be under the suffering evil of the times than under the sinful evil. If you will not run with the stream and walk godlessly, like the rest of the world...

<summary>This page discusses how Christ's prayer for believers provides strength against temptation but does not excuse personal negligence. It offers practical "aids" for avoiding sin, such as shunning debate with the devil, avoiding opportunities for vice, and remembering God's all-seeing eye.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the previous discussion regarding Christ’s intercessory prayer for his followers. It transitions from a call to endure persecution rather than participate in sin, to a new thematic section titled "A Divine Balance," which provides an exposition of 1 Thessalonians 5:21.</meta>

do so, and you may perhaps be subject to persecutions; for it is better for you to lie in a prison-house than to sin by turning a blind eye, protecting, or favoring the horrible godlessness that has recently been committed among us, and is still being committed. Oh, it is a thousand times better for you to suffer to the utmost all the evils that the times might bring upon you, than to be an accomplice to the sins of the times, which are very terrifying and strange.

<margin>Flee to Christ, as to your hiding place.</margin>
Fifthly, whenever you are tempted toward any sin, make your recourse to Jesus Christ; flee to Christ as your hiding place, because you stand firm not through your own strength, but through the strength of Christ. If you now cast your eye upon yourself, you say, "Alas, I have prayed, I have shed many tears, and heard many sermons, and yet I cannot restrain my desires, nor subdue my corruptions." But there is still one single means left for me to use, and that is to flee to Christ and to take to heart his Mediation, shown in his praying for me. Christ prays in Heaven not only to save your soul, but also to sanctify your afflictions and to empower you to withstand temptations; he prays not only for the salvation of your soul, but also for all other things which serve toward that salvation. Oh, it is a great comfort that you have a string on your bow which the whole world cannot break. Though your faith, your heart, and everything should fail, you nonetheless have the prayers of Jesus Christ, which shall never fail. This prayer of Christ must be a strong support for your soul: *I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.* <note>John 17:15</note>

# A Divine Balance
## For All Kinds of Doctrine.
### 1 Thessalonians 5, verse 21.

->Test all things: hold fast that which is good.<-

<margin>The gathering of words is explained.</margin>
In the latter part of this chapter, the Apostle presents many supporting arguments which, if well-observed in the practice of godliness and put into action in our Christian conduct and life, are of great value. He begins from the 14th verse and ends at the 22nd verse. And therein you have twelve or thirteen excellent, concise proverbs, which are like a short summary of our whole duty toward God and man: *Admonish the unruly; comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all; see that no one renders evil for evil to anyone; but always pursue what is good, both toward one another and toward all; rejoice always, pray without ceasing: thank God in everything, and quench not the Spirit, and despise not prophesying, test all things, hold fast what is good: abstain from every appearance of evil.* The words of my text are nearly the last,

<column-break/>

but they are not the least duty which is prescribed here.

The interpreters do their best to provide not only the meaning, but also the connection of these words with the preceding ones; I shall not weary your head with the linkage; only take note of what goes just before my text, namely: *Despise not prophesying.* Prophesying here must not be taken for that great and uncommon gift which the Prophets had, both in the Old and New Testament, through which they were empowered by God to foretell future things by an immediate revelation, and to explain the Scriptures with an infallible Spirit. This uncommon sort of prophesying has now ceased, since God has fully revealed in the Scriptures all that is necessary to be known concerning the state of his church until the end of the world. So, by "prophesying" here, only preaching is understood (1 Cor. 14:31): *For you can all prophesy one by one, that all may learn and all may be encouraged*; that is, preach one after another, for it would create a confusion in the assembly if many spoke at the same time. It is remarkable to whom the Apostle gave this lesson—not to the godless of the world, but to those of Thessalonica, who were not weak Christians or children in Christ (like the Philippians), but strong and mature Christians who had attained a great measure of faith, patience, and sanctification, so that they had become examples to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia (1 Thess. 1:7). They were Christians of the best sort, famous for their faith and godliness, serving as a model and example for neighboring congregations; nevertheless, the Apostle commands them that they shall not despise prophesying—that is, the preaching of God’s Word. In our days, people have arisen who are frivolous and ignorant, who—out of a fanciful and imaginary sense of their own perfection in knowledge and high growth in grace—deem themselves to be far above all instituted worship; that is, above both prayer, hearing God's Word, or receiving the Sacraments. They live together *in the highest* <note>original: "in excelsis"</note> in the highest heavens; you will never see them below the third heaven; their common conversation is of an inexpressible, rapturous fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ; and based on this, they despise all the institutions of the Gospel as lowly principles and as food for young children. But let such people consider that if any congregation or people in the world might have claimed to be above instituted worship, the Thessalonians could have done so, as they were graced in many ways so that they were incomparable; yet the Apostle urges upon them the necessity of using the ministry of the Gospel. Note then from this:

That those who have come to the highest perfection of grace and knowledge attainable in this life must not despise or neglect the instituted worship of Jesus Christ.

Not only does a small child need daily food, but so also does the strongest man...

# A Divine Balance

[The soul] of the world shall falter and die if it comes to lack that. I was amazed when I thought how the Devil has been able to plant this deception in the hearts of men: that they should consider themselves to be above the established means of God’s service, even though the Scripture so explicitly goes against this feeling in 1 Corinthians 14:22: *Thus strange tongues are a sign, not to those who believe, but to the unbelievers; and prophecy is not for the unbelievers, but for those who believe.* Here you see that the Apostle clearly says this: that believers—yes, even strong believers—must not despise prophecies <note>In this context, "prophecies" refers to the preaching and explanation of the Bible.</note>. And David, being a great Prophet, a man after God's heart, rich in gifts and grace, nevertheless longed for the courts of the Lord (Psalm 84:3). It was his earnest longing, his highest comfort; indeed, he considered it the greatest blessedness he could achieve in this world: to be near the Ark of God (which was God’s special dwelling place among men in those days), to behold the face of God in His sanctuary, and to perform the communal services of God. And the Apostle says in Hebrews 5:14: *Solid food is for the mature, who by habit have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.* The "mature," namely, in comparison with those whom he previously compared to children; "by habit," that is, by hearing, reading, and contemplating God's Word; "have their senses exercised," that is, their understanding, judgment, and memory; "to discern both good and evil," that is, to choose the good and to reject the evil. Now the Apostle says explicitly in Ephesians 4:11, 12, 13, that one must continue to hear God's Word preached until the time one enters Heaven. *He gave some to be Apostles, some Prophets, some Evangelists, and some Pastors and Teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ; until we all come to the unity of the Faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.* The use of the ministry of the Word is everlasting, as long as the Sun and Moon endure, until all God’s elect are brought in, until we shall all be perfect men—namely, in the world to come. We must live among the means of grace until we come to glory.

<margin>
1. Reason: Our sanctification is not complete.
</margin>

And the reasons for this are these. First, because our sanctification in this life is not perfect; the last-cited scripture passage indicates as much. In the best of Saints, there is an "old man" and a "new man," flesh and Spirit; although sin has received its death-blow and shall never again reign as King in their soul, it is nonetheless within us as a violent force, and we shall never be completely freed from its resistance until we enter Heaven.

<margin>
2. Reason: Sin lies hidden in the deepest caverns of the heart.
</margin>

Secondly, the heart is deceitful above all measure; it is more full of craftiness than any other thing (Jeremiah 17:9) <note>The original text cites Jeremiah 17:19, but the quote corresponds to verse 9.</note>. The heart of man is the greatest traitor and deceiver in the world; it is so greatly, horribly, and inscrutably godless—who shall know it? Godlessness lies hidden in the secret corners of the

<column-break/>

<margin>
Psalm 19:13.
Proverbs 28:26.
</margin>

heart. There is no one (not even the wisest or the most innocent) who understands his own wanderings. Therefore Solomon says, *He who trusts in his heart is a fool.* Now, the preaching of the Word is a powerful means to find out this forbidden nature and to discover the hidden corridors of the heart (Hebrews 4:12). *The word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and pierces even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and the intentions of the heart.* I wanted to point this out in passing before I come to my text: that while you live in this world, you must use the ministry of the Word and not despise prophecies.

Following this command of the Apostle, my text now follows fittingly; for many would indeed accept the teaching of the Ministers before they test it. Therefore, when the Apostle says, *And despise not prophecies,* he adds to it: *Test all things.* Test, test—and if there be any error in what you hear, then despise it; do not despise the preaching itself, only do this: *Test all things; hold fast to what is good.*

<margin>
The words of this text are unfolded.
</margin>

First, I shall explain the meaning of the words to you. "Test"—the Greek word <term>δοκιμάζετε</term> <note>original: "dokimazete" - to test, examine, or prove</note> is borrowed from goldsmiths, who, when they test money to see if it is good and current or not, bring it to the touchstone. The word also means to test or know through experience, and thus you must go and test every doctrine you hear against the touchstone of God’s Word; this is the true rule by which one shall test them. "Test all things"—by "all things," understand all preached doctrine, all prophecies and sermons that you hear. It is noteworthy that when the Apostle Paul spoke these words, the Gospels were not yet written, nor had they been committed to the general care of God's Church. It is thought that this letter was written thirty or more years before the Gospels; so when the Apostle commanded them to test the preached doctrine, he sent them to the writings of the Old Testament. Then follows: "Hold fast to what is good." "Holding fast" the good is meant in two ways: 1. To hold fast the truths of the Gospel in one's judgment, so as not to fall into error. 2. To hold fast the power of the Gospel in practice, so as not to fall into sin.

<margin>
1. Hold fast the good in judgment so that you do not run into error.
</margin>

First, hold fast in your judgment the truths of the Gospel, so that you do not run into error; this is set forth in 2 Peter 3:17: *You therefore, beloved, knowing these things beforehand, beware lest you also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own steadfastness.* That is, in judgment. There must be a foreknowledge of the truths of the Gospel before you can come to steadfastness in grace; and besides knowledge, there is also required watchfulness and care if we wish to retain the Gospel truths. So you must then hold fast the doctrine of the Gospel in your judgment, so as not to fall into erroneous principles. It is "childish," says Saint Paul in Ephesians 4:14, to be moved by the tide and carried about by every wind of doctrine—to be "easy-believing" or light of faith, and to be unstable like those who stumble.

<summary>This page argues that all believers, regardless of their spiritual maturity, must remain engaged with the "means of grace" like preaching and scripture. It introduces an exposition of the command to "test all things" (1 Thessalonians 5:21), comparing the process to a goldsmith testing metal with a touchstone.</summary>

# For all kinds of Doctrine.

<margin>Keep the good in practice, so as not to fall into sin</margin> Secondly, by this it is pointed out that we must keep the good in practice, so as not to fall into any sin, to keep your course of sanctification steady and unchanged, as it is written in Philippians 2:15, 16: *That you may be blameless and sincere, being children of God, without rebuke in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world; holding forth the Word of life;* <note>Philippians 2:15-16. To "hold forth the word" means to demonstrate the Gospel through one's behavior.</note> that is, in an irreproachable, holy, and humble walk of life. Someone keeps the good when he directs his life according to the guidance of God’s Word; for it is a vain and useless knowledge which is not brought into practice; and practice in our Christian walk is difficult and heavy; it requires close wakefulness, therefore we must be carefully concerned to be steadfast in our practice of that which we are convinced in our judgment to be the truth and the will of God, which is revealed to us in His Word, so that the meaning of the words is: Test all Doctrine of that Minister under whom you live, by the Word of God, whether it be true or false, healthy or unhealthy; and what you find to be the truth and in agreement with God’s Word, embrace that and accept it: keep that in your judgment, so that you do not fall into any contradictory opinions, and also keep it in your practice, so that you do not come to transgress in any evil dealing or conduct: and what you find to be false and sinful, reject that. And thus you have a brief, cursory explanation of the words. Then regarding the first part, **test all things**, I shall draw this observation, namely: That it is the duty of all hearers of the Word to test and examine all kinds of Doctrine that they hear; St. John commands this in his first Epistle, <margin>honor.</margin> Chapter 4, verse 1: *Beloved, believe not every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God: because many false prophets have gone out into the world;* <note>1 John 4:1</note> that is, test the Doctrine of such Preachers who claim to have the Spirit and preach through the spirit; whether it is true or false. Erring Teachers also boast of the Spirit, so we must test from what Spirit their Doctrine proceeds; we must not, like that foolish person Solomon speaks of, believe everything which is published under the glorious name of the truth: but we must think that God’s Church has always been plagued with false Teachers; in the time of Jeremiah there were those who presented the visions of their own brains as sound Doctrine; and the Apostle Paul often complains of false Teachers who transform themselves into Angels of light; it is the cunning of the Devil to often transform himself into an Angel of light, and because his wares do not sell well on his own Market, he tries to bring them to God’s Market (for that is the Preaching of the Word), thinking that no one will hold him suspect there. Have we then not great reason to test all kinds of Doctrine that we hear?

In the handling of this Doctrine, I shall first present some warnings; secondly, the Reasons for the Doctrine; thirdly, some directions concerning the testing of that which you hear.

<margin>gain</margin>
<margin>Everyone must not take the liberty upon themselves to test all Preachers.</margin>
The first warning is this. When the Apostle commands testing all things, it is not his aim that all people should take the liberty to go and hear everyone, and so test all Preachers; as Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), a central figure in the Protestant Reformation.</note> well remarks on this passage; for by doing so, one might more easily suck in an error than accept the truth; indeed, the Scripture is explicitly against this: If you hear someone preaching the truth, you must not follow those who are infamous for spreading errors, 2 Timothy 3:3-4. *For the time will come when they will not endure sound Doctrine; but having itching ears, they shall heap to themselves teachers according to their own lusts, and shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.* <note>2 Timothy 4:3-4. The text cites chapter 3, but the quote is from chapter 4.</note> And in the second Epistle of John, at the 10th and 11th verse: *If there come any unto you, and bring not this Doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed: for he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds.* And Matthew 24:23: *If any man shall say unto you, Lo, here is the Christ, or there; believe it not: for there shall arise false Christs and false prophets, and shall show great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.* And verse 26: *wherefore if they shall say unto you, Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth: behold, he is in the secret chambers; believe it not:* False prophets shall arise, and what shall they say? Look, here is the Christ; not as if Christ were there in person, but in the Doctrine. Some will say, He is in the Desert; for these false Teachers used to draw the people out into a desert place, to reveal their errors and heresies there all the more unencumbered; but the truth seeks no <margin>Truth seeks no corners. <note>original: "Veritas non quærit angulos."</note></margin> corners or nooks. But do not go out, says Christ: if they say to you, He is in the secret chambers, believe it not. That which is honorable is public, but evil <margin>Flaws are hidden by the night. <note>original: "Nocte latent mendæ."</note></margin> wants to be covered, and therefore they seek secluded secret chambers: Darkness best matches the works of darkness. For this reason, the Scripture commands not only to take heed which Preacher and in <margin>Thieves extinguish the lamp. <note>original: "Lucernam extinguunt fures."</note></margin> what manner you hear, but also *what* you hear, for so the Evangelist expresses it; Mark 4:24, *take heed what you hear.* A Physician may well be authorized to practice, and yet prescribe dangerous potions: someone may be a true Teacher in respect of his office, and yet a false Teacher in respect of his Doctrine, and thus be rejectable; we must not only look at the messenger, but also at the message. And if anyone (whoever he may be) proclaims a Gospel other than that which you have received, let him be accursed, Galatians 1:9. This erroneous and deceptive Doctrine is the Devil’s weeds, and the preaching of the same is the Devil’s seed-time, and if we do not want these weeds to grow in our field, then we must not be present where the Devil sows them; for we must know that a Christian can be poisoned unto death as easily as die of hunger: It then belongs to Christians to see what they hear, so that they do not take in poison instead of healthy food, and soul-destroying opinions instead of the unadulterated Milk of God’s Word.

<summary>This page argues that believers must test all religious teachings against the Word of God to avoid spiritual error and maintain a holy life. It warns against the curiosity of listening to known false teachers, comparing deceptive doctrines to poison and weeds sown by the Devil.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of 1 Thessalonians 5:21, transitioning from the definition of "testing all things" to specific warnings and reasons for why believers must be discerning regarding the sermons and doctrines they hear.</meta>

# A Divine Balance

1 Peter 2:2. *As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word,* <note>1 Peter 2:2. The author contrasts "sincere milk"—pure biblical teaching—with the "imagined opinions" of men.</note> not the imagined opinions and feelings of frivolous men. Will you look carefully to the food for your body, and not to the food for your souls? Should you be so careful that it is truly bread with which you are fed for physical strength, and yet not even take care that your souls are not fed with dross and poison? See then what you hear, and whom you hear, for sin first entered through the ear; and the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 15:33: *Evil communications corrupt good manners.* This is the first warning: when you are commanded to test all things, you are not thereby given the liberty to hear all kinds of preachers.

<margin>
2. Warning.
We must not be doubters in religion.
</margin>
Secondly, when the Apostle says, *Test all things,* he does not wish for people to be inconstant in Christianity, or doubters in religion, or "wandering stars" <note>A reference to Jude 1:13, describing false teachers as unstable stars.</note> who are never firmly established in the truths of the Gospel—like "seekers." For they may rightly be called such, as they never stand still but always search out new "truths" through their "new lights," which in the end are commonly found to be nothing other than old errors. The Colossians are exhorted to strive to be rooted and established in the faith. (Colossians 2:7).

<margin>
3. Warning.
We must not bend the Scripture to our feelings, but the contrary.
Whatever is taught in Scripture is truth; whatever is commanded is goodness. <note>original: "Quicquid in Scriptura docetur, veritas, quicquid præcipitur bonitas."</note>
</margin>
Thirdly, in testing all sorts of doctrine that you hear, be certain that you do not bend the Scripture to your feeling, but your feeling to the Scripture; for the Scripture teaches nothing but the truth and commands nothing but good. Many force the Scripture to say that which was never the intent of the Holy Spirit, in order to give a gloss to those deceptive feelings which they spread. They place the Scripture, as it were, upon the rack <note>A "pijn-banck" or rack was a torture device used to force a confession; the author suggests false teachers "torture" the text to make it "confess" things it doesn't say.</note> to make it confess what was never its aim. So it was of old with the heretics, and this is still put into practice in our days. They deal with the Scripture as a certain man did with the bench of Delphi, <note>Likely referring to the Oracle of Delphi, where ambiguous prophecies were interpreted to suit the listener's desire.</note> which he made to speak whatever suited his mind. But I warn you: do not bring your opinion to the Scripture, but strive to grasp the meaning of the Holy Spirit from the Scripture.

<margin>
4. Warning.
Do not be too trusting in your own feeling.
Proverbs 4:26.
</margin>
Fourthly: In testing the doctrine you hear, do not lean too much on your own understanding; do not consider yourself infallible. Do not trust too much in your own opinion in differing matters, especially if they conflict with the judgment of those who are outstanding in gifts and grace. Weigh the Scripture thoroughly and seek God through prayer before you firmly establish anything in doubtful matters: *Ponder the path of your feet.* <note>Proverbs 4:26.</note>

Having now dealt with the warnings, I shall give the reasons why people must test the doctrine they hear.

<margin>
1. Reason.
There is a close resemblance between erring and true teachers.
</margin>
First, because erring and corrupt teachers can be very similar to those who preach the truth. One reads of two painters, Parrhasius and Zeuxis, <note>A famous anecdote from Pliny the Elder about a contest to see who was the most realistic painter.</note> who competed against each other to see who was the best in that art. One painted grapes so naturally that birds flew down to peck at them, thinking they were real grapes. And the other painted a curtain so skillfully

<column-break/>

that his fellow painter came to push it aside, thinking it was a real curtain. There is such a close similarity between healthy teachers and seductive teachers that it is not easy to make a distinction between them.

But all that glitters is not gold; you have a remarkable text for this in 2 Corinthians 11:13, 14: *For such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ; and no wonder, for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light.* False apostles can transform themselves into the likeness of apostles of Christ, and servants of the Devil—brokers for Hell—can put on the appearance of the servants of Jesus Christ. There is, then, great reason why you must test all kinds of doctrine you hear, whether it agrees with God's Word or not.

<margin>
2. Reason.
The Scripture predicts that there will be many false teachers.
</margin>
Secondly, because God’s Word foretells us that under the New Testament there will be as many (if not more) false teachers as in the Old, and more in the last days of the world than in previous ages. This appears clearly from 2 Peter 2:1: *But there were also false prophets among the people, even as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing on themselves swift destruction.* They were of old under the Law; they shall also be with you under the Gospel. Although the Pharisees who corrupted the Law are dead, nevertheless the same spirit lives in men and shall live until the end of the world. The Apostle gives this as a reason why we must test such doctrine as we hear: because in the times of the New Testament many false teachers shall appear. 1 John 4:1: *Beloved, believe not every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.* Do not believe every person who says he has the Spirit which teaches him the doctrine he preaches, but test whether it agrees with God's Word or not. The reason he gives is because many (not few) false prophets have gone out—not just in some corner or part of the world. Truly, in former times, the nest of heresies was in one part of the world, namely in the Netherlands, and particularly in Amsterdam; <note>Amsterdam was famously tolerant in the 17th century, leading contemporary critics to label it a "nest" for every conceivable sect and heresy.</note> but now they have gone out into the whole world. Test then the spirits whether they are of God; test before you lean upon it, before you believe.

False teachings are spread very craftily.
</margin>
