# A Divine Balance

1 Peter 2:2. *As newborn babes, be very eager for the rational, unadulterated milk,* <note>The "unadulterated milk" refers to the pure, uncorrupted Word of God, as opposed to human traditions or errors.</note> not for the imagined opinions and feelings of frivolous people. Will you look carefully at the food for your body, and not at the food for your souls? Will you be so diligent to ensure it is truly bread with which you are fed for physical strength? And will you not even take care that your soul is not fed with husks and poison? See then what you hear, and whom you hear, for sin first entered through the ear; and the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 15:33, *Evil company corrupts good morals.* This is the first warning: when you are commanded to test all things, you are not thereby given the freedom to hear all types of preachers.

<margin>
2nd Warning.
We must not be doubters in Religion.
</margin>
Secondly, when the Apostle says, *Test all things,* he does not want people to be unstable in Christianity, doubters in divine service, or wandering stars, but to be firmly established in the truths of the Gospel. He warns against being "seekers"—for so those may rightly be called who never stand still, but always search out "new truths" through their "new lights," which in the end are commonly found to be nothing other than old errors. <note>The "Seekers" were a radical religious group in the 17th century who believed all organized churches had lost their authority; "New Lights" refers to those claiming fresh, direct revelations from God.</note> The Colossians are exhorted to strive to be rooted and built up in the faith. Colossians 2:7.

<margin>
3rd Warning.
We must not bend Scripture to our own opinion, but the contrary.
<note>original: "Quicquid in Scriptura docetur, veritas, quicquid præcipitur bonitas." — Whatever is taught in Scripture is truth, whatever is commanded is goodness.</note>
</margin>
Thirdly, in testing all kinds of doctrine that you hear, be assured that you do not bend the Scripture to your opinion, but your opinion to the Scripture. For the Scripture teaches nothing but the truth, and commands nothing but good. Some force the Scripture to speak that which was never the intent of the Holy Spirit, in order to give a semblance of truth to those wandering opinions which they spread. They lay the Scripture, as it were, upon the torture rack <note>original: "pijn-banck" — The author uses the metaphor of judicial torture to describe how some interpreters force the Bible to "confess" to meanings it does not contain.</note> to make it confess that which was never its intent. So it was of old with the heretics, and this is still put into practice in our days. They deal with the Scripture as a certain man did with the oracle of Delphi, making it speak whatever suited his mind. But I warn you: do not bring your opinion to the Scripture, but strive to grasp the meaning of the Holy Spirit from the Scripture.

<margin>
4th Warning.
Do not be too trusting of your own opinion.
Proverbs 4:26.
</margin>
Fourthly. In testing the doctrine you hear, do not lean too much on your own understanding; do not consider yourself infallible. Do not trust too much in your own opinion in various matters, especially if they conflict with the judgment of those who are outstanding in gifts and grace. Weigh the Scripture thoroughly and seek God through prayer, so that you establish something firm in doubtful matters: *Ponder the path of your feet.*

Having now dealt with the warnings, I shall give the reasons why people must test the doctrine they hear.

<margin>
1st Reason.
There is a close resemblance between erring and true Teachers.
</margin>
First, because erring and corrupt teachers can be very similar to those who preach the truth. One reads of two painters, Parrhasius and Zeuxis, who competed against each other to see who was the best in that art. <note>Parrhasius and Zeuxis were famous Greek painters of the 5th century BCE, known for their extreme realism.</note> The one painted grapes so naturally that birds came down to peck at them, thinking they were real grapes. And the other painted so skillfully

I

<column-break/>

a curtain, that his fellow painter came to push it aside, thinking it was a real curtain. There is such a close similarity between sound teachers and misleading teachers that it is not easy to distinguish between them.

But all that glitters is not gold; you have a notable text for this in 2 Corinthians 11:13, 14. *For such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ; and no wonder: for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light.* False apostles can transform themselves into the likeness of apostles of Christ; and servants of the Devil, brokers for Hell, can take on the likenesses of the servants of Jesus Christ. There is then great reason why you must test all kinds of doctrine that you hear, whether it agrees with God’s Word or not.

<margin>
2nd Reason.
Scripture foretells that there will be many false Teachers.
</margin>
Secondly, because God’s Word foretells us that under the New Testament there shall be as many (if not more) false teachers as in the Old, and more in the last days of the world than in previous ages. This appears clearly from 2 Peter 2:1. *But there were also false prophets among the people, even as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing on themselves swift destruction.* They were of old under the Law; they shall also be with you under the Gospel. Although the Pharisees who corrupted the Law are dead, nevertheless the same spirit lives in men, and shall also live until the end of the world. The Apostle gives this as a reason why we must test such doctrine as we hear; because in the times of the New Testament many false teachers shall appear, 1 John 4:1. *Beloved, believe not every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.* Do not believe every person who says he has the Spirit, or that the Spirit teaches him the doctrine he preaches; but test whether it agrees with God’s Word or not. The reason he gives is because many (not few) false prophets have gone out—not just somewhere in a corner or part of the world. Surely, formerly the nest of heresies was in one part of the world, namely in the Netherlands, and especially in Amsterdam; but now they have gone out into the whole world. Test then the spirits whether they are of God; test before you rely on them, before you believe.

<margin>
3rd Reason.
False teachings are spread very craftily.
</margin>
Thirdly, test all doctrine you hear preached, because false teachings and heresies are very cunningly and craftily wrapped into the minds of men by deceivers. No greater trickery is practiced by a clever juggler than by these false teachers; they are shrewd and cunning in turning away the hearts of men, as the Apostle shows in Ephesians 4:14. *That we should no longer be children, tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in the cunning craftiness of deceitful plotting.* The word in Greek is very emphatic: <note>original: "ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ" (en tē kybeia) — literally "in the dicing," referring to the cheating or sleight of hand used by professional gamblers with dice.</note> *by trickery with the dice.* The word is borrowed from the dishonest gambler, who with a die—

# For All Sorts of Teaching.

...can throw the dice <note>original: "belsteen," likely a variation of "dobbelsteen" (die/dice)</note> however they wish. These teachers can make the people believe errors as easily as a cunning gambler can cheat with the dice. We have many such sophisticated and crafty deceivers among us; otherwise, it would not be possible for the truth of God to be so greatly perverted as it currently is. It is noteworthy, in Revelation 9:8, that the locusts <note>In 17th-century Protestant commentary, the "locusts" of Revelation were often interpreted as the Catholic clergy or religious orders.</note> who came up from the East had faces like the faces of women. Interpreters explain that these are the Jesuits and the agents of Rome: they had faces of women, by which they enticed, attracted, and bewitched people through their follies. The Apostle speaks of such men in Romans 16:18: *For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.* Just as a foul harlot paints and whitewashes her face, so do these men whitewash their damnable errors with eloquent entanglements; sometimes they promise to satisfy your itching ears so much with such eloquent words that you are moved to wonder. Sometimes they also promise high privileges and unspeakable advantages through that which they teach—just as the Devil did to our first ancestors: *you shall be as God.* Error must have sweet words to coat itself, as well as beautiful, pleasant, eloquent, and crafty ways of speaking. Through sweet words, they seduce the hearts of the simple. And in 2 Peter 2:1, the Apostle places their cunning before our eyes in the introduction of destructive heresies. If Peter had lived in our time, he would have been considered a sharp and harsh man for calling these heresies, even "destructive heresies"; but they were introduced secretly, and he says, *many shall follow their pernicious ways; and through feigned words, they shall make merchandise of you* (verses 2 and 3). This had to happen with feigned words, under
<margin>Distinguishing evil from good, and good from evil. <note>original: "Int. mala a bonis, & bona a malis."</note></margin>
the shining cover of truth and novelty; they will mix some gold among their copper, some truths among their falsehood; they will make their bait sweet to catch you all the faster. For if error were introduced nakedly, hardly anyone would want to accept it; it would have such a hideous appearance. Therefore, they clothe it with the appearance of truth and godliness.
<margin>Reason: there is an aptitude in our nature through error... human nature is prone to levity. <note>original: "natura hominum levitatis fida"</note></margin>
Fourthly, you must test every doctrine you hear before you believe it, because through human gullibility, even the best minds could easily be led away by novelties and deceived by error. We are by nature like the sand of the sea, which is driven by every wind; and like the reed, which is moved by every gust of the wind. You have a notable teaching regarding this in 2 Corinthians 11:3: *But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.* The Devil did not wish to use a blunt or simple creature, but a crafty serpent, to deceive Eve so that she would eat of the forbidden fruit. Now the Apostle says, I am afraid that the Devil, through fine and crafty temptation, will draw your senses away from the truth of the Gospel. This indicates that there was an aptitude in their nature to be led away into error.

<column-break/>

<margin>Matthew 13:11, 12.</margin>
And what is more, even the holiest and most understanding in the mysteries of God are only enlightened in part (1 Corinthians 13:12). And although they do not willfully deceive you, it can nonetheless happen through the remnant of ignorance and obscurity within them that they take error for truth. Therefore, no one’s piety or learning should blind us so far that we would believe all he says without bringing it to the touchstone of the Word. For we must not build our faith on human authority, but on Divine authority. We must follow those of Berea and daily search the Scriptures to see if the teachings we hear are truly the truth of God. They were praised for this in Acts 17:11. Oh beloved, accept nothing on the faith and authority of the preacher; weigh everything in the scales of the Sanctuary. You must deal with the doctrine you hear just as you do with gold; no one wants to receive gold without weighing it. Oh, there is as much falsehood in opinions as there is in gold; therefore, weigh and test all things. It matters not what this or that man says, whether it be Cephas or Apollos, even if they are outstanding in learning and godliness; but that which God says in the Scriptures, that you must accept. For those are the Rule of our Faith, and whatever does not agree with this, reject it as the dross and scum of man's corrupt brain; do not accept it as the gold of God's pure word.
<margin>1 Corinthians 1:11.</margin>
<margin>Whatever does not have authority from the Holy Scriptures is rejected with the same ease with which it is approved. <note>original: "Quid de Scripturis sacris auctoritatem non habet, eadem facilitate contemnitur qua probatur."</note></margin>
Someone will now say: you have now given several reasons why we must not believe the doctrine we hear before we have tested it; but what rules and helpful means can you give us? How could such a weak and ignorant Christian as I am be capable of testing and judging the doctrine I hear? *This is the labor, this the work.* <note>original: "Hic labor, hoc opus." A famous phrase from Virgil’s Aeneid, referring to a difficult task.</note> Well, I shall endeavor to give you a general and specific answer to this great question. I hope that it will be of great use to us in these heretical times, in which false teachers and false doctrines are so very abundant.
<margin>General rule.</margin>
<margin>Let the Scripture be a touchstone to test all doctrine against.</margin>
First, take this general rule: Ensure that you make God’s Word a touchstone <note>A touchstone is a dark stone used to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak they leave when rubbed against it.</note> to test and probe every doctrine you hear; and if anything is preached (even if it were by an Angel from Heaven) which does not agree with God’s Word, do not believe it. This is also what the Prophet Isaiah prescribes to us in Isaiah 8:20: *To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.* By the "law and the testimony," we must understand God’s Word, for that is God’s testimony; and if anyone speaks otherwise than according to God’s Word, it is a clear and manifest sign that there is no light or truth in him. I give you this rule because there are a multitude of people in these days who reject the written Word of God and run to inspirations and revelations to test doctrines with; however, those are not certain rules. Through this means, they take the deceits of Satan for Heavenly inspirations. ### A Divine Balance-Scale

<margin>
* According to the English Translation. <note>likely referring to the King James Version/Authorized Version</note>
</margin>
...was brought to Heaven, when we were with him on the Holy mountain. And we have a * **more sure prophetic word.** The written Word of God is more certain regarding us than if we heard a voice from Heaven. And this is the reason why—when the Rich Man <note>Referring to the parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16</note> wanted his Brothers to be warned by an extraordinary means, so they would not end up in Hell, and therefore prayed that Lazarus should rise from the dead to warn them more strongly, thinking then they would believe;
<margin>
Luke 16:31.
</margin>
Abraham sends him to Moses and the Prophets, and says, *if they do not hear them, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.* If we heard a voice from the Air, we should not believe it, but only that which we find written in God's 
<margin>
Deut. 29:29
</margin>
Word. *The secret things belong to the Lord our God; but those things which are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this Law.* I say all this to this end: to show you that those who so greatly pretend to have "Revelations" and abandon the written Word of God are now on the path to falling into the deceptions of Satan and heavy misfortunes.

<margin>
2. General Rule. Clear principles of truth must be held fast rather than disputed.
</margin>
A second general rule regarding the testing of such Teachings as you hear is this, namely: clear principles of truth must be held fast rather than disputed. It is a rule and a Maxim of Faith in <term>Philosophy</term> <note>the study of fundamental nature and logic</note> that one must not argue against basic principles; this is also the truth in <term>Theology</term> <note>the study of God and religious belief</note>. We must not dispute over such foundational articles as: Whether Christ is the Son of God; whether the Scripture is God's Word; whether there shall be a resurrection of the body, a salvation for the Saints, damnation for Sinners, a coming judgment, or an eternal life. Such foundational principles must be held fast and not debated.

<margin>
3. General Rule. Hold no opinion until you have tested it.
</margin>
Thirdly, do not stubbornly maintain an opinion until you have thoroughly tested it. Such is the inconstancy of men's minds in these heretical times that often one Sermon will turn them away from the truths of the Gospel more than twenty Sermons will confirm them in it.

<margin>
Objection.
</margin>
But someone will say: many who are learned and Godly differ in these things; one says this is the truth, another holds that for the truth; how shall I, poor creature that I am, judge which Teaching is the truth or not?

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
I answer: just as I have guided you in general, so I will also give you some specific rules and aids by which you shall test all Teachings you hear.

<margin>
First Rule.
</margin>
Firstly, whatever God's Word expressly commands to believe and accept—or that which necessarily flows from Scripture through a natural consequence, even though it is not found in Scripture in so many words <note>original: "totidem verbis"</note>, or that which agrees with the true sense of any place in Scripture, even though it does not seem to accord with the literal sense of another place in Scripture, or also that which agrees with the end and purpose of the Scripture: This Teaching is sound and must be accepted.

<column-break/>

But on the contrary: that Teaching which is not found in the Scripture and is not established upon it, which also cannot be drawn from the Scripture with good reason through a necessary consequence, but is built upon the traditions and inventions of men; those who add to or take away from the Word; those who twist and pervert the Scripture; or whatever Teaching cannot endure the test of the Word nor the light—that is false and abominable.

<margin>
Second Rule.
</margin>
Secondly: whichever Teaching most exalts the grace of God in Christ and humbles man, attributing all glory to the free grace of God—that Teaching is sound.

But on the contrary: that Teaching which nullifies the grace of God in Christ and exalts the corruption of man, and which sets <term>free will</term> <note>the idea that humans can choose good or evil without divine aid</note> against free grace—that Teaching is unsound.

<margin>
Third Rule.
</margin>
Thirdly: whichever Teaching exalts God's will as well as His grace, and shows as much what God wants us to do as what He has promised to do for us—that Teaching is a true Teaching.

But on the contrary: that Teaching which exalts God's free grace and meanwhile grants people the liberty to live as they please—indeed, which sets God's will for obedience directly against God's grace for salvation—that Teaching is a false Teaching.

<margin>
Fourth Rule.
</margin>
Fourthly: that Teaching is a sound Teaching which honors the attributes of God; God's justice as well as His mercy; God's holiness as well as His grace; and which holds as good all those ways which God has prescribed for us in Scripture to walk in—namely, faith and conversion, Godliness toward God and love toward men—I say, that Teaching is sound and good.

But on the contrary: whichever Teaching robs God of the glory of one of His attributes, which makes God either unmerciful or unjust, etc., or which despises any law in which God has commanded us in the Scripture to walk, or which separates the two Tables of God <note>referring to the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments: duties to God and duties to neighbors</note> from one another, Piety from love, acts of <term>justification</term> <note>being declared righteous before God</note> from acts of <term>sanctification</term> <note>the process of becoming holy</note>. Though a Teaching might strongly advocate for love toward men, if it does not recognize or teach the practice of Godliness toward God; or if it pretends to have much Godliness and yet does not teach the practice of love and justice—that teaching is false and corrupt.

<margin>
Fifth Rule.
</margin>
Fifthly: whichever Teaching reveals the sinfulness of idle thoughts and covetous imaginings as well as of sinful works—that is a true Teaching.

But that which only seeks outward reform and does not reach to the cleansing of the heart—that is an unsound Teaching.

<margin>
Sixth Rule.
</margin>
Sixthly: that Teaching is sound which accepts all truth—the directing truth as well as the comforting truth, the commanding truth as well as the promising—and which proclaims both the Law and the Gospel.

But on the contrary: whichever Teaching pleases the corrupt nature of man and is easy for flesh and blood, and which paves the way to unrestrained looseness and worldliness—that Teaching is unsound.

<margin>
Seventh Rule.
</margin>
Seventhly: all such Teaching as necessarily tends to bring a good Conscience into a good state, teaching that we... only...

<meta>This page continues the author's "rules" for discerning true doctrine from false, building on the previous page's argument that the Bible is the only "more sure prophetic word." <header>for all kinds of Doctrine.</header>
<page-num>111</page-num>

must be established upon Christ's merits for our salvation, and not upon our own good works; that Doctrine is healthy.

But any Doctrine that leaves a sorrowful and troubled conscience without any good foundation to lean upon, teaching people to hang their salvation upon the changeable will of man—this is not only a comfortless but also an unhealthy Doctrine.

<margin>Eighthly</margin>
Eighthly, whichever Doctrine tends toward the promotion of Godliness <note>Dutch: *Godtsaligheyt*; refers to a life of active piety and devotion</note>, and which (as the Apostle speaks in 1 Timothy 1:1) possesses the knowledge of the truth which is according to Godliness; which is useful for the perfection of sanctification; which makes us diligently take care that we work out our salvation with fear and trembling; which is helpful to the work of grace in our souls; which tends toward the instruction of the judgment, the reformation of the heart, and the conforming of one's life to the whole will of God—that Doctrine is true and good.

But on the contrary, whichever Doctrine tends toward licentiousness and "free-spiritedness" <note>The author is likely attacking 'Antinomians' or 'Libertines' who believed that because they were saved by grace, the moral law no longer applied to them</note>, causing people to neglect God's institutions and to become weary of the worship of the assembly, and to despise the religious duties of the household and of each individual in private; those who misuse God's grace as an excuse for wantonness; who highly exalt the death of Christ but nullify His life; who say much of Christ's blood and His Priestly office, but pay no heed to the Commandments of Christ and His Kingly office; who cause people to trust in mercy while making them careless regarding conversion; who set Christ up as highly merciful but allow people to continue in their sins, or at best, bring them to a form of Godliness without its power—this is an erring and dangerous Doctrine. Truth always promotes Godliness, but erring doctrine fights against it. 2 Timothy 2:16: *Avoid godless and empty chatter, for they will increase unto more ungodliness.* We find in our days that the fruits of such empty chatter and argumentative disputes are such destructive sentiments as these: namely, that a person must not weep over sin, that he must not confess sin, and that he must not pray for the forgiveness of sins. In this way, three parts of Prayer are taken away. Likewise regarding God's decree: that if they are ordained to salvation, they shall be saved even if they live according to their own whims; and if they are ordained to damnation, they shall be damned even if they did all they could. Whereas the Doctrine of election and reprobation ought to be a spur to pursue sanctification. Likewise, regarding the Law of God: that it has no use for believers. Many such destructive Teachings have sprouted from empty disputes; all of which tend toward greater ungodliness, which sufficiently proves they are false, for the truth always promotes the practice of Godliness in the life of a Christian.

<margin>Lastly</margin>
Lastly, true teachings will be found true when they are tested. Truth does not fear the test; error fears the light and creeps into houses, not daring to come forward in public; it takes captive the weak women who are burdened with sins, as the Apostle speaks in

<column-break/>

2 Timothy 3:6. But it does not dare to oppose or confront an understanding Christian. And this is why the Turks <note>In the 17th century, 'Turks' was a general term for Muslims or the Ottoman Empire</note> forbid anyone to dispute against their Quran; this is also why the Church of Rome does not allow the common people to read the Bible, but they must (so to speak) play their faith on another’s mouth <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to mindlessly repeat what another says without personal conviction</note> and believe what the Church believes. And so they ensure that their errors and Idolatries are swallowed down, which, if they were brought into the light, would expose their weakness and sinfulness.

The short summary of all this is this: Whenever you hear any Doctrine proposed, compare it with God's Word; and if you find that it goes against any part of the Old or New Testament, do not believe it; for it is not truth, but error.

These rules and directions regarding the testing of heard Doctrine can be very profitable to you in these loose and erring times, if God the Lord gives your hearts the grace to apply them well.

In truth, my Conscience does not tell me that I have presented anything to you contrary to Scripture; but nevertheless, believe nothing of what I preach until you have tested it; and if you find anything not agreeing with the written Word, reject it. *Test all things; hold fast that which is good.*

### The Closest Examination
## Of a Good Christian.
->Acts 16: v. 30, 31.<-

> And he said, Dear Sirs, what must I do that I may be saved? And they said, Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ: and you shall be saved.

This text is presented by way of a questioning; the manner of its form indicates that this question comes from a startled and bewildered mind, and a troubled and desperate soul, and that regarding a matter of the very greatest weight. There are many precise and varied questions which people investigate nowadays: but this question from this poor Jailer <note>original: *Stockwaerder*; the keeper of the prison in Philippi</note> is about the greatest matter anyone can ask; namely, he asked what he had to do to be saved?

The question seems to be an expression of someone who is in great distress and dejection of spirit; and truly the matter about which this question is asked is such that the whole world ought to be startled. As a certain dignified Theologian answered someone who came to him asking, "Sir, I am troubled concerning my salvation"—"Well, friend," he said, "it is a matter that the whole world ought to be startled over." So also this poor man cries out to Paul and Silas, *What must I do that I may be saved?*

I shall not spend time on the explanation, but I shall [present] all that I...

<meta>This page continues the sermon on the conversion of the Philippian jailer (Acts 16). # The Closest Examination

<margin>
2. Observation from the condition of the person who poses this question.
</margin>
...to bring these words into practice. Before I come to the Doctrine which I intend to treat from this text, three coinciding circumstances regarding the words are to be observed, from which three remarks arise. First, from the consideration of the state of the one who poses this earnest question; it is a Jailer <note>Dutch: *Stock-waerder*; literally a 'warden of the stocks'</note>, a profession which in these days is especially considered dishonorable, because the followers of Christ are most often held in the bonds from which oppressors and perpetrators of violence commonly escape. Nevertheless, see here a Jailer or Turnkey <note>Dutch: *Suppier*; a keeper of a prison</note>, the object of God's forgiving mercy: note from this:

<margin>
Mark 2:17.
</margin>
That people of the most despised status in the world can also be the objects of God's forgiving grace. Salvation is not confined to the ranks of the rich and prominent of the world; but sometimes even the lowliest are those to whom God shows His mercy. Forgiving grace sometimes extends to the most wicked and most outstanding sinners of the world; Christ was not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance <note>original: "Christus was niet gekomen om te roepen rechtveerdige, maer sondaers tot bekeeringe"</note>.

<margin>
2. Observation from the occasion of the Jailer's conversion.
</margin>
Secondly, from the reflection on the occasion or manner of this Jailer's conversion; it says that around midnight a great earthquake suddenly occurred; and the Jailer was woken from his sleep, and when he stood up, he saw that all the doors of the prison were opened, and thinking that all the prisoners had fled, he was greatly dismayed and distressed, fearing what would happen to him. This was made by God into a means to make this man strive for salvation, so that, although he thought the escape of the prisoners would cause the loss of his life, his care was now what he should do to preserve his soul. He said: Dear Sirs, what must I do that I may be saved? Note from this:

That God through His providence <term>Providence|The theological concept of God's intervention and guidance in the world</term> often knows how to arrange it so that afflictions are frequently a means to make people strive for salvation. If this poor man had not thought that he had lost his prisoners, God knows whether he would not have lost his soul, and whether he would have ever sought salvation. I have read of a Scottish theologian who, being in great distress of sickness, thanked God the Lord for it; for, he said, this sickness of my body has been a means to the preservation of my soul. God is accustomed to making one affliction or another into an instrument to cause people to seek after salvation.

<margin>
3. Observation. From the great change that this providence worked in him.
</margin>
Thirdly, here is to be noted the great change which this providence worked in the Jailer. The poor man was previously very dismayed when he thought that the doors of the prison were opened; and it says in verse 27 that he drew a sword and would have killed himself. Yet now we hear no more talk of killing himself; but all his care is how he shall preserve his soul. Note from this:

That when people once begin to seek Heaven diligently, a great change then manifests itself in their passions and inclinations. This man's

<column-break/>

fear and care was now not how he should get his prisoners back, but only what he must do to no longer be a prisoner of Satan; not how he should keep other people in bonds, but what he must do to release himself from the bonds of the Devil. Oh, how wonderful is the change which conversion works in the soul! It changes not only one's interaction with others, but even the very passions and inclinations of the heart are changed.

I point out these remarks only in passing, for they are not the main objective of the text.

<margin>
The Jailer's question arises from fear.
</margin>
Now I shall come to the treatment of the Jailer's question, and of the Apostle's answer.

First, the Jailer's question is: Dear Sirs, what must I do, that I may be saved?

This troubled question arises from two fountainheads <note>Dutch: *springh-ader*; literally a "spring-vein," referring to the source of a stream</note> or from two kinds of passions in man.

<margin>
From hope.
</margin>
First, it springs from fear. For he spoke while trembling greatly, and said: Dear Sirs, what must I do? Intense questions contain within them a mixture of fear. As if he said: I might lose both my life and my soul at once; oh my lords, do tell me how I may but preserve my soul, and then my life is of no consequence. There was fear mixed with this question: what must I do, since I have done evil?

Secondly, it flows from hope; for he would never have been inclined toward it if there had not been some hope of grace. The question "what shall I do?" makes known some measure of hope: We do not ask about things that are impossible, for example, how we might climb into Heaven, or how we might fly through the air like a bird, because these things cannot be done by us. But one asks about things that are reachable; so this question "what shall I do?" expresses that there was still some hope in him.

<margin>
Two parts in the Text.
</margin>
The text contains within itself two particular things. 1. The question of a troubled soul: "what must I do that I may be saved?" 2. A healing, satisfying answer to this question: "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and you shall be saved."

<margin>
6 particular things to note in the manner of speaking he used.
</margin>
Before I now draw the Doctrine from the Jailer's question, note with me six particular things regarding the manner and form of expression.

1. He does not say "what evil shall I do"; he had already done so much evil, he did not want to heap sin upon sin; but he says "what good shall I do."

2. He does not say, "which good words shall I speak?" or "what good confession shall I make?"; but "what good shall I *do*." Good words or a good confession cannot bring a man into Heaven: those who cry "Lord, Lord" <note>A reference to Matthew 7:21</note> shall never enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

3. It does not say, "what *might* I do," as if it were indifferent and he were free to do it or not; but he saw there was a necessity to do something—"what *must* I do?"

<meta>Catchword: Waer (Where)</meta>

<summary>This page analyzes the conversion of the Philippian jailer, highlighting how God uses earthly afflictions and crises—like an earthquake and the fear of professional failure—to redirect a person's soul toward the necessity of salvation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Philippian jailer’s conversion. The previous page discussed how God’s grace reaches even those in "lowly" or "dishonorable" professions, like a jailer, and how an earthquake served as the catalyst for his spiritual awakening.</meta>

->## of a good Christian.<-

4. It does not say: "What must another do?" but rather, "What must **I** do?" Just as I cannot live by the food which another person eats, so I cannot reach Heaven through the good works which another person performs.

5. It does not say: "What must I know?" but "What must I **do**?" There are often high speculations and great sciences in the brains of men when there is no virtuous disposition in their hearts. Truly, it is not knowledge, but doing that shall bring a man into Heaven. *If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.* <note>Original: "Indien ghy dese dingen weet, zalich zijt ghy so ghy de selve doet." A reference to John 13:17.</note> The Devils know more than all the children of Men; they know much good, but they do much evil.

6. It does not say: "What must I do to get my prisoners back?" but "What must I do to obtain Heaven, to be saved?" And certainly, this is the most weighty question of all. These, then, are some observations based on the manner of speaking which the Jailer <note>original: "Stockwaerder"</note> uses here.

<margin>The Doctrine.</margin>
**The Doctrine is this.** That the children of men must, as a matter of necessity and with the utmost care above all things in the world, investigate this: namely, what they must do to be saved. In the handling of this proposition, I shall first set forth some warnings; secondly, I shall give you the reasons; and then I shall apply it to us all.

<margin>I. Warning. It is a necessary good to do.</margin>
The warnings to be taken into account here are as follows. *First:* although it is most necessary for the children of men to investigate what they must do to be saved, they must nevertheless be warned that although we must investigate what we must do, we must not fool ourselves into thinking that we shall be saved *by* the doing. This is expressed very well by the Man of God, *Job*, when he says; <margin>Job 7:20.</margin> *If I have sinned, what shall I do to you, O Watcher of mankind?* <note>original: "Hebbe ick ghesondicht, wat sal ick u doen; O menschen Hoeder?"</note>

This question contains within it an absolute denial: "what shall I do to you," that is, I can do nothing to satisfy your justice, to still your wrath, or to obtain your love and favor. Lord, I have truly sinned against you, and if you require restoration and satisfaction from my hands, I do not have the slightest strength to do so.

*Job* speaks like a poor, ruined bankrupt to his rich and angry creditor, who seizes him for his debt, and whom he is in no way able to satisfy; and therefore he throws himself down at his feet and cries out: "My Lord, I well acknowledge that I owe you much, but I have nothing at all to pay; I cannot satisfy you in the slightest for that which I owe you." So it is with all men after the fall of Adam. God gave us whole things to keep, but we have lost everything, and we have become bond-breakers with total debts: we owe God a thousand times ten thousand Talents <term>Talent: an ancient unit of weight and high-value currency; here representing an unpayable spiritual debt</term>, and we cannot, of ourselves, satisfy the Divine Majesty in the slightest for all the wrong and dishonor we have done him through our sins. It is true, we might be able to serve God in payment of our current duty, but we can do nothing to pay the old debt which we owe him. Therefore, although everyone must indeed investigate "what must I do to be saved," remember nonetheless that no one shall be saved because of his doing.

<margin>II. Warning. No one is saved without the doing.</margin>
Secondly: though no one is saved *because* of his doing, nonetheless everyone must investigate "what must I do," because no one can be saved *without* the doing; just as St. *Augustine* also says: *Although God created you with-*

<column-break/>

*-out you, He will not save you without you.* <note>original: "Hoewel Godt u gemaeckt heeft sonder u, soo en sal hy evenwel u niet zalich maecken sonder u." A famous quote attributed to Augustine of Hippo.</note> Certainly, my doing is not the *cause* why God saves me, but it is a *reason* without which God will not save me. God saves no one because of their doing, yet God will save no one without their doing. God is not so indulgent in the giving of Heaven that He would throw it into the lap of someone who will do no labor for it. Heaven is the end of a racetrack, and unless you run, you shall never obtain it. Heaven is a reward of life, but unless you are faithful unto death, you shall never obtain it.

<margin>3. Warning. Heavenly concern does not exclude lawful worldly care. Socrates.</margin>
Thirdly: this investigation into salvation does not exclude a lawful striving and care for worldly things. God never intended for Heaven to so occupy and busy your care and consideration that you should look nowhere else but toward heaven. No; you can seek Heaven and not neglect worldly things as well. You do not need to do as *Socrates* did, who, because his riches hindered him from studying Philosophy, threw them all into the sea, saying: "I shall destroy you so that you do not destroy me." You do not need to reject your station; you may well care for both worldly and Heavenly things; but with this oversight: that your first and foremost care be concerning Heaven and the Heavenly, and that your worldly care be subordinate to that. These are the warnings.

Now follow the reasons for the Doctrine.

<margin>First reason: because the soul is so excellent.</margin>
First: we must above all things investigate what we must do to be saved because the soul is the most noble thing in the world. Scripture gives it this title: "the precious soul." The Body is but the shell, and the soul is the Pearl; the Body is the box and the soul the Jewel; therefore, make it your special work to see how you shall keep your soul, because more depends on that than on the whole world. *Julius Caesar* used to say to *Cicero* that he was negligent in his own affairs and diligent in those concerning the common welfare; so we too must be somewhat "negligent" in things concerning our bodies, in comparison to those concerning our souls.

<margin>Second reason. Heavenly care is the right path to bodily welfare. God does not always hear according to our will or pleasure, so that He might always hear for our salvation.</margin>
Secondly: seeking the preservation of the soul is the right means to provide for the welfare of the body. No one is wise for himself if he is not wise for his soul. *Matthew 6:33.* *But seek first the Kingdom of God, and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.* See that you first and above all "buy" Heaven; the other things God will sufficiently throw in, just as *Solomon* was also given riches and honor (*1 Kings 3:13*). Truly, God does not always grant us the specific temporal blessings for which we pray and which we think we need, for He knows better what we require than we do ourselves; but although He does not always hear according to our will, He nonetheless always hears according to our need. For, says the Apostle (*1 Timothy 4:8*): *Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come.* Regarding the blessings of this life, they are given in such measure as they serve our good; but regarding the future life, they are given absolutely and without any condition. It is remarkable what we read in *Exodus 1:21*: *And it happened, because the midwives feared God, that He provided them with houses.* The midwives feared God, and God cared for them. Do you but take care for your soul, and God will certainly take care for your body.

<meta>This page continues the sermon on the Philippian jailer’s conversion. The previous page established that investigating how to be saved is a necessary duty; here, the author provides specific reasons for this urgency and begins to apply these truths to different types of people.</meta>

### The Closest Investigation

<margin>
Third Reason.
Because the Devil seeks to destroy the soul.
</margin>
Thirdly, you must strive to preserve your soul because the Devil strives so greatly to bring it to destruction. *1 Peter 5:8.* "Be sober and watchful, for your adversary the Devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour," <note>original: "verslinden"</note> or literally, whom he might swallow down or gulp up in one go. Satan envies our restored state—that we shall enjoy that blessed Paradise which he once possessed and from which he was cast out. Therefore, he is our irreconcilable mortal enemy. He tempts and disturbs us constantly out of his infinite hatred for God and godliness. Just as the leopard <note>original: "Luppaert"</note> has such an innate hatred for mankind that if he only sees a painting of a person, he will tear it to pieces; so it is with the Devil. If he sees even the image of God in us, he seeks by all means to scrub it out.

<margin>
Chrysostom.
</margin>
Now Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an important Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note> says: if the Devil is standing on guard, will you then sleep? If the Devil is walking around, will you then sit still? If the Devil is diligently investigating which souls he may devour and bring to ruin, should not the children of men make it their business to investigate how they might preserve their souls?

<margin>
Fourth Reason.
If you lose your soul, you lose everything.
</margin>
Fourthly, seek after this, for if you lose your soul, you suffer the greatest loss that can be imagined; no loss reaches so far. To lose the soul is to be deprived of God, of Christ, of a Kingdom, and to be deprived of all the company of the Saints and the Angels for eternity. Oh, that word "eternity" makes this loss very heavy; it is a loss which can never be restored or recovered. If you lose your soul, you lose everything; it is an everlasting loss which is impossible to take back.

<margin>
Chrysostom.
</margin>
Chrysostom notes this very well, saying: Nature has arranged the parts of the body so that a person has two eyes, two feet, and two hands, so that if someone loses one eye, he can see with the other; or if he loses a leg, he can walk with the other; or if he loses a hand, he can work with the other. But, he says, God has given you only one soul, and if you lose that, you lose everything. Oh, that this reflection might make you ask: "What must I do to preserve my soul?"

<margin>
First useful application, for the reproof of three sorts of people.
First, those who only investigate speculative questions.
</margin>
Now I come to the useful application. If it is true that one must investigate this above all else: "What must I do to be saved?" then this serves first for the reproof of those who constantly ask about matters of lesser weight, but never about the means of salvation. Nowadays there are multitudes of people who tire their heads and are infatuated with mere speculations or theories and various questions, but who never press this question upon their souls: "Lord, what must I do so that I may be saved?" How justly those deserve to be accused who, regarding Christianity, only strive after precise, pleasant, and subtle questions <note>The author is likely criticizing those who enjoy academic theological debates but ignore personal piety.</note> which only serve to darken the clear truth of the Gospel, and meanwhile do not think once of this weighty and necessary question: "What must I do to obtain Heaven?" Truly, we live in an age

<column-break/>

that is full of controversial questions, and in which all the foundations of Religion are called into doubt. But unless God prevents it, these common questions will cast out this necessary question: "What must I do to be saved?" Among all questions, there are two that are most necessary for the people to ask, and most comforting for the Minister to answer. The first: "What shall I do to be saved?" The other: "How shall I know that I will obtain salvation?" These are the weightiest questions of all. And just as Christ says (speaking of our love for God and our neighbor): *This is the first and greatest Commandment, and the other is like it,* so I say also: this is the first and greatest question: "What shall I do to be saved?" and the other is like it: "How shall I know that I shall be saved?" The first is the foundation of all our happiness, and the second of all our comfort.

<margin>
Secondly, those who only strive after earthly things.
Psalm 4:6.
</margin>
Secondly, it shall serve for the reproof of those who focus their attention on the body and that which belongs to its welfare, but never strive for their salvation. There are many people in the world who cry out with the fleshly-minded: "Lord, who will show us any good?" but they never ask how they themselves might become good. These people are like the man who went to the Doctor asking how he could drive away the pain in his finger, but never once investigated how he might heal the consumption of his lungs. Many people inquire eagerly after common worldly matters, but not how they might obtain a right to Jesus Christ, how they might escape Hell, and attain Heaven.

<margin>
What folly it is to be anxious about those things which you will have without being anxious, and not about those which you will not have unless you are anxious. <note>Original Latin: "Quæ stultitia est de iis solicitum esse, quæ habebis non solicitus, & de iis non quæ non nisi sollicitus."</note>
</margin>
Now, what folly and madness it is for someone to be very careful over those things which he would have even without that care, and to be neglectful and careless regarding those things which are not promised to him without constant care! For grace and glory must not be expected without seeking and diligent searching. But external things shall be "thrown in" <note>original: "toe-geworpen"</note> to us if we seek the Heavenly things.

<margin>
Matthew 6:33.
</margin>

<margin>
Thirdly, those who seek to bring themselves to damnation.
</margin>
Thirdly, it serves for the reproof of those who earnestly seek how they might bring themselves to destruction, and not how they shall be preserved. The drunkard asks where Wine and strong Beer are to be found; the adulterer (as Solomon says) looks for where the house of the harlot may be. Thus there are many who investigate how they shall ruin their souls, but oh, how few there are who cry out with this poor Jailer: <note>original: "Stockwaerder"</note> "Dear sirs, what must I do so that I may be saved?"

<margin>
Second useful application: to examine whether you are in a state of salvation.
This can first be known by the way God deals with such souls.
1. Manner and order of dealing.
</margin>
The second application shall be for testing, so that you may investigate for yourself whether you have already answered this question—whether you are already assured within yourself that God has indeed brought you into the state of salvation. Now, to know this, consider the following things:
First, whether God has dealt with your soul in that manner, method, and order which He uses with those whom He intends to save. Here you shall say: "What are those ways and manners of dealing that God enters into with a sinner whom He intends to save?" I answer:
First, God enlightens the understanding of that person and makes him see that his sins are exceedingly sinful and that he himself is most miserable.

You have a very excellent text for this in <note>The book of Job is often cited in 17th-century sermons to illustrate the internal struggle of the soul before God.</note> Job 33:27, 28, 29, 30. *He shall look upon men and say: I have sinned, and perverted what was right, and it profited me not; but God has redeemed my soul, that it should not go into the pit; so that my life beholds the light: see, all these things God works two or three times with a man; that he may turn back his soul from the pit, and he be enlightened with the light of the living.* It is God’s usual way of working that when he redeems a sinner from Hell, he shows him his sin in the **Mirror of the Law** <note>The "Mirror of the Law" is a common theological metaphor: just as a mirror reveals physical stains, God's commandments reveal moral "stains" or sins.</note>, making him see that he is sinning beyond measure, and that he perceives his own sinfulness, namely how he has perverted what is right. Paul says of himself that he was alive without the law, but when the commandment came, he saw his sin as sinning beyond measure. Is then (says he) that which is good become death to me? Far be it. But sin has become death to me: so that it might be revealed as sin, working death in me through that which is good; so that sin might become exceeding sinful through the commandment. Sin is in its own nature so exceedingly evil that one can give it no worse name than to call it **sinning sin**. Beloved, if God has dealt with you in such a way that he makes you see that your sins are sinning beyond measure, and that you yourself are beyond measure wretched and miserable, know that God is accustomed to begin this work with the soul which he intends to bring into Heaven.

<margin>1. Method of dealing.</margin>
The second method that God uses to preserve the soul of a sinner is this. God places him in a state of **Spiritual dejection** and despair, so that he regards himself as a lost creature, entirely powerless to save himself; nor does he know who will undergo this work for him; this appears clearly from the text: *Dear sirs, what must I do to be saved?* A question of astonishment and confusion of the mind. When God once throws a person out of his own self-sufficiency, self-righteousness, and self-ability, this is a good step toward Heaven.

<margin>2. Method of dealing.</margin>
A third way that God enters into a sinner is when he offers Jesus Christ to his soul as the most delightful object in the entire world. He sees that sin is sinning beyond measure, and he himself is beyond measure miserable, and then he sees that Jesus Christ is beyond measure desirable. Well, you who feel this testimony in your soul—that God has dealt with you in these ways—know this for your comfort: that God is accustomed to meet those souls in this manner whom he intends to save.

<margin>

1. Impression on the heart.
1 Cor. 1:18.

</margin>
Secondly, whether God has brought you into the state of salvation, you shall be able to discern from these **impressions** <note>In this context, "impressions" refers to the lasting marks or changes the Holy Spirit makes on a person's character and desires.</note> which our Lord Christ works on the hearts of those whom he wishes to save: now these impressions are fourfold.

First; God lets the power and glory of the Word fall upon the **Conscience** <note>original: "Conscientie"</note> of that person whom he wishes to preserve at one time or another with great conviction. For the word of the Cross is indeed foolishness to those who are perishing; but to us who are saved, it is the power of God. The power of God in his Word shall be felt upon the Conscience of that person whom God brings into a blessed

<column-break/>

state. Therefore the Apostle says expressly: *For this cause also we thank God without ceasing, because when you received the Word of God which you heard from us, you received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the Word of God, which also works in you who believe.* God’s Word has an active power and a glorious authority over those who shall be saved. It is powerfully working in those who believe, who are thereby changed into its own likeness; it effects that which it prescribes; yes, it strengthens the soul so that it can achieve every duty, no matter how difficult for flesh and blood, and so that it hates every sin, no matter how pleasant or profitable.
<margin>Heb. 4:12.</margin>
The Word of God is *living and powerful, sharper than any two-edged sword*, as the Apostle speaks; it binds the Conscience effectively, it improves and directs the judgment, it subjects the will, and the sinner cannot endure against it.

<margin>2. Impression on the heart.</margin>
The second impression that God makes on the heart of the one who shall be saved is this: he is brought to an obedient disposition to keep God’s Commandments; God’s Law is not burdensome to him, but delightful and sweet; he has a general readiness for all of God's commands, as David speaks and as the Apostle says in Hebrews 5:9: *And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him.*

<margin>3. Impression on the heart.</margin>
Thirdly, if God brings you into a saved state, he makes this impression on your heart: that you strive as much for a **sanctified nature** as for the salvation of your soul. Titus 3:5: *Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost.* And John 3:3: *Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.*

<margin>4. Impression on heart.</margin>
<margin>The second part of the text is explained.</margin>
The last impression is this: he will bring you into a state of believing; he will make you hold fast to Christ through faith. And this leads me to the second point which the Apostle gave as an answer to this poor man, who cried out what he should do to be saved: namely, *Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and you shall be saved.*

<margin>Objection. No one can believe by their own power.</margin>
At first glance, someone might think that the Apostles' answer in no way sets the heart of this troubled man at rest. Paul and Silas command him to believe. Might he not have answered back: "Just as little as I can make a world, perform miracles, or move mountains, so little can I believe by my own power; why then do you command me to believe?"

<margin>Answer. God promises to give what he commands.</margin>
To this I answer: although it is indeed so that every Commandment of God is equally difficult for flesh and blood—so that someone could as easily create a World as keep a Commandment rightly, or as easily defeat an entire army as one single lust—yet know this for your comfort: this is the tenor of the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangeliums"</note>. When God the Lord demands anything from the hands of his elect children, he brings some power into their souls through that command, to strengthen them for the performance of that Commandment. If God commands someone to believe and gives him the power to believe, then the work will soon be done. And in the Prophet Ezekiel, God commands a person to make a new heart; now a man can no more make himself a new heart than he can make a new

Just as it is written in Micah 7:18, 19: *Who is a God like unto you, who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of his heritage; he retains not his anger forever, because he delights in mercy. But God shall give you a converted heart, for He has promised to give *repentance and forgiveness of sins.* I pray you, take note of this: that the commands in the Scripture are no proof of what a person *can* do, or should do by their own natural strength. But such commands are laid upon people to let them know what God wants to do for His elect. If you put into practice the sanctifying powers that God gives us, then God will add His helpful grace to it, to strengthen us for that which we cannot do of ourselves. Therefore we must pray with **Saint Augustine**: 
<margin><note>original Latin: "Da quod jubes & jube quod vis."</note> Give what You command, and then command what You will.</margin>
Furthermore, observe with distinction the difference between the answer which **Paul** and **Silas** give to these questions, and the answer which **Peter** gives in Acts 2:38. Peter said to them: *Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.* Paul and Silas give this as an answer: *Believe and you shall be saved.* Peter gives this as an answer: *Repent, and you shall be saved.* God indicates something special by this—that these different answers are given by the Holy Spirit to the same question. Both their answers are true. Peter says, *Repent, and you shall be saved,* to show that such faith which is not accompanied by repentance is but a presumptuous confidence. 
<margin>Faith and repentance must be joined together.</margin>
Paul says, *Believe, and you shall be saved,* to point out to you that repentance which is not accompanied by faith is merely a legal sorrow <note>The author distinguishes between "legal sorrow"—grief caused only by fear of punishment—and "godly sorrow" which leads to true change.</note>. Therefore one says *Believe*, and the other says *Repent*, to show that you must join those two together. If only this answer had been given—*Believe and you shall be saved*—then people might have said, "This is a short way to Heaven; one needs only to believe." Peter says *Repent and you shall be saved* to show that both must be put into practice by Christians; that **Faith** and **Repentance** must go hand in hand if one intends to be saved. I touch upon this all the more readily because there are some people who are very fond of believing in Jesus Christ, but not at all fond of repenting and bewailing their sin. Such sins would make it so that Peter’s answer would be no answer at all. Besides these, there are also others who place everything in repentance; they are in spirit

<column-break/>

troubled and grieved in the mind; they wish that *their heads were waters and their eyes fountains of tears* <note>A reference to Jeremiah 9:1, expressing deep mourning.</note> in order to make a bargain and reconciliation with God; but they do not rest at all upon Christ through faith. Now, these sins would make it so that Paul’s answer would be no answer at all; but remember that you must repent and so be saved with Peter, and that you must believe and so be saved with Paul.

However, I shall only speak briefly of the answer which Paul and Silas give here. Take from it this Doctrine: 
<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
**That it is the bounden duty of all who expect salvation to believe in Jesus Christ.**

But I think I hear some already saying: "If this is so, well then, surely salvation can be obtained by small efforts <note>original: "klepne moeren," likely meaning small pains or easy steps.</note>; for do we not all believe in Christ? God forbid that anyone should be so godless that they would not believe in their Savior." I answer: certainly there are many who have a *kind* of faith, namely a historical, a speculative, a common, dead faith; such a faith as **Simon the Sorcerer** <note>A biblical figure from Acts 8 who "believed" but was rebuked for seeking to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.</note> had; such as the stony ground <note>Refers to the Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13), where seeds on stony ground sprout quickly but wither because they have no root.</note> had; such as the devils have, who *believe and tremble.* A person can have this faith and still go to hell.

But there are few in the world who have a living, precious, and unfeigned faith, which in the Scripture alone is considered a true faith in Christ; and whoever has the same shall never perish, but have eternal life. There are few who want to accept Christ as He is offered in the Gospel: namely, as much as a **King** to rule them as a **Jesus** to save them. There are few who are willing to accept the naked Christ with His cross as well as Christ with His throne. There are few as ready to surrender themselves to Christ for **sanctification** as they are to accept Christ for **justification** <note>Justification is being declared righteous by God; sanctification is the ongoing process of being made holy.</note>. Most people love the priestly office of Christ to obtain salvation for them, but they do not love the kingly office of Christ to fight against their corruption. They would gladly have Christ take them into Heaven, but they do not want to receive Christ into their hearts. In the day of adversity, when they lie on their sickbeds and the terrors of death seize them, then they cry out for nothing but Christ; but in the day of prosperity, when the world smiles upon them and riches and well-being surround them, then Christ is held in low esteem by them; they see no beauty in Him for which they should desire Him. For there is not one godless person in the world who wants to accept Christ according to the prescriptions of the Gospel, aside from their own well-being and outward prosperity. Indeed, what is more, most people think that believing is the easiest of things—that it is merely "believing," that it is in their power to believe at whatever time they wish, and that they can believe early enough when they lie on their deathbeds. Poor people! They do not consider that God works faith in the soul by the same **Almighty power** through which He raised Jesus Christ from the dead, as the Apostle shows in Ephesians 1:18, 19: *And what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the...*

# Of a Good Christian

It is as impossible for a person to cause themselves to believe through their own strength as it is to create a world or to give themselves their own being. Note here also that every kind of outward agreement with God’s Word is not true faith; although **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621) was a Roman Catholic Cardinal and a key figure in the Counter-Reformation; the author is here critiquing the Catholic view of faith as mere intellectual assent.</note> says that to believe is solely and simply to agree with the Word. But if saving faith consisted only in a simple agreement that the Scripture is the truth, then there would be a great multitude of believers in the world; but God shall never claim such "believers" as His own.

<margin>
Description of saving faith.
</margin>
Secondly, consider that faith is not a bare agreement; no, rather the nature of faith consists in this: It is a grace from God wrought in the heart of a humble sinner, who perceives that their sins are enough to damn them, and that all their own righteousness is too little to save them; therefore, they go out of themselves, and they rest and lean entirely upon the righteousness of Jesus Christ, and through this, they expect salvation.

If we were now to look over all the children of men, where would we find those who believe in Jesus Christ in this way? How few are there in the world who feel the burden of their sins? Who see that all their righteousness and religious observations <note>The original Dutch uses "Godts-dienst-plegingen," referring to formal acts of worship or religious duties.</note> amount to nothing at all in the matter of justification? Who find in their souls an earnest longing for the Lord Christ, to be found in Him, not having their own righteousness? Who roll their burdened souls onto Jesus Christ, resolving that if they are to perish, they will perish there. Certainly, beloved, if people tested their hearts against this description of faith, very few believers would be found.

<margin>

1st Consequence.

<margin>

</margin>
Learn from this to take good care that you do not chase after empty trifles and worthless trinkets, and that you do not meanwhile neglect the greatest matters of eternal life. It was a sign of a foul spirit in **King Sardanapalus** <note>A legendary Assyrian king often depicted in early modern literature as a symbol of decadence and the neglect of duty.</note> that he wished to sit among the women, spinning and carding wool, while he ought to have been ruling and observing the affairs of the Kingdom. Many people are of such a base and ignoble nature that they waste their time, their strength, and their labor in useless outward works, and meanwhile neglect the great and weighty matters of the Heavenly Kingdom.

<margin>
2nd Consequence.
</margin>
Secondly, if only a few closely investigate how they shall be saved, then we may conclude from this that only a few shall be saved. There are many in the world who never come as far as that wealthy young man <note>original: "Borgerlijcken Jongman," referring to the Rich Young Ruler.</note> of whom it is written in **Matthew 19:16**, who asked, *What good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?* and who never asked with the **Jailer**, *What must I do that I may be saved?* Oh beloved, if the greater part of humanity does not even ask after Heaven, how few shall then arrive in Heaven?

<column-break/>

<margin>
Second Utility.
</margin>
But secondly, from this answer that the Apostle gives to the Jailer’s question—*Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ*—base your salvation upon Christ; lean upon His blood, His merits, and His righteousness; thus learn what a great benefit and what a privilege the children of men enjoy, that they live under the <term>Covenant of Grace</term> <note>The theological concept that God saves humanity through faith in Christ's sacrifice rather than through human perfection.</note>; for although they cannot be saved through their works, they can nonetheless come to it through that which Jesus Christ has done for them. You cannot be saved through all your doing, but certainly through believing, resting, and trusting in Jesus Christ, waiting for salvation through that which He suffered in your place and for your benefit. If we had remained under a <term>Covenant of Works</term> <note>The belief that salvation is earned by perfect obedience to God's laws, as was required of Adam.</note>, then this would have been our rule: *Do this and you shall live;* but the Covenant of Grace says, *Believe and you shall live.* The condition of the Covenant of Works is that we ourselves must show God a neat and perfect righteousness; the righteousness of another would not be enough; also, in this Covenant, a little would not be accepted for much—the will for the deed—but the judgment of acquittal would only be announced if you were without any blemish and completely righteous. But the Sentence of Damnation would be pronounced if you were found unrighteous in even the smallest matter. This Covenant speaks not a word of hope or help, mercy or peace to the poor lost sinner; but judges him as cursed because of the slightest transgression, and for the smallest departure from God’s righteous Law; and there is no place left for repentance or grace. Adam made

This saying of the Woman was a proverb among the Jews / when someone had performed something praiseworthy / they used to cry out / saying / blessed is the womb that has borne you. <meta>This page continues the practical application of the Covenant of Grace, shifting from the theological merits of Christ to the lived experience of "blessedness." It specifically interprets the biblical encounter between Jesus and a woman in the crowd (Luke 11:27-28) to explain that spiritual obedience is a greater blessing than even the physical act of mothering the Messiah.</meta>

->True Blessedness.<-

The usefulness of this is to teach you that whoever God has blessed with good children must be exceedingly grateful to God; for it is a greater blessing for you than if God had filled your house with silver and gold. And you, whom God has so greatly afflicted that He has caused wicked children to come forth from your loins <note>original: "lendenen," a traditional way of referring to biological descendants</note>; oh, weep under the heavy hand of God, that He has made you into instruments to bring children into the world who will increase the number of the damned in Hell.

So much has been said regarding the words of this woman, who said, "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked." But Christ answered and said, "Yes, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it." Christ said "yes," those are blessed; He does not say that His mother was not blessed, but so that this woman would not attribute too much to His mother—thinking she was blessed only because she had carried Him in her womb—He therefore said: "Come, I will tell you who is truly a blessed man or woman; it is those who hear God’s Word and keep it." Christ did not wish to accept her praise, but He gently corrected her. Notice from this that you must take care that you are not "tickled" <note>original: "gekittelt," meaning to be enticed or puffed up by flattery</note> with pride when you hear yourself or your kin being praised. Christ would by no means indulge the praise of this woman. She believed that the Virgin Mary was the most fortunate woman in the whole world, but Christ says, "Yes, blessed are those who make a matter of conscience of hearing God’s Word and keeping it." A faithful hearer, who is obedient to Christ, is in doing so more blessed than the Virgin Mary was merely for having brought Christ into the world, although that was the most blessed birth that ever occurred.

Oh, how this foresight ought to be a spur to us, to hear and to do all that we hear, since we are so blessed in doing so.

<margin>1. Observation.</margin>
I shall observe several things regarding the way and manner of speaking that Christ uses here. First, it does not say, "blessed are those who hear the Word of God," for there are many types of hearers who are not blessed; rather, blessed are those who hear God’s Word and *keep* it—those who incorporate it into their souls and are thus transformed into its likeness. There are four kinds of hearers spoken of in Matthew 13 <note>The Parable of the Sower</note>, of which three do not attain salvation. Not all hearers reach blessedness, even though they hear one and the same Word of God: it is not the hearing, but the keeping and observing of God’s Word that makes one blessed.

<margin>2. Observation.</margin>
Secondly, notice also that it does not say, "blessed are you who believe," although it is also true that all true believers are blessed; nevertheless, it is not said that way, so that people should not think that mere faith is enough to make them blessed, or that they are now above hearing God’s Word, praying, and receiving the Sacraments. Many in these days are occupied and infected with such high-minded pretensions.

<margin>3. Observation.</margin>
Thirdly, it also does not say, "blessed are you who keep the Word of God," while cutting off the hearing; rather, the hearing of

<column-break/>

God’s Word is included therein. "Blessed are you who hear and keep." Many people think they have already reached a great perfection of life and conduct by keeping Christ’s commandments, but they shut out the hearing; they neglect to hear the Word. Yet those are truly blessed in the eyes of Jesus Christ who hear the Word of God and keep it.

<margin>4. Observation.</margin>
Again, it does not say, "blessed *shall* you be" who hear and keep the word; but "blessed *are* you." This is to point out that you shall not only be blessed when you enter Heaven, but that in doing so, you are already blessed while you are here on earth. The Apostle says: <margin>Romans 6:22 <note>The original OCR lists Rom. 6:12, but the quote corresponds to verse 22.</note></margin> "But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, you have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life." Oh man, if you are blessed, you have your fruit already, before you come to eternal life.

<margin>5. Observation.</margin>
Again, it does not say only, "blessed are you if you hear and keep," but "if you hear the Word of God and keep it." You may hear people who preach damnable errors, and you may quickly imprint those in your heart; but in that case, you are closer to a curse than to a blessing. It may be that some hear many sermons and act accordingly, but if these do not agree with God’s Word and are not established upon the Scripture, they will sooner bring a curse upon their necks by that hearing than a blessing. Therefore the Holy Spirit says here: "blessed are those who hear the Word of God and keep it." By this, people ought to be taught to take good heed to *who*, *what*, and *how* they hear—that they hear nothing other than the Word of God, and then keep that which they hear. We read of teachers who shall introduce destructive heresies, and that many shall follow their destructions: <margin>2 Peter 2:1, 2, 3</margin> for so Peter says: "But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction. And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of. And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not." Thus, those who hear such people who introduce destructive heresies are not blessed. The Scripture does not attribute blessedness to all hearers, but only to those who hear God’s Word and keep it.

<margin>In the English Translation.</margin>
Again, it does not say, "blessed are also those," but "yea, rather, blessed are they," <note>This refers to a nuance in the English King James Version of Luke 11:28: "Yea rather, blessed are they..."</note> or more accurately, "those are truly blessed." Christ does not say, "My Mother is a blessed woman, and those people are also blessed who hear God’s Word and keep it"; but Christ says they are *more* blessed, as if He said: "I consider those men and women more blessed than my own Mother, who was the instrument to bring me into the world." Oh, how this reflection ought to inflame our hearts and stir us to a diligent hearing of God’s Word and a conscientious working out of what we hear; there is no comparable saying in the entire Bible.
