Under what a sleepiness and lethargy <note>Dutch: "paddicheit"; literally "toad-like nature," implying slow, cold, or sluggish.</note> of spirit do most people lie. Many people are as **David** was (1 Kings 1), who, when he was old and well-stricken in years, was so cold that no clothes could warm him. And even though ordinarily the words of the wise (as **Solomon** says) are like nails and goads—they are like nails to fix us fast in...

They only crawl like snails on the way to Heaven; while they can nevertheless run like a heavenly body <note>original: "Hemel"; likely a metaphor for the speed of the celestial spheres or stars.</note> in the ways of sin.

It is the observation of a Rabbi that the snail, above all other creatures of God, was declared unclean because of its creeping and slow gait: God looks upon you as an unclean man, and as an unclean woman—those who have a creeping and slow spirit in the matters of Christianity. There are many people for whom no life appeals except a vain life; they are never so weary as when they are weary of doing good and performing their duties: an hour in the sermon, a day of fasting, or a little time in prayer wearies them to the highest degree, whereas in the ways of vanity and pleasures they are never weary.

It was the saying of that Epicurean <note>A follower of Epicurus, here used to describe someone devoted to ease and pleasure.</note> Marcus <margin>I wish this were working. <note>original: "utinam esset rare [laborare]"; a famous anecdote where Lepidus, reclining in the shade, wishes that such ease were considered "work."</note></margin> Lepidus, who, lying under the shade of a tree on a day when the sun shone, stretching himself out, cried out: "Oh, would to God that this were working, to live so easily." There are many people as foolish as he was: they can wish, "I would to God that sitting in the tavern were the way to go to Heaven; I would to God that on the Sabbath day, walking in the field or sitting before the door were the way to Heaven." Many people would very much like to be saved easily! Therefore, how ought this to stir up that great weariness and sluggishness of man's spirit, that they do so little in the matters that concern their souls?

Beloved, you have reason to labor, because so many are bound <note>Meaning bound for judgment or excluded from grace.</note> who have labored for Heaven and have never entered Heaven. *Many shall seek to enter in, but they shall not be able* (Luke 13). Have you not then good reason to be on your guard? Yes Beloved, even if—(this is a supposition that <margin>[Fragmented Latin text regarding the state of man and the years of life]</margin> Ægidius <note>Likely Blessed Giles of Assisi, known for his pithy spiritual sayings.</note> proposed, though it is not true, nevertheless, I take it as such)—even if all the world should be saved except for one person, yet, says he, you have reason to labor to be saved, so that you might not be that one person who would be damned. If all the world should be saved, and only one man alone should be damned, I have reason to labor with all my might that I might not be that one man. So you have here great cause not to lie under sluggishness in matters concerning the soul. You have much to do, and perhaps but little time: if you knew the greatness of your work and the shortness of your time, you would perhaps not postpone the work of your salvation now. It was the proverb of the young King Charles of Sicily <note>Charles II of Anjou (1254–1309), though the quote is a common memento mori attributed to various rulers.</note> lying on his deathbed: "I have hardly begun to live, and woe is me, now I am forced to die." Beloved, many of you have cause to speak thus; you have hardly done any good work that can give you any evidence of being blessed with Christ hereafter: perhaps you have not yet even begun to be a Christian, and you may soon be called to die; and what a torment that would be for you, that you have hardly begun to live the life of grace, and

<column-break/>

yet must lay down the life of nature. This diligence concerns many things. 1. Concerning the obtaining of grace. You have a great work to do here to obtain grace; whatever you get, get understanding. And the difficulty of obtaining grace is a proof of the excellence of grace (as we say) in nature. The worst things appear most before our eyes and are found most cheaply: stones and mud you have everywhere, but things of an excellent nature require more effort to reach: if you want gold, you must dig in the earth; if you want pearls, you must dive into the sea: thus nature has made the most excellent things difficult to reach. This shows the excellence of the things concerning the soul, that they are very difficult to obtain (Prov. 2:4): *Seek for wisdom as for silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures.* 2. Not only is diligence required to obtain grace, but also to keep it; and it is no less an art to keep grace than to obtain it, as there are so many temptations that lie in your way. <margin>It is no less a virtue to protect what is won than to seek it. <note>original: "Non minor est virtus, quam quaerere parta tueri"; a quote from Ovid's 'Ars Amatoria'.</note></margin> And then 3. To watch over your heart, which conspires against your grace and against your soul: Prov. 4:23. *Keep your heart* above all that is to be guarded, for out of it are the issues of life. 4. In the searching of your heart: Psalm 64:6 <note>The text cites 64:7, following different verse numberings in older Bibles.</note>: *The heart is deep*; and Psalm 77:6. All these things considered, you have cause to labor diligently in all matters of your soul.

Having thus finished this doctrine, I now pass over to those particular parts toward which our diligence must be applied. *Be diligent:* for what purpose? *To make your calling and election sure.* From which I shall draw the second doctrine, which is this:

### 2. Doctrine.

That Christians who make a profession of the Gospel ought to apply great industry and diligence to make this sure to their souls: that they are powerfully called and eternally elected. *Be diligent to make your calling and election sure.*

Now, I cannot handle this doctrine in its entirety, but I must necessarily take it in parts, and handle it point by point, so that I may thereby present the power of the whole doctrine in its application. And since "Calling" stands first, I shall now handle that in a few sermons. And the doctrine from it shall be this:

### 3. Doctrine.

That Christians ought to apply great diligence to make this sure to their souls: that they are powerfully called.

Beloved, this is a matter of great weight that I now have before me, especially in this deceitful age in which men throw themselves into a deep pit of [presumed] mercy, and often take up faith and Christ on "good faith" <note>Meaning a superficial or unexamined belief.</note>. It is proper that you who live under the Gospel test and prove your calling by the Gospel—whether it is a true calling or not. There may well be an outward calling, where nevertheless, through the working of the Spirit on your hearts, there is no inward calling.

In the handling of this doctrine, I shall show you these three things.

# Of our Effective Calling

First, what effective calling is.
Second, why great diligence is required of you to make your calling sure to your soul.
Third, by what marks <note>original: "Merckteyckenen"; refers to diagnostic signs or evidences of spiritual health.</note> you may be assured in your own heart that you are effectively called.

First, what effective calling <note>original: "krachtige Roepinge"; also known in theology as "effectual calling," this refers to God's internal work that successfully draws a person to faith, as opposed to a general invitation.</note> is. You say that we must make it sure; therefore, what is its nature? For an answer, you may take up this description.

Effective calling is the fruit of **GOD’S Election**, whereby **GOD**, on account of His free grace, works a wonderful change in the heart of an elect person through the internal operation of the Spirit accompanying the external ministry of the Word; by the power of which the soul is brought from under the dominion of sin and Satan into the state of grace, and thus made fit for the enjoyment of **GOD** in Glory. Now, I shall not recount these parts in particular, but commend them to your memory and judgment to grasp: only in this description are presented four distinctions to differentiate effective calling from that ordinary or external calling which the ungodly also receive through the ministry of the Word. Namely:

1. Effective calling, in the description, is said to be a fruit of God’s Election; but the external and general calling is a fruit only of His general providence. God sends the Gospel among a people, and thereby He calls them to an external obedience and conformity; but effective calling is a fruit of God’s Election.

2. It is said in the description that effective calling changes the heart. Whereby **GOD** works a wonderful change in the heart; but the external calling in no way touches the heart—it only works certain kinds of civil and common changes in one's life.

3. It is said that effective calling is wrought by the internal operation of the Spirit, accompanying the external ministry of the Word; whereas external calling happens only through the word, but in no way through an internal, saving work of the Spirit.

4. It is said of effective calling that it is a calling out from under the dominion of sin; but the external calling is only from the outward acts of sin. Certainly, the word through an external calling may have such power over a person that it restrains and holds him back from the visible and outward workings of sin; but it works in no way upon that drive to draw him away from the affection for sin, whereas effective calling works upon the heart, as much to conquer and cast down the power of sin as its outward workings.

Second, why does God require that we should apply such great diligence in making it sure that we are effectively called by the Spirit of Jesus Christ in the Gospel? There are three reasons why it ought to be so.

<margin>1. Reason.</margin>
First: Because there are many making profession of the Gospel who, without

<column-break/>

foundation, persuade themselves that they are effectively called, when they nevertheless are not. Now, if many people are so deceived, why might you not be also? And if many are so easily deceived concerning this matter, have you not then great cause to be diligent, so that you are not likewise deceived? The Jews of old boasted of their calling and said: *We have Abraham for our Father.* But Christ refuted that; *If you were Abraham's children* (He says) *you would do the works of Abraham, but you seek to kill me, which Abraham did not do.* But they go even higher in John 8:41, claiming they were effectively called: *We have one Father, namely GOD.* No, says Christ, *You are of your father the devil.* Thus many people run into these great errors, believing they are effectively called when they are not. Many are called externally who are not called effectively, Matthew 22:14. Therefore, it concerns you that you are not deceived in this great work.

<margin>2. Reason.</margin>
Secondly, because this natural aptitude is in us only regarding things of some value to the body; you will certainly assure yourself of those and make them sure. If you have copper, or tin, or base metal, your kitchen will serve well enough for that; but things of greater value, like pearls and diamonds, these must be locked away in a cabinet. You want to be sure that they are well-secured. Therefore, how much more ought you to make sure this great and precious jewel of your effective calling, which so much more concerns your immortal soul? When you buy land, you want to be certain that your right to it is good, by having such evidence as can stand in law. You know the merchants; if they venture a great deal or the majority of their means upon the sea, where perhaps some peril lies in the journey, they will run quickly to insure a large part of it. Beloved, that is what you ought to do; your body is the ship, and the merchandise brought into that ship is your soul; and this ship undertakes a great journey toward Glory. Glory is the harbor where this ship must arrive. You shall meet many perils on your way—perhaps storms and tempests of temptation; yes, perhaps you may drag upon the rocks of presumption <note>original: "laetdunckenheyt"; an over-estimation of one's spiritual standing.</note> or upon the sandbanks of despair. Oh, run now to insure that well! What is that? Run to seek the testimony of Christ's Spirit in your own spirit through the word, to demonstrate to yourself on good ground that the ship shall be preserved and the cargo safely brought to Heaven; that the ship, body, soul, and all shall arrive safely in Heaven. Beloved, if men thus secure their worldly state, you have much more reason to secure your souls. For believe this: if you do not secure your soul, and if you suffer shipwreck, you shall immediately become bankrupt; bankrupt before God, and shall lose Him forever. It was said of an old usurer <note>original: "woeckeraer"; a moneylender who charges high interest, here used as a secular example of extreme caution.</note> that when someone came to him to borrow money, he would hardly trust one in twenty; being asked the reason why he was so distrustful? (He said) it is so good to be sure. Therefore, Beloved, shall a usurer go so securely in all his affairs, and in

# To make your Calling sure.
<sig>M 2</sig>

If you are careful when investing money, so that you can say, "It is good to be secured," then I cannot say much more to you than this: it is so much better to be secured by Heaven. It is so good to be assured that you are effectively called through the power of Jesus Christ—to be assured that you are Christians in truth and not in name alone; that you are Christians in deed, and not only in profession. Oh! It is so good to make your calling and election sure.

Thirdly: Christians ought to labor to make it sure because the more you are assured of your effective calling, the more it will increase and enlarge your inward peace and comfort. 1 Peter 1:8 <note>The original text cites 1 Peter 5:8, but the quote—"believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory"—is from 1 Peter 1:8.</note>: *In whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with a joy unspeakable and glorious.* It is worth noting in all the Epistles of the New Testament, where the Apostle speaks of their effective calling to be saints, that in the very next verse he greets them with these words: *grace and peace be unto you.* 1 Corinthians 1:2: *You are called to be saints; grace and peace be unto you.* Romans 1:6–7: *Called to be saints; grace and peace be multiplied unto you.* And so it is in every Epistle; this is to make it known that when a person is effectively called, the more certainty they have of their calling, the more peace they also have in their own conscience. It shall enlarge your peace and increase your inward comforts; therefore, you ought to labor for the assurance of your effective calling.

Thus, having shown you what effective calling is, and why you should be diligent to make it sure, I now proceed to the third question.

What are the **Marks** <note>original: "Merckteykenen"; diagnostic signs or evidences of spiritual life.</note> by which my soul can be assured that I am effectively called through Jesus Christ? To settle this, I shall analyze it through these two general chapters.

First, you may be assured of your effective calling if God has dealt with your soul in the manner He ordinarily deals with those He effectively calls.

Secondly, if the Lord has wrought in you the saving powers or accompanying operations which commonly attend those who are so effectively called. If these two things have occurred, then you may have a seal and assurance in your own heart that you are indeed effectively called. Beloved, it is not a minister’s job to flatter you <note>original: "Pluymstrijken"; literally "to stroke with a feather," meaning to use sycophancy or empty praise.</note>. Among the many in the world, there are but few who are called; among those who are called, there are but few chosen; and therefore, do not flatter yourselves. If you find on the touchstone that you are not among the number of those God has once called, go home and weep over your unregenerate and unconverted state. But before I can speak of this manner of proceeding, I must first present some errors which have been taken up by many errant spirits <note>original: "Dwael-geesten"; a term for heretics or those who spread false doctrine.</note> concerning the way God acts in calling a sinner to Himself.

The first is the error of the **Pelagians** <note>Followers of Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD) who taught that human nature was not corrupted by original sin and that humans could choose good by their own will without special divine grace.</note>, who hold that a man has the power to call and convert himself. Now, this view excludes God entirely from 

<column-break/>

having any hand in it at all. They say that a Christian is able (having only a general cooperation and assistance from God) to call and convert himself.

2. That of the **Arminians** <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius; in this context, the author critiques their view that God's grace can be resisted and that a believer can "fall from grace" after being called.</note>, and they hold this: that effective calling consists only in moral persuasions, and can be resisted by the person who is thus called; and that a man, being called to the state of grace, can fall away from his calling and grace, and thus have no benefit at all from his calling; which is a very comfortless view. Surely, God will never undertake such a manner of proceeding in the calling of His people.

3. That of the **Papists** <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics; here the author refers to the doctrine of "foreseen merits" (God calls those He knows will do good works).</note>; these say that God calls a sinner and ordains them to glory, but it is through the foresight of their good works. God looked ahead to see how good and holy the person would be, and therefore He willed to choose and call them to glory; but this has no foundation anywhere in Scripture.

4. That of the **Familists** <note>A 16th-century mystical sect (the Family of Love) that prioritized internal "revelations" and spiritual experiences over the external Word of the Bible.</note>; and they hold that it is not God's way to call a sinner through the external ministry of the Word, but through raptures and revelations, through divine inspirations and extraordinary workings. But this is not God's usual way of proceeding, although God sometimes acts so, as He did with Paul, who was called in an extraordinary manner; nonetheless, it is not God's usual rule.

5. There is another error, and that is of those who lay a necessity of a certain measure of terror and fear of the law upon the consciences of men, or else they can never be saved. Sometimes ministers have been so sharp (though truly there is no such cause to slander them as is often claimed) that they were of the opinion that men must be humbled in such and such a way, in such a measure, and for such a duration. Now, it is not God’s way to compel in such a specific measure. It is a great error concerning God’s manner of acting in the calling of a sinner; although I must confess that this comes closest of all five to the rule that God keeps in calling a sinner to glory.

Having thus presented the errors, it is now easier to find the truth. I shall now speak of the manner of proceeding God keeps in the calling of a sinner, and shall here present several ways which God enters into with those He effectively calls, so that if He does so with you, you may go home with a seal upon your heart that you are effectively called to grace, and shall one day come to glory.

**First**, when God goes out to effectively call a poor sinner to the state of grace, He ignites a clear light in their soul, by which they can see the abominable and terrifying nature of all their sins, more than they ever did before (Romans 7:8, 9, 10). Paul says there: *Without the Law, I once lived and sin was dead*; that is, before the power of the Word came upon his conscience to convert him, he lived—meaning he thought he was a good man and a righteous man; he thought that sin was dead and annihilated.

Have you ever seen the misery that sin has brought upon you? They were as if in a daze; the word worked on them, and they saw that it was their sins, that they had crucified Jesus Christ; and so they cried out with a great dismay, "Men and brothers, what shall we do to be saved?" When God powerfully calls a person, he wants to leave them to themselves for a little while, until they do not know what way in the world to turn. # Making the Calling Sure <note>original: "Roepinge vast te maecken." This refers to the biblical exhortation in 2 Peter 1:10 to "make your calling and election sure."</note>

As if a person could not be called without these [terrors]. Yet, we read of Lydia <note>Acts 16:14. Lydia is often cited by theologians as an example of a "gentle" conversion where God opens the heart without extreme terror.</note>, that her heart was opened, and she was never distressed nor dismayed; God sometimes works in such an extraordinary way. But I say this: it is God’s ordinary way of doing things, in one measure or another, or at one time or another, to so cast down His people that they shall not know which way in the world to turn themselves. And so it was with these three thousand in Acts 2. They did not know what they should do to be saved.

Furthermore, if you ask me: with whom does God most often perform this work of bringing them into such spiritual distress, with terror and fear regarding their eternal state? I answer first: with those who, before their conversion, lived in the way of wickedness. Let them take heed: if you have been a knotty and stout-hearted sinner against God, God must give you many a blow before He can bend you to His own will. You who are guilty of drunkenness, of adultery, or of a great and bold breaking of the Sabbath; you who have made this world into a stage upon which to play out your wickedness—take heed; and do not boast of your calling. If God has not brought you along this path, you have reason to suspect that you are not yet called. Those who were unrestrained in their lives before their conversion, if they do not find this spiritual distress within themselves, it is not likely that they are called. And therefore, I truly hold your calling to be suspect, you who come leaping out of the way of wickedness into the way of profession <note>The "way of profession" refers to outward religious practice or claiming to be a believer.</note>, and from the way of malice to take delight in hearing sermons and loving the ministers. You who have been opponents of godliness, if you do not show an extraordinary work in your conversion, I greatly doubt whether you are converted or not; because it is God's usual way of doing things to bring those people who were of an evil life before their calling to a great dismay when they are called.

2. You who have often run against the calling of God, and still continually resist it; so that sermon upon sermon and invitation upon invitation cannot overcome you: look to yourselves. God shall give you many a blow, and send you many a sorrowful hour, before He brings you to your peace.

3. With those who have often sinned against their conscience, who, as it were, wrestled with their conscience; who are excessive in sins, not fearing to sin against so much light and so much conviction. Beloved, you shall not enter Heaven so easily: God will first lay many blows upon you and draw sorrowful sighs from you. David says, *Because of your terrors I am afraid, and my bones are dried up.* <note>A paraphrase of sentiments found in Psalm 38 and Psalm 119:120.</note> You are subject to much terror and dismay, you who sin against your conscience. Again:

4. When God has made you see the abominable nature of sin, shown you your misery because of sin, and has brought you into such a state that you do not know how you shall be saved; then fourthly, this is God's way of doing: that He pulls you away from your own ground, and pushes you away from leaning on

<column-break/>

duties <note>In 17th-century theology, "duties" refers to religious acts like prayer, fasting, or church attendance that people often mistakenly rely on for salvation instead of Christ.</note>, from hanging onto grace [as a reward], and from every thing in your own self. This was God's work in Paul. Philippians 3:9, 10. I was (says Paul in verse 5) *circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of the Hebrews:* that is, my father and mother were Hebrews: what then? *And I was blameless according to the law.* Notice how he stood on his own legs and on his own ground; how he thought he was a holy man, a man blameless according to the Law. But now, he says in verse 7, *The things that were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ's sake; yes, certainly, I also count all things to be loss, that I may be found in Christ, not having my own righteousness.* Paul here, before his conversion, clung fast to his holy life and glorious walk; but now that I am converted and see my foolishness, I desire now to be found in Christ, not having my own righteousness. See how God loosens Paul from any good in himself and makes him lean on Jesus Christ: this is also God's work with you. He will loosen you from your own self and make you see that you cannot be your own Savior.

5. After He has loosened you from your own self, He ignites in you an earnest desire and looking out for Jesus Christ. When a poor soul has searched through all duties, and gone to this and that minister to have full instruction from them, and he sees that the duties cannot help him, and that prayer does not help him; then he thinks: I see no one but Christ to lay my head upon, and no one but Christ to whom I must take my refuge. And then he is so greedy for Christ that even if all the paving stones were gold, and the entire structure of his house were diamonds, and all his clothes were set with pearls—none of all these things could stop him or hold him back in his run toward Jesus Christ. And this, I may say, is God's second work: the first three ways of acting can occur in wicked people; they can see their sins, and the misery alongside them, and be in a distress, not knowing which way they shall go. But these last two [cannot happen to the wicked] by any means; they never loosen themselves from themselves, nor do they ever have a desire or longing for Christ.

6. So it is God's way of doing, after all this, to make them find an abundance of satisfaction and rest in Jesus Christ; so that they may say: I see that I have sought my help in one who is mighty; I see that I have taken my refuge in Him who is both powerful and willing to do me good. 2 Thessalonians 2:16. *He has given us an everlasting consolation, and good hope through grace.* Now Beloved, having spoken of all these things, how many have I left here in this assembly with whom the Lord perhaps has pursued none of these ways with their souls? Oh Lord! I am not able to tell you of your miserable state, but I pray you: be on your guard, and do not bind up your souls in arrogance and groundless imaginations; but believe that these are the ordinary ways that God takes with most souls to bring them to Glory.

# Of our Effectual Calling

### 2 Peter 1:10

->Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to make your calling and election sure.<-

---

<margin>3rd Sermon.</margin>
Having finished the first part concerning the signs regarding the manner of God’s dealings with those whom He effectually calls <note>original: "krachtiglijk roept." In Reformed theology, an "effectual call" is an internal call of the Holy Spirit that cannot be resisted, as opposed to the "general call" of hearing a sermon.</note>, I now proceed to the second sort of signs: namely, the saving accompanying works that join a soul which is effectually called. I shall organize these saving works under eight headings.

First, a person who is effectually called by Christ unfeignedly <note>sincerely or without hypocrisy</note> loves the Word of God and the Minister who preaches that Word, whom God uses as an instrument of his calling. First, I say, he loves the Word: John 8:47. *He who is of* GOD *(that is, who is called by God) hears the words of* GOD; *therefore you do not hear them, because you are not of God.* Scripture tells us there that those who are of God and are effectually called by Him hear His Word with an abundance of delight, joy, and love. So also, 1 John 4:5–6: *He who knows God hears us; he who is not of God does not hear us.* And therefore David, when he wished to reveal this work of God upon his soul, said in Psalm 119:14: *I am more joyful in the way of your testimonies than in all riches.* It is as if he did not value riches at all when compared to the Word; verse 72: *The Law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold or silver.* Beloved, if you are converted and called by Jesus Christ, you will love the Word of God which was the instrument of your calling. Therefore, all you who despise the Gospel, who cannot endure the Word being pressed with power upon your conscience; all you who are weary of the established means of worship and find no more taste in the ordinances of God than (as Job says) *there is taste in the white of an egg* <note>Job 6:6. A metaphor for something that is bland, lifeless, or unsatisfying.</note>—that is proof that you are not yet called. What is the reason that one person will rise early, travel far, take great pains, and often neglect his legal calling <note>his daily job or profession</note> just to enjoy the Word, while another person will walk by the church door, perhaps into a tavern, and not go in to hear the Word even once? The reason is that one is called through the Word and the other is not. One is called through the Word and therefore loves it; the other is not called and therefore neglects it. Secondly, he loves not only the Word, but the Minister who was an instrument of his conversion through the preaching of the Word. And therefore it is noteworthy what some theologians observe: that of all the people we read of in Scripture, no one loved Paul as much as Timothy did. *For I have no one like-minded,* says Paul in Philippians 2:22. No one cared for him and for the Church of God as naturally as he did;

<column-break/>

For as a child with his father, he has served me. And what was the reason? It was because Paul was the instrument of Timothy's conversion. Timothy, being a Minister and having attained a great measure of grace, thought that among all the reasons in the world that should move him to love Paul, it was because Paul was the Minister who converted him. Therefore Paul calls him, in 1 Timothy 1:2, *Timothy, my true son in the faith.* And this is why, when the Apostle wished to draw the love of the Corinthians toward himself (since the Ministers of Christ are the means of their calling), he pressed it on this ground: that they were the means who "begot" them in Christ Jesus, 1 Corinthians 4:1, compared with verses 15 and 17: *Let every man so account of us as ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of* GOD. Why should men regard them so? *For though you might have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel.* By this, he wishes to draw their love to him, because he was the instrument who first converted them. Now, put these two things together: a person who is effectually called loves both the Word of Christ, which was an instrument of his calling, and the Minister who preached that Word, who was the means through which he was called. Test yourselves by this: many of you perhaps think that some good and some change has been wrought in you; but truly, let me tell you this: if you are people who do not love the Word, and do not love those ministers whom God made instruments to convert you, you have right cause to hold your calling suspect. For you see throughout the whole of Scripture that their hearts cling with love to those who called them; therefore, those who can despise the Ministers through whose service they were brought home to Jesus Christ have right cause to be jealous <note>anxious or suspicious</note> over their calling and to hold it suspect. Again:

3. If God has effectually called you, He will, through His Spirit, bring you out of the state of ignorance and darkness and give you some measure of knowledge to understand both the mysteries of God and Christ, and the sinfulness of yourself more than ever before. The Apostle Peter indicates this in 1 Peter 2:9: *You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people, that you should proclaim the praises of Him who has called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.* That is, out of ignorance into a great measure of knowledge; and it is called a "marvelous light." 1. Because it is marvelous if you compare the knowledge you shall have under the Gospel with that which people had under the Law. 2. It is marvelous because people stand amazed that after such a long night of ignorance, they should come to such a great measure of knowledge. 3. It is called marvelous because it is so contrary to the state they were in previously; just as a person who had lain in a dark dungeon for a long time and was suddenly called into an excellent palace—that palace would seem much more glorious to him because it is so contrary to that dark dungeon. So also is this work of God when He calls you; it is a marvelous light, because it is so...

# To Make Your Calling Sure

The contrary state is that which you were in before your calling: Isaiah 30:26, Acts 26:18. He has sent His word to call you from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God.

4. It is a **wonderful light**, because no one but the Mediator <note>The "Mediator" is Jesus Christ, acting as the bridge between God and humanity.</note> could create such a light; Isaiah 42:6, 7: *I will give you as a light to the Gentiles.*

5. It is a **wonderful light**, because it is a light that shines out of the darkness; 2 Corinthians 4:6: *GOD who said that the light should shine out of the darkness.*

6. It is a **wonderful light** because it has greater power than any other light; it is called the *light of life*, John 8:12.

Now, this Calling from darkness to light has two branches:
1. A person shall have more light to obtain greater knowledge and clarity in the mysteries of Jesus Christ.
2. More light to know the sinfulness of oneself.

First, he shall have more light to know the mysteries of Jesus Christ: and from this, Paul tells us in Galatians 1:16: *It pleased God to call me by His grace, and to reveal His Son in me.* Giving us to understand that where God calls a sinner by His grace, He reveals His Son in him. Therefore, Beloved, if Jesus Christ has not been made known to your souls, and you do not have a sufficient measure of the knowledge of Christ, you may be convinced of this: that you have not yet been called through Jesus Christ.

But further, He does not only call you to this light to reveal Jesus Christ to you in an obscure way; but you shall have a clear light: 2 Corinthians 4:6. *For God, who said that the light should shine out of darkness, is the one who has shone in our hearts* (not with an obscure but a shining light) *to give the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.* That is: you have a clear light to know God in the face of Jesus Christ; you cannot know God in Himself, but you shall have a light to know Him in the person of Jesus Christ. This then is the first branch: that God shall kindle a light in your soul, through which you shall have a clear knowledge of those things that belong to Jesus Christ.

Again, secondly, this light shall not only reveal Christ to you, but it shall also reveal yourself to you, and your own sinfulness. It is notable of Paul, that before his Calling he was blameless according to the Law; he thought he was a man without faults; but when the word called him, then he cried out: *I see that sin is exceeding sinful.* Then he saw that sin was sin, and that he was a wretched <note>original: "cathijgh," meaning miserable or wretched.</note> and miserable man.

Therefore, Beloved, if any of you do not have this wonderful light in your soul—to know God, or to know Jesus Christ with the matters that belong to Him, or to know the sinfulness of your own heart—take it from God’s perspective that you are not powerfully called. Either these places in Scripture must be struck out, or otherwise your Calling is not sure. Therefore, be on your guard: I would gladly make my service an examination, so that the hypocrites <term>Hypocrites</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, a hypocrite was someone who performed the outward duties of religion but lacked the internal "effectual" change of heart.</note> do not lie and hide under it. You would be better Christians if you better knew the instability and wretchedness of the heart that is within you; therefore (I pray you) watch yourselves. Although I do not want the godly—

<column-break/>

—godly to lose heart because of what has been spoken here, nevertheless I wish that those of you who are not called might have your hearts pricked by what has been said and what will be said.

3. A person who is powerfully called goes out from himself, clings to, and hides himself in Jesus Christ with greater pleasure and satisfaction than he could ever do in all his life before. John 6:45: *Everyone then who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me.* He does not say: everyone who has heard from the Father. Many people hear the word, but they never unite themselves in Christ; but all those who have heard, and through hearing have learned, and are called, come to me, hide themselves with me, cling to me, and take satisfaction and delight in me. Beloved, there are many who hear the Word, yet they never go out from themselves, and they never hide themselves in Christ; but all who hear and learn—that hear and are called through that hearing—they all come to Jesus Christ. Therefore, all of you who, in hearing, cannot find your hearts in love for Christ, and to unite yourself with Christ, and to believe in Christ: you have right cause to keep your Calling suspect, that it is not a powerful calling. In 1 Corinthians 1:24 the Apostle says that there were people who considered Christ foolishness, *but to you who are called, Christ is the power of GOD, and the wisdom of GOD.* That is: you recognize and understand of Jesus Christ that He has as much power as God has in Him, and as much wisdom as God has in Him. And to that end, you hide yourself in Christ, while other men consider Christ foolish and powerless. Uncalled people have low thoughts of Christ: But to you who are called, Christ is the power and the wisdom of GOD: you shall have high thoughts of Christ if you are powerfully called.

4. A person who is powerfully called shall be made capable through the Spirit of Christ to call upon God. 1 Corinthians 1:2: *To the church which is at Corinth, to the called saints, with all those who call upon the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ.* Here the Apostle joins together "the called saints" with these words "all those who call upon the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ." To show that he who is powerfully called to be a saint shall be made capable by the Spirit of God to call upon God. Psalm 27:8: *My heart says to you, You said, seek my face: I seek your face, O Lord.* Regarding this you also read in Acts 9:11, when Ananias doubted whether Paul was truly called or not; and when Jesus Christ wanted to convince Ananias that he was truly called, what means did He use in verse 11? *Doubt him,* but *Arise,* says Christ, *and go to the street called Straight, and ask in the house of Judas for one named Saul of Tarsus: for behold, he prays.* If he were not called, he would never go to God through such a heartfelt way, and humble his soul before God for his past misdeeds; nor would he pray so fervently for the time to come, and labor to be at peace with me. Go to him, *for behold, he prays.* And therefore, all you who have not in some measure received the Spirit to call upon God, and your...

5. If you are effectually called, then God has wrought in your soul a great abhorrence and loathing of all that evil which you committed in the former part of your life, before your Calling, and for which you stand guilty. Hosea 14:8 <note>The text cites verse 9, but in most English Bibles, Ephraim's rejection of idols is in verse 8.</note>: *Ephraim shall say, What have I to do anymore with idols?* This question brings a great abhorrence and indignation against <margin>2 Corinthians 7:11</margin> the same, 2 Corinthians 7:11. The Apostle speaks there of conversion (which is the same as Calling) when people have the work of grace in their hearts: And this is a branch of it; that Godly sorrow works care, fear, and distaste. That is, if any man is a converted man, this conversion shall cause a distaste; that is, he shall be incensed and angry with himself that he was such a vile person before his conversion, as he truly was. Thus it was with Paul; he speaks with abhorrence against those sins he was guilty of before his Calling. *I was a persecutor, I brought the Saints into prison; Yes,* he says, *I was even mad against the Church.* Beloved, you must reckon that your sins are a madness, and are made very heavy, having been committed before God called you. Anselm <note>Saint Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a major theologian of the medieval church.</note> said to his body, "I will tame you, O unruly Beast, with fasting and prayer." We read of one who bit off his own tongue out of indignation because he had denied Jesus Christ with it. Another Martyr <note>Likely a reference to Thomas Cranmer, who held the hand that signed his recantation in the fire until it burned away.</note> thrust that hand first into the fire with which he had signed a recantation: saying, "Burn, O hand that signed that; which might have caused both soul and body to burn in hell." And therefore, you who have no loathsome thoughts against your past deceits, drunkenness, cursing, and swearing, and past wickednesses: Distrust your Calling. You who do not turn your thoughts away from your habitual sins, from your customary pride and customary greed: if you cannot look upon these with indignation, you have great cause to hold your Calling suspect; for if God has called you, He shall also make you angry with yourself, that you were once as vile as you indeed were. Therefore it is, when God speaks of <margin>Isaiah 2:20</margin> Israel's conversion, Isaiah 2:20, that it says they shall cast away their idols: They shall cast away their sins, as with an abhorrence against themselves because they have sinned. And for this reason the Prophet Ezekiel says <margin>Chapter 20:43</margin> in his prophecy, Chapter 20:43: *You shall loathe yourselves for all your evils that you have committed:* so great should be the indignation toward themselves because they had been so vile toward God before their Calling. So says David with indignation, after he was brought back to himself: *Then was I foolish and <margin>Psalm 73:22</margin> ignorant,* Psalm 73:22. Now Beloved, I appeal to you; I wish to judge no one; let your own consciences pass the sentence upon you, but let me appeal to your own selves; have not many of you previously been opponents of Religion; people walking in godless and unholy ways of life? Perhaps you have now come to a

<column-break/>

show of Godliness; you hear the Word, and speak well of the ministers; and rejoice over the present government because you can now carry out your affairs as you wish, but what is in your hearts? Do you have a loathing for your past persecutions and wickednesses? If not, believe me, though you may go far, I fear you shall nonetheless not reach Heaven: your Calling is not sincere if you do not have a loathing and anger against your previously committed sins. And therefore; O what a sorrowful word this is against all unfeeling sinners! That there are people whose hearts have never been touched with the gnawing of remorse over any evil: what a sorrowful word is this for you who have been drunk week after week; and have sworn day after day, and practiced deceit hour after hour, and been unjust time after time: and yet all these wickednesses have never touched the heart? Truly, you have great reason to fear that God, through Jesus Christ, has not yet effectually called you.

6. A person who is effectually called has his soul brought into an obedient state to obey the commands of Jesus Christ: if God has called you by His Spirit, He will not let you wander in your own ways and will, but He will bring you to a surrender of the heart to all His commandments, <margin>Romans 1:5, 6</margin> Romans 1:5, 6. *We have received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith among all nations for His name, among whom you also are the called of Jesus Christ.* The Apostle did not only receive grace for obedience; but it was also thus among them; you have received grace for the obedience of faith. So that, if you are the called of Jesus Christ, then the Lord possesses this work in you, that He brings you to the obedience of faith; that is, He works in your soul an obedient state to obey all the commands of Christ; and therefore if any of you stand up against Jesus Christ with a boldness of heart; let Christ say what He will, and you will do what you please; let Him command what He will, and you will do what you like; you then who so stand up with a resistance of the spirit against Jesus Christ, you have great cause to doubt your Calling. Again.

7. A person who is effectually called through Jesus Christ shall be spoken ill of and hated by worldly people. John 15:19. *If you were of the world, <margin>John 15:19</margin> the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.* But understand me well; I do not say in this mark that every person who is hated and spoken ill of by the world is a called person: but I say, a person who is truly called shall be spoken ill of by godless people. Now the ill-speaking or the hatred of godless people is a pledge of your effectual Calling, if you take it in these qualities; first, if they only speak ill of you because you are Godly, and hate you for your holiness' sake, then it is a proof, just as Christ says, *because I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.* Secondly, if they speak ill of you when you give them no reason to rightfully speak ill of you: so

The author suggests that being slandered without cause is evidence of a godly life.</note> If they speak evil of you without any foundation, then it is a likely proof of your effectual Calling.

8. A person who is effectually called strives and endeavors to walk worthily of his Calling: 2 Thessalonians 2:13, 14 and Ephesians 4:1. *Walk worthily of the Calling wherewith you are called.* And thus I have briefly gone over these eight parts; I pray you, examine by these hallmarks whether you can show to your own souls that you are effectually called through Jesus Christ, or not.

<margin>Use.</margin>
Now, if it is true that God deals with all those whom he has effectually called in this manner previously spoken of, and that he works these aforementioned co-operations? Then, 1. By way of application, this must serve as a cause of dismay to all those who have never yet experienced this manner of God’s dealing upon their souls, nor had these workings within them to accompany their Calling. Oh (Beloved), I wish that I could fix the nail of terror deep into their hearts who have never yet had any of these things wrought in their souls; who have never yet loved the Word, or the Ministers of the same; who have never yet been brought by God out of the state of ignorance into the state of knowledge; who are not yet truly united with Christ; who have never yet had a loathing for the sins they committed before their conversion; who have never yet brought their hearts into an obedient state to take to heart any commandment that God would lay upon them. How heavily shall this reflection lie upon their hearts?

<margin>Use.</margin>
2. Are you effectually called? Labor to be conformed to Him in your conduct who has called you. The Apostle makes this use of this doctrine in 1 Peter 1:15: *But as he who has called you is Holy, so you also become Holy in all your conduct:* make yourselves like Him in holiness who has called you. You have an excellent way of speaking regarding this in 1 Peter 2:9: *Proclaim the praise of him who has called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.* The word expresses more in the Greek language <note>original: "Griecksche Tale"</note>—"proclaim" or "reveal"—(not just the "praise" as we read it, but) the virtues or the graces of him who has called you. If God and Christ have called you, you must then reveal the graces of Christ in your conduct; that is, live as Christ lived, and walk as Christ walked; if you say that you have fellowship with Christ, then you must walk even as he walked. 1 John 1:6.

<margin>Use.</margin>
3. And do nothing that might in any way stain this, your holy Calling; the Apostle urges this in 2 Thessalonians 1:11: *We also pray always for you, that our God would count you worthy of this Calling.* So also, Ephesians 4:1: *I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beseech you that you walk worthily of the Calling wherewith you are called.* Beloved, if you are called, beware of defiling your Calling in any way; all the offenses

<column-break/>

and weaknesses that you commit lie like a blot upon your Holy Calling; although, in truth, there is no reason to slander anyone's profession <note>The "profession" refers to one's public declaration of faith.</note> even though he sometimes happens to stumble in practice. The Apostle removes this objection in Galatians 5:8: *This persuasion,* says Paul, *does not come from him who calls you.* As if he were saying: many people, seeing that the Galatians might become apostates, slander Religion and slander God who calls them; but, says the Apostle, do not slander Him; for this inclination toward their failings does not come from Him who has called them; the fault lies not in your Calling, but in your corruptions. Therefore, it is an unjust accusation to slander God and Religion because some people do wrong.

<margin>4. Use.</margin>
4. If God has called you, and you come to perceive that in your own soul through the hallmarks heard before, my last application is this: that you should live in the exaltation and magnifying of the grace of God in your Calling. You are called, says the Apostle, according to his own purpose and grace; not according to our works. Oh live, live in the magnifying of that grace which has called you.

I could here propose seven or eight observations as to why you ought to magnify that grace. I shall first name them in general. This exhortation would have much power with you if you would consider these three things: 1. From what you are called. 2. To what you are called; and 3. Why you are called. I shall put those first two things together.

1. The consideration of this—namely, from what and to what you are called—ought to greatly stir you up to magnify this grace; and to this end, I shall propose seven parts.

1. A person who is effectually called is called from ignorance to knowledge, 1 Peter 2:9: *You are called from darkness to a marvelous light.* Now, should this not cause you to magnify this grace? That you, who lay there uncalled in your sins, as in a dungeon of darkness, that God called you into a very bright and delightful Palace; your soul was a beautiful building without windows, or without any openings, or they were only wooden windows through which no light came; now God has opened these shutters and let the Sun of Righteousness shine upon your soul; He has brought you out of the dungeon of darkness of your soul to the light of His knowledge.

2. You are called from the way of sin to the way of Holiness. Before your Calling you were slaves of the devil and did his work according to his will; the devil (as Paul speaks to Timothy) had taken you captive at his pleasure; but when God calls you, he pulls you from under the dominion and the territory of sin, and brings you into the way of sanctification, 1 Thessalonians 4:7: *You are not called to uncleanness but to sanctification.* 2 Peter 1:3: *He has called us to glory and virtue.* Before your Calling you were a sewer, or a common gutter of all filth and uncleanness; but when you are called, you are cleansed with the broom of Sanctification; yes, beautifully wrought and adorned as a delightful Palace for your God to take pleasure in. This ought to stir you up to [magnify] that grace...

# Of our effectual calling

...to magnify [God's] grace; that you have been brought from being bond-servants of the devil to being household-friends of God; from being slaves of the devil to being servants of God; from being the devil's laborer, receiving your wages in Hell, to being a workman of God, to receive your reward in Heaven.

3. God calls you from bondage to freedom. During the time you were uncalled, you were in bondage. 2 Peter 2:19 says: *They were the servants of corruption, etc.* You were in bondage to your lusts, in bondage to your passions, and a slave to the world; you were in bondage under the Law, under the curse, the severity, and the condemnation of the same; but now, if Jesus Christ has called you, he has called you to freedom. Galatians 5:13: *You have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh.* Look at your Calling in 2 Timothy 2:26: <note>The text likely refers to being delivered from the snare of the devil.</note> In your natural state, you are in the snares of the Devil; but after your Calling, you are set at liberty; you are freed from guilt, and freed from the bondage of your sins.

4. You are called from a hardened state into an inner communion and fellowship with Jesus Christ. Before your Calling, you were alienated from the life of grace, Ephesians 4:18. You were without God in the world, alienated from the citizenship of Israel, Ephesians 2:12. But when God called you, he called you from the state of a stranger into friendship and the fellowship of Jesus Christ. 1 Corinthians 1:9: *God is faithful, by whom you were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.* You, who before your Calling were without Christ, now, being called, enjoy close communion with his Son.

5. You are called from Satan to God. Acts 26:18: He has sent his word among you to turn you from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God. You are now brought from under the claws of Satan—who was your Lord, Master, and Ruler—under the dominion and obedience of your God.

6. When God calls you effectually, you are brought out of the state of enmity against God, into the state of friendship and reconciliation with God, and with Jesus Christ, and all the things of God. Colossians 3:15: *Let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you are called; and be thankful.* God has called you to peace, and not to wrath. Before your Calling, God and your soul were the oldest enemies in the world; after your Calling, God and you, from being enemies, have become the greatest friends. You are called to peace; therefore, be thankful.

7. You are called from a state of shame to a state of glory. Before you were called, you were in the eyes of God base and shameful creatures; but when God called you, he called you into the state of glory. 1 Peter 5:10: *Who has called us unto his eternal glory.* And 1 Thessalonians 2:12. <note>The author also cites Isaiah 43:4 and 1 Peter 2:6.</note> Since the time you have been precious in my eyes, you have been glorified, and I have loved you, Isaiah 43:4. And 1 Peter 2:6: *To you who believe, Christ is precious;* or as it stands in the Greek language, *he is an honor to you.* <note>original: "hy is een eere voor u"</note> Once you are called into a state of faith, Jesus Christ is not only precious to you and praised by you, but he is also an honor to you. This you must then

<column-break/>

consider: that when you were uncalled, you were in a shameful state, where not the least sign of honor rested upon you; but once you are called through Christ, he also gains honor through you.

8. And finally (which shall be the conclusion), you shall be called from the Earth to Heaven, and from the Grave to Glory; this shall be your Calling after death. Now, put all these eight parts together: to be called from ignorance to knowledge; from Sin to Grace; from Bondage to Freedom; from Alienation to the fellowship of Jesus Christ; from the state of Enmity to the state of Friendship and reconciliation with God and men; from Shame to Glory; and from Earth to Heaven. Should this not, in the highest degree, stir up your joy and praise to magnify and exalt the grace of God in your hearts?

Secondly, just as the consideration of *from what* and *to what* you are called should increase your praise, so also *why* you are called should do the same. Now, why are you called? You are called solely according to the purpose of his own grace—not for foreseen works, nor good upbringing, nor grace in yourselves; none of these moved God to call you. And therefore you come to see that there was nothing in you, considering there are many things in us that might move God *not* to call us. We have often resisted his Calling; we have frequently stifled the movements of his Spirit in our hearts. We have often brought a rebellious heart to the entreaties of the Ministers of Christ; so it is not anything in us, but only his own grace that overcomes and subdues our unholiness, unwillingness, and the boldness that is in us. It is solely the grace and goodness of Jesus Christ. Now, count all this together and ponder it in your heart, and you shall see what a great cause you have to live in the magnification of Jesus Christ.

# Making our calling sure

...a terror to the godless, and a comfort to the godly; so that the one being mingled with the other might be good for both. I begin with the first.

1. The first sad conclusion that I shall propose is this: that there are many people in the world who are outwardly called through the Word to the **profession of Christ**, <note>A "profession" of Christ refers to publicly identifying as a Christian and attending church.</note> who are not **effectually** <term>Effectual Calling: A theological term for an internal call by the Holy Spirit that actually changes a person's heart, as opposed to just hearing a sermon.</term> called by the Spirit to the possession of Christ. My meaning is this: there are many people upon whom the Word of God works to change their lives, to alter their path, and to create an outward show or appearance of godliness, notwithstanding that they never had any **saving grace** wrought upon their hearts, which is the effectual Calling. *Many are called, but few are chosen,* says Christ, *Matthew 20:16.* And this is a mournful conclusion to all of you who are professors <note>In this context, "professors" are people who claim to be believers.</note> and do not have a saving work upon your hearts; to you who flock together to the ministry of the Word and, nevertheless, are not called thereby.

2. That those who are outwardly called through the preaching of the Word to the profession of Christ, and yet not inwardly by the Spirit, shall suffer much heavier condemnation and pains in Hell than those who never heard a word of Jesus Christ, *Matthew 8:11, 12.* *Many shall come,* says Christ, *from the East and West, and shall sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven.* And what then? *But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness, there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.* Now, who are understood here by the "children of the kingdom"? Not those for whom Heaven is prepared, but the professing Jews, who were called children of the kingdom because they enjoyed a greater, clearer, and bolder measure of the things of God—which showed them the way to the kingdom of heaven—than other people did. And when Christ calls them the "children of the kingdom," he calls the heathens "children of the world." Now, many of the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness; indeed, if there is a place that is more wretched than another, it shall be for the children of the kingdom—those who were, as it were, nurtured in God’s arms through the established means of worship. The children of the kingdom shall have a more miserable portion and a sadder place in Hell than other people who never enjoyed the ordinances of Jesus Christ. Oh, what a sad word that is for you who live where the established means of salvation are so abundant: that you could be called children of the kingdom, and yet be thrust into the uttermost darkness!

3. That there are many people who are only outwardly called to a bare profession, who make themselves believe and nourish such thoughts in their own hearts that they are effectively called by Jesus Christ, though they never had any saving work of grace upon their hearts. Of this I spoke some weeks ago, regarding *John 8:41.* The Jews firmly imagined that they had Abraham as their father; and when Christ convinced them otherwise, 

<column-break/>

they went higher and said, "We have God as our Father." And yet in verse 44, Christ says to them, *That they were of their father the Devil.* Beloved, so you also can be deceived by firmly imagining to yourselves that you are effectively called, when you are only outwardly called.

4. That it is most unlikely, among all people in the world, that those who—in their own feeling and their own eyes—judge themselves to be good, without seeing their defect and the necessity of Jesus Christ, are effectively called by Jesus Christ. This I prove from *Matthew 9:13.* *I am not come,* says Christ, *to call the righteous, etc.* <note>The full verse is "I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."</note> Notice who these are: that is, Christ did not come to call the Pharisees, who were righteous in their own eyes and firmly imagined that things went well with them, and did not see that they had need of a Mediator, Intercessor, and Savior; *I am not come to call the righteous.* Jesus Christ excludes that sort of people from his Calling—those who are high-minded in themselves and lean on their own goodness, without having any lack of Jesus Christ. Therefore, all you who think that since you were born you have had a strong faith in God, that you live honestly among your neighbors and give everyone their due, and therefore do not see that you have need of Christ in your days; may the Lord be merciful to you, for it is more unlikely that you are called than any person in the world. In *Matthew 21:31* there stands a parable of a man who had two sons; he commanded them both to work in the vineyard. One son said, "I will not work," he was stubborn; the other son said, "I shall work," and he did not do it, and so his saying was worse. Now these two sons are a representation of two sorts of people within the bounds of the Church. Some are godless and stubborn people; these answer and say like the first son, "We will not work." The others are professors, people who make a good profession, but they do not answer their profession with their practice. Now notice: which of the two will the Father accept? They said to him, "The first," the most stubborn one, who said "I will not go," but afterwards went. *Verily,* says Christ, *I say unto you, that the tax collectors and the harlots shall go before you into the Kingdom of Heaven.* Notice how Christ applies this parable from their own mouths: you who are Pharisees, who are righteous and glorious in your own eyes, I shall sooner call harlots, adulterers, and the worst of people than you. Tax collectors <note>original: "Tollenaers"</note> and harlots; tax collectors were the worst sort of people there were. They sat at the receipt of custom; <note>The "receipt of custom" was the tax office.</note> their calling brought them to extort much from the people and to have their eyes blinded here and there with gifts and bribes. Nevertheless, these people would go into Heaven before others who made an honest profession of Christ. Again,

# Of our effectual [Calling]

...dwell in the same house with you, who hear in the same assembly of the congregation with you, or sit on the same bench with you; that you shall hear that these are **effectually called**, while you remain uncalled. This shall greatly increase your sin and damnation. *Matthew 21:32.* John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; (that is, you were not called through his ministry <note>original: "dienst"</note>); what then? But the tax collectors and harlots believed him. What further? But you, seeing this, did not afterward repent so as to believe him. Notice how Christ reasons here; He insists upon it that these people heard the same sermons that the others heard who were converted. He says, you see that harlots are converted (casting His eye upon Mary Magdalene and others), and yet you do not convert, nor do you believe. Now you see the one and the other, and yet, even though you see them, you do not repent so that you might believe. Beloved, this is a sad conclusion for you, that you shall see others convert—when you perhaps lie together in one bed, sit on the same bench, hear the same sermons in one and the same assembly of the congregation—yet they are converted and called, and you are not. This shall greatly increase your sin and damnation.

6. That it is God’s **ordinary way** <term>Ordinary Way: The standard, established method God uses to work in the world (preaching and scripture), as opposed to "extraordinary" miracles or direct revelations.</term> concerning those whom He intends to call effectually, to call them through the ministry of His Word. *2 Thessalonians 2:13, 14.* There it is said that they were called in sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth through the Gospel to the obtaining of the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ. They were called through the belief of the truth; that is, through the faith and love of the preached word. Faith comes by hearing. Faith is the first grace of a Christian’s **Calling**, and that comes by hearing. *Romans 10:17.* So also, *Acts 26:17, 18.* When Christ wanted to call and convert the Gentiles, He did not do it without means, but He used the service of Paul: *Go, teach the Gentiles, and bring them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to GOD.* God always does it through the preaching of His Word. Now this is a sad word for three kinds of people.

First, it is a sad word for those who have never sat under the powerful preaching of the Word; they are outside of God’s ordinary way to be saved.

Secondly, it is a sad word for those who come to enjoy the Word and yet despise it; therefore, it is not likely that they are called.

Thirdly, it is a sad word for those who abandon the ordinary way of God’s calling through the preaching of the Word and come to rely upon raptures, revelations, inspirations, and extraordinary means to be called by God. Alas! They are outside God’s ordinary way of Calling; for God usually keeps to this path, that He calls a soul through the preaching of His Word. *Luke 15:23.* When the Prodigal Son was effectually called home to his Father, his Father did not

<column-break/>

immediately comfort him himself, but he sent his servants and said: *Go, bring forth the best robe and put it on my son.* This son is the sinner, the Father is God Almighty, the servants are the **Ministers**. Now God does not do His work by Himself alone, but He hands that over to His ministers; and they shall put on the ring and the robe; they shall be instruments through the ministry of the Word to work grace in the heart. That is why in *1 Corinthians 1:12* some were rebuked who said, *I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Christ.* Why were they rebuked here for saying they were of Christ? Is it blameworthy to call upon Christ? No; the offense is not simply that they magnified Christ, but this was the fault: that they so called upon Christ without being willing to use the ministers and the instituted means of divine service, and in that they were to be rebuked. For Christ does not want to call anyone without means through revelation and raptures, but works the conversion and the Calling of a sinner through the ordinary way of the preaching of the Word. And therefore, this is a sad word for all who are outside the way of God’s Calling, or for those who do not have God’s word, or for those who have it and never seek to enjoy it.

7. That for those people who enjoy God’s Word for a long time and are not effectually called by it, it is probable that they shall never be called. To prove this, I commend to you the passage in *Luke 13:6, 7*, where Christ tells you of a **Fig Tree**. He came for three years to seek fruit upon it but found none; the dresser of the vineyard prayed that He would spare it one more year, and if it then brought forth no fruit, He should cut it down and cast it into the fire. Now, this fig tree represented the professing Jews, who lay for such a long time under the ministry of Christ and His Apostles; and when this fig tree was spared one more year and brought forth no fruit, it would be cut down. And so Christ did; it seems He cursed it, saying: *Let no fruit grow on this tree forever.* Now you will ask, what is the meaning of this? Beloved, if a fig tree brings forth no fruit in four years after it is planted, it is likely it will never bring forth fruit. This parable applies here in this way: that if people have for a long time remained the same through the ministry of the Word, though some sparks have been sought in them, and after all this they have not converted, then likewise the curse of the fig tree shall come upon the hearts of such people; the Word does such people no more good, and grace grows no more in such people's hearts; *let no fruit grow from that tree forever.* And further, this parable holds in this: that if you live a long time under the enjoyment of the Word and are not converted, it is a proof that you shall not be called. And this is a **heart-cutting observation** for all old people, who have outlived these ministers and have seen their ministers laid in the grave; their ministers have worn out their strength and consumed their lungs in preaching to them, and they are now still

# To Make Our Calling Sure

...so Godless, so unrestrained, and so heedless of God’s grace as to hear it; truly, if it is so with you, you are in a very sad state; you run the risk of never being called by Jesus Christ.

<margin>
Augustine: *Book on the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 14.
<note>original Latin fragment: "Surgunt indocti et rapiunt caelum... nos... detrudimur in gehennam." Translated: "The unlearned rise up and take heaven by storm, while we with our learning are thrust down into hell."</note>
</margin>
8. That God, in the distribution of His grace, does not **ordinarily** let the **effectual Calling** <term>Effectual Calling: A theological term meaning an internal call by God that successfully draws a person to faith, as opposed to a general outward invitation.</term> pass over the Rich in this world; but much more over the poorest sort and kind of people that there are. I remember that Augustine in one of his books says this: "the unlearned people snatch Heaven away from us great learned ones." And certainly, just as it was in his time, so it is also now: People of great learning, who understand the Scripture and have knowledge of languages, are cast into Hell, while unlearned and poor people obtain Heaven. God has chosen the lowliest of this world to be rich in faith. In all the distribution of His grace (although He calls some rich men so that he may thereby further the work of grace and bring some luster to His People), nonetheless God's effectual Calling does not so commonly go toward the rich as toward the poor of this world. The poor, says Christ, receive the Gospel; the wise Scribes and the Doctors among the Jews and the Rich Pharisees despised Jesus Christ, whereas the poor and ignorant People who did not know the law followed Him. *1 Corinthians 1:26.* **For you see your calling, brethren, that not many wise, not many noble, not many mighty are called; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world, and the weak things of the world, and the ignoble things of the world, and the despised things of the world, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are.** Here you see this conclusion perfectly confirmed: that God’s effectual Calling does not ordinarily or commonly go toward the great of this world, but toward the poor and lowliest sort of people, who ordinarily are most drawn to the Gospel. And the reason for this is:

First: To make His grace great through the Rich. If Christ called only and primarily the Rich people, many would think that the riches and honor of man moved Christ to call them. Now, Christ, to defend and exalt His grace, calls poor, despised people, so that everyone may perceive and see that there is no reason or anything at all why God should cast the eye of His favor upon him.

Secondly: To glorify and reveal His power, that He wishes to protect a portion of poor, despised people among so many mighty and rich enemies, who are never powerful enough to overcome them.

Thirdly: Because rich people are subject to more temptations against the effectual Calling than poor people. The rich think: "Should I be called to be a professor of faith? I might lose my wealth, put my status in peril, and obscure my honor." These are great temptations for rich people that hinder their Calling. Therefore you read in *Mark 10:22* of a Young Man that when Christ called him, it says **he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.** He did not want to follow Christ, who had nowhere to lay His head. Many people, out of fear of losing their status, lie under these heavy temptations which prevent them from being 

<column-break/>

called; and so also for their honor. People think that they would obscure their honor if they made their profession among the rich. *Galatians 2:2.* **I set before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles: and particularly to those who were in high reputation, lest by any means I should run in vain.** It is as if he said: the people of quality and standing did not want to confess Christ openly; they were afraid they would lose their honor and credit. And therefore Paul was forced to accommodate them so far as to preach to them in private. For this reason, Nicodemus, a great man, came to Christ by night.

9. If you are only called outwardly to the **confession of Christ**, and not inwardly to the **possession of Christ** <term>Confession vs. Possession: A common 17th-century distinction between merely saying one is a Christian (confession) and actually having Christ in one's heart (possession).</term>, then God will, at one time or another before you die, discover the hypocrisy of your heart and the instability of your Calling. There are many who are called now, and man cannot distinguish whether they are effectually called or not; but nonetheless, before you die, you shall experience one thing or another that will give you a right ground for suspicion that you are not called to salvation—either by falling into some error, or by running into some scandalous sin, or the like.

Lastly: If God has not purposed or effectually called you, you may take this for an **Infallible truth**: that God has never purposed to justify you, nor to save you. **Those whom He called, them He also justified**, and no others; **and those whom He justified, these He also glorified**, and no others. So the justification and the glorification hang upon the Calling, *Romans 8:30*. And thus I have finished these ten sad Conclusions.

I shall now change my argument and turn my speech to a second sort of people, and I shall present to them ten **comforting Conclusions** to comfort you who are the called of Jesus Christ. And before I present them, I shall first show you here why it is necessary that the Ministers preach comfortingly to you who are effectually called. Because, firstly, after you are effectually called, you are more subject to the persecution of men. Secondly, the temptations of the devil. Thirdly, a stronger wrestling with your corruptions from within than you were previously. Therefore you have need of comfort.

1. I say, after you are called, you are subject to meet more persecution from men than you were before. *Hebrews 10:32-33.* **But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after you were illuminated, you endured a great fight of afflictions; partly while you were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions, etc.** They suffered nothing at all before, but after they were enlightened, they endured a great fight of afflictions. Do you not therefore have great need of comfort?

2. After your Calling, you are more subject to the temptations of the devil than you were before. When the devil finds all things in peace, he leaves men alone; but when he finds a man escaping from his claws to be called, then Satan disturbs and storms against him. *1 Peter 5:8, 10.* Your
