Yet it was against these that the Devil so raged: do you not then have great need of comforts, seeing that you are all the more subject to the temptations of the Devil?

And thirdly: You shall encounter a stronger and more powerful working of inward corruptions in your own heart; just as Paul, before his calling, was not troubled by his corruptions; sin did not make him restless; the mighty and strong workings of his lusts never wearied him: but when the commandment came, then sin became alive again: When the power of the word came upon his conscience with authority, then he saw that sin became alive again and gained strength over him. Beloved, I shall now appeal to any of you whom God has called to grace and glory: did you find sin to be as strong before you were called as you did afterward? And were the workings of your inward corruptions as violent then as they are now? Therefore, upon these three grounds, you have need that comfort be preached to you.

I come now to the **Conclusions** which I shall set down for the comfort of all those who are effectually called.

1. That Jesus Christ powerfully calls a poor Sinner before the Sinner looks toward Jesus Christ. If the Heaven of God were seen as an inheritance for us only on this condition—that you, who first transgressed, must be the first to seek reconciliation—we would never have ended the dispute between God and ourselves; but see, here is mercy, and here is a ground of comfort: that, although we are the first in transgression, Christ is the first to seek reconciliation. Jesus Christ powerfully calls poor sinners before they call out or look toward Jesus Christ in any way.

<margin>Isaiah 65:1</margin>
> I was found by those who did not ask for me, I was found by those who did not seek me; to the People who were not called by my Name, I said, behold, here I am, behold, here I am. 

Here you see that Jesus Christ first goes out to call you, before you go out to call Him. Oh, what a comfort this is; Christ does not wait until you look for Him, but Christ casts an eye upon you before you look for Him. We read of **Matthew the Tax-collector**, that while he was looking at his money and at the receipt of the tribute, at that very time Jesus Christ looked upon his soul. We read of the **Disciples of Christ**, while they were mending their Nets and looking at their Fish, that Jesus Christ took the opportunity to catch them with the Hook of the Gospel. We read of **Paul**, that while he breathed persecution against the Church of God and raged with haste against the Saints of God, he was called at that time to be a Saint: so this is very comforting. In His powerful calling, God looks toward a Sinner before a Sinner looks out for Christ. God looks toward you first, enlightening you through Preaching, and grips you in your Conscience through the commandment before you look back to Him.

2. That Jesus Christ has powerfully called you, while He has left many thousands in the world of greater understanding, better

<column-break/>

disposition, having more natural good and less evil in them than you have in yourself; and yet He has rejected them and called you. Jesus Christ has rejected entire lists of Heathens, while He has called you who are of a second-rate and passionate nature. Jesus Christ has passed by many a sharp-witted mind, and many an ingenious scholar, and many of exceptional subtlety, who—if they had been granted the grace to apply themselves—might have brought more honor to God; and it may be that He has called you, a poor, ignorant, foolish creature. It may be that Jesus Christ has rejected many who had less sin in them than you have in yourself. Jesus Christ rejected many a magnificent Heathen while He chose to call **Mary Magdalene**, who had seven devils in her; Christ rejected **Simon Magus** <note>A sorcerer who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit (Acts 8).</note>; He rejected **Agrippa**, a half-converted Christian; He rejected **Herod**, who heard **John the Baptist** gladly; He rejected **Felix**, who trembled at a sermon; and He rejected **Ahab**, who humbled his soul before God; yet it may be that He calls you, who have never had such workings in your hearts as these men had: oh, what a comfort of comforts is here!

3. When God calls a soul and brings it into the state of grace, He does so willingly for His own name's sake; at a time when there was nothing in you to move Him to call you; at a time when there was more in you that might have provoked Him never to call you; nevertheless, His own grace constrains Him, and His own Mercy obliges Him to call you. **2 Timothy 1:9**. *We are called according to his own purpose and grace, not according to our works.*

4. That among all people, it is most probable that those who are most sensible of their own insignificance, and who most clearly see their lack and need of Jesus Christ, are the ones being called. When Christ rejects civil, righteous people—people who rely on themselves and are modestly well-behaved—it is by no means probable that they are being called; but for such people who are sensible of their own Godlessness and see that they lack Jesus Christ, it is most probable among all people that they are being called.

<margin>Matthew 9:13</margin>
> I have not come to call the righteous; but who then? But Sinners to repentance. 

All people are Sinners, but He means those who see their sins and see that they need Christ to forgive their sins and to subdue them; for the words imply this: *those who are healthy have no need of a Physician, but those who are sick.* Those who are sick of their sins and see their weaknesses, such people seem most likely to be called by Jesus Christ. And therefore, this is very comforting for you, all you who are mournful Christians, who let your heads hang over the feeling of your sins, who see that sin is exceedingly sinful; this is the end for which Christ came into the world: namely, to call you to glory.

5. That a person may be chosen by God from all eternity, and yet live a long time in the course of sin before God calls him, though he shall surely be called before he dies. 

<margin>John 10:16</margin>
> I lay down my life for the Sheep; and I have

It highlights that God's calling is based on His own grace rather than human merit or natural intelligence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Conclusions" section regarding the comfort of those who are "effectually called" (those whom God has actively drawn to faith). It addresses common anxieties, such as not knowing the exact moment of one's conversion or feeling too "near-sighted" to see God’s favor clearly.</meta>

-> ### Making one's Calling Sure <-

...other sheep which are not of this fold; these I must also bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one flock, and one Shepherd, etc. <note>This refers to John 10:16, a famous passage about Christ gathering people beyond his immediate followers.</note> The meaning is this: Christ calls those who are already converted his sheep; but these are not all of them; rather, I have others who are not yet converted, whom I nonetheless shall convert and bring into one flock. So it is that Christ has his sheep even among those who are not yet converted nor called; and although you may often walk a long time in the way of sin, yet before you die, you shall be powerfully called and brought into the sheepfold of Jesus Christ.

6. A person can be powerfully called even when they cannot find any immediate or firm proof of their calling in their own understanding. This is the manner of speaking introduced by Peter,
<margin>2 Peter 1:9</margin>
2 Peter 1:9: *He who lacks these things is blind, and cannot see afar off.* This is spoken of a godly person—of a person whose election is certain, but who does not add grace upon grace to make his calling sure. Such a person is "near-sighted" <note>The original Dutch *bysiende* literally means near-sighted or myopic; here it describes someone who can see their immediate sins but cannot look "far off" to see God's eternal plan for them.</note> and cannot see from afar; that is, he cannot see into Heaven to know that his name is written there, and he cannot have a clear and strong comfort regarding his standing with God. Many a godly person may be powerfully called and yet be near-sighted, lacking the power to behold the glory of their effectual calling with an open face.

7. A person may have a firm assurance that they are powerfully called, and yet not know the time when, nor the manner how, nor the instrument <note>In this context, "instrument" refers to the specific preacher, sermon, or Bible verse that triggered the conversion.</note> through which they were called. And this is a very comforting conclusion. There are some who define conversion so narrowly that if a person cannot say the time when, or the manner in which, or the preaching through which he was called, they say he is not yet converted. This is all too strict a teaching; the Scripture confirms this further: namely, that a person can have a firm assurance of his effectual calling even if he does not know the time, the manner, or the instrument by which he was called.
<margin>Mark 4:27</margin>
Mark 4:27: *And he said, "So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knows not how."* The sown seed here is the work of grace, for "so is the kingdom of God," says Christ. This seed sprouted; the person perhaps cannot say the day when he sowed it, nor how it sprouted, yet this seed sprouted and he knows not how. So also a person may have the seed of grace sown in his heart—which is the effectual calling—and it grows up, yet he knows not how, nor when he was called.
<margin>John 9:19, 20</margin>
So in John 9:19, 20 (I say it only as a comparison) where it speaks of a man who was healed by Jesus Christ—that blind son whose eyes were opened by Jesus Christ. What did his parents say? *We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind; but by what means he now sees, we know not; or who has opened his eyes, we know not.* Beloved, so I may say of a poor sinner; a poor sinner is

<column-break/>

just like this blind son; we know that we are born blind, knowing neither God nor ourselves. We know, if we are converted, that we now see; but how this happened, or through whom it happened, a person cannot always measure so precisely.

But now, this conclusion does not hold in all cases; if a person has been a godless person <note>This refers to someone who lived a notoriously wicked or "profane" life before turning to God.</note>, then it is impossible, according to the ordinary way, that such a person could be powerfully called without knowing the time when he was called. But regarding others who have been brought up from their childhood in a godly household, and from their childhood until their dying day have never broken out into any scandalous sin—these people cannot give an account of when or through whom they were called, and yet their calling may be effectual. And therefore, it is all too strict a teaching to insist on such harsh requirements for conversion; for God has various ways and degrees of working, even though they do not all appear before our eyes.

8. That those who are called by Christ shall be preserved by Christ, so that they do not fall away from their calling, but are brought to the state of glory; and that is another comforting conclusion. You are not called by Christ and then left to yourself and the wide world, as Adam was. Adam was called by God to the state of happiness, but he was left to himself to stand by his own strength; but you are not so. You are not only called by Christ, but you are also preserved by Christ; so that once having been called to it, you shall not fall away from grace.
<margin>Jude verse 1</margin>
Jude verse 1: *Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ... to them that are called, sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ.* Here then is your comfort: that you are not called by Christ and then left to yourself, but you are preserved by Christ—called and preserved in the state of grace until you shall come to Glory. So it is written,
<margin>1 Thess. 5:24</margin>
1 Thessalonians 5:24: *He who calls you is faithful, who also will do it;* that is, bring you to that Glory to which you are called.

9. When Christ has intended to call a poor sinner, neither their poverty nor their godlessness shall hinder the calling of Jesus Christ. Not your poverty;
<margin>James 2:5</margin>
*God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom.* James 2:5. Nor your godlessness; poor Christians think, "Oh, I am so vile, I am so sinful and unholy, that I fear Christ will not want to call me." Why? This shall not hinder. Mary Magdalene was a prostitute, possessed by seven devils, yet she was called. Manasseh, a blood-shedder who made the streets of Jerusalem overflow with blood, was nonetheless called. Paul, a persecutor, a blasphemer, a man who raged against the church of God, yet mercy happened to him. Why indeed? So that he might be an example to those who would be called thereafter. So here is your comfort: when Jesus Christ has intended to call you, neither your poverty nor your godlessness shall withstand His calling, nor turn the thoughts of His mercy away from you.

# Concerning our Effectual Calling

§. 10. That although no one can look into God's decree regarding election and reprobation <note>Reprobation refers to the theological concept of being rejected by God or not chosen for salvation.</note>, nevertheless, if you can only prove your <term>Effectual Calling</term> <note>Effectual Calling is the theological idea that God’s inward call to a person’s soul is so powerful that it certainly leads to their salvation.</note>, then you may be assured of your Election and of your glorification. Although no one—I say—can enter into the secrets of God to know His hidden decrees, nevertheless, if you can find on good and Scriptural grounds that you are effectually called, then you may be assured that you are eternally chosen and shall hereafter live in glory. Romans 8:30: *Whom he predestined, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified.* And therefore, comfort your hearts with these consoling conclusions regarding the Effectual Calling.

->2 Peter 1:10<-

*Wherefore, Brothers, be all the more diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.*

<margin>5th Sermon.</margin>
The doctrine which I still have at hand in the continuation of these words is this: that Christians ought to apply great diligence to make this sure to their souls—that they are effectually called through Jesus Christ. In the treatment of which, on the last Lord’s Day, I set down twenty conclusions: ten with respect to the wicked and uncalled people, and ten conclusions for the comfort of those who are effectually called through Jesus Christ. I shall now proceed to dispatch six <term>cases of conscience</term> <note>A "case of conscience" was a common teaching method used to resolve specific moral or spiritual doubts that a believer might face.</note> which I shall handle concerning the Effectual Calling. Three of these concern those people who are not effectually called, and three touch upon the believers who are called by Christ here to grace and to the hope of Glory in the world to come.

The first three cases concerning wicked people are these:

First, whether a wicked person has the power to resist his own Calling?

Secondly, what temptations the devil suggests to keep a wicked person from receiving and embracing the Calling of Jesus Christ?

Thirdly, what deceits the devil uses to deceive the hypocrites and to make them presumptuously believe that they are effectually called when they are not?

The other three cases touch upon godly people: namely,

First, whether a person who is effectually called can in any way be assured of it?

Secondly, if a person can be assured, what is the reason then that many a godly person is not assured of his Effectual Calling?

And then thirdly, how he can obtain the assurance of his Effectual Calling? I begin with the first, concerning the wicked people who are not called; and the case is this:

First, whether a wicked person—a person who is not yet called—has the power

<column-break/>

to resist and hold back his own Calling?

Now, so that you may understand the answer to this, I must propose this distinction: that there is a twofold Calling of Christ.

An external Calling, and an active [or working] Calling.

First, the external Calling, which is such a Calling by which Christ, in the ministry of the Word, signifies and declares what He desires that people should do. Now, wicked people can resist this sort of Calling—this Calling, I say, and this revealed will of God, declaring what grace He wants the person to practice and what sin he should leave behind. Therefore we read in Acts 7:51: *You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit;* there he means the preaching of the Word through the service of his Apostles. So also, Proverbs 1:24: *I have called and you have refused,* etc.

But now secondly, there is an active [effectual] Calling, and that is such a Calling by which God not only makes known to a person what he must do, but along with the signifying of His will, He gives the person the power to do the thing to which He calls him, accompanying the Word with His Spirit, making the heart pliable and obedient to Jesus Christ.

Now, no one can resist this Calling; this grace is irresistible, and a person cannot resist this powerful Calling through the working of the Spirit. All the resistance of the heart and all the boldness of the will must bow and be subject to Jesus Christ. John 6:37: *All that the Father gives me,* says Christ, *shall come to me.* They shall not be powerful enough to resist Jesus Christ, but they shall come to Him. So also Isaiah 55:10: *Just as the rain and the snow come down from Heaven, and do not return there, but water the earth, and make it bring forth and sprout; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do that which pleases me, and it shall be prosperous in the thing for which I sent it.* Just as the whole world cannot prevent the rain from falling down upon the earth, so also no one in the world can prevent the benefit of the Word from blooming in his soul, if God has purposed to convert and call him.

Now, the answering of this case in such a precious way shall provide a twofold use.

<margin>1st Use.</margin>
First, a use for the condemnation of those wicked people who have often resisted the signifying or external Calling of Jesus Christ. When Christ has made it known—"this is my will, I want you to leave that way and walk in these ways"—Christ makes His will known in the ministry of the Gospel; nevertheless, though Christ lets His will be known, you want to do what pleases you; this is a great condemnation for you.

<margin>2nd Use.</margin>
Secondly, the answering of this question serves for the comfort of the elect who are not yet converted. Do you belong to the election of God? Before you are converted, you have a rebellious will,

# To Make Our Calling Sure

a rebellious heart and a presumptuous spirit against God; your heart is as hard as a diamond, as hard as a rocky crag. Nevertheless, here is your comfort: all the rebelliousness of your spirit and all the defiance of your will shall not be powerful enough to keep you from converting grace, nor to keep <term>Calling Grace</term> <note>The specific favor from God that draws a person toward salvation.</note> away from you. When God has purposed to call you, He shall come with power alongside His calling, and make you do what He commands you, and make you embrace that to which He calls you. If Christ did not use an <term>Effectual Calling</term> <note>Original: "werk-same Roepinge" – a call that actually produces the intended result in the heart.</note> as well as an outward calling, then no one in the world would ever be called. And this is the reason that in hearing the same sermon, and following the same preacher, one person is converted and the other is not. The reason is this: that the calling of the ministry is only a "signifying" call to the subjects <note>Original: "bewoorpene," referring to those who are the targets of the sermon.</note>, only making known what God wants them to do; but there is no power joined to the invitation to make the person able to do that to which Christ calls him; and therefore one is called and the other is not. So much for answering the first case.

<margin>The Case.</margin> Second, what assaults does the devil give to those who are uncalled, so that they should not receive and embrace the calling of Jesus Christ unto grace and glory? To answer this, I shall only present four inspirations of the devil wherewith he ensnares a person, so that they should not devote themselves to the calling of Jesus Christ; and likewise as I present them, so shall I also labor to take them away. Namely:

1. The first assault the devil shall suggest is to you who are still young; and to you he shall suggest that you are still too young to embrace the calling of Jesus Christ. It shall be time enough later; you are now still far too young to cut off your pleasure, to kill your lusts, and to commit yourself to such a narrow way as that to which Christ calls. And through this assault, the devil prevails particularly well with young people. I am reminded of what <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian known for his dramatic conversion after a wayward youth.</note> says: that this assault of the devil kept him for seven years from embracing the calling of Jesus Christ. The devil said constantly in his heart: "you are still too young to leave your drunkenness; you are still too young to leave your harlots," until he finally cried out, "How long shall I still say 'it is too early'? Why do I not convert myself now on this day?" This assault, I say, has taken such a hold on many that they thought they were still too young to come to Christ. And to this end, the devil shall suggest to you that old and lying proverb: *A young saint, an old devil.* <note>A cynical proverb of the time suggesting that those who are overly religious in youth will become wicked in old age.</note> If this were true, if you are young devils, then you shall become old <term>Beelzebubs</term> <note>A name for the devil or a high-ranking demon.</note>. And therefore, seeing that this is an inspiration which has great power over many hearts, I shall set down six observations to draw you away from this assault, so that it may have no power over you.

First, if the devil assaults you and says that you are still too young to listen to the calling of Christ, note that the devil can give you no certainty of your life. If

<column-break/>

the devil could assure you of a long life, and said that you would live to a high old age, then you might listen to his assaults with more tranquility. But your life does not depend on the disposal of the devil; God has the power over your life. The outcomes of life and death are in His hand. You may die uncalled in your youth; you can then be as surely damned as you are dead. You could be like those people in Job 36:14: *Their soul shall die in youth, and their life among the unclean.* And therefore, although the devil assaults you with the idea that you are still too young, since he cannot assure you of your life, you have no reason to listen to his assault.

Second, even if the devil could assure you that you would live to a high old age, nevertheless take note of this: that delaying your calling and the work of your conversion in your youth may so provoke God that He hardens your hearts in your old age, so that you shall have no heart to think upon the calling and invitation of Jesus Christ, nor to embrace it. Jeremiah 22:21: *I spoke to you in your great prosperity, but you said, I will not hear you; this has been your way from your youth, that you have not obeyed my voice.* God spoke, but they would not hear; and this they did from their youth. Therefore God would never speak again. God hardened their hearts so that they never accepted nor embraced the calling of Jesus Christ. So also in Isaiah 6:9-10: Because the Jews from their youth were rebellious against God's Word, *Go forth,* says God, *make their ears heavy, and their hearts fat, and their eyes blind, that they may not be called, and convert, and I heal them.* Let this therefore be a second observation: that delaying your calling until your old age may so provoke God that He never gives you a heart to embrace His calling.

Third, even assuming this—that you could have a guarantee of your life, and be assured that when you reached old age your hearts would not be hardened—nevertheless note this: the more sinful and wicked the days of your youth have been, the more unrest of spirit and terror of conscience they shall bring forth when you have become old, even if you are called and converted through Jesus Christ. Job 13:24-26: *You hide your face, and hold me for your enemy. You shatter me like a driven leaf, and pursue me like dry stubble.* Now, why does Job complain thus? Note these following words: *For you write bitter things against me, and you make me inherit the sins of my youth.* It seems that when Job was a young man, he was a godless person and committed many sins in his youth; and this makes him cry out in his old age, saying that God held him as an enemy, and that God shattered him like a leaf driven by the wind. O Beloved, the sins of your youth—even though you are converted like Job—shall nevertheless produce a great unrest and a great terror in you when you have grown old. The lusts of your youth, and the vanity of your youth, and the sensual pleasures of your

### Of our powerful

youthful days; they shall lay a foundation of sorrow when you have come to gray hairs and have approached your grave; Job 20:11. And therefore, consider it so, that you should convert and be called while you are young, and have no cause to postpone the <term>Calling of Jesus Christ</term> <note>The internal invitation by God to a person's soul to seek salvation.</note>, seeing as the sins of your youth shall bring you such terror and unrest of mind. From this it comes that David, after he was called through the power of the Word, cries out in Psalm 25:7: *Lord, remember not the sins of my youth*; the sins of his youth before his Calling were the ones that troubled and embittered his <term>Conscience</term> <note>Original: "Conscientie" — the internal sense of right and wrong.</note>. It is the saying of a certain author, that the 
<margin>What were the empty joys of youth, these are the bitter burdens of old age. <note>Original Latin: "Quæ fuerunt inania juventutis gaudia, hæc sunt acerba senectutis gravamina."</note></margin> 
pleasurable vanities and delights of youth shall bring a heavy burden and bitter torment to old age. Beloved, the more wickedly you burst forth in your young days, the greater and deeper a foundation of unrest and sorrow you lay in your souls against your final days, even if you should be called through Jesus Christ.

4. If the Devil suggests to you that you are still too young to embrace the invitation of Jesus Christ: then take note that Jesus Christ shall receive it as a greater kindness from your hands if you accept His calling while you are still young, Jeremiah 2:2. *I remember,* says the Lord, *the kindness of your youth, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.* Notice how the Lord speaks, and how kindly He takes it, that they followed God in their youth; the Lord wants to remember that, and accept the same as a kindness, if you—while you are still young, while there is marrow in your bones and strength in your limbs—will embrace the ways of Jesus Christ. It is an observation that some make regarding the beloved disciple John, in John 20. He is called the disciple whom Christ loved, and who leaned on His breast; Christ loved John above all the other eleven disciples; and the theologians give this reason: that John was the youngest of all the disciples, he was converted and called by Christ while he was still a youth, and Christ, seeing that a youth followed Him, took that very lovingly from his hands, and called him to be His beloved disciple. Just as parents do, who set small children on their laps, whereas they do not do such for the older ones; so with John, who was a youth, Christ wants to let him lie on His breast and in His bosom, thereby expressing His friendliness toward him.

Now, how ought this to ward off this temptation—that you are still too young to follow Christ—seeing that Christ takes it so lovingly from your hands if you come to embrace this calling in time? Indeed, Christ takes it so kindly that He loves bare modesty and civic decency in young people; and therefore it says in Matthew, when Christ saw that youth and 
<margin>Matthew 16:20 <note>This likely refers to the story of the Rich Young Ruler found in Matthew 19:20; the marginal reference in the original manuscript appears to be a common early modern citation error.</note></margin> 
he said to Him, *All these things have I kept from my youth up:* That Christ looked upon him and loved him. Christ showed a general love to the youth who from his youth had only been a modest man; and if Christ loves modesty, much more shall He love godliness and true sincerity. It is noted of Timothy, that regarding one particular man, Paul

<column-break/>

expressed more love to Timothy than to anyone else: read through the entire Scripture, you shall nowhere find that Paul expresses so much love to anyone as to Timothy; he calls him *Timothy my son, Timothy who has served me as a child,* and *Timothy my dearly beloved*; and why all this? The reason is because Timothy was converted from his childhood and knew the Scriptures, 2 Timothy 3:15. He was converted from the time he was a child, and called through the ministry of the Word from Paul's mouth, and this ignited Paul's heart with love for him. You read in the book of Leviticus that when God required an offering, He did not want an old sheep, but a young lamb, a lamb of one year old, one of the youngest lambs of the flock: and this signified not only that Christ, our sacrifice, should die and suffer for our sins in the flower of His life, but it was also to show that Jesus Christ regards it as a cursed offering when you do not want to be of His sheepfold while you are still young lambs. O Beloved, Christ takes this exceedingly kindly if you come to embrace His calling in your youth.

Fifthly, do not give yourself over to this temptation of the Devil, seeing that although you might be converted in your old age, nevertheless Christ can receive it as nothing other than very unpleasant from your hands, that you postpone Him until the end of your life, and that you (if even any part remains) save the worst part for His service. You know when Christ stood all night before the door of His Bride, until His head was filled with dew and His locks with the drops of the night; He goes away because she did not come, and would not stay standing any longer. O, how poorly (do you think) will Christ take it, that He shall wait year after year; and that you nevertheless will not embrace His calling!

It says in Isaiah: *I have stretched out my hand all day long to a rebellious people, but they would not hear:* and Malachi 1: *Offer a lamb and that which is blind to your Governor, shall he have a delight in it?* Christ must necessarily take this very poorly, that you give the Devil the flower, and to Christ only the mangled and weak part of your life; that the Devil should suck out the marrow of your youth, and that you give God only the dry bones, a fainting head, dim eyes, and a weak body, and consequently a very weak service to God; just think how poorly Christ shall take your service to God which is so conditioned.

Lastly, note this: that from your day of birth until the day of your death, you have little enough time to carry out the work of your salvation, even if you lived ever so long; and therefore you have no cause to postpone the calling of Jesus Christ. And so these things are spoken for instruction, to ward off the first temptation: that you are still too young to embrace the calling of Jesus Christ; and this I do for the sake of the young people, that they may be on their guard not to be ensnared by this deceit of the Devil.

To ward off this suggestion of the *Devil*, I shall set down six points in response. As:

First, *God* never intends that our external vocation should in any way hinder us in the work of our conversion. *God* never intended that our affairs here on earth should prevent the necessary preparation for *Heaven*. But *God* has so arranged our vocations here in the world that He has made and ordained them—our general and powerful *Calling*—to be subordinated to the great work of *God’s* glory and our own *Salvation*.

<margin>Genesis 6:9</margin>
It is written of *Noah* that he walked with *GOD*, and that he was upright in his generations. And yet *Noah* was kept busy by *God* for some time—namely, for 120 years—in a manual labor vocation to build an *Ark*, thereby showing that *God* never intended that *Noah’s* making of the *Ark* should in any way hinder his walk with *God* or hold back the work of his *Soul*. Even though you have a vocation here to carry out, and a *Household* to provide for, *God* never intended that your external vocation should prevent your internal and powerful *Calling*.

Secondly, note this, you who plead thus: whether you do not spend more of the time of your external vocation in the work of sin and of *Satan* than in the matters concerning your soul. There is many a man who can pretend that he has no time to pray, nor any time to hear a *Sermon*; he must attend to his vocation; yet he can well enough pursue a harlot, and frequent the *Tavern*; yes, he can well spend a whole day for his pleasure, and yet spare no time nor find opportunity to listen to *Jesus Christ*. This ought then to be a great conviction to you, who pretend that you must attend to your vocation, while you can neglect your vocation to follow your pleasurable and idle ways, and yet can spare no time to make your souls blessed.

Thirdly, you who pretend that your external vocation in the world is an excuse as to why you cannot listen to your powerful *Calling* through *Jesus Christ*; note this: that this excuse has damned many a soul before you, and consequently shall also damn you, if you do not take heed. This is an old pretext; <margin>Luke 14:18, 19, 20</margin> When *Christ* called a number of people there to come to Him, what excuse did they have? One says, I have bought five *yoke of oxen*, I must go to test them; I have bought a *Field*, says the other, and it is necessary that I go out and see it. I have

married a *Wife*, and therefore I cannot come, says the third. These were all worldly vocations, and yet these vocations kept them back from *Heaven* and kept them away from *Jesus Christ*. You read in <margin>Acts 24:25</margin> that when *Paul*, through a powerful *Sermon* on the coming *Judgment*, terrified the *Conscience* of *Felix*, *Felix's* heart trembled; but note now how *Felix* postponed the power of the *Word*: For this time now, he says, I have no time; go away, and when I have obtained a convenient time, I shall call you to me to speak of it. As if he said, I must now go do some other things regarding the matters of my Kingdom, and I can make no opportunity now to hear you: and thus, through some external work, he stifled the power of the *Word* from his heart and had no convenient time to embrace *Jesus Christ*.

So also in <margin>Deuteronomy 28:38 to 46</margin>: You shall carry much *Seed* out into the *Field*, but you shall gather little in, for the *Locust* shall consume it; that is a curse: *Vineyards* you shall plant and dress, but you shall drink no *Wine* nor gather anything, for the *Worm* shall eat it; that is another curse: *Olive trees* you shall have in all your *Borders*, but you shall not anoint yourself with *Oil*, for your *Olive tree* shall cast its fruit; that is the third curse. Sons and Daughters you shall beget, but they shall not be yours; all your trees and the *Fruit* of your *Land* shall be consumed. **6.** To you who pretend that your outward profession is a reason why you cannot listen to the *Calling of Christ*: take this as your answer—to tell the truth, it is not the necessity of your work, but the rebelliousness of your will and the sloth of your spirit that is the cause of your not heeding the *Calling of Jesus Christ*. If it were a person's profession that truly burdened them, they would take no pleasure in sin; therefore, it is not their profession, but the wickedness of their heart. They love neither Christ nor His ways, but they think that working toward conversion is too heavy a task; and therefore they bring forth this excuse. **John 5:40**: *You will not come to me that you might have life.* When the will is lacking, says **Doctor PRESTON** <note>John Preston (1587–1628), an influential English Puritan minister and master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge.</note>, then a "blue excuse" <note>A Dutch idiom (blauwe excuse) meaning a flimsy, transparent, or poor excuse.</note> is put forward. When the will is lacking to walk in God’s ways, a groundless pretext will be made to excuse one's negligence. And thus these points are said to repel the second suggestion—namely, that people must attend to their worldly business and therefore have no time to look toward the powerful *Calling of Jesus Christ*.

<column-break/>

**3rd Suggestion.** Thirdly: The *Devil* argues that if you accept the *Calling of Jesus Christ*, you will be subject to great **Poverty** and **persecution** in this world, and therefore you must not listen to His *Calling*. To this end, he will even bring forth *Scripture*. First, regarding poverty, the *Devil* will insist on **Matthew 8:19, 20**, where Christ says: *The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.* The *Devil* will press this scripture upon you, telling you that if you follow Christ, you are subject to poverty, want, and the "beggar’s bag." We read similarly in the history of **Lucius**, the first Christian King of England <note>A legendary 2nd-century King of the Britons said to have introduced Christianity to the island.</note> (and in truth, the first Christian King of any nation, to the honor of England, as **Gildas** <note>A 6th-century British monk and chronicler.</note> tells us in his life). This King, although he was converted to Christianity, was nonetheless attacked for many years with the thought that Christians were poorer than the Romans, who did not accept Jesus Christ, and he could hardly ward off this temptation. The Romans were richer and the Romans were more warlike; he was assaulted with such temptations. **Agolantus** <note>A fictional Saracen king from medieval legends of Charlemagne.</note>, a heathen Prince, having been taken prisoner by the Emperor and brought to his court, saw thirty or forty poor people dressed in rags walking in the palace. He asked the Emperor who those poor people were; the Emperor answered him that they were followers of Jesus Christ. "Are they such as these?" he said. "If Christ keeps his followers in such a lowly state, then I never want to follow Jesus Christ." The poverty of Christ’s followers kept him back from Christianity. There are many people today, especially those **Courtly Dandies**, who—seeing a group of poor, simple women going about with a Bible under their arm, embracing and loving the faith—find it such a great offense that they will not follow Christ because of the poverty one is subject to in the ways of Jesus Christ. And then also regarding **persecution**: that one is not only subject to want, but also to the loss of one's freedom, property, name, and life. **Matthew 10:38**: *You must take up your Cross.* These are hidden conditions for flesh and blood, and they struggle exceedingly against men, holding them back from embracing Christ. Now, to ward off these assaults of the *Devil* so they take no hold on your hearts, I shall set down six points in response.

**First**, that the servants of God from ancient times have preferred to choose poverty and persecution with the people of God rather than to enjoy the vanities and advantages of this world with wicked men. This is what **Moses** chose. **Hebrews 11:24, 25**: *By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt.* Now that Moses had "come to years," it was no childish act, but a mature and deliberate deed; nor was it a forced act, but Moses "preferred" it—it was an act...

It is said of Mr. Philpot <note>John Philpot (1516–1555), an English Protestant martyr during the Marian Persecutions.</note>, while in his **Coal-house** <note>original: "Koolhuys"; a dark, cramped storage cellar at Windsor used as a temporary prison for those accused of heresy.</note> at Windsor—a dismal and dark place—that someone said, "I would rather be with Philpot in the Coal-house than with Bonner <note>Edmund Bonner (c. 1500–1569), the Bishop of London notorious for his role in the persecution of Protestants.</note> in his Palace." When asked why, given that one place was so miserable and the other so beautiful, he answered: "Because Bonner's conscience makes his Palace into a Coal-house, but Philpot’s God and Philpot’s Christ make his Coal-house into a Palace." And **Beloved**, this is the truth; though someone were a beggar, if he is only **Rich in faith**, he is the happiest person in the world. Even if a person begged for his bread from door to door, if he can but "beg" for Christ and have Him, and "beg" for grace and receive it, he is the richest person on earth. Therefore, this is my first answer: that the servants of God have preferred to choose oppression with the people of God, rather than to enjoy the pleasures of the ungodly.

**Second.** Suppose you did encounter poverty and persecution in following Christ; nevertheless, take note that Jesus Christ repays you for that abundantly with that **inward peace** and that **inward joy** with which He fills your heart entirely, against all the outward oppressions you may encounter in the world. **John 16:33**: *In the world you shall have tribulation,* but pay attention to the strengthening: *in Me you shall have peace; therefore be of good cheer, I have overcome the world.* Though you have oppression in the world, yet you have joy and peace in Me; and therefore, why should you be offended?

**Third.** Note that although you lack many things in the world, the *good* shall nonetheless not be lacking to you. **Psalm 84:11** <note>The Dutch text cites verse 12, following the numbering in some older translations.</note>: *The Lord will give grace and glory; He will withhold no good thing from those who walk uprightly.* If riches are good for you, you shall not lack them; if a high status is good for you, it shall not be lacking, for He will withhold no good thing from those who walk uprightly.

**Fourth.** A graced heart, if it has a portion or can find that it has a true right to Christ—even if it lacks much in the world—thinks that it lacks nothing at all; for it has all things when it has Christ. It will not complain of any poverty when it is endowed with the riches of Heaven. **Luke 22:35**: *And Christ said to them, "When I sent you out without purse and bag and shoes, did you lack anything?"* Note the question: if a fleshly-minded person had to answer this, what would he have said? What else? Send a person out without a purse, and he will lack money; send him without a bag, and he lacks food; send him without shoes, and it is a bad situation for a poor man who has no shoes on his feet. Thus a fleshly person would have said: "Yes, Lord, we lacked money, and we lacked food, and we lacked shoes." But ask the Disciples: *did you lack anything?* They said, **"Nothing."** And why was that? Because the Disciples knew that they had an assured portion and right to Jesus Christ, and al-

<column-break/>

though they might have desired these outward comforts, they did not lack Christ’s comforts and grace. Therefore, even when they had neither purse, bag, nor shoes, they lacked nothing. Therefore, **Beloved**, if you were of the same nature as these Disciples, you would also say the same; so that if you can but find that you have a firm and true portion in Christ, even though you lack many comforts of this world, you would say that you lack nothing. *Did you lack anything? And they said, nothing.*

**Fifth.** You who use poverty as an excuse, take note of this: that the poor are usually the very people whom Jesus Christ calls to embrace His Gospel. *The poor receive the Gospel,* says Christ, *and blessed are you who are not offended.* *Not many wise, not many noble are called, but God has chosen the poor of this world,* **1 Corinthians 1:26**, and in **James** <note>James 2:5: "Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith...?"</note>. God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith. Therefore, **Beloved**, do not use this as an excuse to keep yourself away from Christ, seeing that these are usually the people upon whom Christ bestows His love most, and takes delight in making them rich in grace, who are poor in goods.

**Sixth.** Note that if you abandon the *Calling of Jesus Christ* on this ground, you will be subject to a greater poverty and worse persecutions than you could ever be in embracing Christ. In following Christ, you are only subject to an outward poverty; but through the neglect of Christ’s Calling, you are subject to becoming poor in grace, and becoming such a **Beggar** who is not endowed with even one drop of grace—and then you are true beggars. Just as we say: it is a poor man whom God hates. He who does not have Christ and the treasures of Heaven within himself is subject to a thousand times more poverty than he can be by embracing the *Calling of Christ*. **Revelation 3:17**. Indeed, he is subject to a worse persecution because he neglects Jesus Christ out of fear of persecution. **Psalm 83:15** <note>The text cites verse 5, but the quote "persecute them with fury and wrath" matches verse 15.</note>: *The Lord shall persecute them,* says David of the ungodly, *with fury and wrath.* All the persecution of men extends only to the body, but this persecution from God extends to the soul.

**Seventh, and finally.** This ought not to hinder you from following Christ, considering that although you might be poor and be persecuted, Heaven will nonetheless make all this good to you. **Hebrews 11:35**. Heaven will repay your poverty when you are endowed with the riches of Christ; Heaven will repay your persecution when the weary shall rest there, and the oppressed shall be at peace. And let this much be spoken regarding the **third suggestion of the devil**, namely: "If you embrace the Calling of Christ, you shall be subject to much poverty and persecution here in this world."

### 2 Peter 1:10.

Therefore, Brothers, be all the more diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.

<margin>6th Sermon.</margin>
The teaching that I still have at hand is this: That Christians ought to employ great diligence to fix this in their souls—that they are effectively called through the power of Jesus Christ. In following this, I have resolved one case of conscience and now have the second case at hand; namely, what suggestions the Devil uses to keep people from embracing the Calling of Christ. I have proposed and answered the first of these.

**Fourthly**, there is yet another suggestion. When the Devil sees that none of the previous excuses take hold, he brings forth a fourth temptation to discourage people from embracing Christ's Calling, which is this: "Well," says the Devil, "if you accept the Calling of Jesus Christ, you will cut yourself off from all the fruit and comfort of your life; you will never have another happy day as long as you live on this earth. You see those people who claim to be converted and listen to sermons—what heavy-headed and melancholy people they are! They are not as cheerful and pleasant as others who do not walk so **precisely** <note>The Dutch term *precies* refers to the "Precisians" or "Puritans," believers who lived according to strict moral and religious rules.</note>. If you follow Christ and His Gospel, you will say goodbye to all your happy days, it will bring you into a sorrowful humor, and all your best days will be over." Therefore, this **smear** <note>original: "vlecke"; literally a "stain" or "blot," here used to mean a defamatory rumor or reproach.</note> must be wiped away: the claim that the ways of Christ are sad and melancholy ways. This has been a smear from century to century and from generation to generation—a snare the Devil has used to keep people away from Christianity. It comes to my mind that this was one of the craftiest inventions used by the **Antichrist** <note>In the context of 17th-century Protestant preaching, "the Antichrist" was a common polemical term for the Pope or the Roman Catholic hierarchy.</note> to support and maintain his Kingdom. The **Papists** <note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics.</note>, to frighten people away from Christianity and the Protestant Religion, kept their teachings tied to this idea: that the Spirit of a **Calvinist** <note>A follower of the Reformed tradition of John Calvin.</note> is a sad and heavy-headed Spirit. Therefore, they discouraged all nations from turning to this Religion, and the Priests had to announce in all the churches of Rome how sad and melancholy those became who converted to the Calvinist Religion; this powerfully held the people back from embracing the truth. This smear has passed from hand to hand and often exerts great power over the souls of those who belong to the true Religion, making them think they must not be too "forward" in the practice of Religion, for fear that it would cause melancholy and sad thoughts in them.

Now, to ward this off, I shall briefly stand upon only four or five main points.

**First**, whereas you say they are melancholy and sad people who are called by Jesus Christ to the confession of His ways, I answer thus: that among all people in the world, they have the greatest cause for joy and

<column-break/>

<margin>Psalms</margin>
gladness, and they are truly the most cheerful people in the world. It is evident that they have the greatest cause for joy. When the Disciples triumphed because they could cast out devils, heal the wounded, and perform miracles, Christ said: "Oh no, do not rejoice in that, but rejoice much more that your names are written in Heaven" (Luke 10:20). It is as if Christ said: "All the gifts and extraordinary talents of the spirit are not such a cause for joy, even if you have them all; but here is your joy and cause for gladness: that your names are written in the **Book of Life** <note>A biblical concept (e.g., Revelation 20:12) referring to the record of those predestined for salvation.</note>; that you are in Christ, and that your souls shall be saved." And so Paul tells us in Philippians 4:4: "Rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, rejoice." The Apostle did not want to say that with a single command, but he doubled his expression to show that they were the people whose sins were forgiven and whose souls were reconciled; who had the right to Glory, whose Names were written in the Book of Life; and these, among all people in the world, have the most cause for joy and cheerfulness. And they not only have the most cause, but they also truly rejoice the most, and have more true joy in their hearts in one day than a godless person can have in all his life (1 Peter 1:8). They rejoice with an unspeakable and glorious joy. Whatever joy you have in the world, the tongue is able to express it; but the tongue is not able to express that inward joy which the Godly have in their hearts through the understanding of the right they have to Jesus Christ. Psalm 4:7: "O Lord, lift up the light of Your countenance upon us; You have put more joy in my heart," etc. Proverbs 14:13: "A good conscience is a **continual feast**." <note>The author is paraphrasing Proverbs 15:15: "He that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast."</note> People are never more cheerful than when they are at a feast; the Godly carry a pure conscience within them, and that makes them so cheerful and pleasant, as if they were continually at a great and costly banquet. It is true, they do not rejoice with such unrestrained joy as godless people do. The godless rejoice in Sin, and that they cannot do; godless people rejoice in their lusts, in their drunkenness, in their adultery and ways of sin—the Godly people dare not do that. Such joy as that is the foundation of sorrow; this joy (like that of the **Prodigal Son** <note>original: "verlozen Sone"; referring to the biblical parable of the son who wasted his inheritance on "riotous living" before returning in repentance.</note>) in a dissolute way of life is the foundation of sadness and will meet you when you come to die.

**Secondly**, even if that [sadness] were true, nevertheless take note of this: the sadness that Godly people have is such a sadness that they will have no cause to repent of it; rather, it is for them a foundation of future joy. 2 Corinthians 7:9, 10: "I rejoice," says the Apostle, "because I made you sorry." What? "I am glad to see you a sad people?" Yes, because the sorrow with which I made you sorry was a sorrow never to be repented of; you will never have grief over that sadness. And therefore Paul wanted to do that, because it was a sorrow never to be sorrowful about; yes, it is not only such a sadness...

...never to have any regret over; rather, it is a sorrow that lays the foundation for a greater future joy; *those who sow with tears shall reap with shouts of joy.* <note>A reference to Psalm 126:5.</note> But now, all the joy of a godless person is a joy to be regretted. They must repent of all their foolish jests and all their delightful pastimes; it will then be a sorrow for them to remember these things. In contrast, the sorrow of the **Godly** is never such that it should be regretted.

**Thirdly**, it is true that they may be sorrowful, but they are sorrowful over sin—for which you, who are uncalled, have just as much reason as they do, and perhaps much more. If a godly person is sorrowful over sin, it shall never be harmful to him. Certainly, *the sorrow of the world produces death,* says the Apostle, *but the sorrow according to God produces a conversion to salvation that brings no regret.* <note>original: "De droefheyt der Werelt werckt de Doodt... de droefheyt nae Godt werckt een onberouwelijcke bekeeringe tot saligheyt." A translation of 2 Corinthians 7:10.</note>

**Fourthly**, it may be that they are sorrowful, but why is that? They are not sorrowful because they are good, but they are sorrowful because they are still so "bad" <note>meaning, still prone to sin or imperfection</note>. It is not their profession of faith that makes them sad, but rather that they cannot profess Christ better or more zealously; that is their sorrow. And that sorrow ought to be in all of us—that we cannot serve God better and cannot bring more honor to God.

**Fifthly**, they are sorrowful, but it is not for themselves; it is for you. They are not sorrowful because they are good, but because you are so bad. They are sorrowful over your sins, because they constantly see you uncalled, drunken, and godless, and see that you dishonor God and bring your soul to damnation. This makes them sadder than they otherwise would be. **LOT** tormented his righteous soul because of the godlessness of the Sodomites. <margin>2 Pet. 2:8.</margin> **JEREMIAH’s** eyes ran with tears because of the injustice of the people among whom he lived. And so also **PAUL**, "I have told you often, and I say it now even weeping, that there are those among you who live godlessly and do not walk according to the truth." <margin>Philip. 3:17, 18.</margin> Paul did not weep because he was miserable, but because he saw so many who were godless and lived abominably. **DAVID** likewise: <margin>Psalm 119:136.</margin> *Streams of water flow from my eyes because they do not keep your Law.* <margin>Ezech. 9:4.</margin> So also Ezekiel 9:4.

**Lastly**, although you see that some people are sorrowful and melancholy, do not think ill of the ways of God for that reason; seeing that this way, among others, most invites one to joy and gladness in the Lord. *Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.* <margin>Phil. 4:4. And John 16.</margin> *These things I have spoken,* says Christ, *so that your joy might be full.* It is the aim of Christ to give you more joy in the profession and following of Christ than you ever had before. There is, then, no reason to accept a high judgment from the temptations of the Devil against the ways of Jesus Christ when He calls you to profess His Gospel. <margin>1. Deception.</margin>

# Concerning our Effectual [Calling]

...to hear the commandments with pleasure, yet not the threats of the Word; in this case, this hearing is no proof of your **Effectual Calling**. <margin>Mark 6:20</margin> There it is written of Herod that he heard John the Baptist gladly, and did many things: this was his "partial" hearing. He heard him with joy in many things, but he did not want to do *all* things. Now, if you ask, where did Herod fail? Herod heard the word with joy. This was nevertheless no proof of his Effectual Calling. Where did he go wrong then? Note: compare this scripture passage with <margin>Luke 3:18, 19, 20</margin>. It is true that Herod heard John the Baptist gladly so long as he preached of ordinary things, but when John rebuked him for his sins, and told him that he was an adulterer, then he could not bear to hear John preach. Verse 18: *And John, exhorting them in many other things, preached the Gospel to the people; but when Herod the Tetrarch was rebuked by him because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, and for all the evils Herod had done, he added this above all else: that he shut up John in prison.* Then he no longer wished to hear John. Note how the Scripture portrays a godless person: Herod heard John gladly when he preached of comforting and general things; but when John came to rebukes and convictions, then he no longer wanted to hear him; but added this sin to all the others, that he shut John in prison. So, to be a partial hearer—to hear only one part of the Word and not everything—cannot be proof of the Effectual Calling. Such a temperament in people is revealed in <margin>Isaiah 30:10</margin>: *Speak to us smooth things, prophesy deceits.* There were many who could take pleasure in hearing "smooth" and comforting sermons, but they could not bear to hear a true declaration of God’s judgments against them because of their sins. They gladly hear some parts of God’s will, but not all; the promises, yes, but not the rebukes: this is no proof of the Effectual Calling. <margin>Ezekiel 13:17, 18</margin> There were certain lying prophetesses who preached there, but what did they do? *They sewed cushions for the elbows* <note>A biblical metaphor for providing false comfort or making people feel "at ease" in their sin.</note>, and the Lord rebuked them for it, saying they hunted souls. To preach "smooth" teachings and most-desired comforts is merely to sew cushions for the elbows and to hunt the souls of men. Now, many people like to be smoothed over and flattered <note>original: "geplugmstrijkt" - literally to be stroked with feathers, meaning to be coddled or complimented</note> in their sins; therefore, being a partial hearer is no sign of your **Effectual Calling**.

3. To hear the Word with pleasure is no proof of your Effectual Calling in the event that it is a wavering and inconstant hearing. To take pleasure in hearing the Word because there is no danger in hearing it; this may give godless people pleasure to do, yet if times of persecution arise, they will be wavering and cease their hearing. <margin>Matthew 13:20, 21</margin> It is written there regarding the stony places, that the seed sown in stony places are those who *receive the Word with joy* (there is their pleasure in hearing), but having no deep root, in time of persecution they fall away. The Scripture

<column-break/>

here dissects a person, showing that they may hear the Word with joy at certain times—when the current of the times makes Religion popular <note>original: "te meê balt" - to go along with or roll with the times</note>, or when the Word takes hold among a people. But if persecution attacks the Word, and the prison-house threatens the hearing, then you would see how weak their pleasure in hearing the Word would be. And in this case, you may have pleasure in hearing the Word, yet it is no proof of your Effectual Calling.

4. In the event that your hearing is a self-interested hearing: in this way, many people may hear the Word with pleasure: why? Because through the hearing of the Word, they can obtain judgment <note>meaning a reputation for discernment</note>, praise, and noble honor, and this may cause them to take a wonderful pleasure in hearing. <margin>Luke 12:1</margin> There were many thousands of the multitude gathered together to hear Jesus Christ, so that they trampled one another; yet Christ says of them, <margin>John 6:26</margin>: *You seek me, not because you saw the signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.* It was not out of love for Christ’s person, or His service, but only because they saw that Christ satisfied so many people with a few fish; seeing that miracle, it caused them to come to the ministry and the word of Jesus Christ. Many people may hear the Word when personal gain accompanies the hearing—to get more business, or to make their neighbors have a better opinion of them; this is a self-interested hearing, and in this case, you may hear and yet not be effectually called. There is a way of speaking in <margin>Hosea 7:14</margin>: *They do not cry to me with their heart, but they howl upon their beds; they gather themselves for grain and new wine.* Here was a people who gathered for the Ordinances of God; but what was their goal? There was a scarcity and hunger at hand, and therefore they wanted to use those duties as means to prevent hunger and to obtain grain and wine. Here was a self-interested goal, and thus people may hear, yet have no proof of their Effectual Calling.

5. If your hearing is a divided hearing, and your pleasure a divided pleasure, that can be no proof of your Calling. It is like this: a person may create pleasure in hearing, yet if that person divides and distributes their pleasure—partly to sin, and partly to the Word—this can be no proof of their Effectual Calling. In the place just touched upon, <margin>Hosea 7</margin>: *They assemble themselves and howl upon their beds, but they rebel against me, says the Lord.* There they divided their pleasure; they wanted to serve God in His worship, but they also wanted to be rebellious against Him. So also in <margin>Isaiah 58:3, 6, 7</margin>: They took pleasure in humbling themselves before God, but in these fast-days of theirs, they found pleasure in sin. Now, to have a divided love—to take as much pleasure in sin as in the established means of Religion—that can be no proof of the Effectual Calling; and your hearing of the Word in these five cases is but a mere deception. Yes, but you will say: "This persistence, even if it is no proof of our effectual calling, we can go one step higher; we do not only take delight in hearing the word, but we love the godly who are effectively called to grace and glory; and if we love them, we hope that it is a proof that we are also so called." Now, to speak of that: I answer, it is clear in God’s Word that every kind of love for the people of God is no proof of the effectual calling, but there can just as well be a hypocritical and imitated love as any other grace. Therefore the Apostle insists in <term>Romans 12:9</term> <note>The text cites Rom. 12:9</note>: *Let your love be without hypocrisy*; indicating that people can just as well feign their love as any other grace. <term>1 John 3:18</term>: *Let us not love with words, nor with the tongue; but with deed and truth.* So also in <term>1 Peter 1:22</term>: *Having then purified your souls for unfeigned brotherly love*: indicating that there can also be a hypocritical and false love. So that every kind of love is not a proof of the effectual calling. And this I will make good through this proof: because there are various acts or expressions of love which those people who are not effectively called may show toward godly people. Now, if an uncalled person can show many expressions and acts of love to a person who is converted, then the mere showing of love to a godly person is no proof of your effectual calling. I will tell it to you briefly; I want to bring it into six points. As:

1. A person may often be in the company of the godly, yet not be effectively called. 2. They may also speak well of the people of God. And this John tells us in <term>1 John 3:18</term>: *Let us not love with words, nor with the tongue.* This "loving with words and tongue" was to speak well of the godly; this ungodly people can do.

3. They may write letters of recommendation on behalf of the godly. 2. To measure your love toward them according to their grace: that you love that person most who has the most grace. That is a proof of the effectual calling, seeing that it is the grace in the person and nothing else that you love.

# [Of Our] Powerful [Calling]. 158

[...powerful] Calling, for then it is evident that grace, as grace, is the object of your love.

Finally, to love a person in such a way as to specifically have compassion for him in your heart—to have a heart that suffers with him in his suffering, as in **1 Peter 3:8**: *Be compassionate toward one another, loving the brothers.* This shows that your love is genuine when it carries sympathy and compassion for others.

<margin>
3. Deception.
</margin>

I move now to a third deception, which is truly a peculiar delusion that has deceived many, especially those who make a profession of the Gospel, leading them to believe they are effectively called when they are not. And that is: because they find a change in their conduct—that they are not the same people they were in days past. Through this, the Devil makes them believe that they must certainly be effectively called, and he brings forward the scripture passage **1 Corinthians 6:9, 10, 11**: *Such were some of you, but you are washed, etc.* Now, this is such a common deception among many people in the world that if they have any hope of Heaven, it is on this ground: that they are no longer who they were in previous times. I will therefore allow myself a little time to speak on this matter, and I shall set down six or seven points in which I will show that this ground, taken so generally, is no infallible proof of a person’s effectual Calling.

**First**, because there are many gradual changes which do not reach or result in a saving change of the human heart. Just as there is a change from a Heathen to a Christian—in this way Julian <note>Original: "Julianus." This refers to Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman emperor, who was raised Christian but tried to revive Roman polytheism.</note> was changed, yet he was never called through Jesus Christ. So also there is a change from being a persecutor to being a supporter of Religion; thus we read that Valerius Maximinus <note>Gaius Valerius Maximianus (Galerius), a Roman emperor notorious for his brutal persecution of Christians. Christian historians claimed his body rotted away while he was still alive as divine punishment.</note> was changed, who was the most wicked persecutor of all men in his time. The hand of God lay so heavy upon him for that sin that his intestines rotted within him, and worms crawled out of his body, so that in the terror of his conscience he made a great outcry to his nobles who stood around him, advising them to be warned by his example never to persecute the Christians like that again. Now, these were great changes, and yet they were only gradual changes that leave men far short of those saving changes which God works in those who are effectively called. And **thirdly**, there is a change from ungodliness to profession <note>The act of publicly declaring oneself a believer.</note>, and yet that is one step below a saving change. **Fourthly**, there is a crossover from profession into sincerity and the actual possession of Jesus Christ. Now, those deep steps fall short of a saving change; therefore, every change of life is not a proof to a person that they are effectively called, since there are many gradual changes that do not reach as high a level as this: to be changed unto salvation.

**Secondly**, there may be a change in the life when there is no change

<column-break/>

in the nature or in the heart; **Matthew 23**: *they may cleanse the outside of the cup, when it is full of uncleanness within.* <note>Matthew 23:25-26. The author uses this famous imagery of the "Whited Sepulcher" to describe moral behavior that hides an unchanged heart.</note> The life, deeds, and outward course of a person may be changed when the heart is not changed, and the nature remains constantly the same.

**Thirdly**, there may be a great change in a person's life, arising not from a change in their nature, but from the time in which they live. The times have changed, and therefore they have changed; the times no longer favor superstition, and therefore they do not show their superstitious heart; the times do not favor ungodliness, and therefore they do not wish to be ungodly. Beloved, the change in a person's life may often come from the change of the times in which they live, and yet this change is no proof of a changed heart, or of the effectual Calling through Jesus Christ.

**Fourthly**, a change in your life may come from a change in your sin, and not from a change in your heart. It works like this: a person may in past times have been a drunkard, he may have been an adulterer, he may have been a wicked person, and he may change these sins for other sins. He may change his drunkenness into greed, and become a covetous man of the world. He may change his adultery into idolatry and be a superstitious person. He may change his ungodliness into hypocrisy and be a hypocrite. He may change his loose practices into a corrupted judgment and be an erring spirit <note>A term often used for a heretic or someone who holds false doctrines.</note>. Now, this is not a change of the heart, but only a change of the sin. You do not have the same sins you had before, but you have other sins in their place; and thus a person may have a change in his life, flowing from a change in his sins, which nonetheless is no proof of the effectual Calling. **Jeremiah 2:36**: *Why gadabout you so much, changing your way?* The people of Israel were always wanting to change: now they held with God, and then with Baal; now with true worship, and then with false worship. They were quite willing to always change their sins, but never to leave sin; they only wanted to change their old sins for another kind of sin. And so there are many people today who are changed; they are converted from their wickedness and have come to a profession of faith. It may be that they no longer have such gross sins as in times past; in past times they set themselves against Religion, but now they profess it; but even though they have left their opposition, they now have a sin that is more prominent than the others. Many people who were loose in practice have changed that into being corrupted in judgment. This is not a change of the heart as long as it remains so: therefore, hold it as the truth that there can be a change in the life while the heart remains constantly unchanged.

1. Rule.
</margin>

**Fifthly**, there may be a change in a person’s life arising from a change of the opportunity to sin, and not from a change in the heart. Just as a lion will run and roar up and down, tearing its prey when...

he runs wild; but put that lion in a corner, and there he is quiet, and shall do no harm. Lastly, many people may change their lives because they have now come into better company; perhaps their company is now more pious than in times past, and that may work a change in their lives. Seventhly, and lastly, every change is not a proof of Effectual Calling, because there may be a change in life proceeding from a wrong principle and tending toward an evil end. For example: a man may change his life out of a wrong principle; what is that? I shall name two wrong principles of change in unregenerate men:

First, people may change their lives because of some present afflictions <note>Original: "berduckingen"—pressures or oppressive circumstances.</note> that lie upon them here in this life; their sighs may urge them to change their ways, and not to be so wicked as in former days. *Jonah 1:5*: when they were in the ship in the storm, everyone cried out to his god. What a change was here! Yet the change was only for the sake of necessity; they were in peril of death, and therefore they became so "godly." Every man, when necessity and sighing lie upon him, will turn toward God and become a man of a different mind. And so was Pharaoh: when God sent him ten heavy plagues, the plagues forced Pharaoh to confess his sin and to seek Moses to pray for him; and yet this change in Pharaoh was only because of the present affliction lying upon him, which caused this change. *Jeremiah 22:23*: *O you who now dwell in Lebanon, how gracious will you be when pangs come upon you?* When the pains and the sighs lay upon them, then they would be a "gracious" people. There is many a man who changes his life when God sends pains, and death, and sickness upon him; these are forced ways that God uses to make a godless and stout-hearted <note>In this context, "stout-hearted" means stubborn or prideful against God.</note>

<column-break/>

sinner change his life. *Isaiah 16:12*: there it stands, *When it is seen that Moab is weary, then Moab shall go into my Sanctuary to pray.* What a change was here in Moab? Moab was an idolatrous people, who hated the people of God and were enemies of all godliness; yet when they were weary, and God’s hand pressed hard upon them, then they wanted to worship. *Ezekiel 24:12*. So you clearly see, even though people change their lives, if this change only arises from that present affliction under which they lie, and because God’s hand over them forces them to change their course, this is no proof of a saving change, and consequently no evidence of your Effectual Calling.

Secondly, people may change their lives from this origin: namely, because of that terror of Conscience that seizes them through the understanding of hell and the wrath of God; and from this origin, even a Heathen may change his life. It was noted by someone on the passage of **PETER**: *It has happened to them as the dog has returned to his own vomit, etc.* <note>Reference to 2 Peter 2:22.</note> Regarding these words, he makes this note: that the dog in vomiting is compared to a godless man who leaves his sin. Now, says the author, when the dog vomits, it is because of a sickness and distress that is in his stomach; and when he has that anguish, he unburdens and relieves himself by vomiting; not as if he had a loathing for his food, for if he could rid himself of this distress, he would gladly keep the food in his body to nourish him. So also a godless man: he may spit out, vomit up, and forsake his sins—but why? It is not because he hates his sins; no, certainly not; he would gladly keep them as a tasty morsel under his tongue; but it is because those sins cause a terror and restlessness of the Conscience. He cannot deceive, nor follow his lusts, without the Conscience pursuing him. Now, if you change your sin only to stop the mouth of the Conscience, and to satisfy the Conscience, that is no proof of your Effectual Calling.

<margin>4. Deception.</margin>
Fourthly, people are tempted by the devil to harbor these vain imaginings <note>Original: "verwaende inbeeldingen"—presumptuous fantasies or delusions.</note>—that they are effectively called when they are not—because they are despised by worldly people and spoken ill of by them. Now, they think, "I would never be despised by godless people, and there would not be evil spoken of me, if I were not called by my God."

Now, to address this precious work, I answer that all contempt from the godless cannot be a proof of God’s effectual calling, since a person may be spoken ill of on two different grounds: there are some people who suffer as Christians, and some as evildoers. We can suffer either for Christ’s sake, or for our own sake; the distinction is set down in *1 Peter 4:15, 16, 17*: *Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters; but if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed.* So that there...

Using examples like Pharaoh and King Joash, the author warns that even the "terror of conscience" can produce a false repentance that mimics true salvation.</summary>

->Of our effectual [calling]<-

some people may be punished for their own evil that they have done, and so they suffer no more than they have deserved; but others suffer for their confession, because they confess Jesus Christ. Therefore Christ calls them blessed in Matthew 5:11: *Blessed are you when men revile and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake:* this is a proof of your **effectual Calling** through Jesus Christ.
