### 2 Peter 1:10

*Therefore, Brothers, be all the more diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.*

<margin>7th Sermon.</margin>
The Doctrine that I still have at hand, drawn from these words, is this: **That Christians ought to employ great diligence to make this sure to their souls: that they are effectually called through Jesus Christ.** In the pursuit of this, I have gone over many points and untied some cases of conscience in respect to the godless. I now intend at this time to settle some more cases of Conscience touching those who are effectually called through Jesus Christ: As—

1. Whether those people who are effectually called through Christ into the state of grace and hope of Glory can obtain in this life an infallible and firm assurance of their own effectual Calling?
2. If it is certain that it can be obtained in this life, what is the reason that many Christians, who are effectually called, doubt so greatly and hold their own calling suspect; and go about so sadly for the lack of their assurance?
3. What must chiefly be done to make this so sure to your own souls, that you are effectually called through Jesus Christ.

First, whether it can be obtained in this life, that people who are effectually called through Christ can have a firm and infallible assurance of their own Calling? To untie this <note>The author uses the metaphor of "untying" a knot to describe solving a difficult theological problem.</note>, I shall briefly prove the same by two extremes, both of which are untrue concerning this question.

<margin><note>original Latin: "Si quis dixerit hominem renatum teneri ex fide ad credendum fecreto effe ex numero Prædestinatorum, anathema fit."</note> If anyone says that a reborn man is bound by faith to believe he is secretly among the number of the predestined, let him be cursed. Session 6, Canon 15.</margin>
The first is that of the Papists <note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics.</note>, who to the extreme deny all such things—namely, the assurance concerning a person's Calling, justification, or election by God—and they keep all their followers in doubt, establishing as a certainty that most people can only have a "guessing faith" <note>Term: <term>Gissend' ghelove</term>, referring to the Catholic doctrine that one can have a moral certainty or hope of salvation, but not an absolute "infallible" certainty without special revelation.</note> and a hope or a guess that they shall be saved. And it is from this that they made this Rule in that Papal Council of Trent: that if anyone says that he is bound by faith to believe that he is certainly in the number of God’s called, or justified, or elected, let him be an *Anathema*, let him be cursed. That person who would want to so assure himself, him they hold as cursed. And the reason why they

<column-break/>

do that is because they push another error—namely, the "falling away from grace"—which they would not be able to maintain if they did not hold this so. This is the first extreme.

Secondly, the other extreme is that of the Lutherans; they, being on the contrary side against the Papists in this matter of assurance, in order to refute those who deny all assurance, run into this extreme: that they hold that assurance is of the very nature of faith, and that he who has faith also has assurance. But this is another extreme, and a comfortless doctrine for doubting Christians, if such were true. Therefore, to hold the truth in the middle between these two extremes, I shall set down this proposition as an answer: **That although sometimes those persons who are effectually called may be without a particular assurance of their own Calling, nevertheless this assurance is to be obtained by Christians in this life; and that Christians can be assured of their own effectual Calling.** And this I shall prove by three means.

First, because the Apostle commands it here in my Text: *Be diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.* Now, this is a rule in Theology: that no one is bound to do a thing that is impossible; and therefore, that which is charged upon us, and which we are bound to do, it is clear that such is possible and can be made sure.

Secondly, because it is the ministry of the Spirit of Jesus Christ to work this particular assurance in the hearts of those who are effectually called: that they are in the state of grace and shall be brought to Glory. 1 Cor. 2:12: *We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we might know the things that are given to us by God.* 1 John 5:10: *He that believes in the Son has the witness in himself;* a witness to his own soul that he believes. Eph. 1:13, 14: there the Spirit is called a Seal; *You are sealed with the Spirit of promise;* and in verse 14 He is called the Earnest <note>An "earnest" or "pledge" is a down payment that guarantees the full amount will be paid later.</note> of our inheritance. Now, a Seal and an Earnest are to give greater assurance to the promise; now, the Spirit of God here is given to the believer as a Seal and an Earnest, that just as they have the first fruits in grace, they shall have their harvest in Glory. 1 John 4:13: *Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.* It is the ministry of the Spirit of Jesus Christ to assure our hearts in this matter. Rom. 8:16: *The same Spirit witnesses with our spirit that we are children of God.*

Thirdly, particular servants of God in the Scripture, who have been partakers of this grace, have had this firm assurance of their effectual Calling. I shall bring forth only three examples. First, of Paul: the Scripture tells us of him that he had a clear proof of his effectual Calling, Gal. 2:20: *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me, who has loved me and given himself for me.* There he had a particular assurance that Christ loved him and [gave] himself...

has surrendered to Him. So also 2 Timothy 1:12: *I know whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him* <note>original: "mijn Pandt by hem weggelegent," referring to a deposit or "pledge" entrusted to God.</note> *against that day.* Likewise 2 Timothy 4:8: *I have fought the good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness.* Indeed, not only Paul, but likewise also Job, Job 19:25: *I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:* he knew that Jesus Christ was his Redeemer. And so also David who says, *You are my God, therefore I will praise you,* Psalm 118:28, and Psalm 23:6: *Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.* So then, put this together: God commands it; it is the Spirit's ministry to work this assurance in the heart; and since specific servants of God have had this assurance, why then can it not be obtained? But if you say, "these were no ordinary servants of God; they were servants of a higher rank and order; but can common, weak Christians know this as well?" Yes, indeed. Therefore—

Fourthly, not only did specific saints have it, but also the people of God in general; they have declared in the Scripture that they enjoyed this particular assurance of their **effectual calling** <term>Effectual calling: the theological concept that God's internal invitation to salvation is powerful enough to ensure the person responds in faith.</term> and of the salvation of their state through Christ. I will give but a few examples. Isaiah 63:16: *Doubtless thou art our Father.* They did not doubt it; they were so convinced that they did not waver. Isaiah 45:24: *Surely, shall one say, in the Lord have I righteousness and strength.* "Surely": a word of trust; they were assured that they had righteousness for their justification in Christ Jesus. So also 2 Corinthians 5:1: *We know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, eternal in the heavens.* They knew that when they came to die, they would see God in the heavens; not only Paul, but also other godly Christians with him. Likewise, Hebrews 10:34: *Knowing in yourselves that ye have a better and an enduring substance in heaven.* They were assured in themselves that when they should die, or lose their goods here, God had prepared for them a better and enduring substance in the heavens. Likewise 1 John 3:19: *By this we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him.* So verse 14: *We know that we have passed from death unto life,* etc. So then, what could be more clearly proven than this: that this assurance can be obtained in this life? Since God commands such a thing, since it is the ministry of the Spirit to work it, since specific Christians have had it, and since the people of God in general have enjoyed and confessed that assurance.

<margin>Excellent.</margin> If it is so, then, that this assurance can be obtained in this life, how greatly are our opponents, the <term>Papists: a historical, often polemical term for Roman Catholics</term>, to be rebuked! They keep their followers in doubt, telling them they must live without the assurance of their own state; that their souls must hang in fear and doubt all their lives; that the most they can have is only a guess. Oh! into what an abyss of comfortless-

<column-break/>

-ness they throw them! Beloved, the Lord, in the book of Deuteronomy chapter 28, speaks of it as a curse that one's life should hang in doubt; it is an even greater curse that the souls of men should hang in doubt, that men should not know whether they shall be saved or damned. It is a hell on this side of hell; and therefore they are greatly to be rebuked who hold their followers fast with the idea that they might perhaps be saved and perhaps not; while the Scripture is yet so clear in this matter.

Secondly, do not let thoughts of the impossibility or the difficulty of attaining this assurance discourage you from seeking it. It is not impossible, though it is indeed difficult; and the difficulty, far from taking away your courage, ought to awaken your efforts to make your **Calling** and **Election** sure.

Thirdly, since this assurance can be obtained in this life, investigate the cause of why you, who are **effectually called**, have not yet obtained this assurance. This brings me now to the handling of the second case of **Conscience**, seeing that this assurance can be obtained. Therefore—

Secondly: what is the reason that many Christians, who are **effectually called** through Jesus Christ, live in so much doubt and fear regarding their **effectual calling**?

To answer this, I shall set down these three points: that the doubts which arise in Christians concerning their **effectual calling** bloom from this threefold fountain:

Either first: from some apparent defect that they imagine in the *manner* of their calling. Or

Secondly: from some apparent defect that they imagine in the *means* of their calling. Or else

Thirdly: from some apparent defect that they imagine in the *workings* of their calling; these three grounds can arise, from which many Christians who are **effectually called** doubt their calling and are not assured of it.

First: it arises from some apparent defect that they perceive to be in the *manner* of their calling: they say, "I am not called in such a way as I see others are." For instance: they think, "I see that when other people are converted, their humiliation is very great; I see that they have a terror of **Conscience**, that they are worked upon by the fear of the Law, that they are exceedingly humbled before God. Now, as for me, I never found that manner of God’s working in my soul; I never found that I could clearly see my sins or be greatly humbled over them; I never found in myself that humiliation and fear of the Law that I hear many people speak of; and this makes me doubt whether I am indeed **effectually called** or not." Now, to take that away, I shall say only three things in answer.

First: that it is true that God takes this path with some; nonetheless, God is not bound or limited to one and the same way of working with everyone. What is it to—

### Confirming Our Calling ###

<center>O 4</center>

...other means. One of these three [might say]: "I was converted," (says one) "by living in a godly household, among good Christians; seeing their example was what first won me over." Or (says another), "I was drawn by reading a chapter in the Bible, or in some other good book; and that first worked upon me." Or (says a third), "it may be that though it was through the Word, it was the Word preached by a godless man, who has now become a wandering spirit <note>original: *dwaelgeest*; likely referring to a preacher who has fallen into heresy or "wandered" from the truth</note> or godless in practice; and this causes no small second-guessing." The Word preached from the mouth of a godly minister is God's ordinary path; but [you say] "I was entirely outside that path, and therefore this makes me doubt the truth of my **effectual calling**." Now beloved, I pray you, lend me your attention for a little while; for I would gladly, as much as I can, make this teaching a comfort to everyone who is called. I shall speak of these things in order, and show you that even if one of these was the means of your calling, you nevertheless have no reason to doubt your **effectual calling**.

**First**, you doubt your calling because the means were, you say, not hearing a sermon or the preached word, but living among good Christians; and seeing their example and their life, you came through these means to love the ways of God. And those were the first means that converted you. Beloved, I do not doubt that I speak to a great multitude who cannot say that a sermon converted them, but only that they were won to the ways of God to embrace the truth through this path. Now, what shall I say to such people as these? What? I shall say this much: that although the Lord uses His preached Word as the ordinary means to convert souls, God is not bound in His calling to His preached Word; rather, He may use other means to convert your soul.

**Secondly**, and more particularly, we find in **Scripture** that living among good people and seeing their example, both in life and in worship, are often powerful means to convict, and sometimes to convert. And if you can find this in **Scripture**, then you can have an abundance of comfort. It has often been a means to convict: *1 Peter 3:16*. "They will be ashamed for speaking ill of you, when they behold your good conduct in Christ." When they see that you live in Christ and walk after Christ, they shall be ashamed—ashamed of what they have done and what they have spoken—and that will convict them. So also, *1 Peter 2:15*. And the **Apostle**, when he speaks of the fit and orderly conduct of worship, *1 Corinthians 14:23, 25*: "If an unbeliever should come in among you, and he sees your order," he says, "he shall fall on his face, and will be convicted, and declare that God is truly among you." Seeing this (says the **Apostle**), that godly people are holy in their life and holy in their worship, even though he is an unbeliever, he shall fall down and say that God is truly among you. This is then regarding the convic-

<column-break/>

tion. But further, God sometimes blesses the gracious life and blameless example of Christians so that they are means to convert some, even when the **Gospel** [preached] cannot do it. You will think this is very comforting, if only it could be proven. I will recommend but one **Scripture** passage to you to prove what a blessing it is to live in a good household where the husband or wife, or everyone in the household, is godly: *1 Peter 3:1*. "You wives, be submissive to your own husbands," what then? "So that even if some are disobedient to the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives." A remarkable passage! There were entirely godless men, so that all the sermons they heard could not convert them; yet the **Apostle** tells them, if the wife led a godly and holy life, that her life would sometimes be more powerful to convert her husband than the Word. And this, beloved, purely takes away your first pretext—namely, that because you are converted by example and by living among good Christians and seeing their conduct, that this won you over—this is then no reason to let your courage fail, seeing as the Lord sometimes (I say) blesses the examples of a gracious life to gain those people who are assigned to **Jesus Christ**.

**Secondly**, they go even further. There is another poor soul who has been brought to **Jesus Christ**, and what does that one say? "I doubt the means of my calling, because preaching never worked upon me; the first thing of all that ever won me over was the reading of some chapters in the Bible, or of some books by holy men, and that first made me hate sin and love the ways of God, and look to His word for my salvation." I do not doubt that many Christians have found that the reading of the Word was the first means to gain their hearts. And therefore, to take this away likewise, I shall say two or three things in answer. As:

**First**, that God is not bound to any means, but that He can work with the smallest means to bring a people to **Jesus Christ**. If Peter's conversion was through a rooster—a crowing rooster—and a glance from Christ's eye, why may Christ not use the reading of **Scripture** as a means of a man's calling? If God can raise up children for Abraham from stones, why can God not also do that through His Word, to make the read Word a means in His hand to work the same? God can do all things with nothing at all, without means; He can make great things happen through weak means.

**Secondly**, and more particularly: although ordinarily preaching and the hearing of the preached Word are ordained by God, and He has primarily crowned them as instrumental means to convert souls, God has nevertheless sometimes blessed the reading of the Word likewise as a means to convert souls. However, beloved, I do not wish to do as the **Prelates** <note>The "Prelates" refers to the high-ranking clergy of the Church of England (Bishops) during the 17th century, whom Puritans often criticized for preferring set prayers and liturgy over fervent preaching.</note> did, who would gladly have brought the people to reading in order to abolish our sermons. Preaching is a nobler work, and ought...

# Of Our Effectual [Calling] #

-> L 4 <-

<meta>catchword: First,</meta>

[the preached word] ought to be highest in our thoughts; nevertheless, if God wills to take an unusual path, who can rebuke Him? If God wills to do this through the reading of a chapter, and not through a preached sermon, who can withstand God? If He wills to show His power through weak means, who shall resist that? God sometimes honors the reading of the Word—to give courage to the practice of reading—by making it a means of some people's calling. I have read of **St. Augustine**, that he was converted not by hearing a sermon, but by opening the Bible and reading the passage, **Romans 13:13**: *Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness.* <note>original: "niet in brasseryen ende dronckenschappen, niet in slaep-kameren ende onduchtigheden"</note> And the reading of that verse worked upon him. I have read of **Cyprian** <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> that he was converted by reading the prophecy of **Jonah**, hearing there of God's mercy in preserving such a godless people, and of God's grace toward Jonah when he was wrongfully angry with God. I have likewise known another famous Minister, who, walking through a bookbinder's shop, was converted by reading a "Sermon on Conversion" which cost only two English pennies; and he has since been a famous Minister, converting many hundreds of people to **Jesus Christ**. **Junius** <note>Franciscus Junius (1545–1602), a Reformer</note> was converted by reading the first chapter of **John**; so also the **Chamberlain** <note>The Ethiopian Eunuch in Acts 8</note> was converted by reading **Isaiah 53:7**. Beloved, God is not bound to any single way to save man; He who worked upon Augustine through the reading of a verse, and upon another through the reading of a sermon, can also do the same with you. Reading is an ordained means from God, and God is not bound to anything, but He may likewise use it as a means of your **effectual calling**. <term>Effectual Calling: The theological belief that God's internal call to a person's soul is powerful enough to ensure they come to faith.</term>

**Thirdly**, "Yes, but," says another doubting soul, "perhaps I was not visited through the sight of the godly people I lived among and the observation of their example, nor even through the reading of good books; but I was first visited by hearing a certain Minister whom I now see has fallen into error <note>original: "dwalinqe"</note>; or a Minister who has become lawless in his conduct (perhaps in these present times he has joined the ranks against the Kingdom) and has become vile of life; and because the Minister who visited me was evil, it makes me doubt whether the work in me is not an unstable and an evil work." This likewise troubles many Christians. To which I briefly answer:

**First**, granted that the Minister who visited you was evil, nevertheless, the wickedness of the Minister is no proper ground to make us doubt our Calling. For then we would never be certain of our Calling. A person can be certain of his own conversion, even though he cannot be certain of the conversion of the one through whose means he was called.

**Secondly**, again, it is clear in Scripture that God may use Ministers who are themselves godless to convert others. Regarding the Ministers of the seven churches of **Asia**, no doubt some of them were evil men. Paul says to you in **1 Corinthians 9:27**: *I*

<column-break/>

*discipline my body, lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.* Showing that a person may preach to others and may be a means to save others, and yet not be saved himself. So also **1 Corinthians 13:1**. Ministers in this regard may be compared to **cooks**; a cook may prepare and let pass through his hands a multitude of dishes to set upon a great and stately table, yet of all those dishes he hardly tastes one himself. So also Ministers: they may prepare many dishes for their listeners, yet not once lick their fingers or even taste this spiritual food themselves. Just as in the building of the **Ark**, there were many men who built Noah's Ark to save others, who were themselves drowned; so also many men may build an Ark through the preaching of the Word and the ways of God to save other people's souls, while they themselves may drown. From this, the Scripture tells us of stars that fell from Heaven; many Ministers, who seemed to be godly Ministers like the stars in their generation, nevertheless fell away and became godless and evil. I think of **Doctor Pembleton** <note>Likely Henry Pendleton, an English preacher who famously recanted his Protestant faith to become a "Papist" under Queen Mary I</note>, a famous Minister in the days of **Queen Mary**, and a man whose ministry converted many Christians; yet at the last, he himself became a **Papist**. <term>Papist: A 17th-century term for a Roman Catholic.</term> Now, these Christians neither mistrusted nor ever doubted their conversion because the man who converted them was an evil man; they could well be a good people, even though he was an evil Minister. So this is no ground at all; although I confess it is not ordinary that God makes godless men the means of conversion—for God ordinarily crowns the word most in the mouth of a godly Minister—nevertheless, God may, I say, sometimes use them as a means to convert souls. I shall give you these reasons to prove that a godless person may convert souls, and that God does not bind conversion to a godly Minister.

**First**, because the power of the word does not depend on the man, but on **Jesus Christ**; and Christ may use whom He pleases.

**Secondly**, if only a good person could convert, then it would follow that we could be just as certain of another person's conversion as we are of our own; which is a thing that is entirely untrue. For if only a godly person could convert, then if I were certain of my own conversion, I would also be certain of the conversion of the one who worked it in me; which cannot be. Therefore, this should not lay a stumbling block in your way because you see that the Minister who worked upon you is not a good man, since conversion is not bound only to a godly Minister.

**Thirdly**, the third ground from which doubts arise in those who are once called is from certain seeming defects they imagine to be in the accompanying matters that attend or in the effects that follow the **effectual calling**. And this makes them afraid that they are certainly not powerfully called. I shall name four of these to you.

# Making Our Calling Sure #

<meta>catchword: are</meta>

First, (says a doubting Christian) I hear in the Scriptures what effects follow and accompany a person who is effectually called, and I do not find those worked in my soul. For example, first, I understand that when a person is effectually called, they will be made capable by God to call upon Him in prayer. I find in the Scripture, **1 Corinthians 1:2**, that all who are called to be saints shall call upon the Lord in every place. But alas, woe is me, I do not find this in my soul. I find that all the days of my life I have a clumsy, dead heart, without desire or proper form for prayer; and therefore I doubt whether I am effectually called or not. Now, I shall set down three things here in answer.

First, you perhaps judge that you are not fit to pray because, although you have inner stirrings <note>original: "bewegingen," referring to the internal movements of the soul or Holy Spirit</note> in prayer, you lack the outward expressions. Now, if you judge yourself unfit for prayer solely because you lack expressions, you judge wrongly, seeing that prayer must be judged by the stirrings and not by the expressions. Expressions are but a breathing out of nature; a naturally light tongue may easily pour out expressions; on the contrary, the stirrings in prayer are the breath and fruit of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, do not judge that you cannot pray because you do not have such flowing expressions as others may use, for the true essence of prayer lies in the heart. Therefore it stands that when the Spirit of God teaches a person to pray, He does not teach them with expressions alone, but with **groanings that cannot be uttered**, **Romans 8:26**. When the Spirit moves the heart and makes you sigh out and cast forth your desires and petitions, then you pray best of all.

Secondly, you who judge yourself unfit to pray and think you are not called because you cannot call upon God, I will say this to you: that the best of God's children have found a great difference in their souls regarding the fulfillment of their duties; the best of God's children do not always pray the same way. Sometimes the stirrings of the godly in prayer are as fast as the **chariots of Amminadab** <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 6:12, often used to describe spiritual swiftness or fervor</note>; at other times they drive as heavily as the **chariots of Pharaoh** when the wheels were off. Sometimes God’s people are burning in their stirrings, as hot as fire; at other times they are frozen in their stirrings, as cold as ice. None of God's people are always the same in their progress toward God in prayer, **Psalm 77:4**. These are the words of **Asaph**: *O Lord, my soul is overwhelmed within me, I am troubled, and I cannot speak.* The man was so troubled that he could not speak; yet Asaph spoke these words with his mouth. But the meaning is: although Asaph was a godly man, he was so overwhelmed with heaviness that he could not speak to God, that he could not call upon God with that inward power of the spirit. Even though you may sometimes call upon God with feeling, nevertheless, when heaviness rests upon you, your heart can be out of its proper frame.

Thirdly, God's people are often sub-

<column-break/>

-jected to a state of abandonment and of restoration in their spiritual stirrings, and then they are out of their routine for prayer; when you lose the stirrings, then the wheels of prayer are shot off. It often happens with God's people that they are brought into a weak and faint state, that they are in such powerlessness as if they had neither the beginning nor the working of a spiritual life. **Revelation 3:2**: *Strengthen,* says the Holy Spirit, *the things which remain, that were ready to die.* God's people may be a dying people, and then the tongue falters when it dies. God's people may be in a dying state; though they do not die entirely in grace, they may be so weak in their spirit that they cannot cast out their desires to God as they used to do. **2 Chronicles 17:3**: *Jehoshaphat walked in the first ways of his father David*, implying that David's first ways were better than his last. So also many people's former ways may be good, yet sometimes in the end before they die, they may have complete deficiency and deadness of spirit upon them.

Fourthly, if a person only mourns that they cannot call upon God, God sees that as a calling unto Him; if you can but sigh out your desires, and weep because you do not weep, and pray that you might pray, the Lord hears your prayer. That is the most pleasant music you can make in the eyes of God. Therefore **David** says, **Psalm 6:9**, *The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping*; there is a voice in tears as well as in words. If the Lord sees you weeping over your own distress and mourning over your own deadness, the Lord looks upon this with a more pleasing eye than if you could pour out the elevations of your tongue with the most fluent and pleasant expressions.

# Making our Calling Sure #

-> [that which] they wished to do. And therefore Paul complains in Romans 7: *The thing that I want to do, I do not do.* <note>original: "Het gene dat ick wil, dat en doe ick niet." A reference to the internal struggle between the spirit and the flesh described by the Apostle Paul.</note> Paul himself, who was a pillar in God’s House, tells you that he could not reach the very act of obedience which he desired in his heart; and therefore, if you willingly wish to do more than you actually do, God accepts the little that you perform. <-

Thirdly, although you cannot produce many days of obedience to God, nevertheless, where there is a readiness of mind and heart, God accepts that intention of the mind as the deed itself, according to 2 Corinthians 8:12: *For if the readiness of mind is there, it is acceptable according to what one has, and not according to what one does not have.* And let this much be said regarding the second case of conscience: why people who are effectually called doubt their own Calling so greatly.

<margin>Wisdom</margin> Thirdly, since Christians ought to apply great diligence to make their Calling sure; where then should this diligence of ours be occupied? Or in what channel should it run, so that we might be certain of our effectual Calling? This is a very weighty question; and in resolving it, I shall answer it in these two general parts:

First, if you wish to obtain certainty of your effectual Calling, you must apply all diligence to keep away those things which hinder you from making your Calling sure. And,

Secondly, be diligent to put into practice those duties which may help you to confirm that you are effectually called.

First, you must keep away those things which entirely hinder you from being assured; and these obstacles which must be cleared away I shall categorize into six main points. Namely:

First, you must be diligent to keep the way of <term>Melancholy</term> <note>In the 17th century, melancholy was viewed as both a physical ailment caused by "black bile" and a spiritual state of despair or gloominess.</note> out of your thoughts; this is a natural obstacle to assurance. Melancholy is a humor in man arising from "black blood" that circulates through the body, which naturally causes mistrust and fear in the minds of men; this humor being in the body works greatly upon the state of the soul. Now, if you are of a melancholy humor and thus prone to mistrust and fear, this will be a great hindrance to having the joy and comforts of the Lord in your hearts, and the assurance of His love. It is an observation that <term>Perkinsius</term> <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), a highly influential English Puritan theologian.</note> has regarding Nebuchadnezzar, when he ate grass like a beast; writing on that passage, he thinks that Nebuchadnezzar was in a deep melancholy, and that it so possessed him that he could not tell if he was a man or a beast; although (he says) he did not actually eat grass, yet the deep confusion of senses that possessed him made him think that he had turned from a man into a beast. Beloved, melancholy in a Christian will make him think of himself that he is a hypocrite where he is actually a saint; and therefore beware of melancholy, a heavy and sad humor; it is a very great hindrance to this grace of assurance. I present this here simply as a natural remedy.

<column-break/>

Secondly, a mind filled with worldly cares and running after earthly concerns is a great hindrance to assurance. The cares of this life (Matthew 13:15) are compared to thorns. Now, thorns choke the seed because they draw the "sap" that is in the seed to themselves, and thus the corn does not grow where thorns sprout. The cares of this life are like thorns in this regard: they have a "drawing-back" power to suck the sap out of your spirits and draw it to themselves, so that you cannot have the sap of your Spirit to gather your "evidences" <note>In Puritan theology, "evidences" were specific signs or traits in one's life that proved they were truly saved.</note> for Heaven. The more you are preoccupied with the world, the less you shall reach the clear proofs of your eternal state; the cares of this life pierce the soul with many sorrows, and when a person is pierced with many sorrows, they are in a very unfit state of mind to be awakened into spiritual joy. The more you occupy yourself with the businesses of this world, the less you shall be in the comforts of Heaven. It comes to mind what the saying of a Pope was when he lay on his deathbed:

> When I was a hard-working, preaching Minister, I had hope for my Salvation; when I became a Cardinal, I doubted it; but when I became Pope, I despaired of it; so was I ensnared by the businesses of this life.

Beloved, so may I say to you: when you were but ordinary Christians in the world, you were on the path to obtaining assurance of your salvation; but since you have been taken up with the businesses of the world, it so ravishes your minds that you are not in a settled state of mind to have any firm certainty of heart regarding your eternal state. It is an observation of the Philosophers that the Sun is eclipsed by the intervention of the Moon, because the Moon comes between the Sun and our sight. Beloved, the Sun of your comforts is eclipsed by the Moon (this is a symbol drawn from the words of Revelation 12:9). Now, if the "Moon of the World" comes between your comforts and you, it will miserably eclipse and darken your comfort. Nothing in the world hinders your comfort in assurance so much as the worries and cares regarding the things of this world.

Thirdly, beware that you do not harbor the guilt of any known sin upon your Conscience. Keeping sin on the Conscience is a great obstacle to your inward comforts. You shall never be assured as long as you do that; and therefore, if you ever want to have assurance, clear that away. It is an observation of <term>Mr. Hildersham</term> <note>Arthur Hildersam (1563–1632), a prominent nonconformist clergyman and author.</note> regarding Psalm 51:12, 14. What does David do when he prays for assurance? Saying:

> Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation, and let thy free Spirit uphold me.

Give me back my comforts and my evidences. What path does he take? Read verse 14:

> Deliver me from blood-guiltiness, O God.

This is as much as to say: as long as sin lies on the Conscience without being repented of (as it was for nine months), so long did David lack the joy of the spirit and the comforts...

### Of our effectual [calling] ###

blessings of Heaven; and therefore, when he comes to renew his comforts and to restore his assurance, he prays to God—while praying for assurance—also that He might deliver him from blood-guiltiness; <note>A reference to Psalm 51:14, where King David prays for deliverance from the guilt of his sins after his affair with Bathsheba.</note> as knowing that if that sin remained upon his conscience without repentance and without being forgiven, he would never regain the joy of God's Spirit. Beloved, you shall never have the assurance of your **effectual calling** <note>In Reformed theology, "effectual calling" refers to God's internal work of drawing a person to salvation.</note> until your consciences are freed from having any sin upon them with your consent. There is an observation that *Aristotle* has regarding earthquakes: that they are caused by winds trapped in the hollows and empty places of the earth; which, having no place to exit, burst forth and overturn houses, mountains, and everything in their path. Sin, when it sits upon the conscience without repentance, is like the wind in the earth; it will make the heart tremble, so that there shall be no calm, rest, or composure of mind, which would be present if the sin were gone. Of this we read in *Isaiah 33:14*: *The sinners in Zion are terrified; trembling has seized the hypocrites.* The sinners were terrified; those who had guilt upon them, their sins caused terror and fear; and the *hypocrites*, who were internally convicted of their own sins, trembling seized them; but the upright and sincere of heart were not so. This is to show that it is a great hindrance to inward peace and to the assurance of your eternal state if you harbor sin in your conscience without repenting of it. And it is right with God that it is so; because if you keep sin in your hearts—which always fights against Heaven—then it is right with God that He should be at odds with you.

Fourthly, beware that in a state of despondency, you do not cast your eye upon others who are more outstanding in grace than you, and who surpass you in the ways of godliness. It is true, for a person who is given over to spiritual pride and even self-deception regarding their own goodness, it is useful for them to look at those who surpass them in grace, in order to humble them further. But regarding a person who lies under distress of mind and under doubts concerning their eternal state, such a person must not look at others who are more excellent in grace than they are; because that would sooner increase despondency than work any assurance. If you look at the glittering rays of the Sun when it shines in its full strength, the more you look at that rising and shining Body, the more it will blind your eyes, so that you will see only blurry things on the Earth. So it is also with Christians; some Christians shine like so many Suns in the Firmament; their graces shine and glitter so much that if you look at them, they will make your eyes blurry and blind, so that you cannot see those small sparks and glimmers of grace that are in your own hearts. Therefore, if you wish to obtain assurance, beware of casting your eye too much upon those who surpass you in grace.

<column-break/>

Fifthly, beware that you do not make perception and feeling a touchstone <note>A "touchstone" was a stone used to test the purity of gold or silver; here it means a standard for judging one's spiritual state.</note> by which to test your effectual calling; perception and feeling will deceive you in the matter of effectual calling. I may here allude to the passage in the Book of *GENESIS*: you know old *Isaac*, whose eyes were dim, and because of his old age he fell into a mistake through feeling; he had *Jacob* by the hand, and through feeling, he thought it was *Esau*. Beloved, many of us are dim-sighted in our comforts and graces; and if we trust in feeling, we may be deceived just as *Isaac* was. You may think, when you have *Jacob* by the hand (I mean grace in the heart), that it is only an *Esau*—that it is but a castaway. Therefore, beware of making your feeling the touchstone to test your Calling. A child is born, yet it does not know it is born; it lives, yet it does not know it lives; and it is even so: a Christian may be born again, living the life of grace, and yet not be sensible of it.

Sixthly, be diligent to remove this obstacle: namely, **pride** in your gifts and clinging to your graces. That pride and arrogance are not only murderers of comforts, but they likewise murder our graces. If God sees you swelling with pride because you are abundant in grace, He will soon prick that swollen boil. It is the observation of a modern-day theologian <note>Likely referring to a contemporary Puritan or Reformed author.</note> that spiritual elevations of the soul after obtaining assurance inevitably expose a Christian to great despondency or to great sins. Scripture mentions that pride in your gifts is not only an enemy to comfort, but an enemy to grace; not only an enemy to comfort because of grace, but against the actual possession of grace. *Habakkuk 2:4*: *If a man's soul is lifted up, it is not upright in him.* And *James 4:6*: *God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.* So pride is not only an enemy to your comforts, but also to the true obtaining of grace; when the vine-branches grow too luxuriously, they shall be pruned. And thus you have here the first sort of Helps set down; if you wish to obtain assurance, you must be diligent to shun those things that may be obstacles to you in obtaining the assurance of your Calling.

Secondly, the second sort of Helps, if you wish to obtain assurance, is to use diligence in practicing those things which may be aids and advancements in obtaining assurance concerning your effectual calling. I shall mention only six or seven points here.

First, exalt the evidences of faith above present feeling. If you once set yourself to dispute with the Devil, he will over-reason you and stop your mouth. The Devil is a crafty debater; it is not without peril, says *Doctor Preston*, <note>John Preston (1587–1628), an influential English Puritan divine and master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge.</note> with...

# Making your calling sure #

to dispute with the devil; the devil will out-dispute and over-persuade you. It is the work of a Christian to elevate the proofs of faith above their present feelings. Insofar as you wish to obtain assurance, you must do as Abraham, the Father of the faithful, did when he had to believe in a matter which both his feelings and his reason might have told him would never happen. It is said of Abraham in *Romans 4:18-19*: *That he believed in hope against hope.* He elevated faith above feeling. And how was that? God promised Abraham a son; reason and feeling might have said to Abraham: "Abraham, you are a hundred years old, and your wife is ninety-nine; her womb is barren; it is not likely that you shall have children." But Abraham did not reason-cavil <note>The original Dutch *redenkavelde* implies a form of argumentative quibbling or debating against God's word.</note> in this way, but he placed the arguments of faith above his own reason, and elevated the promises and the Word of God, and claimed them for himself; Abraham believed in hope against hope. 

Beloved, you ought to do the same; even though you say that you have a "barren womb," meaning it is not likely that grace shall grow within you, and even though you are old, or weak and fragile Christians, nevertheless elevate the proofs of faith regarding God's love, God's power, God's providence, and God's promises; that is the way to make your comforts clear and full. I may here apply what <term>Foxus</term> <note>Referring to John Foxe (1516–1587), author of *Actes and Monuments* (popularly known as *Foxe's Book of Martyrs*), a famous history of Protestant martyrs.</note> relates in his memorable histories of a godly woman who was called during the reign of <term>Queen Mary</term> <note>Mary I of England (r. 1553–1558), often called "Bloody Mary" by Protestants for her persecution of their faith.</note> before <term>Bonner</term> <note>Edmund Bonner, the Bishop of London, notorious for his role in the interrogation and execution of heretics during the Marian Persecutions.</note> and others who sat in judgment over those of the Religion. They saw that she, although a poor and simple woman, nevertheless held fast to her confession and would not deny her religion. Finally, Bonner sent some learned doctors to dispute with her and to reason-cavil over the details of certain points she held. Seeing them, she warded them off with these words: "Well, you are school-learned men, and you come to dispute; I must tell you plainly, I cannot dispute, but I can burn for my religion." 

Beloved, I would also have you answer the devil in this way when he comes to dispute and bicker with you regarding your comforts: say that you cannot dispute, but that you can believe; and that you expect your help from Jesus Christ, from One who is mighty. Thus, elevate the arguments of faith, and this shall greatly strengthen your comforts. *Luke 8:42*: There came a ruler to Jesus Christ and pleaded with him on behalf of his daughter, who lay dying. And while he was requesting this of Christ, another messenger came to him saying: "Your daughter is dead, do not trouble the Master." What did Christ say when He heard that? *Fear not, only believe.* It was as if He said: feeling and reason might say it was a useless thing to pray to Christ for his daughter since she was dead; but, says Christ, do not bow under feeling and reason; *fear not, only believe,* and the work shall be done. So I say to you: do not consult with flesh and blood, but elevate the proofs of faith above your present feeling, and this is the way to obtain the assurance of your comforts.

<column-break/>

Secondly, **Keep your conscience pure,** so that no sin may harbor there; thus you are on the path to obtaining full comforts. God, says David, will speak peace to His people, but let them not turn again to folly. <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 85:8.</note> It is as if he said: although God speaks of peace and assures you of your forgiveness and salvation, if you nevertheless return to sin, God can speak of breaking your peace and change His friendly countenance into a wrinkled and angry face. Guard yourself against sin, and keep your conscience pure; that is the way to have a firm peace in your heart. *Job 11:14-15*: *If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and do not let injustice dwell in your tents. For then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear.* A remarkable passage! That if you put sin far away, then you shall be secure before God and not fear; that is, you shall not be subject to those fears, doubts, and anxieties to which other men are subject. *Hebrews 10:22*: *Let us draw near to God with a true heart, in full assurance of faith.* Now, what shall a man do to come to God in full assurance? Note the following words: *having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience.* Here is the way: if you are cleansed from an evil conscience, you may come boldly to God in full assurance. On the contrary, alas, if your conscience tells you that you are a fornicator, and that you are a deceiver, and that you are a liar, and that you are a dissolute person, then you cannot come with full assurance; you might come with a sense of <term>presumption</term> <note>original: *laetdunkentheyt*, meaning an arrogant or false sense of confidence in one's standing with God.</note>, but not with the assurance of faith. Therefore, keep your conscience pure from harboring any sin, and that is the way to have a heart full of joy.

Thirdly, **Be diligent to maintain fellowship** with the godly and most experienced Christians among whom you live; this is a very special way to increase your comforts. You read an excellent passage in *2 Corinthians 1:4*: *We are comforted by God,* says the Apostle, *so that we may be able to comfort others with the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted by God.* Godly Christians will comfort you through the same comforts with which they themselves have been comforted. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort. If the godly have any inward comforts from God, they will share their experiences with you and tell you, just as David did in *Psalm 66:16*: *What God has done for my soul.* There is no better way than to maintain fellowship with godly Christians who have knowledge. <term>Mr. Bradford</term> <note>John Bradford (c. 1510–1555), a preeminent English Reformer and martyr who was famously humble and often struggled with his own sense of unworthiness.</note>, that famous martyr who lay in prison for the confession of Christ—the history says that he lay for a long time under the torments of the mind and the terror of conscience, so that he could not find a powerful and clear proof of his effectual calling. Many people came to him and could not set him at rest. But there was a poor weaver, an old and experienced Christian, who used to keep Mr. Bradford company in the prison house. Through constant fellowship with this poor man, he obtained more...

### inward comfort ###

inward comfort than he had ever hoped to hear in all his life. Beloved, I speak this to you to make you strive all the more for the dignity of a **Godly company**; for the more you associate with Christians who enjoy the light of God’s countenance and the steady assurance of His favor, the more you are on a ready path to increase your own comforts and assurance.

**Fourthly**, submit yourself to the judgment of others and be willing to allow them to pass a sentence upon you. When you are asleep or lying in a faint, you cannot tell yourself what you did, but others must tell you; so it may also happen with the Godly. They may be in such a state of **spiritual faintness** that they are not fit to judge their own condition. In such a case, submit yourself to the judgment of others; they may see grace in you when you cannot see it yourself. Thus was <term>Mr. Throgmorton</term> <note>Likely referring to Job Throgmorton (1545–1601), a prominent Puritan activist and suspected author of the Marprelate tracts, known for his spiritual struggles.</note> comforted by the testimony of several Godly Ministers.

**Fifthly**, exercise your grace daily, for that is the way to obtain assurance. The Holy Spirit presents this means in the chapter from which my text is taken: "add grace to grace." I recall that <term>Beza</term> <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin in Geneva.</note> writes concerning this text that in the **Geneva translations**, these words are inserted: *Diligently strive, through good works, to make your calling sure.* Whether this is exactly so or not, I cannot say for certain, but of this I am sure—and the preceding and following parts of the text will clearly confirm it—that the way to make your calling sure is to add grace to grace. For after the Apostle had spoken of adding grace to grace, he introduces this: *Diligently strive to make your calling sure.* This indicates that the more you work upon your grace, the more you shall enjoy comfort.
<margin>Isaiah 32:17</margin>
*Isaiah 32:17: The work of righteousness shall be peace.* Not just the habit, but the **work**; if you work righteousness, and work upon your grace and increase therein, that shall be peace; and the working of the same shall be quietness and assurance forever. So also *John 16:24: The more you pray, the more your joy shall be fulfilled,* so that the more you exercise grace, the more you are on the path to obtaining assurance.

**Sixthly**, if you wish to obtain assurance, spend more time strengthening your **evidences for Heaven** than in calling them into doubt. It is a great fault of many Christians that they spend much time in doubting and not in strengthening their comforts. They persuade themselves that they are unbelieving and say: "Lord, how could I believe? How could I take hold of the promises, being such an unholy and unregenerate creature?" And by this, they persuade themselves so far that they dare not hold fast to Christ, whereas it ought to be your work to bring yourself to Christ through reason as much as you can. Labor to strengthen your comforts, and reason thus: "Why should I not believe in Christ?" So did David in *Psalm 42: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?* Is not the mercy of God greater than the sin in the creature? Is

<column-break/>

there not ripe grace where there is guilt? Are there not mountain-sized mercies where damnation is deserved? You ought to build up your comforts through reasoning, rather than casting them down, and spend more time strengthening them than pulling them into doubt. You would consider a man very foolish who held a **deed** to much land, yet would create difficulties and doubts for himself and use no means to make his right to it secure. And truly, many Christians are just as foolish regarding Heaven; they have, if I may say so, a good warrant and seal that God shall bring them into Heaven, and yet they pull it into doubt and cast themselves into unbelief. Beloved, this ought not to be; you ought much rather to strengthen your comforts than to doubt them.

**Seventhly**, be diligent in a serious consideration of the **Covenant of Grace**. Beloved, all the doubts of a Christian arise from an ignorance of the Covenant of Grace. And so that I may speak a little of this here, I pray you to follow me in considering this Covenant. If you do so, you shall see particular supports within it to hold up your hearts against discouragement, and to strengthen us in a way of assurance regarding your effectual calling.

**First**, the **Covenant of Works** commands perfect obedience upon pain of damnation; but the **Covenant of Grace** commands and accepts an *imperfect* obedience, provided it is sincere. There is your first support.

**Secondly**, the Covenant of Works is not satisfied with good desires unless there are good works; the Covenant of Grace accepts the **good will** and the good desires. When the deed is lacking, it is satisfied with the will in place of the deed.

**Thirdly**, the Covenant of Works demands that you must obey the will of God perfectly in your own person; the Covenant of Grace demands only that you obey it in the **Person of Jesus Christ**. If Christ has obeyed for you, it is accepted, even though you do not do it perfectly yourself.

**Fourthly**, the Covenant of Works demands that you obey the whole will of God through your own strength; the Covenant of Grace accepts it even if it is not our own strength, but the strength of Christ brought forth in the doing of any spiritual work.

**Fifthly**, the Covenant of Works demands the fulfillment of the condition before it gives the promise; just as it says, "Do this and live." You cannot live, says the Covenant of Works, unless you do this. But the Covenant of Grace sets forth the **promises first**, and then shows you the effects of faith. First, accept the promise, and then continue and practice the condition of that promise. First, believe, and then take hold of Christ, even though you are unworthy and a miserable creature. If you, after you have accepted Him, wish to be conscientious in putting those obligations into practice, He shall accept...

### 2 Peter 1:10

->Therefore, Brethren, be the more diligent to make your **Calling** and **Election** sure.<-

<margin>Sermon-</margin>
The doctrine that I still have under hand in the continuation of these words is this: that a Christian ought to apply a very great diligence to make this sure to their souls, that they are **powerfully called** <note>In Reformed theology, "effectual" or "powerful" calling is the internal work of the Holy Spirit that brings a person to saving faith.</note> through Jesus Christ. In the handling of which I have gone over many points and resolved various cases of **conscience**. I have only two more cases to untie, and then I shall wind it all up for a general application.

->Therefore<-

**Fourthly**. When or at what time does God most of all fill the soul of His people with the assurance of their powerful calling? And then:

**Fifthly**, wherein lies the distinction between the assurance that a godly person has of his powerful calling, and those conceited imaginings that the godless have—that they are powerfully called, when they are nevertheless not?

**First**, when or at what time does God give His people the greatest and strongest assurance of their powerful calling? To answer this, I shall comprise all that I have to say under four headings: that God usually gives the strongest assurance to His people in four cases or times.

**First**, after the Lord has greatly humbled the hearts of His people and broken them for sin's sake, then He usually gives the greatest assurance of a person’s powerful calling and of the blessedness of his future state. When you can say with David, *Psalm 38:4*: *There is no peace in my bones because of my sin.* When you can say like the Psalmist, *Psalm 51:10*: *That the bones which you have broken may rejoice,* then it is the time for God to make you break out in joy, when He has broken your hearts with sorrow. God had broken David's heart through the feeling of that impurity he had committed. "O!" says David, "you have broken my heart; now let my broken spirit rejoice"; and God gave him comfort, and restored to him the joy of His salvation. You have a way of speaking in *Psalm 34:19*: *The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and He saves the crushed in spirit.* The Lord is near to them to do what? Not only to deliver them from outward distresses, but also from inward sorrows; to give them inward joy and inward comforts, so that the bones He has broken might rejoice. The Lord is near to those who are of a broken spirit to comfort them. *Luke 4:18*, there it is said that the Spirit of the Lord was upon Christ to do what?

<column-break/>

It was to bind up the brokenhearted and to comfort those who mourn. So also *Isaiah 61:1, 2, 3*: *To comfort those who mourn, and to bind up the brokenhearted.* When the Lord has broken you under sin and humbled you under the sight of your wickedness, then it is the time that God wants to break out toward you with great joy. *Matthew 11:28*: *Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.* The "rest" there does not only refer to our rest in Heaven—that we shall rest there from sin, and rest from sorrow, and rest from temptations—but "I will give you rest" likewise refers to the promise in this life. So, if you are burdened, and you consider your iniquities a burden too heavy for you to bear, then Christ has promised you peace—an inward peace in your conscience, for the assurance of your eternal state, for the assurance that you are called to the state of grace and shall come to the state of glory.

You know that when the earth is plowed, the clods are broken; and the breaking of the clods makes the corn take deeper root, so that it can sprout up with greater growth. It is likewise when you "break up," as the Prophet speaks in *Jeremiah 4*: *The fallow ground of your hearts*; when you break the clods of your heart through **humiliation**, this makes a way for the corn and grain—that precious grain of **assurance**—to sprout and grow to a fuller measure. Thus, you are out of God’s way for having strong assurance if you have never been humbled by the sight of sin. I say it is God’s ordinary way. I do not deny that God can bring you into Heaven even if you do not have the full working and order of the Law upon you; nevertheless, God will never give you such strong assurance and such elevated comforts as He gives to those broken in spirit. Look through the whole of Scripture, and you shall find that those who were most broken in heart were the strongest in comfort. A house that has the deepest foundations seems to be the strongest building, whereas tents and small huts need less grounding in the earth. It is likely that God may make you like a small hut, although not deeply founded; but you shall never be raised up into a beautiful building, to become a strong Christian in the matter of comfort and assurance, if God has not grounded you low in humiliation. It is a true rule in grace: *he who sows in tears shall reap in joy.* The deeper you are in sorrow, the higher you shall be raised in joy.

**Secondly**, after the people of God have been troubled, driven, and made weary by the strong assaults and temptations of the devil, then it is God's time to fill His people with the greatest joy and the most comfort. You know that a water mill goes fastest when the stream runs strongest. Beloved, God lets the stream of temptation run strongly against you to make your mill go—so that you might grind your lusts into dust, and that you might grind your sins like corn over a millstone. God makes the flood strong at the sluice to make your comforts stronger and your graces firmer.

And so that I may speak a little of this here / I pray you / that you follow me / to consider the Covenant of Grace; which if you do / then you shall see five particular supports in the same / to hold up your hearts against despondency / and to strengthen you in a way of assurance regarding your **powerful calling**.

**First**, The **Covenant of Works** commands perfect obedience on pain of damnation / but the **Covenant of Grace** commands and accepts an imperfect obedience / if it is but sincere: there is your first support.

**Secondly**, The Covenant of Works is not satisfied with good desires / unless there are good works; the Covenant of Grace accepts the good will / and the good desires; when the deed is lacking / it is satisfied with the will for the deed.

**Thirdly**, The Covenant of Works requires that you must perfectly obey the will of God in your own person; the Covenant of Grace requires only that you obey it in the **Person of Jesus Christ**; if Christ obeys for you / it is accepted / even though you do not do it.

**Fourthly**, The Covenant of Works requires of you that you obey the whole will of God through your own strength; the Covenant of Grace accepts it / though not our own strength / but the strength of Christ is brought forth in the doing of any spiritual work.

**Fifthly**, The Covenant of Works requires the fulfillment of the condition / before it gives the promise; namely / *do this and live*: you cannot live / says the Covenant of Works / without you doing this: but the Covenant of Grace first proposes the promises / and then it requires the condition: it invites you first / take Christ / and believe first / and then it shows you further the effects of faith. First / accept the promise / and then hold forth and practice the high worth of that promise. First / believe / and then accept Christ / even though you are unworthy / and a miserable creature / if you / after you have accepted Him / will be conscientious / to put into work those obligations that lie upon you / he will accept you.

Now, the more a Christian is shaken by stormy temptations, the more the Lord uses it to ground and establish him more firmly in strong comforts and assurance.

*Thirdly*, when God has some **extraordinary work** that His people must do or suffer, then is the time that He fills His people with the greatest assurance. If God brought His people under outward suffering and gave them inward fear, they would not be fit to undergo that state with joy and patience. Therefore, when He calls His people to any extraordinary measure of suffering, then is the time that God comes to fill them with more than common comforts. I have read in the **Book of Martyrs** <note>Likely referring to 'Foxe’s Book of Martyrs', a famous collection of accounts of Protestant martyrs.</note> of **Mr. Robert Glover**, a renowned man in his generation, who, during the time of his imprisonment, was greatly troubled in his mind by a lack of assurance. I am now as full of joy as my heart can hold." All the time he was in the prison, he was troubled and very distressed, until God brought him to an eminent suffering—namely, to undergo death—and then he was filled with comfort. So I have also read of one **Adolphus Clarenbachius**, who was a man subject to melancholy and lay under many doubts and fears; but as soon as he was brought to the stake, he declared openly to the people: "I have by nature always been of a sad humor, but I confess now before you all, that I think there is no more joyful heart in the whole world than mine." So it is that when they must undergo

The more you slacken in your fellowship, the more you shall wither in your assurance, and the more your comforts shall die. Fellowship with your God has two parts in it. ### Making our Calling Sure

...that he might miss his comfort. A person who has this assurance knows the worth of that assurance; he knows how quickly it is lost and how difficult it is to regain. This makes him very **tender** <note>In this context, 'tender' means sensitive or easily wounded by the presence of sin.</note> toward sin. <margin>2 Corinthians 7:1</margin> *Since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves.* When a godly person knows that God is his God (for that is the promise spoken of in the preceding verse), knowing that he belongs to God and the promises belong to him, this knowledge causes him to cleanse himself from all defilements, both of the **flesh** and of the **spirit**, so that he holds onto no sin in his mind nor any sin in his actions. A person who has this assurance is made very tender toward sin. But now, a person who has **presumptuous imaginations** <note>original: "verwaende inbeeldingen," referring to a false, arrogant self-confidence in one's salvation.</note> of his own goodness—his imaginations make him all the bolder and more reckless to run into sin. He makes no difficulty of sinning, and he does not shrink from falling into one sin today and another tomorrow, practicing godlessness day after day; he is bold and headstrong in every sin. <margin>Jeremiah 3:4, 5</margin> *Will you not from this time cry to me, ‘My Father, you are the guide of my youth’; will he reserve his anger forever, and will he keep it continually?* But what does God say? *Behold, you have spoken and done evil things as much as you could.* It is as if He said: "You cry to me, ‘My Father’; you persuade yourself that God is your Father, and yet you speak and do as much evil as you can." God brands them here as a **conceited people**. To persuade yourself that God is your Father and yet to do as much godlessness as you can—to be drunk as often as you can and to swear as often as you can—alas! you deceive your own heart in this, for God cannot be your Father in that regard. Beloved, I pray you, as we go over these distinctions, that you would lay them upon your own hearts and see if you may be distinguished from these presumptuous imaginations that are now so common in the world.

Secondly, a person who has an **effectual assurance** <note>A 'powerful' or 'working' certainty of faith.</note> of his effectual Calling meets with more attacks and trials from the Devil to damage his peace than other men who have only a counterfeit assurance. Just as you know that those shops which have the best wares and the richest treasures, such as **goldsmiths' shops**, are most subject to theft, while men do not bother with a small, cheap stall. Those ships which are most richly laden are most subject to the peril of **pirates** <note>original: "Zee-roovers"</note> on the sea, while your small boats, laden with goods of less value, escape. So it goes also with Christians. The Christians who are most richly laden with the treasures of assurance, who have that precious jewel in their heart, are most in danger of the Devil’s assaults; he is there like a pirate to set upon them with violence to harm them. The Devil envies those most who have the greatest assurance, so that he never leaves them in peace, but hunts them like a partridge over the mountains through dejection-

<column-break/>

-ness, through suggestions, and through various trials. Through the **fiery arrows** of Satan, through distrust, through cast-in scruples, and through the crafty reflections of fleshly reasoning—through consultations with flesh and blood and through a lack of a comforting feeling. The Devil continually brings these things forward to see if he can dampen their comforts and cause them to **cast away their confidence**, which has a great reward. Therefore, the Apostle commands that Christians should not cast away their boldness (a borrowed way of speaking, as some believe, taken from a ship at sea: when the merchants are at sea and their ship is driven upon the waves by storm and tempest, and it appears they will suffer shipwreck, the ship being heavily laden, they throw their merchandise overboard to save their lives. Now some, by this comparison, believe that the Devil similarly drives a poor soul in the matter of comfort, like a ship driven by the wind on the sea. Now, if you are driven on the sea of trial and on the waves of torments and attacks, **do not throw your merchandise away**; do not throw your comforts away). This indicates that godly people are often attacked and stormed; so that even if the Devil cannot bring you into Hell, he would dearly love for you to have a **Hell in your conscience** as long as you live. He envies not only your blessedness but also your comforts. On the contrary, those people who harbor such imaginations that they are called when they are not—the Devil lulls them to sleep; he leaves them without fear and never disturbs them. <margin>Luke 11:21</margin> *When a strong man, fully armed, guards his palace, his possessions are safe.* That is, when the Devil of Hell has total possession of a man’s soul, he is not tempted by it; his thoughts are at rest. When the Devil sees that a man builds on a sandy and evil foundation, he will never shake it through trial, lest by the shaking the man should wake up to look for a better and lasting good. When the Devil sees you hushed to sleep in a **golden dream** of conceit, he will never wake you through trial, but let you sleep, because he knows that sleep will be a sleep of death. Just like a man who lies down and sleeps on a steep cliff and dreamily enjoys visions of crowns and kingdoms, but jumping up hastily in joy, breaks his neck and rolls into the depths of the sea; so it is with a man who harbors unfounded imaginations of his good state. That which a fleshly man uses as proof that he is in a good state is actually an indubitable demonstration that he is in a bad state. You will see a godless man, when he hears that a godly man is troubled in his mind and wounded in his spirit, he will tell you that he (thank God) has never been troubled since he was born; that the Devil has never made him uneasy, and that he has had a strong faith for as long as he can remember. Alas! Beloved, this is a mournful sign; you make this a sign of your comfort, whereas in truth it is a...

<summary>This page distinguishes true spiritual assurance from false presumption, noting that true assurance leads to a hatred of sin while false assurance leads to recklessness. It also explains that the Devil specifically targets those with genuine faith, whereas he leaves the self-deceived in a "golden dream" of false peace.</summary>

### Of our Powerful Assurance

...is proof of your lack of a firm **assurance** <note>In this context, 'assurance' (Dutch: versekeringe) refers to the internal certainty that one is saved and in a right relationship with God.</note>; for if your assurance were good, the devil would never leave you in peace, but would constantly labor to make you cast away your confidence. But because your assurance is bad, he desires that you cherish it continually. We say that the **oxen** who are fattened in the grassy meadows are closest to the slaughter; while the poor, lean ox, who wears the yoke daily and is beaten, and must work every day, lives long and is in a better state. Those people whom the devil leaves at rest, and never attacks, are like those fat oxen; they never come under the blows and the yoke, and are never disturbed. It is an evidentiary argument that they are near to slaughter and under a great peril of their souls. But those who are under the yoke, who are often attacked, and upon whom the **thorn of Satan** <note>original: "den prickel des Satans," an allusion to the "thorn in the flesh" mentioned by the Apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:7.</note> lies; that is an argument that their comforts are right and their insights are good, because they are so assaulted and attacked by the devil.

Thirdly, true assurance is more or less present in the soul of a person according to whether that person holds more or less **fellowship with God**. If a person lets their walk with God go and becomes careless, clinging to outward things and becoming estranged from God, he will at last become a stranger to himself and likewise to his comforts. But if a person keeps himself close to God and strictly to his duties, so that he can return and bring himself to converse with God in a more constant and earnest manner—being well-prepared and readily practiced in the established **means of grace** <note>term: 'means of grace' (ingestelde middelen van den Godtsdienst), referring to activities like prayer, scripture reading, and the sacraments through which God strengthens faith.</note> so that he can pour out his soul into God’s bosom—that person is on the way to having his comforts increased. On the contrary, those people who have a false comfort and imagination, whether they are much or little with God, it is all the same to them; their comforts are always the same. Come to a person who has false comforts: he is the same at all times; he is in the same thoughts as he was three, four, or seven years before. Ask him in any week of the year, on any day of the week, at any hour of the day, and he will tell you that he has the same comforts and constantly the same evidences: that he has a strong faith in God and has it continually; that he has a strong hope to be saved and has it continually; that he is always the same in his comforts, even though he changes so much in his fellowship with his God. This is proof that his imaginations are false, seeing that the fellowship and the walk of a Christian with God feeds his comforts. Now, just as the body is weaker or stronger depending on how much or little it is fed, so it is with your comforts; as much as they are nourished by your walk with God, so much they become weak or strong. Now let a godless person become ever so vile and ever so sinful, it never breaks his peace; he always has hope and assurance, and he constantly trusts in God even though he always sins. This is proof that his comforts are unstable. You have a **vivid example** <note>original: "levende schilderye," literally a 'living painting' or 'vivid picture.'</note> of this in <margin>Micah 3:11</margin>. *Their heads judge for bribes, and their priests teach for hire, and their prophets divine for money; yet they lean upon the Lord,*

<column-break/>

*saying, Is not the Lord in the midst of us?* That is to say, even though they had those sins among them and walked in such a way, nonetheless they wanted to hope in God to be saved after all this. Therefore, beloved, you shall find that God will fail you; although He will never fail an assured Christian, nonetheless He will fail that person who leans on Him when he does not belong to Him. When you neglect your walk with God and sail forth into an abyss and sea of pleasures, and yet can constantly say that you remain the same in your comforts and the same in your imaginations, it is proof that all your comforts are false and your insights are unstable.

Fourthly, the **effectual assurance** of your state supports the soul under the greatest sorrow and suffering that it can encounter here in the world. <margin>Hebrews 10:34</margin> *They took the plundering of their goods with joy, knowing in themselves that they had a better and an enduring substance in heaven.* What made them so joyful when they saw their houses plundered before their eyes and their goods taken from them, other than this: that they knew in themselves and had assurance in their own hearts that Christ was theirs, and that Heaven was theirs; and this made them endure the plundering of their goods with joy. So also in <margin>Psalm 119:50</margin> *This is my comfort in my misery, for your promise has made me alive.* That is: it supports my heart when I am oppressed, that I have a word to build upon, that I have assurance, that I have a share in the promise to build upon; this quickens me and supports me in my sorrow. So also in <margin>Psalm 119:81</margin> *My soul faints for your salvation, but I hope in your word.* That is: I have built hope and trust on your Word, and that restrains me from fear, from fainting, and from despondency under my oppression. Likewise in <margin>Isaiah 33:24</margin> *No inhabitant shall say, "I am sick"; for the people who dwell there shall have forgiveness of iniquity.* The sense of the forgiveness of their sins will take away the sense of outward suffering. Beloved, assurance will hold up the heart and support it under all sorrows. Assurance in a Christian is like **oil**. Now, if oil stands in a sea of water, the oil will never stay beneath but will always float on top; so also this oil of comfort and this oil of assurance will lift you up to the very top, even though you might be thrown into a flood of anxieties and a sea of sorrows. I have read in the writings of **Latimer** to **Ridley** <note>Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley were famous English Protestant martyrs burned at the stake in 1555. Their correspondence from prison was widely read as a model of Christian courage.</note>, those renowned martyrs, a remarkable saying regarding this. "Sometimes," he says, "when I live in a settled and steadfast assurance regarding the state of my soul, it seems to me then that I am as bold as a **lion**; I can laugh in all anxieties, no oppression makes me fear. But when I am darkened in my comforts, then I am of such a fearful spirit that I would likely run into a **mouse hole**." Beloved, so it goes with the godly; when they lack the assurance of their state and the certainty of their calling, every oppression strikes them down and every anxiety makes them terrified. Oh! But when they can...

It also highlights how this assurance provides supernatural strength during persecution, as seen in the examples of the martyrs Latimer and Ridley.</summary>
