### Making your Calling Sure

...can live in a settled assurance of their portion in Christ, and of their hope through him; they are as bold as lions, and they are sustained with comfort amidst all the sorrows and sufferings they encounter. But now, those people who have false <term>imaginations</term><note>The Dutch "inbeeldinge" refers to a self-deceiving or illusory sense of security, often translated as "delusions" in 17th-century religious texts.</note>, their imaginations cannot support their hearts in times of oppression, loss, or distress; and because it is not a soul-saving and inward comfort, it can never produce an inward peace. The comforts of the ungodly, when they come to suffer, are like a garment that is poorly woven. Let a man wearing a well-made garment be caught in a heavy rainstorm, and it will never shrink; but a garment that is poorly woven, once it is in a heavy rain, it shrinks immediately. It is the same with a man's comforts; bring comforts that are "well-wrought" into a rainstorm of oppression, and that man shall not shrink under his affliction. But bring a poorly-wrought and unstable assurance, and it will shrink, fail, and withdraw, and it will not support the heart under the sorrows and the sufferings that arise. The boastful <note>Henry Pendleton was a 16th-century English clergyman who famously told a soon-to-be martyr that he would "fry his fat flesh" before recanting his Protestant faith, yet he did recant as soon as he faced personal danger.</note> Pendleton boasted that his fat flesh would roast in the fire before he would forsake his religion; yet when he was put to the test, he fell away immediately.

<margin>Galatians 2:20</margin>
Fifthly, a firm assurance, wherever it is found, makes the heart very humble toward God and man, and makes a man very small in his own eyes. There you have a <term>mark</term><note>A "mark" (merck-teycken) is a diagnostic sign used by believers to test whether their faith is genuine.</note>; *I live,* says Paul, *by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.* Here is his assurance. What then? does it make Paul puffed up? No, indeed; it makes him very small: *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me.* Paul comes to himself—I live—no, not so; it is not I who lives, but Christ who lives in me. See how Paul was delivered from a bold pride and an uplifting of the spirit within himself. "It is not I who lives." The thoughts of his comforts make him come to himself and appear small in his own eyes. In contrast, alas, false imaginations puff up the soul with pride, and make a man boastful and high-minded, so that they cry out, just as Jehu did to Jonadab, "Is your heart right, as my heart is?" "Come and see my zeal for the Lord." They make him bold, just as Jehu was in his false imaginations.

<margin>Psalm 26:3, verse 4, etc.</margin>
Sixthly, firm comforts and a powerful assurance stir the soul to walk before God in the way of holiness. *Your lovingkindness is before my eyes;* that is, I am as certain of God's lovingkindness toward me as if I saw it with my own eyes. What then? *And I walk in your truth.* I walk before you with a holy and upright heart; I do not sit with vain persons (verse 4, etc.). So you see that David wanted to walk in the way of holiness because he had within himself a proof and assurance of God’s love.
<margin>1 John 3:3</margin>
So also, *everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure;* that is, a person who carries the hope and

<column-break/>

thoughts of Heaven—his hope makes him a Christian who seeks to purify his own heart and to be holy, just as Christ is holy. That is the nature of true assurance.
<margin>If you say "it is enough," you have perished. <note>original: "Si dixeris sufficit, periisti"</note> Augustine, Sermon 18 on the words of the Apostle.</margin>
But now, regarding false assurance: someone who has it does not look toward holiness at all. He thinks that he is "well enough," that he has obtained that which every wise man would trust in, without bothering himself any further. Indeed, he is so far from binding himself to walk in the way of holiness that he would rather use it as a reason to walk in the way of license and wickedness; because grace is "abounding," therefore he is "abounding" in sin. This is the evil use that false comfort makes of the grace of God. And therefore, Beloved, look through your hearts. Does the comfort and the assurance that you hope to have and enjoy make you strive more after holiness? So that you can say, just as David did: *I see your lovingkindness before me, and therefore I shall love your ways and hate sin?* Or can you say that you have comforts, and therefore you want to run into sin and wallow in ungodliness? It is a proof that your comforts are not true comforts.

Seventhly, true assurance is obtained and maintained through great diligence and industry. The best things are the hardest to obtain and the most difficult to keep. Stones can be found in all places; but before you can obtain Gold, you must delve deep and labor to dig deep into the bowels of the Earth. Weeds grow easily, but the beautiful flowers in your garden must be watered often and carefully looked after, or else they will not grow. Beloved, this weed of a false imagination and assurance is a weed that will grow under every hedge and wax in every garden without any looking after; whereas, alas, the flower of true comfort and soul-saving assurance is so difficult to make grow. And when it has grown, it is difficult to keep it so that it does not wither and wilt. Assurance costs a man many years of waiting, the shedding of many tears, and much praying before he can obtain or maintain it; whereas, alas, false assurance is easily obtained and easily maintained. A man can obtain self-conceit without any effort at all; the devil will incite you to both—to the obtaining and the maintaining of it. Therefore, you who so easily obtain your comforts without prayers, and keep your comforts without effort, you may be certain that they are but false comforts.

<margin>Isaiah 57:19</margin>
Eighthly, true assurance is obtained through the Word and is founded upon the Word. It is obtained through the Word: *I create the fruit of the lips; Peace, peace to him who is far off, and to him who is near.* (Isaiah 57:19). The "fruit of the lips"—that is, the fruit of the Minister's preaching. The Word which proceeds from the lips of a godly Minister, God has ordained and made as the way to work and create "Peace, peace"—that is, a firm peace in the hearts of his people. And the same...

### 2 Peter 1:10

Therefore, Brothers, be all the more diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.

<margin>Preaching.</margin>
The doctrine that I still have at hand, drawn from these words, is this: that Christians ought to apply a very great diligence to make this sure to their souls, that they are powerfully called through Jesus Christ. In the pursuit of this, I have handled several parts; I come now to the conclusion of this doctrine to make a special use of all that has been said, and then to pass over to that other part: to make your Election sure. The <term>use</term><note>In 17th-century sermons, "use" refers to the practical application of a theological point.</note> of which I shall speak will only be a use of admonition and instruction. My admonition will be directed to two sorts of people. First, to those who enjoy and are assured of their powerful Calling; who are called and are certain that they are called. Second, to those who have sometimes enjoyed this assurance, but have now lost or obscured the comforting feeling of their assurance. In these two main sections, I shall expand my reasoning.

<margin>Application.</margin>
First, the admonition and counsel that I shall give is to those who are assured of their powerful Calling; who have done that work which the Apostle commands here, who have made their Calling sure, and through an indubitable proof can also say so. And these I would advise toward three special duties.

First, you ought to be instructed to use your assurance rightly.

Second, to preserve the same carefully.

Third, to apply your assurance daily. This is a profound work that lies upon you who come to enjoy that precious jewel of assurance.

First, you must take care that you use and maintain your assurance rightly. A thing that is hardly obtained, if the same is not well-managed, a person can easily lose it. To use assurance well is the greatest art of a Christian. And so that I may speak modestly regarding this instruction, I shall set down eight points, being accompanying matters, or gracious qualities, which must accompany you in the state of assurance; as:

First, you must use your assurance with humility, if you are to use it 

<column-break/>

well. Assured Christians must be humbled Christians. The higher you are in comforts, the lower you ought to be in spirit. You know the fullest <term>ears of grain</term><note>The original uses "Coren-ayren," referring to wheat or similar cereal crops.</note> hang their heads lowest to the ground, while the light and flaunting weeds that have nothing of value in them stretch their heads high. Assured Christians are like your full and ripe ears of grain; the fuller they are of this fruit of the Spirit—assurance—the lower they hang (and ought to hang) their heads. Empty vessels boom <note>Meaning they make a loud, hollow noise when struck.</note>, but the full ones, even though you strike them, give no sound. It is those Christians who are most empty of faith, and most empty of assurance, who make the most noise and are most proud of their gifts and graces; whereas assured Christians, who are like full vessels of the best liquid, make the least noise. The more God has filled you with this comfort, the more you ought to appear in humility, just as Paul did when he said, *Christ loved me and gave himself for me*; when he was fullest of comforts, then he was most filled with humility, and said, *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me.*

Second, you must use your assurance with a high valuation of God's comforts in you. A person who has received a benefit, if he does not value it, it causes the person who gave it to him to repent of his gift, or to take it away. When David had assurance, notice how he valued it: Psalm 63:4 <note>Original: "Uwe goedertierentheydt is beter dan het leven." In modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 63:3: "Because your steadfast love is better than life."</note>. *Your lovingkindness is better than life.* He valued the comforts of his God and the light of God’s countenance better than life. And Psalm 4:7 <note>In English Bibles, Psalm 4:6-7.</note>. *Lift up the light of your countenance upon me, and that shall gladden me more than the time when their grain and wine increased.* David valued the comforts of God's Spirit more than any other comfort in the world. Assured Christians who use assurance rightly must value it highly and hold it worthy. The reason is that you will not easily part with your assurance for a base, minor pleasure or an unproductive sin, if you once know the value and worthiness of it.

Third, your assurance must cause your heart to be <term>weaned</term><note>To "speenen" (wean) means to lose the taste for or dependency on worldly things in favor of spiritual ones.</note> from the comforts of this World. 2 Corinthians 4, the last verse compared with Chapter 5:1. The Apostle says there: *We do not look at the things which are seen, which are temporary.* What made the Apostle not look at worldly things? He gives the reason. *For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were broken, we have a building from God, eternal in the heavens.* It is as if he said: that is the reason why we do not notice the world as worldly people do; for we know, when we leave the world, that we have a Heaven to enter into. The assurance of the happiness of their future state makes them esteem the world little, as a thing not worthy to be gazed upon; people who have assurance can say just as Philip said to Christ, John 14:8. *Lord, show us the Father,* says Philip, *and it is enough for us.* Thus says a gracious heart,

Lord / O sweet Jesus / only show us Your favor; only assure my soul / that Your Father is a reconciled Father to me in Yourself; that He is my Father as well as Your Father; only show me the Father / and it is enough for me; though I have little or nothing in the world / it shall be enough for me. Gracious hearts / who live there in the enjoyment of <term>assurance</term><note>A theological term for the internal certainty that one is saved and in God's favor.</note> / they ought to live with a heart weaned from the comforts of this world. People who have tasted Honey or some other sweet morsels / they have no taste for all other things / even if they are pleasant in themselves: So also people who have tasted of this Honey of God's love / and the sweetness of this grace of assurance; it shall make all the things of this world tasteless to them / no matter how pleasant and good they are in themselves. If a person looks into the Sun / it blinds his eyes / so that he cannot distinguish the colors around him; so also he who beholds the light of God's countenance / cannot look upon the things here below. I may here cast my eye upon that place in Luke 5:39. *No one,* says Christ, *who drinks old wine, immediately desires new; for he says, the old is better.* His meaning is this / no one / who has had a taste of Christ / and communion and company with Christ / and has lain under the ministry of Jesus Christ; no one who has drunk this old wine / shall say / the new is better; that having other comforts and other pleasures is better; no one shall say that / says Christ. And so He compares His ministry / and His teaching / and the comfort that God's people have through it / to old wine: Beloved / so I say / people who have drunk a draught of this Wine of comforts / and who are firmly assured / and have had a proof that the Lord is gracious, none of them shall then say that the world and the comforts here below are better. No indeed / the assurance of God's love ought to wean a person's heart from all the comforts of the world. Just as the old Jacob said / when in his great old age he saw his son Joseph / after he had often prayed and shed many a tear; *it is enough / my son Joseph still lives.* Just as Jacob conducted himself regarding Joseph / so ought a Christian to conduct himself regarding Christ. If he can say / my Joseph, my Jesus lives in my heart; when I have Him then I have enough; this comfort ought to lift up his Spirit. Paul, when he was caught up into the third Heaven / was so Ravished that he did not know whether it was in the Body or not; so are the people of God caught up with Heavenly comforts / that they are not minded toward these earthly things.

<margin>To whom Christ begins to grow sweet, for him the world must necessarily become bitter. <note>original: "Cui incipit dulcescere Christus, ei necesse est amarescere mundum."</note></margin>
It is the saying of Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential medieval abbot and mystic.</note> / to whom Jesus Christ has once become sweet / so that he can taste the sweetness of His love / and the sweetness of His mercy / the true sweetness of the love of Christ shall make the world bitter to him.

Fourthly, You must use your assurance with a tenderness of Conscience against sin. Assured Christians ought to be tender, conscientious Christians. Psalm 85:9. *God shall speak peace to His People,* note the duty; *but let them not turn again to folly.* They must not run back into

<column-break/>

sin / they must be tender regarding sin / and then God shall speak peace to His people. Sin (as I once told you) shall be like the wind in the bowels of the earth. The Philosophers say that earthquakes / and eruptions / are caused by the wind that is locked in the bowels and hollows of the earth / which having no place to come out / turns mountains and houses upside down: Beloved, sin in the heart shall do likewise / it shall make it tremble and shake if it is in there; it shall make the grave of your comforts / and the resurrection of your fears. Therefore Christians who are assured / they must guard themselves from sin / if they wish to keep their comforts / they must guard their hearts / so that sin is not received into their Consciences. Beloved, those who are assured Christians / they know how difficultly they obtained this assurance / and know how sweetly they enjoy this assurance / and that shall make them very tender / so that they do not lose for a minor craving a thing that was so hard-won and is so sweetly enjoyed; so that they do not lose their previous evidences / and bring their previous terrors back to life.

Fifthly, Your assurance must be used with patience in bearing any outward affliction / that you might meet in the world. Assured Christians must be patient Christians / Hebrews 10:34. *They took the plundering of their goods with joy, knowing that they had a better and lasting possession in the heavens;* and that makes the Saints of God disdain and despise all loss / that they meet in the world. Take a person who was at Sea / and he had precious Jewels and Pearls with him / if that person could only be assured that he would keep his own life and his Jewels / even if he lost the small chest and the box / that would not much upset him: you who are assured of Heaven / you can never lose that Pearl / your soul; you might lose the shell / your life; you might lose the chest / but you shall never lose the Jewel; and shall that upset you? If you are an assured Christian / be assured that whatever storm of temptation reaches you / you shall only lose the box / and never the Pearl. This ought therefore to make assured Christians patient Christians / whatever they might undergo here in the world. I have read a Story in the memorable history of Foxe <note>John Foxe's "Actes and Monuments," popularly known as the Book of Martyrs.</note> / of a woman / who when she came to be examined for her Religion before Bonner, that bloody Bishop <note>Edmund Bonner, the Bishop of London under Queen Mary I, known for his harsh persecution of Protestants.</note>; he threatened her / that he would take away her husband from her, so she said / Christ is my husband; I shall take away your child: Christ / she said / is better to me than ten sons; I shall rob you / he said / of all your outward comforts; yes but / she said / Christ is mine / and you cannot rob me of Him. These thoughts sustained the woman's heart / in the robbing of everything / and the taking away of everything / that nevertheless Christ was hers / and that they could not take Him away from her. O Beloved, when your soul lives in the assurance of God's love and of your calling to grace and glory; this shall make you wonderfully patient to bear whatever you might yet [suffer] here in the world.

# From our powerful [assurance]

Meanwhile, a human being—a Christian—who knows that God is his Father, who has not only the crumbs of outward blessings but whole pieces of inward heart-comforts, and who can drink from a draught of inner solace; who knows that he has a God and Heaven, that he has Christ and Glory; yet he cannot be as cheerful as a poor little bird. Truly, it is a striking reflection. Often, the people called by Jesus Christ, who have a foundation and assurance of their eternal happiness through Him, still cannot be as joyful as a poor little bird. The birds in the morning hours will sweetly warble and sing as if nothing weighed on their hearts, while a Christian is mournful and wearying <note>The original Dutch *vermoept* likely implies moping or wasting away one's life.</note> his life in discontent and sadness. This does not befit a Christian. Assured Christians <note>In this context, "assurance" refers to the deep spiritual certainty that one is saved and loved by God.</note> ought to be cheerful Christians.

Ninthly, assured Christians ought to be thankful Christians. For to give a person only a promise is worthy of gratitude, but when someone not only gives that promise but also assures that he will fulfill it, that is worthy of even greater gratitude. Beloved, if God had only promised you Heaven and given no assurance of it, it would be worthy of gratitude. But when God gives you His impressed seal, which seals you until the day of redemption, and when God gives you an assurance in your own heart that you shall go to Heaven and go to God, this ought to make you live much more for God in your spirit. It is the saying of David: *My soul praises the Lord for His wonderful loving-kindness.* You have loving-kindness, and you have wonderful loving-kindness; my soul praises God for the same. David did not want to withhold God’s praise, seeing that God did not withhold David’s heart-comforts. In Heaven we shall break out in wonder because we possess good things; here we ought to break out in thanksgiving because we have them in expectation. Thus I have finished the first part of my instruction to you who are assured Christians: that you ought to labor to use your assurance rightly.

<margin>It is no less a virtue to guard what has been acquired than to seek it. <note>Original Latin: *Non minor est virtus quam quærere parta tueri*, a line from the Roman poet Ovid.</note></margin>

Secondly, all you who are assured Christians ought to be instructed to carefully keep and preserve your assurance. It is no less an art, says the poet, to preserve a virtue than to obtain it. It is said of Hannibal <note>Hannibal Barca (247–181 BC), the Carthaginian general famous for his military genius, who won many battles against Rome but was criticized for not capitalizing on his victories to win the war.</note> that he was a skilled soldier in winning victories, but had no understanding of how to keep them once they were won. The same may be said of us: Christians can obtain assurance, but they have no understanding of how to keep it once they have obtained it. I must therefore press this point now, so that you might be careful to preserve your assurance. And to speak of this, I shall set down two parts: that in order to keep your assurance, there are some things you must do, and some things you must shun and guard yourself against.

<column-break/>

First, there are some things you must do, and these I shall summarize under two or three main points.

First, in order to keep your assurance, you must keep yourself very close in fellowship with God, practicing the duties of godliness. The more you keep grace, the more you will keep your comforts. And so that I may expand on this instruction here, I shall summarize these duties under four main points and show you from Scripture that keeping close to God in the use of these four duties will be a ready way to keep your assurance within you.

First of all, keep yourself close to God in the duty of prayer. John 16:24. *Pray*, says Christ, *and your joy shall be full.* Pray, that your joy may be fulfilled; indicating that if you keep yourself close to God in the duty of prayer after receiving assurance, your souls shall be made full and complete with joy.

Secondly, keep yourself close to God in the duty of frequently reading God's Word. Through frequent reading of the Word, you will often encounter promises and supports for your comfort. This is the reason that people diminish in comfort: because they do not read God's Word frequently. You cannot read a single chapter without finding there a support for your faith and a prop for your assurance. Holding steadfastly to the Word is the way to preserve your assurance, 1 John 5:13. *These things have I written to you who believe in the name of the Son of GOD, that you may know that you have eternal life.* These things I have written to you, not only so that you might have life, but so that you might know it. Through reading the writings of John, John tells them they could better know that they would live in eternity and be eternally blessed. Keep yourself close to God in the reading of His written Word, and that will be of great use. Since promises are spread through the "veins" of the Scripture, you can hardly read a passage of Scripture without there being a promise or a support for your faith in one way or another.

Thirdly, keep yourself close to God in a constant, conscientious hearing of His Word; and this is a great means to obtain assurance, Luke 1:76. *You shall be called a Prophet of the Most High, for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare His ways.* That is, you shall go to prepare the hearts of the people so that they may receive Jesus Christ who follows after you. This was spoken of John the Baptist. And what was the effect of hearing John preach? *To give His people knowledge of salvation, in the forgiveness of their sins*; not only to give them salvation, but to give them knowledge and assurance of this salvation. Do lead your life under the ministry of the Word, and under the ministry of John the Baptist, who preached repentance and humility <note>The original Dutch *bernede-ringhe* likely refers to *vernedering*, meaning humiliation or abasement before God.</note>; for that is the ministry which will give the greatest assurance of your salvation.

Fourthly, keep yourself in fellowship with God in a daily testing and examination...

# Making your calling sure.

...searching of your own hearts; Galatians 6:4. <note>The author quotes: "For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself. But let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone."</note> If someone thinks they are something when they are nothing, they deceive themselves; but let everyone test their own work, and then they shall have glory in themselves. That is, let a person examine themselves and test their heart; this shall be a means to work joy in the heart, so that they shall have comfort and joy within themselves in the assurance of their blessedness. Beloved, what is the reason that you do not maintain your assurance? The reason is because you do not keep yourself close to God in these holy duties of communion; you do not keep yourself near to God in prayer, in reading the Word, and in the searching of your own hearts—in the testing of your comforts and of your own state—and that is the reason that you are not more assured and firm.

Secondly, if you wish to maintain your comforts, then keep your Conscience <term>Conscience: In this period, the conscience was viewed as a "witness" or internal judge that reflected one's standing before God.</term> clean from harboring the guilt of sin; Job 11:14-15. If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away: if sin is in your conduct, away with it. Let there be no sin in your heart, nor in your house; then shall you lift up your face without spot, and shall be steadfast and shall not fear. This shall quiet your spirit and protect your heart from fear, and it will keep you in a firm assurance if you keep your conscience clean.

Thirdly, if you wish to maintain your assurance, gather and heap together all the experiences that you have had from God in your heart in times past. *I considered the days of old,* Psalm 77:6 <note>Original: "I have considered the days of old, the years of ancient times."</note>. Reflect on all the experiences you have had of God, of Christ, and of your own grace, and of the fruits of God’s Spirit in your own soul; and that shall wonderfully uphold your assurance. Romans 5:4, the Apostle tells us there: *experience works hope.* The more experienced you are, and the more you heap your experiences together, the more you strengthen your hope; and the more hope is strengthened, the more assurance is obtained. These are the things you must put into practice, if you wish to maintain the assurance of your powerful calling in your hearts.

Secondly, there are some things which you must shun and of which you must beware, if you wish to make the assurance in your hearts lasting. And these I shall comprise under six headings.

First, beware that you do not give yourself over and wallow in fleshly joys and pleasures. There is nothing in the world that consumes spiritual joy and that powerful assurance in your hearts more than giving yourself too much to fleshly joy and voluptuous pastimes, which drag the heart away. The more your joy runs into that channel of fleshly pleasures, the less it runs toward God and toward the comforts that are above; godly sorrow is the seed of spiritual joy.

Secondly, beware of the sin of worldly-mindedness, if you wish to maintain your comforts. There is nothing in the world that dispels your comforts more than an earthly mind which constantly gapes at the things of the world. What the Philosophers say of the eclipse of the sun—

<column-break/>

—that it is caused by the intervention of the Moon between the Sun and our sight, is true in this case. The Moon is a symbol of the world. If the world comes between Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, and our sight, it will darken our vision of Jesus Christ and bring an eclipse upon our comforts and graces. Those people who dig deep into the bowels of the earth are often smothered and stifled by the vapors that rise from the Earth; so it is also with Christians—those who are always gaping at and rooting around the things of the world. It is a thousand to one if a vapor does not rise from those worldly things that smothers their comforts and extinguishes their graces; the world pierces through with sorrow, therefore your joy must necessarily stifle. A candle, though it may shine before everyone's eyes, if you place it under the earth (even if there is no gust of wind), the vapors will stifle the light of the flame. Beloved, though you shine like candles in your comforts, if you bring them under the Earth, a clod of Earth will stifle your candle and dampen your comforts. There is nothing that leads a Christian to a greater loss of their assurance than worldly-mindedness.

<margin>2 Peter 1:11.</margin>
Thirdly, guilty slothfulness in the duties of Religion. If you become sluggish in your duties, you shall become sluggish in your comforts; few duties and few comforts go together. If someone loosens the rigging of his ship and lets down the sails, that ship cannot move forward with a swift motion, especially if the wind and the tide are against it; the ship must necessarily go backward. Believers who are assured Christians are like a ship under sail; they go against wind and tide, against nature and against corruption, against temptations, against the devil, and against everything. Now, if you loosen your sails and become slothful in your duties, you shall soon become weak in your comforts. Whatever waits upon your graces and relaxes your duties will diminish your assurance and darken your comforts; and therefore, beware of sloth in your duties: Oh! do not diminish your work when you have the greatest encouragement.

Fourthly, beware of spiritual pride. If you once begin to admire yourself, then you lose yourself. If you are once proud of your graces, it is a provocation for God to take away your comforts and cause you to lose your graces—I mean to lose them not in their essence, but in the comfort and exercise of them. Pride is a great murderer of a Christian’s comfort.

<margin>Ephesians 4:30.</margin>
Fifthly, beware of grieving the Spirit of God; *grieve not the Holy Spirit,* says the Apostle, *whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.* The Spirit of God is a sealing Spirit; Oh! do not grieve this Spirit. The Spirit deals with us just as we deal with Him; if we grieve the Spirit of God, God will visit you, and your spirits shall be grieved, so that you shall not maintain the joys of the Lord in your hearts in assurance of...

# Of our powerful calling

...His love and favor toward you. You read in Isaiah 63:10: *They have grieved his holy Spirit, therefore he turned to be their enemy—he himself fought against them.* <note>original: "Sy hebben sijnen heyligen Geest smerten aenghedaen, daerom is hy haer in een vyant verkeert..."</note> Beloved, although God may be your friend, he shall nonetheless be angry with you as an enemy and seem to fight against you as far as you grieve his Spirit. If you grieve God’s Spirit, God shall grieve your spirit; and when your spirit is grieved, you must necessarily lose your **consolations**. <term>Consolations: Internal feelings of peace, joy, and spiritual security provided by the Holy Spirit.</term>

Finally, beware of the sins of **hypocrisy**. False grace shall bring forth a false joy. False hearts must necessarily have false comforts. You shall never retain true comfort as long as you have an unsound heart. The upright of heart shall leap for joy, so that they shout for joy upon their beds; they shall do that, but the hypocrites shall not. Beware therefore of that sin, and then you are on the path to preserving your assurance.

### 2 Peter 1:10

->Therefore, Brothers, be all the more diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.<-

<margin>11th Sermon.</margin>
The doctrine which I still have at hand is this: that Christians ought to apply a very great diligence to make this sure to their souls, that they are effectively called through the power of Jesus Christ. <term>Effectual calling: A theological concept where God's internal invitation to salvation is so powerful that the person inevitably responds with faith.</term> In the handling of which I have come to a "use of instruction" for those who are assured of their powerful calling, and I gave them three instructions. First, that you must use your assurance rightly. Secondly, preserve it carefully. Thirdly, that you must apply your assurance daily; of which last one I still have to treat. And regarding this third instruction to apply your assurance daily, I shall give you only three main points: which, if you make use of them, you may apply your assurance every day and bring the same from a small to a great measure. Specifically:

First, if you wish to do that, then apply your graces. The more you increase in grace, the more you shall grow in comfort. Grace and comfort are **Twins**, so that the more the one grows, the better the other increases. From this you read that in the greeting of every Epistle, the Apostle sets those two together: *grace and peace be multiplied unto you in Christ Jesus,* 1 Corinthians 1:3. <note>The author likely refers to the standard Pauline greeting found across the epistles.</note> Wherein the Apostle makes the multiplication of grace to be the multiplication of peace. The more you multiply and grow in grace, the more you shall increase your peace—the inward peace of the conscience: they are both joined together. You have a Scripture passage, 2 Peter 1:5, 11, compared together: *add to your faith virtue, etc.* The Apostle urges there our diligence to add grace upon grace; that is, to apply grace. And what shall follow? Verse 11: For doing that, you shall

<column-break/>

never stumble; for so an entrance shall be richly provided for you into the everlasting Kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. You shall not only go into Heaven, but an entrance shall be richly provided for you to come therein; you shall have an abundance of assurance and inward peace before you arrive there. And to give you a particular instruction here, there are principally these three graces that you must put to work.

First, put to work the grace of **humility**. <term>Humility: Often translated as 'vernederinge,' meaning a lowliness of mind or self-abasement before God's majesty.</term> Isaiah 57:15. The Lord promises there to revive the spirit of the humble. It is a special promise to that grace: that God shall revive you, and give you, if you have the same, a new life. The "reviving" there is not understood as the first life of grace, but as a life of comfort. They had grace before, but God would give them a life of comfort; he shall renew your comforts to you if you are a humble people. For this reason it says in James 4:6: *The Lord gives grace to the humble.* Yea, *He gives more grace.* The Lord gives more grace to a humbled person than to anyone in the world. Now, the more grace you have, the more comfort you must necessarily have. Humility is a foundation of greater grace, therefore it must necessarily be a foundation of greater comfort. That building whose foundation lies lowest is among all the most beautiful and finest buildings above the earth; so also those Christians who lay a foundation in humility, they are likely to be built up into a very beautiful building in comfort.

Secondly, put to work the grace of **faith** in believing, and that is the way to increase comfort, 1 Peter 1:8: *In whom, though now you see him not, yet believing, you rejoice with a joy unspeakable and full of glory.* Although they never saw Christ, yet believing in Christ and putting their faith to work, they had not only an ordinary measure of comfort, but they had more comfort in their hearts than they could express with their tongues: They rejoiced with an unspeakable and glorious joy. So also Romans 15:13: *Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Spirit.* Believing makes you full of all joy, and makes you abound in the same. The more you are in believing, the more you shall be in assurance.

Thirdly, put to work the grace of **love** toward Jesus Christ. John 14:23: *If a man love me, my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.* If you begin the love toward Jesus Christ, God the Father and God the Son shall make their dwelling in your hearts. Now, he must necessarily be a comforted Christian who has such good guests as God the Father and Jesus Christ to come to him and make their dwelling with him. Just as you know, to your friend whom you love, and you know that he loves you, you shall share all your secrets: so shall God the Father, if he knows that you are his friend and sees that you love him, he shall [share] all his hid-

# Making your calling sure.

...make consolations available to you; you shall not lack consolations if you increase in love for Jesus Christ.

**Fourth,** put into practice the grace of **Godly sorrow**; <note>Godly sorrow: A theological term for "repentance," referring to a deep sadness for one's sins rooted in love for God rather than just fear of punishment.</note> you shall never find sweeter music in consolation than when you lie down in tears. Just as the sound of a trumpet is never more pleasant than when played upon the water, so too when God sees the water of repentance and Godly sorrow flowing from you, then you are likely to hear the sweetest melody in the understanding of God’s love; *Psalm 126: Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.* You shall have not only a little, but a handful of joy; just as reapers cut down whole handfuls of corn. And as you know it is with seed—even if you sow but one grain of corn, a dozen grains can come from that one seed. So also, if you sow but a little Godly sorrow, one grain of Godly sorrow can be a root of a great deal of spiritual joy.

<margin>The Spirit of God is a delicate matter. <note>original Latin: "Res delicata est spiritus Dei"</note></margin>
**Second,** if you wish to properly establish your assurance, maintain a clean **conscience**, both before God and man. A good conscience is a continual feast, *Proverbs 15:15.* I may say of assurance, just as an ancient Father says of the Holy Spirit and its consolations: the Spirit of God is a delicate matter; every sin will hold back the consolations of the Spirit. Now, if you harbor sin in your conscience, you shall never thrive in consolation; every sin will restrain the comforting movements [of the Spirit]. And just as philosophers say that when the air is foggy, it arises from the vapors that exhale from the earth, making the air as misty as it is; so also it is the impurity drawn from our earthly hearts that creates such a foggy mist between our consolations and us, and between God and us. You must keep your conscience clean, otherwise you shall never keep the heavens clear. Heaven will be clouded if the heart is impure. *Job 11:14, 15.* If there is wickedness in your hand, put it far away; if there is sin in your conscience, do not harbor it, for then you shall lift up your face without blemish, and you shall be steadfast and not fear. You shall not only not fear, but you shall have a degree of assurance. You shall be steadfast if you put sin far from you. A stained and defiled conscience will never be in a Christian who is strong in assurance. You shall never grow in assurance if your conscience harbors sin.

**Third,** if you wish to properly establish your assurance, maintain close fellowship with God. Nothing feeds consolations as much as a Christian’s holy walk, *Isaiah 32:17.* The work of righteousness shall be peace, and the effect of righteousness shall be quietness and assurance forever. If you walk in the works of righteousness and on the path to maintaining close fellowship with God, that shall be peace, and that shall be quietness and great assurance. Notice how the Holy Spirit ascends by 

<column-break/>

steps; (saying) not only peace and quietness, but also assurance: you shall have the highest degree of peace and the highest degree of consolation if you walk diligently in the way of holiness with God. And so much has been spoken to the first sort of people, who live in the enjoyment of the assurance of their powerful calling.

I have now a word for those people who live in lack of this assurance, who perhaps in times past had some glimmering and dim sight of consolation regarding their eternal state, and yet are now very clouded and darkened in their consolations, or have now lost the consolations they once had—what they should do to regain them. And for their instruction, I shall say only four things.

**First,** that you should set yourselves to the work of **examination**. **Second,** to the work of humiliation. **Third,** to the work of prayer. And **fourth,** that you should set yourselves to the work of meditation. These four aids shall, through God's blessing, be very useful in restoring your usual consolations to you.

**First,** my advice to you shall be that you set yourselves to the work of examination. <term>Examination: The spiritual practice of "self-testing" or looking inward to see if one's faith and behavior align with God's word.</term> When you have lost something, the first thing you do is look for it, where you lost it, so that you might find it again. If you have lost this precious jewel of assurance, be just as wise for yourself; set yourself to the work of examination. Scripture points this out to you, *Galatians 6:4.* Let every man prove his own work, and then he shall have rejoicing in himself. This is the way to bring in spiritual joy and consolation—to deal frequently with one’s own heart. David, when he lay under a bad condition, notice how he deals with his soul: *Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?* He puts his heart to the touchstone. And here, in the work of your examination, I would recommend five things for your testing.

**First,** examine how you obtained your assurance.

**Second,** how you established your assurance.

**Third,** how you used your assurance.

**Fourth,** examine what might have provoked God to take your assurance away.

**Fifth,** and lastly, examine what you would give to God if you might regain your previous and usual assurance. Lay these examinations to your hearts; as:

**First,** put it to an examination: how you obtained your assurance. It may be that it was such an assurance as you have had since you were born from the womb: which you obtained without care and without pain; and if it is so, it is **presumption**, and not assurance. <term>Presumption: A false, unearned confidence in one's spiritual safety that does not come from a genuine relationship with God.</term> And if you have lost it, it is well. It is better to be in a disconsolate state than in a presumptive state.

**Second,** examine how you established your assurance. It may be that you...

<meta>This page continues the numbered instructions for maintaining and investigating one's spiritual assurance. The previous page discussed the importance of a clean conscience and godly sorrow. This page focuses on troubleshooting why a believer might lose their sense of God's favor.</meta>

<page-num>184</page-num>
<header>Of our effectual [calling]</header>

...which is only founded upon yourself, and not upon Christ. It may be that you founded it only upon the imagined delusions of your own heart, and not upon the firm evidence of God’s word; if it is so, that your assurance had a poor foundation, it is no wonder if God turns it upside down. If it is not rightly founded, it shall not last long. Therefore, examine upon what ground you have established your assurances; and if you find that the foundation of your consolations was poorly laid, then you must once again uproot it entirely.

**Thirdly,** examine how you used your assurance. It may be that you used your assurance with pride, and not with humility; it may be with negligence and carelessness of the Spirit, and that you took no notice of those attachments and impulses which might diminish your consolations; and if it is so, it is no wonder if the devil sows weeds among your wheat; it is no wonder that the devil has stolen away your consolations if you lay down your watch.

**Fourthly,** examine what particular cause there was in your hearts that might provoke God to cloud your consolations and take your assurance away from you. And so that you might be somewhat instructed in this examination, you may trace the cause of your darkening and the removal of your assurance to these two main headings: either it was the commission of some great transgression, or otherwise the neglect of some weighty duty; that may provoke God to darken your consolations.

### First, the commission of some great transgression.
Great sins lay a foundation for great discouragements in tender consciences. Great sins devastate the **conscience**; turning that which was like a well-adorned and beautiful garden into a desolate wilderness. Great lapses ordinarily bring dark eclipses upon the soul. And so that I might lead you to this examination, I would advise you to investigate what particular sin it was, and how you might know the transgression that provoked God to take your consolations away from you. For instance:

**First,** if it is the case that God took away your consolation immediately after the commission of some great sin, then you may be certain that that sin was the cause. 
Or:

**Secondly,** if the commission of a sin brings upon you more than an ordinary measure of hardness of heart, then you may be certain that that was the sin. 
Or:

**Thirdly,** if any sin made you sluggish in spiritual duties, that was the sin that provoked God to take your consolations away from you. And through such an examination as this, you may find out and firmly guess the particular provocation.

And I would truly wish that you would search out these particular transgressions; and they are ordinarily these four, which move God to take away the consolations of a people:

**First,** the sin of harshness and lack of compassion of spirit toward doubting Christians. If a soul casts a proud and harsh eye upon poor Christians, and has no compassion for doubting souls, then God may, because of that sin of lack of compassion, bring that person to that same state <note>Meaning: God allows the person to experience the same spiritual doubt they refused to pity in others.</note> in which he could not feel compassion for other people.

**Secondly,** the sin of grieving the Spirit; if you grieve God's Spirit, God shall grieve your spirit, *Isaiah 63:10*. 
Or:

**Thirdly,** the sin of spiritual pride; that may very ordinarily be the sin. 
Or:

**Fourthly,** the sin of worldly-mindedness, or the vehement pursuit of the things of this world. Just as digging deep into the Earth puts a man in danger of being suffocated by vapors; so also digging and rooting in the world brings but a vapor over the consolations of Christians and often suffocates their assurance. Just as the Sun is eclipsed by the positioning of the Moon between it and our sight, so also if the world once comes between the **Sun of Righteousness** <note>Sun of Righteousness: A traditional title for Jesus Christ, derived from Malachi 4:2.</note> and you, it will darken the Sun so that you shall not see the glory of Jesus Christ, and shall not perceive nor obtain that share in Jesus Christ that you had in time past.

**Secondly,** <note>This "secondly" refers back to the two main headings: commission of sin vs. omission of duty.</note> you must examine another cause; if it is not the commission of some great transgression, yet it may be the neglect of a necessary and weighty duty; the Lord may bring you to discouragement as well for neglect as for commission. If someone leaves but one wound unbandaged, he may die just as well as if you struck him on the head with a chisel. Beloved, if you leave your wounds unbandaged and your discouragements unexamined, and let everything run to uncertainty; if you break off your duties, it is just with God that He breaks off your consolations. If you do not keep your watch, it is no wonder if you are overtaken. There are many Christians who become careless in communion with God, who love rare reading, rare praying, and rare examination of their own hearts; alas! those people who throw away their duties make God, in His judgment, stop up the path of their consolations.

**Fifthly,** in the work of your examination, ask yourself what you would be willing to do, provided that God would restore your previous evidences to you; if you can bring your hearts to this state—that you think no trouble is too much to take on, no cost is too much to give, that nothing would be too difficult for you which God would have you do, if only He would give you your accustomed consolations—if you find this state of spirit in you, that is the right way to bring your consolations back again, and to restore the virtue of your salvation to you.

**Secondly,** <note>A new major step in the process of recovery.</note> set yourself to the work of **humiliation**: <note>Humiliation: In this context, a spiritual discipline of humbling oneself through fasting, prayer, and confession to seek God's favor.</note> the only way to regain what you have lost is mourning over your loss. *Jeremiah 31:18, 19, 20.* See how...

# Making the Calling Sure

...that Ephraim comes to have his consolations restored when he complains of his own lack of comfort. I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself, says God; and he says: Is not Ephraim my dear son? I saw him strike his thigh <note>This refers to Jeremiah 31:19, a traditional gesture of shame and repentance.</note>, humbling his soul for his sins; and since I spoke against him, I still earnestly remember him, and I will surely have mercy on him. Here you see the complaining Ephraim; at the right time of his complaints, God restores his consolations to him. We hear many complaining about their outward losses, but who complains about the loss of inward consolations? David, after he had lost some consolations through the sin of adultery, composed seven Penitential Psalms—psalms of complaint and repentance; and one of these he calls "A Psalm of Remembrance." <note>Likely referring to Psalm 38 or 70, titled "to bring to remembrance."</note> And as a certain author well observes: when David came to renew his consolations, he wrote a psalm to bring to mind those sins which might provoke God to take His consolations away from him. So also, Beloved: let it be your work to compose such psalms in your inner chambers, and let your practice bring to mind those sins that provoke God to darken your consolations, and let that humble you. If you cannot find the specific sin, labor to humble your souls for every sin, and then be assured that you cannot miss the mark.

<margin>Psal. 51:8, 10.</margin>
**Thirdly,** do you wish to restore your usual consolations? Set yourself to the work of prayer. You find that David took this course: *Lord, make me to hear joy and gladness, that the bones which You have broken may rejoice.* — *Create in me a clean heart,*
<margin>v. 12.</margin>
*and renew a steadfast spirit within me.* (v. 12) <note>original: Psalm 51:10, 12</note> Here you live by David’s praying, how he pours out his soul in prayer, that God would renew in him the joy of His salvation. And here, in the work of prayer, I would instruct you in only three things:

**First,** pray for a discerning sight of those sins which provoke God to take your consolations away from you.

**Secondly,** after you have obtained that sight, turn the strength of your prayers mostly against those sins which so provoke God to cloud your consolations. Pray against them as against the deadliest enemy you have in the world.

**Thirdly,** pray to obtain those graces that you might be admitted into spiritual consolation—such as the graces mentioned before: the grace of godly sorrow, the grace of humiliation, the grace of faith, and of love for Jesus Christ. If you thus set yourself to the work of examination, of humiliation, and to the work of prayer, then you are on a likely path to having your consolations restored.

**Fourthly,** set yourself to the work of reflection; and in this work, I shall recommend to you four considerations which you must take into your thoughts, which may be very helpful and of great use to you in restoring your consolations. Such as:

**First,** let your reflections dwell on the fact that you are sometimes not as capable judges of your spiritual state as others might be. Such as:

<column-break/>

**First,** in the time of desertion, when God has forsaken you and is angry with you.

**Secondly,** in the time of temptation, when the devil's assaults are powerful against you.

**Thirdly,** in times of falling, when you have fallen into some great sin; at such a time, you are not such capable judges of your own state, but bystanders may see more of your own godliness and your own sincerity than you can do yourself; just as the proverb says: *The onlookers often see more than he who plays the game;* <note>A common Dutch and English idiom of the period regarding perspective.</note> it is true in this case. An observer may see sincerity glistening in your practice and your graces shining in your conduct, when you cannot see it yourself. A child, when it sobs and cries, can see nothing in its book; so also, when Christians are sad, mournful, and melancholy, they can hardly read any of their evidences. Mr. Throgmorton <note>Likely Job Throgmorton (1545–1601) or a similar Puritan figure known for spiritual struggles.</note> received his assurance through the testimony of a group of godly ministers, who said they could stake their own souls in place of his soul. Let this, therefore, come into your reflections: that often the bystanders and the Christians who observe your conduct and see your deeds may see more ground for consolation in you than you can do yourself.

<margin>Psal. 77.</margin>
**Secondly,** reflect and think upon the consolations that God gave you in times past, and bring them to mind. Do as David did (Psalm 77): *I considered the days of old, the years of ancient times.* Bring to mind the days of old: did God not show you His face? Did God not carry you in the palms of His hands? Did God not give you many a kindness from His countenance and many a pledge of His love, even through your very sighs? Did God not place many a seal upon your heart, that your consolations were true, your evidences clear, and your intentions sincere before God? Beloved, bring to mind the former state of your spirit, how you were in times past; and this reflection, being supported by God’s Spirit, can be a great means to restore your consolations to you; past virtues must be present encouragements.

<margin>From that which we are born, by the same we are nourished.</margin>
**Thirdly,** reflect on by what path it was that you obtained your previous consolations and assurance; and God will help that same path to restore your consolations again. What the physicians say of the body—<note>original: "Ex quo gignimur, eodem nutrimur"</note> *that we are nourished by those things from which we are healed and generated*—so I say of consolations. That very same thing which produced the consolations will restore your consolations again. Now think on this in your practice and observe: by what path did I obtain my consolations in years past? Did I obtain my consolations through godly sorrow, through mournful yearning for God, and through weeping over the terrible wanderings in my practice? Now take that same course to renew your evidences. Go and weep in your inner chamber over your evil conduct before God. Go and complain of your sins; cry after your Father, and tell Him that you are grieved to your very heart that He has become such a great stranger to your soul. Did you formerly obtain your assurance by frequently humbling your soul...

# Of Our Effectual Calling

...before God? Set yourself again to the work of humbling. Did you formerly obtain your consolations through walking closely with God? Improve your paths and direct your ways toward your Creator in times to come; that is the right way to restore your consolations, which was the first means by which you obtained them.

Fourthly, let your thoughts dwell on those comforting promises in the Gospel, which offer the greatest comfort to a downcast soul. Truly, I am convinced that the reflections of Christians—which focus more on their own failings, their own jealousies, and their own mistakes than on the promises of the Gospel—have often been a great occasion for them lying so long under the spirit of bondage <note>The "spirit of bondage" refers to a state of spiritual fear or legalism where one feels like a slave to sin or judgment rather than a free child of God.</note> and under a dark eclipse in the absence of the consolations of God's Spirit. Therefore, let your thoughts dwell on those promises that offer the greatest comfort to a downcast and forsaken soul. And to this end, I shall name five or six of the most comforting promises in God’s Word:

As in Isaiah 57:15: "The Lord who dwells on high and in the holy place, who gives life to the spirit of the humble, and to the heart of the contrite." <margin>Isaiah 66:8</margin> So also Isaiah 66:8 <note>The author likely intended Isaiah 66:2, which matches the quoted text better than verse 8.</note>: "The Lord dwells in the Heavens, and with those who are of a humble and contrite spirit, and who tremble at his word." <margin>Psalm 34:19</margin> With those, God shall dwell. So also Psalm 34:19 <note>In many English Bibles, this is Psalm 34:18.</note>: "The Lord is near to those with a broken heart, and he saves the crushed in spirit." <margin>Luke 4:18</margin> Likewise in Luke 4:18: "Jesus Christ is anointed—that is, appointed by God the Father—to preach the Gospel to the poor, to heal those who are brokenhearted, and to comfort the mourning." <margin>Isaiah 66:10</margin> So also Isaiah 66:10: "Be glad, all you who have been mourning." <margin>Hebrews 12:12</margin> And Hebrews 12:12: "The Lord shall lift up the sluggish hands and the weak knees." 

I shall end with that remarkable and very glorious Evangelical promise in <margin>Isaiah 35:3, 4, 5, 6</margin> Isaiah 35:3, 4, 5, 6: "Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the stumbling knees." God says this to weak Christians, whose legs can hardly carry their bodies, and whose hands can scarcely reach to their mouths. Say to the weak Christians in grace and consolation, and confirm and strengthen them: Say to the fainthearted of heart, be strong and do not fear; poor, fearful, doubting souls, who fear every temptation and every trial, and who fear they shall lose the reward of their labor: say to those fearful hearts, be strong and do not fear. See, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of GOD; he will come and deliver you. Then shall the eyes of the blind be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. This is not understood as referring to physical eyes, but to those who were blind and could not see the <term>mysteries of Christ</term> <note>original: "verbogentheden Christi"; referring to the deep spiritual truths of the Gospel</note> and could not read their own consolations; then shall their eyes be opened. And the deaf, as Isaiah says—those who refuse to be comforted, who will not listen to any comfort, but stop their ears against all comforting teachings and only open a way for sorrow—their eyes shall be opened. And the lame shall leap like a deer; the poor, lame 

<column-break/>

Christian who halts in his consolations—who is now believing, but a moment ago was stumbling; now joyful, who a moment ago was despairing—that poor, lame person shall leap like a deer; and the tongue of the dumb shall shout for joy. That poor person who could not speak a word of his own graces, or of his own consolations, or regarding his own evidences—the tongue of that dumb person shall shout for joy. O Beloved, here is your work, if you wish to be a Christian and restore your consolations: set yourself to the work of meditation, to think upon these precious promises of the Gospel which offer the most comfort to a downcast, humbled sinner.

### 2 Peter 1:10

->Therefore, Brothers, be all the more diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.<-

<margin>12th Sermon.</margin>
The doctrine that I still have at hand is this: that Christians ought to apply a very great diligence to make this sure to their souls, that they are effectively called through Jesus Christ. In the pursuit of which I have gone over many points. There remains now regarding this subject only one application to handle, and then I shall move on to a third doctrinal point drawn from these words. <margin>Application</margin> It shall be an application of consolation from all that has been said regarding the assurance of our effectual calling; I shall only direct my reasoning toward setting down six or seven comforting conclusions for those Christians who are effectively called, and yet perhaps do not have a sensible assurance of their own calling.

First, take this as the truth: that assurance is necessary, not for the <term>being</term> but for the <term>well-being</term> of a Christian. <note>In Puritan theology, "being" refers to the basic state of salvation (having faith), while "well-being" refers to the comfort, joy, and peace that comes from knowing for certain one is saved.</note> It is not necessary to one’s state, but to one’s comfort. It is not necessary as food is to life, but only as a medicine is to the body. A person cannot live without food; but a person can certainly live without medicine. Assurance is but a comforting cordial for the soul; grace is like the food to keep the soul alive, even if you lack assurance—this cordial—to support you.

Secondly, that many of God’s dear children can lie for a long time in lack of this assurance regarding their effectual calling. In Psalm 88, it is said of Heman, in verses 14 and 15: "Lord, why do you cast off my soul? And hide your face from me?" <margin>Psalm 88:14, 15</margin> Note his complaint: "I am perishing." Was this only a temporary abandonment, or was it constant? Indeed, verse 15 says: "From my youth up I suffer your terrors; I am distracted; your fierce wrath goes over me." Heman lay under this abandonment from his childhood onwards; for he tells you here of his state, that he was not just troubled for a day, two, or three, after which his oppressions were over; but from his youth up he lay under this deprivation, so that he...

# Making Your Calling Sure

<header>Making Your Calling Sure.</header>

He thought that God had cast off his soul and that he bore God’s terrors <note>original: "verbaertnissen"</note>; yet this man did not doubt his spiritual state, for he was the man—as Ainsworth <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622) was a prominent English scholar and Nonconformist theologian known for his Hebrew studies.</note> believes—who composed this Psalm. Certainly, God never honored a godless man to be a writer of Holy Scripture. The Psalm is called a "golden Psalm," and it is so named because he intended to teach troubled consciences that they may lie under great terrors from their youth, and under a sad doubting regarding their eternal state, and despite this, they still have grace and a Foundation. Heman <note>Heman the Ezrahite is the traditional author of Psalm 88, which is noted for its tone of deep despair and lack of a happy ending.</note> does not merely seem as if he had a common disturbance of the mind, but he seems as if he lay under an extraordinary weight of God’s wrath. Verse 7: *You have laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the depths; your wrath lies hard upon me.* He lay and sank, as he believed, under the feeling of God’s wrath. This is therefore a comforting conclusion: that the godly may lie in a state of spiritual desertion not just for a moment or in flashes, but for a long time, many years together. For some believe Heman was over sixty years old when he wrote this Psalm; yet from his youth until this age, he lay under these terrors and doubtfulness.

Thirdly, many of God’s dear children may lie submerged under spiritual desertion and a lack of assurance for so long that they may refuse and resist comforts when God offers them in the Gospel—and yet, despite this, they may still possess grace. Just as a person who is raving due to a fever or some other severe sickness, even if you bring him a heart-strengthening medicine that might lessen his illness, he will in a fit throw the glass against the wall, even though it is the only means to his health. So it is with the godly; they are often so accustomed to sadness through the lack of assurance that they may refuse comforts when God offers them. Psalm 77:3: These are the words of Asaph, *My soul refused to be comforted.* A remarkable statement: although comfort was presented to him, his soul refused it. Here then, Beloved, this may be a great support for you—that you can be so long accustomed to doubts that you might refuse comfort when God offers it, and yet nonetheless be a heart that has received grace.

Fourthly, and this is even more comforting: rather than God letting His people live and die without assurance, He would rather work assurance in them through a miracle or through an unusual and extraordinary way. You have a famous example of this in a noblewoman who once lived in this city (the story is told by Mr. Bolton <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631) was a famous Puritan rector and author.</note>), a Mrs. Honywood <note>Mary Honywood (1527–1620) was a real historical figure known for her long struggle with religious melancholy.</note>, who was a renowned professor of religion and a woman who for many years was very troubled in her mind for lack of assurance. Finally, a minister came to her, who did his best to fix her hope and comforts in Jesus Christ;

<column-break/>

and as he pressed the promises upon her, she took it very poorly that he should offer her any promise to which she thought she had no right. Having a Venetian glass <note>Venetian glass was prized for its beauty and extreme fragility.</note> in her hand, she held that glass up and said, "Speak to me no more of salvation, for I shall be as certainly damned as this poor Venetian glass shall be broken against the wall," throwing it with all her might against the wall to break it. But it pleased God, through a wonderful providence, to preserve the glass entirely whole. Seeing this, the minister took up the glass and said, "See, God must work faith in you by a miracle before you will believe." And from that day on, says the history, she was a woman very strong in the assurance of God’s love. Here you see how God met the weakness of His poor servant. Rather than let you live and die without assurance, God would rather bring it about through a miracle. It might be that this woman would have died unassured if God had not strengthened her through an unusual path. I have likewise read in the *Book of Martyrs* <note>Referring to *Acts and Monuments* by John Foxe, a popular history of Protestant martyrs.</note> of Mr. Glover <note>Robert Glover was a Protestant martyr burned at Smithfield in 1555.</note>, that all the time he was in prison, he was in a state of spiritual desertion and very clouded in his comforts, and could not have any grasp of God’s love for his soul. Indeed, when he came to Smithfield <note>The primary execution site in London for those condemned for heresy or treason.</note> and saw the stake and the fire with which he was to be burned, he cried out, *I have found Him! I have found Him!* and he confessed of himself that he was as full of joy as his heart could hold. The Lord made the sight of the stake an entry into a present joy. Someone might have thought that the sight of the stake would have made his courage sink; instead, he became most confident then.

Fifthly, although grace in your heart is unchangeable, the *feeling* of your own grace is subject to great change. Grace in itself is unchangeable. All the devils <note>original: "duppelen," contextually referring to the powers of hell.</note> of hell cannot pluck the smallest believer out of Christ’s hand. *These whom you have given me, I will keep,* says Christ, *and no one shall pluck them out of my hand.* The foundation of God stands sure; although your knowledge, which you build upon that foundation, may not be certain to you. *The Lord knows those who are His,* even though you may not know it. Grace itself is not changeable, although your feeling of grace is subject to many alterations and changes. Although grace itself is an immovable foundation, our feeling of grace is not. In our feeling of grace, we are like the air—sometimes clear, sometimes cloudy. We are like the sea—sometimes ebbing, sometimes flowing; decreasing in comforts as much as increasing in grace. Believers, in their feeling of grace, are like the trees of the field—sometimes blooming, green, and growing; at another time the leaves fall off, and then they are like a dry log. So are Christians regarding their feelings; the grasp and the feeling of their grace is subject to much change, even though their grace is not.

Sixthly, that lack of assurance...

# Of Our Powerful Calling

<header>Of our powerful</header>

is not actually a hindrance to the salvation <note>original: "salicheyt"</note> of a Christian, although it is a hindrance to the comfort of a Christian. It is in no way a hindrance to your salvation; you may certainly be saved, even if you are not assured. For first, this lack of assurance is no barrier to your free access to the Throne of Grace: you may freely come to present your requests to God, even if you are not assured whether they will be accepted. As one author says: even if God does not show you His face, He may still lend you His ear when you come to Him in prayer. God lends an ear in prayer to many a Christian, even though they see neither His face nor the radiance of His favor. Secondly, your lack of assurance will not hinder your success in prayer; you may go away with an abundant answer, even if you do not go away with a fullness of consolation. 

When Benjamin was with Joseph in Egypt, he had a token of Joseph’s love—a golden cup <note>The biblical account in Genesis 44 describes a silver cup, but the author here uses "golden cup" as a metaphor for hidden grace.</note> in his sack—even though he did not know it. This is a living representation of how the love of our Joseph, Jesus Christ, is carried toward His "young Benjamins." He may place a token of love in your hearts and give you a golden cup and grace, although you do not know that the grace is there. Finally, it does not prevent your reconciliation; you may be reconciled with God, even though you do not know the agreement has been made. There may be a true friendship between God and a believer, even though there may seem to be some enmity. *You hold me for your enemy,* says Job, yet God did not do so, although Job thought it. Zion says, *The Lord has forsaken me, the Lord has forgotten me.* But God had not done so, for He says immediately afterward, almost in the same breath: *Even if a mother should forget her nursing child, yet I will not forget you.* Thus, there may seem to be some dispute when there is no enmity at all between God and you.

Seventhly, those Christians who have reached the strongest and highest level of faith have nevertheless had much weakness and many struggles mixed with their faith.

> Lord, I believe, help my unbelief. <note>original: "Heere, ick geloove, komt mijn ongeloovicheyt te hulpe." Mark 9:24.</note>

Yet that man had reached a high degree of faith, as in 1 Thessalonians 3:10: *Night and day praying exceedingly that we might see your face, and might perfect that which is lacking in your faith.* Now, you must not consider these Thessalonians as if they were newly converted or a people weak in faith; rather, the strength of the meaning lies here: that even though these Thessalonians were the most excellent Christians in the world, they still had a great lack in their faith. Therefore, compare this with 1 Thessalonians 1:7-8: *You became examples to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia, for from you the Word of the Lord sounded forth... in every place your faith toward God is spread abroad.* The people spoke everywhere of the great measure of faith that was among the godly people of that Church; and yet, although their faith was so 

<column-break/>

extraordinary, and they were such outstanding Christians, they nevertheless had some defects and weaknesses in their faith. See also Psalm 55:5 and Psalm 77. So there is a very great comfort here for believers: that the strongest Christians have had great infirmities accompanying their faith.

Thus I have now dealt with these seven comforting conclusions. Since I do not want a deceived sinner to puff himself up with presumptuous imaginings <term>presumptuous imaginings: the Dutch "laet-dunckende inbeeldingen" refers to a false or arrogant sense of spiritual security</term> of his own happiness when he is a loathsome person marked for Hell, I have two or three more conclusions to propose for all those who harbor unstable and presumptuous imaginings of their powerful calling <term>powerful calling: also known in theology as "effectual calling," the idea that God’s internal call to a person's soul is irresistibly effective</term> when they are not, in fact, called. 

First, you who carry presumptuous imaginings of your powerful calling when you are not called: take up this conclusion to terrify your hearts—that it is likely you will never be powerfully called by Jesus Christ. No one is so unlikely to be truly called by Christ as the person who thinks he is called when he is not. Matthew 9:13: *I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* "The righteous"—that is, those who thought they were righteous and who, in their own eyes, thought they had grace and were as good as the best—*I am not come,* says Christ, *to call them.* But "sinners"—that is, sinners who see their sin and see that they need a Savior, and are sensible of their lost and ruined state without Christ—Christ has come to save them and call them to repentance. You, who harbor presumptuous imaginings of your powerful calling, are the least likely of all people in the world to be called.

Secondly, while you live in this world, you are total strangers to that inward and spiritual joy which every true believer feels and experiences in Jesus Christ. You do not partake in the same joys and sweet enjoyments of the heart that every upright believer has in Jesus Christ. A person who has assurance on a good foundation is so filled with joy that it will support him against all kinds of suffering and sorrow which he may meet here in the world. For him who has assurance, no suffering can make his heart sink. Just as Adolphus Clarenbachius <note>Adolphus Clarenbach (c. 1490–1529) was a German Protestant reformer burned at the stake as a martyr.</note>, when he was burning at the stake, was so filled with the assurance of God’s love that he said of himself, *I think in my heart that there is no more joyful heart in the world than mine.* And so also another Martyr, burning at the stake, said, *I taste so much sweetness, and find that I am now so enlightened in the flame, as if I lay on a bed of Roses.* <note>This quote is famously attributed to the English martyr James Bainham (died 1532).</note> The fullness of his joy in the assurance of God’s love made him willing to undergo all torments. When Mr. Sanders <note>Lawrence Saunders (1519–1555), an English Protestant martyr.</note> was imprisoned in jail, and Bainham <note>James Bainham, as mentioned above.</note> was in the fire, he said, *I feel no more than if I were lying down in my bed.* In contrast, you who harbor false imaginings: your hope will shrink when you come to suffer.

It then warns that those with false or arrogant spiritual confidence are often the furthest from true repentance and lack the sustaining joy found in true martyrdom.</summary>
