# Making Calling Sure

<header>Making Calling Sure</header>

suffer; like a garment in the rain that is not well woven, your deception shall not lift up your spirit to such a high degree as these others have reached. This is your misery: you shall never have that sweet peace and joy in your heart which the believers have, who are assured upon Scriptural grounds.

Thirdly, take this to your terror: that you shall be cast into hell before you are even aware of it. It is the saying of Mr. Bolton <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631) was a noted English Puritan clergyman and scholar known for his works on comfort and conscience.</note>: the person who takes up a false imagination of his powerful Calling when he is not truly called is like a man who is in a pleasant dream, dreaming that he is a King, and that he has a Kingdom, and that he possesses treasures of gold and silver; but when he wakes, behold, the man has nothing at all. He compares him to a man sleeping on the mast of a ship; he is in a golden dream, and dreams of kingdoms and of thousands that he possesses, and perhaps in a moment a wind arises, the ship is tossed upon the waves, the man falls from above and he drowns. So it goes with many people, who nourish golden dreams and hopes that Heaven is theirs, and that Christ is theirs, when in an instant they roll down from above and are cast into Hell, before they are even aware of it. This ought to be a solemn reflection for your heart—you who harbor arrogant imaginings of your powerful Calling, though you are not called at all.

Thus, I have handled in eleven sermons this Doctrine regarding the powerful Calling. I now move on to the third and last point of Doctrine drawn from these words; and that is:

->That Christians ought to apply a very great diligence to make this sure to their souls: that they are eternally chosen by GOD for life and Salvation. Be diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.<-

There are many useful points to handle in the delivery of this Doctrine; I shall only pursue a few in the time remaining. First, I shall show you what Election <note>original: "Verkiesinghe"</note> is.

Secondly, whether a man can be certain of his own Election, since Election is an act of eternity. How can a man be certain of that which took place in God’s decree before we even existed? Thirdly, by what marks can a man infallibly judge that he is chosen?

In handling this Doctrine, I shall begin with the first, namely: what is Election?

So that you might know this, I shall set down this short description of it.

Election is an eternal decree or purpose of GOD, whereby He has freely chosen out of the mass of the human race a small number of people, who shall come to eternal life and Salvation through Jesus Christ. That is Election.

In this description, these things are to be noted. First, I call it an eternal purpose; because although a man

<column-break/>

is not justified from eternity, nonetheless he is chosen from eternity. God has from eternity a purpose that a man should be justified, and called, and saved. Election is from eternity, although Calling, Justification, and Sanctification are not so. Therefore you read in the Scripture, when it speaks of Election, in Ephesians 1:4: *He has chosen us in Christ before the foundation of the world.* But it is never said thus of Justification. God has a purpose to make us blessed, and a purpose to call us in time, and a purpose to justify us from eternity, although the working out of this purpose is fulfilled at the proper time.

Secondly, I call it a purpose whereby He has freely chosen. And this I do in opposition to that Papist <note>The author uses "Papist" as a common 17th-century Protestant term for Roman Catholics.</note> proposition: that God foresees or chooses man for salvation based on the foresight of good works. A very improper view, which takes away the freedom of this act of God’s Election. 2 Timothy 1:9 says: *Not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace.* Thirdly, I say: whereby GOD has chosen a few out of the heap of the human race to obtain life and salvation. This is in opposition to those who hold to a universal redemption and universal grace, just as Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184 – c. 253) was an early Christian scholar whose views on universal salvation—that all beings, even the devil, might eventually be saved—were later deemed heretical.</note> and many after him who have been tainted with this error, holding Election to be universal. And so also many of the Papists. Now the Scripture tells us that *many are called, but few are chosen.* Election means a choice; now a choice, the word itself, indicates a rejection of one and an exception of another. The word Election indicates that all shall not be saved. Origen held that all people would be saved; that Election would extend to every person. Yes, that even the devils on the day of Judgment would be saved: which is a view that ought not to be named among Christians; for Election pertains only to a few. Fourthly, I said: that it is to bring them to eternal life and salvation; therefore it is called an ordaining to eternal life. Acts 13:48.

<margin>2. Question.</margin>
Secondly, can a Christian in this life be assured of his eternal Election, seeing that Election took place in God’s decree before he ever existed, or before the World was? Therefore, since we do not know God’s decree and counsel, how can we be assured of our eternal Election? The Papists strike this Doctrine down entirely. And it is from this that in the Council of Trent <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the formal Roman Catholic reply to the doctrinal challenges of the Protestant Reformation.</note> this rule was made: That if anyone should say he was bound to believe that he was of the number of those whom God had ordained or chosen for eternal life, let him be accursed. They did their best to strike down assurance, and held that everything a man can have must only be a "conjectural assurance," or some such hope of salvation, and nothing else. Now so that you...

# Of our powerful [Calling]

...might not wander astray in this matter, see what the Scripture speaks in this case. That, although Election is an act of God from eternity, nevertheless a believer can certainly and perfectly know his own Election. And this I shall prove with various passages of Scripture. Read Luke 10:20 <note>original: "Lucæ 10. 20"</note>. Rejoice not in this, says Christ to his disciples, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice much more that your names are written in Heaven. That is: do not rejoice that you can perform miracles; a thing which even the godless can do who are not elected: but rejoice much more that your names are written in the Book of Life; that is: that you are chosen for salvation in God’s decree. Now, how could they rejoice unless they knew it? So also 1 Thessalonians 1:4. Knowing, beloved brethren, your election of God. The Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> holds it for certain that the believers knew they were chosen. So also Ephesians 1:3, 4, 5. The Lord has blessed us with all spiritual blessings in Christ, just as he has chosen us in him before the foundation of the world. Who has predestined us to the adoption of children through Jesus Christ. Many more Scripture passages I could bring forward, but in the mouth of two or three witnesses, it is enough to confirm all truth.

But now, although the Scripture is so clear, nonetheless there are some objections which seem to go against this truth, which I must answer. The Papists <note>A historical term used by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics, often in a polemical or debating context.</note>, as far as I have read in their writings, I find five objections which they draw from Scripture against this truth—namely, that a person can be assured of his Election. For they say: it is an act of God which happened before we even existed; how then can we be assured of it? I shall therefore, beloved, first bring forward those Scripture passages which they pretend overturn this doctrine, and then take away that which seems to oppose it. The first place they insist upon is 1 Peter 1:17. Walk in fear during the time of your stay here. This Scripture passage, they say, commands us that we should pass our time with fearing; and if it is so, then we cannot be assured of our Election, but we must fear all the days of our life whether we are chosen or not.

To this I shall briefly answer. You must know the fear which the Holy Spirit insists upon here—that men should walk their time in fear—is not understood as a fear concerning our Election; but it is understood as a fear of sin; that we must not sin against God, but fear God, and show we fear God by shunning our sins. And if you ask how this is evident, I make it clearly evident thus: because in verse 18 it is said, Knowing that you were not redeemed by corruptible things, like silver or gold, but by the precious blood of Christ, etc. Now, this verse clearly confirms that they knew they were redeemed by the blood of Christ, and so consequently knew their Election. Therefore, the Apostle does not insist on a fear to cast down the knowledge of their Election; walk your time in fear, that is: fear to anger God, and fear to sin against him.

<column-break/>

Another objection which they bring forward is this: the Scripture, they say, commands us many times to fear; and truly fear and assurance cannot exist together. Proverbs 28:14: Blessed is the man who fears continually. Now, if a man must fear continually, then the most a man can have is hope; and thus he hangs between hope and fear all his days. To which I answer:

That fearing continually, to which Solomon attaches blessedness, is not understood as a fear regarding someone’s Election, but only as a fear of sinning against God. And if you ask me how that is evident, read the entire verse. Blessed is the man who fears continually, but he who hardens his heart shall fall into mischief. Now notice: it is evident by the contrast that the fear there is not a fear of our eternal state, but only a fear in contrast to that hardness of heart in the godless, who go forward in sin.

Another place they bring forward is 1 Corinthians 10:12. Therefore, let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. Now, they say, the Scripture tells us there that no one stands as firmly as he thinks regarding his Election, but he must take heed; he can fall away from grace and be damned. Now, to answer this, I shall set down two things.

First, the Apostle does not speak there of people who have a firm assurance of their Election; but to people who lie in fleshly security <note>A term for a false sense of spiritual safety based on worldly comfort or pride rather than true faith.</note> and have deceptive imaginings of their good state; and that is evident in the text; for he says, he who *thinks* he stands, he does not say, he who *stands*; for such a one cannot fall; but he who *thinks* he stands. Those people who feed conceited and groundless imaginings that they are in a good and blessed state, let them take heed that they do not fall.

Secondly, by "falling" it is not understood here as falling away from grace, or falling away unto the end after Election, for that is impossible; but it is only understood as falling into sin. And so this is the meaning: he who thinks he stands—that is, he who thinks he is strong in grace and stands on his own legs—let that person take heed that he does not fall into sin. Now, a person may take heed that he does not fall into sin, and yet in no way call his assurance into doubt. If you now ask how I make it evident that this is the target and aim of the passage, I answer by the preceding part of the text. Read the previous verses: And let us not tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted him; and do not murmur, as some of them also murmured; all these things happened to them as examples, and are written for our warning. Therefore, let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. It is as if he said: you have seen here that some people fall into sin; you have heard that some people murmur, that some tempt Christ; this ought to discourage you from falling into sin and bearing the punishment they bore. But what does this have to do with the denial of assurance, that people cannot be certain of their Election?

# Making your Calling sure.

Yet another passage that they bring forward is found in Philippians 2:12. **Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.** Now they say, if a person must work, and carry out the work of his salvation with fear and trembling, then a person certainly cannot be assured of his Election in this life. To which I answer:

First, that the "fear and trembling" spoken of there is not a fear and trembling that opposes the assurance of our Election; rather, it goes against that fleshly security <note>In this context, "fleshly security" refers to a dangerous spiritual overconfidence or complacency.</note> and that sinful leaning upon one's own strength. This is evident from the following words: **For it is God who works in you both to will and to work.** And therefore, seeing you have no strength and no power of yourself to do anything, fear and tremble for that reason.

Secondly, fear and trembling can certainly coexist with this grace of assurance; for we read in Psalm 2:11, **Rejoice with trembling.** You can fear and yet be joyful. So also in Psalm 5:8, **But I will enter into your house through the greatness of your mercy, I will bow down toward your holy Palace in your fear.** Here fear and trust in the mercy of God are joined together to show that fear and assurance may very well exist with one another. But then they object: how can that be? For John says, **perfect love casts out fear,** 1 John 4:18. I answer that although John says perfect love casts out fear, John does not say that *imperfect* love casts out fear. Now, in this life our love is imperfect, and therefore mixed with fear; but in Heaven our love is perfect, and thus casts out fear. So this does not work against us, but a person can have a firm assurance of his eternal Election.

Yet another passage they object with is Romans 11:20. **Be not high-minded, but fear.** To this I answer: these words are not spoken regarding fearing our Election—that we should fear whether we are elected or not. Rather, they serve to cast down all feelings of our own righteousness, as if we were accepted by God for that reason, and to keep us from boasting over the rejected Jews, now that we have been grafted in in their place.

Yet another Scripture passage (which is truly the most special pillar they lean upon) is found in Romans 11:34. **Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?** Here the Papists <note>A term used by the author to refer to Roman Catholic opponents.</note> say the Scripture challenges anyone in the world to come forward and say that he knows God's mind; by "God's mind" is understood God's decree. And Paul here challenges everyone, saying that no one knows the decree of God from eternity. Therefore, if no one knows the mind of the Lord, then certainly no one knows his own Election, for that is God's mind and God's decree. They hold this to be an irrefutable argument.

To satisfy you regarding this Scripture passage, I shall set down three things.

First, when it is said that "no one knows the mind of the Lord, nor has anyone been his counselor," it confirms that no one knows the mind or the decree of the Lord regarding *other* people's Election. The Apostle does not say this as if

<column-break/>

no one knew God's mind concerning his own, but concerning another man's Election—who is elected and who is not; for that is the aim of the passage. The Gentiles thought that all the Jews were damned people; and they judged and boasted over them. Now Paul says, no one knows the mind of God regarding others, whether they shall be saved or damned while they are in this world.

Secondly, no one knows the mind of the Lord in this sense: that is, to give the reason for God's decree, why God decreed this and that; why God chose Peter and not Judas. No one knows the reason for God's decree and of his ways.

Thirdly, no one knows the mind of the Lord—that is, no one knows God's decree—by looking at the decree alone, but by looking up from God's hidden will to his revealed will; and thus we may know his decree. I make use of the passage in Romans 10:8. **Do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into Heaven?** That is to bring Christ down from above. But what does it say? **The Word is near you, in your mouth.** Trust in that. It is as if he said, let no one think to know God's decree by going up into Heaven and searching there in God's decree, for that he cannot do; but look to the Word, and there you shall find whom God has chosen and decreed to make blessed, 1 Corinthians 2:16. No one can know it by merely looking at the decree, but if we compare God's decree with his Word, and see from the Word those who are chosen, then we can easily know who is chosen or not. This brings me now to the third Chapter: how a person may be assured in his own soul that he is chosen to life and salvation by God the Father.

### 2 Peter 1:10.

->Therefore, Brothers, be the more diligent to make your Calling and Election sure.<-

In the continuation of this matter, you may remember the last Doctrine that I drew, which was this: that Christians ought to apply a very great diligence to make this sure to their souls: that they are eternally chosen to life and salvation by GOD the Father. In the handling of which I have shown you: 1. What Election is. 2. That the People of God can make their Election sure, even though it took place from all eternity.

I shall now show you how the People of God may be assured in their own hearts that they are eternally chosen. And to obtain this knowledge or assurance of our Election here, I do not only take it as far as the Papists do, who say that you may have a mental image which they call *Fides conjecturalis* <note>Latin: "conjectural faith"—a Catholic theological concept of a hope of salvation that falls short of absolute certainty.</note>, a "guessing faith," or a hope that you might be saved; but they do not want to go as far as the words of my Text, to be sure of it. one's own soul can be made fast.

<margin>No one is bound to the impossible. <note>original: "Nemo tenetur ad impossibile." This is a legal principle used here to argue that since God commands us to be sure of our salvation, it must be possible to achieve that certainty.</note></margin>
For no one is bound to an impossible matter; and seeing that it is a matter required of us—to be assured of our <term>Election</term><note>Election: The theological doctrine that God chooses specific individuals for salvation before the beginning of the world.</note>—Scripture never binds our obedience to that which is in itself impossible. I do not only drive it this far, but even further: what an elect person ought to do to be certainly persuaded that he is eternally chosen by God for the obtaining of life and salvation. I am now handling a doctrine to be trembled at while you hear it. And in the untying of this question, you must take up this rule: that you cannot obtain assurance by climbing up into God’s decree, but by descending into your own hearts, examining them by the Word to see whether those saving operations, which God works in an elect person, have been wrought in your souls or not. And that is a way to come to a firm and certain knowledge of your Election. The knowledge of your Election is not to be obtained by climbing up into God’s decree—for who has made you His counselor? Nor is it commanded to you through a revelation; that is an unstable ground, and by it you could just as easily fall into <term>fanaticism</term><note>original: "geest-drijverge." Referring to 'enthusiasm' or the belief in private revelations outside of the Bible, which the author views as dangerous and deceptive.</note> as into a presumption of your Election. And it does not happen through revelation, nor against nor without the Word. Whatever testimony there is, if it does not come from the Word, you may suspect it of being deceitful. Now, the proven way (although I know it is much spoken against) to go about examining whether you are in the number of God’s elect is to examine in your own hearts whether those things are wrought in you which are wrought in those whom God has chosen for life and salvation. And I shall content myself here with naming six Saving Operations.

First, every person who is elect shall, sooner or later, be <term>effectually called</term><note>Effectual Calling: An internal call by the Holy Spirit that certainly results in a person’s conversion, as opposed to a general outward call to everyone who hears the Gospel.</note> and savingly converted by the power of the Word. This the Apostle sets forth in 1 Thess. 1:4, 5: **Knowing, beloved brothers, your Election by God.** How would one know that? Verse 5: **For our Gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit.** That is, our Gospel was not in words only, to tickle your ears and then leave you at rest; but our word was in power, being supported by the operation of the Spirit, unto your conversion. All people who are elect must, sooner or later, undergo this work, to have the power of the Word with authority upon their conscience for their effectual calling. So it stands in Rom. 8:30: **Whom He predestined, these He also called.** And therefore, Beloved, whoever you are, if you live and die without the power of the Word having passed over your soul unto your effectual calling, then you may well conclude in your hearts that you are not chosen by God for the obtaining of life and salvation. For whom He predestined, those He also called.

Secondly: A person whom God has chosen for life, God shall, through a renewing and regenerating grace, sooner

<column-break/>

or later sanctify. And this differs from the previous point only in degrees, for Calling is sanctification begun. Now, when God chooses a person, He not only begins the work of grace, but He carries it out in the way of sanctification. Of this you read in 2 Thess. 2:13: **We are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brothers beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth.** If God has chosen a person from the beginning unto salvation, the Lord does so through sanctification: not *because* of sanctification, as the <term>Papists</term><note>Papists: A historical, often polemical term for Roman Catholics. The author is rejecting the Catholic view that God chooses people based on the good works He foresees they will do.</note> say, or because of foreseen faith, but it is *through* the same as a means by which we are brought to salvation; sanctification shall run through our lives like water through a gutter. So also in 1 Pet. 1:2: **Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through Christ, in sanctification of the Spirit.** Likewise in 2 Tim. 2:21. And therefore, Beloved, if people live and die and do not have the power of sanctifying grace upon their hearts and consciences, and the operation thereof in their lives, without doubt those people are not elect; since you clearly see there that God will work this in such people at one time or another. Jude 4.

Thirdly, the people who are chosen by God for life and salvation shall, sooner or later, be brought to the state of faith. Acts 13:48: **And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.** There is no one who is ordained to eternal life but that he shall be brought to faith. And therefore, those people who live and die in the state of unbelief are not elect. For this reason you read in Titus 1:1 that faith is called **the faith of God’s elect**; signifying that all who are elect shall have faith before they die, and no one else shall have faith but they alone. And therefore it is called in a special way "the faith of God’s elect," being assigned to them alone.

Fourthly, in that person who is elect, God shall, sooner or later before he dies, work in his heart a special delight and an upright love for the preached Word. This you have expressed in John 8:47: **He that is of God heareth God's words; ye therefore hear them not, because ye are not of God.** To be "of God" means to belong to God through Election. Now, to the one who is of God, God shall in time cause him to hear His Word with delight and love; but he who takes no delight therein is not chosen by God. 1 John 4:5, 6.

Fifthly, the Lord shall, sooner or later, work in the heart of an elect person a love for the people of God, and compassion for those who are not chosen by God. Coloss. 3:12: **Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies and kindness.** By that manner of speaking, the Apostle seems to signify clearly: "put on, as the elect of God," etc. As if it were a matter ordained for, and inseparable from, an elect person after his effectual calling: that he has inward stirrings of mer—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "six workings" or signs of grace that allow a believer to be sure of their eternal Election. The previous page established that such certainty is possible through self-examination rather than trying to read God's secret mind.</meta>

### Making [one's] Calling Sure.

<columns>
...that He would have mercy on those who are not called, and kindness toward those who are called. For a person who is once <term>chosen</term><note>chosen/elect: Referring to "Election," the belief that God selected certain people for salvation before the world began.</note>, and has the execution of that <term>Decree</term><note>Decree: God's eternal and unchangeable plan for the universe and the salvation of souls.</note> in his <term>effectual Calling</term><note>effectual Calling: A theological term for when God’s grace successfully draws a person to faith.</note>, it is natural for him to have inner stirrings of mercy.

First, God will work upon a chosen person, sooner or later, changing what he was in times past to a new course of life and obedience. 1 Pet. 1:2. *You are chosen according to the foreknowledge of GOD the Father in the sanctification of the Spirit unto obedience.* Although you were previously disobedient, serving various lusts, nonetheless, if God has chosen you, He will bring you to the course of obedience. Rom. 8:2. *He has predestined us.* To do what? *To be conformed to the image of His Son.* God intends that the person whom He has chosen for life should be conformed to Jesus Christ, and that he shall live a different manner of life than before; that although he was previously subject to sin and Satan, he shall nonetheless then walk in the ways of the obedience of Jesus Christ.

Having thus briefly ended these main points, I have only four or five warnings to present, in order to keep what has been said within the bounds of truth. Such as:

First, take note that these six workings do not extend to children who die while they are still children, but to men and women who are of age. A child cannot use reason while it is a child; it cannot have observed any of these points in itself—at least not in the same way and manner as those of age do. A child, when it is a small child, does not experience conversion in such a way as a man does, although it has something equivalent to it; something like sanctification, and also something like that faith which those of age possess; but what that is, and how it is wrought, no man can measure. Therefore, in urging these workings, I say that they do not extend to children who die in their infancy, but only to people who have come to the <term>years of discretion</term><note>years of discretion: The age at which a person is considered old enough to understand right from wrong and be spiritually accountable.</note>; if those people live and die without having these six workings, they may conclude that they cannot be among the elect.

Secondly, that the lack of these six workings for a time is no proof that a person might not be chosen; for before conversion (which is God's first dealing with the sinner), a chosen person can be as vile and as wicked as any godless person living. Just as the Apostle Paul tells us, Tit. 3:3. *For we ourselves were also sometimes disobedient, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, etc.* Also 1 Tim. 1:12. So the lack of these workings for a time is no proof that a person is not chosen, for then it would follow that an unconverted person was not a chosen person, which would go against the entire contents of the Scripture; but a person living and dying without these work-

<column-break/>

-ings does not belong to the Election of grace.

Thirdly, I do not insist on having these workings in <term>actuality</term><note>original: "dadelijckheyt." Refers to the outward performance of religious acts or the current feeling of grace.</note>, if only you have them in <term>habituality</term><note>original: "hebbelijckheydt." A theological term meaning the underlying disposition or "habit" of the soul, even when not actively being felt or performed.</note>. My meaning is this: a person can be chosen and yet not do any thing that corresponds to an effectual Calling, nor have any delight and love for the Word, nor do anything in the way of sanctification; yet if you have these things habitually, in the disposition of the same, these can be testimonies or proofs of Election.

Fourthly, I do not insist that having these workings <term>sensibly</term><note>sensibly: Meaning "perceivably" or something that can be felt with the emotions.</note> is the only proof of Election, if you only have them effectively. There are many people who have them effectively when they do not have them in their own understanding.

Fifthly, I do not insist on having these workings in high degrees, so long as you have them sincerely. My meaning is this: that a person may be chosen; indeed, he may not only be chosen in God's eternal decree, but the execution of that decree may have passed over him, so that he may be effectively called, and yet he may not have all these six workings in a great measure or at the highest degree; but he may have them sincerely, so that they are like a pledge to his own heart of his eternal Election.

And having thus handled this third question, I now pass over to another, hanging upon the previous one, which is truly a very terrifying subject, and a matter to tremble over while it is being handled, and it is this: what apparent guess can be given of a person, that he is not within the bounds of God's Election? This is a very weighty matter, and it must be handled with great seriousness and caution, being a matter concerning the salvation or the damnation of all people on earth. And therefore I pray you to look to yourselves. God's decrees are in Heaven, and it is only an effectual work of grace in your hearts on Earth that can give you proof that these decrees are for your good, as a good that is wrought as a proof of God's intention to save you; so the contrary work may be a proof of God's intention never to save you, but to leave you outside the bounds of God's eternal Election. Nothing can be established perfectly and with certainty, but many apparent guesses can be given of those people who are not within the bounds of God's Election; of which I shall mention only six or seven types. And I wish from God that none of you who are before the Lord this day had your names written in this <term>black Book</term><note>black Book: A metaphorical list of the reprobate, or those predestined for damnation, contrasting with the "Book of Life."</note>, so that you have no righteous cause to fear that your names are not written in the Book of Life.

# Of our effectual [calling]

to make [us] blessed. I do not say every falling away, or every straying inclination, but a total and final apostasy; when a person falls and does not rise again; when a person runs away from God and does not return. The Scripture points out concerning such a person that he is not within the bounds of God's <term>Election</term><note>Election: The theological concept that God chose specific individuals for salvation before the creation of the world.</note>. Heb. 10:38, 39. *If anyone withdraws himself, my soul has no pleasure in him.* The translators note that in these words there is a figure of speech <note>The author is referring to a "litotes," where a point is made by denying its opposite; "no pleasure" actually means "great wrath."</note> in which less is expressed than is intended: "my soul has no pleasure in him." It is as much as if God said, "my soul shall hate him," or "I shall hate him exceedingly." But we are not of those who withdraw themselves unto destruction, but of those who believe to the saving of the soul. These words clearly give us to understand that those people who withdraw without returning, withdraw themselves unto destruction—unto <term>damnation</term>; "but we are not of those," says the Apostle. And here then, Beloved, this word strikes anyone who is before God this day: have you left the narrow way, and have you fallen into the way of godlessness and unbridled living? Have you fallen away from your God, and do you never think to return? I shall not judge you; but if you live and die in that state, it is an undoubted proof that you are not within the bounds of God's <term>Decree</term><note>Decree: God's sovereign and eternal purpose regarding the fate of souls.</note> to make you blessed.

Secondly, those people who make the mercy and goodness of God an argument to further stiffen themselves in sin; such people are likely not the persons whom God has chosen for life and glory. In the Epistle of Jude, verse 4, it speaks of people who *change the grace of God into lasciviousness.* And what does the Apostle say of them? That they are people who *were of old ordained to this same judgment.* The Scripture sets it there as a marking-sign of a person who was of old ordained to damnation: when he shall persevere in that sinful state of changing God's grace into unchaste behavior—that is, taking arguments from the grace, mercy, and goodness of God to walk in the ways of sin. And therefore take heed, and mourn from the heart, all you who are inclined to misuse the doctrine of grace; and because God is good, you therefore wish to be evil; because God is merciful, you therefore wish to be sinful. If you die in that state, the Scripture declares that you are those people who were of old ordained to damnation.

Thirdly, a person who walks in the way of sin willfully, with haughtiness, and knowingly against his <term>Conscience</term>, and stubbornly without resistance; and therein perseveres and so lives and dies—that person is not within the bounds of God's Election. There is a way of speaking in Psalm 59:6: *Be not merciful to any of them, O Lord, who treacherously practice iniquity.* It says in some translations, *Be not merciful to those who practice godless ill-will*, or *willful godlessness*. Now, there is this rule which the theologians give: that these prayers which were made by David are rather prophecies of that which would happen, that which actually

<column-break/>

prayed that it might happen. Just as when David prays against the Jews in Psalm 69:23: *Let their table become a snare before them, and make their loins continually to shake*; which was a prophecy, and it happened so. And so he prays here that GOD would not be merciful to those people who practice godless ill-will; which is as much as a prophecy that God will not be merciful to the person who has practiced willful godlessness. And therefore, Beloved, all you who live thus, and intend that you wish to die so, and perhaps die so, and yet stubbornly sin, so that—let God command what He can—you will do what pleases you; let the Minister say what he will, you will do what you desire; who sins against knowledge and against Conscience, and without any resistance, and intends to live and die in the course of sin: may the Lord be merciful to such people, for certainly there would need be no Bible if such people came within the bounds of God’s Election.

Fourthly, the person who, through living under the powerful ministry of the Word, becomes more hardened in the heart and worse in life; if a person becomes such, it is a proof that he is not within the intention of God's Decree. Matt. 13:14, 15. *By hearing you shall hear, and by no means understand; and seeing you shall see and by no means perceive; for this people’s heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed; lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them.* Here is the judgment that God speaks upon such sinners: that they shall have eyes and not see, they shall be ignorant, their hearts shall become gross, they shall be incapable of taking any impression of the Word upon them. And what is the end of all this? *Lest they should be converted, and I heal them*; indicating that if God lets you—who live under the ministry of the Word—have dark eyes and hard hearts, it is a proof that God has no intention to save you, and therefore His intention is to damn you. So also, John 12:40. *He has blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart: that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted.* Here it is set down as an act of God, that God has hardened their hearts and blinded their eyes so that they are not converted, indicating that if people live and die in this state—having lived year after year under the powerful ministry of the Word and yet becoming more blind in judgment, more godless in life, and harder in heart after twenty, thirty, or forty years of hearing than they were before; so that the Word only draws out their godlessness, makes them more godless, and makes them resist godliness all the more—may the Lord be merciful to such souls, for certainly if God leaves you thus, it is a proof that He never intended to save you, for the Lord deals thus with such persons so that they might not be saved. There is a passage, Rom. 11:7. *That which Israel seeks; that it has not obtained, but*

By "the election" is understood the *elect* (the <term>abstract</term><note>abstract: A grammatical term; here, the author explains that the word "Election" is used to refer to the group of "Elect people."</note> being placed for the <term>concrete</term>). Just as often in the Scripture, "the circumcision" is placed for "the circumcised"; and so also here, "the election" is placed for "the elect." The elect have obtained it: what have they obtained? They have obtained Salvation and Glory; but the others, who were not chosen, were hardened. The Lord makes this a hallmark of those who are not chosen: that they are a blind people and a hardened people. Giving us to understand that those people who are not chosen—though they shall live under the preaching of the Word—shall nonetheless be blind in their minds, hardened in their hearts, and godless in their lives; and the ministry of the Word shall never improve them. If any of you are such a person, oh, that the Lord would make you tremble this day; tremble that God's thoughts may not be to do you good on another day.

Fifthly, when God gives a person over to the power of <term>delusion</term><note>delusion: In this context, a spiritual blindness or a "strong delusion" sent as a judgment.</note>, not only to believe lies themselves, but to teach lies to lead others astray; when the Lord lets them live and die in that state, the Scripture sets that as a proof of those who are not chosen by God for life and glory. For this reason, you shall read concerning that great delusion of the Antichrist in *2 Thessalonians 2:10, 11, 12*: *That God shall send them a strong delusion, that they should believe a lie, that they all might be damned who believed not the truth.* It is made into a brand of damnation when God shall give them over to believe a lie. Although a godly person may die holding a mistaken opinion (for every error is not a sign of damnation), yet errors that are fundamental—which strike at the Foundation of Religion—in which people walk so far that they never repent of their errors: the Scripture sets that as a sign of a person whose soul is in a world of peril. Read that passage, *2 Peter 2:1, 2, 3*: *There were also false prophets among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you.* And which are those? *Who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them.* (Not every error is a <term>heresy</term><note>heresy: A belief or opinion profoundly at odds with established Christian doctrine.</note>), but these people shall bring in damnable heresies. *And many shall follow their pernicious ways.* Now, what is their sentence? *Whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.* Their damnation did not sleep, but damnation has been waiting for them a long time, and they were in peril of the same. So that, Beloved, it is a great danger for people to be proponents of errors, especially when they are gross and tangible; and when they—as the Scripture speaks—may be called damnable heresies. It is a proof, if those people live and die thus, that they are not within the purpose of God's decree to do them good.

Sixthly, those people who live and die in a continual despising and opposing of the Gospel and the powerfully

<column-break/>

preached Word of God; it is a terrifying sign that they are not within the bounds of God's election. *1 John 4:5, 6*: *You are not of God, for you hear not His word.* So also *John 8:47*: *He that is of God heareth God's words: ye therefore hear them not, because ye are not of God.* Therefore, you do not belong to Him. But even more powerful to this end is that passage in *Acts 13:46, 47, 48*: *It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.* Now compare this with *verse 48*: *And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.* The contrast says this: as many as God intended to save, they praised God's Word, and they rejoiced and were glad in His word; but those who were not ordained to salvation, they thrust the word of the Lord away from them; they despised it and opposed it, and could not endure the word of the Lord. Therefore the text says: *The Jews stirred up the devout and honorable women, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts.* It was said to Amaziah in *2 Chronicles 25:16*: *I know that God hath determined to destroy thee, because thou hast not hearkened unto my counsel.* Thus you see that the Scripture makes this a hallmark of a person who is not kept within the bounds of God's Election to be brought to life and glory: to live and die in opposition to the Word of God.

Seventhly, we may say this with greater certainty and firmness: that a person is not within the bounds of God's election who commits the <term>sin against the Holy Spirit</term><note>sin against the Holy Spirit: Also known as the "unpardonable sin," traditionally interpreted as a willful, knowing rejection of God's grace and truth after having received it.</note>. *Matthew 12:32*: *It shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come.* This is an incomprehensible sin, *1 John 5:16*. Now, I know well that there are many who limit this sin only to the Pharisees, as if they alone were guilty of it. There are others who say that this sin is seldom committed, so that many theologians speak favorably of it. But Beloved, I am certain that this sin is committed more often than many people in the world believe; and many people have fallen into this sin who still have a good opinion of their own souls. The sin against the Holy Spirit is simply this:

It is a willful and premeditated act by a <term>professing believer</term><note>believer: One who claims to follow the religion or "professes" it openly.</note> of the Religion, through which he not only falls away from his profession; but he knowingly runs in the way of sin, against his conscience, stubbornly against counsel, and maliciously against JESUS CHRIST. This is briefly a description of this sin. Now I am certain that there are many in the world who have professed the Religion, who, if they are not in this sin, are nevertheless very near to it. I have now, from this somber Doctrine, only a few comforting propositions to set down, and then to conclude as follows:

1. That although these points may give you an indication of those who are not within the boundaries of God’s Election, nonetheless no one is bound to convince themselves that they are not chosen. For I have presented these main points not to cause any godly person to doubt their Election, but to terrify the godless, who live in a manner entirely contrary to the Children of God.

2. That a person may come very close to the worst of these sins and yet still be a chosen person. "We were," says Paul, "once disobedient, led astray, serving various lusts and pleasures," <margin>Titus 3:3 and Ephesians 2:2</margin> "formerly you walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, of the Spirit that now works in the Children of disobedience. Only see to it that you do not live and die in these sins; for if that is the case, there is no hope of grace.

3. That for those people who doubt their Election—simply because they do not find the saving workings of Election in their hearts and lives—it is actually more an evidence that they *are* chosen than that they are not. This is because people who are not chosen never look back at their Election to make it sure; they rely entirely on a vague sense of God's mercy and grace, and never look for holiness. Sin never disturbs them, godlessness never grieves them, and the lack of holiness never appalls them. Therefore, the doubting of your election, arising from the sins of your conduct, is rather a sign that God has chosen you for life and glory.

4. Election often covers those who are the worst sort of people in the world. Election reaches those who have been evil in their lives before they were called. And through this, God magnifies the riches of His grace. Election passes over the "civilly righteous" people—the sensible, moderate people—and commonly reaches people who were scandalous, unrestrained, unholy, and godless before they were called. <term>Matthew 21:31</term>. Harlots and tax collectors shall go before you into the Kingdom of God. Manasseh, who was a cruel murderer and an idolater, yet Election reached him. Mary Magdalene, a common harlot, out of whom Christ cast seven devils, yet Election reached her. Rahab, a harlot; Paul, a persecutor and blasphemer, a man harmful to the Saints; yet <term>Acts 9:15</term> he was a chosen vessel of God and obtained grace. God,

<column-break/>

in order to make the riches of His grace the greatest, lets Election reach the worst people who are in the world. And this ought to be a great comfort to you; although you may have been drunkards, Sabbath-breakers, adulterers, and godless, yet if you can now but embrace Jesus Christ and look toward Heaven—if you can now but weep over your state and have repentance for your former failings and come to Jesus Christ—Election has reached people as evil as you are. And even though you may now be godless in your life, you may nonetheless be the objects of God’s Election.

# Making [our] Calling Sure

### R 3

his principles; then the fault lies within themselves that they shall not be saved. And this the theologians call **universal redemption**.

Now, against this, I shall set down various passages of Scripture and then remove the objections that seem to strengthen this [universalist] view.

First, regarding the passages of Scripture. In the *Epistle of Jude, verse 4*, you read of certain men who were of old ordained to condemnation. Therefore, it is certain that all men cannot be saved. *1 Thessalonians 5:9*: Some men are appointed to wrath, but we to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, all men cannot be within the purpose of God’s primary aim to save them. *Matthew 22:14*: Many are called, but few are chosen. So also *Romans 11:7*: What Israel seeks, it has not obtained, but the elect have obtained it, and the rest were hardened. And *2 Timothy 2:20*: There are vessels of honor and vessels of dishonor. Scripture makes this a distinguishing act in God: that He has chosen some for life, and that He has, from eternity in His counsel, appointed others to wrath and condemnation. These passages of Scripture completely overthrow this [universalist] opinion. And indeed, the very word **Election** refutes it, as it signifies the taking of one and the passing over of the other.

But let us now look a little into the arguments of Scripture that they misuse to strengthen this false opinion of theirs.

One passage is *1 Corinthians 15:22*: "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive." Now they say: every human dies in Adam; every mother's child has become subject to death through the Fall of Adam; even so shall every human be made alive in Christ; the Lord intends that every human should receive a benefit through Jesus Christ.

Now, to remove this, I shall answer it by showing you the true target and aim of this passage of Scripture. This general manner of speaking—of being "made alive"—does not have its regard toward the salvation of the soul, but toward the **resurrection of the body**. And thus the sense is this: That just as in Adam, through the power of his sin, every human dies a natural death, so shall they all be made alive in Christ; that is, so shall every human rise from the dead through the power of Christ. Now, if you ask how I can prove this is the aim of the text, I answer that the words themselves make it manifest in *Verse 21*: "For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead." That is, just as through the one man Adam death came, so through that one man Christ shall be the resurrection from the dead. "For as in Adam all die, etc." So you see here that this is brought in as a confirmation of the 21st verse, signifying that this being "made alive" does not regard the life of the soul, but only the resurrection of the body; that just as Adam, through his sin, brought death upon all men, so also shall Christ, through His power, awaken all men from the dead—

<column-break/>

each in his own order. How could it ever be proven that this "making alive" refers to the life of the soul? It can mean no more than this: that all who are condemned are condemned as if in Adam’s loins; and all who are saved shall be saved as if in the loins of Jesus Christ. And so, this does nothing at all to confirm that which they call **universal election**.

Yet another passage of Scripture (irrefutable, as they think) is found in *Romans 11:32*, where it is said: "God has bound all men over to disobedience, so that He may have mercy on them all." Now they say: if God has performed an act to make men see their disobedience, and has intended through this act to have mercy on them all, then God has intended in His counsel to save them all.

Now, to this "that He may have mercy on them all," I answer: this manner of speaking ("all") must not be taken in an indefinite sense, as if God had bound all [individual] men under disobedience; rather, God makes all **believers** see their own misery, so that He might have mercy on all those who believe. If you ask how I prove that this is the meaning of the text, I answer: Scripture confirms that clearly in *Galatians 3:22*. "The Scripture has bound all men under sin" (the very words touched upon before); but what is the definition? Shall all men be saved? Oh no, for pay attention to the following words: "The Scripture has bound all men under sin, **that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe**." Now, although Paul does not say it exactly like this to the Romans, nonetheless, the words being the same, the definition holds firm in both places. So it is clear that "so that He might save them all," or "have mercy on them all," is not understood as everyone in general, but everyone with the definition Paul sets here: all those who believe.

Yet another objection, or passage of Scripture, which they misuse is *1 Timothy 2:4*: "Who desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." <term>Origen</term><note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian theologian who was later criticized for suggesting that all created beings, perhaps even the devil, might eventually be saved.</note> misused this text very grossly, maintaining from this that it is the aim and the will of God that all men should be saved. Now, to remove this objection, we must first distinguish **God's will**, and then the word **"all."** "Who desires all men to be saved."

First, regarding God's will: the <term>Scholastic Teachers</term><note>The "School-Leeraers" or Scholastics were medieval and early modern theologians who used logic and philosophy to define Christian doctrine.</note> provide this distinction: that there is a **will of God’s good pleasure**, and there is a **signified will of God**.

Now, the **will of God’s good pleasure** is that effectual purpose in God to save a person; and there is no one whom God, in this sense, wills to be saved who shall not be saved. But in that sense, God does not will that all men be saved.

But secondly, there is **God’s signified will**, whereby God in the Scripture offers salvation to every person who will accept Jesus Christ. And thus, God’s signified will excludes no one from salvation; but the Ministers, even if they preached to ten thousand people, so—

# Of our effectual [calling]

This is God’s **signifying will**; and although God tells you through this what the Ministers must do—namely, to present Christ and salvation to everyone—it nevertheless by no means follows that the **decreed will** of God’s good pleasure is wrapped up in this, or that all people shall actually be saved. <term>Perkins</term><note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch.</note> in his writings makes this distinction: that there is an **absolute will** of God, and in that sense He does not will that all people be saved; and a **conditional will** of God, which is that insofar as someone believes, they shall be saved. For God does not begrudge anyone's salvation; there is enough grace in God to make every person in the world blessed.

But secondly, a more distinct answer can be given to this passage: *God wants all men to be saved.* "All" is sometimes taken **distributively** and sometimes **collectively**. In a **distributive** sense, it would mean every individual human under Heaven; and in that sense, God does not will that all men be saved. But secondly, in a **collective** sense, it means all sorts and conditions of people; and in this way, God intends to save all—that is, some from every sort and from every state of people in the world. And this is evident if you consider the preceding words of the text: "He wants all men to be saved," that is, some of all sorts. Some Kings, some great Personages, some Rich, and some Poor, some Princes, and some Beggars. And the Apostle therefore commands them that they should pray for all men. "Pray," he says, "for Kings, and all who are in high positions," because God wants all men to be saved. This is as much as if he said: pray for Kings, because God, according to His grace, may save Kings just as well as poor people, who have fewer worries and fewer distractions in the world, and fewer <term>distractions</term><note>The original Dutch "afteckingen" refers to things that draw the soul away from God.</note> in their own souls than [Kings] have. God wants them all to be saved: salvation shall come to all sorts of people, and therefore you may lawfully pray for them. <term>Calvin</term><note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the French reformer whose 'Institutes' defined the theology of the Dutch Reformed Church.</note> also interprets this passage intelligently in this way: that God wants all sorts of people to obtain salvation through Jesus Christ; but it must not be extended in general, as if every man or woman without distinction would be saved. 3. "All" in contrast to the times of the Old Testament—*Romans 16:25*.

<margin>Application.</margin> Now, is it true that Election is not universal, but that some people are chosen and others are rejected? Do not rock yourselves to sleep in a **carnal security**, for it may be that you are in God's decree to be saved, or it

<column-break/>

may be not. Perhaps you may be in God’s thoughts to make you blessed; perhaps He may have decreed to damn you; and this ought to urge you toward that work to which my Text calls you: to strive to make your Calling and Election sure.

2. The second question is this: can someone who is one of the elect fall away from their election and be damned, or not? Regarding this point, the Protestant theologians have had great differences with the **Arminians**<note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius who argued that grace could be resisted and election was conditional upon faith.</note> and **Papists**<note>A common historical term for Roman Catholics.</note>. I shall not treat this through the disputes, but only—as best befits the pulpit—show you those firm passages of Scripture and reasons which confirm the truth, and then answer the most powerful objections they bring forward to the contrary.

**Question:** Can a person who is chosen fall away and afterwards be lost? To this I answer: **No.** A person who is once chosen can never be lost. And to prove this, I shall bring forward passages of Scripture and reasons. *Matthew 24:24*: Christ tells us there of a delusion that had crept in so easily that (if it were possible) they would deceive the elect. Signifying that it is impossible to deceive the elect in such a way that they would fall away until the end. So also *John 6:37*: "All that the Father gives me shall come to me"—that is, all those whom God the Father has intended to save through Christ shall come to Christ. *Verse 39*: "This is the will of the Father who sent me, that of all He has given me, I should lose nothing." This is the Father's will and the command to Christ: that all those whom He has given to Christ by His decree to save through redemption, He should not lose any of them. And Christ says, "I have lost none of them." So also *John 10:28, 29*: "I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish for eternity, and no one shall pluck them out of my hand; my Father who gave them to me is greater than all, and no one can pluck them out of my Father's hand." By "the hand of His Father," He understands His decree; that God, through His decree, intends to save so many, and Christ redeems so many for His Father, tells us that as many as God the Father has decreed to salvation, no man nor devil is powerful enough to pluck them out of the hand of His Father. Likewise *Romans 11:2*: "God has not cast off His people whom He foreknew." That is, God casts off none of those whom He has previously ordained; none of them shall be lost. Many more other passages of Scripture I could bring forward to show that a person who is once chosen shall not be lost in eternity, such as *2 Timothy 2:19*, *1 Corinthians 1:8, 9*, and *2 Thessalonians 3:3*. But I shall name reasons as well as passages of Scripture. And

First, if election were changeable, then God would have to be changeable; nothing is more absurd than to think that. If God’s decree were changeable, then God’s essence and nature would likewise be so, since election is nothing other than God Himself choosing: for everything in God is God. Thirdly, should this be true, then Paul's <term>Golden Chain</term><note>A theological term for the sequence of salvation described in Romans 8:29-30, where each link—predestination, calling, justification, and glorification—is seen as an unbreakable connection forged by God.</note> would be broken. Romans 8:30. *Those whom he predestined, these he also called: and those whom he called, these he also justified: and those whom he justified, these he also glorified.* Now, should this chain break—that those He has chosen, He has also called, and those He has called, He has also justified, and then stop there (as the <term>Papists</term><note>A historical term for Roman Catholics, used here to contrast the Reformed view of eternal security with the Catholic view that grace can be lost.</note> hold) and the people be afterwards damned—then the largest and most prominent link would be lost, namely: *those whom he justified, these he also glorified.* And this would thereby bring an absurdity upon the Scripture.

Now, to answer some passages of Scripture that they misuse (which at first sight may seem praiseworthy to you) to maintain that a person can be one of the elect, and brought to Christ, and yet afterwards be damned. The first passage is John 6:70. *Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?* Now, they say, there were twelve chosen, and one of them was a devil who was lost; indicating that people may be chosen, yet notwithstanding this, be lost. To which I answer:

That there are two kinds of election. First, an election to some particular office or ministry. Secondly, there is an election to grace, life, and glory. Now, when Christ says, *have I not chosen you twelve?* it is understood as his election to a ministry, to the place of an Apostle to be his Disciples. Now, it is true that a person can be chosen for some particular office in the Church of GOD and yet be lost and damned; but these words have no regard to the decree of GOD from eternity, only to a temporal election of twelve men to a temporal ministry, namely, to the ministry of an Apostle.

Another Scripture passage they misuse is found in Exodus 32:32. It was Moses' prayer: *If you will not forgive their sins* (Moses says to GOD) *then blot me now out of your Book, which you have written.* Now they say, this Book is GOD’S election: and Moses prays here that God would blot him out of his Book. Indicating, they say, that

<column-break/>

a person can be chosen and written in that Book, and yet afterwards be lost and blotted out.

To which I answer: That this prayer of Moses is only a wish, or a supposition, just as a wish of Paul’s was, when he wished to be cut off from Christ for his brothers, who were his kinsmen according to the flesh. Now, a person can imagine great mountains, and things that have never been, nor ever shall be: mere imaginings do nothing to the essence of the matter. So it is here, that Moses makes a supposition in an emotional prayer; this by no means confirms that his name could be blotted out of the Book of Life.

Secondly, <term>Rivet</term><note>André Rivet (1572–1651) was a highly influential French Huguenot theologian who taught at the University of Leiden.</note> explains it thus: that there are two kinds of Books of Life. The Book of Life is sometimes taken for an eternal counsel and decree of God, as in Philippians 4:3. Sometimes for a particular providence of God over people, in protecting them among the living. So we read in Psalm 139. *All these things* (says David) *were written in your book.* Meaning, not in the Book of GOD’S decree, but only in the Book of his providence, that all the members of David’s body were all under the providence of GOD, so that no one could harm him. And so Rivet and others believe that by the Book of Life here is understood that GOD would blot Moses out of the Book of his particular protection, and let him die just like other men, rather than have this evil come over the people of Israel. Just as if he said, erase my name from among men, and protect me no longer.

Again, they bring against this that which is said in Psalm 69:28. *Let them be blotted out of the Book of Life.* Now, they say, that is GOD’S election, and to be blotted out indicates that a person can be chosen and yet be lost.

To this I answer, as before, that the Book of Life in that place does not refer to the decree of GOD’S election, but only to the Book of his providence; that God would not protect the wicked in his providence in the same way as he did his own people. There is another manner of speaking in the Scripture that helps this explanation. Like Ezekiel 13:9. *They shall not be written in the records of the House of Israel.* What is that? That is: let them no longer be known as Israelites, nor be counted among the people. It seems to me that <term>Ainsworth</term><note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622) was an English scholar and pastor in Amsterdam, famous for his detailed annotations on the Bible.</note> compares Psalm 69:28 with this passage in Ezekiel 13:9. And he holds the meaning to be one and the same: that to be blotted out of the Book of Life is nothing other than to be out of GOD’S protection, to be blotted out of the register of the living, and to have one's life brought into peril of death. And David wishes this wish upon those wicked men.

But then they further object from Revelation 22:19. *If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, GOD shall take away his part out of the Book of Life.* Here, they say, by the Book of Life is undoubtedly understood GOD’S decree; and the Scripture says, he who takes away from the words of the Book, GOD shall blot him out of the

To which I answer: I confess that in this place the Book of Life is taken for God’s decree; and that a person can be said to be deleted from this Book / and yet it by no means follows that a chosen person can be condemned. Let me give you here the words of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for the Reformed tradition, especially regarding the doctrines of grace.</note> on this passage / which is a very clear and sufficient answer. That a person can be said to be deleted from the Book of Life in two respects:

**First**, That his name shall not be written in the Book of Life. The Scripture often has this manner of speaking. Just as it is said in **Matthew** <note>Refers to Matthew 5:19.</note>: He who does evil and teaches men to do so, he shall be the least in the Kingdom of Heaven. Signifying / not as if he should come into Heaven / but that he should by no means come there. To be the least there is not to be there. So also here / to be deleted / is here as much as to say that they were never in it.

**Secondly**, A person’s name can be said to be deleted from the Book of Life / not as if it were so in deed and truth / but in their own feeling; they thought they were chosen / and that their names were written there / they had a strong feeling of it; and even though they are now deceived and have a misunderstanding / yet God will one day let them know / when they are in Hell / that their names are deleted from the Book of Life. Again—

Yet another passage of Scripture they misuse / is **1 Cor. 10:12.** *He who thinks he stands, take heed lest he fall.* Now they say / if it were impossible for a chosen person to fall / and to fall away unto the end / to what end then is this warning of the Apostle? It would be a needless warning / if it were impossible to happen.

To which I answer two things. **First**, The Apostle does not say / he who stands / take heed that / etc. But the Apostle says / he who *thinks* he stands take heed lest he fall, signifying / that those people / who think they are chosen / and think they are in a good state / ought to take heed / that they are not lost for all eternity.

**Secondly**, take heed lest he fall. This falling is not understood here as a falling away from grace unto the end / and of a falling into Hell / and being lost; but the falling here is only a falling into sin / and a chosen person should take heed regarding that. A chosen person / although he stands firm in God’s decree / yet he ought to take heed all the days of his life / that he does not fall into sin. If you ask me how I make that clear; I answer / from the preceding part of the Text. This is the conclusion or the warning that the Apostle gives regarding the falling away of several examples of the people of God / who in former ages sinned against God. Just as some who tempted Christ, and fell in one day twenty-three thousand, others committed fornication, and rejected him in the Wilderness. And still other such sins being reckoned up / so the summary of all is / that consider—
<meta>catchword: seeing</meta>
<sig>A 3</sig>

<column-break/>

ing that they who were God’s People fell into sin / and were punished / therefore you who think you stand / and think that you are chosen / ought to take heed that you do not fall into sin / even as they did. And thus have I now finished with the untying of this second question.

**Thirdly**. Whether God chooses anyone to salvation upon the foresight of his faith / or good works: Foreseeing that those people would believe / and that he therefore chose them to salvation; and that other people would not believe / and that he therefore rejected them to damnation. Whether / I say / God in his eternal decree has chosen anyone to eternal life upon foreseen works? The **Papists** <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics.</note> and the **Arminians** <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius, who argued that God's election is based on his foreknowledge of who would choose to believe.</note> join together here to maintain this. The reason / they say / why God has chosen some / and others not / is / because God from eternity foresaw that those people would be holy / and believe in Christ / and therefore God chose them to salvation. These are the harsh accusations they charge God with.

To untie this I shall answer it with a denial / namely, that God / in the choosing of a certain number of people to life and salvation / has not done that upon the foresight of any good works / which he saw would be in them; be it faith / conversion / sanctification / or any other grace. It is true / that many of the **Papists** do not say so crudely that it was the foresight of good works in general / but only the foresight of faith, and so say the **Arminians** as well.

But now / to overthrow this groundless opinion / I shall / first / set down some passages of Scripture to confirm this, that God in choosing people to salvation / has not done so upon the foresight of good works / and then present the reasons: and then afterwards take away those objections which seem to obscure this truth.

**First**, Regarding the passages of Scripture that confirm this / for that we have **Rom. 11:5.** *Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the Election of grace.* Signifying / that the remnant which is saved / is only according to grace / and not according to foreseen works. So also **Ephes. 1:5, 11.** *He has chosen us according to the good pleasure of his will.* God’s pure good will was the moving cause of man’s election / but not anything in man. So likewise / **Rom. 9:11.** *That the purpose of **GOD** which is according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls.* So also **2 Tim. 1:9.** *Not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace.* According to his good pleasure / and according to his good will toward the human race / on that ground stands election.

But now to add some reasons here / why it cannot be / that God in his own counsel should decree to make people saved / upon the foresight of their works / so I shall name four or five. As /

<margin>2 Tim. 1:9.</margin>
**2 Tim. 1:9.** *We are called not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace.* And then regarding justification: we are also by no means justified because of our works, but by his grace; for *by the works of the Law shall no Flesh be justified.* Now, if calling and justification are not from works, much less is election from works, or from foreseen works, which are not yet effective within us.

**Secondly**, because it would then follow that children who die in their infancy cannot be chosen. For a child being in the mother’s body, if it has life, it has a soul, and so it must either be saved or damned. But a child, while it is in the Womb, does neither good nor evil. Now, if God chose men to eternal life based on foreseen works, then the children who die in their Mother’s body could not be chosen, because there are no works that God could foresee in them. And then this would be a very comfortless Doctrine for Parents whose children die in their youth.

**Thirdly**, then man would have the right to boast before his God, just as if he could attribute salvation to himself. If God were bound to choose men for salvation upon the foresight of good works, then man might say: "I do not thank God, but I thank my faith, and I thank my good works, for which God has chosen me for glory"; and thus the poor man would boast against his Creator.

<margin>1 Cor. 1:27, 28.</margin>
**Fourthly**, because God has chosen the basest men, while others who had more natural dignity and goodness were passed by. **1 Cor. 1:27, 28.** *God has chosen the foolish things of the world, that he might shame the wise: and God has chosen the weak things of the world, that he might shame the strong. And the base things of the world, and the despised, God has chosen,* etc. And **Matth. 11:25.**
<margin>Matth. 11:25.</margin>
*I thank you Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them unto babes.* Those who had the greatest worldly wisdom and natural abilities—who stood out most in outward strictness and moral virtues—are rejected, while those who were but children in understanding, and who were often, regarding their morality, the basest, are chosen; which is a clear proof that election is not grounded upon faith or upon foreseen works; for then the best would have been chosen before all others.

**Fifthly**, our works bring no proportion to that for which God has chosen us; we are chosen for eternal glory, but our works are finite, imperfect, and no more than our bounden duty; indeed, they are not done by our own strength, but by the power of God’s grace, and therefore they cannot be

that which moves God to choose us.

It is true—understand me well—I confess (and so also all theologians that exist confess this) that God makes man blessed for Christ's sake, but God does not choose man for Christ's sake, but purely for the sake of His good pleasure. God, in choosing man for eternal life, has no regard for Christ as if Christ were the moving cause.
<margin>1 Pet. 1:20.</margin>

<margin>Eph. 1:4.</margin>
**Eph. 1:4.** as in a general Person; God first chose Christ in order, and all believers in him; but it is not for Christ's sake, but according to His own will. For example: suppose a Kingdom were newly established, a King is chosen, and his successors to follow after him; therefore all the following kings are chosen in him, namely, the one who was first chosen; so also are we chosen in Christ. God chooses a man just as freely as if Christ had never died; nevertheless, God makes no one blessed except for Christ's sake; and this makes the election on God's side very voluntary. God does not look upon Christ, nor the good works that we have, but it is only His own good will that moves Him to make some blessed and to pass others by. Thus much be said to confirm this point. There are now some objections that lie in the way, which must be cleared away.
