->### Making one's Calling sure.<-

[one would not] use his prayers, nor also use holy duties; so says <note>John Preston (1587–1628) was an influential English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch.</note> Preston: if you neglect the <term>means</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, "means" (middelen) refers to the tools God uses to work in a person, such as prayer, reading the Bible, and attending church.</note>, it is a sign that you are not chosen; because, when God has chosen you for the end [salvation], He has also ordained you to the use of the means. I have read a story of an Italian, who, lying on his deathbed, sent for a Physician, the most excellent and famous artist of all Italy; this man was of that opinion of which I now speak: that since God’s decrees were unchangeable, a person might live just as he pleased, and still be saved; and that, let a person live as holily as he could, if God had decreed his damnation, he would be damned; and let a person be ever so godless, if God had decreed his salvation, he would be saved; and that also the decree of God took away the use of all means, so that people had no need to use any means, but only to leave it to God. The Physician, being a man experienced in the mysteries of Religion, after he had asked him about the state of his body and where the sickness lay, and the sick man desiring that he should prescribe him some medicine; the physician gave him this answer, saying: "God has decreed how long you shall live; therefore, whether I give you a medicine or not, if God has decreed that you shall die, you shall die all the same; and if He has decreed that you shall live, even though I give you no medicine, you shall nonetheless live." And this answer (says the historian) took such a place in the Italian, that it converted him from his opinion, and he cast upon this saying a right and well-grounded reason. This is therefore my answer: that if such <term>reasonings</term> <note>The original Dutch "reden-kavelingen" implies a sort of logical quibbling or sophistry.</note> as these are unreasonable in temporal things, they are much more so in spiritual things.

Secondly, I would say this to you who pretend such a thing: that at that very same moment in which God decreed to bring a person to eternal life, at that same moment God also decreed that this person should be holy before he died; that he should use all holy and sanctified means which are fit for his salvation, Romans 8:29. *For whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son.* God the Father, in that same decree in which He ordained a person unto life, also ordained that those chosen people should be conformed to Jesus Christ in life. <note>The text cites Ephesians 4, but the quote "chosen us... before the foundation of the world" is actually found in Ephesians 1:4.</note> Ephesians 4: *He has chosen us in Christ, before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy, and blameless before Him in love.* God has decreed that our life should be holy; He ordains holiness as the means, just as well as Heaven as the end. So also Ephesians 2:10: *We are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God has prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.* So likewise, 2 Thessalonians 2:13: God, before the world was, at that same moment in which He ordained and chose the person for

<column-break/>

salvation, also ordained that the people should live here on the earth a holy and blameless life. Now then, regarding the fact that people make this objection—that since God has decreed the person for eternal life, that therefore the person may live as he pleases—that is absurd: for if the person lives as he pleases, it is a proof that God has not ordained them to eternal life, because God, in decreeing the person to life and salvation, decreed that they should walk in the way of sanctification, and that they should live holily in this world.

Thirdly, suppose it were granted that God had decreed to damn you or me; that God in His purpose had decreed that He would not save us, nonetheless God, as a Creator, is entitled to our service. God, as a Creator, may demand your bounden duty from you. Although God should damn us, nonetheless, as He has created us, He deserves obedience and duties of gratitude from us. And therefore under this name alone, even if no other consideration were looked at, this ought to obligate you to a righteous life; and this ought to urge you to your bounden duty, even if God never made you saved. Adam, being in the state of innocence, even if he were never to come into Heaven, nonetheless as he was made and created by God, he was bound to lead a holy life. And so it is with every person who lives, insofar as we are Creatures, and have a being from God, and have the comforts of this life from God; all these things bind us to obedience and a righteous life toward God, even if He were to cast us into hell when we have done all that. And let this be enough for the untying of the fourth question: that God’s decree, regarding the election of the person to eternal life, in no way encourages the person to live as they please, upon the aforementioned grounds. I go now over to the fifth question.

Fifthly, what temptations does the devil throw into the mind of the godly, to make them doubt in themselves that they are not chosen by God, when they are in fact chosen; so that he makes them think that they are "reprobate silver," when they are vessels of honor fit for their Master's use? Perhaps I may speak to some whose souls are troubled in this case. I shall bring the answer to this into three main points, and as I present them, labor to carry them away, so that they may not be a righteous cause or reason to make you doubt your Election.

First, the devil tempts the godly with this: that surely you cannot be chosen, because before your Calling you were so exceedingly sinful and godless in your life; such exceedingly godless, base, and evil people, that surely such as you (the devil will say) cannot come within the bounds of God’s purpose to be saved.

Secondly, the devil will tell you that surely you cannot be chosen for eternal life, because after your Calling in Jesus Christ, you have so foolishly fallen into deadly and offensive crimes and sins.

-># Of our powerful [Calling]<-

And thirdly, because God constantly follows His people with external and great tribulations: from this, the devil will conclude that you are not the chosen and beloved of God. He often brings these three great temptations upon tender <term>Consciences</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, a "tender conscience" refers to a person who is very sensitive to sin and easily distressed by the fear of God's judgment.</note>, solely to create a world of doubts and disturbances in the chosen vessels of mercy. I begin with the first.

First, the devil tempts you by saying that you are certainly not chosen because your life was exceedingly godless, and you were such horribly wicked people before you accepted the profession of Jesus Christ. The devil lays this before many a poor soul as a stumbling block.

In order to satisfy you in this matter, I shall set down four points in response.

First, many of the servants of God, before their <term>Calling</term> <note>The "Calling" (Roepinge) is the moment a person is effectively summoned by God's grace to faith and repentance.</note>, were very wicked, unholy, and openly godless people. And they were, nonetheless, within the bounds of God's <term>Election</term> <note>"Election" (Verkiesinge) is the Reformed doctrine that God chose certain individuals for salvation before the world began.</note> to life and glory. Cast your eyes upon Paul, and there you shall find what he was before his Calling. He tells you of himself: "I was a blasphemer (a terrible sin), I was a persecutor, and an oppressor of God’s Church; I took people captive for the profession of the Name of Jesus (these were great sins)." Yea, he says even more: "I was exceedingly raging against the Church of God." A man who raged with a high hand against the people of God. Now, what could be more base than he? And yet, you shall find that this man was a chosen vessel of mercy. Yea, you shall find that God—in order to strengthen the confidence of people regarding their Election—places a scandalous person and Election together, to make people see that a scandalous life before conversion is not harmful to a person's Election. Acts 9:13, 14. And Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many of this man (speaking of Paul), how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem. We have heard from many what a wicked man this is, and that he has power from the chief priests to bind all who call upon your name." And that this man has also done that and fulfilled his commission. Here was a godless person: but notice now what the Lord says: "Go thy way," says God, "for this man is a chosen vessel unto me." Here you see that Ananias lays his misdeeds and godlessness before the Lord; and yet, "Go thy way," says God, "go thy way, for he is a chosen vessel unto me." We have similar examples in Manasseh and Mary Magdalene. This is, therefore, my first answer: that many of God’s servants, before their conversion, were people of a very evil and godless life, and were nonetheless within the bounds of God's Election to salvation.

Secondly, although people were openly godless in their lives before their Calling, nonetheless, if this open godlessness moves them to labor more excellently in grace after their Calling, this is a sign of Election rather than of rejection. This is remarkable in Paul; he was an openly godless man before his Calling, but now this outstanding godlessness before his Calling

<column-break/>

moved him, after he was converted, to labor to surpass all others in godliness; and the worse he was before, the more he labored to be holier afterward. Just as he previously labored to take people captive for the profession of Jesus Christ, so now after his Calling, he is very zealous to draw people to Jesus Christ; he was very diligent in doing evil before his Calling, and this made him—after his Calling, as he himself says—labor more than they all. And so also Mary Magdalene, who was a base woman before her Calling, and one who was a common prostitute; a woman out of whom Jesus Christ cast seven demons; and yet this woman, after her Calling, labored to be more outstanding in godly sorrow than any woman before or after; she washed Christ's feet with her tears and dried them with her hair. You do not read of such a thing in Scripture regarding any other woman. And this was a very good sign: when your open godlessness in the ways of sin before your Calling sets you so much to become more excellent after the Calling, this is a very good proof or encouragement that you are within the bounds of God's Election; and therefore, you have no cause to lose heart. Suppose that you—before the Word took hold of your conscience—were guilty of great sins, unfit even to be named in the assembly; if you now wish to honor and praise God all the more, and wish to walk more humbly, and labor to surpass others in grace just as you formerly did in sin—this is a great sign that you are within the bounds of God's Election.

Thirdly, you who have been scandalous in your life before your Calling, know for your comfort that God in His eternal counsel prefers to make unholy, godless, and evil people the objects of His Election rather than "civilly honorable" people <note>The author distinguishes between people who are merely "civil" (respectable or law-abiding by worldly standards) and those who are truly transformed by God's grace.</note>—rather than those people who lead a glorious, civil, and modest life here in this world. And the Lord does this on this ground: to all the more magnify the goodness and the riches of His own grace in choosing people for eternal life. For if God were to choose only moderate and civilly righteous people in the world, people would think that it was a person's modesty and civility that moved God to choose them; and therefore, to cast down these thoughts, God rather allows Election to run toward those people who have been openly godless and sinful in their lives, rather than toward those other people. Manasseh, an openly bloodthirsty man, nonetheless came within the bounds of God's Election, while many a civil person was left outside. Mary Magdalene, a common prostitute, was nonetheless chosen, while many a noble, chaste woman was cast into Hell. Matthew 21:31, 32. There Christ tells a parable of two people. One said that he would not go nor follow Christ, but he did it anyway; and the other said that he would go, but he did not go. Now, which of the two did the will of Christ? And they said, "The first." And Jesus said to them, "Verily I say unto you, that...

you, that the Tax Collectors and the Harlots shall go before you into the Kingdom of God. But you will say: was this common? Was this only for a specific time? Therefore, pay attention to the following words: "For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; but the Tax Collectors and the Harlots believed him." John came preaching, and you would not believe—you <term>Pharisees</term> <note>The Pharisees were a Jewish sect known for strict, outward observance of religious laws, often contrasted by Jesus with those who had sincere, inward repentance.</note>, you strictly moral people who do not break out into such scandals as other people do—you would not believe, says Christ; but Tax Collectors, people who were very inclined toward oppression and improper gain, they embraced Jesus Christ, where moral people would not. This, therefore, ought to be another comfort to you: that <term>Election</term> <note>The theological concept that God chooses specific individuals for salvation based on His own grace rather than their merit.</note> often runs toward the unholiest sort of people sooner than toward civilly righteous people here in the world; and God does this to make the richness of His own grace great.

Fourthly, it does not matter what you were before your <term>Calling</term> <note>The moment an individual is spiritually summoned by God to faith.</note>, provided that you are a holy people after your calling; your former failings shall in no way be harmful to your future blessedness. *1 Corinthians 6:9, 10, 11.* "Neither Fornicators, nor Idolaters, nor Adulterers, nor the Effeminate, nor Thieves, nor the Covetous, nor Drunkards, nor Revilers, nor Robbers shall inherit the Kingdom of God; and such were some of you," etc. Here you see a register of vile sins heaped together, "and such were some of you"; but now you are washed, now you are sanctified, etc. So it does not matter what you have been before your conversion, even if guilty of great sins, as long as you are now a renewed and sanctified people; *Titus 3:3.* "For we ourselves were also sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy," etc. So were you formerly; but when the kindness and love of GOD appeared to you, after they were converted, they were no longer so. So these four points clearly take away this objection: that it does not matter what you were before your conversion. If you are now a converted people, mourning your sins and amending your ways, your previous evil life shall be no hindrance at all to your election. Truly, I must necessarily say this: that you who have been the most outstanding in sin, God expects this from your hand—that you should be the most outstanding in grace, the deepest in humiliation, and the most excellent in godly sorrow, even though your previous sins in no way hinder your election.

Secondly, if the devil cannot fix this upon you, then he will attack you with this storm: namely, with your frequent falling into offensive, shameful, and gross sins after you have accepted the profession of Jesus Christ. And the devil will sing this very closely: perhaps the sins before your conversion were not so great; but now, since you have followed the Sermons, and since you have confessed Jesus Christ, and since that time you have foolishly fallen into gross and offensive sins; surely this cannot exist with grace, and cannot fall within

<column-break/>

<margin>Persons who are within the bounds of God's election.</margin>
I confess this is very sad and dangerous; I shall nonetheless set down three things to uphold you, so that you may, notwithstanding this, be within the bounds of God's election. Namely:

*First*, that various persons who were within the bounds of God's election have foolishly, after their calling, fallen into gross sins. *Lot*, after he was called, fell into incest and drunkenness; *David*, after he was called, fell into Adultery; *Peter*, after he was called, fell into a denial of *Jesus Christ*. Yes, you read of *Solomon*, *1 Kings 11:9*, that his heart had turned away from the Lord the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice. Yes, that He had revealed Himself to Solomon and had converted him; yet after that time, he did evil against his God. Yes, you read further, *Nehemiah 13:26, 27*, that foreign women caused Solomon to sin, even though he was beloved by his God. Although he was loved by God and chosen by Him, nonetheless his wives drew his heart away from the Lord. You have a similar manner of speaking in *Numbers 14:23*. "After all these works and miracles which I have done among them, and My signs which I did in Egypt and in the Wilderness, they have tempted Me these ten times," says the Lord. After they were the Lord's through the covenant, and after they were a redeemed people; even after they had tempted Him many times by sinning against Him, nonetheless many of them were chosen vessels of mercy. So I say that many of God's servants, after their calling, have foolishly fallen into offensive sins and yet have been within the bounds of God's election.

Secondly, if your falling into great and offensive sins does not contain these four sinful parts in itself, then your falling into sin after your calling can coexist with election. *First*, if you do not fall into the sin willfully. Secondly, if you do not fall into the same sin frequently. Thirdly, if you do not fall into the sin with delight. And fourthly, if you do not remain lying in your sin without repentance. If these parts are mixed with your sinning after your calling, they cannot coexist with election. *First*, if you fall into sin willfully, so that you rush into the sin like a horse into battle. Secondly, if you fall frequently into the same sin, then it is perilous and dangerous. It is true, *Peter* denied *Christ*, but it was only in a gust of temptation. *David* fell into adultery, but it was never more than once; *Lot* was guilty of drunkenness, but it was only once: for the servants of God, although they fall, they do not fall frequently into the same sin if it is gross and offensive. Thirdly, if you fall into the sin with delight, so that you seem to take pleasure in the sin you fall into; if you, as Job says, keep the sin under your tongue, deeming it sweet and delightful to you. And lastly, if all this is capped with an unrepentant heart, so that you have no heart to have remorse over the sins you fall into—may the Lord be merciful to you; for surely if you fall into sin with these ingredients, you are not

It also addresses the danger of falling into sin after conversion, providing biblical examples like David and Peter to show that even the elect can stumble, provided the sin is not willful, frequent, or unrepented.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the resolution of the second "storm" or case of conscience: the fear that falling into sin after one’s calling disqualifies them from being among the elect. It then introduces the third "storm": the belief that ongoing suffering and affliction are signs of God's rejection.</meta>

within the boundaries of God's mercy to be saved. But now, even if you fall into sin—if it is not willful, but through the power of temptation; if it is not with delight, but with a displeasure against the sins into which you fall; and that as soon as you fall and see your sins, you have repentance and rise up again—even if you happen to fall in this way, it shall be no obstacle to your <term>Election</term> <note>The theological concept that God chooses specific individuals for salvation based on His grace.</note>.

Thirdly, falling into sin after one’s <term>Calling</term> <note>The moment an individual is spiritually summoned by God to faith.</note> and after having made a profession of Jesus Christ can coexist with Election in these four cases: First, if the sins into which you fall are clearly seen. Second, if they are feelingly lamented. Third, if they are strongly resisted. And lastly, if they are daily worked and prayed against. Although you fall into sin, nevertheless, in these cases, sin shall not condemn you or be an obstacle to your Election. And thus I have finished the second case of conscience. Only let me touch upon this one thing before I depart from it (for I do not want you to turn this Doctrine into a doctrine of license; but I would have you lay it to heart): that if any of you fall foolishly into sin after your conversion, believe this—that God will make you suffer for it. Although not in Hell, you shall nonetheless have a Hell in your conscience; you shall have a true foretaste of Hell, a wounded conscience; and God will expect a deep humiliation and a great repentance if you sin after making a profession of Jesus Christ. It may have that effect on you, just as it did with David, who cried out, *I have no rest in my bones because of my sin.* <note>Original reference: Psalm 38:3.</note> God will give you no rest night or day because of sin, if you run into it after your profession of Jesus Christ.

Thirdly, people doubt their Election because God pursues them with constant afflictions and lays upon them the constant blows of His heavy wrath; and this makes many a godly person think that they are not in the number of God’s chosen. To which I shall briefly answer:

That this is nothing other than a temptation, and not the truth; and that was the same dispute that Job's friends had with him: they wanted to fix this upon Job—that he was a <term>reprobate</term> <note>Someone rejected by God and destined for damnation.</note> and a hypocrite because God afflicted him so. But Job defended his integrity and showed his grounds: that God was his friend and that He did not reject him, even though He afflicted him. But to speak more specifically:

<margin>Ecclesiastes 9:1, 2.</margin>
First, no one can infallibly and certainly judge God's purpose regarding a person's Election or rejection based on any of God's dealings with their bodies in the things of this life. For "no man knows either love or hatred by all that is before them. All things come alike to all. One event happens to the righteous and to the wicked; to the good, so also to the sinner; to him who swears as to him who fears an oath." <note>Original quote from Ecclesiastes 9:1-2.</note>

Secondly, the afflictions from God are so far from being grounds or proofs

<column-break/>

that a person is not chosen, that in some cases they may be proofs that he is a true chosen one of God.
<margin>Hebrews 12:6, 7.</margin>
"For He scourges every son whom He receives; if you are without chastisement, then you are bastards and not sons." "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent."
<margin>Revelation 3:19.</margin>
In some cases, the afflictions of God are signs of God's love rather than the opposite. This is true: 1. Insofar as the afflictions are a spur to you, to reawaken your pace on the way to Heaven. 2. Insofar as your afflictions are like <term>pruning knives</term> <note>Original: "snoep-messen," referring to the pruning of vines to encourage growth.</note> to prune and cut away the luxuriant sprouts and workings of sin in the heart. 3. Insofar as the affliction is a testimony to restrain you and make you walk in a close fellowship with God, and not to stray or wander from Him. 4. Insofar as the affliction is like an axe to chip away that rust which clings to your nature. 5. Insofar as the affliction serves as a furnace to refine you from that dross of corruption that is mixed with your service to God. In these cases, afflictions are so far from being grounds to doubt your Election that they should rather give you proof that you are a true chosen one of God.

Thirdly, that God, according to His wisdom, often subjects His own people in this life to greater afflictions than He causes the godless and reprobates to undergo. God does not want to give the reprobates their Hell here, so that He might give it to them hereafter. God does not want to give the elect their Heaven here, in order to make Heaven more desirable to them while they live here, and more welcome when they arrive there. It pleases God, in the distribution of His providence among men, to let His own people lie under more outward sorrow than the godless do.
<margin>Psalm 73:5, 7.</margin>
"Their eyes stand out with fatness... they are not in trouble as other men, neither are they plagued like other men." <note>The author quotes Psalm 73:5 and 7 to show that the wicked often live easy lives.</note> The Lord in His governance deals with the godless in such a way that they are not plagued and afflicted as the godly are here in this world. And therefore, affliction is certainly no proof of God's displeasure, or that they are not within the boundaries of God's purpose to do them good.

### 2 Peter 1:10

Therefore, Brothers, be all the more diligent to make your **Calling** and **Election** sure.

<margin>16th Sermon.</margin>
The Doctrine that I still have at hand is this: that Christians ought to apply a very great diligence to make this sure to their souls—that they are eternally chosen to life and salvation by GOD the Father. In the pursuit of this Doctrine, I have covered various points; I now have only one question to satisfy concerning **Election** <note>The theological belief that God predestines certain individuals for salvation.</note>, and to wrap up this Doctrine by proposing some explanatory propositions which are very useful for making the Doctrine of Election clear. The question that must be resolved is this:

What are those deceits of the devil by which he introduces arrogant imaginations into the minds of men, making them think they are chosen by God when they are not? To answer this, I shall bring everything I have to say under these three main headings.

First, the devil makes godless men believe they are chosen on this ground: because they do not break out into such gross, scandalous, and outstanding sins in their lives as many other people do around them. And therefore, the devil maintains them with this: "Surely, if you were not chosen, you would be as evil, as base, and as wayward as anyone. Now, seeing that God restrains you, so that you do not do such things in your life as other men do, this can be a comforting proof to you that you are in the number of God’s chosen." And this deceit deceives thousands of people, especially idle and "civil" <note>Meaning socially respectable or law-abiding but lacking internal spiritual life.</note> people; they run blindfolded toward Hell, and nourish in themselves the hope of life and salvation, never feeling the contrary until they come to death and into Hell. I shall explain that this is a deceit by setting down four or five points. As:

First, that many people are mentioned in Scripture who were not within the bounds of God’s Election, who nonetheless were people of a blameless and glorious life, not stained with any gross and scandalous sins. Read Luke 18:11, 14, concerning the **Pharisee** <note>A member of a Jewish sect known for strict, outward adherence to religious law.</note>; he thanks GOD that he was no robber, adulterer, miser, drunkard, nor as godless as the tax collector. Here you see a man who speaks boastfully and truly, that he was not a man who broke out into such sins as other men did; yet what kind of man was this—a chosen vessel? Certainly not. Read verse 14. The Text tells you there that the tax collector went down to his house justified rather than he, the Pharisee. Although he was free from scandalous and gross, outstanding sins, yet he was not a justified man, and consequently not a cho-

<column-break/>

sen man. You read of the **Hypocrites** in Matthew 23, that they "cleansed the outside of the cup and the dish," that is, that they cleansed their conduct and the outward man from gross scandals, and yet within were full of filthiness; and Christ tells us that they were Hypocrites, and that they would have their portion in Hell. And if you were to look through the histories written of the Scribes and Pharisees, and some people among the Jews, they would relate to you what wonderful, holy-living people they were; they were constant in their duties, they fasted twice a week, and prayed every day on the street corners; no one was as strict in observing the **Sabbath** <note>The day of rest and worship.</note> as they were. They wished to walk cautiously so that they would not be ensnared by these high distractions <note>original: "hoog-werfelen"</note>; and yet these people, who were so strict and attentive, were people who did not have a drop of grace in them. Although they were a people who were thus well-mannered in their lives, yet the Scripture tells us of them that harlots and tax collectors would go into Heaven before them. This is, therefore, the first point: that many people in their lives have been free from gross scandals, and yet were people who were not chosen by God for life and salvation.

Secondly, that a man’s conduct may be free from scandalous sins, yet if that freedom from scandals comes from an evil source, then it can be in a person who is not chosen. As I shall make clear. There can be a freedom from gross sins proceeding from a three-fold source, and he may nonetheless be a person who is in the state of damnation and rejection. Namely: first, there can be a freedom from scandals proceeding from a *religious upbringing*; secondly, from a *natural temperament*; and thirdly, from the power of *restraining grace*. First, there can be a freedom from gross sins proceeding from the power of upbringing. So it was with the young man in the Gospel, Matthew 19:18, 19, 20. When Christ said to him what the Law was: *You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall love your neighbor as yourself, you shall not kill, you shall not give false witness,* etc. Then the young man said, *All these things have I kept from my youth.* He was a Pharisee, and his parents, being very strict in their lives, brought him up that way from his youth; and yet this was not a chosen man (verse 22). Secondly, a man can be free from scandalous sins arising from a sensible natural temperament. A man’s temperament can sometimes be outwardly averse to certain sins. **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer (c. 46–119 AD), here cited for his moral integrity despite being a "pagan."</note>, a Heathen, could say: "I would rather it be said that there was no such man as Plutarch in the world, than to say that Plutarch was unchaste, or a drunkard, or a swearer." A man’s natural temperament can sometimes be free from gross sins, and he nonetheless not be a chosen man for that reason. And then thirdly, a man can be free from gross...

<meta>This page continues the sermon on the assurance of salvation and the doctrine of Election. The previous page discussed how avoiding outward sin is not a definitive proof of being chosen by God. This page transitions into a systematic explanation of Election through ten propositions, specifically addressing the limited number of the elect and the common misconceptions about God's mercy.</meta>

-># Making [our] calling sure.<-

[...barm]merciful God is; yet God's saving mercy does not extend so far as to include all creatures that live, which He has made. You read in Isaiah 27:11: *It is a people of no understanding: therefore he that made them will not have mercy on them, and he that formed them will show them no favor.* Here you see that the Prophet tells them that God, who made them, shall damn them; and that God, who formed them, shall show them no mercy. Thus, God's mercy does not extend to all the works of His hands; for if it were so, the devils might claim salvation just as well as men; for God made them when they were glorious angels just as He made men. And therefore, if all the works of God's hands could claim salvation, then they might also come within the bounds of God's Election, just as wicked men do.

And thus you see that in these various sermons I have dealt with the doctrines of Effectual Calling <note>In Reformed theology, "Effectual Calling" refers to the work of God's Spirit whereby He convinces a person of their sin and draws them to Christ.</note> and Election. I shall now clarify this matter a little by setting down ten propositions, which shall serve to explain the doctrine of Election in its many parts, and then I will conclude.

**First**, That all men are not the objects of God's Election. And this proposition refutes the opinion of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar. He is famous for the theory of "apocatastasis," the idea that eventually all beings, including the devil, will be saved.</note>. Origen was of the opinion that the entire human race would be saved; yes, that even the devils would all be saved through Christ. A very groundless and unheard-of opinion; for all men are not chosen for salvation. Jude tells us in his Epistle that there are some who were long ago marked out for this condemnation; and if it is so, certainly they cannot come within the bounds of God's Election. In 1 Thessalonians 5:9, there are some appointed to Wrath; *we are not among those*, says the Apostle, *but we are appointed to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.* All men are not objects of God's Election to eternal life.

**Secondly**, That God has made the smallest portion of men the objects of His Election. God has, in His own counsel, chosen the smallest part of the men in the world for life and salvation. And this is a very proper doctrine. *Many are called, but few are chosen,* Matthew 22:14. Romans 11:5, *A remnant according to the election of grace.* And to follow this chapter a little further, I shall set down two things under this proposition: First, that only a few rich people are chosen by God for life and salvation. Secondly, that also only a few civilly-honorable <note>The term "civilly-honorable" refers to people who live moral, law-abiding lives in society but lack internal spiritual transformation.</note> people are chosen by God for life and salvation. There are but few rich people who come within the bounds of God's purpose to be saved, 1 Corinthians 1:26: *Not many mighty* (he does not say "not any," but "not many mighty"), *not many noble, not many great of the world are chosen.* You read in Matthew 19:24, *That it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a

<column-break/>

needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.* That it is easier for a camel. It is not to be understood in the sense that some explain it: That there was a gate in Jerusalem called "The Needle’s Eye"—a small and low gate through which camels, when loaded, could not pass, and therefore the burden had to be unloaded and the camel had to bow down before it could go through. Some think that Christ's saying refers to what Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major French Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> says, that instead of <margin>kamēlos</margin> <note>original: "καμηλος", meaning camel.</note> a camel, they read *kamilos*, a cable, which, if it were unraveled, could be stuck through the eye of a needle; but the knot is not untied by this explanation, but rather cut. But these words were a proverb among the Jews, who used this as a saying: that when someone spoke of things that were improbable or unbelievable, they said, "That can happen as easily as a camel can go through the eye of a needle." And Christ, having His eye on that proverb, says that rich men who hang and lean upon their riches, and would rather lose Heaven, and Christ, and soul and all creatures, than their riches—Christ says it is an impossible thing for such rich men to come into Heaven. Just as I once recounted what Buchanan <note>George Buchanan (1506–1582) was a Scottish historian and tutor to King James VI and I.</note> said, lying on his deathbed during an embassy to King James: "I am now going to the place where few Kings come." And beloved, that saying is true, for *not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble has the Lord chosen.* Secondly, few civilly-honorable people come within the bounds of God's Election to be saved. Modest people who lean on their civility and modest honor, and on their fair dealings; few or none of those come into Heaven. *The tax collectors and the harlots shall go before you into the kingdom of heaven,* Matthew 21:32. Harlots and tax collectors believed in Me when you did not believe, says Christ.

**Thirdly**, That although God in His own counsel has decided upon or chosen only the smallest number of men for life and salvation, yet this in no way contradicts the mercy of God, nor does it diminish or accuse the mercy of God. Men might think as if God had certainly laid aside all His bowels of mercy. What? Would God create such a world full of men, as He has done, and save only a few of them? Men might think as if God were a hard Master, who took pleasure in the destruction of men, who had forgotten to be merciful; such accusations they would be ready to lay upon God. But now, beloved, that God has chosen such a small number for life, this in no way accuses the mercy of God. And I demonstrate it thus: because God was not bound to save anyone; therefore, you cannot accuse God of unmercifulness or of unfaithfulness, even if He saved no one. It was a mere
<meta>The word "mere" (enckel) is a catchword for the next page.</meta>

->Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? hope in God, for I shall yet praise him; he is the ...... health of my countenance, and my God.<-

ALTHOUGH the Psalms are contained in one Book, which is called the Book of Psalms (Acts 1:20), in Hebrew they are nonetheless distinguished into five Books.
The first Book of Psalms begins in Hebrew with the first Psalm, and ends with the 41st Psalm, being concluded with "Amen, yes, Amen."
The second Book of Psalms the Hebrews begin with Psalm 42, and end the same with Psalm 72, which is also concluded with "Amen, yes, Amen," and "the prayers of David the Son of Jesse are ended."
The third Book of Psalms begins with the 73rd Psalm, and ends with the 89th Psalm, which one also finds concluded with "Amen, yes, Amen."
The fourth Book of Psalms begins with Psalm 90 and ends with Psalm 106, with "Amen Hallelujah."
My Text is contained in that Psalm which begins the second Book; the Interpreters differ in finding the occasion of this Psalm: In general, the Interpreters agree in this, that it was written by David, either when he fled from Saul (for then David was greatly troubled, and driven from his House and Home, and by his enemies driven from Public Worship) and was forced to hide himself in the holes and caves of the earth: when he was in that sorrowful state, it is thought that he composed this Psalm. Or it was composed <margin>2 Sam. 15:14.</margin> at that time when he fled from his Son Absalom, when he was in danger of losing his life. At one of these times, the Interpreters think that David composed this Psalm.

<column-break/>

And it seems closest to the truth that it was composed when David was deprived of public worship.
But I come now to the words themselves: *Why are you cast down*, etc. My Text contains a moving <term>Soliloquy|A spiritual practice where a person speaks to their own soul or heart, often used in Puritan devotion to examine one's internal state.</term> or self-talk, which the Psalmist makes to his Soul, as if they were two Friends, while he reasons with himself, just as the supernatural and noblest part of Man conducts reason with the lowliest and most outward part of Man (*Why are you cast down*, etc.). Just like a Man who speaks to someone whom he wishes to convince. So here David, in order to speak with his own Heart, uses such reasons as one would use to someone in grief and heaviness, when his soul is disquieted and dejected; *Why are you disquieted within me?* etc.
These words are then a self-talk, through which he seeks to encourage himself to be of good cheer in all his grief. These words are exceedingly useful for your souls. One finds that David did the same at other places and times as well, Ps. 103:1, *Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless His Holy Name.* See how the Psalmist addresses his soul, to praise the Name of God. And at another time, when he rebukes his own soul for his negligence and <margin>Ps. 73:22.</margin> failings before the Lord, he says, *I was a beast before him*: and the Scripture tells us that the People of God have rebuked their own hearts before God over a sin; whenever they found the least fault in themselves, then they accused themselves of the same: *Why are you cast down, O my soul*, etc.
In general, I shall take these four things into consideration regarding these words.
I. Why, or what the reason might be, that...

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

...that these words are used three times in this and the following Psalm? <note>Love is referring to the refrain "Why art thou cast down..." which appears in Psalm 42:5, 42:11, and 43:5.</note> For in the whole Book of Psalms, one will not find two verses of the same length, except in the 6th verse of the 42nd Psalm, and in this Text the 12th verse, and in the 5th verse of the 43rd Psalm, where the same words, *why do you bow yourself down*, etc., are found. There is no Psalm that uses such a repetition of words as this one, except for the 107th Psalm, where it is frequently repeated: *let them praise the Lord for his goodness.*

Well, what might this signify to us, that David so often mentions his own soul—that it goes as if it would bow down, being neither restful nor quiet? Truly, the repetition of these words indicates to us the weightiness of the matter. Matters of lesser weight are spoken of least and are merely touched upon; but over matters of great weight, reflections linger longer, and they are presented and repeated with greater earnestness and diligence; as in these words: *Why do you bow yourself down, O my soul? and why are you disquieted within me?*

**II.** When, and on what occasion, were these words spoken? It was at that time when David was persecuted by Saul, when he was banished from his house, from public divine service, and from the stately assembly of the believers (verse 2). For this reason, his soul bowed itself down and was disquieted within him, as he had a holy longing for God and His courts. Verse 3: *My soul thirsts for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God's face?* This is a matter that troubles David’s mind. David was in difficulty and anxiety when there was oppression over the Church of God, as one difficulty followed upon another. Verse 8: *Deep <margin>Tribulation begets tribulation. Musculus.</margin> <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563) was an influential Protestant reformer and biblical commentator.</note> calleth unto deep at the noise of your waterspouts.* One wave of sorrow followed another, just as the waves of the sea strike against one another; thus does one unrest give birth to another.

Secondly, when he composed this Psalm, the troubles of the Church weighed upon him at that time, specifically concerning the strong enemies who confronted him. Psalm 42:10 <note>The Dutch text says Ps. 10, likely a shorthand or misprint for Psalm 42 verse 10.</note>: *Why do you forget me? why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?* Nevertheless, in this his sad and restless state, he utters this bursting soliloquy: *Why are you disquieted within me?* etc.

Note here (in passing) that often the people of God, in the midst of their greatest sorrow, must bring these holy reflections to their soul’s attention, so that they are not too greatly disturbed in troubles. Therefore David says (notwithstanding that he was in great turmoil): *why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?*

In the same way, Paul also wrote most of his Letters in bonds, in prisons, and in great troubles: nevertheless, in the midst of them, his heart was filled with joy to his great comfort. So also was David’s heart better disposed when he was in the Cave than when he was in his Palace; and although troubles pressed upon him, yet he speaks to his soul, that it should not be troubled.

**III.** David’s troubles proceeded from the Devil and wicked men who oppressed him. The wicked oppressed him and the Devil tempted him; yet David 

<column-break/>

rebuked his own heart and nothing else. David does not lash out against Saul or against Absalom, but he rebukes his own heart: *why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?* Although the Devil tempts us and the wicked plague us, as instruments of punishment for sin, yet we must, like David, rebuke our own soul. David had cause to accuse Absalom and Saul, but he does not do it, only rebuking his own soul. *Why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?* etc.

**IV.** Remember that the words in the original language stand in the active voice: <gloss>מָה-תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי וַתֶּהֱמִי עָלָי</gloss> <note>original: "Mah-tishtochachi nafshi va-tehemi alay" — Why do you [yourself] bow down, my soul, and [yourself] moan within me?</note> *Why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?* and not *why are you bowed down?* Just as Arias Montanus translates it: *why have you humbled yourself? why do you depress yourself, my soul?* <note>Benito Arias Montanus (1527–1598) was a Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> Lorinus Proverbs 12:25. <note>Jean Lorin (1559–1634) was a Jesuit commentator known for his work on the Psalms and Proverbs.</note> The words being taken thus indicate this: that God's people can be too greatly dejected over the feeling of sin, and that they themselves particularly labor toward this defect. It is neither God nor the Devil who bows you down, but *why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?* Man often causes himself more unrest and sorrow than God lays upon him or the Devil inflicts upon him.

In the words themselves, three parts are to be noted.

**I.** Here is a twofold distress to be lamented, differing in degrees from one another; to be disquieted is more than to be bowed down: *why do you raise a tumult?* <note>original Latin: "cur tumultuaris?"</note>

**II.** Here is a twofold duty to be practiced: to hope in God and to praise God.

**III.** Here is a double encouragement in these distresses: *He is the health of my countenance, and my God.*

*Why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?* The believers cause themselves disquiet. Neither God through what He sends, nor the Devil through temptation, disturbs us as much as we trouble ourselves. Proverbs 12:25: *Heaviness in the heart of man bows it down.*

1. Sometimes bowing down is taken in a good sense; when the soul humbles itself before God over sin and judgment; as we see in 2 Corinthians 7:6: *God, who comforts the humble,* etc. Namely, those who humble themselves over sin and the feeling of their misery. On such an occasion, David nowhere, and certainly not here, rebuked his soul.

2. It is sometimes taken in a bad sense, when the sorrow over sin is not moderate, so that it is greater than God requires or commands; where such sorrow is found, it must not be coddled but rebuked; just as David rebukes his own soul over it in this text: *Why do you bow,* etc.

The explanation and treatment of these words can serve as a particular benefit for God's people: I shall therefore seek to spend some time upon them: I will begin for this time with the first part of this text. *Why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?*

The Doctrine that I shall draw from these words is this:
The children of God, although they <margin>Doctrine.</margin> cannot be cast away, yet they may well be cast down. <note>Love is making a wordplay on "verworpen" (rejected/cast away) and "neder-geworpen" (cast down).</note> *Why do you bow yourself down, O my soul?*

# Of a Broken Soul

<unclear>Da</unclear>vid’s soul was thus cast down in this Psalm.

I. He mourns because he was forced to be absent from public worship, so that he could not gather in the place where God is served. See his desire in the 3rd verse of this Psalm: *My soul thirsts for God, for the living God: when shall I go in and appear before God’s face?* See also verse 5. *I remember these things and pour out my soul within me, because I used to go with the multitude, and walk with them to the House of God,* etc. David was now deprived of public worship, and that caused him to mourn.

II. His soul was pressed down under the feeling of the sin which he had committed against God, and the evil fruits of that sin, remembering what he had done against God. Thus, he felt the <term>wrath of God<note>A common theological concept referring to the divine response to sin, often felt as deep internal guilt or anxiety.</note></term> in the pondering of his sin.

III. He lay under the <term>eclipse<note>original: "Eclipsis"</note></term> and sorrowful suspension of Divine favor, verse 10. *I will say to God, my rock, why have you forgotten me?* The awareness of the withholding of God's grace cast David's soul down within him. Seeing as he missed the feeling of God’s love and the light of His countenance, that caused him to mourn so.

IV. He mourns over the oppression and victory with which the enemies of the truth overcame God’s people, verse 4.

V. He was more grieved over the sin than over the hardship that struck him; since the Name of God was blasphemed and dishonored by other men. This caused him to complain, verse 11: *With a death-stab in my bones my adversaries taunt me: while they say to me all day long: where is your God?* Also verse 3: *My tears have been my food,* etc. All these things indicate that he was more troubled by spiritual disturbances than by physical oppression. The blasphemy against God is a death-stab in his bones, whereas the misery was but a scratch. This must teach you all that whenever you are at any time restless and cast down, you must be more concerned, with David, over spiritual things than over outward oppression. The dishonoring of God’s Name is to David a death-stab in his bones.

In the handling of this doctrine, I shall show for what reasons the souls of the children of God—who were not rejected—were nonetheless cast down. And this shall be the foundation of the following account; it lies then in these four things:

1. Although they are not rejected, they can nonetheless be cast down over the greatness and hideousness of sin: that is a great cause why the souls of God’s people are bowed down.
2. Because they miss the favor of God and the feeling of the forgiveness of their sins.
3. Over the visitation and miserable state of the Church and the people of God.
4. Over the outward oppression which they themselves feel.

These I shall only name, because they are the foundation of the following account.

First: the soul of the children of God is cast down, although not rejected, by the sight and feeling of sin. The reason why I handle this matter is

<column-break/>

so that it may be as a consequence of the forgiveness of sins.

In the handling of this doctrine, regarding the bowing down of the soul under the sight and the feeling of the greatness and hideousness of its sins, many things are to be noted.

1. I shall show what this casting down over sin is.
2. What kind of people God bows down and humbles over the sight and feeling of sin.
3. When God’s people can be said to be too much dejected over the sight and feeling of sin.
4. How one shall distinguish the dejection of the children of God over sin from the dejection of ungodly people over sin: for both the godly and the godless are sometimes dejected over sin.
5. What the reason may be why the souls of the children of God are dejected over sin, even though they are not rejected.
6. What rules the people of God have to observe, so that they are not too much dejected under the burden, sight, and feeling of sins, and thus do not fall into despair.

1. I shall begin with the first, namely what this dejection over sin is. I said in the beginning that there is a dejection over sin: first, when God humbles the soul over sin, and this is a dejection for good, when the sorrow over sin is mixed with faith. Secondly: there is also an evil dejection over sin; when the soul is so pressed down under sin that it does not lift itself up to Christ, to see with the eyes of faith the forgiveness of sins, and thus with confidence to apply to itself the forgiveness of sin through Jesus Christ. This kind of dejection is blameworthy.

2. What kind of people God bows down under sin: this I shall show you in nine or ten things. There are nine or ten kinds of people whom God humbles over sin.

1. These who have been public and shameful sinners before their conversion, leading a godless life: God ordinarily brings them home through stormy alarms in their conscience. Such was <term>Manasseh<note>A King of Judah described in the Bible (2 Chronicles 33) as being extremely wicked before undergoing a dramatic conversion while in captivity.</note></term>, outstanding in sin and hideous in unrighteousness, but greatly humbled over the weight of his sins. God uses sharper and rougher means to win over gross and public sinners, those who set their faces against Heaven and are raging and heated persecutors of God and His Truth, who willfully and stubbornly continue in sin. When God calls such to conversion, then He humbles them deeply over their previous sins and provocations.

<term>Paul<note>The Apostle Paul, who prior to his conversion was known as Saul of Tarsus.</note></term> was a great and public sinner before his conversion, being a great persecutor of the Congregation and people of God; he was an unrighteous man and a blasphemer; it was all the same to him what injustice and pain he caused the Church of God: he persecuted the people of God from one city to another, throwing them into prison, seeking to root out both the Christians and the Religion so that they might no longer be remembered. David had cause to accuse Absalom and Saul, but he does not do it, rebuking only his own soul. *Why are you cast down, O my soul?* etc.

Remember that the words in the original text are in the *active* voice: <term>תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי וַתֶּהֱמִי עָלָי</term> <note>Hebrew: "Why do you cast yourself down, my soul, and why are you disquieted within me?"</note> *Why do you cast yourself down, O my soul?* and not *Why are you cast down?* Just as Arias Montanus <note>A famous 16th-century Spanish scholar and Bible translator.</note> translates it: *cur humiliasti te? cur deprimes te anima mea?* <note>Latin: "Why have you humbled yourself? Why do you depress yourself, O my soul?"</note> Lorinus <note>Jean Lorin, a Jesuit commentator.</note> on *Prov. 12:25*. The words being taken thus, they indicate this: that God’s people can be too greatly dejected over the feeling of sin, and that they themselves specifically labor toward this failing. It is neither God nor the Devil who casts you down, but *why do you cast yourself down, O my soul?* Man often causes himself more unrest and sorrow than God lays upon him or the Devil inflicts upon him.

In the words themselves, three parts are to be noted:

I. Here is a twofold distress to be lamented, differing in degrees from each other; to be disquieted is more than to be cast down; *cur tumultuaris?* <note>Latin: "Why are you in an uproar?"</note>

II. Here is a twofold duty to be practiced: to hope in God and to praise God.

III. Here is a double encouragement in these distresses: *He is the health of my countenance, and my God.*

*Why are you cast down, O my soul?* Believers cause themselves unrest. Neither God through what He sends, nor the Devil through temptation, troubles us as much as we trouble ourselves. *Prov. 12:25:* **Heaviness in the heart of man makes it stoop.**

1. Sometimes "bowing down" is taken in a good sense: when the soul humbles itself before God over sin and judges itself; as we see in *2 Cor. 7:6*: *God, who comforts the humble,* etc. Namely, those who humble themselves over sin and the feeling of their misery. In this instance, David has nowhere, nor here, rebuked his soul.

2. It is sometimes taken in a bad sense: when the sorrow over sin is not moderated, so that it is greater than God requires or commands. Where such sorrow is found, it must not be coddled but rebuked; just as David rebukes his own soul over it in this text: *Why are you cast down,* etc.

The explanation and handling of these words can serve a particular usefulness for God’s people: Therefore, I shall seek to spend some time upon them. I shall begin for this time with the first part of this text. **Why are you cast down, O my soul?**

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
The doctrine that I shall draw from these words is this:

The children of God, although they cannot be cast *away*, can nonetheless be cast *down*. *Why are you cast down, O my soul?*

->### of a contrite Soul.<-

...for a soul was thus cast down in this Psalm.

I. He mourns because he is forced to be absent from public worship <note>Dutch: *openbaren Godts-dienst*, referring to communal religious services</note>, so that he may not gather in the place where God is served. See his desire in the 3rd verse of this Psalm: 
> My soul thirsts for God, for the living God: when shall I go in and appear before God’s face?

See also verse 5. 
> I remember these things and pour out my soul within me, because I used to go with the multitude and lead them to the House of God, etc. 

David was now deprived of public worship, and that caused him to mourn.

II. His soul was pressed down under the feeling of the sin which he had committed against God, and the evil fruits of that sin, remembering what he had done against God: thus he felt the vengeance of God in the pondering of his sin.

III. He lay under the eclipse and the sorrowful suspension of Divine favor, verse 10. 
> I will say unto God, my rock, why have you forgotten me? 

The awareness of the suspension of God's grace threw David's soul down within him: since he lacked the feeling of God’s love and the light of His countenance, it caused him to mourn so.

IV. He mourns over the oppression and victory with which the enemies of the truth overcame God’s people, verse 4.

V. He was more disturbed over the Sin than over the hardship that befell him: because the Name of God was blasphemed and dishonored by other men. This made him complain, verse 11. 
> With a death-blow in my bones my adversaries taunt me: while they say to me all day long: where is your God? 

Also verse 3. 
> My tears have been my food, etc. 

All these things indicate that he was more moved by spiritual troubles than by physical displacement. The blasphemy against God is a death-blow in his bones, whereas the misery was but a mere scratch <note>original: *schabbe*, meaning a scab or a minor skin irritation; used here to contrast a superficial wound with a deep one</note>. This must teach you all, that whenever you are at any time restless and cast down, you must be more concerned—like David—over spiritual things than over outward displacement. The dishonoring of God’s Name is to David a death-blow in his bones.

In the handling of this doctrine, I shall show for what reasons the souls of God's children, who were not rejected, were nevertheless cast down. And this shall be the foundation of the following narrative; it lies then in these four things:

1. Although they are not rejected, they can nonetheless be cast down over the greatness and the abominableness of sin: that is a great cause why the souls of God's people are bowed down.
2. Because they lack the favor of God and the feeling of the forgiveness of their sins.
3. Over the visitation and the miserable state of the Church and the people of God.
4. Over the outward displacement <note>Dutch: *verruckinghe*, referring to being forcibly moved or exiled</note> which they themselves feel.

I shall only name these, because they are the foundation of the following narrative.

Firstly; the soul of God's children is cast down, though not rejected, over the sight and feeling of sin. The reason why I handle this matter is,

<column-break/>

so that it may be as a consequence of the forgiveness of sins.

In the handling of this doctrine, concerning the bowing down of the Soul under the sight and feeling of the greatness and abominableness of its sins, many things are to be noted.

1. I shall show what this casting down over sin is.
2. What kind of people God bows down and humbles over the sight and feeling of sin.
3. When God's People can be said to be too greatly contrite over the sight and feeling of sin.
4. How one shall distinguish the contrition of the Children of God over sin from the contrition of ungodly people over sin: for both the godly and the godless are sometimes contrite over sin.
5. What the reason may be why the souls of the Children of God are contrite over sin, even though they are not rejected.
6. What rules the People of God have to observe, so that they are not too greatly contrite under the burden, sight, and feeling of sins, and thus do not fall into despair.

1. I shall begin with the first, namely what this contrition over sin is. I said in the beginning that there is a contrition over sin: first, when God humbles the soul over sin, and this is a contrition for good, when the sorrow over sin is mixed with faith. Secondly; there is also an evil contrition over sin; when the soul is so pressed down under sin that it does not lift itself up to Christ, to see with the eyes of faith the forgiveness of sins, and thus with confidence apply to itself the forgiveness of sin through Jesus Christ. This sort of contrition is blameworthy.

2. What kind of people God bows down under sin: this I shall show you in nine or ten things. There are nine or ten sorts of people whom God humbles over sin.

1. Those who have been public and shameful Sinners before their conversion, leading a Godless life: God usually brings them home through stormy alarms in their conscience. Such was Manasseh, outstanding in sin, and abominable in iniquity, but greatly humbled over the weight of his sins. God uses sharper and rougher means to win over gross and public Sinners, who set their faces against Heaven, and are raging and hot persecutors of God and His Truth, who with a stubborn heart proceed in sin: When God calls such to conversion, then He humbles them deeply over their previous sins and provocations.

Paul was a great and public sinner before his conversion, being a great persecutor of the Congregation and People of God; he was an unrighteous man and a blasphemer; it was all the same to him what wrong and shame he did to the Church of God: he persecuted the People of God from one city to another, throwing them into prison, and sought to blot out both the Christians and the Religion, so that they might no longer be remembered. Paul being thus a public Sinner, and so outstanding in sins, as he...

->### Balm of Gilead, or the Healing<-

When someone is brought to themselves through <term>conversion<note>Dutch: *bekeeringe*. In this context, it refers to a complete turning of the heart toward God.</note></term>, God often deals with them strictly and sharply. He humbles them greatly by revealing their own unworthiness and the magnitude of their sinfulness. God throws such a person down, just as He met Paul on the road while he traveled to carry out his evil plan of tormenting God’s People. God, I say, threw him to the earth upon his face, causing him to cry out in *Acts 9:6*: "Lord, what will you have me do?" Read more of this in that chapter. The reason for this treatment is that since his cruelty was public, God also wished to make his conversion from sin public. Because his sin was not only against the great God, his conversion is not only great; but since his sins were a great offense to those who feared the Lord, the greatness of his humbling is revealed to those who were scandalized by the course of his sinful life. This humbling and terror is his spiritual <term>penance<note>Dutch: *penitentie*. Here used as a public showing of regret or outward proof of a change of heart.</note></term> before the world, making his conversion visible. And if I now speak to any among you who have been or still are outstanding in sin and godlessness, such that you have heavily transgressed: when God eventually calls you to conversion, He shall humble you deeply through the sight and feeling of sin; so that just as your sins have been great, so also shall your sorrow over them be great.

What we read in *Acts 16:14* and *29, etc.* is worth noting: we read there of two persons who were converted, yet in different ways.

One reads of Lydia in *verse 14*: "A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, so that she took heed of the things spoken by Paul."

This woman was converted in a gentle way and manner, through coming to hear Paul’s preaching, at which time God opened her heart. Here was conversion without any mention of terror or the stirring of the conscience, or of a casting down and deep humbling over sin. There is no mention of a humbling arising from the feeling and possession of her former life; rather, she was brought to God through a soft and friendly path.

But in the same chapter, you read the history of the conversion of the <term>Jailer<note>Dutch: *Stock-waerder*, literally "keeper of the stocks."</note></term> in *verse 29*: "Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas: 30 And said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" This was one who previously had handled Paul and Silas harshly, throwing them into the inner prison and fastening their feet in the stocks (*verse 24*). When God now wished to convert him, He made him fear and quake, and his conscience tremble, and his heart ache; and springing in, he fell at their feet and asked how he might be saved. And all this happened because of the godlessness of his actions. This is thus the method God maintains to convert bold and neck-strong sinners to Himself.

I may say, just as Solomon said in another context in *Ecclesiastes 10:8*: "He who digs a pit shall fall into it: and he who breaks through a wall, a serpent shall bite him." I

<column-break/>

know that the passage specifically looks upon those who tread underfoot and break the wall of government, whether of Kingdom or Church, and that they also shall be broken sooner or later. But let me apply it to this occasion nonetheless. You, O Man, who break the hedge of God’s commandments, transgressing every command through your sinful life, be assured that a serpent shall bite you, and that you shall fall down at the sight and feeling of your sin; you shall be stung and bitten by the feeling of God’s vengeance. When God converts you, He shall humble you more in repentance than other men. Therefore remember, O Man, that if you take pleasure in committing atrocious and outstanding sins, God shall also deal with you by humbling you deeply over your sins when He calls you to Him.

II. God casts these down most over sin: those who fall back into the same sin after they were converted. They wound Religion; God also wants to wound their hearts and break their peace. God brings such things back upon their heads and presses it upon their hearts, yes, making their conscience troubled, and thus God punishes them extraordinarily for it. Sin was to David before his conversion like a small thorn in the flesh, but after his conversion, sin was like a death-stab in his bones; so that he had no rest because of his sins. Hear him speak after his conversion regarding his sins in the matter of Bathsheba and Uriah in *Psalm 51*. Sin is like the crushing of his bones (*verse 10*). He prays to God for a restoration of the joy of salvation (*verse 14*). Previously, sin might have broken his sleep, but now it breaks his heart. <term>Tertullian<note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage.</note></term> calls these *peccata devoratoria* <note>Latin: "devouring sins" or "swallowing sins."</note>, offensive sins, swallowing sins. He who falls foolishly shall walk with difficulty and be restored with hardship. In *Psalm 30:9*, David says to the Lord: "What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit? Shall the dust praise you? Shall it declare your truth?" Although he went with his foot into the grave, he nonetheless thought that his soul would not be saved. Therefore, beware of falling into great sins after God has done great things for your soul.

III. The third sort of people whom God strikes down over their sin are those who are of a <term>melancholic humor<note>In the 17th century, "humors" were believed to dictate temperament; "melancholic" referred to a person prone to sadness or heaviness of spirit.</note></term>. The devil has more power over melancholic people than over any sort of people in the world, to plunge them into sorrowful fear, greater abandonment, and heavier terror than those people who are lively and of a cheerful humor.

IV. God strikes these more over their sin: those who are of a rough and hard disposition. When God converts such people, He ordinarily lets them be more dismayed over their sins than those who are of a softer temperament, who do not need as much humbling as others. You know that the hearts of men are compared to stones: it is also known to you that one stone is broken sooner than another; so also some hearts are softer and more tender than others. Some hearts are like flint-stones, upon which many a heavy blow must be brought to break them, while other hearts are like soft stones, which break with the smallest blow. When God...

->### The State of a Stricken Soul<-

God shall bring bold-hearted sinners—those who make a habit of sinning—to <term>conversion<note>Dutch: *bekeeringe*. A total turning of the heart and life toward God.</note></term>; to do so, He uses hard blows to break and humble their stony hearts. It is with sinners much as it is with wood: one piece is easily hewn, while another is more <term>knotty<note>Dutch: *quastiger*. Referring to wood that is difficult to work with due to knots; used here as a metaphor for a stubborn or difficult personality.</note></term> and requires more strikes to make it square and fit for use. So it is also with the nature of some people; it is much rougher and more knotty, requiring a greater measure of humbling than others do.

V. God humbles those who are not converted until their old age deeply over their sin. When such people are converted, God keeps them long stricken under the feeling of their sins. It is right for God to do this so that, just as they have long persisted in sinning, God keeps them long under the feeling and fear of the guilt and the weight of sin. If one wishes to cut a sprout from a tree, one only needs a penknife; but if one wishes to hew off a branch, an axe is required. Now, all the sons and daughters of men are from the old trunk of the <term>old Adam<note>A theological reference to the fallen state of humanity inherited from the first man, Adam.</note></term> and are grafts of a natural stem; we are all chips of that old block. Old sinners are those who have spent the most time of their lives in sin. God will strike more blows to cut you off from your old root, from your worldly way of life; God wants to use such means and keep you longer under the feeling of your sins to humble your proud heart. Whereas a young child—one whom God converts from their youth—God will not strike as severely over their sins as He does the one He converts in their old age.

VI. God strikes those very severely over their sins who harbor and indulge in many <insert>known</insert> sins in their hearts which are not known to the world, and of which no one in the world can have knowledge but they alone. These God humbles greatly when He converts them; God stirs up a silent storm of sin in their <term>conscience<note>Dutch: *Conscientie*. The internal moral compass through which the author believes God speaks to the individual.</note></term> over their misdeeds. Just as it is with the wind: while it is spread out in the air, it does no damage; but when it is gathered together in the bosom of the earth, it overturns house and yard and all things. So it is with sin: as long as sin (although it is in you) is only (like wind in the air) scattered and dispersed through repentance and humbling, it does you no harm. But when sin is pursued and harbored in your bosom, in your heart, and is cherished and tolerated by you in your soul, then it shall be in your soul like a wind in the earth, to cause heart-shaking and conscience-shaking, and thus causes great turmoil in your mind. Therefore, O man! whoever you are who treads the path of sin and pleases yourself in known sins for which no one can accuse you but God and your conscience, know that God will one day deeply humble you over those sins if He is to convert you to Himself.

VII. God casts down over sin those who turn away and fall away from religion—those who profess the truth and then deviate from that profession. When

<column-break/>

God wants to bring these people back, He humbles them to the dust over their sins; <margin>Proverbs 14:14.</margin> according to the saying of Solomon: *The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways; but a good man shall be satisfied from himself.* Just as the backslider has been filled with the pleasures of sin, so shall he also be filled with his own ways—namely, with terror of conscience, anguish of spirit, unrest of mind—and his own turning away shall be a torment to him. God wants to humble such a person low when He brings him back; <margin>Jeremiah 2:19.</margin> *Your own wickedness shall chastise you, and your backslidings shall reprove you: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that you have forsaken the Lord your God,* etc. It may be that you have turned away from the truth, but God will make your own turning away punish you. I shall present to you the well-known history of <term>Francesco Spiera<note>original: "Fransiscus Spira." An Italian lawyer (c. 1502–1548) who famously fell into deep despair and died believing he was damned after recanting his Protestant faith.</note></term>: he professed the truth, and thereafter he fell away from the profession of the truth; although his conscience assured him that he sinned, nonetheless he sinned so heavily that he sinned against his conscience, the <gloss>representative of God</gloss>. Read the history, and you shall see what a gnawing and terror of conscience this sin caused; it laid him under the terror and the feeling of divine vengeance for his apostasy. All you, then, whoever you are who falls away from the profession of the Gospel: God will meet you and fill you with terror, and your turning away shall punish you, and your wickedness shall chastise you.

VIII. God humbles those under the feeling and weight of sin whose nature is easily puffed up with spiritual pride; such as these God humbles greatly when He brings them to conversion. As the Psalmist says of wicked and godless men, they stand on slippery ways and <margin>Psalm 35:6, 73:16.</margin> slick places. Whoever dwells in high places does not remain standing long; and what is said of outward pride is especially true of spiritual pride. God brings the proud to the depths of Hell, as one reads in Isaiah 14:11-16. <margin>verse 11.</margin> *Your pride is cast down into Hell, with the sound of your harps: the maggots shall be spread under you, and the worms shall <margin>verse 12.</margin> cover you.* Verse 12: *How are you fallen from heaven, O morning star, son of the morning! How are you cut down to the ground, <margin>verse 13.</margin> you who weakened the nations!* Verse 13: *And you said in your heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: and I will sit upon the mount of the congregation, on the sides of the north.* <margin>verse 14.</margin> Verse 14: *I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.* <margin>verse 15.</margin> Verse 15: *Yet you shall be brought down to Hell, to the sides of the pit,* etc. This was spoken against the King of Babylon to destroy his outward pride. Those who think to set their nests in the heights, God shall bring such into the dust. So then, O man, because you have become spiritually proud on the strength of your natural gifts, know that if God has purposed to bring you to Himself, He will humble you before Him in the feeling of your sins. Those who are puffed up by the delusion of their own worthiness, God wants to humble...

**IX.** God humbles those whom He intends to make instruments in His Church—for the building up, strengthening, and comforting of <term>stricken souls<note>Dutch: *verslaghen Zielen*. Refers to individuals overwhelmed by the weight of their sins.</note></term> and restless consciences. These individuals God plunges into the sight and feeling of their own sins. More cost and effort is spent on the Vessels of the Sanctuary than on any other ordinary vessels for common use. Likewise, God spends more effort (if I may speak so) on those He wishes to make vessels in His Church, fit for His Service. Such a person will have to endure greater trials and temptations for his humbling, so that he might be more capable of comforting and reassuring others who are stricken and troubled in their minds. The <term>star-gazers<note>Dutch: *Sterren-kijckers*. An archaic term for astronomers.</note></term> who lie low in pits and valleys have the clearest view of the stars; so too are those most fit to comfort others who have themselves been under God’s discipline. It is noteworthy regarding **Luther**: there was no man in his age who was so restless, tried, and plagued by the temptations of the Devil, and so troubled by the sight of his sins, than Luther; indeed, the Devil appeared to him in a physical form and desired to fight him hand-to-hand. Yet, in all this and through these means, Luther became the most capable and willing in the Church to bring comfort to the oppressed.
