## II. SERMON.

->Psal. 42 : 12.<-

> Why do you bow down, O my soul, and why are you restless within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him, He is the <unclear>......</unclear> salvation of my countenance and my God.

THE third Question is: When can God's people be said to be too much cast down over their sins? Truly, being stricken and humbled over sin is good and necessary; when then can a child of God be too much cast down over sin? David did not rebuke himself for being humbled over his sins, but because he was *too much* cast down.

A child of God can be said to be too much cast down over sin in these nine circumstances:

**I.** A person is too much cast down over sin when his humbling causes him to cast away all hope of forgiveness: when he lies so low under the burden of his sins that he has no hope they will be taken from him. Then the humbling over sin is too great, as it makes one say (as in Jeremiah 2:25), "It is hopeless," and that you are cut off. This is too great a measure of humbling: when the godly, doubting, say what the godless say mockingly—that their sins are too great and their situation too desperate for there to be any hope or help for them in God; that there is no salvation

<column-break/>

to be expected for them, nor any means for them to escape. This is to be too much cast down over sin: this is the way to cut off all hope. The hope of the Saints in Heaven is also cut off, but it differs greatly from this manner of cutting off. Their hope is changed into a perfect enjoyment of what they previously hoped for; they have no more hope because they are *above* all hope. But the Saints on earth must always maintain their hope against all <term>dejection<note>Dutch: *mismoedigheydt*. A state of being disheartened or lacking courage.</note></term>, and steadfastly hope for the forgiveness of their sins. It is better that the thread of our lives be cut than the anchor-rope of our hope; despair is the cutting off of all hope. To be so stricken over one's sins that one has despairing thoughts without hope of grace—that goes too far.

**II.** That person is too much cast down over sin who neglects his <term>required duty<note>Dutch: *schuldige plicht*. Religious obligations such as prayer or attending services.</note></term>. When a man <term>argues<note>Dutch: *reden-kabelt*. To debate or reason internally, often in a circular or negative way.</note></term> thus against himself: "Why should I pray and practice other holy duties, when I know that God will not hear? He will not hear my prayers, though I pray as long and as often as I want." And likewise regarding the confession of sins: "Why should I confess my sins? I know that God will not forgive them anyway." And "Why should I desire grace? I know that God will give me no grace." And "Why should I hear sermons? I know that God will not hear me, nor accept my service, nor shall I gain any benefit by all that I do or hear." These reasonings, O man, are very sinful and indicate a high degree of excessive humbling over sin. Just as despair cuts off all hope, so does such sinful imagination cut off all effort. When a man is so stricken over sin that he is negligent in observing his duty, it shows there is too great a casting down of the Spirit. Despair is a total eclipse of the mind with black smoky vapors rising from the burning pool of terrible terrors.

<margin>Psal. 77. 5.</margin>
**III.** The state of being stricken over sin is too great when someone is so cast down over sin that he is unfit for holy duties. The godly are sometimes thus overtaken; see it in Asaph, Psalm 77:5: *You hold my eyes awake; I was stricken and did not speak.* Asaph’s soul was so restless and overwhelmed that he could not speak; as if he meant to say, "I wanted to pray, but I could not pray," so disturbed was he over his sins. Then indeed your humbling is too great, when the sight of your sins makes you unfit for the practice of the duties of godliness: this is not necessary, but sinful.

<margin>Hos. 5. 15. Jerem. 3. 21. Nehem. 9. 1. 4.</margin>
<margin>Jud. 2. 4, 5.</margin>
The right disposition of the soul toward humbling over sin is so far from making the soul unfit for holy duties and prayer, that it, on the contrary, makes the soul fit to pray to God (Hosea 5:15; Jeremiah 3:21; Nehemiah 9:1, 4). Therefore it is said that the people of Israel wept, pleaded, and sacrificed (Judges 2:4, 5). When the sight and feeling of sin, and the humiliation over sin, fills your heart with fitness for prayer, then it is necessary and good; but when your soul becomes unfit for prayer and supplication through it, then it is sinful. There it stands

### IV.
A person is too much stricken over sin / when their mind is incapable or unwilling to receive and apply comforting counsel from God's Word / which is offered to them in such circumstances. If there is in you a greater readiness to embrace the terrifying threats of judgment against sin / than to receive any good signs set down in the Gospel / and clear promises for the peace and comfort of a disturbed spirit; when you are more capable of troubling yourself over sin / than of strengthening yourself against the unrest of your mind over sin; in such a case you are too much stricken over sin. Just as upset stomachs in children would rather be fed with lime and filth than with nutritious food <note>This refers to the historical medical belief that certain illnesses caused "depraved appetites" for non-food items</note>: Likewise / if / when comfort appropriate to your state is presented to you by the Ministers of the Gospel / you then do not apply it to yourself / but push it away; remember then that you are all too much stricken over sin. When the concern over sin so bows you down / that all the good words from the Gospel applied to you / cannot make you glad / then you are too much stricken over sin.

<margin>
Mark 9:50.
Matthew 5:13.
Have salt in yourselves, and keep peace with one another. Preserve good teaching / therefore Christ says / you are the salt of the Earth.

If you see a pot boiling / and it boils too strongly / when you throw salt into it / so it shall cease from boiling so strongly. Likewise / if your passions so increase / that all the Teachings of the Gospel / and the precious comforts / which are in the same / cannot sweeten these passions / and pacify your conscience / comfort your soul and support your spirit / then your dejection over sin is far too great / since no ailment of the soul is so great / that there is not enough comfort in the Gospel to refresh such a soul over the same. When God shall call you and say: *Come unto me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest*, Matthew 11:28. and you refuse to come to Jesus Christ and push all comfort away from you / then you are too much stricken over sin.

### V.
A person is too much bowed down under the weight and feeling of sin / when the sorrow over Sin becomes a cause for harming the Body and distressing it through sickness: Likewise, melancholic people are too much subject to this distress / and in this they are much to be rebuked. These make their tears their Food and Drink; being so filled with tears / that they cannot eat their Bread with joy. There are many godly souls who are so distracted with sorrow over sin that they have no comfort nor joy of heart. Job 20:25. *The sword is drawn, it comes out of the body, and the glittering point comes out of his gall: terrors are upon him.*

<column-break/>

Some people lie in the bitterness of their souls / so that they cannot eat even a morsel of bread with pleasure, Job 21:25. God does not require so much sorrow over sin / that one should eat without the comfort of his life and should overturn the joy of the day / and be so restless that one cannot sleep at night nor take any delight in the day. As is testified of Asaph. Psalm 77:5. *You held my eyes awake, I was stricken and did not speak.* When it is so with you / that you are thus troubled and stricken / then it goes too far. The Lord has commanded you to mourn / not to weaken and crucify your Body but your lusts: He commands you to weep over the strength and life of sin / but not over the strength and life of your Body: God does not require that a person shall kill his Body to save his Soul through humiliation and sorrow over sin.

### VI.
A person is too much stricken over sin / when he is so humbled by the feeling and sight of sin / that he has no desire at all to follow his own <term>calling<note>Dutch: *beroepinge*. In this era, "calling" referred to one's daily work or social duties, which were seen as divinely appointed.</note></term>: this is a sinful sorrow. The sorrow over sin is not only sinful / when it draws a person away from the duties of godliness / but also when it draws a person away from his calling in the world: and the reason is this / according to the saying of the Theologians; because God requires no duty regarding our general calling as Christians / which cannot exist alongside our particular calling as human beings. Therefore if the disturbance of your mind over sin is such / that it does not let you pay heed to your calling in the world as a human being: such sorrow over sin is not deemed necessary by the Scripture; but this is an immoderate and all too great dejection over sin.

### VII.
One is too much stricken over sin / when the lovely / wonderful and comforting attributes of God are terrifying and fearful to a person: when one so thinks on sin / that one does not think on the attributes of God, the grace and mercy of God; the longsuffering and patience of God; and the faithfulness of God. When the person so remembers God / as if He were entirely and only just / entirely and only vengeful without mercy. The godly are sometimes overtaken by this fault / just as Job was. Job 23:15. *Therefore I am troubled at His presence,* etc. Here Job tells you of the unrest of his mind under which he lay / so that it frightened him away from God / and he was troubled at His presence: when he thought of God / he was troubled by it. Someone might think / that to think on God is comforting; as when a person thinks that God is merciful to forgive sin; faithful to keep His Covenant with His People; generous to fulfill His People; powerful to protect His People; He is mighty to save them to the uttermost. To think of God in this way / one would think is comforting. But that face / that presence / which Moses could not endure to be near / that Job could not endure to behold; the cause was the guilt of his sins and his fear and doubting within him; which cast him down too much. # Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

Asaph says in Psalm 77:4: *I thought of God and was troubled.* <note>original: "maeckt-te ick misbaer," meaning to make a lamentation or to be visibly/audibly distressed</note> How is this! Did the thoughts of God trouble Asaph? Yes, *I thought of God and was troubled. I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed.* He might have reasoned with himself thus: I remember that this God is a glorious and terrible God, a sin-avenging God; He sees me, He marks all my steps and knows all my ways, and He will repay all my deeds. Therefore, when I thought of God, I was troubled. Yet the thoughts of God comforted David's soul in Psalm 94:19: *In the multitude of my thoughts within me, your comforts delight my soul.* But I (says Asaph), when I thought of God, I was troubled. And Job says: *When I think of God, the Almighty, I am terrified of Him.* When thinking upon the attributes of God disturbs a person and does not refresh or comfort them, then the sorrow of being stricken over sin is too great.

**VIII.** When, under the sorrow of sin, you cannot look up to God and praise Him for common blessings or special grace: God gives you blessings; indeed, He enriches you with great blessings and follows you with favors, daily kindness, and His faithfulness is toward you every moment; He gives you the world according to your will; and for all this, God receives no glory from you—this shows that you are far too stricken over sin. Otherwise, the unrest and humiliation over sin, when it is moderate, serves as a cause to serve God, to praise and prize Him for common blessings and special graces. It makes us glorify God and inclines our hearts to serve Him and thank Him for the blessings received. But when blessings do not have these effects on you, and when sorrow over sin does not work in this way, then it is an immoderate sorrow and a far too great dejection over sin. When God gives you grace to stand against manifold temptations, and to keep you from committing various sins, and to help you against spiritual numbness <note>original: "verdooventheden," referring to a state of being spiritually dazed or insensitive</note>, and to strengthen your heart—and all this cannot lift your heart from under its sorrow to praise God—this is a sinful sorrow. If a person lies on their knees, they can see the Heaven above and the Earth below; but when a person lies flat on their face, they can see neither the Heaven above nor any creature, but only the Earth beneath them. Likewise, when God makes you kneel over your sins, you can see a gracious, faithful, merciful God and a compassionate Father; and then you can see the blessings God bestows upon you, and praise and glorify Him for them. But when you throw yourself to the Earth through sorrow and lie on your face over sin, being too much humbled under the sight and feeling of sin, in this condition God receives no praise, nor do you receive any comfort.

**IX.** When your sins make you despondent about holding onto Jesus Christ, then you are too much stricken over sin: that person is truly sick unto death when their affliction will not allow them to send for the Physician. A troubled

<column-break/>

person often says, doubting, what the ungodly say mockingly: *There is no help for me in God.* This is a sinful sorrow. Whereas true sorrow and Evangelical <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to a gospel-centered approach focused on grace rather than legalistic terror.</note> humiliation over sin, instead of taking away the soul's courage to go to Christ, actually drives the soul to go to Christ, and to rely on Christ, and to prize Christ above all that is in the world. But it is a sinful sorrow when it draws the soul away from Christ and robs it of the courage to go to Him and to highly value and praise Him. Just as we must not—along with the <term>Antinomists</term> <note>From Greek *anti* (against) and *nomos* (law). A group who believed that under grace, the moral law is of no use or obligation.</note> or those set against the Law—fix our eyes only on free grace and mercy without looking at sin; so too we must not, like a doubting and despairing Christian, look so much at sin that we fail to fix our eyes on Christ.

Thus, I have now set down in nine points when a person is said to be too much stricken over sin.

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
I come now to the usefulness of this, namely **I.** for Comfort, and **II.** for Prevention.

**I.** It may first of all serve for comfort; if it is so that God's people are too much stricken over the feeling and sight of sin, then the first comforting observation for God's people is this: that God never wants to reject His people, although He sometimes casts them down. Although you are stricken, nevertheless comfort yourself, for you shall never be rejected. Psalm 94:14: *For the Lord will not cast off His people, neither will He forsake His inheritance.* He casts His people down over sin, but He will never reject His people. This makes the Apostle say in Romans 11:1: *Has God cast away His people? God forbid.* Verse 2: *God has not cast away His people which He foreknew.*

<margin>Luke 24:28.</margin>
Secondly, it is true that God's people may seem to be cut off, when in fact they are not. It happens with them as it did with the two disciples when Christ met them; in the end of Luke it seems He wanted to leave them, as if He would go further. But Christ had not intended to leave them. So God may also do to your soul; He may seem to withdraw from your soul, but He will nevertheless never forsake it. He may seem to want to hide His face, but He will never truly and entirely withdraw Himself from your soul. So Psalm 74:1: *O God, why have you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?* Psalm 77:8: *Will the Lord cast off forever?* Psalm 89:39; Leviticus 26:44. This was not actually so, but only in appearance. God does not reject His people, although He casts them down. The Church thought indeed that God had cut her off, but it was not actually so. <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for both Catholics and Protestants.</note> had a good observation on John 14:4–5: *Where I go you know, and the way you know. Thomas said to Him, Lord, we do not know where You are going, and how can we know the way?* Here there seems to be a contradiction or a counter-speech between Christ and Thomas. But Augustine has a good observation on these words; they say they do not know, and Christ says that they surely do know. Well, how shall this be reconciled? The meaning then is this: the disciples and Thomas did not know their own knowledge...

Thirdly, it is not the measure, but the sincerity of the humiliation <note>original: "vernederinghe," referring to the state of being humbled or brought low by conviction of sin</note> over sin, to which grace is joined: the promises are made to grace; not to strong grace, but to true grace; not to the measure and length of the humiliation, but to the sincerity of the same. Scripture does not assign the promise to faith insofar as it is a strong faith; but to a weak and small faith (provided it is sincere), even if it were but as a mustard seed: indeed, the greatest promises are assigned to the smallest measure of faith. It may be, O Christian, that you do not have a great measure of faith, provided you have a small and weak faith; comfort yourself, for all the promises are assigned to the beginnings of faith: it may be that you do not have faith like a grain of wheat; if it is but as a mustard seed, the promises are for you. It may be that you do not have streams of tears, provided you have one tear, some sorrow over sin—such is acceptable to God. Although it is false, what the Libertines and Antinomians <note>Libertines and Antinomians were radical religious groups often accused of believing that the moral law was not binding on Christians under grace</note> say, that the promises are made to sinners as sinners. It is also false that they are made only to sinners who are exactly so deeply humbled and distressed. Many souls are damned for the total lack of grace, but no person is condemned for missing certain degrees of grace. The promises are made to sincerity, and not to the degrees or steps of grace: true grace, although it is weak, is reckoned by God to have a share in the promises: Therefore, let this comfort you.

Fourthly, let it comfort you that God has not only made promises to the humbled, but also *of* humiliation: Do you have a hard heart? God has promised that He will break your heart: God has promised to take away your stony heart, and to give you a heart of flesh. God has promised to take away the old heart, and to give you a new heart. You have this promise in Ezekiel 11:19: *I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within them; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh.*

## II. So much for comfort; I come now to the usefulness of cautionary instruction.

1. In handling this doctrine—that God's people can be cast down over the sight and feeling of sin—I do not wish to handle it as many hypocrites do, who push aside all manner of humiliation over sin. Because some people are too greatly distressed over sin, they do not want to be humbled over sin at all. To follow this path <note>meaning to avoid all sorrow for sin</note> is the surest way to break out into all unbridled license and to fall from one extreme to the other.

<column-break/>

2. Labor so to dispose the inclinations of your mind that when you humble yourself and are sorrowful over sin, you take care not to cut off the sorrow over sin immediately, unless you are certain that you have attained such a degree of humiliation over sin that brings you to lie at the feet of Christ, but no lower. Christ requires that you shall be so humbled that you lay yourself at the feet of Christ in the sight and feeling of sin; but the Devil seeks that you might be so stricken over your sins that you might lie in Hell. Jesus Christ wants you to be sorrowful over sin so that you may be restored from sin; but the Devil wants you to lie so low in humiliation over your sin so that you might never be restored. Take heed, then, of such sorrow over sin; do not humble yourself as much as the Devil and your own wicked heart might desire. And this is all for the third question.

> Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, who is the... salvation of my countenance, and my God.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
4. The fourth question, which stands to be noted in order, is this: Seeing that God's people can be too greatly stricken over sin, and too greatly humbled over the sight and feeling of their corruption, what might be the reason that evil and ungodly men are not always stricken over their sins? While the godly can be too greatly stricken here over sin, and yet hereafter shall not be rejected because of sin; and while the ungodly shall be cast into Hell for sin when they die, yet they are not always stricken over sin while they live? What reason can be given for this?

To answer this question, I shall set forth six points in reply.

The first reason why the ungodly—although they shall be rejected—are nonetheless not stricken over sin: this arises from their ignorance of the dangerous and damnable nature of sin. They have a blind understanding and a mute conscience; they do not see such a great evil in sin as the godly do. Although the ungodly know sin in general, it is nonetheless only a general knowledge of sin in the head; but they have no particular, experienced, and discerning knowledge of sin and the dangerous nature of sin in their heart and conscience: and from that, it comes that they are not stricken over sin. This general knowledge of sin may cause them to be rejected, but it does not cast them down; and this is the reason that they do not see the surging sinfulness of sin, and they take no notice of the evil and damnable nature of sin, according to what Jeremiah says, Jeremiah 2:22-23: *How can you say, I am not defiled, I have not gone after the Baals? See your way in the valley, know what...*

**II.** Thus much for comfort; I come now to the usefulness of prevention.

1. In handling this doctrine—that God’s People can be cast down over the sight and feeling of sin—I do not wish to handle it as many "Deep-spirits" <term>Dyp-geesten: likely referring to radical spiritualists or intellectualists who over-spiritualized theology</term> do, who shove aside all manner of humiliation over sin. Because some people are too greatly stricken over sin, they wish not to be humbled over sin at all. Not to pursue this matter further, that is the very spring that leads to breaking out into all unrestrained license, falling from one extreme to the other.

<column-break/>

2. Labor to set the inclinations of your mind so that when you humble yourself and are sad over sin, you take care not to cut off the sorrow over sin immediately, unless you are assured that you have reached such a level of humiliation that it causes you to lie at the feet of Christ, but no lower. Christ requires that you shall be so humbled that you lie at the feet of Christ in the sight and feeling of sin; but the Devil seeks that you may be so cast down over your sins that you may lie in Hell. Jesus Christ wants you to be sad over sin so that you may be restored again from sin; but the Devil wants you to lie so low in humiliation over your sin that you might never be restored. Take heed, then, to such sorrow over sin; do not humble yourself as much as the Devil and your own evil heart might desire. And thus much for the third question or issue.

***

# III. SERMON.

-> Psalm 42 : 12 <-
<note>In modern English Bibles, this is usually Psalm 42:11</note>

> *Why do you cast yourself down, O my soul, and why are you restless within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him, He is the help of my countenance and my God.*

The fourth question, which stands to be noted in order, is this: Since God's people can be too greatly cast down over sin, and too deeply humbled over the sight and feeling of their corruption, what might be the reason that the wicked and godless people are not always cast down over their sins? Since the godly can be too greatly cast down here over sin, and yet hereafter shall not be rejected because of sin; and since the godless shall be thrust into Hell for sin when they die, why are they nonetheless not always cast down over sin while they live? What reason can be given for this?

To answer this question, I shall set forth six points.
<margin>Answer</margin>

The first reason why the godless, although they shall be rejected, are nonetheless not cast down over sin: this arises from their ignorance of the dangerous and damnable nature of sin. They have a blind understanding and a silent conscience. They do not see such a great evil in sin as the godly do. Although the godless know sin in general, it is nonetheless only a general knowledge of sin in the head; they have no particular, experienced, and discerning knowledge of sin and its dangerous nature in their heart and conscience. And from this it follows that they are not cast down over sin. This general knowledge of sin rejects them indeed, but does not cast them down. This is the reason that they do not see the exceeding sinfulness of sin, and they take no notice of the evil and damnable nature of sin, according to what Jeremiah says in Jeremiah 2:23: *How can you say, "I am not defiled, I have not followed the Baals"? See your way in the valley, know what you...*

<meta>This page continues a sermon or treatise regarding the spiritual state of the soul. While the previous page addressed the "distressed soul" seeking comfort, this page analyzes the opposite condition: why the "ungodly" or "unrepentant" do not feel the weight of their sins.</meta>

### Balsam of Gilead, or the Healing ###

you have done, you light, swift female camel <note>original: "Kemelinne"; a reference to Jeremiah 2:23, comparing a sinner's wandering to a camel in heat</note>, who twists her ways. The Jews were very sinful and excelled in godlessness; nevertheless, they said that they were not sinful, or at least they did not know they were so: It is because of the lack of knowledge of their ways and the sinfulness of their conduct that they were not stricken with remorse over their sin. When a man meets a lion in the wilderness, he is afraid of it; the reason is that he knows the lion is a harmful animal. But when a man sees a lion painted on the wall, he is not frightened by it, because he knows it cannot harm him. So it is when a man looks upon sin: if he does not look upon it as a lion in the wilderness, which will surely destroy him unless he guards himself against it—for to look upon sin as a lion painted on the wall has no power to alarm him—they see sin only in general through intellectual knowledge, but not in particular through experience.

**The second reason is this:** It springs from the presumption or imagination of forgiveness, grace, and mercy; when the godless hear the thunderclaps and curses of the Law pronounced against sin by the ministers of the Gospel, intended to awaken them from the sleep of sin and carelessness; when they hear of the strict justice of God, and that He is God who avenges sin, and that He will by no means hold the guilty innocent, but will reward everyone according to his ways and works: What does the godless man do in this situation? Does this awaken his conscience to see the evil of sin? Not at all; but he frames it in another way: out of presumption and the imagination of God’s forgiveness and mercy, he blesses himself in his heart, saying,

> I shall have peace, even though I walk according to the dictates of my own heart. <note>Deuteronomy 29:19</note>

As if he would say, "Let sin trouble whom it will; let it strike down those who wish to be struck down; it shall never strike me down, nor disturb me." What! Should sin disturb my conscience and destroy my peace? Or what! Shall I mourn and trouble myself when it is not necessary? While others seem to break their hearts over it, it shall not break my sleep; for I hope that it shall never damn my soul. I hope, although I sin, that God will forgive my sin; and although I am sinful, I know that God is merciful. And so they go on, through presumption, in the way of sin, without any disturbance or dejection over the sight and feeling of sin.

**The third reason** why the godless are not always stricken over sin arises from the hardness and hardening of their hearts, and from the searing of their conscience. There is a sort of person of whom one may say, in regard to sin, that they have become unfeeling, according to the saying of the Apostle in Ephesians 4:19:

> Who, being past feeling, have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.

And as Paul says in 1 Timothy 4:2, having their own conscience seared as with a hot iron. When people have so accustomed themselves to sin that sin hardens their hearts, it is no wonder then that they are not stricken over sin.

<column-break/>

**Fourthly,** that the godless are not stricken over sin arises from this: that they drown out the rebukes of their conscience when it reproves them for sin. When a person has this intent—that although they shall be rejected because of sin, yes, even cast into Hell for it—he still does not want to be stricken over sin. Instead of breaking off their sins at the admonition and reproof of their conscience, they weigh down and enlarge the same by stifling their conscience so that it cannot do its duty. Thus did Cain; when he began to be troubled over sin, and his conscience began to reprove him for the evil he had committed, what did Cain do? Did he let his conscience do its duty? Not at all; he enlarged and heightened his sin, and stifled his conscience, Genesis 4:13:

> My punishment <note>original: "misdaedt" (misdeed/guilt). Older translations often rendered this as "My sin is greater than can be forgiven."</note> is greater than can be forgiven.

And he goes on to stifle his conscience, verse 16:

> And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord, and dwelt in the land of Nod.

He went out from the presence of the Lord and stifled his conscience by the building of cities. And from this it comes that men are not stricken over sin, because they drown out the rebukes and reproof of the conscience. Thus the theologians explain the passage in the 11th verse of the Epistle of Jude:

> Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain.

And that was when his conscience rebuked and troubled him over the murder of his brother and the shedding of his blood; that he, to stifle and quiet his conscience, went to build cities. And thus, O man, you who walk in the ways of godlessness, and your conscience reproves you for your evil conduct, by telling you that your conduct is neither good nor upright, but that your ways are unrighteous and sinful; and that you, by habituating yourself to an evil walk, drown out the rebukes and reproofs of your conscience and take pleasure in continuing in the way of godlessness; this is a great cause why the godless are not stricken over sin in this world.

**A fifth reason** why the godless are not stricken over sin in this world is this: because they abuse the long-suffering <term>long-suffering: God's patient restraint in delaying punishment to allow for repentance</term> and forbearance of God. You have a notable passage on this in Ecclesiastes 8:11:

> Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.

Because God does not immediately punish the godless for his godlessness: because a drunkard is not immediately punished for his drunkenness; a swearer for his cursing; and a fornicator for his impurity, etc., therefore their heart is full to do evil. When the godless abuse long-suffering and forbearance to indulge themselves in sin, from this it comes that they are not stricken over sin.

**Sixthly,** a sixth reason is because the godless have such poor thoughts of God’s omnipresence. Although the godless are not Atheists in doctrine, so as to deny that God sees all things, nevertheless such is their feeling. Many people are in fact Atheists because they live so godlessly, as if God did not see everything and did not know their godless dealings.

->### of a contrite Soul. ###<-

<margin>Job 22:13, 14.</margin> You have there an explicit passage from Job 22:13, 14. Therefore you say, "What does God know of it? Shall he judge through the darkness? The clouds are a hiding place to him, so that he does not see." It is as if they said that God did not know or see their godless and sinful ways, as if the clouds were a covering between God and them, so that he could not see their evil ways. This is the reason why their sins do not disturb them: and thus I have finished the fourth Question, why the Ungodly are not contrite over their sins.

The fifth Question is this: Seeing that the Ungodly are not contrite, and yet they shall one day be rejected for the same in Hell, according to the given reasons: what may be the reason why the Godly—who shall not be cut off nor cast into Hell for their sins' sake—are nonetheless very contrite over the sight and feeling of their sins?

In answer to this Question, I shall give seven reasons.

The first is taken from the nature of sin and the justice of God, considering them together. What then is the nature of sin? This is the nature of sin: Sin is in its own nature a resistance, a strife and a quarreling against God—a battle to cast God down and to place oneself in His stead. It is the nature of sin to tear God from Heaven and from His Throne, and to place oneself there. Now God also wishes in justice to quarrel and fight against sin, and to show Himself stronger than sin and Sinners, and thus to cast them down. <margin>Job 15:25, 26.</margin> That such is the nature of sin you can see in Job 15:25, 26. *For he stretches out his hand against God, and behaves violently against the Almighty. He runs against him with his neck, with his thick high-raised shields.* Here Eliphaz describes a Sinner who, in his sinful ways, attacks his Enemies like a Soldier; he strengthens himself against him, and runs at him with all his might, so that he may overcome him: So also does an ungodly Man; he strengthens himself and runs at God, as it were, with all his might to overcome him and push him from his throne: Therefore it is right for God to condemn sin and to humble the Sinner. The Sinner casts God's Law behind his back. But it is the nature of sin to cast God behind the back: Yet God will in justice reject the Sinner through condemnation, or humble him through humility.

Secondly, God casts the Sinners down under the sight and feeling of sin, so that the Children of God might reject sin with greater indignation: and therefore God humbles them all the more through humiliation. When a man has a knife in his hand and falls with it, so that he hurts himself, he will immediately throw the knife away. Now so it is in the ways of sin and godlessness; when you take sin in your hand and walk in an uncertain path; if you fall into sin, you then take knives in your hands, and so falling into sin, you wound yourself. God makes it so that the knife of sin stabs you in the heart, and wounds your conscience and Soul; so that you, seeing that sin stabs you like a knife in your fall, you would throw it away with

<column-break/>

greater loathing. <margin>Isaiah 30:19, 22.</margin> One reads of the sorrow over sin in Isaiah 30:19, 22. *The People shall dwell in Zion, at Jerusalem; you shall weep no more, surely he will be gracious to you at the voice of your cry; as soon as he hears it, he will answer you.* Here is God's promise regarding their humiliation: thereafter in verse 22: *You shall also defile the covering of your silver graven Images, and the ornament of your golden molten Images: you shall cast them away like a menstrual cloth <note>original: "Maenstondigh Kleedt"</note>, and say to each of them, Begone.* God makes His People mourn over Sin, and casts them down and humbles them under the sight and feeling of sin, and makes them show themselves over the sin, and then throw away the sin like a menstrual cloth: And just as it is with Nurses, when they want to wean their Children, they smear something bitter on the Breast, such as wormwood or gall, so that they might cause the children to leave the Breast; So God smears something bitter on that which we consider sweet: he places bitter drinks on the breast of our sinful pleasure, so that he might thus wean His People from sucking any more at these poisonous Breasts, which we, according to our corruption, prize so highly. <margin>Luke 15:16.</margin> You read of the prodigal Son <note>original: "verlooren Soon"</note> in Luke 15:16. When he was brought to such great distress that he desired to fill his belly with the Husks <note>original: "Draf"; the waste pods fed to livestock</note> that the swine ate. After he came to himself, he desired to eat bread and to be as a hired servant in his Father's house. When God makes sin painful to His people, just as it went for the prodigal Son in his absence from his Father's house; when they are hindered by their sins as the prodigal Son was; when they then come to themselves, they rejoice with the prodigal Son to praise their Father's house. So when the Soul is deeply humbled over sin, then they prize Christ very highly. <margin>James 4:8, Joel 2:12.</margin> It is noteworthy that wherever the humiliation over sin is spoken of, there is also added a loathing and a separation from sin. James 4:8, Joel 2:12.

Thirdly, God places the Sinners under the sight and feeling of sin because such causes the Soul to cast itself upon and rest upon Jesus Christ. It is our deficiency that first makes us seek for and rest upon Jesus Christ, because we see that without Jesus Christ we are lost: It is with us as it was with the Lepers <note>original: "Melaetsche"</note> of whom we read in <margin>2 Kings 7:3, 4.</margin> 2 Kings 7:3, 4. Now there were four Leprous Men before the entrance of the gate: who said to one another, "Why do we stay here until we die? If we say, 'Let us enter the City,' the famine is in the City and we shall die there, and if we stay here we shall also die: now then come and let us fall into the Camp of the Syrians, if they let us live, we shall live, and if they kill us, we shall but die." Oh, apply this in this situation: here is the case; if I die in a Christ-less state, then I am lost forever: and if I am at ease in the trust of this world, that can bring me no salvation: I will therefore run to Jesus Christ, so that I might have support there, and relieve myself of my burden by resting on Jesus Christ in his promise.

When God sees that a person is puffed up with pride over their talents, then God hides His gifts and shows them their sin, and humbles them. So it was with Paul; he was a man of exceptionally great gifts beyond other men, indeed above all men, except for Christ alone. Fifthly, so that He might thereby bring the hearts of His people to a clearer sight and livelier feeling of the grace of forgiveness. The more God casts His people down over the sight and feeling of their sins, and the deeper He humbles them through lowliness, the more they desire to exalt God for the grace of forgiveness. After a man has been tossed about much at sea by a tempest, he prizes the harbor. God deals with His people just as is told of the stargazers <note>Original: "Sterre-kijckers"</note>; they do not stand on the tops of high mountains when they wish to behold the sky, but they lie or sit in the lowest valleys; not in the places closest to Heaven, but in the lowest places furthest away from Heaven. So God also deals: He does not forgive His people at all times as if on mountains; but He lays them low in the Valley of Humiliation, and casts them down over the sight of sin, so that their hearts through faith might have a clearer sight and livelier feeling of the free mercy and forgiving grace of God. God casts you into the low pits of humiliation so that you might thereby see the mercy and grace of God more clearly. Mercy and forgiving grace were precious when they lay deep under oppression and were lowly

Sixthly, so that He may make them acknowledge that there is more evil in sin than there seemed to be pleasure in the contemplation of sin. It is a remarkable example that you read in Ecclesiastes 7:25, 26: "I turned my heart to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom and the reason of things, and to know the wickedness of folly, and the foolishness of madness. Here Solomon applies his heart to find out the deceit of sin, as if to say: "I have sought to know the secret snares and hidden nets which sin lays for sinners; and I have especially labored to know the secret villainy of the sin of adultery." And when God made him see the evil of that sin, and cast him down over the sight of it, then he could say: "I found a more bitter thing than death, a harlot whose heart is nets and snares." And then he could see that it was folly, wickedness, and madness. When God casts His people down over the sight and feeling of sin, He thereby ensures that they see and must acknowledge, with Solomon, that sin is more bitter than death. Indeed, that in the smallest sin there is more evil than there seems to be pleasure, profit, and satisfaction in the pursuit of it. The hearts of God's people have never tasted the bitterness of sins until God first lays and casts them under the weight, sight, and feeling of sin; and by these means, God makes them see what a bitter thing sin is.

Seventhly, God does such things so that He might terrify the godless from the pursuit of sin. God does this in mercy to them, if only they would notice it. May not the godless man reason with himself thus? "If God treats His own people so because of sin, what can I expect from God's hand? If God casts His own people down under the feeling and sight of sin, what can I expect from His hand, since I rejoice in sin for whose sake His people suffer so?" Truly, if God so casts down His own people under the sight and feeling of sin, then I may well expect that I shall be rejected because of sin. If they are cast down to the ground because of sin, then I shall surely be cast into Hell for sin’s sake. If He casts them down into the feeling of Hell, truly He will cast me down to the possession of Hell. Have I then no reason to be dejected over sin, since I shall be rejected for it? If His own people shed tears over sin, then I shall shed my blood over sin. If they are dejected over sin, who shall not be wholly...

->of a Contrite Soul.<-

rightfully rejected for the same; shall I then not be contrite over sin, whose sins cause me to be rejected? So I say that God, in this smiting of His own People, shows His mercy to the godless, so that they might thereby be kept from sinning against God. Thus, in these seven points, I have answered the fifth Question: why God's People, who shall not be rejected, are yet contrite over the sight and feeling of sin.

The sixth and last Question, which I am to handle, is this: What Rules must God's People observe, so that they are not too greatly smitten over the sight, feeling, and burden of sin, nor too deeply cast down under the same?

To answer this Question, take note of these points.

The first Rule is this: Do not expect as much sadness and contrition over sin as some other people may have had. The reason I give you this Rule is because some of God’s people might say: I must be contrite over sin in such or such a way; I must have such a degree or such a measure of humiliation, since I see that others have such; I must have such a sight of sin and be so humbled over sin because others do so; should I not do the same? Shall I not lie so humbled? Shall I not be as lowly as I see others are? I have as many, as great sins as they, and my sins are accompanied by as gruesome circumstances as theirs. Therefore, why should I not be as humbled as they? Mark then: If others have been more contrite than you, how does that affect your humiliation over sin? For another man's manner, degree, and measure of humiliation is no rule by which you must humble yourself; for it may be that others, who have had such a measure of humiliation and contrition over sin, have been more outstanding in sin; and that they are rougher by nature, and more stubborn of humor than you. It may be that your mind is more docile, more flexible, and more yielding, which can be more easily watched than another's; therefore, such a degree and measure of humiliation is not required of you as is required of others. It may be that you cannot bear what others can; the ballast keeps the Ship, but it would overload a small Boat. Therefore, do not reason with yourself by comparing your contrition over sin with that of others, lest you cast yourself down too much over sin. Other men may have heaped up more sin together than you have; and perhaps you have not so dulled your Conscience, nor committed those sins which they have committed, and have not so laid waste to your conscience as they have done, and have not led such an evil life as they.
<margin>1 Peter 1:6</margin> Therefore, you do not need as great a measure of humiliation over sin as they truly need. You have an example of this in 1 Peter 1:6: *For a little while (if need be) being grieved through manifold temptations.* <note>The author uses this verse to show that spiritual sorrow is measured by God according to what is "necessary" for the individual.</note>

God sees in His wisdom that some people need—yes, more greatly need—a larger measure of affliction and contrition over sin than other people do. It may

<column-break/>

be that some people have more spiritual pride regarding their gifts and graces, and more guilt lying upon them than you do.

The second Rule is this, as an instruction: Rest, being satisfied in your Conscience, even though you do not find the *measure* of your humiliation, as long as you find the *end* <note>In this context, "end" refers to the purpose or goal (Latin: *finis*).</note> of your humiliation; be at rest and content in that. If your humiliation makes you desire to be truly humbled over sin; and that you desire to behave yourself lowly before the face of God; if you desire to have a loathing of yourself over the sinfulness of your Nature and life; and if you wish to amend your ways, and your dealings which are not good, and to walk more loftily with your God: if you do so, even though you do not have such a measure of humiliation and contrition over sin as others, yet you have the *end* of humiliation, and you may rest satisfied in your Conscience. If that humiliation makes sin bitter and makes Jesus Christ dear to your Soul; I tell you, O poor Soul, although you do not have this degree of humiliation, you are nonetheless acceptable to Jesus Christ, and shall for all that go to Heaven. And I tell you again for your comfort, that no one ever went to Hell and lost Heaven over the lack of degrees of grace; but many descend to Hell and miss Heaven over the lack of the *truth* of grace. No one ever went to Hell over the lack of such or such a degree of contrition or humiliation over sin; but many descend to Hell because they lack the least measure and truth of humiliation. If there is faith in you, and grace in your Soul, even if it is but as a Mustard-seed <note>A reference to Matthew 17:20, where the smallest amount of true faith is shown to have great power.</note>; a small Sprout of grace in the Soul shall grow in your soul to a Harvest of glory as your reward. Yes, God rewards the Soul with no less a reward than glory for a little grace; Heaven is not promised to the Soul upon such or such a degree of grace—to have so much faith, so much humiliation, and so much contrition over sin, and so much love for Christ (although one must strive for this, such as a strong faith in God, great love for God, etc.)—but Heaven is promised to a weak faith, a small love, etc., if only they be sincere. Therefore, when you find the ends of humiliation, you may be content, even though you lack the degrees of the same. This is the second Rule.

The third Rule, so that the Souls of God's People should not be too greatly smitten over sin, is this.

Cast yourself with confidence upon Jesus Christ, to obtain Life and Salvation, and whatever then comes, do not be too greatly smitten and cast down over sin.

What is the reason why so many a poor Soul is so greatly smitten over sin? It is this: because they do not dare to give themselves entirely over to Christ, and to roll themselves upon Him for preservation. Although the greatness of sin requires a greatness of Tears over sin upon the thought of it; nonetheless, it is not necessary that Christ should shed more Blood for the sin; He has no more to die.

### Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

...die to satisfy for sin; Christ has paid a perfect and sufficient Ransom <note>The word "Ransom" here refers to the theological concept of "Atonement," where Christ's death pays the debt for human sin.</note> for sin, and needs to die no more, even if you do not shed all the tears that you ought to shed over sin, over the body of sin, and the remnants of corruption that are within you. It is the nature of the godless—and indeed, sometimes even of the godly—to run to extremes regarding sin. Therefore, observe this Rule, and it shall be a means to restrain you from becoming too greatly despondent over sin.

First, it is innate to the godless that they are so far from being struck with remorse over sin that they are never troubled or humbled by it at all; instead, they go from sin to sin, from one step to another, until they are eternally lost, and they do this without fear.

Secondly, but on the right hand <note>Meaning "on the other side of the issue."</note>, the godly easily stray to the other side; while the godless do not wish to be remorseful for sin at all, the godly tend to strike themselves too hard over the sight and feeling of sin. Scripture mentions the godless—that they are not troubled by sin at all, as you may read in Job 21:14, 15. Nothing troubles their conscience when they die; see verse 13: *They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave.* Yet are they in any way humbled before God? Read verses 14 and 15: *Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him?* Therefore they say "depart from us"—and why? Because they live in joy, merriment, and tranquility of heart; and they think little of sin, much less of being humbled by the feeling of it. Therefore they seek neither God nor His ways: so you see that the godless are not struck with remorse over sin at all.

But the godly, on the other hand, are very ready to make their state bitter through an all-too-great despondency over sin; this is possible, and the godly are very easily led to it. 2 Corinthians 2:7: *So that contrariwise ye ought rather to... comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.* When a child of God, because of the bitterness of his soul, casts himself down too much over sin; just as he was subject to it who was banished from the Church for his sins; while he was under the censure which he suffered for his sin, the Apostle feared that he would be too greatly depressed by an all-too-great sorrow. Therefore, although the godless think lightly of sin and are not humbled at all by the sight and feeling of it, you must guard yourself so that, in mourning your sins, you do not cast yourself down too far. And thus I have concluded these six Questions.

I shall now conclude this Teaching with a word of application.

<margin>1. Application.</margin>
Is it so, then, that the children of God are cast down over sin, even though they shall not be rejected because of sin? Indeed, can a godly person be so struck by sin that he cries out with the Psalmist: *Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me?* Although the godless live in merriment all their days, and are never troubled or struck by the sight and feeling of

<column-break/>

sin: then I shall speak to the godless for a little while.

1. You who live in a habit of godlessness, in ways of wickedness, allowing yourselves to live according to the imagination of your own evil hearts—take note and speak thus to your soul: What! Are the godly cast down, though they shall never be rejected? And are they cast down, who shall never be cast away? What will you do then, who heap sin upon sin and commit iniquity upon iniquity, multiplying your abominations, yet your hearts have never been troubled, nor has your conscience ever knocked at your door because of the wickedness of your actions? Consider this: many can be cast into hell for sin's sake who were never remorseful for sin; and if you continue constantly in the way of sin, what will become of you?

But you might say: what is to be done, and what means must be used to bring the soul into such a state that it is struck by sin, and that we might be humbled over the sight and feeling of sin? There are three ways that God uses to strike and humble the souls of sinners over the sight and feeling of sin.

The first is this: God lets a light into the understanding, and sets to work that great Officer of God within man—his conscience—which so smites the heart and convicts the whole soul of the evil in its actions, and makes the man single out his sin, yes, even the "Master-sin," his beloved Delilah <note>A reference to the biblical figure Delilah; used here as a metaphor for a "favorite" or "darling" sin that seduces the soul.</note>, the lust of his heart, which has made him most guilty of violating the righteous Law and which leaves him most exposed to the vengeance of God. He singles out that sin which has been his companion all his days. God does not merely make him look at sin in general (since a general sight of sin in the soul only produces a general conversion from sin), but God, through the light that He places in the understanding and conscience, picks out your sin, your most beloved sin, and as it were, brings it to your understanding so that it might comprehend its guilt and weight. Therefore you also read of some in their first conversion, Acts 2:37: they were guilty of many sins they had committed; but God, through the working of their conscience, picks out one sin in particular—that sin, 그that iniquity of which they were most guilty, and that was the crucifixion of the Prince of Life. You can see this in verse 36: *Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.*

That was the sin that hit home in their hearts, as you can read in verse 37. <gloss>they were pricked in their heart <note>original Greek: "katenygēsan tē kardia"</note></gloss>. Hearing this, they were struck in their heart. Here they were caught in the sin of which they were most guilty; God caused their consciences to bring it in a particular way, and this troubled and pricked their heart. Although they were guilty of many great sins, God nevertheless laid this one great sin alone upon their heart, so that they might be most remorseful for this sin above all. Similarly, when the Samaritan woman came to Jesus Christ as He sat by the well, speaking of her husbands, He told her what her sin was, John 4:18.

<summary>This page discusses the balance of remorse for sin, warning the godly against excessive despair while rebuking the unrepentant for their lack of concern. It introduces the "Master-sin" concept and how God uses conscience to convict individuals of their specific, most cherished sins.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual remorse, concluding the section on how God humbles a person through the sight of their sins and beginning the fifth sermon on dealing with a disquieted soul.</meta>

of a stricken Soul.

"The one you have now is not your husband." <note>A reference to Christ's conversation with the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4.</note> Christ told her plainly what her sin was; he told her that she was a harlot; and she went and said, *that he had told her all that she had ever done*, verse 29. Christ did not say in general terms that she was a sinner; but he picked out her great sin, of which she was most guilty, and thus worked upon her heart and conscience: her conscience told her so, and she understood the truth of it; and this struck her <note>Original: "versloegh," meaning to be struck down with remorse or contrition.</note> because of the same. So then, if God gives you the grace to be remorseful over sin, he will place a sound <note>Original: "luyt," literally a sound or tone, suggesting a resonant conviction in the mind.</note> in your understanding, and make your conscience active to single out your beloved sin, the greatest sins of which you stand guilty; so that you may be humbled over them.

The second way that God enters in to humble a man over sin is this: God awakens the movements of the soul to remember the aggravations and horrible circumstances with which the sin is clothed. Job 36:9. *Then he shows them their work, and their transgressions, that they have exceeded.* God does not only show sinners their sins, that they are great sins; but he also shows them the weightiness of their sins; it is not a passing vision of the greatness of their iniquity and transgression; but he makes them know them rightly; he makes them know that their sins are clothed with horrible circumstances, such as that they have sinned against the <term>means of grace</term> <note>Religious practices like prayer, preaching, and sacraments believed to convey God's favor.</note>, against love, against the light and the gnawing of conscience over those sins; all this happens to humble you and bring you low over your sins.

The third and final way that God enters in to humble a man over sin is this: God makes the conscience do its duty in a person, not only by singling out a particular <term>master-sin</term> <note>The specific sin to which an individual is most naturally inclined or "addicted."</note>; but also to bring to memory those sins of which you stand guilty before God; and to set them before your sight, and especially that master-sin and beloved sin, and to humble you and bring you low before God over them, until the sin shall be mortified within you: Sin must not only be seen and the affections awakened to the memory of the horrible circumstances with which it is clothed, and that they are exceedingly great: but the conscience must keep them in memory for so long, until they are killed and brought under subjection: These are the three steps that God uses to humble a man through the sight and feeling of sin. Now then, all you who are still strangers to this work, who do not yet know what it means to be stricken over sin, strive to have these three points worked upon your soul, so that you may thus be remorseful over the sight and feeling of sin. And thus I have finished this Doctrine regarding remorse over sin.

### V. SERMON.

->Psalm 42 : 12.<- <note>In most modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 42:11.</note>

->Why art thou cast down, O my soul, and why art thou disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, who is the ....... health of my countenance and my God.<-

<margin>1st Doctrine.</margin>
Before I come to the second part of these words, I shall remark upon the manner of speaking which the Psalmist uses in this text: and then draw some teachings which the words afford us. You see that the manner of speaking is a <term>soliloquy</term> <note>Original: "alleen-spraecke," a speech made to oneself.</note>, which is a way of speaking to oneself as if between two friends; **Why art thou cast down, O my soul?** From which manner of speaking, take this observation.

That such soliloquies, as the Psalmist uses here, are necessary duties, in which believers must be much occupied, and must exercise themselves. The Psalms are full of such soliloquies. Psalm 103:1. *Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name*, so also verses 2, 22. Psalm 104:1. *Bless the Lord, O my soul*. Psalm 34:2. *My soul shall make her boast in the Lord*. Psalm 146:1. *Praise the Lord, O my soul*. And many other places in the Psalms concerning the praising of God. All these make known to us that divine soliloquy which the saints and servants of God have used to praise God; See not only these divine soliloquies recounted here, but also the works of Augustine, Bernard, Gerardus, Bishop Hall, <note>References to St. Augustine, Bernard of Clairvaux, Johann Gerhard, and Joseph Hall—theological writers known for their meditative and "soliloquizing" styles.</note> and others, who have had divine soliloquies between God and their own souls in private; Therefore let this be your concern, and make it a matter of conscience to be much in these soliloquies, so that in secret your soul speaks with your God: it is the duty of Christians to confer with others; and God takes note of this also: likewise it is your duty to confer with your soul between God and your soul. David sometimes praises God, and sometimes rebukes himself; sometimes he addresses his soul to praise God; and sometimes he scolds his soul because it is too cast down, **Why art thou cast down, O my soul? Are you at any time disquieted in your mind?** then use these holy habits of the holy man, **Why art thou cast down, O my soul.** Are you sometimes sluggish in any duty? then say to yourself, it is better to be a servant of God than a slave of the Devil, and thus awaken your soul to a proper readiness to undergo that duty which stands before you to do, and to serve your God; it is better to live in peace with God and a good conscience, than to live in the service of the Devil, which causes disquiet of the mind and terror of the conscience; and say in the conversation with your soul by yourself: what am I? what is my condition? am I one of the elect, or am I a castaway? am I an heir of glory, or of Hell? am I a child of God, or a child of wrath? am I in the state of grace, or in the bonds of iniquity? Such conversations as these with your own heart shall be means to [strengthen] your heart...

<meta>This page continues the fifth sermon from the collection titled "Balm of Gilead," focusing on how a believer should respond to spiritual dejection. It moves from the necessity of self-examination to the specific practice of "holy reasoning" with one's own soul to combat excessive despair.</meta>

-># Balm of Gilead, or the Healing<-

to awake out of the sleep of carelessness, to pay attention to your own state; this is your bounden duty. Let it be your business to enter into a conversation with your own heart, as David did; but I shall not pursue this point further. There is something more to be noted in these words, and that is the manner in which David speaks to his own soul, and how he reasons <note>Original: "reden-kavelt," meaning to argue or debate logically with oneself.</note> with his own heart, saying: *Why are you cast down, O my soul?* From this manner of speaking, observe this doctrine.

<margin>2. Doctrine.</margin>
That a child of God must rebuke his own soul and use holy reasons against excessive dejection over sin. I draw this from the Psalmist’s way of speaking; he reproves his own heart and argues with his soul over this matter: *Why are you cast down, O my soul?*

In treating this doctrine, two points are to be noted.

I. That a child of God must rebuke his own heart and use holy reasons against excessive dejection over sin.

II. It must be shown in what manner you must use these holy reasons against excessive dejection over sin.

I. **Why shall a child of God rebuke his heart and use holy reasons against unorderly and excessive dejection over sin?**

1. Because he is the primary actor and promoter of his own casting down; being the first instigator of this sorrow, he must lay the fault and blame upon himself. The words are in the *active* <note>Original: "Activo." The author notes that the soul is performing the action of "bowing down" itself.</note> voice: *Why do you cast yourself down?* Thus, you are the one cast down; you are the worker of your own dejection. You bow yourself down; therefore, rebuke your own heart and use holy reasons against the immoderate and excessive bowing down over sin. God commands his people to believe in Him, to sustain their souls and lift them up to God; and yet they are sometimes subject to bowing themselves down and throwing themselves down through immoderate and excessive dejection over sin. If the Devil does not cast them down through his temptation, then they cast themselves down. *Why are you cast down, O my soul?*

2. This is the readiest and most powerful way to rescue oneself from that downcast condition: by rebuking one's heart for excessive dejection. Holy reasons shared with a man’s own soul are powerful arguments to pull a man’s soul out of that downcast state. If he were to leave himself alone in this downcast state, he would soon dive so deep into such an occasion and immoderate dejection over sin—into such a wave of misery—that he would not be able to be rescued from it. Just as it is good for a man to reason with his own heart when he is assured of salvation, so it is also when he doubts it. There is as much "why are you cast down" in sorrow as there is "why do you exalt yourself" in comfort.

II. **In what manner must the people of God use these holy reasons against the immoderate and excessive dejection of the soul over sin?** There are seven ways in which the children of God must rebuke their hearts and use these holy reasons against immoderate sorrow and dejection over sin.

<column-break/>

1. The children of God must reason with themselves in this way: "O my soul, I am not eternally rejected by God for being humble before God; why then shall I be too much dejected over sin?" Psalm 94:14. *For the Lord will not forsake his people, nor will he leave his inheritance.*

Although God does not say "I will not cast my people down," he says nonetheless, "I will not reject them." Romans 11:1. *Has God cast away his people? God forbid.* The Apostle denies it strongly in verse 2: *God has not cast away his people whom he foreknew.* Since God does not cast away his people, why then shall I be too much dejected? Let the godless and the reprobate, who shall be cast away forever, let them be too much dejected; but not I, since I shall never be rejected, although I may be struck down for a small moment, according to what is written in Isaiah 54:7, 8. *For a small moment have I forsaken you, but with great mercies will I gather you. In a little wrath I hid my face from you for a moment; but with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on you, says the Lord your Redeemer.* This humiliation over sin is but for a short time; but He will not reject forever.

II. Reason thus with your soul against your downcastings and say: "Jesus Christ has willingly and meritoriously laid down his life for me, and has humbled himself very deeply to be my Savior; therefore, O my soul, why shall you be too much dejected over sin?" It is true, O my soul, if you had been required to die and work out your own redemption to be your own preserver; and if the weight and exceeding burden of your sins had been laid upon your own shoulders; and if you in your own person had been required to satisfy Divine justice; if you had been bound to keep the whole Law perfectly; and if you had to make a full restoration for the wrong and evil you had committed, and had to offer the fruit of your body for the sin of your soul—even then, this would not have produced the least satisfaction, nor brought about the smallest repayment or restoration for the evil. If such were your situation—that you had to be your own <term>Mediator</term> <note>A go-between; in Christian theology, Jesus is the mediator between God and humanity.</note> and advocate, and that you had to shed your blood for your sins—if this were your case, then you would have cause to be so outstandingly dejected over sin. A finite creature cannot satisfy infinite justice. Micah 6:7. *Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?* Such is, in any case, no sufficient ransom for my deliverance. But it is entirely otherwise; forgiveness <note>Original: "quijt-scheldinghe," referring to the pardoning or canceling of a debt.</note> is your lot. Here, O my soul, is your case, which can provide you with abundant comfort: the blood, even the precious blood of Jesus Christ, is given for sins so that you should not be too much dejected over sin. And you may draw an abundance of comfort and satisfaction from this consideration.

->### of a dejected Soul.<-

1. Observe within yourself, O my soul, that Jesus Christ did not shed his precious blood for himself, but for you: he has laid down his life as a Good Shepherd for the sheep, *John 10:15.*
2. Observe, that God the Father has accepted this giving of his life in this regard, *John 10:17.* Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life.
3. Observe within yourself, O my soul, that just as there are great reasons to enlarge and weigh down sin, so also there are great reasons to enlarge the grace of God in Christ. Is your sin great? The grace of God is greater. Does your sin deserve great plagues, even eternal death? The death and the merits of Jesus Christ are of an infinite worthiness to merit life, even eternal life. Are your sins the sins of a human? The <term>satisfaction</term><note>Original: "genoeghdoeninghe," a theological term referring to Christ paying the debt of sin to God's justice.</note> of Jesus Christ is a satisfaction of God; if your sins deserve the contempt of God, Christ’s death deserves and obtains the favor of God. In a word, just as Christ’s person surpasses your person, so Christ’s obedience infinitely surpasses your disobedience; therefore the Apostle Paul says in *Romans 5:16:* But the gift of grace is from many offenses unto justification. The Apostle indicates here that although there is a great debt in sin, there is nonetheless greater grace and merit in Christ; for just as through Adam came sin and death, so through Jesus Christ comes righteousness and life; just as the wages of sin is death, so the gift of God's grace is eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord, *Romans 6:23.* There is not so much guilt in sin to condemn as there is merit in Jesus Christ to save. Therefore, why do you bow yourself down, O my soul? Jesus Christ has given his life for me; and in the laying down of his life he has fully satisfied his Father for sin; and although more tears are required over sin by means of humiliation, nonetheless no more blood is needed for sin by means of satisfaction; therefore, be not too greatly dejected over sin.

III. Reason with your own soul in this way, so that you are not too greatly dejected over sin, O my soul; observe, that excessive dejection prevents your soul from applying holy duties toward the subduing and killing of sin. It is the policy and craftiness of the Devil to pull man toward extremes: sometimes the Devil possesses a person so much with the reigning power of sin, that they never think upon the guilt of sin; and sometimes he possesses them so with the weight of sin, that they are not able to look up toward the forgiveness of sin. I may say to you, as God said to Joshua, *Chapter 7:10:* Stand up: why do you lie thus upon your face? It was proper that Joshua was dejected over the misfortune, but not that he should be drawn away from pursuing the enemy. Therefore reason and say, O my soul, it is not fitting to be over-much dejected over the guilt of sin, but lift yourself up against it by relying upon God.

IV. Reason thus with your soul; O my soul, observe, are not these bowings-down of the mind, this over-great dejection over sin, an exceeding

<column-break/>

diminishment of the free grace and mercy of God, and of Christ’s merits? If a thirsty man comes to the sea, the great Ocean, to seek water, and when he arrives there, he lies down with these thoughts: that all the waters of the sea cannot quench his thirst; this man would be saying that the sea is but a small puddle. So if you, being troubled and too greatly dejected over sin, think that the grace of God and Christ's merits cannot comfort your dejected soul, this greatly belittles the great Ocean of God’s grace and Christ’s merits, since you think that your sins surpass and overcome his mercy and free grace. In the time of the Law, the <term>Mercy Seat</term><note>Original: "Versoen-decksel," the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant, representing the place where God's mercy meets human law-breaking.</note> entirely covered the Ark, in which the Law lay; to show that when a man broke not only one Commandment, but every commandment of the Law, all such things were nonetheless covered with grace; and notwithstanding the breaking of the Law, they had the Mercy Seat to which they could go; although they break the entire Law, all the commandments of God, this Law is nonetheless covered over with atonement; the grace of God is greater than your humiliation. The Red Sea drowned Pharaoh and all his host as easily as a single man would sink. Likewise can the Red Sea of Christ’s Blood drown every sin (even if they were mountains of transgression) as well as the smallest sin. *Psalm 25:11.* For your Name's sake, O Lord, pardon my iniquity, for it is great. In the Hebrew it is a word with an emphasis; we read "for it is great," but it can be read "although it is great."

V. Reason thus with your soul; Why will you bow yourself down, O my soul? Since the dejection of the soul also throws down the body. There is such a sensitivity between the body and the soul, that the one cannot be troubled and dejected without the other being so as well: For when the Body of Christ was troubled, then also was his soul distressed; when the People of God are melancholy and have restless thoughts, it also troubles and disturbs the body as well as the mind; it weakens the body and diminishes the joy they should have in God, and disturbs the whole man; and therefore it is noteworthy what David says (which I shall place here for those who are troubled over the dejection of their minds under sin, for those who so greatly distress themselves over sin that they disturb and trouble the body). *Psalm 32:3, 4.* When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. 4. My moisture is turned into the drought of summer. It stands even more clearly in *Psalm 38:3, 4.* <note>Original references Psalm 38:4-5, but quotes match 3-4 in many English versions.</note> There is no soundness in my flesh because of your anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin. 4. For my iniquities are gone over my head: as a heavy burden they are too heavy for me. Upon such great dejection follows a physical disturbance and sickness, *verse 6.* I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly. *verse 7.* For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease: and there is no soundness in my flesh. Many commentators maintain that this unrest in the mind, his bowing down under sin, was the cause of his physical ailment. So also *Psalm 39:8, 9.* Deliver me from all my transgressions, etc. There you have his inward dejection, his un-
