<meta>This page continues the "holy reasoning" that a believer should use to comfort their soul. The previous page focused on the infinite value of Christ's sacrifice compared to the weight of human sin; this page addresses how to handle the physical and emotional toll of excessive sorrow.</meta>

->## Gilead's Balm, or the Healing<-

rest regarding sin: and verse 11: *Remove your plague away from me; I am consumed by the blow of your hand.* <note>The author is quoting Psalm 39:10-11, where the Psalmist asks God to relieve the physical suffering caused by his guilt.</note> When God rebukes someone for sin, He makes them see their guilt in the face of sin, so that they do not persist in it. But if you bow down too low under the obsession with sin, it does not only disturb your mind, but also damages the body. I recount this, not because I want anyone to reject <term>godly sorrow</term><note>A theological term for repentant sadness that leads to spiritual growth, as opposed to "worldly sorrow" which leads to despair.</note> over sin, but so that they may be able to keep it within proper bounds; for sorrow over sin in a proper measure does not trouble the mind, nor does it upset the body. Rather, it is the all-too-great sorrow over sin that casts down the soul and causes disorder in the body; therefore, engage in <term>holy reasoning</term><note>Original: "reden-kabelt," literally "reason-cabling," referring to a structured internal dialogue or a chain of logic used to combat spiritual despair.</note> with your soul against it.

VI. Reason thus with your own soul: Observe, O my soul, that opposition to sin is more pleasing to God than an all-too-great despondency over sin. Christians are ready to think and believe that when they are so utterly crushed and terrified by sin, they are doing something great; and yet, in the meantime, they do not fight against their lusts or stand firm against sin. To be humbled and crushed by sin only so far as it gives the soul courage to fight against sin—that is pleasing to God. When the children of Israel fled before the men of Ai (Joshua 7), Joshua fell on his face and tore his clothes. Then God said to Joshua in verse 10: *Get up: why do you lie thus on your face?* So God says to you when your soul is bowed down and too much crushed by sin: why do you lie on your face so defeated by sin? Stand up. Say the same to your soul: why do you lie on your face? Why do you cast yourself down? Why do you mourn all too much over sin? Stand up. God would rather see the soul upright and fighting against corruption than lying down in despondency over sin. It is with your soul as it is with a soldier: a commander would rather see his soldiers standing upright and fighting against the common enemy than lying wounded on the earth, complaining about their wounds. So also God would rather see the souls of His people upright and fighting against their corruption and lusts—the common enemies of their salvation—than lying on their faces on the ground, being all too much crushed by sin.

VII. Reason thus with yourself, O my soul: why do you bow down under the sight and feeling of sin? Notice that God has promised His promise of acceptance not to the degree or level, but to the *sincerity* of the humiliation. Therefore, do not lie so low under such mournful despondency, for God promises great things to the smallest measure and level of faith. Though your faith be small and your gifts meager, God nevertheless accepts the smallest and lowliest measure and degree of grace. Although many go to Hell for a lack of sincerity of grace <term>in habitu</term><note>Latin: "in essence" or "as a settled character."</note>, nevertheless no one is lost for a lack of degrees of grace <term>in actu</term><note>Latin: "in practice" or "in the performance of an act."</note>. If there are but the smallest beginnings of grace, it is pleasing to God. Even if it is only a faith like a mustard seed,

<column-break/>

it is nevertheless faith. A small tree may be called a tree just as well as the largest; even if it does not have such height, it is still a tree. So also a small grace, a small seed of faith like a mustard seed, is as truly and properly called a true faith as the strongest faith. God has His bottle for those who shed few tears as well as for those who make their head a fountain of water; <note>References to Psalm 56:8 ("put my tears in your bottle") and Jeremiah 9:1.</note> though your grace be but like a bruised reed and a smoking flax-wick, yet the bruised reed shall not be broken, nor the smoking flax-wick quenched (Isaiah 42:3). Though the grace be tender, small, and meager, like a bruised reed and smoking flax, God will strengthen the one and cause the other to kindle. He will not reject these small beginnings of grace, even though they show themselves so obscurely that they can hardly be seen. Although God makes no promise to sinners as long as they remain in that state, He nonetheless makes them to sinners who have grace, however tender and meager it may be.

<margin>Useful application.</margin> The usefulness of this is as follows: to make it known to you that the Scripture does not only command you to rebuke your heart and use holy reasons against an all-too-great despondency over sin, but that you must also reason with yourself out of faith. Many Christians want to reason why they should believe, be comforted, and be humbled; but as to why they are *all too much* crushed, they have no reasons at all, other than that they must do so, and that they must have the one as well as the other. What reasons can these Christians give—who make a conscience of all their ways and seek to walk fruitfully on all sides and live in the use of the <term>ordinances</term><note>Religious rituals or requirements, such as prayer, attending church, or the sacraments.</note> and walk with God in all their ways—what reason do they have to be all too much crushed over sin? Therefore, if you want to reason toward faith and comfort, you must also argue against all-too-great despondency over sin; for you have no reason for this. You must show a reason for your despondency just as much as for your hope and assurance. Ask the wicked regarding Heaven: they will tell you they are certain of Heaven. But ask them for a reason why they think so; they can bring forth none at all; therefore, that is presumption. In the same way, the godly, under the despondency of the Spirit, will easily say that they shall go to Hell and be cast out of Heaven. But ask them for a good reason; they can give none at all. And this is a sin on the other side. I want to ask those double-minded Christians with attention: while you think that you shall go to Hell, can you say that you have no more reason in you than the rejected wicked have? Can you say that you are guilty of such spite which is impossible to exist alongside the beginnings of true grace, and that something rules in you which can never befall a child of God? These are some reasons; but if such things are not found in you, then you have no cause to be so despondent. Yet even if you must rebuke your heart for all-too-great despondency over sin, you must not reject all humiliation over sin: for to be crushed over sin is...

<summary>This page argues that while sorrow for sin is necessary, excessive despair is spiritually and physically harmful. It encourages the reader to "stand up" and fight sin like a soldier rather than lying paralyzed by guilt, noting that God values the sincerity of faith more than its intensity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how a believer should regulate their sorrow. The previous page established that while "godly sorrow" is necessary, it becomes harmful when it consumes the body or drives the soul to despair. This page provides specific tests to determine if one's grief over sin is healthy or has become a "sinful sorrow" itself, before transitioning into a new sermon on the absence of the feeling of God's love.</meta>

### of a dejected Soul.

...highly—but to be all too greatly crushed over sin is itself a sin. There is a certain duty upon which you must set your heart, but you must not let your heart bow down too low. And if you ask me, "How shall I distinguish these duties?" I answer with these four points:

1. You must not rebuke your heart for bowing down under sin if the measure of your humiliation serves the purpose of that humiliation. The purpose of humiliation is two-fold: First, to make sin bitter; second, to make Jesus Christ precious. If your humiliation achieves these two ends—namely, that it makes sin bitter to your soul and Jesus Christ precious—then your humiliation is right. You must not rebuke your heart for this, but rather cherish and embrace it. But when your humiliation makes sin neither bitter nor Jesus Christ precious, but instead unsettles your mind, throws your soul down, and drives you away from Christ, it has gone too high; it is not serving these two ends and thus becomes sinful.

2. You should cherish this broken-heartedness when you join the feeling of God’s love and favor together with your humiliation over sin. This is when your heart is positioned so that with one eye you see the sin, and with the other, you see God’s love and forgiving mercy. But those who stare so constantly <note>Original: "ster-oogen," literally "star-gazing," meaning to fixate or stare intently.</note> at their own corruption and sinful misdeeds that they are never able to see God’s love and free grace—forgiving sins through the promises of the Gospel—this is sin, and for this, you must rebuke your heart.

3. Your dejection is not too great when it concerns the evil of the sin more than the danger of the punishment. When your brokenness is more about the sin committed than about the dangerous state of your soul, then it is not too great. But if your dejection is more because you have made your state dangerous than because you have sinned, that goes too high. When a person commits a sin and is crushed, saying, "I shall go to Hell and lose my blessed state in Heaven," fearing Hell as a punishment more than mourning over the sin as sin, then this sorrow over sin is too great. But when your sorrow is more for the sin and the dishonoring of God than for the fear of punishment—if this is the unrest of your soul—you need not rebuke your heart for it.

4. This humiliation and dejection over sin must be welcomed when it has this effect: that it causes you to justify God and condemn yourself, justifying God in all His dealings. But if, under the humiliation of your mind, you harbor evil thoughts of God, to murmur and be dissatisfied, these thoughts must not be fed but rebuked. However, when you can justify God in all His dealings toward you, these workings of the Spirit must not be rebuked but cherished. Job 39:37: <note>In modern English Bibles, this passage is found in Job 40:4-5.</note> *Behold, I am too insignificant; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand upon my mouth.* verse 38: *Once have I spoken, but I will not answer; or twice, but I will proceed no further.* It is as if Job wanted to say, "In the trouble of my mind, I have often spoken against God, once and twice against God; but I will lay my hand on my mouth and justify God, and condemn myself, and acknowledge myself insignificant in my own eyes." This is what Job teaches us to do. And when you, 

<column-break/>

under your dejection over sin, justify God and condemn yourself, acknowledging God to be righteous in all His doing and acknowledging yourself insignificant in your own eyes, then this dejection over sin is not too overwhelming. You must cherish it and by no means rebuke your heart for it. Thus, I have finished the first ground for why God’s people are dejected over sin.

## V. SERMON.

->Psal. 42 : 12.<-
<note>In the King James Version and most English Bibles, this is Psalm 42:11 or 43:5.</note>

>Why do you bow down, O my soul, and why are you restless within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him; he is the . . . . . . salvation of my countenance and my God.

THE second question is: Why are God’s people bowed down? This concerns the lack of the feeling of God’s love and favor. In treating this matter, I shall proceed in this way:
I. I shall show you why God allows His people to be bowed down over the feeling of a lack of God’s love and favor.
II. I shall show you that although this is your situation, there is nonetheless no great cause for the bowing down, unrest, and dejection of the soul in this state.
III. I shall set down some theological rules for what a Christian must do and what path they must take so that they might obtain the love and favor of God.
IV. I shall show the utility and application.
I. I shall show you why God allows His people to be depressed under the feeling of a lack of God’s love and favor; and although God loves them, yet it can be that they do not know the love and favor that God bears toward them. I will bring the reasons under four headings:
I. It arises from the person themselves.
II. It comes from God.
III. From the Devil.
IV. It comes from other people.
These many are the four general causes why God’s people are bowed down under the lack of God’s love and favor in their souls.
I. It arises from the person themselves, and that in these five respects:
1. From the abundance of natural melancholy in a person's body. <note>"Melancholy" was understood in the 17th century as both a physical ailment (an excess of "black bile") and a spiritual trial of profound sadness or depression.</note> Overpowering melancholy in a person darkens the understanding and unsettles the senses; it disturbs reason, grieves the soul, and clothes it with mourning. When these things come together, they press a person down and withhold from them the feeling of God’s favor. Melancholy is the mother of discomfort and discontent, and it is the nurse of doubts. Remember the history which you read in Dan. 4:33 regarding Nebuchadnezzar: *he ate grass like the oxen;* he did not know if he was a beast or a man. His senses were unsettled, his understanding darkened, and his reason had departed from him. In the same way, natural melancholy makes a child of God think they are a child of the Devil when they are actually a child of God; it makes them think they are a native of Babylon, while they are in the

# of a broken Soul.

There is no greater curse upon your grace and comfort than this: if you refuse obedience to God, God shall in justice refuse you peace and comfort. He who will not work, shall not eat; just as this is true in worldly things, so it is also true in spiritual matters. If you do not perform your **bounden duty** <note>The original Dutch "schuldigen plicht" refers to an obligatory moral or religious requirement that a believer owes to God.</note> toward God, then God will also withhold from you the comfort of grace. If you do your duty toward God, then you shall eat of the promised Land. If you will not let the Spirit of God work the work of sanctification within you, then God will not let you enjoy the comfort of His Spirit in your Soul. You know what **Solomon** says: he who slumbers shall have Poverty. If you are spiritual sluggards and do not perform your bounden duty toward God, be assured that you shall have spiritual poverty and a lack of comfort. Remember what **Christ** says in the Gospel: that it is the faithful Servant who shall enter into the joy of his Lord. If you will not be faithful in your bounden duty, you cannot expect to be filled with inward joy. Grace, *says Baxter* <note>Richard Baxter (1615–1691) was an English Puritan known for his practical writings on the "afflicted conscience."</note>, is neither seen nor felt in the Soul, except when it is in action; the lack of action must necessarily cause a lack of assurance. Although these bounden duties do not "earn" grace, grace nonetheless stands and falls with our diligence in our bounden duties. I may explain this through a common comparison: there is fire in the **Flint**, but the fire is not seen within it; but strike the steel and the stone against each other, and then you shall see the fire. So too there may be grace in the soul of a Man, but unless the Spirit of God strikes upon the Soul, like the steel upon the stone—unless the Spirit of God works with the spirit of Man in his bounden duty—no grace is seen, and so the Soul lies under the mournful workings of the soul, under the lack of assurance of God’s Love.

5. This arises from the fact that they look more for comfort than for grace; and this is the reason why they lack more comfort than they ought to lack; they look more at the **signs** <note>Commonly called "marks of grace" in Puritan theology—outward evidence that one is truly saved.</note> that show them what they are, than at the **commandments** which tell them what they must do. When Christians seek more after **privileges** than after their bounden duty, it is right for God to withhold their comfort. When Christians labor more to know that they are **justified** <term>Justified: A theological term meaning being declared righteous in the eyes of God.</term> than they use the means to become righteous; to know that they are in the state of grace, rather than using the means prescribed to them to obtain grace, this is a reason why God withholds the comfort of the Spirit from them.

And thus I have shown you the first cause why God’s People are bowed down under the weight of the withholding of God's grace from the Soul.

II. The second reason why God’s People are depressed under the lack of God’s favor comes from God Himself. God may withhold the enjoyment of His Love and favor from you, and that: 1. Because of His **sovereignty**. Assurance is given out of His good will, and the withdrawal of it shows the absolute nature and freedom of His will. May God not do with His own People 

<column-break/>

what He wills? God has by His power created day and night; God gives not only days of comfort and refreshment to His People, but He also gives **nights of desertion** <note>The original "nachten der verlatingghe" refers to periods of spiritual darkness where a believer feels abandoned by God.</note>; these are acts of God’s power and sovereignty over His People, to show that, whenever it is God’s will, He can take away the day of comfort and withhold His love and favor from the souls of His People; so also, if He wills, He can give us assurance through the power of His sovereignty. God may do what pleases Him, and no one may say: why do You do so?

II. God does this to reveal His wisdom and loving-kindness to His people; for through this withdrawal and withholding of comfort and the hiding of His face:

1. Through this, He restrains His People from loathing the comfort and joy; if God continually gave them the light of His countenance and the full assurance of faith; if God continually let out the rays of His glorious love upon their souls, they would be subject to loathing and would trample upon grace, and take little notice of the friendly Love of God and of the Divine benefits bestowed upon them. Therefore, God sometimes judges it necessary to hold back His favor, and His love, and to withdraw the comfort thereof, so that they might value it more highly and receive it better when they do enjoy it.

2. God withdraws His Love and favor from the Souls of His People out of wisdom, so that He might thereby let His People see and notice that there is truly more evil in sin than there appeared to be good in the contemplation of sin. Man commits sin so that he may obtain some apparent good from it, such as the pleasure of the lust of his eyes, or to obtain some other human good; but God lets him see and find—through the withholding of His favor and grace, and the light of His countenance—that there is more evil in the loss of God's Face than there appeared to be any good in the contemplation of sin and the pleasure thereof.

3. God withholds His favor out of wisdom to ward off the **pride** and **self-conceit** of a Man, so that they should not be puffed up by their gifts and graces, or by the strength and degrees of their grace. **Job 33:17**. *That he may withdraw Man from his work, and hide pride from the Man.* Why so? Because a Man can be proud in the work that he does, being full of high and noble thoughts of himself; therefore God withholds His work, so that He may withhold pride from him; and this is an act of Wisdom and goodness in God.

4. God does such things so that He may the more deter His People from sinning against Him, so that their comfort may not be darkened again. I must reason thus before I commit any sin: that if I do this, I break the righteous Law of God, and if I break the Law of God, then God will break my heart and peace; thus I shall take care not to sin against God, seeing that by committing the same I must lie under the feeling of God’s wrath.

5. God does it so that He may let Man experience that assurance is not **essential** to Holiness; although God’s People have grace, and they believe and...

# 226 Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

<note>original title: "Balzem Gileads" — a biblical reference to Jeremiah 8:22, commonly used in the 17th century to describe spiritual medicine for a distressed soul.</note>

6. God does it / so that a person may see the difference between Heaven and Earth; God saves the best for last: God does not judge it useful that man should have a steady joy in this unsteady world / that he should be full of joy on this empty Earth / nor that it should be a lasting joy in this passing world / but he preserves such things until His People come into Heaven; if the People of God, while living here in this World / had the fullness of joy and a steadfast comfort / then they would not long for Heaven; therefore it pleases God to mix sorrow with consolation / and to hide his face to that end / so that they would look toward Heaven; to let them see the difference between Heaven and Earth. Thus you see the second Reason / why God withholds His favor from His People / which is taken from God's wisdom.

III. God withholds from His People the feeling of His favor out of justice / laying them under the feeling of His wrath: God wants to punish His own People for sin by withholding His love and favor. Although He will not punish them with Hell and in Hell / nonetheless He wants to and may punish them with the feeling of Hell / and lead them under the feeling of wrath. I shall set before you certain points on how God punishes His People for sin with the feeling of a lack of assurance.

1. God punishes His People for the Sin of grieving His Spirit; if you grieve the Spirit of God / God will then grieve and trouble your spirit; if you send the Spirit of God sorrowful to Heaven / then God will place sorrow in your spirit upon the Earth; and if you must be comforted / how can you expect any comfort / when you send Him away sorrowful / who should refresh your Soul? Therefore when God has withdrawn His face from you / conclude then that you have grieved His Spirit.

2. God withdraws His love and punishes His People for sin / for their carelessness and lack of understanding / which His People have regarding God and His fear; just as children become playful, willful, and irreverent when the Father is away / yet a commanding severity takes away the playfulness: so are God's People like playful children forgetting God and His fear / and therefore He deems it necessary that we should see His sourness as well as His friendliness; He wants to punish His People with the loss of His favor for their Sin / just as much as He wants to smile upon them in the light of His countenance; God wants to look sourly at His children sometimes / so that they may see the wrinkles of His forehead / (if I may speak in a human way) too much familiarity breeds contempt: the **Persian Kings** <note>Ancient Persian monarchs were famous for their seclusion; it was often a capital offense to approach them without an invitation, which maintained their aura of divine authority.</note> avoided familiarity and were seldom seen / so that they might be more greatly honored.

<column-break/>

3. God does it so that He may punish the severity / and unmercifulness / which people hold toward others who are troubled in their minds: there are many Christians who have obtained the assurance of God's favor and their salvation / they look upon others / who are surrounded by fear and unrest of mind / and who lie under temptation / they look at them from afar / and do not grant them any more love or bowels of mercy <note>A common 17th-century idiom meaning deep, heartfelt compassion.</note> / than they do to those who have no grace at all: God then / to heal this defect / withholds His favor / and withdraws the light of His countenance / and lets them lie under doubts and fear / so that they may learn to be merciful toward the dejected / and so that they should no longer be so unmerciful toward them; not judging them and crushing the **bruised reed** <note>A reference to Isaiah 42:3: "A bruised reed he will not break." It refers to a person whose spirit is fragile and weakened by suffering.</note>.

III. <note>The original text repeats the numbering "III" for this new section regarding the Devil.</note> I come now to the third reason / why God's People lie down under the realization of the lack of the love and favor of God toward their Souls. It arises from the Devil and this out of his malice and out of his cunning. The Devil, since he cannot make the Children of God smash their Souls to pieces on the rock of presumption / therefore he labors to drown their Soul in the whirlpool of despair: since he cannot prevent a Child of God from entering into his Master's joy in the next world / therefore he tries to prevent his Master's joy from entering into them / in this world: the Devil would rather play a small tragedy / than none at all: knowing that he cannot prevent them from going to Heaven / therefore he seeks to prevent Heaven from coming to them; since he cannot prevent you from having grace / therefore he seeks / as long as he can / to withhold from you the feeling of grace. This is the third Reason / why God's People lie down under the lack of the light of God's countenance.

IV. The fourth kind of reason / why God withdraws the Light of His countenance is this / it arises from other People and that partly from good / partly from evil People.

1. It arises partly from good People.

I. Good People sometimes despise the company of doubting and weak Christians; when they perceive it thus in themselves / "I am a disturbance to the company of the good"; and when good People then stand far off and do not seek the company of weak Christians / this makes them say / "truly God does not remember me for good / would Christ want to keep fellowship with me / and not despise me?" These reasons rise up in the hearts of good People / weak Christians are made so by the strangeness and the contempt of Spirit in good People toward those / who are weak: It is hard to be very merciful / until we have felt the pain ourselves. Women / who have never experienced **childbirth** <note>original: "Barens-noot." A comparison often used to describe the "labor" of spiritual rebirth or deep trials.</note> / cannot be so compassionate with those who are in the pangs of birth: a Christian who has never been tempted / cannot be very merciful toward those / who lie under a great and strong temptation; those / who have never been under strong doubts and fear / cannot be compassionate with those who are in doubts and fear.

2. It is to give them more experience in order to comfort afflicted Souls /

# of a Dejected Soul.

<margin>2 Cor. 1:4.</margin> The Apostle shows one of the purposes of their affliction: *Who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves were comforted by God.* verse 6. *But whether we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation.* This was so that they could comfort those who were under spiritual affliction with that same comfort with which they themselves were comforted by God; a Student may read much—yes, entire Books—concerning spiritual endurance, and of the doubts and terrors under which other Christians have lain, yet from all that reading he shall not be as fit to comfort sorrowful souls, because the experience is lacking to him. A Scholar can read Books on the Art of Seamanship, and yet not be a good Skipper; rather, it is experience that makes someone a good Skipper. Likewise, someone can read books on endurance and yet not be fit to comfort those who are in suffering, because they lack the experience that others have who have been in such a situation. These, who have been tempted; these, whose Conscience has been disturbed; these are the most fit to come to the aid of those who are in such a condition. God chooses broken vessels to pour comfort into, so that they might, in turn, pour it out into others.

II. It arises from evil People; the wicked cause the unrest of Soul in the dejected; Although God allows His People to be bowed down and dejected, God does such things:

1. To strike a godly fear into the wicked regarding their eternal state: Must not the godless man reason thus within himself? If I see such a Man, who follows the Ordinances of God; who lives and walks carefully in the ways of God; who makes it a matter of Conscience how he shall live in his calling; who labors to keep his heart toward God and to maintain fellowship with him; who will not and dares not commit any known sin; who prays with his Household; who seeks to kill sin and keep his Body in subjection and to grow in the ways of God and in goodness: if I see such a one lying under terrors, doubts, and unrest of spirit, and so dejected, fearing that everything is in vain and that he will lose Heaven at the last; what will then become of me? What shall I think of myself, whose ways are not like his ways? He has followed the Ordinances, I have not; he has carefully sought to walk in the way of God, where I have made no Conscience of such things; he has conscientiously sought to live in his calling, which I have never done; he dared not commit known sins, while I gave in to Sin and hid it in my bosom; he labored to kill sin, while sin has ruled over me as a Lord; he sought to be fruitful, but I am unfruitful; I do not hate my heart, nor do I do my guilty duty; nor do I make it a matter of Conscience to walk holily and humbly with God as he does; and yet, look, he is restless and dejected over the lack of God’s favor; what then shall I think of myself? If this Man lies under the feeling of vengeance, shall I not fear that

<column-break/>

I shall have to lie under the burden of God's Wrath? If he fears Hell, shall I not fear Hell? And when they see this, it is only to wake them from the sleep of carelessness, and to make them alert to the presumption and imagination of their salvation: and in a certain respect it is a mercy to the godless that the good are dejected and restless, so that they may look upon their own hearts and ways, to improve them and be converted.

2. God does it as a Judgment upon the godless; the Lord lets His People be depressed over the absence of His Divine favor as a Judgment to the World, so that it may be a stumbling block for the World on the way to Heaven; when they shall say of themselves, "I and my company—there are no such merry People in the world as we are; we can be joyful; we cheat and deceive in our trade, and we can do this and that, and yet not be restless in our conscience all year long: and look at these who follow the Ministers and go to the Ordinances, and hear the Sermons, and love the Bible; look how their heads hang, how they are restless in their minds and dejected, and have hardly any comfort all their lives." What could the Reason be that they continue so in their evil ways and yet are not restless, while God's People in their strict <note>original: "precysen" — referring to the "precisians" or Puritans who were very strict in their religious observance.</note> walk are so very dejected? It was so in the days of Calvin: <note>original Latin: "Spiritus Calvinianus est spiritus melancholicus"</note> "The Calvinist spirit is a melancholy spirit." The spirit of the Christian is a sad spirit, and this has been a stone of stumbling for many Papists <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics.</note>, who did not want to follow a sad Religion.

### VI. SERMON.

->Psalm 42 : 12<-

> Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, he is the . . . . help of my countenance and my God.

I will now show you why the People of God should not be so very dejected, if they have a comforting assurance of God's Love.

In treating this matter, note these nine points.

<margin>Nine comforts against desertions.</margin> I. Remember that God's withdrawal of the feeling of his love and favor from the Soul is not always an act of his justice to punish sin, but that it is sometimes an act of his sovereignty. When it is for sin's sake—just as you have grieved God's Spirit, so this grieves the soul—it is neither comforting nor meritorious; But when you suffer from God as though by the act of his power, then there is not such great turmoil, nor cause for dejection; rather, you must comfort yourself in that state, since God may sometimes withdraw and withhold his love and favor solely through an act of his sovereignty. In the thank-offerings Oil was mixed, but not in the sin-offerings, because there is no peace or comfort in suffering for our sins. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page 227 regarding "spiritual desertion"—the experience of a believer feeling abandoned by God. While the previous page focused on how this suffering prepares one to comfort others, this page examines the different theological reasons why God withdraws His presence: as a just response to neglect, or as a loving test of the soul's devotion.</meta>

# Gilead's Balm, or the Healing

read of the abandonment of the church <note>The "church" here often refers to the individual soul of the believer, personified as the "Bride."</note> in the Song of Solomon chapter 5:5, 6.
> I rose up to open to my Beloved, but my Beloved had withdrawn himself... he was gone; my soul failed when he spoke; I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.

This was an act of Justice in Christ to withdraw himself from her; Jesus Christus knocked until his head was filled with dew and his locks with the drops of the night, and she did not open for him. Therefore, Christ treats her with "un-right" <note>The author uses "ontrecht," implying a withdrawal of the usual "rights" or favors of the relationship.</note> to punish her sin through an act of Justice, because the Bride did not let Christ in when he knocked. You also read of the abandonment of the church, not as an act of Justice to punish her sin, but as an act of his power. Song of Solomon 3:1.
> By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loves: I sought him, but I found him not.

If then your conscience tells you that you are diligent in your divine services, and that your heart is upright, and that you labor to walk precisely, and yet you still cannot see the appearance of your comfort, you may then perhaps—yea, without perhaps—say it is not an act of Justice, but an act of his power, that he withholds his favor and the light of his countenance from your soul.

### II.
God may withdraw his love and favor from the soul, not because of any displeasure he has toward her, but indeed out of Love, to test his people’s love for him; like a mother, a tender-hearted mother, who sometimes runs behind the door and hides herself in a corner, not because she is angry with her child, but to test the strength of her child’s love in seeking its mother. In this way, God withdraws his love from the soul of his people, not because he is angry, but it is out of love for his people, to test the strength of his people’s gifts and their love in seeking him. God tests the power of your gifts of grace in following Christ and your love in longing for Christ. It was so with Joseph, of whom it was said in Genesis 42:7: *He behaved like a stranger toward them and spoke harshly to them, namely his brothers.* Verse 17: *and he put them all together in custody for three days.* All his dealings with his brothers were not out of a lack of love for them, but to test the affections of his brothers and to bring to their memory their previous unkindness <note>Referring to the brothers selling Joseph into slavery years prior.</note>. Thus God often deals with his own people; he withdraws his love, and withholds his favor, and keeps back the light of his countenance, to test the strength of his people’s gifts of grace, and the power of his people’s love for him. See such a thing in Luke 24:28, when two disciples went to a village and Christ came to them and walked with them, and when they came near the village where they were going, Christ acted as if he would go further; but this act of Christ was to test the love of his two disciples, whether they would compel him to stay with them. So God withdraws the rays of his love and withholds his divine favor for this purpose: to test the love of his people, how they long for him and how much they desire his love in their souls.

### III.
God holds back his favor because sometimes there is more of his Fatherly love in the withdrawal of his love than in the manifestation of his love to the souls of his

<column-break/>

people, and that in these two circumstances.

1. When man, in the enjoyment of the feeling of God’s love, becomes proud, then it is a mercy to withhold his love and favor; if he cannot enjoy the feeling of God’s love without the feeling of a spiritual pride, in this circumstance it is then a great love. Job 33:17: *That he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man.* So that man does not become proud of God’s grace and comfort, God withholds from him the comfort of his grace; in this circumstance it is a great goodness of God to be weaned from the love of God, for if they possessed it constantly, they would become proud. A small boat cannot carry a large sail without sinking; nor a weak vessel <term>weeck Vat</term> <note>Meaning a fragile container, like a clay pot or glass bottle.</note> hold strong moisture without breaking. Some of God’s people are like small vessels; you know that small boats are like weak vessels. Weak Christians are not capable of bearing strong comfort; pouring strong liquid into weak bottles is a means to break them; likewise, placing great revelations and strong comforts in a weak soul would quickly break it. God sees that his people sometimes are not capable of bearing and properly using comforts and divine revelations; and in this case, it is a great grace to withhold them from you when you cannot bear them. For the lack of comfort makes you more fiery for Christ. Often the enjoyment of comfort makes you careless, whereas the lack of comfort makes you more diligent in desiring it.

<margin>He does not desert unless he is deserted; he deserts instead so that he might not be deserted; therefore he seems to desert because he does not wish to be deserted. <note>original: "Non deserit nisi deseratur; deferit potius, ne deseratur; ideò videtur deserere, quòd vult deseri."</note></margin>
Just as it is a cruel mercy for a godless person to have hope and an imagination of heaven and yet go to hell; so is it a merciful cruelty that a godly person lies under the fear of hell and yet goes to heaven.

2. The withholding of God’s love and favor is in love when it makes you praise Jesus Christ more in the absence than in the enjoyment of him. The Lord often brings his people to great lack and need, so that they would praise his mercy all the more, and be more diligent to seek it; and so that they would not become proud when they have it. You read in Deuteronomy 32:13: *He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the increase of the fields: and he made him suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock.* God did not give him water, but God gave him honey; it would have been grace had God given him water to drink when they were dying of thirst; but when Moses speaks of this, he says that God gave him honey to suck; since they felt the lack of a lesser grace, God gave them a greater favor. Thus it is also in the spiritual realm: when we in our distress see the lack of grace in our soul, Oh! then the soul sighs for even a small grace; the smallest crumb of comfort then refreshes the soul; the lack of spiritual grace makes us see the worth of that grace; the loss of God’s favor and the lack of the light of his countenance makes the

<meta>This page continues the pastoral advice for a "stricken soul"—someone feeling the heavy weight of spiritual desertion. ->### of a stricken Soul.<-

The soul praises the enjoyment of the same; the lack of Christ’s love, shining in the soul, makes the soul see, feel, and acknowledge that the love of God in Christ is exceedingly precious. When the withdrawal of the light of God’s countenance works these gracious effects in the soul, then it is a great love and favor toward the soul. <note>The author argues that feeling God's absence can be a "favor" because it teaches the soul to value His presence more highly.</note>

IV. So that you should not be too greatly dejected, observe: That God’s people, although they do not always have the consolation and the feeling of comfort in their souls—so that their souls are sometimes without the feeling of comfort—nevertheless, God’s people are never without the *cause* of consolation in their souls. Just as a man has a right to an inheritance, even though he cannot read the deeds of the same; so do those have a right to an inheritance who are sanctified through faith in Jesus Christ, even though you do not tangibly enjoy your inheritance. It was the same with Hagar <margin>Genesis 21</margin> as it is with many doubting Christians. She wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba; when the water in the bottle was gone, she cast the child under one of the shrubs and sat down opposite him and wept. There was a well of water near her, but she did not know it; but when God opened her eyes, then she saw the well. So it is with many poor souls; salvation is close by them, very near to their soul, and the soul has no sensory knowledge of it, but easily thinks that it shall perish through the lack of salvation and through the want of comfort and the consolation of God in Christ. It is worth noting what is said of Joseph’s brothers; they were greatly loved by their brother, so much so that they even had a sign of it with them—they had the money in their sacks—and yet they did not know it, nor did they recognize their brother. Thus a poor soul may enjoy a sign of God’s love and a pledge <term>onder-pant: a "down payment" or earnest money signifying a future full delivery</term> of His eternal love toward their souls; and yet they may not know this sign and not feel the lovely friendship of God toward their soul.

V. Remember this for your support: that no one among God’s people always retains an equally great feeling and manifestation of God’s love in their souls. Rather, it goes with the souls of God’s people, in regard to comfort, as it goes with the sea—sometimes ebb, sometimes flood; and as it is with the air—sometimes misty, sometimes clear; and as the seasons of the year—sometimes winter, sometimes summer. As it is with nature, so it is also situated with grace. Nothing in nature always keeps the same form and perfection, and so it is in grace; no child of God under Heaven always has the same measure of consolation in his soul. Just as Samson did not always have the same great strength, so a Christian does not always have equally great consolations.

VI. When God sometimes withholds His love, favor, and the light of His countenance, remember that God never does such a thing unless He sees great reason and necessity for doing so. <margin>1 Peter 1:6</margin> You read in 1 Peter 1:6: *In which you rejoice; though now for a little while (if need be) you are grieved by manifold temptations.* That refers to suffering for the sake of the Gospel; so I may also say to you: if it is necessary, you shall be in sorrow because of the lack of God’s love in Christ; if you have need of sorrow, then you shall have sorrow; if you have no 

<column-break/>

need of sadness, then you shall have no sadness. The philosophers say that the wind and thunder are just as necessary as the sunshine, for by them the air is purified <note>original: "gesupyvert," meaning cleansed or purged</note>. When God then sometimes thunders upon your soul and roars like the wind against your soul, God sees some necessity therein to deal with you thus—to purify your soul from sin and the love of the world, to humble your pride, to subdue your lusts, and to purge out the negligence of your spirit, by which you might also make others sluggish. God sometimes withholds the light of His countenance and the consolation of grace from your soul so that you should not be proud of the measure of your grace; and sometimes God does such things to kindle in you compassion toward others in their oppression, so that you might thus use your gifts. God may let you lack the comforting operation of the Spirit so that you might all the more obtain the sanctifying operation of the Spirit. Therefore, comfort yourself in this; for if God saw no necessity for this oppression, He would never let you lie in such a sorrowful state.

VII. Note this for your comfort: that Christ was under spiritual abandonment just as you are. Christ Himself cried out, *My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?* Matthew 27:46. <margin>Matthew 27:46</margin> Here was a <margin><note>original Latin: "Erat subtractio visionis non unionis"</note> withdrawal of the vision, not of the union.</margin> withdrawal of the feeling, while the union remained. And you must do no more than cry "my God, my God" during the absence of God’s favor. Jesus Christ did this to sanctify your death; He was buried to make your grave a bed of roses; He was tempted to sanctify your temptations; He was abandoned to sanctify your abandonments. He drank deeply from the cup; you only sip from it. He was under terrors, abandonments, and temptations so that He might come to the aid of those who are tested; thus, through experience, He was made fit to help His people in similar circumstances.

VIII. The apparent loss of God’s favor is not harmful to the state of grace; for it does not hinder you from going to the Throne of Grace; it cannot prevent you from glory. You may hope and wait upon God in your conduct; and although you do not enjoy the light of His countenance, this shall not prevent your access to the Throne of Grace. The lack of Christ—and not merely the lack of comfort—is what makes the Throne of Grace a throne of justice and vengeance. You may lack the face of God to comfort you, but you shall not lack the hand of God to help you. God may lend His ear to your prayers even when He refuses you the shine of His countenance. It is the *truth* of grace and not the *feeling* and *sight* of grace that brings the soul to Heaven. It may be that as long as you live, you are without your Master’s joy; but be assured that you shall come to your Master’s joy when you die. Though you have no Heaven in your soul while you live, your soul shall nonetheless enter into Heaven when you die.

IX. So that you should not be too greatly dejected over the lack of comfort, remember that when you come into Heaven, you shall then have comfort enough. God preserves the fullness of comfort for the fullness of glory—

<margin>1. Objection.</margin>
There is an objection to be answered / which is this.

I think I hear a poor Soul say / If I thought that God, in the hiding of his Face from my Soul and in the withdrawal of the comfort of his Spirit from me; if the absence of the Light of his face were only an act of his sovereignty and power / and to test my Love / to try the trust of my heart in hoping upon him / and to incite me all the more to a longing for Christ (if it were so) I would then not be so greatly disturbed; but alas, what shall I do? My conscience tells me / that because of my sins God withdraws the light of his face and the consolation of the Spirit from me / and that he deals thus with me for that reason; my conscience testifies to me / that I have grieved the Spirit of God and sent him sadly away to Heaven / and therefore it is right for God to let me live mournfully here on the Earth in a comfortless condition; I have committed great sins to take away my comfort / and for the guilt of my sin God hides his face; and this is the sad objection and reasoning of many poor Souls.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
There are then four things / why a Child of God must not be so greatly dismayed / although he lies struck down under sin.

1. If you cannot keep the feeling of God's Love / provided you keep the feeling of your sins / through which you have lost the feeling of God's Love; to have much of the latter / although you have little of the former: to grow in humiliation / even if you increase little in consolation / such is still a great grace. <note>original: Hos. 14, 6</note> Hosea 14:6: *I will be like the dew to Israel, he shall bloom like the Lily: and he shall strike out his roots like Lebanon.* You who bloom like the Lilies / even if you do not bloom so much in the enjoyment of comfort / if you only grow downward / and strike out your Roots downward through the sight and feeling of sin / and increase in humiliation / such is a great grace: It is better and more blessed to shoot the roots of grace downward in growing through the sap of humiliation / than to grow upward and bloom in the feeling of the grace of forgiveness; the Reason for this is this / because the one is absolutely necessary for the preservation of the Soul / but the other is only necessary for the comfort of the Soul / Therefore the one is more necessary than the other: if it were in my choice / I would rather have the lack of the feeling of the forgiveness of sins / than the lack of the feeling of my sinfulness: God would rather see his People in mourning clothes / than in clothes of joy—

<column-break/>

—oy. Though God does not see your face full of joy; if he but sees your eyes full of tears / such is pleasing to him: Although you lack the light of God's face / if you but have the feeling of your sinfulness / which hides the Light of God's favor from your Soul / you do not have such great reason to be so dismayed over your sins.

2. When you are dismayed over your sins / if you then can truly love Christ / you need not be discouraged / even if you do not know for certain that Jesus Christ loves you; although you do not know that you are loved / if you but love Christ in his time / you need not then be disturbed: Even though you do not clearly see Christ / if you but believe in him / and through faith apply Christ to your Soul; if this is your work / and you can testify to such / then you may assure yourself that Christ also truly <margin>1 John 4:19</margin> loves you / although it does not seem so: the reason for this is certain / since we cannot love Christ / unless he first loves us; a person being disturbed in his mind / lacking the assurance of God's Love / who says that he does not know what the testimony of God's Spirit has to say / and what he [has] in his Soul / if he can only say that he relies and believes upon and in Christ / and that he desires to love Christ; then I say to you / although you cannot tangibly feel the Love of Christ in your Soul / if you can only heartily love Jesus Christ / be assured / that Christ also loves you.

3. Do I speak this day to someone who is encompassed with sin in the lack of the feeling of the consolation of the spirit / and can neither see nor feel the revelation of God's Love / as others do? ...to praise God; The Psalmist says in Psalm 44:17-19 <note>The Dutch text cites verses 18-20; in modern English Bibles, this corresponds to verses 17-19</note>: "All this has come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor dealt falsely with your Covenant. If you can also say / even if God covers me with a **Shadow of Death** / and there is a **Cloud** between God and my Soul / nevertheless I fear to sin against him / to provoke him / and to depart from his ways; in this you may comfort yourself / even though you feel that Christ has turned his back to you / and yet you say / I will not for the whole world cease to live for Christ in the way of love and obedience.

<margin>Objection:</margin>
Is it so / that many Souls are too greatly dejected over sin / and you say that they sin in this / and that they must labor against the unrest and dejection over sin : but does this not lay a foundation for presumption <note>original: "verwaentheyt" — a spiritual arrogance or false sense of security</note> in many minds / so that they imagine their salvation / and does this not make them bold in sinning against God, seeing as you say / that they must not be so distressed?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
It is true / if this Doctrine is not well-refined and handled wisely ; for just as it may comfort one Soul / so it causes presumption in a hundred / for in some circumstances / when God withholds his favor / and hides his face from the Soul because of your sins / then you have cause to mourn in this / and that in these five cases.

1. You have cause to let your head hang with sadness / when you lack the feeling and the revelation of **God’s Love** to your Soul / and at that time you also lack the sight and the feeling of your sin; when you have a restless spirit / and at that time do not have a restless conscience; you lack the feeling of Christ’s Love to your Soul / and yet at that time you lack the sight and feeling of your sins against Jesus Christ. Many people are in this case; These people must say / that they do not know / where they shall go, to Heaven or to Hell; whether they are children of God / or children of wrath; whether Christ loves them / or not / yet no Sin disturbs them / but they presume grace and forgiveness / where you know above all / that between you and Hell is but a step; and in this case / your state is very sorrowful.

2. You / who say that you lack the feeling of God’s Love / and yet at that time you do not lack the feeling of the loss and absence of that Love; When a Man does not know if God loves him or not / and that he at that time is not concerned about all this / whether his state be a lost state / that he loses grace / and loses Heaven / this is a sorrowful case / to be in such danger / and yet to be unfeeling about such danger.

3. Your case is mournful / in the circumstance when you lack the feeling of Christ’s Love to your Soul / and at that time you then lack the act of love; and to express your Love toward Christ / you seem to want to know if Christ loves you or not / without ever trying to know or examine if you love Christ / or not ; but instead of loving Christ / you murmur against God / against Christ / where you ought to trust in him / there you murmur against him / and you

<column-break/>

do not say with Job chapter 13:15 <note>original: "Job cap. 13. 15."</note>: "Behold, though he slay me, yet will I trust in him" <note>original: "Siet, soo hy my doode, soude ick niet hopen ?" — literally, "would I not hope?"</note>. If under the feeling of God’s Love / you lack Love for Christ / then your case is very sorrowful.

4. At that time when you miss the consolation of the Spirit / and when you then also do not have the observation of the Spirit / then your case is mournful / when you not only lack comfort / but you also lack grace / such makes your condition sorrowful; to be restless over the lack of comfort / and not to be restless over the lack of grace. Oh go into your own heart! you who miss the consolation / do you also miss grace? have you no tenderness of conscience? no gnawing of your Spirit? no desire for duties? no zeal for God? no faith / to live through? no hope / to rely on Christ? no Love for Christ in your Soul? no repentance over sin? in this circumstance your state is very mournful.

5. When you have lived for a long time under the loss of consolation and in restlessness of your mind and disturbance of your Spirit / and yet you live thus without examining how you shall escape from that sorrowful state / and how you shall obtain the consolation / which you lack; to miss consolation and grace / and to live thus without attaining them / but to do as **Cain** did / to follow the World / and to follow the profits and pleasures of the world / and all that to strike your Conscience on the mouth <note>a 17th-century idiom meaning to silence or suppress the conscience</note> / for you take no trouble to awaken grace in your Soul and to quicken your heart / so that you may enjoy the joy of Heaven ; and the consolation of grace / the Love of God / and the light of Christ’s countenance; the revelations of his love ; and the assurance of your salvation ; when you then do not look back for any means of grace or consolation / such makes your case very sorrowful.

And thus I have concluded this part / that God’s People have no reason for doubting / even if they are dejected over their sins, or over the lack of God’s favor to their Soul.

I shall now set down some scriptural rules / to help a child of God / who lies cast down under the lack of the assurance of God’s Love / to obtain again the feeling of God’s Love.

Now then for your help in this matter / I shall give you these two lessons.

I. You must put away the things / which cause a withholding of God’s favor and Love from you; which cast you down.

II. You must consider such things / which may advance you in obtaining the comforting feeling / and certain assurance of God’s Love.

I. Concerning the first / here are eight things to be avoided / which cause this suspicion of God’s Love.

<meta>This page continues the pastoral advice for a soul suffering from spiritual desertion. The previous page concluded a defense against the idea that excessive sorrow over sin leads to presumption; this page provides practical steps to restore a sense of God's love and comfort, identifying specific spiritual and physical obstacles.</meta>

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

1. Strive to ward off natural melancholy; there is such a natural sympathy between the Soul and the Body that a disturbance in one causes a stroke in the other. It is no more a wonder that a conscientious man, overtaken with melancholy <note>In this period, "melancholy" was understood as both a physical imbalance of "humors" and a state of deep depression or fear.</note>, fears and doubts, etc., than that a sick man groans, or that a child weeps when it is struck. If there is melancholy in the body, there will also be a stroke in the soul—that is, the abandonment and disturbance of the mind. In Christians, this sometimes begins from natural melancholy. This must then be warded off if you wish to regain a comforting feeling and assurance of God’s Love. The Physicians say that natural melancholy has sorrowful effects for those who listen to it, such as fear, trembling, terrifying dreams, and being subject to mournful perceptions. The Devil can speak when your perception is disturbed, and he knows how to change this and make you fear for your salvation. The Devil is a cunning spirit, and when the natural constitution is thus disturbed, he can turn a natural ill into a spiritual one.

2. You must put away spiritual pride, according to Job 33:17: *That he may withdraw man from his work, and hide pride from man.* If these swelling humors of pride are in your spirit, God will <margin>2 Corinthians 12:7</margin> send you a messenger of Satan to buffet you. Men of a haughty spirit, says Preston <note>John Preston (1587–1628), a highly influential English Puritan theologian.</note>, lie open to sorrowful abandonments and dark eclipses of their comfort. It is God’s custom, when he sees a man proud and puffed up beyond measure and the degrees of his grace, to then strike down their pride; he then withholds from them the comfort of his grace. Pride is not only a ban on grace, but also on comfort; God resists the proud. The Greek word <note>original: *antitassetai*. This term implies a military confrontation.</note> signifies that God sets himself in battle array against him. Beloved, God sets himself in battle array against a proud man; therefore, if you seek to regain the certainty and assurance of God’s Love, put away pride.

3. If you wish to regain this comforting assurance, then put away the bluntness and deadness of heart in holy meditations. When the form and liveliness of our spirit is diminished in meditation, then the comfort of God’s Spirit will also be withheld. Little meditation and little comfort go together; when the movements are dead and the heart is forfeit in meditation, then the assurance will be darkened, and the comfort will eclipse. Fireless meditations are answered by God with sternness and not with kindness.

4. Fleshly joy and comfort in creatures <note>meaning "created things," such as wealth, status, or worldly pleasures.</note>, and in the things of this world, unnerve spiritual joy; the Sun, when it shines upon the fire, prevents the fire's burning. If you have the sunshine of comfort in this world, it is a hundred to one that your affections have any light or warmth; comforts are made warm by grace; the more heat in your affections, the more strength also in your comforts. Fleshly pleasures take away the heart, and when the heart is gone, then it is also finished with the comfort.

<column-break/>

Hosea 4:11. *Whoredom, and wine, and new wine, take away the heart.* To sit swilling and babbling by the jugs, and to follow wantonness—this takes away the heart. Fleshly joy is entirely contrary to spiritual joy; a man shall never have joy in the Holy Spirit while he overflows with fleshly and idle pleasures in the things of this world.

5. Beware of grieving the Spirit, if you wish to keep the comforting assurance of God’s Love. Isaiah 63:10: *But they rebelled, and vexed his Holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought against them.* If you cause pain to his Spirit in Heaven, then he will <margin>The Holy Spirit is a delicate thing; he treats us just as he is treated by us. — Tertullian.</margin> cause your spirit to grieve here on Earth. God’s Spirit will deal with us just as we deal with him; if you grieve God’s Spirit, he will also grieve you; he will pour no joy into your spirit if you grieve him. If you torment God’s Spirit by resisting the holy movements of the Spirit, then he will also torment your spirit by withholding the comforting movements of the Spirit. It is noteworthy that the Spirit of God in Scripture is not only called a Comforter, but also the Holy Spirit; therefore, it is in vain to believe that the Spirit will be a Comforter to you if you resist the office of the Spirit insofar as he is the Holy Spirit. Therefore, you who cause pain to the Spirit by resisting his holy movements, you shall never obtain the comforts of the Spirit.

6. Ward off all unmercifulness and lack of compassion of spirit toward others who are troubled in their minds. Many Christians are like the harts <note>male deer</note>, which have a habit that when one hart is wounded by the woodsman, they all abandon it together and leave the wounded hart to care for itself. There are also many such uncompassionate people who, when a person is troubled in his mind and has the arrows of God's wrath sticking in his Soul, run away from him and abandon him. Many people lack this tenderness and the bowels of mercy toward the tempted and troubled souls; they are full of rebuke, contempt, and harsh treatment. Because of this hardness and lack of compassion, God also causes eclipses in their souls. If you then seek to obtain comfort, be compassionate with tempted and troubled souls, and that is the way to obtain comfort.

7. Beware of wantonness <note>original: "dertelheydt" — meaning a lack of proper reverence or a frivolous attitude.</note> and fearlessness toward the Divine Majesty and power. When parents dandle a child on their knees, their child will easily become wanton; therefore, parents are often forced by a stern look to prevent this wantonness. If God always showed us a friendly being, such would cause a contempt of God; therefore, God sometimes shows himself with Majesty and a seeming displeasure, with wrinkles in his forehead, and all this to improve the spirit of wantonness that sticks in his People. The Persian Kings avoided all familiarity with their subjects and were only seen twice a year, so that the subjects would not despise them if they saw them often. So God also hides himself from them, so that his People do not become wanton.

8. If you do not wish to be cast down under these...

these desertions / take away from you all worldliness; being overloaded with creatures <note>In 17th-century theology, "creatures" refers to any created thing—people, possessions, or worldly desires—as opposed to the Creator.</note>; and having your hearts filled with the world; if you are so disposed / then you shall never enjoy a comforting assurance of God's Love. A person / who is worldly-minded / cannot be strong in assurance; if you keep your eye at a proper distance from the earth / then you can see far; but if you lay your eye upon the ground / then you can see but little: Beloved / keep your heart at a proper distance from the Earth / then you shall see far into the feeling of God’s favor; but if you let your eye / I mean your Soul / stay near the world: then you see nothing; you shall not perceive the feeling of God's Love / if worldliness has the upper hand in you: Place a Candle above the ground / and it shall shine clearly / but place that same Candle under the ground / and it shall burn but dimly / the damp of the ground hinders its light. going to the Promised Land: how God, who has been good / shall still be good. After that I will remember the Land of Hermonim; in that Land Sihon / King of the Amorites / and Og / King of Bashan were conquered / which you read in Joshua 12:1, 2. Some believe Mizar <note>original: "Missar"</note> to have been a small hill near Mount Sinai / where the Law was given. I will remember God's goodness in giving His Law to His people; here David remembers God's lovingkindness of old / to obtain for himself comfort and peace in his mind. In this way he also does in Psalm 77:12. I will remember the works of the Lord: yes, I will remember your wonders of old. Think on old mercies / and old privileges of favorable Love / and that is the way to lift up your heart with courage.

4. Use the arguments of faith against present feelings: Abraham would never have believed God's promise; if he had not used arguments of faith against present feelings and preoccupations <note>original: "besessen" - refers to one's current state of mind or worldly attachments</note>. Theologians apply that of Isaac to the occasion of desertion: How! did Isaac fail in accepting Jacob before Esau? Theologians apply this / that through feeling God's People think / that they are Esaus / and that they are rejected and hated by God, while they are nevertheless the Beloved of the Lord; although feeling and current state may tell you; my weaknesses are many; my corruptions are strong; my heart is hardened; my affections are dead / which God well knows; I cannot believe; I cannot have comfort: believe nevertheless / that God is free; that God is merciful; that God accepts the will for the deed; that he accepts the imputed righteousness / as if it were an inherent righteousness: thus use arguments of faith against present feelings. If you reason thus the Devil shall trouble you no more; although I do not have the faith of proof / yet I will nevertheless strive for adherence <note>original: "aenklevimghe" - a theological term for clinging to God despite a lack of emotional "proof"</note> / relying myself on Christ; Reason thus.

5. Follow this Rule; let your comfort rather be grounded on an unchanging covenant / than on your own feeling / and withered affections; this is a Rule of great utility. Beloved / should Christians build their eternal comfort on their felt affections / their comfort would be ebb and flow / going up and down; their affections are sensory / sometimes hot as fire / sometimes cold as the Air; the Pulse of the Body beats sometimes hard / sometimes faint / so also do the affections. If you then build your comfort on your affections / then you shall have no steady comfort / but constantly go up and down; but build rather your comfort on the eternal and unchanging covenant / on such a Covenant / that accepts the will for the works / the desire for the deed / the intent for the fulfillment. So then build your comfort rather on the unchanging covenant / than on the flowing affections / this is the way to obtain and keep everlasting comfort.

6. Keep this Rule; In some occasions / particularly in desertions and temptations / it is safer to submit yourself to the Judgment of others / than to follow your own Judgment. Am I deserted? am I tempted? am I troubled in my mind?

<column-break/>

why? it is better for me if my own Judgment can give me no comfort / that I then submit myself to the Judgment of others / who are experienced Christians / if they, having taken notice of my life / and manner of doing / then minister comfort to me; To these I am duty-bound to submit myself in case of desertion or temptation. <margin>Mr. Frogmorton.</margin> It is told of a Minister of the Word in England / that he was for a long time troubled in his mind / so that he could not comfort himself / until he had the judgment of learned Ministers / and through their testimony he received comfort. Mr. Bradford <note>John Bradford (1510–1555), a famous English Reformer and martyr.</note>, could not be comforted; except through the testimony of another Martyr / John Carelesse <note>original: "Jan Carelesse"</note> assured Mr. Bradford that he was a holy and good Man, the testimony of John Carelesse set the conscience of Mr. Bradford very much at rest. Thus Nathan's testimony comforted David; and Ananias's testimony comforted Paul <note>original: "Paulum"</note>. The passions of sadness and fear blind the Judgment / and make it unfit to judge, 2 Kings <note>original: "2 Reg."</note> 5:12, 13. When Naaman was under a bad judgment and passions / then his Servants could tell him / what was best for him to do. Sometimes then in case of desertion and temptation it is a good and certain Rule / rather to rest in another's judgment than in one's own.

7. Keep this Rule; Never go to wrong means / and ways to soften / and to satisfy the unrest of your mind. Cain / when he was troubled in his mind over his sin / and in terror of Conscience / Cain to soften this unrest went to building; Therefore some theologians explain that clause in the Letter of Jude verse 11, *They have gone the way of Cain*, thus / as to soften and deaden the unrest of their conscience through outward pleasure / and worldly business; Some with Saul play music; do not follow this course to use sinful and wrong means for softening the unrest of the mind: As a person in a fever drinks cold liquid / it cools a little for a while / but afterwards it increases the heat: So when a person is hot from God's wrath / why do they run to sin / which nevertheless increases the heat? just as someone who is stung by a Bee / would run to a bush of nettles / and rub himself with them to soften the sting of the Bee: Beloved / when a person is stung by God's Wrath / and he then runs to sin to heal himself / he is like one / who rubs himself with nettles / to soften the stinging of the Bee: like a Man / who wants to support his falling House with a burning piece of wood. Beloved / when you are troubled in your mind; then to run to joys / Music / building / buying and selling / and not to approach God on your knees, this is not the way to obtain comfort again / but it is the way / to increase your sadness and to cause greater distress of Conscience. A joyful meeting may soften the unrest of the mind for a time / but it shall return with...

# of a dejected Soul.

...with the more terror as it did before; therefore take care that you use no sinful means to regain the rest and peace of mind.
8. Strive more to do your duty than to acquire comfort: It is a fault in many Christians, that they spend more time in needless complaints over the lack of comfort, than in holy consideration of their duty. If God’s People would only observe this rule, to spend more time in considering their duty than in acquiring comfort, their comfort would be more easily obtained, and their duty better performed. When a house is on fire, we must not inquire how it caught fire, but we must labor to extinguish the flame: In the same way, when a person has second thoughts <note>original: "achter-dencken" - here meaning doubts or suspicions</note> about their state, and mourns over the lack of consolation, they must not rest in a fruitless weeping, but they must make an effort toward consolation. Psalm 30:8. *You hid your face, I was terrified.* Verse 9 follows: *To you, Lord, I cried,* etc. David did not spend as much time in fruitless weeping as he did in holy consideration.
9. Strengthen your evidence more than you weaken it; many spend more time calling their evidence into doubt than in strengthening it. In the unrest of the mind, a person will often devote themselves to reading terrible threats; to reading such places of Scripture and such good books which contain many terrors, and they reject the promises and consolations; by this, one strengthens the Devil's hands and weakens their own. If you find your heart to be arrogant <note>original: "laetdunckig" - conceited or self-important</note> and self-deceiving, then it is good to apply the threats and terrors to yourself to awaken you; but when a person is restless in their mind, then to avoid the promises and to impress the threats of Scripture upon oneself—I say that this is a means more to weaken the consolations than to strengthen them; if you do not find your affections above <note>meaning: spiritual affections focused on heaven</note>, why do you run to your inclinations? Why, it may be that you say, I cannot mourn when I want to mourn; I cannot pray, but I want to pray; I cannot hear profitably, but I would like to hear better. It is a Rule that the theologians <note>original: "Godts-geleerde" - the "God-learned," often translated as "divines"</note> give: that if a believer cannot have comfort from the *act* of grace, he must then look to obtain comfort from his general inclination. It may be that you cannot pray well, but to what end do you pray? Is it not to obtain communion with God and more strength against sin? If you then cannot find that the evidence is strengthened through the consideration of grace, then you may find evidence through your inclination toward virtue. Thus I have finished these two great cases of the dejection of believers: namely, knowing the greatness of sin, and then secondly, the desertion and the Divine withholding of God's Love.

### VIII. S E R M O N.
->Psal. 42: 12.<-

> Why do you bow down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him; he is the ....... health <note>original: "verloſſinghe" - literally "deliverance" or "rescue"</note> of my countenance and my God.

I have now come to the second part of the Psalmist’s sadness. *Why are you disquieted in me?* A simile taken from the Sea, to show the

<column-break/>

unrest that is in a godly person. The manner of the Psalmist’s speaking is like an expostulation <note>a reasoning or earnest protest</note> and complaint; and from this I shall draw this observation.
<margin>Doctrine.</margin> That the godly must rebuke their hearts over, and use a holy reasoning <note>original: "reden-kavelinge" - a structured debate or argument with oneself</note> against, all disordered unrest of the Soul.
In which handling of this point in general, I shall show what those things are over which the Soul of a child of God is disquieted.
That which disquiets the Soul of a child of God is:
I. The prosperity of the wicked. II. The weightiness <note>or "difficulty"</note> of God's Church. III. Outward visitation in their body. IV. Inward corruption in their heart.
I will spend this Sermon on the first, to teach that the godly must rebuke their Soul over the disquiet concerning the prosperity of the wicked.
I know no outward thing in the world that disquiets the Soul of the godly more than the prosperity of the wicked. Regarding this point, I shall handle it in this manner.
I. I shall show that the godly are easily disquieted in their minds over the prosperity of the wicked.
II. I shall show you reasons why you should reason against and rebuke your Soul for the disquiet over the prosperity of the wicked.
III. I shall set down some observations by which you may reason against the disquiet of the Soul over the prosperity of the wicked.
I. The godly have their Souls much disquieted over the prosperity of the wicked. There are four or five proofs of the godly in this; In David the Father, and in Solomon the Son, you have a discovery of this unrest of the Soul.
I. In David the Father. Psal. 73:3 and 12, 13. Where the Psalmist seems to say, "It is in vain that I am godly, since I see that the wicked are so prosperous in the world." It is a great stumbling block <note>original: "Steen des aenstoots" - stone of offense</note> in the way of the godly toward Heaven, to see that the wicked are prosperous; the godly are sometimes seized with this, becoming despondent and disquieted in their Soul to see the prosperity of the wicked in this world.
II. Solomon was disquieted over the same matter, Eccles. 10:6, 7. *Folly is set in great dignity: but the rich sit in low place. I have seen servants upon horses: and princes walking as servants upon the earth.* To see servants riding on horses, etc., that is, to see the wicked promoted and having prosperity; and to see the godly despised and in a low state—this disquieted Solomon.
III. See this in the Prophet Jeremiah; he was very disquieted over this, Jerem. 12:1. *Righteous are you, O Lord, when I plead with you; yet let me talk with you of your judgments: why does the way of the wicked prosper?* etc. He wants to reason with God; what does he say to God? "Let me speak with You of Your judgments; why does the way of the wicked prosper?" Jeremiah would gladly have known a reason from God why the way of the wicked was prosperous.
IV. A fourth proof you have in Job cap. 21:7. *Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power?* etc.
Thus you see four proofs from the best of men,
