# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

between David, Solomon, Jeremiah, and Job.

V. I can also give you one from the Holy Prophet Habakkuk 1:13. *Why do you look upon those who deal treacherously? Why do you remain silent when the wicked swallows up the one who is more righteous than he?* Here the Prophet reasons <note>original: "redenkabelt" - a term for debating or arguing a case</note> with God as to why God does such things; that He, who is of pure eyes, would watch the wicked prospering in his evil way.

Thus you see the precious first part: that the godly are easily troubled in their souls when seeing the prosperity of the wicked.

## II. The second matter is that I show you the reasons why the godly ought not to be troubled or disturbed in their souls when they see the prosperity of the wicked.

->The reasons are four.<-

1. Do not be troubled by the prosperity of the wicked, because God gives him prosperity as a snare. Proverbs 1:32. *For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them.* It makes them careless and satiated in pleasures. Hosea 13:6. *After they had their pasture, they became full; when they were full, their heart was exalted; therefore they have forgotten me.* Their gold, silver, wool and flax, and clothing enrich and strengthen their sins. Do you then, Beloved, want to envy the prosperity of the wicked? Would you envy a man who has a silk rope with which he hangs himself? God gives prosperity to the wicked as a silk rope to hang him eternally; therefore, do not lose heart, even if they have prosperity in this world.

2. Be not troubled, for the curse of God is in the prosperity of the wicked; Job gives this reason in Chapter 5:2-3. He calls these people "fools" who envy the prosperity of the wicked in this world; for Job says: *I have seen the foolish taking root: but suddenly I cursed his habitation.* Beloved, it is better to have poverty with a blessing than abundance with a curse. The wicked have the curse of God in all their prosperity. Solomon gives you this reason so that you should not be troubled. Proverbs 3:31, 32, 33. *Envy thou not the oppressor: and choose none of his ways. For the froward is abomination to the Lord: but his secret is with the righteous. The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked: but he blesseth the habitation of the just.* Even if you see the wicked become wealthy through the oppression and trampling of the poor, do not envy him; for the curse of the Lord is in his house. This is a good reason not to be troubled by the prosperity of the wicked. It is noteworthy what was said of Esau in Genesis 27:28. *Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth.* <note>"Fatness of the earth" refers to the best, most fertile lands and material wealth.</note> A great promise; yet you read: *Jacob have I loved and Esau have I hated.* Jacob had only a poor staff, and Esau had the fatness of the earth. You can be poor like Jacob, with only a stick and a staff, and yet be loved with Jacob; and the wicked may have the fatness of the earth like Esau, and yet God hates them. Therefore, do not be troubled by the prosperity of the wicked. God may give you rest in this world and an abundance of riches; what does God say in Zechariah 1:15? *I am very sore displeased with the heathen that are at ease.* He mixes 

<meta>translator note: the catchword "gelt" is the conclusion of the verb "mengelt" (mixes)</meta>

<column-break/>

His corn and curse with the abundance of the wicked. Therefore, do not be troubled by the prosperity of the wicked.

3. Their prosperity costs them dearly; they lose a soul to win the world. They lose the joy of Heaven for earthly prosperity; it is a costly exchange. Would you envy a man who, to buy a house, lost his life? Yet the wicked, to buy luxury, lose their souls. I have read of a soldier, when an order was given by the General that no one should plunder the land; the soldier plundered a vineyard, taking a cluster <note>original: "krap" - a bunch of grapes</note>; and as an example he was hanged. Some envied the man the cluster; "Do not envy me," he said, "for I must pay dearly enough for it." I apply this: you may see the wicked around you eating the fat and drinking the sweet of the land, while you eat the bread of oppression and drink your tears. Oh, do not envy him, for his luxury is the pain of his blood; it costs him dearly enough.

4. Do not be troubled by the prosperity of the wicked, for this would put you in danger of wanting to be wicked yourself. The person who is disturbed by the prosperity of the wicked is also tempted to become wicked so that they might also be prosperous. Take note where the Scripture speaks of the godly not being disturbed by the prosperity of the wicked; it places this caution upon it: so that you do not become wicked as they are wicked. Proverbs 3:31. *Envy thou not the oppressor: and choose none of his ways.* A notable text in which David tells you what danger he was in when he was troubled by the prosperity of the wicked; you have it in Psalm 73:2. *My feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.* David shows that he envied them and that he had almost fallen into the same fault. You have an excellent passage in verse 19: *How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors.* Wherein he shows that their prosperity in the preceding verses is not lasting. Beloved, to see someone break their covenant and act treacherously, and then see them still prosperous—if you then envy them, you are in great danger of sinning just as they do, so that you too, like them, might be prosperous.

## III. The third question is: What observation shall a person use to reason against the disquiet of the soul over the prosperity of the wicked?

->Beloved, I shall name six observations<-
->to still the disquiet over the prosperity<-
->of the wicked.<-

<margin>Six observations against the disquiet over the prosperity of the wicked.</margin> 1. Consider within yourself that it is a more difficult thing for the godly to use prosperity well than to use adversity. You know it is more difficult to carry a cup filled to the brim with wine without spilling than it is to carry a cup that is only half full. It is more difficult to bear prosperity without sin than adversity. Therefore in the Scripture one sees that those who were good in adversity were evil in prosperity. The children of Israel were good in Egypt, but were evil in Canaan, Deuteronomy 32; as soon as God had delivered them and given them the land of Canaan, even then they rebelled against him. When they became sated and full in the promised land, then they kicked back against God. When David was in an ordinary state, when he was persecuted by

# Of a Dejected Soul

<margin>
One is in more danger from prosperity than from adversity.
</margin>

When Saul pursued David like a partridge over the mountains, David was good; but when David came to the throne, then he became an adulterer and a murderer, whereas he was previously a man of a very restrained life. Therefore the Scripture says of Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 17:3 that he walked in the former ways of his father David, indicating that his former ways were his best ways. I have read in the works of Saint Bernard, Chapter 12, book 2, to this effect: that there is more danger in prosperity than in adversity. It is an observation by Cornelius a Lapide <note>a Flemish Jesuit priest and exegete (1567–1637)</note> regarding Proverbs 1:32: that the word *Shalvah* <note>original Hebrew: **שלוה**</note>, which in Hebrew means prosperity, is read by the Arabic translator as *investigatios* <note>Latin: investigations or trials</note> and by the Seventy translators as <term>exergasmos</term> <note>original Greek: ἐξεργασμός — a working out or thorough testing</note>; and the reason for this is that prosperity reveals a person's true condition, just as we say of the <term>Magistracy</term> <note>original: Magistraets ampt — a high public office</note>, *The office shows the man* <note>original Latin: "Magistratus indicat virum"</note>. When a person comes to public office, it will show what kind of person they are; so I may also say, prosperity will show what is in a person, and will truly find them out. Therefore

<margin>
Anselm: Tribulation proves patience alone, but prosperity examines all the virtues.
</margin>

Anselm says in his Proverbs: adversity tests only patience, but prosperity tests all the virtues. It tests your love, whether you love God or the world; it tests your zeal, whether you want to leave Christ or your status. Do you then, Beloved, want to envy a person who has prosperity in the world, when it is such a difficult matter for the godly to use that prosperity well? It is said of Pope Pius V that he was called godly because, in the judgment of many, when he was a common man, he was held to be godly; but when he became a Cardinal, he doubted his salvation; and when he was Pope, he despaired of being saved. Beloved, when you are in a common state, then you live more holily and pray more richly than you do now; God had more service from you then than He does now, since you have become great in the world. It is an observation that Bernard has regarding Psalm 91:7: *A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand: it shall not come near you.* The direct sense of this passage is that the godly would not fall in that plague at that time; but Bernard says, I may apply it to prosperity: at the right hand ten thousand shall fall through prosperity, where not even a thousand shall fall through adversity. Beloved, where adversity strikes down a thousand, prosperity strikes down ten thousand.

2. Remember that the prosperity of the wicked hastens their end and ruin: do you then want to envy someone’s prosperity when you see that it hastens their downfall? Psalm 37:1-2. *Fret not yourself because of evildoers, neither be envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb.* The more a flower blooms, the closer it is to wilting. When the wicked flourish most broadly, then they are nearest to being cut down; therefore, fret not yourself over evildoers, for they shall soon be cut down. Proverbs 24:19-20. *Fret not yourself because of evil men, neither be envious of the wicked; for there shall be no reward to the evil man; the lamp of the wicked shall be put out.* Their prosperity will

<column-break/>

hasten their destruction, but not their reward: there shall be no reward for the wicked. Would you not consider that man a fool who, being an heir to many thousands of pounds a year, should envy a stage actor <note>original: "Comediant"</note> with a lump of gold in his hand and dressed in a royal robe, even though he does not own a foot of land? Although he has the form, the appearance, and the attire of a king or nobleman on the stage, he is nonetheless an heir to nothing. So it is with the wicked: though they are costly dressed and live luxuriously every day, lacking nothing and enjoying more than their heart can wish; they are only the possessors, but you, the godly, are the heirs. The ox that must work lives longer than the ox that walks in fat pastures, for being there hastens its slaughter. When God places the wicked in fat pastures, He hastens their downfall.

3. Remember that another man's prosperity does not result in your harm or disadvantage; therefore, do not envy their prosperity. Even if a wicked man had much, because of his abundance you do not have any less; your portion is not smaller because another's is larger. The fruitfulness of Leah was no cause for Rachel's infertility, yet she envied her. Why do you envy the wicked because they become rich? It is indeed foolishness, since their prosperity is not harmful to you.

4. Consider that in this life you have a prosperity which the wicked do not have, and in the life to come you shall have a prosperity which the wicked shall not have.

There are two parts to this observation, the first is this:

1. That in this life you have a prosperity which the wicked do not have. 3 John verse 2: *Beloved, I wish above all things that you may prosper and be in health, even as your soul prospers.* Even if your body does not prosper, but is sick; even if your status is not prosperous, but you fall short, so that the work of your hands cannot satisfy your belly nor clothe you; even then your soul can prosper. According to the words of the Psalmist, your soul may flourish like green herbs. Psalm 92:14: *Those that be planted in the house of the Lord shall be given to grow in the courts of our God. Verse 15: They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing.* The grace of the Spirit may increase in you, even if things do not go well for you according to the world. Although the wicked are prosperous in the body, they are not prosperous in the soul: they increase in luxury and goods, but not in grace. It is a remarkable text in Psalm 106:15: *And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul.* The quails were a delicious food which satisfied their bodies, but their souls [failed] <note>The OCR "<unclear>stof</unclear>" likely refers to the soul being diminished</note>; their souls progressed in nothing, their grace did not increase, and their souls perished from hunger. Even if your status does not increase, as long as your graces grow, this must comfort you and free you from all unrest in the inner man.

2. In the coming life, you shall enjoy a prosperity that no wicked person shall have; this observation must take away all unrest. Thus the Psalmist does in Psalm 17:14-15. David speaks of the men who have their portion in this life, they have children enough, and money enough for all their children, to leave their surplus behind:

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

Let us consider: what does David do now to prevent the vexation and unrest of his soul? Note the following words: *But I shall behold your face in righteousness,* etc. <note>Psalm 17:15</note> His meaning is: I see them prospering here; they have many children and enough for all of them; but as for me, this satisfies me—that I shall behold Your countenance. That is to say, when my body shall be raised in the Resurrection, then I shall enter Heaven, and this satisfies me. This thought set David’s soul at rest.

5. Consider that prosperity makes the wicked worse, and adversity makes the godly better; here, too, are two parts.

1. Prosperity makes the wicked worse. God exalted Pharaoh to a high station; it was to make him worse; all of Pharaoh's luxury served only to harden his heart further. Proverbs 1:32: *The prosperity of fools shall destroy them.* Hosea 13:6: *When they were fed in their pasture, they became full; once they were full, their heart was exalted; therefore they have forgotten me.* Prosperity makes the wicked worse; it is a spur to arrogance, an ignition for his temper, and a rejection of God's gifts of grace.

2. But adversity makes the godly better; it peels him away from the world and makes him look toward Heaven; it makes sin bitter to him; it causes him to spend more time in godliness. It makes the good better; as Themistocles <note>An Athenian politician and general (c. 524–459 BC)</note> said of himself, *I would have been lost, if I had not perished.* <note>Original Latin sentiment: "periissem nisi periissem" — meaning his downfall was actually his salvation.</note> Many godly people may say the same: if such a misfortune had not befallen me, I would have been drowned in the world. O Beloved! This observation will greatly take away your unrest: prosperity makes the wicked worse, and adversity makes the godly better.

6. Remember that the wicked do not always have contentment and comfort in their abundance and prosperity in this world; though the wicked are prosperous and overflowing with wealth, they nevertheless have a mingled dissatisfaction, vexation, and insatiability alongside their abundance. Would you envy a man who has a silver staff, but a diseased leg? Alas! Beloved, a wicked man may be clothed in silver, but you do not know what pain stings beneath that silver garment. It may be that a leather jerkin and a simple garment hold more inward contentment of soul for one who earns only 12 stivers <note>A small Dutch coin</note> a day, than for one who earns 100. I have sometimes seen those who wore fine shoes, but they confessed that the shoes pinched them. Beloved, the wicked may be dressed more finely than others and have more in the world than others, but God may distress them with a restless conscience, knowing they obtained their status through oppression and unjust gain. Would you then envy a wicked man? If the godly knew the vexation and the horror of conscience which accompanies the abundance of the wicked, they would in no way desire their abundance; they would rather die as beggars than live as rich men. We read of Haman in Esther 5:13: *Yet all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the King’s gate.* He was the King’s favorite; he had more influence with Ahasuerus than the entire Court; yet a trifle <note>original: beufelinge</note> consumed all of Haman’s comfort and contentment, and made him lie on his bed in sorrow, so that

<column-break/>

he would not be comforted because he could not obtain a bow of the knee from Mordecai. What a small thing makes the wicked dissatisfied! We read of Ahab: he had the best kingdom in the world, the Kingdom of Israel, yet he could not satisfy himself because he did not have Naboth’s vineyard; therefore he was sick. There is a notable passage in Ecclesiastes 5:9-12: *He who loves money shall not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves abundance with increase: this is also vanity. When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what profit is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes? The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep. There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their own hurt.* Also true is the saying of Christ in Luke 12:15: *Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consists not in the abundance of the things which he possesses.* You may have abundance, but the comfort of your life does not consist in your abundance. The godly have more comfort, inward peace, and contentment with a little morsel <note>original: klepuken</note> than the wicked with all their abundance. See Psalm 37:16 and Proverbs 15:16. There can be great treasures and great troubles; there can be little of the world and yet great peace within it. Therefore, do not be troubled because the wicked are prosperous in the world.

### ->I shall now give you a word of application.<-

<margin>Use.</margin>
Since it is so, the People of God must rebuke their own hearts and use reasoning against the unrest of the soul caused by the prosperity of the wicked. From this then flows:

1. Do not wonder so much at the prosperity of the wicked in this world; do not think that prosperity is such a happy state. It is not worthy of being envied; it ought not to give a single disturbed thought to a good man’s mind. The wonder that someone feels over a natural matter should not trouble another person just because they do not have it as well.

2. If I then must not be troubled because the wicked are prosperous, I conclude from this that I must not envy or be troubled over the gifts of grace given to the godly. If I must not envy the wicked’s increase in wealth, then I must also not envy the godly’s increase in goodness. It is the greatest wickedness in the world to envy another man’s graces; it is a devilish sin; it makes a man into a devil—it makes him a fleshly devil. Because another’s gifts surpass yours—that another preaches better than you—will you envy him for that? Augustine calls this a devilish sin in his commentary on Psalm 139 <note>original: over Psalm 139</note>, because it is essentially the sin of the Devil in Hell. The Devil, out of pure spite and envy, begrudges the good of Mankind. Beloved, many are of this humor, that they envy and are troubled over another man’s good; this is the Devil’s sin. Just as the Philistines envied the good of God’s people, as they did in Genesis 26:15: *And all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth.* It is a strange

the Philistines behave by doing themselves harm, provided that the children of God should enjoy no advantage: What did they do? They stopped up all the wells, and hindered themselves from enjoying the benefit of the water, so that God's People should have no water. Why do the wicked act thus? They envy another's enjoyment of good; they envy God's People not only their luxury, but even their grace: Cain envied Abel, because his Brother's works were righteous, and his own were wicked.

3. If it is so, that we must rebuke all envying and unrest over the prosperity of the wicked, then I conclude from this that it is just in God’s eyes to let the wicked envy the prosperity of the Pious, since the Pious often envy the prosperity of the wicked. David envied Saul's prosperity, and God, to repay David's sin, allowed Saul to envy David; Why does Saul pursue David like a partridge over the mountains? O Beloved! God pays us with our own coin; Isaac envied the prosperity of the Philistines, and God allowed the Philistines to envy Isaac; they stopped the wells and would give him no water; the cause was only envy, for they said: "you are stronger than we, and have more goods than we," and therefore they refused him water. This is then just for God to allow: that the wicked envy the prosperity of the Pious, because the Pious sometimes sin by envying the prosperity of the wicked.

4. If it is so that we must not be disturbed by the prosperity of the wicked, then I draw from this that prosperity is no sign of a good cause, or of good people; I must not envy them. One reads in the 73rd Psalm that the wicked are prosperous; that their houses are free from fear; that they do not fall into hardship like other Men; nonetheless, neither they nor their cause are good. Truly it is a great vanity when a man takes Success and prosperity as an infallible sign of a good cause. Why do we condemn the Papists <note>A historical term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics.</note> if we think that prosperity is a sign of a good cause and of good people? We would then have to agree with the Papists and set prosperity as a mark of the visible Church. Beloved, some have become like Papists; they make prosperity a sign of the true Church; and many among us make it a sign that God approves of what they do, because they have prosperity. All our Divines <term>Godts-geleerde: theologians or scholars of divinity</term> have written against the Papists on this point, and say that adversity and persecution are more likely signs of God’s Church than prosperity.

->### IX. SERMON.<-
->Psalm 42: 12.<-

>Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, he is the ... salvation of my countenance and my God.

<margin>2. Use.</margin>
I come now to the second application: an exhortation to move you all to rebuke your heart because it is disturbed by the outward prosperity of the wicked; and so that I might prevail upon you in this, I shall give you these three considerations. I. Note to

<column-break/>

what ends God allows the prosperity of the wicked in this world. II. Consider the ends that the wicked have in their prosperity in this world. III. Note the ends why God does not want the Pious to be disturbed and restless over the prosperity of the wicked; and what the ends are why God does not allow His People to be so prosperous in the world. If these three considerations are thoughtfully weighed by God’s People, they would take away all murmuring, troubles, and disturbance of the hearts of God’s People when beholding the prosperity of the wicked in this world.

1. If you wish to soften the disturbance of the mind over the prosperity of the wicked, only observe the ends why God lets them be prosperous in the world: There are six ends which God has in view here, all of which serve to soften and still the disturbance of the minds of God's children over the prosperity of the wicked.

1. God allows the wicked to be prosperous in this world so that they might have more opportunity to commit sin and wickedness: whereas otherwise, if they were in a poor and despised state, they would not have such great opportunity to bring forth the sins and wickedness which are in their hearts. If these Vineyards of Sodom and these fruits of Gomorrah were never warmed by the Sun of prosperity, we would not see these sour grapes and clusters of bitterness that are within them. It pleases God then, for ends best known to Him, to multiply the prosperity of the wicked to bring forth the sin and also the malice that lies hidden in their hearts, and thus to make it openly seen. Do we not have a clear proof of this in Hazael <note>A courtier of Syria who murdered his king to take the throne (2 Kings 8).</note>, when he was in power and prosperity? That was a fitting opportunity to discover and bring to light that wickedness which lay hidden in his heart. The Prophet said to him <margin>2 Kings 8:12</margin> *You will set their strongholds on fire, and kill their young men with the sword, and dash their children in pieces, and rip up their women with child.* But what did Hazael answer? verse 13. *But what is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?* and Elisha said: "The Lord has shown me that you shall be King over Syria." And so you shall do this; he was not able to do all that villainy as long as he was in a poor and lowly state; but when the world was favorable to him, and he had prosperity, and became great in power in the world, then there was a great opportunity to bring this wickedness to light. Just as we also see in our days: if there were not such great unrestrained freedom and a common excuse among us, we would not have the heart for such wickedness; and the wicked would lack the opportunity to commit such wickedness as is now known to the world; and God’s People profit by this, for through these things they see what sticks in the heart of Man. <margin>Daniel 8:24, 25</margin> It is said of Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Greek king of the Seleucid Empire known for persecuting the Jews.</note>: *His power shall be mighty... and he shall destroy wonderfully, and shall prosper, and practice: and shall destroy the mighty and the holy people. And through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand; and he shall magnify himself in his heart...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding why the Pious should not be troubled by the prosperity of the wicked. It provides five specific reasons for this divine arrangement, drawing on biblical examples and metaphors.</meta>

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

...en: and in quiet rest he shall die there many, etc. If this man had not been a King, nor great in power or prosperity, then the wickedness of his heart would not have been uncovered; but through his prosperity, he had the opportunity to bring forth the malice of his heart and make it known to the world. In **Job 12:6**, mention is made of the tents of robbers who have rest: God allows them to be prosperous so that they may see the malice that sticks in their evil heart. Just as a downpour falling on the earth brings to light the reeds that otherwise would not be seen. The Serpent, in the fable, when it was frozen, could not sting; but when it was warmed in the bosom, then it could sting. The meaning is: when men are in a poor and lowly state, they can do no harm because they have no power; but when they are warmed by the prosperity of the world, then they damage and offend.

2. God lets the wicked be prosperous so that their mouths might be stopped, and they should have nothing to say when God goes against them in Judgment; when God shall say to them: "I gave you benefits, and you did not observe your duty toward me; I gave you prosperity, but you gave me no glory for it." And God will say, "Such a one, who had no riches, no prosperity in the world like you had, nevertheless observed his duty and gave me more glory than you ever did. I have been beneficial toward you, but you have not been humble before me; you have had much from me, but give me little in return." This prosperity will then be an argument to stop their mouths, so that they shall not know a single word to say against it.

3. God lets the wicked be prosperous to this end: so that He might see whether His People will love God for His own sake, and love Christ for His own sake; whether they can love a <term>naked God</term> <note>meaning God Himself, stripped of any worldly rewards or material blessings</note>, a naked Christ, and a naked truth. For their own sake, God tests His People to see if they will love holiness, grace, and the ways of God just as well when they are paved with thorns as when they are strewn with roses; and to see if His People will love Religion when Religion is persecuted; and whether they shall love holiness and a precise walk when it is mocked and the confessors of the same are despised; and whether they shall love Religion more when it has no power nor prosperity, than sin and the way of vanity with prosperity, advantage, and pleasure. And this is one end why He tests His own servants by letting the men of this world be prosperous: to see if they shall love God for His own sake.

4. So that thereby the downfall of the wicked might be hastened and made heavier; what is the purpose of putting an Ox in a fat pasture, other than to fatten him against the time of slaughter? So God also places the wicked in fat pastures of prosperity and riches in this world, to fatten them against the slaughter-time, and to make them a sweeter meal—not only for the worms in the Grave, but for the Devils in Hell. God lets the wicked be prosperous, and have the world according to their will, yet it is to bring them the sooner to the place of darkness. **Psalm 92**: When the wicked spring up as grass, and the workers of

<column-break/>

iniquity flourish, it happens so that they may be destroyed forever.

5. So that the prosperity of the wicked might be a shield and protection for His own People. What was the reason that **Cyrus**, a wicked man <note>Cyrus the Great, King of Persia, though a pagan, was used by God to end the Babylonian captivity</note>, should increase so much in strength and power, and that he should disturb the Chaldeans and Babylonians? He was a heathen, and God used him for the preservation of His People; by Cyrus's hand, the Jews were delivered from imprisonment. One might ask, why was Egypt such a grain-rich place in the seven years of famine, when all the nations around her had hunger? God's purpose was so that they might have provisions to maintain His People, **Jacob** and his sons. The Land of **Canaan** was never so fruitful as in that year when the Jews inherited it. What was the reason? God did not love the **Canaanites**; but they built houses, and God's People came to inhabit them; they planted vineyards, and God's People ate the fruit thereof; it was for their sake that God allowed them such things. God loved neither **Pharaoh** nor the Canaanites; but God loved His People, and for their sake He did all this; He let them be prosperous and become great in the world, so that His People might enjoy the lands of their possession.

You shall find that there are three texts that make this very clear. The first is **Proverbs 14:22** <note>In most English Bibles, this is Proverbs 13:22</note>: *The wealth of the sinner is laid up for the righteous.* The wicked may sell their gains to the Devil <note>original: "Huyvel", likely a variant or typo for "Duivel" (Devil)</note> and throw their souls into it, and all this to obtain some luxury in the world; and God may allow him to be prosperous in his ways and to obtain riches through sinful means; but what then? The end is: it is laid up for the righteous. God often directs it so that what the wicked obtain, the Godly enjoy. So you also read in **Job 27:16, 17**: *Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare raiment as the clay; He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver.* This is the portion of the wicked: to heap up silver like dust and prepare clothing like clay; but the righteous shall divide it, and the innocent shall put it on. God will not let the Godly be tempted so far that they would have to win the world <note>meaning through sin</note>, but He lets that temptation come upon the wicked; but when they have done so, then His People shall have the enjoyment. The third and last to this end is **Proverbs 28:8**: *He that by usury and unjust gain increaseth his substance, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor.* 

Therefore we see how many men go to Hell to obtain riches, and then they leave them for the Godly and the criminal. Shall this then disturb a Godly person? It may be that you see the wicked obtain riches; but he runs the peril of losing his soul to get them, and you enjoy the benefit after him. A child who sees his Father’s shepherd having many sheep—will that child envy him? He only keeps them until his Father dies; likewise, the rich obtain the world and run the peril of their souls, and they do not know who shall enjoy what they have obtained; for the Godly have a right to that which God lets the wicked enjoy. I do not say that they have a civil right...

# Of a Contrite Soul.

have a right; for they have only a spiritual right to that, and to the whole world; for the whole world is given to you for your best; and although the **wicked** are permitted to be prosperous in this world, do not be troubled by it.

6. God does such things for the **spiritual welfare** of His People; when God's People see that the wicked are prosperous in the world, and that they themselves are not prosperous in the world, this gives them occasion to live the *life of faith*: If God showed signs of displeasure to everyone who angered Him, and signs of favor to everyone who pleased Him, then we would live by *sight* and not by *faith*; but now, at the time when they see that they are persecuted, and holiness is mocked, and the **professors** <note>Those who publicly declare or "profess" their religious faith.</note> of the same live lowly in this world, and they see the wicked flourish and grow in the prosperity of the world, and that they are not plagued like other men, but live in all the delights of the world, and have more than the heart can wish; this then gives God's people occasion to live by faith.

7. God lets the wicked be prosperous in the world for this end: so that, living in such power and prosperity, they might be ordained by God to do God some **service** in this world: Thus you read that **Jehu** did God some service in the world while he lived in prosperity; and God repaid him for it, for he and his descendants would hold the Kingdom for four generations: and for his temporary service, God gave him a temporary reward.

II. Just as you have noted the ends of God in permitting the wicked to be prosperous, so you must also consider the ends of the wicked living in prosperity; and by the observation thereof, you shall not be disturbed by their prosperity: and this appears in these points.

1. If you consider that outward prosperity is the **entire portion** that God has allotted to the wicked; they have no other part, nor shall they ever have another happiness than in this world: therefore, do not envy their prosperity. **Job 9:24**. *The earth is given into the hand of the wicked.* A wicked man enjoys the Earth, but he enjoys no more; this is his whole Heaven, his whole salvation, his whole portion, his whole comfort; he shall have no Heaven to reward and receive him, no God, nor Christ, to smile upon him, no grace which is crowned with glory; nothing is given to him but only prosperity in this world. Just as **David** prays in **Psalm 17:14** to be delivered from *men of the world, whose portion is in this life, whose belly You fill with Your hidden treasure.* God gives them their treasure in the world; God gives them no treasures of Heaven; they shall never see His face, they shall never enjoy the light of His countenance; no communion with the Father and Son, no joy nor comfort of the Holy Spirit; no true peace of conscience; never shall they have any part among those sanctified through faith in Christ: they have the Earth in their hand, but nothing of Heaven in their heart. They exercise dominion in the world, where they are slaves of the world; they rule others, where they are slaves under the will of Satan: these men have the treasures of the world, the portion

<column-break/>

of slaves; but they shall never have the inheritance of the Sons: Therefore do not envy them.

2. Do not envy their prosperity for this reason: because the **curse of God** is in all their possessions. **Prov. 3:31**. *Do not be envious of a man of violence: and choose none of his ways:* The reason is in verse 33: *The curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked.* So also **Job 5:3**. *I have seen a fool taking root: but suddenly I cursed his dwelling.* God's curse goes with the prosperity of the wicked: do not then envy that which God curses: even if they have good things from God, they nevertheless do not have a single good thought from God; they have nothing from Him but curse and wrath.

III. The **ends of God** with the Pious, why He withholds prosperity from them, are:

1. So that God might give His People **better things** than the outward prosperity of this world; He gives good things to the evil, but better things—spiritual and Heavenly riches—to the Pious: He refuses harmful things to His People, but He grants them good things; God keeps them empty of the world so that He may fill their hearts with grace and with Jesus Christ; God lets you enjoy little of the world so that He may give you more of Himself. God did not want to give **Moses** the land of Canaan, a temporary good, but He gave him Heaven, a spiritual and eternal good: likewise, God refuses you outward prosperity to give you inward grace, to have an inheritance among the sanctified through faith in Christ; this He wants to give you, but refuses you the outward inheritance in this world: He clothes you poorly with the world, so that He may clothe you richly with the righteousness of His Son: He has a **Benjamin's portion** <note>A reference to Genesis 43:34, meaning a significantly larger or specially favored share.</note>, a rich portion for His Children; a portion that lies not in dusty rubbish, but in the spiritual blessings in Heaven; God does not want to fill your House with rags, but He wants to fill your heart with Himself: He gives you little in this world so that He may give you the forgiveness of sins, the Love of Christ, Heaven and glory, and everything that serves to make you eternally happy in Heaven.

2. God refuses His People prosperity in this world because He sees that they can hardly use prosperity well. **David** was exceedingly good when he was in a lowly state and under persecution, but when David obtained the Throne, and became great, rich, and powerful, then he heaped one sin upon another. Likewise **Solomon**, what an abundance of sin did he heap up, not being able to use prosperity well; his luxury did him more harm than his wisdom did him good. If God gives you prosperity in the world, it is a hundred to one if you use it well: if God gives you full sails of prosperity and fills you with the world, it would overturn your small vessel. Therefore God refuses you that which He allows the wicked to have to their own destruction. Prosperity in the world destroys more than troubles, bonds, and persecution do; more are killed by prosperity in their chamber than by the sword in the field: So it is then a mercy from God to refuse His People that which is harmful to them.

# Gilead’s Balm, or the Healing

1. To justify those people who are prosperous in evil ways.
2. To condemn those who are not prosperous in this world while on good ways.

1. Do not condemn those who have no prosperity in a good path: it can happen that the Church of God, which has God, Christ, the truth, and everything on its side, nonetheless has no Victory; for if you were to condemn someone for this, you might for the same reason condemn Christ and the ancient Church; and for the same reason, you would justify the **Turk** <note>Historically used to refer to the Ottoman Empire or Muslims in general.</note> and the **Pope** and damn Christ, if you based your judgment on victory and the winning party; for the enemies have often overwhelmed the Church. Judge not by prosperity, and so that you might free yourself from unjust judgment, this observation arose. It is a borrowed way of speaking, taken from Trees, the one applied to Christ, the other to **Nebuchadnezzar** the King of Babylon, Daniel 4:22. From verse 4 to 12 mention is made of the vision where the King saw a Tree in the midst of the Earth, and its height was great, verse 10. The Tree became great and strong, and its height reached to Heaven, and it was seen to the end of all the Earth, verse 11. Its leaves were fair, and its fruits many, and there was food in it for all; under it the beasts of the field found shadow, and the birds of the Heavens dwelt in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it, verse 12. This must be understood as Nebuchadnezzar and his Kingdom, which spreads itself over the whole Earth. Of Christ, it is spoken in Isaiah 53:2, 3. He grew up before his face like a tender plant, and like a root out of a dry ground: He had no form nor glory, etc. This is the testimony of this Tree, by which Christ was meant; and in this Tree there is no form that we should desire Him: This Tree was not to be compared to the Kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar in power, greatness, and wealth in this world, and yet Christ had to be a despised plant. Likewise, when you see the people of the world prosperous in this world, do not then condemn the lowly plants in this world, for you would be damning Christ, the Church of God, and the generation of the righteous.

2. And do not justify the **wicked**, even if they are prosperous in the world: you must not therefore judge their cause to be good because they have prosperity. The **Papists** <note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics.</note> set their prosperity as a proof of the truth of their Church, and that they are on the right path. Many hold this for a constant sign, and are ready at every opportunity to justify evil deeds with this saying: "Do you not see that they have prosperity?" And all violations of the covenant, and all ungodliness and sinful deeds, they are ready to justify because they have prosperity, and no one lifts a hand against them, and they have everything going for them. This is as bad a matter as that of the Papists; they set prosperity as a proof of the goodness of their cause, and of the truth of their Church. When **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse, a Greek tyrant famous in moral literature for his sacrilege and subsequent claims that the gods favored him because of his success.</note> had robbed the Church, and taken away everything they had, he could then say, to justify his deed, "See how favorable the Gods are to me." He made his prosperity a proof to

<column-break/>

justify his church-robbery. When men have the full sails of worldly prosperity, and they are successful in an evil way, and no one disturbs them, and all is well with them, and they have the world at their will, then they can laugh in their sleeves and think that the God of Heaven justifies them in all their doing. They have the weapons and the power of the world on their side; but we have the truth and God on our side; and although the Church and the People of God now lie in the dust, and are trodden under the feet of the wicked, yet the time shall come that the Church and the People of God shall have the upper hand: Therefore, do not justify the wicked in an evil way.

3. Labor to be abundant in grace, just as you are abundant in blessing. We read of an Altar that **Moses** made, and we also read of an Altar that **Solomon** made, which was four times larger than that of Moses, because Solomon had more wealth and peace than Moses: Moses’ Altar was made in the Wilderness, Solomon’s in the Land of Canaan. I shall apply this: You, to whom God grants much wealth and causes to be prosperous in this world, whose state is four times greater than others; God also requires four times more service from you, as He does well by you more than others. You, whose state is great, and who enjoy your annual income without hardship or labor, God expects of you that you shall devote yourself to His glorification, to honor Him according to what He requires of you, more than He expects from laborers; although they too must serve God in practicing those duties which God demands of them; they must carve out so much time from their calling to serve their God; they must deprive their belly to practice their divine services. This is a good exchange, to deprive one’s body to preserve one’s Soul. It was said of the **Athenians**, [they had] the best land and the best Laws, <note>original: "Frumentis uterentur, legibus nequàquàm."</note> *they use their grain, but by no means their laws.* Take care then, that your abundance does not make you forget your duties.

4. Do not wonder at the prosperity of the wicked.
<margin>Augustine, Epistle 70: <note>original: "Hec bona ne putentur mala, dantur bonis, & ne putentur summa bona, dantur & malis."</note> These goods, so they are not thought to be evil, are given to the good; and so they are not thought to be the highest goods, they are also given to the evil.</margin>
**Augustine** says: So that worldly goods are not considered evil, they are given to the good; on the other hand, so that they are not held as the highest good, they are also given to the evil. If there is a thing that is better than others, the worst men shall never have it. Grace is the best good of the world, therefore the best people shall have it. Now the wealth of the world is the lowest kind of wealth, and therefore the wicked shall be prosperous in it. Prosperity is not the highest good, since God commonly denies the same to His beloved children, and He grants it to the worst. If He then denies it to His children, and grants it to slaves, it is proof that it is not the best good. So much for the first part, why God’s People are easily cast down.

I come now to the second point / for which God’s People are dismayed / namely over the miserable state of the Church, and the People of God in this world. Although some would make us believe that the state of the Church was never more glorious than in these days; nevertheless, whatever they say / he / who looks into the matter rightly / and diligently examines the state of the Church / shall easily see and notice that the state of the Church is very low / and that the glory and the appearance of the Church was never more destroyed than now / and we may well say / where is now our glory? and we see the glory as if standing on the threshold / and ready to take its wings and fly away like a Bird; and our eyes shall yet see it / if God does not prevent it; for do we not see a Cloud of troubles and sad visitations hanging over our heads / ready to fall upon us in these regions of the world / and they shall also surely fall upon us / if God does not hold them back? So I do not wish to recommend to them a Stoic insensitivity and a foolish bluntness concerning the miseries of the Church; just as you must not be like the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that taught indifference to pain or misfortune; here the author warns against being cold-hearted.</note> / not at all being moved over the hardships of the Church / having no compassion with your Brothers' misery: you must not be an indifferent Gallio <note>A biblical figure from Acts 18:17, used here as a name for someone who cares nothing for religious struggles.</note>, not being dismayed or touched by the troubles of the Church: but I want you to be grieved and concerned with the troubles of the Church, yet with moderation in a holy feeling and humbling of the heart over the troubles of the Church.

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

->Daniel 8:27. *Then I, Daniel, became weak, and was sick for some days.*<- What was the cause that this good Prophet was weak and sick for several days? It was the dismay of his soul because he foresaw through his prophetic spirit the troubles that would come upon God’s People; that the Church would suffer much under the reign of Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Hellenistic king who persecuted the Jews in the 2nd century BCE.</note>, and for this reason, he was sick for some days: which hardship did not strike the Church of God until many years after his death, as seen in verse 14. Nevertheless, this hardship made him weak and sick; and thus you have proof of godly men who have been dismayed over the hardships of God’s Church even before they arrived.

2. There is also proof of godly men who were dismayed over the hardships of the Church when they were actually upon them; when they saw **gray signs of decay** <note>original: "grauwe happen," likely a metaphor for signs of aging or impending ruin like gray hairs.</note> upon the head of the Church, and hardship and commotion overwhelming her: this troubled their spirit. One reads in 2 Samuel 1:11, 12: When David heard that the Philistines had fought against and conquered the People of God, then David took hold of his clothes and tore them; and likewise all the men who were with him. And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening: for Saul, and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. So you also have to this end a complete proof in Nehemiah 1:2, 3, 4. When the mournful condition of God’s People was told to him, then that good Nehemiah wept. Here you see then how the godly have been struck with sorrow when they heard that hardship had come upon the Church and the People of God.

Thirdly, I shall show you the distinction between a proper compassion for the troubles of the Church, and a sinful unrest over the hardships of the Church; the one is our required duty, the other is sin.

1. A proper compassion for the Church in troubles makes prayer lively for the good of the Church; you read of the Psalmist when the People of God were in great dismay that he was sorrowful, yet his sorrow drove him to the Throne of Grace to pray for them, Psalm 137:1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Although the suffering of the Church makes you sorrowful in spirit, it must not make you dead in prayer. Those who are compassionate toward God’s Church in her oppression also have prayers in their heart for her when she is in trouble, so that it might be taken away. On the contrary, those who are too greatly sorrowful over the troubles of the Church will complain to men and make their sorrow known to them; but their sorrow makes their heart unfit to go to God with prayer and supplication so that the hardship might be removed. These who are so pressed down with sorrow, complaining to men and not to God, it is proof that their sorrow is disorderly and sinful, whereas well-ordered sorrow makes the soul go to God with prayer, so that the hardship and troubles might be turned away from the Church.

2. These men who mourn moderately over the hardships of the Church still retain some good hope for the restoration of the Church. Therefore you read in Lamentations <note>original: "Thren." for Threnoi, the Greek/Latin title for Lamentations.</note> 3:31, 32, 33: *The Lord will not cast off forever: but though he cause grief, yet*

<column-break/>

*will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he does not afflict nor grieve the children of men from his heart.* <note>The author interprets "from his heart" as "willingly" or "by his own desire."</note> Here you see that although the Church was in great oppression, they had compassion for her and mourned over her; nonetheless, they had hope in God in all of this; they could see and notice that God’s heart was toward them, even though his hand seemed to be against them: he did not grieve them from his heart. As if they said: God does not visit us by his will, but it is for the sake of sin, which he hates in his own People, and he is as if bound to scourge his children; it is not his custom, but a "strange work"; it comes not from the heart, but from the hand. Therefore they can still hope for deliverance out of troubles while in sorrow. But sinful dismay cuts off all hope: just as you may read in 2 Kings <note>original: "2. Reg." for 2 Regum.</note> 7:1, 18, 19. Elisha said to the people, when there was famine in Samaria and he told them of the great hardship that would come upon them, and thereafter he said: *Tomorrow about this time shall two measures of barley be sold for a shekel, and a measure of fine flour for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.* Here he spoke of great abundance: but a captain had answered the Man of God and said, *Behold, if the Lord should make windows in heaven, might such a thing be?* and he had said, *behold, you shall see it with your eyes, but shall not eat thereof.* Many people are just as this man was, so cast down with too great a sorrow over the suffering of the Church; when the Church of God is low, and its enemies powerful, then they easily think that she is so small and her wounds so great, and her enemies so strong, that it is impossible for her to be restored. Lamentations 3:18, 19: *Then I said, my strength is perished, and my hope from the Lord. Remembering my misery and my wandering, the wormwood and the gall.* When their sorrow and suffering lasted long in Babylon, and they saw no prospect of deliverance, no visible means of their restoration and deliverance from captivity, then they were overloaded with sorrow; they said "our hope is perished from the Lord." Ezekiel 37:11: When they were like dry bones in the valley, and they thought it was impossible that dry bones should have flesh and that sinews should be brought upon them: they thought they were entirely lost, and that they would never be delivered from their hardships: and this stirred up bitter weeping in their spirit.

3. Moderate sorrow stirs up holy contemplations, so that according to your opportunity and calling you promote the deliverance of the Church: such as you read in Jeremiah 51:50: *You who have escaped the sword, go away, stand not still: remember the Lord from afar, and let Jerusalem come into your mind.* As if the Prophet said: Jerusalem is in trouble and under great and sad visitation—do what you can for her! Do not stand still, but exert all your strength in every opportunity for her preservation. On the contrary, when a man is seized with a sinful sorrow, he will not exert his strength for the People of God who sit in trouble, but he sits down and says: I will do nothing for Religion, nor for the cause of God; and he thinks that he has already done too much, and he regrets everything he has done; this is a sinful

4. These, who mourn so moderately, are more distressed over the troubles of the Church and the difficulty of the People of God than over their own difficulty: David’s difficulty in his own person was but as a thorn in his flesh; but the troubles and suffering of the Church were like a sword in his bones <margin>Psalm 42:11.</margin> Psalm 42:11. *As with a sword in my bones, my adversaries reproach me; while they say unto me all the day long, where is your God?* You also read the same of Elijah, 1 Kings 19, verse 14. *It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.* v. 10. *I have been very jealous for the Lord God of hosts, for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant,* etc. Here you see how this good man mourned over God’s Church: *they have slain your prophets with the sword,* etc. This disturbed him and dismayed his spirit. But immoderate grief is more concerned with a private cross, sorrow, and loss: the loss of status and position, or some personal visitation in your body, dismays them more than the great troubles in which the Church finds itself. This is a sinful grief. To remove this immoderate grief, then, so that you should not sin in mourning over the difficulties of the Church of God, I shall give you these five observations, which is the fourth point I proposed as helpful means against despondency.

<margin>Five observations to take away sinful grief over the misery of the Church.</margin>
I. First, do not be immoderately distressed over the difficulties of God’s Church, because the Church increases in number through troubles and persecutions. The blood of the Saints shed in persecution is the seed of the Church, and from that very seed many grow. Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage, who was martyred during the Roman persecutions.</note> is read as a martyr, and many were converted through his martyrdom, as much by his suffering as by his preaching. The persecutors, by throwing someone into prison, and killing someone, and through banishment, think thereby to root out the rest, both the believers and the Religion; but God, by His Almighty hand, directs it so that such is a means to cause the multitude of God's People to increase. If a child sees a man cutting off some branches of the trees, he thinks that the man wants to ruin that tree: but it is not so, for by the pruning of the trees, they grow the better. The wicked may thus cut down a tree here and there, and prune the branches; but God ensures by these means that the Church grows more in number, and better than she did before; just as it was with the Church of the Jews: they went down into Egypt in a small number; but their slavery and imprisonment made them increase more in number in Egypt than even in their own land. Exodus 1:7. *And the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty; so that the land was filled with them.* Do you wish to know the number of those who came into Egypt? They were 70 souls; but 600,000 men came out of Egypt. How the goodness of

<column-break/>

God manifests itself through His providence for the good and preservation of His People! So much so that even persecution turns out for their best to cause them to increase and grow. To the Jews, the land of Canaan was given; yet through their sins they were dragged captive to Babylon. In 2 Kings 24:16, you read of 7,000 who were carried away captive: and in the kingdom of Zedekiah there were 4,600, and in total there were not even 12,000; all these were brought captive to Babylon. One would think that in their captivity they would not increase but decrease: but it was so directed by God’s Almighty power that they increased greatly, fourfold more in number, and they came out of captivity 42,360. Thus they increased in seventy years. This is the great foresight of the Lord, making it so that the People of God increase in persecution. Not only in former times, but in these latter times, the persecutions have been so great and hot, that they thought not to leave the name of a Christian upon the Earth without persecution; but the more they persecuted, the more the People of God multiplied; so then, be not too much dismayed over this, since such serves for the growth of God’s People.

<margin>Wooden chalices, golden priests; now golden chalices and wooden priests. <note>original: "Lignei calices aurei sacerdotes; nunc aurei calices et lignei sacerdotes."</note></margin>
II. If the number of God’s People does not increase, then remember and be assured of this: that the gifts of grace of God’s People increase through persecution. The children of Israel were better in Egypt than in their own land; better in the wilderness than in the land of Canaan: as was also said of the Roman Church in former times, when she had wooden chalices, then she had golden Bishops; but now she has golden chalices, and wooden Bishops. Likewise, when the Church of God is in outward prosperity, when she experiences good times in the world, then she is very poor in grace, and very near to carelessness and slumbering in the way of God. Canticles 4:16. *Awake, O north wind; and come, you south wind; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out.* You know that the north and south winds are against each other, and these two opposites make the fruits of the garden grow: The north wind signifies affliction, and the south wind signifies prosperity. It is the north wind—the sharp persecutions and other visitations—that most causes the gifts of grace of the Church to grow. The Church of God grew better in grace under the pagan Emperors than under Constantine the Christian Emperor, because her tranquility caused her to fall into error and heresy: when their bodies were prosperous, then their souls were not prosperous. On the contrary, when they were under the pagan Emperors, under great and heavy persecution, although their bodies were in trouble, their gifts of grace nevertheless increased greatly. When Popery took the upper hand, and the People of God sat in great temptation, their grace nonetheless grew green and fresh: as Molin <note>Likely Pierre Du Moulin (1568–1658), a prominent Huguenot minister and author.</note> says; "when people were banished for reading the Bible, then we burned with fire to read the same; but now the Bibles are like old almanacs, which lie moldering in a corner, while the playing cards—the Devil’s catechisms—are worn out by constant use."

# Gilead's Balm, or the Healing

<margin>
The destruction of one church was the building up of many. <note>original: "Vnius ecclesie destructio multarum fuit ædificatio." From the Annals of Baronius or a similar ecclesiastical history.</note>
</margin>
While the Church of God is shaken in one place, the Lord God establishes and strengthens it in another. This must comfort you: the scattering of one church is the building up of many other churches. You may read on this subject in Acts 8:1, concerning the great troubles and persecution of the Church within Jerusalem, and how they were all scattered. Now, what fruit came through this persecution? Verse 4: *Therefore those who were scattered went everywhere preaching the word*, so that a church was also established in Samaria. In many places that had never heard the Gospel before, it was proclaimed because of the hot persecution within Jerusalem. The troubles and persecutions of God’s People in England by the Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials, likely referring to the Anglican hierarchy during the era of Puritan migration.</note> have been a great cause for the planting of the Gospel in other parts of the world, such as in New England and America, places which had never heard it before. The same congregations in Asia were scattered by Heathen persecution; but through their scattering, the Gospel was transplanted into Africa, and into Europe, and since then into America. So, when God allows the Congregation to be persecuted in one place, she nevertheless gains ground by moving to other places through these troubles; and although she is persecuted in one Kingdom, she is confirmed in another Kingdom through her transplanting.

IV. Consider that such infallible promises have been made to the Church of God regarding her perseverance, that she shall never be uprooted by any persecution, fury, or violence of the godless. She may be persecuted, but she cannot be destroyed; she may be ducked down, but she cannot be suppressed; she may be discouraged, but not despairing. The Church of God cannot be persecuted in such a way that she would be uprooted by the godless. Therefore you read what Christ said to Peter in Matthew 16:18: *You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church* (that is, upon Christ), *and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* All the violence of Hell and the cunning of the Devil cannot overcome the Church; much less shall the Earth and men, through persecution, overcome and uproot the Church, or push her off from the rock on which she is built. It is recounted that in the year 1620, when the war began in Germany <note>The start of the Thirty Years' War.</note>, a large stone fell upon a great copper statue of the Apostle Peter standing in St. Peter's Church in Rome. On the statue was a scroll with this writing: *You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and to you I will give the keys, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Tu es Petrus et super hanc petram ædificabo ecclesiam, & tibi dabo claves, &c."</note>. The stone broke the statue into pieces so that not one letter of the entire inscription remained unharmed, except for these words: *I will build my Church* <note>original Latin: "ædificabo Ecclesiam meam"</note>, which remained entirely undamaged. God has made no promise to any Kingdom, Nation, or Republic that they should remain forever; rather, they can and shall be destroyed. No one can say they are certain that their Monarchy will exist forever; but of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ, God says that despite the malice of the Devils in Hell, and the power and cunning of men on Earth, it shall stand, because God has promised that He will preserve His Church. *Upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* Therefore, do not be too greatly troubled.

<column-break/>

<margin>
For the works of God must not be judged before the fifth act. <note>original: "Nam est judicandum de operibus Dei ante quintum actum." A common theological metaphor comparing God's providence to a five-act play where the resolution only comes at the end.</note>
</margin>
V. Behold the end and the consequence of the Church's suffering. If we only looked at the beginning and not at the end of the oppression, then we might be dismayed by it; but look at the end of the suffering and what follows it, and tell me then if you need to be so greatly dismayed. When a Father or Mother strikes a child, it is to make that child better. Likewise, when we see God striking His Church with the rod of discipline, God's aim in this is not to destroy His People, but so that they might smell better, like spices <note>A common metaphor: spices release their scent when crushed.</note>. Therefore, do not be too disturbed by the difficulties of the Church. We must not judge the works of God until the very last. If we had read at the time of creation and seen nothing else but the wild and empty earth, and the darkness upon the Abyss, we would have seen no beauty in it; but what do you think now of the world and of Man after everything was perfected? What a glorious building it is! Likewise, when you look at the first beginnings of the troubles of the Church, you cannot judge her; but if you observe

<margin>
Jeremiah 31:18.
</margin>
the Church at the end of the persecution, when the troubles have ended, then you shall see her full of glory and beauty. The beginnings are sad for God's People because of the troubles of persecution, but the end is good.
"When the Martyrs went to their deaths, they
"said: we shall have a sad breakfast, but
"a joyful supper; for our outcome shall be
"good and our reward great; we go to Christ.
Just as Joseph said to his brothers in Genesis 50:20: *You thought evil against me, but God meant it for good.* So I may also say to the godless persecutors of God's Church: you think evil against her, but God thinks it for good. You think to persecute, destroy, and uproot the Church from under Heaven; but God intends to preserve and establish her on the Earth (notwithstanding your persecution) until the end of the world. The ends of God and the ends of the godless are different; they think to do evil, but God's ends are grace and mercy. The Physician draws blood from a man, and the leech also sucks blood from a man, yet their ends are different. The leech does it to satisfy itself, but the Physician does it to heal the man. So it is also between the ends of God and the godless in the persecution of the Church; God allows such things to purify her from sins, but the godless do it to destroy her and to carry out their malice against her. Therefore, do not be too greatly disturbed by the difficulties of God's Church.

### XI. SERMON.

->Psalm 42: 12.<-

> Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, he is... the help of my countenance, and my God.

Since it is so, that the Godly are troubled by the difficulties of God's Church, there are three sorts of people at whom I shall aim the arrow of my rebuke.
I. Here are those to be rebuked who are of an entirely different temperament, who do not take the difficulties of the Church to heart; they let Religion sink

or struggle; whether the **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelium"</note> stands or falls; whether the Church prospers or not, they care nothing for it. These people are a stain and a blemish upon the Church; they enjoy the Church's benefits yet are not troubled by its difficulties. It is noteworthy that when the Holy Spirit counts the tribes of **Israel** <margin>Revelation 7:4–9</margin> **Rev.** 7:4–9, He leaves out one tribe, namely the tribe of **Dan**. Theologians <term>Gods-geleerde: Scholars of divinity or theologians.</term> are very busy trying to find the reason why God’s Spirit omits this tribe. The best opinion regarding this omission is due to certain failings: first, because the tribe of **Dan** fell away from true worship and gave itself over to idolatry. <margin>Judges 18:30</margin> **Judg.** 18:30: *the children of Dan set up for themselves that carved image.* Secondly, because the tribe of **Dan** did not take the difficulties of God’s Church to heart; while the other tribes risked their lives in the field, the tribe of **Dan** remained in the ships <note>A reference to the Song of Deborah in Judges 5:17.</note>; they did not want to leave their dealings, trades, and commerce. Theologians give this as a reason why God brands that tribe and why the Spirit of God does not count them among the other tribes. It is deserving of punishment that when the difficulties of the Church increase, you then abandon the Church and refuse to help her, but instead remain constantly "aboard ship" in your business and commerce. God hates neutral people.

## II. 
A second sort who should be rebuked are those who, instead of being troubled when things go badly for the Church, then rejoice and are merry. Thus we read of **Haman**, that monster among men, **Esth.** 3:15. While **Esther**, **Mordecai**, the daughters of the city, and the **Jews** fasted, prayed, and wept for their lives in this danger to the Church, the King and **Haman** sat down to drink; they were glad and rejoiced while God’s Church was in great danger. Scripture here brands the King and **Haman** for sitting down to eat and drink while the city of **Susa** <note>The capital of the Persian Empire.</note> was in confusion. So you also read of those careless people <margin>Amos 6:7</margin> **Amos** 6:7: *Therefore they shall now go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed.*

## III. 
A third sort is so far from being troubled by the Church's difficulties that they are aggrieved <note>The original "bezoekt" here implies a sense of being plagued or troubled by the Church's survival.</note> that it does not go worse for the Church and Religion; there are many such people nowadays. <margin>Psalm 37:12</margin> **Ps.** 37:12: *The wicked plotteth against the just, and gnasheth upon him with his teeth.* The gnashing of teeth is a sign of bloodthirstiness; because they cannot have their way through their plots, they gnash their teeth and grumble against good ministers; they are upset that it is not worse for godliness and religion. This is a torment of the spirit to them. A remarkable text is <margin>Neh. 2:10</margin> **Neh.** 2:10: *When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.* See what poison and malice is in the hearts of these men; it displeased them greatly that a man had come to seek something good for the children of **Israel**. These people gnash their teeth, and it grieves them that any loss should arise because of Religion and the Church; nothing displeases them more than that.

## IV. 
I come now to the third matter over which God’s People are often troubled, and that is

<column-break/>

concerning outward visitation <term>visitation: In this context, a "visitation" refers to trials, afflictions, or punishments sent by God to test or correct a person.</term> and sorrow. These outward visitations are often a great cause of dismay and displeasure among God’s People; and this is the third great cause of unrest. In this, when I say that visitations are great causes of unrest, I shall distinguish the outward visitations of God’s People into two kinds. First, there are *privative* <note>original: "privative" — referring to the loss or lack of good things.</note> or depriving visitations; that is, certain outward things which God’s People lack, and these trouble them greatly. It may be that they are poor and of low status; that they lack friends; that they are sick and lack help; and that this pinches them more than it does other people; and this troubles them greatly. Second, there are certain *positive* <note>original: "positive" — referring to the presence of actual afflictions or evils.</note> or inflicted evils under which they lie. I shall speak of the first, so that God’s People may not be troubled when they lack those good outward things. I shall then give you six observations.

## 1. 
Be assured that you will not lack those things whose enjoyment God sees to be useful for you. If God saw that the thing you lack were useful to you, be assured that He would not withhold it from you; are you poor and do you lack food? Be assured that God knows the lack of luxury is best for you. <margin>Psalm 84:11</margin> **Psalm** 84:11 <note>The OCR says verse 12, but in most English Bibles this is verse 11.</note>: *No good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.* If it is good for you, He will not withhold it from you; He who did not begrudge you His own Son will not begrudge you the trifles of worldly goods, if He saw such were for your good.

## 2. 
Remember that God lets His people lack some things so that He may give them better things in their place. I shall give you but a few proofs of this; look at **Job**, when he scraped himself on the ash-heap and mourned his great loss: one would have said that **Job** was a very cursed man. Read the register of his loss in the first chapter, how God let him be stripped of all his possessions; 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, etc.; truly a great loss. Yet all that **Job** lost was given back to him double. **Job** lost 7,000 sheep, God gave him 14,000 back; he lost 3,000 camels, and God gave him 6,000 back; and so with everything, except for the children, who were not doubled. If God takes some benefit or status away from a person, He gives it back to them double before they die. Does God then do you wrong, my Beloved? Truly, no He does not. We see this also in **David**; when he lost his son born of **Bathsheba**, he was very grieved over the loss of his son; but God gave him a better benefit in place of that bastard; God gave him **Solomon**, a legitimate child. **David**, who was to be King, lay beforehand like a hermit in a cave. So then, if God allows a great lack of some outward benefits to come upon you, you must think that God allows it to happen so that you may enjoy better benefits in their place. This observation set the heart of **Isaac** very much at rest. We read that his mother **Sarah** died, and that God gave him **Rebekah** as a wife, and that he <margin>Gen. 24:67</margin> loved **Rebekah**; thus was **Isaac** comforted after his mother’s death. **Isaac** lost his mother, and he received a wife in place of his mother. If God allows you to lack a mother, children, or some office, God will provide you with another benefit in their place, and let this set your heart at rest.

### Balm of Gilead, or the Healing.
