3. Observe that although you lack external, pleasant blessings, you nevertheless do not lack the better blessings, the spiritual blessings. You may lack crumbs, but you do not lack **Christ**; it may be that you lack food for your belly, and that you are not fed with delicacies as many worldly people are, but you may be fed with **Christ**, that **Bread of life**, through faith. It may be that you do not have such costly clothes as other people have, but you do not lack the **Robe of righteousness** of **Jesus Christ**. You may lack the possessions of this world, but you do not lack an **Inheritance** among the sanctified in the world to come. You may lack health, but you have a healthy soul; your soul fares well, just as **John** says of **Gaius**.
<margin>3 John verse 2.</margin>
One reads in Proverbs 14:14: *The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: but a good man shall be satisfied from himself.* <note>original: "Die af-keerigh van herten is / sal van sijne weghen versadight werden, maer een goet Man van zich selven."</note> It may be that nothing from the outside can satisfy you; that you undergo much trouble in this world, rise up early, eat your bread with sorrow, and that you nevertheless cannot obtain enough to fill your belly and clothe your nakedness; yet if you are one who has received grace, speak to yourself thus: "Although I lack these external things, yet blessed be God, who is my portion; although I have no inheritance in this life, yet I am an heir of the **Kingdom of Heaven**." This will take away the unrest that arises in your mind.

4. Consider that if God gave you these external things which you lack, the giving of them would be a greater snare and curse to you than the lack of them is. It may be that you lack luxury, or that you have a closed womb and no heirs; if God gave you these blessings which you lack, the granting of them would be a greater snare to you than the deprivation. I shall give you two or three clear proofs. One is **Rachel**, who was exceedingly impatient <note>original: "over-duldig," here meaning excessively distressed or suffering under the weight of her desire.</note> over the lack of children.
<margin>Genesis 30:1.</margin>
*Give me children, or else I die.* God gave her her desire, but notice how God punished her for it, so that she died in childbirth.
<margin>Genesis 35:18.</margin>
**Genesis** 35:18. Beloved, this must teach you to be careful not to be so discontented and restless when you lack something. You have another proof in **David**, who greatly desired the life of his child born of **Bathsheba**; he wept and fasted so that the child might not die. But if this child had continued to live, the life of this child would have been a greater snare for **David** than his death could be; for it would have been a constant reminder of **David's** shame, for everyone could have said, "there goes **David's** bastard." We see that harlots consider unchastity a shame and therefore commit a greater wickedness by murdering their children, so that their godlessness might not be known. So it was also in **Absalom's** situation: he rebelled against his father, and by his polite treatment of the people, he took away their freedom; by which means he had almost taken the kingdom from his father. They took up arms against each other; but **David** said:

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing.

3. Observe that although you lack outward, pleasant benefits, you nevertheless do not lack the better benefits, the spiritual benefits. You lack the crumbs, but you do not lack **Christ**; it may be that you lack food for your belly, and that you are not fed with delicacies as many worldly people are, but you may be fed with **Christ**, that **Bread of life**, through **Faith**. It may be that you do not have such costly clothing as other people have, but you do not lack the **Robe of the righteousness of Jesus Christ**. You may lack the possessions of this world, but you do not lack an **Inheritance** among the sanctified in the world to come. You may lack health, but you have a healthy **Soul**; your soul fares well, just as **John** says of **Gaius** <margin>3 John 1:2</margin> **3 John verse 2**. One reads in **Proverbs 14:14**:
> The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways, but a good man shall be satisfied from himself. 

It may be that nothing from the outside can satisfy you; that you undergo much trouble in this world, rising early, eating your bread with sorrow, and that you still cannot obtain enough to fill your belly and clothe your nakedness. Nevertheless, if you are one who has received grace, speak to yourself thus: "Although I lack these outward things, yet God be praised, who is my portion. Although I have no inheritance in this life, I am nevertheless an heir of the **Kingdom of Heaven**." This shall take away the unrest that arises in your mind.

4. Consider that if **God** gave you these outward things which you lack, the giving of them would be a greater snare and curse to you than the lack of them is. It may be that you lack luxury, that you have a **closed womb** <note>original: "gesloten Baermoeder," referring to infertility</note> and no heirs. If **God** gave you these benefits which you lack, the granting of them would be a greater snare to you than the deprivation. I shall give you two or three clear proofs. One is *Rachel*, who was impatient over the lack of children <margin>Genesis 30:1</margin> **Gen. 30:1**: 
> Give me children, or else I die. 
**God** gave her her desire, but notice how **God** punished her for it, so that she died in childbirth, **Gen. 35:18**. Beloved, this must teach you to take care not to be so discontented and troubled when you lack something. Another proof you have in *David*, who greatly desired the life of his child born of *Bathsheba*; he wept and fasted so that the child might not die. But if this child had continued to live, the life of this child would have been a greater snare for *David* than his death could be, for it would have been a constant memorial of *David’s* shame; for everyone could have said, "there goes *David’s* bastard." We see that harlots consider unchastity a shame and therefore commit an even greater wickedness by murdering their children, so that their godlessness might not be known. So it was also in *Absalom’s* situation: he rebelled against his Father and, through his polite encounters with the people, stole their favor <note>original: "hypsheydt," referring to his courtly charm used to win over the Israelites</note>; by which means he had nearly taken the Kingdom from his Father. They took up arms against one another; but *David* said <margin>2 Samuel 18:5</margin> **2 Sam. 18:5**: 
> Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom. 
If *David* had obtained his desire, that *Absalom* were not killed, he would have been a constant threat to his Father, for he had already partially

5. Remember that displeasure and disturbance of the soul under an external **Cross** and difficulty makes the enjoyment of present benefits bitter: an impatient person, who is impatient over one difficulty, loses the enjoyment of a hundred comforts. An impatient man may have a good wife, lovely children, and a wealthy state, but if he is impatient over one difficulty, that makes it so that he can have no comfort in anything. What a poor state this is: impatience over one difficulty consumes the comforts of a hundred benefits. An impatient person can rightly be compared to a **Hedgehog**, which, in order to bring provisions into its hole, goes after it has rained heavily into an orchard and rolls itself in the fallen apples, and thus fills its quills with apples and brings them to its hole; but if, in the bringing to its hole, just one apple falls off, it shakes off all the rest. Even so is an impatient man; God may overload him with many benefits, but if God then takes away but one blessing, he throws down the comforts of all the benefits that God has bestowed upon him. This is the evil fruit of this disturbance of the soul under external difficulty.

his Cross, suffering, and sorrow of the Body. When Peter saw the transformation of Christ's appearance, **Matt. 17:4**, he said to Jesus: "Lord, it is good that we are here; if you will, let us make here three Tabernacles." <note>A reference to the Transfiguration, where Peter wished to build shelters (tabernacles) for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah.</note> Theologians observe that Peter did not demand a Tabernacle for himself, but he said that it was good to be there, and that on a barren mountain where there was neither food nor lodging; such things he had forgotten. Having a vision of Heaven, he said that it was good to be there on a barren mountain. It has been experienced that the birds that fly lowest mourn the most, but the birds that fly highest are the best: the Dove peeps, the Crane chirps, the Raven croaks, but the Eagle makes no sorrowful sound. Theologians draw this lesson from it: that downcast people who cry like the Ravens and peep like the Doves when they are oppressed should instead be like the Eagles, flying to the joy of Heaven through your thoughts and meditations; this shall keep you from mourning. If things go poorly for you in the world, there is nothing better to take away all disturbance of the soul over physical crosses and difficulties than to transport your soul to the joys of Heaven. This

<margin>
"Walk through Paradise in your mind, and you will not be in the wilderness for so long." <note>original: *Paradisum mente deambula, & tamdiu in eremo non eris.*</note>
</margin>

„ advice Jerome gave to a hermit: "Walk 
„ through Paradise in your mind, and so 
long you shall not be in the wilderness." If you only come to walk in Heaven once or twice, you would not be so disturbed by the difficulties on Earth, **2 Cor. 4:17**. For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, works for us a far more exceeding eternal weight of glory. The weight of Glory makes the Apostle consider heavy tribulation to be light; therefore he calls it a light affliction; eternal glory makes the Apostle consider long tribulation to be short. If you then wish to consider tribulation to be no burden, remember the weight of Glory; if you do not wish to consider tribulation long, remember what an eternity there is in glory.

The second rule is: If you do not wish to be inordinately troubled by tribulation in this world, labor so that your hearts may be greatly troubled over sin. When a person bleeds too much from his nose, the Master Physician opens a vein to divert the blood. <note>A reference to the historical medical practice of bloodletting to balance the humors.</note> Beloved, when you are too sorrowful over worldly tribulation, make a diversion of the sorrow; open the sluices of your tears over sin, pour them out over sin, and then you shall be less grieved over the world. This is the reason why people are so greatly grieved over tribulation: because they are too little grieved over sin and spiritual numbness. It is a true rule: Godly fear drives out slavish fear; likewise, spiritual disturbance drives out the worldly kind. They who are greatly troubled over sin are no longer disturbed over any matter in the world, except for sin.

The third rule: do not place too great a Love on any comfort in the world; if you wish to keep your disturbance regulated, keep your Love well-ordered also. It is remarkable what we read of Jacob, **Gen. 37:34, 35**. Then Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth around his loins: and he mourned for his son many days. And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him: but he refused to be comforted, etc. What was the

<column-break/>

reason that this good old man was so exceedingly grieved over his son? In verse 3 it is said, Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he was the son of his old age. That Jacob loved Joseph more than all his children made him more sorrowful over Joseph than over all his children. If he had not loved Joseph as much as he did, he would not have been grieved beyond measure when he thought he had lost him. Labor then to have a moderate Love regarding worldly comforts. A person can endure the trimming of his nails, but not of his fingers. Why? Because he looks upon the nails as an excess <note>A superfluity or something extra.</note>. Look upon the world as a trimming of the nails, for it is but an excess; you can well go to Heaven without the abundance of worldly comfort; and do not grieve so much if God takes some comfort away from you. People use the world like the skin of their hands and not like a glove, which they can easily take off; therefore when God takes it from them, it is distressing to them. Just as it is with a painting: if it is in a frame, you can hang it up and take it down without damaging the painting; but if it is glued to the wall, you cannot take it down without tearing the painting. If your heart is also as if in a frame, God can then pull you away from the world and not disturb you; but if you are glued and pasted to the world, that shall disturb you beyond measure when the world is taken from you.

The fourth rule: Look upon the comforts of the world as unnecessary, or at best, as uncertain things, **Luke 10:42**. "One thing is needful." Christ says that grace alone is necessary. Grace is a necessity for a Christian; other things are non-essentials. <note>The original term "onbetaemlyckheden" suggests things that are fitting or convenient but not essential.</note> If God then takes from you the non-essentials, and does not take away the necessities, and if he leaves you grace, Christ, and Heaven, why then are you restless? Look upon the comfort of the world as changeable; not as an anchor on the bottom of the Sea, but as the weather vane on the Mast of a ship, which turns with every wind. Socrates did not mourn when his child had died; he said, "I know that I have begotten a mortal." This is the reason that people are so disturbed over the loss and the cross of this world: because they do not look upon the world as being perishable.

<margin>
"Know that I have begotten a mortal." <note>original: *Scito me genuisse mortalem.*</note>
</margin>

The fifth rule: Consider within yourself that disturbance under tribulation can do you no good, but great harm. It can do you no good, just as Christ tells you that you cannot add one cubit to your height; through all your thoughts you cannot bring any comfort to your life; through all your disturbance, you do not lighten your burden, but you make your grief heavier. The damage of disturbance under tribulation is two-fold. First, it makes the tribulation heavier; second, it makes it longer.

1. It makes it heavier in weight, and more in number, than it otherwise would be. A child that is patient under his Father's chastening has few and soft blows, but a stubborn one gets many. When God sees that a person grumbles and murmurs and is disturbed under tribulation, then they cause themselves more blows. **Prov. 27:3**. "A stone is heavy, and the sand is weighty: but [a fool's wrath is heavier than them both]."

### of a Smitten Soul.

the anger of the fool is heavier than both. This anger is not only heavy toward another, but heavy for himself: the affliction shall lie heavier upon him than a heap of stones or sand. A small bundle of folly causes a small bundle of rods. A man under a burden, if he continues steadily, shall carry his burden all the lighter; but if he falters and stumbles under his burden, he exhausts himself all the more.

2. We make our affliction last longer through our distress under it; the Father lashes that child longer who cannot kiss the rod and confess his fault, than he does another. Beloved, we prolong the days of our misery through impatience and distress under the striking hand of the Lord.

The sixth rule is this: compare the present blessings that you enjoy with the present afflictions that you suffer. *Ecclesiastes 7:14.* In the day of prosperity enjoy the good, but in the day of adversity, consider, etc. When you are prosperous, think thus: God has set adversity over against prosperity, so that I should not be too sensitive; then in adversity, do not be dejected, since God has set prosperity over against adversity. Perhaps you have lost a child; do you have no more? It may be that you have lost your status; do you not have health in your body and comfort in your outlook? Always look upon your blessings in this way whenever any cross meets you in the world.

The seventh rule is this: notice God’s hand in all the difficulty that meets you in the world. *Psalm 39:10.* I was silent, I will not open my mouth, because you have done it. Remember that God's ear hears all the murmurings of your tongue, and you shall not murmur against God in your distress. This is a powerful means; simply notice God’s hand in all that meets you.

The eighth rule is this: if you do not wish to be distressed by affliction, do not do that which renews your sorrow or reminds you of your grief. There are many people who aggravate their own sorrow and make their wounds bleed anew by dwelling on their cross and suffering. This is noteworthy regarding *Rachel* and *Jacob*. *Genesis 35:17-18.* And it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, the midwife said to her: Do not fear, for you shall have this son also. And it came to pass, as her soul was departing (for she died), that she called his name *Ben-oni*; <note>original: "Ben-oni," meaning "Son of my sorrow" in Hebrew.</note> that is, Son of sorrow; but his father called him *Benjamin*. <note>original: "Benjamin," meaning "Son of the right hand."</note> That is, Son of the right hand. Now why would *Jacob* not call him *Ben-oni*? Because the child’s name would remind him that his wife had died in childbirth. Therefore he changed the name that the mother had given him, *Ben-oni*, into *Benjamin*, the son of my right hand. Therefore it is folly in those who look at and speculate upon the paintings and clothes of their deceased friends; all these things are nothing more than a renewal of sorrow.

The ninth rule: notice the end <note>The "end" here refers to the final goal or purpose intended by God.</note> that God intends in your visitation, and the measure of it. The ground of impatience is that people notice the "measure"—how much—and the "time"—how long—they are afflicted, but they do not remember *why* they are visited. I shall explain this with a parable. A physician and 

<column-break/>

an enemy can perform the same act upon a man; but you know that a man will allow the physician to draw blood from him, yet he will not allow his enemy to do the same. The reason is that he knows the purpose of the physician is to heal him, but his enemy would do such a thing to kill him; nevertheless, they both let him bleed. Therefore, Beloved, notice that God's purpose for your soul in sending affliction is to heal you (and to cleanse your soul from sins); let then the "end" outweigh the "measure"; however much or however long you are visited, this shall take away all unrest and disorderly distress of your mind.

The tenth and last rule: remember that God in His wisdom will moderate all visitations that come upon you in this world according to your ability, so that you shall be able to bear them. *1 Corinthians 10:13.* No visitation has taken you, etc. <note>Referring to the verse stating God will not allow one to be tempted beyond their strength.</note> If God lays heavy burdens upon you, He shall give you strong shoulders. *Seneca* says: if the affliction is heavy, it is short; but if it is long, it is light. <note>A paraphrase of the Stoic maxim *Dolor si gravis brevis, si longus levis*.</note> God moderates the visitation. *Job 14:1.* A man born of a woman is of few days and full of unrest. The restless days are short; though they be full of unrest, they are nonetheless short. How sad it would be if misery and length—a multitude of difficulties and a multitude of days—came together. God shall then measure out the affliction according to your ability. *Isaiah 28:27.* For the vetches are not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cartwheel rolled over the cumin; but the vetches are beaten out with a staff, and the cumin with a rod. <note>This agricultural metaphor illustrates that God uses gentler methods for delicate "seeds" (people) and does not crush them with heavy machinery.</note> The *finis* <note>Latin: "end" or "conclusion."</note> is that God does not wish to tax a weak people with strong visitations, but that the visitations shall be moderated according to their ability; this God has promised. *Isaiah 27:8.* In measure you have contended with him, etc. If a man cannot endure a storm, then He shall hold back His harsh wind; He shall diminish the measure of the affliction. Let this set your soul at rest, that God moderates all His dealings with you according to your strength. Thus you have here set down ten rules for enduring affliction without disorderly distress of the soul.

<margin>Question</margin>
But since we must not be like unfeeling sticks and blocks under our visitations, and since God Himself has permitted some distress and sorrow over affliction, how shall we know if we are immoderately distressed over outward afflictions?

<margin>Answer</margin>
1. When the outward affliction swallows up the comfort of present blessings, then you are too greatly distressed. We see this in *Ahab*; *Ahab* had a flourishing kingdom and a precious palace, yet he could take no pleasure in all these things because he could not obtain the vineyard of poor *Naboth* for himself; that shows an all-too-great distress in him. So we also read of *Rebekah*, *Genesis 27:46.* And *Rebekah* said to *Isaac*: I am weary of my life because of the daughters of *Heth*. A very impatient saying—that a temporary affliction makes you say, "I am weary of my life"; just as many people, when things go against their wishes, say, "I am weary of my life," although they nevertheless enjoy many blessings. Such sayings are trappings of distress; do not let a difficulty rob you of all rejoicing in this world. *Jacob*

->of a dejected Soul.<-

Your fierce wraths go over me: your terrors make me perish. See how this man increases his complaints because of his troubles and great afflictions that struck him in both soul and body. So one also reads of Job’s disturbances, how greatly he was unsettled because of his personal troubles. Job 23:15. *Therefore am I troubled at his presence,* etc. From all of which it appears that God’s people are easily unsettled by their troubles and sins.

II. In what occasion are the People of God most troubled and distressed over sin? A person is not always distressed and troubled over the guilt of sin, but there are certain occasions in which God allows their conscience to be more troubled and distressed over sin than is ordinary.

There are then seven particular occasions in which the conscience is greatly distressed and troubled over sin. <note>The author lists five on this page, likely continuing on the next.</note>

<margin>1 Kings 21:27.</margin>
1. The first case is from the consideration of some threatened judgment: The awareness of some great judgment brings the guilt of sin into memory, and then the conscience is greatly troubled. Thus we read of the ungodly that they are troubled in their conscience, 1 Kings 21:27. When it was said to Ahab that he would be rooted out, then the guilt of sin came before him, and his conscience was unsettled, and his spirit dejected. *And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth <note>Coarse fabric worn as a sign of mourning or repentance</note> upon his flesh, and fasted,* etc. In the same way, Jehoshaphat’s and Hezekiah’s hearts and consciences were unsettled in such a case.

<margin>2 Chron. 33:10, 11, 12.</margin>
2. A second case is when God places them under great oppression; when it is not merely nearby, but already upon them; a proof of this you have in Manasseh, 2 Chronicles 33:10, 11, 12. When Manasseh was in prosperity, God spoke to him, but he did not listen: but when the Lord brought him among the thorns and afflictions, when he was in prison, then he sought after the Lord, then he reflected, and earnestly entreated the face of the Lord his God. So you also read of Joseph’s Brothers; they attempted to destroy their Brother, and because of this sin their conscience was not troubled or moved in the time of their prosperity, but when they came to Egypt to buy grain, and they were placed in prison, then they thought of their sin committed against their Brother, and then they began to say, <margin>Gen. 42:21.</margin> Genesis 42:21. *We are verily guilty concerning our brother,* etc. So it can also be that some people live seven, ten, or twenty years in a sin, and yet do not repent, but when they lie under a great visitation and trouble, then the conscience awakens, and then they are exceedingly moved; this is then the time that God seizes to unsettle their soul and conscience over sin. So one reads of Adoni-Bezek <margin>Judges 1:7.</margin> Judges 1:7. what cruelty he had practiced toward 70 Kings, cutting off the thumbs of their hands and their feet; in his prosperity this did not disturb his conscience, but when he was in hardship and imprisonment, then he thought of his sin, and then he said, *as I have done, so God hath requited me.*

3. The third case is: When a person is under a sin-searching and rebuking ministry of the word, and particularly when his

<column-break/>

sins were rebuked; this is a time when God moves the conscience over sin. When a person comes to hear, and he is touched in his sins by the preached word, then God awakens the conscience to stir the soul. You read of such among the unconverted Heathens, when one of them comes into the Church to hear the word, 1 Corinthians 14:25. *And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God,* etc. That is, he shall confess his sins and acknowledge his guilt.

<margin>Acts 24:25.</margin>
So you also read in the Acts of the Apostles, when Paul preached of righteousness, temperance, and of the Judgment to come, Felix became very afraid. It seems that Felix’s sin was unrighteousness, intemperance, and drunkenness; through the preaching of the word, Paul touched upon his sins, of which he was most guilty, and thus made his heart tremble. So also when Peter preached the Gospel to the Jews, and told them that they had crucified the Lord of life, <margin>Acts 2:37.</margin> Acts 2:37. it is recounted what followed; *when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart,* etc. This was the time that their conscience told them they were guilty of such a sin.

4. The fourth case is: when God awakens the conscience to rebuke a person for great and beloved sins, which he cherishes and allows to lie unrepented in his heart: When God then awakens the conscience, that is the right time for a person to be distressed over sin. One reads that Delilah said to Samson, <margin>Judges 16:18.</margin> *The Philistines be upon thee*; he lay and slept in her lap, he had lost his strength, because God had departed from him. If you are likewise rocked to sleep and are ensnared in sin, and give yourself over to a known sin; if you are careless and sleep in a pleasant sin, the time will come, as Delilah said to Samson, *the Philistines be upon thee*: so the conscience shall also say, stand up man, for the devil is upon you, and Hell is near you, and destruction approaches you, and then the conscience shall terrify you and unsettle you over your committed sins. Just as Eliphaz said to Job, chapter 22:9, 10. *Thou hast sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken. Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee.* It was true in Doctrine, but false in its application to Job.

5. The fifth case is: when a person, out of fear of loss or out of hope of gain, is driven to do something against the testimony of his conscience: if those people belong to God, then He will unsettle them over this great evil: we have many proofs of this. It is remarkable in Bilney <note>Thomas Bilney (c. 1495–1531), an English reformer who recanted his Protestant views under pressure but later retracted his recantation and was burned at the stake</note> in King Henry’s time, the eighth, when he was sentenced to die, he signed the Popish Articles to save his life; but History testifies that he was troubled over that sin in his conscience for two years together, and he never enjoyed any praiseworthy day in breadth and rest until he retracted the signature, preached the truth, and was burned. So it was also with Dr. Cranmer <note>Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556), Archbishop of Canterbury, who famously recanted his recantations before his execution</note> out of fear of losing his life, signing his recantation; but he soon broke his promise and retracted what he had done; he never had rest in his conscience until he [burned] his recantation

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

So also Baynham <note>James Bainham (died 1532), an English lawyer and Protestant martyr.</note>, a legal scholar, signed the Popish Articles; but he had no rest in his conscience until he acknowledged the truth again. Beloved, take heed then, that you sign nothing against your conscience to preserve your life or status.

6. The sixth case is: when a person falls away from the fundamentals of Religion into an evil way, the conscience troubles and rebukes him for his backsliding. <margin>Prov. 14:14.</margin> *The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways, but a good man shall be satisfied from himself.* Just as a good person is filled inwardly with peace of conscience and with tranquility of mind in his upright walk; so, on the contrary, a backslider shall be filled with the unrest of Conscience in his evil ways. <margin>Jer. 2:19.</margin> *Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God,* etc. The sin of apostasy <note>Renouncing one's religious faith.</note> will, above all sins, trouble the sinner's conscience, and disturb his peace, and unsettle his soul; if God turns His back on you, He makes your conscience like a great dog, to fly in your face because of your turning away from God; the Conscience will tell you what you have done in your godless departure from God; then your conscience shall be worse than the biting of a dog, for then your Conscience shall seize its moment to make known to you your sin against God.

7. The seventh case is: when a person lies on his sickbed or deathbed; that is the final time that God uses to wake the sleeping sinner, and to awaken the conscience, and to trouble him over his committed sin. It may be that you live as a Drunkard, or as a Whoremonger, and are not troubled; but when you lie on your sick- or Death-bed, and your Conscience awakes, can you then die as a Drunkard or Whoremonger and not be troubled? Take heed then of these sins. <margin>Prov. 5:8.</margin> *Remove thy way far from her: and come not nigh the door of her house.* Here is a warning for young people concerning a Harlot. verse 12. *and thou mourn at the last,* etc. This is the final opportunity in which the Conscience troubles you for your sins; if you listen to God, He will at the last make you mourn over the evil you have committed. <margin>Job 21:25.</margin> *And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure.* Oh, the bitter pangs that are in many souls when they die, where another thinks that he departs in peace.

### III. I now come to the third point, to show the difference between the distress of the Godly and the Godless; for the Godless are also sometimes troubled in their minds over the sins they have committed, since God has placed a Conscience in man to rebuke him for sin.

In handling this matter, I shall show thirteen or fourteen differences between these two.

1. The Godless are indeed troubled over sin, yet only over great and gross sins, not for small and secret ones.

<column-break/>

Paul, before his conversion, was never troubled over concupiscence <note>The inclination of the soul toward sensible good; here, secret sinful desire or lust.</note>, which is secret corruption and the lust of the heart; therefore he says <margin>Rom. 7:7.</margin> 
> I had not known lust, except the Law had said, Thou shalt not covet.

He thought all was well with him as long as he refrained from gross sins, but he did not regard the small and light sins. The unconverted see sins as we see the Stars in the night; we may see the largest Stars, but the smallest we do not see. So also the Godless, by the light of their natural conscience, see the gross, great, and shameful sins, but they do not know the small, narrow, and secret sins and lusts of the heart. But look at the Godly, there you find a great difference; their trouble of conscience differs much from this; for their Conscience is not only troubled over sins as large as camels, but also over sins as small as gnats; not only over Mountains of sins, but also over Molehills of corruption; small and slight sins unsettle their spirit. Hezekiah humbled himself greatly, even though it was only an inward sin: the lifting up of his heart in pride. This is a proof of true grace: when the soul is humbled over inward and secret sins. Thus David's heart smote him after he had numbered the People: it is doubtful what particular sin this was, since it is lawful for a King to count his People, but it was a secret sin of the heart—a pride of heart, or some other sin; because of this, his heart smote him. These sins that do not disturb the sleep of the Godless, break the heart of the Godly; that which is but dust on the finger or glove to the Godless and does not trouble him, is to the Godly like a sting in the kidneys, to unsettle him.

2. The second difference: many of the Godless are troubled over sin, over some outward act of sin, but they are not troubled over the inward form and nature of sin, that evil disposition of the heart toward sin. We read that the Godless have often been troubled over reigning sins, but they are not troubled over the sin of their nature. Cain was troubled over the murder of his Brother; Balaam over his Sorcery; Ahab over his Idolatry; Judas over his betrayal; and Saul over his cruelty; but none of these, nor any other Godless person, has ever been troubled over original sin, over the corruption of their nature. But the Godly man's distress over sin concerns not only the deed, but also the form of sin, over the natural corruption which is the Fountain from which all sinful deeds flow: this is what greatly unsettles them. Such you read of Paul <margin>Rom. 7:24.</margin> 
> O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? 

Looking at those sins, wherein people were accustomed as a punishment to bind together a Dead and a living Body <note>An ancient Roman punishment where a living prisoner was tied face-to-face with a corpse until they died of infection.</note>; he speaks here of the Body of his corrupt nature, which was to him like a dead man bound to a living man; whereas before his conversion, he did not mourn over any inward corruption, nor even make mention of his corrupt nature. Are you troubled over sin? Can your conscience assure you that your distress is as much over the...

# [of a troubled Soul.]

...the corruption of your nature as well as over your sinful life. Are you disturbed by the corrupt Fountain <note>The "Fountain" refers to original sin or the inherent sinful nature, while the "stream" refers to individual sinful acts.</note> as much as by the corrupt stream that flows out of it? If you are thus moved over sin, then all your struggling with sin shall end with a victory over sin on another day.

3. The third distinction: The **Godless** are moved over sin, but their distress over sin is more about the evil of the punishment than the evil that is in the nature of sin itself. They are restless over sin, but it is because sin ruins the soul, not because it stains the soul; because God pursues the sin, but not because He hates it; more because it is against God's justice, which is provoked, than because it is against God's Holiness, which is dishonored. The **Godless** are moved and disturbed because God threatens sin, not because God forbids sin; because Hell exists because of sin, not because Hell is *in* the sin. But the **Godly** hate sin and loathe sin more because it is against the Nature of God, and because God hates it; more because it is against God's command than because God punishes it. It is like a Child who will not touch a coal because it would make his hand black; the Child will not grasp the Coal because it is a fiery coal and would burn his fingers. So it is also with the **Godly**: they will not touch sin because it is of a staining nature; but the **Godless** are like a Child that will not touch the sin only because it would burn. If you can then say that you hate sin because God hates it, and that you do not hate it for the punishment of sin but for the evil of sin; not for the damning power of sin, but for the staining power of sin; in this case, your restlessness over sin shall not harm you.

4. The fourth distinction: Although the **Godless** are moved and disturbed over sin, this disturbance does not make them leave the sin; instead, when the anxiety of the sorrow is over, they run back to the sin again. They may sometimes be disturbed over sin, but it is only for the time that the trouble lasts, and no longer. We read in **Jer. 18:12**: *But they said, There is no hope: but we will walk after our own thoughts, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart.* Their conscience knocked at them a little over the sin, but they nonetheless wanted to follow the sin. But the **Godly** reason thus with themselves: if such sins disturb my soul, and upset my conscience, and hinder my communion with God, and break my peace, shall I then touch them? No, I will cast them away like a filthy garment, and leave them, and say to them: get away from here! This is another distinction: the **Godly** break off from sin; but the **Godless**, even if they are restless, they still continue in the sin as soon as the trouble is over.

5. The **Godless** experience a temporary restlessness over sin, but this only causes a delay in the act of sin; it does not make the soul loathe the sin. It may be that, because of the natural <term>conscience</term> <note>The 17th-century idea that even non-believers have a basic moral compass that causes guilt.</note>, there is a cessation of sin, so that he does not commit that same sin again for a long time; but this does not birth a loathing of the sin in the soul; rather, when the commotion is over, the cessation is

<column-break/>

ended, and then he goes his way to sinning again. You have proof of this in Pharaoh, <margin>Exod. 8:15.</margin> **Exod. 8:15**: *But when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them.* When he was in distress and trouble, then his sin was set aside; but when the trouble was gone, then he hardened his heart again. So, when conscience flies in the face of the **Godless** and tells them that they have sinned in this or that way, they labor to quiet their conscience and say they will leave their godless ways and live so no more; yet when the trouble of the conscience is over, they return again to their old sinful ways. This is the condition of the **Godless**. <margin>2 Pet. 2:22.</margin> **2 Pet. 2:22**: *But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.* The **Godless** are like dogs; when they have a sickness in their stomach, they are troubled and vomit it out; but when the distress is over, they return to the vomit. So do the **Godless**: when Conscience seizes them, and moves them, and punishes them, then they want to vomit out their sins and say they will do so no more; but when the pain and trouble is over, they return to their previous sins. The restlessness of the soul in the **Godless** is like a prison to a Thief; the Prison prevents the Thief from committing his robbery, which he would commit if he were free; but it does not change his thievish inclination toward that sin. So it is also with the conscience of the **Godless**: it may punish, rebuke, and restrain them from the commission of prominent and great sins; but it does not change the sinful inclination that is within them, nor does it awaken a true defense against sin. It is noteworthy of Balaam, <margin>2 Pet. 2:15.</margin> **2 Pet. 2:15**: *Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness.* He loved the profit, and the pinches of his natural Conscience were so great upon him that they restrained him from receiving this sinful profit; but when Peter notes the sin of Balaam, he says that he *loved* the reward of unrighteousness, even though he did not receive it. It is no thanks to you, O godless one, that you do not commit the sin (it may be that you do not commit it because your conscience rebukes you), but do you have no love or pull to commit it? Do you have a lust for Adultery? Although you have no opportunity, nonetheless if you love it and delight in thinking about it, this is sin in you before God. Do you have a lust for Drunkenness, and do you love strong drink, but have no opportunity to commit that sin? It is no thanks to you; for the Love of the sin makes you guilty, and God shall judge you for it.

But the **Godly**: they are moved over sin, and they seek not only to put away the act, but also the inclination toward sin. <margin>Psal. 119:104.</margin> **Psal. 119:104**: *Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way.* The Psalmist, through pondering the sweet commands of God, came to an understanding of the nature and evil of sin, and therefore he hated all sins and false paths; not only false paths in the outward commission of sin, but the false paths...

It uses biblical examples like Pharaoh and Balaam to show that an unrepentant heart only stops sinning temporarily while under duress.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the godly and the godless regarding a troubled conscience. The previous page established that the godly loathe sin for its nature, while the godless fear it for its punishment. This page focuses on where each seeks comfort and how they prioritize spiritual versus physical suffering.</meta>

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

...paths of the secret movement of sin in his own heart, and of the nature and inclination toward sin.
6. When a godless man is disturbed by sin, he does not go to God's Word to obtain comfort and take away the sadness and disturbance; instead, he goes to sinful and fleshly pastimes and worldly pleasure to drive away the restlessness of his soul and conscience. You read this in Genesis 4:15, 18. There you read that Cain, lying under the restlessness of his mind over his sin—indeed, even to the point of despair, so that he said his sins were greater than could be forgiven—what does he do under this disturbance? What course does he take? Does he go to God for satisfaction and the removal of his troubles? No, he takes a strange course (verse 16): Cain went out from the presence of the Lord, and (verse 17) he built a city. By his "going out from the presence of the Lord" is understood his departure from the ordinances <note>In this context, "ordinances" refers to established religious rites, worship services, and the community of the church.</note> and the Church of God toward worldly and fleshly delights; not that Cain can go out from the essential omnipresence of God—no man can do that. So also Ainsworth <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622) was a famous English scholar and nonconformist theologian whose "Annotations" on the Bible were highly influential in the 17th century.</note> understands this verse: that what is meant here is his abandonment of the place of the Divine Word and public worship. To a godly person, it is the greatest joy in the world thus to come into God’s presence, to come to the ordinances in the church of God—a joy of which Cain was now deprived, though he ought to have run to them to take away this disturbance of the mind. Instead, he went away to build cities in the world, that he might thus quiet his conscience. But for the godly, when they are troubled by sin, running to the pleasures and pastimes of the world cannot comfort them, nor bring any joy or peace of conscience; rather, they know they must hear God’s word, pray, and seek God’s face publicly and secretly in His ways, according to His will, in paths He has sanctified for that purpose: to pacify troubled consciences. You read that Jonah was troubled by the sin of fleeing from God’s presence and not obeying His voice; under this restlessness over sin, his heart fainted within him. But did Jonah go to worldly, sinful, and fleshly pleasures to take away this restlessness of his soul? No, says the text in Jonah 2:7: *When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the Lord: and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple.* He saw that no way was suitable to pacify his conscience except in God’s way, which He has sanctified for that purpose. The godly present their supplications to God and address themselves to Him in the way of His worship to heal their disturbed souls; and they strive to bind themselves to God’s Love in Christ through His promise. The godly might say that sin in their heart and the pollution of their soul visits them; but they seek an admission to God’s presence to rejoice their souls and to have Him tell them that their sins are dead <note>Meaning the guilt of the sin has been removed and its power over the individual broken.</note>; and to promise peace to their conscience; and to bring joy to their heart, contentment to their soul, and rejoicing to their spirit, which makes the soul rejoice and be glad in God’s presence.

<column-break/>

### XIV. SERMON.

-> Psalm 42. verse 12. <-

> *Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.*

I have already set down six distinctions regarding the disturbance that springs from the natural conscience in the godless over sin, and the disturbance of the soul over sin that is found in the godly.

7. The seventh distinction is: the godless are restless over sin, but it is because it causes outward visitation <note>The author uses "visitation" to mean God's active judgment or physical trials sent as punishment.</note>, and not because it causes the inward and spiritual withdrawal of God’s countenance. When God visits them with outward sorrow, then they consider what evil they have done and how they ought to improve it; yet it is more out of fear of death than out of love for righteousness. This makes them say: I must cleanse myself, not because sin is unclean, but because it visits my body and takes away my peace. If sin did not torment the body, they would never torment the soul of the godless with its will. The godless are like someone whose lungs are wasting away, yet who complains to the physician about a small pimple on his finger. People are disturbed by visitations that are mere trifles; but when they decrease in grace and approach eternal death, that does not disturb them. People who are thus more disturbed by affliction than by the inward withdrawal of God’s countenance may aptly be compared to a duck in a pool of water; let only a small stone be thrown into the water, and the duck will dive; but let it thunder in the Heavens, and the duck is not afraid. I shall make this use of it: the godless are like ducks; let God but once blow upon their outward man or visit their body, and this makes them dive, bow, tremble, and makes them afraid; yet let the Heavens be mournful, let God hide His face—if the sin did not disturb their body, it would never disturb their conscience. A godly person is disturbed by the affliction for the sake of the sin, but the godless are disturbed by the sin for the sake of the affliction; the affliction disturbs them concerning the sin. The godly are of an entirely different disposition; they are disturbed by sin more because of the inward withdrawal of God’s countenance than because of the outward affliction of the body. Psalm 30:8: *Lord, by thy favor thou hast made my mountain to stand strong: thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled.* David had trouble in his kingdom and in his person at that time; but this did not go to his heart so much as the hiding of God’s face. The heaviest blow of God’s hand did not disturb David as much as the hiding of God’s countenance: the outward affliction was but like the scratch of a pin in David’s flesh;

<summary>This page argues that while the godless seek to quiet their consciences through worldly distractions and only fear sin's physical punishments, the godly seek God's presence and fear the spiritual withdrawal of His favor above all else.</summary>

# of a contrite Soul.
->Y 3<-
<meta>catchword: yet</meta>

...but the withdrawal of God's countenance was as a sword in his bones.

8. The eighth distinction is: The ungodly, amidst their distress over sin, complain more **about** God than they complain **to** God; but the godly complain more **to** God than **about** God when they are distressed by sin. It is the habit of the ungodly to complain miserably *about* God, rather than humbly *to* God, when they are in terror of conscience under the distress of sin. Revelation 16:9: *Men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God.* When God allows the fire of His wrath to heat the conscience of a man because of his hostility toward the church, this causes him to blaspheme the Name of God. Isaiah 8:21: *It shall come to pass, that when he is hungry and very angry, he shall curse his King and his God, looking upward.* The ungodly complain about God—that He is a hard Master, that He shows no mercy to His creatures, only harsh judgments. The terror of conscience makes them quarrel with God as if He were unjust; they complain about Him, that His decree is biased, that His mercy is lacking, and His justice is cruel; but they do not complain humbly *to* God under the distress of their souls. An ungodly person is very vividly depicted for us in Job 15:24, 25, 26: *Anguish and distress terrify him: they overwhelm him, like a King prepared for battle. For he stretches out his hand against God,* etc. Just as one man will rush at another in anger to harm him, an ungodly man, in the terror and trouble of his soul, arms himself against God even in his complaining. This is the nature of the ungodly in the terror of their conscience: to think ill of God; to complain *about* God, but not *to* God. But a godly person, when he is troubled by sin, his nature is to complain *to* God. Lamentations 1:18: *The Lord is righteous, for I have rebelled against his mouth.* <note>original: "monde weerspannigh" - literally "rebellious against his mouth/word."</note> Here is a complaint *to* God, not *about* God: "You are righteous, but I have sinned." Psalm 51:4 <note>The Dutch text cites Psalm 51:6 following an older numbering system.</note>: *Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight: so that you are righteous in your speaking, and pure in your judging.* It is as if he wanted to say: "I will accuse myself and condemn myself now that my conscience flies in my face, but I will justify God and not judge Him." This is the nature of a godly person under the distress of mind over sin: he complains *to* God, but never *about* God.

9. The ninth distinction is: The ungodly, in the distress of the soul over sin, complain more about their trouble to men than to God. Thus did Judas, after he had betrayed his Master (Matthew 27:4). He came to the Chief Priests and Elders, saying: *I have sinned, betraying innocent blood.* But we read nowhere that Judas went to the Lord and said, "I have betrayed your Son, I have sinned, betraying innocent blood." Haman was also thus distressed when he could not get Mordecai to kneel before him; yet he recounted to his wife and friends what had happened to him, but not to God. When Saul was also thus distressed and tormented in his spirit, he told his servants that an evil spirit terrified him; but we do not read that Saul went to God to be delivered from this distress of the heart. This is the mark of the ungodly: sin blows upon him,

<column-break/>

conscience flies in his face; he complains of this to men, but he does not complain to God, saying: "my soul is distressed, my conscience is wounded." He cannot go to God to pour out his complaints. But the godly complain more to God than to men. Sometimes it may happen in certain heavy cases that they speak to others to resolve some doubts, but God hears their mourning and sighing in secret. The Psalmist testifies to this clearly in Psalm 61:2: *From the end of the earth I cry to you, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to a Rock that is too high for me.* Jonah 2:7: *When my soul was overwhelmed within me, I thought of the Lord, and my prayer came to you, in the Temple of your holiness.* Jonah was distressed over his sin, yet he thought of the Lord, and his prayer came to Him; he complained more to God than to men when he was under trouble.

10. Concerning the tenth distinction: The ungodly are indeed distressed over sin, but this does not make them conscientiously and powerfully seek the <term>mortification</term> <note>mortification (doodinghe): A traditional theological term for "killing off" the power of sinful habits through spiritual discipline.</note> of these sins over which they are troubled. They are more concerned about the *guilt* than about the *power* of sin. If they can ward off the guilt of sin, then they are not concerned about the power and dominion of sin. This is the mark of the ungodly. Thus Pharaoh was distressed by the guilt of sin while God punished him, but the power that held his hardened heart never distressed him. So it is with the ungodly: their distress over sin does not make them seek the killing and subduing of sin. But the godly are of an entirely different nature; they seek more to kill the sin than to set their conscience at rest; more to subdue the power of sin than to take away the guilt of sin. He knows that he must either kill sin or be killed by it; if he does not kill sin, sin will kill him. Therefore, his work is as much to cleanse his conscience as to satisfy it; as much to ward off the power as the guilt of sin.

11. The eleventh distinction: The ungodly, when they are in distress of soul over sin, are rich and abundant in promising to leave the sin while the distress is upon them; but when the trouble is over, they run back to the same sin with greater earnestness and desire. This is shown to you in Deuteronomy 5:27, 28: *Go near, and hear all that the Lord our God shall say: and speak you to us all that the Lord our God shall speak to you, and we will hear it and do it. And the Lord heard the voice of your words when you spoke to me, and the Lord said to me: I have heard the voice of the words of this people, which they have spoken to you; everything they have spoken is good.* When the people heard the terrifying manner of God in giving the Law—in thunders and lightnings—they promised much to Moses: *Everything the Lord our God says to you, we will hear and do.* But God said in verse 29: *O that they had such a heart, to fear me, and keep all my Commandments every day, that it might go well with them and their children forever.* It is remarkable that as soon as this distress had passed a little, the people were more wicked than they had been before; they fell back into murmuring and murmured ten times against God, who had delivered them. This is the mark of the ungodly: even when the trouble of conscience distresses them, their sins remain with them. Oh, how they promise...

<meta>This page continues a series of numbered distinctions between the ungodly and the godly regarding the "trouble of the soul" or a distressed conscience. The previous page discussed how the ungodly complain *about* God, whereas the godly complain *to* God during spiritual distress.</meta>

# Balm of Gilead, or the healing
### of a contrite Soul.

<column-break/>

nevertheless, that such people will be as they are, that they will lead a life and refuse to remain as they were; but let their distress be removed, then you shall see that this restraining of their conscience shall make them more diligent to commit sin than they were before. Man's sins are compared to an **Oven** <margin>Hosea 7</margin>. Fire spread in the open air does not burn so fiercely; but in an oven, it burns very hotly. In the ungodly, when sin is held within their heart (notwithstanding the distress of the soul over sin), when this fire then catches air, it burns with even more heat and violence. When the conscience dams up the sin until the distress is over, then sin masters the soul with even greater strength. In the godly, it is different; when the distress of the soul over sin is over, a godly person fears to run back to that same sin again; although the distress is gone, he still remembers how distressed he was. I will say even more: I still remember what it is like to lie under the weight and heaviness of sin. Therefore, this makes the conscience fearful, so that he does not dare to go toward sin as in former times.

12. The twelfth difference: The ungodly, under the distress of their souls over sin, more easily apply to themselves the **comforts** of the Word than the **threats** and commands of the Word when they are troubled by the ministry of the Word. <margin>Deuteronomy 29:19</margin> *And it shall come to pass, when he hears the words of this curse, that he shall bless himself in his heart, saying, "I shall have peace, even though I walk according to the dictates of my heart," to add the drunken to the thirsty.* <note>This biblical idiom refers to someone stubbornly continuing in sin ("drunkenness") while ignoring their spiritual need ("thirst").</note> They could claim peace for themselves, but they would not claim the threats, even though they walked according to the whims of their hearts. The ungodly, under the terror of conscience, would rather apply comfort to themselves, even if it is without foundation, than claim the threats, even though those are their portion. <margin>Jeremiah 3:4, 5</margin> *Will you not from this time cry unto me, "My Father, you are the Guide of my youth"? Will he keep his anger forever? Will he reserve it to the end? Behold, you have spoken and done evil things as much as you could.* They did as much evil as they could, yet they presumed to say that God was their Father and that God was concerned with them. This is the mark of an ungodly person: to claim the comforts, but not the threats of the Word. But the godly are more inclined to apply the threats than the promises of the Word to themselves. <margin>Psalm 77:3</margin> <note>In many English Bibles, this is Psalm 77:2.</note> *In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my hand was stretched out in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted.* Asaph <note>A biblical psalmist known for his honest portrayals of spiritual doubt and depression.</note> could claim the terror for himself, but he refused to be comforted. Observe also from daily experience how a conscientious person, under the distress of the soul over sin, will always remember the terrible threats of the Scripture, but he does not claim any promises for himself that might take away the soul's distress over sin.

13. The thirteenth distinction: The ungodly, under the distress of the mind over sin, turn to sinful ways and means to pacify the conscience and take away the soul's distress; therefore, they use four sinful means, which the godly dare not do:

<column-break/>

1. They avoid a soul-searching and sin-rebuking ministry of the Word; you see this in Felix <margin>Acts 24:25</margin>. *As he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, "Go your way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for you."* Paul told him of two sins of which he was most guilty: namely, drunkenness and injustice. When he dealt with him so directly, he made his conscience tremble and his heart distressed. Felix said, "Go away, I will hear you at another time." Paul had disturbed him; therefore, Felix shunned the continuation of the rebuke. But a godly person does not dare to do this; a godly person loves that Word which searches and awakens his conscience. See this distinction between Felix and the converts in the Acts of the Apostles; Felix commands Paul to leave and shuns the rebuke of the Word when his conscience is tested; but when the converts were distressed over sin and pricked in their hearts over the killing of Christ, they loved the Apostles and clung to them, and brought their possessions to the Apostles' feet. The godly dare not do as the ungodly do in this point.

2. The ungodly, to ward off the unrest of the conscience, go to a multitude of worldly business; you read of this regarding Cain <margin>Genesis 4:17</margin>. God’s people dare not do such a thing; they do not dare run to the world to soften the distress of their conscience; but they go to God’s Word; they withdraw into a corner and search God’s Word to see what God’s Word says to them in that day of their distress. <margin>Proverbs 12:25</margin> *Heaviness in the heart of man makes it stoop: but a good word makes it glad.* I bow under sorrow and trouble, but only a good word from God can comfort me.

3. The ungodly, under distress, use this sinful way: they go to sinful pleasures to soften the distress of the mind. Saul called for musical instruments <margin>1 Samuel 16:17</margin> to sweeten the distress of his spirit. When the Israelites sacrificed their children to Moloch <note>An ancient deity associated with child sacrifice by fire.</note>, they drowned out the cries of their children with the sound of drums and pipes; so also do the ungodly with their conscience. God’s people dare not do this; they know that fleshly pleasures can no more pacify a troubled conscience than a silk stocking can heal a leg suffering from sciatica; they do not dare tumble into sinful pleasures, but they go to the promises and rejoice in them.

4. The ungodly go to evil company, to merry feasts, or to that which can make them forget their distress; thus did Herod <margin>Mark 6:18</margin>. *For John had said unto Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."* Shortly after John had stirred his conscience about having his brother’s wife, Herod called for merry company—his nobles and military commanders—so that he might forget the distress of his spirit. But the godly go to the godly and to God <margin>Psalm 61:3</margin> <note>Psalm 61:2 in English versions.</note>. *From the end of the earth will I cry unto you, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.* Thus do the godly behave.

->Again, the ungodly look more toward comfort<-

# of a contrite Soul.

**Column 1**

than their bounden duty; if God gives them rest and peace, they ask for no grace; but the people of God look more to their bounden duty than to comfort in the disturbance of the conscience. When the converted were troubled in their spirit, they did not cry out for comfort, but asked after their duty; they cried out, *Men and Brethren, what shall we do to be saved?* <note>original: "Mannen Broeders wat sullen wy doen, om salig te worden." A reference to Acts 2:37.</note>

Thus I have finished the third point: the distinction between the distress in the godly and the ungodly.

IV. The fourth question is: why are the people of God so greatly troubled over sin, so much so that they are more moved by sin than they are comforted by the sight of their grace? Sin shall not damn their souls; why then does sin so greatly disturb their conscience?

There are five reasons for this.

1. It arises partly from the softness of the heart and tenderness of the conscience, which is planted by God in His people; the eye is disturbed by a small movement <note>meaning a speck or irritant</note> where the hand is not moved by much larger things; the eye is the most tender part of the body; so also God's people have a tenderness of conscience. Sin is to their conscience as a movement is to the eye, which greatly disturbs them. It is worthy of note that as God promises that He will keep His people as the apple of His eye, Deut. 32:10, so also God's people are said to keep the Law of the Lord as the apple of their eyes, Prov. 7:2. Beloved, a speck <note>original: "vlaes," referring to a film or mote</note> causes pain to the eye; you must keep the Law as the apple of your eyes; the apple of the eye is the most tender part of the whole body; a violation of the Law through sin must disturb you as much as a speck in your eye, if you keep the Law as the apple of your eye.

2. God's people are troubled over sin because they see that they sin more against God than they are obedient to God; therefore sin disturbs them. Grace is like the gleanings of the vineyard <note>The small amount of grapes left after the main harvest</note>, but sin is like the full harvest, Job 15:16. *How much more abominable and filthy is man, who drinks iniquity like water.* God's people see their sins as mountains, and their graces only as molehills; my lust burns like a flame, but my grace only as a smoldering coal; my sins are like a full flood, but my graces like a low ebb: this makes God's people restless over sin. Disturbance of the soul often occurs in the godly, just as the moth is ordinarily found in the finest clothes; the worm is in the rose sooner than in the thorn.

3. Because sin is more visible to their souls than their graces, they are therefore more moved by sin. You read Gal. 5:19: *Now the works of the flesh are manifest; which are adultery, fornication, etc.* But when the Apostle gives you the list of the fruit of the Spirit, he does not say the fruits of the Spirit are manifest, but the works of the flesh are manifest: to show (as one well notes) that man can more easily distinguish and have a sight of his sins than a godly person can have a sight of his grace.

4. The fourth reason is taken from the consideration that Christ's soul was troubled over sin, even as it was imputed to Him <note>imputed: a legal term meaning Christ took the credit/blame for our sins even though he didn't commit them</note>, though not as an inherent unrighteousness. Now is

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

*my soul troubled,* said Christ; He suffered not only in His body on the Cross, but also in His soul in the Garden. His soul was not troubled over His own sin, for no guile was found in His mouth. Now then, Beloved, Christ was troubled over your wounds; this makes the godly look upon themselves: shall Christ be troubled over my sins, which were only imputed to Him, and should I not be troubled over the sin that clings to me?

5. So that God's people might all the more taste and see the evil and bitterness of sin in the course of their lives, and might all the more guard themselves from the commission of sin in the future. This is a reason that Solomon gives in Eccl. 7:25, 26. *I applied mine heart to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom, and the reason of things, and to know the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness: And I found more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands.* Solomon desired to know the evil of sin; and he says, I found it to be more bitter than death; Solomon speaks this through experience, that he found sin more bitter than death. Beloved, this is God's purpose, why God wants to let man unbind the wickedness of sin; and why He lets him be troubled in his conscience over sin, so that they themselves might find it to be more bitter than death, and that they might avoid and shun those same sins which have pained them so much. Thus I have also finished the fourth question.

### The fifth question in order is this: when can God’s people be said to be too much disturbed over sin?

There are seven points to open this: four of those I shall gather from one place, Psalm 77:2, 3, 4 <note>original: "Psal. 77. 3. 4. 5." following different numbering</note>. *In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted. I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak.* Here it is revealed in four ways when a person's contrition and disturbance over sin is too great.

1. When a person is so disturbed over sin that he is not only unfit to receive comfort, but is also unwilling to receive the comfort that belongs to him, verse 3. *My soul refused to be comforted.* This was sin in him; it was a weakness in Asaph <note>Asaph: the traditional author of this Psalm</note>, when he was troubled in his mind, that he refused comfort. God wants the restlessness over sin to be an exercise of the gifts of grace, not to extinguish the certainty of grace; when the disturbance over sin...

# Gilead’s Balm, or the Healing

**Column 1**

causes an **eclipse** <note>original: "Ecclipſis," referring to a spiritual darkness where God's favor is hidden</note> of grace, and not a path to grace, then it is too great.
2. When the lovely and glorious attributes or properties of **God** are shown to the soul of the **godly** under a terrifying form. Verse 4: *I thought of God, and I made a lamentation; I pondered, and my soul was overwhelmed.* <note>Reference to Psalm 77:3–4. In the author's view, thinking of God should bring comfort, so if it brings only terror, the distress is out of balance.</note> Thoughts of God ought to comfort a soul in the unrest of the mind; but when a person, in the distress of the mind, causes the attributes of **God** to terrify him, then it is too great. *Job 23:15.* Therefore I am troubled at His presence: consider, and be afraid of Him. **Adam**, after he had fallen, hid himself from God’s face: *Gen. 3:8, 10.* Beloved, if you cannot think of God, or if thoughts of God disturb you, this is an all-too-great distress in a godly person.
3. When a person is so troubled in his soul over sin that he deprives himself of the natural refreshments which God grants him; when he cannot eat, drink, or sleep. This is set down in verse 5: *You held my eyes waking.* <note>Psalm 77:4 in English Bibles.</note> His meaning is, I am so troubled in my conscience over the guilt of my sins that I cannot sleep at night when I lie upon my bed; I can neither eat nor sleep; I cannot use the natural refreshment of sleep which God grants me; just as worldly anxiety is described in a greedy man. *Eccl. 5:11.* The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep. This is a proof of all-too-great worldly anxiety and distress in a person over the world, when a person is so infatuated with the world that he cannot take his rest at night.
4. When the distress of the soul over sin makes a person faint-hearted or unfit for religious duties, then they are disorderly and distressed beyond measure: this lies in verse 5. *I was overwhelmed and spoke not.* He was so overwhelmed with fear and trouble in his spirit that it made him despondent and unfit to pray. It follows then, that all those troubles that are so immoderate that they make him refuse comforts and cause him to be troubled when he thinks of God, and make him unable to sleep or pray, this was his weakness. These are the four proofs from this Psalm.
5. It is then immoderate when a person is so distressed over the sight of sin that he has no inclination nor heart to follow his calling to which God has called him in this world—that he can take no delight in his wife or children or station. When a person is so distressed that he cannot follow his calling, then it is sinful; the reason for this is that God commands nothing regarding our common calling as Christians that conflicts with our particular calling as human beings. Herein lies the craftiness of the devil: if he can keep a person from his calling through unrest of the mind, he then has a better opportunity to watch over an idle person.
6. When the distress of the soul over sin is detrimental to the health of the body; just as I hate robbery for a burnt offering <note>Isaiah 61:8; the author argues that God does not want a sacrifice—even a spiritual one—that involves "robbing" the body of health.</note>, it is also no offering to God which is detrimental to the body’s health; this was a weakness in Heman, *Psalm 88:4.* My soul is full of

<column-break/>

troubles, and my life draws near to the grave. Heman’s distress of soul was so great that it weakened his body and brought him to nothing but much weeping: so you also read of distress in *Psalm 31:10, 11.* Be merciful to me, O Lord, for I am in trouble: my eye is consumed with grief, my soul and my belly. For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing; my strength fails because of my iniquity: and my bones are consumed. There was a mixture of weakness in this, although it was over sin; for God does not require the bones to be consumed and the strength to be lost.
7. Finally, when a person is so distressed over sin that he is entirely despondent about clinging to Christ; when they say doubtingly what the enemies say mockingly: *there is no help for him in God.* When the sort or degree of the mind’s distress is so great that they [the ungodly] attain its end, then it is too great; what is the end of the mind’s distress over sin? The end is to make sin bitter to us and to make the soul look toward Christ. Thus I have given you the main points of this topic.

VI. The sixth question: you will easily ask me, if it is so that the godly are so greatly troubled in the soul over sin, what then is the reason that the ungodly live so joyfully under such a heavy burden of sin, and even have not a troubled thought nor a distressed heart all their days? That they cannot be in distress like other people? What is the reason for all this? This is a useful question which must be well noted.
There are ten general causes.
1. It comes partly from the wickedness and craftiness of the devil, that he does not trouble these souls—whom he hopes to damn when they die—over sin while they live; this is made known to you in *Luke 11:21.* When a strong man armed keeps his palace, all that he has is in peace. By the "strong man armed," the devil is understood; by the "palace" is meant the heart of an ungodly person; by "all that he has is in peace" it is made known that the thoughts of the ungodly are at peace; nothing disturbs him. When the devil possesses their hearts, he seeks to keep all his thoughts in silence and peace. **Stella** <note>original: "Stella," referring to Diego de Estella, a 16th-century Spanish Franciscan author.</note>, although a Popish author, has a good observation here: *one thing is to be observed here* <note>original: "unum est hic observandum"</note>: we must note one thing here, the great craftiness of the devil; the soul that he has in possession of that conscience, he does not want to trouble; to this end he labors (*he says*) *so that it suffers no sting of conscience* <note>original: "uti nullum conſcientiæ ſtimulum patiatur"</note>. The devil deals with the ungodly as the Babylonians did with the Jews in captivity: they wanted to make them sing. When the devil has the ungodly captive, he desires then that they should sing and be at rest, and that they should not be distressed all their days.
2. A second reason is: it arises from that gross ignorance which is in the ungodly person’s mind and understanding, through which he does not see the evil of sin and its heaviness; a blind mind and a dumb conscience go hand in hand together. If the understanding of man lacks an eye to see the evil of sin distinctly, the conscience will lack a hand to strike.
