# of a Contrite Soul.

**Column 1**

over sin; if sin were greater in a man’s eyes, the sorrow over sin would be greater in a man’s heart. It is worth noting the comparison of two Scripture passages: **Psalm 51:5**, *I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me;* and **Psalm 38:18**, *I am ready to halt, and my sorrow is continually before me.* How did it happen that the **Psalmist** <note>The author of the Psalms, usually referring to King David.</note> had continual sorrow over his sin, other than that he had the sight of his sin continually before him? It is the sight of sin that lets sorrow and dismay over sin into the mind. What is the reason that a man who sees a **lion** in the wilderness is terrified, but if a man sees a lion painted on a wall, he is not moved? The reason is that he knows a lion in the wilderness is of a biting and cruel nature, therefore he has fear of it; but he does not recognize such evil in a painted lion, and therefore he is not dismayed by it.

Beloved, if the ungodly could look upon sin as a loose lion in the wilderness that will fly into their face, the sight of sin would then move them; but they look upon sin as a painted lion; they do not see that it is so hateful and heavy. This is a great cause why men are so little troubled over the guilt of sin.

3. It springs from a hardness of heart and a searing of the conscience. **Romans 2:5**: *But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God.* To make it known to you that it is from the hardness of the heart and the searing of the conscience <note>The Dutch "toe-schoeppinge" refers to a conscience becoming calloused or "seared with a hot iron," making it lose all feeling.</note> that a man cannot repent, nor make confession, nor be dismayed over the evil he has committed, and of the guilt under which he lies. Calloused flesh is not sensitive to the touch of a pin; it is raw flesh that is sensitive. The seared consciences of men make it so that sin is no sword within them.

4. It arises from a constant habit of sinning; the habit of sin hardens the heart and sears the conscience. It is in this situation just as it is with someone who first learns a trade. He comes to the work with a soft hand, and when he begins to work with hard tools, he cannot work without pressing his hand and getting blisters upon it; but when he has been at the trade for many years, through constant work his hand is hardened, so that he can handle the work without getting blisters. It is exactly so with a sinner. Before a man is used to an evil way, the conscience is tender and full of gnawing; but to make a habit and trade of sin hardens the conscience and makes it fall away to nothing. Just as in a **Blacksmith's House**, a dog that first comes into the house cannot endure the sparks flying about his ears; but when the dog is used to it, then he sleeps peacefully. When the ungodly long accustom themselves to sin, the leaping of the flames from the fiery furnace-breath <note>original: "Oven-vongen"</note> flies about their ears, but it does not dismay them. All this arises from a habit of evil.

5. It arises from the ungodly deafening the testimony and rebukes of their conscience; as if quenching the Spirit in His holy move-

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

-ments toward the good. This causes **God** to withhold the holy movements of His Spirit. The deafening of the conscience makes it so that God no longer lets the conscience dismay you, but that you are given over to a foolish dullness and insensitivity of the conscience.

6. It springs from a misunderstanding that the ungodly adopt: that the dismay of the conscience over sin is an enemy of all worldly joy, and that once a man is dismayed in his mind over sin, he will never have another happy day, but that his head will hang and he will lead a melancholy, sad life. Beloved, the ungodly's pretexting of this holy unrest with these prejudices is a particular reason why they are no more moved over sin than they are. This is made known to us in **Ecclesiastes 7:4**: *The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.* The ungodly are afraid to be in the house of mourning, to mourn over their committed evil, because they think they would never have happy and comforting days in the world. The **Papists** <note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics used by Protestants.</note> bring this prejudice against the **Protestant** Religion: that *the Calvinist spirit is a melancholic spirit.* <note>original Latin: "spiritus Calvinianus est spiritus melancholicus."</note> Beloved, the way to have a well-ordered joy and comfort in the world is to have a Godly sorrow and an Evangelical mourning over the evil that you have committed in the world.

7. It springs from a groundless presumption that the ungodly have regarding the grace of forgiveness. Thus says an ungodly man: "If I have the hope of Heaven when I die, why do I need to be dismayed over sin? I hope it will not damn my soul; therefore I will not dismay myself. I will not lay sin upon my heart, for God will not charge the sin to me. I shall go to Heaven when I die; why then should I break my peace while I live?" This is a great reason for those who are not dismayed over sins. **Deuteronomy 29:19**: *And it come to pass, when he heareth the words of this curse, that he bless himself in his heart, saying, I shall have peace, though I walk in the imagination of mine heart.* God does not bless them, but they bless themselves. They presume upon mercy, Heaven, and blessing; therefore it is that they are not dismayed to add drunkenness to thirst. They can heap sin upon sin, but they cannot add sorrow to sorrow over sin.

8. The eighth cause is that men are at rest with a flattering and "untempered mortar" <note>original: "loosen kalck," a reference to Ezekiel 13:10–11, meaning flimsy or deceptive teaching.</note> coating the ministry of the Word. Men who, under the pretext of preaching pure grace, the love of God, and the merits of **Christ**, comfort everyone in all their sermons, make the way to Heaven wider than God has made it. God Himself gives this reason in **Isaiah 8:11**: *For the Lord spake thus to me with a strong hand, and instructed me that I should not walk in the way of this people.* They spoke of peace where they were in troubles. **Jeremiah 23:13, 14**: *And I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria; they prophesied in Baal, and caused my people Israel to err. I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem a horrible thing: they commit adultery, and walk in lies: they strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness: they are all of them unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah.*

->**Gilead’s Balm, or the Healing**<-

9. The ninth cause is because they have the help of outward prosperity and blessings in the world; this can be applied as much to the distress of the soul as to physical distress. Specifically, prosperity holds a person back from being troubled in their mind over the guilt of sin. **Hosea 12:8** <note>The Dutch text cites Hosea 12:9, but in most English Bibles this is verse 8.</note>: *And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance: in all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me that were sin.* They were a godless people, yet their prosperity so hardened their hearts in the evil way of sin. You have proof of this in **Pharaoh**; nothing hardened his heart more than prosperity. The fact that God raised him up to be a King hardened his heart. When men are overloaded with prosperity, they have no ears to listen to the gnawing of the conscience. **2 Chronicles 33:10**: *And the Lord spake to Manasseh, and to his people: but they would not hearken.* In prosperity, he would not listen to the knocking of his conscience until God laid him in chains; then he listened.

Lastly, men are not dismayed over sin because they do not perceive the omnipotence and the all-seeing eye of God. Although men are not atheists in the sense of arguing that God does not see all things, they are nonetheless atheists in regard to their lives, living in an evil way as if God did not see it. **Job 22:13-14**: *And thou sayest, How doth God know? can he judge through the dark cloud? Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven.* The Lord does not see it, the Holy One does not notice it; is there not a cloud between us and Him? The ungodly consider sin a small thing—"tut," they say, "the Lord does not notice it." What is the reason that men regard sin so lightly? Because they think God pays no attention to sin. Sin neither troubles nor dismays them because they think God does not see it; they do not consider God's Omnipotence.

I shall now briefly give you some useful points from what you have heard concerning the godly dismay <note>The Dutch "ontsteltenisse" refers to a state of being profoundly shaken, unsettled, or troubled in spirit.</note> over the guilt of sin.

For examination or testing: you have heard much regarding the distress of the soul which is found in the reprobate. The use of this is to exhort you to self-examination, so that you may be assured in your conscience that the distress of your soul over sin is an Evangelical <note>In this 17th-century context, "Evangelical" refers to a response prompted by the Gospel of grace and love for God, rather than "Legal" distress prompted only by fear of the Law and punishment.</note> and saving distress over sin, and is not the kind of distress that arises from the natural conscience in the ungodly. To satisfy you in this, I will set down certain signs.

1. Do you find in yourself that the distress of the soul is more over the evil that you have committed than over the punishment that you must suffer? My meaning is this: if you are more troubled over the sin than over the punishment to which you have made yourself liable by committing the sin; if you are more dismayed over the sin because it robs God of His glory than because it robs you of glory; then this is an Evangelical grace.

2. If you are more dismayed over the sin of nature <term>sin of nature: Original sin, or the inherent sinful inclination humans are born with, as opposed to "actual" sins committed in daily life.</term> than over the sins that break out in your life; if the sin of nature troubles you as much as the sin of your actions. We find nowhere in the entire Scripture that a godless man had any gnawing of conscience over the sin

<column-break/>

of nature. You, then, who can say that the sins of nature trouble you as much as the sins of your actions—this is a proof of an Evangelical distress over sin. **David** revealed this grace when he composed that penitential **Psalm 51** concerning the sin of adultery with **Bathsheba**. David did not only bewail the unchaste act, but he also mourned his impure nature.

3. You may be at peace if you are as much dismayed over the sight and guarding against the power of sin as over the guilt of sin. I am grieved not only because sin is so dangerous, but also because sin is so powerful in me.

4. The distress over sin is Evangelical when the degree of your mind’s distress is useful and helps to promote the purpose of that distress. That purpose (as I have told you) is to make sin bitter and to make **Christ** more worthy. If you then have such a degree and step of soul-trouble as to make sin bitter to you and Christ dearer to you, this is truly an Evangelical humiliation to which the Gospel exhorts us.

5. You may assure yourself that it is an Evangelical trouble of the mind when you are dismayed over sin as much because it is committed against a merciful God as because it is committed against a righteous God. A godless man can be troubled over sin committed against a righteous God, because justice will avenge the sin and the sinner. But a godly man says, "God overwhelms me with mercy"; when he can then mourn and be dismayed over sin, that is Evangelical. **Hosea 3:5**: *They shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days.* I may apply here the fable that **Plutarch** has in his *Moralia* <note>A collection of essays and transcriptions by the Greek philosopher Plutarch.</note> of the **Sun and the Wind** contending over who could make a traveler take off his cloak. Beloved, the storms and tempests of God's wrath may make an ungodly man leave off sin and be dismayed over sin; but when the Sun of God's Love makes the heart melt and causes you to cast off the rags of sin, this is a proof of an Evangelical distress.

Lastly: It is an Evangelical sorrow and dismay over sin when you can be just as dismayed over the sin that you know is forgiven as over the sin you know is not forgiven. If you are of this temperament, then a forgiven sin will fill your heart with trouble, so that you will bathe the sin in your tears of contrition, even though you know it is washed in the blood of Christ for forgiveness.

I shall now give you some practical instruments as rules. My work this morning will be to prescribe some rules to those who are greatly troubled in their minds over sin. The rules are of two kinds: some are instructional rules, and some are comforting rules.

<meta>This page continues the previous discussion regarding the "distress of the soul" over sin. While the previous page focused on why the ungodly do not feel this distress, this page provides practical rules for the believer to manage and remedy "disorderly" or excessive sorrow, directing them toward Christ’s grace and the support of the Christian community.</meta>

### of a contrite Soul.

I first begin with the instructional rules;

<margin>
Rules to prevent and to remedy the disorderly sorrow over sin.
</margin>

1. If you are too greatly unsettled by the guilt of sin, then observe this rule: take those troubled thoughts you have concerning the guilt of sin and spend them instead on the *power* of sin that is within you. This is a holy diversion <note>original: "diversie," meaning a strategic redirection of thoughts</note> and turning—to always be occupied with the power of sin. If Christians were more unsettled by the power of sin, they would be less unsettled by the guilt of sin: the devil does not care if the professors of Religion are restless Christians, as long as they are not Christians who have died to sin.

2. Keep your conscience <note>original: "ghewisse," an older Dutch term for conscience</note> pure, so that you do not add guilt upon guilt; for to add guilt upon guilt is the way to heap terror upon terror in your conscience. Guilt in the conscience causes this mournful fear, amazement, and dejection of the soul. If the conscience does not shut sin out, then sin will shut the door of the conscience from the outside. This is a rule given by **Bernard** <note>likely St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic</note>: the conscience must be comforted, yet it must first be purified and made clean. This rule is also given by **Eliphaz** in **Job 11:14**: *If iniquity be in thine hand, put it far away, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacles.* Beloved, this is the way to keep fear out: keep sin out. If the Conscience is not a swept and clean House, it will plague you and keep you unsettled. Do not think that the turmoil of the mind will be removed if the Conscience is not purified. **Proverbs 29:6**: *In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare; but the righteous doth sing and rejoice.* By the "snare," Solomon understands the terror of the conscience, which is evident by the contrast (the Interpreters say that in the Proverbs of Solomon, one contrast explains the other). Just as the righteous man here sings and is joyful in his grace, so the godless man has a snare in his sin: he shall have terror of conscience at the sight of sin. **Proverbs 15:15**: *All the days of the afflicted are evil: but a merry heart is a continual feast.* A good conscience has joyful days; but sin in the conscience is a means to awaken your despairs and fears, and to bring all your spiritual hope to the grave.

3. Watch out that you do not run to sin to soften the distress of the soul over sin; this is a third rule. To run to idle pleasures and fleshly delights to drown out the voice of the conscience—what is this other than running to the devil for a plaster <note>a medical bandage or ointment</note> to heal the wounds of your soul? Beloved, those people who go to sin to take away the distress of the mind are entering a path that pushes the conscience back, so that it may fall upon them all the more fiercely and cruelly later. It is just as if a thirsty man wished to quench his thirst with a poisonous drink. When you lie under God's wrath, and you drink a draught of sin to soften it, what are you doing but drinking so much venom? Many, when they are under distress of mind, run to sin for relief, but therein is a Serpent that offers them even more pain.

4. Fix your thoughts on the evidences of your grace when your heart is all too greatly unsettled by

<column-break/>

the sight of sin. Just as the distress of the conscience at the sight of sin restrains a person from becoming proud of his gifts of grace, so the sight of grace shall prevent a person from being too greatly unsettled by sin.

5. Ponder more in your reflections the comforting promises of the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangeliums"</note> than the threats of the **Law**. If I were speaking to a careless sinner, I would give him a completely opposite rule: that he should rather consider the threats of the Law than the promises of the Gospel. But a Sinner weighed down under the wrath of God must consider the promises of God's word more than its threats. **Proverbs 25:12**: *As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear.* The good word of the promises makes a poor soul joyful, one who stoops under the weight of sin. If a pot boils too fiercely, throw a handful of salt into it, and it will stop the pot's boiling; when your soul is stirred and restless over the distress of sin, throw in a handful of the salt of the Gospel's promises, and that shall still the turmoil of your soul. The promises are called by some the "instruments of Christian peace"; they are called God's proclamation of forgiveness to poor Creatures; they are like a Treasure in which one can read all his privileges. Therefore, meditate on them well.

6. Compare your sins with the merits of **Christ’s righteousness**, and you shall find that there is more in Christ’s righteousness to save than there is in sin to damn. Christ’s righteousness is imputed to a believer so that the guilt of sin should not be laid to his charge. Just as Christ’s Person is greater than your person, so also is Christ’s righteousness above your righteousness. The Apostle makes this known to us in **Romans 5:15**: *the free gift exceeds the offense.* Compare these then in your thoughts, and that shall be a means to take away the distress of your heart.

7. Reveal and disclose that sin which most disquiets your soul to a wise, compassionate, and experienced Christian; giving light to your sorrow through lamentation is a fit means to lighten the mind. If God, in the state of innocence, deemed it proper that Adam should not be alone but that he should have a helpmate, how much more do we in this Valley <note>The "Valley of Tears," referring to earthly life</note> need the help of another? If God deemed it useful, when Christ was in anguish, to send an Angel to comfort him, how much more then do believers need comfort when they are in spiritual distress, conflict, and temptation? The Apostle commands in this regard that they should comfort one another. **1 Thessalonians 4:18** and **5:14**: *Comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all.* God commands Christians to perform this mutual act of love: comfort one another. Just as in an arch that is artfully built, although all the stones hang downward, nonetheless one stone supports the other so that they do not fall. Beloved Christians, who are living stones in Christ’s spiritual building, you must be like the stones in an arch: though one stone hangs down, the next must nevertheless hold it up. This is what Solomon says in **Ecclesiastes 4:9, 10**: *Two are better than one... for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.*

# Balm of Gilead, or the Healing

<margin>3. Caution.</margin>
In this, three precautions are to be observed.

1. You must not reveal the sin that disturbs your conscience to everyone, but to an experienced Christian. **Judas**, when he was restless in his mind over betraying **Christ**, went to the High Priests and Pharisees and confessed to them that he had sinned by betraying innocent Blood; yet they had no compassion for him. In the same way, you might go to some with your complaints who would laugh at you and send you away with mockery. Go then to those who are compassionate and wise regarding the spiritual state of a Christian. Beloved, in physical illness, one does not tell every neighbor that they are sick, nor does one reveal their weakness to all, but one makes it known to a Doctor. It is not right, for a troubled mind, to run to everyone—to people who have no mercy, experience, nor wisdom to speak a word at the right time to a weary soul. Many people are like a herd of deer: when one deer is shot, all the rest run away from the wounded deer and leave it to worry for its own life. When a person is wounded in their conscience, and the arrows of the **Almighty** stick in them, then people think it is merely "melancholy" <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" was often used as a medical diagnosis for what we might call clinical depression or anxiety, sometimes dismissed by others as a physical ailment rather than a spiritual trial.</note> within them, and they shun and flee from them. Go then to those who have "bowels of mercy" <note>original: "ingewanden der barmherticheyt," a biblical idiom meaning deep, heartfelt compassion</note> toward you.

2. You must not disclose every particular sin for every small disturbance, unless your disturbance is very pressing and tormenting to your soul. Beloved, you do not always go to the surgeon when your finger hurts or if you have a small scratch; likewise, you must not disclose your particular sin for every light disturbance of the mind. Confession should not be made to another except when, after using all other means, you cannot comfort yourself, or when your soul is bitterly grieved within you. Only then, in case of great necessity, must you make your sins known to another.

3. When you follow this rule, beware in the revealing of your mind to someone that you do not deal hypocritically with that person. People sometimes come to the Ministers and tell them that they are unsettled in their minds, but they do not want to say what it is that pricks their conscience; instead, they reveal some other minor things, but do not state the actual matter that disturbs them. The tiger does not cry out near its nest, but far from it. Many people behave so that you shall not find their "nest"—they do not wish to reveal their beloved sins.

8. The eighth rule is this: when you are unsettled over sin, go then to **God** through **Christ** in prayer, to set your conscience at rest and to speak peace to your soul. When you are troubled, we <note>referring to ministers or fellow Christians</note> may come to speak peace, but it is God who *gives* the peace. This is one of God’s chief honors: that He is a God who comforts the downcast (**2 Corinthians 7:6**). *But God, who comforts the humble, has comforted us by the coming of Titus.* He is a God who creates peace out of nothing. It is remarkable what we read in **Isaiah 8:11**: *For the Lord spoke thus to me with a strong hand, and He instructed me not to walk in the way of this people.* When God wanted to comfort the Prophets against the accusations and conspiracies of the enemies of God’s Church, He spoke to them with a "strong hand." The tongue is the instrument of speech, not the

<column-break/>

hand; we speak with our tongues; we can speak comforting words to someone, but we cannot make you believe them. But the Scripture says that God speaks with His hand, because He can *do* what He says. His word is like Christ’s word was in **Matthew 8:26**: *Then He arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.* Beloved, God’s word has a "hand"—it can perform what it says. Go then to God through **Jesus Christ** in prayer. There are two things that you must desire from God in prayer if you wish to have the disturbance of your mind remedied:

1. Desire to have a share in the **Blood of Christ**, which earns your peace (**Colossians 1:20**): *And having made peace through the blood of His cross, by Him to reconcile all things unto Himself, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven.* There is peace with God and a peace in your conscience; this is a certain consequence of Christ’s negotiation with His Father in Heaven. This was foreshadowed under the Law (**Exodus 12:23**): *The Lord will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when He sees the blood upon the lintel and on the two side posts, the Lord will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come into your houses to strike you.* The blood of the Paschal Lamb sprinkled on the doorposts of any house was a sign that there was peace and safety for that house. If you then have the Blood of this **Paschal Lamb**, Jesus Christ, sprinkled on the doorposts of your conscience, this shall be a sign that there is peace and safety for your house; the striking angel shall pass by.

2. Pray to be a participant in **Christ’s Spirit**, which works peace. Therefore the **Holy Spirit** is called the **Comforter**. He is called the Holy Spirit to show that His office <term>office: a formal duty or role assigned to a person</term> is to work holiness in us. He is called the Comforter to show that also, on the other hand, His office is to comfort His people. Thus, I have hastily run through these instructional rules to take away the excessive disturbance of the soul over sin.

<margin>Rules of Comfort.</margin>
Secondly: I will now set down some rules of comfort which shall comfort the soul of the godly who are truly tormented and restless over the guilt of sin. There are six comforting rules to give comfort to the godly who are unsettled over sin.

1. Take this rule to hearten you: if the power of sin is not master over you, you may be assured that the guilt of sin shall never damn you. Therefore think: if sin does not have a reigning power over you, it shall also never have a damning power over you. O you Christian, dead to sin! You may be unsettled over what you committed when you were a child; but have you killed this sin? Those sins that you have rooted out shall never damn you. It may be that you are unsettled over the guilt of sin whose power you have already destroyed; lift up your hope; the guilt of sin shall never damn you if the power of sin does not reign over you.

2. It is better for a Christian to have his soul too unsettled over sin than to be too little or not at all unsettled. It is better to have a disturbed and terrified conscience than a numb <note>original: "domme," meaning dull, senseless, or unfeeling</note> conscience. Better to have a

## of a Smitten Soul.

A wound with raw and living flesh is healed sooner than a wound with dead flesh <note>The author uses a medical analogy common in the 17th century: "dead flesh" refers to necrotic or gangrenous tissue that has lost all sensation, whereas "raw flesh" is painful but still vital and capable of healing.</note>. If your conscience is dead flesh, you shall not be healed as quickly as if your conscience were raw and bruised flesh. It is a sign of leprosy if there is dead flesh in the sore; a clouded and dull conscience indicates an unclean leper who is still in the state of Nature <note>The "state of Nature" refers to the human condition before receiving God's grace—a state of spiritual death or indifference.</note>. It is better that the conscience be God's Lieutenant-Governor, being all-too-busy, too much rebuking and accusing you, than to have no duty of the conscience to awaken you. This is another observation to comfort your smitten soul.

<margin>Micah 7:19.</margin>
3. Consider that God's mercy and Christ's merits, in the forgiving of the guilt of your sin, are much greater than the greatness of your guilt. Romans 5:15: *But not as the offense, so also is the free gift. For if through the offense of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many.* The meaning is that the gift of Jesus Christ, and the worthiness of this one man, far exceeds the guilt and the evil of sin. It is written in Psalm 32:10:
> He that trusteth in the Lord, mercy shall compass him about.
My guilt and sin are great, but God's grace and mercy are yet greater. When God is said to forgive sin, it is testified of Him that He casts the sins into the depths of the Sea. The Red Sea could drown Pharaoh and his host just as easily as a single man. Beloved, the Red Sea of Christ's Blood can cover a heart full of sins just as well as a single sin. The Sea covers the whale just as it covers the tiny fish; the Sea of Christ's blood covers great sins as well as small ones. David makes an argument from this in Psalm 25:11:
> For thy name's sake, O Lord, pardon mine iniquity; for it is great.
It is noted that the Ark, in which the Moral Law lay, was entirely covered with the <term>mercy seat</term> <note>The "mercy seat" (Dutch: *versoendecksel*) was the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant; the author argues that just as the lid covered the stone tablets of the Law, Christ’s grace covers our breaking of that Law.</note>. This was to show that Jesus Christ, the grace of God, and the merits of Christ bring about a reconciliation that covers all the breakings of the Law. The mercy seat is broad and large enough to cover everything; therefore, let such things comfort you.

4. Consider that the more unrest of the mind you have now over the feeling of sin, the less you shall have thereafter. God deals with His people as landowners do with their tenants: when the landowner takes a large "entry fee" <note>original: "bate," referring to a premium or lump sum paid at the start of a lease.</note> for the beginning of a house or land, he takes a smaller rent thereafter. God takes a large entry fee from you at first: He makes the sin cost you many tears, and many nights and days of unrest. The larger the fee God takes from you, the fewer annual rents of sorrow He expects from you. The more you are distressed for the present, the less woe and pain shall be your portion hereafter. Am I restless now? It may be that I shall have greater peace when I die, so that in the declining

<column-break/>

of my days I might have joy and peace in faith. Think then: if God, at your first coming to Christ, makes you pay dearly for your sin and makes it cause you pain, you shall have less sorrow and trouble in the time to come.

5. If you are distressed in your mind over sin, take this heart-comfort: the more you are distressed over sin, the nearer you are to struggling out of the claws of the devil. When the devil makes your conscience keep silent, it is a proof that the devil and sin possess you entirely. When the devil has a long stay in someone, he will not disturb them so much. In Mark 9:26, it is said that when the devil came out of the child, he tore him greatly, and the child became as if dead. When the devil possesses a person entirely, then he does not disturb them. As Stella <note>Likely Diego de Estella (1524–1578), a Spanish Franciscan mystic and author widely read in the 17th century.</note> says: the devil does not let him feel even a prick of the conscience. But when the devil is about to go out and the sin is being cast out, then the devil tears the man and lays him down as if dead; this is a characteristic of the devil. Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Church Father whose commentaries on the Book of Job were foundational for medieval and early modern theology.</note> says in his exposition of Job: "The devil works great terrors and doubts of the heart for this reason, because sin is being cast out of the heart." Let this then comfort you: when the devil disturbs you more than ordinary and your conscience is terrified, so that you are a burden to yourself—Beloved, this is a proof that the devil and sin are being cast out. Comfort yourself then, saying: "I hear the voice of my conscience daily, it makes my guilt known to me; praise be to God, I hear my conscience roaring; the more hope I have that the devil and sin are being cast out."

6. Take this for your comfort: that more promises in the Gospel are made to such a person than to any other sort of people in the world. I could give you a multitude of promises to people in this situation. Matthew 11:28:
> Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Also Isaiah 4:10, 11, and 35:4, and 57:15. I could give you such texts as these, where God gives abundant promises to those who are restless in their minds over sin. When children are well, they have only toys to play with; but if a child is sick, then the Mother goes to the cabinet and seeks fine things to quiet the child. Beloved, it may be that healthy Christians go on their way comforted and now and then have a glimpse of God's countenance, but God’s rich cabinet of promises is opened for the sick. When a poor sinner fears that his sins are not forgiven, then God comes with a promise to comfort him, that his sins are forgiven. The healthy children are well-loved by the parents, but the sick child sits on the lap; the healthy children may have bread and butter, but the sick child has comforting things <note>Likely referring to delicacies or medicinal treats given to soothe an invalid child.</note> to cheer him. Beloved, God’s sick children—who are sick over sin and are very distressed in their minds—them God sweetens with consolation to satisfy their troubled spirit. Oh! let these comforting words sink into your heart.

### of a Stricken Soul.

Turn <note>The Dutch "keere" suggests a turning or comparison between types of conscience.</note> toward a wounded and prickling conscience, rather than a clouded and insensitive conscience regarding sin. There is more hope for a soul in spiritual sickness who is restless and feels the accusation of their conscience—lying under the distress of its own remorse—than for one who lies in a spiritual "death-sleep," sleeping and snoring in their sin, which never disturbs them. A wound with raw and living flesh is healed sooner than a wound with dead flesh. It is better that the conscience acts as God’s Deputy—too busy, too much rebuking and accusing you—than to have no duty of the conscience awakened within you. This is another consideration to comfort your stricken soul.

3. Consider that God’s mercy and Christ’s merits, in forgiving the guilt of your sin, are much larger than the greatness of your guilt. **Romans 5:15**: *But the free gift is not like the offense. For if by the one man’s offense many died, much more the grace of God and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, has abounded to many.* The meaning is that the gift of **Jesus Christ**—the dignity of the Person—far exceeds the guilt and the evil of sin. It says in **Psalm 32:10**: *He who trusts in the Lord, mercy shall surround him.* My guilt and fault are great, but God’s grace and mercy are even greater. When God is said to forgive sin, it is testified of Him that He casts sins into the depths of the Sea. The **Red Sea** could drown **Pharaoh** and his army just as easily as a single man. Beloved, the Red Sea of **Christ’s Blood** can cover an army of sins as easily as a single sin. The Sea covers whales as well as tiny fish; the Sea of **Christ’s blood** covers great sins as well as small ones. **David** makes an argument from this in **Psalm 25:11**: *For Your name’s sake, O Lord, pardon my iniquity, for it is great.* It was noted that the **Ark** in which the Moral Law lay was entirely covered by the Mercy Seat <note>The "versoen-decksel" or Mercy Seat was the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant, symbolizing where God meets humanity through atonement rather than judgment.</note>, to signify that **Jesus Christ**, the grace of God, and the merits of **Christ** bring about a reconciliation covering all the breakings of the Law. The Mercy Seat is broad and large enough to cover everything; therefore, let yourself be comforted by this.

<margin>Micah 7:19</margin>
4. Consider that the more unrest of mind you have now over the feeling of sin, the less you shall have afterward. God deals with His People as landlords do with their tenants: if the landlord takes a large entry fee for the moving into a house or land, he takes a smaller rent thereafter. God takes a large "entry fee" from you at first: He makes sin cost you many tears, and many nights and days of unrest. The larger the fee God takes from you, the less "annual rent" He expects from you. The more you are distressed in the present, the less fearful pain shall be your portion hereafter. Am I restless now? It may be that I shall have greater peace when I die, so that in the passing

<column-break/>

of my days I might have joy and peace in faith. Think then: if God, at your first coming to **Christ**, makes you pay dearly for your sin and causes you pain, then you shall have less sorrow and trouble in the future.

5. If you are distressed in your mind over sin, take this comfort: that the more you are distressed over sin, the nearer you are to wrestling out of the claws of the devil. When the devil makes your conscience wring, that is a proof that the devil and sin [no longer] entirely possess you <note>The author suggests that a peaceful sinner is one the devil already "owns," while a struggling sinner is one the devil is losing.</note>. When the devil has a long stay in someone, he will not distress them so much. In **Mark 9:26** it is said that when the devil came out of the child, he tore him greatly, and the child became as if dead. When the devil possesses a person entirely, he does not distress them. As **Stella** <note>Likely referring to Diego de Estella (1524–1578), a Spanish Franciscan mystic and author popular in the 17th century.</note> says: the devil does not let him feel a single prick of conscience. But when the devil is to go out and sin is cast out, then the devil tears the person and lays him down as if dead; this is a characteristic of the devil. **Gregory** <note>Saint Gregory the Great, often cited for his commentaries on Job.</note> says in his explanation of **Job**: "Therefore the devil stirs up great terrors and doubts of the heart, because sin is being cast out of the heart." Let this then comfort you: when the devil distresses you more than ordinary and terrifies your conscience so that you are a burden to yourself—Beloved, this is a proof that the devil and sin are being cast out of you. Comfort yourself then, saying: "I hear the voice of my conscience daily; it makes my guilt known to me; praise be to God, I hear my conscience roaring; the more hope I have that the devil and sin are being cast out."

6. Take this for your comfort: that more promises are made in the **Gospel** to such a one than to any other kind of people in the world. I could give you a multitude of promises to people in this situation. **Matthew 11:28**: *Come unto me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.* **Isaiah 4:10, 11** and **35:4** and **57:15**. I could give you many such texts where God gives overflowing promises to those who are restless in their minds over sin. When children are well, they only have "prickles" <note>likely "toys" or "trifles"</note> to play with; but if a child is sick, then the Mother goes to the cradle and seeks fine things to quiet the child. Beloved, it may be that healthy Christians go their way comforted and now and then have a glimpse of God’s face; but God’s rich cabinet of promises is opened for the sick. When a poor sinner fears that his sins are not forgiven him, then God comes with a promise to comfort him—that his sins are forgiven. The healthy children are well-loved by the parents, but the sick child sits on the lap; the healthy children may have bread and butter, but the sick child has comforting things to console him. Beloved, God’s sick children—who are sick over sin and are greatly distressed in their minds—those God satisfies with comfort to soothe their distressed spirit. Oh! let these comforting words sink into your heart.

<header>Gilead’s Balm, or the Healing [of a Smitten Soul]</header>

## XVII. SERMON.

->Psalm 42, verse 12.<-

> Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him; he is the... salvation of my countenance, and my God. <note>In modern Bibles, this is usually Psalm 42:11. The "salvation of my countenance" is an older way of saying God is the one who brings a healthy, joyful look back to a person's face.</note>

I shall now give you some other rules for those who weep and say, "Lord help me, I am so far from being too much troubled that I find my heart not troubled at all; I do not find my soul even troubled over many chief sins for which I am guilty." Therefore, I shall give you some instructive and some heart-comforting rules.

First, I shall show how a child of God—who does not find their soul sensibly touched or "Evangelically troubled" <note>The author uses "Evangelically troubled" to describe a specific kind of sorrow: one prompted by the Gospel and a love for God, rather than "legal" trouble prompted only by a fear of punishment or hell.</note> over committed sin—may obtain that their soul might be Evangelically troubled over sin.

1. Do not be restfully satisfied with a general and confused sight of sin, but strive to find out the most prominent of your hard-heartednesses, in order to have a particular and distinct sight of them. This is the course that God’s People have held. Acts 2:37. *And when they heard this, they were pricked in the heart, and said to Peter and the other Apostles, "Men and brothers, what shall we do?"* Peter did not say here in general terms that they were sinners; but from among all sins, he singled out one: *You have crucified the Lord of Glory.* And when they heard that, then they were pricked in their hearts; he singled out that sin so that they might bring their hearts to brokenness and contrition.

<margin>John 4.</margin> When Christ wanted to bring the Samaritan Woman to a state of remorse and trouble over sin, Christ singled out one sin from all her other sins, and told her that she was a harlot. The Scripture lets us know that the singling out of that one sin made her see all her sins; for the woman said in verse 29, *Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did.* Yet Christ had only spoken of her adultery. Do you then likewise: what is that "Delilah" <note>A reference to the biblical Delilah who brought down Samson; here used as a metaphor for a "darling sin" or a secret vice that one is reluctant to give up.</note> in your bosom that delights you? Single out that sin, and that is the way to obtain a clear sight of all your wickedness; a general and confused obsession with sin only produces a general humiliation. It is the ruin of many souls to be satisfied with a general obsession with their guilt; they live and die without any remorse in their consciences that serves toward salvation. He who writes of Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal. Protestant writers often used him as a foil to argue against the Catholic view of "good works" and sinless living.</note> says of him that when he died, such was the innocence of that man that he could not name a single sin in himself that he should confess. This did not arise from the man's actual innocence, but it sprang from a confused sight and observation of his ways, because he had only a general view of his sins. You read of Ahimaaz, that he ran as a messenger to bring the news of what had

<margin>2 Sam. 18:19.</margin> happened. David asked him, "What news?" and Ahimaaz said, "I saw a great tumult when Joab the King's servant and I your servant were sent off, but I do not know what it was." Many people do the same with their sin as he did with his message; they are troubled over sin, but

<column-break/>

<margin>Dan. 2.</margin> they know nothing except in general; they do not know what the sin is. Just like Nebuchadnezzar: he called his wise men and sorcerers together and said, "Tell me the interpretation of my dream, for I have dreamed, but I do not know what it was." Some people say they have sinned, but they do not know what sin they have committed, or what particular sin they have done.

2. Look upon small sins as being clothed with great weight. Beloved, this is the reason why people are not troubled; they look at their small sins as "small," but they do not see them as clothed with a multitude of hateful circumstances. Granting that your sin was a small sin, invisible to the world, yet if you will clothe and surround this sin with circumstances—it may be a sin against your conscience; against great grace; a sin committed against many promises. Justinus <note>This likely refers to St. Augustine (Latin: *Augustinus*), as the famous story of the stolen pears is found in Book 2, Chapter 4 of his *Confessions*.</note> takes this course in the second book of his *Confessions*, Chapter 4, regarding his robbing of an orchard: "I did such," (he says) "not forced by hunger or poverty, but out of wantonness; for I stole that of which I had enough of my own, yes, and even better," etc. And thus he magnifies his sin. Beloved, if you do not find your souls troubled over sin, then clothe them with aggravating circumstances. Thus we read of one who wanted to magnify his sin; he said, "It is true the devils have sinned, but they have not sinned against a Savior as I have done; Adam sinned, but he did not sin against Christ as I have done." Magnify a small sin in this way, and this will work humiliation.

3. Read while contemplating forgiving grace. It is true that the godless misuse forgiving grace to become arrogant; yet forgiving grace, when rightly applied, is the right way to break and trouble the soul. Beloved, lay yourself in Christ’s arms, on the bed of His Love, and that is the way to break your stubborn heart. A child of God cannot help but bathe his sin in the tears of contrition when he knows that his sins are bathed in Christ’s Blood for forgiveness.

I shall now also give you some rules of comfort, which are these. Is there then comfort for a person who finds his heart hard, and who seldom or never finds his soul troubled over the feeling of sin?

I. Be comforted if that which you lack in "Godly sorrow" over sin is fulfilled by you through "Holy care" and watching against sin. If a child of God does not have a weeping eye over sin, but he has a waking heart against sin, that is pleasing to God. If there are no tears in your eye over sin, as long as there are weapons in your hand to fight against sin, such pleases God to the highest degree. The Chief Leader of our salvation, Jesus Christ, would rather see a warring weapon against sin than a weeping eye over sin; this is a comfort.

II. A second comfort is this: that the lack of being troubled over sin does not always arise from a hardened conscience, but often from an ignorant mind. If the conscience has an eye to see the sin, then it will also have a hand to strike because of the sin. The conscience then lacks a hand because the person's judgment <note>In this context, "judgment" refers to the faculty of the mind that evaluates and understands facts.</note>

<meta>catchword: lacks (ont-)</meta>

It also offers comfort, suggesting that a proactive struggle against sin is more important to God than the physical act of weeping.</summary>

it lacks an eye to distinguish evil.

III. A third comfort is this: that even if a godly person is not distressed over sin for a certain time, there is nevertheless a great difference in that situation between them and the godless. He may not be distressed, but he *wishes* he were distressed; a godless person is not distressed, and he wishes never to *be* distressed. A godly person may not mourn, but he *wants* to mourn, and he loves that Minister who touches his heart; but a godless person cannot bear him. There is then a great distinction between the one and the other: a godly person does not dare to strike his conscience on the mouth <note>original: "zijn gewisse niet om de mont slaen"; an idiom meaning to silence or forcefully suppress one's inner voice</note>; a godless person, when the conscience begins to disturb him, does whatever he can to still the cry of his conscience. When the conscience arrests a godless person regarding guilt, they do not run to God; they make the conscience drunk with fleshly pleasures and idle amusements, so that they might thereby escape the arrest of Conscience. But the Godly dare not do so; instead, they say to the Conscience: "Exonerate me when I do well, and accuse me when I do poorly." This is the conduct of a godly person.

IV. Take this for your comfort: although you are not as distressed over sin as you wish, you nevertheless have as much as is acceptable to God. This is a firm rule in Theology: that the **desire for any grace is the grace itself**. A true desire for conversion *is* conversion; a true desire to mourn over sin *is* mourning over sin. If you only once wish for a distressed heart, that is then a Holy distress. This is a great mercy, that God in the Scriptures considers the desire for any grace as the grace itself. It is remarkable what we read in Nehemiah 1:11.

<margin>Nehemiah 1:11</margin>
> O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants, who delight to fear your name, etc.

Compare that place with Chapter 5:15 ("But the former governors who were before me burdened the people, etc. but I did not do so, because of the fear of God") to notice that the *delight* to fear God is the *fear* of God; a desire to convert is the conversion; a longing to be distressed is a Holy distress, as long as it is a whole, sincere, and insatiable desire for some grace. Thus we read of Abraham; when God dealt with Abraham, what did God say to him?

<margin>Genesis 22:16</margin>
Because you have done these things; therefore I will do thus and so with you—even though he had not yet actually offered his son. Theologians say from this that the desire in God's estimation is as the deed itself. Therefore, when Paul recounts Abraham's deed, he says:

<margin>Hebrews 11:17</margin>
By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. Beloved, it would be a great terror for the godless if the Scripture said to us that the desire for sin is sin; this is the same before God. Therefore Christ says in Matthew 5:28: *That whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.* The desire and the deed are one before God, although it is not so among men. God regards the desire of the eyes as an unchaste thought. 1 John 3:15: *Everyone who*

<column-break/>

*hates his brother is a murderer.* God regards the desire to kill someone as a murder. Now, on the other side, it is a great comfort for the Godly that the desire for grace is the grace itself. I recount this for you who are sad because you cannot mourn; you who do not mourn, but indeed desire to mourn.

->So much regarding the Rules of Comfort.<-

<margin>Utility.</margin>
I shall give you only this application, and thus I shall end this teaching on the disquietude of souls. This is a utility of "prevention," so that you guard yourselves against falling into evil misunderstandings regarding the soul's distress over sin. The devil might present something that is neither grace nor distress of the mind over sin; from which I want you to guard yourself, so that you might not be misled in these matters.

I shall give you five misunderstandings to guard against.

<margin>Cautions or Preventions.</margin>
1. Guard yourself that you do not mistake natural **Melancholy** <note>In the 17th century, "Melancholy" was viewed as a physical illness caused by an imbalance of humors (fluids), often resulting in what we would call clinical depression today. The author is distinguishing medical depression from spiritual conviction.</note> for a Divine sadness and distress of the mind over sin. Many people, whose temperament is sad, heavy-hearted, and fearful, think that Melancholy is a Divine sadness; yet there is a great distinction between natural Melancholy and spiritual disquietude.

1. Natural Melancholy has many imaginings in the fantasies, but spiritual disquietude arises from the conscience, based on the feeling of God’s wrath and the greatness and wickedness of sin.

2. Melancholy is cured by a Physician <note>original: "Medecijn meester"</note>; but all the Physicians in the whole world cannot still the disquietude of the godly soul.

3. Melancholy makes a person sad, but he cannot say why; but a person in spiritual troubles says: "It is sin that presses my conscience, and such a fall grieves my soul." A melancholic person cannot do this; he cannot say, "It is this specific grief that I am guilty of."

4. Melancholy is recognized by one's natural complexion: a heavy eye, a sad face; but spiritual distress in the Conscience can exist in one who has a cheerful, joyful, and friendly appearance. Therefore, the theologians note of David that when the Scripture says he was "ruddy" <note>David's "ruddy" appearance (1 Samuel 16:12) was traditionally interpreted by theologians as a sign of a naturally healthy, cheerful disposition, highlighting that his internal spiritual sorrow was not due to a naturally gloomy personality.</note>, such a sign indicates joyfulness and cheerfulness; yet he was grieved and sighing under the distress of the soul over sin.

5. Melancholy diminishes the strength of the body, but sadness over sin does not.

6. A melancholic person cannot take delight in God, nor in his required duty; whereas a person under the distress of the mind—although he is distressed over sin—nevertheless rejoices in God and delights in his calling. Divine sadness and spiritual joy are not contradictory things, but are helpful to one another.

II. Guard yourself, that you do not think that a distress of the mind over sin is that which is only a distress over some outward difficulty in the world. When a person is distressed over the loss of a child, or over the loss of his city, many...

### III.
A third consolation is this: although a **Godly person** <term>Godly person: a "Godtsalige," referring to someone living a life of active piety and devotion to God.</term> might not feel unsettled over their sin for a certain time, there is nevertheless a great difference in that situation between them and the **godless**. The Godly person is indeed not unsettled, but they *wish* they were; a godless person is not unsettled, and they wish they might *never* be unsettled. A Godly person does not mourn, but they want to mourn, and they love that Servant of the Word <note>The "Servant" refers to the minister or preacher.</note> who touches their heart; but a godless person cannot endure him. There is then a great distinction between the one and the other. A Godly person does not dare to strike their conscience on the mouth; but the godless, when their conscience begins to unsettle them, does everything they can to silence the cry of their conscience. When the conscience seizes a godless person for their guilt, they do not run to God; they instead make the conscience drunk with fleshly pleasures and vain delights, so that they might escape the arrest of Conscience. But the Godly dare not do so; instead, they say to their Conscience: "acquit me when I do well, and accuse me when I do poorly." This is the conduct of a Godly person.

### IV.
Take this for your consolation: although you are not as unsettled over sin as you wish, you nevertheless have as much as is pleasing to God. This is a fixed rule in Theology: that the **desire for any grace is the grace itself**. A true desire for conversion is conversion; a true desire to mourn over sin is to mourn over sin; if you only wish for a troubled heart, that is then a **Holy disturbance**. It is a great mercy that God, in the Scripture, considers the desire for any grace as the grace itself. It is remarkable what we read in Nehemiah 1:11: *O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name,* etc. Compare that place with Chapter 5:15: (*But the former governors that had been before me were chargeable unto the people... but so did not I, because of the fear of God;*) to notice that the *desire* to fear God is the fear of God itself. A desire to convert is conversion; a longing to be unsettled is a Holy unsettling—if it is but a whole, upright, and insatiable desire for grace. Thus we read of Abraham;

<margin>Genesis 22:16</margin>
When God dealt with Abraham, what did God say to him? *Because thou hast done this thing...* because of which I shall do so-and-so with you; yet he had not actually sacrificed his Son. Theologians say here that the desire in God's estimation is the same as the deed itself; therefore, when Paul repeats Abraham's

<margin>Hebrews 11:17</margin>
deed, he says: *By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered up Isaac.* Beloved, it would be a great terror for the godless if the Scripture spoke to us this way: that the desire for sin is sin itself. This is how it is with God; therefore Christ says in Matthew 5:28: *That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.* The desire and the act are one with God, although it is not so among men. God regards the desire of the eyes as an unchaste act; 1 John 3:15: *Whosoever hateth his*

<column-break/>

*brother is a murderer.* God regards the desire to kill someone as a murder. Now, on the other hand, it is a great comfort for the Godly that the desire for grace is the grace itself. I relate this for you who are sorrowful because you cannot mourn; you who do not mourn, but indeed desire to mourn.

---

### Thus much regarding the Rules of Consolation.

<margin>Utility.</margin>
I shall give you only this application, and thus I shall end this teaching on the disquieting of the soul over sin; and that is a utility of prevention, so that you guard yourself against falling into evil misunderstandings regarding the soul's disturbance over sin. The devil might present something that is neither grace nor a true unsettling of the mind over sin; from which I want you to guard yourself, so that you might not be misled in these matters.

### These misunderstandings I shall give you to guard against.

<margin>Cautions or preventions.</margin>
1. Guard yourself that you do not mistake **natural Melancholy** <term>Melancholy: in the 17th century, this was seen as a physical illness caused by an imbalance of "black bile," leading to gloominess. The author distinguishes this physical condition from spiritual sorrow.</term> for a Divine sadness and unsettling of the mind over sin. Many people, whose temperament is sad, heavy-minded, and fearful, think that Melancholy is a Divine sadness; yet there is a great difference between natural Melancholy and spiritual disquiet.
1. Natural Melancholy possesses many images in the imagination, but spiritual disquiet rises out of the conscience, from the feeling of God’s wrath and the greatness and wickedness of sin.
2. Melancholy is cured by a Physician; but all the Physicians in the whole world cannot still the disquiet of a Godly soul.
3. Melancholy makes a person sad, but they cannot say why; but a person in spiritual trouble says this: "it is sin that presses upon my conscience, and such a fall grieves my soul"; which a melancholic person cannot do—they cannot say "it is such a corruption of which I am guilty."
4. Melancholy reveals itself in the physical complexion—a heavy eye, a sad face; but spiritual disturbance in the Conscience can exist in one who has a cheerful, joyful, and friendly being. Therefore, Theologians note concerning David that when the Scripture says he was "ruddy" <note>original: "voor dachtich," likely a transcription error for "van een schoon gelaat" or similar, referring to 1 Samuel 16:12.</note>, it is a sign of joy and cheerfulness; nevertheless, he was sorrowful and sighing under the unsettling of the soul over sin.
5. Melancholy diminishes the strength of the body, but sorrow over sin does not.
6. A melancholic person cannot delight themselves in God, nor in their required duty; whereas a person under the unsettling of the mind, although they are disturbed over sin, nevertheless rejoices in God and delights in their calling. Divine sadness and spiritual joy are not conflicting things, but are helpful to one another.
II. Guard yourself that you do not think it is an unsettling of the mind over sin which is only an unsettling over some outward hardship in the world. When a person is unsettled over the loss of a child, or over the loss of their city, many...

->**Healing of a Smitten Soul.**<-

...deceive themselves in this, and take this worldly sorrow for a spiritual disturbance; if that were true, then **Ahitophel** <note>A counselor to King David who betrayed him and later hanged himself in despair (2 Samuel 17).</note> would have been disturbed over sin, for he came home grieved and hanged himself. Then **Haman** <note>The antagonist of the Book of Esther who was distressed by his loss of status before being executed.</note> would have had a Godly sorrow, for he was disturbed over his cross in this world; he came home grieved and told his friends what had happened to him. Beloved, you must not regard worldly disturbances as spiritual troubles; but do this: when you find your heart overwhelmed with worldly disturbances, try to lead them toward spiritual troubles, to shed tears over sin when you shed tears over the loss of your worldly estate. Turn that flood of tears to weep over sin; turn the mill of Godly sorrow to grind your heart to dust in the feeling of sin. It is a deepening of tears to shed them over every matter. Beloved, to shed tears over worldly things is to be excessive in tears.

### III. 

Beware that you do not think yourself disturbed over sin simply because it causes shame among men; many reprobates are disturbed over sin—but why? It is not because God is dishonored by the sin, but because they suffer shame through their sins; this is not an Evangelical disturbance. Many people are like **Judah**, Gen. 38:23. Then Judah said: "Let her keep the things for herself, lest we be laughed at." As if he wanted to say: if the woman should say that I had committed adultery with her, then I would suffer shame; leave her alone. Thus people also cry out; they want their conscience to leave them alone, and they want to leave the sin alone, so that they might not be shamed. If it is such that the hiding of a sin can hide their shame, then they do not concern themselves with it. The Heathens go further; <term>Seneca</term> <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> says: "Even if I knew that all the people of the world would be ignorant of what I might do, I would still not wish to sin, and that because of the ugliness of sin." <term>Tullius</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman.</note> has a remarkable passage, and it is to be wondered at that the Heathens reached so far; he says: "Though I thought that all my sins could be hidden from the whole world, we must nevertheless do nothing greedy, nothing unchaste, nothing unjust; we must do no evil, even if the world never saw us." Many are more grieved over sin because it brings them to shame; this is not a spiritual and Evangelical disturbance over sin.

### IV. 

Do not consider that to be a right disturbance over sin which is more over the punishment than over the evil of the sin; more because there is a Hell *for* the sin than because there is a Hell *in* the sin. **Cain** was more disturbed over the punishment than over the sin; he cried out, "My punishment is greater than I can bear"; but Cain

<column-break/>

did not cry out, "My sin is greater, which I have committed."

### V. 

Do not consider that to be a right disturbance of the soul over sin which is only over great and gross sins, without having any gnawing over secret and lesser evils. For many people, if one stares them in the face <note>Meaning a blatant, obvious sin.</note>, even though all their other sins never disturb them, they nevertheless conclude that this is a Godly sorrow and Evangelical gnawing. Alas; Beloved, **Judas** was disturbed over one sin, but not over other sins; he was disturbed over his ill-gotten goods. But to be disturbed over one sin, and not over all sins, is not an Evangelical disturbance; he who is not disturbed over all sins of which he knows himself to be guilty, is disturbed over no sin. Behold the godless: you shall find them many times disturbed over great wickednesses, but never over lesser ones. These sins, which disturb the hearts of the Godly, shall not even break the slumber of their sleep. He can go his way cheerful and rejoiced under the guilt of these sins which disturb the soul and break the peace of the Godly every day. These sins are like ornaments to the godless, which they wear like a golden chain around their neck; they wear and display their pride, they consider sin to be their ornament. That which is one man's ornament is another's torment; his pride, lust, and his complimentary oaths are his delight; but it is a torment for the Godly. Therefore, do not consider that disturbance of the soul to be a Godly disturbance.

### VI. 

Do not consider that to be an Evangelical trouble over sin if it does not concern original sin as much as actual sin. <term>Master Bolton</term> <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631), a prominent English Puritan clergyman and author.</note> testifies of a High German in his time, who was a great professor of religion, and he was once overtaken by drunkenness. I went to that man to show him the evil of drunkenness, to make him see what a beastly sin it was; I labored to show him what this was; I tried to make him see the wickedness of a drunken nature. He readily admitted to me that drunkenness was an evil sin, but he would not admit the godlessness of his nature. This man bewailed the act of drunkenness and fell into other sins; but at last, God moved this man again, and being disturbed, he sought out the same man and said: "Now I believe your words; I find an unchaste, adulterous, and a drunken heart; I see now that it is worse than a drunken act"; and after that, he fell no more into the same sins.

Thus I have, in seventeen sermons, run through the distress of which the Psalmist here complains:

> Why art thou cast down, O my soul, and why art thou disquieted in me?

> Colossians 3, verse 4.
> When Christ, who is our life, shall appear; then shall ye also appear with him in glory.

<margin>1st Sermon.</margin>

Before I can treat these words in particular, I must point out three things regarding the letter in general: first, to what people it was written; secondly, when; thirdly, by what occasion it came to be.

First, the people to whom this Letter was written were the Colossians, inhabitants of a city named Colossae, a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor <note>An ancient region in what is now central Turkey.</note>, as appears in Chapter 4, verse 16. There they are commanded to read this letter in the Church of Laodicea, which indicates that Laodicea was located close to this Church of Colossae. Now, Laodicea is said in Revelation Chapter 1, verse 11, to be one of the seven Churches of Asia; consequently, the inhabitants of this place also lived there. So much is said of the Persons. We read in the Histories (they are but human accounts, and therefore I give them to you as such) and ancient Authors testify to it, that this Church of Colossae, after the death of Paul, fell into terrible errors; and that they were therefore, by God’s righteous judgments, together with Laodicea and Hierapolis (shortly after Paul’s death under the Emperor Nero), overtaken by an earthquake which destroyed the dwellings and inhabitants of this city; from which I—if it were true—give you only this observation: That the best Congregations do not stand so firmly that they cannot be scattered if they come to teach errors.

Secondly, as for the time when it was written, it is evident that Paul wrote it when he was in prison in Rome; and from this we must learn that experiences in prison are the clearest experiences. For read this Letter; there is not a Letter in the Scripture that contains more matter for practice in the Christian life than this one written by Paul in prison. I could also remark something from the fact that Paul, when he was in prison among the Heathens, had the freedom to write for the strengthening of God's Church, namely: That the Heathens showed more mercy to Christians when they lay imprisoned than our persecutors in these latter days have done to the Godly, when they were given neither pen, nor ink, nor paper; when their friends were not allowed to visit them, but when they were

<column-break/>

locked in a dungeon, deprived of all liberty; they were more cruel and wild than the Heathens were in former times. Paul, though he was in prison, nonetheless had the freedom to write to the Church. But

Thirdly, the occasion by which this Letter was written was this: Paul being in prison, Epaphras, who was the Teacher of that Church of Colossae, came to visit him in the prison at Rome. From this conduct of the Church, I might observe this: That when God’s children are imprisoned for a good cause, a prison should not estrange them from one another. See, Epaphras having come to Rome, relates to Paul the state of that Church, and Paul acknowledged that, as he had heard from Epaphras, they were growing in the Gospel. And besides that, he told him in Chapter 2 of evil Teachers, who were becoming numerous in that Church; that though they had been converted to the faith, some wandering spirits were troubling these Saints with Philosophical disputes <note>Refers to "philosophy and vain deceit" mentioned in Colossians 2:8.</note> and Mosaic church-customs <note>Legalistic adherence to Old Testament ceremonies.</note>, attempting to turn their minds away from the simplicity of the Gospel. And upon hearing this, Paul writes this Letter to them, to confirm them in the faith they had accepted. The matter of the Letter will fully explain its foundation; for it deals primarily with those things which most serve to be worked out in the service of God.

I shall not weary you with the book in general; it is only very necessary in the first explanation of my Text that I show you the aim and the sense of the same. I shall not bring you further back than to the Chapter from which my Text is taken, and let you briefly look over the three preceding verses; as you survey them, you shall notice the aim and the connection of these words.

First, draw your heart away from the world; for Jesus Christ is the Head, He is risen, and has ascended into Heaven, and sits there at the right hand of His Father; and if the Head is in Heaven, where then should the members be but where the Head is? <meta>This page continues the opening sermon of Christopher Love's series on "The Glory of Heaven and the Terror of Hell." ### Christ is the Life

Secondly, *Seek those things which are above / for ye are dead / verse 3.* That is, you are dead to sin; you have a different kind of life than the world has / namely, a life of grace. Just as a dead man does not contemplate sweet songs / nor the pleasant displays that might be performed for him; so you ought also to be as if dead / not preoccupied with anything here below / for you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. You have a life hidden in Christ / men cannot see it / and they do not know the excellence and glory of it.

Thirdly, *Thus he says / why they should not set their hearts on things here below (a powerful motivation for the godly) because they shall live a glorious life with Christ one day.* Now if they were to have a glorified life in the other world / then it is reasonable / that they seek those things / which belong to that life and that world / and not only things / which are in this despicable world: And this motivation is in my Text / *When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory.* So you see the connection of the words / now note the meaning thereof.

In these words, three things are to be explained / First, what it means / that Christ is said to be our life: Secondly, what it means / that Christ our life shall be revealed? Thirdly, what it means / that we shall then be revealed with him in glory?

First, what is understood by / *Christ who is our life?* I answer / Christ Jesus is called our life / not essentially / as if we shared in that same essential life / which Jesus Christ has / but he is said to be our life causally or effectively / that is / he is the Author and cause / and disposer of our Christian life. Now there is a two-fold life in a Christian / and Christ is the two-fold cause of this two-fold life. 1. There is a life of grace / which we call sanctification / of which Christ is the cause. 2. There is a life of glory / which we call glorification / which we shall enjoy with Christ / when the world has ended: of both these lives Christ is the cause / he is the working cause / and the meriting cause; through his death he has obtained / that we should live eternally; so that the meaning is clear; Christ is our life; that is / he is the Author of this life / and through his death the meriting cause of our eternal life / since he died / to destroy him / who had the power of death / namely the devil.

Secondly; what does that manner of speaking imply / when Christ who is our life shall be revealed? Answer: In Scripture mention is made of three kinds of special revelations of Jesus Christ. First, there is a revelation of Christ in the flesh bodily / of which one reads in 1 *John 3 verse 8.*

<column-break/>

Which they will not admit / but they say / that Christ shall appear on earth before this time of glorification.
