# Appearance for Judgment.

If Christ were to personally reign here for a thousand years / I shall reduce the arguments against it to seven main points.

1. From this, it would follow that there must be two Ascensions of Christ: for as is known / Christ ascended to Heaven from the Mount of Olives forty days after his rising from the dead. Well / if Christ were to come down to Earth for a thousand years / he would also necessarily have to ascend to Heaven again / because the Scripture says / that Christ must come again from Heaven / when he comes to judge. Philippians 3 verse 20. So he would then have to ascend for a second time / and so there would then be two Ascensions / which, you can well imagine, is entirely unfounded in God’s word / as it has neither footing nor place there.

2. This absurdity would follow: that there would be two resurrections. For those who hold this view / say / that when Christ comes for these thousand years / the dead who were Martyrs / shall rise; so there will then be two kinds of resurrection / one for the good at that time / and another for the wicked on the last day / which, how it conflicts with Scripture / will appear from John 5 verses 28, 29: *The hour is coming in which all who are in the grave shall go out, the good to the resurrection of life, the wicked to the resurrection of damnation.* The Scripture places the resurrection of the righteous and unrighteous at the same hour: furthermore, the Scripture says / that when the resurrection occurs / Christ shall deliver up his Kingdom / and not receive a Kingdom.

3. If this were granted / then one would certainly know the time / in which the day of judgment would be. And why? Because according to their view, Christ must come to judgment at the end of those thousand years / and then they could say a thousand years in advance / when the day of judgment will be; which greatly conflicts with Scripture: for Christ himself tells us / that neither he as man / nor the Angels in Heaven know the day or the hour.

4. This absurdity would follow / that many sayings in the Scripture would be made false / which speak of the state of God's people while they live in this world. What does the Scripture say? *In the world you shall have tribulation, but in me you shall have peace,* John 16 verse 33. And *those who want to live godly shall be persecuted.* 2 Timothy 2 verse 12 <note>Though the text cites 2 Timothy 2:12, the quote "those who want to live godly shall be persecuted" is usually found in 2 Timothy 3:12.</note>. And Hebrews 12 verse 6: *Whom God loves, he chastens,* and *we must enter into the Kingdom of Heaven through many tribulations,* Acts 14 verse 22. Now, if this view were granted / that Christ shall reign for a thousand years / in which time there will be no persecution or tribulation / or difficulty at all; (Indeed, some say that there will also be no sin there) then you see well from those sayings / how greatly this would be against the Scripture: for as long as you are in this world / you shall be subject to difficulties / tribulations, and persecutions / which that view completely throws down.

5. If Christ were to reign on Earth for a thousand years / then it would follow / that some on Earth must live for a thousand years one after another without dying; this view proposes this / which conflicts with the frailty of human nature / being made only of clay / and against the Scripture / which says that the oldest man who ever was / was Methuselah, and he did not live a thousand years. Indeed, David sets man's life shorter / that if a man lives eighty years, his life is but labor and trouble / which differs much from a thousand / and yet this view being held / the other must necessarily follow.

6. If this were established, it would follow / that Christ, while still in the world, has not yet had a visible Kingdom; for those who are of this opinion / say / that Christ had not yet a visible Kingdom / until this one of a thousand years / in which he shall rule on Earth.

7. And finally, it would follow / that Christ would leave his Church in as miserable a state after the thousand years as before / if not in a worse one; for after a thousand years the Devil would be loosed, and deceive the nations: Now it is not believable / that Christ, having reigned for a thousand years / would ascend to Heaven again / and leave his Congregation and the Nations to be deceived and overcome by the Devil.

The next thing I must do / is to prove from the Scripture / that there shall be no such appearance of Christ / of which these men speak; to confirm this / I shall cite three Scripture texts; the first is Hebrews 9 verse 28 / where it stands / *to those who look for him for salvation, Christ shall be seen a second time without sin.* Just as Christ in his first appearance appeared with sin / truly with our sins being imputed to him / <note>original: "toe-gerechent"</note> <gloss>Theological term meaning our sins were legally credited to Christ's account so he could pay for them.</gloss> not with inherent sin / for in this way Christ did not sin / but he was in his first coming made to be sin / because our sins were laid upon his shoulders by imputation; But for the second time he shall appear without sin / that is / then there shall be no sin laid upon him / but he shall come in a time of salvation: note / the Scripture sets only two kinds of appearance of Christ / namely / 1. His first appearance in the flesh / God revealed in the flesh. 2. His second appearance for judgment / he shall appear a second time for salvation; But if one granted a thousand years / and that Christ would reign personally on earth / then this Text would have to be changed / to say Christ shall appear a third time. The first time in the flesh / the second time for a thousand years / and the third time to come for judgment; But the Scripture (as if rejecting this view) speaks only of the second appearance of Christ / namely / when he shall come for the salvation of man. Yes / but they object and say / that this place is for them / and that this second appearance of Christ is his appearance to reign for a thousand years; therefore they think / that they are on the strongest side: to which I answer / and shall prove it from two reasons in the Text / that nothing else is spoken of here / but of Christ's coming for judgment / as appears from the context of verse 27. *It is appointed for man once to die, and after that the judgment,* and then come these words / *Christ shall appear a second time without sin for your salvation;* so that it is clear / that this appearance of Christ is on the day of judgment / as the context indicates. 2. Because the Text says / *he shall be seen for your salvation;* yet those who hold / that Christ will come to Earth for a thousand years / know that it will not be for their complete salvation / for they are on Earth / and they are not fully blessed / until Body and Soul are in Hea-

# Christ’s Glorious [Appearance]

is; therefore, this appearance of Christ must necessarily not be understood as referring to a thousand years, but of his coming for judgment, when Body and Soul shall be preserved by him.

<margin>Acts 3:20, 21</margin>
The second text is Acts 3, verses 20 and 21: *He shall send Jesus Christ, who was preached to you before, whom the Heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God has spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.* I wish to urge this text against this opinion <note>The "opinion" refers to the Millenarian view of a literal 1,000-year reign.</note>—namely, that the Heavens must receive Christ, which is to say, contain and hold him, just as he is now bodily in Heaven—and for how long? Until the time of the restoration of all things.

Those who hold that opinion intend to pull this text to their side, claiming that this "time of the restoration of all things" is the period of the thousand years. But I shall show that this time of restoration, until which Christ must be kept in the Heavens, cannot be taken for that time of Christ’s reign which they imagine, and that for two reasons. 1. Because at the time of those thousand years, everything would not yet be restored; for as long as there is sin in the world, all creatures lie under a curse because of sin. However, even then there would be sin in the world, for the godless shall be in the world, and Satan shall be released again; thus there can be no restoration of all things then, since sin subjects the Creature to the curse and to bondage.

<margin>Rom. 8:22, 19</margin>
The Apostle explains it in Romans 8, verse 22: *We know that the whole creation groans together and travails in pain together until now; and not only this, but we ourselves also await the adoption as children, namely the redemption of our body.* Compare that with the 19th verse: *The creature, as if with its head lifted up, awaits the revelation of the children of God.* Here the Apostle tells us that the creature groans and lies under a curse, and will do so until all the sons of God are revealed, until all the elect are saved; which cannot be before the Day of Judgment. The Apostle explains it here thus: until that day in which all the elect of God shall have their bodies glorified, until that day the Creature lies under the curse. So, this "restoration of all things" can be understood as no other time than the time of Christ’s coming for judgment; and until that time, Christ must be kept in Heaven; Heaven must receive him. 2. This time of restoration cannot be the time of a thousand years because all the Prophets indeed prophesied of the restoration of all things, but nowhere of a thousand years: they only give testimony of the former. Thus, this cannot be that time; it must therefore be taken for Christ’s coming for Judgment, and until that time the Heavens must embrace Jesus Christ.

<margin>Col. 3:4</margin>
The third text is here in our own words, Colossians 3, verse 4: *When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall we also appear with him in glory.* When Jesus Christ appears in glory, then all the elect shall be glorified with him; which necessarily can be no other time than when Christ shall appear to judge the World. So much has been said

<column-break/>

to satisfy those doubts, and as proof that Christ shall not personally reign on earth for a thousand years with his Elect before he comes to judge the World.

The fifth and last doubt is: whether Jesus Christ, when he shall appear in glory to judge the world, will take any length of time to carry out the judgment of the world?

In answering this, I could present to you the loose and unfounded thoughts of many. I remember reading in the Turkish <term>Alkoran</term> <note>The Quran.</note> that they expect a Christ, although their <term>Mahomet</term> <note>Muhammad.</note> has deceived them; and they believe that this Messiah will judge the World, and that he will be occupied with it for fifty thousand years. This is their ridiculous thought, which has neither proof nor reason in it. The <term>Millenarii</term> <note>Millenarians; those who believe in a literal 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth.</note> (following them somewhat) say that Christ will judge the World for a thousand years, but this has no basis or certainty in Scripture at all. As for what the Scripture declares regarding the time, it seems to sufficiently indicate that Christ will not take up much time in judging the World. For take note: the sayings in Scripture regarding Christ’s coming for Judgment do not propose a long row of years, but never more than a day; and so we often read in Scripture. It is called "a day of wrath."

<margin>Rom. 2:5</margin>
*They treasure up wrath for themselves against the day of wrath,* Romans 2, verse 5. And "a day of the righteous judgment of God."

<margin>Acts 17:31</margin>
And Acts 17, verse 31: *God has appointed a day in which he will judge the world by a man, Christ Jesus.* And Christ speaks of a shorter time than a day, saying: *Of this day and hour no one knows, not the Son of Man, nor the Angels in Heaven.* So the Scripture sufficiently teaches that Christ will take very little time to pronounce the Sentence of acquittal over the elect and of damnation over the godless. I shall give you only this reason:

When Judges sit for a long time over the judging of persons or matters, this proves two things in them: either that they see no proof brought against the evildoers, or else that they are doubtful in their thoughts as to what judgment they should pass over such criminals. But neither of these two things can apply to Christ; for Christ knows all deeds; there shall be no defense or proving on the day of judgment. There shall be no Lawyer to plead for you; no testimony to prove for you. Your own conscience shall be your witness to testify against you; it shall be your Book.

<margin>Rom. 2:15</margin>
Man's conscience shall condemn him on that day, Romans 2, verse 15. So it most accords with Scripture to believe that Christ will not use a great length of time to bring this work to an end—to judge the World, to damn the godless, and to pronounce his elect blessed.

Now, the Utility <note>The practical application or moral lesson.</note> of all I have said regarding this Doctrine of Christ’s glorious appearance to judge the World shall be a utility of terror.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the Second Coming of Christ. # Appearance for Judgment

To all souls who have a guilty conscience; to all you who do not have your Judge as your Jesus, as your friend; who have no right to Jesus Christ; who have not made your peace with your God: O, this day of Christ’s coming for judgment ought to be a day of terror for you. It ought to make the blood rush to your face, your limbs to tremble, and bring horror and dismay upon you when you think of the deadly proceedings that shall be carried out against unconverted souls on that day.

I have read a saying of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"; St. Jerome (c. 342–420 AD) was a Latin Church Father best known for translating the Bible into the Vulgate.</note>, which he says of himself:
> Whether I eat, whether I drink, or whether I do anything else, it seems to me I constantly hear the voice: "Arise, O man, and come to judgment."

Beloved, it seems to me you ought to hear that voice, just like Jerome; you ought to hear it when you are occupied in your lusts, in your deceits, and in your other sins. O, if you heard this voice then! "For this, O man, shall you come to judgment; for this, O man, shall sentence be passed upon you on the last day." What a fearsome bond this would be to hold you back from those sins into which you are now ready to run. This doctrine of Christ’s future appearance to judge the world ought to be a means for all kinds of people to keep them from sinning against this God. The Holy Apostle makes this use of it in Acts 17, verses 30 and 31:
> God now commands all men to repent; Why? Because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a Man whom he has ordained;

and Acts 24, verses 15 and 16: "Because God has appointed a day for judgment, therefore," says Paul, "I desire to maintain a good conscience." O beloved, keep your consciences pure; for on this day, Christ shall disclose all your secret adulteries, and all your robberies and deceits which you have committed in this world. Let Paul’s argument then be yours, and say: "I want to maintain a good conscience, because God has ordained a day in which he shall judge the world through Jesus Christ."

And just as this doctrine of Christ’s appearance for judgment ought to be a means to make you labor against all sin, so also specifically against these five sins:

1. It ought to keep you from **drunkenness**. "Take heed" (we read in the 21st chapter of Luke <note>The source text cites "4. cap. Luce," which appears to be a printer's error for Luke 21:34.</note>) "lest at any time your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness, so that this day come upon you unawares." You who always want to be in such company, you who cling so to this sin, who love drink so much—think on this: the Day of Judgment shall fill that mouth of yours with fire, which you now fill with water <note>In this context, "water" is likely used generically for strong drink or liquid.</note>. In that day, you who are now so sated with wine and beer shall not have one drop of cold water to cool your burning tongue. Let this restrain you, all you who are inclined toward this sin.

2. Let Christ’s coming for judgment be a deterrent to you from **adultery**. Hebrews 13, verse 4: "Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." The Lord shall judge every sinner, but these especially. God shall judge you for your deceit and for all that you have done in the body, 2 Corinthians 5,

<column-break/>

verse 10. But God shall judge the adulterer in an extraordinary way. 2 Peter 2, verses 9 and 10: "God knows how to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished; but chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness." *Chiefly them.* For this reason Solomon says that those who are hated by God go to the harlot. Therefore, O you adulterers, fear if you have defiled your body, and let the day of judgment disturb your consciences, if anyone here before the Lord is guilty of this sin.

3. This doctrine ought to keep you from all **mockery and contempt of God’s children**. Jude verse 15:
> Behold, the Lord Jesus shall come with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment against all, because of all the hard words.

Take note: the Day of Judgment shall be a terrible day for you, because of all your slandering and mocking of the godly.

4. Christ’s appearance to judge the world shall be a terrifying day for all **ignorant and disobedient** people who do not obey the Gospel of Jesus Christ. 2 Thessalonians 1, verses 7 and 8:
> The Lord shall be revealed from Heaven with his mighty angels, in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore I pray you (I know that I speak to a mixed multitude, to all kinds of people) lay this to your heart; if any of you be guilty of this sin, how can you look your Judge in the face when God specifically tells you that he comes to condemn you for these sins?

5. And finally: it must withhold you from the sin of **oppression and cruelty**. James 2, verse 13: "Judgment without mercy shall be upon him who has shown no mercy." If you want mercy to be shown to you on the day of judgment, then show mercy while you live in this world. "Judge not, that you be not judged." The Day of Judgment shall fall hard upon all of you, you oppressors, who cause the faces of the poor to waste away through usury <term>charging excessive interest on loans</term>, robbery, and violence. Woe, woe to you on that great day. So much has been said of this second Doctrine.

I proceed now to this third and final observation which these words yield, taken from these last words: *then shall you also appear with him in glory.* The observation from this is: **That Jesus Christ has reserved the full glorification of his elect until the time of his glorious appearance to judge the world.** When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall you also be revealed with him in glory.

In handling this doctrine, I shall follow this plan: 1. I shall show what it is for the elect to be fully glorified by Jesus Christ; 2. why Christ has reserved this fullness of their glory until he shall come to judge; and then I shall conclude everything with an application.

I begin with the first: what is understood by the full glorification of the elect? For an answer, take this description: The full glorification of the Saints of God is the most blessed and most happy, indeed also unchangeable state, which God out of his free grace through Jesus Christ—

# 308

->The Appearance of the Saints<-

Christ has prepared for the elect in Heaven, to be enjoyed after the day of judgment, at which time the body shall rise from the grave and be reunited with the soul. Thus, both soul and body shall be delivered from all sin and misery, and shall share in the glory with God, with Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, with the Saints and Angels for eternity. This is what we call glory: that reunion of body and soul, through which both shall become participants, enjoying the glory—the special communion with the three persons of the Godhead, with all the Saints and Angels, for eternity.

This appearance in glory, or this full glorification of the elect, consists of two things. 1. The glorification of the body, having risen from the dead and being reunited with the soul. 2. The glorification of the soul. I shall begin with the first branch, namely the glorification of the body. When Christ shall come to judge the world, the bodies of the elect shall be glorified as well as their souls. And in speaking of the glorification of the body, I shall demonstrate two things: 1. Why the body as well as the soul must be glorified; 2. In what this glory of the body consists, or what specific things make the bodies of men "glorified bodies."

First, why must the bodies of the elect be glorified in the heavens as well as their souls? I answer for three reasons.

1. Because their bodies have suffered for the sake *of Christ* <note>original: "Christi"</note>; *Galatians 6 verse 17.* "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body"; that is, he suffered for Christ and was scourged for him. Now, if the body suffers for Christ, then it is just that the body is also glorified through Christ. If the body, through suffering, resembles a crucified Christ, so it is just that the body, by being glorified, resembles a glorified Christ; for this reason then shall the elect be glorified.

2. The body has a share with the soul in all the good deeds and holy exercises that the soul performs; *2 Corinthians 5 verse 10.* You shall give an account of all that has happened in the body, whether it be good or whether it be evil; while you are in the body, so the body participates in all religious duties. While the soul prays, the eye looks up toward Heaven, the lips move, the hands are lifted toward Heaven, and the whole body is at work. If then the body does its part with the soul in these exercises, so shall the body also have a share with the soul in glory.

3. Then there is that natural sympathy <note>The author uses "zamen-gevoeligheyt," a literal translation of "sympathy," meaning "feeling together."</note> that exists between the body and the soul; therefore shall the one be glorified as well as the other. That sympathy exists because of the close union between soul and body, such that the soul can suffer nothing without the body suffering the same. If the soul is sorrowful, the face is pensive, the mind is oppressed, the head is heavy. If the mind is joyful, the face is also pleasant; such a natural sympathy or "suffering-together" exists between soul and body. And if that is so, then that natural pull shall also be in Heaven, so that when one is glorified, the other shall be as well.

<column-break/>

Secondly, I shall point out to you wherein the glory of the bodies of the elect shall consist; to that end, I shall present seven glorious ornaments which the elect in Heaven shall enjoy, which your bodies here in this world cannot enjoy.

1. This makes the bodies of the elect glorious on the day of judgment: that their bodies shall be spiritual bodies; *1 Corinthians 15 verse 44.* "A natural body is sown, a spiritual body is raised." The body, while it lives here and also when it dies, is only natural; but it shall rise from the grave as a spiritual body. When I speak of a natural body, I mean a body which requires natural refreshment to sustain life, such as food, sleep, clothing, and the like; and when I say that the body in Heaven shall be spiritual, I do not mean it as *Proclus* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who held that the celestial body was made of light or ether.</note>, the Platonic philosopher, believes—that the bodies of men shall be changed into air or wind. Nor do I mean it as if the essence of our bodies would be taken away and they would become spirits, which errors *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD) was a historian and bishop who defended the physical reality of the resurrection against Gnostic or purely spiritual interpretations.</note> refutes; *Book 2, Tome 1, against Heresies, page 182.* For we shall have these hands, these eyes, and these feet in Heaven which we now have on Earth; "for with these my eyes," says *Job*, "shall I behold my Savior." When I then call it a spiritual body, I mean to say this: your bodies shall not be like natural bodies that require external refreshment; you shall have no need of food, no sleep, no clothing, but you shall be (as Christ says) like the angels in glory; *Matthew Chapter 22 verse 31.* You shall not marry, nor be given in marriage; you shall have no need of husband, nor wife, nor estate, nor house; but your bodies shall be spiritual, refreshed by the spiritual enjoyment of God. When Christ comes to judge the world, your bodies, which are now natural, shall be made spiritual.

2. Your bodies shall be immortal bodies. Now you have a mortal body, and a dying body, and therefore that name may be given to you: that you are a mortal human, whose breath is in his nostrils. Now you have a dying body, which every moment is subject to falling away into dust and earth; but when Christ comes to judgment and you appear with him, your bodies shall become immortal. *1 Corinthians 15 verses 42, 43.* "The body is sown in corruption, and it is raised in incorruption; this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." These bodies of yours shall be incorruptible and immortal; never shall they die. If I nevertheless say that the bodies of men shall be immortal, note: 1. That the bodies in Heaven shall not be as immortal as God is; for He is essentially immortal. God’s essence is immortal; but we are immortal not essentially, but entirely through the grace of God, keeping us in that immortal state; therefore the Scripture speaks thus of God, *1 Timothy 6 verse 16.*

The only wise, and only immortal God: God alone is essentially immortal; but the elect of God are immortal in their bodies through the grace of God, which preserves them in that state. 2. You must make a distinction between this immortality and that which Adam had before he sinned; he was immortal, but only in such a way that he was subject to death at every moment under a certain condition, and so he died; as long as Adam did not sin, he would be immortal, but if he sinned he would die: but the believers are immortal in a different way than Adam, because they are immortal through *Jesus Christ*, so that it is impossible that they should ever die. 3. We are not immortal in the same way as the Angels: for they are so through the grace of creation, being spiritual beings; but our bodies are such through God's special ordinance, and the perfect renewal of God's image in us. 4. We are not immortal in the same way as the Devils are; for the Devils and the damned in Hell shall be immortal and never die, neither their bodies nor their souls, but that is a miserable immortality; it would be good for them if they were not immortal; it would be good for them if they could die; because their life is a miserable life/ but our life is a glorious life; we shall live in Heaven in glory with *Christ* and the Angels, and not in misery in Hell with the Devils and damned Spirits. This then is your Privilege, your prerogative: your bodies, just as they shall be spiritual, shall also be immortal bodies; they shall never die.

3. The bodies of the elect shall have this glorious gift: they shall be <term>impassible</term> <note>original: "onlydelyke," meaning incapable of feeling pain or being harmed</note> bodies; they shall not be susceptible to any suffering. Here in this world you are subject to much suffering, much sorrow, many diseases; here you suffer sometimes through poverty, through hunger, thirst, cold and nakedness; here you are subject to imprisonments and diseases, fevers, the stone <note>a historical term for kidney or bladder stones</note>, strokes, pleurisy, and a world of other diseases; here your bodies are passible <note>subject to feeling and suffering</note>, but in Heaven you are subject to no sorrow or suffering at all. In Heaven you shall cause sorrow and sighing to flee from you: here is your body, as the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or a similar classical authority</note> calls it, like a hospital, full of weaknesses; all the parts of the body are here subject to suffering; but in Heaven the body shall not be so. Here the body is, as *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author known for his Natural History</note> calls it, a Warehouse of all kinds of diseases; *Pliny* says that in his time the body of man was subject to three hundred kinds of diseases, but now I may say three hundred times more; the body in this world is subject to many thousands of weaknesses, but here is your glory, that you shall be delivered from all these in Heaven; no suffering shall come to the elect.

4. The bodies of the elect shall be beautiful. *Philippians* 3, verses 20-21. *Our citizenship is in Heaven; from whence also we look for the Savior, who shall change our lowly body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body.* Just as *Christ* was beautiful, so shall the bodies of all believers be glorified like *Jesus Christ*. Here your bodies are lowly, being made of poor material, and tending toward a lowly end, namely to destruction, where the worms shall gnaw your flesh, and from whence it comes; *Eliphaz* in *Job* calls it a house of 

<column-break/>

clay, *Paul* an earthly house, the Philosopher a wicked hut; the Preacher <note>Ecclesiastes</note> says in Chapter 12 verse 7: *Dust shall return to the earth as it was*, subject to evil and stinking diseases, a place full of filthiness, a Warehouse full of all weaknesses; but there you shall be glorious; *Christ* shall make your lowly bodies conformable to his glorious body. It is the word of *Thomas Aquinas* <note>a highly influential 13th-century theologian</note>, That if there be any ugliness in the body in this world, all shall be taken away and covered with beauty on the day of judgment. Just as if someone were a monster, or had a hunched back, or lacked a limb, or such like, in that day all these deformities shall be taken away. Your bodies shall be beautiful, like *Christ's* glorious body.

5. Their bodies shall be swift in movement. Here our bodies are sluggish and heavy: We are here like exhausted Horses, who go slowly in all godly contemplations, and must be driven with spurs to all good duties: But there you shall go swifter than the *Chariots of Amminadab* <note>A biblical reference to legendary speed from the Song of Solomon</note>, in all the ways of God; then you shall ascend in the praise of your Redeemer and in his service, with greater speed than the winged Birds that fly in the Heaven. That shall be your benefit, when you shall be in glory: Your bodies shall be light and swift.

6. Your bodies shall be pure bodies, and that is certainly also your prerogative: for even if your bodies were immortal, impassible, beautiful and swift; if they were nonetheless sinful, sin would be your stain in Heaven. But this is your glory: your bodies shall be pure in Heaven, and have no spot at all. *Romans* 8 verse 23: *We wait for the redemption of our body.* Now you are shackled and surrounded with sin, and attached to temptations; but then your bodies shall be delivered, sin shall no longer lead you captive, it shall no longer entice you nor hold you fast. Then you shall have no occasion for that complaint of *Paul's*, *Romans* 7 verse 24: *O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?* You shall be set free: for that time shall be the redemption of your body, a deliverance of the same from sin and sinful practices.

7. Your bodies shall be glorious bodies, so says my Text. You shall appear with him in glory: And so says *Paul* in another place, *Philippians* 3 verse 21: *He shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto Christ's glorious body*; so it stands in 1 *Corinthians* 15 verse 43: *It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory*: and *Matthew* 13 verse 43: *Then shall the righteous shine forth as the Sun, in the Kingdom of their Father*; so also *Romans* 8 verse 18; *Daniel* 12 verse 3. So you see now both why the body shall be glorious, and in what the glory of this body consists.

Well, by way of Application, is it so, that you who are God's elect, shall one day be glorified both in your body and in your soul through *Christ Jesus*! Oh so let me persuade you, that you do not let your bodies be instruments of your Savior's dishonor, for these bodies shall be so glorified by him. Let not these bodies of yours dishonor your *Christ*,

<margin>VII. Sermon.</margin>

THE Teachings that I have drawn from these words were three; The first two I have handled and finished. The last one I am still upon is this: That Jesus Christ has postponed the full glorification of his elect until that time when he himself shall appear in glory to judge the world. When he appears, we shall also be revealed with him in glory. In my introduction to this, I showed you, 1. What this appearance in glory is. 2. That this glory consists of two parts, namely: 1. The glory of the body, and 2. the glory of the soul. Of the body I told you that it would have seven glorious adornments at that time of Christ's appearance.

Now I come to the second Point, to treat of the glory of the soul; namely, that, just as the body shall be a glorified body (as the Apostle speaks, *your lowly body shall be conformed to the glorious body of Christ*), so also shall your souls, you elect, on the day of Christ's appearance, be glorified souls.

How should I now venture to speak of the glory of the soul, as Gregory <note>Likely referring to Gregory the Great (c. 540–604) and his work *Moralia in Job* (Books on Morals).</note> says in his *Books of Morals*; If a mortal man speaks anything of that eternal bliss of the Saints in glory, he does as much as if a blind man were debating about the Light, which he has never seen, and consequently can speak nothing distinct about it. We shall hereafter know more than the Scripture speaks of it, or your hearts can conceive; so that I may break out into that ecstasy of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 2 verse 9: *Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and it has not entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him.* The eye has seen many wonderful things in nature; it has seen crystalline mountains and rocks of Diamonds; it has seen gold mines and rain of Pearls, and lands 

<column-break/>

full of spices (so say the travelers and the writers of geography); the eye has seen (as Mr. Bolton <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631), a well-known English Puritan clergyman and author.</note> speaks) the Pyramids of Egypt, the Temple of Diana, the Tomb of Mausolus, which by the geographers are placed among the wonders of the world; and yet the eye, which has seen so many wonders in the world, could never sufficiently look into the glory of Heaven. Nor has the ear heard it; the ear of man has heard the most delightful and most ravishing choruses, but never has the ear heard that sweet and pleasant Music which shall be in glory; and it has never entered into the heart of man; and what can the heart of man not conceive? man is made so magnificent that he can grasp everything that is, was, or ever shall be. Man can conceive that all the Stones of the Earth are changed into Pearls, and all the grass into Jewels; he can conceive that all dust is changed into Silver and the entire Earth into a lump of Gold. Man can conceive that the Air could be Crystal, every Star a Sun, and each of those Suns ten thousand times greater and brighter than it is now. So much a man can grasp, but in no way can he grasp what the glory of Heaven is, which God has prepared for those who love him. Therefore you cannot expect that I should speak much of that which the Scripture says so little of, and all that it says of it is but in obscure words; But I shall in moderation and truth speak a little of what the Scripture proposes concerning the glory of the soul when this life is at an end.

All that I shall say of it, I shall include under two heads.

This glory consists first of something which is a privation <note>In the sense of a removal or absence of negative things.</note>, and secondly of something positive. Something privative—that is, the soul shall be delivered from everything which can make it miserable. Something positive—for the soul shall be clothed with everything which can make it blessed. These are the two principal adornments of the soul.

First, The soul shall be delivered from everything which could make it miserable, namely these three: sin, the causes of sin, and the punishments or effects of sin: only these can make your soul miserable; and from all these shall your souls, when they are in glory, be delivered, which you are not here.

In the first place, You shall be delivered from sin; Here you complain like Paul, *O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?* Here you cry out like the Bird of Paradise, of which Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder). In early modern lore, it was often believed Birds of Paradise lacked feet and thus could never land, symbolizing a soul longing for heaven.</note> speaks, which always desires to fly in the Air, and when it is fastened to the Earth with a cord, it complains and cries day and night because it is held there. Here you are like this Bird, surrounded by a world of corruptions, but when you are in glory, you shall cast off this burden which now presses upon you; when you are in glory, you shall shake off this body of sin, and you shall only gleam and shine with the glory of the Divine nature. Here sin makes War upon you; *The flesh lusts against the Spirit*, Galatians 5 verse 17. But then the battle shall be at an end, and you shall destroy everything in

victory. Here the beautiful soul is smeared with spots and stains of sin; then you shall be without blemish, namely at the appearance *of Christ; 1 Thess. 5:24, 1 Tim. 6:14.* Second, just as you shall be freed from sin, so you shall also be freed from the causes of sin. *Adam* was in the state of innocence free from sin, but not from the incitements and temptations to sin; that was his misery. *Satan* was there to tempt him; but when you are in Heaven with Christ in glory, you shall be freed from all opportunities for any sin. In this world, three temptations come against you. 1. The corruption of your nature. 2. The suggestions of the Devil. 3. The allurements of the world; from all of which you shall be freed.

1. The corruption of your nature is the first temptation to sin: here you carry with you sinful foundations and dispositions of the heart, so that even if the Devil let you go, you would still sin against God; your own nature would tempt the Devil to tempt you. But in glory you shall shake off the body of sin and be clothed with a Body from Heaven; when you are glorified, you can no more sin than the Body of Christ can do, for your lowly bodies shall be like Christ’s glorious body. This shall be your blessedness in Heaven.

2. You shall also be freed from the suggestions of the devil. Here the devil goes about us, seeking whom he might devour. *1 Pet. 5:8 <note>The original text mistakenly cites verse 18; the reference to the "roaring lion" is 1 Peter 5:8.</note>, Heb. 2:14.* There the Lion shall lie bound in eternal chains and locked in an eternal dungeon. Here the devil steps on your heels <note>original: "treet op uwe haken," literally "treads on your hooks/heels," meaning to trip someone up or harass them.</note> and he often overcomes you through his temptations; but there God shall shortly tread Satan under your feet, *Rom. 16:20.* Shortly; namely, when you shall appear with Christ in glory, you shall tread on the neck of the devil, who now treads on you through his temptations.

3. You shall be delivered from the allurements of the world. Here, the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and the pride of life, and the things of this world, allure one to sin against God, *1 John 2:16.* But when you are in glory, you are above the world; the world with all its allurements and attractions shall be burned with fire. *Galeph the Philosopher* <note>Likely a reference to Galen or a similar classical authority. This analogy refers to the "sublunary" vs. "ethereal" spheres in ancient meteorology.</note> says that above the middle-region of the Air there is nothing but rest, stillness, and fair weather; and below are rushing winds and violent storm-weather; so it is in Heaven; there you shall have nothing but stillness and peace! Well, put this all together: here is your blessedness consisting in removal <note>term: "weg-neemen" (removal/privation). The author is describing "privative" blessings—happiness defined by the absence of evil.</note>, that when you are in glory, you shall be freed from sin and the incitement to sin; then you shall be delivered from a corrupted nature, from a tempting Devil, and from an alluring world; and there you shall be a conqueror over those things that overcome you while you are here. It is a good allusion of which you read in *1 Kings 6:32*, where it says that there was a Palm tree on the door where one entered into the Holy of Holies. You ask now, what did it mean that a Palm tree was there? The Scripture explains it. The Holy of Holies was an example of Heaven, as the Scripture takes it to be in *Heb. 9:12*: Christ having entered once with his blood into the Sanctuary,

<column-break/>

has brought about an eternal redemption. There, the Sanctuary is understood to mean Heaven, for Christ went into Heaven after his death, after he had finished the work of our redemption. A Palm tree is a symbol of victory over enemies; so it says in *Rev. 7:9*: Those who overcame rode on white Horses, with Palm branches in their hands. <note>The text conflates the white horse of Rev 6 or 19 with the palm-bearers of Rev 7:9.</note> Riding on white Horses is a sign of victory, and the Palm branches in their hands signify the triumphing because of that victory. Now, just as there was a Palm tree at the entrance of the Holy of Holies, so you also, in your entrance into that Holy place, shall carry these Palm branches in eternal glory; you shall have true and substantial testimonies that you are victors over sin, the devil, and the world; and this is your happiness taken in a privative sense <note>term: "berovende zin" (privative sense). In theology, this refers to the removal of all negatives/evils as a form of bliss.</note>. But

Third, you shall be freed from all consequences and evil effects of sin. While you are here, no matter how holy you are, having nevertheless a remnant of sin in your nature, you shall have the consequences and punishments of sin, whether loss, or a cross, or at last death; for all men shall die, because they have all sinned; Death has passed through to all men, in which all have sinned. But on the contrary, when you are in Heaven, in that place of glory, all the consequences of sin shall be brought to naught: in respect to the body, all sicknesses and weaknesses; and in respect to the soul, all sorrow and punishment. You are delivered from the wrath to come, which is the portion of the damned, but you are freed from all those consequences. *1 Thess. 1:10.* So you see then the privative good which the soul shall enjoy in Heaven.

Now I come to the positive goods <note>term: "stellige goederen" (positive goods). In contrast to the "privative," these are the actual joys or gifts granted to the soul in heaven.</note> which the soul shall enjoy when she appears in glory with Jesus Christ. These I shall bring under three heads. 1. There shall be a beatific seeing of God. 2. An actual enjoyment of God. 3. There shall be a perfection of all graces. These are the three general gifts of which the Scripture speaks.

First, there shall be a beatific vision, or seeing of God. *Matth. 5:8.* Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. So also *1 John 3:2*: When he shall be revealed, we shall see him as he is. Here we see only what God is not—not unrighteous, not weak, not unwise—but then we shall see him as he is. So it says in *Job 19:25, 26, 27*: I know that my Redeemer lives, and that he shall stand at the last over the dust; and I shall behold God with my eyes. And in *1 Cor. 13:10*, this seeing of God is placed alongside the enjoyment of God and communion with God. Many texts express this, that one shall see God. If you now ask me, what is it to see God so that it constitutes the greatest happiness of the soul in glory? I answer, this seeing of God contains two things.

1. It contains an actual enjoyment of the favor and Love of God towards us in Christ; so it is called in *Matth. 18:10.* Joseph said to his Brothers: You shall not see my face, unless your brother be with you, *Gen. 43:3.* That is, do not expect...

not that I shall show you love or favor; for God will not show his face to those who do evil—that is, the face of his love and favor. God will show him no love but rather wrath who does evil. So, in the Scriptures, to **see God** is to enjoy the favor of God. When someone was removed from favor by the Romans and condemned to die, their face was immediately covered to show that the Judge had no favor or mercy for that person; and the Scriptures perhaps refer to that Roman custom, indicating that God does not want to see a sinner—that is, he bears them no favor.

2. A perfect knowledge of God in his nature; and that is the most significant thing which this word "to see God" intends to convey; not as if we should see his Divine essence with physical eyes, for those cannot see God's essence. But understand that "to see God" is with the **Eye of the understanding**; you shall see God with more perfect knowledge than you do now. Now you know him only darkly, in a **Mirror**; you know him only as in a **Riddle** <note>original: "Raadsel," referring to the "darkly" or "enigmatically" of 1 Corinthians 13:12</note>—the depth of the Persons in the Godhead and the Unity of two natures in Christ; these are riddles for flesh and blood. But when you are in glory, you shall know God more perfectly and have a complete apprehension (though not a comprehension) <note>The author distinguishes between "vatting" (grasping/apprehending) and "om-vatting" (fully encompassing/comprehending), as the finite mind can never fully contain the infinite God.</note> of the nature, attributes, and Majesty of God. This is your first blessedness.

**Secondly**, because seeing without enjoying gives little comfort, there shall be a true enjoyment of God; you shall enjoy God as far as your natures are capable. Now you are adorned with the divine nature, yet you have some spots and stains by reason of the sin that is in you; but then all the stains shall be wiped out, and you shall have the divine nature shining gloriously in you. Here you have, it is true, an enjoyment of God, but you enjoy God *mediately* through the ordinances; but then you shall enjoy him *immediately* face to face.

<margin>1 Cor. 13 verse 10.</margin> 2. You enjoy God here in part; you enjoy but a little bit of God. But there you shall enjoy God without measure; here you have the fullness of a bucket, there you shall have the fullness of a sea.

3. Here you enjoy God in spurts; there are interruptions in your path; now you lose God, then you find him in an ordinance; but in glory you shall enjoy God without any ceasing, and therein lies the great difference between this present and the future enjoyment of God in glory.

4. Here you have God in expectation, but there you shall have him in possession.

**Thirdly**, there shall be perfection of all graces once you come into this place of glory; here you have perseverance, but no perfection in grace, as it is written in **1 Cor. 13 verses 9, 10**: *We know in part, and we prophesy in part, but when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part shall be done away.* Here your graces are not complete, but once you are in Heaven, all your imperfections shall be made perfect; and among the perfection of your graces, there are three outstanding ones that shall shine gloriously in Heaven: the grace of **Love**, the grace of **Knowledge**, and the grace of **Joy**. Although all other graces shall be per-

<column-break/>

fected, nevertheless the Scripture speaks to us particularly of the perfection of these graces.

**First**, the grace of **Love** (where all other gifts and miracles shall cease) shall be made perfect; and as **Anselm** <note>Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher.</note> says: *they shall love God more than themselves, and one another as themselves.* Then your love shall flow in a single channel <note>original: "pyp," literally a pipe or tube, meaning the love is no longer divided but focused.</note>. Here you divide your love between God and man, between God and your comfort, between God and your status; but then all your love shall be gathered into God as into the center point.

**Secondly**, your **knowledge** shall also be perfect; here you know in part, only in an imperfect mirror; but then you shall know God as he is, and you shall see all those rays of glory and Majesty which your dark eyes cannot see now.

And then **thirdly**, your **joy** and delight in God shall be perfect; that grace shall shine wondrously in Heaven, and for all your sorrows and sighings which you have had because of sin on earth, your joy shall be all the greater to sing Hallelujahs to your God in Heaven. This shall be the great blessedness of you all who are God's elect.

**Utility.** Now, is this true? Are these the glorious adornments of the Soul? Well then, oh you all who are already chosen and called and justified by the blood of Christ, you all who shall be glorified in body and soul by Jesus Christ, let this Doctrine be a bond for you, that you do not so dishonor your souls that you would make them dwellings for unclean lusts. Oh, these souls, which shall receive so much glory—let them not be holes or pens for unclean beasts, nor cages for unclean birds to rest in. Do not let your souls, I say, which shall contain such great glory, be made into inns for sins, which sins are the cause of so much shame. In your understanding there is now ignorance—and I speak it to your shame—some of you have no knowledge of God. In your will there is rebelliousness; Christ may say what he wants, but you want to do what pleases you. In your hearts there is hardness; in your passions there is disorder; you love what you should hate, and you hate what you should love; you love the sin you ought to hate, and you hate God whom you ought to love. Oh, do not defile your souls through such ways, since they shall be glorified through Jesus Christ. I recall that **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46 – 120 AD).</note> has a story of **Alexander**, who, being invited to run in the racecourse among the common crowd as a common person, gave this answer: *Were I not,* he said, *the son of a King, I would not care what company I had; but since I am the son of such a Prince, I must join myself with such company as might in some way correspond with my birth.*

I could make use of this: just as Alexander was, so you are Kings and Princes in all lands, sons of the Great King of Kings and of the Lord of Lords. Well now, sin, being a vagabond and an idle beggar, wants to seek to consort with you; lust wanted to have your heart, and sin wanted your—

You do not wish to open your soul so wide as to be a lodging-place for sin, as it may have been in former days.

I shall draw this utility <note>In this context, "utility" refers to the practical application or moral benefit of a theological teaching.</note> from the discussion of these words.

Now I shall come to certain doubts which will be properly handled regarding this matter of our appearing with Christ in glory. These doubts or questions are many; I shall now only speak of the first, which is this:

**Whether all those who appear with Christ in glory shall have an equal amount of glory.** Or otherwise: **Whether there shall be different levels of glory in Heaven.**

I shall satisfy you in this question in an affirmative manner, stating: That God’s elect, although they shall all come to glory, nevertheless shall not all have the same level of glory; but some shall have more than others. Before I proceed to discuss this further, I will first open the question—namely, what it regards—so that, being thus stated, it may be better distinguished.

Therefore: 
1. When I propose whether there are levels of glory in Heaven, the question is not to be understood in terms of **duration**, as if one godly person would be in glory for a longer time than another; for they shall all together be in glory for all eternity. 
2. The question is not to be understood in terms of **freedom**, as if they would not all be equally freed from all evil; for it is undoubtedly true that all the elect shall be freed from every kind of sin and evil. 
3. They shall all be equally glorified in terms of **God’s Love**: God will love everyone to the end equally. 

But it shall only not be so—as Gerardus <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a highly influential Lutheran scholastic theologian often cited in Dutch Reformed works.</note> notes—in terms of **application**. Some will grasp more of God, enjoy more of God, know more of God, and understand more of His nature and being than others. This is the only point the question regards. Having thus presented these warnings, I shall do three things in the discussion of this: First, I shall give you Scripture passages to confirm it. Secondly, I shall add reasons for it, and then take away the most notable objections that may seem to have force against this truth.

**First**, as far as Scripture is concerned, see Daniel 12, verse 3: *The teachers shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who justify many, like the stars, forever and ever.* Now note: how glorious is the shining of the stars—which the philosophers say are a round gathering-together of their heaven to shine more gloriously—above the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the expanse of the sky; the author is comparing the general glow of the sky to the specific, brighter light of individual stars.</note>. Just as the stars are a more beautiful part than the rest of their heaven, so some shall shine like the firmament, others like the stars, those glorious and beautiful bodies. Just as there are degrees between the glory of the firmament and that of the stars, so shall there also be degrees between one glorious saint and another. So also, 1 Corinthians 15, verses 41 and 42: *There is one glory*

<column-break/>

*of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differs from another star in glory; so also shall be the resurrection of the dead.* And this is not only (as some wish to limit it) a parable of our dying and rising again, but also (as the theologians <note>original: "Godt-geleerde," literally "those learned in God."</note> well observe) of the most glorified state of the saints when they rise: so that just as one star differs from another in glory, it shall also be so in the resurrection of the dead. So it stands in Matthew 19, verse 28: *That the Apostles shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* Now, Christ tells us in the following words that all the elect shall come to eternal life; but some men shall be there on thrones, judging the tribes of the Earth. The Apostles, who had followed Jesus Christ in distress and oppression, would have a more eminent manner of glory than others who had fewer gifts and graces than they.

As for the **Reasons** to prove that this is true, I shall propose only four.

**First**, since there are levels of torment in Hell, there shall also (by way of contrast) be levels of glory in Heaven. That there are levels of torment in Hell appears from Luke 12, verses 47 and 48: *The servant who knew his Lord’s will and did not do it shall be beaten with many stripes. But he who did not know it, and did things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes.* So also Romans 2, verse 9: *Tribulation and anguish shall be, first upon the Jews, and then upon the Greeks.* First the Jews—that is, primarily the Jews: they shall be particularly condemned and tormented in Hell who rejected Jesus Christ and His Gospel. So also Luke 10, verse 12, and in other places of Scripture, as where Christ would say to the sinners: *Your portion shall be with the hypocrites.* Indicating that they would lie under greater torment than others. Well, by way of contrast, if there are levels in Hell, it follows that there shall also be levels of glory in Heaven.

**Secondly**: There are different levels of Angels in Heaven, so it follows that there shall also be different levels of saints. There is a variety of Angels in Heaven: there are Cherubim, Seraphim, Angels, and Archangels. Cherubim and Seraphim are the lower sort of Angels; the Archangels are the higher sort, having different levels of glory; although each has as much glory as they can hold, nonetheless it is not in an equally great measure. Now, the Scripture says *that we shall be like all the Angels*; and consequently, as the Angels in Heaven have different glory, so shall the glory of the saints also be varied.

**Thirdly**, there is a variety of measure of gifts and graces among the godly on earth; therefore there shall be levels of glory in Heaven. 2 Corinthians 5, verse 10: *God shall reward everyone according to his works.* Some people have more...

Guillaume Bucanus was a prominent Genevan professor of theology in the late 16th century.</note> that just as God distributes his gifts unequally among men, so God shall crown his gifts unequally, so that some shall have more glory, and some less. *1 Corinthians 3, verse 8.* And Timecius says, since the labor and grace of men differ, so their reward and glory shall also differ. And this is made known in *Luke 19, verses 16 and 17.* The man who had ten talents and had gained ten more would have power over ten cities; and he who had five talents and had gained five more would have power over five cities. There you see, one man had more than the other. And this parable <term>parable: a simple story used to illustrate a moral or spiritual lesson</term> makes this known: these talents were gifts; the profit from these talents was the application of these gifts to the glory of God; and just as he who had applied his gifts the most received the most, so he who most applies his grace here shall have more glory hereafter.

Fourthly, in Heaven there shall be various degrees of glory, as this is a wonderful awakening and stimulation to become outstanding in grace. There is no greater awakening to duty or grace than glory; if, then, the degrees in glory wonderfully spur and awaken one to be outstanding in grace (for how can it be otherwise when people think: "the more I enjoy of God here, the more I shall enjoy him hereafter; and the more I labor here and put my graces to work, the more outstanding I shall be in glory"), then they shall be there in that glory. Thus, just as men are different in their grace here, they shall be different in glory hereafter.

As for the objections, although many seem to oppose this here, there is nonetheless only one that seems to touch the heart and life of this truth. And that is *Matthew 20, verse 10*, where you find the parable of the Master of the house, who called laborers into his vineyard; and calling them to himself, the History says, he gave each a penny <note>The "penny" refers to the Roman *denarius*, a standard day's wage.</note>. He who came at the first, the third, or the sixth hour had no more than he who came at the last hour; for he who came then received a penny just as well as the first. Therefore, they say, all people in Heaven shall have equal glory and salvation. To speak then on this passage, I shall propose this thesis: That this parable of the Master of the house, giving each a penny—both those who labored least and those who labored most—has absolutely no reference to the glorified state that the elect shall have in Heaven. This I shall clearly prove: for if by the Penny each received, glory were understood, then it would follow that murmurers <note>In the parable, the early workers complained or "murmured" about the equal pay.</note> would be saved, and that people who are not among the elect would be glorified, which you can easily see is absurd. And to make this apparent, read the 16th verse of this chapter: *So the last shall be first, and the first last; for many are called, but few chosen.* That is the conclusion of the parable.

Now, if those who in this vineyard were
<meta>catchword: called</meta>

<column-break/>

called, and each one of them had a penny, and if that were glory, then it would follow that many would have glory who, by the decree of God, are not among the elect. Therefore, this parable certainly does not represent the state of glory that the elect shall have at the coming of Christ. What then does this make known (they will say)? I answer: by the giving of a penny to everyone is understood the giving of gifts on earth. That everyone had a penny means that everyone had a sufficient gift that they could very well apply for God. And (as Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602) was an influential English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch.</note> explains it well) that everyone has a penny indicates that everyone works in the use of the "means" (for there, says Perkins, was their calling, a calling in the Church to put the established religious services to work). Every person who works in the use of the means shall obtain something; and it may so happen that those who were converted more quickly obtain less grace than the newly converted and those who came at the eleventh hour. The newly converted may well obtain as much grace and gifts here on earth as those who were converted at the beginning of their lives. And so it hits the mark of the parable for this purpose: that people should not boast of their gifts; for it can happen, I say, that sometimes those who come later to conversion shall receive their penny—gifts just as great, if not more, than yours.

But since some appearance of reason might still be brought against this, I shall propose some cautions to satisfy those difficulties that might arise against this truth.

1. Although there shall be degrees of glory, this distinction nonetheless does not flow from any merits of our virtues, but only from the simple arrangement of God’s grace. God wills it to be so, therefore it shall be so. It is not as the Papists <note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics; the author is distinguishing his Reformed view from the Catholic doctrine of merit.</note> say, that there are degrees of glory because grace is deserving, and that the more grace one has, the more glory one shall merit through their grace. This is to maintain "meritorious" and "supererogatory" works <term>works of supererogation: in Catholic theology, actions believed to go beyond what God requires, earning extra merit</term>, but this must not be. Further,

2. Though there are degrees of glory, this does not mean that there shall be deficiencies of glory in Heaven in any glorified person; but each shall be as full of glory as he can be. Perkins explains it clearly thus: take, he says, a small vessel and a large vessel and throw them both into the sea; both shall become full, yet there is not as much in the small one as in the large one, even though they are both full. So, he says, the godly are like two vessels, but one, by reason of enjoying God, is more capable of holding more of God than the other. Nevertheless, the least saint shall be full of glory; he who has the least glory shall have sufficient glory, although not as great as some glorified saints. So degrees of glory are no proof of any lack in any persons who have less glory than others.

3. Degrees of glory in Heaven breed no envy, as degrees of grace do on earth; for here one envies another who is above him in grace or gifts, but it shall not be so in Heaven; but...

The Doctrine, as you may remember, which I am still addressing, is: That Jesus Christ has laid away the full glorification for his elect until the time when he himself shall appear in glory to judge the world.

In the treatment thereof, I have pointed out several things to you, which I entrust to your memory, and now I proceed.

But if you do not consider this enough to resolve the doubt, before I speak specifically to the question, I shall first present several ways of speaking by which the Scripture portrays this place of glory, Heaven, where the bodies and souls of the elect shall be glorified. # The Appearance of the Saints

I have gathered these scriptural passages together so that when you read them scattered here and there, you may know their purpose: namely, to use various expressions to represent the glory and blessedness of the elect when they are in Heaven.

As for the specific treatment of the place where this Heaven shall be, there are various opinions. Some hold that this place shall be on earth; that there shall be a new Heaven and a new Earth, and that the elect shall live and be glorified there. They believe that the promise (*Matthew 5:5*, "That the meek shall inherit the earth") shall only be fulfilled in glory. They give this reason: because this world was the place of their grace, it shall also be the place of their glory; here was the place of their dishonor, and so it shall also be the place where they shall be honored before God and his Angels. But Scripture nowhere allows this in any way.

There are others who hold that the place shall be both in Heaven and on earth; for, they say, where God’s presence is, there is Heaven. Heaven is not bound to any specific place, but where God is, Heaven shall be.

Now, although it is true that God makes Heaven, nevertheless it is not so in this case; this answer is too general and does not climb high enough to satisfy this present question.

Others believe (and this is but a fantasy) that every Saint shall be a Star, and that the stars are said to be innumerable because the Saints are innumerable; they believe that every Star shall be a seat in glory for the Saints to sit in. This was the opinion of some Jewish Rabbis, and in truth it is but a loose and groundless opinion which they build upon that passage in *John 14:2*, where it says, *In my Father's house are many mansions*. "See," they say, "there is not just one place or dwelling for every glorified Saint, but many; and therefore every Star shall be as a dwelling for every Saint to shine within." Now, although this seems to greatly showcase the glory of the Saints in Heaven, it nonetheless cannot be permitted, as it has no foundation in Scripture; for we must not be wise above that which is written. Scripture does not declare that these many mansions are various Stars; thus, there is no ground for us to accept it. But so that you may know the place a little more closely and distinctly, I shall give you this distinction, which is grounded in Scripture: there are three kinds of Heaven: 1. The Heaven of the Air, 2. The Heaven of the Firmament, and 3. The Heaven of the Blessed.

The first Heaven is the Air, which is the expanse from the Earth up to the Moon; and this is called Heaven in Scripture because the birds flying in the air are called "Birds of the heavens" (*Matthew 6:26*), because they fly in the Air, which in Scripture is called Heaven, and from whence descend Hail, Rain, Snow, and other such things (*Deuteronomy 7:11*). The Philosophers also call it the Heaven; but this is not the place where the elect shall be.

The second Heaven is the firmament or 

<column-break/>

expanse; so it is named by God himself, *Genesis 1:14-15*. Namely, that place which contains within itself the various Planets and other Stars, with their orbits (*Deuteronomy 17:3*). The Philosophers can speak much of these two kinds of Heavens, but not a word of the third. Therefore,

The third Heaven is the Heaven of the blessed, which is above all these Heavens (*Deuteronomy 10:14*). It is more glorious and beautiful than all these Heavens are, or the Sun or Moon or Stars above us. It is called the "third Heaven" by *Paul*: *I was caught up into the third heaven.* We must not take this to mean that God was enclosed in some imagined place: for his infinite being cannot be contained. *Bernard* <note>Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic and theologian.</note> says, *he is nowhere and everywhere* <note>original: "nusquam est & ubique est"</note>; he is nowhere, because no place can contain him; he is everywhere, because no place can exclude his presence. *1 Kings 8:27.*

*Aristotle*, the most keen-sighted in the mysteries of nature—whom they call Nature’s secretary—nevertheless said that beyond the moving heavens, there was no body, nor time, nor place, nor *vacuum*, or emptiness; but God’s word assures us (whatever he may say) that the highest Heaven shall be the place of our blessedness, above all the visible and moving heavens. It appears clearly from Scripture that the place of the glorified Saints is not on the Earth, nor in the Air, nor in the Stars (as the Rabbis would have it), but it is a place above the Sun, Moon, and Stars. Scripture indicates this frequently; read *Deuteronomy 4:39*, *The Heavens above, and the Earth beneath*; and *seek those things which are above* (*Colossians 3:1*), *where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God*. *Exodus 20:6*, *In the Heaven above, or in the Earth beneath*; so that the place where the elect are blessed is above the Earth.

There are also some who believe that it shall be in the Air, because of that text, *1 Thessalonians 4:17*, *We shall be caught up to meet the Lord in the Air, and so shall we ever be with the Lord*. But it is not there either: for Scripture says that it is above the Stars, and the Stars are far above the Air. Therefore *Solomon* calls all men to the task, saying, *the height of the Heaven, the depth of the Earth, and the heart of Kings is unsearchable.* <note>term: unsearchable <gloss>beyond human ability to measure or fully understand</gloss></note> *Proverbs 25:3.* There is an unbelievable distance from the Earth to the Starry Heaven; Astronomers calculate it at 16,338,562 miles. It must necessarily be high, since some Stars are nineteen times larger than the Earth, and the Sun is one hundred and sixty-six times larger. The floor of Heaven is speckled with bright-shining lights and beautiful Stars: one might perhaps know how high it is to the Stars, but it can never be known how high it is to this Heaven of Heavens, above the Stars, of which *Paul* speaks. And this third Heaven, above the Stars, is the place of blessedness where the elect are. Take for that purpose only this one passage, *Ephesians 4:10*, *He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens*. Jesus Christ ascended far above all heavens—that is, above this first and second Heaven of which we have spoken; far above those has Christ ascended.

-># in glory with Christ.<-

Beloved / we do not know exactly what place it might be / but Scripture gives us this light / that it is a place above the Sky / above the Sun / Moon, and Stars / to which Jesus Christ has ascended. If we were to dive deeper into this mystery / we might, like the fly coming too close to the candle / burn our wings / if we desired to see more than the light of Scripture reveals to us.

Scripture tells us / that Heaven is that clear and glorious expanse far above the visible heavens / called the "third heaven" <note>Referring to the Pauline concept in 2 Corinthians 12:2 of a realm beyond the immediate atmosphere and outer space</note>; where God reveals His glory to the blessed Angels and Saints. Thus Ursinus <note>Zacharias Ursinus (1534–1583), a leading German theologian and co-author of the Heidelberg Catechism</note> and others agree with this sentiment.

To conclude this question / let us take this lesson from it: If it is so / that this place / where the elect dwell in glory / is made so beautiful by these descriptions / that it is called the Heaven of Heavens / a Kingdom / a future city / a glorious inheritance / and so on—if this is the place: then let this admonish and awaken you / O you children of men who live upon the earth / that you do not lose this glorious place. Even though we cannot fully describe what it is; nonetheless, we can easily say *that* it is / and how glorious it is / you can easily guess from those various ways of speaking which Scripture uses here. Is it a Kingdom? Oh / do not lose this Kingdom for trifles. Do not be like Tiberius / who was called the "wicked Biberius" <note>original: "d'argen Biberius"; a pun on the Emperor Tiberius's name and the Latin *bibere*, "to drink," referencing his reputation for alcoholism</note> / because he was willing to put his entire Kingdom in peril for a drink. Oh, do not lose Heaven for the sake of the Earth; do not lose a Kingdom for a trifle; for this place / where the elect shall be in glory / shall be a Kingdom. Is it called Abraham’s bosom? <note>A traditional term for the place of comfort in the afterlife</note> Oh, do not lose the chance to sit in Abraham’s bosom / only to lie now in Delilah’s bosom / or to lie now in the bosom of your harlots. Is Heaven called an eternal house / an eternal house in Heaven? Is that your place? Oh then, beloved / do not lose that eternal house / which lasts for eternity in the Heavens / by looking instead toward your magnificent and glorious houses / which one day shall not have one stone left upon another / but shall lie down in the dust. Is your Heaven called a glorious inheritance? If that is the place; then do not sell this inheritance / like the unholy Esau, for a bowl of pottage <note>original: "schotel moes"; referring to the biblical story of Esau trading his birthright for a meal</note>: do not exchange all these glorious possessions for things that are worth nothing. Here / beloved / I could move you strongly: If the place / where you shall be glorified / is so glorious / then do not lose this glorious place. Should I compare all the beauties of the world to this / they would all fall far short of this place / where you shall be made blessed. Though you may gaze upon mountains of crystal / mines of gold and diamonds; nevertheless, they all fall short of this incomprehensible glory / which you shall enjoy in Heaven.

Let this then persuade and move you / not to go and lose such a glorious place as Heaven is / for a single desire / or for the fleshly vanities of this world. Make this your lesson. And thus I have finished with the second Question.

Another or third doubt concerning this glorious state / (which is a little more hidden and obscure) is this / whether the Saints

<column-break/>

who shall be glorified by Christ in His appearing / shall know one another? And whether those who know one another now / shall also know one another / when they come into Heaven? This is a point / which indeed holds some curiosity in its discussion / yet in its truth is very comforting and very profitable.

Before I answer this doubt specifically / I shall present to you the sentiment of Luther. Gerhardus <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian</note> relates in his "Commonplaces" a remarkable story of Martin Luther; he says that during the last supper / which Luther held in this world / being with a company of Christian friends / this doubt was proposed / whether one would know the other in Heaven? And whether they would know him / when they should arrive there? After a short silence Luther gave this answer: 1. Just as fellowship / he said / is comforting on earth / so I do not doubt that it shall also be in Heaven. 2. Just as fellowship here would not be so comforting / if there were no knowledge and friendship / so the fellowship in Heaven would not be so comforting / if we did not also know one another. 3. Just as Adam, when he was in the state of innocence / had such perfect knowledge / that he knew his wife Eve / although he had never seen her before / having been asleep / and although he did not even ask / where she was from / or who she was / but said / "This is bone of my bone." If Adam knew this perfectly / then this knowledge in Heaven shall be much more perfect: we shall not only know our friends / but also Adam, whose face we have never seen / and those glorified Saints / whom we never knew on earth. Thus far goes Luther. And Mr. Bolton <note>Likely Robert Bolton (1572–1631), an English Puritan clergyman</note> relates a story of Augustine, that he gave this comfort to a widow / who was grieving over the loss of her husband / "You must trust in God / and be comforted in this / that you are only cut off from him for a small while / and then you shall, above all others, most enjoy your husband in the Heavens; and you need not doubt this; since there shall be no strangers in Heaven." Yes, you shall not only know your husband / but all the elect shall know you / and you them / and this is the great glory / which we shall have in Heaven. But now you will say / I have only presented the sentiment of two men / but what strength does Scripture give to confirm this? Well / follow me a little / and I shall present these propositions in general / that the blessedness and perfect knowledge of the elect shall be such / when they are glorified / that they shall know one another in Heaven; a friend shall know his friend / yes, you shall know those whom you never knew on earth / you shall know Abraham whom you never saw / you shall know Isaac and Jacob, and Paul, and all the glorified Saints / once you come into glory. To confirm this proposition / I shall bring forward six arguments.

First / Since the Scripture tells us / that the Apostles knew the glorified Saints in Heaven / while they were still on Earth / it follows that when we are in Heaven / we shall know the glorified Saints much more. Now we find in Scripture / Matthew 17 verse 3. That Peter, James, and John / knew Moses and Elijah in Heaven; The text tells us /
