# Hellish Terrors.

it is certain that one shall suffer more pain and torment than the other. And I shall establish this from Scripture and from Reason. Some will have greater pains, some less; nevertheless, they shall all have enough to make them miserable. To satisfy you with the Scripture, read Matthew 10, verses 14 and 15:
> Whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when you depart out of that house or city, shake off the dust of your feet. Verily I say unto you, it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city.
Note now: the Scripture tells us that Sodom and Gomorrah bear the punishment of eternal fire (Jude verse 7). Although they are in Hell, it shall nevertheless be more tolerable for them than for those who live in the days of the Gospel in unrepentance and godlessness; so it also stands in Matthew 11, verse 22:
> I say unto you, it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment than for you.
Christ speaks there against Chorazin <note>A city in Galilee where Jesus performed many miracles; it is used here as an example of those who witness God's work but refuse to change.</note>, a city that enjoyed the Gospel and in which Christ’s miracles were performed; nonetheless, through all these they were not converted or improved. Therefore Christ says:
> It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon (being two pagan places) in the day of judgment than for you.
So one reads in Luke 12, verses 47 and 48:
> That servant who knew his Lord’s will, and did it not, shall be beaten with many stripes.
And in Matthew 23, verses 14 and 15, Christ says:
> those who under the pretense of long prayers devour widows' houses shall receive the heavier judgment.
Indicating that—though all who have lived godlessly and died unrepentant will be damned—nonetheless, the hypocrites shall receive a greater and heavier judgment.

If you now ask me the reasons why there are degrees of pain in Hell—in some more, in some less, though in all enough—then I answer:

First, because some commit greater sins than others. Now, it is right with God to repay everyone according to what they have done; and consequently, those who have transgressed more shamefully and more frequently must also be tormented more in damnation. Christ tells us in John 19, verse 11:
> You could have no power against me unless it were given to you from above; therefore, he who delivered me to you has the greater sin.
Without doubt, God’s justice is so set against sin that those who have the most sins will also have the greatest pains. John 15, verse 22, Christ says:
> If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.
Some people’s sins are small as splinters <note>original: "splinters"; in English Bibles usually translated as "motes" or "specks".</note>, others are large as beams (Matthew 7, verse 4). Some sins are small as gnats, others are large as camels (Matthew 23, verse 24).

Secondly, because there are degrees of Glory in Heaven. Just as those who are outstanding in grace shall have the greatest degrees of Glory in Heaven, so shall those who are most shameful in sin have the greatest pains and punishments in Hell.

<column-break/>

Nevertheless, as I said just before, they shall all have enough, despite there being degrees of Glory in Heaven. As Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian often cited in Dutch Reformed works.</note> explains this: Cast two vessels into the sea, one larger, one smaller; they will both be filled, although the small vessel will not contain as much within itself as the large one. So also among the glorified Saints: some shall be able to contain more, some less glory; yet they shall all be full. So shall it also be with the damned. Some who have been the foulest sinners shall suffer more outstanding pains, and some shall suffer less; yet they shall all have enough to suffer, as much as creatures can bear. I could also bring forth the testimonies of the Church Fathers. **The punishment for each is as much heavier as each has more heavily sinned.** <note>original: "Tanto gravior singulis pœna, quanto gravius quisque peccavit."</note> Augustine, *On the Merits of Sins*, chapter 13. 2 Corinthians 5, verse 10. Let us now apply this. Oh, tremble, all you who run headlong into the foulest sins and transgressions, who give yourselves over to wantonness, to commit all uncleanness greedily; you shall suffer the greatest pains in Hell. *As much as she has glorified herself and lived luxuriously, so much torment and sorrow give her,* it says in Revelation 18, verse 7. Even if the least measure of the pains of the damned is sufficient to make them miserable, nonetheless, woe to you who heap up for yourselves the greatest measure of God’s wrath. But passing over this, I come to the fifth question; since it is indeed good to hear a Preacher speak of Hell, so as not to feel Hell, and to shun the sin that leads there; then take note, I pray you.

The fifth Question is: Since there are degrees of pains for the damned in Hell, how could we know who those are of whom the Scripture says shall have the greatest pains in Hell? This is a very fearsome matter; yet the Scripture speaks of it fully. And truly, I must tell you; my flesh trembles in speaking of this Doctrine to you, and I wish of God that your hearts and minds might tremble and shake in hearing the same, so that we might indeed not be of that damned heap that shall be cast into the deepest part of Hell.

All that I shall say regarding this, I will contain in seven particular main points. There are seven sorts of people of whom the Scripture says that if they live and die unrepentant of these seven sins, they shall have a greater punishment in the pains of Hell than others. Who are they?

First, those people who themselves do not wish to live in a holy walk of life, and also, as far as in them lies, do not suffer <note>Meaning "permit" or "allow."</note> others to live holily. Whoever they may be, they shall receive greater damnation. Matthew 23, verse 13:
> Woe unto you, says Christ, for you will not enter into the Kingdom of Heaven yourselves, and you will not let those enter who would enter.
As much as is in you, you hinder them; truly, says Christ, you shall receive the heavier judgment. Therefore, beloved, let this word disturb you. All you who are parents of children, and perhaps do not want to be holy yourselves, and also cannot suffer that your children should be so. All you who are masters of households, who

I pray you, take this to heart: for certainly, unless you repent of this, you shall receive greater damnation than other men.

And you, Capernaum, who are exalted unto heaven, shall be brought down to hell.* These two cities, *Capernaum* and *Chorazin*, of which Christ speaks, were cities where Christ and his disciples preached often, and where they performed many great and wonderful works, as appears from verse 20: *Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not.* Here Christ performed powerful miracles; indeed, the first time Christ spoke publicly in the world was at *Capernaum*, yet these people did not repent. What does Christ say to them now? *It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for you.* You shall have greater pains in Hell than those poor heathens who lived in *Tyre* and *Sidon*. So I may say: God shall say, tribulation and anguish and wrath shall be for the unholy heathens, but first for the professor <note>In this context, a "professor" is someone who "professes" or openly declares their faith, rather than an academic teacher.</note>, first for the Christian, first for the inhabitant of *London*, for them above all people of the world. Therefore I heartily pray you, take note of it, all you who live under the Gospel without improvement of your life, take this to heart; for this is your sentence: you shall receive heavier damnation from your God.

### Hellish Terrors.

[The scripture] speaks in Luke 12, verses 47 and 48, of two kinds of people, saying: "The servant who knew the master's will and did not do it shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who did not know it shall be beaten with few stripes." Ignorance will not excuse the sin, although it will certainly (as the theologians say) diminish the punishment; it will not take the punishment away entirely. Ignorance excuses the sin from certain levels of pain, but not from the pain altogether. Those who did not know the will [of God] shall be beaten with few stripes; they shall have some punishment. But he who knew his Lord’s will and did not do it, thereby sinning against his conscience, that person shall be beaten with many stripes.

Let this then be a sorrowful word for all of you who perhaps have long made a profession of faith and have gained a great measure of knowledge, yet despite all your knowledge, you are like the Heathen Woman <note>original: "Heydensche Vrouw"; this refers to Medea in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, a common classical reference in 17th-century preaching</note> who said of herself: <note>original: "*Video meliora, &c.*" — "I see the better things [and approve them, yet I follow the worse]"</note> **I see better things, yet I follow the worst?** If this is the case with you—you know what God is, you know what sin is, and what Hell is; you know what an evil thing it is to sin against God, and yet you are willing to risk sinning against your conscience—Oh, that you had hearts to take notice! If the Lord God does not bring you to repentance in time, you shall receive more stripes than others. Ignorant people who never knew Christ shall be punished; but you shall receive greater punishments than they.

Fourthly: those who, through their evil life and example, have stirred others to live godlessly and to go to Hell as well as themselves, shall be more terribly tormented than others. If any of you have been such a person, know this: you shall be damned not only for your own sins, but also for the sins of other people. Read Luke 16, verses 27 and 28: when the Rich Man lay in Hell (the text says), he begged Abraham that someone might rise from the dead to warn the living and tell them what kind of place Hell was. "No," said Abraham, "they have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them." God will not perform miracles now; let them listen to the ministry and preaching of the Gospel; if they do not hear those, they shall never be saved. "But no," said the Rich Man, "let him go; for I have five brothers, let him testify to them, so that they also do not come into this place of torment."

What was the reason, then, that the Rich Man so desired that his five brothers should not come to Hell? It did not come from the fact that the Rich Man had love for their souls; for in Hell there is no love for souls; those who are in Hell wish that the whole world was there with them. But he desired it on this ground and reason: because while he lived on earth, he had been a cause of sin for his brothers through his evil example. He knew that since he had stirred them to much evil by his example, their coming into Hell would increase his own pains. All commentators clearly indicate that this is the meaning: namely, that it was self-

<column-break/>

love, and not love for them, that made him speak so.

Well, I pray you, let this word take hold among you: are there not many among you who have given bad examples to others? Have not your children, while they were young, learned to swear from their stammers when they heard you, who are their fathers, swearing in their presence? Have not your children learned to speak unchastely and flippantly by hearing you do so? Have you not taught your children to be impure because they have seen you walk in such unjust ways? Have they not learned to be godless by seeing you be so?

O beloved, if you live and die unrepentant of the sins of your evil example, you shall not only be cast into Hell by God, but your torments shall also be greater than those of other men. I recall that Augustine, in one of his books, offers this prayer: <note>original: "Heere bevryt my van myne zonden van andere" — likely referencing the concept of "aliena peccata" or "other men's sins"</note> **Lord, deliver me from my sins of others.** And he does this on this ground: that when he should come to Judgment, he would have to account not only for his own sins but also for the sins of others. Since he had given the opportunity for it through his example, he would be punished for their sins as well as his own.

Fifthly: those who live and die unrepentantly in the sin of adultery shall be tormented above other men. You who now burn in your lusts shall one day burn in hotter flames than others. 2 Peter 2, verses 9 and 10: "The Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation and to keep the unjust for the day of Judgment to be punished." But who? **Most of all those who walk after the flesh in unclean lust.** The Lord God wants to keep all the unjust for judgment, but primarily those who walk in the lusts of uncleanness. Therefore it says in Hebrews 13, verse 4: **Whoremongers and adulterers God shall judge.** God shall judge all men, but these particularly. If you are adulterers, God shall judge you and give you a greater measure of pain than others. If then any of you, whether woman or man, has been guilty of this sin, repent in time; for believe it, if you do not repent, you shall be punished more than others. Those who make a habit of giving themselves to unchaste desires—if they live and die unrepentant of those sins—their portion in Hell shall be deeper and heavier than that of others.

Sixthly: those who are hypocrites and take up the profession of religion merely to be a "huyk" <term>huyk: a traditional hooded cloak, used here as a metaphor for a disguise</term> and a cover for coarser and more abominable sins in their life and conduct, shall receive the greatest damnation. An exceptional saying is found in Mark 12, verse 40: "Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites, who make a show of long prayers" (making long prayers was not a sin, but it was under a show and a cover for an evil end, and therefore it was sin) "so that you may devour widows' houses." That was their sin; they wanted to commit violence in their courts of law and outward dealings; and so that people would not think they were so base and godless, they wanted to take on the mask of holiness, and pray much and confess outwardly, so that people would have no suspicion of them...

### Hellish — Terrors.

[They] would have [the reputation] that they were so cruel: and what does Christ say of them? Those who under the appearance of long prayers perform [evil], shall receive a heavier Judgment.

Seventhly, those who persist in a state of unrepentance and hardness of heart against that long-suffering and patient God—who has shown them much kindness—shall receive greater torments than others. *Romans 2, verse 5:* Do you despise the riches of his kindness, and forbearance, and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath as a storehouse. Every person here is indeed offered the grace of God; but whoever meanwhile lives unrepentantly because God is patient, that person gathers wrath for themselves like a treasure against the day of wrath. The reason is that the more God's forbearance is abused, the more his wrath is ignited to punish that abuse. *Patience, when offended, turns into fury* <note>original: "Læsa patientia fit furor"</note>. Therefore, we see that no men are so deadly in their anger as those who are usually gentle. Therefore the Scripture tells us: Moses was endowed with patience, he was the gentlest man on Earth; yet being provoked by the Israelites, who served the molten Calf, he was so carried away by indignation that in his anger he broke the two stone Tablets which had been given to him by God's own hand. The offending and despising of God’s forbearance will so provoke and disturb God that he shall justly multiply and increase your pains. Thus far I have entered into this sorrowful point of doctrine; may the Lord God make it an instrument to bring you into Heaven and to deliver you from this place of torment, which shall be the portion of all who do not fear God and do not walk in his fear.

The doctrine which I drew from these words at the beginning was this: That the consideration of this (that God has an absolute supremacy over his creatures to cast their bodies and souls into Hell) ought to awaken a respectful fear in the hearts of God's Children.

In the handling of this chapter, I have gone through five questions, which I discuss solely to awaken slumbering sinners and to increase the joy of the glorified Saints upon hearing of these eternal pains from which they have been delivered. I now move on to the stated question.

The sixth question is: where is Hell? In answering, I say there are various opinions about it; I shall present the thoughts of several people to you and then explain what most agrees with the word of truth. All agree on this: that there is such a place, *for everything that is finite must necessarily be in some "where" [location]* <note>original: "Omnia enim finita necesse est esse in aliquo ubi"</note>

<column-break/>

[some] "where." Some believe that this place of the damned is in the air; we find this to have been the opinion of Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century theologian and bishop</note> and of some others after him, and they base this on these two passages: *Ephesians 2, verse 2,* where it says that the Devil is the prince of the power of the air; so then, they say, the place of Hell is the air. The other Scripture passage is *Ephesians 6, verse 12,* where it says: "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the air." Now, wherever the Devils are, they imagine, Hell itself must be. To dismiss this—that Hell is not there—I answer regarding the first Scripture passage, *Ephesians 2, v. 2,* that the Devil is called there the Prince of the power of the air, not to make known where Hell is or where the damned are, but only to indicate that God has at times allowed the Devil to have power over the air, to stir up winds and storms and tempests in the air; God has given the Devil that power, that he can cause a storm-wind to arise, just as he did in *Job 1, v. 19:* The devil caused a great wind to come from across the wilderness, and struck the four corners of the house in which Job’s children were feasting. This saying, I say, only points out that God gives the Devil so much power that he can stir up tempests in the air, or otherwise, go up and down in the air; and therefore he is called the Prince of the Air; it does not in any way refer to the place where the damned are. Regarding the other passage, *Ephesians 6, verse 12:* "We wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, etc." (That is, against the Devils, ruling in the darkened minds of the ignorant) and against spiritual wickedness in the air—that is, we struggle against the Devil, who is a Spirit full of wickedness and who fights against us in high places (so the English translation has it). In the original text it says only *in the heavenly things* <note>original: "èn tois epouraniois"</note>; which is not to say "in the air," but "in the heavenly," which word being placed alone, to complete the sense, must receive the word "things," just as in *Hebrews 8, verse 5:* *the heavenly things* <note>original: "ton epouranion"</note>. So "in heavenly things" here means in our heavenly graces: see there the Devil's wickedness, that he opposes himself against our heavenly graces and against our journey toward Heaven; and therefore he is called a spiritual wickedness. So this passage by no means supports or advocates for the opinion that Hell is in the air; the Text only says that this is the supreme wickedness of the Devil, that he sets himself against us as we go toward Heaven, and that he opposes himself against our graces which lead there, *2 Corinthians 4, verse 4.*

2. Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar</note> says that Hell is beneath the globe of the Earth, but that is not provable, since as many people live down there <note>A reference to the Antipodes, or people living on the opposite side of the world</note> as we do here.

3. A third opinion is that Hell is in the Valley of Jehoshaphat <note>A valley near Jerusalem mentioned in biblical prophecy</note>, and that from *Joel 3, verse 12.* But what I said to refute the opinion that Christ would come there for Judgment shall also have force against this opinion.

### Hellish — Terrors.

[The view] held by many learned men is that Hell is at the center, in the bowels and the middle of the Earth. They base this on the fact that in Scripture, Hell is called a pit, a pool, and a depth; therefore, they believe that this is the place itself, and that the damned are held together there in the center of the Earth. But this has no firm foundation in God’s word; thus, it cannot be confirmed by it.

There is another opinion (which has an appearance of reason) that Hell might be at the bottom of the Sea; so say Keckerman <note>Bartholomaeus Keckermann (1572–1609) was a German Reformed theologian and philosopher.</note> and others, and they ground this on Matthew 8 verse 29 and Luke 8 verse 31. There it says that the Devils, when they were cast out, begged Christ that they might go into the swine, and the swine plunged off the steep bank into the Sea. The Devils went there; therefore, Hell is there. To this, it serves as an answer that this cannot be the meaning of the passage, for it would then follow that the swine had entered into Hell; which is against reason and against Scripture. For only rational creatures—men, women, and Angels—can enter Hell, and not other creatures that have not sinned; these are the thoughts of many regarding this passage. Those who write about this with the most caution say only in general: "that Hell is a subterranean place" <note>original: "gehennam esse locum subterraneum"</note>, just as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> says in his *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 24. The Apostles, who preached to the Heathens, called Hell "Hades" <note>original: "ades"</note>, which is a place under the Earth ordained for punishment. Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet, often cited for early descriptions of the underworld.</note> says that Hell is as far beneath the Earth as Heaven is above it.

Now I shall present to you, in words of moderation, what the Scripture says concerning this matter.

The Scripture does not recount the specific place where Hell is located; it only assures us of two things in general which one must believe. First, that there is such a place, which is distinct from Heaven; it is not there where Heaven is—you may freely believe that. Secondly, you may freely believe, with a foundation in Scripture, that this place, wherever it is, must be below Heaven, somewhere down low. So you read in Proverbs 15 verse 24: *The way of life is above for the wise, that he may depart from Hell below.* And in Luke 8 verse 31, the Devils pray to Christ: *Lord, torment us not, and send us not away into the abyss.* Hell is in the depths, somewhere below Heaven and also below the Earth; therefore they say: *Lord, send us not into the abyss,* which is to say, "torment us not, and send us not into the place of the damned." But where the specific place is exactly, regarding that the Scripture is silent; and where the Scripture has no tongue to speak, there you must also have no ear to hear. If anyone asked further, I might say, like Socrates: "I have never been there myself, and I have never spoken to anyone who came from there."

But what might be the reason why God hides the place where Hell is, and does not make it manifest or known to the world? There may be five reasons that move God to do so.

1. God does it to prevent the presumption of many; if men knew the spe-

<column-break/>

cific place, some would be so meticulous that they would not be satisfied in their minds until they had searched out the place where Hell is. To prevent this curiosity, then, God has not revealed the place.

2. So that men, if they knew the place, would not fear Hell more than the sin that leads to Hell. It is God's will that they should fear sin more than Hell; as Anselm <note>Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a philosopher and theologian who served as Archbishop of Canterbury.</note> rightly says: "If Hell were on one side and sin on the other, you should fear entering into sin more than entering into Hell." If men found this place and heard the shrieks of the damned and saw the torments prepared for sinners, they would be more fearful of the place than of the sin that leads there. To prevent this, then, God hides it.

3. Because God wants faith to be used and exercised; because God wants to bind you to believe that God has prepared such a place, even if we do not know distinctly what and where it is.

4. God does this, furthermore, to rouse men from carelessness and to make them fear sin in every place; God does not tell you where the place is, for you might descend into Hell before you are aware of it; therefore, God does not want to let you know where Hell is, in order to rouse you from carelessness.

5. God hides this so that men would not expect extraordinary means and ways for their conversion, but so that they would apply themselves to the ordinary preaching and working of the Word. I might give the same answer that Abraham gave to the Rich Man <note>A reference to the Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus in Luke 16, where the rich man begs for a ghost to warn his brothers.</note> when the Rich Man desired that someone should go to tell his brothers how he was being tormented. "No," says Abraham, "God will perform no miracles in that regard. They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them." Here Abraham rebuked the Rich Man and said that God would not perform miracles for the conversion of men, but they must apply themselves to the ordinary means of the Word. If men saw the flames of the hellish fire hitting them in the face, this might trouble their conscience and change their expression somewhat. But it does not please God to show you the signs of Hell, or to give knowledge of where Hell is, until you are in it—you who are not chosen and do not belong to God. To bring this question to a practical use, know then:

First, it ought to be your wisdom to strive more to avoid Hell than to find the place where it is. If you do not labor to shun Hell, know this for certain: wherever Hell is, it shall find you, to receive you into eternal torments. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note> makes this use of it: "Let us not seek where the punishment is, but how we may flee it." <note>original: "μὴ ποινὴν ζητῶμεν, ποῦ ἐστίν· ἀλλὰ πῶς αὐτὴν φεύγωμεν." *Homily 31 on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 16.*</note> If someone’s house were on fire, he would not seek how it had happened, but how he might extinguish it.

Secondly, although it is uncertain where the exact place of Hell is, nonetheless you can know for certain that sin is the high road that leads to Hell. You may not know the place for certain; however, this is very certain:

### Hellish — Terrors.

Sin shall lead you to Hell. Proverbs 7:26.
> The house of a harlot is a way to Hell, descending to the inner chambers of death.

And the more excessive you are in sinning, the more you run toward the place of the damned with a bastard coachman <note>A metaphorical "driver" or guide leading one astray.</note>.

Thirdly, do you not know exactly where Hell is? This ought to teach you to guard yourself against sin in every place; for Hell follows sin on its heels. If you sin against God, God knows how near Hell is to you. You have a notable saying, Genesis 4 verse 7, where God says to Cain, "If you do not do well, sin lies at the door"; that is, the punishment that fits the sin. So I say to you, if you walk in the ways of sin, if you drink yourself drunk, swear or bicker, see, Hell lies at the door, damnation lies at the door; you do not know how near to Hell you are if you sin against God. Guard yourself then from sin in every place; for you do not know where the true place of Hell is.

Fourthly, although we do not know where Hell is, nonetheless we are certain of this: that there are some who carry the likeness of Hell with them wherever they go. A guilty and burdened conscience, united with an unholy, godless life, is the living image of Hell itself.

## The Seventh Question: What are the pains of the damned in Hell?

Beloved, this is a question that makes my heart tremble to speak to you of what the Scripture says regarding it. Nevertheless, I must be faithful to the Text and to the truth in handling this sorrowful matter. And I pray you, lend me your attention for a little while, as I declare to you what the pains of the damned in Hell are. All that I have to say, I shall contain under two heads.

The pains of the damned are of two kinds: either privative <note>original: "berovende" — a punishment consisting of the loss of something good, such as the sight of God.</note> or positive <note>original: "stellende" — an active, sensory punishment like fire.</note>; or punishments of loss, or punishments of feeling (as the Scholastic teachers <term>School-Leeraars</term> <note>Theologians from the Middle Ages who used systematic logic to explain Christian doctrine.</note> call them). And even if someone had the tongues of Angels and of Men, yet he could not sufficiently reveal the extreme miseries of a tormented soul in respect of these two heads. And that I might break out as the Philosopher did in speaking of Hell, I say: If all the Land were Paper, and all the water in the Sea Ink, and all the grass in the Field Pens, and every grain of sand on the Shore of the Sea Scribes, it would all be too little to represent the pains of Hell. But let us only say what the Scripture says, which says enough of these pains to make you shun the ways that lead there.

First, then, the pains of the damned are privative; they lose something, and this punishment of loss makes the pains of the damned great. Their loss consists of five particular things of which they are deprived.

1. The godless in Hell are deprived and banished from the gracious presence of God. And if there were now a thousand worlds (says Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential early Christian preacher.</note>), the loss of the favor of one God would be more than [the loss] of a thousand worlds. This is the greatest pain of a damned person, that he is without God. God’s presence makes Heaven into a Heaven; God’s absence (namely, of His favor) makes Hell more of a Hell than it already is. "Depart from me, you cursed." This is a

<column-break/>

great torment of the damned, that they must part from God and from Jesus Christ forever. If Absalom reckoned it so great a misery to be cast off by his Father for a time, that the text says, "He was weary of his life," 2 Samuel 14 verse 32, how heavy will it be for the damned that they shall not see that God is their Father, and that for eternity? To lose God is the greatest loss there can be, and this you shall lose if you are cast into Hell.

2. They lose not only God and Christ, but also the company of the Saints and the Angels forever. Here they enjoy the company of God’s Saints, but the time when they are in Hell is the time of their separation, Matthew 22 verse 13, Matthew 24 verse 41. "Depart from me, you cursed, with the Devil and his angels." And if they are not to be with those, they must necessarily be separated from the Saints.

3. You shall lose Heaven, the place of blessedness. Luke 16 verse 26. "There is a great gulf" (said Abraham) "between us and you, so that you cannot come where we are"; you are utterly lost. Now, if Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman orator famously devastated by his exile from Rome.</note>, being banished from Italy, so bitterly mourned his banishment that as often as he looked toward Italy he fell to weeping; and if Demosthenes <note>The Greek orator Demosthenes (384–322 BC), who also suffered under the pain of exile.</note> took his banishment from Athens so heavily that he began to weep as often as he saw it; if this grieved them so much, how then shall the thoughts of being banished from Heaven grieve you, if it shall be your sad lot to be cast into Hell?

4. You lose not only God and Christ and the Angels, but (which is not the least part of your misery) you lose all pity from God and Christ, and from all God's Saints. It is still some comfort in misery to be pitied by a friend, but in Hell you shall lose every kind of mercy. God shall not pity you; He shall laugh at your destruction, He shall mock when your fear comes, Proverbs 1 verse 26. The Godly shall not pity you; they shall rejoice in seeing God's power and glory in your damnation, Psalm 52 verse 8, Revelation 14 verse 10. It is a saying of Augustine: "Neither Creator nor creature shall be moved with any compassion over the damned in all their pains." When you burn in your flames, when you howl in your pains, then God shall laugh over your destruction, and then the Saints of God shall sing and be glad that you are a vessel of His justice, and that His power and justice are thus made known in you. Here, when you are in misery, mercy is shown to you, but in Hell there is no one who takes pity on you, and so your misery is the greater.

5. You shall lose all hope of being restored and of getting out. We say, "If it were not that I had hope, my heart would break." Here in the world, no matter how godless you were, there is always some hope as long as you are in the land of the living; but in Hell there is no hope, you are now beyond rescue; once you come into Hell, your heart may break from sorrow, for there is no hope of ever getting out.

Thus you see a glimpse of what you [will lose] in Hell...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the pains of the damned, transitioning from a general introduction to a detailed examination of the "positive punishments" (physical and mental suffering) rather than just the "punishment of loss" (separation from God). It outlines the first four of eight specific characteristics that make the suffering of Hell unbearable.</meta>

### ->Hellish — Terrors.<-

...you shall choose hell. But secondly—and this will perhaps touch your thoughts more—you must observe the punishments of sensation, which we call positive punishments or pains, which the bodies and souls of men suffer in Hell. And here I pray you, listen with a little attention to the speaking of these distinct things.

There are eight observations which make the positive pains of the damned so great and terrifying.

1. The variety of those pains. 2. The universality of those pains. 3. The intensity <note>original: "hoogte" - height or degree</note> of the pains. 4. The continuity of the same. 5. The company with whom one is tormented. 6. The quality of the place where one is. 7. The cruelty of those who shall torment you. 8. The eternity of all this. These eight considerations shall make you tremble, if you do not have hearts of stone.

**First**, note the **variety** of the pains; you shall be tormented not in one way, but in a hundred, a thousand, yes, ten thousand different ways. When you are sick here, perhaps you have one kind of sickness at a time—perhaps the stone <note>A common and excruciating historical term for kidney or bladder stones.</note>, the plague, or some other ailment. But you do not have several at once. Now, imagine if you were plagued and seized at once by the plague, and the stone, and the gout, and the fever—how wretched you would be! Well, in Hell there is not one kind of pain, but many kinds: there is an unquenchable fire to burn you, a pool of sulfur to stifle you, eternal chains to bind you, utter darkness to terrify you, and a worm of conscience to gnaw at you eternally. The Lord God has caused a multitude of torments to fall upon a man; and this makes the pains of Hell most terrifying.

**Secondly**, there is not only variety but also **universality** of pains; not only many kinds of pains, but the same shall also universally afflict the body and the soul, all parts of the body and all faculties of the soul: and this makes the pains of Hell the more fearsome. Perhaps here on Earth you have your sickness, but though some members are in pain, the others are nonetheless free; though it is not well with your body, your head can nonetheless be free; though your head aches, your lung and liver may be healthy; and though those ache, your arms and legs may be free; there is no sickness that puts the whole body in pain at once. But in Hell it is not so; there all the parts of your body and the powers of your soul shall be tormented, if you end up in that sorrowful place.

All the parts of your body shall be punished: the eye shall be tormented with the sight of the Devils; the ear with the screaming and terrifying outcries of the damned in the flame; the nostrils shall be filled with the smell of sulfur, even unto stifling; the tongue shall be tormented with the flame. In a word, the entire body shall be punished with the flames of Hell-fire; there is no part of the body—neither hand, nor foot, nor tongue, nor eye—that shall not be subject to these flames.

Yes, not only the body, but also all the faculties of the soul shall be tormented. Your imagination shall be plagued by the thoughts of your present

<column-break/>

pain: your memory shall be tormented with thoughts of Heaven and the blessedness which you have lost; you shall remember what a fit opportunity you had to be saved, that you lived under the Gospel, that you heard the ministers of Jesus Christ often admonish you to repent, and you would not allow yourself to be persuaded. Your mind shall plague you by the observation of the time you have misused: in a word, your understanding shall torment you in the thoughts of your past pleasures, present pains, and future sorrows, which shall last for eternity; and your conscience shall plague you with a constantly gnawing worm.

A **third** observation which makes the pains of hell very grievous is the **extraordinary intensity** of those pains. The fire of hell burns so violently that all the waters of the sea cannot extinguish it. Imagine that someone is unwell in every part of his body, and he is moreover troubled in his mind; if his pain is not extreme, it is somewhat bearable. But if someone's body is sick, and his soul is troubled, and all this is at the highest degree—how then shall such a man find death better than life? Well, Beloved, in Hell it is so; there you shall have pains in the uttermost and highest degree. The torments on Earth in the highest degree—take for instance the stone, gout, breaking on the wheel <note>A form of execution where a criminal's limbs were shattered with an iron-shod wheel.</note>, burning at a stake—are but flea bites <note>original: "blopbeeten," likely "vloois-beeten"</note> in comparison with those protruding pains which your body and soul must suffer in Hell; there you shall lie under such a heavy weight of God’s wrath as your natures can possibly bear. There the fire shall be a hundred times hotter than the fire of Nebuchadnezzar <note>Refers to the biblical story in Daniel 3, where the furnace was heated seven times hotter than usual.</note>, which was seven times hotter than usual; there is the very highest pain. Beloved, who can suffer all kinds of pains in every part, and those in the highest degree? Nonetheless, you shall have to suffer them all if your lot is there. If lying under the guilt of your sin for only an hour or two fell so heavily upon the Son of God that it made him sweat drops of blood, what shall the extremity of your pains in hell make you sweat?

**Fourthly**, note the **continuity** of those pains. Even if the pains of hell were many, universal, and extreme, if there were only now and then a pause, it would be some comfort. He who is tormented with the gout or the gravel <note>Small stones or crystals in the kidneys or bladder.</note>, as long as he still has some rest, finds therein a great refreshment for his body. But in Hell, this is your lamentable state and misery: there are pains without any ceasing. When you have swallowed sulfur for one day, you must begin again the next day; when you have lain for one day under the raging of an angry God, you must be pressed under the weight of His wrath again the next day: there is never any rest. Revelation 20 verse 10: *They shall be tormented day and night.* It comforts a sick man if he can rest in the morning, even if he cannot sleep at night: but in Hell there is no rest night nor day; there is no ceasing of the pains. Revelation 14 verse 11. The reason why it is so continuous is this: because in Hell they continually sin and blaspheme God, for cursing is the language of Hell. If they then sin without ceasing, they must also...

The author uses vivid analogies to earthly illnesses and biblical references to emphasize that Hell's torments far exceed any earthly suffering.</summary>

# ### ->Hellish Terrors.<-

...punished without ceasing. Just as the damned have no forgiveness of sins, so they have no release from pain, no respite from being punished, nor any permission to catch their breath. Therefore, Hieronymus <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a prominent Church Father known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> says: "When the damned sin in Hell, their sinning is like oil, and God's wrath like fire." As long as you throw oil into the fire, it will not stop burning: as long as they persist in sinning in Hell, so long shall the fire of God's wrath burn them continually. For in John 3:36 it is written: *the wrath of God remains on you*; and that is why the pains of Hell have no respite.

**Fifthly**, the company with whom you shall be tormented makes the pains of Hell heavy and dreadful. Good company for a sick body greatly lightens one's pain and makes one forget their sorrow; but if someone then has bad company, it does not suit them—that company torments them as much as their sickness. In Hell, it would be a mitigation of your pains if you only had good company; but now you have no other company there than Devils and damned men, just like yourself. And just as it is a pain here to see or hear what others suffer, so it shall be a pain for the damned in Hell to see the torments and hear the screams of the damned around them. Beloved, you would consider the life of that person wretched who was forced to live in a hospital <term>Gast-huys: historically a place for the poor and sick</term> among the crippled, or in a workhouse <term>Tucht-huys: a house of correction or prison</term> among thieves and rogues, or in a madhouse <term>Dol-huys: an early form of asylum</term> among the insane. Well, hospitals, workhouses, and madhouses are all places that have better company than the damned in Hell; your company shall make your existence there very wretched, and your pains shall be greatly increased.

> I would rather (says Bernard) <note>original: "Malo... fornacem calentissimam ferventem intrare, quam Diabolum in sua propria forma videre." St. Bernard of Clairvaux was a 12th-century mystic and abbot.</note> enter a most glowing, boiling furnace than see the Devil in his own true form.

**Sixthly**, the quality of the place shall make your pains very heavy. Beloved, if someone were placed in a location where there is no good company, but where the place was nonetheless pleasant, it would still be bearable; but to be banished from a pleasant place to a prison of darkness, that is truly wretched—and so it is in Hell. Perhaps you have here on Earth magnificent houses, delightful gardens, fertile vineyards, and pleasant buildings. But from those beautiful places you must be thrust into Hell, which is a prison, a bottomless pit, a cavern of darkness, a lake of fire and sulfur, a fiery oven that burns for eternity. Oh Beloved, the quality of the place shall make Hell terrifying for you.

**Seventhly**, the consideration of the cruelty of those whom God has ordained to be your tormentors in Hell shall greatly weigh upon the pains of Hell. And who are they? Well, read Matthew 18:34. The Devils are called your tormentors; they torment the ungodly, they torment the souls in Hell. Beloved, it would soften a person's pains a little, even if he were condemned to suffer some punishment, if the man who carried out the punishment were merciful—if he wished to spare him as much as he could; if someone

<column-break/>

were to be burned in his hand, if the man who was to burn him spared him and barely touched him, he would consider it a great stroke of luck. It would reduce your pains somewhat if there were only merciful creatures in Hell. But who are your tormentors? They are the Devils in whom there is no pity <note>original: "ontfaming" - likely "ontferming" (mercy/pity)</note>, who will not spare you, but will torment you as much as they are able, and as much as you are able to bear. Know this for certain: your tormentors will not pity you, but they will load you with rivers of sulfur and mountains of fire to the uttermost. This then makes the pains of Hell altogether bitter, that your tormentors are full of cruelty. Just as when someone is condemned to die, the sight of the executioner <term>Scherp-rechter: literally "sharp-judge," the official executioner</term> shall itself make his heart tremble—especially if he is a cruel man—so the very sight of the Devil, who shall be your executioner, will distress and terrify you to the highest degree. I remember the word of Anselm: "I would rather" (he says) "endure all the pains that art or nature can invent, than see the Devil with my bodily eyes; yes, even to see him when he distresses and torments the damned." Well, Beloved, guard yourselves against Hell, for if you ever end up there, your tormentors will have no compassion for you; they will not spare you, but they will focus their efforts on how they might increase your pains.

**Eighthly** and lastly, the **Eternity** of all this makes the pains most heavy of all. Beloved, when someone lies on their sickbed, this is their comfort: even if he has heavy pain and is grievously tormented, unable to rest night or day, he nonetheless hopes it will not last long—either he will be cured, or he will die, and so his pains will be ended. But this consideration cannot comfort you in Hell: you shall be in pain there, and you shall be in pain there for eternity. And here (says Mr. Bolton) <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631), a famous English Puritan clergyman known for his vivid preaching on the afterlife.</note> this word "eternally" shall break the hard hearts of a sinner; your pains are many, they are universal and extraordinary, and they shall moreover last forever. Eternity makes everything wretched to the highest degree.

Let us briefly bring the handling of this question to use.

First: Is this true, Beloved, that the pains of the damned are privative—that you then lose God, and Christ, and Heaven, and Glory, and the Saints, and all mercy and hope of restoration? If you lose all this in Hell, this then clearly shows the madness and folly of those who are willing to undergo the peril of losing God and Christ and Heavenly Glory; and who are willing to run the risk of falling into these pains of Hell, and all this only for a pleasant folly or a fleshly desire. Oh, the great folly of many in the world, who would rather lose God than lose a single desire, or leave their Lord, or forsake their profit which comes through unjust gain. I remember a story of Lysimachus <note>Lysimachus (c. 360–281 BC), a Macedonian general and successor to Alexander the Great.</note>, King of Macedonia, who while leading an army, when the weather was so hot and dry that the entire army was about to die of thirst, was forced to surrender himself and his army and kingdom into the hands of his enemies for a drink of water; and when he had drunk this water...

It concludes by warning that trading eternal salvation for temporary worldly pleasure is a supreme act of folly.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Hellish Terrors," specifically focusing on the eighth characteristic of hellish pain: its agonizing nature compared to the fleeting pleasures of sin. # ### ->Hellish Terrors.<-

...then he burst out thus: "O, what a brief pleasure this is, that I have lost a glorious Kingdom for a single drink of water!" <note>This refers to Lysimachus, a successor of Alexander the Great, who reportedly surrendered his army and kingdom to the Getae in exchange for a drink during a drought.</note> Truly, you have more reason to complain than *Lysimachus* had. You lose the Kingdom of Heaven perhaps for a drink of water, or for a bowl of wine; because you want to drink one glass too many, or want to gain one penny <term>stuiver: a small Dutch coin</term> too much, you are willing to lose Heaven for it. Because you want to swear one oath too many, you are willing to lose a God for it; O, for how little profit are men willing to do this? This is a proof of the hasty folly and unthinking madness of which men are guilty.

**Secondly**, these pains of the damned are privative <note>meaning "consisting of a loss"</note>, since one loses God; and are there eight considerations in this? If this is true, then it seems to me that all of you who are outside of *Jesus Christ* ought to be all day long in the state of *Belshazzar*, *Daniel 5:5*. When he saw the writing hand on the wall, he was so terrified that his knees knocked against one another. O beast! O man, be afraid! O woman, who are ordained to be a vessel of eternal wrath, how can you endure these various pains? How can you lie under the heavy wrath of an incensed God? This consideration ought to draw tears from your eyes, blood from your hearts, and especially sin from your lives—that you hear and see how grievously the damned are tormented.

**Thirdly**, is this the portion of the damned in Hell? This then ought to teach you that although the pains of Hell are hideous, nonetheless sin is worse than the hellish pains. Hell is not as evil as sin, for sin made Hell; that which made Hell into a Hell is surely worse than Hell itself. Even though you have heard of these hellish pains, I still do not want you to fear the pains more than the sin. Rather, fear the sin as the cause more than Hell, which is the effect; for sin is worse than Hell. And when you take an oath into your mouth, or drink and swallow immoderately, then think: you would have done better to have swallowed a drink of sulfur-water than to commit that sin. Therefore, Beloved, do not let the hearing of these pains sink into your thoughts in such a way that you would regard sin as something small; rather, fear sin more than Hell. I recall a saying of *Chrysostom* <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an early Church Father known for his preaching.</note>: "It is more fearful," he says, "to dishonor *Jesus Christ* than to be tormented with the pains of the damned." And *Mr. Bolton* <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631), an English Puritan clergyman.</note>, as I recall, brings up the saying of *Anselm* <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109).</note to this end: "If," says he, "sin was on one hand, and Hell on the other, I would rather go into Hell than run into sin." And *Edmund* <note>likely St. Edmund of Abingdon (1175–1240).</note>, the follower of *Anselm*, expresses himself thus: "I would rather run into a fiery oven, or throw myself into a pool of sulfur, than knowingly commit a sin against God." Beloved, I mention these only to this end: so that you would not look upon Hell as worse than sin, and so that you would not judge the pains of Hell too harshly; for sin is ten thousand times worse. Hell is a creature <note>in the sense of a "created thing."</note>, but sin is not; God made Hell, but the Devils made sin. God created Hell, but He never made sin; God considered Hell better than sin, otherwise He would never have 

<column-break/>

made a Hell to punish sin. Even if you have heard all these hellish pains, let sin always be worse in your eyes than all those pains.

**Fourthly and finally**, I pray you all: do not run the risk, for the pleasure and profit of sin, of going into those eternal pains. Suppose that through your unjust gain you increased your status, or suppose you had a rich income—if you simultaneously lose a God, what gain have you made? If you lose a soul, what profit does it do you? If you lose Christ, what does it benefit you? Oh, do not put yourselves in danger of running into those eternal pains just to enjoy the pleasure of sin for a time. A certain man says: "He is a right fool who plays the thief; perhaps he is busy for only an hour in stealing the goods, and he may lie for a whole year in shackles because of it, and then finally reach the gallows for it." But oh, how much greater fools are they who, perhaps for the pleasure of an hour, or at the longest for a lifetime of unjust gain and sinful living, lie in the prison of hell—not for a year, but for all eternity! Such are much greater fools. Therefore, I pray you, let these pains of hell sink down upon your heart. And if you will think of the hellish pains while you live here, then this shall be the way to keep you from these pains when you die. It is a pleasant word from *Bernard* <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153).</note>: "Let us," he says, "go to Hell while we live, so that we do not go to Hell when we are dead." A very good word. And I wish from God that you would do so: that you would go home today and think on what you have heard of the punishments of loss and of sense; and perhaps the thoughts of this will so cause you to walk in your life that you shall then be kept from hell when you shall die.

> But rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Hell.

<margin>XIV. Sermon.</margin>
**T**he observation that you can remember from these words is this:
That the consideration of this (that God has an absolute power over men and women to cast their bodies and souls into Hell) ought to work in the hearts of His people a fear and reverence of God.

In the handling of this, I have already passed over seven questions. The eighth question is this: whether the pains of Hell are eternal or not? Whether they shall last forever, or have an end? This I shall answer first in general, and then in particular.

First, I say in general: The pains of the damned are eternal pains; for proof I shall give you Scripture and reason. 1. As far as Scripture is concerned, *Matthew 18, verse 8 and Jude, verse 7*; there the fire is called an eternal fire which torments the ungodly. *Matthew 25, verse 46*, they are called eternal pains which shall last always; and *2 Thessalonians 1, verse 9*, they shall suffer as punishment eternal destruction from the face of the Lord; and *Daniel 12, verse 2*, And they shall awaken

# ### ->Hellish Terrors.<-

...to eternal horror. Combine these alone: eternal fire, eternal pain, eternal destruction, and eternal horror, and you shall then clearly see from the Scripture that the pains of the damned must be eternal.

2. As for the reasons, I shall mention only a few:

1. These pains must be eternal because God's justice, which has been wronged by sins, can never be fully satisfied, and the ungodly must be tormented until God's justice is satisfied. *Luke 12, verse 59*. The ungodly shall be in Hell until they have paid the last <term>penningsken: a mite or very small penny</term>. If he then cannot give God His due, nor make amends for the sins he has committed, he must lie in Hell for that long. But it is impossible for the ungodly to pay the last penny to satisfy God for the wrong he has done Him. Therefore, *Jesus Christ*, God and Man, had to come down in the place of the elect to satisfy God for the wrong they had done Him through their deeds and their sins on Earth. And for this reason, the pains of the damned must be eternal.

I have read a history of the Emperor *Tiberius*, who, being angry with one of his courtiers, was asked by the same: *That his punishment might be shortened and quickly ended, so that he might know what he could rely upon.* The Emperor answered: *No, man, I am not yet a friend to you.* Beloved, so God also says: for the ungodly wrong God’s righteousness, kindness, and supreme majesty; they do not wish to be subject to His commands; and yet they still expect that their pains might soon end. But no, He says, and He answers as *Tiberius* answered his criminal: I have not yet restored you to my favor; you and I are not yet friends; you have not yet made good the wrong you have done me; therefore, you must still suffer.

2. The ungodly shall sin for all eternity, so their pains must also be eternal; as long as there is sin in a person, the Lord will torment that person, for sin and punishment cannot be separated from each other. Sin is like oil, and God's wrath like fire: as long as you throw oil into the fire, the fire cannot stop burning. As long as sin is in someone's nature, a person cannot be free from their suffering; *Revelation 14, verse 11*. *The smoke of their torment shall go up forever and ever.* The ungodly sin in Hell for eternity, and therefore they shall be punished eternally; their curses are their songs, their wailing is their melody, and blasphemies their hymns; they blaspheme God, who made them, for throwing them eternally into Hell. *Revelation 16, verses 9, 11, 21*. Since they are cursed by God, they blaspheme the name of God. There they blaspheme His righteousness because He has judged them, and His Son because they feel His hand; there they condemn His mercy because they have not tasted that mercy, and there they shall curse the blood of *Christ* because that same blood has saved thousands, but not them. Hell consists solely of blasphemies and sins: they sin there eternally against God, and therefore they shall be eternally tormented by Him.

<column-break/>

3. The godly shall be in eternal joy, so the ungodly must suffer eternal pains: their state shall be exactly opposite to that of the godly; the pains of the one shall last as long as the joy of the other; just as the one serves for the glory of God's grace, so the other shall be for the glory of His justice; the ungodly sin continually in Hell against God, yet they never have a heart to repent of the sins they commit against God; thus they must be punished forever. If people continue in sin and have no heart to repent, so God must continue to punish them; for God will not stop punishing as long as a person uncontrollably <note>original: "onbeheerlijk"</note> continues in sins. A certain writer says: the damned shall be continually sorrowful, but it will only be for their punishment; they shall never be converted so that they might receive forgiveness and grace. Thus far I have spoken in general, but now in particular, which shall explain and lay open the matter further. And here I will show you that everything that serves in any way for the pain of hell is eternal, and therefore the pains must also be eternal. I pray you, listen to me attentively for a little while while I present these sorrowful things to you; I shall contain it under eight heads alone.

1. The God who damns the ungodly is an eternal God, so the pains must also be eternal. *As long as there is a God, so long shall there be a Hell,* says *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an important Early Church Father</note>. *Isaiah 33, verse 14*. *Who among us can dwell with an everlasting fire?* God is an eternal God, and so He burns and torments the ungodly in eternity; so it is written in *Romans 16, verse 26*: *The commandment of the everlasting God.* If then that God, who torments the ungodly, be an eternal God, then their pains must last as long as God is, that is, they must be eternal. Mr. *Bolton* <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631), a prominent English Puritan known for his vivid preaching on the afterlife</note>, writing about this, has this expression: *Suppose that all the mountains of the earth were mountains of sand, and that as many more mountains were added until they touched the Heavens, and a tiny bird came once every thousand years to take one grain of sand from this mountain; in this way, countless years would pass before that heap of sand would be consumed and taken away, yet this time would have an end.* And it would be a stroke of luck for man if Hell were no longer than this time. But such is the misery of man in Hell: he shall have no more hope of getting out when he has been there for millions of years than he had when he was first thrown in; for his pains shall last eternally and have no end; for the God who damns him is an eternal God.

2. The fire that torments the ungodly is an eternal fire. *Jude, verse 7*. *They suffer the punishment of eternal fire.* Likewise, *Isaiah 30, verse 33; Isaiah 66, verse 24*. And if this is so, then the pains must also necessarily be eternal.

3. The prison that receives the ungodly is an eternal prison, a prison that shall never fall into ruin, that shall never be broken or dug through by thieves; it is a prison that shall so enclose you that you shall never escape from it. *Jude, verse 6*. There Hell is called *eternal chains of darkness*. When you are in the dark, you do not know which way to go;

# ## ->Hellish — Terrors.<-

...to eternal horror. Put these together: eternal fire, eternal pain, eternal destruction, and eternal horror—and you shall then clearly see from the Scriptures that the pains of the damned must be eternal.

### 2. Regarding the reasons, I shall cite but a few:

1. These pains must be eternal because God's justice, which has been wronged by sin, can never be fully satisfied, and the ungodly must be tormented until God's justice is satisfied. *Luke 12, verse 59*. But it is impossible for the ungodly to pay the last penny to satisfy God for the ways he has wronged Him. Therefore, *Jesus Christ*, God and Man, had to come down in the place of the elect to satisfy God for the wrong they had done Him through their actions and their sins on Earth. And for this reason, the pains of the damned must be eternal. If men continue in sin and have no heart to repent, then God must continue in punishing them; for God will not cease from punishing as long as a person continues dishonorably in sins. A certain writer says: the damned shall be continually sorrowful, but it shall only be because of their punishment; they shall never be converted so that they might receive forgiveness and grace. Thus far I have spoken in general, but now I speak in particular, which shall explain and lay open the matter more. And here I shall show you that everything which in any way contributes to the pain of hell is eternal, and therefore the pains must also be eternal. ### 1. The God who damns the ungodly is an eternal God, so the pains must also be eternal. And it would be a happiness for man if Hell were no longer than this time. # ### ->Hellish Terrors.<-

...you shall; if you are bound in chains of darkness, then you are beyond hope of escape; and this represents the state of Hell: that once you enter, you shall never depart. Therefore it is called a bottomless pit; when someone is sinking, he will not stop sinking until he reaches the bottom. So it is in Hell; once you are locked inside, you shall never come out.

4. The Worm, which gnaws the conscience of the ungodly, is an eternal worm. *Isaiah 66, verse 24. Mark 9, verse 44.* There the worm shall not die. This worm is not a natural worm, like those that gnaw a man's flesh in the grave, but it is the biting and accusation of the conscience; this is the worm that shall gnaw continually and shall devour a person's peace. Even the pagans, though they had no Scripture, nevertheless had a glimpse of this through the light of nature. I have read in Virgil, a pagan poet, that he speaks of a certain Tityus, whose liver was gnawed every day by a vulture, and at night his liver was restored and grew back so that the bird might satisfy itself upon it again the next day. <note>original: "Tytius" — In Roman mythology, Tityus was a giant punished in the underworld by having two vultures perpetually eat his liver, which was considered the seat of passions.</note> By this, they depicted Hell and the gnawing of the conscience there. This vulture, being your conscience, shall consume your peace and torment you with thoughts of terror, and this you shall have until time shall be no more. Put all this together now: God, the Prison, the Fire, and the Worm are eternal; the pains must therefore also be eternal.

5. The loss of God, of Glory, and of Jesus Christ, is an eternal loss. You know that when friends part, even if only for a while, their parting wrings tears from them; but when they part never to see each other again, what a bleeding of sorrow their parting then causes! When you die, you do not part for a time, but for eternity; you say an eternal adieu to God, to Christ, and to all the Saints in whose company you live here. You bid them farewell, never to see them again, and never to enjoy their company more; you must then be cast into a dungeon of darkness, never to see the Sun; into an abyss, never to come out; into the company of Devils, never to be with Christ and His Saints. Your loss is an irreparable loss: You shall see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven, but you shall be shut out. Your loss shall be an eternal loss; therefore your pains must necessarily be eternal.

6. Sin, the cause of the pains of Hell, is eternal, so the pains must also be eternal. If you establish the cause, the effect must also be there; take away the cause, and the effect shall cease. Since sin, which is the cause of Hellish pains, lasts forever (for the ungodly shall throughout all eternity blaspheme God, blaspheme Hell, blaspheme His justice, blaspheme His mercy, and blaspheme the blood of Jesus Christ), then the pains of Hell, which proceed from sin, must also be eternal.

7. The sentence pronounced over the ungodly is an eternal sentence: *Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire.* A sentence which, like that of the Medes and Persians, cannot be revoked.

<column-break/>

8. The body and the soul, the subjects of the pains, are eternal. The body here is mortal and subject to corruption; here it must die, but in Hell neither body nor soul shall die. Your soul, being subject to the pains, is an eternal soul. *Revelation 9, verse 6.* No one shall be able to make an end of his own life or the life of another. Put all this together now: Your God is an eternal God, Hell is an eternal prison, the fire is an eternal fire, the worm is eternal, the soul and the body are eternal, sin is eternal, and the cause of everything is also eternal. Tell me now, can it be contradicted that the pains of the damned must be eternal?

### Lessons.

If it is so, that the pains of the damned are eternal, then first: this provides matter to refute that groundless opinion of Origen, who held that although there is a Hell and although the ungodly are tormented (for he allows that), nevertheless on the Day of Judgment there would be no Hell; but that all—not only ungodly men but also the Devils—would be saved. <note>This refers to the doctrine of "Apocatastasis" or universal restoration, attributed to the early church father Origen.</note> A very coarse opinion; for if these pains are eternal, and the ungodly must be tormented eternally, then this opinion of Origen must necessarily be false—that Hell shall be brought to nothing, and that all the ungodly, and even the Devils, shall be saved. This opinion is clearly and nakedly overthrown by this.

Secondly, are the pains of Hell eternal pains? This must teach you who live on earth to beware of coming into danger of suffering these eternal pains for the sake of temporary vanities. If you sin, you can only sin for a short time; if you obtain unjust gain, you enjoy it only for a time; but if you are damned, you shall be damned for all eternity. Beware then that you run no risk of falling into eternal pain for this reason. As it is said: *You can buy gold too dearly*; so you can buy these worldly vanities too dearly. When Demosthenes was enticed to impurity by the prostitute Lais, and she demanded ten thousand reals for the pleasure of one night, Demosthenes reflected and gave her this answer: *I do not wish to buy regret so dearly.* <note>Demosthenes was a famous Greek orator; Lais of Corinth was a renowned courtesan. The quote is often translated as "I do not buy repentance at such a price."</note> If Demosthenes, a pagan, could answer a temptation so, then I wish that you, who are Christians, would answer it more strongly. You are enticed to sin by the Devil; if you consent to it, you may run the risk of losing God and Christ, and of falling into these eternal pains. Rebuke your heart then, and say: "I do not intend to buy pleasure so dearly; I do not intend to lose God and Christ and run the risk of suffering eternal pains for the sake of one sin." Cast off temptations with these intentions.

Thirdly, this provides matter for the condemnation of all despairing people who wish themselves in Hell before God wants them there. How many are there who hope that God will damn them, sink them, and cast them down. Alas, poor people! They do not know what they wish for their souls. Yes, some people not only wish themselves in Hell but even want to kill themselves and send themselves to Hell before God...

### ->Hellish Terrors.<-

we would have there. If someone only knew what this place of torment is, he would never have such words in his mouth. Well, if you do not know, I shall tell you; when you wish that God would damn you, you wish for nothing other than this: That God should take you from a pleasant world, from a place of delight and agreeableness where you have your pleasure and refreshment, and that He should send you into a place of darkness, a cavern of darkness, an abyss where you shall never see light; that God should banish you from His presence so as never to have a good sight of Him again; that God should send you into unquenchable fire to burn you, into a pool of sulfur to stifle you, and to have the Devils as your tormentors, where your pains shall be without end, without rest, without remedy. This is wishing yourself into Hell; therefore, let the consideration of this—that the pains of Hell are eternal—rebuke all those who cry out for God to damn them; for, alas! you wish for the greatest misery that can come upon you, whether here or in the world to come.

Fourthly, learn from this, all you who are redeemed through *Jesus Christ*, learn to patiently endure the temporal afflictions that God imposes upon you here; even if they are ever so heavy, though you have the pain of <term>the gravel</term><note>A historical term for kidney stones or bladder stones, notoriously painful before modern medicine.</note> for a month, the pain of the gout for a year, or sickness and weakness of the body all your life long; nevertheless, thank God that He has delivered you from the greatest pain of all; these are but flea-bites compared with the pains of the damned. If God has then freed you from the pains of Hell, be patient, even if God should afflict you ever so much while you are here in this world. The Apostle makes this use of this doctrine in *1 Thessalonians 1, verses 6 and 10*, compared together: "You received the word in much affliction with joy." Here they were greatly afflicted, and yet they rejoiced; on what ground? Because they awaited God’s Son from Heaven, namely *Jesus*, who has delivered us from the wrath to come. This is the reason for their joy in affliction: because they waited for *Jesus*; as if he were saying, "O blessed be God, who has delivered us from the wrath to come, from the greatest pains." For this reason, we may be joyful

<column-break/>

and patient under the afflictions we encounter in this world for the sake of *Christ* or for the confession of the *Gospel*. We are delivered from the greatest pains, so we may well bear the lesser ones. O all you redeemed of the Lord, this doctrine of the pains of Hell ought to greatly strengthen you to suffer any affliction here, since your afflictions are not eternal: God has delivered you from eternal pains, which are greater than any you shall ever suffer in this world.

Fifthly, are the pains of the damned eternal pains? Oh, then labor while you live in the world so that you do not perish eternally, so that you do not cast yourself into this hellish pool from which there is no escape; while you are here, there is hope, but hereafter there is no hope. Labor while you are here so as not to fall into an eternal state of misery. *Zeuxis* the Painter, being asked why others ran so hastily through their work and finished so much, while he took so much trouble and spent so much time to complete and perfect his work,

<column-break/>

answered: "Others work for profit, but I paint for eternity" <note>original: "propter æternitatem pingo"</note> so that my works may be seen in eternity, that succeeding ages may behold them. How I wish that people were like this Painter! Others wish to sin, to swear, to make unjust profit, and they do not concern themselves with how; but why do they do so? Because they are only out for their profit; they look only at the world and its pleasures. But you, you must work for eternity, and therefore you ought to live so that you might be blessed for all eternity, and not be cast into these eternal flames.

The ninth Question is, since the pains of the damned are eternal, whether it can stand with God’s justice to damn a man forever because he sins only for a time. Flesh and blood might rise up here against its Maker and say, "I might die in my youth, I might perhaps not live ten years, and then perhaps be damned forever; is this right with God?" Another may say, "I might die after having lived only a short while, and I would perhaps receive as great a punishment as the oldest man; is this justice in God, to damn a man forever who has only sinned for a short time?" Thus the godless plead against God. To answer this, I say: yes, it is right that God damns a man eternally, even if he sins only for a short while here in the world. And to prove this, I shall present only four or five particular points.

First, in defense of God's justice, I answer that punishment must not be calculated by the length of time in which the fault was committed, but by the nature of the deed. For example, suppose someone breaks into a house; perhaps he was not occupied there for an hour, yet it is right for the authorities to keep that man in prison until the assembly for the execution of justice is held, and this for much longer than he was busy in the act. Someone being angry with another can give him a death-blow in a moment; that man can be kept in prison all his life, and it is well if he gets off so easily, although the deed was done in a minute's time. If now a man can punish for a long time according to the gravity of the deed, will you restrict God? Shall God be restricted in that which men have freedom to do? If a man may be punished all his life because he does something evil in an hour, shall God not also be allowed to do that?

Secondly, because sin is against an infinite God; since the sin is committed against an infinite Majesty, it therefore deserves an eternal punishment. You know that in the same deed, the punishment is increased or decreased according to who the person is against whom the evil is done. If you strike a common man, you may at most be called before the law once and pay a small fine; but if you strike a Prince, you might end up on the rack, or in prison for all your life, because it is an eminent person against whom you...

<summary>This page argues that eternal damnation is a just punishment for temporal sins because the gravity of an offense is determined by the status of the victim (God) rather than the duration of the act. It encourages believers to endure earthly suffering patiently, viewing it as minor compared to the eternal pains from which Christ has delivered them.</summary>
