# ->Hellish Terrors.<-

offense. If the sin were against an ordinary person, it would not have been right for God to impose extraordinary punishments; but because the sin is against God, who is infinite and eternal, it is therefore just for God to impose eternal pains. Since the wicked sin against God—who is the highest good and an infinite person—by a Divine right, the punishment for that evil can be laid upon them forever; so says Tauler <note>original: "Taulerus"; Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361) was a famous German mystic and theologian.</note> in his *Sermons* <note>original: "Homil."</note>.

Thirdly, if a man lived forever, he would sin forever; therefore God, seeing this disposition in man, can justly punish him for eternity, even though he sins only for a time. Man sins for the duration of his "eternity" <note>Referring to the whole of a person's life or their eternal soul's intent.</note>, so God may punish for the duration of His eternity; these are the <margin>Moralia, Book 34, Chapter 16; Dialogues, Book 4, Chapter 44. <note>original: "Moral. lib. 34. cap 16. lib. 4. Dial. cap. 44."</note></margin> words of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note>, *Moralia, Book 34, Chapter 16 & Dialogues, Book 4, Chapter 44.* Man sins as long as he can (says Bernard) <margin>Letter 153 to Guinarus <note>original: "Epist. 153. ad Guinarum"</note></margin>, *Letter 153 to Guinarus*, and so God will also punish as long as He can. If a man wishes to sin eternally, then it is just for God to bind and punish him, and to make him suffer eternally.

Fourthly, because the wicked, even if they can no longer sin upon Earth, carry their sins with them into Hell after their death; there they continue in sinning without conversion, and there they increase their blasphemies and rebellions against God continually, more than they ever did on earth. Put all of this together, and you cannot in any way rebuke God’s justice for imposing too hard a punishment on the wicked, nor charge your Maker with cruelty and injustice.

Fifthly, the wicked have lost an infinite good for the sake of sin, and have set themselves against an infinite good; therefore they must suffer an infinite evil. Since the wicked despise the infinite grace and mercy of a God, and the infinite merits of a Christ, and the infinite offers of God's grace, they are therefore justly cast into eternal punishment. You have received infinite loving-kindness from God, kindness beyond number; if you sin against these infinite graces, then it is just for God to punish you with infinite pains; for the nature of your punishment must correspond with the nature of your offense. It is the word of an ancient writer: *That if there were ten thousand Hells, and ten thousand times more pain in those Hells than there is now, it would not be enough to satisfy God's justice for the sins of men.* The wicked, even if they suffered ten thousand times more than they do, could not sufficiently satisfy or appease God's justice for the wrong they have done Him through sinning. Therefore, it is in no way unjust to damn someone eternally, even if they lived only a short time to sin here.

### Applications.

If it is true that it can consist with God's justice to damn a man eternally, even if he lives in sin in this world for only a short time, then let this serve:

First, for instruction. This should teach you the evil and the hideous nature of sin; if sin were not so detestable, it would never have such unendurable punishment attached to it. You can know the lion by its claw <note>A common proverb meaning the whole can be judged by a small part; here, the severity of the punishment reveals the severity of the crime.</note>; so too you can know sin by its punishment. If sin incurs so great a guilt

<column-break/>

and deserves such a heavy burden of wrath to be laid upon the sinner, then sin—sin itself—must be a very great evil. Do not, then, look upon sin with light thoughts; it would have been better for you to have run into Hell than into sin. Sin is worse than Hell, for it is sin that made Hell a Hell. If the pains are eternal, and God justly condemns men to those pains for a year of sinning, then see that sin is truly evil. When you see a man being dragged on a sled toward the gallows, you do not think that man is an ordinary rogue or murderer, but some detestable traitor of the State. From the greatness of the punishment, you guess the greatness of the crime; so you may guess of sin, that it is an exceedingly sinful and wicked act, since such an exceeding and unbearable burden is attached to it. Therefore, I pray you, behold sin with loathing <note>original: "verſoepinge", likely a typo for "verfoeyinge".</note>, and look at it in its heavy nature. We look at sin through a diminishing glass; we see it smaller than it is. But you ought to behold sin with a magnifying glass, and see how it is accompanied by eternal punishments; and consequently, it must necessarily be very great.

Secondly, learn from this that small and young children, even if they live but a day, are in as great a danger as men who live a hundred years. For God shall not punish you for the sake of time, but for the hateful nature of sin. And the reason why I draw this conclusion is to take away that blind feeling of the people: they call children "innocents," as if they were without guilt and sin, and many a woman wishes to be where that child is, even though that child could be damned. Now, do not misunderstand me; I do not say that all children are damned, for God has hidden ways to work grace in them and to make them blessed, just as He has public ways and means to make others blessed. Nevertheless, I say: God may justly punish children, even if they live only two minutes in this world, for the sin of their nature <note>A reference to "Original Sin," the belief that all humans are born with a sinful nature inherited from Adam.</note>.

Thirdly, is God just, even if He punishes men for all eternity because they sinned for only a little while? Then take note of this, you young men and young women who are here before God this day: you have lived long enough in sin to deserve eternal pains, however young you may still be. Let these thoughts rest in your hearts: *I have lived long enough to end up in Hell.* Then stop and stand still; go no further in sin, so that you do not aggravate and increase your own pains.

Fourthly and lastly, learn from this not to accuse God of cruelty, that He is a hard God; do not accuse Him of being unjust. For here you see, in the handling of this question, God's justice fully explained: namely, that He may condemn you to eternal pains, even if you have sinned in this world for only a short time.

However, this refers to their eternal salvation: that although the number of the Jews be as the sand on the seashore, yet only a few of them shall be saved. You merchants, when there is a remnant <note>The Dutch word "overblijfsel" means both "remnant" and "survivor."</note> left of a large piece of cloth, are accustomed to give it at a lower price; the remnant is not valued as much as the whole piece. Even if the Jews were innumerable, yet only a remnant of them would be saved. And if that is so, then you can easily judge where the multitude must go.

**1. Objection.** "What," some say, "shall the majority of God’s creatures be damned and bear the pains of Hell? This cannot be believed; how can this be true? For it says in Genesis 15, verse 5, that God came to Abraham and said to him: *Look up toward the Heavens and count the stars, if you are able to count them,* and He said to him: *So shall your seed be.*" God told Abraham that his seed would be like the stars—an innumerable multitude. "Well," they say, "if God promised this to Abraham, would most still be lost? How can this be?"

To this I answer first: That this promise in Genesis 15, verse 5, does not refer to the eternal salvation of all the seed of Abraham. Rather, it is a promise that refers to an eternal grace; namely, that Abraham would have an innumerable seed which would eternally be admitted to the privileges of the Church, which would be regarded as a Congregation of God, and not as if they would all be saved. That this is the meaning, you will find explained by the Apostle in Romans 9, verses 6, 7, and 8: *They are not all Israel, who are of Israel*; that is, they shall not all be saved who come from the loins of Abraham or Jacob. *Neither, because they are Abraham’s seed, are they all children; but in Isaac shall your seed be called*; that is, in Christ shall all the elect <term>elect: those chosen by God for salvation</term> be saved. *Not the children of the flesh are the children of God.* It is as if he said: It is true, Abraham has an innumerable seed according to the flesh, but this number does not consist solely of children of God just because they came from the loins of Abraham; only those who come from Christ and have a share in Him shall be saved through Him, and not all the seed of Abraham.

2. The meaning of this passage cannot be that all the seed of Abraham would be saved; for this would contradict other passages of Scripture, such as those that say: *Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet only the remnant shall be saved* (Romans 9, verse 27). And: *They are not all Israel, who are of Israel* (Romans 9:6). Therefore, not all who came from Abraham’s loins and were shown to be God’s people through an outward sign shall be saved.

**Objection.** "Yes, but," they say, "one reads in 1 Timothy 4, verse 10: *God is a savior of all men.* If God then saves all men, how can your proposition be true, that the majority shall suffer the pains of Hell and the vengeance of eternal fire?"

<column-break/>

To answer this, I must distinguish between types of salvation <note>The Dutch "behoudenis" can mean "salvation," "preservation," or "safety." The author is distinguishing between physical safety and the salvation of the soul.</note>. God can properly be called a "savior" in two ways: first, by giving an outward and temporal preservation; secondly, by giving eternal salvation. When it says there, *God is a savior of all men*, it is not understood in this sense as if He wished to save the souls of everyone; for this salvation is restricted to the elect (Hebrews 9, verse 28 and Hebrews 5, verse 9). But it is understood only as an outward and bodily preservation; namely, that God is a God who preserves the bodies of His children and of the wicked from many perils and deadly needs in this world. That it is taken thus here, I shall demonstrate as follows:

1. From the aim of the passage: *He is a savior of all men.* The words that precede it are: *We labor and suffer reproach.* In order that the Apostle might support the hearts of God's children under outward suffering and bodily reproaches, he tells them: *God is a savior of all men*; that is, God delivers all men at one time or another from many perils in which they find themselves.

2. Because the Scripture in this place indicates another manner of salvation for the elect, beyond that by which He saves all men; for so it stands in verse 10: *He is a savior of all men, but especially of those who believe.* It is as if he said: God preserves all men from many perils and diseases, but in another way He preserves the godly and the elect who believe. In a special way He preserves them, implying that the salvation spoken of here cannot be understood as the salvation of the soul.

3. Because otherwise this passage of Scripture would contradict other passages of Scripture which say that not all men shall be saved through Jesus Christ. And it is a true rule in divinity <note>Theology.</note> that the meaning of one scriptural text cannot be that which is crosswise and contrary to the meaning of another; since the Scripture was given by one and the same Spirit, it speaks everywhere with harmony, and not with a dispute or conflict between passage and passage. Now, when other passages say that God will not save everyone, but that the majority shall be lost, you can take it as granted that this cannot be the meaning of the passage—as if everyone would receive eternal salvation through Christ.

By virtue of this truth, I can draw from this eight specific instructions and applications.

First: Is it the lot of most men to suffer Hellish pains? Then learn from this the unsoundness of that view of the Roman Church <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note>, as if "universality" <note>The "catholicity" or sheer number of followers.</note> were a mark of the true Church. This cannot be, since the greater part of men shall be lost and damned; therefore, to make universality a banner and mark of a true Church is an unsound and groundless view.

Secondly: This condemns the view of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253), an early Christian theologian who famously hypothesized that all beings, including the devil, might eventually be reconciled to God.</note>, who held that all men, yes, even the devils, would be saved; which is an unsound and entirely irrational and un-

...to me, as a Minister of the Gospel, to speak to you in defense of my Lord and Master Jesus Christ; specifically, that although the majority of men and women shall be damned, this in no way brings blame upon God’s mercy or the merits of Jesus Christ. And this I shall make clear to you in five propositions.

First, to you who make this objection, I wish to say, just as the Apostle did: *Who are you, who accuses your Maker, or who answers back to God? Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why have you made me thus?* Romans 9, verses 20 and 21. There the Apostle makes this comparison: if the potter makes a vessel of clay, shall the pot say, "Why have you made me so?" The potter would take that poorly from the potsherd. Well, God has a greater power over man than the potter has over a potsherd; if the clay might not say such a thing, much less should you argue against God in this way: "Why have you damned me?" or "Why was I made to be saved?" This is a quarreling and a resistance against which the Apostle reasons, saying that God will not and shall not endure such a thing. You must not open your mouth against God for this reason.

But
Secondly, God damns no one unless there was sin in that person which deserved greater damnation than God lays upon him; therefore, you cannot accuse God of any cruelty. Romans 9, verse 22: *What if God, wanting to show His wrath and to make His power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction?* <note>In the theology of this period, "vessels of wrath" refers to people destined for destruction due to their own sin and God's sovereign choice.</note> God sends no one to Hell until his sins have prepared him and made him fit for it. The ungodly shall be damned because they are vessels of wrath made fit for destruction; shall God not send them to the place for which they are fit? Those who sin on Earth, who dishonor God on Earth and make sin their pleasure—such people are neither fit nor prepared for Heaven. Heaven would be a Hell for them; those who do not love godly exercises <note>Refers to spiritual practices like prayer, worship, and Bible study.</note> on Earth would not love them in Heaven either. How can you now open your mouth against God when He tells you that He has perhaps endured you for many years before you were damned? And when He casts you into Hell, He says that you are prepared and made fit for Hell; that is then your sorrowful portion. We cannot, then, accuse God of any unmercifulness, since the Lord damns no one unless sin is in him, which prepares him for Hell and makes him a vessel of wrath, made fit for destruction.

Thirdly, that which is consistent with God's decree is also consistent with His mercy. Now, with the decree of our God, it is consistent that the majority should be lost; thus, it does not conflict with His mercy. For this is a certain rule: God's decrees cannot go crosswise or against His attributes; and since mercy is one of His attributes, the decree does not conflict with it. For then God would fight against Himself, which is unthinkable.

<column-break/>

Fourthly, it so little accuses God's mercy when He damns the majority of men, that through it, God’s mercy receives greater luster than otherwise. Romans 9, verses 22 and 23: *What if God, wanting to show His wrath and make His power known, endured the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction; that He might make known the riches of His glory on the vessels of mercy, which He had prepared beforehand for glory?* As if he said: "What? Does the damnation of souls bring blame upon God’s mercy?" No, it glorifies His mercy, so that God might show the riches of His grace to all the vessels of mercy—the elect of God—in that so many should be lost, and yet they are saved.

Fifthly, God would show more mercy if He saved but one single person in the world than He would show "extreme injustice" <note>The author is using a rhetorical argument here: since all are sinners, God could justly damn everyone. Saving even one person is an act of pure, undeserved mercy.</note> in damning the entire world. The reason is: if God saved one person in the world, He would therein show much mercy, since that person does not deserve salvation; he is not worthy to be delivered from Hellish pains. But if God damned the entire world, He would show no extreme or harsh injustice, since *the whole world has sinned and falls short of the glory of God.* All men have forfeited any right to glory and to Heaven, so that if God damned them all, He would not be an unjust God. Therefore, O man, to speak against God’s mercy—what is this other than being bold and quarrelsome against your Maker? What is this other than pleading with the Papists <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics, used here to criticize the idea that humans can "earn" their way into heaven through good works.</note>, as if good works deserved Heaven and moved God to save us and not to damn us? Whereas you see that it is mercy in God if He made but one person saved; it is justice with God if He damned them all. Therefore, it is mercy whenever God saves as many as He does; if He willed to save only a few, it would still be mercy; and if He willed to save only one, it would still be mercy. Thus, the mercy of God is greater in saving as many as He does save. God was not bound to make any of His creatures saved; God would not have been unmerciful if He had not shared even a drop of His lovingkindness. He might have kept His goodness within Himself and enjoyed it, just as He did before the Creation; He is not bound to give anything to anyone.

**Uses.** <note>The "Uses" (Nuttigheden) section of a sermon or treatise provides practical applications of the doctrine for the reader's life.</note> First, how this must serve to convict you who have entertained evil thoughts of God! You have thought ill of God because He laid physical oppression upon you; yet you see that you ought not to think anything against God even if He laid Hell and the weight of His wrath upon you, or if He burned your soul with fire and sulfur. How, then, should this convict you? You have had the gout, the stone <note>Kidney or bladder stones, a common and excruciating ailment in the 17th century.</note>, or some other affliction in this world, and you thought that God was a hard Master; you foolishly accused God for this His doing...

<meta>This page continues the author’s theological defense of God’s righteousness. Following the previous page's discussion on why God is not to be blamed for the damnation of the many, the author concludes that even in Hell, God’s mercy is evident because human sin deserves even greater punishment than what is inflicted. # ->Hellish Terrors.<-

...there you see that if God throws you into Hell, you must not accuse Him. A certain writer says: "Lord, make me miserable on Earth, I shall still say You are a merciful God; yes, throw me into Hell, I shall still continually acknowledge Your mercy; even in the deepest pit of Hell, I shall still say Your mercy still extends to me; for my sins have deserved more pains than a Hell can impose on me." Believe it: if our natures could bear more pains than the Devil can inflict on us, sin deserved that; therefore God is a merciful God who does not impose more on you.

Secondly, do the condemned have any cause to think ill of the mercy of God? Oh, what reason you have then to acknowledge and remember the greatness of the riches of His mercy—you who are freed from damnation, you who are delivered from wrath, and called to obtain salvation through Jesus Christ! 
<margin>Ephesians 2, verses 5, 6, 7.</margin> 
You have greater reason to exalt God’s mercy than the condemned have, although they have no reason to open their mouths against His mercy. Now follows the twelfth Question.

The twelfth Question is: Whether after this life, besides Hell, there is another place of torment in which the souls of men and women are tormented? I consider it necessary to deal with this here, because the Papists <note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics, used here by the Protestant author to distinguish his theology from theirs.</note>, to draw your thoughts away from Hell, maintain that there is a Purgatory <term>Purgatory: from the Dutch 'Vagevyer', literally 'cleansing fire'</term>, which they say is a place of torment after death, under the Earth, above Hell, in which there is a fire nearly as terrible as the hellish fire, where the souls of men must remain for a time as in a prison house or dungeon to be purified after this life, since they were not fully purified in this life; so that through that purification they might be made fit to go into Heaven. Thus they say that the souls of the pious do not go straight to Heaven when they die, but into Purgatory, and are tormented there some hours, some twenty, some a hundred years, and thus purified, and after that they go into Glory. Of this Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit theologian and Cardinal during the Catholic Counter-Reformation.</note>, that great advocate of the Papists, writes much. The origin of this opinion was thus: it began in the year 595 after Christ’s birth, and was first brought up by Pope Gregory the First <note>Pope Gregory I, also known as Gregory the Great.</note>, who held that for certain small faults or venial sins, one must be in the fire there before the day of Judgment. To maintain this Purgatory, the Papists gather great heaps of straw <note>A metaphor for weak or flimsy arguments.</note>, some slight and flickering proofs from the Scripture.

The first and foremost Scripture passage upon which they build this opinion is 1 Corinthians 3, verses 11, 12, 13, 14, 15:
> No one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. And if anyone builds on this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw: each one’s work shall become manifest; for the Day shall declare it, because it is revealed by fire; and the fire shall test what sort of work each one’s is. If anyone’s work remains, which he has built on it, he shall receive a reward. If anyone’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall

<column-break/>

be saved, yet so as through fire.

Here the Papists believe they have an undeniable ground to prove this. *He shall be saved, yet so as through fire*; that is, they say, he shall go into Purgatory, and that shall deliver him from the hellish fire, and he shall come to Heaven a little while after. Before I give you the meaning of the passage, I shall take away their deceptive reasoning and show that by "fire" in this place, Purgatory is not understood, and that for these reasons:

1. If they take the word "fire" in this place literally, then they must also take the other words so, namely "wood," "hay," "straw"; but these cannot be taken literally, but must be understood metaphorically; consequently, the word "fire" must be as well.

2. It says there that the fire shall burn and test the *work*; "each one’s work shall be tested," not the person. However, Purgatory does not burn the work, but the Soul; so it cannot be taken in this sense.

3. It says here that through fire each one’s work shall be made *manifest* (public); but what happens in Purgatory is not manifest—we do not know what happens there. Thus, this fire cannot be Purgatory, because this is a fire that makes things manifest; therefore it must be some other fire.

4. It says there that *everyone’s* work shall be tested; but the Papists themselves say that not everyone shall come into Purgatory—for example, the Martyrs.

5. In this passage, the worker loses his work; but in Purgatory, as they define it, no work is lost.

To give you now the objective and the meaning of these words—*If anyone builds on this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, etc.*—know that by this "foundation" is understood Jesus Christ, and by the "builders," the Teachers. Those words describe two kinds of building materials: some who build on it gold, silver, and precious stones, and some who build on it wood, hay, and straw. That is, there are two kinds of Teachers: some preach Jesus Christ and make Him their foundation, yet they lay upon it wood, hay, and straw—that is, they preach corrupt and bad doctrines in minor matters. Others there are who lay gold and precious stones on it—they preach in everything the true and sound doctrine, keeping at the same time to Jesus Christ their foundation. Well, the text says: each one’s work shall be tested by the fire, but the person shall be saved, yet so as through fire. In this place, by "fire" is understood the fire of the Word and of the Spirit; and it is a manner of speaking, referring to a refiner, just as one refines metal and skims the dross off gold or silver. So shall the fire of the Word consume the erring opinions and unsound doctrines (which are here called wood, hay, straw), and it shall burn up the drossy and corrupt opinions. And when the fire of the Word shall consume these errors, then the person who held such errors shall perhaps have his soul saved, if he is reborn through the Word and leaves his error. This is the correct sense of the passage. And it is not strange that the Word is called "fire" here, for the Lord God calls it so Himself. <margin>Jeremiah 23, verse 29.</margin> <note>Jeremiah 23:29: "Is not my word like as a fire? saith the Lord; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?"</note>

<meta>This page continues the author's refutation of the Catholic doctrine of Purgatory, which was introduced at the end of the previous page. # ->Hellish Terrors.<-

"Is my word not like a fire," says the Lord? "And like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?" So also says *Jeremiah* in Jeremiah 23, verse 29, that the word in his heart became like a burning fire. And it is common in the Scriptures to call the Word of God "fire"; thus, in this instance, the word "fire" must be understood as the "fire of the Word." Just as fire skims the dross from good metal, so shall the fire of the Word consume all unhealthy teachings and separate error from sound doctrine. <note>The author is likely responding to a specific Catholic argument that uses biblical references to "fire" to justify the existence of Purgatory.</note>

The Papists <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics, used here by the Protestant author.</note> hold many other passages to support the existence of Purgatory, such as *Matthew* 12, verse 32: "Whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the one to come." By "the age to come," they say Purgatory is meant. So the meaning would be that a person who commits that sin shall receive no forgiveness here, nor shall Purgatory cleanse him of it there. I answer: by "the age to come" is not meant some time immediately after death, but it refers to the Day of Judgment; so that the person who commits that sin shall have no forgiveness here, nor on the Day of Judgment. For that is how the phrase "the age to come" is understood in Scripture, in *Luke* 20, verses 34 and 35: "The children of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who shall be accounted worthy to obtain that age, and the resurrection from the dead, shall neither marry nor be given in marriage." Here, Christ uses "the age to come" for that time when the dead shall rise, which is the Day of Judgment. Thus, by "the age to come," one does not understand a time in which the souls of men shall lie in Purgatory, but that time when Christ shall come to judge the world; and at that time, he who sins against the Holy Spirit shall receive no forgiveness, but shall be condemned to Hell for that sin.

2. By "the age to come," a Purgatory is not indicated, but it is used in an exclusive sense; "it shall be forgiven him neither in this nor in the coming age," meaning it shall *never* be forgiven him. So *Mark* explains this passage in *Mark* 3, verse 29: "Whoever shall blaspheme against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is guilty of eternal judgment." Here he shows that this saying means nothing other than "it shall never be forgiven him"; therefore, it can in no way serve the Papists as if "the age to come" were proof of Purgatory. So much for the objections.

Now I shall present reasons and Scriptural texts against this opinion:

### First, the reasons.

1. Such a place of torment as Purgatory cannot exist; for such a place would greatly diminish the merits, the suffering, and the blood *of Christ*, as if *Christ's* blood could not cleanse the soul from the guilt of all sin, but that we still needed Purgatory to do this work. 1 *John* 1, verse 7: "The blood *of Christ* cleanses us from all our sins." *Christ's* blood is a Christian's Purgatory. *Hebrews* 1, verse 3: He brings about the purification

<column-break/>

of our sins. I say then, if this [Purgatory] were allowed, much would be detracted from the power of *Christ's* blood, as if it could not fully wash away the sins of man.

2. This would fall short of the satisfaction <term>Satisfaction: the theological concept that Christ's death fully paid the debt of human sin to God's justice.</term> *of Christ*, as if *Christ* had not fully satisfied the wrath of His Father, but that a person nonetheless had to be cleansed first before he entered Heaven.

3. This accuses God of cruelty: that He would torment His children for sins that have already been forgiven.

4. This would lay the utmost injustice upon God: that He would want double satisfaction for a single crime. For *Jesus Christ* has satisfied His Father for all the sins that the elect had committed against Him. If the Father now punished the elect in Purgatory, He would unjustly punish a person for those sins for which *Jesus Christ* had fully satisfied Him.

5. Through this, one would then make "merchandise" <note>The author is referring to the sale of indulgences or the practice of paying for masses for the dead.</note> of forgiveness, as one sees happening in the Roman Church. For these reasons, then, it cannot be allowed that there would be a place of torment for the elect after this life has ended.

Secondly, many Scriptural texts are also against this, such as *Philippians* 1, verse 23: "I desire to be unbound and to be with *Christ*." The Apostle clearly says that after he was unbound [by death], he would be with *Christ*. Therefore, the first Christians did not celebrate their birthday, but their death-day as a joyful day. Likewise *Ecclesiastes* 12, verse 7: "The body returns to the earth, and the Spirit to God, who gave it." The Spirit does not go to Purgatory, but immediately to Heaven. When the body of one of the elect is dead, it goes to the grave, and his spirit—his soul—returns to God, who gave it. And in *Luke* 16, verse 23 it is written: "*Lazarus* died, and he was carried by the angels into *Abraham's* bosom." Likewise the Thief on the Cross: "Today you shall be with me in Paradise." He did not go to Purgatory, but to Paradise, which is to say Heaven; this is evident if you compare that passage with 2 *Corinthians* 12: 3, 4: "I was caught up into Paradise, into the third Heaven, where *Jesus Christ* is in glory." See also 2 *Corinthians* 5, verses 6, 7. Many other texts could be cited to overthrow this groundless opinion. Furthermore, there will be many on earth on the Day of Judgment who will never enter Purgatory. Thus, there is no such place.

Well then, is there no other place besides Hell to torment people in? Is there no Purgatory to cleanse you of your sins that you have committed here? Then this provides a twofold benefit.

### First, for the comfort of you who are godly.

Fear no pains when you shall die. I confess, I would not want to be a Papist for anything in the world, even if there were no error but this in all their teaching: namely, that when I lie sighing on my deathbed under some grievous illness, I would then have to consider, "I must go lie in the fire and burn for ten, twenty, or a hundred years." Death would be a terror to me, if I thought—

I thought, "I must go into the fire for a thousand years, or thereabouts, even if I escape hell." Oh, uncomforting doctrine, which these wicked Papists <note>A common, often derogatory, period term for Roman Catholics.</note> preach, to keep the consciences of their listeners in terror! ### Matthew 10, verse 28.

But rather fear him, who is able to destroy both soul and body in Hell.

<margin>Sixteenth Sermon.</margin>
The Doctrine which I drew from these words was this:
That the consideration of this—that God the Father has absolute supremacy over men and women to cast soul and body into Hell—must work a reverent fear of God in the hearts of His children.

In the handling of this, I have resolved many doubts; now I proceed to what remains to be said concerning this matter. I have come to the thirteenth Question, which is this:

The thirteenth Question: Did Jesus Christ personally descend into Hell, into this place of torments, yes or no? There are various opinions on this. I shall, according to my weak measure which has been given to me, present that which most agrees with the truth and Scripture: And thereafter, I shall point out Scriptural texts that have caused some to think that Christ descended into hell, into this place of torment.

To answer this, I shall provide this proposition: That Jesus Christ did not descend into Hell, into that place of the damned, and I shall establish that from three Scriptural reasons.

First, Christ did not descend into hell; for Luke, who is the most meticulous historian of all the Evangelists, who intended to fully declare everything that Christ did or suffered, makes no mention of this deed, of His personal descent into hell; yet he says, in Luke 1, verse 3: *I know all things that Christ began both to do and to teach* <note>original: "Ik kenne alle dingen die Christus begonnen heeft beyde te doen, en te leeren"</note>; compare Acts 1, verse 1. Now, if Christ went to hell, into the place of the damned, undoubtedly Luke and the other Evangelists would not have omitted such a remarkable deed, since they spoke of things that are less remarkable which Christ performed.

Secondly, if Christ descended into hell personally, it would have to have happened either in the body or in the soul. His body could

<column-break/>

not go into hell, for it was laid that same night by Joseph of Arimathea in the grave, and the text says in Matthew 12, verse 40: *As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, so shall the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.* And as for His Soul, it could not be in hell, for it says in Luke 23, verse 43: *Today you shall be with me in Paradise.* Now, how could Christ say to the Thief, "today you shall be with me in Heaven," if His soul did not go there? Therefore, since neither body nor soul was in hell, Christ was not there.

Thirdly, there was no end <note>The author uses "end" here in the sense of a "purpose" or "goal."</note> for which Christ would do this; and Christ would perform no deed that did not have some good purpose attached to it. I say there was no apparent purpose why Christ should descend into hell; for if Christ had descended, it must have been for one of these three purposes: either, as the Papists hold, to bring souls out of hell; or to make further satisfaction for the sins of His people on earth; or to conquer and overpower the Devil; none of these three could be the purpose; for:

1. Christ’s purpose for going into hell could not be to pull souls out of it; why? Because it is a rule in Theology that souls once in hell shall never come out, Luke 16, verse 26. There Abraham says, *Between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, so that those who want to pass from here to you cannot.* After death there is no redemption; after death there is no conversion or hope of grace once a person is in hell. This then cannot be His purpose, since one who is once damned cannot be made saved.

2. To make further satisfaction for the sins of the Elect could not be Christ’s purpose, since Christ had fully satisfied God's wrath in dying on the Cross; therefore one reads in John 19, verse 30, when Christ took the gall and vinegar to drink, that He cried out, *It is finished*; the work of your salvation was finished in the dying of Jesus Christ; therefore Christ did not need to go into hell to do anything more for your redemption.

3. Christ had fully conquered the Devil by dying on the Cross, Colossians 2, verse 15. *He has despoiled the Principalities and Powers, and He has triumphed over them on that same Cross.* The Apostle knew that Christ had conquered the Devil in dying, otherwise he could not thus triumph over him in bringing him down. Likewise, Hebrews 2, verse 14: *Christ has through His death destroyed him who had the power of death, that is the Devil.* So Christ did not need to go to hell to destroy him; for He had done it on the Cross. Thus, these reasons can strengthen you to believe that Jesus Christ did not descend into hell, this place of the damned.

There are four objections, or arguments of proof, which are brought against this by those who maintain Christ’s descent into hell.

# ->Hellish - Terrors.<-

...of the Resurrection of the Body. But what then is understood by Hell? *You shall not leave my Soul in Hell.* <note>Psalm 16:10 and Acts 2:27.</note> Know, that "Hell" does not always signify the place of the damned, although it is sometimes taken as such; but here it signifies the Grave. When the Apostle says then, *you shall not leave my soul,* that is, you shall not leave my Body in the grave; and so the following words explain it: *nor let your Holy One see corruption.* Although other men shall lie rotting in their graves, yet (says Christ) you shall not let my body perish, nor lie rotting in the grave, since His Body was to rise again on the third day; see Acts 13, verses 35, 36. This text, then, being understood according to its own purpose, shall in no way strengthen the Papists <note>A term used historically by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> in their opinion of Christ’s descent into Hell.

Fourthly, they bring another proof from 1 Peter 4, verse 6: *For to this end was the Gospel preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit.* Here the Papists say that the Scripture says the Gospel of Christ was preached to the dead—to the damned in Hell—so that they might live to God, and that they might come out of Hell and be saved; thus they explain the passage. But I shall give you the true sense of the passage: some understand "the dead" in this place to mean those who are spiritually dead, even though they live naturally—those who are dead in their sins and transgressions. For the Scripture calls those who live "dead men" when they are ungodly, as in 1 Timothy 5, verse 6: *She that follows her pleasure is dead while she lives;* and Revelation 3, verse 1: *They had the name that they lived, but they were dead.* So, I say, some explain this place: the Gospel was preached to the ungodly, who lived a natural life but were dead in their sins, and some of those were converted by that Gospel, and were to be judged according to men in the flesh, but would live to God in the Spirit. 

But I do not hold this to be the right sense of the passage; rather, I believe that Calvin <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), a principal figure in the development of Reformed theology.</note> and Piscator <note>Johannes Piscator (1546–1625), a German Reformed theologian.</note> come closer to the aim of the Holy Spirit. They say that by "the dead" are understood those same ones mentioned in chapter 3, verse 19, namely, those of the ancient world, who were then dead [when Peter wrote]; that the Gospel, through the ministry of Noah, was preached to the ancient world while they lived, but who were dead when Peter wrote this Letter. And this Gospel was preached to them so that they might be judged according to men in the flesh; that is, the Gospel was preached to some of the ancient world who, although they were judged in the flesh—that is, perished in the body by the Flood, as everyone knows—nevertheless were converted by the preaching of Noah, and lived to God. This is their explanation. Well, this in no way refers to Christ’s descent into Hell. For the word does not say that Christ went there, but that the Gospel was preached to them by means of Noah’s ministry, by which means some of the ancient world were saved and not all were lost.

I have dwelled on this so long because there are 

<column-break/>

so many Scripture passages that the Papists bring up to strengthen this opinion, and you see how plausible the texts are upon which they ground it. And hereupon I wish to give you this warning: that you guard yourselves from accepting an opinion just because, at first glance, the proponents of that opinion cite Scripture. Believe me, if a Papist were to speak with many of you about Christ’s descent into Hell and pressed these Scripture passages against you, perhaps you would not be able to answer him; yet it does not follow that you must side with them. There is not a wandering spirit <note>A term for a heretic or teacher of false doctrine.</note> in the world but that he uses Scripture to maintain his opinion. Guard yourselves, then, I say, from believing every opinion just because its proponents bring up Scripture texts to prove it, unless you have well-examined the opinion itself and tested it against the Scripture. But I will pass over this now.

**Utilities.** <note>Practical applications or lessons for the reader.</note> Well, is this truth then established, that Christ did not descend into Hell, into the place of the damned, even though that seems to be implied somewhat by our Article of Faith?

1. Then learn from this that, although Christ did not travel to Hell, He nevertheless suffered much of the **hellish pains** on the cross for your sake, which you would have had to suffer if He had not suffered all this. You must not value Christ’s love any less because He did not descend into hell for you; for He suffered much of Hell for your sake, in lying under the weight of sin and of His Father’s wrath.

2. Know also that, although Christ did not descend into Hell, He nevertheless suffered enough to deliver you and keep you from Hell: Colossians 2, verses 14, 15; Hebrews 2, verse 14.

3. See to it how you understand that Article of Faith regarding Christ’s descent into Hell; for if you understand it as Christ’s personal descent into the place of the damned, then it is an untruth; yet if you understand it as Christ’s powerful descent in suffering something which corresponds to the pains of Hell, this can be true. So much has been said regarding the thirteenth Question: whether Christ personally descended into Hell, or not?

### The Fourteenth Question is, Whether there is actually fire in Hell, or not?

Beloved, I considered this a very necessary piece to speak upon, so that you might be all the more deterred from your sins; if Love cannot do it, then may the Fire do it. I confess, regarding this Question there are various opinions. Most that I have consulted on this matter give this answer, which I also believe mostly agrees with the truth: that just as we do not know for the present where Hell is, so also for the present there is no fire in it. But that on the Day of Judgment, Christ shall come to Judgment in flaming fire, and that this fire shall burn the ungodly for all eternity. Although there is no fire in Hell now, nevertheless the Scripture gives enough indication that after the Day of Judgment there shall substantially be fire, in which the ungodly shall eternally...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of Hell, moving from the definition of the word in the Apostles' Creed to the physical and spiritual reality of hellfire and its properties.</meta>

# ->Hellish Terrors.<-

...be burned. It is the word of *Gregory* <note>Pope Gregory I, also known as Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note>; If, he says, God shall condemn the ungodly to the fire on the Day of Judgment, why shall that fire not last eternally to torment the damned? <note>original Latin: "Si in igne damnabit reprobos, quare non in igne cruciabit damnatos."</note> One could see no reason why there should be no fire after the Day of Judgment. I know that some theologians hold that there is fire burning in Hell even now; but I believe that the same could hardly be established from Scripture; although it is true that Scripture speaks of eternal and unquenchable fire; yet that can be said figuratively, to represent that they shall be burned by the wrath of God, which wrath torments the Soul just as fire torments the Body. Others hold that when the Body shall be in Hell, there shall not only be the worm of conscience to torment the Soul, but also fire to burn the Body. It is a remark of a theologian that I have read: He says, just as we cannot now say where the place of Hell is, so we cannot now say whether there is fire in Hell or not; but on the Day of Judgment we shall know where Hell is, and whether there is fire or not; but in all probability, Hell shall be on Earth; the godly shall be taken up into Heaven; and there the ungodly shall be tormented with fire, in the place where they made it the site of their sinning; God shall make the Earth the place of their Judgment, and when Christ comes for Judgment, the World shall be set ablaze for all eternity by the breath of God.

### Objection,

The fire cannot be physical, because it shall afflict the Soul; for all that is physical works by touch, which cannot occur between the Soul and a Physical fire.

I answer first: The fire may work through a supernatural power, if not through a natural one; and although there is no physical contact of dimension, there can nevertheless be a contact of essence and of power.

Secondly: Hell can be considered in two ways: first in itself, and second in respect to the primary worker whose instrument it is; and thus it can work upon the soul; just as the heat of nature has the power to make things hot, but from the Soul it has the power to change nourishment into our own substance. And although *Augustine* in *City of God, Book 21, Chapter 10*, doubts whether there is physical fire in Hell now, he nevertheless does not doubt that there shall be physical fire there after the Resurrection.

But Beloved, though there shall be fire in Hell, know nonetheless that this fire is very unlike that fire which burns in our hearths; if you were to take it so literally, then the other words must also be taken literally, such as worms and sulfur. But no; it is unlike our fire in its very properties.

First, our fire has light as well as heat, but the fire of Hell, says *Gregory*, indeed has heat to burn a person, but it has no light. <note>original Latin: "Cremationem habet, lumen non habet vim comburendi retinet, illuminandi amisit." / Translation: "It has burning, it has no light; it retains the power of consuming, it has lost the power of illuminating."</note> In the hellish fire there shall be the black-

<column-break/>

-ness of darkness forever, *Jude verse 13.* The Poet describes it as *Cimmerian* darkness <note>A classical reference to a mythical people said to live in perpetual mist and darkness near the entrance to the underworld.</note>, being a stretch of land in Italy between Baiae and Cumae, where the *Cimmerii* live, being so surrounded by hills and overshadowed with overhanging Mountains that the Sun never comes there.

Secondly, our fire, whatever it consists of, consumes and turns things to ash; but the hellish fire is not of that nature; you shall burn there eternally and never be consumed; it would be good for one of the damned if the hellish fire would burn him to ash; but this is his misery: the fire of hell shall eternally burn his Body, but never consume it; he shall always be dying, and never be dead; our fire consumes and destroys all that is cast into it, but your Body shall not be consumed in Hell.

Thirdly, our fire is kindled by a man and can also be extinguished by a man; he who made the fire can put it out if it pleases him; but the hellish fire is not kindled by a man: for so it is written in *Isaiah 30 verse 33*, "The breath of the Lord shall kindle it like a stream of brimstone," and *Job 20 verse 26.* Neither can it be extinguished by a man; therefore it is called an unquenchable fire by *Luke*; they shall be cast into the unquenchable fire.

Fourthly, our fire does not have such a terrible power to torment as the fire of Hell has; our fire, as *Polycarp* says in the *Life of Sebastian*, is but as fire painted on a wall, which cannot burn you; but the fire of hell is of such a tormenting power that the Body is punished thereby with unbearable pains. Let us now draw this together in a short application.

### Useful Lessons.

First: Is it so, that it is debated whether there is fire in hell now or not, even though it is provable that there is? Then let this serve us to rather avoid the hellish fire than to dispute over it so precisely; do not struggle so much regarding the hellish fire as you take care to escape it. I recall that Mr. *Bolton* <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631), an influential English Puritan clergyman.</note> offers this reasoning: Suppose there is no fire in Hell, nevertheless I assure you that you shall be roasted with fire; the fire of God’s wrath shall torment you more than physical fire can do. Therefore, do not investigate the hellish fire so much as you strive not to go there. I have read a story of a fool who, seeing his house burning, stood and stared to know how the fire got in, and where it burned, in what place, and what things, but was not concerned with extinguishing it—this was his folly. So also you, who go about noting whether there is fire in hell, and how it is kindled, and how it is durable, and yet never seek by a godly life to avoid it—you are more foolish than he.

Secondly: Learn from this that although there is fire in hell, this can in no way terrify you who are God’s Elect, who have a right to Christ Jesus. Christ has extinguished the power of these flames in respect to you; although they shall burn and roast the ungodly, they shall nevertheless never touch you.

<meta>This page continues the sermon on the terrors of Hell, specifically focusing on the physical nature of hellfire and how the blood of Christ acts as the only remedy to extinguish its spiritual flames. # ->Hellish Terrors.<-

...of Israel. I have told you once that *Nebuchadnezzar's* fiery furnace was a type <note>In 17th-century theology, a "type" is a historical event that foreshadows a spiritual reality.</note> of Hell; that fire did not singe a hair of the heads of those three youths, but it burned those who threw them into it. So too, although the godless wish you in Hell and would gladly have you there, yet you need not fear, for the hellish fire shall not singe a hair of your head. You are then delivered from that fire through the right you have in *Jesus Christ*; because you have a share in *Christ's* blood, so shall that blood extinguish the hellish fire for you, and it shall not burn you. *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author whose "Natural History" was often cited for its curious scientific claims.</note> says in one of his writings that nothing in the world extinguishes fire as quickly as salt and blood; and therefore in many countries where blood is obtained in abundance, they use salt and blood rather than water to extinguish a fire. If you throw a mass of water into the fire, the fire will immediately work it out and break through; but throw blood on it, and it shall quench it in a moment. Beloved, I relate this only for this end: that although there be fire in Hell, you may indeed obtain *Christ's* blood; and I can assure you, whatever [physical] blood can do, the blood of *Christ* shall extinguish the flames of hell, so that none of them shall burn or destroy you. Therefore, oh, see that you gain a share in the blood of *Jesus Christ*.

Thirdly, if it be so that there shall be fire in hell—though it may be disputed whether there is fire now or not—well, oh then, guard yourself against those fiery sins that shall bring you into this place of fire; for fiery sins, says *Bernard* <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a medieval mystic often quoted by Protestant preachers for his emphasis on personal piety.</note>, give birth to fiery pains, yes, the fire of hell, to torment you. See to it then, if you burn in a fire [of sin] on Earth, you shall one day burn in the hellish fire. Do you ask now from what fire you must guard yourself here? I answer: First, guard yourself from burning in the fire of fury and wrath, like a madman; guard yourself from burning in that violent passion of the heart. When your passions are set on fire, your fiery sins shall bring forth fiery judgments. Secondly, guard yourself from the fire of lust; guard yourself also from that fire, for the fire of pleasures would one day bring you into the hellish fire. You know what the Scripture says of fornicators who burn in their lusts: it is better for them to marry than to burn, *1 Corinthians 7 verse 9*. There are some who burn through their pleasures and desires for harlots; well, if you burn in lust, see to it that those desires do not one day cause you to burn in Hell. You know what *Solomon* says in the Proverbs regarding an adulterer: that he with whom the Lord is angry shall fall into the mouth of the harlot <note>Refers to Proverbs 22:14, suggesting the harlot is a trap for those already under God's judgment.</note>, *Proverbs 22 verse 14*, and that he who goes to the strange woman shall not ponder the path of life, *Proverbs 5 verse 5*. Beloved, if you wish to burn in your pleasure, you are in very great danger of burning in hell, unless God gives you a heart to truly and uprightly repent of your sins. Well, then let the consideration of the fiery pains of hell work in you a concern to avoid fiery and burning lusts. I have read a story of a young maiden who, being tempted by a lustful young man to the act of impurity, and who persisted very much in doing that foul deed, gave him this answer: "If you," she said, "will give me one thing that I desire, then I will grant your...

<column-break/>

...request." He said that he would indeed do so. "Well, I desire," she said, "that you hold your finger in a candle for a whole hour, to burn." "Oh," said he, "that is unreasonable, what you demand of me." "It is so," said she, "but your request is yet much more unreasonable: namely, that I should satisfy you in a matter for which I would burn not just for an hour, but eternally in the unquenchable fire of Hell." Beloved, I stand here for this purpose: if perhaps the love of *Christ* and the love of grace might not compel you to hate sin and obey God, at least the fear of Hell may make you remember your sins and fear Him. Oh, that God would sanctify the thoughts of hellish pains to your hearts! *Mr. Dod* <note>John Dod (c. 1549–1645), a prominent English Puritan whose practical divinity was highly influential in the Netherlands.</note> says: "If hellfire is to make anyone look toward Christ, then these thoughts of the fire of Hell must be maintained and kept alive." And truly I urge this only to this end: that if *Christ's* loving-kindness, loveliness, and beauty cannot entice a gnarled and stiff-necked heart, at least the hearing of these pains of the damned might make it terrified. When you are then tempted toward any lust, take note of this: that to burn in hellfire shall be intolerable, and the thoughts of this fire shall powerfully restrain you from fiery lusts. I have read of a young man who was very inclined to impurity, and who prayed much to God for the <term>mortification</term> <note>The spiritual practice of "killing" or subduing sinful desires through discipline and prayer.</note> of those burning lusts that he had within him. And he said of himself: As often as he felt lust arise within him, he ran to the fire, stuck his finger in the flame, and burned it, and then reasoned with himself thus: "Well, my soul and my body, if you cannot endure for a moment of time that your finger is in the fire, how then will you endure for all eternity that not only your finger, but also your whole body lies eternally in the flames?" And by this means, he says of himself, he gained great strength for the killing of his burning desires. Well, oh beloved! I pray you (I know that I speak to a mixed people, and perhaps to many who burn in their lusts), let one fire burn out the other: let the hellish fire consume the fire of sins and cause you to avoid it: for (to end this with the word of *Bernard*), fiery sins shall bring you into fiery pains.

Fourthly, if it be so that there shall be fire in Hell, then see here God's righteous judgment, who shall punish your bodies—which have been instruments of sin—as well as your souls. God shall not only punish your souls with a <note>The "worm of conscience" is a traditional image for the internal, psychological torment of guilt that never dies.</note> worm of conscience, but He shall also punish your bodies with fire. Your eyes, which have been full of impurity and adultery, those very eyes shall be struck into flame with fire. Your mouths, which have taken in drink with excess, shall swallow fire and sulfur in abundance. Your limbs, which have burned in impurity and lust, shall one day burn in the fire of Hell: this body shall burn in Hell by the righteous hand of God. Well, oh see then whether the pleasure of sin, coming through the body, can outweigh the pains of this fire. Perhaps...

...burns your body in unripe lusts; but shall these pleasant dalliances be worth a burning fire? Perhaps you can now swallow an abundance of Beer and Wine; but will this be able to cool the palate of your mouth when your whole body shall be on fire? Consider whether all the pleasant sins, which you, being here, commit in the body, shall outweigh those fiery pains which you shall have on the last day. And thus it has been, I confess, a sorrowful subject over which I have preached for so long: nevertheless, God will perhaps bless it for some of you. Some are moved by love, some by fear. God tells us in the Scripture that the Teachers are various and walk in various ways; some are <term>Boanerges</term> <note>original: "Boanerges"; a Greek-derived name meaning "Sons of Thunder," used in the New Testament to describe those who preach with power and intensity.</note>, Sons of Thunder, and some are <term>Barnabases</term> <note>original: "Barnabassen"; meaning "Sons of Consolation," referring to those who preach with gentleness and comfort.</note>, Sons of Consolation. The Scripture tells us that we must make a distinction, having compassion on some, but saving others through fear, in verses 22 and 23 <note>Refers to the Epistle of Jude, verses 22-23.</note>. The Scripture indicates clearly enough that we must preach fearsome doctrines to frighten people away from sin and from Hell. And I also wish from God that this doctrine may have those effects on the godless and the impious, who walk the path and do those things which lead to Hell, and yet think nothing of it.

->Matthew 10, verse 28.<-

->But fear him much more, who can destroy both soul and body in Hell.<-

<margin>XVII. Sermon.</margin>
In treating this text, I have drawn this Doctrine from it:
->That the consideration of this—that God the Father has an absolute supremacy over Men and Women to cast soul and body into Hell—must work in the hearts of His Children a reverent fear of God.<-

In the handling of this, I have searched through six sermons; that which remains concerning this Doctrine, I shall now dispatch.

The fifteenth Question, in order, which I shall answer is this: Since the Scripture clearly points out to us that there is a Hell, and that the godless who are already dead are in Hell, when did God make Hell? We read that God in the beginning created Heaven and Earth, and what the works of His hands were in the six days; but we do not read when God made Hell. I confess, this is a precise <note>In this context, "precise" means overly curious or technical.</note> question, and those who treat the same speak of it only briefly. I shall present to you the thoughts of some: <term>Lud. Mollina</term> <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note>, an old writer, gives this opinion and says that Hell was made on the third day, although the Scripture says nothing of it; he gives this reason: because on the third day the Earth was adorned with its beauty, and since Hell is in the center-point of the Earth, so also was Hell made when the Earth was thus adorned. But this has no firmness at all: for even if one takes for granted that Hell is in the center-point of the Earth, the Scripture nowhere specifically agrees to this. Another wri-

<column-break/>

-ter says that Hell was made before the six days, before Earth or Heaven was made. And the occasion for this opinion was given to him by a question which was proposed by an old writer: "What did God do before He made the world?" This learned writer gives him this answer: "God prepared Hell for such curious questioners as you are, who want to sniff through the secrets of God and know those things which you are not permitted to know" <note>This is a famous anecdote often attributed to St. Augustine in his "Confessions," though he mentions it to criticize the flippant nature of the answer.</note>. I do not accept this as a truth either, for certainly God delighted and satisfied Himself in His own glory before the world was made. Hell was a creature <note>A "creature" in 17th-century English refers to anything created by God.</note>, and no creature existed before the world was made: for the Scripture tells us that Heaven and Earth were made in the beginning. Some among the Rabbis say that Hell was made on the seventh day, and that although God rested from His labor on the seventh day, He nonetheless made Hell then, so that the godless should never rest, even though God wanted to let His own people rest. But this is also quite contrary to the Scripture, for the Scripture says that God rested on the seventh day, which He could not have done if He had made Hell.

<term>Kornelis vander Steen</term> <note>Better known by his Latin name, Cornelius a Lapide (1567–1637), a Flemish Jesuit priest and renowned exegete.</note> is of this opinion (and it is the most probable) that Hell was made on the first day, and for this reason, which may seem to come very close: because the Angels fell on the first day; for so the theologians generally write about this. "It is very clear," some say, "that they fell before the sixth day; for on the sixth day there was already a devil to tempt Adam." Adam did not live a single day in innocence; but the very day in which he was made, he sinned; not one night did he remain in honor (Psalm 49, verses 12, 13). Well, as soon as the Angels fell, they were cast into Hell, so that we can give no more probable opinion than that the fall of the Angels and the making of Hell happened at the same time. Upon their fall, Hell was created to receive them. On the first day the Angels fell, and then Hell was made to receive the fallen Angels.

The sixteenth question is: What is understood by that part of the pains of the damned in Hell, that they shall have a <term>worm of conscience</term> <note>A traditional metaphor for the internal, gnawing remorse of the soul.</note> that shall never die and that shall gnaw their conscience eternally? (Mark 9, verse 44; Luke 13, verse 28). And second: what pain is expressed by the <term>gnashing of teeth</term>? Since this is a great part of the pains of the damned, it is good to investigate what is represented by these phrases.

As for the first, Beloved, I shall not give you those absurd thoughts of some who mean that there shall be a physical worm that shall gnaw the flesh of the body after the Resurrection. But by the worm that shall never die is understood that gnawing and terrifying of the Conscience which shall come upon a damned soul because it lies under the wrath of an avenging and incensed God eternally. Although the godless here on Earth have unfeeling and seared Consciences, so that sin never grieves them, nor does their Conscience ever upset them; nonetheless, the Conscience in Hell shall be like a worm to them, always gnawing them, and distressing them, and making them restless and terrified, because they lie under God's wrath forever without hope of escape.

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth sermon on the terrors of Hell, transitioning from a discussion on the fire of damnation to the internal torment of the conscience and the specific meaning of the "gnashing of teeth" described in the Gospels.</meta>

# Hellish Terrors.

...come. Just as worms continually gnaw at a dead body, so shall sins gnaw at the conscience; and even the Heathens, through the glimmering light of nature, saw something of this. I recall that **Virgil**, a Heathen Poet, speaks of one **Tityos** <note>original: "Titius"; a giant in Greek mythology punished in Tartarus by having his liver pecked out by vultures.</note>, whose liver was gnawed every day by a flying vulture, and every night it was restored and grew back again, so that the bird might feed upon it again the next day. The Poets imagined this to be what Hell is; they could not speak of it clearly because they did not have the Scriptures, yet they did not guess poorly or fail to depict what the Scripture calls "the worm of conscience," which shall never die.

**Usefulness.** Is this so? Well, oh how careful you ought to be while you live here on earth to maintain a good conscience! For believe it: the more you defile your conscience here and the more you burden it with guilt, the more you shall feel the gnawing of that worm in Hell. Therefore, I pray you, beware of harboring guilt in your conscience. I remember that **Luther**, in his Commentaries, has this saying: *That the person who carries the guilt of sin in an awakened conscience without repentance, carries a Hell with them on earth.* And truly, you do little less if the conscience is awake. You who heap sin upon sin, lust upon lust, deceit upon deceit; if you load all this upon your conscience, take heed, for the conscience shall be a gnawing worm to you one day. The conscience shall one day torment and gnaw at you more than it does now. Perhaps your conscience is now made unfeeling and has fallen asleep; but this worm shall never die; it shall gnaw and plague you at the last day without ceasing.

**Secondly,** What is understood by that part of the pain of the ungodly expressed by the "gnashing of teeth" in Hell? Some imagine that it shall proceed from the cold that will be in Hell; for although there shall be fire, they believe some shall freeze from the cold. I consider this to be but a dream. I shall give you three reasoned guesses as to why the pains of Hell are presented under this expression of gnashing of teeth.

<margin>Luke 13, verse 28.</margin>
**First,** the gnashing of teeth shall proceed from that irreconcilable enmity which the ungodly shall bear in their hearts toward all those who shall be saved. They shall gnash their teeth out of envy because others are saved while they are damned. **Luke 13, verse 28:** *There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth:* And what is the reason? *When you shall see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of God, but yourselves cast out.* You know that men bite their teeth in envy when they see the happiness of someone they hate; so do the damned spirits gnash their teeth because they envy the elect their salvation and glorification.

**Second,** the damned in Hell shall gnash their teeth out of fury against **Jesus Christ**, because He would not save them as He did others. To gnash the teeth is the posture of a man who is in mad wrath and distress. Here the ungodly are said to gnash their teeth to show that they bear an irreconcilable wrath and indignation against **Jesus**

<column-break/>

**Christ**, because He would not redeem them through His blood; and also against **God**, because He would not save them through His mercy. Oh, that they cannot take revenge on **God** and **Christ**! That they cannot thrust Him out of Heaven! That is why they gnash their teeth so. They not only envy you your glory, but they are also rebellious against **God** and **Jesus Christ**.

**Third,** they gnash their teeth out of the realization that during their lifetime they had the opportunity to obtain Heaven and Salvation, yet they neglected it. Just as we know, men bite their teeth when they have lost a suitable opportunity that would have brought them profit, by which neglect they now suffer great loss. So the damned are said to do here, when they consider that they lived under a godly ministry, that their sins were revealed to them, and they were urged toward a godly life, yet they stifled all those movements and stopped their ears against all the rebukes of the Word; that although **Christ** was offered to them on easy conditions, they nevertheless would not embrace Him. Oh, this shall greatly torment the damned: simply thinking that they had many opportunities for grace in this world, yet neglected them all.

**Usefulness.** Is this so? That the gnashing of teeth proceeds from envy toward the happiness of the Saints and from resentment toward **Jesus Christ**—is this their pain? Oh beloved, if any of you envy the happiness of the godly on earth, or have any resentment against **Jesus Christ**, or are filled with any malice regarding the salvation of the Godly in Heaven, then you are doing the very work of Hell. This is what is done in Hell: hating **Jesus Christ**, hating the conversion of souls, etc. If you then envy the good of souls, you do the work of Hell; the Devils and the damned do so—they gnash their teeth out of envy because other souls are glorified and they are damned.

Thus I have handled these sixteen questions; I shall pull everything together and give you some general Uses flowing from this entire Doctrine for the exercise of godliness.

-> **This Doctrine of Hell, and of its pains, is very useful for the ungodly and the godly.** <-

**First,** it is very useful in respect to the ungodly in two ways: 1. For the terrifying of the ungodly; 2. For the rebuking and restraining of sins in the ungodly. In these two respects, this doctrine is wonderfully useful.

**First,** it serves to terrify and unsettle the souls of careless and unfeeling sinners; and to work that terror, I shall present six terrifying observations that an ungodly person can draw from this Doctrine of Hell.

1. Because most men and women whom God has made shall have this sorrowful portion: to be tormented in the flames of Hell. But since I have spoken of this previously in an answer to the tenth question, I pass over it by merely naming it.

2. Because many are tormented in Hell who have done more good than many...

# Hellish Terrors.

...many of us who now live on earth and still hope for Heaven. Just look at the Scriptures. A humbled **Ahab** is in this place of torment, <note>1 Kings 21:29; Ahab was a king of Israel who repented briefly after a prophecy of doom, yet was still judged for his wickedness.</note> *1 Kings 21 verse 29.* He humbled himself, and perhaps many of us have not had a single hour of true humility since we entered the world. A repentant **Judas** is now in Hell, *Matthew 27 verse 3.* **Judas** felt remorse and returned the silver coins; nevertheless, the Scripture says **Judas** has gone to his own place—that is, to Hell, *Acts 1 verse 25.* And perhaps many of us, since we were born, have never had a contrite and repentant heart. A weeping **Esau** is now in Hell; he sought the blessing with tears, and he found it not, *Hebrews 12 verse 17.* And many of us have not yet shed a single tear over our sins or our miseries while we have been in the body; their faces are like flint, from which water could come as easily as tears from them. A fearing and trembling **Felix** is now in Hell, <note>Acts 24:25; Felix was a Roman governor who trembled with fear while listening to the Apostle Paul preach about judgment.</note> *Acts 24 verse 25.* Many of us tremble no more at a sermon than the pews in which they sit or the stones upon which they stand. A half-converted **Agrippa** is now in Hell, who was halfway turned and moved by the Word; and many of us have felt no change in our souls through the Word since we have lived. Well, Beloved, how ought this to bring terror to a godless person? A humbled **Ahab** is there, and you are not yet humbled; a repentant **Judas** is there, and you are not yet unsettled; a trembling **Felix** is there, and you are not yet moved in your conscience upon hearing the Word! What a sorrowful word this shall be for you: that many are now in that place of torment who did more good in their lifetime than you have ever done?

3. Hell, who nevertheless was no drunkard, and you are perhaps one. The **Pharisee** is now in Hell, who was no adulterer; perhaps you are one. The **Pharisees** are now in Hell, who did not profane the Sabbath so, and perhaps you, since your birth, have not yet hallowed a single Sabbath to God. Oh, how this must leave you stunned! Certainly, if your conscience is not greatly surrendered to insensitivity, then these observations shall deeply unsettle you.

4. Note that many have taken more trouble to go to Hell—to this place of the damned—than many of us have done to go to Heaven. At one o'clock, when she came to the meal expecting nothing but merriment, this old man began to weep. Truly, beloved, you may well speak of yourselves in this way. When you see noble, worldly people who, as **Habakkuk** says, weary themselves in vain (or in vanities), *Habakkuk 2 verse 13;* who sit up entire nights to play cards, to gamble, and to drink; when you see people who are untiring in the ways of sin, then you may fall to weeping and say: "This person has sat up longer and spent more time to go to Hell than I have spent going to God in my inner chamber." And this must be a terrifying observation for you: that many take more trouble to go to Hell than you do to go to Heaven.

# Hellish Dread.

You do the works of the Devil. From all this, you can see that you may well hope and believe that you are children of God, while you are nonetheless children of the Devil; and that you think you are on the way to Heaven, when you are actually walking the straight path to Hell. And should it not deeply dismay you that many people will suffer the pains of Hell who, in reality, hoped to enjoy the glory of Heaven?

This is the punishment of a damned soul: that they depart from Jesus Christ; *Depart from me.* The "punishment of loss" <note>term: "punishment of loss" (poena damni); a theological term referring to the pain caused by the permanent separation from the presence of God, often considered the greatest suffering in Hell.</note> is, above all punishments, the greatest pain for a damned soul. "No," says Christ, "depart from me, you cursed, *into the fire.*" "Yes, but oh Lord," they say, "if we must go away and into the fire, let it only be for a short time." 4. "No," says Christ, "it shall last forever; depart, you cursed, *into the everlasting fire.*" "Oh, but Lord, if we must be cursed and go into the everlasting fire, let us at least have good company, which might somewhat ease our sorrow and make us forget our misery." 5. "No," says Christ, "you shall have only the Devils and the cursed, damned spirits as your companions; *Depart, you cursed, into the everlasting fire, with the Devil and his angels.*" These are the best companions a damned soul shall have. This is the sorrowful sentence which shall be passed over a godless sinner; and once it is spoken, it is irrevocable; it cannot be called back. Put these six observations together, and what do you think? Who would want to go to Hell for the sake of a sin? Who would damn his soul for the sake of a harlot? Who would want to lie under this fearsome sentence for the enjoyment of a fleeting lust?

But as for the godly and upright hearts, they need not be dismayed at all; for they are delivered through Jesus Christ from this coming wrath.

May the Lord grant that you may know more of Hell now, so that you may feel less of it hereafter.
