# On the Omnipresence and Omniscience of God, presented in several sermons, on 2 Chronicles 16, verse 9. By **Mr. CHRISTOPHER LOVE.**
->Translated by M. J. K.<-

> **2 Chronicles 16, verse 9.**
> For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is perfect toward him; herein you have done foolishly; therefore from henceforth you shall have wars.

My text is a part of that divine message which Hanani the Seer brought to Asa, King of Judah. Asa, being in a time of need and difficulty, mistrusted his God and ran to Ben-hadad, King of Syria, for his help and assistance against Baasha, King of Israel. When Asa thus mistrusted God’s providence—despite his previous experiences of God preserving him and his people—the Seer Hanani brings these words of the text as a reason why Asa had no cause to distrust God and thereby lean on outside help for the preservation of his Crown and Kingdom. Your eyes, he means to say, were upon Ben-hadad the king of Syria, but your eyes should have been upon the Lord for His help; for *the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth*, etc. This is the occasion of the words; in the words are two parts: 1. A reason why he should not have set his eyes on the King of Syria, but on God, for *God’s eyes run to and fro*, etc. 2. An announcement of a heavy 

<column-break/>

judgment upon Asa because of his reliance on the King of Syria: *From henceforth you shall have wars.*

The words themselves are not obscure; I shall now only give you an expanded explanation, namely of the first part of this verse: *The eyes of the Lord*. This does not mean that God actually has instruments, members, and parts of the body, since He is a <term>pure Spirit</term> <note>meaning a being without a physical body</note>; so He has no eyes, but it is spoken after the manner of men. Just as God is sometimes attributed a hand—as we seize something with the hand, so God takes hold of a matter—so an eye in God signifies that inseparable and certain observation and knowledge which God has over all men, and over all things that have been, are, and shall be in the world. *The eyes of the Lord* generally signify two things: First, an act of observation in God, through which He has a precise insight into all that has been or shall be. Proverbs 15, verse 3: *The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good*; there, by the eyes of the Lord, is understood God's noticing of all creatures. Secondly, *the eyes of the Lord* are taken in Scripture for a more particular preservation by God over some creatures, Psalm 33, verses 18 and 19: *Behold, the eye of the Lord is upon them that fear him, upon them that hope in his mercy; to deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine*; here God’s eye is placed for His protective eye, just as in the previous place it was for His observing eye.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of God, transitioning from the internal "fear of God" to the doctrine of His Omniscience and Omnipresence. It specifically interprets the biblical metaphor of "God's eyes" as His perfect knowledge of human actions and thoughts.</meta>

# Of the Omnipresence

eye. In this passage, it must be taken in both senses; the eyes of the Lord run through the whole earth; that is, Asa <note>Referring to King Asa of Judah in 2 Chronicles 16:9.</note>, you have no reason to distrust God in your distress, since God saw well in what straits you were thrown, and you had the eye of His protection to deliver you, and He would indeed have delivered you if you had trusted in Him.

**Secondly**, what does it mean to say that God’s eyes run through the whole earth? This way of speaking signifies two things. First, the speed or readiness of God's knowledge. God does not know things by degrees, <term>step by step</term> <note>original: "per prius & posterius," meaning "by what comes before and what comes after."</note>, as we do through reasoning, drawing one thing from another or the unknown from the known; but He knows and sees everything <term>at a single glance</term> <note>original: "uno intuitu"</note>, in an instant. Secondly, it signifies the universality of His knowledge: they run through the entire earth. There is not one part, not one dark corner, not one hiding place in your heart that God does not see; His eyes run through the entire earth. So, there you have the explanation of the first part of the verse.

**The observation is this**: That it is an essential attribute in God to see and know certainly, unfailingly, and universally all people and all things throughout the whole earth. In short, take the point of doctrine as follows: **That God is an All-seeing God.** Perhaps you think that this is a common teaching which everyone believes and which does not require much work. But before I have come to the end, I shall show you how many are guilty of practical **atheism**—namely, those who do not live as if there were an All-seeing God in the world. I shall then prove that God is an All-seeing God: **Proverbs 15, verse 3**: *The eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the evil and the good.* **Job 34, verses 21, 22**: *For his eyes are upon the ways of man, and he sees all his goings. There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves.* **Psalm 44, verse 22**: *Would not God search this out? for he knows the secrets of the heart.* In the **139th Psalm** is a summary of God’s knowledge and All-seeing eye: that He knows all deeds, all thoughts, etc. **First**, He knows the thoughts, verse 2: *You know my sitting down and my rising up; you understand my thoughts from afar.* **Secondly**, He knows the words of men, verse 4: *For there is not a word on my tongue, but behold, O Lord, you know it altogether.* **Thirdly**, He knows the works of men, verse 3: *You encompass my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways.* Here then is a summary of the All-seeing eye of God: the words, works, and hearts of men fall under the observation of God.

I shall handle this text in such a way that I bring it entirely toward instructions for the practice of godliness.

First, I shall give you the arguments from which it appears that God is an All-seeing God; here I shall present them to you from the Scriptures.

**First**, it appears that God sees and knows everything because God has made and created everything. God Himself gives this proof, **Psalm 33, verses 13, 15**: *The Lord looks from heaven; he sees all the sons of men. He fashions their hearts alike; he considers all their works.* What proof 

<column-break/>

does the Scripture give of this! Well, He fashions the hearts of men, and He considers all their works. That God fashions man is a proof that His eyes behold the deeds of the children of men. Likewise, **Isaiah 29, verse 16**: *Your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter's clay: for shall the work say of him that made it, He made me not? or shall the thing framed say of him that framed it, He had no understanding?*—indicating that God, in making and forming the world, must be a God of knowledge and understanding. For example: he who makes a clock knows its defects; he knows which wheel is better and more precise than the others; so also God, who made the world, must necessarily know everything that is in it. Similarly, **Psalm 94, verses 8, 9, 10, 11**: *Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? he who formed the eye, shall he not see? he who chastises the nations, shall he not correct? he who teaches man knowledge: the Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are vanity.* This is said to refute the **atheists** who said that God did not see it, nor take notice of it; He who made man’s eye is Himself nothing other than an eye. This is the first proof: God must know everything, for He made everything.

**A second argument** can be taken from the immensity and omnipresence of God; God is present in all places, so He must see everything; and He is so omnipresent that no one can hide himself so that God cannot see him, for God says, *Do I not fill heaven and earth?* God's omnipresence is a proof of His omniscience. **Psalm 139, verses 2, 3, 7**: *You know my sitting down and my rising up; you understand my thoughts from afar; you encompass my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways; where shall I go from your Spirit? or where shall I flee from your presence?* This He proves here also, for *if I make my bed in hell, behold, you are there.* God's omnipresence proves His omniscience: He is present in all places, so He must know everything; the Lord God also uses that proof in **Jeremiah 23, verse 24**: *Can anyone hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.*

**A third proof** of God’s All-seeing eye is that God fully knows the spiritual wickedness of the devils and the cursed spirits; if God knows all that happens in hell, all that spiritual wickedness proceeding from those spirits—well, it is easier to know the heart of a man than the heart of the Devil. For our bodies express what is in our hearts; he who has a lustful, gluttonous body can know that he has a lustful heart; he who has a bloodthirsty hand can know that he has a bloodthirsty heart; but the Devil has no body through which to express the evil hidden in his heart. **Proverbs 15, verse 11**: *Hell and destruction are before the Lord: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?* <term>Cornelius a Lapide</term> <note>original: "Kornelis van der Steen," a Flemish Jesuit priest and exegete (1567–1637) famous for his commentaries on nearly all books of the Bible.</note> says that there it is not taken for the grave, but he understands by it—and most interpreters with him—the damned spirits who are there in...

### Of God's Omniscience

... lie in destruction. Hell and destruction joined together <note>original: "Hel en verderf"; these terms frequently appear together in the Dutch Bible to translate the Hebrew "Sheol and Abaddon," referring to the depths of the grave or the place of the lost.</note> signify damnation. He argues **from the greater to the lesser** <note>original: "à majore ad minus"; a logical principle stating that if a rule applies to a more significant case, it certainly applies to a less significant one.</note>. If God knows that which is more difficult, He knows much more that which is easier. If God knows what is in Hell—the spiritual wickedness of the damned who have no bodies to express what evil is in their nature—then it is much easier for Him to know the hearts of men.

A fourth proof of God's All-seeing eye is evident from this: that a person's own conscience is aware of the most hidden things. Well, if a creature of finite capacity and understanding knows that which is least apparent and most secret, surely the Creator must know much more. Scripture also provides this proof in 1 John 3, verse 20:

> For if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and He knows all things.

If a person's heart—that is, the conscience—condemns them for that evil of which the human eye takes no notice, then God knows even more. If man’s conscience is so quick in perceiving that it knows the most hidden things, then God knows all things much more. If the conscience knows so much, God knows far more. So much for the demonstration or proof; now I will give you the reasons for this teaching, which are these two.

There are two unbreakable and undeniable reasons why God must be an All-seeing God.

**First**, otherwise God could not govern or rule the world. If there were anything in the world outside the sight of God’s eye, that same thing would be outside the reach of God’s hand. God would not be able to rule men and affairs here below if He did not see or know all that happens on earth. Therefore, in Scripture, God’s ordering, ruling, and preservation of His creatures is introduced as a proof of His All-seeing eye. Because He sees everything, He can also direct and govern all His creatures. There are two texts for this; one is Psalm 66, verse 7:

> He rules forever by His power; His eyes keep watch over the nations; let not the rebellious exalt themselves.

God the Lord rules by His power; this is God's governance. But what makes Him capable of this? For "His eyes keep watch over the nations." If God’s eye did not see the nations, His hand could not rule them. The nations are unruly; and if God did not have the wisdom to see them, He could have no power to control them. He could not rule the world were He not an All-seeing God. The other text is Proverbs 24, verse 12:

> If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not He who weighs the heart perceive it? And He who keeps watch over your soul, does He not know it? For He shall repay every man according to his work.

Thus, God must necessarily know everything; otherwise, He could not be a fit Person to rule the world.

The **second** reason is: because God could not judge the world rightly if He were not an All-seeing God. Romans 2, verse 16: "In the day when God shall judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ, according to my gospel." If God did not know the secrets of men, He would have to judge in bulk. Ecclesiastes 12:14: "For God shall bring every work into judgment,

<column-break/>

with every secret thing, whether it be good or whether it be evil." If God did not search out the mysteries, He could not be a perfect Judge of the world. Job 34, verses 21 and 22:

> For His eyes are upon the ways of man, and He sees all his goings. Surely He does not lay more upon man than is right, that he should enter into judgment with God.

God is an All-seeing God so that He may be a fit Judge of the world. Because He sees everything in truth, He can judge everything according to justice, and thus men cannot challenge Him in judgment. These, then, are the reasons why God is an All-seeing God. Before I proceed to a third question—namely, **what kind of seeing** this sight of God is—I shall gather what I have said into some practical applications. The usefulness which I shall treat is two-fold: 1. To rebuke and restrain the conscience so that one guards against hidden sins. 2. To be a great awakening and a spur for you toward holy exercises.

**First**, this teaching serves to sharply forbid and bind your conscience and mine, that we guard ourselves against all hidden sins, even if you had ever so much opportunity or secrecy to commit them. Scripture makes this general use of it in Psalm 44, verses 21 and 22:

> If we had forgotten the name of our God, or stretched out our hands to a foreign god, would not God search this out? For He knows the secrets of the heart.

They made God’s knowledge of the hearts of men a restraint and a hindrance, which is why they did not want to forget God. It was Seneca's <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> advice to his friend Lucilius that, whatever he did, he should imagine that Cato <note>Cato the Younger, a Roman statesman known for his moral integrity; Seneca suggested using such a figure as a mental "witness" to one's conduct.</note> or some other excellent Roman was watching him. But in particular, this teaching serves to restrain various kinds of sins: namely,

**The sin of impurity.** Even though you might have a suitable opportunity and secrecy to commit it, remember nonetheless that God's eye sees you. Paphnutius <note>Likely referring to Saint Paphnutius the Ascetic, who famously converted a courtesan by pointing out that while she could hide from men, she could never hide from the eye of God.</note> made this observation a great help in resisting the temptation to wantonness: that he could be brought nowhere where God’s eye would not see him. You have a remarkable text that can also serve to restrain this and all other hidden sins, Leviticus 19:14:

> You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God.

Suppose someone did both of these; suppose he cursed a deaf man who cannot hear him; suppose he placed a stumbling block before the blind; well, the blind man cannot see. But God is not deaf; He hears. God is not blind; He sees. Let the sight of the seeing and hearing God bring a fear upon your conscience. You must not wrong a deaf or a blind man, for God hears and sees you, and you must fear your God. Guard yourself against unknown sins, even if all people were as if they were deaf, never to hear your wickedness, and as if they were blind, never to see your wickedness; well, remember that God hears and sees everything.

Scripture is most abundant in this: that it makes the All-seeing eye of God a restraint on the unclean lusts of the flesh. You have a full text for this in Proverbs 5:20-21.

# Of the Omnipresence

...crystalline glass could see: God sees everything, and yet not as one indistinct blur, as if everything were but one thing. God does not see as man sees; man does not see things as they truly are, but God sees them exactly so.

**Thirdly**, God’s sight is **impartial**; ours is not, for we see partially and one-sidedly. By this I mean: sometimes we see evil in others and we "see it through our fingers" <note>original: "door de vingeren"; a Dutch idiom meaning to look the other way or tolerate something.</note>; sometimes we see good in others and we oppose it. But God sees with an impartial eye; where He sees evil, there He punishes it, and He repays everyone according to their wicked way. **Psalm 10, verse 14**: *Surely You have seen it, for You observe trouble and grief, to repay it with Your hand.* You are of purer eyes than to behold evil, **Habakkuk 1, verse 13**. Likewise, He beholds all the good that is done, and He rewards it, **Matthew 6**.

**Fourthly**, God sees everything with a **preserving and observant sight**. The Lord God does not see things as we see them; we see them in passing and without notice. We see the dust upon which we tread, but we pay it no mind; we see many things in the world, but we do not retain what we see. The Lord God sees things, and that with much observation; He remembers everything He sees. **Job 11, verse 11**: *For He knows vain men; He sees wickedness also; will He not then consider it?* God’s sight is an observant sight; He pays attention to the deeds that have been done, and in what proportion He must give to one according to his evil, and to the other according to his good. We see our face (says James) in a mirror and we forget what manner of people we were; we forget what we see, but God does not; God retains what He sees.

**Fifthly**, God’s sight is a **swift sight**. God does not see and know things gradually by steps, as we do; but God sees them through a pure act of His understanding, through a simple act of beholding. Your thoughts are swifter than an arrow from a bow; indeed, but the Lord God is infinitely swifter in knowing all things; He sees your thoughts faster than you could understand any clockwork <note>original: "hoorwerk"; likely referring to the complex internal mechanism of a watch or clock.</note>.

**Sixthly and lastly**, God’s sight is an **eternal sight**. **Acts 15, verse 18**: *Known unto God are all His works from eternity.* God knew what men would think before they were born; from all eternity God had a view of what would be intended in the hearts of men. **Psalm 139, verse 2**: *You understand my thoughts from afar.* The interpreters understand this to mean the eternity of David's thoughts—all were manifest to God from all eternity.

Thus I have given you six properties of God’s sight.

I shall now handle an **objection**: I think I hear someone say, "Why is it necessary to give these proofs that God is an all-knowing and all-seeing God? For we believe this doctrine, that the eyes of the Lord are in every place, beholding the good and the evil."

To answer something to this objection, I say: it is true that there are very few within the Church who deny God's all-seeing eye in their intellect; but I may say, as the Apostle did in another case, **Titus 1, verse 16**: *They profess that they know God, but in works they deny*

<column-break/>

*Him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.* In words, all men profess that there is a God; they also profess all the attributes of God—His Omnipotence, His Omnipresence, and the like. In their intellect, they occasionally admit this, but in their works, they deny these and other similar attributes. And to do no one an injustice, I shall give ten proofs from Scripture of **atheistic people**, whose way of life tells us that they think there is no God in the world, and that there is no God whose eyes run through the whole earth.

The **first proof** of this practical atheism in the hearts of men is this: when a person allows himself **hidden sins**. See here a full passage, **Ezekiel 8, verse 11**: *Then He said to me, "Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? For they say, 'The Lord does not see us; the Lord has forsaken the land.'"* Another remarkable passage is in **Job 31, verses 26, 27, 28**: *If I have beheld the light, etc., and my heart has been secretly enticed, or my mouth has kissed my hand* (that is, by way of worship) *that also were an iniquity to be punished by the Judge; for I should have denied the God that is above.* The secret practice of idolatry (and likewise of any other sin) is a proof of atheism in the one who practices it. Therefore, you who take the liberty to go to your beloved Delilahs <note>original: "Dalilaas"; a reference to the biblical Delilah, symbolizing seductive or secret sins that rob a person of spiritual strength.</note>, who can fondle them in the lap of your affections, you who can harbor any hidden wickednesses and give yourself over to the practice of them—you are **atheists in practice**. A certain harlot, tempting a young man to impurity, used among other reasons the secrecy of the place, that no one would see her; to which he answered: "You miserable creature, do you fear the sight and the presence of man, and are you not afraid of the eyes of God?" It is a certain proof of atheism in the heart of the thief and the adulterer that they rejoice in their wickedness while they escape the observation of man; they fear nothing else. In **Job, chapter 24, verse 17**, it says: *For the morning is to them even as the shadow of death; if one knows them, they are in the terrors of the shadow of death.* If someone makes no conscience <note>To "make conscience" of something is to feel a moral or religious obligation regarding it.</note> of hidden evils, they can only keep them from the knowledge of man; but that God sees his sins neither disturbs nor terrifies him. This is sheer atheism; that someone gives himself to hidden sins and is not moved by it comes from the exercise of atheism in his heart.

A **second proof** of practical atheism in the heart is a constant **neglect of the performance** of those exercises that belong to a godly walk. Truly, you do not then think that there is a God who sees you. **Psalm 10, verse 4**: *The wicked, through the pride of his countenance, will not seek after God; God is not in all his thoughts* (so the English translation has it). If someone will not seek God, it is because God is not in his thoughts. We then desire that God should depart from us; we do not desire the knowledge of His ways; we then think that God does not see...

### Concerning the Omniscience of God.

...through a dark cloud. **Job 22, verses 13, 17**: *You say, "What does God know? Can He judge through the thick darkness?"* Thus, if someone spends their life without calling upon God, or without going to God within their household, you are surely drifting toward atheism.

A **third** mark or proof of practical atheism <note>The author uses "practical atheism" to describe people who believe in God intellectually but live as if He does not exist or cannot see them.</note> is a carelessness of the human spirit in performing specific spiritual exercises. Even if you cannot entirely neglect these exercises, if you perform them with total negligence, it is the same as doing nothing at all. When someone persists in an outward Christian conduct—perhaps praying every day with their family and hearing sermons every day of the week—yet fails to examine their conscience or account for *how* they hear and *how* they pray; how casually, how foolishly, and how half-heartedly they pray throughout their lives; surely such people think there is no God in the world who sees it. **Isaiah 29, verses 13, 15**: *For the Lord has said, "Inasmuch as this people draws near to Me with their mouths and honors Me with their lips, but has removed their hearts far from Me, and their fear toward Me is taught by the commandment of men: Woe to those who seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord, and their works are in the dark; they say, 'Who sees us?' and 'Who knows us?'"* So it follows that when someone approaches God only with their lips but never cares for the condition of their heart during worship, they are effectively saying, "Who sees us? Who knows us?" And God must try to pull them out of that mindset with reason; for *shall the thing made say of him who made it, "He did not make me"? Or shall the thing formed say of him who formed it, "He has no understanding"?* (verse 16).

O beloved, perhaps I speak to many who take too little concern over this; those whose consciences work just deeply enough that they dare not leave their household devotions undone, yet they perform them very carelessly and thoughtlessly. You read in **1 Samuel 2, verse 1**: *Hannah prayed and said, "My heart rejoices in the Lord."* What was the reason her heart went with her, that she did her work so heartily? It was because she noticed that *the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by Him actions are weighed* (verse 3). God has a touchstone and a scale to judge our devotions, both in terms of their quality and their quantity. In **Psalm 11, verse 4**, it says: *The Lord’s eyes behold, His eyelids test the sons of men.* <note>The "eyelids" of God is a poetic way of describing a squinting, focused gaze that scrutinizes the hidden depths of the heart.</note> Surely then, if you are so careless in holy exercises, it is a sign that you do not believe God’s eyelids are testing you.

A **fourth** mark of this practical atheism is that you do not think God sees all the world because you are impatient when no blessings immediately follow your religious exercises. **Isaiah 58, verse 3**: *"Why have we fasted," they say, "and You have not seen? Why have we afflicted our souls, and You take no notice?"* This is also presented in the book of Job, **Job 21, verses 14, 15**: *"Depart from us... what profit do we have if we serve the Almighty?"* Because they did not receive a timely return or immediate blessing upon their earnest desires, they became 

<column-break/>

weary of waiting upon the Almighty God. Beloved, you who have an impatient heart—perhaps you have prayed so often and heard so many sermons, and yet you see no returns proportional to your praying and hearing, and therefore you wish to cast aside your prayers and reject the hearing of sermons; well, this flows only from atheism in the heart. You have an example of this in **2 Kings 6, verse 33**. Joram had waited on God for deliverance, and it did not come; whereupon he broke out in these words: *"Look, this evil is from the Lord; why should I wait for the Lord any longer?"*

A **fifth** mark of practical atheism is relying on sinful remedies and means to be saved in times of need and danger. Asa had a hint of this sin <note>King Asa of Judah was generally a good king, but in his later years, he relied on political alliances and physicians rather than God.</note> when Baasha, King of Israel, came against him; he went to Ben-hadad and pleaded with him to break his covenant [with Baasha] and assist him. Now (says Hanani the Prophet), *the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show Himself strong.* So also when Saul went to a medium <note>original: "Toveresse" - a witch or sorceress, specifically the Witch of Endor.</note>, acting as if there were no God to go to: this is proof that his heart believed there was more help in the Devil than in God. Note that expression in **Isaiah 47, verse 10**: *For you have trusted in your wickedness; you have said, "No one sees me."*

A **sixth** mark of practical atheism is when one harbors hypocrisy and vanity in their heart regarding the profession of religion. The Apostle says, *God is my witness.* A person must take God as their witness; we must not make religion a cloak <note>A "dekmantel" or "covering mantle"—using religious appearance to hide true intentions.</note>, for God is our witness. See what our Savior says to the Pharisees in **Luke 16, verse 15**: *You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for what is highly esteemed among men is an abomination in the sight of God.* This indicates that they were people who, in their own way, professed religion solely in the sight of men to gain the applause of the people, but God knew the heart. They did not think of God's knowledge, and that caused them to indulge in this vain ambition and hypocritical profession of religion. Truly, it is the forgetting of God that makes people take the liberty to be hypocritical in the ways of Christianity.

A **seventh** mark of practical atheism is imagining that God is merely an idle spectator of what happens in the world. It is pure atheism when someone says that God leaves the world to itself—that people may do as they please, and that however people hold power in their hands, God only looks on. It says in **Zephaniah 1, verse 12**: *And it shall come to pass at that time that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and punish the men who are settled on their dregs, who say in their heart, "The Lord will not do good, nor will He do evil."* This is atheism: to think that God does not concern Himself with the world. It is like when people choose the strongest party, the one with the most power, thinking that God is just watching and that He will not involve Himself or correct the evil He sees. But the Scripture says, in my text: *That God does not see things wrongly...*

### Concerning the Omnipresence <note>The Dutch title is *Al-tegenwoordigheyt*, which literally means "Omnipresence," though the text focuses heavily on "Omniscience" or God's all-seeing eye.</note>

...to walk, as if not to concern Himself with them; but His eye shall set His hand to work, for the Lord God shall show Himself strong to those who are upright of heart. This is a living sign.

The **eighth** proof of practical atheism—thinking that God’s eyes do not run through the whole world—is when someone imagines that God overlooks their evil because of their prosperity, and considers their ways to be good; this is a true hallmark of this age. **Psalm 73, verses 11, 12**: *They say, "How would God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?" See, these are the ungodly, yet they have rest in the world; they increase in power.* When people have prosperity in the world, increasing in goods while others are sick and they are healthy, or others are poor and they are rich, they then think that God approves of their ways. This is another proof of practical atheism.

A **ninth** proof of practical atheism is mistrust of God in times of need. Hagar was in misery, yet she said, *You, O God, see me*, **Genesis 16, verse 13**. When someone in danger distrusts God, you think God does not see you; you weep, perhaps, in a corner, and you think that you shall never escape these troubles; the reason for this is that you think God does not see you. **Isaiah 49, verse 14**: *But Zion said, "The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me."* The Church thought that God had forsaken and forgotten her, which was a scent of atheism. God was moved to declare this doctrine to her: that His eyes are always upon her; otherwise, they thought that God had abandoned her. Beloved, I pray you, go and examine your heart, and see what atheism remains within it; and look at your deeds, and see if many of them do not cry out loudly, saying: "Surely, there is no God who pays attention to the world."

The **tenth** and final mark is when one imagines that God looks upon the wicked, who are prosperous in their ways, with approval or by turning a blind eye. Beloved, we find this presented in **Malachi 2, verse 17**: *You weary the Lord with your words. Yet you say, "In what way do we weary Him?" In this: that you say, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and He has delight in them," or "Where is the God of justice?"* Beloved, if one allows this to arise in their heart—that when the wicked are prosperous in their ways, God looks upon them with a wink or with approval—this is to render God without eyes; this is to justify the wicked, and to make God their partner and a patron of human godlessness. And this is the final mark of practical atheism in this respect. So much shall be said in answer to that objection.

I shall now give you only a word of counsel: if it is so, that God has an all-seeing eye, then give place, I pray you, to words of encouragement. I wish to stir you all up to make this a great help for yourselves, to urge you toward the practice of godliness and the confession of Religion: that God’s eyes alone run through all things. Let it stir you to Christianity, even in the inward parts. **Psalm 119, verse 168**: *I keep your precepts and testimonies; for*

<column-break/>

*all my ways are before You.* There is the inward practice of Religion—that is the argument or the foundation. I watch my life and my heart; I watch Your commands; and, dearly beloved, I shall keep Your commands, for all my ways are before You. Your ways and mine are before the Lord; O, then be well occupied in the innermost part of Christianity, not only in the outward acts of worship, but be much taken up in your heart and concerned with God and His ways. **Song of Solomon 2, verse 14**: *O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.* O, let God hear your voice in a secret corner; be much in secret exercises, particularly in the most inward parts of those exercises. Use this as a motive for the secret giving of alms (**Matthew 6, verse 4**) and for secret prayers (**Matthew 6, verse 6**). Furthermore, let this doctrine lay a great terror upon your soul, so that you guard yourself against sinning against God in secret. I recall the advice of Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> to someone: that whenever he was tempted toward any dishonest act, he should imagine that Cato <note>Cato the Younger, a Roman statesman known for his integrity.</note> or some other eminent Roman had their eyes upon him. If the thought of this was such a proof that men ought not to commit such evil deeds, how much more should the thought of God cause you to avoid every evil way, since the eye of God sees you? I come now to the treatment of three "uses" <term>uses: Practical applications of a sermon or text.</term>: 1. of instruction, 2. of comfort, 3. of terror.

First, the **Use of instruction** shall be partly for doctrine, and partly for practice and exercise.

First, for doctrine: if it is so, that it is an essential attribute of God to know all things, then I conclude two things from this:

1. That although the Devil knows much, he nevertheless does not know everything. The Devil is a Spirit who, because of his long experience, can know much; he walks to and fro on the earth (**Job 1, verse 7**) and thereby notices and knows many things; nevertheless, the Devil does not reach the point where he would know everything; this is God’s unique attribute. **Jeremiah 17, verses 9, 10**: *The heart of man is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked; who can know it? I the Lord search the heart, I test the mind, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.* As a theologian rightly notes: if we did not betray our own souls into Satan's hands, the Devil would have to guess in bulk what temptation he should suggest to us; before our actions, he could never know what is in our hearts. The Devil’s knowledge is great, and God’s knowledge is far greater. Now, although the Scripture often makes known to us that great knowledge and science which the Devil possesses, nevertheless the Devil does not know the heart, nor things to come; rather, this is made an attribute of God, to distinguish Him from false gods. **Isaiah 41, verses 22, 23, 24**: *Let them bring them forth, and show us what shall happen; let them show the former things, what they be, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the omniscience of God, specifically how God’s perfect knowledge of the future distinguishes Him from false idols and how this knowledge applies to both Christ’s divinity and the lives of believers.</meta>

-> and God's Omniscience. 375 <-

Let them hear; declare things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods; yes, do good and do evil, that we may be dismayed and behold it together. Behold, you are less than nothing, and your work is worse than a viper; he is an abomination who chooses you. <note>This is a paraphrase of Isaiah 41:23–24, where God challenges idols to prove their divinity by predicting the future.</note> This is presented here as an **incommunicable attribute of God**—to make future things heard and to foretell them infallibly and certainly. Now, it is true that the Devil can, in some ways, foretell future things for which a natural cause can be given (even if it is hidden from us), partly through his knowledge of the temperaments of our bodies and the nature of things, partly through his presence in most places (since he is present in all conspiracies and deliberations), and partly through his understanding of the Prophets in the Scriptures. 

Plutarch says in the *Life of Alexander* that when Alexander was to go to war against Darius, he went to the oracle to know who would be the victor. The Devil knows the letter and the matter of Scripture better than anyone; therefore, one of the later theologians says regarding that history that he believes the Devil knew it from the prophecy in **Daniel 11:3**: *Then a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion, and he shall do according to his pleasure.* The Devil knew that this was spoken of Alexander. Sometimes the Lord God reveals it to the Devil, just as what the Devil revealed to Saul in **1 Samuel 28, verse 19**. But God’s knowledge is not through conjectural guessing; rather, it is an immediate and infallible knowledge of future things. Therefore it stands thus in **Isaiah 46, verse 10**: *Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, "My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure."* The Lord God declares certainly and infallibly the end and the outcome before the beginning.

2. From this, I conclude that wherever this attribute is found, it is a reason to prove divinity there. For this reason, theologians firmly prove the **Divinity of Christ** against the <term>Arians</term> <note>The Arians were followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal or fully equal with God the Father.</note>. The Scripture says this of Christ: that He knows all things, so He must necessarily be God. **Luke 6, verse 8**: *But he knew their thoughts, and said to the man who had the withered hand, etc.* **John 21, verse 17**: *And he said to him, "Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you."* So also **John 2, verses 24, 25**: *But Jesus did not commit himself to them, because he knew them all; and had no need that anyone should testify of man, for he himself knew what was in man.* Just as a gardener, who knows what seed he sows, also knows what herbs will sprout up on every bed of his garden.

3. If God sees and knows all things, I conclude from that that God sees the sins in His own children. The Psalmist indeed says our iniquities are covered—that is, in respect to His justice they are covered—but not in respect to His all-seeing eye. One text may seem to contradict this, which is **Numbers 23, verse 21**: *He has not beheld iniquity in Jacob, neither has he seen perverseness in Israel.* To this text I answer: 1. Among those who best 

<column-break/>

understand the Hebrew language, some translate the words in a different way than they are translated in our Version. For they translate it thus, more according to the Hebrew text: <note>original Hebrew: *lo hibbit aven bejakob, velo raah gnamal bejiſchrael*</note> *He shall not endure the wrong against Jacob, and he shall not suffer the affliction of Israel.* Thus says the learned master <term>Gataker</term> <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654) was an English theologian and critic known for his deep knowledge of Hebrew and Greek.</note>, who defends this text at length. 2. The text does not speak of the godly Israelites alone, but of their entire body, the greater part of whom were godless; so if that text proved what they want, it would also prove that God sees no sin in the godless. 3. The meaning is: God does not see sin in such a way that He would impute it to their eternal damnation, but He saw it in order to send their temporal punishment upon them, as is evident from the 25th Chapter. 4. Other Scripture texts speak of God seeing sin in His own. **Psalm 69, verse 6**: *O God, you know my foolishness, and my sins are not hidden from you.* **Psalm 90, verse 8**: *You set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your countenance.* **Psalm 44, verses 21, 22**: *If we had forgotten the name of our God, or stretched out our hands to a strange god, would not God search this out? For he knows the secrets of the heart.* That cannot be the true meaning of the Scripture text which makes it contradict many other Scripture texts. 5. The meaning of that passage is this: that God does not see sin in Jacob nor perverseness in Israel; that is, God does not see it in them so as to deliver them into the hands of Balak to curse them. In this way, He does not behold sin in Jacob or wickedness in Israel. It is true that God does not look upon sin and grace in the same way. Sin He sees only <term>by way of simple understanding</term> <note>original Latin: *per modum simplicis intelligentiae*</note>, that is: through a single knowledge, <term>not through knowledge joined with approval</term> <note>original Latin: *non per scientiam conjunctam cum approbatione*</note>. But nonetheless, He sees the sin in His people.

**Secondly**, for **Practice**, this doctrine gives us these three conclusions: 

1. Since God is an all-seeing God, live then in such a way that you notice that the all-seeing eye of God is constantly upon you. This would be a restraining and binding of all godlessness. It is a strange rule that <term>Seneca</term> <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> gives: <note>original Latin: *Sic vive cum hominibus, tanquam Deus videat sic loquere cum Deo tanquam homines audiant*</note> *Live with men as if God saw, and speak to God as if men heard.* **Psalm 16, verse 8**: *I have set the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.*

2. Let the all-seeing eye of God bring you shame and sorrow in the memory of your secret sins. **Ezra 9, verse 6**: *O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to you, my God; for our iniquities are increased over our head, etc.* **2 Samuel 12:12** compared with **Psalm 51:6**: In Samuel the words are, *You did it secretly,* and in the Psalm it stands, *Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight.* In Samuel it says that David sinned in secret, but when David considered it in his <term>Penitential Psalm</term> <note>Psalm 51 is traditionally known as a "Penitential Psalm" written by David after his sin with Bathsheba.</note>, he said it was before God's eyes. That made him offer so many sighs of repentance; that made him leave behind a memorial of his shame and sorrow; for that which...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on God’s attributes, specifically moving from God’s omniscience (all-knowing nature) to the practical application of His omnipresence (all-presence) and how the awareness of His "all-seeing eye" should govern human behavior and provide comfort to believers.</meta>

-> On Omnipresence <-

What had happened in secret was nonetheless done before God’s eyes.

3. The all-seeing eye of God ought to move you to be conscientious in your calling and profession, in which God has placed you. It is a point of reasoning in the Scriptures that rulers and authorities ought to be conscientious in their office, because the eyes of the Lord are upon them. **2 Chronicles 19, verse 6**: *And he said to the judges, "Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the Lord, who is with you in the judgment."* The eye of the Lord watches how you rule and govern. Furthermore, it is also a reason for ministers. **2 Corinthians 2, verse 17**: *For we are not as many, who peddle the word of God; but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.* <note>The author emphasizes that a preacher must be sincere because he acts under God's direct observation.</note> This a minister must do: preach in sincerity, because God sees him. This also applies to masters. **Colossians 4, verse 1**: *Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.* So it serves for servants, to make them serve their masters in simplicity of heart. **Colossians 3, verse 22**: *Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eye-service, as men-pleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God.*

### A second benefit is for the comfort of the godly.

This point, which I am now handling, yields matter of comfort to godly Christians in six cases and states.

First, **Is God’s eye an all-seeing eye?** then take comfort, all you who are often in secret exercises <note>“Secret exercises” refers to private prayer, meditation, and personal devotion.</note>, who often come before the throne of grace; when no eye sees you, no ear hears you, take this comfort: that God’s eye sees you in secret, and His eye causes His ear to open to hear. The seeing of His eye is always united with the hearing of His ears. **Psalm 34, verse 16**: *The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry.* Peter repeats similar words in **1 Peter 3, verse 12**: *The eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers;* or in their prayer: <term>eis deēsin autōn</term> <note>Original: "εἰς δέησιν αὐτῶν" — a Greek phrase meaning "unto their prayer."</note>. The Lord God sets His eye as if upon the heart itself. It was a great comfort that David received upon this foundation in **Psalm 38, verse 10**: *Lord, all my desire is before thee; and my groaning is not hid from thee.* Desires are but hidden and quiet wishes of the soul, not expressed through words; the Lord God accepts all those hidden wishes. The voice of the Church is guided by Christ, and that with delight, when she is *in the secret places of the stairs, in the clefts of the rock.* **Song of Solomon 2:14**.

Secondly, this serves for comfort to all of you who are disturbed in mind and conscience over hidden sins. Just as men may be ignorant of your woe and miseries—where a new shoe pinches, no one knows but he who wears it—know this for your comfort: that although men here may not know your sadness and the disturbance of your conscience, nonetheless your God remembers all your hidden complaints regarding your hidden sins. The Lord’s eye sees all your hidden, lamentable complaints which your soul pours out under great sins and powerful

<column-break/>

cravings. David’s complaint was in **Psalm 38:4, 9, 10**: *There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin. I am feeble and sore broken: I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart. Lord, all my desire is before thee; and my groaning is not hid from thee.*

Thirdly, this doctrine can be for comfort in the case of all external oppressions which God lays upon you in this world. Suppose God lays upon you miseries and afflictions that others do not know; others do not know how poor you are in the world; others do not know how hard it is for you to obtain meager food; but remember your God sees you. And this was Hagar’s comfort; you have a remarkable text in **Genesis 16, verse 13**: *And she called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, "Thou God seest me": for she said, "Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?"* Suppose you were driven out into a fearful wilderness with Hagar; O, remember and bring to mind the words of Hagar: "O God, You know in what oppressions I have been cast."

Fourthly, this doctrine shall give comfort in the case that one is oppressed and treated harshly by men; the Scripture makes this an end for which God’s eyes run through the world. **Psalm 113, verses 6, 7**: *Who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven, and in the earth! He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill.* **Acts 7, verse 34**: *I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people which is in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and am come down to deliver them.* There is a doubling in the words, *I have seen, I have seen*, to indicate the perfect sight that God has of all the oppressions of His people. The Lord sees, the Lord sees; it is a full sight, a compassionate sight; therefore the word is doubled. O, remember that when the Israelites were under harsh taskmasters, and when they sighed under the heavy burdens and hard dealings of men, then the Lord said, "I have seen, I have seen their oppressions in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and am come down to deliver them." In **Deuteronomy 26, verse 7** it says: *And when we cried unto the Lord God of our fathers, the Lord heard our voice, and looked on our affliction, and our labor, and our oppression.*

Fifthly, the all-seeing eye of God comforts you in the case of innocence and uprightness of heart, notwithstanding all the slanders, smearing, and false accusations with which you are burdened. **Jeremiah 12, verse 3**: *But thou, O Lord, knowest me: thou hast seen me, and tried mine heart toward thee.* He was accused as a man who set the state in turmoil and who was ill-disposed toward the city; yet it was a great comfort to him that he could appeal to Heaven: "You, O God, have known me and seen me, and You have tested my heart toward You." It is a great comfort, whatever evil is falsely laid to your charge, if you have uprightness and perfection of heart toward God; well, God sees that your heart is upright, sound, and good, and that can comfort you just as it did David in **Psalm 17, verses 2, 3**.

Sixthly and lastly, this serves for comfort in the case of all conspiracies and cruel deliberations of enemies against the Church of God...

God; perhaps this atheism <note>In this period, "atheism" often referred to "practical atheism"—living as if God does not see or care—rather than a philosophical denial of His existence.</note> creeps into the hearts of men. **Isaiah 29, verse 15**: *Woe unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord, and their works are in the dark, and they say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us?* God's eye shall nonetheless discover them all; not only what men have done, but also what the wicked intended to do against the Church; the Lord knows all hidden plots and counsels. **Psalm 11, verses 2, 4**: *For, lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart. The Lord is in his holy temple, the Lord’s throne is in heaven: his eyes behold, his eyelids try, the children of men.* This could then be a great comfort: that God’s all-seeing eye takes notice of all the intentions and cruel designs against the Church of God, and that He causes their intentions to fail; they cannot carry them out, because God sees them and their devised plots; He breaks and hinders the same. **Daniel 11, verse 27**: *And both these kings' hearts shall be to do mischief, and they shall speak lies at one table; but it shall not prosper: for yet the end shall be at the time appointed.* This is prophesied of two kings, Antiochus and Ptolemy. <note>The author refers to the historical conflicts between the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt, as interpreted through the lens of biblical prophecy.</note> Who can know their hearts? No one but God; He who knows all hearts knows theirs also; although these two kings were a great scourge to the Holy Ones, nonetheless they would not prosper. Oh, under what a hiding place do we live then? We live under an eye that sees everything, and under a hand that does everything; and who would not want to lie under such a screen, under the shadow of such wings? Thus have I finished the benefit of comfort in these six mentioned cases.

I have but one benefit remaining, and that is for the terror of the wicked; although they may imagine, as the atheists did in the Psalm, saying: *Who is the Most High, can He see through the thick clouds?* though they might say, *What eye sees us, and who knows us?* let them nonetheless realize that God’s eye runs through the earth; yet perhaps they believe this in their minds, that God does this. But let them further know that God looks upon the wicked in a different way than He does His people, and that in four respects.

First, God looks upon His people with an eye of mercy; *in all their affliction he was afflicted, through his love and through his grace he redeemed them,* **Isaiah 63, verse 9.** But the wicked He looks upon with an eye of wrath <note>The original Dutch *verborogenthept* is likely a printer's error for *verbolgentheydt*, meaning wrath or indignation.</note>; He sees them, but He does not take pity on them, **Psalm 7, verse 12.** God is a righteous judge, and a God who is angry with the wicked every day. God shall judge the righteous, but against the wicked He shall pass judgment. God searches the heart and tries the reins, and He shall avenge the wrong done to the righteous; He so looks upon the wicked that He is daily angry with them. **Isaiah 66, verse 14**: *And when ye see this, your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall flourish like an herb: and the hand of the Lord shall be known toward his servants, and his indignation toward his enemies.* The Lord God

<column-break/>

sees the whole world, but He sees His servants in such a way that His hand shall be for their good, to deliver them; and He sees the wicked, to be angry against them. This is the first.

Secondly, just as God looks upon the pious with an eye of mercy, so He also looks upon them with an eye of preservation and keeping; but upon the wicked He looks with an eye of ruin and destruction. **Psalm 33, verses 18, 19**: *Behold, the eye of the Lord is upon them that fear him, upon them that hope in his mercy; to deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine.* But the eyes of the Lord are upon the wicked for destruction. **Amos 8, verse 9**: *And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord God, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day.* His eye is a discerning eye, for the preservation of the one, and for the destruction of the other. Therefore one reads of Christ’s eyes, **Revelation 1, verse 14**: *His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow; and his eyes were as a flame of fire.* God’s eye is a consuming eye, burning the wicked like stubble, whom He sees and beholds.

Thirdly, God’s eye toward His own opens His ear to His own. **1 Peter 3, verse 12**: *For the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers.* God’s eye opens His ears to all their prayers and to all their cries. But on the contrary, God’s eye closes His ears to the prayers of the wicked; He opens His eye to see their sin, to punish them; but He does not open His ears to hear their prayers, to accept them, comparing **Ezekiel 8, verse 12 and verse 18** together. *Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The Lord seeth us not; the Lord hath forsaken the earth:* *therefore will I also deal in fury: mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: and though they cry in mine ears with a loud voice, yet will I not hear them.* God’s eye closes His ears; were it not that God saw how evil the wicked are, God would hear them; but God sees how bad you are; His eyes close His ears to all your prayers. You find this both put together in **1 Peter 3, verse 12**: *The eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers: but the face of the Lord is against them that do evil;* as if he said, God’s eyes open His ears to the prayers of His servants, but God’s eyes close His ears to the prayers of the wicked; indeed, His face and power are against them.

Fourthly and finally, God’s eye toward His own opens His hand for their blessing and deliverance from many dangers: but God’s eye closes His hand of grace and blessing, and opens His avenging hand against them. **Acts 7, verse 34**: *I have come down to deliver the pious:* but for the evil, God’s eye opens His avenging hand. <meta>This page continues the discussion of God’s all-seeing eye, transitioning from the concept of His observation to the practical application of His power on behalf of the faithful. It explores the theological definitions of "perfection" and "omnipotence."</meta>

# Of Omnipresence

translation) so that **God’s** looking upon the ungodly draws out an avenging hand; but **God** looks upon the godly to deliver them, to open a strong hand, and to rescue them. **The Text states: The eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him.** <note>The author is quoting 2 Chronicles 16:9.</note>

And this now brings me to the next part of my text: *to show himself strong*, etc. Of which I shall now treat and speak: 1. That God's eye sets His hand to work. God is no idle spectator, merely watching the persons and things that occur in the world; rather, He takes a side, He chooses a party. He is not only a seeing God, but He is a strong God; and this strength shall not always be a hidden strength, but it shall, in certain cases and for certain persons, be revealed. Therefore my text says: *For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong to those whose heart is perfect toward him.* To show himself strong, etc. Of these words, I shall give you a brief explanation.

1. What is understood here by God "showing Himself strong." 2. What is meant by a "heart that is perfect toward Him."

First, what is understood here by God showing Himself strong? To answer this briefly: the strength of God is an attribute in God through which He can do whatever pleases Him. Whatever God has a will to do, He has a power to do; and this is the strength of God. When it says here that God shows Himself strong, the meaning is that God—when He, in His wisdom, deems it fitting to rescue, refresh, and deliver His oppressed servants—then reveals His strength. The Scholastic theologians <note>Refers to "School-leeraars," the medieval and post-Reformation academic theologians known for precise, often complex logical distinctions.</note> have pedantic disputes concerning God’s power: Whether God's power is absolute, such that He can do everything? I answer: all that God *wills* to do, He can do; but He cannot do *everything*—He cannot commit sin, He cannot lie (*Titus 1, verse 2*), and He cannot deny Himself. He cannot make contradictory things true, for to do such things would be a proof of imperfection and not of strength. But all that God wills, that He can do; and the Scripture gives you this description, *Psalm 115, verse 3*: *But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.* *Ephesians 1, verse 11*: *In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will.* **What God wills to do, that He does.** *Augustine* <note>original: "Augustinus"</note> says that some things are impossible for God; but herein is the perfection of God’s omnipotence: that He can do all that He wills. Some things [like lying or sinning] come from weakness and not from power; if God could do these, He would not be almighty. Thus, God cannot do them. **Nothing is impossible for God, except that which He does not will to do, whether in Heaven or on earth.**

Secondly, what does it mean to "show Himself strong to those whose heart is perfect toward Him"? To understand this word "perfect" <note>The Dutch uses "volkoomen" or "volmaakt."</note>, know that God’s children can be called perfect in two ways: in respect of justification <term>Justification: being declared righteous before God through faith.</term>; thus they are, in the narrowest sense and meaning, perfect. All their sins are perfectly forgiven, and all their

<column-break/>

persons are perfectly accepted. This the Scripture teaches, *Hebrews 10, verse 14*: *For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified*; that is, He has perfectly justified them and freed them from the guilt and punishment of their sin. So, the godly are perfect in respect of justification. 2. We can be called perfect in respect of sanctification <term>Sanctification: the ongoing process of being made holy and turning away from sin.</term>. In this sense, only Adam in Paradise was perfect, as well as the spirits of the perfectly righteous in Heaven. But in my text, the Lord is not "strong" only for those who are perfect through a legal perfection—those who have no sin. For *Job* says, *Job 9, verse 20*: *If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me: if I say, I am perfect, it shall also prove me perverse.* <note>The author cites Job 9:20; the OCR transcribed "19. 20."</note> Beloved, you must further know regarding this perfection of sanctification that it is twofold: 1. A perfection of parts. 2. A perfection of degrees. This latter [perfection of degrees] no one possesses on this side of Heaven, that is, on earth; but every believer in this world has the perfection of parts. Although every part is not thoroughly sanctified, they are nonetheless sanctified in every part. There is then a perfection of parts, even with these various degrees in our sanctification. This then is the sense of the Scripture when it says the Lord shall show Himself strong to those whose hearts are perfect with Him: that is, to those who have any measure of true grace, God will show Himself strong on their behalf. Perfection is taken in the Scripture for sincerity; for the Hebrew word signifying "perfection" or "perfect" also signifies "upright" and "uprightness" (*tham* <note>original: "tham" (תָּם) - a Hebrew root for integrity or completeness.</note>), so that an upright man is, in God’s accounting, a perfect man. But here is a question to be answered, namely this:

-> Question: Since we know that all men here on earth are imperfect, how and why are they called "perfect" in the Scriptural manner of speaking? <-

-> Answer: For four reasons. <-

1. Because they are perfect in comparison. If you compare a godly, upright man with men who are openly ungodly, or those who are secretly hypocritical, in that respect they are perfect; for the ungodly have no grace, and they [the believers] have grace in some measure. *Genesis 6, verse 9* states: *These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.* He was a perfect man in his generations—perfect in respect to the ungodly among whom he lived, but not simply perfect [in an absolute sense], for then he would have had no sin. He was perfect in respect of that sinful age in which he lived. <note>original: "volmaakt in suo genere, non in genere entium, sed in genere hominum, eo loco & tempore viventium" — perfect in his kind, not in the kind of [all] beings, but in the kind of men living in that place and time.</note>

2. He can be called perfect in respect of his aim and desires. *2 Corinthians 13, verse 9*: *For we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong: and this also we wish, even your perfection.* A godly person desires to be a perfect man; he wishes he could shake off the body of sin. Indeed, in respect of this desire of the soul—to have no sin, and to have a perfect measure of grace—one can be called a perfect man. *Psalm 119, verse 106.*

### and the Omniscience of God.

"I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep the judgments of your righteousness": and verse 112, "I have inclined my heart to perform your statutes forever, even to the end." <note>The author is quoting Psalm 119:106 and 112.</note> Well—because the desire of a godly soul is to have more grace than she currently possesses: in that respect, the Scripture grants a title based on the best part—that because of his desire, he is a **perfect man**.

3. He can be called perfect in respect of God's acceptance: God looks upon him as a perfect one; God accepts his will for the deed. Just as he expresses his will through his deeds, so God names men according to their best part.

4. Even if he has no perfect grace dwelling within him, he nevertheless has **perfect righteousness** imputed to him. In this respect, he can be called a perfect man. And these are the reasons why a man, although imperfect, may nonetheless be said to be perfect.

From these words, *To show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him,* many observations can be drawn. From the connection, *The eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong,* note:

**First**, That God is no idle spectator, merely watching what happens, or letting the world fall off its wheels and hinges and letting everything turn upside down while leaving men to their own devices; rather, **He has a hand, as well as an eye.**

**Second**, That God's eye sets His hand to work. Even if God were great in power, if He had no counsel or plan to put His hand to work, it would not be so remarkable. But God's eye runs through the earth to show Himself strong.

**Third**, That God is not only an all-seeing God, but also an **Almighty God**; therefore He is called the <term>Mighty One of Jacob</term> <note>The author refers to the title *Abir Ya’akov*, highlighting God’s role as the protector of His covenant people.</note>; that *Epithetum* <note>original Latin: "epithet" or "title"</note>, that surname was given to Him.

**Fourth**, From the words *To show himself strong*, note that God has more strength than He shows in the world. God the Lord did not show all His power in the making of the world. After God has shown much strength, He still has more; His power is not drawn out to its furthest height. I say this only so that you might have high thoughts of God.

**Fifth**, God's eyes run through the earth to show Himself strong: But sometimes He hides His strength and will not reveal it. Habakkuk 3, verse 4: "And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power." <note>The "horns" are often interpreted as rays of light or symbols of power emanating from God.</note> God sometimes hides His power, just as we hide and hold something back with our fist.

**Sixth**, *To show himself strong*, note that there are certain special seasons in which God wills to reveal His strength and power most fully. God is always strong, but He does not always show His power and strength.

**Seventh**, *To show himself strong to those whose heart is perfect toward him.* Note: God's children can take comfort from the attribute of God's strength. It must be an arrow in the heart of one who lives godlessly that this God, whom you have angered, is a strong God; this ought to make you tremble.

<column-break/>

God's people alone can draw comfort and suck sweetness from the attribute of God's strength. God's strength is for them, just as it is against the godless; thus God's power was made known to Pharaoh.

**Eighth**, Note that God's strength is for the benefit of His own people: God the Lord is strong because His people are weak.

**Ninth**, *For those whose heart is perfect with him.* I said that by "perfect," "upright" is understood. From this, note: that an **upright heart**, according to the sense of the Scripture, is a **perfect heart**. Thus I have given you many points and teachings. I shall gather all these flowers into an **Atelier** <note>The author uses the word for a workshop or studio to describe the synthesis of his points.</note>, and the doctrine that I shall handle is this:

**That there are certain special times in which, and certain special persons for whom, God will show and prove His strength for their preservation and deliverance out of all perils: To show Himself strong to those whose heart is perfect toward him.** In handling this doctrine, I shall 1. Give you two or three warnings to understand the teaching well. 2. I shall present to you some seasons in which God wills to exercise His strength for certain chosen people for their deliverance; and then I shall give you some applications. First, regarding the warnings, they are three:

1. That God is always strong, even if He does not always prove His strength. I told you just now from Habakkuk 3 that God's power is sometimes a hidden power.

2. When God's power and strength are no longer exercised for the benefit of His servants, one must not think this is because God has no more power or could not do more. No; it is because we are neither fit nor ready to receive more. Many call God's power and the strength of the Almighty, of the **Mighty One of Jacob**, into doubt because they see that the godless prosper in this world, and that the pious suffer much adversity and misery here. This makes them think that surely, if God had power, He would work to change this. But alas! We are not fit to receive more strength and power. In Psalm 59, verse 12 <note>Psalm 59:11 in English versions.</note>, one reads: "Slay them not, lest my people forget: scatter them by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield." If God gave grace in certain times, we would sometimes forget our graces and benefits; therefore God's hand is held back—not because God cannot do more, but because we are not fit to receive more from God. This is why God does not reveal His strength more for the sake of His own. It must not be attributed to God as if He lacked the power to act, but rather that we are not fit to receive more; yet God can certainly do more.

3. Take this warning: that God is strong for His servants whose heart is upright toward Him. This must not be limited only to outward preservation (though truly the primary aim of the text is that God is strong for His own for their temporal preservation). I say, we must not limit God's strength to preservation from outward enemies, but it must be extended to all spiritual things: such as 1. To bring down all your strong lusts.

### On the All-Presence

2. to resist strong temptations. 3. to help you in the performance of holy exercises <note>“Holy exercises” refers to spiritual disciplines such as prayer, meditation, and worship.</note>.

1. It [God’s strength] must be extended to the subduing of our strong desires. *2 Corinthians 12:9. He said to me, my strength is sufficient for you; for my strength is made perfect in weakness.* Whether this [the "thorn in the flesh" mentioned by Paul] was the sin of uncleanness or indwelling sin <note>“Indwelling sin” is a theological term for the inherent human inclination toward wrongdoing.</note> is somewhat difficult to determine; at any rate, it was some internal weakness, and not outward illnesses, as some have claimed, wherein God's power is revealed—when you are weak in resisting your strong lusts and in subduing the powerful workings of nature. Remember then, that the Lord God shows and exercises His strength in your weakness.

2. Just as God's strength is extended to the overcoming of your strong lusts within you, so it is also extended to resisting the temptations of the Devil. *Ephesians 6:10-11. Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the Devil.* We have power in God's power and strength, and we are strong in His might, not only to bear persecutions, but also to resist the Devil's schemes; therefore we read in the Scripture, *Psalm 138:3. In the day when I cried, you answered me, and strengthened me with strength in my soul.* Here is comfort: that God's strength is not limited or restricted to outward protection (though that is also a great mercy), but that it extends to your soul, to fortify it with power.

3. God's strength is extended for the benefit of His own, to perform difficult services and exercises that are too heavy for our own strength; we are in a state of weakness and helplessness. *Romans 7:5. For when we were in the flesh, the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death.* This indicates that a person is not only without grace, but also without the strength to obtain grace and to do good. Well, in this case, we have need of God's strength to help us in performing our holy exercises. Paul says in *Colossians 1:11, Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness.* Giving us to understand that the glorious power of God is extended to strengthen His own, that they might abound in good works. Thus I have given you three warnings.

The doctrine, as you see, is this: That there are certain special times in which, and certain special persons through whom, God will show and exercise His strength for the deliverance and preservation of His people. I have first given you the warning.

Secondly, what are those times in which God exercises His strength to deliver and preserve His people? There are many signs of these special times in which God reveals and exercises His strength.

First, when the Church and God's people are brought to the lowest ebb, then God takes pleasure in showing and exercising His strength. *Isaiah 25 [verse 4]: For you have been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast*

<column-break/>

of the tyrants is like a storm against a wall; when the darkness is greatest upon them, then is God's strength most for them. So also in *Ezekiel 37:11. Then he said unto me, Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel: behold, they say, Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost: we are cut off.* We are dry bones; is it likely that these bones should receive sinews, flesh, and life again? Our hope is lost—which refers to the return from the captivity of Babylon; nonetheless, when they say, "we are dry bones," behold, says the Lord, I shall make my power known, and bring life into them again. The meaning is: I shall deliver my people from captivity, even if they were in a very low state; so that this is a proper time; when God's people are at their lowest, then it is God's time to make His strength and power manifest in them. It was a saying of Greenham <note>Richard Greenham (c. 1535–1594) was an influential English Puritan whose works were widely read in the Netherlands.</note>, that if God's people were low enough, and God's enemies high enough, the Church would not lack deliverance for a single hour.

A second time is when the raging, the cruelty, and the confidence of the enemies of His people are at their greatest and highest; then God's power is shown for their preservation and for the destruction of their enemies. *Exodus 3:7. And the Lord said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows.* There was a proverb among the Jews, that when the number of bricks was doubled, then God came <note>This refers to the biblical account where Pharaoh increased the workload of the Israelites (requiring them to find their own straw for bricks) just before God intervened through Moses.</note>. When God saw that their cry was heavy and their oppression great, then the Lord said, *I have seen your afflictions, and have come to help you.* When their oppressions were cruelest, and their oppressors most bold; for they say, "Who is the Lord, that we should fear Him?"

A third time is when all visible power and strength of the Church and the people of God has perished, and there is much visible power against them; then it is God's time to show His power and strength for the benefit of His Congregation and people. Take a text for this, *Deuteronomy 32:36. For the Lord shall judge his people, and repent himself for his servants, when he seeth that their power is gone, and there is none shut up, or left.* And *Isaiah 63:5. And I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold: therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me; and my fury, it upheld me.* When all strength was gone, then God's strength came; then my arm—that is, my strength—brought salvation. When the Church cried: "By whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small" <note>A reference to Amos 7:2.</note>; he was small, and no one could help Jacob up. Well, says God, Jacob shall arise, even if he cannot see by whom. Just as the Apostle said, so let God's people say: when they are weak, then they are very strong; when they have no visible means to support them, and when there is much power against them, then is the special time that God makes His strength manifest against the enemies of His people; then God reveals His strength for their preservation and deliverance.
