-ken / so that they would give a full blow / to break the lock of the chain / but those behind / misunderstanding that / thought it was said / so that they should retreat / and they fled immediately / although no one pursued them; and the City was preserved. 2. God uses the mistake of his own people / when they are not thinking of it. Augustine, that famous instrument in God's Church / had the Donatists <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa that Augustine of Hippo famously opposed.</note> the Heretics as his enemies / they could not suffer that Augustine should so rule in God's Church / when he then went to preach / in a neighboring City / they planned to lay in wait / and kill him. Now there is one who relates / that Augustine got a guide / to show him the way / and the guide often went that way, yet through carelessness he missed a path / and thus went a wrong way / leaving the ordinary path; God used this error of the guide / to preserve Augustine's life: for only a few stations further lay the bloodthirsty men / to cut Augustine's throat. This shows God's power in the world / that he uses a simple mistake for the preservation of that famous and worthy instrument. O seek to broaden and widen this in your mind / so that you may worship God's power / which he has in so many ways for your preservation. And in this you have evident fruits of God's strength.

Sixthly, God the Lord demonstrates his strength for the benefit of his servants / by sometimes preserving them through contradictory means / means that in all appearance would destroy them; and certainly the theologians make this the greatest proof of God's power. When there was no way in this world to preserve Daniel in an ordinary manner / how does God preserve Daniel? he does it through contradictory means; there were Lions / that had been kept hungry; Daniel is thrown into the Lions' den; and the Lions' mouths were closed; God used the Lions / so that they should preserve Daniel; the men wanted him dead / but God uses the Lion / a more cruel and fierce beast than a man / as a means for Daniel's preservation. Likewise / God uses a contradictory means for the preservation of Jonah; he was swallowed by a Fish / it is said / that the food / which all creatures take / is changed into substance in less than three days / but Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the Whale / and yet he was kept alive; therefore the theologians say / he was a living man in the grave. Even so Christ willed / to show the power of his Divinity / to restore the sight of a man through contradictory means / John 9 verse 6. *When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay.*

Seventhly, God shows his power sometimes for the protection of his people / by restraining the natural inclination of the Creatures: Thus God preserved Peter; he had to walk on the water / and it would not drown him; so God preserved the three young men / they had to walk in the fire / and it would not burn them; fire would always burn / and water drown; but God / to show his power / sometimes stops the natural course; the God of nature wants many Creatures

Whether this be truly so, I cannot say; but I am certain that such a person is a fool who, when God presents him with the glory of Heaven, the assurance of God's love, and the salvation of his soul, regards children's toys and trifles above them. God the Lord proves that this is a spiritual foolishness in **Proverbs 17 verse 16**: *Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no heart to it?* <note>The original Dutch uses "verstant" (understanding), but the sense is having no will or heart for it.</note> God gives him much money in his hand; He gives him many convenient opportunities to save his soul and to enter Heaven, but he has no heart to apply them. In this, Esau showed his foolishness, who sold his birthright for a bowl of pottage, **Hebrews 12 verse 16**: *Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.* Cardinal Bourbon <note>Charles de Bourbon (1523–1590), a powerful French prelate and member of the royal house.</note>, having obtained great income in Paris, confessed to his friends that he would not trade his part in Paris for his part in Paradise. Many place their part and portion in the World above the glory of God; and thus the Gadarenes proved their foolishness when they valued their Swine above their Savior. This is the first proof.

A second proof of natural foolishness is that a fool always wants to be busy and play with harmful instruments; he wants to handle knives, and he wants to be busy with sharpened tools, or be near the water. This is very much like spiritual foolishness: that a person can joke and play with sharp tools, with whetted knives—that is, that he can joke with sin; this is foolishness. Abner said, *Let the young men now arise, and play before us,* **2 Samuel 2 verse 14**, when they were about to fight. So the godless joke with sins, as if it were but a joke to go to hell. Oh, you who play with sin, you are a right fool. **Proverbs 10 verse 23**: *It is as sport to a fool to do mischief.* And **Proverbs 14 verse 9**: *Fools make a mock at sin.* Beloved, you know that one considers it stupidity and foolishness in the dull fly <note>A common metaphor for a moth.</note> that it flies and plays around the candle so long until it has burned itself. Many, like the dull flies, play around hell and fly around hell; for when you sin, you play around hell, for then there is nothing but a small breadth between Hell and you. Oh, what foolishness it is in you to joke with that which shall destroy you, damn your soul, and burn you eternally. Plutarch <note>A famous Greek historian and biographer (c. 46 – 119 AD).</note> tells of a foolish child in Lacedemonia <note>Sparta.</note> who so loved to play with a fox that although the fox sometimes bit and tore him, the child nonetheless would not leave it; but at last, the Fox tore the entrails out of the child's body. Yet when the child's parents then came and took the fox away, the child screamed. Oh beloved, there are many more fools besides this Lacedemonian child. The Devil, that old fox, shall tear your entrails out if you play with him, and he shall damn your soul forever: yet you wish to play with him continually.

It highlights how the wicked "play" with the danger of sin and hell, much like a moth with a flame or a child with a wild animal.</summary>

->### and God’s Omniscience.<-

A third proof of a **natural fool** <note>In this period, a "natural fool" referred to someone born with intellectual disabilities, used here as a metaphor for the "spiritual fool" or sinner.</note> is that it is his nature to care only for the present and not for the future. He cares for nothing as long as he has food to fill his belly and clothes to cover his nakedness; a natural fool looks no further. This is an apt parable for a **spiritual fool**, of whom it is written in *Luke 12*. He cared only for this present life and laid up goods for it, but he never took care to lay up treasures for eternal life. And note what follows in *verses 20 and 21*: *But God said to him, "You fool! This night your soul will be required of you; then whose will those things be which you have provided?" So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.* That is to say, not only is this specific man a fool, but so is everyone who gathers treasures in this life for himself and is not rich toward God. Mark this well: Jesus Christ calls everyone a fool who piles up riches for himself—money-bag upon money-bag, hundred upon hundred—yet never lays up grace. I pray you, look back upon your own heart and see if some remnants of this foolishness do not remain among you. *Jeremiah 17, verse 11:* *As a partridge gathers eggs but does not hatch them, so is he who gets riches, but not by right; it will leave him in the midst of his days, and at his end he will be a fool.* A partridge is a dim-witted bird; she makes her nest in the grass, and even a child passing by can find it. And such are the greatest and richest men in this respect; they shall be found to be the greatest fools. *See Psalm 49, verses 11 and 12.*

A fourth comparison between natural and spiritual foolishness is this: A natural fool wants to be most busy and active with the most childish trifles and useless things, while neglecting matters of the greatest weight. We count it foolishness in our children when they run up and down the fields to catch butterflies while neglecting to go to school. If we consider it foolishness in our children to act so, surely our Father will count it foolishness in us if we occupy ourselves with such trivial things. So it was foolishness in **Domitian** <note>The Roman Emperor Domitian was famously said by historians to spend his spare time catching flies with a stylus.</note> that he, like a child, wanted to catch flies when he should have been carrying out the affairs of his state. It was also foolishness in **Archimedes** to draw lines in the dust <note>A reference to the mathematician Archimedes, who was so focused on a geometric problem drawn in the sand that he ignored the Roman soldier who eventually killed him during the Siege of Syracuse.</note> when he should have been protecting the city against the attacks of the enemy. This foolishness possesses the minds of many in the world; trifling and crude things take up their time, their strength, and their hearts, causing them to neglect the great matters of the world to come. Certainly, to live in this world in such a way that one neglects the next is proof of great foolishness.

Fifthly, a natural fool is an ignorant creature, and yet very unteachable and unmanageable. **Aristides**, a natural fool, was so dull that he could not learn to count beyond the number five. In the same way, spiritual fools are ignorant of God’s will; they do not know, and they do not *want* to know, which is proof of spiritual foolishness. *Proverbs 23, verse 9:* *Speak not in the ears of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.* Though your words be

<column-break/>

ever so wise, a fool will despise them; a spiritual fool is ignorant, and yet he cannot be taught or managed. *Jeremiah 22, verse 21:* *I spoke to you in your prosperity; but you said, "I will not hear." This has been your manner from your youth, that you did not obey my voice.* Beloved, if you are an ignorant person who does not know and does not want to know, who is not holy and does not want to be holy, who does not understand and does not want to understand—you are deeply possessed by a great measure of foolishness.

Sixthly, a natural fool is ignorant, but has a high opinion of himself; he easily thinks that no one leads as good a life as he does, and that no one has as much peace of heart as he. In this, he resembles a spiritual fool, who is an ignorant and godless man yet still has a great opinion of himself. *Proverbs 12, verse 13:* *In the transgression of the lips is the snare of the wicked.* *Proverbs 14, verse 16:* *A wise man fears and departs from evil; but a fool rages and is confident.* He thinks his way of life is safest and his own paths are best. I have read a notable story concerning a natural fool as proof of his folly, and it shall serve to explain spiritual foolishness. **Gilbertus** <note>Likely referring to Gilbertus Cognatus or a similar collector of moral anecdotes.</note> tells of a fool who, being sent to a woodpile to bring home an armful of wood, went to the bottom of the pile and began to heave and shake it to pull some sticks out. But he could hardly pull one out, and though he was advised by bystanders to go to the top of the pile where he could get the wood with great ease, he would not. He kept plucking and pulling at the base of the pile and did not stop until he pulled the entire woodpile down upon his head, which knocked the brains out of his skull. So it is with spiritual foolishness; you do that which will damn your soul, which will ignite the whole woodpile to burn with you. When someone tells you this, and you will not stop but wish to follow your own course, this is spiritual foolishness. Oh, how many there are who, like the fool, will bring the woodpile down upon their own heads! How many there are who keep such a course as inevitably leads to their ruin, despite all the counsel given for their correction.

Seventhly, it is a characteristic of a natural fool to take more pleasure and delight in gaudy ornaments than in modest clothing for the body; just as natural fools take more delight in multi-colored hat-bands than in honest attire. This is so prevalent in our days; had these people lived then, one would have thought they were fools. They think it is proof of their brilliance and finery, but truly it is proof of their foolishness. So too, when someone reaches a prosperous state through much effort, he thinks it is his wisdom; but if the Psalmist is believed, it is proof of his foolishness and an aggravation of his misery. *Psalm 92, verses 6 and 7:* *A senseless man does not know, nor does a fool understand this: that when the wicked spring up like grass, and when all the workers of iniquity flourish, it is that they may be destroyed forever.* It is a certain mark of a spiritual fool to [be]

->## Of the Omnipresence<-

...to amuse oneself in trifles <note>original: "sodderpen," an archaic term for nonsense or trivialities</note> and trivialities, and to neglect the weighty matters of salvation.

The usefulness of this teaching is: First, that to do evil is to act foolishly; thus I conclude that no godless person is a wise person. *Proverbs 1:7*: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction.* A person does not begin to be wise until he begins to fear God. *Psalm 111:10*: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; all those who follow His precepts have good understanding.* It is as if no one had a good understanding except he who does what he knows to be right; this is the reason for the saying in *James 3:13*: *Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in the humility that comes from wisdom,* indicating that a person leading an evil life is a true fool; he is not wise if he is godless.

Secondly, I conclude from this that although the pious are considered fools by the world, nonetheless, no one is truly wise but them. The godless are wiser in their generation than the children of light—that is, in worldly matters. How does he fare on the "busy side" of life? <note>Likely referring to worldly success or material gain.</note> No; for in God's account, regarding the matters of the other world, he is the wisest man who gathers for another life when this one comes to an end. In Sparta, the Kings were only made Kings for a single year, and after that, they had to be banished and live in poverty. But one King was wiser than all the others; because he saw that he must hold his Royal power for only a year, he sent his goods ahead—during his time of power and plenty—to that place where he would be banished, and so he lived in abundance all his days. Those are the wisest who think of the time of banishment <note>A metaphor for death and the afterlife.</note>; when the Lord God takes you out of this evil world, you who lay up grace, you are the wisest who strive to have a well-grounded portion in Jesus Christ; this is the greatest proof of wisdom. Thus you now have a passing explanation of the proverb of Hanani the Seer to King Asa: "In this you have done foolishly."

I come now to the last part of the text, namely, the Seer's proclamation of the terrible Judgment upon King Asa in these words: *For from now on wars shall be against you.* I confess, I am reluctant to handle this particular detail, as it is a point that touches upon these present times and may cause many thoughts in many people. *Therefore, from now on wars shall be against you.*

Well, beloved, note in these last words these three parts: 1. Here is the proclamation of a truly terrifying Judgment: *you shall have wars.* 2. The gravity of the Judgment: *you shall have wars*—not a single battle, but wars from many places, at many times. The gravity also lies in this: that this Asa had wars before he acted foolishly, but in those he gained the upper hand (*2 Chronicles 14:9, 12*). But this proverb means to say: you shall have wars, and you shall have the worst of it in those wars, as indeed happened to him. War is a judgment, but to have war, and to be defeated, and to have the goods of the Kingdom diminished thereby—that is the Judgment; so it was with Asa. 3. Here the timing of this judgment is emphasized: *From now on you shall have wars.* Some believe it began in

<column-break/>

the tenth year of his reign, but that thereafter his entire reign, which lasted 31 years, was a bloody time. "Until this time," says God, "you have lived in a peaceful Kingdom, but from now on you shall have wars." 4. The meriting cause—why God brought this war into the land—is indicated by the word **Therefore**. And why was it? Four types of causes can be given as an answer to this **Therefore**:

1. Because Asa robbed God's Temple of its treasure, and of that which was to maintain the service of God at Gilgal. You see this in *2 Chronicles 16:3*: *There is a treaty between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. See, I am sending you silver and gold; go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel so that he will withdraw from me.* "I send you silver and gold"—it is not recounted there where it was taken from. But compare this place with *1 Kings 15:18*: *Then Asa took all the silver and gold that was left in the treasuries of the Lord’s temple and of his own palace. He entrusted it to his officials and sent them to Ben-Hadad.* Here was Asa’s wickedness: all the money and treasures that were laid up in the Bank <note>The "Bank" refers to the sacred treasury or storehouse of the Temple.</note> for the maintenance of God's service had to go to the maintenance of the War. And if, proportionally, a War is brought about because one takes away what maintains God's service, and leaves no equal maintenance in its place, then the Lord shall have a dispute with every nation that does this.

2. A second meriting cause was that Asa entered into a covenant with an unbeliever, with a Heathen; and in such a covenant that he relied on an unbeliever, that he helped him against his Brothers, the children of Israel. Therefore Hanani says to him in *verse 7*: *At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said to him: "Because you relied on the king of Aram and not on the Lord your God..."* Why should you run to a Heathen King to join yourself with him, when the Lord fought your battle before and struck down an army of a thousand thousand? <note>Refers to the defeat of the Cushites in 2 Chronicles 14.</note>

3. Asa incited Ben-Hadad to break his covenant with Baasha, the King of Israel (*verse 3*). Between Baasha and Ben-Hadad there was a covenant that they would practice no acts of hostility against one another. Well, for this cause—that he advised another to break his covenant, a covenant between man and man—therefore God sends war upon his Kingdom.
From this I may infer: If it is so, that inciting another to covenant-breaking shall be avenged by God, what then will God do to the breakers of a covenant made with God? O good God! What have we to expect over the entire Land? We have broken the solemn covenant that was made, more so than any since the world began. Certainly, if God is in Heaven, He will avenge this wickedness; and perhaps the sin is so general that He shall punish the covenant-breaking with the breaking-in of the sword.

4. Asa relied on an arm of flesh <note>A biblical idiom for human strength or military power as opposed to divine aid.</note> in his danger, and not on God to be delivered; and this Hanani announces to him. These were the causes of the War that Hanani threatened would come over Judah: *Therefore from now on there shall be wars against you.*

<meta>This page continues the discourse on King Asa's folly and the consequences of relying on human strength over divine wisdom. ->### and God’s Omniscience.<-

...various points of doctrine can be drawn from here.

*Therefore from now on you shall have wars.* Asa alone sinned, yet God punished the entire Kingdom. Note from this, firstly, that God sometimes punishes a whole realm for the sins of its King and Rulers, even if the people themselves are not guilty. *2 Chronicles 28, verse 19*: *For the Lord humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel, for he promoted wickedness in Judah and was unfaithful to the Lord.* He humbled the people because of Ahaz's sin. So too in *2 Samuel 24, verses 15 and 17*: *So the Lord sent a plague on Israel from that morning until the time designated, and seventy thousand of the people from Dan to Beersheba died. When David saw the angel who was striking down the people, he said to the Lord, "I am the one who has sinned and done wrong. These are but sheep. What have they done? Let your hand fall on me and my family."* It was David's sin. Conversely, sometimes God punishes the Authorities for the sins of the people; it went poorly for Moses, the leader of the people, because of the sins of the people, *Psalm 106, verse 32*. I recount this to teach us to mourn when we see Rulers living godlessly, for God may punish the people of the land for their sins; sometimes the people corrupt their rulers, and sometimes the rulers corrupt the people. So it was with Asa: Asa sinned, and the people were brought to ruin. *From now on, wars shall be against you.*

Note secondly, the precise times when wars begin are fully determined by God; the time is set by Him when wars shall break into a land.

Note thirdly, that God never brings a judgment upon a person or a people unless there is a cause. God might punish the nations and turn Kingdoms upside down, and no one might say to God, "Why do you do this?" But God deals with the nations not according to His absolute power, but according to His justice.

Note fourthly, that leaning on an "arm of flesh" <note>This is a biblical metaphor for relying on human strength or military power instead of God.</note>, breaking a covenant, and conspiring with God's enemies angers God in the highest degree. Relying on human strength and entering into conspiracies with known enemies of God is the path and the door to a bloody war. *2 Chronicles 28, verses 16 and 20*: *At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria for help. Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria came to him, but he gave him trouble instead of help.* He brought wars and distress into his Kingdom, but no one helped him. The Lord is strong enough to give people their due if they only use right paths and employ only right instruments for the work; but if anyone uses evil means, God will make them feel the pain of it. But the observation I shall draw from this text is: **That there are certain particular sins which are the bloody causes of war in a Kingdom.** *Therefore from now on, etc.* Before I handle the doctrine, I must here open and remove two or three difficulties.

First, how can it be said that this message of Hanani <note>Hanani was a prophet who rebuked King Asa for relying on the King of Syria instead of God.</note> threatened against Asa was fulfilled—namely, that he would have wars in his

<column-break/>

Kingdom—since we read in the following verses of this chapter that Asa died, yet we read of no wars that Asa had after the war with the Lubim and Ethiopians, which was before that time? Scripture remains silent about any wars after that period. Now, as to whether this was fulfilled, I answer: although it is true that in the Book of Chronicles no mention is made of wars that Asa had, and that there is only a short summary of the history, nonetheless, this is the perfection of the harmony of Scripture—what is missing in one place is fulfilled in another. Even if there is no mention of this judgment in the Book of Chronicles, it is nonetheless in the Book of Kings. *And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days,* *1 Kings 15, verse 32*. And after Baasha's death, with Omri <note>The original text says "Othan," likely a transcription error for Omri or a reference to the ongoing conflict with the Northern Kingdom.</note> and Ahab. There is then the express and particular fulfillment of this fearsome prophecy of Hanani: *From now on you shall have wars against you.* Thus the interpreters untie this knot.

Secondly, here is another difficulty. Verse 1 says: *In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah.* Other scriptural texts say that Baasha was dead long before that time. *1 Kings 16, verses 6 and 8*: *Baasha rested with his ancestors and was buried in Tirzah. And Elah his son succeeded him as king. In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king of Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years.* How can this Scripture be true, that one says Baasha came up against Asa in the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, and yet he died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign? Interpreters say, to reconcile this, that when Baasha came up against Asa, it was the thirty-sixth year of his reign—that is to say, the thirty-sixth year of the Kingdom of Judah since the separation of the ten tribes from the house of Judah. At that time Baasha came up against Asa, which was actually only the sixteenth year of Asa's personal reign. This is the truest reconciliation that interpreters give of this apparent contradiction.

Thirdly: How can Scripture say, *from now on you shall have wars*, and that with Baasha, seeing that Baasha died twenty-five years before Asa died? For Baasha died in the sixteenth year of Asa's reign <note>based on the chronological reconciliation mentioned above</note>, and Asa reigned for another 25 years beyond that. How can it then be true that Asa had war from then on all his days? I answer: it is indeed true that he did not have wars with Baasha all his days, but he nonetheless had wars with those who came in Baasha's place, so that he was never at rest until the day of his death; therefore the threat was fulfilled.

But I shall focus my thoughts on the text which applies more to practice: *Therefore from now on you shall have wars against you.* The observation is this: **That there are certain particular sins that cause bloody wars in a Kingdom.** *Therefore from now on, etc.* For the proof and explanation of this point of doctrine, I shall point out which specific sins those were in Israel that from time to time caused bloody wars in that land, so as to see how this corresponds with the godlessness of this generation; and I shall list seven or...

->### Of the Divine Presence<-

...name eight particular sins that brought bloody wars to Israel.

The **first sin** that brought bloody wars to Israel was when the party in power, through the force of the sword, drove from their possession those who had a true right to rule the Kingdom. I shall give you some clear examples of this: You know that God rejected Saul because of his godlessness, so that he should no longer be King, and He chose David to be King over Israel. David had a calling from God; now, what did Abner do? A man of war, he wanted to make Ishbosheth King over Israel and cast David out, so that he should not be King. Note the outcome of this; it was a bloody war. *2 Samuel 2, verses 8 through 17.* So too in *2 Samuel 3, verse 1*: *Now there was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. But David grew stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker.* A second example is Rehoboam, who, as you know, was David’s grandson and had a right to the Kingdom of Israel through lawful succession; but Jeroboam obtained the strength of the sword and, in a conspiracy, shook ten tribes away from the house of David. What was the outcome of this? *1 Kings 14, verse 10.* <note>The author likely intended to cite 1 Kings 14:30, which mentions the constant warfare.</note> *And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days.* A third example is in Athaliah, who created a schism and slaughtered all the royal blood, except for a young Prince who was hidden by his aunt. *2 Chronicles 22, verses 10, 11, and 12.* And what discord did this provoke in Judah and Jerusalem? This was made known by the proverb: *And all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet after they had slain Athaliah with the sword.* *2 Chronicles 23, verse 21*, and *2 Chronicles 24, verse 7*. The sons of that godless woman Athaliah had broken into the house of God. Another conflict was between Tibni and Omri, *2 Kings 16* <note>Actually 1 Kings 16:21-22</note>. The Kingdom belonged to Tibni by right, but those who held the power of the sword in their hands made Omri King, and he reigned, although he had no right; but he had the soldiers on his side, and with them he carried it out. *1 Kings 16, verses 21 and 22*: *Then the people of Israel were divided into two halves: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri. But the people who followed Omri prevailed over the people who followed Tibni. So Tibni died and Omri reigned.*

A **second sin** that provoked bloody wars in Israel was covenant-breaking. See this in *Leviticus 26, verse 25*: *And I will bring a sword against you that will execute the vengeance of the covenant; when you are gathered together within your cities, I will send pestilence among you; and you shall be delivered into the hand of the enemy.* God has a dispute with those who break the covenant, and He will avenge Himself upon those who do so. *Isaiah 24, verses 1, 5, and 6*: *The land is defiled by its inhabitants, because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant. Therefore the curse has devoured the land, etc.* God speaks there of the fruits of war. Why was all this? The land defiled, etc. They have broken the covenant that should have been everlasting; they broke the law, and therefore war broke

<column-break/>

in upon them: read the fourteenth verse of the preceding chapter, and *Jeremiah 34, verses 17, 18, and 20*: *I will deliver you to trouble among all the kingdoms of the earth. And I will give the men who have transgressed My covenant, who have not performed the words of the covenant which they made before Me, when they cut the calf in two and passed between the parts of it* <note original="met het kalf dat zy in twee hadden gehouden">This refers to an ancient ritual where a sacrifice was split in half, and the parties walking between the pieces invoked a curse upon themselves if they failed to keep the oath.</note>—*yes, I will give them into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their life. Their dead bodies shall be meat for the birds of the heaven and the beasts of the earth.*

A **third sin** that caused bloody wars was a general apostasy from the purity of religion. You have a notable text for this in *Judges 5, verse 8*: *They chose new gods; then there was war in the gates; was there a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?* Even if there were no shield or weapon of war among forty thousand men, nevertheless, when they chose new gods, wars immediately came. It is not the honor of a people to have weapons of war; rather, it is the shame of a people—it is a proof of the cruelty of men toward one another. It is remarkable that those Kings who looked after religion, to keep it in its luster, reigned most peacefully in their Kingdom. *2 Chronicles 14, verses 5 and 6*: *He took away the high places and the sun-images* <note original="Zonne-beelden">likely idols or pillars dedicated to sun worship</note> *from all the cities of Judah, and the kingdom was quiet under him. And he built fortified cities in Judah, for the land had rest, and he had no war in those years, because the Lord had given him rest.* Asa had no wars in his realm for the first ten years because he reformed the service of God; when he first came to the crown, he was zealous for the service of God; then his kingdom was quiet before him, and he had no wars in those days. Likewise, *2 Chronicles 17, verse 10*: *And the fear of the Lord fell on all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, so that they did not make war against Jehoshaphat.* When Jehoshaphat threw down the idolatrous images, the people feared the Lord, and Jehoshaphat had no wars; those Kings who viewed Religion as their greatest and foremost work had their Kingdoms made most peaceful by God, whereas conversely, that people who repeatedly fell away from religion were punished by God with the sword.

A **fourth sin** that brings bloody wars into a kingdom is carelessness <note original="zorgeloosheydt">here meaning spiritual complacency or indifference to warnings</note>, when crying sins are committed and terrible judgments are threatened. You have a notable text for this in *Jeremiah 5, verses 12 and 17* <note>The OCR cites verse 27, but the text matches verse 17</note>: *They have lied about the Lord, and said, "It is not He; neither shall evil come upon us, nor shall we see sword or famine." ... And it shall eat up your harvest and your bread, which your sons and daughters should eat; it shall eat up your flocks and your herds; it shall eat up your vines and your fig trees; it shall impoverish your fortified cities, in which you trust, with the sword.* So also *Jeremiah 14, verses 15 and 16*: *Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who prophesy in My name, though I did not send them, and who say, "Sword and famine shall not be in this land"—by sword and famine those prophets shall be*

Therefore, thus says the Lord of Hosts: "Behold, I will visit punishment upon them; the young men shall fall by the sword, and their sons and their daughters shall die of hunger." Simply because the men of Anathoth had placed Jeremiah in prison and mistreated him, therefore their young men shall die by the sword and their children by hunger. Contempt and a lack of profit under the established services of God brings the sword into a Kingdom. A striking text stands here, if you consider it well:

<margin>Rev. 6: 2, 4.</margin>
*Revelation 6: 2, 4.* And I saw, and behold, a white horse, and he who sat upon it had a bow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering and to conquer. And another horse, and to him who sat upon it was given power to take peace from the earth, and that they should kill one another; and there was given to him a great sword. By the white horse, they <note>Commentators of the era.</note> understand the swift delivery of the Gospel; by the one who rides upon it, Christ and His Apostles; by his going out conquering and to conquer, the converting of souls. But what follows in verse 4? That after the white horse, a red horse came, which represented the wars of the Roman Emperor. And the text says, "He who sat on the red horse had power to take peace from the earth, and to make them kill one another." The meaning is this: since Jesus Christ, riding upon the white horse, preaching and spreading the Gospel, did not convert the people nor make them come in and embrace the Gospel; therefore, a red horse followed to avenge the quarrel of

<column-break/>

the white: the sword and war followed to take peace from the earth, because the people did not accept the Gospel of peace. Take note, then: if the white horse of the Gospel finds no place in the hearts of the people, the red horse of war will follow to avenge the rejection of the white. The first battle that took place was at a location which, in these recent wars, was called Scherpenheuvel <note>Literally "Sharp Hill," a famous pilgrimage and battle site in the Southern Netherlands/Belgium.</note>, but the Valley where the two armies fought was called the **Valley of the Red Horse**. Theologians make good use of this, noting that the first great battle in these recent wars happened precisely in that place named the Valley of the Red Horse—as if God wished to bring this passage from Revelation to our minds: that if one misuses the white horse of the Gospel and does not receive it into one's heart, God will send the red horse of war to avenge the quarrel of the white horse. Likewise, if you have days of freedom when the Gospel is preached and spread, yet you live contemptibly, unholily, and unprofitably under it, this can provoke God the Lord to send the red horse, and one upon it to take peace from the earth so that they kill one another. Ursinus <note>Zacharias Ursinus (1534–1583), a key author of the Heidelberg Catechism.</note>, in the preface to his Catechism, says that England’s fruitlessness under the Gospel in the days of King Edward <note>Edward VI (r. 1547–1553), who established Protestantism in England.</note> brought the indignation under Mary <note>Queen Mary I (r. 1553–1558), who persecuted Protestants.</note>.

A **sixth sin** is the withholding of and opposition to the power and purity of Religion: this is a sin that stirred up wars in Israel. You shall find a remarkable example in the Jews themselves—for I speak only of that people—*Matthew 23, verses 37, 38.* Jerusa-

<margin>Matth. 23 verses 37, 38.</margin>

Behold, your house is left to you desolate. Why did the Jews suppress Christianity? Why did they oppose Christ? Simply on this foundation: for, they said, Christ is an enemy to Caesar, and they feared that if they embraced Christianity, the Romans would come and destroy their place and take it away. They rejected Christ; about forty years later, Titus Vespasianus <note>The Roman general, later Emperor, who besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> came to Jerusalem and destroyed their place and people. Thus was Christ's prophecy fulfilled: "Your house is left to you desolate." The Jews thought this was a clever plan to keep their place and home, but God turned it into a means of their extermination because they opposed Religion. Maximus <note>Likely Galerius Maximianus or Maximinus Daza, Roman Emperors known for persecuting Christians.</note> made an Edict to suppress Christianity within his jurisdiction, and immediately a bloody war arose in his territory in which he had the worst of it; thus, resisting the Gospel of peace brings in raging war.

->Of the Omnipresence<-

Eighthly and lastly, the sin of oppression and injustice caused wars in Israel. *Micah 2, verses 2, 3, 4, 5.* And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage. Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, against this family do I devise an evil, from which ye shall not remove your necks; neither shall ye go haughtily: for this time is evil. In that day shall one take up a proverb against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, and say, We be utterly spoiled: he hath changed the portion of my people: how hath he removed it from me! turning away he hath divided our fields. Therefore thou shalt have none that shall cast a cord by lot in the congregation of the Lord.

### The Utility is / 1. Of warning, 2. Of counsel, 3. Of comfort. <note>In 17th-century preaching, the "Utility" or "Use" (Nuttigheydt) was the section of the sermon where the minister applied the biblical doctrine to the daily lives of the congregation.</note>

First, for warning, and that in two ways.
First, consider the sword <note>The "sword" is a common biblical metaphor for war and violent conflict.</note> as one of God's heaviest judgments: the Lord recounts sharp judgments in His word, and the sword is the sharpest, as seen in these following observations.

1. When David had his choice, whether he would have the sword, or famine, or the pestilence, he by no means wanted to choose the sword, indicating that it was the worst of all three. <note>This refers to 2 Samuel 24, where King David is offered three punishments for his pride in numbering the people.</note>

2. The sword leaves a people worse than they were at first; another judgment makes God's people better, just as when God sends a famine in the land, it makes men look up toward Heaven: they see then God's hand; when they behold the plague, this makes them look upon God; but the sword makes men wild and beastly. I have not come across a history, whether Ecclesiastical or Secular, in which I find that the sword has made a people better; rather, it has made them worse, more cruel, and more savage toward one another: the savagery and desolation that the sword brings will hardly be forgotten in a hundred years; it is a terrible judgment.

3. The sword causes other sharp judgments; for famine and pestilence are commonly the companions of the sword. *2 Kings 6, verse 25.* And there was a great famine in Samaria: and, behold, they besieged it, until a donkey's head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a kab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver. The sword brings famine; so you also read of the sword in Jerusalem, when the sword of the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians.</note> was upon them. *Lamentations 4, verses 4, 5.* The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them. They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills. Well, beloved, see it as the very heaviest judgment, should God bring the sword to you again.

Secondly, be warned that whenever God brings the sword into a peaceful Kingdom, you must view that as the punishment for certain crying sins, and as the fruits of God's extraordinary wrath kindled against you; when the sword comes, which is such a devastating judgment, it is a consequence of certain punishments for certain unusual sins. A full text for this is found in *Job 16, verse 29.* <note>In modern Bibles, this is Job 19:29.</note> Be ye afraid of the sword: for

<column-break/>

wrath bringeth the punishments of the sword, that ye may know there is a judgment. It is wrath that brings the punishment of the sword. How so? That you may know there is a judgment, not a general Judgment, but that God judges you for your crying sins. Beloved, I pray you, see this as the punishment for certain crying sins, as the consequences of God's wrath, that the sword has been in this peaceful Land: Or if it should yet again be drawn from the sheath (which God forbid), but if it happened, see it as the consequences of God's wrath.

### The second Utility is for counsel.

There are certain particular sins that bring the sword; take then a word of counsel.

1. Make peace with God, and then, if the sword comes, it shall do you no harm. *Isaiah 27, verses 1, 5.* In that day the Lord with his sore and great and strong sword shall punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea. Or let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me; and he shall make peace with me. If the sword comes to war against you, then run and hide yourselves, and make your peace with God; that is the greatest point of wisdom, so that when there are troubles without, there may be no troubles within. If my peace is made with God, I need fear no enemy outside of me.

2. Strive to have a true right and portion in Jesus Christ. *Micah 5, verse 4.* <note>In modern English versions, this is Micah 5:5.</note> And this man shall be the peace, when the Assyrian shall come into our land. If the sword is drawn, and Christ is yours, then Christ does not ask about the war: It is worthy of your notice, *Isaiah 9, verses 4, 5.* For every battle of the warrior is with confused noise, and garments rolled in blood; but this shall be with burning and fuel of fire. For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, etc. <note>The author interprets the prophecy of Christ's birth as the ultimate comfort even in the midst of bloody warfare.</note> The meaning is, that the promise that Jesus Christ would be born into the world should make the people rejoice: Though there are garments rolled in blood, if you can nevertheless prove that Christ is given to you, a war need not disturb you.

3. If God should send bloody wars among us, take this counsel: let it hold you back from carnality and lustfulness. *Ezekiel 21, from verse 9 to verse 15.* Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus saith the Lord; Say, A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished: Should we then make mirth? etc. When God brings a sword (which God prevent), let it keep you from sensuality.

4. If God from now on should send wars among us, let not your heart cling to any pleasure or possession that you enjoy here. War is a shaking judgment: It shakes people out of their state, so that they need not set their heart upon it. Oh! do not let your heart hang upon anything here below! *Ezekiel 7, verses 12, 13, 15.* The time is come, the day draweth near: let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn: for wrath is upon all the multitude thereof. For the seller shall not return to that which is sold: Although

# and the Omniscience of God.

their life was still among the living; because the vision, concerning the whole multitude of the land, shall not return, and no one shall strengthen his life through his iniquity. The sword is outside; and the plague and the hunger are within; he who is in the field shall die by the sword, and he who is in the city, him shall hunger and plague consume. <note>This opening paragraph paraphrases Ezekiel 7, warning that worldly wealth cannot save a person during divine judgment.</note> The buyer rejoices that he has made a good bargain; but (He says) neither is necessary, for you shall not return to that which you have, for the sword shall thrust you out of your possession. Let then your heart not cling too much to anything that you enjoy here.

**The Third Utility** is of comfort. First, even if God willed from now on—as punishment for our iniquities—to cause us to have wars, know nonetheless for your comfort that God in every age, and until the end of the world, shall preserve a remnant from the power of the sword; though the sword be bared and drawn, and though the enemies be ever so mighty, nonetheless God has in all ages and shall until the end of the world preserve a remnant from the strength of the sword, *Job* 5, verse 20. In famine He shall deliver you from death, and in war from the power of the sword, *Ezekiel* 14, verses 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. When I bring the sword upon that same land, and say, "Sword, go through, through that same land," so that I root out from it humans and beasts; even if these three men were in the midst of it, as surely as I live, speaks the Lord God, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone would be delivered, etc. Petitioners and Saints of God, such as *Noah*, *Daniel*, and *Job* were, shall keep their lives, even if the sword consumes many in the land.

**Secondly**, even if wars come, take nonetheless this comfort: that the war cannot harm those who have made their peace with God. It is worthy of your consideration—and the interpreters take great pains in its reconciliation—2 *Chronicles* 35, verses 23, 24. And the archers shot King *Josiah*, then the King said to his servants: "Carry me away, for I am sorely wounded," and his servants took him away from the chariot, and carried him in the second chariot that he had, and brought him to Jerusalem, and he died, and was buried in the graves of his Fathers, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned over *Josiah*; there it stands that *Josiah*, that pious King, died by the sword of the King of Egypt; he died in the war,

<column-break/>

he was wounded in the battle, and so he died. Now compare this text with 2 *Chronicles* 34, verse 28: *Behold, I shall gather you to your Fathers, and you shall be gathered to your grave in peace.* <note>King Josiah is often cited in 17th-century sermons as the model of a "pious prince" whose death was a national tragedy.</note> Here God promised to *Josiah* that he would go to his grave in peace. How can this be? Beloved, in a threefold way the fulfillment of this promise is made good:

1. Some theologians say the promise, "you shall go to your grave in peace," rests on a hidden condition: namely, if you keep His ways and do not go to war; if God does not command you to go to war, then you shall die in peace.

2. Others say that he would go to his grave in peace because the promise was not to him personally—that he would die in peace—but that he would see his Kingdom in peace; for so he did, as he went out from his Kingdom to wage war.

3. But other scholars give a third answer, which serves my purpose; the promise says that *Josiah* would go to his grave in peace, and the following chapter says he died in the war. Even though *Josiah* died in the war, he died nonetheless in peace, to show that a godly person dying in the war by the point of a spear suffers no more damage to his soul than if he died in his bed; though he died in the war, he died nonetheless in peace. This is for your comfort: though you might come to die in a war, if your peace is made with God, then you die in peace.

**Thirdly**, this is for your comfort: whatever preparation there may be for war, whatever probability there may be of a future war, or of the long duration of war in a Kingdom, God nonetheless has a supreme power over all nations; He can suddenly suppress it all. Let there be apparent war preparations, nonetheless God has a supreme power, and He can hinder it. There is an excellent passage in *Psalm* 46, verse 10: *Who makes the wars to cease unto the end of the earth, breaks the bow, and snaps the spear in two, burns the chariots with fire.* This was Luther’s Psalm. <note>Psalm 46 was famously the inspiration for Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God" (*Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott*).</note> God needs only to speak a word, and the wars are quiet and gone. So you must look to God, who has power and headship over all people; He can soften and take away all the intemperances of the times. And let this much be said regarding this time and text. *For the eyes of the Lord run through the whole earth, to show Himself strong to those whose heart is perfect with Him; you have done foolishly in this; for from now on there shall be wars against you.*

# The Sinner’s Testament to his Descendants. The Patient Watchman:

### And

# A Christian’s Appointed Hiding-
place. Presented in several Sermons by Mr. CHRISTOPHORUS LOVE. Translated by M. J. K.

<margin>First Sermon.</margin>

> Lamentations 5, verses 7, 8.
> 
> Our Fathers have sinned, and are no more, and we bear their iniquities; servants rule over us; there is no one who can snatch us out of their hand.

<note>Christopher Love (1618–1651) was a prominent English Presbyterian minister and Covenanter who was eventually executed for his involvement in a plot to restore the monarchy.</note> This Book is a renowned part of the Scripture, much used and highly esteemed among the Jews; once a year it was read in the Jewish Synagogues, namely on the ninth of July, because on that day of the month the City of Jerusalem was taken and the Temple burned. There are many differences among the interpreters regarding the occasion of the writing of this book, but I shall summarize everything briefly; 1. It is not a prophetic lament over the misery that would befall Jerusalem in the future; the Papist <note>The author uses "Papist" as a common 17th-century term for Roman Catholic interpreters.</note> interpreters say that Jeremiah prophesied what happened to Jerusalem through Titus Vespasian: but no, it is a lament over the past, not over the future. 2. It is not a specific lament over the suffering of any particular person; some apply it to Christ, Chapter 1, verse 12. Others to Josiah, that it is a lament over his death because of Chapter 4, verse 20. <note>original: "Sed res ipsa clamat, majorem calamitatem hic deplorari"</note> "The matter itself cries out that a greater calamity is lamented here," says Calvin. This Book was written in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, when he was carried away captive by Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon. So as not to overlook the entire book, which is filled with mournful lamentation, I shall only speak of this Chapter. Here is a complaint about the shaming of their name, verses 1, 2. About the restoration of their state, verses 2, 3. About the loss of nearby friends by the sword and pestilence, verses 3, 4. About famine, verses 4, 5. About their slavery and subjection under their enemies, verses 5, 6. And about the fact that they were punished for their Fathers' sin, in my text, which describes the destructive effect of sin upon the persons themselves who commit it: *Our Fathers sinned and are not,* and 2. Upon their descendants; sin brings a punishment upon them: *We bear their iniquities.*

Notice from this that sin robs man of his being in this world: sin is the primary murderer of men; it destroys generation after generation from the face of the earth; sin, coming into the world, drove men out of the world. Romans 5, verse 12.

<column-break/>

Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and death passed to all men, because all have sinned.

The Doctrine from these words is this: It is consistent with the righteousness of God to punish children or descendants for sins committed by their ancestors. Exodus 20, verse 5. *For I am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the Fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation.* Deuteronomy 5, verse 9. *Lord, you repay the iniquity of the Fathers into the bosom of their children.*

Before I go on to show how it is consistent with God's justice to punish descendants for the sins of the ancestors, I shall, for warning, present seven or eight propositions or statements that shall serve to explain the doctrine.

1. God may, through His sovereignty, punish any creature, even the best, and yet He shall not be unrighteous: He who made every creature may destroy every creature: He may do with His own what pleases Him: that which does not conflict with His sovereignty does not conflict with His righteousness. Ezekiel 18, verses 2, 3, 4. *What do you mean, that you use this proverb concerning the land of Israel: saying, the Fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge: as surely as I live, speaks the Lord God, you shall no longer have occasion to use this proverb in Israel: behold, all souls are mine, as the soul of the Father, so also the soul of the Son is mine; the soul that sins shall die.*

2. Although God has a supreme power to punish every creature, even the holiest, nonetheless He does not put the acts of His supreme power into effect, punishing anyone unless sin is found in them, whether <term>original sin</term><note>inherited sin from Adam</note> or <term>actual sin</term><note>sins committed by the individual</note>, which deserves such punishment.

3. Commonly, God punishes such children for their Fathers' sins who imitate their Fathers' sins. Psalm 49, verse 14. *This their way is a folly to them; yet their descendants have a delight in their words:* what follows? they shall be punished together, verse 15. *They are appointed like sheep for the grave, death shall feed on them.* Likewise Daniel 5, verses 21, 22. Daniel first tells Belshazzar of his Father <note>Nebuchadnezzar</note> that because his heart was lifted up, he was deposed from his throne, and driven from among the children of men, to dwell with the wild donkeys, and to eat grass like the oxen, until he acknowledged, etc. And you, Belshazzar his Son, have not...

# To his descendants.

you have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this; but you have lifted yourself up, etc. <note>The author is referencing the downfall of Belshazzar in Daniel 5:22-23.</note> What follows? verse 28. Your Kingdom is divided, and it is given to the Medes and the Persians. Matthew 23, verses 31, 33. See, I send to you Prophets, etc. and some of them you shall kill and crucify, and some you shall scourge; so that upon you may come all the righteous blood that has been shed on the earth: From the blood of the righteous Abel, to the blood of Zechariah, whom you killed between the Temple and the Altar. Jeremiah 7:18. The children gather wood, and the Fathers kindle the fire, and the Women knead the dough, to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven <note>original: *Melechet des Hemels*</note>, etc. to provoke me to anger, etc. <note>original: *Ideo, iniquitates eorum portaverunt, quia imitatores eorum in nequitia extiterunt* — "Therefore, they bore their iniquities, because they stood as imitators of them in wickedness."</note> This was also the case with Jeroboam.

4. God, in His justice, can sometimes punish the children or descendants for their Fathers' sins, in which they had no part; nevertheless, they share in the punishment. So it went with Achan’s children, Joshua 7; with the children of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram; and with the children in Sodom. Without doubt, there were many young children in Sodom burned with fire who could not have imitated their Parents' sins: So also many drowned in the ancient world. Numbers 14, verse 33 states: Your children shall wander in this Wilderness forty years, and shall bear your whoredoms, until your dead bodies are consumed in this Wilderness. 1 Kings 14, verse 10. (God says) I will cut off from Jeroboam every male <note>original: *die aan de wandt pist* — a literal 17th-century biblical idiom for "every male."</note>, I will take away his descendants, etc.

5. God may punish the children for the sins of their ancestors which were committed many years before their birth, as cited before in Matthew 23, verse 35. And 2 Kings 21, verses 11, 12. Because Manasseh, King of Judah, has done these abominations, doing more wickedly, etc. Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will bring such evil upon Jerusalem and Judah, that whoever hears of it, etc. It was 55 years and six months after the sin of Manasseh that this threat was fulfilled in their captivity. 1 Samuel 15:2, 3. Thus says the Lord of Hosts: I have remembered what Amalek did to Israel, how he set himself against them on the way when they came up out of Egypt. Now go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that he has, and do not spare him; but kill both man and woman, child and infant, etc. It was for a sin of the Amalekites committed about four hundred years before, Exodus 17, verse 8, long before these Amalekites were born whom Saul was to strike. We may come to suffer for sins committed three or four Generations before us, as appears from the Second Commandment: So it is held that the Jews suffer to this day for the sins of their Forefathers.

6. God sometimes punishes the descendants themselves for the iniquities of godly Parents: So the child generated unlawfully <note>referring to the child of Bathsheba</note> was punished with death for David’s sin, 2 Samuel 12. So ten tribes fell away from Reha-

beam because of the sins of Solomon his Father, 1 Kings 11, verse 35.

1. **Utility**, for the rebuking of the murmuring of our hearts against God, as if He were unjust in doing this. Ezekiel 18, verses 2, 3, 4. It is just as if the Doctor gave Medicine to the child when the Father is sick.

Especially look forward, that you do nothing to bring a punishment upon your descendants; we are more inclined to use telescopes <note>original: *perspectif-glazen*</note> than mirrors. We would rather see other people's sins than our own; see what you do, for it shall cause the descendants to repent if you break the covenant; if you subscribe to one thing this year, and the contrary the next year; shall your sin not find you or your descendants out? Surely it shall. **Question.** How does it appear that it can stand with God’s justice to punish the children for the sin of the parents?

**I answer.** Origen, not knowing how to reconcile this with other Scriptural texts, says that this saying is to be understood in an allegorical and improper way, and not according to the letter; by "Fathers" he understands the Devil <note>original: *pater peccati diabolus est* — "the father of sin is the devil"</note>, and by his "children" he understands the godless: he sins in tempting us, and we yield to him, and are thus punished: this cannot be: for 1. the law does not look to the Devil, but to men; 2. the contrast shows the contradiction. God’s justice can be defended if one notes these particulars.

# The Sinner’s Testament

Verses 2, 3, 4. What do you mean by using this proverb: "The fathers have eaten **sour grapes**," etc. <note>original: *onrijpe druyven*; a reference to Ezekiel 18:2, where the proverb suggests children are punished for their parents' actions.</note> As surely as I live, says the Lord God, you shall no longer have occasion to use this proverb, etc. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine. He may do with His own what He wills, and whatever does not conflict with His supremacy does not conflict with His righteousness.

2. For the most part, children follow the sins of their fathers for which they were punished; now, it is very just that if they follow their sinful example, they are punished for their own sins as well as for ours; this is evident from the previously mentioned texts, Psalm 49 verse 14, Matthew 23 verse 31 to verse 36, and Jeremiah 7 verse 18.

3. Even if children do not commit the specific sins of their parents and do not follow them, they nevertheless possess <term>original sin</term> <note>original: *erf-zonde* — the theological concept that all humans inherit a sinful nature from Adam.</note>, which deserves punishment from God; in this way, **Zanchius** <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), a prominent Italian Protestant Reformation theologian.</note> affirms God’s justice.

4. Children are parts of their parents; now, just as it is lawful among men to whip the back for what the hand has stolen—punishing one limb for a sin committed by another—so it is just with God to punish the child, who is a part of the father, for what the father does. **Perkins** <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note> on Galatians.

5. Children are often the occasion for parents to sin; they say, "What shall I do for my wife and children?" Since the children are the occasion, even if by accident, they are nonetheless justly punished. **Josiah** did rightly when he broke the **Bronze Serpent**, even though it was erected by Moses at God’s command (Numbers 21 verse 8), because it had become an occasion for idolatry (2 Kings 18 verse 4). Is God then not righteous, etc.?

6. We consider it just among men to punish children for the faults of their parents, such as when the estates of traitors and rebels are confiscated; their children, who had no hand in the treason, are disinherited, and often their blood is shed as well. Shall God have less freedom than men?

7. If God left the children in this life and to their own devices, they would sin just as their fathers sinned. Song of Solomon 2 verse 15:
> The **little foxes**, which had not yet spoiled the vineyard nor eaten the lambs, had to be killed because they would want to do so.

8. Through God’s mercy, children share in the good of their parents before they do good or evil; thus, the great God in His justice may make them partakers of the punishments before they have done good or evil. Theologians distinguish the ways in which someone can be guilty of being punished for another’s sin: 1. By **accrued guilt**, when I encourage the perpetrator of a sin to do it, as David did in the case of Uriah. 2. By **guilt through occasion**, thus David was punished for giving an occasion or cause to the enemies of God to blaspheme; the child died. 3. By **civil guilt**; thus innocent persons, such as young children, by virtue of civil bonds, become partakers

<column-break/>

of many temporal judgments, etc. So it was with Achan’s children.

9. Consider what relationship God has to His Church, and you shall see the cause why He may punish the children for the parents. God is as the Husband, the Church as His Bride; if the Bride plays the harlot, He may cast her out the door with the children. Hosea 2 verses 1, 2, 3: 
> Contend against your mother, contend, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband, and let her put away her whoredoms from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts, lest I strip her naked, etc. I will not have mercy upon her children, for they are children of whoredom.

->*The Utility of Warning.*<-

1. This is just as true of **political parents** <note>Meaning civil leaders or kings.</note> as of natural ones. 2 Chronicles 28 verse 19: The Lord humbled Judah because of Ahaz, king of Israel; he was King of Judah, yet he is called King of Israel because he followed their ways. So also 2 Samuel 24: David sinned in counting the people, yet the people suffered, up to 70,000.

2. This is not only true of natural parents who immediately precede us and generated us, but also of our **ancestors**—grandfathers or great-grandfathers. 2 Kings 21 verses 11, 12: The sin of **Manasseh** was punished in **Jehoiakim**, though he was his great-great-grandson; for Manasseh’s immediate son was Amon, his grandchild was Josiah, his great-grandchild was Jehoahaz, and his son Jehoiakim was carried away into captivity. So God avenged the blood-guilt of Israel upon the House of Jehu. Hosea 1 verse 4: Jehu reigned 28 years <note>The text says 17, but historically Jehu reigned 28; his son Jehoahaz reigned 17.</note>, and Jehoash his son 16 years, and Jeroboam his son 41 years; and in the days of Zechariah this blood was avenged, for he was struck down by Shallum, and he was the last of Jehu’s lineage, yet Jehu was the great-great-grandfather of Zechariah’s father. 2 Kings 15 verses 9, 10.

3. This is true not only of fathers, but of **mothers** as well; God may punish the children for the sins of their mothers. There is a text that indicates this, Psalm 109 verse 14:
> Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered by the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out.
That is, let the sins of his mother be laid upon him as well as the sins of his father.

**Objection:** Deuteronomy 24 verse 16:
> The fathers shall not be put to death for the children; neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers; every man shall be put to death for his own sin.
**Answer:** This text defines only the power of the **Magistrate**: he may not put the father to death for the children, nor the child for the father; but this does not affect God in the least. This is evident in 2 Kings 14 verse 6: The children of the murderers he did not kill, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses, where the Lord commanded: the fathers shall not be put to death for the children, etc. In the **Kingdom of England** there is a law: if a woman be with child, she shall not be put to death until she is delivered. <meta>This page continues the theological debate regarding whether children are punished for the sins of their parents. It follows a discussion on original sin and the nature of God's justice. # To his descendants.

...was to be accused of killing a Peter Wakefield <note>Peter of Wakefield (or Peter of Pomfret) was a 13th-century hermit executed by King John of England after prophesying the King's downfall. His son was also executed alongside him.</note> for treason, and along with him all his children, even though they had no hand in it, so that no one from that lineage would ever rise up again.

2. **Objection.** Ezekiel 18 verses 2, 3: *What do you mean by using this proverb, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge"? As surely as I live, says the Lord, you shall no longer have occasion to use this proverb in Israel.* And verses 19, 20: *Yet you say, "Why? Does not the son bear the iniquity of the father?" Indeed, the son who has done what is right and just, and has kept all my statutes and observed them, shall surely live. The soul who sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.* **Answer.** 1. **Thomas Aquinas** <note>A hugely influential 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note>, to reconcile this with other texts, says that this passage in Ezekiel speaks of eternal punishments of the Soul; one shall not be condemned for another’s sins. However, those texts in Exodus and elsewhere are to be understood as temporal judgments <note>Physical or earthly punishments rather than eternal damnation.</note> over the soul. Yet **Zanchius** <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), an Italian Protestant Reformer.</note> rejects this as insufficient; for this text speaks as much of temporal punishments as those in Exodus. 2. This promise must be limited to that people in that specific case; they complained that Manasseh sinned and they suffered; God promises that they would not be led away into captivity like that again: so says **Weemse** <note>John Weemse (1579–1636), a Scottish minister and Hebrew scholar.</note>. 3. **Zanchius** gives the best reconciliation: this is not against a general truth spoken of in many places, but God only rebukes that proverb as sinful, since it was spoken (1) in murmuring against God, and (2) falsely, as if they were innocent, when they were not. 4. This text proves at most that children, if they see and notice their father’s evil and do not do the like, shall not be punished for their parents' sin. Ezekiel 18 verses 14, 15, 16, 17: *Now look, if he has a son who sees all the sins his father has done, and considers, and does not do the like... He shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live.* This then does not extend to children, nor men of years, who follow their father’s sin: so says **Perkins** <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note>. 5. **Calvin** says, *That the child shall not die solely and absolutely for his father's sin, but when he adds to his father's sin; then he may be justly punished for both his own and his father's sins.* It is true; had the child no sin of his own, neither actual nor original, he could not be punished for his father's sin.

3. **Objection.** Jeremiah 31 verses 29, 30: *In those days they shall say no more: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge." But everyone shall die for his own iniquity; every man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth shall be set on edge.* **Answer.** They shall not use the proverb while murmuring and thinking ill of God, nor while erring and considering themselves innocent and God unjust. The naturalists

<column-break/>

observe that when someone eats sour grapes and makes a sour face, one who stands nearby becomes affected through sympathy, and his teeth are set on edge merely by the sight. **Aristotle** section 7, problem 41, 5. In their sense, the proverb would then cease, but not the matter itself, as Jeremiah later explains in Jeremiah 32 verse 18: *You recompense the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them.* Jeremiah 23 verse 34: *And as for the prophet, or the priest, or the people who shall say, "The burden of the Lord," I will even punish that man and his house.*

4. **Objection.** *For every man shall bear his own pack; every house shall stand on its own foundation.* **Answer.** 1. The manner of speaking is not exclusive, as verse 2 says: *Bear one another’s burdens.* 2. Primarily, everyone must give an account of himself, but not to the exclusion of others: we must not say like **Cain**, *Am I my brother’s keeper?* Romans 14 verse 12: *Every one of us shall give account of himself to God.* So also 1 Corinthians 11 verse 28: *But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.* That saying does not exclude everything; otherwise, a servant might say, "Everyone must examine himself, why do you need to examine me?" So a child might say to his father. 3. Yes, we must also give an account for another, Hebrews 13 verse 17: *Obey those who rule over you, and be submissive, for they watch out for your souls, as those who must give account, that they may do it with joy and not with grief.* Ezekiel 33 verses 7, 8, 9: *So you, O son of man: I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel... If I say to the wicked, "O wicked man, you shall surely die!" and you do not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked,* etc.

5. **Objection.** *The holiness of the parents is not credited to the children; shall then their wickedness be credited to them?* **Answer.** 1. Just as the holiness of a father cannot save a child, so the sin of a father cannot damn a child. 2. God does good to children for the sake of the holiness of their parents; thus God may rightfully do them harm for the sins of their parents; I may say as **David** said, *Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, to whom I may show kindness for Jonathan's sake?* So, etc. 1 Kings 11 verse 34: *However, I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon's hand, but I will make him prince all the days of his life for the sake of my servant David.* Genesis 49 verse 26: *The blessings of your father have excelled the blessings of my ancestors.* Psalm 112 verse 2: *The generation of the upright will be blessed.*

# To his descendants.

...was to be accused of killing a Peter Wakefield for treason, and all his children with him, although they had no hand in it, so that no one from that lineage would rise up again. <note>The author likely refers to Peter of Wakefield, a hermit executed by King John of England in 1213; the inclusion of his children in the punishment was a historical example of extreme "blood guilt."</note>

2. **Objection.** Ezekiel 18, verses 2, 3. *What do you mean by using this proverb: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge"? As surely as I live, says the Lord, you shall no longer have occasion to use this proverb in Israel.* And verses 19, 20: *But you say, "Why? Does the son not bear the iniquity of the father?" Surely the son, who has done what is right and just, and has kept all my statutes and done them, shall surely live; the soul who sins shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.* **Answer.** 1. **Thomas Aquinas**, to reconcile this with other texts, says that this text in Ezekiel speaks of eternal punishments in the Soul; it shall not be condemned for another’s sins; but those texts in Exodus and elsewhere are to be understood as <term>temporal judgments</term> <note>original: *tydelyke oordeelen*; punishments occurring during earthly life rather than in the afterlife.</note> upon the soul. However, **Zanchius** <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), an Italian Protestant reformer.</note> rejects this as insufficient; for this text speaks as much of temporal punishments as those in Exodus. 2. This promise must be limited to that people in that specific case; they complained that Manasseh sinned and they suffered; thus God promises that they shall not again be carried away into captivity in such a manner: so says **Weemse**. 3. **Zanchius** gives the best reconciliation: that this is not against a general truth spoken of in many places; but God only rebukes that proverb as sinful, because it was spoken 1. in grumbling against God, 2. falsely, as if they were innocent when they were not. 4. This text proves at most this much: that children, if they see and notice their fathers' evil and do not do the same, shall not be punished for their parents' sin. Ezekiel 18, verses 14, 15, 16, 17. *Now look, if he has fathered a son who sees all the sins his father has done, and considers, and does not do likewise... He shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live.* It is not then extended to children, nor men of years, who follow their father's sin: so says **Perkins** <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note>. 5. **Calvin** says, that the child shall not die solely and absolutely for his father's sin, but when he adds to his father's sin; then he may be justly punished for both his own and his father's sins. It is true, if the child had no sin of his own, neither <term>actual</term> nor <term>original</term>, he could not be punished for his father's sin.

The naturalists

<column-break/>

note that when someone eats sour grapes and makes a sour face, one who stands nearby becomes affected with <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: *mede-gevoeligheyt*; here meaning a physical reflexive response or shared sensation.</note>, and his teeth are set on edge merely by the sight. Aristotle, section 7, problem 41. 5. In their minds the proverb would cease, but not the matter itself, as Jeremiah later declares in Jeremiah 32, verse 18: *You repay the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them.* Jeremiah 23, verse 34: *And as for the prophet, or the priest, or the people who shall say, "The burden of the Lord," I will even punish that man and his house.*

4. **Objection.** For everyone shall bear his own pack; Each house shall stand on its own foundation. **Answer.** 1. The manner of speaking is not exclusive; verse 2: *Bear one another's burdens.* 2. If I say to the wicked, "O wicked man, you shall surely die," and you do not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked from his way,* etc.

5. **Objection.** If the holiness of the parents is not credited to the children, shall then their wickedness be credited to them? **Answer.** 1. Just as the holiness of a father cannot save a child, so the sin of a father cannot damn a child. 2. God does good to children for the sake of the holiness of their parents, so God may then rightly do them harm for the sins of their parents; I may say as **David** said, *Is there anyone left of the house of **Saul**, that I may show him kindness for **Jonathan's** sake?* So, etc. 1 Kings 11, verse 34: *However, I will not take any of this kingdom out of **Solomon's** hand, but I will make him a prince all the days of his life for the sake of my servant **David**.* Genesis 49, verse 26: *The blessings of your father exceed the blessings of my ancestors.* Psalm 112, verse 2: *The generation of the upright shall be blessed.*
