# The Sinner’s Testament

nevertheless, He does not visit the sins of the fathers upon the children, except only for the sin of *Idolatry*. For this sin, men primarily make this excuse: that they must adhere to a false religion for the sake of their wife and children; therefore, God threatens the children. The time is limited to the fourth generation, since men live long enough to see their third generation, *Genesis 50 verse 14* <note>While the text cites Genesis 50:14, the theological concept of visiting sins to the fourth generation is most famously found in Exodus 20:5.</note>. The Jews say, "An ounce of the golden calf," etc. The Second Commandment.

2. The sin of Adultery. *Numbers 14:33.* Your children shall bear your harlotry until your dead bodies are consumed in this wilderness. This can refer to both physical and spiritual adultery <note>In biblical language, "spiritual adultery" refers to idolatry or unfaithfulness to God's covenant.</note>, *Numbers 25 verses 1, 9.* The people began to commit harlotry with the daughters of the Moabites: and those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand. David’s impurity was the cause of his child’s death, *2 Samuel 12.* *Deuteronomy 23 verse 2.* No bastard shall enter the congregation of the Lord, even to his tenth generation. Not as if he were excluded from their holy gatherings, but that he was kept only from serving in any office there. Even if he were circumcised, he was nonetheless not admitted to full fellowship to enjoy all the privileges of free-born Israelites. This was to show how abominable the sin of adultery was; indeed, the children of a bastard could not enter there until their tenth generation. See also *Isaiah 65:3, Proverbs 6 verse 26.*

3. The sin of covenant-breaking, *2 Samuel 21 verses 1, 3.* Saul struck down the Gibeonites when the children of Israel had sworn an oath to them; and seven of his sons were hanged long after Saul’s death.

4. The sin of persecution of the godly. God’s curse follows the households and descendants of persecutors. *Matthew 23 verses 31 to 36.* You witness against yourselves that you are children of those who killed the prophets; you then also fill up the measure of your fathers; behold, I send to you prophets, some of them you shall kill and persecute, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of Abel, to—*Numbers 20 verses 20, 21.* Edom refused to let Israel pass through his borders: and the Psalmist, *Psalm 137 verse 7,* prays for the curse upon their descendants: Lord, remember the children of Edom on the day of Jerusalem. So also *Genesis 27 verse 45.*

5. The sin of bloodshed, *1 Kings 21:21.* The blood that Ahab bartered made his descendants food for dogs: I will take away your descendants, and I will root out from Ahab everyone who urinates against a wall <note>A literal biblical idiom (Hebrew: *mashtin bi-qir*) used to denote all males in a household.</note>, *Jeremiah 15 verse 4.*

6. The sin of oppression: That one obtains someone’s goods through violence and deceit, *Habakkuk 2 verses 9, 10. Proverbs 20:21.* When an inheritance is hurried at the beginning, its end shall not be blessed: *Proverbs 12 verse 11.* Wealth gained from vanity shall be diminished. <term>A Lapide<note>Cornelius a Lapide (1567–1637), a Flemish Jesuit scholar famous for his comprehensive Bible commentaries.</note></term>, on *Proverbs 20 verse 21,* notes that the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, who were so hasty to take possession on the other side of the Jordan, were the very first to be devastated by Hazael, the King of Assyria. *2 Kings 10:33.*

<column-break/>

*Proverbs 21 verse 6.* To labor for treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vanity of those who seek death: passed down from father to son. *Et. Jeremiah 17 verse 11.* <note>original: "Et." is likely an abbreviation for "Also" or "And."</note> Like a partridge that gathers eggs but does not hatch them, so is he who gathers riches, but not by right: in the midst of his days he must leave them, and in his end, he shall be a fool. In gathering goods, many lay up treasures of wrath for their children.

7. Contempt for Authority and for the Ministry of the Word. *Numbers 16 verses 32, 41.* And the earth opened her mouth and swallowed all the men who belonged to Korah <note>Korah led a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron.</note>. And the entire congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, and there died (besides those who had died because of the matter of Korah) 14,700, the descendants of those who rose up against the Authority and the Ministry, *verse 49.*

8. The pretense of reformation and of the common welfare, solely to advance one's private profit: so it went with Jehu, *Hosea 1 verse 4.* God threatens to avenge the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the House of Jehu.

-> The First Utility is for the comfort of the Godly. <-

1. Although you are temporarily punished for your father’s sin, you cannot, however, be eternally punished for their sins. 2. You shall be saved by another’s righteousness: you are punished for Adam’s sin, yet you are made blessed through Christ’s righteousness. 3. The curse is not everlasting but is limited to a certain time, and then it breaks off; it is only to a third or fourth generation: thus Josiah broke off the curse, so that it did not come in his days. 4. Not all punishments are either for our sins or for the sins of our elders: some punishments are for testing, like Job’s afflictions; or otherwise, so that God may show His Sovereignty and Power over all creatures. It was a common error to think that all punishments were for the people's own sins or for the sin of the elders. *John 9 verses 2, 3.* Christ’s disciples asked him, saying, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?" But it was for neither, *verse 3.*

-> The Second Utility is for exhortation; and it is threefold: 1. To the Children. 2. To the Parents. 3. To all. <-

The first exhortation is to the children. 1. See to it that you do not let the sin run in the blood; do not follow your father’s sin. Esau hated Jacob, *Genesis 47 verse 45.* And the Edomites, who were Esau’s descendants, hated all the descendants of Jacob. *Psalm 137 verse 7.* Lord, remember the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who said there, "Raze it, raze it to its very foundation." We read in *Numbers 23 verses 20, 21* that they refused to let Israel pass through their borders. God complains of children who follow their fathers in sin. *Jeremiah 7 verse 18.* The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, to offer to other gods. *Hosea 4 verses 12, 13.* My people ask their wood; for the spirit of harlotry deceived them, that they go whoring away from under their God: upon the heights of the mountains...

### To His Descendants

...they offer sacrifices; therefore your daughters commit harlotry, and your daughters-in-law commit adultery. <note>original: "gen offeren zy..." Likely referring to Hosea 4:13-14.</note>

2. Regard it as a heavy judgment to be punished for the unrighteousness of your parents. **Job 21 verse 19**: God lays up his violence for his children; he repays him that he may know it. **Psalm 109 verse 14**: Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out.

3. Lament the unrighteousness of your elders. **Psalm 79 verse 8**: Do not remember our former transgressions <note>The author clarifies this as "that is, those of our forefathers."</note>. **Nehemiah 1 verse 6**: I and my father’s house have sinned. **Leviticus 26 verses 39, 40**: They shall pine away in the iniquity of their fathers. Daniel confesses in **Daniel 9 verse 16**: For our sins, and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem has become a reproach.

4. Thank God, you who are born of good parents. **Genesis 49 verse 26**: The blessings of your father exceed the blessings of your ancestors, reaching to the end of the eternal hills; they shall be on the head of Joseph. **Psalm 112 verse 2**: The generation of the upright shall be blessed.

5. Thank God that you break off the sins of your forefathers, as Josiah did, and the sons of Korah—who was an evil man, yet his sons were very pious.

6. Thank God that, although you come from the <term>loins</term> <note>A biblical term referring to one's physical ancestry or biological descent.</note> of godless parents, they have nonetheless not pressed a curse upon you. **Numbers 26 verse 11**: But the children of Korah did not die. Although Korah was wicked, his children were good. One often finds them mentioned with honor, as in **Psalms 42, 44, 45, 46, 47, 49, 84, 85, 87**, and **1 Chronicles 9 verse 19**. However, the descendants of Dathan and Abiram suffered along with them.

7. Do not follow the sins of your forefathers. **Jeremiah 7 verse 18**: The children gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough to make sacrificial cakes for the Queen of Heaven—that is, for the Sun <note>While the author identifies the "Queen of Heaven" as the Sun, historical scholarship usually identifies her as the goddess Ishtar or Astarte.</note>. When the Israelites married the women of Ashdod, the children spoke the language of Ashdod, following their parents: **Nehemiah 13 verse 24**. Thus they fill up the measure of their fathers: **Matthew 23 verse 32**.

8. See to it that you are not godless while being sprung from pious parents; this increases your sin and brings shame upon your ancestors. It is noteworthy in **Judges 18 verse 30**: The children of Dan set up the carved image; and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests for that image. Now, Jonathan was the son of Gershom, and Gershom was the son of Moses (**Exodus 2 verse 22, 1 Chronicles 23 verse 15**). The Jews observe that he is not called the grandson of Moses, for that would have been a dishonor to Moses; instead, he is linked to Manasseh, being called a son of Manasseh because he followed him in his idolatry. So it is stated in <note>original: "Weemse, fol. 95" Referring to the works of John Weemse (c. 1579–1636), a Scottish theologian.</note>. It is a shame to have wicked and idolatrous children, according to **Proverbs 10 verse 1**: A foolish son is the grief of his mother; and **Proverbs 26 verse 15**: A child left to himself shames his mother. Such children do not only damn their own souls, but they also grieve the hearts of their parents. Esau’s sin is said to have been a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and Rebekah: **Genesis 26 verse 35, Genesis 27 verse 46**.

<column-break/>

We have similar examples in **2 Chronicles 28 verse 19**: God humbled Judah because of Ahaz, the king of Israel. He was king of Judah, yet he was called king of Israel because he imitated the wicked kings of Israel in their malice. He was descended from Jotham, son of Uzziah, son of Amaziah, and it would have been a dishonor to his forefathers that such a one as Ahaz should be born of them, who stood marked with such a stigma; this is that King Ahaz.

9. Lament and bewail the sins of your forefathers. **Daniel 9 verse 16**: For our sins, and for the sins of our forefathers, Jerusalem is a reproach. Belshazzar is accused of not having done this: **Daniel 5 verse 22**: You, Belshazzar, his son, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this.

10. It is a shame for evil children if they descend from pious parents. **2 Chronicles 36 verses 5, 12; Ezekiel 18 verses 10, 13; Jeremiah 22 verses 15, 16**. Consider Nadab and Abihu from Aaron, or Hophni and Phinehas from Eli.

->The second Admonition is to the Parents.<-

1. Do nothing by which you provoke God to punish your descendants. If you do not watch over your own souls, at least avoid sin for the sake of your children. See to it that you do not leave a curse behind for the descendants of your loins and for the fruit of your womb. Many children might rather wish, says Mr. Burroughs <note>Jeremiah Burroughs (1599–1646), a prominent English Congregationalist and Puritan preacher.</note>, to have sprung from dragons and vipers than from such parents who have left them a curse as their inheritance. It was a terrible legacy that Joab left his children in **2 Samuel 3 verse 29**: some would die of a discharge, some of leprosy, some would lean on a staff due to lameness, some would fall by the sword, and some would beg for their bread. So godless parents leave to some of their children their swearing, to some their Sabbath-breaking, to some their adultery, and to some their oppression and unrighteousness. Let this restrain you: "I shall not only wrong my own soul, but also my descendants." While such parents lay up treasures, they also lay up wrath as a "treasure" for their children; the children shall be heirs of their sins as well as their lands. Gehazi left a talent of silver to his descendants, but he also left them leprosy: **2 Kings 5 verse 27**. Do not, therefore, take such an obligation upon yourself.

2. If you have done anything that might justly anger God, oh, repent of it early; you may thereby ward off the punishment from your descendants.

3. Grieve over the fact that your children inherit both sin and punishment from you; if they had no sin, they would have no punishment.

4. It is an oppression—and so parents must regard it—that they live to see their children follow them in evil, but not in good. Neocles did not live to see the noble victory achieved by his son Themistocles; nor Miltiades to see the battle won in the field by his son Cimon; nor Xanthippus to hear his son Pericles preach and reason; and Ariston never heard the lessons and disputes of his son Plato. But men, said Plutarch, live to see their children carousing, swilling, gambling, whoring, and similar evil dealings. <note>original: "Plutarch. Mor. p. 24" Referring to Plutarch's *Moralia*.</note>

# The Sinner’s Testament

It is a great comfort for parents if they live in such a way that none of their descendants will suffer because of their wrongdoing. **Numbers 27 verse 3**: The daughters of Zelophehad said, "Our father died in the wilderness, and he was not in the company of them that gathered themselves together against the Lord in the company of Korah; but he died in his own sin, and had no sons: why should the name of our father be taken away from among his family?" He did not die in the uprising with Korah, which would have brought a stain upon us; rather, he died in his own private sins, which made him liable to death as all men are. But (says Attersoll <note>William Attersoll (d. 1640), an English Puritan theologian known for his commentaries.</note>) he did not commit such sins that would bring punishment upon his descendants. 

6. Those parents are to be blamed who strive to amass wealth for their children through injustice and oppression. **Habakkuk 2 verses 11, 12**: The stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it; woe to him that builds a town with blood, and establishes a city by iniquity. **1 Kings 14 verse 10**: Jeroboam thought to lay the foundation for the greatness of his descendants this way, yet he destroyed them with it. God says, "I will cut off from the house of Jeroboam <term>him that pisseth against the wall</term> <note>A common biblical idiom in the 17th century referring to every male member of a household.</note>." They do worse than those in **Leviticus 18 verse 21** who let their seed pass through the fire for Moloch; read also **Chapter 20 verse 2**, which says such parents must be put to death. Manasseh was guilty of this sin, **2 Kings 21 verse 6**. "A bloody husband you have been to me," said Zipporah in **Exodus 4 verse 26**; so might these children say, "A bloody father you have been to us." 

7. Good parents can find comfort even if they have wicked children, like Eli and Aaron; likewise, good children can have evil parents, just as in Abijah the son of Jeroboam "some good thing was found toward the Lord," **1 Kings 14 verse 13**. Abraham sprang from idolatrous seed, **Genesis 12 verse 1**. Hezekiah was the son of Ahaz. Jephthah, who fought the battles of the Lord, was a bastard, the son of a harlot, **Judges 11 verse 1**, **Hebrews 11 verse 32**.

The third admonition is to everyone: 
1. Be convinced of this truth: justify God and condemn yourself, acknowledging that you are of a sinful descent from sinful parents. God is righteous in all that is brought upon you. Plutarch condemns Alexander the Great for slaughtering the Branchidae <note>An ancient Greek clan of priests.</note> because of what their ancestors had done many centuries before in surrendering the Temple of Miletus; yet he justifies the Gods in such actions. He gives seven reasons why the Gods may punish the child for the sin of the parents in his treatise <note>original: "de seranuminis vindicta"</note> *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance*. A child is bound by the power and right of succession and inheritance to pay the father’s debts; thus, the descendants of Hercules were rewarded for the good he had done; why then should the descendants of the wicked not be punished? 

2. Declare God righteous in your thoughts for punishing descendants for Adam’s sin. I conclude this with even more force, <note>original: "a fortiori"</note> by much stronger reason: If God is righteous in punishing for the sins of parents who are private persons, how much more is He righteous in punishing for the sin of Adam, who is a <term>public person</term> <note>In theology, this refers to Adam as the legal representative of all humanity.</note>?

<column-break/>

### Lamentations 5 verse 8

> Servants rule over us; there is none that doth deliver us out of their hand.

<margin>II. Sermon.</margin>
In these words, two parts are to be noted: 1. An intolerable misery under which the Jews lie: "servants rule over us." 2. The hopelessness of their situation according to all human evidence; there was no one who could snatch them out of their hands.

**Question:** Who is understood by these "servants"? There are many guesses regarding this; I will not trouble you with the various thoughts of men on this matter. Hugo and Lyranus <note>Referring to the medieval commentators Hugh of Saint Cher and Nicholas of Lyra.</note> say they were the Ammonites and Edomites, who had previously paid tribute to the Jews. Most interpreters say they were the Chaldeans, called "servants" for these reasons: 
1. Because they came from Ham, whose descendants were to serve the Jews as descendants of Shem. **Genesis 9 verse 26**. Cush and Nimrod were the two sons of Ham; the first ruled in Babylon, the capital of Chaldea, just as London is of England, **Genesis 10 verses 6, 8, 10**. They were thus their servants, yet now they had become their rulers. 
2. Because of their slavish and lowly state, they are called "the worst of the heathen." **Ezekiel 7 verse 24**: "I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses," etc., to represent their despicability. 
3. They were a thieving people. **Job 1 verse 17**: they stole Job’s camels. 
4. They were great sorcerers, **Daniel 2 verses 2, 10**. The King sent for these Chaldeans to tell him his dream. 
5. They were known drunkards. **Habakkuk 2 verse 15**: "Woe unto him that giveth his neighbor drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also." This is spoken against the Chaldeans. 
6. They were proud and greedy, **Habakkuk 2 verse 5**: "He is a proud man... who enlargeth his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied," and **verse 9**: "Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high"; spoken in the manner of the Chaldeans. 
7. They were a very raging and cruel people; **Ezekiel 23 verse 25** states, "They shall deal with thee furiously: they shall take away thy nose and thine ears; and thy remnant shall fall by the sword." 
8. They lived by violence and robbery, **Habakkuk 2 verses 6, 8**: "He increaseth that which is not his." And **Habakkuk 1 verse 9**: "They shall come all for violence," etc. Read **Deuteronomy 28 verses 49, 50, 51**.

To the misery of the Jews, this was added: "they were first a priestly kingdom," <note>original: "erant prius regnum sacerdotale"</note> says Calvin, but now they are under servants.

**The Doctrine is:** It is a heavy and lamentable judgment when the government of a State or Kingdom is changed and loosened, and when men of slavish descent and status rule. Read **Ezekiel 19 verses 11, 12, 14**: "She had strong rods for the scepters of them that bare rule" (that is, she had many Princes).

# To his descendants.

His strong rods are broken and dried up; the fire has consumed them (this refers to the Royal tribe, as seen in **2 Kings 25 verse 7**). There is no strong rod left in him to be a scepter for ruling; this is a lamentation, and it has become a lamentation. This refers to the Chaldeans <note>The Neo-Babylonian Empire, which destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE.</note> when they took the Jews away into captivity. God threatened this as a heavy judgment in **Daniel 4 verse 17**: that God intended to set the "basest of men" over the kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar. Solomon complained of this in his day in **Ecclesiastes 10 verses 5, 6, and 7**: "There is another evil I have seen under the sun; a fool is set in great dignity, but the rich sit in low places. I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth." Indeed, it falls hard upon a distinguished man, as in **Job 30 verse 1**: "But now they that are younger than I have me in derision (Job says in a lamenting manner), whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock."

**Question:** Why is it such a lamentable judgment that servants rule?

**I answer:** 1. Such a state or Kingdom must necessarily be in an unstable and restless condition. **Proverbs 30 verses 21, 22, and 23**: "For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat; For an odious woman when she is married; and a handmaid that is heir to her mistress." 2. It overturns the order of nature when one sees a child ruling over the Father, the maidservant over her Mistress, or the manservant over his Master—likewise in a Republic <term>commonwealth or civil society</term>. **Proverbs 19 verse 10**: "Delight is not seemly for a fool; much less for a servant to have rule over princes." 3. It frequently causes bitter contentions and bloody wars within a Kingdom, of which you have several powerful examples in Scripture. In **Judges 9 verse 18**, Abimelech, a lowly man and the son of Gideon’s maidservant, took over the government (verses 2 and 3); he slew seventy of Gideon’s sons, who had more right to the rule than he. But what followed? See verse 23: "God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem." And in verse 35, he sowed it with salt—that is, he made it a wasteland. **Psalm 107 verses 33 and 34**: "He turneth a fruitful land into barrenness"; the original text says "into saltiness," as in **Zephaniah 2 verse 9**. So we read of Omri, who was made King by the soldiers in **1 Kings 16 verse 16**. But what followed? Read verse 21: "Then were the people of Israel divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni to make him king; and half followed Omri, etc." Much blood was shed over the taking of the Crown for three and a half years <note>The original Dutch uses "viertehalf," an archaic way of saying three and a half (the fourth half).</note>.

**2. Question:** Why does God send such a heavy Judgment?

**Answer:** 1. Because when men do not serve God, they shall serve lowly men, and those shall rule over them. This very reason is given in **Deuteronomy 28 verse 48**: "Because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things; therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the 

<column-break/>

Lord shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst, and in nakedness, and in want of all things: and he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck, until he have destroyed thee"—namely, the Chaldeans. Those who despise serving the Lord, it is just that they serve the vilest of masters. <note>original Latin: "Qui Domino servire contemnunt, justum est, ut vilissimis servant Dominis."</note>

2. Because men do not submit themselves to the rule and government of Christ in His Church, God destroys the government in the Civil Polity. The stone cut out of the mountains without hands <note>A reference to the prophecy in Daniel 2 regarding Christ's kingdom.</note> breaks all kingdoms to pieces that set themselves against him. The Jews rejected him and said, "We will not have this man to reign over us; we have no king but Caesar. Away with this Jesus, for then the Romans will come and take away both our place and nation" (**John 11 verse 48**). And this was the very means by which they lost both their place and their people. **Matthew 24 verse 15**: "When ye therefore shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, stand in the holy place." What this was can be understood by comparing it with **Luke 21 verse 20**, where it says: "And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh." The Romans were a lowly people and detestable to the Jews, and yet because they rejected the reign of Christ, the Romans gained dominion over them. They had Roman Judges, which is why Christ is said to have been crucified in Rome <note>Likely an interpretation of Revelation 11:8, suggesting the authority that killed Him was Roman.</note>, because it happened through a Roman Judge (**Revelation 11 verse 8**).

**Application.** This is a judgment for those who rule and for those who are ruled.

1. It is a judgment for those who rule; let the following be noted: 1. Their guilt makes them afraid of their own shadow. Gaal sought to take control, and Zebul said to him, "Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men" (**Judges 9 verse 36**). He was terrified by every little shadow; such are all usurpers and unlawful seizers of authority. 2. Their own party shall desert them. The divisions rise so high among those on their side that they destroy one another. **Judges 9 verse 23**: "So God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech." 3. Unlawful commanders do not live long. In **Judges 9 verse 22**, Abimelech reigned only three years. They come to an untimely end, for which reason God is remarkable in His Judgments: He slew the seventy sons of Gideon upon one stone (**Judges 9 verse 5**). Zimri slew Elah, King of Israel, yet reigned only seven days and was burned in the King’s house (**1 Kings 16 verses 15, 18**). Jezebel said in **2 Kings 9 verse 31**, "Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?" Shallum, the son of Jabesh, slew Zechariah, the son of Jeroboam, and he reigned no more than a month; then Menahem slew him and reigned in his place (**2 Kings 15 verses 13, 14**). And Menahem reigned only ten years and was struck (**verse 17**). Athaliah took the Kingdom by force, and she reigned only six years (**2 Kings 11 verse 16**).

# The Sinner's Testament

<header>To his descendants.</header>

...and left alone, she who hopes in God, and continues in supplications and prayers day and night. God draws us away from help or hope in the creature <note>In this context, "creature" refers to anything created, particularly human allies or earthly resources, as opposed to the Creator.</note>, so that we may set our hope on God.

### 3. What reasons for comfort can be given to God's people in such a state?
**Answer 1.** God has no need for the help of creatures; He does not need to seek that out to bring about the deliverance of the Church; but He commands deliverance, Psalm 44 verse 5: *Command the deliverance of Jacob.* **2.** God prepares it, and it shall come to pass, Isaiah 26 verse 1: *God appoints salvation for walls and bulwarks.* **3.** Or He creates the deliverance. Isaiah 65 verse 18: *I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy.* Creation is a bringing forth out of nothing; there was no one to help God in the work of the Creation of the world; likewise, no one is needed for the salvation of the Church. This is the first reason for comfort. **2.** That it is the most visible time for God to undertake the deliverance of His Church when there is no one else to deliver. 2 Kings 14 verse 26: *The Lord saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, and that Israel had no helper;* and what follows? verse 27: *Then He delivered them by the hand of Jeroboam, the son of Joash.* Psalm 72 verse 12: *He shall deliver the needy when he cries, the poor also, and him who has no helper.* Deuteronomy 32 verse 36: *The Lord shall judge His people; for He shall see that their power is gone, and there is none shut up or left.* Isaiah 63 verse 5: *I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold; therefore My own arm brought salvation.* **3.** The Lord God may raise up men as deliverers for His Church of whom we little dream; when the Jews were in Babylon, who would have thought that Cyrus, King of Persia, would be their deliverer? Yet he was: Isaiah 45 verse 1, 4. Isaiah 13 verse 17: *I will stir up the Medes against them,* and then Isaiah 14 verse 1, 2: *For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel; and He will set them in their own land, and the nations shall take them and bring them to their place,* that is, the Persians shall yet bring the Jews to Jerusalem. Acts 7 verse 25: *He <note>Referring to Moses</note> supposed his brethren would have understood that God by his hand would deliver them: but they understood not.* Yet he was, after being hidden for three months, laid in a chest of rushes <note>A basket made of papyrus or reeds</note> at the river’s edge. So too was David taken from the sheepfolds to the glorious throne, and in place of the shepherd’s staff he received the Royal scepter; yet God made him a great deliverer of His people! **4.** It is all the same to God whether He delivers His Church through small or great means, or through small means or none at all; He is not bound to any means: 2 Chronicles 14 verse 11: *And Asa cried unto the Lord his God, and said, Lord, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power.* Likewise 2 Chronicles 20 verse 12: Jehoshaphat prays in his distress, saying: *O our God, wilt Thou not judge them? for we have no*

<column-break/>

*might against this great company that comes against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon Thee.* To show His power, God sometimes ordains it so that impressive means shall not deliver, but rather unimpressive means. There was an army of Midianites, like locusts in multitude; their camels were without number, as the sand by the seaside; Gideon raised up 32,000 men against them, but he was only to use 300 of them, and that not with weapons of war, but with pitchers and torches; a barley loaf overturned the tent of the Midianites, Judges 7 verse 13, 14. It is written, *The least of the flock shall draw out the Chaldeans,* Jeremiah 50 verse 45, and Isaiah 26 verse 6 says, *The feet of the poor, and the steps of the needy, shall tread down the lofty city.* Yes, even without means; *The mighty are taken away without a hand,* Job 34 verse 20. **5.** If men cannot or will not deliver, then God shall do it, Esther 4 verse 14: *If you altogether hold your peace,* said Mordecai to Esther, *then shall relief and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place.* But, etc.

### Usefulness.

even if you have no helpers: for **First**, when you have no helpers on earth, you have a great deliverer in Heaven, who is more than all your enemies. So likewise, for how many do you count God?

Five Kings of the Amorites were gathered into a great army against the children of Israel; and it is written, *God cast down great stones from Heaven upon them, and they died;* and more were killed by the hailstones than by the sword of the children of Israel, Joshua 10 verse 5, 11. Judges 5 verse 20: *The stars in their courses fought against Sisera;* likewise the Sun stood still at Gibeon, and the Moon over the valley of Ajalon, until they had avenged themselves upon their enemies, Joshua 10 verse 13, 14.

So Saul pursued David, when a messenger came, saying, *Haste thee, and come; for the Philistines have invaded the land,* 1 Samuel 23 verse 26, 27, 28. So the Persians warred with the Babylonians and destroyed them, and by that means the Jews were delivered from their captivity. **2.** By changing the disposition of the enemies of the Church. # The Patient WATCHER.

->Lamentations 3 verse 26.<-

->It is good that a man should hope and be quiet for the salvation of the Lord.<-

The title of this book shows you the matter that is treated within it. The Prophet Jeremiah makes / in the name of the Church / a bitter complaint about the miseries and darkness that had come over Jerusalem / verses 1, 2, 3, &c. It was written

<column-break/>

about the beginning / or in the first year of the captivity: And although the Jews were to remain in Babylon for a full 70 years / nevertheless / says the Prophet / It is good that a man should hope and be quiet, &c. **Doctrine.** Under the saddest appointments of the Lord, it is good that a man should quietly wait for the deliverances of the Church. Psalm 52 verse 11. I will wait on your Name (says David) for it is good before your saints.

**1. Reason.** Because the Lord God waits for suitable opportunities to deliver His people. Isaiah 30 verse 18. The Lord will wait, that he may be gracious to you; for the Lord is a God of judgment. That is / to know when it is the most suitable opportunity / to help His Church out. Blessed are all they who wait for Him. Deuteronomy 32 verse 35. To me belongs vengeance, and recompense; in the time when their foot shall slip. 1 Peter 5:6. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time; *that he may exalt you in due time* <note>original Greek: "ina upso-se en kairo"</note>, at the right and proper time. God will not wait for His enemies' time / that would be too long; nor for His people's time / that would be too fast; but for His own time / which alone is the right time.

**2. Reason.** Because when deliverances are unprovable / indeed impossible in our eyes / they are not so in God's eyes: What is heavy in our eyes / is light for God's hand / to work that out. Zechariah 8 verses 5, 6, 7. The streets of that city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets. Because it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people, should it also be marvelous in my eyes? says the Lord of hosts. I will deliver my people from the land of the rising, and from the land of the setting of the Sun.

**3. Reason.** Because never is more patience needed / than when everything goes against us. Psalm 59 verse 10. Against his strength I will wait upon you, for God is my high retreat <note>or defense</note>. You accepted the plundering of your goods with joy, knowing that you have in yourselves a better and enduring possession in Heaven, and verses 35, 36. You have need of patience, so that after you have done the will of God, you might receive the promise. To this James awakens us. James 1 verses 3, 4. Knowing, he says / that the trying of your faith works patience, but let patience have a perfect work, that you may be perfect and entire, lacking nothing. This the Prophet put into practice. Micah 7 verse 1 to verse 8. Woe is me, for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, &c. The godly man is perished out of the land, and there is none upright. They all lie in wait for blood; the best of them is like a brier, and believe not a friend, and trust not in a chief friend; for the son dishonors the father. **3. Question.** What observations serve to keep the heart still in waiting upon God under particular difficulties?

**Answer. First.** Pay attention as much to the end as to the degree of your suffering: Now there is a twofold end / 1. <term>Finis intentionis</term> <note>The purpose or goal intended by God.</note>, an end which God aims for through all the afflictions. # A Christian’s Instruction.

<meta>catchword: And</meta>

If you mourn over sin, then weep as much as you can. Be like ice before the Sun, which quickly melts and turns into water: you who are children of God, know that you have greater things and of higher weight to spend your tears on than any outward difficulties; you have daily stumblings <note>original: "struypelingen," meaning minor sins or spiritual slips</note>, many sins and corruptions which are not yet killed nor brought under subjection, and the loss of the light of God’s countenance to mourn over; your sorrows do not run right unless they run in this channel: when your tears flow in a way to stifle your lusts and corruptions, to consume and weaken them, then are your sorrows right and regulated.

Lastly, I pray you let me advise you not to err regarding your sorrows, by thinking that you mourn and are grieved over your sins when it is only over outward oppressions. Many people, when their neighbors ask them why they are so sad and melancholy, and weep so much, will immediately say that it is over their sins and stumblings, and over their corruptions which are too strong for them, or the like; where in reality it is only over some cross <note>historical: "kruys" or cross refers to any heavy burden or trial sent by God</note> and outward hardship which has befallen them; and therefore, do not consider that sorrow to be a sorrow over your sins which is only or particularly over some outward oppression that has come upon you.

<margin>Second Sermon.</margin>

**W**e come now to the third Question, with which I shall spend this entire afternoon, and it is this: that I shall present to you twelve considerations to moderate your immoderate and excessive sorrow over any worldly miseries or oppressions, and how we shall keep ourselves in order and moderation of Spirit; which the Apostle here commands us, namely, to weep as though we wept not. Today, I may say to you, that God does not want us to be numb and unfeeling under any oppression from His hand; yet just as we ought not to be

<margin>† The Stoics held that one should be moved neither by prosperity nor by adversity.</margin>

† Stoic, so also we must not be immoderate in our sorrows: And therefore, in my Meditations, I have reflected on these various considerations, being the most excellent to moderate improper sorrow.

<margin>Various considerations to moderate improper sorrow.</margin>

First, consider or reflect that in your life you have had more mercies to rejoice over than grief to discourage you. This consideration greatly strengthened Job to support his spirit under oppression, Job 2: 10. "Should we receive good from God," (he said) "and not receive evil?" I have read a story of a man fifty years old, who, when he was forty-

<column-break/>

eight years old, did not yet know what sickness was: But in the last two years of his life he was very sickly, and in his sickness very impatient; but at last he reflected on the matter within himself and said, "The Lord could have given me forty-eight years of sickness and only two years of health; but He has done the contrary, and therefore I would rather wonder at God’s mercy, giving me so long a time of health, than be vexed or murmur against Him over giving such a short time of sickness." The Lord always leaves us more mercies than He takes from us: And therefore, how it ought to support our souls, seeing that our mercies have been more and greater than our oppressions. Even though the Lord now visits me with sickness, yet I have had more years of health than sickness: though I have lost friends, yet let me consider that they lived with me for a long time: though this or that comfort is taken from me, yet I have more of them still left to me. The Scripture is very sensitive to how we are so inclined to mourn all too much; and therefore it prescribes this rule to us to moderate our sorrows, Ecclesiastes 7 verse 14. "But in the day of adversity, consider": Why? What must we consider? "That God also has set the one over against the other": That is, although you are now in some oppressions, yet God has previously given you mercies, and it may be that He will give you prosperity again: He has weighed your present oppressions against your former mercies, and if you set the mercies you have enjoyed against the oppressions you currently suffer, you shall find that the account of your mercies exceeds the number of your oppressions. When David, in such immoderate sorrow over his son, cried out, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! O that I, I, had died for thee, Absalom my son, my son!" 2 Samuel 18: 33. If he had then said likewise, "O Solomon my son, my son!" and seriously considered what a good son he still had living, this would have been a great means to quiet his soul. The consideration of those manifold mercies that we have enjoyed will be an excellent means to uphold our hearts in any oppression under which we lie.

Secondly, if you want to keep yourself in check regarding your sorrows, then consider that God sometimes takes away the bodily comforts and satisfactions of His people to prepare a way for a greater mercy and blessing in their place. This is very noteworthy in the case of David; God took away by death a child that was conceived in illegitimacy <note>original: "on-echt," referring to the child born of David's affair with Bathsheba</note>, and He gave him in its place a lawfully born and a better child, a Solomon: Indeed, this consideration upheld David’s heart, Psalm 71 verses 20, 21. "Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth. Thou shalt increase my greatness, and comfort me on every side."

# A Christian’s Instruction.

And if this were seriously considered, it would be a means to keep our hearts upright during losses and difficulties: although this or that comfort is taken from you, it may nonetheless be that God intends a good end in it, to pave the way for a greater mercy in its place. Would you be angry at a man who wanted to throw down your smoke-filled huts <note>The author uses "roock-hutsen" to describe a humble, drafty dwelling, contrasting it with the "stately palace" God intends to build.</note> from over your head, and in their place wanted to erect a stately palace? For every mercy that God takes from you, He shall give you a greater one: just as the Prophet said to **Amaziah**, who had spent his wealth on the Israelites, *The Lord is able to give thee much more than this* <note>2 Chronicles 25:9</note>. Thus God dealt with **Job**, as you can see in the first and the last chapters of that same book; when compared together, the Lord deprived **Job** of his entire estate and all his goods, but gave him twice as much as He had taken from him: seven thousand sheep were taken from him, and God thereafter gave him fourteen thousand in their place; he lost three thousand camels, but thereafter he had six thousand; he lost five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, but received double back again afterward. And this case of **Job** may serve Christians in all ages as an example and a ground for courage, to wait upon God with a humble submission under all His dealings. *Ye have heard of the patience of **Job**,* says the Apostle James, chapter 5:11, *and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.* This example of his ought to hold up our hearts in times of oppression: the Lord takes away small mercies to make room for greater ones. It is very noteworthy how this consideration worked upon **Isaac**; his mother **Sarah** had recently died, and to fulfill his loss, God gave him **Rebekah** as a wife; and it is said in Genesis 24:67, *that she became his wife, and he loved her, and so he was comforted after his mother’s death.*

<margin>Esth. 5: 10, 11, 12, 13.</margin>
Thirdly, consider that immoderate grief over the loss of one consolation embitters all your other present consolations; and therefore, guard yourself against throwing this bitter gall among your comforts. Immoderate grief is like a worm in a nut, which eats out all the sweetness of the kernel and leaves nothing but the shell: so shall immoderate grief take away all the sweetness of your present comforts. Thus it was with **Haman**, Esther 5:10–13. *And he sent and called for his friends, and **Zeresh** his wife. And **Haman** told them of the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the **King** had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the **King**.* Now, you cannot think otherwise than that this man was a prosperous man. Yes, **Haman** said further, *Moreover **Esther** the queen did let no man come in with the **King** unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and tomorrow am I invited unto her also with the **King**.* *Yet all this,* said he, *availeth me nothing, so long as I see **Mordecai** the Jew sitting at the **King’s** gate,* for he will show me no honor nor obedience. 

<column-break/>

<margin>Gen. 37: 35.</margin>
In this was the curse of God upon him, that he could enjoy no mercy with comfort because **Mordecai** did not honor him. Likewise, we see this in the example of **Jacob**, previously recounted in Genesis 37:35. Immoderate grief over one oppression loses the comfort of all our mercies.

<margin>Prov. 14: 14.</margin>
Fourthly, to moderate excessive grief: consider that you have within you a greater reason for exceeding joy than any thing outside of you can be a cause for immoderate grief; as in Proverbs 14:14: *A good man shall be satisfied from himself.* A godly man, whatever happens to him in the world, always has reason for rejoicing within himself.

<margin>Luke 13: 21.</margin>
We read in Luke 13:21 <note>The author likely intends Luke 17:21, "the kingdom of God is within you."</note> when the disciples were focused on a temporary, blooming kingdom, that Christ told them that the Kingdom of God was within them: if we have the grace of Christ, etc., even if we had nothing else, that is a greater cause for exceeding joy than any other deprivations can be grounds for immoderate grief. Notwithstanding that they have nothing here on earth, yet God is their portion, and they have an inheritance with the saints in light preserved for them. Notwithstanding that they have not a single penny of money in their purses, yet they have a true treasure which moths cannot corrupt, nor the thief dig through to steal. What does it matter if they have no bread at home in their pantries <note>original: "spinden," meaning a larder or food cupboard</note>, when they are fed every day with the precious body and blood of Christ? What does it matter if you are besmirched and scandalized in your good name, when nonetheless your names are written in the Book of Life? You always have more cause for joy within you than reason for grief outside you.

<margin>Gen. 33: 11.</margin>
Genesis 33:11. *I have enough,* says **Esau**; **Jacob** also says, *I have enough*; but the word signifies as much as *I have everything*: yet **Jacob** was poorer than **Esau**: "He has all things who possesses the One who possesses all things." <note>original: "Ille habet omnia qui habet habentem omnia." This Latin maxim suggests that having God is equivalent to having everything.</note>

<margin>Gen. 30: 1.</margin>
Fifthly, consider that if God had continuously granted you that consolation (over whose absence you mourn so immoderately), it might perhaps have been to visit you with a greater misery and hardship. There is a remarkable example of this in Genesis 30:1. You read there of an impatient woman, **Rachel**, who, because she had no children, was so overcome with passion and grief that she cried out to her husband, *Give me children, or else I die.* Well, this woman obtained her desire; but she who previously cried out, *Give me children, or else I die,* when she now had children, she died in childbirth.

<margin>Gen. 35: vss. 16, 17, 18.</margin>
Genesis 35: verses 16, 17, 18. *And they journeyed from **Bethel**; and there was but a little way to come to **Ephrath**: and **Rachel** travailed, and she had hard labor. And it came to pass, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also. And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing (for she died), that she called his name **Benoni**,* etc. She died after her son was born. God can turn those comforts (which we desire) into miseries for us. If God had given **David** the life of his child, it would have been a living monument

<meta>This page continues a list of "considerations" meant to help a believer moderate their grief. The previous page discussed how God often replaces a lost blessing with a greater one, using the examples of Job and Amaziah.</meta>

# A Christian’s Instruction.

<columns>
...would have been to his shame; for everyone who knew the child would have said, "There goes David’s Bastard." I heard a godly preacher tell a story of how he once went to visit one of his neighbors (whose child lay on its deathbed) to comfort her. But she was so sorrowful and so overcome with grief that she would in no way be comforted. The preacher said to her, "Woman, why are you so deeply distressed? If your child were to live, God might perhaps make him a mockery and a torment to you through his godless and sinful way of life." She answered that she did not care about that, if only he might be made well, even if he were to be hanged afterward. This son of hers recovered, and was afterward hanged for some evil deed that he had committed. Well now, would it not have been a greater mercy, and a thousand times better for her, to have seen him buried beforehand than to come to such an unfortunate end? I relate this only to show you that God can change those comforts, for which we have such high regard and which we prize so much, into miseries and difficulties; and therefore, this ought to moderate immoderate grief over the loss of any worldly comforts.

**Sixthly**, consider that all those miseries and distresses in the world over which you mourn, though they be ever so great, are nonetheless very short; and this is the argument which the Apostle uses here in this text: *Brethren* (says he) *the time is short, so that they who weep should be as if they wept not* <note>1 Corinthians 7:29-30</note>. Though your afflictions be ever so heavy, they shall nonetheless not last long; be therefore patient and long-suffering under them; though they be ever so great, yet because they are short, they are bearable.

<margin>
All things that are brief ought to be bearable, even if they are great. Cicero. <note>original Latin: "Omnia brevia tolerabilia esse debent, etiamsi magna sint."</note>
</margin>

The Apostle expresses this in 2 Corinthians 4:17: *For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.* And God says: *For a small moment have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I gather thee. In a little wrath I hid my face from thee for a moment; but with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee,* Isaiah 54:7-8. Our afflictions are always counted by days and hours, but our mercies by years, to show that the time is but short in which we endure afflictions here; they vanish quickly like the clouds, through which the Sun soon breaks. When **Athanasius** <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian often exiled for his beliefs.</note> was banished, he said that it was but a little cloud and would immediately pass over. A martyr said to his companion, "Just close your eyes, and when they are opened, it shall be in another world."

**Seventhly**, consider that immoderate grief is not the way to restore or diminish your afflictions; but rather provokes God to continue and increase them. This I showed you this morning. Just like a stubborn child who grumbles, stamps, jumps, and whines, or the like; this behavior is not the way to make the Father stop chastising him, but rather to give him more lashes: so also, the more immoderate we are in our sorrows, the heavier afflictions God will at times lay upon us. That which Christ says of worrying in Luke 12:25—*Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit to his stature?*—may also be said to this end: Which of you can, through immoderate grief, diminish anything of your afflictions? The means to ward off our afflictions

<column-break/>

is to accept the punishment for our sins. A child who submits himself, and prays for the forgiveness of his misdeed, and promises improvement, protects himself thereby from many a blow.

**Eighthly**, consider that the worldly comfort, over whose loss you mourn so immoderately, is no better than that which a godless person can enjoy, and you yourself may well be without it. If it is for lack of wealth, honor, children, etc.—well, all these things the godless may have; and therefore, why do you want to upset yourself so much over missing that which a reprobate can enjoy? But if it were over the loss of **Christ**, or **Heaven**, and eternal salvation, then we truly could never mourn enough over that loss; but in the absence of these outward blessings, we come to lose nothing more than that which the wretched or the cursed may enjoy. Those things over which we mourn are not of such substance and value as we often come to esteem them. I have read a story of two godly men who met one another, namely one **Anthony** and **Didymus** <note>Referencing St. Anthony the Great and Didymus the Blind, a famous scholar in Alexandria.</note>. Now, **Didymus** was blind, yet of a noble lineage. **Anthony** asked him if he was not grieved by his blindness. "Yes," said **Didymus**. "But," said **Anthony**, "do you want to trouble yourself over the lack of that which flies and dogs can have, and not rather rejoice to have what the angels possess?"

**Ninthly**, to make your immoderate grief decrease, consider that whatever loss or affliction God sends upon you here in the world, He intends your profit through that loss; and therefore, why should any adversity dismay you? Since God aims for your welfare through all adversities, so that you shall at last have to say: *It is good for me that I have been afflicted,* Psalm 119:71. And, *In faithfulness thou hast afflicted me.* It is the observation of **Salmeron** <note>Alfonso Salmeron (1515–1585), a Spanish Jesuit theologian and one of the founding members of the Society of Jesus.</note> on John 3: Suppose that a man threw a precious pearl or diamond to you, and it bruised your hand; if you could have that diamond through it, would you consider that an injustice? Well, so God deals with us; He turns our losses into gain, and all our miseries into comforts. Suppose that a man (who had many debts, and greatly needed money, even to buy bread to eat) went to one of his friends and made his state known, and begged him for some assistance: if this friend of his went to his chest, and took a large bag of money out of it, and threw it to him, commanding him that he should take it; even if this bag happened to hurt him, do you think he would take it ill? No, certainly. Well, so also every affliction which God lays upon us shall turn out for our good. We may say as **Joseph** said to his brothers: *Though you meant it for evil, God nonetheless meant it for good* <note>Genesis 50:20</note>. When someone comes to wrong us, we may say to him: "Although you intend to damage me, God will nonetheless work out the good for me through the same." The Lord does not intend any harm with the afflictions He lays upon us, but rather the good. All afflictions have, like **Jonathan’s rod**, honey at the end <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 14:27, where Jonathan tasted honey from the tip of his staff and was refreshed during a battle.</note>; and therefore let us bear them patiently. You would be very angry if an enemy drew blood from you: but if a Doctor, for your heal[th]—

# A Christian’s Instruction.

<columns>
...for the sake of your health and for your own good, [He] took even more away from you, you would not consider that a crime. Therefore, be advised to be patient and long-suffering under all worldly miseries and difficulties, because God intends through these very things to promote your benefit and your spiritual gain, so that just as your afflictions are abundant, so also your comforts in Christ might be even more abundant.

**Tenthly, Consider** that those who are better than you have been in as bad or worse condition than you are in this region; and therefore, let this diminish and moderate your sorrows. It is indeed true that if we were in such a bad and miserable state that no one had ever been in the like before, then we might have some excuse for our immoderate sorrow; but there is no one among us who is oppressed alone. Those who are much better than we are have had as great miseries and difficulties as we have ever had. 1 Peter 5:9. There the Apostle exhorts them to resist the Devil with steadfastness of faith, *knowing that the same sufferings are accomplished in your brotherhood that is in the world.* There is now no one in such a miserable state but that there are others who have been, are, or shall be in as wretched a condition as you. *No temptation has overtaken you except such as is common to man; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able.* 1 Cor. 10:13. Have you lost a great estate? Well, Job lost more than you ever did; he lost seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys; he lost all that he had, so that not even any outward comfort was left to him. And therefore, since the same affliction has come upon others, why should you not be content? But you will say, "I have lost my children." Well, Job lost more children than you ever did; he lost ten children in one day, who were taken away by an untimely death; yet it may be that you also have lost as many children, but they went in peace to their graves, and therefore this can comfort your heart; others have been in a worse state than you are in now, and yet they underwent it patiently. Job did not sin, nor did he open his mouth against God, notwithstanding all the afflictions that lay upon him.

And so also our Lord **Jesus Christ**, Matt. 8:20. He was a Man of Sorrows; *the foxes have holes,* He said, *and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.* **Jesus Christ**, although heir of all things, was nonetheless as poor as you have ever been; and therefore, let these reflections support your heart in all the afflictions that might come upon you here in the world; for the Lord knows what a bloody cloud is still hanging over our heads.

**Eleventhly**, to keep down your immoderate sorrow over the loss of any physical comforts, consider that your sorrow is never right unless it is over sin; your sorrow is not right and runs in a wrong channel until it is in

<column-break/>

this circular course, namely, over sin. If you mourn over the things of the world, you let your sorrow run into a bad gutter, and you prevent it from running where it ought to run. It is a pity to use sweet water to wash a filthy place; sin ought to be the primary object of our sorrow, and our tears are kept out of their rightful channel when we do not mourn more or less over sin. God has promised to gather all those tears which we shed over sin into a bottle, and no others; the tears which we shed over worldly things are but in vain, they overflow and do not come into God's bottles. And truly, brothers, there are no afflictions here that are worthy of our sorrows or tears. Would you not consider him a madman who would go and throw pearls or diamonds at a pear tree <note>original: "peere-boom"; likely a metaphor for wasting something precious on something of little value</note>, and thus come to lose them? So also, it is a pity to throw away tears over the things of the world, and to squander such precious treasures over every minor occasion.

**Twelfthly**, consider that your immoderate sorrow over the world will prevent and hinder you from mourning over sin; just as when a vein is opened in the arm <note>a reference to the medical practice of bloodletting</note> and the blood flows out there, it prevents and holds it back from running in its ordinary channel; so also, when you are in a vein of sorrow and displeasure over worldly losses or miseries, that prevents and holds back the natural course of your tears, so that you cannot mourn over sin.

And thus I have finished these twelve reflections or considerations, as well as these three questions. I have shown you when your sorrow is immoderate, and I have given you some reasons why Christians ought not to mourn immoderately over the things of this world; and I have now presented to you twelve reflections or considerations to withhold you from immoderate mourning over the loss of any outward comfort.

Sermon.

Three rules to moderate the loss of worldly comforts.

**I** have now, fourthly, one more question to handle: namely, to show you what rules or means you must use to keep your sorrows over worldly miseries within bounds, to weep as if you did not weep. I shall likewise give you eleven or twelve instructions here for the fulfillment of this duty.

**First**, if you want to keep your sorrow in check, use this helpful remedy: those things, the lack of which makes you so immoderately sorrowful, look upon them as mere nothingness. But you will say, "It is a childish thing for a man to value nothing"; well, many such childish things we do very often; we are sorrowful,

# A Christian’s Instruction.

<columns>
...mourning and weeping over mere trivialities. If we were to consider this earnestly when we mourn the loss of this or that comfort, it would moderate our sorrows, since they are but mere trivialities.

But you will say, "Oh! my business is failing me, I have lost so much of my goods; and do you call this a mere nothing?"

Yes, for that is what the Scripture calls it. Solomon says in Proverbs 23:5: *Will you set your eyes on that which is not? For riches shall certainly make wings for themselves, and fly away.* And if this is so, why should we set our hearts so strongly upon them, or mourn so much when we lose them? When King Agrippa came to pass judgment on Paul, Acts 25:23, it is said that he came with "great pomp." But in the original text it says he came with "great fantasy" <note>original Greek: *meta pollēs phantasias*, meaning with much show or pageantry</note>. All worldly pomp and comforts are such fantasies and trivialities compared to the great and weighty matters of salvation. *Only one thing is needed,* says Christ in Luke 10:42, and that is to have a share in Him. It is not necessary for you to have riches and honor in the world; the only thing necessary is to obtain Christ. Therefore, why should we spend our time and effort on that which is not bread, and after that which will not benefit us, being mere trivialities?

How childish was Haman <note>A high official in the Persian Empire (Book of Esther) who plotted against the Jews because a single man, Mordecai, refused to bow to him.</note>, when he had so many advantages and honors—the King's favor, sitting at the King's table, riding his horse, etc.—yet was so grieved and upset because Mordecai would not show him respect? What a poor and small reason this was to ruin all his comforts! And Ahab, etc., because he could not have Naboth's vineyard, though he had so many of his own. These people are so easily overwhelmed with sorrow over minor and trivial trifles. Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Roman Stoic philosopher whose writings on endurance and emotion were very popular with Christian authors.</note> compares such people to a man who has a stately house, beautiful orchards, and gardens with much fruit, and yet becomes distressed over the falling of a little foliage.

**Secondly**, if you wish to keep your sorrows in check, then take care not to give place to an improper or unauthorized love for any comfort you enjoy here. If you love the enjoyment of a thing too much, you will mourn its loss too much; therefore, never let your hearts be attached to any comfort here. Let worldly comforts be to you like gloves on your hands, and not like the skin on your flesh. You cannot pull the skin from your flesh without great pain and torment, but you can pull your glove from your hand without any danger. If your hearts are too attached to the love of worldly things, the loss of those things which you love so immoderately will produce immoderate sorrow and pain. A person will never mourn the loss of that which he hates, but only that which he loves; and you can never keep your sorrows in check if you do not keep your love in check. It is like a painting: if you put it in a frame

<column-break/>

and hang it against the wall, you can easily take it down again; but if you fasten or glue it to the wall, you cannot take it down without damaging it and breaking it into pieces. So too, if your love is attached to the world like a painting glued to the wall, you will not be able to part from worldly things without great sorrow, gloom, and torment. It is said of Jacob (when he heard that his son Joseph was dead, Genesis 37:33, 35) that he wept and would not be comforted; and the reason was that he loved Joseph exceedingly, more than all the others. His immoderate love for Joseph made him mourn so greatly over the loss of him.

<margin>I know that I have begotten a mortal. <note>original Latin: *Scio me genuisse mortalem*. This is a famous Stoic saying attributed to Anaxagoras upon the death of his son.</note></margin>
**Thirdly**, regard all comforts here below as loseable and uncertain. God in His wisdom has not granted permanence to any comfort here below. Look upon your comforts as changeable and fleeting. Have you lost a child? Well, say: "I knew beforehand that I had fathered a mortal child." It is appointed for us all once to die, and the comforts we enjoy here in the world are not like an anchor in the seabed that holds fast in a storm, but like the flag on the top of the mast, which turns with every wind. Therefore, since you are subject to change every moment in your greatest comfort, why should you mourn so immoderately over its loss, and be so distressed over that which you could lose, and know not how soon? A person ought to possess fleeting things loosely, and never pave a way to certain sorrows over the loss of such uncertain comforts.

**Fourthly**, if you wish to keep your sorrow in check, consider that you have no cause to mourn the loss of worldly things if God leaves you enough for the necessities of life, even if He does not leave you an abundance for the pleasure and delight of your life. *Having food and clothing, let us be content with that,* 1 Timothy 6:8. If you have bread, though no banquet, be content with that. If you have clothes, though no ornaments, be content nonetheless. If you have food and clothing, however meager, being just enough to preserve your life, then you have no cause to complain, but to be at peace. Jacob was a richer man than any of you who hear this today; yet he says in Genesis 28:20: *If you will give me bread to eat and clothing to put on, it shall be enough for me.* If the Lord gives us food and clothing, even if the food is ever so humble and the clothing ever so poor, we should nonetheless be content and say, "it shall be enough for me." Though God gives us no abundance for our pleasure, yet if He gives us enough to support our needs, we should be content; and therefore, in that matter, you have no cause for immoderate sorrow.

# ->A Christian’s Instruction.<-

<columns>
...keep [their grief], when they have lost a loved one <note>original: "Vrient," which in this context includes close friends and family</note>, a husband, or a wife, or parents, or a child. They will continue to look at the painting, or the clothes, or some other object belonging to their deceased friend, which renews their sadness and makes their wound bleed again; do not do that which can bring your sadness back to your memory. It is a notable example, and very remarkable for this purpose, which is found in Genesis 35:17, 18. There it is said of Rachel that when she was dying, and her child being born, she named him *Ben-oni*, the Son of my sorrow <note>Rachel named her son *Ben-oni* out of her birth-pangs and impending death.</note>; but note now, Jacob would not let him be called by that name which the mother gave him; instead, he called him *Benjamin*, the Son of my right hand <note>Jacob renamed the child to shift the focus from the sorrow of his wife’s death to the strength and support the son would provide.</note>. And the theologians give this reason for it: that if Jacob had allowed the child to be called by that name, it would have been a means to bring the loss of his wife to his memory every time he heard it—she who died while she was in labor with him—and thus it would have renewed his sadness and pain over it. Therefore, we ought not to bring our afflictions to memory in such a way as to renew our sorrows.

Sixthly, if you wish to keep your sorrows in check, then live much in the meditations and reflections on Divine things. The reason why you mourn so much over the things down here is because you no longer reflect on the things above; if your thoughts were raised to the contemplation of Divine and Spiritual things, the joy of the same would swallow up your sadness over the loss of any thing here below. Adam, in his state of innocence, conversed so with God that he did not see his own nakedness. I have read of the Eagle <note>The author uses the eagle as an allegory for the soul's ascent; while other creatures focus on their earthly distress, the eagle seeks the sun.</note> that its nature and condition is contrary to all other birds: for all other fowl, when they are offended or in some discomfort, will cry out and make a clamor; just as the Crane will chatter, the Dove will mourn, and the Ravens will croak; and all other creatures will make a noise when they are harmed or in want. But now, the Eagle will fly upward toward the Sun, and there delight itself with its warm rays. Oh, my beloved, if only you would be like the Eagle, to soar upward to Heaven in your meditations! and to work up your thoughts to Spiritual and Heavenly things; Oh, this would greatly soften your sorrows over the loss of any outward comfort.

Seventhly, labor to mourn more over sin; then you shall grieve less over external afflictions. When your conscience is once touched with a penitent sorrow over sin, that will cause the mourning over the loss of worldly comforts to cease. O Beloved, when you let your sorrows run out over sin, it will keep them away from any other object, because when the soul is once set to weep over sin, then sin shall be seen and noticed to be so great an evil, that no evil in the world has such a ground of sadness as sin. And therefore, if you wish to weep over external difficulties as if not weeping, then weep more over sin, and over the

<column-break/>

corruptions which are in your own heart; I may say of sadness just as it is said of fear in Isaiah 8, verses 12, 13,
> *And do not fear their fear, and do not be terrified; the Lord of Hosts, Him you shall hallow, and let Him be your fear, and let Him be your dread.*

They who fear the Lord shall not fear men; they who have a godly fear shall have no worldly fear. So also, if you have a divine sorrow over sin, it will preserve you from immoderate worldly sorrow; and therefore I wish, when you begin to seek out your sorrows over the loss of worldly comforts and the things which go against you here below, that you would then consider that you have greater evils to mourn over, and much greater cause to let your sorrows run in the channel of sins, than over any external miseries or afflictions.

Eighthly, if you wish to soften the immoderation in worldly sadness, then weigh your external deprivations against your internal and spiritual enjoyments; and your external miseries against your internal comforts; and then see if the scale of your spiritual comforts does not far outweigh the other. And if God makes your spiritual mercies exceed your external afflictions, then you have more cause for rejoicing than for mourning. David followed this course, 2 Samuel 23, verse 5. Although, he says,
> *my house is not so with God; yet He has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and sure: for this is all my salvation, and all my desire, although He does not yet make it grow.*

It is as if he would have said: though I have no abundance of worldly happiness, yet I do not ask for it, seeing God has made an everlasting covenant with me, and has ordered everything surely; though all things are lost from without, yet all is well within. God has made a covenant with me, and that is all my desire, and all my salvation; so that if you would now, like David, weigh your external miseries against your internal comforts, you would see there more cause for internal joy than for external sadness. A good man (says Solomon) shall be satisfied from himself, Proverbs 14, verse 14. He has within him that which shall bring him comfort, whatever his state might be.

You who are smitten with worldly sadness, reason thus with yourself: although my state is sad, and I lack the necessities of this life, and have no house to live in; or if I have one, it is but a poor smoky hut <note>original: "rook-hutjen," referring to a very humble, primitive dwelling.</note>; nonetheless, why should I be saddened, since I have a *house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens*, 2 Corinthians 5:1. Although I have no dwelling here, Christ has nonetheless gone into Heaven to prepare a place for me there. Although I am a man of low estate, and can hardly make ends meet with all my effort and labor; nonetheless God is my portion, and I have an inheritance among those who [are] in Christ...

corruptions which are in your own heart. I may say of sorrow what was said of fear in Isaiah 8, verses 12 and 13: *And do not fear their fear, nor be afraid. The Lord of hosts, Him shall you hallow; and let Him be your fear, and let Him be your dread.* Those who fear the Lord will not fear men; those who have a godly fear will have no worldly fear. So also, if you have a divine sorrow over sin, it will preserve you from immoderate worldly sorrow; and therefore I wish, when your sorrows over the loss of worldly comforts and the things which go against you here below begin to break out, that you would then consider that you have greater evils to mourn over, and much greater cause to let your sorrows run in the channel of sins, than over any outward miseries or sighs.

**Eighthly**, if you want to soften the immoderation of worldly sorrow, then weigh your outward deprivations against your inward and spiritual enjoyments; and your outward miseries with your inward comforts; and see then if the scale of your spiritual comforts does not far outweigh the other. And if God makes your spiritual mercies exceed your outward sighs, then you have more reason to rejoice than to mourn. David follows this course in 2 Samuel 23, verse 5: *Although, he says, my house be not so with God; yet he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and sure: for this is all my salvation, and all my desire, although he does not yet make it sprout.* It is as if he would have said: though I do not have an abundance of all worldly happiness, yet I do not ask for it, since God has made an everlasting covenant with me, and has ordered everything surely; though all things are lost from without, yet all is well within; God has made a covenant with me, and that is all my desire and all my salvation. So if you, like David, would now weigh your outward miseries against your inward comforts, you would see there more cause for inward joy than for outward sorrow. *A good man*, says Solomon, *shall be satisfied from himself* (Proverbs 14:14); he has within him that which will bring him comfort, whatever his state might be.

You who are struck down with worldly sorrow, reason thus with yourself: "Although my state is sad, and I lack the necessities of this life, and have no house to live in—or if I have one, it is but a poor smoky hut—yet why should I be distressed, since I have a *house not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens*" (2 Corinthians 5:1). Although I have no dwelling place here, yet Christ has gone before me into heaven to prepare a place for me there. Although I am a man of low estate, and can hardly make ends meet through the year with all my trouble and labor, yet *God is my portion, and I have an inheritance among those who in Christ...*

# ->A Christian’s Instruction.<-
