...are sanctified through faith, **John 14:2**. Although I have debts, and when I walk the streets I am in constant fear of being arrested and imprisoned <note>Debt was a common cause for imprisonment in the 17th century; the author uses this legal anxiety to contrast earthly debt with the "debt" of sin.</note>, yet my greatest debt is paid; **Christ** has satisfied Divine justice for me: and I shall never go to the eternal prison of hell. Although I have no money in my purse to buy bread, yet I have a treasure in Heaven which shall never be exhausted; although I hardly have clothes to cover my nakedness, yet I have the long robe of **Christ’s** righteousness to cover my sinful nakedness: and although I hardly have food and drink to fill my belly, yet I am fed by the Bread of Life, the Lord **Jesus Christ**. Although I am harmed in my good name, scandalized and slandered, yet my name is written in the book of life: and although I never have a foot of land to enjoy here, yet I am an heir to a Kingdom. A disguised Prince is poorly received in a foreign land. But it does not trouble him much; why? Because he is an heir to a crown, and knows that when he is in his own Kingdom, he will have honor enough. Beloved, let these internal and spiritual enjoyments soften all worldly sorrow, noting that if you weigh your spiritual enjoyments against your outward deprivations, and your internal comforts against your outward losses, the former will infinitely outweigh the latter.

Ninthly, would you keep your sorrows in check? Then make much of the mercies which you receive, and little of the afflictions you suffer; it is the nature of a sorrowful spirit to think too much of its afflictions and too little of its graces. But if you wish to keep your hearts from immoderate sorrow, you ought to magnify and expand God’s mercies toward you, and diminish your sorrows in your memory; you will thus increase your thankfulness and decrease your sorrows and murmurings. Consider within yourself that the smallest grace you enjoy is more than you are worthy of, and the greatest affliction you suffer is less than you deserve. Likewise, reflect within yourself that you brought nothing into the world, nor can you carry anything out; and that if you escape the future torments of hell, it is a greater mercy than if you were to enjoy all the treasures and pleasures of the world. But many people, if they encounter even one day of adversity, look so closely at their misery and so enlarge their sorrows that they never think of that multitude of mercies which **God** has heaped upon their heads. You have more reason to rejoice that **God** gives you the smallest grace than to be upset when He sends you the greatest affliction.

Tenthly, compare your afflictions with others, who endure greater afflictions with more patience and have been less sorrowful than you. Remember the patience of **Job**, and the end the Lord brought about for him: you have

<column-break/>

never lost as much as **Job** did; he lost seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she-asses; he lost seven sons and three daughters, and all in one day; he suffered great misery in his body and lay on the dung-heap, and yet he was patient under all these afflictions. Well, reflect now that better men have had greater miseries, difficulties, and afflictions than you, and yet had greater patience and less sorrow and pain than you. The Apostle **Peter** exhorts people in a suffering state to patience, *knowing that the same sufferings are accomplished in your brotherhood that is in the world*, **1 Peter 5:9.** And **Paul**, **1 Cor. 10:13.** *There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.* Indeed, **Jesus Christ** himself underwent many afflictions and miseries, and yet *he opened not his mouth, but as a sheep that is dumb before its shearers, so he opened not his mouth.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:7, describing the Messiah's silent endurance of suffering.</note> Those who have greater grace have less mercy <note>Likely meaning "outward comforts" or "earthly leniency" in this context.</note> than you; and those who have fewer sins have greater afflictions.

Eleventhly, to moderate your sorrow and keep it in check, remember that it is better for you when you are at your worst than it is for the ungodly when they are at their best. If this reflection went to your heart, it would greatly soften your immoderate sorrow: *The little that the righteous man has is better than the revenues of the wicked.* **Prov. 15:6.** *In the house of the righteous is much treasure, but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble.* Note that it is not said: "In the *revenues* of the righteous is a great treasure," but, "In the *house* of the righteous." A righteous man’s house may be a poor hut, a beggar’s house, and in the same not a chair to sit on, or a fire to warm him, or food to nourish him, etc. Yet **Solomon** says, *In the house of the righteous is much treasure.* But do the wicked also have treasures? No, *In the revenues of the wicked is trouble.* He does not say, "In the house of the wicked," but, "In their revenues there is great trouble." There is the curse of **God** on everything that a wicked man enjoys. The poor beggar’s hut of the righteous holds more treasure and salvation than the great revenues of the ungodly. A godly person at their worst is better than a wicked person at their best. **Prov. 16:8.** *Better is a little with righteousness, than great revenues without right.* A little with the fear of **God** is better than the much that a wicked man has. Why then will you not take this to heart? Even if you suffer under great afflictions and have lost your means, wife, children, or anything else; yet, if you are a godly person, I dare assure you that in your worst state you are better than a wicked man at his best. Although there is little or nothing in your house, yet there is great treasure; and although there is much in a wicked man’s house, yet there is also great difficulty and sorrow. I have only one more reflection to discuss.

Twelfthly, if you wish to soften your grief over worldly miseries, then consider that you will live much more happily by being satisfied with what you have, than by mourning too much over what you do not have; for by such means, you pierce yourself with many sorrows. A man can be very rich and conduct a great trade <note>original: "neeringe," referring to commercial business or livelihoods</note>, and yet the same man can be a miserable person, having a hell in his conscience and a hell in his household. And therefore, if you cannot bring your circumstances to your mind, then you must bring your mind to your circumstances; for the comfort of a man's life consists not in riches, but in being satisfied with one's state. Therefore, thank God rather for what you have, than mourn and be grieved for what you do not have: for this is the way to make your life comfortless, full of difficulty and sadness. Therefore, take the Apostle’s advice, **Hebrews 13:5**: *Let your conduct be without covetousness: and be content with such things as you have. For He has said, I will never leave you, nor forsake you.* And thus I have finished these twelve remedies or considerations to keep your sorrows in check. We come now to the application, which serves to rebuke those who can mourn over every slight loss—not even worth considering—that happens to them in the world; whose heads are like fountains, pouring out rivers of tears over some worldly miseries or oppressions: and yet when God calls for mourning, weeping, and <unclear>humility</unclear> <note>original: "haal-heyt." This may be a typo for "kaal-heyt" (baldness/shaving the head), a biblical sign of repentance mentioned in Isaiah 22:12 alongside weeping and mourning.</note>, their heads are then like rocks, which cannot pour out a single drop. Although they can mourn over small and light oppressions, yet they cannot pour out a tear over their sins, nor over the sins of the People; these people are rightly to be rebuked for their misplaced sorrow.

<margin>IV. Sermon.</margin>
I proceed now in the handling of this Doctrine: since Christians ought to guard themselves against immoderate sorrow, and to weep over worldly oppressions as if they wept not; then this teaching shall serve you for these three warnings, from which three cases of conscience shall arise.

First, guard yourself that you do not fall into this error: for when you are in immoderate sorrow over worldly crosses—to pretend to have nothing more than a natural feeling of your oppressions; the reason why I give you this warning is because there is a natural inclination in man, when they are rebuked for their immoderate sorrows, to excuse the same and say, "Will you not give me the freedom to mourn over my sins, and to be sensitive to God's

<column-break/>

hand upon me?" and other such excuses <unclear>besides</unclear>.

<margin>1. Case of Conscience.</margin>
Now, because man is so inclined to err in this matter, I shall handle this case of conscience regarding it: namely, wherein the distinction appears between a person who only has a natural sensitivity to the hand of God upon him, and a person who is immoderately mourning and grieved; between a gentle <note>original: "minnelijke," meaning moderate or affectionate</note> sorrow and a fretful torment of the Spirit; and this I shall show you in these following six points.

First, where there is only a natural feeling, and a gentle mourning over worldly miseries, it will rather refresh the soul and give courage for religious duties, than in any way disturb or distract her; and therefore it is that you so often find in the Scripture that weeping goes together with prayer and supplication; and thus it is said of **Jacob**, *that he wept and made supplication*, **Hosea 12:4**; and **Jeremiah 3:21**, *A voice was heard upon the high places, weeping and supplications of the children of Israel*; so also, **chapter 31:9**, *They shall come with weeping, and with supplications will I lead them.* Likewise **Judges 2:4, 5**, it is said that the children of **Israel** at **Bochim** <note>The name "Bochim" literally means "Weepers."</note> lifted up their voices and wept, and sacrificed there to the Lord. All these places show that the sorrow which is only a natural feeling of God’s hand will rather refresh and encourage the soul to her duty than make her unfit; but on the other hand, immoderate sorrow makes a person unfit for prayer, the hearing of the word, or any other holy duties. As is seen in **Asaph**, who was so overwhelmed with sorrow that he could not speak, **Psalm 77:4**; and **Exodus 6:9**; then your sorrow is immoderate, when it makes you unfit for the exercise of holy duties.

Secondly, where there is only a gentle sorrow and a natural feeling of worldly miseries, there is kindled in that person's heart a mutual sympathy for other people's difficulties; that person will carry bowels of compassion <note>A 17th-century idiom for deep, gut-level empathy.</note> toward other people who are in difficulties, as well as themselves. *Did I not weep,* says **Job**, **chapter 30:25**, *for him that was in trouble? was not my soul grieved for the poor?* But now, where sorrow is immoderate, you will think so much upon your own difficulties that you will not have mercy on those who are in like difficulty with you.

Thirdly, where there is only a natural feeling of worldly miseries, there remains in that soul a sense of those manifold Mercies (which you enjoy) as well as of the oppression and suffering under which you are; the natural sensitivity to oppressions does not take away the comfort and the enjoyment of present mercies: there is a sense of the mercies which you enjoy as well as of the oppressions you suffer. But now, in immoderate sorrow, the feeling of your difficulty and misery takes away and embitters all your previous and present mercies. As is seen in **Numbers 16:13**, *Is it a small thing that you have brought us up out of a land that flows with milk and honey, to kill us in the...*

The Desert? It is my sin which is the cause of all my sorrow / pain and tears / and I hope that you will allow such a thing to be done. Yes / mourn over your sins in God's name; but because people are so inclined to deceive themselves in this matter / I shall therefore treat another <term>Case of Conscience</term> <note>A "Case of Conscience" is a specific spiritual or ethical problem that requires a resolution based on religious principles and self-examination.</note> regarding this.

<margin>The 2nd Case of Conscience.</margin>
Namely, how you can distinguish when a person mourns immoderately / whether he weeps over his afflictions or over his sins? Rather over his difficulties and worldly miseries / than over his corruptions, crimes and sins against God / I shall here present to you four clear discoveries of such a person.

<margin>Indicators of people who mourn over the affliction rather than over the sin.</margin>
First, a person mourns under worldly miseries / rather over his sins than over his afflictions / if he mourned and wept over his sins before he was afflicted. It is proof that your sorrow is rather over the sin / than over the affliction / if sin broke your heart / when you were in prosperity / and because of the sin you could have no rest nor peace within you: and thus David mourned over his sins / when he drenched his bedstead with his tears / over the dishonoring of **Bathsheba**, for he then had no affliction or misery lying upon him. And yet David roared in the disquiet of his soul, and had no rest in his bones because of his sin. When David sat upon the Throne in worldly honor and prosperity / even then he could lie down in the dust and spiritual shame / and this happened before the child was sick. And therefore if you find upon your examination that you mourned and wept over your sins and corruptions / before you had this or any other difficulty lying upon you / so you may conclude / that your sorrow is more over the sin than over the worldly afflictions; but now / where a person pretends to mourn over the sin / yet his sins have never before disturbed him in all the time of his life / nor have his corruptions ever grieved his heart / or burdened his conscience before / this shows that such a person mourns and weeps more over his afflictions / than over his sins.

Secondly, a person mourns rather over the sin / than over the affliction / when he takes more care to put away his sins from his soul / than the afflictions from his body. When it is the greatest desire of your souls / and the most care of your hearts / to have your sins rather than your afflictions taken away from you. **Hosea 14:3**. *Take these words with you, and return to the Lord: say to him; take away all iniquity, and give us good;* they did not say / O Lord take the afflictions away. Although they then had many; but Lord take away the iniquity of your servants, and give the good; it is a sign that he does not mourn over the sin / but over his misery / who would rather be delivered from his difficulties than from his sins. Thus it was with **Pharaoh** when the judgments of God lay upon him / such as the Thunder / Hail / Lightning / Lice / and the death of the Cattle / Etc. Then he said to **Moses**; *Pray fervently to the Lord, (for it is enough) that there be no more Thunder of God nor Hail,* **Exodus 9:28**. He requests of Moses that he should pray to God to take the plagues away from him / but

<column-break/>

he never desires or requests that his sin / and the hardness of his heart might be taken away. In which you might cry out / O Lord do take this misery / or those afflictions away from me; but you never can pray to be delivered from your sins / and to bring your corruptions under subjection: this is proof that you mourn more over the affliction than over the sin.

Thirdly, When the committing of a sin / and the deliverance from an affliction stand against one another / if you then would rather have the affliction continue over you / than commit a sin: that shows that you are grieved rather over the sin / than over the affliction. As for example / when a person is brought to a lowly state / and is greatly diminished in the world / so that his trade fails him / and his lineage has perished / if that person is more disturbed over his sin / which has brought him into that state / than over the affliction itself / then he will not commit a sin to restore his loss again / even though he knows / that the committing of such a sin would do the same; so also in some other occasions: just as I have read a History of a Nobleman / whose Son and Heir was thought to be bewitched / and therefore he was advised by some to go to a Sorceress / to help his Son and to un-bewitch him; so he answered / no / by no means / for he would rather have the Sorceress have his Son / than the Devil. But if you make no Conscience of committing a sin / to take your afflictions away from you / if you will break the determination of the commandment to avoid a small foul path of afflictions / so it is a sign that you are more grieved over your miseries and difficulties than over your sins / and that you never mourned so much over your corruptions / as you have done over your chastisements, **Job 36:21**. Those who in their distresses go to the Sorceresses / Soothsayers and Devil-artists / (like **Saul** to the Witch at **Endor**) show that they mourn more over the afflictions than over the sins.

Fourthly, If you mourn over the sin / then the true joy / which proceeds from the forgiveness of sins / shall swallow up your sorrow / which comes upon you through any worldly misery or affliction / and shall likewise make you undergo the same with patience. The person mourns most over the sin / who / when his sins are forgiven / is least grieved over the external afflictions; if the comfort of the forgiveness of his sins rejoices him more / than the continuation of any affliction can grieve him: as in **Isaiah 33:24**. *No inhabitant shall say, I am sick, for the people that dwell therein, shall have forgiveness of iniquity.* These people were like a ship in a great tempest / their mast broken / their sails lost / and all their rigging was gone: Well! What was it then? Nevertheless / *No inhabitant shall say, I am sick*, because the Lord has forgiven them their sins. He does not say / They shall not say / that they *were* sick; But / They shall not say / that they *are* sick, because their sins are forgiven. The tasting of the forgiveness of their sins would take away the feeling of the pains of their present sorrows. Now / when it is thus situated with you /

She prayed and said: Let your handmaid find grace in your eyes: So the Woman went her way, and she ate, and her countenance was no longer as it was. Because she had poured out her heart in prayer to God / she was comforted / and she went her way / and was no more sorrowful. Then is your sorrow upright / when you go on your knees to God in your sorrow / and that this same act comes to set your heart at rest. Or/

Secondly, <note>The original text repeats "Ten tweeden" (Secondly) here, likely as a sub-point to the fourth indicator or a printer's error in the original manuscript's numbering.</note> When the promise of God comforts you: Thus it was with David, <margin>Psalm 119: 50.</margin> This is my comfort (says he) in my misery: for your promise has made me alive; that is / the word of the promise. So also verse 92. If your Law had not been all my delight, I should have perished long ago in my affliction. And verse 107. I am very greatly afflicted, Lord, make me alive according to your word. Then is your sorrow moderate / when prayer to God / or the promise of God / sets your Hearts at rest; and then are your sorrows immoderate / when all the promises in the entire Bible / you being under some tribulation / cannot set you at rest; nor can any prayer comfort you. And thus it was with Job, <margin>Job 9. Cap. verse 16.</margin> in his 9th Chapter verse 16. If I call (says he) and he answers me, I shall not believe that he has given ear to my voice. And therefore / beloved / take note / you who have been overtaken by these worldly miseries and difficulties / and no prayer has ever been able to comfort you / nor promise set you at rest / it is a proof that your sorrows were immoderate.

Fifthly, where there is only a natural feeling of worldly miseries / there that soul justifies God / notwithstanding all his tribulations / and judges himself / acknowledging his own sins to be the cause of all difficulties. Here you have an example in the Lamentations of Jeremiah. <margin>Cap. 1. verse 18.</margin> Chapter 1. verse 18. The Lord is righteous in all the evil that has come upon us. And <margin>Dan. 9: 14.</margin> Daniel 9: 14. The Lord is righteous in all that has come upon us; for we have not obeyed his voice, and have done what is evil in his eyes. So also David, <margin>Psalm 51: 3.</margin> Psalm 51: 3. I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Then is your sorrow right / when you can justify God / and take the shame upon yourself. But now / where the sorrow is soul-fretting and immoderate / there the Sinner lashes out against God / and would rather justify himself; there the Sinner considers God very harsh

<column-break/>

and cruel in his dealings / murmurs against him / thinks ill of him / and of his ways. And thus it was once with Job, <margin>Cap. 16. verse 17.</margin> Chapter 16. verse 17. He has broken me with a tempest, and multiplied my wounds without cause. He blamed God / and justified himself; which showed that his sorrow was unregulated and immoderate. You have a notable passage of this in Isaiah 8. verse 21. <margin>Isa. 8. verse 21.</margin> there it is said / that when God shall bring tribulations and difficulties upon the land / that they shall then curse their King, and God when they shall look upward. They shall be so overcome by sorrow / that they shall curse God / and justify themselves. So also Proverbs 19: 3. <margin>Prov. 19: 3.</margin> The foolishness of man (says Solomon) shall pervert his way, and his heart shall fret against the Lord.

Sixthly, where there is only a natural feeling under God’s hand / there shall be an inclination to listen to the comforting counsel of God’s Word / so as to uphold the heart under tribulations; and therefore it is said / <margin>Job 33.</margin> Job 33. when God laid tribulations upon him / that he opened his ears to counsel. When you are so tamed by tribulations / that you want to hear the voice of the rod, and the voice of the word, and listen to the counsel that is presented to you / to uphold you / and to support your souls / then is your sorrow regulated / and such as God desires: But now / where the sorrow is unregulated / there that person is not fit to receive any instruction / from a friend who stays near him to comfort him. Thus it was with Asaph <margin>Psalm 77: 2.</margin> Psalm 77: 2. when he was so overwhelmed with sorrow / that his soul refused to be comforted. They are then like Rachel, <margin>Matt. 2: 18.</margin> who would not be comforted / Matthew 2: 18. A voice was heard in Ramah, much lamentation, weeping, and wailing: Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they were not. The Women of Bethlehem mourned and wept / and would not be comforted / which showed their sorrow to be immoderate. When no promise in the Bible / no comfort nor support of the word / shall lighten and set the heart at rest / that shows that such a one is too much overcome by worldly miseries with sorrow / fretting and pain.

And thus I have finished with the first warning, namely to beware when you are too much grieved over worldly tribulations / that you then do not say / that it is nothing more than only a natural feeling of God's hand upon you.

Secondly, if it is so that we must not be immoderate in our sorrows over worldly miseries; but must weep as if we wept not: then beware that you do not judge that to be a mourning over sin / which is only over outward difficulties. Beloved / the reason why I give you this warning / is / because of that inclination which is in man / that when they have lost a Husband / Wife / Children or goods, etc. / to be so extremely unsettled and dismayed. If you ask them / why they mourn and are so very grieved: They will answer / that it is over their sins / and say / will you give me no liberty to mourn over my sins?

It is my sin which is the cause of all my sorrow / pain and tears / and I hope that you will permit me to do so. Yes / mourn over your sins in God's name; but because people are so inclined to deceive themselves in this matter / I shall therefore treat another case of Conscience regarding this. Namely, how you can distinguish when a person mourns immoderately / whether he weeps over his tribulations or over his sins? Or rather over his difficulties and worldly miseries / than over his corruptions / crimes and sins against God / I shall here present to you four clear discoveries of such a person.

<margin>Signs of a person who mourns more over sin than over tribulation.</margin>
Firstly, a person under worldly miseries mourns more over his sins than over his tribulations / if he mourned and wept over his sins before he was afflicted. It is proof that your sorrow is rather over sin / than over tribulation / if sin broke your heart / when you were in prosperity / and because of sin you could have no rest nor peace within you: and thus David mourned over his sins / when he drenched his bedstead with his tears / over the dishonoring of Bathsheba, for he then had no tribulation or misery lying upon him. And yet David roared in the disquiet of his soul, and had no rest in his bones because of his sin. When David sat upon the Throne in worldly honor and prosperity / he could nonetheless lie down in the dust and spiritual shame / and this happened before the child was sick. <note>Referring to the son of David and Bathsheba, whose illness and death followed David's repentance.</note> And therefore if you find upon your examination that you mourned and wept over your sins and corruptions / before you had this or any other difficulty lying upon you / then you may conclude / that your sorrow is more over sin than over worldly tribulations; but now / where a person pretends to mourn over sin / whereas his sins have never before in all the time of his life disturbed him / nor have his corruptions ever grieved his heart / or burdened his conscience before / this shows that such a person weeps and mourns more over his tribulations / than over his sins.

Secondly, a person mourns more over sin / than over tribulation / when he takes more care to put his sins away from his soul / than the tribulations from his body. When it is the greatest desire of your soul / and the most care of your heart / to have your sins rather than your tribulations taken away from you. Hos. 14:3. <note>In modern Bibles, this is Hosea 14:2.</note> *Take these words with you, and return to the Lord: say to him; take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously;* <note>original: "neemt weg alle ongerechtigheyt, en geeft het goede"</note> they did not say / O Lord take away the tribulations. Although they were then burdened by them; but Lord take away the iniquity of your servants, and give what is good; it is a sign that he mourns not over sin / but over his misery / who would rather be delivered from his difficulties than from his sins. Thus it was with Pharaoh when the judgments of God lay upon him / such as the Thunder / Hail / Frogs / Lice / and the death of the Beasts / Etc. Then he said to Moses; *Pray fervently to the Lord, (for it is enough) that there be no more mighty thundering or hail,* Exod. 9:28. He requests of Moses that he should pray to God to take the plagues away from him / but

<column-break/>

he never desires or requests that his sin / and the hardness of his heart might be taken away. In which you might cry out / O Lord do take this misery / or those tribulations away from me; but you can never pray to be delivered from your sins / and to bring your corruptions into subjection: this is proof that you mourn more over the tribulation than over the sin.

Thirdly, when the committing of a sin / and the deliverance from a tribulation stand against one another / if you then would rather have the tribulation continue over you / than commit a sin: that shows that you are more grieved over the sin / than over the tribulation. As for example / when a person is brought to a low estate / and is greatly diminished in the world / so that his trade fails him / and his family has perished / if that person is more disturbed over his sin / which brought him into that state / than over the tribulation itself / then he shall not commit a sin to restore his loss / even though he knows / that the committing of such a sin would do so; likewise in any other circumstances: just as I have read a story of a Nobleman / whose Son and Heir was thought to be bewitched / and therefore was advised by some to go to a Sorceress / to help his Son and to un-bewitch him again; he answered / no / by no means / for he would rather the Sorceress had his Son / than the Devil. <note>The father likely meant he would rather his son suffer a physical affliction than for the father to sin by dealing with the devil's agents.</note> But if you make no Conscience of committing a sin / to take your tribulations away from you / if you will break the decree of the commandment to avoid a small painful path of tribulations / then it is a sign that you are more grieved over your miseries and difficulties than over your sins / and that you never mourned as much over your corruptions / as you have done over your chastisements, Job 36:21. Those who in their distresses go to Sorceresses / Fortune-tellers and practitioners of the Devil's arts / (as Saul went to the Witch at Endor) show that they mourn more over the tribulations than over the sins.

Fourthly, if you mourn over sin / then the true joy / which proceeds from the forgiveness of sins / shall swallow up your sorrow / which comes upon you through any worldly misery or tribulation / and shall likewise make you undergo the same with patience. The person mourns most over sin / who / when his sins are forgiven / is least grieved over outward tribulations; when the comfort of the forgiveness of his sins rejoices him more / than the continuation of any tribulation can grieve him: as in Isa. 33:24. *No inhabitant shall say, I am sick, for the people that dwell therein, shall have forgiveness of iniquity.* These people were like a ship in a great tempest / her mast broken / her sails lost / and all her tackle was gone: Well! What was it then? Nonetheless / *No inhabitant shall say, I am sick,* because the Lord has forgiven them their sins. He does not say / they shall not say, that they were sick; But / *They shall not say, that they are sick,* because their sins are forgiven. The tasting of the forgiveness of their sins would take away the feeling of the pains of their present sorrows. Now / when it is thus situated with you /

so it is a proof that you are more troubled by sin than by tribulation. But a person is moved more by his tribulations than by his sins when he wishes to be sorrowful, even though he is assured that his sins are forgiven and it is manifest that he is an heir of glory. All the convictions he has regarding the forgiveness of his sins do not in the least soften his impatience. And this is as far as concerns the second warning, namely, that you must take care not to regard as mourning over sin that which is only over some outward difficulty or tribulation.

But before I proceed to the third warning, grant me the liberty to apply this to your hearts with a word or two; what has been discussed regarding these two cases of Conscience <note>A "case of conscience" (Latin: *casus conscientiae*) refers to a specific spiritual dilemma where a believer seeks to apply moral laws to a particular situation.</note> must serve first as a reproof, and then secondly as an exhortation.

**Use.** First, for a reproof of those who, instead of weeping over tribulations as if they wept not, <margin>30</margin> mourn immoderately as if their entire body were a lump of ice that turns entirely into tears when the Sun of tribulation shines upon it. How many people are there who are so easily drawn to immoderate sorrow by worldly miseries? We commonly say a person must weep so that he waters his plants; and you know, when you make your plants in your garden too wet, you drown and kill them. So also, when you weep too much over your tribulations, you drown your plants and ruin your beasts, and make them unfit for any spiritual use.

Secondly, it reproves those who, when they come to mourn and weep over their sins and the desolation of their hearts, stand so stiff regarding their tears that they weep as if they wept not. A minor outward sigh or a forced tear is the greatest sorrow many people have over sin; man is like a cloud and will easily pour out tears over some outward tribulation, but regarding sin, he is like a rock and cannot let a single drop fall for it, nor for the displeasure and dishonoring of God. Many are like Louis XI, King of France, <note original="Lowys de elffste Koningh van Vrankrijck">Louis XI (r. 1461–1483) was often depicted in Protestant literature as a superstitious or hypocritical figure.</note> who always wore a crucifix on his hat, and when he committed a gross and heinous sin, he took it from his hat and bowed before his crucifix and prayed for forgiveness; that being done, he thought all was well for the time being. Most people are inclined to have a poor and outward sorrow over their sins: well then, how do you understand the Apostle’s <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> order and instruction here? When you weep over sin as if you wept not, yet you are exceedingly immoderate in your worldly sorrows.

**Use.** Secondly, it must serve as an exhortation; see then that you behold your sins as greater matter for sorrow and pain than all the tribulations that happen to you: O weep, and weep again over them; for your sins are worse than all your external difficulties; and to better encourage you to this duty, consider then:

<column-break/>

First, that sin is the cause of all your miseries and tribulations; had it not been for sin, you would have undergone no suffering: therefore mourn rather over the cause than over the tribulation itself.

Secondly, tribulations are not as evil as sin, considering that God is the Author of all our tribulations; but sin is such an evil that God does not desire it, even though there is no evil in the City that the Lord does not do; <note>A reference to Amos 3:6, distinguishing between "evil" as suffering (which God permits) and "evil" as sin.</note> that is, He is the Author of the evil of tribulation; yet He does not desire to be the Author of sin.

Thirdly, consider that all outward tribulations can coexist with grace; but some sins are entirely intolerable and cannot coexist with grace. Let your tribulations be ever so great, you can nonetheless, despite all this, be a godly person; you could be as poor as Job, or as miserable as Lazarus, and endure whatever the tribulations must be, yet all this can coexist with grace; but not all sin can coexist with grace, such as the sin against the Holy Spirit, the sin of final impenitence, or final obduracy and hardness of heart; these cannot coexist with grace, and therefore you have more reason to mourn over sin than over tribulations.

Fourthly, consider that tribulations only touch the body, but sin touches the Soul; tribulations can only make the outward man miserable, but sin will destroy the Soul, and the Soul is the most precious part; be therefore convinced and rather lament over your sins and <unclear>corruptions</unclear> / <unclear>o</unclear> <unclear>a</unclear> <unclear>...</unclear> / <unclear>... re</unclear> weep.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "cases of conscience" regarding spiritual sorrow. Having previously warned against mistaking worldly grief for godly sorrow, the author now addresses the specific danger of excessive or immoderate sorrow for sin, defining the boundaries where healthy repentance becomes spiritually harmful.</meta>

# Een Christens onderrichtinge.
# ->A Christian’s Instruction.<-

...so that some might not be in any way swallowed up by too abundant sorrow.

**Secondly**, take this as a conclusion: that there are but few in the world who mourn and are sorrowful over their sins too much. Where there is one who sins by mourning too much over sin, there are thousands and ten thousands who sin by being too little sorrowful; there are but few who are immoderate in their sorrows over sin.

**Thirdly**, consider that none but comfortless, doubting, and despairing sinners are too sorrowful over their sins. Hardened sinners do not mourn at all, and steadfast Christians shall not be too sorrowful; only despondent and despairing sinners are all too sorrowful.

<margin>
3. Case of conscience; namely, when a Christian can be said to be all too sorrowful over sin.
</margin>

Here we now come to the third case of conscience: namely, how or in what case a person can be said to weep and be too sorrowful over sin.

I shall reveal this to you very briefly.

**First**, that sorrow over sin is immoderate which makes a Christian look so much at his corruptions <note>In this context, "corruptions" refers to the inherent flaws and sinful tendencies of human nature.</note> that he overlooks his graces. A child mourns too much when it whines and cries so, and fills its eyes so with tears, that it cannot see its letters nor read its book. So a Christian also mourns too much over his corruptions when he cannot see, nor thank God for, the blessings He gives him.

**Secondly**, you mourn too much over sin when it condemns and obscures your evidences of Heaven; when a Christian casts his eyes so upon his sins, and discovers such cause for sorrow and pain from them, that he never looks into his own heart to see what cause for joy he has there—in enjoying the assurance of his part and portion in Christ, and a rightful title to glory. Beloved, God does not want one grace to overthrew another. Sorrow over sin is a grace; but God does not want this grace to push out spiritual joy. When a Christian so mourns over sin that he casts away all hope of Heaven, then his sorrow is immoderate; when he so mourns and weeps that he cannot read his evidences <note>Evidence refers to the "proofs" or signs in a believer's life that they are truly saved.</note> of Heaven.

**Thirdly**, sorrow over sin is immoderate when it discourages the soul from coming to Christ for pardon and forgiveness; when a person so mourns over sin that he does not dare venture toward Jesus Christ to look up for mercy, and to apply a promise to his comfort. When a sinner goes to work in this way, then he mourns immoderately. If the children of Israel, when they were bitten by the fiery serpents in the wilderness, had not had the boldness to look upon the bronze serpent, they could have had no healing. So also, when our sorrow over sin makes us so that we cannot look up to Christ for forgiveness, then it is disordered and immoderate. Sorrows and tears over sin are never well-placed until they are like water-streams to drive us toward Christ.

**Fourthly**, sorrow over sin is immoderate when it so overwhelms you that you can take no comfort in the outward blessings which God has given you, such as food, land, grain, wine, or the like.

<column-break/>

When a Christian's sorrow so stifles his soul that he cannot take that outward joy and that permissible pleasantness, which God allows, in worldly comforts, then your sorrow is immoderate. Although many believe that God allows sin to be so bitter to them, yet it is not so; you must be sorrowful over sin, and yet take comfort in the outward blessings which God gives you.

**Fifthly**, sorrow over sin is immoderate when it makes a person unfit to receive the comforts of the Gospel; when a Christian sees his sin as so great and his state as so sorrowful that if you apply the promises of the Gospel to him, they are as if of no value to him, and he thinks they do not belong to him, and therefore can take no comfort nor taste in any of them. When a person, because of his sins, sets himself entirely and obstinately against the comforts of the Gospel, then his sorrow is immoderate. Thus it was with Asaph, *Psalm 77:3*. *I was troubled* (he says) *and my soul refused to be comforted.* <note>The author quotes the Dutch Statenvertaling version of Psalm 77; in most English Bibles, this is verse 2.</note> When a person is in a sorrowful state and yet refuses to be comforted, then his sorrow is immoderate.

**Sixthly**, sorrow over sin is immoderate when it makes a person unfit to fulfill his required duty, whether in his general or particular calling <note>A "calling" or "vocation" refers to one's station in life. The "general calling" is the duty shared by all Christians to pray and worship; the "particular calling" is one's specific job or role in society.</note>. When it makes him unfit for the duties of his general calling as a Christian, so that he cannot pray, nor read, nor speak, nor hear God's Word, but lies alone in a corner and will not allow anyone to comfort him or associate with him—that sorrow which makes a person unfit for holy duties is a disordered sorrow. *Psalm 77:4. I was overwhelmed and did not speak.* Namely, in prayer to God. And so again, that sorrow which makes a person unfit for the duties of his particular calling as a man, so that he cannot work, study, do his trade, or attend to his private affairs—that sorrow is an immoderate sorrow. God requires of us to work in our callings as well as to work out our salvation; and therefore, that sorrow which hinders and makes us unfit for it is too excessive and immoderate. And thus I have shown you when sorrow over sin is immoderate and all too disordered. I have given you only the main points of the matter, and so I have now finished with the resolution of the third case of conscience.

**Use.** We come now to the application: if it is so, that a Christian should take care not only to avoid mourning too much over tribulations, but also over sin, then take care that you do not twist this teaching. Take care not to be obstinate, perverse, and hardened of heart in sin. Although I tell you that Christians must not be immoderate in their sorrows over sin, yet I do not say that the godless should be obstinate and bold of heart in sin, and should not [mourn] over sin at all—

...to mourn. No; it would be good for them if they could weep bitterly over their sins; and therefore, you obstinate and bold sinners, take care that you do not abuse this teaching. And conversely, you upon whom sin weighs as your greatest burden, and to whom every molehill of sin seems like a mountain: take care not to be so crushed by sadness that you can see no comfort at all in Christ, nor in the promises of salvation through him. Instead, behold the Lord Jesus Christ, and see that there is more in Christ to save you than there is in yourself to condemn you. Although there is an abundance of corruption within you, there is nevertheless a perfection of satisfaction <note>In 17th-century theology, "satisfaction" refers to Christ's payment for human sin on the cross.</note> in Christ; he is mighty to save all those who shall come to God through him. All you who have laid hold of Christ, and weep neither too much nor too little over your sins, do not say: "I wish neither to mourn nor to shed any tears at all over them." For just as the blood of Christ was shed for our sins, so we must keep our tears to pour out over them; yet we must not be so grieved by them as to be discouraged from going to Christ, or to let our evidences of Heaven be darkened.

We have now only one application of exhortation <note>A "use" or "application" was the part of a sermon where the preacher gave practical advice to the congregation.</note> remaining, and with that, we shall conclude this topic. If it is the bounden duty of Christians to weep as though they wept not (for that is the aim of the text), then let me, for the sake of Christ’s mercy, advise all of you who are God’s people to strive to follow this Apostolic rule: that you carry yourselves in mourning as those who have a better hope and better things to look toward than anything here below. And just as I have previously given you twelve considerations to soften and restrain your immoderate sadness, I shall now give you seven or eight more considerations to preserve you from excessive grief; which, if you take them earnestly to heart, can be great aids in keeping you from breaking out into immoderate sorrow, no matter what condition may befall you.

<margin>
Various considerations to preserve a person from immoderate sorrow.
</margin>

**First**, reflect or consider that immoderate sorrow over worldly miseries is proof of a total lack of grace, or otherwise of an exceptional weakness of grace. **First**, it sometimes signifies a total lack of grace. In this situation, it is with a Christian as it is with the rusty hinges of a door: when you open or close the door, they will creak and make a noise; but if you rub some oil on them, it is finished. So it is often with Christians: God cannot touch them with the rod of affliction without them crying out, being immoderate in their sorrows and impatient under God’s hand; and the reason for this is that they do not have the oil of grace. Or, if it is not proof of a total lack of grace, it is nonetheless a sign of a great weakness of grace. I have often noticed in the streets that the wheels of a new wagon will make a noise and a racket as it goes along; but an old wagon moves along quietly. So also, if you—when God sends you afflictions—are like the new wagon, if you cry out and

<column-break/>

mourn immoderately under His hand, it is proof that you are but a new and a weak Christian. "He who faints in the day of adversity," says Solomon, "has little strength." <note>original: "heeft kleyne sterckte" — a reference to Proverbs 24:10.</note> But a Christian who has been long practiced and is well-experienced in difficulties and afflictions—you may lay a great and heavy burden upon him, but he will not make an outcry over it.

**Secondly**, to preserve yourself from immoderate sorrow, consider that whatever events befall you in the world, they are but the revelations and executions of God’s will, which is the rule of order and righteousness; His dealings are in themselves right and good. If God’s will is done, even if it conflicts with your own will, it does not matter. This was what kept David from immoderate sorrow, 2 Samuel 12:21, 22. David’s servants wondered why he fasted and wept for his child while it was alive, and when it was dead, he stood up and ate bread and was no longer grieved. And David said: "While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, who knows if the Lord might be gracious to me, that the child may live? But now it is dead; why should I fast now? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me." Now I see that the will of God is accomplished; why should I be grieved about that? "I was dumb, I did not open my mouth; because you did it," Psalm 39:10.

**Thirdly**, consider that before your conversion, you never mourned over the lack of grace and spiritual mercies. Why then, after your conversion, should you weep over worldly things when you enjoy spiritual mercies? Consider: "Before my conversion, I was content with outward worldly comforts, and was never disturbed over the lack of grace, the hope of Heaven, or the lack of reconciliation with God; I was never grieved over these things." And seeing that when I was without Christ, I did not mourn over the lack of these things, shall I now, when I have Christ, be grieved over the lack of ordinary and common blessings of worldly things? It is the bounden duty of a Christian to take revenge upon himself with a holy indignation: "If before my conversion I could not mourn over the lack of grace, then I will not now—while I have grace—be grieved over the missing of outward comforts," seeing that there is infinitely more reason to mourn over the lack of spiritual than temporal mercies.

**Fourthly**, to keep worldly sorrow out, consider that God never sends His people any outward misery or oppression except it be on account of sin, whether for punishment or for the prevention and purging of sin.

**First**, for the punishment of your sins; and if it is for the punishment of your sins, then if you mourn over anything, mourn over your sins which were the cause, rather than over the affliction, which is but a consequence of your sins. ...the mourning. No; it would be good for them if they could weep bitterly over their sins; but for you, obstinate and presumptuous sinners, beware that you do not misuse this doctrine. And again, you who hold sin as your greatest burden, and to whom every molehill <note>Original: "mol-hoop." The author uses this image to contrast small sins with the "mountain" of guilt a sensitive conscience might feel.</note> of sin is like a mountain, beware of being so dejected by sorrow that you can see no comfort at all in *Christ*, and in the promises of salvation through him. Instead, behold the Lord *Jesus Christ*, and see that there is more in *Christ* to save you than there is in yourself to condemn you. Although there is an abundance of corruption in you, there is nevertheless a perfection of satisfaction <note>A theological term (original: "genoeg-doeninge") referring to Christ’s atonement being "enough" to pay the debt of sin.</note> in *Christ*; he is powerful enough to save all who shall come to God through him. All you who are *Christ’s* own, weep neither too much nor too little over your sins. Do not say, "I wish neither to mourn nor to shed any tears at all over them"; for just as the blood of *Christ* was shed for our sins, so we ought to pour out our tears over them. Nonetheless, we must not be so grieved over them as to discourage ourselves from going to *Christ*, or to obscure our evidences of Heaven.

<margin>Various considerations to preserve a person from immoderate sorrow.</margin>

We have now only one more useful exhortation, and with that we shall depart from this subject. If it is the bounden duty of Christians to weep as if not weeping (for that is the aim of the text <note>The author is referencing 1 Corinthians 7:30: "and those who mourn as though they were not mourning."</note>), then let me, for the sake of the compassions of *Christ*, advise all of you who are God’s people to strive to follow this Apostolic rule: that you would carry yourselves as those who have a better hope, and better things to look forward to, than any things here below. And just as I have previously given you twelve considerations to soften and restrain your immoderate sorrow, I shall now give you seven or eight more considerations to preserve you from immoderate grief. If you take these earnestly to heart, they can be great helps in keeping you from breaking out into immoderate sorrow, whatever state may befall you.

**First.** Consider or reflect that immoderate sorrow over worldly miseries is a proof of a total lack of grace, or otherwise of an exceptional weakness of grace. First, it sometimes signifies a total lack of grace. In this situation, it is with a Christian as it is with the rusty hinges of a door: when you open or close the door, they will creak and make a noise; but if you rub some oil on them, it is finished. So it is also often with Christians: God cannot touch them with the rod of affliction but they cry out and are immoderate in their sorrows, and impatient under God’s hand; and the reason for this is that they do not have the oil of grace. Or, if it is not proof of a total lack of grace, it is nevertheless a sign of a great weakness of grace. I have often noticed on the streets that the wheels of a new wagon make a noise and a racket as they move along, but an old wagon moves forward quietly. So also, if you—when God sends you afflictions—are like the new wagon; if you cry out and

<column-break/>

mourn immoderately under His hand, it is proof that you are but a new and a weak Christian. He who faints in the day of adversity, says *Salomon*, has small strength. But a Christian who has been long accustomed and is well-experienced in difficulties and afflictions—you may lay a great and heavy burden upon him, but he will not make a fuss <note>Original: "beslag," meaning a stir or a commotion.</note> over it.

**Secondly**, to preserve you from immoderate sorrow, reflect that whatever miseries befall you in the world, they are but the revelations and executions of God’s will, which is the rule of order and justice. His administrations are in themselves right and good; if God’s will is done, even if it conflicts with your own will, it is of no consequence. This was what kept *David* from immoderate sorrow, *2 Samuel 12:21-22*. *David’s* servants wondered why he fasted and wept for his child while it lived, yet when it was dead, he stood up and ate bread and was no longer grieved. And *David* said: "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, 'Who knows, the Lord may be gracious to me, that the child may live.' But now he is dead; why should I fast now? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me." Now I see that the will of *God* is fulfilled; why should I be grieved over it? "I am mute, I will not open my mouth; because You have done it," *Psalm 39:9*.

**Thirdly**, consider that through your conversion, you never mourned over the lack of grace and spiritual mercies. Why then, after your conversion, should you weep over worldly things when you enjoy spiritual mercies? Remember: "Before my conversion, I was content with outward worldly comforts, and was never disturbed by the lack of grace, the hope of Heaven, or the lack of reconciliation with God; over these things I was never grieved." Since I did not mourn over the lack of these when I was without *Christ*, shall I now, when I have *Christ*, be grieved over the lack of the ordinary and common blessings of worldly things? It is the bounden duty of a Christian to take a fierce indignation against himself. If I could not mourn over the lack of grace before my conversion, then I will not now, while I have grace, be grieved over the missing of outward comforts, seeing as there is infinitely more reason to mourn over the lack of spiritual than temporal mercies.

**First**, as a punishment for your sins; and if it is as a punishment for your sins, then if you mourn over anything, mourn over your sins which were the cause, rather than over the affliction, which is but a consequence of your sins. ...with humiliation; but look with loathing upon sin: we have no reason to complain about our afflictions. <margin>Lamentations 3:39.</margin>
> Why then does a living man complain? Let every man complain because of his sins.

In this matter, you ought rather to mourn over your sins than over your punishments.

And secondly, if it is not for punishment, then it is for the prevention of sin, to keep you back from sinning: And this was the end for which God punished Job, <margin>Job 33:17.</margin> it was so that He might turn man from his work and hide pride from the man. Therefore, though God takes away your status, friends, or any outward comfort, as long as it is to prevent sin and to keep you from Hell and damnation, you have no reason for sorrow. If the Doctor lets your blood <note>Original: "bloet laat." Bloodletting was a standard medical practice intended to balance the body's fluids and prevent inflammation.</note> to prevent pleurisy, would you be angry with him for it? Certainly not; so too God never takes any outward comfort from His people except in His mercy, so that He might prevent sin thereby.

Or,

Thirdly, if it is not for the punishment or prevention of sin, then it is for the purification of sins, as in <margin>Isaiah 27:9.</margin> "Therefore by this shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged; and this is all the fruit, that he shall take away his sin." A man will not be grieved that the Physician makes him sick and causes pain in his bowels, because it is done to cleanse him of those evil and harmful humors <note>The "humors" refers to the ancient medical theory that health was governed by four bodily fluids; an imbalance or "evil humor" was thought to cause disease.</note>. Beloved, your miseries are but **Purge-pills** to cleanse you of your deceits. All worldly afflictions are either for the punishment, prevention, or purification of sin, and therefore we have cause to bear them with patience.

Sixthly, consider that God turns all worldly miseries and losses for His people into spiritual gain; you shall never be a loser through your afflictions. Just as when a poor man who is in debt and has a great lack of money comes to a rich man and makes his condition known, praying for assistance; if that rich man immediately goes to his chest, fetches a bag of money, and throws it to him, the poor man would not look upon this as a wrong or an injustice done to him, but would rather be thankful for it. So God turns all our seeming miseries and afflictions into actual and spiritual gain. <margin>Philippians 1:19.</margin>
> I know, says Paul, that this shall turn to my salvation.

<margin>Romans 8:28.</margin>
> And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, namely to them who are called according to His purpose.

Although we cannot see how it shall happen, we are in this matter like little children, who, when they see a beautiful heap of sweet roses lying on the table, and their mother goes and puts them in a mortar and crushes them all to pieces, the child will cry and think the mother is destroying them; nonetheless, she does it to make a **Conserve** <note>Original: "Conserf." A sweet, medicinal preserve made by crushing herbs or petals with sugar.</note> from them, so that they might be more wholesome and durable. So we; we think we have comforts like beds of roses, and when the

<column-break/>

Lord takes the same from us and breaks them all to pieces, we are inclined to judge that they are all destroyed and ruined, and we are grieved thereby, whereas God intends to work the same out for our greater benefit and advantage.

Seventhly, read of the contemplation and the holy meditation of the joy and the glory of Heaven. And this shall be a great means to keep worldly sorrow out; the glory and the blessedness of Heaven shall so transport the soul of a Christian with spiritual joy that he shall not easily be overwhelmed with worldly sorrow. I have read in one of the **School-Teachers** <note>Refers to the Scholastic theologians, such as Thomas Aquinas or others who taught in the medieval universities.</note> who was of this opinion: that the reason why Adam, in the state of innocence, was so indifferent to his nakedness was because he was so taken up with exceptional fellowship and communion with God. So also, if you were now taken up with a greater elevation toward God and the realization of Glory, even if you had nothing here in the world, you would nonetheless think that you lacked nothing. The state of glory and blessedness in Heaven shall make you look over the head of all miseries and afflictions here below. It is said of Paul that he was caught up into the third heaven and saw unspeakable things; but whether it happened in the body or out of the body, he could not say.

That is, he saw so much glory, and was so taken up with Heavenly joys, that he could not say whether he was in the flesh or not; it made him forget all his difficulties and miseries that he had here below. I am reminded that I have read in Jerome what advice he gave in his time to a young man who was so greatly oppressed with sorrow and pain over worldly miseries.
> Just go, he said, now and then on a journey or two into Paradise, and then you shall never think of the wilderness, nor be troubled by the miseries of the Desert.

Oh, beloved! If only your soul had this heart of divine speculation and meditation, so that you might have an experienced knowledge of the joys of Heaven! Oh, this would keep you from mourning any more over worldly miseries. When Christ was transfigured on the Mount, Peter said to Him:
> Master, Master, it is good for us to be here; let us make here three tabernacles: one for Thee, one for Moses, and one for Elias.

He was so lifted up by the vision of Heaven that he never thought that he was then on a barren mountain, or from what lack and distress they had been driven there. I have repeated to you before what I have read of the **Eagle**: that she is not like other birds that fly in the sky; for while all other birds, when they are injured or hungry, will cry, mourn, and make a fuss, the eagle, when she is injured, will fly upward to comfort herself with the warm rays of the sun. Oh, beloved! If you would, like the eagle, fly upward in divine meditations and thoughts of Heaven’s glory and blessedness; Oh, this would greatly strengthen you against worldly sorrow!

<margin>Isaiah 27:9.</margin>
Thirdly, **If it is not for punishment or prevention of sin, then it is for the cleansing of sins;** as through this the unrighteousness of Jacob shall be reconciled, and this is all the fruit: that He shall take away his sin. A man shall not be sad that the Physician makes him sick and causes pain in his bowels, because it is done to cleanse him of those evil and harmful humors <note>In early medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to control health and temperament.</note>. Beloved, your miseries are but Purging-pills to cleanse you of your corruptions. All worldly afflictions are either for punishment, prevention, or the purging out of sin; and therefore we have cause to bear them patiently.

<margin>Philippians 1:19.</margin>
Sixthly <note>The text skips "fourthly" and "fifthly," likely continuing a numbered list from a previous section or column not shown here.</note>, **Consider that God turns all worldly miseries and losses into spiritual gain for His people; you shall never be a loser through your afflictions.** Just as when a poor man who is in debt and has a great lack of money comes to a rich man and makes his state known to him, praying for support; if that rich man immediately goes to his chest and fetches a bag of gold and throws it to him, the poor man would not look upon this as a wrong or an injustice done to him, but would rather be thankful for it. So God turns all our seeming miseries and afflictions into actual and spiritual gain. <margin>Romans 8:28.</margin> I know, says Paul, that this shall turn to my salvation <note>original: "ter Zaligheydt gedyen sal"</note>. And Romans 8:28: And we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good, namely to those who are called according to His purpose. Although we cannot see how it shall happen, we are in this matter like small children, who, when they see a beautiful heap of sweet roses lying on the table and their mother goes and puts them in a mortar and stamps them all to pieces, the child will cry and think that the mother is wasting them; notwithstanding, she does it to make a Conserve <note>A medicinal jam or preserve made from crushed petals and sugar.</note> out of them, so that they might be more useful and durable. So we think that we have comforts like beds of roses, and when the

<column-break/>

Lord takes the same from us and breaks them all to pieces, we are inclined to judge that they are all wasted and spoiled, and we thereby ruined; whereas God intends to work the same out for our greater benefit and advantage.

Seventhly, **Read in the contemplation and the holy meditation of the joy and the glory of Heaven.** And this shall be a great means to keep out worldly sadness; the glory and the blessedness of Heaven shall so carry away the soul of a Christian with spiritual joy that he shall not easily be overwhelmed with worldly sadness. I have read in one of the Scholastic Teachers <note>Referring to the "School-Leeraars," medieval theologians like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus.</note> who was of this opinion: that the reason why Adam in the state of innocence was so unaware of his nakedness was because he was so taken up with a special intercourse and communion with God. So too, if you were now taken up with more frequent interaction with God and the possession of Glory, even if you had nothing here in the world, you would nevertheless think that you lacked nothing. The state of glory and blessedness in Heaven shall make you look over the head of all miseries and afflictions down here. It is said of Paul that he was caught up into the third Heaven and saw unspeakable things; but whether it happened in the body or out of the body, he could not say.

**That is, he saw so much glory, and was so taken up with heavenly joys,** that he could not say whether he was in the flesh or not; it made him forget all his difficulties and miseries that he had here below. I am reminded that I have read in Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), a prominent Church Father.</note> what advice he gave in his time to a young man who was so greatly oppressed with sadness and pain over worldly miseries. "Go but now and then," he said, "on a journey or two into Paradise, then you shall never think of the wilderness, or be troubled by the miseries of the desert." Oh! beloved, if only your soul had this heart for divine <term>speculation<note>In this context, it refers to deep theological meditation or contemplation, rather than financial risk.</note></term> and meditation, so that you might have a worthy knowledge of the joys of Heaven! Oh! this would keep you from mourning any longer over worldly miseries. When Christ was transfigured on the Mount, then Peter said to him: "Master, Master, it is good for us to be here; let us make here three tabernacles, one for Thee, one for Moses, and one for Elias." He was so lifted up by the vision of Heaven that he never thought that he was then on a barren mountain, or from what lack and distress they had been driven there. I have told you before what I have read of the Eagle: that she is not like other birds that fly in the air; for where all other birds, when they are injured or hungry, will cry, mourn, and make a fuss, there the Eagle, when she is injured, will fly upwards to comfort herself with the warm rays of the sun. Oh! beloved, if you would, like the Eagle, fly upwards in divine meditations and thoughts of Heaven’s glory and blessedness, Oh! this would greatly strengthen you against worldly sadness.

Eighthly, remember that your sins demand more tears from you than you are capable of shedding; therefore, do not waste them on the things of the world. Beloved, if you could dissolve yourself in tears over your sins, it would all be too little to express your sorrow and grief over them; indeed, even if every tear you shed were an ocean or a sea, it would be too little to pour out over sin. Tears are sweet waters, and it is a pity to wash houses <note>The author uses "houses" or "earthly places" as a metaphor for worldly concerns, suggesting that precious tears of repentance shouldn't be wasted on mundane grief.</note> with them; save them for your sins, for they have a better and greater need of them. And even if you had still more tears, it would all be too little: Yes, even if your head were a fountain, and your eyes rivers of tears <note>A reference to Jeremiah 9:1: "Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears."</note>, they would all not be enough to pour out over those manifold sins and iniquities that you have committed against God.

And thus I have concluded the first part of my text: *and those who weep, as though they wept not.*

->1 Cor. 7: 30, 31.<-

> And those who weep, as though they wept not; and those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and those who buy, as though they possessed not; and those who use this world, as not misusing it. For the fashion of this world passes away.

<margin>VI. Sermon.</margin>
WE proceed now to the second part of the Apostolic instruction: *And those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not.* If your state here in the world is sorrowful, miserable, and full of sighing, then it is your bounden duty to *weep, as though you wept not.* But when you catch a wind of prosperity and happiness, and enjoy the comforts of this world in abundance, then you must *rejoice, as though you rejoiced not*; that is, you must rejoice with moderation and discretion. And the point of instruction that I shall give you here is this:

*Doctrine:* That it is the bounden duty of Christians not only to take care that they are not immoderate in worldly sorrow over outward miseries, but that they must also take care that they are not immoderate in worldly joy over outward comforts. We can greatly enjoy all comforts under the Sun.

In the pursuit of this doctrine, I shall dispatch these two or three questions:
1. I shall show you when your joy is immoderate.
2. I shall propose some rules to keep your joy in check, so that you are not too greatly rejoiced in the comforts of this life.
3. I shall give this to you by way of utility and application.

For this time, I shall not come to the handling of any of these things; but I shall first, according to my ordinary method, set down six or seven resolutions.

And first, take this as a resolution: that although Christians must take care—

<column-break/>

<margin>Various resolutions regarding immoderate joy over worldly comforts.</margin>
—that they are not immoderate in their joy over worldly comforts, nevertheless, you must know that God allows you to rejoice in the outward comforts which He gives you here in the world. Solomon says in Eccl. 3:4, *There is a time to weep, and a time to laugh.* And chapter 9:7, 9, *Go your way, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart... enjoy life with the wife whom you love.* So also chapter 7:14, *In the day of prosperity be joyful.* As also Deut. 12:7, *And there you shall eat before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you put your hand unto, wherein the Lord your God has blessed you.* This resolution is necessary for sorrowful, melancholic Christians who, even if they enjoy an abundance of worldly comforts, nevertheless do not wish to rejoice in them at all. Beloved, God allows you to rejoice.

Secondly, consider that religion does not call out or abolish worldly joy, but only regulates and moderates it. It is not like a weeding hook <note>original: "Wiet-mes"</note> to pull up your joy by the root; but like a pruning knife <note>original: "snoep-mes" — in this context, a tool for trimming excess growth.</note> to prune away the immoderation of it, and to preserve your joy in its proper fitness. I present this to you for those prejudices that many people take up against religion or godliness, as if it made a person melancholic. They are inclined to think that once they begin to be religious, they must then abandon and forsake all worldly comforts, and forever shake their hands of all the pleasures of this life. Beloved, religion does not abolish your joys, but regulates them; indeed, being religious increases your joys rather than diminishes them in any way. When God made a covenant with Abraham, He promised him a son, and God gave him his name, saying, *you shall call his name Isaac,* which signifies "laughter" <note>original: "Isaak, welke lacchen betekpent"</note> (Gen. 17:19). This is to show that after you are in a covenant with God, you may have joy and pleasure; and therefore, do not harbor such evil thoughts of religion as to imagine that you must shake your hands of joy when you take up religion.

Thirdly, take this as a resolution: that the worldly joy of the wicked is often mixed with more internal stings and pains of the spirit than the worldly joy of the godly, as is seen in Prov. 14:13, *Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.* And 2 Cor. 5:12, where the Apostle speaks of some who *gloried in appearance, and not in heart.* The joy of the wicked is only in appearance, and not in reality. When they are in their greatest joy and delight, even then they have some internal stings and distress of conscience which embitters and unsettles them. A man can have a fine shoe on his foot, but no one knows where it pinches him except the one who wears it. The joy of the wicked is like the sorrow of the godly: the joy of the wicked is only in appearance—

Fourthly, a trivial matter will disturb the worldly joy of the godless more than the joy of the godly: I mean that outward worldly joy which he has here in this world. How quickly was Haman’s joy broken off, Esther 5:13, notwithstanding he had such great cause for joy in the glory of his riches / and the multitude of his children / and his promotion in the Court above all the Princes and servants of the King: Nevertheless, because poor Mordecai did not bow / nor show him any reverence / he was so displeased that he could take no pleasure in all that he possessed. <margin>Joys to be punished. <note>Original Latin: *Gaudia punienda*.</note></margin>

Such things are meant to be grieved over; these people go to hell with joy.

Secondly, You must also not rejoice in the sins of other people / they are never permitted by God to be a matter for your joy; it is said of love in 1 Cor. 13:6 / that **it does not rejoice in iniquity, but it rejoices in the truth.** That is / love toward someone / gives us no cause to rejoice in their sins but in their well-doing. Romans 1, at the end / those are not only condemned by God who do the same things as the godless; but also those who have pleasure in those who do them. Not only covenant-breakers, merciless, whisperers, backbiters, haters of God, Revilers, proud, boastful, inventors of evil

things, etc. Not only those / who do these things / but they also are condemned who have pleasure in those who do them. This is rather a cause for sorrow / than for joy. Psalm 119:136. **Rivers of water run down from my eyes, because they do not keep your law.** And 2 Pet. 2:8. there it is said that Lot **tormented his righteous soul** by seeing and hearing the godless deeds of the lawless. And on this ground Mr. Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch.</note> condemns the comedians or stage-players / they are for the most part displays of human roguery and godlessness / to stir the spectators to joy and pleasure / and are therefore unlawful / and ought not to be used.

Thirdly, You must not rejoice at all over the punishment of sin / in irrational creatures. And on this ground this author also condemns the use of bull-baiting or bear- and cock-fighting / because it is a rejoicing in that which is a product of sin; for it was sin that first brought the enmity between the bear and the dog / and between creature and creature: sin was the cause of all discord and contrariety between the creatures / and therefore it is not permitted for us to rejoice in that which is a consequence or effect of our own sin. Truly / regarding bull-baiting / more could be said / it can make the bull more fit for human food <note>There was a contemporary folk belief that "baiting" or stressing a bull before slaughter made the meat more tender.</note> / but to make the bull bite simply out of pleasure / is unlawful: likewise falconry and hunting are permitted / because those creatures cannot be caught without it. But all those who take pleasure in stage-players / and make the sin of other people the matter of their joy / or who frequent or practice bear- and cock-fighting / and such like / are to be rebuked here; and be advised that you desist from it in the future.

This author likewise condemns / on this ground / the nobles who keep fools <note>Refers to the practice of keeping "natural fools" (people with intellectual disabilities) as court jesters for entertainment.</note> in their houses / to be a game and a pleasure to them. This is not permitted by God / because it is a rejoicing in that which is a punishment of sin in another creature.

Fourthly, You must not rejoice in goods that are ill-gotten: God never allows you to rejoice in goods which are not rightly obtained. Psalm 62:11. **Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.** And Hab. 2:13, 14, 15. **You are of purer eyes than to behold evil, and cannot look on iniquity: wherefore do you look upon those who deal treacherously? If, in buying and selling, you overreach or deceive a person, and when you have obtained a good penny’s worth, you then **laugh in your fists** <note>original: "in u vuysten te lacchen"; a Dutch idiom meaning to chuckle secretly or gloat over a deceptive success</note>—oh, that is very evil. Fifthly, You must not rejoice over the oppressions and the suffering of God’s People: this is what the Lord condemns the **Edomites** <note>The descendants of Esau, often portrayed as the historical enemies of Israel</note> for, Obadiah 1:12: **But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress.** And so forth; and so the Lord threatens Mount Seir and Edom because of their hatred toward Israel, and their rejoicing over them in the day of their distress, Ezekiel 35:15. **As thou didst rejoice,** says God, **at the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so will I do unto thee: Mount Seir, and all Idumea, even all of it, shall be desolate.** And Micah 7:8, there the Church says: **Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise.** Proverbs 17:5: **Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished.** Lamentations 1:21.

Sixthly, You must not even make the miseries and the suffering of your enemies a reason for your joy. Proverbs 24:17: **Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth.** Job was so conscientious in this that he entirely forsook such a practice, Job 31:29: **If I rejoiced,** he says, **at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil**
