**found him**: neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul. Job disapproves of such ways as these: you ought not to make the oppressions and the suffering of your worst enemy whom you have in the world the matter of your joy. But if you look upon them as the enemies of God and of His Church, then you may laugh at their destruction, insofar as they are God's enemies: as David says, **I hate those who hate Thee, yea, I hate them with a perfect hatred.** You must hate no one insofar as he is your enemy or does you any wrong; but you ought to hate him and rejoice over his destruction insofar as he is God’s enemy: none of these six things should be a reason for a Christian's joy.

Lastly, take this as a conclusion: that there are some times and seasons in which it is not seemly to be joyful, even in lawful things; I shall name them to you very briefly.

First, on public and solemn Fast-days and days of humiliation; then must the bride go forth from her chamber, and the bridegroom from his inner room. At such times, expressions of joy are untimely.

And no greater regard for His glittering sword than for a rod that grows on a tree. Nehemiah 1:4, 5: there it is said of Nehemiah, who was the King's cupbearer, that although he was never before sad in the presence of the King; nevertheless, when he heard that the remnant of the captivity were in such great affliction, and Jerusalem’s wall broken down, and her gates burned with fire; that he then sat down, wept, and mourned certain days: and was fasting, and praying before the God of Heaven: and would in no way rejoice.

Thirdly, when God's hand comes to press heavily upon any particular person or household where you live; it ought then to be a house of mourning, Ecclesiastes 7 verse 2.

Fourthly, after a great **falling away** <note>original: "af-val"; apostasy or backsliding</note> from God, after you have fallen into some great and foul sin or transgression, then it is no time for rejoicing. For this you have an excellent passage, Hosea 9:1: **Rejoice not, O Israel, for joy, as other people: for thou hast gone a whoring from thy God.** Other nations may rejoice, but you may not, because you have gone a-whoring after other gods. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of joy and sorrow, specifically addressing how even a person as favored as King David could find no pleasure in his earthly status or talents until his sins were forgiven. It transitions from general observations to the "Seventh Sermon," which warns against immoderate worldly joy using the text of 1 Corinthians 7:30-31.</meta>

# A Christian’s Instruction.

was reconciled. It is very remarkable what you read of David in Psalm 38 and Psalm 32:3, after he had fallen into the sin of impurity <note>original: "onreynigheydt"; here referring to David's adultery with Bathsheba</note>; what a sorrowful man he was for a long time. "I have no rest in my bones," he says, "because of my sin; I roar in the disquiet of my heart." But was all of David's joy turned to wickedness? Yes; for although he had many mercies which could have promoted his joy, he nevertheless could take no comfort in any of them.

There were yet three specific circumstances which could have moved David to break out into worldly joy.

First, he was a King, and sat upon the throne in state, honor, and dignity; yet this could not gladden his soul; rather, he humbled himself and mourned in the dust.

And secondly, David was a musician, a man skilled in playing the harp (1 Samuel 16:17-18); yet the melody of his music could not refresh his heart.

Thirdly, he was by nature of a cheerful disposition, ruddy of face <note>original: "rootachtig van aangesichte"; a reference to the biblical description of David’s youthful appearance</note>, and cheerfully inclined; and yet all these advantages could not make him rejoice. His sin unsettled, defeated, and lay so heavily upon his conscience that, notwithstanding he was a king, a musician, and of a cheerful humor, yet all this could not gladden him, nor could he rejoice until his sin was forgiven. So much for the sixth conclusion.

Seventh, that a person whose humor is cheerful lies open to various evils, such as desire, lightness of spirit, an overflow of words, and the constant seeking of company, etc.

Eighth, mark that there can be an excess in spiritual joy as well as in worldly joy. Although you may think this a very strange conclusion, it is nonetheless true: Christians ought to guard themselves against being immoderate in their spiritual joy just as much as in their worldly sorrow. They are immoderate when spiritual joy makes them thoughtless and imprudent in their duty, when it makes them too eager or hasty, causing them to neglect their calling <note>original: "beroep"; one's daily work or station in life</note>, or to live above the ordinances <note>original: "ordinantien"; the established rules and practices of the church</note>, and the like. In these instances, spiritual joy is immoderate, which I shall prove to you with two passages of Scripture. The first is Acts 12:12, 13, 14. Many were gathered together there, praying in the house of Mary the mother of John; and as Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a maidservant came to listen, named Rhoda. And recognizing Peter's voice, she did not open the gate for joy, but ran inside and announced that Peter stood before the gate. The maidservant was so glad that Peter was at the door that she could not open the door; which in her was a proof that her joy was immoderate, because it made her so thoughtless that she did not open the door when Peter stood outside knocking. She did not open the door for joy—that is the first text to prove that your joy

<column-break/>

can be immoderate. The other passage we find in Luke 24:39-41. This was spoken here after the resurrection of Christ from the dead. When His disciples were together, Christ came and stood in their midst, and showed them His pierced hands and feet, so that they might believe it was He, and that He had risen from the dead; and it is said there that they believed it not for joy. This was a spiritual joy—that Christ had conquered death, hell, and the grave, and had risen from the dead—yet they were so joyful that they could not believe it, and therefore their joy was immoderate. I say this only with regard to young converts, that they can have many sins mixed into their joy. And so, having handled these eight conclusions, I shall proceed to the dispatching of those questions which will be more profitable in the continuation of this teaching: That it is the bounden duty of Christians not only to guard against being immoderate in worldly sorrow over outward miseries, but that they must also take care that they are not immoderate in worldly joy over outward comforts.

->1 Corinthians 7:30-31.<-

>And they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not; And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.

### VII. Sermon.

At this time, I shall speak briefly of these two things. First, I shall show you when your worldly joy is immoderate. And secondly, I shall propose some rules to you to keep your joy in check.

1. Question. When is worldly joy immoderate and unregulated?

<margin>It is shown in eight parts when worldly joy is immoderate.</margin>

Answer. I shall show you this in these eight parts.

First, worldly joy is immoderate when it prevents Godly sorrow over sin; when a person is of such a cheerful and merry humor that he cries out, "Away with sadness!" and "Cast away care!" and refuses to be sorrowful, nor ever wants to have any serious thoughts about sin. Such joy as this is immoderate and sinful. One grace does not overthrow another; when worldly joy overthrows sorrow for sin, then it is unregulated. Thus it was with Belshazzar, Daniel 5:2. He spent his days in mirth and joy; he drank from the golden vessels of the Temple; he made a great feast for his thousand lords; and he was merry with wine. But what was the end of it all? That you can see in the 20th verse: **His heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride.** His joy was immoderate because it hardened his heart and kept him from mourning over sin...

Eighthly, **when people run to worldly joy and pleasures in order to quiet and stifle the miseries and terrors of their consciences.**

When a person has a conviction of conscience—which disturbs and burdens him over some great evil he has done in his life—and he then runs to his recreations and pleasures, or joins merry company to shake off his gloom: this shows that his joy is immoderate. Thus Saul displayed a cheerful and unshakeable spirit in 1 Samuel 16: 15, when an evil spirit from the Lord terrified him. So it was with those idol-worshippers who sacrificed their children to Moloch <note>an ancient deity associated with child sacrifice</note>; they had musical instruments, but for what purpose? Well, it was first to drown out the screams of their children, and secondly to stir themselves to joy and gladness so that their consciences would not terrify them over such a cruel murder as the sacrifice of their children. Well (now beloved), when a sermon has worked upon your soul and touched you unto life, and the Word of God has come upon you with power and worked effectively in you to discover and convict you of your sins—if you then run to your recreations and pleasures, to company, and to theatrical plays <note>original: "Comediant-spelen"</note> or the like, to stifle the thoughts of your sins and to divert and choke the terror and agitation of your consciences: this is a sign that your joy is immoderate and sinful. First, consider that you have better things to rejoice in than anything in this world. You have your election, calling, redemption, and glorification <term>heerlijckmakinge: the final state of perfection in heaven</term>. You have all these objects or grounds to stir you to joy and to fix your pleasure upon. Would someone rejoice in six pennies if he could have as many pieces of gold in their place? Or would someone delight or rejoice in so many pebbles if he could have pearls instead? Or will someone rejoice in a common stone who possesses a diamond? Oh my beloved! You have things of greater value than anything in this world to rejoice in. There is a much greater difference between the things of Heaven—the eternal mercies—and these outward comforts here below than there is between copper and gold, between pebbles and pearls, or between the sun and a candle. And therefore consider: I have a God, Christ, Heaven, and blessedness, forgiveness, reconciliation, sanctification, justification, redemption, and glorification. I have all this to rejoice and be glad in; and therefore, why should I rejoice so much in the things of this world? The disciples of Christ thought themselves to be something and were puffed up because they could cast out devils and perform miracles; but Christ said to them: *Do not rejoice that the devils are subject to you; but rejoice much more that your names are written in heaven* (Luke 10: 20). The more someone is taken up with the esteem and contemplation of Heavenly joy, the less he will estimate or value earthly comforts. The higher one stands, the smaller the things below appear. # A Christian’s Instruction.

2. And those who buy as if not possessing. <note>This refers to 1 Corinthians 7:30, which advises believers to remain spiritually detached from worldly goods.</note> Learn from this that Christians should maintain such a disciplined affection for the things they have obtained through buying and selling, as if they possessed nothing at all.

I shall go over this last teaching only briefly, but I shall emphasize the first one more strongly: That it is the bounden duty of Christians to take care that they do not transgress the rules of Scripture in buying and selling.

And my beloved, please follow me now for a little while, and listen diligently to the handling of this doctrine. This morning I shall set before you some Scriptural rules which you ought to observe in buying; and in the afternoon I shall give you some Scriptural rules for which you must watch, so that you do not transgress them in selling.

<margin>Various Scriptural rules and warnings concerning Buying.</margin>
I shall spend this hour giving you ten special Scriptural rules, which you must take care not to transgress in your buying. As follows:

First, if you do not wish to transgress Scriptural rules in buying, then beware that you do not disparage those goods which you intend to buy, in order to drive the goods to a low market price, and thus to get them at a better bargain, for less than they are worth. For this you have a well-known passage, Proverbs 20:14: *It is naught, it is naught, says the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasts.* In the time of Solomon, people were so ungodly that when they came to the market to buy something, the buyer said, "it is bad, it is bad" <note>original: "het is quaat, het is quaat"</note>; notwithstanding the merchandise was very good and salable, and the seller had set a reasonable price for it. But when he had gone away, then he boasted; that is, he boasted of the good bargain he had made, and what a good contract he had secured, or the like. This then is the first warning to be observed in buying: namely, that in buying you do not disparage the merchandise when it is good and marketable, to get it at a better bargain.

Second, do not say, nor insist, that you will not give more for any goods than you first offered, when afterward you must give more, and do indeed give more. It is a common custom among people to enter a shop and offer money for some goods; the buyer says, "I will not give one penny <note>original: "stuyver," a small Dutch coin</note> more," and the seller says, "I will not take a farthing <note>original: "oortjen," a small copper coin worth a quarter of a stiver</note> less." And yet the buyer gives more than he first offered, and the seller takes less than he had previously held out for. Although this is a common practice, it can nevertheless not be approved as good. It is a very obvious lie and a great sin; therefore, beware of it. If your word has once passed, you are bound by it, and you sin if you give a single penny more.

Third, do not give bad money for the goods you buy. It is said of Abraham, whose upright dealings and deeds are recounted as an example and pattern

<column-break/>

for following generations, when he bought the Cave of Machpelah from Ephron, the son of Zohar the Hittite, Genesis 23:16. The text says, *That he weighed to him for the same four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.* And therefore, my beloved, when you buy any goods, if you then give copper for silver, or counterfeit gold for upright gold, where you know it to be such, then you transgress the rules of Scripture; it is nothing better than pure deception. I say this because there is now a deceitful world among us regarding the giving of poor and false money.

Fourth, in buying, keep this rule: do not give less for any goods than you judge in your conscience they are worth. It is an oppression in buying when you seek to bring any goods below their proper price. You ought to give as much as you judge in your conscience they are worth. Thus did Abraham, when he bought the Cave of Machpelah from Ephron: *That he may give it to me for the full price,* he said, Genesis 23:9. So also David, when he wanted to buy the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite; and David said to Ornan, *Grant me the place of this threshing floor, that I may build an altar therein unto the Lord; thou shalt grant it to me for the full price,* 1 Chronicles 21:22.

Fifth, do not postpone the time of payment regarding the goods you take on credit <note>original: "burgt"</note> for a long time, when it is in your power to pay for them. You have this rule in Proverbs 3:27, 28: *Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Say not unto thy neighbor, Go, and come again, and tomorrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.* This is spoken here with respect to buying and selling; when a person has sold goods and is forced to go again and again for his money, and yet cannot get it. That this is the purpose of this proverb is clear from these words: *Withhold not good from them to whom it is due.* Although this text is applied to works of mercy, it likewise has its regard for dealings in the world, or the buying of any goods. If you owe someone money for any goods you have bought from him, you ought to pay your debt, and not let the creditor run day after day for his money, and still let him go away without it when it is within your power to pay. This goes against the defaulters <term>Bankeroetiers: specifically those who dishonestly avoid paying debts they have the means to settle, rather than those who are simply impoverished</term> who borrow money and take up goods, and make no conscience of paying what they owe for them. If people had but some sparks of honesty and good nature in them, they could never be at ease in the world until they had paid everyone their own. Phocion <note>An Athenian statesman known for his incorruptible character and frugality.</note> would not hold a banquet until he had paid Callicles what he owed him. The Prophet Elisha was so conscientious in this that when he multiplied the poor widow's oil, 2 Kings 4:7, he commanded her: *Sell the oil, and first pay thy debts, and then live thou and thy children on the rest.* Not to pay one's debt is presented in Scripture as a sign of the wicked, Psalm 37:21. The wick-

Sixth, do not buy up a commodity entirely by yourself, so that no one else has any besides you, in order to sell it according to your own pleasure: this is a great oppression and a ruin of the common good <note>original: "gemeene-beste"</note> and of all trade. You shall find that the Scripture itself condemns this,
<margin>Proverbs 11:26.</margin>
where it speaks regarding the grain-buyers—those who had enough money to buy a great quantity or multitude of it. For thus the text says: *He who withholds grain, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him who sells it.* There were grain-buyers at that time who, when grain was cheap, wanted to buy up all they could get and keep it until it became expensive again; they wanted to hold the grain until it was dear, and then sell it. Now Solomon says, he who does such a thing—well, the people shall curse him, but they shall bless those who sell it. So it is no sin in itself to buy up certain goods, provided you give a good bargain and sell at the ordinary price; that is no sin. But for a person to buy up certain goods solely to increase and hike the price is such an oppression that the people shall curse the person who does so. In this matter of monopolizing, people may well be compared to a great Oak Tree, which spreads its branches so far that a small tree cannot grow beneath it. So many people hoard goods so greatly that poorer people cannot live by them, which is a gross oppression and a great godlessness.

Seventh, if you do not wish to transgress the Scriptural rules, then in the buying of a ware, take no profit through the fault or mistake <note>original: "faute ende abuys"</note> of the seller. For instance, if you came into a shop and bought so many yards of cloth, and the shopkeeper happened to give you more than was your due, or take less money than he ought to have; you may not take any advantage in this situation. For if you take anything more from him than you have bought, it is theft; or if you give him anything less than your contract, it is theft. And you have this in
<margin>Genesis 43:12.</margin>
Jacob: when there was a famine in the land, he sent his sons to Egypt to buy grain. When they arrived there, Joseph recognized his brothers and he put their money, which they brought to buy the grain, back into the mouths of their sacks and sent them home. When they found their money in their sacks, they announced the same to their father, who commanded them to go back and carry to him the money they had brought away in the mouths of their sacks; for, says he, perhaps it is a mistake. Here was conscientiousness; when a person gives you more than your due, or you do not give him what is his: in neither of these cases may you make any profit. For if you do so, the Lord considers it nothing better than extortion and deceit.

<column-break/>

Eighth, do not engage in commerce on the Day of the Lord. It is quite true that in cases of pressing necessity, such as the protection of life, whether for humans or beasts, it is permitted; but to buy those things for which there is no necessity, and without which you could well manage until Monday: in this situation you sin if you buy anything on the Day of the Lord. That day is the Heavenly Market-day.
<margin>Nehemiah 10, verse 31.</margin>
Nehemiah entered into an oath, and the people with him, *That if any people of the land brought wares or grain on the Sabbath to sell, they would not buy from them on the Sabbath.* Now although some are ready to object and say that this Sabbath spoken of here, in which they were so strict, was the Sabbath of the Jews; I answer: it is true, it was the Sabbath of the Jews; but nevertheless, the Gospel gives you no freedom to profane and violate the Christian Sabbath, for it is your bounden duty to maintain the same now as strictly and closely as then. And therefore, in my finding, I cannot see but that it is a sin for a person to buy either wine, pepper, mustard, or any other such trifles <note>original: "tryfelinge"</note> without which they could well do; it must necessarily be unlawful and sinful to buy any things which you could well do without or lack. In that situation you sin if you buy on the Day of the Lord; and therefore I pray you, rather go without such minor things than to buy them on the Day of the Lord and transgress the Scripture.

Ninth, in the buying of any ware, do not exploit <note>original: "arbept niet op," literally "do not work upon"</note> the necessities of a poor person who needs money, to make him sell it at such a low price that he cannot live by it; this is a very great sin and oppression. Frequently the rich take advantage of the necessities of the poor; for they must sell their goods, perhaps to buy food, or for more materials to give themselves work. Now the rich do not want to buy their goods unless they can have them cheaper than they can afford to give them; this is a great oppression. Therefore it is
<margin>Leviticus 25:14.</margin>
said, *Therefore when you sell anything to your neighbor, or buy from your neighbor's hand; let no one oppress another.* there is oppression in buying just as much as in selling, when someone takes advantage of the poverty of a poor person and wants to make him give a better bargain than he can, or else will not buy anything from him at all. Oh! beloved, how few there are in the world who are conscientious in their buying in this regard.

Tenth, if you do not wish to transgress the rules of Scripture in buying, then beware that you do not buy those things which are not fit or are unlawful to be bought or sold. As first: do not buy spiritual things, such as the gift of the Holy Spirit, church properties, etc. For these things may not be bought. This is called Simony <note>original: "Symoni," referring to Simon Magus from Acts 8:20, who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit.</note>, Acts 8:20. When Simon...

# A Christian’s Instruction.

<note>original: "Magus"</note> Simon Magus wanted to have bought the gift of the Holy Spirit; "Your money perish with you," said Peter, "because you thought that the gift of God could be obtained through money." <note>This refers to the sin of "Simony"—buying or selling church offices or spiritual influence—named after Simon Magus in Acts 8.</note> Secondly, do not buy stolen goods; it is not fitting that they should be bought. If you know that those goods which are for sale are stolen goods, they may not be bought, but must rather be returned. I fear that this is a sin of which many people make no conscience; as the common proverb goes, "the holder is as bad as the thief": let me likewise say to you, the buyer is as bad as the thief. Thirdly, do not buy mementos or remnants of idolatry, such as crosses, rosaries <note>original: "Paternoster"</note>, crucifixes, images and the like; these ought not to be bought. Fourthly, do not buy people as slaves: this is what is rebuked in <margin>Amos 8:6.</margin> "That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes." So also in <margin>Deuteronomy 24:7.</margin> "If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and makes merchandise of him, or sells him; then that thief shall die": you may not steal a person and sell him.

And so you see that I have very briefly run through these ten points. And oh! my beloved, I must tell you that it is the grief of my heart that there are few of you who stay within the bounds of these points; but that you have transgressed in one or another of them in your buying.

I shall now only make a short application of what has been said, and so I shall end.

First, then, by way of exhortation, in the fear of God: O all you who buy and sell in the world and do business <note>original: "neeringe"</note>, beware of this stumbling block <note>original: "Kotssteen," literally a stone one trips over</note>, so that your souls do not suffer shipwreck upon it. I shall show you this afternoon what you gain through your unrighteous practices or dealings, and therefore shun such ways; and let me warn you in true hope, among all your buying in the world, I pray you to buy what Solomon commands you to buy: <margin>Prov. 23:23.</margin> *Buy the truth, and sell it not.* <margin>Apoc. 3:18.</margin> And that which Christ counsels you to buy: *I counsel you to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that you may be rich; and white raiment, that you may be clothed, and that the shame of your nakedness does not appear; and anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see.* And buy that for which the good merchant sold everything <margin>Matth. 13:44.</margin> that he had to obtain—namely, the Pearl in the field. So also you, sell everything that you have to buy this precious Pearl, the Lord Jesus; but do not deceive yourselves when I command you to buy spiritual things, and do not think they are to be obtained with money; but I wish that you would labor for them and <margin>Isa. 55:1.</margin> strive after them: *O all you thirsty, come to the waters, and you who have no money, come buy and eat, yes, come buy without money and without price, wine and milk.* These things are not to be bought with money, but with effort, labor, and earnest prayers to God for them. You must give your garments of sin and sorrow for this white garment of Christ’s righteousness. And let the market-day

<column-break/>

of your souls <note>A metaphor for the time during one's life when salvation is available.</note> not slip away so without buying at a price for the profit of your souls; buy the truth, and sell it not; buy the pearl of grace; strive for spiritual things, and do not consider the things of the world to be worth so much, and grace and Christ, heaven and happiness, and glory to be worth nothing. There is nothing in the world for which we can give too much—one can buy gold too dearly—but Christ and grace we can never buy too dearly; one can never give too much for them. Having one hour of the enjoyment of Christ will inevitably repay all the hardships, miseries, and losses that we undergo here for His sake. And therefore, beloved, do not waste so much time, nor take such trouble for these perishable things here below—for these additions and circumstances of happiness—and spend no longer so little time and effort on these perfections and the essential parts of salvation, and on the obtaining of a part and portion in Christ, in His righteousness, merits, and satisfaction. Diogenes <note>A Greek philosopher known for criticizing social vanities.</note> mocked the foolishness of the people in his time: <note>original Latin: "Quod res pretiosas minimo emerent venderentque vilissimas plurimo"</note> *That they bought precious things for very little and sold the vilest things for very much.* They valued the most precious things little, and held the worst at a high price. Woe to those who block up the trade of religion: <margin>Luke 11:52.</margin> *Woe to you, lawyers! for you have taken away the key of knowledge: you entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in you hindered.*

Secondly: is it so, that in buying wares we ought not to transgress the Scriptural rules? Then let this be a cause of humiliation for some of you, that the Word of God has met you this day. Oh beloved Christians, go home and humble your souls before God, and praise His Name that His Word has found out your transgressions. Go home, my beloved, and do not act so godlessly anymore; if you have transgressed the Scriptural rules in any of these points, then go home and confess your sins to the Lord, and amend your life, so that the Lord does not blow a curse over what you have obtained, and says of your businesses as He <margin>Ezek. 28:18.</margin> once did of those in Ezekiel 28:18: *You have defiled your sanctuaries by the multitude of your iniquities, by the iniquity of your traffic; therefore will I bring forth a fire from the midst of you, it shall devour you, and I will bring you to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all them that behold you.* So that the Lord does not say, when you have obtained so many clothes in your chest, and so many wares or merchandise in your shop, that they are but the fruits of your sins, and the price of your soul, and that you shall have a covenant with death and eternal hellish damnation.

# A Christian’s Instruction.

> *1 Corinthians 7: 30, 31.*
> *And those that weep, as though they wept not; and those that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and those that buy, as though they possessed not;*
> *And those that use this world, as not abusing it. For the fashion of this world passes away.*

<margin>*IX. Sermon.*</margin>
I come now to the second part, namely, that you must guard yourself against violating the scriptural rules in the selling of any goods. and just as the Scripture is very abundant in presenting the rules regarding buying, so it does not fail to give rules and instructions regarding selling; I shall name nine or ten of them for you.

<margin>*Scriptural rules regarding the selling of any goods.*</margin>
First, if you do not wish to violate the rules of Scripture, do not use many unnecessary words in the selling of any goods. The Scripture is very abundant on this occasion: as in *Genesis 23:9*, when Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah from Ephron, there was but one word between the two of them; Ephron said it was worth so much, and Abraham gave it to him immediately. So also in *Zechariah 11:12*: "For I had said to them, if it be good in your eyes, bring my hire; and if not, forbear. And they weighed for my hire thirty pieces of silver." An abundance of words is unnecessary. In the multitude of words, says Solomon, there wanteth not transgression. <note>Proverbs 10:19</note> Just as there is sin in the abundance of words in ordinary discourse, so it is also in trade. I do not say this as if I would have people stand in their shops as stiff as a block; but that they should not be excessive, wicked, or boastful <note>original: "schuym-bechtig," literally frothy or foamy</note> in their words.

Secondly, do not over-praise your goods when you know in your conscience that something is lacking in them: this is a great fault in a seller, when he uses an abundance of fine words to sell his wares. Just as it is a sin in the buyer to say "it is bad, it is bad" <note>Referring to Proverbs 20:14, where a buyer disparages an item to lower the price</note>, so it is also bad in the seller to say "it is good, it is good," when he knows it is not so.

Thirdly, in the selling of your goods, use no false weight or measure; and do not keep a deceitful scale or a deceitful measure. *Amos 8* <note>The text says Amos 5, but the quote is from Amos 8:5</note>, there the Lord rebukes those who say, "When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat? making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit." <note>The "ephah" was a dry measure for grain, and the "shekel" was the weight used to measure the money received.</note> So also, *Proverbs 20 verse 10*: "Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the Lord." That is, the Lord has an abomination for those who use these false weights and measures in selling; and therefore the Lord gave a special law in Israel to all who did any trade, *Deuteronomy 25 verses 15, 16*, that they should

<column-break/>

not deal with any deceit in their weights and measures, *verses 13, 14*: "Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small. Thou shalt not have in thine house divers measures, a great and a small. But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee. For all that do such things, and all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the Lord thy God." This is not to be understood as referring to various kinds of weights, such as pounds, ounces, ells, yarn, and so forth; or many of the same kind, if they all have their right measure; but of various weights of the same kind, yet of an incorrect and unequal measure. And therefore guard yourselves, beloved, against incorrect and false weights or measures, *Micah 6:10*, there the Lord God says: "Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure <note>original: "epha"</note> that is abominable?" Money that is obtained through unrighteous or false weights and measures is called "treasures of wickedness."

Fourthly, you must make it a matter of conscience, not only that you do not speak falsely, but also that you do not speak with a "back-door" <note>original: "achter-deure," meaning a deceptive loophole or excuse</note> or double-meaning. It is a remark that someone has on these words, "That no man deceive his brother"; many craftsmen, he says, although they will not lie, they will nonetheless speak with double-meanings. Many people, to rid themselves of some goods, will have a partner, a friend, or another who offers them money for it, and then they say to the first buyer who comes along, that such a man has just offered so much for it, in order to make the buyer give that much; furthermore they say, "it cost me so much," where it may be that among those same goods they had others of higher price and greater value, and that for the same price, and perhaps a long time to pay, whereas the buyer gives ready money; and many such similar ambiguities they use to deceive people.

Fifthly, in the selling of any goods, do not take advantage of the ignorance or the simplicity of the person who comes to buy the goods from you. If you notice that he is inexperienced and has no knowledge of the matter, then deal with him rather the better than the worse; the Lord threatens to punish the youths who leap over the threshold: who fill their masters' houses with violence and deceit, *Zephaniah 1 verse 9*. So also *1 Thessalonians 4 verse 6*: "That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter" (says the Apostle), "because that the Lord is the avenger of all such." Likewise *2 Peter 2 verse 3*, the Apostle, speaking there of false teachers, says, "And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you." Thus do the false craftsmen in their shops. It is a great sin that a person takes advantage of the ignorance of the buyer, in order to sell his goods at a higher price because of it.

# A Christian’s Instruction.

<margin>Amos 8:6.</margin>
Sixthly, take care that you do not adulterate your goods, nor rob them of their natural goodness and excellence in order to profit more from them. The *Scripture* condemns this in *Amos 8:6*, where they sold the "refuse of the wheat." The grain-buyers wanted to pick out the best grains and then sell the refuse and the worst, for which reason God rebukes and condemns them. This is also the point of the Prophet in *Isaiah 1:22*, when he says, "Your silver is become dross: your wine is mixed with water." They mixed the wine with water and the silver with dross. The *Scripture* condemns the practice of stripping goods of their natural virtue and then selling them at as high a price as if they were not adulterated—indeed, as if they were of the finest quality.

<margin>Isaiah 1:22.</margin>

<margin>Proverbs 11:26.</margin>
<margin>Nehemiah 5:2, 3.</margin>
Seventhly, do not be among the first who raise the market price and increase the cost of any goods. I informed you this morning that this is a very great fault; *Proverbs 11:26* says, "He that withholdeth grain, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it." It is a great oppression for the commonweal <note>original: "Gemeene-beste," referring to the public good or commonwealth</note> when people drive up the price of grain, or of any other goods, when there is no necessity, as seen in *Nehemiah 5:2, 3*.

<margin>Amos 8:5.</margin>
Eighthly, do not be so vehement in the selling of your goods that you do not consider yourself satisfied with selling on the six days of the week, but feel you must also sell on the Sabbath. Do not be like those in *Amos 8:5* who said, "When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat?" These filthy and greedy money-grubbers <note>original: "Mest-bekens," a derogatory term for those obsessed with material gain</note> were so consumed by their profits that the six days in the week were not enough for them, but they wished to sell on the Sabbath as well. <margin>Neh. 13:21.</margin> *Nehemiah 13:21* shows that Nehemiah was very diligent to restore and reform this; when the merchants came within Jerusalem to sell their wares on the Sabbath day, he testified against them and contended with the nobles of Judah, saying to them: "What evil thing is this that you do, and profane the Sabbath day?" And he warned the merchants and sellers of all kinds of goods that if they did it again, he would lay hands on them; so from 그at time on they came no more on the Sabbath. This also condemns your common tap-houses and small, trifling shops <note>original: "klepne Kleuter-winkeltjes," referring to small shops selling minor or vanity items</note> which make no matter of selling small and insignificant things on this day, which is nevertheless a great sin.

<margin>Hosea 12:8.</margin>
Ninthly, when your deceits and unjust dealings in your selling are found out and discovered, do not then justify yourself in your deceit. Even if you come to tell some people that they are selling their goods more dearly than others, they still do not wish to be convinced of it; or if you tell them that the merchandise you bought from them is not good, they will say it is as good as can be given for that price, like those in *Hosea 12:7-8*. In the merchant's

<column-break/>

hand is a deceitful balance; he loves to oppress. Yet *Ephraim* says, "Truly I am become rich, I have found me out substance: in all my labors they shall find none iniquity in me that were sin." Although the deceitful scales were in his hand, he nevertheless says, "No one can accuse me of sin or unrighteousness in my dealings."

Tenthly, do not sell those goods which are not saleable, nor fit to be sold. As:

First, spiritual things may not be sold; when Simon Magus wished to obtain the gift of the Holy Spirit with money, the Apostle said to him: "Go your way, may your money perish with you." <note>original: "u gelt zy u ten verdervye," referring to Acts 8:20</note>

<margin>Acts 19:19.</margin>
Secondly, do not sell any monuments or remnants of idolatry, such as crucifixes, images, rosaries <note>original: "Paternosters"</note>, books of incantation, and the like: these are not permitted to be sold. *Acts 19:19*: "Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver." These books spoken of here were books of incantation <note>original: "Bezweer-boeken"</note>, and although they were of great value, they nevertheless did not wish to sell them, but burned them.

<margin>Deuteronomy 24:7.</margin>
Thirdly, do not sell human beings as slaves. *Deuteronomy 24:7*: "If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you."

Fourthly, you may not sell yourself to commit godlessness, as Ahab did. In this way, sorcerers sell themselves to the Devil to be his servants; and so do all dissolute and loose-livers <note>original: "ongebondene Loos-teecken," likely referring to those living without moral restraint</note>. Remember, beloved, that you are not your own; but that you are bought with a price, even with the precious blood of *Jesus Christ* <note>original Latin: "Jesü Christü"</note>: therefore glorify God in your body and spirit, which both are God's.

Fifthly, you may not sell stolen goods. These may not even be bought; for if they were not bought, they would not be sold.

Sixthly, you may not sell things which cannot be used except with sin; such as powder to whiten the face <note>original: "poeijer om het aangezicht te blanchetten," referring to lead-based cosmetics or vanities</note> and the like. It is true, one may sell those things which are sinful only as a consequence of their use; but we may not sell such things which are only for sinful uses, or which cannot be used without sin.

And thus I have finished these ten points, wherein you must not transgress the rules of the *Scripture* in your selling.

I shall now proceed to handle some cases of conscience concerning trade and commerce in the world.

# A Christian’s Instruction.

<margin>Cases of conscience regarding buying and selling.</margin>
First, regarding the Buyer, he may ask: how shall I know when I am buying a certain Ware at a good price? And the Seller may likewise say: how shall I know when I am selling a certain Ware too dearly?

I answer: that although it is true that the *Scripture* does not explicitly state how much you may profit—whether one, two, three, or four pennies <note>original: "stuyvers," a small Dutch coin</note> on a shilling <note>original: "schellink," a coin worth six stuyvers</note> more or less—nevertheless, you ought not to profit more than what is ordinarily gained on such merchandise by people of your own trade. You ought to keep to the prices as the Market goes, and as those things are commonly valued or sold in the place where you live.

Secondly, sell as those who are the most conscientious in their ways; as far as they go, you may also go.

**Objection.** But may someone not, in certain circumstances, sell some Wares more dearly than they are worth?

<margin>In what case someone may take more for certain Wares than they are worth.</margin>
**Answer.** In some extraordinary circumstances, it is permitted. First, in this situation: suppose someone has a quantity of Goods with him, and God ordains through His providence that the place in which he lives is besieged, so that those Wares are very scarce. In this situation, he may certainly raise his price. Thus it was in the Siege of Samaria, where an Donkey’s head and Dove’s dung were sold for a great price, whereas before they were worth nothing, *2 Kings 6:25*. But when that occasion is removed again, the Ware must return to its previous price.

Secondly, if someone is requested and pestered to sell certain Wares that he does not wish to part with, and cannot well keep them without his own loss, but being overcome by the constant pestering, he finally resolves to sell the same to his neighbor; in that situation, he may take more for it than it is worth. But in the general and ordinary course of trade, to take more than is customary in that place is a sin.

<margin>The Second Case.</margin>
Secondly, whether someone, when he sells a Ware on credit <note>original: "op dag," meaning to pay at a later date</note>, is bound to give it at as good a price as if he sold it for ready money.

Mr. Perkinsius <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch</note>, in his first Book on the Eighth Commandment, defines this case and judges it to be a sin to sell more dearly on credit than with ready money. But certainly, this opinion cannot stand with natural reason, and therefore I shall give you my own judgment in this matter.

First, I judge that in a trade there is no violation of equity to take more for certain Wares when the Buyer requests time for payment than if he gave ready money; and my reason is this: because it is damaging and hindering to the Seller to part with certain Wares without money; and therefore it is permitted for him to take more, as can be seen in *Leviticus 25:14-15*. Therefore (says God) "And if you sell anything to your neighbor or buy from your neighbor's hand, you shall not oppress one another."

<column-break/>

"According to the number of years after the Jubilee you shall buy from your neighbor, and according to the number of years of crops he shall sell to you." This is the same matter here; if you sell your Wares to be paid on a term of years, you may sell it more dearly; but if you sell it for ready money, then you ought to give it at a better price. Ahab did not want to take Naboth's Vineyard away from him, but said to him, "Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a vegetable garden, because it is near my house; and I will give you for it a vineyard better than it; or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its worth in money," *1 Kings 21:2*. Note here: if he had taken ready money, he would only have had the value of it; but if he did not want money, he would have had a better Vineyard for it. So I can see nothing in the *Scripture* why this would not agree with equity—namely, that someone takes a little more for certain wares than they are worth when he does not receive ready money for them. But nonetheless, in these circumstances, you may not take advantage of the necessity of a poor person, and you must ensure that you never take more than that long period for payment warrants.

<margin>The Third Case.</margin>
Thirdly, when someone has sold certain wares and the Buyer has no money to pay, whether it is permitted in that situation to take some pledge as security for his money?

**Answer.** God allows it, in such a situation, to take a pledge for the security of his money. *Deuteronomy 24:10, 11, 12*: "When you lend your neighbor anything, you shall not go into his house to get his pledge. You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you lend shall bring the pledge out to you. And if the man is poor, you shall not keep his pledge overnight." *Proverbs 20:16-18*. It is indeed permitted to take a pledge; yet you may not go into that person’s house to take his pledge yourself, but your debtor must bring it out to you—namely, that thing which he can best spare—until he can pay the money. But nonetheless, the Lord forbids taking someone’s clothing or a millstone as a pledge, *Deut. 24:6, Exodus 22:26, Job 22:5, 6*. If a poor person has no more clothes than those he is wearing, it is cruelty to take them as a pledge; or the millstone, or any other thing with which that person earns his living; this is sin. But he must take what his debtor can best spare until he pays. So it is permitted for a Creditor or Money-lender to take pledges—namely, when his debtor can spare the same without any damage to his life or livelihood.

<margin>The Fourth Case.</margin>
Fourthly, when someone has sold certain Wares and his debtor makes no conscience of paying him for them, whether it is permitted to arrest such a one and bring him before the Law?

**Answer.** If someone is not able...

**Question.** When do Christians give place to immoderate love or affection for their riches and possessions (which they have acquired through their trades)?

**2. Question.** Why ought Christians to be so careful not to give place to the immoderate love for the goods and riches they have acquired?

<margin>When the love or affection for the world is immoderate.</margin>
First, you give place to the immoderate affection or love for your riches in the world / when your earnest endeavors and pursuits after worldly riches / hold you back from all other endeavors toward spiritual things. Thus was the love immoderate in those **tradesmen** <note>original: "Ambachts-luyden," referring to craftsmen or skilled laborers</note> of whom mention is made in Matthew 22 verse 5 / who, when the King had prepared a great wedding for his son, and sent out his servants to call the invited guests to the wedding, saying that all things were already prepared and ready for them, but they, disregarding it, went their way, this one to his field, that one to his merchandise. This is a sign that their hearts are too much attached to worldly things. When Martha, Luke 10:42, was busy about many worldly things / although it was a demonstration of her love for Christ / nevertheless because she neglected / to listen to the voice of Christ / he said to her, "Martha, Martha, you are troubled and disturbed about many things; but one thing is necessary: but Mary has chosen the good part, which shall not be taken away from her." When you are so diligent in your calling / that you never read God's Word / nor pray in your families / or in your private chamber / then your love for the world is immoderate.

**Secondly**, when your hearts are so occupied with your trades and worldly affairs / that you cannot take those ordinary and lawful recreations and delights in the blessings you enjoy / then you give place to immoderate affections for worldly things, Eccl. 5: verse 11. <note>original: "Eccl.", likely Ecclesiastes 5:12 in modern bibles</note> The sleep of a laborer is sweet, whether he has eaten little or much: but the satiety of the rich will not let him sleep. that they (out of concern for profit / fear of loss / or hope of increase) cannot eat their bread at the proper time / nor take their natural rest or sleep: that is a sign that their hearts are too much attached to the world. Eccl. 2: 26. He gives them restlessness / vexation / and heaviness of mind. The Psalmist compares the greedy by a vivid likeness / Psalm 59: 14, 15. **Thirdly**, you give place to your immoderate affections for your riches / when that which you possess in the world / fills you with carelessness and fleshly pleasure. What did that rich man say in the Gospel? <meta>This page continues the sermon's application of the biblical principle "to buy as if not possessing" (1 Corinthians 7:30). The author is transitioning from the theological definition of "immoderate love" for wealth to practical advice for different classes of people in the marketplace.</meta>

# A Christian’s Instruction

Let your possessions be like gloves upon your hands, which you can easily and without effort pull off; so that when God calls for any of your comforts, or strips you of them all, oh, then you shall be willing to leave them and part from them, and be able to say with Job, *The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord*, Job 1:21. Otherwise, it will be a great misery and a sorrowful oppression for you to be robbed of those enjoyments which have taken full possession of your heart.

And thus I have finished the teaching of this part of the text: *and those who buy, as though they possessed not.*

We come now to the application, and the usefulness of this doctrine shall extend to three kinds of people.

If it is so, that Christians ought to take care that they give no place to an immoderate love for the riches and possessions they have acquired in the world, then I have something to say:

First, to those who buy and sell and conduct some trade in the world, and apply great effort, yet God does not come to bless their endeavors with any increase; they buy, but possess nothing at all; they toil and slave in the world, but do not get ahead.

Secondly, to those who buy and sell and come to possess riches in the world, but through dishonest gain.

Thirdly, to those who buy and sell and obtain great riches, and do so through lawful, honest, and praiseworthy ways. In speaking to these three kinds of people, I shall spend two sermons, and will now begin with the first.

First, then, to you who buy and sell, and are diligent in your temporal callings, and yet God does not come to bless you with increase; you buy, but do not possess, and with all your effort, labor, sweat, and slaving in the world, you can hardly make it to the end of the year; you cannot improve your condition, nor barely <note>The original "pers" likely means "hardly" or "with pressure" in this context.</note> have enough by the end of the year. To such as you are, I have two things to say.

First, some things by way of instruction.

Second, some things by way of consolation.

<margin>Advice or instruction for those who exert great effort in the world and yet are barely able to prosper.</margin>
First, by way of instruction: I wish that you would first look around you and earnestly consider whether your poverty does not come from your own self, and whether it is not your own fault that you do not prosper or become rich in the world. Beloved, there are many ways in which a man can conduct a trade and yet not become rich. Such as:

1. Does your poverty not spring from your own misunderstanding in carrying out your calling? Psalm 112:5: *A wise man guides his affairs with justice.* So also Ezekiel 28:4: *By your wisdom and your understanding you have gained wealth for yourself.* Great wisdom and understanding are required in carrying out a business, which perhaps you 

<column-break/>

lack, and therefore your misunderstanding errs in buying and selling, and in the storing of your wares; thus you keep yourself behind in the world.

Secondly, it may be that you conduct your business, and yet are so lazy and negligent in it, and do not stay close to it. Now Solomon says to the sluggard, Proverbs 6:11: *So shall your poverty come upon you like a traveler, and your want like an armed man.*

Thirdly, it may be that you are a lover of "company" <note>This likely refers to idle socializing or tavern culture.</note>—that what you win with your trade, you go and consume in the tavern, so that what you win on one side, you spend again on the other. Proverbs 28:19: *But he who follows frivolous people shall be filled with poverty.* It may be that you consume your goods in excess and gluttony. Proverbs 23:21: *For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.*

Fourthly, it may be that you attend to your calling and acquire much money, but are nevertheless a greedy and stingy person, who will not have mercy on the poor to give them any assistance in their needs; that is the way to become a beggar. Proverbs 11:24, Solomon says: *There is one who scatters, and yet increases more;* he who gives to the poor and distributes when no one hears or sees, he shall increase his abundance. *But* (he says) *there is one who withholds more than is right* (that is, withholds from the poor), *but it leads to poverty.* When God sees that you invest your talent well, and use what you have for His honor, then He will give you even more; but if not, then He will also take from you what you have, and give it to others who will use it better.

Secondly, you who buy and sell and yet do not get ahead, take this for your instruction: beware that you do not murmur about it, nor hate the riches and pride which others in the world have. *Do not fret yourself* (says David, Psalm 37:7) *because of him whose way prospers.* David himself almost slipped into this mistake, Psalm 37:2–3. <note>The author likely means Psalm 73:2-3, where David/Asaph admits his feet almost slipped when he saw the prosperity of the wicked.</note> And Jeremiah disputes about this matter with God, Jeremiah 12:1. Riches and possessions are the portion of the godless, and are all that they have; and therefore do not hate them, but have pity on them, because they are only being fed like oxen for the day of slaughter. Should you be grieved that you go on foot, while another rides to the place of execution?

Thirdly, you who find you can lay nothing aside here in the world, labor only to lay up treasures in Heaven. If you cannot attain riches here, seek only for grace. If you cannot get gold, buy nevertheless the gold that Christ speaks of, Revelation 3:18. <note>original: "Apoc. 3 : 18"</note> *I counsel you* (says Christ) *to buy from me gold refined in the fire, that you may be rich.* If you obtain no goods, see that you obtain grace. If you obtain no riches, see that you obtain Christ: If you do not obtain the earth, see that you obtain Heaven.

# A Christian’s Instruction

And so much by way of instruction for you who buy and sell, and do not get ahead; but I have another word or two for you by way of consolation.

First, keep yourself fully content with your state; and if you see that God, through your trade, does not let you get ahead, then know that God sees it is for your best. Psalm 84:11 <note>The Dutch text cites verse 12, following different numbering.</note>. *The Lord shall give grace and glory; no good thing will he withhold from those who walk uprightly.* Now, it may be that the Lord sees that if he were to give you riches and great possessions in the world, it would be to your harm—that your riches would be your ruin, and your goods your woe, and your prosperity a snare for you, Eccl. 5:13. And therefore, in his great mercy, he withholds that from you. We ought to look upon all the comforts that God takes from us as so many graces and mercies, because God takes from us that which would ruin us.

Secondly, God, in the distribution of outward blessings in the world, judges in his wisdom it is best that the godly have the least portion, and the godless have the most in these worldly possessions. Psalm 73:5. *The godless are not in trouble like other men; neither are they plagued like other men. Their eyes bulge with fatness; they have more than heart could wish.* They spend their days in joy and cheerfulness. But on the other hand, God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom, James 2:5. The wisdom of the Lord our God is greatly revealed in thus distributing his blessings. God acts here like a nobleman <note>original: "Edelman"</note>, who does not want his own son to go from house to house to collect his annual rents; but for such a lowly task he uses his servant, and the servant often has money enough when the son has none. Eccl. 9:11. *I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding.* The godless shall indeed have riches, where the wise and understanding shall have none: God in his wisdom sees that it is better that wise people barely have bread to eat, while the foolish have an abundance; that the understanding shall have want, where the godless have more than their hearts could desire. Now, will you murmur and complain, when God sees that such a condition is necessary for you?

Thirdly, notice for your comfort that God gives you better riches than they have, and although he gives the godless the possession of these outward comforts, yet you have the true right and title <note>original: "op-schrift"</note> to these possessions. Now, who would be so foolish as to think the steward <term>Rent-meester: a person employed to manage an estate and collect rents</term> and dispenser luckier than the heir? The steward has them only in possession; but the heir has them in ownership. And notice, that if you are one who belongs to the election of grace; although you are ever so poor here, yet you have the only true and lasting riches; you are enriched with the treasures

<column-break/>

of wisdom and knowledge, grace, and the happiness of God's right hand. And although God shows you no pebbles <note>original: "key-steenen" (common stones)</note>, Revelation 2:9, if he nonetheless gives you pearls, then you have no reason to complain: although God shows you no riches, if he nonetheless gives you his grace and Christ, Heaven and Glory, then you have no reason to murmur against him. Acorns are good enough for the pigs, but the bread is for the children.

Fourthly, notice that the poorer you are in the world, the more fit you are for the service of God. A lean ox is more fit to work than a fat ox: well, if God keeps you poor and humbled, seeing it is only to make you more fit for his service, why should you be upset about it?

Fifthly, notice that the less God gives you in this world, the freer you are from cares and anxieties; *but those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition,* 1 Timothy 6:9. Now, which is best: to walk in a broad way in which a snare lies before you, or in a narrow way where you may go safely and without fear? And therefore, beloved, if God gives you only a small portion in this world, well, say then: the fewer cares, difficulties, snares, and anxieties I have, to which rich people are subject. Genesis 13:2: there it is said of Abraham that he was very rich; in the Hebrew it says "very heavy" <note>The Hebrew word "kābēd" means both heavy and wealthy/glorious.</note>; so also are those who are surrounded with riches. The prophet Habakkuk expresses it as being surrounded with "thick clay"; they are so loaded with worldly enjoyments that they cannot run the race that is set before them on the way to Heaven.

Sixthly, notice that it may be that you have more peace, comfort, and contentment in the little that you possess, than the godless sometimes have in their great abundance; you often have more true comfort in your want and poverty than the godless in all their fullness. Psalm 37:16. *A little that a righteous man has is better than the riches of many wicked.* Proverbs 15:6. Beloved, those to whom God gives abundance have all that "fat" <note>wealth/abundance</note> which is necessary with them, yet they may have one thing or another that plagues and upsets them; the state of poverty, want, and disfavor can in some circumstances be more comfortable. A satin coat <note>original: "Sartijne kleedt"</note> can cause a rich man more pain <note>Likely referring to the discomfort of stiff, formal courtly dress or the social pressures it represents.</note> than a coarse wool frock <term>Pye-rok: a rough, heavy woolen coat worn by commoners</term> causes a poor man.

The abundance and the riches which the godless have, God often mixes with worry and difficulty; but now a poor person, although he has only a little, nonetheless has the blessing of the Lord upon it. Proverbs 10:22. *The blessing of the Lord, it makes rich: and he adds no sorrow with it.* And Ecclesiastes 4:6. *Better is a handful with quietness, than both the hands full with labor and vexation of spirit.* Small means with peace and contentment is better than twice as much with

<margin>Sermon XI.</margin>
I come now to the further application of the usefulness of this teaching: That it is the bounden duty of Christians to be on their highest guard against giving any place to an immoderate love or affection for the goods and possessions they have acquired in the world through buying and selling. The second sort of people, then, to whom I promised to speak, are those who buy and sell in the world and have acquired goods and possessions for themselves honestly and justly. Concerning these things I have to say to you:

1. I shall give you some warning instructions.
2. Some astonishing reflections.
3. Some useful exhortations regarding the riches you have acquired justly and honestly.

### I begin with the warning instructions.

<margin>Various warning instructions for those who have justly obtained great means in the world.</margin>
First, you who have obtained riches and treasures in the world, I wish that you would often bring your former poverty in the world to your remembrance. The Lord commands the Israelites to do this in Deuteronomy 8:1-2. There God says to them: *Every commandment which I command you this day shall you observe to do, that you may live, and multiply, and go in and possess the land which the Lord swore to your fathers. And you shall remember all the way which the Lord your God led you these forty years in the wilderness, to humble you, and to prove you, to know what was in your heart.* And to keep you from pride and haughtiness of heart. I remember what Plutarch relates of Agathocles <note>Agathocles (361–289 BC) was the Tyrant of Syracuse. Born to a potter, he rose to great power but allegedly kept earthenware on his table to remind him of his humble origins.</note>; who (when he had become a Prince or Sovereign from being a potter’s son) always wanted his food served in earthenware dishes to humble himself and to bring his low and simple origin to remembrance, so that he would not become proud or puffed up. So ought

<column-break/>

you also, beloved, to frequently bring to your own remembrance and look upon your former poverty and low estate. It may be that there are some among you who, when they first came to this city, hardly had clothes on their bodies, but who now go dressed in silk and satin; you ought to remember from where you came. Thus did David, Psalm 78:70: *And he chose David his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds; from following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.* This is mentioned here by the Psalmist as a holy reflection to humble his heart; and this is the first instruction.

Secondly, if God has given you riches through your trade, do not attribute anything in your calling to your own industry and diligence, but to the blessing of the Lord upon your efforts. And the reason for this is: because though a man rises early and goes to bed late, and takes ever so much trouble in the world, if he does not have the blessing of the Lord, it shall nonetheless all be of no avail. Deuteronomy 8:17-18: *And you shall not say in your heart, My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth; but you shall remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth.* Beloved, you must guard against attributing your riches to your own industry; for without the blessing of the Lord, nothing can succeed well. Guard against "burning incense to your own net" <note>This refers to the practice of worshiping one’s own tools or skills as the source of success, rather than God.</note> when you have become rich in the world. Habakkuk 1:16: *Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous.*

Thirdly, do not be proud of the riches God has given you. To the rich in this present world, the Apostle says (1 Timothy 6:17) to command them *that they be not high-minded.* The worm of pride often breeds in the hearts of rich people. It is a difficult thing to keep your heart humble when your status is high, and to keep yourself from pride when God has exalted you above your brothers. Ezekiel 28:4-5: *With your wisdom and with your understanding you have gotten you riches, and have gotten gold and silver into your treasures. By your great wisdom and by your trade you have increased your riches, and your heart is lifted up because of your riches.* When God exalts you in riches, guard yourself then that you do not exalt your heart in pride.

<margin>Pride is the worm of riches. <note>original Latin: "Vermis divitiarum superbia est."</note> Augustine. It is a difficult thing not to give over one's character to wealth... <note>original Latin: "Ardua res haec est opibus non tradere mores..."</note> Martial.</margin>

Fourthly, do not trust in your riches and possessions as if they were powerful enough to protect you from danger and to deliver you from difficulties, etc. *The rich man’s wealth,* says Solomon, *is his strong city, and as a high wall in his own conceit.* Proverbs 18:11. Matthew 19:23: *How hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter into the Kingdom of God!* Juvenal could say: *A man's credit is proportional to the amount of money he keeps in his chest.* <note>original Latin: "Quantum quisque sua nummorum servat in arca, tantum habet & fidei."</note> Your silver and your gold cannot protect you from the wrath of God.

Fifthly, you who have obtained great riches and possessions, do not view yourselves as owners, but as stewards of the manifold blessings of God...

Beloved, God is the Owner of all that you possess; *All the beasts of the forest are mine, and the cattle on a thousand hills.* He is the true Owner; you are but the <term>steward<note>The original Dutch 'Rent-meester' refers to an estate manager who handles accounts for a landlord; the author uses this to emphasize that wealth is a temporary loan from God.</note></term> of your abundance. Luke 16, verses 11, 12: *If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous <term>Mammon<note>A biblical term referring to wealth or material profit, often personified as a false god or a corrupting influence.</note></term>, who will commit to your trust the true riches? And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?* So also verse 9: *Make to yourselves friends of the unrighteous Mammon.*

Sixth, if God has blessed you with great means, you may possess them; but do not let your riches possess you. And do not become vain; as your power and wealth increase, do not set your heart upon them. Your eye, hand, or tongue may be set upon them; but you must not set your heart upon them. Let your spirit come no closer <margin>*I do not surrender myself to things, but lend myself to them. Seneca.* <note>original: "Rebus non me trado sed commodo. Seneca."</note></margin> to them than your hands. A pagan could say that although he lent himself to his riches, he nevertheless would not surrender himself to them. Worldly possessions are like a rose in a man's hand: if you hold it gently, it will retain its fragrance, scent, and color for a long time; but if you crush it and handle it roughly, it will soon lose its color and sweetness. So too, if you use your riches well, you shall possess them the longer; but if you set your heart too much upon them, you shall soon lose them. And thus I have finished these warning instructions; I shall now present to you some astonishing reflections.

<margin>Various astonishing reflections for those who are rich in the world.</margin> First, you who have acquired great means in the world, however honorably you did so, consider nevertheless that God, in the distribution of His graces, generally distributes the blessings of eternal life among the poorer and lowlier people rather than among the rich and people of great possessions. 1 Corinthians 1, verses 26, 27: *For ye see your calling, brethren,* says the Apostle, *how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.* (He does not say "not any," but "not many.") Godly rich people, like stars of the first magnitude, are thinly sown in the firmament; *but God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; and base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen.* So also James 2:5: *Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom?* It is very remarkable that among the seven Churches of Asia, the best Church was the poorest, and the worst among them was the richest. The Church of Laodicea was the worst of all the Churches, for she was lukewarm, neither cold nor hot. And yet,

<column-break/>

the text says *that she was rich, and increased with goods, and had need of nothing,* Revelation 3, verse 17. And the Church of Smyrna, which was one of the best Churches, Revelation 2, verse 9—yet Christ says of her: *I know thy poverty, (but thou art rich).* Although they were outwardly poor, they were nonetheless inwardly rich. God ordinarily bestows His grace upon the poor more than upon the rich; and therefore, let this be an astonishing reflection for you. Just as God in ancient times chose lowly and poor creatures for sacrifices—He chose neither the Lion nor the Eagle, the Lion being the King of Beasts and the Eagle the King of Birds—but the Lord chose the Lamb and the Dove: poor, simple, lowly, and innocent creatures, not as noble nor as highly regarded as the Lion and the Eagle. So also in His election to grace and glory, He chose the Lamb and the Dove—that is, poor and lowly people—rather than men of great riches and possessions in the world.

Secondly, consider that in the first and primitive preaching and planting of the Gospel, it was a rare thing for a rich man to embrace Christ and follow Him. Matthew 11:6: *The poor receive the Gospel;* they were the ones who embraced Christ. So also John 7:48, when the servants and the soldiers who came to seize Christ heard Him speak, they were convinced and said: *Never man spake like this man.* Then the Pharisees answered them: *Are ye also deceived? Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?* As if they would say: "It is not worth anything to you." In Matthew 27:57, it is said that Joseph, a rich man of Arimathea, was himself also one of those who followed Christ. It is recounted as a matter of wonder that Joseph, who was a rich man, would follow Christ. Mark says that he *went in boldly unto Pilate,* Mark 15:43. But John says, *he was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews.* The poorest and lowliest sort of people, the poor fishermen, received the Gospel most of all.

Thirdly, consider that where one person is made better by their abundance and riches in the world, there are multitudes who are made worse by the same. And therefore, let this reflection astonish you. Solomon says, Ecclesiastes 5, verse 12: *There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt.* Beloved, where riches make one man better, they make a thousand others worse.

I recall what I have read of <note>Pius Quintus is Pope Pius V (reigned 1566–1572).</note> Pius V, who recounted of himself: that when he was a man of a lowly and humble state in the world, he then had a very good hope for his salvation; but thereafter, having been promoted to Cardinal, he began to doubt it greatly and to call it into question; but thereafter, being raised even higher and made Pope, he then began to despair and lose hope of it entirely.
