...possessions and advancements in the world made him worse and worse. Might not some of you also truly complain: "When I was poor and in a humble state, I thought constantly of praying in my household, of hearing and reading God's Word, and observing God's ordinances; but now that I have become rich, my household goes without prayer, and my worldly affairs hinder and keep me from the service of the Lord—from reading, hearing, and praying, both in public and especially in my household. I am now much worse than when I was poor, and I have repaid the Lord with evil for all His mercies." Honor changes people's manners; while they increase in riches, they decrease in grace. God's people are generally better in a state of oppression than in prosperity. And so you shall find that David was much better when he was hunted here and there by Saul like a <term>partridge<note>The original Dutch 'Velt-hoen' refers to a wild game bird, echoing 1 Samuel 26:20 where David compares himself to a partridge being hunted in the mountains.</note></term> on the mountains, than when he sat upon the throne. And therefore it is said in 2 Chronicles 17:3 that Jehoshaphat walked in the former ways of his father David; it seems his latter ways were not so good. Many people in their final days, as they become old and rich, are then possessed by their very riches; and it may be that these are in their hearts even when they are not yet in their hands. Therefore, consider earnestly within yourself whether your first days in the world were not your best, and whether your last and richest days are not your worst. It was noted of the children of Israel that they were better under slavery in Egypt than in the land of Canaan, where they lacked nothing; for then they became proud and forgot the Lord. And therefore Moses gives them such a warning in Deuteronomy 8, from verse 7 to 15.

Fourthly, consider this, beloved: that your riches and possessions in the world, though ever so lawfully and honorably gained, nevertheless place you under a greater difficulty in entering Heaven than other men. This you see in Matthew 19, verses 23 and 24, when Christ said to the young man that if he wished to be perfect, he must go and sell all that he had and give to the poor; so he went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions. Then Jesus said to his disciples: "Truly I say to you, that a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven. And again I say to you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God." Upon what hard conditions can a rich man hope to go to Heaven? Some are of the opinion that the word which is translated here as "Camel" actually signifies a <term>cable<note>A common historical linguistic debate suggests the Greek word 'kamelos' (camel) was a misspelling of 'kamilos' (thick rope or cable), implying a heavy rope trying to pass through a needle's eye.</note></term>, and <term>Mr. Perkins<note>William Perkins (1558–1602) was a prominent English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch and highly influential in the Further Reformation movement.</note></term> is also of this opinion; for, he says, although a cable cannot go through the eye of a needle as it is, nevertheless, if the cable is <insert>unraveled</insert> or untwined, there is a possibility of getting it through. So also, if men unravel themselves from the world and live with weaned affections from their riches and possessions, that is the way for them to enter Heaven. Heaven is compared to a stately palace with a narrow gate; the expression shows

<column-break/>

the great difficulty for rich people to enter Heaven. Mark and Luke present it with a <term>pathetic<note>In this historical context, 'pathetic' means 'full of passion' or 'deeply moving,' rather than the modern sense of 'pitiful.'</note></term> expression: "Oh! how hardly," etc. But Christ says, "That which is impossible with men, is possible with God." The riches of the world are confusing and alluring vanities, and they bring you under too great a difficulty to enter Heaven; it is a hundred to one whether they shall confuse and ensnare you.

Fifthly, consider that you, to whom God has given riches and possessions in the world, are subject to more accountings, disturbances, and agonizing worries or anxieties than poor people. For if they have but food and clothing, they have no cause to complain of their poverty, because they are free from those anxieties and difficulties which happen to the rich. Who would desire silk stockings if he had to have the <term>gout<note>A painful form of arthritis historically associated with wealthy diets rich in meat and alcohol.</note></term> in his legs beneath them? And truly, the gout is a disease that commonly follows wealthy folk. Who would desire a <term>satin doublet<note>A 'wambays' or doublet was a close-fitting jacket; satin was a luxury fabric restricted to the upper classes.</note></term> or a purple garment if he had to have a leprous and unhealthy body beneath them? So it is better for you to be poor as you are, than to have riches and with them so many difficulties, miseries, and oppressions. Hear what the Apostle says in <margin>1 Tim. 6:9</margin> 1 Timothy 6, verses 9 and 10: "But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is a root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows." And in <margin>Eccl. 5, verse 11</margin> Ecclesiastes 5, verse 11: "The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep." <margin>Chap. 2, verse 26</margin> Chapter 2, verse 26: "God gives to the sinner the task of gathering and heaping up riches." He meets with great sorrow and difficulty from which a poor man is free; and therefore riches are compared to thorns; you can hardly grasp them with your hands without them pricking and wounding you. A rich man has constantly three <term>vultures<note>The author uses 'Grijp-vogels' (birds of prey) as a metaphor for the psychological toll of wealth.</note></term> feeding on his heart: great care in acquiring, fear in preserving, and grief in parting; and this prevents his rest. It is remarkable that the same word which in Hebrew signifies "commerce" also signifies "difficulty," <note>The author likely refers to a perceived linguistic link in Hebrew between terms for trade/merchandise and those for distress or trouble.</note> to let us know that those who ensnare themselves in worldly affairs shall meet with great anguish, difficulty, and torment.

Lastly, consider that your riches often choke the power and the workings of God's Word upon your souls. In Matthew 13, verse 22, it is said of the <term>thorny ground<note>Reference to the Parable of the Sower, where seeds falling among thorns represent people who hear the Word, but worldly cares and the deceitfulness of wealth choke it.</note></term> that the deceitfulness of riches chokes the word and makes it unfruitful. Can corn grow in a hedge of thorns? No more can the Word bear fruit in a heart that is filled with worldly cares.

Instructions for obtaining God's blessing upon our riches, and thereby preserving and increasing them.

...to never become rich, or never to strive for a great status in the world; but you must not misunderstand me, and conclude from this that it is a sin to be rich; it is dangerous to be rich, but not a sin; it is a snare and a temptation, and therefore it is your bounden duty to take care how you obtain your riches, and how you use them.

Secondly, because there is a danger in riches, do not therefore cast your riches away, nor squander them idly or uselessly, and do not cast the blessings of the Lord away from you. This is told of <term>Crates the Theban<note>Crates of Thebes (c. 365–285 BCE) was a Cynic philosopher who famously renounced his fortune to live a life of poverty in Athens.</note></term>, who said of his riches: *I will destroy you, lest you destroy me.* <note>Original Latin: "Ego perdam te, ne tu perdas me."</note> And this brings me to the third point which I promised to handle, namely to give you some useful instructions and admonitions: what you must do to have the blessing of God upon your riches, and thereby both to preserve and to increase them.

1. Interweave your possessions with grace; obtain grace to be mixed with your goods, and obtain the true riches mixed with your worldly riches; and this is the way to preserve them and to invest them well. The Psalmist says in Psalm 112, verses 1 and 3: *Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who has great delight in His commandments. His seed shall be mighty upon the earth; in his house shall be wealth and riches.* When God commanded Solomon that he should ask of Him what he desired (2 Chronicles 1, verse 12), he did not ask for riches, but for wisdom and knowledge, and an understanding heart. Then God said to Solomon: *Because this was in your heart, and you have not desired riches, goods, nor honor, nor the soul of those who hate you, nor have you desired many days, but have desired wisdom and knowledge for yourself, that you might judge my people; therefore,* said God, *wisdom and knowledge is given to you; moreover, I shall give you riches, and goods, and honor, such as no kings who were before you have had, and after you none shall be like you.* Beloved, you ought first to seek the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all other things shall be cast unto you. The way to preserve and increase your riches is to obtain grace in your hearts.

Secondly, use a portion of your income for godly and Christian uses, for the promotion of Religion, and do it during your life. Proverbs 3, verses 9 and 10: *Honor the Lord with your substance, and with the firstfruits of all your increase (that is) give it to godly uses; and what then? So shall your barns be filled with plenty, and your winepresses shall overflow with new wine.* As a sign of thankfulness to God for His blessing, set aside a portion of your income for His honor, for good and godly uses.

Thirdly, give a portion of your income over to the practice of charity, for the relief of the needs of the poor. Proverbs 11, verse 24: *There is one who scatters, to whom*

<column-break/>

yet more is added: and one who withholds more than is right, but it leads to want. A stingy withholding leads to poverty: God can easily blow away goods that were well-earned, if they are poorly kept. Works of mercy, when they are done discreetly, are never a hindrance, but rather a promotion of a person's outward income. Just as with other gifts, the good use of them brings an increase: so also in this. In 2 Corinthians 9, verse 10, the Apostle calls the works of charity "sown seed." No field is so fertile to sow in as the poor <term>Members of Christ<note>A common 17th-century term for fellow believers, especially those in need, referring to the "Body of Christ."</note></term>: no seed is better than mercy. Yet you must give with discretion (Psalm 112:5). A wise man is merciful, but he conducts his affairs with justice. You should be prudent, and observe how much you ought to give according to your power or ability, and no more: and when, and to whom you must give—not blindly to <term>every Tom, Dick, and Harry<note>Original Dutch: "jan rap en zijn maat," a derogatory idiom for the rabble or common riff-raff.</note></term>, to all the beggars who run along the streets without any distinction; but to those poor people who attend to their calling, and if they are able, apply all effort to get through the world—to such as walk holily and religiously. If you give thus, I want to assure you that at the end of the year you shall never be the poorer, or at least at the end of your life. But to be a stingy person is the way to become a poor person.

All things poorly obtained are quickly lost: so also, the things that are poorly kept shall not last long. If you want God's blessing over your possessions, then be very compassionate of heart toward the poor: and do not give only to those who come to beg of you, but go and find out where the poor are, provide them support, and help them. A generous man (says the Prophet Isaiah, Chapter 32, verse 8) devises generous things, and stands by generous things. You ought to seek out where the person is whom you can do the most good with help and assistance. *Cast your money upon the water, and after many days you shall find it again* (Ecclesiastes 11, verse 1). <note>The author quotes Ecclesiastes 11:1, usually translated as "Cast thy bread upon the waters," but substitutes "money" (gelt).</note> There is a common proverb regarding fruitless commands: we commonly say, "I might as well have thrown my money in the water." Although it may seem so, that you have thrown your money as good as into the water, you shall nevertheless find it: God will surely repay it to you before the year is out, with a good profit, for all that you have given to the poor for Christ's sake. And therefore, do not be stingy to the poor; do not give only a piece of bread at your door so that your neighbor may see it, but give in secret, when no one sees you, and give to those who have most need of your love; and this is the way for God to both bless and increase your riches.

Fourthly, and lastly: you who are blessed by God in your endeavors and increased in your possessions, always attend to your calling conscientiously and diligently. If God has blessed you up to this point, then do not now use any unjust or false means to [gain] even more...

<meta>This page continues the twelfth sermon from the previous page, specifically addressing those who have acquired their wealth through dishonest means. The author transitions from identifying the problem to offering practical "instructions" for the conscience-stricken listener.</meta>

# A Christian’s Instruction. 460

...obtained through oppression, violence, or deceit, and then employ or spend it on good uses—O, remember! that the Lord will not be pleased with it: **This is the first instruction.**

Secondly, hasten toward restitution <note>Restitution: the act of returning something to its rightful owner.</note>. If you wish to be saved, then give back to those whom you have wronged. God would rather you give it back to those you have treated unjustly than that you build hospitals with it, or spend it on any other godly or charitable use. *If I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation,* (said Zaccheus) *I restore him fourfold,* Luke 19:8. When Sultan Selim’s advisor told him to spend the great wealth (which he had taken from the Persian merchants) on building notable hospitals for the support of the poor, the dying Turk commanded instead that it be returned to the rightful owners. When Henry III, King of England, sent a pack of letters to the monks of the Minorite Orders to clothe them, they sent them back with this message: That he ought not to give alms from that which he had unrighteously taken from the poor, nor would they accept such a ghastly gift. See Leviticus 6:4.

Thirdly, when your conscience tells you that you have acted unrighteously, do not justify yourself in the pursuit of dishonest gain. This was the great sin of Ephraim, Hosea 12:7–8. <note>The Dutch text cites verses 8–9, following the versification in contemporary Bibles.</note> *The merchant uses dishonest scales; he loves to defraud. Ephraim boasts, "I am very rich; I have become wealthy. With all my wealth they will not find in me any iniquity or sin."* He justifies himself, despite the deceitful scales being in his hand. But do not do so; for even if you do, God will nonetheless not justify you. *Shall I count them pure* (says God, Micah 6:11) *with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?* No, by no means; I will not do it, says the Lord.

<margin>Six terrifying considerations for those who have obtained their riches dishonestly.</margin>
I proceed now, and shall present to you some terrifying and amazing considerations. O all you who have obtained your riches unrighteously and dishonestly, let these six terrifying considerations go to your heart!

First, consider that riches which are poorly obtained are nothing other than robbery in the sight of God, despite them being obtained in the world through the way of commerce and trade. God views it as robbery, as if you had played the thief and stolen the same from someone’s house, or taken their purse. Psalm 62:10. <note>Cited as verse 11 in the source text.</note> *Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.* Oppression and robbery are one and the same. So also Proverbs 21:6–7. *The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death. The robbery of the wicked shall destroy them; because they refuse to do judgment.* Riches obtained with a false tongue—or a theft with the

<column-break/>

tongue—is called robbery by God; and although we do not reckon it so, God nonetheless considers it no different than if you robbed a man or stole his purse.

And therefore, Beloved, it is very noteworthy that what God required to be given back in Exodus 22:1–4 for goods that were stolen, was the same as what was given by Zaccheus for those things which he had obtained unrighteously, even though he had not "stolen" them in the common sense. Exodus 22:1. *If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.* If someone stole a sheep, the law was that he must give it back fourfold: so David judged, 2 Samuel 12:6. And Zaccheus, although he was not a thief, yet says: *If I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.* Which gives us to understand that things obtained by a deceitful tongue, and riches acquired through oppression, are in the eyes of God no better than robbery. And Beloved, none of you would willingly have the brand of a thief upon you, and truly you are no better in the eyes of God if you have obtained your means dishonestly.

Secondly, consider this terrifying thought: that all the deceit and those dishonest gains which you have made during the week come into remembrance before the Lord on the Sabbath day. You bring the curse of all your sins, which you have committed the whole week, with you on the day of the Lord. Ezekiel 28:18. *Thou hast defiled thy sanctuaries by the multitude of thine iniquities, by the iniquity of thy traffick,* <note>original: "koop-handels" (trade/commerce)</note> says God to the King of Tyre. Beloved, the sins you commit in your trade and in your commerce, they defile your addresses and approaches to God’s presence when you come before Him to worship Him. The sins of your shops defile your prayers and desecrate for you the ordinances of God. The Lord looks upon all your unrighteous gains as if you had defiled His sanctuary. Ezekiel 14:2–4. *And the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Son of man, these men have set up their idols* <note>original: "Dreck-goden" (literally "dung-gods," a derogatory term for idols)</note> *in their heart, and put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face: should I be enquired of at all by them? Therefore speak unto them, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Every man of the house of Israel that setteth up his idols in his heart, and putteth the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face, and cometh to the prophet; I the Lord will answer him that cometh according to the multitude of his idols.*

Oh! Beloved, when you approach in the solemn assembly to make your access to God, O be aware of what unrighteous gain is your Idol, and He Himself shall answer you according to your iniquities, and shall not hear your prayers. Oh! let this consideration terrify you: the sin of your Shops shall defile your sanctuary and keep from you all the profit of your prayers and divine services.

<margin>Job 20:15.</margin>
**Thirdly, consider** that if God ever awakens your conscience, you will be unable to look upon your unrighteous gains without an abundance of unrest, terror, and dismay of spirit. It may be that "stolen waters are sweet" now, and the "bread of deceit" is pleasant to you; but when God comes to wake your conscience—Oh! with what horror and terror shall your soul be seized. Job 20:15 says: *He has swallowed down riches, but he shall vomit them up again.* The riches that someone has acquired poorly shall be like food that lies <margin>Verse 20.</margin> undigested in the stomach, which one is forced to vomit back up. And verse 18: *He shall restore the fruit of his labor, and shall not swallow it down.* Verse 20: *Surely he shall feel no quietness in his belly.* That is to say, in his conscience. The great gluttons of the world, who swallow up riches through oppression, shall feel no peace in their consciences. <margin>Prov. 21:6–7.</margin> Proverbs 21:6–7: *The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death: The robbery of the wicked shall destroy them.* The word which is translated here as "destroy" <note>original: "door-snyden"</note> signifies in the original text "to saw" <note>The author refers to the Hebrew root *garar*, suggesting the wealth tears at the soul like a blade.</note>; which indicates that goods obtained through deceit and oppression shall so disturb and dismay the one who obtained them, just as a saw disturbs and torments a person whose arm or leg is being sawn off. When someone comes to die and reflects: *All this wealth, for which I labored in my life, must leave me on my deathbed;* and that his riches were the price of his soul, obtained by cheating, by swindling his neighbor, by lying, and by oppression—Oh! how shall such a person be able to look God in the face! <margin>Isa. 33:14.</margin> Isaiah 33:14: *Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? Who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings? He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions.* No one who uses dishonest gain and deceives his brother can look God in the face. What a horror and terror of conscience it will be for you when you come to die, to remember that all your riches were obtained with the blood of your soul. <margin>Matt. 27:3.</margin> So it was with Judas, Matthew 27:3.

**Fourthly, consider** that God sometimes punishes those who have acquired great means unrighteously by making them objects of scorn and shame among the people where they live. <margin>Habak. 2:9–10.</margin> Habakkuk 2:9–10: *Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high: Thou hast consulted shame to thy house.* When people join house to house and swindle the poor through oppression, they are planning shame for their own house—not by their intention, but by the outcome. Though their intention is not such, it nevertheless turns out that way; and we see through experience that often the great gluttons and oppressors bring shame upon their own necks in the places where they live.

<column-break/>

**Fifthly, consider** that God, in His righteous judgments, sometimes blows away riches that are dishonestly obtained, even in this life. The riches of oppressors sometimes die before they themselves die. <margin>Prov. 13:11.</margin> Proverbs 13:11: *Wealth gotten by vanity,* says Solomon, *shall be diminished.* Goods that are poorly obtained are called "treasures of snow"; now, the nature and property of snow is that if you hold a ball of it in your hand, it will immediately melt away. So God often causes riches that are unrighteously obtained to melt away like treasures of snow. You have a notable passage regarding this in <margin>Prov. 20:21.</margin> Proverbs 20:21: *An inheritance may be gotten hastily at the beginning; but the end thereof shall not be blessed.* There is a very good observation made by a certain writer <note>The author likely refers to a contemporary commentator like Matthew Henry or an earlier Reformed theologian.</note>: he notes that of all the tribes of Israel, the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh were the most hasty to obtain their possession of the Promised Land. And it pleased the Lord that those who were the most eager to take their possession first, lost their possessions much sooner than any of the others. As you can see in <margin>2 Kings 10:33.</margin> 2 Kings 10:33. I mention this only to show you that even if you are ever so hasty to obtain riches, God can nonetheless quickly take them from you. You have another notable passage on this subject in <margin>Jer. 17:11.</margin> Jeremiah 17:11: *As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool.*

O Beloved, consider that the curse of God waits upon riches that are poorly obtained, and He shall blow them away, perhaps before you die. <margin>Ezek. 22:12–13.</margin> Ezekiel 22:12–13: *In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbors by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord God. Behold, therefore, I have smitten mine hand at thy dishonest gain which thou hast made.* God shall strike with His hand and blow away all dishonest profit.

**Objection.** But I think I hear some rich people saying: "Certainly this is not as you say; for I have obtained profits through dishonesty, and I have acted thus and so, and have obtained great means, and I am still a rich man; I have left each of my children so much per year, and I still have this much in total; therefore, I cannot see that what you say is true."

**I answer:** It is true, a person may sometimes obtain his means dishonestly and yet die rich, leaving his means behind for his children. As may be seen in <margin>Jer. 5:27.</margin> Jeremiah 5:27: *As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great and rich.* God may allow a person to live, to become great and rich, through trade based on deceit.

**Secondly, consider this:** that you can find no true comfort nor peace of conscience in goods that are poorly obtained.

<summary>This page warns that wealth acquired through deceit and oppression brings spiritual torment, social disgrace, and divine judgment, often vanishing like melting snow. It refutes the idea that current prosperity justifies past dishonesty, noting that material success does not equal a peaceful conscience.</summary>

be; although you have obtained them unrighteously, yet you cannot keep them peacefully. <margin>Job 20:15, 18.</margin> The riches that you have swallowed down, those you shall vomit up again, Job 20:15, 18. And surely you shall find no rest in your belly. <note>The author uses the imagery of "the belly" as a metaphor for the conscience, which cannot digest stolen goods.</note>

Our Savior says, *What shall it profit a Man if he gain the whole World, and suffer the loss of his soul.* <margin>Habakkuk 2:10.</margin> By your unrighteous gains you have consulted shame for your house, and have sinned against your soul: and so much regarding the fifth Reflection.

Lastly, Consider that through dishonest gain you run the peril of the greatest loss in the whole World; namely, a precious and immortal soul. In the place previously mentioned, <margin>Habakkuk 2:12.</margin> *Woe to 그 man who obtains his riches with unrighteousness and oppression, he sins against his own soul.* <margin>James 5:3.</margin> *Woe to you rich, your gold and silver is rusted: and their rust shall be a witness against you on the Last Day.* <margin>Habakkuk 2:11.</margin> *The stone from the wall, and the beam from the wood, in the house where you have unrighteously obtained them, shall cry out for vengeance against you.* <margin>a Lapide</margin> <note>original: "a Lapide." The Spider reproaches the Bee for his flitting hither and thither; "Oh," says the Bee, *it is most foolish to vomit out life for the sake of living, to pour out the dearest marrow for the sake of being most provided for, to spend the certain for the uncertain, to lose the great for the least.* <note>original Latin: "stolidissimum est pro vita vitam evomere, providissimae carissimam medullam fundere, pro incerto certum expendere, pro minimo magnum perdere."</note>

And therefore, O Wicked one, consider that you have obtained a fine estate; but that estate shall cost you your soul if you do not govern yourself: oh let this consideration go to your heart, that through your unrighteous gains you put your precious souls in peril.

And thus I have finished these three parts of the utility <note>In 17th-century preaching, the "utility" or "use" was the section of the sermon explaining how to apply the doctrine to one's life.</note> which were directed to three sorts of People: First, to those who buy and sell in the World and can hardly bring the Year to an end. Secondly, To those who through their trade in the World obtain great means, yet unrighteously and dishonestly. And lastly, To those who have obtained great wealth and possessions, and that through righteous and praiseworthy ways. All this I shall now conclude with another short and practical utility, and so I shall end.

I have now already spent four Sermons concerning this business of buying and selling in the World; all that I shall now say as a conclusion to this subject must serve as an earnest exhortation and plea to you all, that you should, in the midst of all your buying and selling in the World, strive to conduct a trade

<column-break/>

for Heaven, and labor just as much to possess grace as Worldly Goods; and to conclude, let these three things be offered for your consideration.

First, Do you not expect some profit and increase through your trades? There is no one among you who does not intend to gain through buying and selling. Oh! therefore do not trade for Heaven if you do not labor therein to grow and become better; the Lord expects <margin>Luke 19:15.</margin> that we should put our Talent to use, and through our trading for Heaven should make a profit. <note>This refers to the Parable of the Talents, where servants are expected to invest what their master gave them.</note> Do you expect profit through your Worldly trades? and does God not expect that you, in your trading for Heaven, should win more grace, more knowledge, more experience, humility, holiness, Heavenly-mindedness, and the like?

Secondly, Would it not be a cause of sorrow to you to continue a long time with buying and selling in the World and yet not increase your estate? Would this not grieve you, Beloved? And shall it not also grieve you that you have for a long time conducted your trade for Heaven, and yet from the time you first began until this moment, you have obtained no profit? And would it not grieve you to decrease in riches after all your labor, trouble, and dealings in the World? Be careful then not to be much more grieved to now be further from Heaven than you were at the first?

Thirdly, Is it not unreasonable that all your pursuits and aims should be to win and provide things for the body, and not to take care for your soul, to provide it with supplies? Beloved, would you not regard him as an unnatural Man who would take care to clothe his slave, and yet let his Son go naked? Even so, is it not unreasonable that you should apply all effort for the body, and not care at all for the soul? Beloved, what a foolishness it is for you to be so diligent to preserve your bodies and never take any care for the welfare of your precious and immortal souls.

And thus I have now gone through three parts of the Text. And *they that weep, as though they wept not: And they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not: And they that buy, as though they possessed not.* <note>The author is quoting 1 Corinthians 7:30.</note>

The next time I shall proceed to handle the fourth and last part. And *they that use this World, as not abusing it, for the fashion of this World passes away.*

<margin>13th Sermon.</margin>
**I**n these words / *and those who use this world, as if not misusing it; for the fashion of this world passes away*; there are these two general parts:
1. A commanded duty.
2. The reason added to it.
First, the commanded duty in these words / *and they who use this world, as if not misusing it*, <note>original: "schema"</note> <term>schema (fashion/form)</term>.
Secondly, the reason added / *for the fashion, or the appearance of this world passes away*. The word <note>The Greek word "schema"</note> signifies a mathematical manner of speaking / which is a mere appearance / and nothing in essence. I shall particularly stand upon the first part of these words / *and they who use this world, as if not misusing it*; but only to learn this /
That all Men, while they use their lawful comforts in this world, must take the highest care that they do not come to misuse them.
This is the Doctrine with which I shall spend this hour. You must not only guard yourself against sinful things / but also against certain lawful things; for although there is no sin in the things themselves / there may nevertheless be a snare in them.
In the continuation of this Lesson, I shall proceed as follows.
1. I shall give you the reasons why you must not misuse the lawful comforts of this World.
Secondly, I shall show you when someone can be said, in the use of lawful comforts, to be misusing them. And lastly / I shall give you some instructions / how a Christian may come to use the lawful comforts of this life / so as not to misuse them.
I shall begin with the first / and show you the reasons why you must not misuse the lawful comforts of this life.
There are four powerful reasons to show this / two of them are found in the Scripture / and the other two are drawn from it.

<margin>Reasons why we must not misuse the lawful comforts of this life.</margin>
First, misuse nothing of that which you use; why? Because nothing of that which you use is your own / but God’s / He is the rightful Owner of all that you possess / and you know well that it is a sort of dishonor to misuse another Man’s goods. All that you have is God’s / the Beasts on a thousand mountains are His, your Corn and Wine is God’s / and if you misuse any of them for excess and drunkenness / then you misuse that which is not yours; this is the first reason / drawn from the Scripture.

<column-break/>

Secondly, there are two reasons found in the Scripture / why you must not misuse the comforts you enjoy; the one goes before my Text / the other follows after. The reason before my Text is this; *but this I say Brothers* (says the Apostle) *that the time is short:* and therefore it remains only, that what you use in the world, you should use it well, since you cannot use it for long: our time is short / and therefore do not misuse your comforts.
The reason now after my Text is / because all our comforts flee from us / wither / and run away / and therefore use this world as not misusing it , *for the fashion of this world passes away*; they fly past with Eagle’s wings / but come <note>original: "komen" (meaning they arrive or are experienced)</note> with Sparrow’s wings / your comforts vanish like smoke; and therefore it was the custom in Rome / that when the Pope went out / an Officer was ordained to burn Flax before him / which made him remember / that all his honor and riches would soon vanish and pass by like smoke. And it was a good reflection that one had while standing by the side of the River; *The Water that I see* (he said) *is now running away, and I see it no more*; so too are Worldly comforts like a running River / and are constantly running away from us : and therefore / since we cannot enjoy these comforts for long / let us then use them well / without misusing them.

<margin>So passes the glory of the world. <note>original Latin: "Sic transit Gloria Mundi"</note></margin>
Fourthly, another reason why we ought not to misuse the comforts of this World is / because Man is by nature more inclined / bolder / and more adventurous to sail forth into the misuse of lawful things / than in the committing of things that are unlawful. More die by food than by poison. It was the judgment of a learned Man / who judged that more went to Hell / by misusing lawful things / than by those things which in themselves are purely sin and unlawful; tangible and gross wickedness can easily be resisted; but who has suspicion or second thoughts regarding lawful things / when someone is eating and drinking? Who has suspicion or second thoughts that his table might be a snare to him? And he who marries a Wife / little dreams that she might loosen his union with Jesus Christ / and he who buys and sells / and does business in the World / has little suspicion that he is then selling his soul : and therefore take care that you do not misuse lawful things / because Man is by nature more inclined to misuse lawful things / than to do those things / the very doing of which is sin and unlawful : you can lose yourself in the keeping of your comforts / *we all perish by lawful things.* <note>original Latin: "licitis perimus omnes"</note> The overindulgence in delicacies and sweet foods has destroyed more than the eating of that which is bitter in taste. It is very noteworthy what is written in Luke 14:18. There were three sorts of Men who made their apology and excuse / why they would not come to the Supper of the great King /

**Answer.** I shall describe it very briefly and show you in four parts / what you must do to use lawful things legally / and to not misuse them.

**First** / If you wish to use lawful things well and rightly / use them in a Spiritual manner / and then you shall not misuse them; use earthly things with a Heavenly mind. Just as the wicked use Spiritual things carnally <note>original: *vleesschelijcken*</note> / so you ought to use carnal things Spiritually / that is, while you are busy with carnal things / you ought to make a Spiritual use of them. Thus did our Savior / when the people came to him for Bread / he took the occasion / to tell them of the Bread of Life and of that Manna that fell down from Heaven, of which a person might eat and not die. So also when the Samaritan Woman was busy at the Water-well drawing water / Christ took the occasion and opportunity to tell her of the Water of Life; of the living Water, of which anyone having drunk, would never thirst again for all eternity. Thus Christ used carnal things in a Spiritual manner. It is permissible for a person to speak and discourse of Worldly things / of buying and selling / and of trade; but in the conclusion some Spiritual and Heavenly things ought always to be touched upon. A person shall never use the World well / until he uses it in a Spirit-

This poor little bird, he said, which knows not where it shall stay, except to rest on a hedge, and knows not where it shall have a morsel of food, or where it shall pick up the first crumb, and yet it can sing and be merry, and therefore why should I (who have enough of the things of the World) be dejected and disturbed with care and anxiety over them?

**Secondly**, Use the things of the World with reflection and oversight / and then you shall not misuse them. From the World, have your oversight upon God. When you enjoy any of the comforts of this life / and find taste and sweetness in any of the creatures / then consider by way of reflection and oversight / that if such taste and sweetness is in the creature / what a sweetness is there then in God the Creator? If you use the World thus / you shall not misuse it. If the creature is so full of goodness and sweetness / oh, how full is God then? If there is such comfort in enjoying the goods here below / oh! what a comfort is there then in having grace in our hearts / and in enjoying those incorruptible treasures which do not perish, which neither moth nor rust can destroy, nor thieves break through to steal. # A Christian’s Instruction.

Seek first the Kingdom of God, and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you, **Matt. 6:33.** Before you seek the world / you ought to seek Heavenly things. Seek first the Kingdom of Heaven / in your judgment and esteem / as the primary and supreme object of your desires and delights. Let the principal meditations of your heart be toward spiritual things; make that your work / for which end you were sent into the world. You may indeed seek after worldly things / but when you have them / then you must use them in service of Heavenly and Spiritual things. You may carry out your calling / out of obedience to God’s command; but let your aim be / to be better suited thereby to maintain your Household / to serve God in that relationship / and in the place in which he has set you / to provide support to the poor / and to comfort the needy / and to sustain others / who lack the help and assistance of your generosity. You ought to have an eye on spiritual things / as being the primary and principal things to look after; and use all your comforts as so many steps <note>The original Dutch uses *trappen*, suggesting a staircase leading upward to heaven.</note> to bring you closer to Heaven. You ought to be submissive to God / in whatever state he has placed you / and not use the world for the world's sake / nor carry out your calling / and buy and sell / solely to obtain profit / and to become rich and great in the World / bringing Religion and godliness into subjection to the world; for that is a very great abuse of the World: but let all things here below second and be subservient to spiritual and Heavenly things.

It is very noteworthy / that where there are five petitions in the Lord’s Prayer for spiritual things / there is but one for bodily and temporal things / and that is / **Give us this day our daily bread**: To teach us and give us to know / that our desires and meditations ought most of all to be toward spiritual things. Furthermore, these are required in the first place / before worldly things / to teach us that worldly things ought to be subject to the spiritual. These are rules here / if you observe them / you shall not misuse the World.

And so I have run through the Doctrine of this subject / I shall only speak a word or two more by way of application <term>toe-eygeninge: a theological term for applying the sermon’s lesson to the listener’s life</term> / and with that I have finished.

**Use.** <note>In 17th-century sermons, a "Use" or "Improvement" is a practical takeaway for the congregation.</note> First, If it is so / that we ought not to misuse the lawful comforts of this life / then this Doctrine (by way of rebuke from God) lays a righteous blame and rebuke upon all men / who misuse the things of this world. It is lawful for a man to eat and to drink / and to enjoy the comforts of this life; but you must not misuse the same to excess / gluttony / or drunkenness / etc.

**Secondly,** this serves as an exhortation: There is no one among those who live in the World / but he must more or less use the World; and therefore my greatest request is / that you would use the world, as not misusing it: And to better persuade you in this / I shall present various considerations to you; but the time has now elapsed / I shall save it for another time.

If man is careful not to misuse an iron instrument / how much more careful shall he be over a silver or golden instrument; if you must not misuse things of a lesser and poorer nature / how much less ought you to misuse things of a higher and more excellent nature. If you ought not to misuse Worldly things / how much less then the Spiritual; and therefore do not misuse the institutions and ordinances of God / do not misuse the Sacraments / nor the Sermons / nor the means of grace / by living unfruitfully and unprofitably under the same.

A person ought to keep to a middle-measure <note>The original Dutch *middel-mate* refers to "moderation" or the "golden mean," a central virtue in Reformed ethics.</note> in the things of the world, and it ought not to matter to him whether he has them or not. But it is not so in spiritual matters; there you must pray as if you were truly praying, as it is said <margin>Faithful prophets.</margin> of Elijah in James 5:17. And you must pour out strong cries to God and hear God’s Word as if you were truly a hearer of it, doing every duty with all your might and strength.

<margin>Ten considerations to move a person to use the world without misusing it.</margin>Admonition. Second Use. Secondly, this doctrine must serve us as an admonition to obey this Apostolic rule and put it into practice: to use the world as if not misusing it. And to make this admonition reach your heart more effectively, I shall set before your eyes ten pressing considerations by way of motives. But, beloved, in view of the coldness of the time <note>Likely referring to the physical coldness of the church building or the season during the sermon's delivery.</note>, I shall greatly shorten my considerations and only give you the core and aim of the matters.

First, if you wish to use the world without misusing it, consider that in misusing the things of the world, you subvert the end which God intends in giving them to you. For the end God intends and aims for is that every creature should lead you to the Creator, so that you might the more wonder at His goodness and magnify and promote His praise and honor. God wants all the blessings He bestows upon you to serve you as a tube or a spyglass <note>The original *buyse ofte verre-kijcker* refers to early telescopes, suggesting that earthly blessings are lenses through which we see God more clearly from a distance.</note> to behold Him more clearly through them, even though you are still at a great distance from Him, 1 Timothy 4:4. For every creature of God is good and must be received with thanksgiving. Just as the dove looks upward at every grain it picks up, so ought a Christian to do. And therefore, if you misuse any of His creatures, you subvert the purpose of the Most High. God the Lord has ordained food to be used to satisfy your hunger, but not to feed your gluttony. He gives you drink

<column-break/>

to quench your thirst, but not to incite you to drunkenness. God has given you clothes to cover your nakedness and to keep you warm, but not to use them for pride <note>original: *hoobaardye*, meaning vanity or haughtiness.</note>; and so it is with all other comforts. This, then, is the first consideration.

Secondly, to keep yourself from misusing worldly things, consider that you are not an owner, but only a possessor <note>The author distinguishes between *eygenaar* (legal owner) and *bezitter* (temporary holder or steward).</note> of the blessings you enjoy in the world. It is true, there is a common proverb among people when you rebuke them for misusing creatures: "Oh," they will immediately say, "may I not do with my own as I please?" Oh, no! Not at all, beloved, for you have nothing that is yours; it is all God's. As can be seen in Psalm 50:10, 11, 12: *For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills. I know all the fowls of the mountains: and the wild beasts of the field are mine. If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fullness thereof.* See also Hosea 2:8, 19. So that when you misuse the things of the world, you misuse that which is not your own at all, but God's. And you know that it is a kind of indecency <note>original: *oneerbaarhept*, here implying a breach of trust or lack of integrity.</note> to misuse another man’s goods. All that you have in the world are but borrowed blessings; God alone has the right and ownership of the same. He only lends them to us for our use and reserves the ownership for Himself. If there is anything (which we call our own among all other things) that might actually be said to be our own, it is surely our body, for that is closest to us; and yet even this is not our own. For the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 6:19, 20: *What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.* When a person borrows something from someone, the lender asks that he use it well. Elisha’s servant <note>The text says "Elifaas Dienst-knecht," but the biblical reference 2 Kings 6:5 refers to the sons of the prophets with Elisha.</note> borrowed only an axe to chop wood, and when the axe fell into the water, he cried out and said: "Alas, my master! for it was borrowed," 2 Kings 6:5. The mercies you have are borrowed rather than given; shall I wound someone with his own weapons? Yet you do so to God when you misuse any of His blessings.

Thirdly, to keep yourself from misusing the lawful comforts of this life, consider what was noted above: that man is more inclined to sin in the use of lawful things than in doing those things which are in themselves inherently unlawful. A greater multitude has died from overindulging the stomach with wholesome food than from taking poison. Beloved, thousands of people go to ruin through the misuse of lawful things.

Fourthly, consider that it is not as easy for a person to repent of the misuse of lawful things as it is for the commission of gross sins, which can be more easily recognized, and...

# A Christian’s Instruction.

->Seek first the Kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you, *Matt. 6:33.*<- While you seek the world, you ought to seek Heavenly things. Seek first the Kingdom of Heaven in your judgment and esteem, as the chief and supreme object of your desires and delights. Let the primary meditations of your heart be toward spiritual things; make that your work, for which purpose you were sent into the world. You may indeed seek after worldly things, but when you have them, you must use them in service of Heavenly and Spiritual things. You may carry out your vocation out of obedience to God’s command; but let your aim be to become more capable through it to provide for your household, to serve God in that capacity and in the place where He has set you, to give assistance to the poor and comfort the needy, and to support others who lack the help and assistance of your generosity. You ought to have an eye on spiritual things as the most important and principal things to look toward; and use all your comforts as steps to bring you closer to Heaven. You ought to be submissive to God in whatever state He has placed you, and not use the world for the world’s sake, nor carry out your vocation, or buy and sell, merely to obtain profit and to become rich and great in the world—bringing Religion and godliness into subjection to the world; for that is a very great misuse of the World. Rather, let all things here below second and be subservient to spiritual and Heavenly things.

It is very remarkable that where there are five petitions in the Lord's Prayer for spiritual things, there is only one for physical and temporal things, and that is: *Give us this day our daily bread.* This is to teach us and give us to know that our desires and meditations should most of all be toward spiritual things. Moreover, these are required in the first place, before worldly things, to teach us that worldly things ought to be subject to the spiritual. These are four rules; if you observe them, you shall not misuse the World.

And so I have run through the doctrinal part of this subject; I shall speak only a word or two more by way of application <note>The original term *toe-eygeninge* refers to "appropriation" or "application," a standard part of a 17th-century sermon where the preacher explains how the listeners should apply the lesson to their own lives.</note>, and with that I have done.

**Use. First,** if it is so that we ought not to misuse the lawful comforts of this life <note>The "lawful comforts" (*geoorloofde vertroostingen*) refer to things allowed by God, such as food, marriage, and work, which are good in themselves but can be abused.</note>, then this Doctrine (by way of a rebuke from God) places a righteous blame and reprimand upon all people who misuse the things of this world. It is lawful for a person to eat and drink, and to enjoy the comforts of this life; but you must not misuse them to excess, gluttony, or drunkenness, etc.

**Secondly,** this serves as an exhortation: There is no one who lives in the World who must not, more or less, use the World; and therefore my greatest request is that you would use the world as not misusing it. And in order not to overwhelm you herein, I shall propose several considerations to you; but the time has now run out; I shall save it for another time.

<column-break/>

<margin>1 Cor. 7 verses 30, 31.</margin>
> And they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not;
> And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.

---

<margin>XIV. Sermon.</margin>
There yet remain several "uses" <note>In the context of 17th-century preaching, a "use" (*nuttigheyt*) is a practical takeaway or lesson derived from the scripture.</note> from this Doctrine: that it is the bounden duty of Christians, in using lawful things, to guard themselves so that they do not come to misuse them. These I shall handle this morning, and save the reasons why (for the fashion of this world passes away) until after the midday.

The uses I shall make of this are only two.
**1. For a warning.**
**2. For an exhortation.**

**Uses. First,** if it is so that Christians in using lawful comforts ought to be careful that they do not come to misuse them—where they ought to use the World as if they used it not—Beloved, then carry these few Warnings with you.

**First warning.** If you must not misuse Worldly things, so much more you ought to beware that you do not come to misuse Spiritual things in the use of them. You must make your life correspond with your confession, and not confess much and live little. And do not use Religion as a cloak for wickedness. You go to Church and observe the ordinances of God; but beware that you do not misuse these exercises and make them a cloak to cover some hidden villainy or godlessness. And do not misuse God's Word, nor use your tongue to mock and jest with the Scripture; and do not misuse your gifts or graces, nor despise or look down upon those who lack them. If a person is careful not to misuse an iron instrument, how much more careful will he be over a silver or golden instrument; if you must not misuse things of a lesser and meaner nature, how much less should you misuse things of a higher and more excellent nature. If you ought not to misuse Worldly things, how much less then the Spiritual; and therefore do not misuse the institutions and ordinances of God, do not misuse the Sacraments, nor the Sermons, nor the means of grace, by living unfruitfully and unprofitably under them.

**Secondly,** take this for your Warning: that these advices and instructions of the Apostle—of weeping as though not weeping, and rejoicing as though not rejoicing, and buying as though not possessing, etc.—must not be extended to any Spiritual duties; but only to the...

<meta>This page continues the "Christian’s Instruction," concluding the tenth point of exhortation and beginning the fifteenth sermon on the fleeting nature of worldly comforts based on 1 Corinthians 7:31.</meta>

# A Christian’s Instruction.

shall be made free, etc. That is, in the hope that the creature shall not always be thus subject to the ungodly, and be an instrument to their sin, and a dishonor to its Creator: the creature is subject, in the hope of being delivered at one time or another from this burden of being used by the ungodly to God’s dishonor.

Tenthly, consider that you cannot use worldly things for long, and therefore you ought to use them well. This is the argument of the text: *But this I say, brethren* (says the Apostle), *that the time is short* (and therefore let those who weep be as though they wept not: and those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not: and those who buy, as though they possessed not: and those who use this world, as though they misused it not). Why? Because the time is short. You cannot enjoy them for long, and therefore you ought to use them well.

And thus, beloved, I have finished these Apostolic instructions; there remain now only the reasons or the motives why we should not use the things of this world unlawfully, because the <term>fashion of this world passes away</term><note>Based on 1 Corinthians 7:31. The original Dutch uses 'gedaente,' meaning the outward form or appearance.</note>. Why must we weep as though not weeping, and rejoice as though not rejoicing, and buy as though not possessing, and use the world as though not misusing it? Why? Because the fashion of this world passes away. The "fashion" of this world: the word signifies a <term>mathematical way of speaking</term><note>The author likely refers to a geometric 'schema' or 'figure' which represents the shape of an object without having its physical substance or volume.</note> (as has been said) which is merely a bare knowledge or appearance, and nothing in essence and substance; such a thing is the world. All the pomp, glory, honor, riches, and highness or greatness of this world are all but fading and vanishing comforts; they are constantly passing by, like a flowing stream. The fashion of this world: the word, says another Author, signifies such a fashion as occurs in a <term>Comedy on the Stage</term><note>A common 17th-century metaphor: the world as a theater ('Theatrum Mundi') where roles are temporary.</note>, where all things are but for a little time to please the eye; a beggar there may well fill the office of a King. So it is with all the comforts, glory, and honor of the world; it is all passing by, like the water of a river; they are constantly running away from you. <note>Guillaume</note> Budæus reads it as: it deceives like an *ignis fatuus* <note>original: "Ignis fatuus"; a will-o'-the-wisp or 'foolish fire' seen over marshes at night.</note>. That is, like a "stable-candle" <note>An old Dutch term for a will-o'-the-wisp.</note>. I would first treat these words in a relative sense, as a reason why we must use the world as not misusing it, because the fashion of this world passes away, from which you might learn:

That the earnest contemplation—that all the comforts and blessings of this world quickly pass by and fade—is a powerful means to move Christians so that they do not set their hearts upon them.

Who would want to set their heart on that which passes by so quickly? Like the running water that swiftly rushes past; even so are the things of the world soon gone and run away, and therefore this ought to awaken Christians not to misuse them, but to use them well, seeing they pass by very quickly.

<column-break/>

But I prefer to treat the words as a pure proposition in themselves, from which the Doctrine shall be this:

**That all the comforts and conditions of this world are passing away from us, even while they are with us.**

This is the Doctrine with which I shall spend an hour this afternoon.

---

->1 Cor. 7: 30, 31.<-

>And those who weep, as though they wept not; and those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and those who buy, as though they possessed not;
>And those who use this world as not misusing it. For the fashion of this world passes away.

<margin>XV. Sermon.</margin>

**T**he fashion of this world passes away. The Doctrine that we have drawn from these words was this: **That all the comforts and satisfactions of this life are passing away from us, even while they are with us.** They are of a changeable and fading nature.

Beloved, so that this general Doctrine may work a little upon your souls, I shall first show you the truth of this Doctrine, and then draw some practical conclusions from it, and so finish this text.

That all worldly things are fleeing away from us, even while they are with us, I shall show you through these three or four things.

<margin>All the comforts of this life are fleeing from us, even while they are with us.</margin>
First, it appears by the <term>induction of the parts</term><note>A logical method where a general rule is proven by examining individual examples.</note>; for if you behold all the states and conditions of men, whether in honor, prosperity, or riches, etc., you shall see all these conditions in a fading and consuming form. Behold Adam in the state of his innocence; his state seemed to be a firm and lasting state, and yet Adam did not remain one night in honor, but became like the beasts which perish. Look also at Solomon, who was the honor and glory of the world; and neither before him nor after him was there any like him; all things of the earth showed him reverence and brought him gifts. 2 Chron. 9:13; there the whole sum of Solomon’s Glory is shown: *Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold; besides that which the chapmen and merchants brought; also all the kings of Arabia, and the governors of the country, brought gold and silver to Solomon.* Furthermore, King Solomon made two hundred <term>bucklers</term><note>Large shields; 'Rondassen' in the original.</note> of beaten gold: six hundred <term>shekels</term><note>An ancient unit of weight and currency; 'Zickelen' in the original.</note> of beaten gold went to each buckler. Likewise three hundred shields of beaten gold; three hundred shekels of gold went to each shield: and the King put them in the house of the forest of Lebanon. Moreover, the King made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold. And the throne had six steps, and a footstool of gold, which were fastened to the throne, and stays on each side of the sitting place, and two

Lions stood by the armrests. And twelve lions stood there on both sides, upon the six steps: the like of it had not been made in any kingdom. Also, all King Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the house of the forest of Lebanon were of pure gold; silver was not accounted for anything in the days of Solomon. For the King’s ships sailed to Tarshish with the servants of Huram: once every three years the ships of Tarshish came in, bringing gold and silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Thus King Solomon became greater than all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom. And all the kings of the earth sought Solomon’s presence to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart. And they each brought their gift: vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments, armor, and spices, horses, and mules, year by year. Solomon also had four thousand stalls for horses, and chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen: and he stationed them in the chariot cities, and with the King at Jerusalem. And he reigned over all the kings from the River <note>The River usually refers to the Euphrates.</note> unto the land of the Philistines, and unto the border of Egypt. The King also made silver in Jerusalem as common as stones; and cedars he made to be as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland in abundance. And they brought horses for Solomon out of Egypt, and out of all those lands. And yet, what became of all his glory and honor? Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like a lily of the field, as Christ says in Matthew 6, verses 29–30. Also, if you look upon all conditions of men in honor, they stand on slippery places and are sliding down every day, as can be seen in Job 20, verses 6, 7, 8, 9: Though his loftiness mounts up to the heavens and his head reaches to the clouds, he shall perish forever like his own dung; those who had seen him shall say: where is he? He shall fly away like a dream, so that he shall not be found: and he shall be chased away like a vision of the night, etc. So also has the Assyrian Monarchy passed to the Persians, and the Persian to the Greeks, and the Greek to the Romans. The state of honor is a fading state.

<margin><note>original: "Divitiæ habent finem suum aut finem tuum."</note> Riches have their end, or you have yours.</margin> Or if it is your portion to be rich in the world, that state is also fading: your riches shall either see their end, or you shall see theirs (1 Timothy 6:17). And set not your hope on the uncertainty of riches; so also Proverbs 23:5: Riches shall certainly make themselves wings and fly away. And Proverbs 27:24: For riches are not forever: or shall the crown endure from generation to generation?

The second proof to show that all worldly things are fading and passing away is this: because the entire world is of a perishable nature, and therefore worldly things must necessarily be so as well (2 Peter 3:10). The heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall burn and melt, and the earth and the works that are therein shall be burned up.

Thirdly, Man—who is God’s masterpiece in the world—is constantly fading and passing away, and therefore so

<column-break/>

much more are the things of the world. Man’s life is but a vapor, but a smoke from the womb to the grave; <note>original: "animantis cujusque vita est in fuga"</note> *the life of every living thing is in flight*. Man has here no continuing city (Hebrews 13:14; Psalm 144:4; Psalm 39:6). And Job, in the last part of the first chapter, says: Naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither. No mention is made of remaining stationary in the world—nothing but a coming into the world and a departing again out of the same.

Fourthly, it appears from those parables <note>The author uses "parables" here in the sense of biblical metaphors or comparisons.</note> by which the world and that which is in it are compared in the Scriptures.

First, the Spirit of God—to make known to us the uncertainty of all things here below—compares the world to a glassy sea mixed with fire (Revelation 15:2). It is compared to a sea because of its rising and falling; and to a glassy sea because of its brittleness and uncertainty, for it is easily broken; and to a glassy sea mixed with fire to teach and show us that the world is always in a consuming state. Now, no one shall look upon the sea except as a very uncertain and unstable element; that drop of water which was here just now is instantly gone and cannot be found.

Secondly, the world is compared to a cloud (Job 30:15). My prosperity (says Job) has passed away like a cloud. Clouds are always fleeing away, and so is the world and all that is in it. And therefore David says (Psalm 104:3) that God makes the clouds his chariot, signifying his readiness and swiftness in his works of mercy or judgment.

Thirdly, the world is compared to a wind (Psalm 78:39). As a wind that passes away and comes not again; so also Psalm 18:10 and 104:3. What is lighter and swifter than the wind? How quickly a wind blows past! So there is also no permanence in any things here below.

Fourthly, the world is compared to grass (James 1:10). For the rich shall pass away as a flower of the grass. For the sun has risen with its heat and has withered the grass, and its flower has fallen, and the beautiful appearance of its face has perished: so also shall the rich man fade in his ways. Not only compared to grass, but to a flower of the grass <note>Meaning something even more fragile than the grass itself.</note>.

Fifthly, it is compared to smoke—and you know that the wind instantly scatters smoke hither and thither (Hosea 13:3). Therefore they shall be like a morning cloud, and like the early dew that passes away. (You know that as soon as the sun shines, the dew instantly vanishes.) Like chaff from the threshing floor, and like smoke that is stormed away from the chimney. There are five parables placed together here in that one verse, so that you see, beloved, that these parables very clearly show and reveal how uncertain, fading, and perishable all worldly honor and comforts are.

I come now to that which I particularly intended, and that is, to put it all into a...

# A Christian’s Instruction. 471

...to wind up the practical application. And all I shall do here is to draw seven practical instructions from this general teaching.

<margin>Practical instructions by way of utility.</margin>
First, if it is so that all worldly things pass us by even while they are with us? Well then, let this consideration wean your affections from all worldly things. Why would you want to love so greatly that which cannot remain with you for long? This is the counsel that Solomon gives in Proverbs 23:5: "Will you set your eyes to fly upon that which is not?" What is it? Though they exist in substance, they do not exist in permanence; for riches shall certainly make themselves wings and fly away. This consideration ought to wean your love from all physical comforts. And though we look upon worldly things with our eyes, we should not do so with our hearts: but let them be fixed, not on the things that are seen, but on the things that are not seen; for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal. 2 Corinthians 4:18. They are not worthy of being gazed upon because they are temporal. In a certain city in Greece named <term>Sparta</term><note>The author uses a historical anecdote about a rotating kingship to illustrate the transience of power.</note>, there was a King who was King for only one year; after that, he lived humbly in a hidden place, and therefore hardly anyone could be brought to accept the position. So too should the consideration of the withering nature of all worldly things move us to withdraw our affections from them.

Secondly, if the fashion of this world passes away, then let this awaken and stir your souls to look toward other things of another world, which are more stable and enduring. <term>Chrysostom</term><note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an important Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note> compares the world to an eel; and you know that the tighter you hold an eel, the sooner it will slip out of your hands. So it is with worldly things: the tighter you think to hold them, the faster they shall slide away from you, and therefore labor to hold fast to Christ, grace, glory, Heaven, and blessedness. Hebrews 13:14: "For here we have no continuing city" (says the Apostle) "and therefore let us seek one to come." Because they had no lasting city here, they looked for one to come, for a city whose builder and maker was God. They looked to the things of another world, which would not perish as this one does. As seen in 2 Corinthians 4:18: "We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal." You have another remarkable passage for this purpose in Hebrews 11:15–17. There it is spoken of the godly Patriarchs, that if they had been mindful of that country from which they went out, they might have had opportunity to return; but now they desire a better, that is, a heavenly one. Because they did not look back to their own country, the land of Canaan, they declared they had a better one in sight, for which they strove—namely, a heavenly Kingdom. The King of Sparta found, during that year

<column-break/>

when he was King, a great treasure for the place of his banishment, so that he might live well there afterward for the rest of his life. So Christians also, while they live here, ought to lay up treasures in heaven. Matthew 6:19–20. Beloved, are the things of this world so vain and uncertain? Well then, let us look toward the things of a better world.

Thirdly, if it is so that this world is so null and perishable, then labor to be convinced of the truth of the same, and let your heart be sensitive to the vanity and uncertainty of all things here below. I may say of the same just as the Apostle speaks in another context, Colossians 2:22: "All these things perish with the using." As soon as you grasp the world, it passes away. We have no more stability in these earthly things than in a flock of birds; I cannot say they are mine, even though they sit in my garden. The glory of <term>Ephraim</term><note>A reference to Hosea 9:11, where the glory of the tribe of Ephraim is described as flying away like a bird.</note> is said to fly away like a bird. The world withers like a small bouquet while you are smelling it, just as snow melts while it is in the hands of children. At the inauguration of the Popes, it is customary for someone to go before him, burning a bundle of straw or flax, crying out,
->*Thus passes the glory of the world,*<-
<note>original: "sic transit gloria mundi"</note>
that is: So the glory of the world passes by. It is a wonderful consideration that a learned man has regarding the names of the two first-born humans in the world, Cain and Abel; we can learn this lesson (he says) even from their names. <insert>Cain</insert> here signifies "possession," and <insert>Abel</insert> here signifies "vanity"; to show that Adam and Eve saw nothing but vanity in all their possessions. Oh! You who are the sons and daughters of Adam, who have much less of the world than Adam had, oh, that you would not set your hearts on the vanities and uncertainties of this world, which pass you by so quickly.

Fourthly, if it is so that all the comforts of this world are passing away, then it shows the folly and madness of those men whose most zealous pursuits are after withering vanities. Oh, what a distraction it is for a man to be so zealous in his pursuit of these passing and withering things, and meanwhile come to neglect things of a greater excellence and durability! And yet there is a world of such foolish and mad people among us, who pursue vanities and neglect eternal riches. Oh, how foolish are many people in the world, who are so zealous about the base and minor things of the world, and meanwhile are negligent in the great heavenly affairs; like <term>Artaxerxes</term><note>Artaxerxes II, a Persian King, was sometimes mocked in historical anecdotes for trivial hobbies while his empire faced crisis.</note>, who kept himself busy making hilts for knives and neglected the most weighty matters of his kingdom; or like <term>Archimedes</term><note>The famous Greek mathematician who was allegedly so focused on his geometric drawings that he did not notice the Roman capture of his city, Syracuse.</note>, who was busy drawing mathematical lines and never took heed to save his city or his life. Histories testify of <term>Caligula</term>, a Roman Emperor (for which reason he was also held for a fool by all those who have written of him), that having prepared a great fleet of ships...
