(as his subjects thought that he would have carried out a great matter, and would have won many kingdoms with the same) he suddenly commanded (contrary to all their expectations) that they go and load all their ships with **mussel shells** and **pebbles**, and so return. <note>This likely refers to the Roman Emperor Caligula, who famously ordered his soldiers to collect seashells as "spoils of the ocean" instead of invading Britain.</note> There are many such foolish people who disturb themselves in the pursuit of mussel shells and pebbles—the withering follies of this world—and neglect the pursuit of the firm, lasting, and substantial riches of the Kingdom of Heaven.

**Fifthly**, is it so, that worldly things are so withering? Then we can see from this the difference and great distinction that exists between earthly and heavenly things. The glory of this world passes away; but you cannot say that of heavenly things. The first wears out like your clothes; the other is like your bodies <note>In the sense of the resurrected, glorified body</note> and is not worn out. *Riches are a fleeting vanity*, Proverbs 21:6. But graces are *enduring riches*, Proverbs 8:18; 1 Peter 1:24. *The grass withers, and its flower falls away; but the Word of the Lord God remains forever.* By the "grass" and the "flower of the grass," we are to understand all the glories of this world, all of which wither and perish; but the Word of the Lord God remains forever. That is, the work of grace, wrought in your hearts through the Word, shall remain into eternity: that shall continue to last, while all the glory of the world passes away. 1 John 2:17. *And the world passes away, and its lusts: but he who does the will of God remains forever.* Beloved, here you see the great inequality that exists between heavenly and worldly things, such as wealth and honor, etc. Suppose you were an heir to a crown or a kingdom; these are but temporary inheritances and last only for a time; but a heavenly inheritance remains into eternity. 1 Peter 1:4. *To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that does not fade away, reserved in Heaven for you.* All your comforts here below are but for a moment: riches and honor are not everlasting, but God and Christ, and Grace, Heaven, and Glory are everlasting: these are comforts that do not perish but remain eternally. Your earthly parents are not everlasting, but your Heavenly Father remains into eternity, Isaiah 9:6. We do not have eternal life here, but in Heaven our life lasts into eternity, Luke 18:30. Here below you are happy one day and sad the next, but in Heaven your joy shall be everlasting. Isaiah 35:10. *And everlasting joy shall be upon their heads.* So also 2 Thessalonians 2:16. *Who has loved us, and has given us an everlasting consolation*, etc. Here your comforts are only for a short time, but in Heaven they remain into eternity. Here your possessions are only passing, but there they are for always and eternal in Heaven: and here you are soon forgotten, and the memory of your names lost; but in Heaven you shall have an eternal memorial, Psalm 112:6.

**Sixthly**, are the comforts of this world passing away? Then know this also for

<column-break/>

your comfort: that the miseries, difficulties, and oppressions of this world are also passing away. *For our light affliction, which is but for a moment*, etc. 2 Corinthians 4:17. Suppose you are a person of a slight and lowly status in the world; what does it matter? For your poverty shall also pass away. Suppose you are sickly and weak of frame; well, your sickness shall also perish. Suppose you are a prisoner and in slavery; well, you shall yet shake off your wearying shackles and prison. Job 11:16. *Your misery shall pass away like a flow of water.* So also Isaiah 35:10. *And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs, and everlasting joy shall be <margin>Every day is bearable <note>original Latin: "Omnis dies tolerabilis"</note></margin> upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, but sorrow and <margin>because it is short <note>original Latin: "quia brevis"</note></margin> sighing shall flee away.* Your miseries and sorrows are just as passing as your comforts. And therefore, beloved, this ought to support and uphold your hearts.

<margin>Why lead [it] to use, when they cannot but lead to punishment? <note>original Latin: "Cur eam ad usum dum non possunt non ad supplicium ducer-"</note></margin>
**Seventhly**, if the pleasures and comforts of this world are passing away, then we ought to take the highest care that we do not, for the sake of having a moment of pleasure, <margin>whether destined to be perpetual <note>original Latin: "num destinari perpetua"</note></margin> cast ourselves into eternal punishments. Beloved, it would be better if there were some proportion and equality between your comforts here and your punishments hereafter; <margin>Riches are fleeting, vain, and perishable <note>original Latin: "Divitiæ sunt caduca, vanæ & peritura"</note></margin> but why should anyone be so foolish that, to obtain a perishable status, he would damn his soul and bring an eternal pain and misery upon his own neck? Riches and the comforts of this life run quickly by; but the punishment for the abuse of the same lasts into eternity. This is like the godless **Esau**, who sold his birthright for a dish of stew. And therefore, O my beloved, be exhorted rather to suffer oppression with God’s people here for a small time, so that you may reign with them in Heaven and be blessed into all eternity, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin here for a time and thereby bring eternal punishments upon yourself in the world to come.

And so, Beloved, in these fifteen sermons, I have run through many points regarding this subject. There remains now only this: regarding the time you still have to live in the world, that those who have miseries, difficulties, and oppressions in the same must *weep as though they wept not*. And those who have riches, honor, and comforts, and enjoy an abundance of all worldly prosperity, let them *be glad as though they were not glad*. And those who buy and sell in the world and conduct trade, it remains only that they *buy as though they possessed not*. And those who use the world in another way, it remains only that they *use it as not abusing it; for the fashion of this world passes away.* <note>The author concludes by paraphrasing 1 Corinthians 7:29–31.</note>

# The Service of Angels to the
## Chosen on Earth
### By Master CHRISTOPHER LOVE; and translated by A. van Laren.

---

->Hebrews 1, verse 14.<-

> Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?

---

<margin>Jesus Christ surpasses the Angels.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring a figure and foliage.</image-desc>
T HE principal aim of the Apostle in this Chapter is to show the excellent dignity of Jesus Christ, surpassing the most excellent of Creatures—namely, the Angels; and he proves this through these six arguments.

1. Argument. First, he sets forth the Dignity of Jesus Christ above the Angels in view of the fact that He has a more excellent Name than the Angels, and that is presented in the fourth verse: *Being made so much better than the angels, as he hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than they.* Jesus Christ has a more excellent Name than the Angels. The Angels are but the **Servants of God**, but **Jesus Christ is called the Son of God.**

2. Argument. That although the Scripture calls the Angels *Children of God* (Job 38:7. *When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy*), nevertheless Jesus Christ is the Son of God in a more excellent manner than the Angels, and of that you may read in the 5th verse: *For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee?* and again, *I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son.* Although the Angels are the Sons of God, yet the Scripture does not say that they are the begotten <note>The author distinguishes between being "created" (like angels) and "begotten" (the unique status of Christ in Christian theology).</note> Sons of God; but of Jesus Christ it is said that He is the begotten Son of God; they are the Sons of God through Creation, but Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God through eternal generation, and therefore far above the Angels.

3. Argument. Jesus Christ is higher than the Angels because they are commanded by God the Father to worship the Son Jesus Christ; and this you also have expressed and set down in the sixth verse: *And again, when he bringeth in the first-begotten into the world, he saith, And let all the angels of God worship him.* The dignity and the honor of Jesus Christ is far above the dignity of the Angels, because the Angels themselves are commanded to fall down, to worship Him, and to obey Him.

4. Argument. Jesus Christ is far above the Angels because the Angels were made by Him, and are but His ministering Spirits; and that is presented in the seventh verse: *And of the angels he saith, Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a*

<column-break/>

flame of fire. And not only are the Angels made by Jesus Christ, but all things are made by Him that are made, both which are in Heaven and on Earth; and He makes His Angels ministering Spirits, and His servants flames of fire, and therefore Christ must necessarily be above them.

5. Argument. There it is said that Jesus Christ sits at the Right Hand of the Majesty of God, verse 13: *But to which of the angels said he at any time, Sit on my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool?* The Angels do not sit at the Right Hand of God, but Christ has sat down at the Right Hand of God; they are only there to serve Jesus Christ, and that for the sake of the chosen of God in the world.

6. Argument. The manner in which Jesus Christ is far above them—namely, in dignity and honor—for so the Text says: *Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?* And thus you see that I have led you by the hand to the words themselves.

**Are they not all ministering spirits?]** This is not a question of doubt, but a clear and strong affirmation. Are they not all ministering spirits? That is: they certainly are. It is to be understood as if the words were spoken in a positive and affirmative manner.

**All]** There are none of the Angels but that they are ministering Spirits for the elect and the People of God who shall inherit Salvation. However, the Papist <note>A historical, often polemical term for Roman Catholics.</note> commentators say that there are some Angels of the higher Orders, such as the Cherubim, who serve God alone because they are of a higher nature; they bring forward Daniel 7:10: *A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him.* But this is merely an imagination. They serve God by serving us. Again, you see that the Apostle tells you that they are all ministering spirits—all without exception.

**Ministering Spirits]** *Lestoyrgika pneumata.* <note>Greek: *Leitourgika pneumata*, from which we get the word "liturgy"; it refers to public or priestly service.</note> *Properly signifies one who most zealously serves the public good, for whom this one thing is proposed: to be as useful as possible to all, and to harm no one.* <note>original Latin: "Propriè significat eum qui bone publico studiosissime servit, cui hoc unum est propositum, quo ad ejus fieri potest, prodesse omnibus, obesse nemini."</note> The word that is taken here for "ministering" signifies a public Servant who presents himself to the utmost, even with all his power to do good in the place where he belongs and wherein he is set; you have the same word also in Romans 13:6: *For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing.* So that these Servants make it their greatest work to do good to the People of God.

<summary>This page introduces a series of arguments from Hebrews 1 to prove that Jesus Christ holds a higher status than angels, who are defined as spirits meant to serve God’s people.</summary>
<keywords>Jesus Christ, Angels, Hebrews 1:14, ministering spirits, salvation, the elect, Christopher Love, divinity of Christ</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sermon by Christopher Love, moving from the superiority of Christ to the specific functions of angels as "ministering spirits." It begins a structured theological examination of how angels serve the "Elect" (those chosen by God for salvation) and refutes certain Catholic ("Papist") doctrines regarding angelic mediation.</meta>

<page-num>474</page-num>
<header>The Service of the Angels.</header>

**Sent forth from God]** *Apostellomena* <note>original: "Apostellomena," a Greek participle</note>, the word stands in the Greek in the present tense, to show that it was not a passing act in God, but a continuous act to all generations; that they should continually be **ministering Spirits** to the chosen of God in the World.

**For the sake of those who shall inherit salvation.]** It has become a special Privilege for them to have Angels who watch over them: Those who are slaves of the Devil shall have no good Angels to watch over them; the Papists <note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics</note> say that God gives wicked men Angels just as well as the People of God, who stand at their service, citing Daniel 10:20: *Knowest thou wherefore I come unto thee? but now will I return to fight with the prince of Persia: and when I am gone forth, lo, the prince of Grecia shall come.*

**1. Answer.** To answer this, note that it is a question whether the Angels spoken of there must be understood as the Angels of God, or whether they are not to be understood as certain great Personages who were sent by God to come to the aid of the Persians against the enemies of God's People.

**2. Answer.** Even if it were an Angel, nevertheless this assistance was not for his own sake, but for the sake of God's People. But I shall not disturb you with points of dispute, but shall come closer to the words themselves. and in the Text there are three points or three parts to be noted.

**First,** The nature of the Angels; they are **Spirits**, not bodies, as Origen, Damascene, and others of the Old Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians from the first few centuries AD</note> have thought.

**Secondly,** Their office or work; they are **ministering Spirits**, they are the Servants of Jesus Christ.

**Thirdly,** The specific persons whom the Angels serve; they are not all men, but those who are and shall be **Heirs of salvation**; and these are the three parts in the Text. I do not intend to weary you with Metaphysics and Philosophical opinions regarding the Angels, concerning their number, different orders, regarding the appearances of Angels, and the taking on of bodies, and so forth. I shall only treat the doctrine of the Angels in the sense that the Apostle intends here.

**Doctrine:** That the Angels of Heaven have a charge and command from God to be of service to the Elect here on Earth: *Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?*

The Doctrine is of great utility and comfort to the believers: Now, in the handling and pursuit of this Doctrine, I shall do these three things.

**First,** Show you wherein the service of the Angels to the Elect consists.

**Secondly,** Why God gives His Angels such a charge and command to serve the Elect and to protect them, seeing that God is powerful enough to preserve them Himself.

**Thirdly,** Whether every individual among the Elect has a specific Angel to watch over him, or whether he has more?

**Question 1.** Regarding the first: What benefit

<column-break/>

do the Elect have through the service of the Angels?

I shall set it down 1. negatively, 2. positively.

**Answer 1. Negatively:** That they are **not our Mediators**; their work has no relation to any part or portion of the Mediatorship with God—to appear before God, to plead there on our behalf, to present our prayers before God—that is Christ's office and not theirs. The Papists hold the Angels as Mediators with God for us, and they boast of this opinion based on Tobit 12:12 <note>A book from the Apocrypha, accepted as scripture by Catholics but not by the Reformed tradition of the author</note>: *Now therefore, when thou didst pray, and Sara thy daughter-in-law, I did bring the remembrance of your prayers before the Holy One,* etc. But this is answered by all Interpreters, that if this were the work of Angels, to present our prayers for us, it would be an old error, similar to the idea that they were God's co-helpers in the work of Creation. But so that no one might be ensnared by this opinion, the Apostle warns the Colossians against this, Colossians 2:18: *Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind.* The Apostle warns them here that they should not be led away to the worship and the Mediatorship of Angels; they are not ministering Spirits in the sense of being our Mediators with God: for that is solely the work of the **Angel of the Covenant**, the Lord Jesus Christ; it is His office alone to appear before God His Father for us; He is the only one who appears before God for us, and through the sweet scent of His Incense He makes our persons and works acceptable to God; so that no Angel in Heaven has any part in the Mediator-Office and intercession with the Father on behalf of God's people.

<margin>First point to establish the service of the Angels regarding the Saints.</margin>
**2. Answer. Positively:** That the Angels are ministering Spirits to serve God's people, the Elect in the World; and to prove this I shall give you these points to consider.

**First,** The Angels are said to be Servants of God's People in this regard: that they are a **bodyguard** to protect the Elect of God here in the World from external danger; You read Psalm 91:9, 10, 11, 12: *Because thou hast made the Lord, which is my refuge, even the most High, thy habitation; There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling. For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.* These words were applied to Christ in the New Testament, as in Matthew 4 verse 6: When the Devil came to tempt Christ, that He should worship him, he brought this Passage: *For he shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.* Although this was applied to Jesus Christ, nevertheless it must also be applied just as well to all believers in the Old Testament before Christ, as in the New Testament after Christ, like Psalm 34 verse 7: *The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him, and*

Likewise, in Genesis 32:2, you read that as Jacob went on his way, the Angels of the Lord met him; and when Jacob saw them, he said, "This is God's host." <note>original: "Gods heyr"; refers to a divine army or camp.</note> Here the Angels are called the host of the Lord who protected Jacob. Only after that could the enemies come and rage as quickly as they wished; and this happened through the service of the Angels, whom God used to protect His people so that they would not be harmed, and also to be a bodyguard for them against outward difficulties in this life. The Angels protect us at every age of life. Mr. Rogers <note>Likely referring to the Puritan preacher John Rogers of Dedham (1572–1636).</note> says that the Angels are the rockers of the cradles of little children (Matthew 18:10). Through an Angel, the chains of Peter were loosened in the prison. Just as the evil angels bring afflictions, so the good Angels help to ward them off.

For they are always ready to be the executioners of God's wrath on behalf of God's people against their enemies who wrong and harm them. And in this we have reason to thank God the Lord for the services of the Angels—that the Angels are so serviceable to God's People living on earth, acting as a bodyguard to protect them while they live in the world.

**The third part.** The Angels are serviceable to the People of God in this: that God has made them instruments to reveal a great part of God's will and mind to the Church of God, which otherwise they would not have known. So you also read in Daniel 9:22 that the vision was made known to Daniel by an Angel: *And he informed me* (that was an Angel) *and talked with me, and said, O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding.* It was an Angel who instructed him about the vision; so it was also an Angel who told him of the death of Christ. Had an Angel not said it, he could never <note>The source text "nopt" is likely a typo for "noyt" (never).</note> have known it in those days, which were so long before the coming of Christ in the flesh. But this was revealed to him through the service of the Angels. The birth of Christ was made known by an Angel (Luke 1:26; Luke 2:16-17). The great Lord of the resurrection of Jesus Christ is revealed by the Angels (Matthew 28:5): *The Angel said to the women, fear not: for I know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified, etc.* We would not have known the manner of His coming to Judgment if an Angel had not told us (Acts 1:11) <note>source cites "Actor. 2:11" but the text matches Acts 1:11.</note>: *This same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.* So through all this, you may see how much the Angels concern us, and that we have to praise God for them, as He, through them, to...

The fourth point. The Angels are powerful instruments in bringing and appointing faithful Ministers to govern and build up God’s people. This is an observation that Zanchius <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), a prominent Italian Protestant Reformation clergyman and educator.</note> has concerning Acts 16:9, 10. *And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; there stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us: And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.* This man of Macedonia was an Angel who appeared to Paul and commanded him to come over to Macedonia to preach the Gospel; for there was much work for him to do there, and through his going, many were brought to the confession of the Gospel; and this was a Calling from God through an Angel. Likewise, you also read that an Angel instructed Philip to preach the Gospel, Acts 8:26, 35. *And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert.* And verse 35: *Then Philip opened his mouth, and preached unto him Jesus.* An Angel of the Lord instructed Philip to preach to the Chamberlain <note>Refers to the Ethiopian Eunuch, a high-ranking official.</note>.

<margin>Here you see that the Angel does not preach to Cornelius himself, but instructs him that he should send for Peter, to tell him what he must do; Cornelius had to go to Joppa to hear Peter preach to him. And Philip had to go to Gaza to preach to the Chamberlain, so that by these means they might bring souls to Jesus Christ; and Zanchius brings this in to prove that it is a special Office of the Angels to protect the Ministers of the Churches and to lead them where their service will do the most good for souls.</margin>
So you also read in Acts 10:3, 4, 5, 6. concerning Cornelius, a devout man, fearing God. *He saw in a vision evidently about the ninth hour of the day an angel of God coming in to him, and saying unto him, Cornelius. The fifth point. That the Angels rejoice over the conversion of an elect person in the world. The Angels in Heaven are gladdened when they see that an elect person is called and brought through conversion to Jesus Christ: this you find presented in Luke 15:10. *Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.* These are the words of Augustine:
> As often as we act well, the Angels rejoice and the demons are saddened; as often as we stray from the good, we gladden the devil and deprive the Angels of their joy. <note>original Latin: "Quoties bene agemus gaudent Angeli & tristantur dæmones, quoties a bono deviamus diabolum lætificamus & Angelos suo gaudio defraudamus."</note>
Augustine says, your being good or your doing good makes the Angels exult and be joyful, and the devils be sorrowful: but

<column-break/>

when you do evil, you please the devil, and rob the Angels of their comfort.

The sixth point. The Angels perform an unknown service in comforting and giving counsel to the Elect when they are in sorrows, difficulties, and distresses; God then employs them, Daniel 8 verse 16: *Make this man to understand the vision,* and Chapter 9 verse 22 <note>The source text says verse 29, but it refers to 9:22.</note>: *I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding.* You also have this presented in Genesis 22 verse 17 <note>The text likely means Genesis 21:17, which describes Hagar’s distress in the wilderness.</note> when Hagar was sorrowful; there it was said that an Angel of the Lord came to comfort her: *And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.* In this sorrowful distress in which she was, the Angel of God came to her and comforted her. So you read likewise in Luke 2:10. When the Shepherds looked toward Christ, they were afraid when the glory of the Lord shone around them; *And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.* So also Matthew 28 verse 5. When Mary went to the Grave of Christ, an Angel appeared to her and said to the women, *Fear not ye: for I know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified.* And to comfort her amidst this fear, he says in verses 6 and 7: *He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay. And go quickly, and tell his disciples that he is risen from the dead, etc.* All this is to show the great usefulness and advantage that the people of God have through the service of the Angels, as here in comforting them and giving them counsel in all confusion and danger.

The seventh point. The service of the Angels is used by God to keep the People of God from committing many sins against God. And to this end, they are very useful. Jude verse 9: *Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.* The Angel would not say where the body of Moses was, because the people of God would have been ready to make his body into an idol. And out of love for them, he would not let the Devil know where the body of Moses was, so that he might not show it to them: so that the knowledge of the same might not have been an occasion to sin against God. So Hagar fled from the face of her Mistress, Genesis 16:6, 9. But an Angel of the Lord appeared to Hagar and commanded her to refrain from sinning; *And the angel of the Lord said unto her, Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands.* If Hagar had continued in the way she was on, she might have committed many sins against God: so that in this also the usefulness of the Angels appears, in doing good to God’s people by keeping them from the occasion of sinning against God.

# The Service of the Angels.

God, to perform our worship; when you are in prayer and in the service of God, then the angels are with you, beholding you, even though you do not see them. Just as the angels behold us in our suffering—*1 Corinthians 4:9* <note>original: "For we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men."</note>—so they also behold our works of worship. This is made known in *1 Corinthians 11:10*: *For this cause ought the woman to have power <note>This refers to a head covering or veil as a sign of being under authority.</note> on her head because of the angels.* Some apply these words to the Ministers, who elsewhere are called "angels," but we may understand it as the angels themselves, because they rejoice in the things of the Gospel. The Apostle speaks here of women, that they should not come into the church without a covering; why? For the sake of the angels, and not for the sake of the Ministers: for it is understood to mean the angels of Heaven. And therefore women must take care how they come into the church, because the angels are spectators and see how you carry yourself; they are fellow-servants of God with you in the Assemblies, and this ought to make you take care how you behave. For although they do not know your hearts, nonetheless they see how you conduct yourselves when coming into the presence of God. The angels behold your unbecoming gestures and manners, and they take note of your frivolous fashions; and therefore this ought to bring a dread over your souls as to how you appear before God in the public Assemblies—that you do not appear before God with your improper fashions and naked breasts like *harlots*, and naked arms like madmen. Such fashions do not become those who worship God, especially since the angels behold us in our worship.

The ninth point. That the angels not only behold us in the church Assemblies, but they are also instruments in the hand of God to stir us up to worship God; and that is the opinion of *Zanchius* <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), an Italian Protestant Reformer.</note> regarding the passage in *Revelation 22:9*: *See thou do it not: for I am thy fellow-servant, and of thy brethren the prophets, and of them which keep the sayings of this book: worship God.* John would have worshipped the angel and fallen down before him, but no, the angel said, "worship God." And here is the reason: for why may the good angels not stir up men to worship God, just as the evil angels move and stir up men to sin against God and make them weary of good duties? And this can happen without diminishing the work of the Spirit: He does it as the Author, but they act as instruments to stir you up to do that good of which the Spirit of God is the Author.

The tenth point. That the angels are made instruments to watch over you when you die; and not only that, but also to carry your souls after death into eternal life (I place these two together). You find this in *Luke 16:22*: *And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom.* Here you see that *Lazarus* died, and that the angels watched over him and carried his soul into Abraham’s bosom in Heaven. Oh, remember then that when we all must die, God has appointed His angels as ministering spirits to watch over you in your sick-bed,

<column-break/>

so that when you come to die, they shall then take your souls and carry them into Heaven.

The eleventh point. The angels are also of service to the Elect in this: namely, that they are sent out by *Jesus Christ* to gather together the bodies of the Elect for the Great Day, to preserve them and bring them before the Lord *Jesus Christ*, so that they may then receive the sentence of acquittal and be taken up into Glory. This point is clearly set forth in *Matthew 24:31*: *And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.* Likewise, *Mark 13:27*: *And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.* Here you now see in this point the work of the angels regarding the Elect clearly set forth: so that they shall not only gather them from the ends of the earth, but they shall also carry you into Heaven, even to the uttermost part of Heaven. I present these things to you so that you may see the great and high Privilege of which the Elect are made partakers through the power of the portion they have in *Jesus Christ*—namely, that God ordains and gives command to His angels to perform for you all these eleven services which I have given you to note at this time.

*Objection.* But an objection may arise in the souls of some people, and they may say: "It is true we have read and heard that the angels in former times performed such services for men, but then they appeared to them in bodily forms, as to *Lot*, to *David*, and to others; but do the angels still perform these same services for the Saints now, just as they did for the Saints of old?"

Now, in answering these objections, two things are to be noted.

*First*, the angels are no less present with us now than they were with God's people of old, although they are more invisible. And the reason why the angels appeared more visibly to the Saints of old was:

*First*, because God's people were then but children and had need of bodily appearances to make them believe and to strengthen them in faith. But the angels are just as present with us in these ages of the world as before; for they are with you in your house for your good and for your advantage—namely, if you are an elect person. Your house is full of angels, although you cannot see them; you cannot lie down, nor rise up, nor do any thing, but you have the angels to guard and protect you.

*Second*, the Scripture does not say that the angels *were* ministering spirits, but that they *are* ministering spirits <note>Referring to Hebrews 1:14: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?"</note>: not that they were so in former times, but that they are always so; and not that they are ministering spirits for the present only, but that they shall be so even for those who shall inherit salvation...

It also clarifies that angels remain active and present in the lives of believers today, even if they no longer appear in physical form as they did in biblical times.</summary>

# The Service of Angels.

...will be; so that the Angels will be serving Spirits in future ages just as they have been in former times / and therefore the Angels do not appear now in human forms. Nevertheless, they now have their office and ministry in as full a measure as they had in former ages / when they were seen in visible forms.

**Question.** But why does the Lord use this Service of Angels with respect to His Elect? <note>The "Elect" refers to those chosen by God for salvation, a central concept in the theology of the time.</note> Can the Lord not protect them Himself?

First, I answer / It is *not out of necessity, but out of good will* <note>original Latin: "non necessitate, sed bona voluntate"</note>. It is not as if God had need of Angels / for God does not; He has no need of any of His Angels / so that He could well accomplish His own glorious ends without them. But because of God's good will and pleasure / He desires that they serve for the good of His elect people / while they live in the world: And there are four ends / glorious and gracious ends / why God wishes to use the Service of Angels for the best of His own people here in this World.

<margin>Four ends for which God wishes to use the service of Angels for the benefit of His own people here in the World.</margin>

**1. Purpose.** The first purpose is this / To reveal the reconciliation and the accord that exists between the Angels in Heaven / and the Saints on Earth. The fall of Man created a discord between the Angels and Men; and Man having thus fallen / and having become an enemy of God / was in enmity and great discord with the Angels: but Jesus Christ reconciled both Men and Angels through His cross. Now / God uses the Service of Angels to declare this / and as a revelation of that Reconciliation / which exists not only between God and man / but also between the Angels and Men. *Colossians 1:20.* <note>original: "And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, I say, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven."</note> Scripture mentions a twofold Reconciliation.

1. Of Men with Men / and so were Jews and Gentiles reconciled.
2. There was a reconciliation in Heaven / between the Angels in Heaven / and the Men on Earth / through Jesus Christ / and so He reconciled both with God: And now / this being wrought and accomplished between Men and Angels / and between Man and Man: God now / to reveal this Reconciliation / uses the Service of Angels / to declare to the World that there is an accord and reconciliation between the Angels in Heaven / and the Saints on Earth.

**2. Purpose.** It is to show the World His great love for His people / and His good will toward them / that He so graciously pleases to give to His own people / such noble Servants as the Angels are. If you will serve God / the Angels shall serve you. This is to demonstrate the great unspeakable love that God bears toward His own people / that these / who are God's own Servants / waiting upon Him around His Glorious Throne / should be appointed by God to serve those who shall inherit salvation.

**3. Purpose.** That it is the restoration of that loss which befell some of the Angels;

<column-break/>

for some of the Angels had fallen / and were cast out of Heaven / the loss was great. Now the Elect / all of whom are saved through Jesus Christ / fill the places of the fallen Angels / both Saints and Angels now make one Body / and both sing God's praise; and all the Saints / when they come into Heaven / are employed in the same work / in which the fallen Angels once were / and the Angels knowing this / that this was the restoration of the loss / that makes the Angels so willing in their service / and protection of God's People / while they live on Earth.

**4. Purpose.** The Lord deems the service of Angels fit / to be used for the good of His elect Children; because the evil angels / namely the Devils / watch the Saints to harm them while they live in the World: and therefore God uses these Angels / for the protection of His Elect / while they live in the World: for the evil angels continually make it their work to persecute them / and if it were possible / to bring them to damnation / and to destroy their souls: therefore God gives His Angels command to protect them / and to preserve the elect from the hatred / storminess / and ill-will of the Devil / who seeks to devour and destroy them. And these are the four reasons why God deems it fit / to use the service of Angels for the sake of the Elect.

The third question is this. But when the Scripture says / that the Angels are serving Spirits / sent out by God to serve them / who shall inherit salvation. Does the Scripture mean / that every elect person has his particular Angel to watch over him / or whether they have more? The Platonists <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato.</note> hold that every person has his Angel / which they call his Spirit, which constantly protects him, and does many other good services: some of the Church Fathers <note>Early influential Christian theologians.</note> lean that way / and most of the Schoolmen <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers, such as Thomas Aquinas.</note> / as *Thomas Aquinas, part 1, question 113, Article 2. To individual men, individual Angels are assigned.* <note>original Latin: "Singulis hominibus, singuli Angeli deputantur."</note> Origen, Basil, and Theodoret were of this opinion. Among today's theologians / Zanchius seems to lean to this side; the principal place upon which he builds / is *Acts 12:15.* They then said, it is his Angel. The History reads thus. When Peter was in prison / and the Church prayed for his release / at the same time he came to the door / and a Maid ran to them / and told them that it was Peter; the Text says verse 15. *And they said unto her, Thou art mad; but she constantly affirmed that it was even so, and they said, It is his Angel.* So they claim from this Text / that every Godly person has his particular Angel to watch over and preserve him: now to give you the right sense and interpretation of this place / I shall handle these three points.

1. I shall give you this answer / that the word translated there as an Angel <term>Aggelos</term> <note>Greek: ἄγγελος, meaning messenger or envoy.</note>, it is as much as to say his Messenger / <term>it is his messenger</term> <note>original Greek: "o' Aggelos auton estin" (ὁ ἄγγελος αὐτοῦ ἐστιν)</note>, for the word signifies a Messenger as well as an Angel. So you find *Luke 7 verse 24.* <term>When the messengers of John had departed</term> <note>original Greek: "Apelthonteon de toon Aggeloon Joo'annou" (Ἀπελθόντων δὲ τῶν ἀγγέλων Ἰωάννου)</note>. When the Messengers of John...

Secondly, the reason given by *Gualtherus* <note>Rudolf Gualther (1519–1586) was a prominent Swiss Reformed theologian.</note> regarding this text / who judges that these words indicate the weakness of the Disciples, following the superstitions of the people of those times, and that they spoke according to the fantasy of the Heathens / who held that every Human had his own protecting God.
Thirdly. *Deodatus* <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a Genevan Protestant theologian known for his Bible translations.</note> gives this interpretation: Among the Jews (says he) there were often appearances of dead Persons, which were thought to be the Spirits of the Persons they represented: So that they / according to common opinion / thought that *Peter* was certainly dead / seeing that his spirit began to appear.
Fourthly. The reasons against this [the idea of a single guardian angel] are these:
First, because it seems to have its beginning from an evil source / namely / from the deceptions of the Heathens / who said / That every human has his good and evil spirit or Angel to watch over them; good Angels to do them good, and evil Angels to do them harm; good Angels to reward them, and wicked Angels to punish them.
Secondly, just as it has an evil beginning / so it also has evil consequences / and it produces evil effects.
First, it agrees with the Kabbalistic <note>Kabbalah refers to a tradition of Jewish mysticism. In this context, the author is criticizing what he views as superstitious or non-biblical traditions.</note> Theology of the fable-telling Jews. They assign an Angel to every Planet / to the Sun *Raphael*, to the Moon *Gabriel*, to *Mercury Michael*, etc. And to the four Parts of the World / to the East *Michael*, to the West *Raphael*, to the North *Gabriel*, to the South *Nariel*.
2. It would seem to give a basis / for every particular Place having its own particular Saint / such as *St. James* for Spain. *St. Denis* for France. *St. Patrick* for Ireland. *St. George* for England. But to maintain this opinion / would open a door for the other.
3. And more particularly: The maintaining of that opinion / would greatly obscure and seem to diminish the advantages which God has given to all his Elect <note>The "Elect" refers to those chosen by God for salvation.</note> / namely / that all the Angels are said to be ministering Spirits to serve them. Now / to set apart one Angel from all other Angels in Heaven / to protect and deliver a particular Person / it would lessen and diminish the Privileges of the Saints. It is said that the Angels rejoice over one sinner who converts / *Luke*

15. verse 10. *In the same way (I tell you) there is joy before the Angels over one sinner who repents.* So also *Luke 16:22.* *And it came to pass that the beggar died, and was carried by the Angels into Abraham's bosom.* <note>"Abraham's bosom" was a common term for the place of comfort in the afterlife where the righteous go.</note> Now if only one particular Angel had been assigned to him / then it would not have been "Angels" / but "Angel"; but it is explicitly said that the Angels carried his soul into *Abraham's* bosom. And these were the Angels of God / who were his bodyguard / to protect him; one Angel was sent to destroy *Sennacherib’s* Army / but many Angels to preserve a Godly Human.
Fourthly. The fourth reason: Why an Angel is not the guard of one human alone / is because wicked humans do not only have one evil Angel / but many evil Angels to watch over them: and therefore if wicked Humans have more than one evil Angel to accompany them / and to watch over them: on the contrary then good People have more than one good Angel to deliver and protect them: for sometimes it is said that a wicked Human has legions of evil Angels; that is many to watch over him / and that many possess one person / as in *Mary Magdalene*. Surely then a good person has more Angels than one to protect him / and to keep him from harm; and if it were allowed / that particular Angels have their charge to guard particular Persons / then it would follow that there are some particular Angels / who are not used for the good / and for the welfare of the Elect. For it must be taken that there are more Angels in Heaven / than there are Humans on the Earth: for if there were fewer Angels than Humans / then every Human could not have his particular Angel to protect him; and if there are more Angels in Heaven than Humans on the Earth / which there certainly are (as *Daniel 7:10.* *Thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him,* etc.) Now if there are more Angels than Humans / and that one Angel alone should serve one human and no more / then all the other Angels / who are more in number / would be of no use / and in no way used for the good of the Elect, the People of God / and so consequently would overturn this Text / which establishes that they are all ministering Spirits / who are sent out for service for the sake of those who shall inherit salvation. And so much regarding this question. There is now only one more part to be spoken of / before I shall give you the usefulness.

# The Service of Angels.

**Objection.** But you may say, you truly speak much from the Scripture concerning the service and the benefit of the Angels to the chosen servants of God. But nevertheless, it makes us doubt whether it is true or not, because we do not know when they were created, nor how they were created; for truly Moses tells us well of the Creation of Man, but he speaks nowhere of the Creation of the Angels.

**Answer.** Now, to the answering of this objection, I shall only set down this point. A word or two concerning the Creation of the Angels. For although the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect active in Judea during the Second Temple period who, according to the New Testament, denied the existence of spirits and the resurrection.</note> deny the Angels and the Spirits, nevertheless there are such Spiritual, incorporeal beings created by God for His glory and for the good of the Elect. Concerning now the time when they were created: it was during one of the six days before man was made; otherwise, there would have been no devil to tempt man. Some attribute it to the second day, and because the evil Angels fell on that day after they were created, therefore nothing was said of that day—that *God saw that what he had made was good.* Others attribute it to the third day, because in *Gen. 1. verse 16* the Heavens were then adorned and filled; but it is most probable it was the first day, when the Heavens were made, just as man was made on the sixth day when the Earth was completed, *Job 38. verse 6.* *Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? Or who laid the corner-stone thereof? When the morning-stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy.* So also *Psal. 148: 2, 3.* When the Psalmist exhorts the Creatures to praise God, he begins with the Angels. *Praise him, all his angels.* But I only touch upon this.

2. Concerning the time of their Creation, it is of no great consequence when they were created; it is not a matter of salvation, or of great doubt, which can arise from this in respect to their Office and ministry. Now that they are created for the good of God's People, the Text is clear on this: that they are all ministering Spirits, sent forth by God for the sake of those who shall inherit Salvation; they are created for God's glory and for the good of His elect; so that you see that the Office of the Angels is to serve for the good of the elect in the World. And thus I have run through the Doctrine of this Text, in which I have shown you wherein the service of the Angels consists, and thereafter I have also given you the reasons why God uses the Angels to serve His people, and showed you that an elect Person does not have one particular Angel to look after him, but more—indeed, all the Angels have a command to serve for the good of the Elect. And so I come now to give you the utility of this Doctrine.

1. **Utility.** Is it so that God has given charge and command to all the Angels in Heaven to serve for the good of the Elect of God? O, how this ought then to stir you up to labor to become heirs of salvation. <meta>Catch-symbol</meta> Why will you 

<column-break/>

presume to continue to be objects of God’s Wrath, and heirs of Hell and damnation, and to be without this bodyguard of the Angels of Heaven, who are ordained by God to serve those who shall be saved? Why shall this not invite you and allure you to come to Jesus Christ and to have a part in Him, so that you may thereby claim this ministry of the Angels for yourself, and thus be protected and preserved by them? Why will you run in the ways of sin and paths of godliness and unrighteousness, and so exclude yourself from this protection of the Angels? God has given His angels command to preserve you in all your ways, *Psal. 34: 7.* If you will come to Jesus Christ to embrace Him; but if you will not walk in His ways, then you may be assured that you shall never be under the protection of His angels.

**Secondly,** it shows you the dignity of God’s people, though they might be but poor and low in this present World; yes, the mockery of men in this World; nevertheless, if you are an elect person, a human in Jesus Christ, then you possess high *Privileges* <note>original: "Privilegien"</note>; you are a person of high dignity, and in high esteem, though not by the World, yet you are so in the *esteem* <note>original: "estimie"</note> and the judgment of God and Jesus Christ. If you are in the state of a poor servant in this World, nevertheless you are an honorable person in the sight of God, and your honor is such that you have glorious servants to preserve and protect you: you have the Angels of God to guard you and to keep you in all your ways. It is said that King Solomon had two hundred Men with Shields, and three hundred Men with Shields of beaten Gold, as his Bodyguard to protect him daily: but you, O godly one, have a greater Bodyguard than Solomon had: you, O human, have all the Angels of God as your Bodyguard, and as ministering Spirits, to preserve you and to lead you in all your ways.

3. This teaches us to praise God, to prize Him, and to wonder at His goodness toward us, that such exceedingly glorious Creatures as the Angels of Heaven are, serve us on the Earth. And having thus spoken in general, I come now to the treatment of those points wherein God uses the service of Angels in a particular manner for the Elect.

<margin>The first particular service of the Angels for the Elect.</margin>
I. The Lord has used the service of Angels to preserve the Elect from bodily sicknesses in times of contagion and general plague. And to confirm this, I shall give you a Scripture passage, which is this, *Psal. 91. verses 10, 11, 12.*

> There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling. For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.

Although it is true that godly people may die of that sickness in a general plague, nevertheless, they are under such protection, above all people in the World: for they are under the protection of the Angels, whom God

# The Service of Angels.

God has sent and given charge to protect them in all their ways: Therefore, it is very noteworthy what the Scripture attributes to the service of the Angels when the Pestilence <note>The Plague</note>, or some other great and fierce sickness is among a people: the Scripture attributes this to the evil Angels, namely, that God allows them to have power to bring and cause diseases among a people because of the sins of the land in which they live; and you find this expressed in Psalm 78, verses 49, 50.

->He cast upon them the fierceness of His anger, wrath, and indignation, and trouble, by sending messengers of evil among them. He made a path for His anger; He spared not their soul from death, but gave their life over to the pestilence.<-

Here you see that God allows the evil Angels to strike the people with diseases and infirmities. Now, just as God allows the evil Angels to do that, so He has also ordained the good Angels to preserve His people in a special way from these plagues. The Devil sometimes has permission from God to touch the body, for thus he struck the body of Job with evil sores. We read in Luke 13, verse 16, of a daughter of Abraham who was bound by Satan for eighteen years. And so God allows the evil Angels here to bring ailments among His people; and just as the Lord allows the evil Angels to bring diseases and disturbances over His people, so He also gives the good Angels command to preserve them from diseases; the Devil has power to stir up and infect the blood by the agitation of those <term>evil humors</term> <note>In early modern medicine, "humors" were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to dictate health and personality. An imbalance was thought to cause disease.</note> which are in the human body, and thereby he causes diseases in the body; and just as the Devils can do this by virtue of the permission they have from God, so God, on the contrary, has given a command to the good Angels to protect His people from those <term>distemperances</term> <note>Illnesses caused by an imbalance or "un-tempering" of the bodily humors.</note> and bodily diseases, by preserving them in times of common infection.

2. The second special service of the Angels for the good of God’s chosen is this: that they have a special influence in the ordering and arranging of matters of war; the Angels do not merely stand as onlookers and spectators to watch it, but they have a special charge from God to protect that side which stands most for His honor; and this you have presented in 2 Kings 19, verse 35, when the Assyrians came against Israel; there it is said that the Angel of the Lord struck them.

->And it came to pass that night, that the Angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand; and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead bodies.<-

Here you see how the Angel of God protected His people and was an instrument of that great success which they had against their enemies; so also in Genesis 32, verse 2, when Jacob was on his journey and in danger, then the Angels met him to comfort him and to preserve him, and he called them the Host of God. Likewise, Psalm 68, verse 18:

->The chariots of God are twenty thousand, even thousands of thousands; the Lord is among them, as in Sinai, in the holy place, etc.<-

Just as 

<column-break/>

chariots in war were a protection to them, so the Angels of God are called the chariots of God for the protection of His people in times of trouble; therefore you read in 2 Kings 6, verse 18, that the Angels of God were a protection to His people in times of war. When Elisha was in great distress (for the enemies had surrounded him on all sides), he prayed to the Lord and said,

->Smite this people, I pray thee, with blindness. And he smote them with blindness according to the word of Elisha, etc.<-

That is, the Angel of the Lord struck the enemies so that His servants might thereby be delivered; there are many who hold that the Angels took on physical forms to settle the quarrel and the dispute between the people of God and their enemies. So also in Zechariah 1, verse 8, there you read that Zechariah saw in a vision a Man standing among the myrtle trees:

->I saw by night (says the text), and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white.<-

The aim of the Prophet is to represent the low state of the church by a Man standing in the depths behind the myrtle trees: by the red, speckled, and white horses, the Angels are understood (says <term>Junius</term> <note>Franciscu Junius (1545–1602), a highly influential Reformed theologian and biblical scholar.</note>), placed there for various works; the red horses for Judgment, the white for Mercy, and the speckled horses represent those who were for the execution of various works, both to protect the Godly and to carry out wrath upon the Godless.

Thirdly, God uses the service of Angels in the arrangement of the solemn state of Marriage, for the comfort and the good of His own people: and this you have set down in Genesis 24, verse 7:

->The Lord God of heaven, which took me from my father’s house, and from the land of my kindred, and which spake unto me, and that sware unto me, saying, Unto thy seed will I give this land; he shall send his angel before thee, and thou shalt take a wife unto my son from thence.<-

As if God will send His angels to arrange a wife for Isaac; the Angels glorify this state so much that they do not think it too much to be used for that purpose.

Fourthly, Their service is to bring holy thoughts into the hearts of God’s people; it is true there is no explicitly stated word of this, but there is a reason for it, and the theologians give this reason to confirm that the services of the Angels serve to bring Holy thoughts into the hearts of God’s people, and yet this is no belittlement of the Spirit of God, since the Lord is the Author thereof, but the Angels are only the instruments in the hand of the Spirit; and that for this reason: because the evil Angels are allowed by God to cast evil thoughts into the hearts of men, John 13:2, Acts 5:3. And therefore, on the contrary, the good Angels have a command from God to bring forth good thoughts in the hearts of God's people. Or else this would follow: that the evil Angels have greater power to make you follow the ways of vanity and to run in the paths of sin;

# The Service of Angels.

...than the good Angels, who through their inspirations cause you to walk in the ways of holiness, and thereby further your path in the course of salvation: certainly, the nature of a good Angel is just as capable, and the power given to him just as great, to deal with our Spirits as the nature or power of an evil Angel. The Apostle gives a warning of this, if not a proof, in 2 Corinthians 11:14, where he says that even the Devil can change himself into an Angel of Light, and that he does this to tempt you and make you walk upon a sinful path. He who is an Angel of darkness changes himself into an Angel of light so that he might ensnare you and pull you toward a fall—even by suggesting good things, yet either at the wrong time or for evil ends. Thus he deceives you and misleads your souls, making you sin under the appearance of doing good. He is an Angel of darkness when he tempts you toward a matter that is absolutely sinful; but he appears to be an Angel of light when he suggests you do that which is good in itself, but out of season. For example: tempting you to pray while you are hearing a Sermon, in order to draw your affections away from the preached word and set them upon another duty. While you are praying, he may tempt you to read. In this sense, he can be called an Angel of light. By this reasoning, they <note>likely referring to other theologians or the "orthodox" view</note> prove that just as the evil Angels tempt you to evil by suggesting evil thoughts in your heart, so too the good Angels have a command from God to bring good thoughts into the hearts of God’s People for their benefit.

5. The fifth way in which God uses the service of Angels for the good of His people is this: that the Lord spreads the Gospel of Jesus Christ through them, and in a singular manner protects those Ministers who preach the Gospel, more than any other person in the World.

First, that the Angels spread the Gospel is set down in Acts 16, verse 9: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; there stood a man of Macedonia, who prayed him, saying, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us." This Macedonian man was an Angel who entreated Paul, and Paul understood from this that he was called to preach the Gospel to that People, and therefore he went. Likewise, you have Acts 8, verse 26: You read there that an Angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, telling him that he should go to preach the Gospel: And the Angel of the Lord spoke unto Philip, saying, "Arise, and go toward the south, unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert." Here Philip had a special calling by an Angel from Heaven to preach and spread the Gospel, which he did; and by this means he spread it in those places, namely through the conversion of such a Person who was of great power and authority, which was a great means to favor Holiness and Godliness; for he was (says the Text) a mighty Lord of Candace, the Queen of the Moors <note>The Ethiopian Eunuch, treasurer to Queen Candace</note>, who was over all her treasure. Philip was

<column-break/>

called by an Angel to convert this mighty Lord to the Faith of Christ.

<margin>The Angels protect the Ministers of the word from misfortunes and difficulties.</margin>
Secondly, that the Angels also protect the Ministers and Preachers of the Gospel from misfortune and difficulties. Regarding this, Perkinsius <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch.</note> has a good observation on Isaiah 6, verses 6, 7, and 8. We read there thus: Then flew one of the Seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: and he laid it upon my mouth, and said, "Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged." After that I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then said I, "Here am I; send me." Now Perkinsius, concerning this Text, speaks thus of the dignity of the ministry: When Isaiah was touched by the Angel, he was then full of courage and assured of protection and the prosperity of his work. Although the Angels are ministering Spirits to protect God’s elect in the world, nonetheless God gives them a more special command to preserve the Ministers more than other men: for if God gives His Angels command to protect all those who shall be saved, how much more does God give His Angels charge to protect not only those who shall be saved themselves, but those who are instruments to bring others to salvation. Thus you read of Paul’s command to Timothy, that he should not be careless nor negligent in discharging his bounden duty, but that he should be diligent in his ministry to use Church discipline, etc. 1 Timothy 5:21 <note>The source text cites verse 22, but the quote is from verse 21.</note>: I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality. The Apostle gives this charge to Timothy before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and before all the elect Angels. But why? What might the reason be? It is because the Angels would be his protectors—not only God and Jesus Christ, but the Angels shall be a protection to you, if you faithfully fulfill your bounden duty in preaching the Gospel. So again in 1 Corinthians 4:9, when Paul spoke there of his suffering, and of the suffering of all the other Apostles: For I think (he says) that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle (or as it stands in the Greek <term>Theatròn</term> <note>Original: "Θέατρον". This refers to a theater or a public arena where spectacles were staged for an audience.</note>, we have become a Stage) unto the World, and to Angels, and to men. God beholds you, and men behold you, and Angels behold you in the station of your ministry: as if the Apostle said, "though you think to do us wrong and lead us with shame, nonetheless God sees you, and the Angels see you, and whatever wrong you do to faithful Ministers, they shall avenge your injustices." Thus God protects those who preach the Gospel. Yea, the Angels are called fellow-servants in Revelation 22:9: "See thou do it not: for I am thy fellow-servant." Just as the Angels are called ministers <note>servants</note>, so are the ministers called Angels.

# The Service of Angels.

6. The **sixth point**, in which God uses the service of Angels for the good of his people, is this: to protect the chosen in times of persecution from the rage and tyranny of cruel persecutors. **Psalm 34:8**, compared with the heading of that Psalm, verse 8: *The Angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and he delivers them.* <note>In most English Bibles, this is Psalm 34:7.</note> Now, when was it that the Angel of the Lord encamped around one who feared the Lord? If you look at the heading of that Psalm, you will find that it was when David changed his appearance before **Abimelech**; it was then he composed this Psalm, when he made himself appear mad to save his life, just as you read the history in **1 Samuel 21:11, 12, 13**. *But the servants of Achish said to him, "Is this not David, the King of the land? Did they not sing of him in the dances, saying: Saul has slain his thousands, but David his ten thousands?"* And David laid these words to heart and was very much afraid of Achish, the King of Gath. Therefore, he changed his appearance before their eyes and acted like a madman in their hands; he scratched at the doors of the gate and let his spit run down into his beard. Here you see what difficulties David was in; nevertheless, this was the time in which he had the promise of the Service of Angels for his protection and preservation, even in that time of persecution. Likewise, **Daniel** was also kept from the mouths of the lions by the service of Angels when he was thrown into the lions' den, **Dan. 6:23**. *My God has sent his Angel (he says) and he has shut the mouths of the lions so that they have not harmed me.* And **Peter** was delivered by an Angel from the memory <note>likely meaning "the expected fate"</note> of the raging cruelty and persecution of **Herod**, **Acts 12:7, 8**. And the **three youths** were delivered from the glowing furnace by an Angel, **Dan. 3:15**. Now, all these examples clearly confirm that God delivers his people from the rage of cruel men through the service of Angels.

7. The **seventh point** is this: that the Lord uses the Service of Angels to protect and keep the chosen in times of temptation from the assaults of the Devil. The Devil tempts you and you do not see it; likewise, the good Angels serve you and you do not see it either. When the Devil tempts you to sin through evil impulses and wicked thoughts, then the good Angels serve to ward off those temptations so that they do not harm you. **Zech. 3:1**; you read there that the Devil stood at the right hand of God’s servant **Joshua**. *And he showed me Joshua the High Priest, standing before the face of the Angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him.* Here you see that the Angel stood by Joshua to oppose the Devil, who came to resist Joshua and to tempt him, showing that just as the Devil is very busy persecuting God's people with his temptations, so the Lord uses the service of Angels to protect them against these temptations.

8. The **eighth point** in which God uses the service of Angels for the good of his people 

<column-break/>

is this: that the Lord, in a very special manner, gives his Angels command to protect the chosen when they come to die. Then God uses his Angels in a special way to watch over you, for this reason: because that is the last work the Angels can do for you in the world. You read in **Luke 16:22** that **Lazarus** died and was carried by the Angels into **Abraham’s bosom** <note>A traditional term for Paradise or the place of the righteous dead.</note>. If this is a parable (which is a matter for debate), it nevertheless serves our purpose very well to show that the Angels carry the souls of the Elect into Heaven when they die. Now, put all these points together and say: what cause do you have to marvel and to worship that merciful God who loves you with such inner affection through his Son, that he appoints, charges, and gives command to his Angels to protect and keep you the entire time of your life in this world. And not only you, but also all the Elect who shall inherit salvation. And thus I have shown you these eight points, in which God in a special way preserves his chosen children through the service of Angels.

<margin>1. Objections.</margin>
Now, there are two more objections to be answered. It seems to me that I see this doctrine struggling and snagging in many people’s spirits, and they may say: *If it is true that the Lord uses the service of Angels in general and in particular, as you have shown us regarding the general and specific benefit the Elect have through them, what then is the reason why Moses, in describing the works of Creation, makes no mention of the Angels?* He tells us of the birds of the air, and of all the beasts of the field, the sun, moon, stars, and of the whole Creation; but not one word of the Angels. And if they are of such use as you have shown, why then was no mention made of the Angels? The wisest men have spent much time in untying this knot and in answering this question. There are three great reasons why Moses did not speak of the Angels on any of the six days, though it is certain they were created on one of those six days.

<margin>First reason why Moses did not speak of the Creation of the Angels on one of the six days.</margin>
First, Moses did not speak of the Creation of the Angels in order to keep the Jews from idolatry—namely, from the worship of Angels. Had he told them of the excellent nature of the Angels and of their strength, power, greatness, wisdom, glory, and excellence, the Jews were so inclined toward idolatry that they would have worshipped the Angels. For they worshipped great figures who had great honor and power and were held in high esteem in the world; they worshipped them as Gods. And that was the reason why God hid the **body of Moses**, and no man to this day can say where it was laid. The Devil and the Angel fought over the body of Moses for this end: namely, that the Devil wished to bring it to light, but the Angel would not allow him, because he knew that the Jews would have worshipped his dead body.

Secondly, Moses remains silent on this doctrine of the Creation of the Angels because, in dealing with the Creation, he only...

# The Service of Angels.

H h 2

...deals with **visible things**, things which can be seen with the eyes and can be understood by the grasp of the common people. You see the heavens above you, and you see the earth beneath you and walk upon it; you see the beasts of the field feeding, and you see the birds of the air flying, and you see the fish of the sea swimming. The Apostle Paul says that God created things **visible and invisible**; and for that reason, Moses did not speak a single word about the **Creation of the Angels**, but left it for the ages to follow.

**Thirdly**, Moses made no mention of the Creation of the Angels because, if Moses had spoken of their creation—being such excellent creatures so far above men—the people would have been inclined to think that the Angels had a hand in, and were co-workers with God in, the creation of the world. This is similar to what the ancient Philosophers held: that the Angels are the movers of the Heavens. Thus, people might have said that the Angels were co-workers with God in the making of Heaven and Earth. But although their creation is left unmentioned, this should nevertheless be no argument to diminish your faith in this truth: that the Angels are created and made as **ministering spirits**, sent out by God for the sake of those who shall inherit salvation. And thus, in these three points, I have answered the first objection.

<margin>Genesis 48:16</margin>
**2. Objection.** If God uses the service of Angels for this purpose, then it must follow (say the <term>Papists|A term used historically by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics, particularly in the context of theological disputes.</term>) that we are bound to honor and worship them. **Bellarminus** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit Cardinal and scholar during the Counter-Reformation.</note> takes great pains to confirm the worship of Angels, and for that purpose he brings forward this passage of Scripture, Genesis 48:16:

-> The Angel who delivered me from all evil, bless these youths, and let my name be named in them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and let them multiply like fish in a multitude, in the midst of the land. <-

These are the words of Jacob, from which Bellarmine wishes to prove that he prayed to the Angel for a blessing; and "his prayer is a part," he says, "of worship, and therefore the Angels ought to be worshipped just as well as God." Now, to answer this objection, I shall set down three things for you.

<margin>Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 3, chapter 11; see also chapter 1.</margin>
**I. Answer.** That by "the Angel" here, as **Augustine** says, is understood not "the Angel of the Lord," but "the Angel [who is] the Lord." <note>original: "den Engel des Heeren / maar den Engel de Heere"</note> It is not to be understood as a created Angel, but it must be understood as the **Creator of the Angels**, namely Jesus Christ, who in the Scripture is called the **Angel of the Covenant**. And

**Secondly**, the reason that **Rivet** <note>André Rivet (1572–1651), a French Huguenot theologian.</note> gives for this is because there is an emphasis in the word—not only because of the emphatic <term>Hammelach|The Hebrew word for "the angel," using the definite article *ha*.</term>—but the word "bless" stands in the singular number. It does not say "an Angel who delivered me," but "**the** Angel who delivered me." This signifies that it is to be understood as referring to Jesus Christ. And besides the Text itself, it is clear in its own right that it is to be understood as God, and not as an Angel of God, in verse 15: *And he blessed Joseph, and said: God, before whose face my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me,*

<column-break/>

*from the time that I was, until this day.* This Angel who delivered me was the **eternal God**. Namely, that Angel whom Jacob worshipped. Who can preserve us from all evil? It is *Angelus Dominus* <note>original: "Angelus Dominus, niet Domini" — Latin for "The Lord Angel" rather than "The Angel of the Lord."</note>, not *Domini*: it is the **Lord of the Angels**, and not the Angels of the Lord.

**Thirdly**, it is just as consistently and certainly said to be God here as in another passage of Scripture. Therefore you read in Genesis 32:26:

-> That Jacob strove and wrestled with an Angel, and he said, "I will not let you go, unless you bless me." <-

By this Angel, God is understood. For Hosea 12:4 states: *By his strength he behaved like a prince with God;* and verse 5: *Yes, he behaved like a prince against the Angel, and prevailed over him; he wept and sought him; at Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us.* And this is said of Jacob’s wrestling with God, who was called an Angel. Therefore, that expression in Genesis 48:16 must necessarily also be understood as God. For you see how one passage of Scripture explains the other—that it must be understood as God and not as an Angel of God. Beyond that, **Chamierus** <note>Daniel Chamier (1565–1621), a French Reformed theologian.</note> says: *Nullam esse invocationem, sed expressum desiderium* <note>original Latin: "That there is no invocation, but an expressed desire."</note>; that is, that it was not a prayer, but only a desire. However, Rivet rejects this. We may pray to God for the protection of Angels, but not to the Angels for the protection of God. And to confirm this even more clearly, I shall give you both Scripture and reason.

**First**, we must not worship the Angels because they are our **fellow creatures**. You read in Revelation 22:9 that the Angel said to John, when John wanted to worship the Angel:

-> "See that you do not do it," (said the Angel) "for I am your fellow servant, and of your brothers the Prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book: Worship God." <-

**Secondly**, they themselves command us to worship God and not them. As in Judges 13:15, 16:

-> Then Manoah said to the Angel of the Lord: "Let us detain you, and prepare a young goat before your face." <-

But the Angel of the Lord said to Manoah:

-> "If you detain me, I will not eat of your bread; and if you will make a burnt offering, then you shall offer it to the Lord." <-

For Manoah did not know that it was an Angel of the Lord. Here you see that the Angel does not want to be worshipped by anyone, because we must worship God alone.

**Thirdly**, the Angels must themselves worship Jesus Christ, and therefore we must not worship them. Hebrews 1:6:

-> And when he again brings the firstborn into the world, he says: "And let all the Angels of God worship him." <-

-> Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and the worship of angels, intruding into what he has not seen, being puffed up without reason by his fleshly mind. <-

# The Service of Angels.

Sf 3
