Now / this Text gives us these three uses.

1. By way of warning.
2. By way of instruction.
3. By way of rebuke.

First / By way of warning, pay attention to these three things.

<margin>1. Utility of the warning.</margin>
1. If it is so / that God gives His Angels command to protect those who shall inherit salvation; then watch out that you do not extend the service of the Angels beyond their covenanted duty; it is true the Angels do well for the *Elect of God* / but do not extend their service beyond what God wants us to have done / that is / watch out that you do not fall into the error of the *Roman Church* : for they say that the Angels of God do not only preserve us here / and carry our souls into Heaven / but that we have yet one more benefit through them / and that is that the Angels are our intercessors <note>original: "voor-bidders"</note> with God / and that for the sake of modesty we may not go immediately into the presence of God / but must go to the Angels / and pray to them that they would intervene with God for us / and they prove this from the book of *Tobit*, yet it is not *Canonical* <note>The author is reflecting the Protestant view that the Book of Tobit is part of the Apocrypha and not the inspired "Canon" of Scripture.</note> : there it is said that the Angels carry our prayers to God / but that shows that it is not a *Canonical Scripture* / because it presents things which conflict with it. Some *Protestants* hold / like *Willet* in his *Synopsis* <note>Andrew Willet (1562–1621) was an English clergyman whose "Synopsis Papismi" was a major anti-Catholic polemic.</note>, that we may do it declaratively to reveal our wounds and works / just as one friend to another / but by no means as *Mediators* / and therefore let this warning take its place in you / namely to watch out that you do not extend the service of the Angels beyond their covenanted duty; and although they are a *Bodyguard* for us / to protect us from danger here in the World / they are nonetheless not *Mediators* on our behalf with God. *Bellarmine* <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and a central figure in the Counter-Reformation.</note> goes to great effort to prove this / and brings to it / *Revelation 8 : 3.* And another Angel came / and stood at the Altar , having a golden censer / and much incense was given to him , that he should offer it with the prayers of all the Saints upon the golden Altar which is before the Throne. *Bellarmine* wants to prove from this that the Angels offer up our prayers to God.

Now take this as an answer: although *Brightman* <note>Thomas Brightman (1562–1607) was an influential English Puritan scholar.</note> understands this as referring to *Constantine* / it is nonetheless clearer that the Angel / spoken of there / must be understood as *Christ Jesus* : and not as a created Angel as *Augustine* explains it. The *Jesuit Blasius Viega* <note>A 16th-century Portuguese Jesuit commentator on the Apocalypse.</note> says, *The following things cannot be suitably applied to anyone other than Christ* <note>original Latin: "Sequentia nisi Christo alteri apte accommodari non possunt"</note>; he says / that the things spoken of here, can be applied to no one but *Christ*. And that in a threefold respect.

First , Because the *Scripture* tells us / that no one but *Jesus Christ* can perform this Office for us / namely to offer up our prayers to God / and to step in for us / no one but *Christ* can be our *Mediator*.

<column-break/>

There is but one Mediator , between God and Man , the Man *Christ Jesus*.

Secondly, It is beyond the power of any Creature to do this work for us / namely to take the prayers of any of God's people and bring the same to God / to make them acceptable before him / and to commend our prayers to God for us.

Thirdly , It appears that *Jesus Christ* alone can do this / because the comparison of this Text fits *Jesus Christ* clearly; for it looks to *Exodus 30 : 7, 8.* There you have the High Priest burning incense on the Golden Altar; And *Aaron* shall burn thereon sweet spices every morning, when he dresseth the Lamps, he shall burn it, and when *Aaron* lighteth the Lamps , at even <note>original: "between the two evenings," a literal translation of the Hebrew term for twilight.</note> he shall burn it : it shall be a perpetual incense before the face of the Lord throughout your generations. The High Priest was a type <note>A symbolic representation or foreshadowing.</note> of *Jesus Christ* / and the Altar a type of his Divinity / and the Sacrifice a type of his Humanity / and the incense a type of his intercession. Now the Altar looked to *Christ* / and the Sacrifice looked to *Christ* / and the incense looked to *Christ* ; and therefore it must necessarily have its regard for *Jesus Christ* / as he is the Angel of the Covenant / and he alone can through his death / suffering and righteousness commend our prayers to God his Father / so that the same might be acceptable to God through him.

It is God who gives his Angels charge over you to preserve you / or else you would always, as long as you live in the World, be in danger of being harmed and destroyed / and therefore God protects you through the Angels / which is a great honor for God / and no lessening of his providence.

# The Saints are Obliged

combined into one verse / transgressions, iniquity, and sin. **Exodus 34:7.** *Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin.* **Micah 7:18.** *Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.* **Leviticus 16:21.** *And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins.* Likewise it is used in **Job 13**, verse 23. *How many are mine iniquities and sins? make me to know my transgression and my sin.*

In these four places these words are used in the Scripture / and in my Text / but nowhere else / as I recall / in the entire Scripture. And because these three words are used here / the interpreters seek to make some distinction between them. There is transgression, sin, and iniquity. I have consulted with many / and the most certain / which I consider best to give you / is / *Peschaj* <note>original: "Peschaj"</note>, transgression; it signifies in the Hebrew disobedience, or rebellion. The Interpreters say / that it is an increase or a heaping up of sin / to a great height. Secondly / *Chattathi* <note>original: "Chattathi"</note>, Sin, signifying an evil of a lesser degree, which is not so terrible; and this is understood only as Sin, wickedness, or infirmity / a common trespass. Thirdly / *Avon* <note>original: "Avon"</note>, iniquity, signifies sin of nature, that corruption of nature, in which a human is born. But the Grammarians in the Latin Tongue / distinguish these words differently: Iniquity (they say) is / that which is done against another person: Sin, that which is done against oneself: And Transgression, that which occurs directly against God. But beloved / the Scripture / in many places / uses the same for one thing: Therefore we must not seek too precise a distinction between these words / *And you forgave the iniquity of my sin.* There is some difficulty regarding the meaning of these words / what it is / to obtain forgiveness of sin from God. By the iniquity of sin, some understand the punishments that the sins deserve. The Hebrew word *Avon*, which means iniquity / also means punishment. It is the same word that was spoken by Cain,

<margin>And the guilt, namely the punishment. <note>original Latin: "Et reatum Sc. pænam."</note></margin>
*My punishment is greater than I can bear.* <note>The author quotes Genesis 4:13.</note> Therefore in some Translations it is read thus / *You forgive the punishment of my sins.* Secondly / others understand here by the iniquity of sin (with which I agree) sin with all its aggravations, with all its sorrowful circumstances; sin with all its wickedness. *You forgave the iniquity of my sin:* So most interpreters understand it / and so sin is discovered in its own color. I shall only briefly run over / at this time / the first part of my Text / *I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord.*

These words contain within them the sense of this Psalm / and are meant to promote the practice and necessity of Christian du-

<column-break/>

-ties. They describe a secret confession of sins to God. Five things are to be noted here / 1. The duty itself / Confession. 2. A deliberate intent to practice this duty / *I said.* 3. The subject of this duty / transgressions, and that with a specific quality / *my* transgressions; not for the sin of other people / but for my own sins; *I said, I will confess my transgressions.* And I remind you that the words in the Hebrew Language signify more / namely / *Amarthi Oodeh alej peschaj Ladonai* <note>Transliterated Hebrew for: "I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord."</note> : *I said, I will confess my transgressions, against myself, before the Lord.* Many people confess their sins / but they do so against God; that is / they make confession in such a way / as if God were the Author of the sins / and accuse him of being a Patron of their wickedness and godlessness: *I said, I will confess my transgressions, against myself, before the Lord.* 4. The object of this duty / the Lord. And this is a golden confession / overturning that which is used in the Roman Church <note>A reference to the practice of auricular confession to a priest rather than directly to God.</note>. The confession of which God and the Scripture speak / is in secret between God and your own souls. When conscience shall suggest your guilt to you / that you have trespassed against your Maker / then complain of and bewail your sins against God / and say / *I will confess my transgressions before the Lord.* 5. Finally / the fruit and the workings of this duty / *And you forgave the iniquity of my sin.* Note the connection / there is a conjunction there / *And* you forgave. He does not use a *so then*, no *therefore*, no causal word / but only the conjunction / *and* you forgave. Not / *I confess my sins, therefore they are forgiven me*; But / *I confess my sins, ve-atthah* <note>Hebrew for "and you."</note>, *and you forgave me.* The forgiveness of sins is not a work / proceeding from any cause in us; but a consequence of something that goes before. Truly the Papists <note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics.</note> pleaded much for these merits / because sometimes causal adverbs are used therein. But this has gone briefly over my Text / and thus much has been set down for the explanation of the words. And in this time I shall only treat one Doctrine / taken from the first part of this Text / *I said, I will confess my transgression before the Lord:* And it is this / That justified persons, whose sins are forgiven, are nevertheless bound, to confess their sins to God.

1. Doctrine. The confession / of which I speak here / is a private confession of our wickedness to God / between God and our own souls: And although it is but a common subject / yet if God shall grant me grace / I shall labor to make a use of this / that it may be to you a profitable edification in a Christian walk / in a holy confession of sins before your God.

There are many questions to be unfolded in the handling of this point.

The first Question is / What are the reasons, why justified and pardoned persons are nevertheless bound, to make confession of sins to God in particular? The reasons are the following.

1. Reason. They must confess their sins to God / because holy confession is a great part of

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of confession. The previous page defined three Hebrew terms for sin—transgression, sin, and iniquity—concluding that regardless of the severity, all must be brought before God. This page moves into the practical reasons why a believer finds relief and spiritual benefit through this act.</meta>

->to confess their sins.<-

their enlightenment and peace in the soul of a sinner; suppressing and indulging in guilt brings a terror and death upon the conscience. Just as the wind, when it is open and swirls through the air, does little damage; but when it is hidden in the hollows of the earth, it causes cracks and earthquakes, throwing things up and down: so also sin, when it is unconfessed, suppressed, and indulged, it causes heart-tremblings in the conscience, and brings great fear and terror.
> **Psalm 32:3.** *When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long.*

The meaning is, David, when he hid his sin, roared with terror when he did not apply his zeal to confess it to God from his soul: But when a person brings their evils to God with an intelligent and clear confession, that unburdens their burdens, enlightens their conscience, and quiets their spirit.

<margin>Spiritual vomiting.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Spiritualis vomitus"</note>
Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for his allegorical interpretations of Scripture.</note> calls the confession of sins to God "the soul’s spiritual vomiting." Now, you know that vomiting gives relief to the stomach when it is pained and burdened with excess. A person is heartsick when he cannot digest: the casting out of the stomach's burden brings relief to the same. When the conscience is burdened, when a person's spirit is troubled, the pouring out of complaints and confession to God lightens the mind. A sinner is like a bloated vessel of new wine, closed at the top; if it has no vent, it bursts: so is a godly person filled up with sin, and if he has no vent of confession to God, his heart is ready to burst.
> **Psalm 119, verse 25.** *My soul cleaveth unto the dust: quicken thou me according to thy word.* **And verse 26.** *I have declared my ways, and thou heardest me: teach me thy statutes.*

As if he had meant to say, (My soul cleaveth unto the dust) I am in a very poor and sorrowful state; but you have told me your ways, I have confessed my sins; you, God, hear me; I then have peace, rest, and am then comforted. This is the first reason. Lordly confession to God gives a great deal of enlightenment and holy rest to the mind.

## 2. Reason.
Furthermore, righteous persons must confess their sins because it pleases God to hear the lamentations and confessions of His own people. Lying on one's face is the best posture for this; and heartfelt weeping is the best ornament that can please God.
> **Jeremiah 31, verse 18.** *I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself, etc.*

That is, confessing his sins to God.
> **Song of Solomon 2, verse 14.** *O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.*

It pleases God to see and hear those complaints and confessions of His servants to Him. So spoke David,
> **Psalm 119, verse 26.** *I have declared my ways, and thou heardest me* with compassion and pleasure.

God sees every person coming with cords around their necks and sackcloth around their loins through a humble confession—just as the servants of Ben-hadad did <note>Refers to 1 Kings 20:31, where the servants of the defeated King Ben-hadad wore sackcloth and ropes as a sign of total submission to King Ahab.</note>—rather than seeing them with costly head-ornaments in self-righteousness. Christ is pleased to hear and see the weeping condition of His children.

<column-break/>

## The third Reason,
why a justified person must confess his sins to God, is because the confession of sin causes the heart to be refreshed through strong and earnest petitions to God.
> **Psalm 32, verse 6.** *For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: surely in the floods of great waters they shall not come nigh unto him.*

Confession refreshes the petition,
> **Daniel 9, verse 20.** *And whiles I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before the Lord my God for the holy mountain of my God, etc. And Gabriel came and touched him, etc.*

Confession is to the soul as the whetstone is to the knife, which sharpens that which is blunt: so confession does to sin; it sharpens our evils through humble petitions to God. The person who will but pray with faith and intelligently confess his sins, making sorrowful and secret acknowledgment of his sins to God, receives great help and refreshment from God through this.

## The fourth Reason is,
Because the confession of sin works a holy contrition and divine sorrow in the heart,
> **Psalm 38, verse 19.** *I will declare mine iniquity; I will be sorry for my sin.*

Declaration works a stinging. Acknowledgment of sin is the very cause that presses the sin upon the conscience, which causes a reddening and shame of the face, and sorrow of the heart.

## There is yet a fifth Reason,
Why righteous people must confess their sins to God, and it is because secret confession of sins powerfully magnifies the Glory of God. It gives glory to God's Justice when I confess my sins and confess that God may justly damn me for them. It gives glory to God's Mercy when I confess my sins and yet His mercy must save me. It gives glory to God's Omniscience when I confess my sin; I acknowledge that God already knows it. Thus, the acknowledgment of sins gives glory to God.
> **Joshua 7, verse 19.** *And Joshua said unto Achan, My son, give, I pray thee, glory to the Lord God of Israel, and make confession unto him, etc.*

## The last Reason,
why we must confess our sins to God, is because a holy confession of sins makes sin un-bitter <note>Meaning "distasteful" or "unpleasant" rather than sweet.</note> to a person and makes the Savior precious to him, when a person casts the sins out of his conscience through a confession. This turning away and this recovery from sin makes the sin un-bitter and the Savior precious. The stronger a desire a sinner has for Jesus Christ, the more he seeks to value Him. And this is all for the first question, namely the reasons for this point.

## The second Question is,
<margin>One must confess his sins in three times.</margin>
But when is a person most bound, and has the proper freedom of Spirit to confess his hidden sins to God? I shall name only three times: As,

1. When God brings a believer under some heavy and outward afflictions, then it is a proper time to [confess] his sins

# The Saints are Bound

to confess to God. <margin>Punishment opens the eyes that guilt shuts. Gregory.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Oculos quod culpa claudit pœna aperit. Greg." Referring to Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope and theologian who wrote extensively on the "Morals on Job."</note> It is a saying of Gregory that sin blinds the eyes of men when they commit it; nonetheless, these eyes are opened by punishments; punishment opens the eyes which the act of sin had closed. Just as you read of the brothers of Joseph, they remained for twenty years as if without a conscience—without pouring out a confession—regarding that evil deed committed against their brother Joseph. But when Joseph placed them in prison, then they confessed their evil. **Genesis 42:21.** Then they said to one another: "Truly we are guilty concerning our brother, whose anguish of soul we saw when he pleaded with us for mercy, but we would not hear; therefore this distress has come upon us."

It may be that you are healthy now and make no confession of your impurity—that you are drunkards, proud, and profane people. But what will you do when God brings you to a deathbed? When God hedges in your ways with thorns, makes your conscience return to you, and brings your guilt to mind? Oh, then it is a suitable time: when God brings a person under any outward tribulations, then he is in a good position to confess his sins. There is a word worthy of your notice in the **38th Psalm**, written by David regarding his bed of sickness and death; you will find that it is a complaint of a heavy illness under which David lay. **Verse 4:** "There is no soundness in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sin." **Verse 6:** "My wounds stink because of my foolishness." <note>The Dutch text cites verse 6 for the "wounds" or "loathsome sores," which matches verse 5 in many English Bibles.</note> **Verse 8:** "For my loins are filled with a loathsome burning, and there is no soundness in my flesh." <note>Matches verse 7 in many English Bibles.</note> Here he lay on a sickbed, for the interpreters say that he composed this Psalm while he was ill.

It is for you to note what title David gives this Psalm: *A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance.* David, when he lay on his deathbed and reflected, said it shall be a "Psalm of Remembrance," to remember his sins and to confess to God his excess committed with Bathsheba; to bring his evil home to himself. Physical sickness makes people fit to make confession to God, to remember their sins, and to bring to remembrance their pride, their haste, and their noble folly—whatever evil sins they may be. Now, it may be that you do not remember these things, but when God brings you under tribulations, you are then fit for this duty: to confess your sins to God and to bring them to remembrance. So it was with the sailors who were in the storm with Jonah; when there seemed to be no hope of being saved, then every man called upon his god. This has given rise to the proverb: *He who has not yet learned to pray, let him go to sea.* So also in **Jeremiah 2:24**: "She is a wild donkey, accustomed to the wilderness, that snuffs up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion, who can turn her away? All those who seek her will not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her." The men of Israel are compared there to a wild donkey, an irrational creature that runs up and down in the wilderness, kicking up its heels. But, says God, though they try to flee from men, yet in their month they shall—

<column-break/>

find them. That is, when the people of Israel were still young and in prosperity, they would not let themselves be caught; but when their "month" came—in their remembrance, in their suffering—then they shall find them; then they shall come to God more to confess their guilt than in former days.

2. When the conscience of a person accuses him with clear and heavy charges, then it is time to confess his sins to God. Just like Judas: when his conscience woke up within him, he confessed before the High Priests and Scribes, saying: "I have sinned, betraying innocent blood." If Judas, upon the awakening of his conscience, confessed his sins, how much more should a believer do so, and it shall profit him. Beloved, the primary use of the conscience in a person is to bring him to his knees, to make him humble in the confession of his ways. The conscience serves to excuse me when I do well, and to accuse me when I do evil, and thus to confess my sins to God. Therefore, note that David says: "I roar all the day long." There was now a noise in his conscience regarding his adultery; then he said: "I will make confession of my transgressions." When the conscience swells with accusation, then the heart makes confession to God. I earnestly pray that you observe these opportune times, and that you perform this duty of confession to God when He brings you under visitation and your conscience accuses you. Oh! Right then is the suitable time for this duty.

3. The third time or opportunity in which a person is bound to confess his sins to God is when God sends home the <term>reproof</term> <note>The Dutch "bestraffing" implies a formal or spiritual correction/rebuke from a minister.</note> of the Ministers of the Word to the soul with conviction. Thus you know David, **2 Samuel 12:13**. He said to Nathan: "I have sinned against the Lord." And this was after Nathan had said to David: "You are the man." The reproof of Nathan had such power on the heart of David that David said: "I have sinned and acted foolishly." Do you go home after every sermon you hear, when you have heard your sins reproved, and take that reproof to heart, and thank God that the Word has contradicted you, pointed out your sins to you, and bound you out like an enemy? If you can go home and follow a helpful reproof with confession, your hearts will then be fit for this good duty: the confession of sins to God.

Although the weakest believer is above the power of sin, nonetheless the greatest believer is not above the confession of sin, because he is not above the committing of sin. As long as a person continues in the committing of sin, so long must he not cease confessing his sins; as long as sin is in the soul, so long must there be a "pumping out" of the same. Confession is to the soul what a pump is to a ship. O! Water leaks into your heart through negligence and carelessness; pump it out through confession. So long as you have not overcome the—

# to confess their Sins.

[...just as one must] commit sin, you are also not above the confession of sin. As long as the natural body gathers corrupt humors <note>In early modern medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament. "Corrupt humors" meant an imbalance that required purging.</note>, there must be purging emetics; if the body gathers long-corrupt humors, it rots. You gather sin upon sin, and heap iniquity upon iniquity; confession is a spiritual purgation, fit to cleanse the heart. See, for this reason it is also highly necessary that reconciled sinners also make confession of their faults.

2. **Use.** When the Scripture says that righteous men must confess their sins, it should be noted that not all confession of sin serves for conversion. Lorinus <note>original: "Lorinus" - Jean Lorin (1559–1634), a Jesuit biblical commentator.</note> notes from Bernard <note>original: "Bernardus" - likely Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic.</note> on these words, *I will confess my transgressions*, that Saul made the exact same confession as David. When Nathan rebuked David, David said, "I have sinned." When Samuel rebuked Saul, Saul likewise said, "I have sinned." Here was a similar confession, but not a similar outcome. David says, "I have sinned," and Nathan said, "The Lord also has taken away your sin." But Saul says, "I have sinned," yet Samuel told him that the Lord had taken the Kingdom from him. <margin>1 Sam. 15:29.</margin> Saul confessed his sins, and yet he was deprived of his Kingdom; but David confessed his sins, and they were forgiven him. Beloved, you could confess your sins with Saul, and yet obtain no forgiveness; you could lose your soul as surely as he lost his Kingdom, even though he confessed his sins.

The third question is this: What theological rules <term>Godts-geleerde Regulen - rules of divinity or scholarly principles of faith</term> are there, according to which we must order our confession of sins before God? **Answer:** There are seven rules that I shall give you regarding this.

**The first Rule** in the Confession of sins to God is this: single out certain secret lusts in your bosom; make special confession of them to God. Do not only make confession of sins piecemeal and in general, but specifically of your favorite lusts, of those sins that most hinder you in a godly course. This wisdom was used by God's people of old; they first singled out that evil of which they were guilty. <margin>Jud. 10 : 10.</margin> Then the children of Israel cried to the Lord, saying: "We have sinned against you, both because we have forsaken our God, and also because we have served the Baalim." "We have sinned against you"—there is a general complaint. "But we have likewise served the Baalim"—there they single out their idolatry in particular. <margin>1 Sam. 12: 19.</margin> And when the people said to Samuel, "Pray for your servants to the Lord your God, that we may not die: for we have added to all our sins this evil, that we have asked for ourselves a king."

They were not satisfied with their old government, but wanted to exchange and change it. That was their **Particular sin** of which they were guilty; they wanted to single this out as well. So also <margin>1 Chron. 21. 17.</margin> And David said to God, "Was it not I who commanded the people to be numbered? Yes, it is I who have sinned and acted very wickedly, but these sheep, what have they done?" etc. He singles out a particular sin under the guilt of which he lay. I may say

<column-break/>

to you as the King of Syria said to the thirty-two captains: "Fight not with small or great, but against the King of Israel." So incline your confession not against the small or great alone, but against those royal desires, against those chief lusts that arise from your disposition. Whether it be Agag <note>Agag was the King of the Amalekites whom Saul was commanded to destroy but spared; here he represents a "pet sin" that one is tempted to keep.</note>, whether it be Delilah <note>The woman who seduced and betrayed Samson; representing a recurring or particularly dangerous temptation.</note>, single them out and fight against them, and make your greatest confessions and complaints against them. Act like soldiers in a garrison; although they watch everywhere upon the walls and occupy all passages, nevertheless, at that place where the breach from the cannon-fire is widest and the storming is hardest, there they most display their strength and resistance. Do likewise: watch against all sin and every slipping of your life, but let your confession toward God go out most against those desires that most harm you and most frequently occur.

**The second Rule** that we are obliged to observe in our confession of sin to God is this: make it a matter of conscience to confess your small and hidden evils as well as your open, great sins. Our secret sins, says the Prophet, are in the light of His countenance. <margin>Psal. 90 : 8.</margin> *You set our iniquities before You; our secret sins in the light of Your countenance.* <margin>Psal. 19: 12.</margin> *Who can understand his errors? Cleanse me from secret errors.*

David did not only confess his murder of Uriah, his adultery with Bathsheba, but he also confessed his small sins. David's heart pained him because he had cut a corner from Saul's robe; it was only an appearance of revenge, as if he wanted to kill with his knife; and that which had the appearance of sin made David's heart ache.

Conscientious people mourn and confess not only open and gross crimes, but they also mourn before God the small and hidden corruptions of the heart. They confess their hidden pride, their hidden worldliness, and their secret murmuring against God; they confess their hidden and small transgressions.

Truly, wicked men fall short here: they confess their great and open sins, but take no notice of their small and hidden wickednesses. There are two examples of this: one in Cain. Cain confessed his murder, saying that his fratricide was greater than could be forgiven him. <margin>Gen. 4: 13.</margin> And Cain said to the Lord, "My punishment is greater than can be forgiven." He made no confession of his hatred, which made him a brother-murderer. He confessed his great sin, but not his secret wickedness. So you read likewise of Judas; Judas confessed the betrayal of the Savior (a great sin), but not his insatiable desire—a hidden sin—which drove him to that evil deed. He says, "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." He complained and also made confession of his betrayal, but he neither confessed nor mourned his immoderate desire and greed, which were smaller and more hidden evils. That is a second rule: make it a matter of conscience to confess small and hidden wickednesses as well as public and great sins.

To magnify your sins, with all their circumstances and aggravations that you can devise; this is what the servants of God have done when they confessed their sins to God. They confessed their sins with all their circumstances, *1 Kings 8:47*, saying, "We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have dealt wickedly." *Lorinus* notes that the word and a humble soul go together in the confession of sin; "we have sinned," there is one word; "we have done perversely," there is the second; "we have dealt wickedly," there is the third. You have a notable example from *Paul, Acts 26:10, 11.* "Which I also did: I imprisoned many of the saints, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death, I cast my vote against them. And I often punished them in all the synagogues and tried to force them to blaspheme; and being exceedingly enraged at them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities."

Here *Paul* magnifies and aggravates his sin: Here are eight amplifications that *Paul* sets forth here to aggravate his sin, thus magnifying it, so that he might humble himself the more.

**First,** they were not common people whom he cast into prison, but they were saints, and to wrong them is a sacred violation.

**Secondly,** he did not cast the people into prison for debt, which may justly be done if he is not able to pay; but "I have imprisoned many of the saints," why? Because they confessed the Name of Jesus of Nazareth, verse 9. Primarily for the confession of *Christ*.

**Thirdly,** if it had been but one or two saints, that would not be much, but it was a great number, "I have imprisoned many of the saints."

**Fourthly,** He further magnifies his sins: to cast them into prison and give them freedom there is not much, but he imprisoned them and guarded the clothes of the prisoners.

**Fifthly,** if he had left it at that, it would still not be all, but he gave his vote to kill them.

**Sixthly,** He goes higher: He also offended their souls, for he forced them to blaspheme God.

**Seventhly,** He further aggravates it; he was enraged against them, "He was exceedingly enraged at them." He raged with madness, with passion, and with great fury against the saints of God.

**Eighthly,** He also persecuted them in foreign cities: He did not kill them, but drove them from wife and children; He made them run and flee for their lives into the outermost corners. This is the nature of true repentance, not to confess sin lightly and carelessly, but to do so with all its circumstances and aggravations. In the confession of sins, we should aggravate ourselves with this, that we have sinned against God's mercies, improvement, warnings, complaints of our conscience, and promptings of the Spirit, &c. And this is a good rule if you will follow it; you have a similar example in the Book of *Da-*

<column-break/>

niel, *Chapter 9, verse 5.* "We have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments and your rules." *Verse 6.* "We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land." There are seven circumstances that *Daniel* uses in the confession of his sins, to magnify them; how does *Daniel* clothe his confession? 1. We have sinned, there is one. 2. We have done wrong. 3. We have acted wickedly. 4. We have rebelled. 5. We have turned aside from your commandments. 6. We have not listened to your servants. 7. Neither we, nor our princes, nor all the people of the land: There are seven aggravations which *Daniel* enumerates in his confession. Thus prayed *David* when he desired forgiveness: "For your name's sake, forgive my iniquity, for it is great."

The fourth rule, in the confession of your sin, is this: in your confession, do not look upon God with mistrust, as upon an angry Judge, but with a firm hope, as upon a gracious Father; to confess sins to God as an angry Judge is to make yourself a damned, malicious person in your confession; therefore, confess to God only as a kind Father; this is what all converts do, they confess their sins to God as a Father. While you have a sorrowful eye on your sin, also have a hopeful eye on grace, as God's children do. To confess to God as a Judge is awful and fearful, but as a kind Father is childlike and sweet, readily receiving forgiveness. *Dan. 9:9.* "To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness, although we have rebelled against him." And so Shechaniah confesses his sins to God, *Ezra 10:2.* "Then Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, addressed Ezra, saying, 'We have trespassed against our God,'" &c. And so says the prodigal, *Luke 15:18.* "I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you."

Although he was a lost son, yet he would go to God as to a Father. In your confession, you must go to God hoping, as to a loving Father. Confession, when it comes to God as to a Judge, brings fear, terror, and trembling to the conscience, but when it is founded on hope and comes to God as a Father, it works a holy breaking of the heart, a holy tenderness and crushing to the conscience. We must confess our sins to God, as an injured person shows his defects and physical deformity to his healer, in the hope of healing.

The fifth rule, which must be observed in the confession of sins to God, is this: do not content yourself with a slight and outward confession, but do it with sorrow, weeping, and concern over your sins. *Psalm 38:19.* "I declare my iniquity; I am troubled because of my sin." *Dan. 9:8.* "O Lord, to us belongs open shame, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you."

### Confessing their Sins. Chapter 11.

Do not confess your sins until shame has filled your face and sorrow has filled your heart: it is a great failing in many people that when they confess their sins, they cry out for God’s mercy in a general sense, thinking they have made a compensation to God for all the wrongs done to Him. But Beloved, do not satisfy yourself with such a confession. In this, we must follow the **Holy Martyr Bradford**, <note>John Bradford (c. 1510–1555) was an English Reformer and martyr known for his extreme devotion; it was said he would not leave his prayers until he felt his heart truly moved by the subject of his petition.</note> who never went to prayer before his heart was troubled and kindled for this duty.

**The sixth Rule** in the confession of sin is this: if you find your heart hardened in the confession of present guilt and sin, then labor to gather and collect old guilt and old sins. This is a necessary practice in a Christian’s walk. Whether it be a man or a woman making confession, it may be that they do not know the sins they committed this past week due to a lack of close observation and regard for their ways. In this case, let them gather what they have done many years before; collecting their old and new sins, not forgetting them but confessing them in humility. So did **David**, in *Psalm 51:5*: <note>In most English Bibles, this is Psalm 51:3: "For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me."</note> *For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.* This was his old sin of adultery, which he now wished to remember. When his heart was as if pierced through, he said, *Lord, remember not the sins of my youth.* He went backward to his youth. I do not write this rule for a godly person who lives under many difficulties, for gathering old sins might cause them to despair; but in the case of spiritual barrenness, if someone lacks the matter of present sins because their heart is unfeelingly bound in prayer to God, in that case, they are bound to collect in their conscience and gather the sins of many years. To go backward to their youth and see what their conscience will bring up to make them humble in the confession of sins to God.

**One last rule**: place more importance on the confession of your **secret sins** to God than on public ones before men. To practice this rule, consider two things:

1. It is not good to confess all the evils you have done before men; and if there were no other proof for secret prayer than this, it would be enough: that it is not good for a person to confess all the sins of their life committed before men. *Zechariah 12:12*: *And the land shall mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of David apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart,* etc. They went to God and confessed their sins individually. You are a poor confessor if you only make confession in public and never in secret; you are but an unfruitful confessor.

2. Again, note this: that although we read of godless men who have made great confessions of sin to God, nonetheless we never read that they made it a matter of conscience to confess their sins to God in secret. **Pharaoh** (you know the history) confessed his sins to Moses and to Aaron, but we never read that Pharaoh confessed the same to God. *Exodus 9:27*: *Then Pharaoh sent for Moses and*

<column-break/>

*Aaron, and said to them, I have sinned this time,* etc.
**Saul** confessed his sins to Samuel, but we never read that he made confession of sins to God. *1 Samuel 15:24, 30*: *Then Saul said to Samuel, I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord and your words,* etc. And verse 30: *Then he said, I have sinned,* etc.
**Judas** confessed his sin, but to whom? To the High Priests and Pharisees; but he never went into a corner or into secret to bewail his blood-guiltiness. So even godless men have made public confessions of sin, but never in secret between God and their own soul; thus they have never known how to confess their wickedness to God. So much for the third question.

**The fourth question** is this: wherein does the difference appear between a godly man’s confession of sins to God and the confession of godless men? There are these eight distinctions:

**First**, holy confession in a godly person makes their soul more active and searching for healing and the forgiveness of sin. Holy confession is diligent. *I confess my sin; but how shall I subdue it? I know the same; but how shall I obtain forgiveness?* It makes us search to obtain remedies for our sins which were present before the confession. *Job 7:20*: <note>Job 7:20: "If I have sinned, what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?"</note> *If I have sinned, what shall I do, O watcher of mankind?* There is his confession: *Lord, what shall I do?* There is his diligence. So did the Jews when they were convicted of their great sins by Peter; they cried out, *What shall we do to be saved?* *Acts 2:37*. But false confession leaves the person empty and careless; they make confession, yet are not concerned with how they shall obtain forgiveness of sin through that confession.

**Second**, holy confession of sins to God in godly people is accompanied by remorse of conscience and a broken heart. *Psalm 38:18*: <note>The Dutch text cites verse 19; in English Bibles, this is usually Psalm 38:18.</note> *I will declare my iniquity; I will be sorry for my sin.* There confession and sorrow are joined together. *Hosea 12:4*: <note>The Dutch text cites 12:5; in English it is 12:4.</note> *Yes, he had power over the angel and prevailed; he wept and made supplication to him.* While the confession is in the mouth, there must be tears in the eyes or sorrow in the heart if the confession is to be sincere.
The godless confess sins but are never truly sorry that they have committed them; they are not ashamed or blushing, as the language of the Prophets testifies.

**Third**, a godly person confessing his sin has more freedom of spirit to confess his secret sins in particular than in public. *I have poured out my soul before God,* says the Psalmist. Confession of sin is a pouring out of the soul before God. He who complains more against secret sin than against public sin is a man who has found grace. The godless only confess their sins before men and not before God.

**Fourth**, holy people confess their sins freely, out of a willingness they have to be freed from sin; but the godless do not. They confess with pain and difficulty, not knowing whether they truly want to or not.

->### The Saints are Bound<-

The godly confess freely and are willing to unburden themselves of their desires; therefore, they acknowledge them before God. <margin>Job 32:18</margin> *I am full of words: the spirit within my belly constrains me.* <margin>Verse 19</margin> *Behold, my belly is as wine which has no vent; it is ready to burst like new wineskins.* <margin>Verse 20</margin> *I will speak, that I may find relief; I will open my lips and answer.* Thus is a godly person in the confession of their sins; their belly is like wine that is not opened; it must be opened, or otherwise the wineskins will burst. They must necessarily confess their sins, which drives them toward God; however, for ungodly people, confession is forced and dragged out of them. It was the plagues of Egypt upon Pharaoh that forced a confession from him; before this, he said, "Who is the Lord?" <margin>Exodus 9:1</margin> It was the distress and terror of conscience in Judas that made him acknowledge he had sinned and betrayed innocent blood. Sailors throw their goods overboard, not because they hate them, but so they do not perish in the storm; likewise, when a storm and tempest arises in the conscience, then people pour out a confession by compulsion, and not voluntarily.

Fifthly, a godly person is conscientious to confess secret and small sins as well as great sins and wicked acts. David confessed his pride and fleshly confidence in the numbering of the people, as well as his adultery with Bathsheba. David acknowledged the cutting off of the corner of Saul’s robe as much as the murder of Uriah. But hypocrites might confess their great sins, yet not their small ones. Cain confessed his murderous act, but not his evil offering; they confess their large sins, but not their small ones. Pharaoh confessed the oppression done to the children of Israel, but not the hardness of his heart. But the godly, even if they have many great and open wickednesses, nevertheless small and hidden evils weigh upon their conscience and unrest their spirit. These do not merely touch the ungodly man's clothes <note>A reference to David merely cutting Saul's robe, which nevertheless smote David's heart, whereas a wicked man would feel nothing even for a greater crime.</note>, but they go straight to the heart; for although there is no unchastity in their flesh, nor any plundering of the world, yet they know they have hidden and inward defilements of the spirit; these they bewail and confess to God.

Sixthly, the godly are distinct and clear in the confession of their particular and specific crimes, so that they might gain mastery over them. Beloved, take note of this: ungodly people are muddled in their confessions and say only in general that they are sinners. Just like Ahimaaz, when he brought the news to David of the battle between Joab and Absalom, <margin>2 Samuel 18:29</margin> <note>Original citation says verse 19, but the quote refers to the report in verse 29.</note> he said, *I saw a great tumult, when Joab the king's servant sent me your servant; but I knew not what it was.* The ungodly tell you indeed that their sins make a "great tumult" within them, but they cannot tell it to you distinctly or in particular, but only in a skimming manner. They confess their sins as Nebuchadnezzar recounted his dream; <margin>Daniel 2:8</margin> he dreamed, but he could not tell what it was. Ungodly people know sin as a person knows something in a dream; when, how, and where—and its aggravating circumstances—they do not know; they have no distinct and clear sight of their failings.

<column-break/>

But the children of God bring forth their specific failings in their confession, as the children of Israel did. <margin>Judges 10:10</margin> In this way, <term>Bellarmine</term> <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and a major target of Protestant polemics who argued for the possibility of a life of perfect righteousness.</note> concealed his ungodliness by saying that he was not ungodly or sinful when he lay on his deathbed; and when his confessor came to him and desired that he should confess his sins, Bellarmine said, "I do not know that I have any sins to confess." This was not the holiness of that man, but boldness and ungodliness, because he did not take heed of his ways. <term>Donatus</term> <note>The 4th-century bishop and namesake of the Donatists, often portrayed by later writers as claiming a state of sinless perfection.</note>, a great ringleader of the Donatists, said, "O Lord, I have nothing that You need to forgive me." Beloved, this comes from hardness—that a person does not see sin—and it rests not on holiness, but on ungodliness and fleshly carelessness. There is a remark someone made regarding Job; Job says, *How many are my iniquities and sins? Make me to know my transgression and my sin.* <margin>Job 13:23</margin> While Job makes this complaint that he had sin, God says that in all this Job did not sin; that is, not absolutely, but by comparison. Beloved, to be constantly in complaint and to be full of the confession of sin does not show that you have more sins than others, but it is proof that you see them more, and therefore you have the fewer sins within you.

Seventhly, godly people confess their sins out of an insight into the feeling of them as being a dishonor to God, rather than as a shame and contempt to themselves. They confess their sins as an uncleanness of nature that dishonors God, rather than for the evil consequences of the same—that it brings damnation to the sinner. <margin>Psalm 51</margin> David says, *Against you, against you only, have I sinned;* it was not just against Uriah that he had sinned, but *against You only have I sinned; I have dishonored You by my sin.* When the Apostles spoke of conversion, they called it a turning to God. <margin>Acts 20:21</margin> *Testifying both to Jews and Greeks, repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.* Suggesting that where true sorrow and confession of sin is, this happens more out of a feeling of sin against God than against oneself. But the ungodly do not yet confess their sins as a dishonor to God, but as a gathered debt, being ashamed of themselves.

Lastly, holy confession of sin in the godly brings a holy fear and sorrow upon their heart, being terrified of committing the sin again after the confession; avoiding every opportunity that might lead them to the sin they previously confessed. <margin>Acts 19:18</margin> Thus you read in Acts 19:18, *And many that believed came, and confessed, and shewed their deeds.* <margin>Verse 19</margin> *Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men,* etc. Those who spoke of their sorcery and devilish arts wanted to burn the books so that they would no longer provide an opportunity to commit those sins again which they had confessed to God. Beloved, this is sincere confession: that when you have once confessed your sins to God in secret and lamented your crimes there, you are then afraid to commit them again, and your soul keeps watch against those sins you have confessed.

It stresses that true confession must lead to a practical avoidance of future sin.</summary>

# The Saints are Indebted

The godly confess freely and are willing to empty themselves of their desires; therefore they acknowledge them before God, as in *Job 32:18*: *I am full of words: the spirit within me constrains me.* Verse 19: *Behold, my belly is as wine which has no vent; it is ready to burst like new wineskins.* Verse 20: *I will speak, that I may be refreshed: I will open my lips and answer.* Thus is a godly person in the confession of his sins; his belly is like wine that is not opened; it must be opened, or else the wineskins will burst. He must necessarily confess his sins, which drive him toward God. However, the confession of the wicked is forced and dragged out of them. It was the plagues of Egypt upon Pharaoh that wrung a confession from him: "Hear this," he said, "who is the Lord?" *Exod. 9:1.* <note>The author likely refers to the general narrative of Pharaoh's resistance and eventual forced admission in Exodus 9:27: "I have sinned this time: the Lord is righteous."</note> It was the anguish and terror of conscience in Judas which made him acknowledge that he had sinned and betrayed innocent blood. Sailors throw their goods overboard, not because they hate them, but so they do not perish in the storm. So too, when a storm and tempest arises in their conscience, men push out a confession through compulsion, and not voluntarily.

**Fifthly**, a godly person is conscientious to confess secret and small sins as well as great sins and wickednesses. David confessed his pride and fleshly trust in the numbering of the people, <note>Referring to the census in 2 Samuel 24, which was considered a sin of prideful reliance on military strength rather than God.</note> as well as his adultery with Bathsheba. David acknowledged the cutting off of the corner of Saul's robe as well as the murder of Uriah. But hypocrites may confess their great sins, but not their small ones. Cain confessed his act of murder, but not his evil offering; they confess their large sins, but not their small ones. Pharaoh confessed his oppression done to the children of Israel, but not the hardness of his heart. But the godly, although they may have many great and open evils, nevertheless small and hidden evils weigh upon their conscience and unrest their spirit. These do not merely touch a wicked man's clothes, but they strike the godly man's heart; for although there is no unchastity in their flesh, no defilement of the world, yet they know they have hidden and inward stains of the spirit; these they mourn, and they complain of them to God.

**Sixthly**, the godly are distinct and clear in confessing their particular and individual crimes, so that they might triumph over them. Beloved, take note of this: wicked men are confused in their confessions, and say only in general that they are sinners. Just like Ahimaaz, when he brought the news to David of Joab’s battle with Absalom, *2 Sam. 18:29*: <note>The OCR lists verse 19, but the quote corresponds to verse 29.</note> he said, *I saw a great tumult, when Joab the king's servant sent me your servant, but I knew not what it was.* The wicked report indeed that their sins make a great "tumult" in them, but they cannot tell it to you distinctly or in particular, but only in passing. They confess their sins as Nebuchadnezzar reported his dream, *Dan. 2:8*. He dreamed, but could not tell what it was. Wicked men know sin like a man knows something in a dream; when, how, and where, and with its aggravating circumstances, they do not know; they have no discerned and clear view of their failings.

<column-break/>

But the children of God bring forth their specific failings in their confession; so did the children of Israel, *Judg. 10:10*. Thus **Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and key figure in the Catholic Counter-Reformation, often criticized by Protestant writers for his views on justification.</note> concealed his wickedness in saying that he was not wicked or sinful when he lay on his deathbed; and when his confessor came to him, desiring that he should confess his sins, Bellarmine said, "I do not know that I have any sins to confess." This was not the holiness of that man, but boldness and godlessness, that he did not observe his ways. **Donatus**, <note>Donatus Magnus (died c. 355), leader of the Donatist schism, who emphasized the personal purity of the clergy to an extreme degree.</note> a great ringleader of the Donatists, said, "O Lord, I have nothing that you need to forgive me." Beloved, this comes from hardness; that a man does not see sin does not arise from holiness, but from godlessness and fleshly carelessness. There is a remark that someone has regarding Job; Job says, *How many are my iniquities and sins? make me to know my transgression and my sin,* *Job 13:23*. While Job makes this complaint that he had sin, God says, *In all this Job sinned not*; that is, not absolutely, but in comparison. Beloved, to be constant in complaint, and to be full of the confession of sin, does not show that you have more sins than others, but it is a proof that you see them more, and therefore you have the fewer sins remaining in you.

**Seventhly**, godly people confess their sins out of an insight into the monstrosity of them, as being a dishonor to God, rather than as a shame and contempt to themselves. They confess their sins more as an impurity of nature that dishonors God than for the evil consequences of the same, such as that it brings damnation to the sinner. In *Psalm 51*, David says, *Against thee, thee only, have I sinned*; it was not only against Uriah that he had sinned, but *Against thee alone have I sinned; I have dishonored thee through my sin.* When the Apostles spoke of conversion, they called it a conversion to God, *Acts 20:21*: *Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.* Showing that where true sorrow and confession of sin is, this happens more out of a feeling of sin against God than against oneself. But the wicked never confess their sins as a dishonor to God, but as an accumulated debt, shaming themselves.

**Finally**, holy confession of sin in the godly brings a holy fear and sorrow upon their heart, being afraid to commit the sin again after the confession, avoiding every opportunity that might lead them to the sin they previously confessed. So you read in *Acts 19:18*: *And many that believed came, and confessed, and shewed their deeds.* Verse 19: *Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men,* etc. They spoke of their sorcery and devilish arts; they wanted to burn the books so that they would no longer provide an opportunity to commit those sins again which they had confessed to God. Beloved, this is sincere confession: that when you have once confessed your sins to God in secret and mourned your crimes there, you are then fearful of committing them again, and your soul keeps watch against those sins you have confessed.

<summary>This page distinguishes true, godly confession—which is voluntary, specific, and focused on God's honor—from the forced, vague, and self-centered admissions of the wicked. It emphasizes that a high awareness of one's own sin is a mark of spiritual health rather than excessive guilt.</summary>

### ...to confess their sins.

A godly person may commit a sin that they have previously confessed; nevertheless, they maintain a fear and terror in their heart, so that this does not happen to them in practice. In contrast, the ungodly confess the sins they have committed, yet they remain bold and unafraid to commit the very same sin again which they have just confessed.

So did the Harlot in Proverbs 7:14. *I have peace offerings with me; today I have paid my vows.* Prayerful promises are a confession that I am indebted to God because of my sins, and a promise to serve that same God. Nevertheless, she shows herself even bolder upon that confession, using it as a means to continue in her ungodliness. To confess drunkenness and afterwards be drunk; to confess <term>unchastity<note>The original Dutch uses 'ontseplinge', likely a variation of 'ontucht', referring to sexual immorality or impurity.</note></term> and afterwards be unchaste, is a bold audacity of the ungodly. Thus Pharaoh confessed his sins in Exodus 9, and afterwards, when the plagues were over, he ran back to the same sin he had confessed; and this is the evil practice of the ungodly. And thus I have finished the fourth part.

->Now I come to the uses.<-

<margin>Use for reproof.</margin> The first use is for reproof: there are three sorts of people who are justly to be reproved here, if it is so that justified persons are bound to confess their sins to God; then this rebukes:

First, the <term>Antinomians<note>A sect that believed that under the gospel dispensation of grace, the moral law is of no use or obligation, and thus confessing sins is unnecessary for the believer.</note></term>, who consider it an unnecessary and useless work for the believer to bring their sins before God or to confess them. And therefore in their prayers (when one hears them in public) they speak entirely of the Majesty of God, of the excellence of Christ, of the glory of Heaven, and of the riches of grace, but not a word of the misery of the creatures; now, to overthrow this idle opinion of the Antinomians, take note:

1. Confession of sins was practiced by all the godly under the Old Testament; and why should we not do it under the New? Daniel 9:4, 16. Daniel prayed to God and confessed his sins; so also did the man of God, Nehemiah, Chapter 1, verse 6 and following: *Let your ear now be attentive, and your eyes open, that you may hear the prayer of your servant, which I pray before you now, day and night, for the children of Israel your servants, and confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against you: both I and my father's house have sinned,* etc. So did David, 2 Samuel 24:10. *And David's heart smote him after he had numbered the people. And David said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O Lord, take away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.* This is the first point to refute that practice.

2. Not only the believers under the Old Testament, but also all converts under the New Testament have made a conscience of confessing sins to God. Matthew 3:6: *And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.* Acts 19:18: *And many that believed came, and confessed, and shewed their deeds.* Luke 15:17: *And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!* Verse 18: *I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I

<column-break/>

have sinned against heaven, and before thee.* This is an adornment of a convert, even if it is but a parable. In the example of the Publican, whom Christ preferred to justify rather than the Pharisee, Luke 18:13: *And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.* Verse 14: *I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other,* etc. Now, beloved, since you have examples in the Old Testament and many in the New Testament, why then should we not perform such a precious part of divine service as this is: confessing our sins in secret to God?

Only acknowledge thine iniquity, that thou hast transgressed against the Lord thy God,* etc.

4. God, in both the Old and New Testaments, has attached and promised many gracious promises to the sincere confession of sins before him. In the Old Testament, Leviticus 26:40, 41, 42: *If they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers, with their trespass which they trespassed against me... Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob,* etc. If they confessed their iniquity, he would remember them. There are gracious promises to those who confess their sins: and it is certain that a person can have no promises in any duty if they do not have them in this one. Proverbs 28:13: *He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.* Job 33:27: *He looketh upon men, and if any say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not,* etc. And in the New Testament, 1 John 1:9: *If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.* Now, beloved, put these four things together: The godly did it in the Old Testament; the converts under the New; God has commanded it; and he rewards it. Therefore, those who regard the confession of sins as an unnecessary work are rightly to be rejected.

<meta>This page continues the critique of religious practices regarding confession. Having addressed those who refuse to confess at all, the author now focuses on the Roman Catholic practice of auricular confession (confessing to a priest), arguing against its historical and biblical validity before discussing the appropriate times for a believer to confess to a fellow human being.</meta>

Thirdly, they say / that the Priest has power upon your confession from *Christ* to pardon you, and to give absolution; see, these things are current regarding <term>Ear-confession<note>Known formally as auricular confession, where sins are whispered privately into the ear of a priest.</note></term>.

And so that you may see the shamefulness and looseness of this opinion / worthy to be rebuked / I shall overthrow the same through these observations.

<margin>Visscher.<note>Likely referring to Johannes Visscher, a 17th-century Dutch theologian.</note></margin>
1. Note the time when this Ear-confession first came into use in the Church / for 800 years after *Christ* / this custom was not yet in the Church of God: and the law of Ear-confession was not instituted until the time of Pope *Innocent* the third / which was about 1200 years after *Christ's* birth: and the first *Council* which confirmed this Ear-confession / was the *Council of the Lateran*, and later the *Council of Trent*. The Church of God in *Primitive* times / did not have such a custom / and therefore this Ear-confession ought now to be driven out of the Church as an ugly abomination.

2. Why then did the Pope institute this Ear-confession? Someone has given these reasons for it.

1. It is a good invention / to know the hidden secrets of men / their thoughts / intentions, and desires / both in Church and <term>State<note>The original Dutch uses 'Politie', referring here to civil government and public affairs.</note></term>.

2. It is a direct means to obtain money for the Pope / according to the greatness of the sin that is confessed / so must the money be, if he is to give Absolution: and therefore a theologian calls it, Money-confession. Oh, this confession is exceedingly fit to know the deliberations of Statesmen / and to bring profit to the Roman Seat / which shows that this practice is unjust.

3. Note what the Scripture says / regarding confession to men, *James 5:16.*
> Confess your faults to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed.

The Scripture does not tell us of a Priest / as the <term>Papist<note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics.</note></term> Church does: but we must confess our faults to one another. If someone has a distressed Conscience or a troubled mind / he must confess that to his neighbor / who can give him some comfort or counsel from the Lord. We are bound to confess our sins to any Christian friend / or member of the Church / whom we judge most fit to advise us / for their wisdom / godliness / compassion, and experience.

Our Protestant interpreters have a good observation against the *Papists*: the Apostle desires / if any be sick among you let him call the Elders of the church, that they may pray over him, *Verse 14.* yet he does not desire that they should confess their sins to the Elders / but to one another: which act does not establish the confession of sins to the Priest. But this is a point of *Controversy* / and thanks be to God / this Church is not burdened with that error: therefore I shall leave it: This is the second sort of reproof / namely / to the *Papists* / who take the confession of sins away from God / and do it to the Priest.

Thirdly, this doctrine rebukes those who / in order to avoid the Papist Ear-confession to the priest / deny all sorts of confession of sin to men / in which

<column-break/>

there are many failings: Many keep the counsel of the devil / and <term>grope among corruptions<note>Original: 'groepen onder de verborventheden', suggesting being stuck or wallowing in secret sins.</note></term>, yet they never open their mouth for counsel or help from other men. There are some particular / and various cases / in which we are not only bound to confess our sins to God / but also to men: but before I treat of those / take these two cautions.

First / you are not bound to confess your sins to men when it is not necessary / but when there is a great and pressing necessity / as when you are extremely troubled in your *Conscience* / and cannot be comforted / in such a case you may make known to men what sins trouble your *Conscience*: but it not being necessary / you are not bound to this. God wills, says *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching.</note>, that we should not go to men, to reveal our shame, but to Him. Unless necessity compels us / and we can in no way help ourselves / we are bound to confess our crimes and failings to men.

Secondly / although you confess your sins to men / you are not bound to do it to everyone: you must confess them to those who are compassionate / who are fit to pray for you / who have wisdom to advise you / who have experience to instruct you / who give counsel / and keep counsel: You are not bound to confess your faults to everyone / but to those who are compassionate of heart / and fit to pray for you. They say / what is that to us? see you to yourself what you have done: So many are not experienced / nor willing to give you counsel; therefore great wisdom is needed to reveal your sins to other men. Thus I have prescribed some cautions for you.

Now / in what cases is it lawful and good to confess one's sins to other men, as well as to God? I shall resolve this for you / in four cases.

First, in case of public scandal to the Church / by your sins / you must confess the same to the Church / of which you are a member; public and great sins require public confession. *David* fell into the sin of adultery / and the sin was known among all nations / in such a way that the enemies spoke evil of *Religion* and of God: What did *David* do then / to wipe out the wrong done to the Church? he makes the *51st Psalm* / not only for his person / but for a public <term>lamentation<note>The original Dutch uses 'gezuych', which can refer to a sigh, a song, or a public declaration of grief/repentance.</note></term>; note the inscription of the same. *A Psalm of David, for the Chief Musician, when the Prophet Nathan had come to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.* This Psalm was sung in the Holy Place and in the Temple / so that the Church of God / damaged by *David's* sin / was hereby again

<meta>catchword: he</meta>

was nourished <note>Original: "gespijst." In this context, it suggests being spiritually fed or restored to the community.</note> because he confessed the same in public. Beloved, this is proper, because the members of a Church are scandalized by such public and known sins; therefore, the conversion must be public. And furthermore, public scandals by any member of the Church bring God's wrath upon an entire assembly if the doer does not confess his sins. Joshua 22, verse 20: *Did not Achan, the son of Zerah, commit a trespass in the accursed thing, and wrath fell on all the congregation of Israel? and that man perished not alone in his iniquity.* Achan sinned alone, but was not punished alone; the wrath remained upon the entire assembly. Therefore, for the good of the assembly and Church of which you are a member, if you commit any public and known sins, you are bound to confess the same: Not that all private sins must be confessed to the Church, but you are obligated to reveal and confess gross and public scandals to the assembly.

Secondly, you are bound to confess your sins to men in the case of a particular wrong done to your neighbor, in offending him. Personal wrongs done to your neighbor must be confessed to him. Matthew 5:23, 24: *Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.* If you have wronged your brother, first reconcile with him. Christ recounts this regarding private and personal wrongs, in which we are bound to make confession and give justice to the one who is wronged. And thus Christ goes further, Luke 17:3, 4: *Take heed to yourselves: If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him. And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.* Christ indicates here that we must confess our sins to our brother whom we have wronged; to specific people against whom we have done some particular evil—not only to God, but also to them.

Thirdly, you must confess your sins to men as well as to God in the case of a violent disturbance of the conscience because of some particular sins committed against God: When your conscience leaps in your face <note>An old idiom for a sudden, stinging realization of guilt.</note>, and you can neither eat, nor drink, nor sleep, nor be at rest, so it oppresses you with terror. If you can obtain no help, nor rest, or stillness in your conscience, then it is good that you go to a faithful and experienced friend, revealing it to him. This is the meaning of the Apostle's saying, James 5 verse 16: *Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed.* That is, when you are in extreme danger and dejection of conscience, unsettled because of sin, then confess your sins to other men and endeavor to pray for the same. And in the confession to men, you are not bound to confess all your sins, but only those particular sins that unsettle your conscience. When you come to a <term>physician<note>Original Dutch: "Medicijn-meester," a master of medicine or doctor.</note></term>,

<column-break/>

you discover to him only those parts in which you are deficient <note>Meaning the parts of the body that are ailing or injured.</note>. You must confess no more to men than those particular wickednesses that most unsettle your conscience.

Fourthly, you must confess your sins to those who have been helpers and sharers with you in sin: To these you must confess your sins as well as to God. There are some interpreters who explain this passage of James 5 in this way: James 5 verse 16, *Confess your faults one to another*; That is, the partakers in sin shall go from one to the other and confess their faults to one another. If you have been a drunkard, go to your comrade and tell him that your heart beats for the sin. You who have been unchaste, if God has disturbed your conscience because of your unchastity, go to your companion in that sin and tell him that God has moved your conscience because of those lusts, and this will likewise awaken his conscience.

Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> relates that the Evangelist John, returning on his journey from Patmos to Ephesus after the death of Emperor Domitian, came into a company of robbers, among whom he found a certain young man who was their captain, whom John converted; and the history says: That this young man, being now converted, went to his former company, who were robbers, admonishing and praying them in the Name of Jesus Christ that they should no longer walk in that way of godlessness. He was disturbed in his conscience, and therefore he gave them earnest counsel: That they, if they loved their souls, must no longer walk in that way of godlessness: and by this means many of those great robbers were converted. In like manner do you to your former company, drunkards, adulterers, etc. Confess your sins, as Demosthenes <note>The author likely refers to a famous anecdote of conversion; though Demosthenes was a Greek statesman, the quote "I am not who I was" is a classic trope of Christian transformation.</note> said to the harlot, "I am not the same as I was before." And it shall easily happen that their conscience is awakened and accuses them, and they consider their godless ways, and that God works a change in them, just as He has done in you.

Here is a use of humiliation in this point, to humble yourself before the presence of God, seeing so much defect in the confession of sins to Him. Now beloved, the defects, not only of the godless but also of the godly in this point, are ten.

<margin>10 Defects in the confession of sins to God.</margin>
The first defect in the confession of sins to God is this: that when they come to confess sins to God, they have such a sterility and confusion in their spirit that they cannot remember or confess the particular sins to Him. Mr. Hildersham <note>Arthur Hildersham (1563–1632), a prominent English Puritan clergyman.</note>, on Psalm 51, has a good note on the words of 1 John 1:8: *If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.* He says: *If we say that we have no sin*: There is no one so bold who will say such a thing, for his own practice shall make his tongue lying; but this is [the case] when we come to God and do not know how to confess our sins before Him, just as if we denied them. We are so confused and sluggish in the consideration of our own ways that we cannot confess them to God in prayer, and this the Apostle rebukes. # The Saints are Bound #
