Thirdly, they say that the Priest, upon your confession, has the power from Christ to pardon you and give absolution; see, these things are common practice regarding **Ear-confession** <note>Also known as auricular confession, the practice of confessing sins privately to a priest.</note>.

And so that you may see the shamefulness and laxity of this opinion—which is worthy of being rebuked—I shall overthrow it with these observations.

1. Consider the time when this Ear-confession first came into use in the Church; for 800 years after Christ, this practice was not yet in the Church of God. The law of Ear-confession was not instituted until the time of Pope Innocent III, which was around 1200 years after the birth of Christ. The first Council that confirmed this Ear-confession was the Lateran Council, and later the Council of Trent. The Church of God in the Primitive times <note>The early era of Christianity, usually the first few centuries.</note> did not have such a custom, and therefore this Ear-confession ought now to be driven out of the Church as an ugly fabrication.

<margin>Fisher</margin> <note>Likely referring to a specific theological writer or polemicist of the era.</note>
2. Why, then, did the Pope institute this Ear-confession? One writer gives these reasons for it:

1. It is a clever invention to know the hidden secrets of men—their thoughts, intentions, and desires—both in the Church and in the State.

2. It is a direct means to obtain money for the Pope; according to how great the sin is that is confessed, so must the money be if he is to give Absolution. Therefore, a theologian calls it **Money-confession** <note>Original: "Gelt-belydenisse."</note>. Oh, this confession is exceedingly well-suited for knowing the deliberations of Statesmen and for bringing profit to the Roman See, which demonstrates that this practice is unjust.

3. Notice what the Scripture says regarding confession to men in James 5:16: **Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed.** The Scripture does not tell us about a Priest, as the Popish Church does, but we must confess our faults to one another. If someone has a troubled conscience or a disturbed mind, he must confess it to his neighbor who can give him some comfort or counsel from the Lord. We are bound to confess our sins to some Christian friend or member of the Church whom we judge most capable of advising us because of their wisdom, godliness, compassion, and experience.

Our Protestant interpreters have a good observation against the Papists: the Apostle desires, *if any be sick among you, let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him,* in Verse 14. Yet he does not desire that they should confess their sins to the Elders, but to one another; which act does not establish the confession of sins to a Priest. But this is a point of controversy, and thanks be to God, this Church is not burdened with that error. Therefore, I shall leave it. This is the second kind of rebuke: namely, to the Papists, who take the confession of sins away from God and give it to the Priest.

Thirdly, this teaching rebukes those who, in order to flee the Popish Ear-confession to the Priest, deny all types of confession of sin to men, in which

<column-break/>

there are many failings. These people keep the devil’s counsel and groan under their secrets; nonetheless, they never open their mouths for counsel or help from other people. There are some particular and various cases in which we are not only bound to confess our sins to God, but also to men. But before I discuss those, take these two precautions.

First, you are not bound to confess your sins to men when it is not necessary; but when there is a great and pressing necessity—such as when you are extremely troubled in your conscience and cannot be comforted—in such a case, you may make known to men what sins trouble your conscience. But where it is not necessary, you are not bound to do this. God wills, says **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, that we should not go to men to reveal our shame, but to Him. Only when necessity compels us, and we cannot help ourselves in any way, are we bound to confess our crimes and failings to men.

Secondly, even if you confess your sins to men, you are not bound to do it to everyone. You must confess them to those who are compassionate, who are capable of praying for you, who have wisdom to advise you, who have experience to instruct you, and who give counsel and keep counsel. You are not bound to confess your faults to everyone, but to those who are compassionate of heart and capable of praying for you. Beloved, if a person is so indiscreet in confession as to do it to everyone, some might easily reproach him for it for an entire year. Chrysostom, in his **Homily of the Rich Man and Lazarus**, gives this reason: *If you confess your sins in the ears of some men, they will throw the same in your face to your shame.* Some men will deal with you as the Pharisees did with Judas. Judas, when he was troubled in his conscience, came to the Pharisees and said, "There is your money; I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." They said, "What is that to us? see thou to that." Thus, many are not experienced, nor do they wish to give you counsel; therefore, great wisdom is needed to reveal your sins to other people. Thus I have prescribed some precautions to you.

Now, in what cases is it permissible and good to confess one's sins to other men, as well as to God? I shall resolve this for you in four cases.

First, in the case of public scandal to the Church caused by your sins, you must confess them to the Church of which you are a member; public and great sins require public confession. David fell into the sin of adultery, and the sin was known among all nations, in such a way that the enemies spoke ill of the Saints and of God. What did David do then to wipe out the wrong done to the Church? He composed the 51st Psalm, not only for his person but for public use; note the inscription of the same: *A Psalm of David, for the Chief Musician, when Nathan the Prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.* This Psalm was uttered <note>Original: "wtert," likely meaning "uttered" or "expressed."</note> and sung in the Sanctuary and in the Temple, so that the Church of God, which had been shamed by David's sin, was hereby again...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the obligation of the Saints to confess. Having previously discussed confession before men for public scandals, the author now transitions to the spiritual mechanics of confession before God, comparing the biblical figures of David and Saul.</meta>

->The Saints are Obliged<-

committed a far lesser sin than David’s sin was—namely, Adultery. Saul spared, merely for his own physical use, the best of the cattle—a small thing, or nothing, in comparison to David’s sin. Nevertheless, see: David was reconciled, and Saul was not. Why? David had confessed, and Saul had not. Saul excused himself and said to Samuel, *That the people had done it, and not he.* This made him punishable. Therefore, beware of failing to confess small sins; for however small they may be, if they remain unconfessed, they damn a person, whereas a great sin that is confessed does not.

The second instruction is this: Do not depend upon the breadth or the most emotional confession you have ever made to God, even assuming you had poured out your soul to God and yet did not become better. You, O man! when you make a confession of sins, act like a beggar: lay your wounds open before God, show your boils and sores, and do not lean upon your confession itself. Just as you must not lean upon your own righteousness, so also you must not lean upon your confession. It is a word worthy of your notice: Saul pursued David like a partridge over the mountains; David cut a corner from his robe; David said, *I have sinned,* and Saul said, *You are more righteous than I.* When Nathan came to David, David said, *I have sinned;* and Nathan spoke, *The Lord has taken away your iniquity.* Saul also said, *I have sinned;* nevertheless, the Prophet Samuel said to him, *The Lord has taken away your Kingdom.* Here the reward is not the same: David’s sin was taken away, but Saul’s Kingdom was taken away. Therefore, do not lean simply upon your confession.

Thirdly, take this instruction: That when you confess your sins to God, and they are terrifying in your eyes, then you are most pleasing in the eyes of God. **Song of Solomon 1:6.** *Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me.* The Church confesses there that she is black and burned by the sun, not lovely. But in verse 8, Christ says: *O thou fairest among women.* Christ looks upon her as the fairest among women. Likewise in **Chapter 2:14**: *O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.* When the poor dove—the Church—sat in the clefts of the rocks, weeping and lamenting like a dove over her sin: Oh, then Christ says, *Come forth, show me your countenance, let me hear your voice.* Christ loves the humblest voice of his people. **Jeremiah 31:18.** *I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself thus: Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the Lord my God.* Job (when he was visited by God with sores and festering boils over his whole body) made these complaints to God in **Chapter 7:20**: *I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?* <note>original: "Menschen-hoeder"</note> I have sinned, says Job: But what does God say of Job? *In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly,* **Job 1:22.** It is not said absolutely that he did not sin; but the meaning is, he did not sin as other men sin. The more 

<column-break/>

you weep, mourn, and are grieved over your sins before God, and the more hideous you deem them in your own eyes, the more lovely you are in the eyes of God. And thus I have concluded the first part of my Text: *I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord.*

Having finished the reasoning of David, I come now to the work of God: *And thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.* <note>The Hebrew word "Selah" is a musical or liturgical sign likely meaning "pause" or "reflect."</note> *Thou forgavest the iniquity,* etc. That is, not only my Sin, but the curse of the same, with all the aggravating and terrifying circumstances. Now, in this work of God, two things are to be noted.

<margin>Veathah nafatha <note>original Hebrew: וְאַתָּה נָשָׂאתָ, meaning "And You forgave" or "And You lifted away."</note></margin>
1. The manner of the presentation of this work of God. The Psalmist does not present it with an *Ergo* <note>original Latin: "therefore"</note>, or "so then": *I said I will confess my transgressions, therefore you forgave the iniquity of my sin;* but rather with an *and*—a coordinating and not a causal word: *I will confess, and you forgive me.*

2. Note further the substance of the reason: The confession was in the intention and in the mind, but the forgiveness is immediate. Take this Doctrine here: That God rewards a holy intention just as much as a completed work in His servants. God forgave: David had only intended to confess—*I said, I will confess my transgressions, and you forgave me.* Oh beloved! what kind of God do you serve! Your earthly masters are not satisfied with your intention in the work if your hands do not labor. You serve a God who accepts the will for the work, the intention for the deed and the fulfillment. The Lord rewards not only holy deeds, but likewise holy intentions in His servants.

The Use <term>Use</term> <note>In Puritan-style preaching, a "Use" is the practical application of the doctrine to the listener's life.</note> of this is:
To the terror of the godless. God shall not only punish them for their evil deeds, but also for their godless intentions. Have you ever intended to be unchaste, intended to strike someone, or secretly laid snares to insult someone? Truly, God will punish you for your intention as well as for your deed. Beloved, it is not only evil what you have done, but also what you want to do. Do you refrain from being an oppressor only because the world would shame you for it? Not a drunkard only because the world blames you? God shall punish the godless for their wicked intentions.

Furthermore, to the Godly: Can you not weep? If only you *want* to weep. Can you not confess the sins? If only you *want* to confess them. Can you not break your heart? If only you *want* to break it. God looks upon your intentions, recognizing them as good, just as well as He does your deeds: Just as David shows here, *I said, I will confess, and you forgave me.*

Thirdly, God looks not only at the intentions of the godless and the intentions of the godly in relation to Him, but also the intention of the Devil, in order to prevent him in his evil. *Simon, Simon* (says Christ) *Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have immediately prayed for you.* The harm was only in the Devil’s intention and desire; and while it was still only in the desire, Christ said, *I have immediately prayed for you.* Oh, marvel at the wonderful harmony of Christ, who crowns your intentions and your desires.

Then the connection of the words...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of confession, specifically focusing on the theological nature of forgiveness. It follows the previous page's instruction that even great sins, when confessed, can be forgiven, whereas small unconfessed sins lead to condemnation.</meta>

->to confess their sins.<-

That there is a necessary joining together between a penitent confession of sin and the forgiveness of the same. I confessed, and God forgave it. You have these passages which impress this upon your thoughts: Proverbs 28:13. *He who covers his transgressions shall not prosper; but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall find mercy.* Job 33:27, 28. *I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not; but God has delivered my soul from going into the pit, and my life shall see the light.*

In the treatment of this point, there are these particular things which I shall handle.

First, what is understood here by the forgiveness of sin. To explain this, three things are necessary to observe.

First: The various names by which the forgiveness of sins is expressed.

1. Forgiveness of sin is the casting of sin behind the back. Isaiah 38, verse 17. <note>original: "Jesa. 38. vers 17"</note> *Behold, for peace I had great bitterness; but you have in love delivered my soul from the pit of corruption, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.* In the Scripture, a thing is said to be cast behind the back when it is forgiven and pardoned. Thus the godless cast God’s commandment behind their back when they do not keep it or wish to obey it. See also Psalm 50, verse 17; Nehemiah 9, verse 17. Likewise, when God is said to cast sins behind his back, he chooses to take no knowledge of them in order to punish them.

2. Forgiveness of sin is called a casting away of sin into the depths of the Sea. Micah 7:19. *He will again have compassion; he will subdue our iniquities; Yes, you will cast all our sins into the depths of the Sea.* This refers to God’s great judgment over Pharaoh and the Egyptian horses when they pursued the Israelites and came to the Red Sea. They thought to pass through it just as the Israelites did, but the Sea fell upon them and they sank down into the abyss. So God says: *I do with sin as I did with Pharaoh; you shall never be plagued by it again, it shall never condemn you again, and you have no need to fear that it shall rise up against you again.* Sin is no light matter that can swim upon the Sea, but a heavy burden. To this refers that which is written in Exodus 15:10: *You blew with your wind, the Sea covered them; they sank as lead in the mighty waters.* Revelation 18:21; Job 7:21. When God pardons sins and casts them behind his back into the depths of the Sea, then the sins are like lead; they can never come up again to condemn a righteous person.

3. Forgiveness of sin is expressed in the Scripture by "blotting out." Acts 3, verse 19. <note>original: "Hand. 3. vers 19"</note> *Repent therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out,* etc. Isaiah 43:25. *I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.* This is a metaphor <term>overspraak|metaphor or figure of speech</term> taken from men; when someone is unable to pay his debt, the Creditor tears the debt-bond <note>original: "Handschrift," referring to a handwritten legal obligation or "chirographon"</note> into pieces and blots

<column-break/>

it out, so that it may not stand against that person in Court. Likewise, the Lord cancels the debt-bond and tears it to pieces, so that neither sin nor the Devil shall have any legal process to condemn those people.

4. Forgiveness of sin is expressed in the Scripture by the discharging and releasing from iniquity. Job 10:14. *If I sin, then you mark me, and you will not acquit me of my iniquity.* Acquittal <term>ontslaninge|acquittal or release</term> is an end of the legal suit, giving you freedom and an open entrance to the Court. The Lord, in the forgiveness of sins, gives the person a free entrance, so that no Proceeding from Heaven shall come against him.

5. Forgiveness of sin is named in the Scripture a "covering" of sin. Psalm 32:1. *Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.* Beloved, if the forgiveness of sins consisted in the total removal of sins from a person, they would never be hidden within us; but now it consists in the covering of sin. God wishes to shelter the sin so that the fierceness of his wrath and the eyes of his anger shall not see it unto condemnation. It is the same word that signifies a garment, *Kefouj*. <note>A transliteration of the Hebrew *Kaphuy* (covered), related to *Kippur* (atonement/covering).</note> Genesis 3:21; Revelation 3:18. If a man had a blemish or a sore on his body, his garment would cover it so that other people do not see it. Beloved, God covers sins as with a garment—namely, with the long Robe of Christ’s Righteousness. Sin is covered by the Righteousness of Jesus Christ.

6. Forgiveness of sin is expressed in the Scripture by the washing and cleansing of sin. Psalm 51:9. *Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.* That is to be understood as: justification <term>rechtvaerdigmakinge|the legal act of God declaring a sinner righteous</term> and forgiveness of sins sets a person before God clean, pure, and without spot. However defiled you are in respect to your sanctification <term>heyligmakinge|the ongoing process of becoming holy</term>, nonetheless you have no defect in respect to your Justification.

7. It is expressed by the "not-remembering" of sin. Jeremiah 31:34. *For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.* This is compared to the escaped goat <note>The Scapegoat or "Azazel" from Leviticus 16.</note> which bore the sins of the people upon its head and brought them into the land of forgetfulness. Thus, the Lord remembers all things, but God is graciously said not to remember the sins in his people when he does not remember them to their condemnation: *I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sins no more.*

8. Forgiveness of sin is expressed in the Scripture by the "non-imputation" of sin. Romans 4:8. *Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.* The word is taken from Merchants, who give a friend money without taking care to record it in the book or not, not charging it to them. God will not impute the sin, nor note it down to their burden. If there are sins, he does not count them. Through these names, it is exceedingly clarified and given to be understood what the forgiveness of sins is.

In the next place, it is to be investigated in how many ways and times sins are forgiven.

### ->The Saints are Bound<-

Firstly, in respect of God’s decree; and so sins are forgiven even before the world began, because God intended to deliver the elect: that for such a number of people, their sins would be forgiven. Thus, Christ is the Lamb slain before the world. <note>A reference to Revelation 13:8, suggesting that in God's eternal plan, the sacrifice was already accomplished.</note>

Secondly, sins are said to be forgiven when the Lord makes the forgiveness of sins manifest.

Thirdly, and most importantly, sins are said to be forgiven when the eternal guilt and damnation of the sin are taken away—when God wipes out the debt of the sin. This is properly what the forgiveness of sin is.

In the third place, it should be noted what is taken away in the sin when God forgives it; and so three things are to be noted.

1. The stain and blot of the sin cannot be taken away through forgiveness; the sin remains sin, even though it is forgiven, for forgiveness cannot entirely undo the sin itself. <note>The author distinguishes between the act of sin (which happened in history) and its legal consequences.</note>

2. The merit of the sin must be noted; it deserves damnation and the wrath of God, even though it is reconciled; this [desert] is not taken away.

3. The ordering and arrangement of a sinner toward eternal punishment must be noted: And this is fully taken away through the reconciliation. When God grants forgiveness of sins, he takes away all obligation to vengeance, death, hell, and damnation. And this is properly the nature of the forgiveness of sin: it is a gracious and free act of God, by which he acquits a sinner of eternal guilt and punishment. He pardons them, though he may truly still discipline them, but not eternally. And thus much for the first part.

Now follows the second part: what kind of confession of sins a person must have, so that the forgiveness of sins will necessarily accompany it—*I confessed, and you forgave.*

I answer in general: not all confession brings with it the forgiveness of sin. Saul confessed his sin, yet God did not take it away, but rather took away his kingdom. The confession that necessarily brings the forgiveness of sin with it has these five conditions.

<margin>Psalm 32:2</margin>
First, a free and sensible confession; not one forced by violence, not a withholding, but a free speaking out. Of this free and sensible confession, the proverb is to be understood: *Psalm 32:2. Blessed is the man unto whom the Lord imputes not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile.* Guile here is not to be taken merely as hypocrisy, but as a rotten, sinful withholding of the sin, when a person does not want to freely and openly confess their sins to God. David wanted to completely and openly confess his sins to God. That confession which is free and done with understanding has the forgiveness of sins attached to it, and not that which only comes from the tongue or is brought forth by force; these are not justified thereby.

<margin>Psalm 38:18</margin>
Secondly, the confession that is accompanied by the forgiveness of sins is a penitent confession, having a sorrow and contrition of heart with it. *Psalm 38:18. For I will declare my iniquity; I will be sorry for my*

<column-break/>

sins. True confession has more of a complaining than a joyful voice; it brings more sorrow and pain to the heart than joy. The instructions that God gave to the leper in the Law, regarding how he should be cleansed of his leprosy, are found in <margin>Leviticus 13:4, 5</margin> *Leviticus 13:4, 5.* Furthermore, the clothes of the leper in whom the plague is shall be torn, and his head shall be bare, and he shall cover his upper lip; moreover, he shall cry, "Unclean, unclean." *Note that he had to cry out twice, "I am unclean, I am unclean." That was his confession, and that he had to do before he could be cleansed.* He had to do two things primarily: he had to tear his clothes, which showed there had to be a brokenness of heart—sorrow of heart joined with the confession of sins. He had to cover his lip, which means there had to be shame along with the sorrow, showing that we have within us a leprosy of sin. The calling out, "I am unclean, I am unclean," is not enough; there must be a stirring of the heart and a shaming of the face. This must go together with this confession if it is to have the forgiveness of sins with it.

<margin>Proverbs 28:13</margin>
Thirdly, there is yet another confession that carries the forgiveness of sins with it, and that is a voluntary forsaking of the sins we have confessed. To confess sins and yet have a rebellious spirit, intending to commit them again, is not a right confession. *Proverbs 28:13. He that covers his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy.* Confession of sin must be joined together with a forsaking of the same if we wish to obtain mercy. One writer <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux</note> calls confession a spiritual vomiting: <margin>Original Latin: Spiritualis vomitus. Bernard.</margin> you know that a person who <gloss>spiritual vomiting</gloss> <unclear>is</unclear> overloaded in his stomach, he willingly wants to be relieved of it because it goes against his nature. So it is with one who makes confession; he thrusts and vomits out the sins upon his conscience, as being a burden that overloads him. Such a confession has the forgiveness of sins with it.

<margin>Psalm 39:1</margin>
Fourthly, the confession that carries the forgiveness of sins with it is joined with a holy awe and fear of running into the <unclear>filth</unclear> <note>original: "bekeele," likely meaning the defilement or mire of sin.</note> of those sins we have confessed to God. *Psalm 38:18.* [I] confessed: I am troubled because of my sin. I said, "I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue." David’s confession worked in him a holy awe and a holy care to guard himself against that sin which he had confessed. To confess one's sins and then run back into them without hesitation does not have forgiveness joined to it.

<margin>Daniel 9:20</margin>
Fifthly, the confession with which the forgiveness of sins is joined makes the soul awake and earnest in petitions and prayers. David confessed his sin, and his confession made him awake to prayer; likewise Daniel: *Daniel 9:20. And while I was speaking, and praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, etc.* Beloved, when the confession of sin is to prayer as a whetstone is to sharpening—when it sharpens your affections and makes them cut into your hearts in prayer—this is a sure sign that such confession goes together with the for-

### ->To Confess Their Sins<-

...the forgiveness of sins. So much for the second part.

The third part is to show you how this joining together of the confession and the forgiveness of sins can coexist with God’s free grace in the forgiveness of sins. How can this be consistent with the freeness of God's grace? The answer is as follows:

1. If we were to place some cause or merit in the confession of sins that brought about forgiveness—as the <note>original: "Papisten"; a common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics</note> Catholics do—this would overthrow the free grace of God. Although we establish a connection between the two, we do not place any merit or any "working cause" in the confession itself. This is my first answer.

2. Scripture makes a beautiful harmony between these two: the confession of sins and God's free grace in forgiving them. This is seen in two respects: first, in respect of the Command; and second, in respect of the Means. First, regarding the Command: God commands us to confess our sins. Now, no command of God intends for us to do something that would diminish His free grace; therefore, this command certainly cannot obscure the freeness of grace in the doing of it.

Secondly, in respect of the Means, confession is a way to obtain pardon. God is the one who performs the work, and Christ is the merit, but confession of sins is a cause which the <term>Logicians</term> call an <term>indispensable condition</term> <note>original: "causa sine qua non"</note>, without which no forgiveness is obtained.
<margin>Psalm 32:5</margin>
> I confessed, and you forgave.

3. Although no one will be forgiven *because* of their confession, nevertheless no one will have forgiveness of sins *without* it. Acts 3:19:
> Repent, so that your sins may be wiped out.
<margin>
Luke 13:3
Acts 3:19
Acts 2:38
1 John 1:9
</margin>
There is no wiping away of sins without repentance; there must be a sorrow and a weeping for sins before they can be forgiven. And the fact that Christ was "broken" for sin does not mean that you should not also be broken because of it. Although He was a "man of sorrows" throughout His entire life, you must nonetheless learn to be sorrowful and humble because of your sins.

4. This knotting together of the confession of sins and God’s forgiveness is not as if the confession had any part in the merit of forgiveness. Although God forgives sins upon confession, He does not do it *for the sake* of the confession. There is more evil in sin (which is an insult to God) than there is good in the confession. And thus much for those three parts, in which it is shown that God's work in forgiveness and the confession of sins go hand in hand.

Now I shall answer some Objections.

The first Objection is this: Why all these exhortations to the confession of sins and the insistence that there is a necessary joining of a person's confession and God's forgiveness? What need is there for confession? Do not God's eyes run throughout the whole earth? Does He not see the evil and the good, and fully know all the wickednesses under the sun? Why do we need to recount them to God, seeing that He knows all things? This is an objection of the <term>Anabaptists</term> <note>original: "Wederdoopers"</note> against the confession of sins. In answer:

<column-break/>

Denying the premise, we do not perform confession of sin solely because of God's sovereign power, but because God *wills* that we confess our sins. He may command us as an almighty God and say, "Come with ropes around your necks; I will lay you in the dust."

2. We do not perform confession of sins to "teach" God our sins, for God knows all things.

3. We do not perform confession as a way of meriting anything, or to satisfy God’s justice for the wrong done to Him. Rather, even though God knows all our sins, we are still bound to confess them for many powerful reasons, such as:

1. To better examine ourselves; to renew our memory, <term>Conscience</term>, heart, and deeds in the remembrance of our wickednesses. We do not confess to teach God, but to teach ourselves, so that we might see the sin more clearly and let it work upon our Conscience.

2. We perform confession because it stirs us up to more sorrow for sin. Psalm 38:18 <note>Cited in text as verse 19</note>.

3. We confess sin on this ground: that by seeing it through confession, we might obtain mercy from God. Confession of sin to God, says <note>Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic and theologian</note> Bernard, is good for this reason: because the greatness of grace is revealed to us as we see the greatness of our sin. If a person never sees the greatness of their sin, they can never see the greatness of God’s grace in forgiving it.

4. So that you might more highly value the merits of Christ. One who never makes confession does not know what power is in Christ’s blood. A surgeon’s skill does not lie in the healing of a slight and fresh wound, but in the healing of a nearly fatal defect. Beloved, an ordinary <note>original: "playster"; a bandage or medical dressing</note> plaster can heal a fresh wound. If you view your sins as a common wound, you will not thank Christ much, nor highly esteem His merit and blood; but someone who confesses their sin with all its dangerous circumstances highly values the merits of Christ.

5. You must confess your sins because the confession of sin gives great glory to the attributes of God. It gives honor to His Omniscience—you acknowledge that God sees your sins. It gives honor to His Patience—that He spares you while you commit the sin and does not strike you down into hell while you do it. It gives honor to His Justice. Psalm 51, verse 4 <note>Cited in text as verse 6</note>:
> Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done what was evil in your sight; so that you are right in your speaking, and pure in your judgment.
It confesses God’s Mercy, and this is what Paul does in 1 Timothy 1:13:
> Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and an oppressor; but I received mercy, etc.
He confesses his sin so as to magnify the abundance of God’s grace and love.

6. Furthermore, the confession of sins is of great use because it unburdens the troubled and disturbed mind. Hiding guilt brings terror and Hell to the Conscience. It is an innocence <note>Used here in the sense of "relief" or "cleansing"</note> when a person can lay themselves open before God in confession; that eases and settles their mind. Job 32:18, 19, 20: For I am...

# The Saints’ Duty

...though he is a godly man, nevertheless he can lie for a long time without feeling his sin, and without his conscience working any disturbance within him. We have a similar example in the sons of Jacob, who were insensible to their sin in the selling of Joseph until nearly twenty years later, when they were troubled in Egypt.

4. Take this as a comfort: that no godly man’s conscience in this world is always equally active in its duty. Sometimes it performs its duty, and sometimes not; sometimes it is a watchful and waking conscience, and at other times it sleeps and slumbers again. It is not always in its "office"—feeling at one time, but hard at another. We see a striking example in David: his heart melted with the feeling of an evil—namely, the cutting off of Saul’s robe—yet at another time, his conscience was not even disturbed by the murder of Uriah. Again, David’s heart struck him for that "idle glory" in the numbering of the people; it was merely a vainglory that he wanted to take pleasure in a mustered army. Yet at another time, David’s conscience could not be terrified by adultery. O Beloved, a man’s conscience leaps and sleeps; it does not trouble itself for any evil if God leaves him alone.

5. A step further: it is possible that the conscience of a pardoned sinner is so deeply asleep that it departs from its duty for a time, so that he consults with his intellect more to be cautious about the sin than to be moved by it. See an example of this in David: when David committed adultery with Bathsheba, he did not set his conscience to work to rebuke him for his sin, but he set his mind to the work of committing that sin. David had four deliberations to commit that sin.

<margin>2 Sam. 11</margin>
First, he sent for Uriah, Bathsheba’s husband, so that Uriah might come and lie with his wife, and thus cover up his impurity.

Second, he made Uriah drunk, and so he thought that when he was drunk, the drunkenness would bring him a desire to go home.

Third, he had Uriah killed, so that no cry would be heard from his side regarding the violation of his wife.

Fourth, David wanted his occupation with wickedness to go even further, for he had pre-arranged the death of Uriah: notice David’s deliberations. A godly man sets his intellect to the work and seeks to be careful regarding the sin, yet he does not always set his conscience to the work to keep him from sin. Oh, how near to Hell a godly man can go, and yet still be going toward Heaven!

6. Still further, take this for your comfort: it may be that the conscience of a pardoned sinner does not gnaw at him for those sins that would make a <term>Heathen</term> <note>original: "Heyden"; referring to someone outside the Judeo-Christian faith who relies on natural law</note> ashamed through the light of natural conscience. This is clearly seen in the history of Abraham, Genesis 20:9. *And Abimelech called Abraham and said to him: What have you done to us? And in what have I offended you, that you have brought a great sin upon me and upon my kingdom? You have done deeds to me that ought not to be done.* For this deceit, Abraham's conscience did not yet gnaw, nevertheless—

<column-break/>

—nevertheless a Heathen, through the light of nature, rebukes Abraham for this. Abimelech, a Heathen, recounted to Abraham: *you have done deeds to me that ought not to be done.*

And thus I have answered this objection at length, in order to set the troubled and dejected conscience at peace. I have shown six steps by which one can go down into the chambers of death, and yet it is possible that a pardoned sinner can have a conscience that departs from its duty.

Now I think I hear a "late-thinking" <note>likely meaning "presumptuous" or "arrogant" in this context</note> heart say: "If it is as you say, that a pardoned sinner may go so near to Hell and yet come to Heaven; if a godly man adds sin to sin and his conscience does not disturb him, then I hope that my sins are forgiven as well as the best."

Now, if this thought lies in anyone who hears me, I shall open this shell. And so that no one should deceive themselves with false deliberations, believing in their forgiveness, I shall show you that although a godly man may have a conscience that departs from its duty and does not gnaw at him for sin, there is a great distinction in this case between a pardoned and an unpardoned sinner. These distinctions are fivefold.

<margin>Levit. 13:10</margin>
1. Although the conscience of the person whose sins are forgiven sometimes sleeps, nevertheless he will not sin as boldly and unafraid against his conscience as a godless person. You find this in the Scripture, but most profoundly in Leviticus 13:10: *If the priest sees that, behold, there is a white swelling in the skin, which has turned the hair white, and there is quick raw flesh in the swelling, etc.* There are two signs of leprosy: white hair in the swelling, and raw flesh in it. The Hebrew Rabbis understand two things by this.

First, the changing of the hair to white in the swelling: by this, they note the persistence in sin—living from youth to old age in sin until the hairs are white and gray.

Second, there was raw flesh in that swelling: by this, they understand the boldness in a sinner committing sin against a living and waking conscience. Another person might be covered in scabs over his whole body, yet he was not unclean, Verse 13: *And the priest shall consider, and behold, if the leprosy has covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean that has the plague: it is all turned white; he is clean.* However, if someone had raw impurity in his flesh or swelling, he was unclean. Notice that a person may have many sins and yet not be unclean in God’s sight; but if he sins against the weighing, gnawing, and pressing of his conscience, he is unclean.

2. This is also a distinction: although the conscience of one whose sins are forgiven does not gnaw for a time for the sins committed, nevertheless they are not stiff or stubborn in quietly pacifying the conscience as the <term>reprobate</term> <note>those considered rejected by God or destined for damnation</note> do. Godless men have a quiet rest and emptiness of conscience, like Saul, 1 Samuel 16:14: *And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of conscience and repentance, specifically addressing how a godly person’s conscience might "sleep" for a time, but will eventually be awakened by God, unlike the hardened heart of the ungodly.</meta>

# To Confess Their Sins

...an evil spirit from the Lord terrified him. Verse 17: *Then Saul said to his servants, "Find me a man who can play well, and bring him to me."* When an evil spirit terrified him—which was actually his <term>troubled conscience</term> <note>The author interprets Saul's "evil spirit" not just as a demonic presence, but as the psychological weight of guilt</note>—Saul called for music so that it might quiet his disturbed mind.

3. Godly people do not seek out pleasurable company to drown out their guilt. In Mark 6:18, John the Baptist said to Herod, *"It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife."* Verse 21: *And when a convenient day had come, when Herod on his birthday gave a feast for his nobles, high officers, and the chief men of Galilee, etc.* Pious people do not avoid a teacher who rebukes them or speaks of death; but consider Felix in Acts 24:25: *And as he reasoned of righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified and answered, "Go away for now; when I have a convenient time, I will call for you."* He could not endure the <term>quickening</term> <note>The "awakening" or "bringing to life" of the moral sense</note> of his conscience through the ministry. If a person is truly pardoned, even though they have sins, they are glad when a teacher touches and awakens their conscience.

4. A pardoned sinner is not satisfied with a weak and flattering ministry, which *puts pillows under his elbows* <note>A biblical idiom from Ezekiel 13:18 referring to false prophets who offer comfortable lies instead of hard truths</note> and says *peace, peace* when there is no peace. Jeremiah 23:13: *I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria; they prophesied by Baal and led my people Israel astray.* Verse 14: *But in the prophets of Jerusalem, I see a horrible thing; they commit adultery and walk in lies; they strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns back from his wickedness; they are all like Sodom to me, and her inhabitants like Gomorrah.* Chapter 8:11: *For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, "Peace, peace," when there is no peace.*

5. They do not use distractions or worldly immersion to forget the life of their conscience, as Cain did. In Genesis 4, Cain, in order to quiet the agitation of his conscience, wanted to immerse himself so forcefully in the world that he might never hear its voice again. A pardoned sinner does not do this; rather, if his conscience shows him guilt, he prays to God that it may speak directly and attentively to his heart.

6. A godly person does not wallow or persist in sin, because the habit of sinning removes the "watchman" of the conscience. Ephesians 4:19: *Who, being past feeling, have given themselves over to lewdness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.* Ungodly people give themselves over to a habit of sin so that they might have no conscience to trouble them. They are like a <term>blacksmith’s dog</term> <note>A common historical proverb: a dog that sleeps in a forge becomes so used to the noise and sparks that it no longer jumps or wakes up</note> which sleeps through the noise or walks by the smith and is not startled by being struck by sparks; he does not catch fire. So it is with the ungodly: they frequent the workshop of sin, and though the sparks of Hell fly around them, they sleep peacefully and 

<column-break/>

do not wake; but the godly do not make a habit of sin, nor do they sleep in their lusts.

7. Although the conscience of a pardoned sinner might not immediately strike him for his sin, he can be awakened from the sleep of sin much faster and more easily than the ungodly. The look in Jesus’ eyes and the crowing of a rooster made Peter weep—he went out and wept bitterly. A rebuke from the prophet made David cry out, *"Lord, I have sinned."* A seared conscience is not so easily moved; it requires great labor before it will hear the rebuke of the Word before death. Much more effort is required to put the conscience of an ungodly man back into its proper office than that of a godly man.

8. There is also this distinction: although the conscience of a godly man may sleep for a time and not be troubled by sin, it will nevertheless disturb him shortly before his end. No godly person in the world remains under the knowledge of his sin without his conscience eventually unsettling him; it will trouble him before his death. But the ungodly live and die in sin, never having a reprimand or rebuke of conscience. Ahaz was terrified by the oppressions sent by God, yet his conscience never troubled him, for he committed even more wickedness against God.

9. Although the conscience of a pardoned sinner sleeps for a time and does not rebuke him for the sin he committed, when it finally does rebuke him, it guards him from sin more because he has <term>dishonored God</term> than out of fear of Hell or any outward judgments. But the ungodly sleep in their conscience, and if it wakes, it is not because sin is evil or a dishonor to God, but because there is a Hell for sin and because terrible outward judgments are coming. When God breaks men through His judgments, then their conscience works, but they never do so out of a true feeling of the sin itself. Take this comparison: throw but a small stone into the water, and the <term>divers</term> <note>Original: "Duykers," likely referring to water-birds or swimmers</note> are startled; but let it rattle and thunder in the Heavens, and they do not fear. A theologian compares this to the conscience of the ungodly: throw a small stone—some present affliction—at an ungodly man, and that will make him terrified and amazed, and trouble his conscience. But let God thunder from Heaven; let the Lord reveal all the depths of His spiritual judgments against sin—how evil sin is, how it dishonors God, and how it brings the soul into danger—and all this thundering from Heaven cannot move him.

And thus I have hastily run through the answers to these three objections, to come to the aid of a dejected conscience, and I end this teaching here.

sins.
</margin>

> *I acknowledged, and you forgave me.* "Forgave," says <note>original: "Musculus"</note> Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), a prominent Reformed theologian</note>, is a word of favor or grace, not of merit. *You forgave:* this shows that the forgiveness of sin is not given as a debt owed, but as a free gift. *You forgave:* What? *The iniquity of my sin.*

# The Saints are Bound to Believe

...sin. The interpreters have various opinions about these words: what it means *when God is said to forgive the iniquity of the sin.* I shall bring them down to these two: Some understand by "iniquity" the punishment of the sin: "I confess my sins, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin." That is: You forgave the punishment of my sin. The reason for this interpretation is because in the Hebrew language the same word *Avon* <note>The Hebrew word *ʿāwōn* carries a dual meaning of both the perversity of the act and the resulting guilt or punishment</note>, which signifies iniquity, also signifies punishment. And therefore they understand by the iniquity of the sin, the punishment of the sin. But other interpreters go directly against this interpretation, because the word is used more often for the sin itself. Furthermore, the entire purpose of that Psalm does not look toward the forgiveness of outward punishment, but toward the forgiveness of the sin in regard to that eternal guilt.

Thirdly, there stands in the text *Selah* <note>A Hebrew musical or liturgical term often marking a pause for reflection or emphasis</note>, which is a sign of wonder, added to this statement, *You forgave, etc.* Truly, it would be no wonder for God to pass by an eternal punishment for those whose sins are never forgiven. What is it then, when it is said here that God forgives the iniquity of the sin? I answer: By the "iniquity of the sin" is understood that God, out of His free grace, not only simply forgives the sin, but also the "iniquity of the failure"—all the malice of the sin, all the terrifying and aggravating circumstances that might in any way enlarge it.

A Teacher, dealing with this Psalm, has this manner of speaking: "To forgive the iniquity of the sins may teach us that there was no light debt to be pardoned; it was the sin, and it was the iniquity of the sin—sin upon sin, the sin enlarged by harmful circumstances. Nevertheless, see the great mercy of God: *You forgave the iniquity of my sin.*" Thus much for the interpretation of the words.

The doctrine is this: That this is the richness of God’s forgiving grace, that He forgives His people not only sin in general, but also their great sins—those which are surrounded by many aggravating and loudly-crying circumstances: *You forgave the iniquity of my sin.* In the handling of this point, I shall keep this order:

First, I shall prove this point by an urging of particular examples, and the application of this through seven uses. This is a doctrine full of comfort. Truly, I know not such a text in the entire Bible that speaks more of God’s grace in the forgiveness of aggravated sins, and so clearly, as this text.

<margin>
God forgives not only small, but also great sins.
</margin>

First and foremost, I shall give you an urging of examples, showing that God does not only forgive His people small sins; but He, out of the richness of His grace, also forgives those sins which are called "The Iniquity of the Sin": sin surrounded by many hateful, aggravating circumstances. To prove this, take the example of David, who spoke these words; and Peter, Paul, and many others who sinned against the conviction of their conscience and against the mercy of God—these have had their sins forgiven.

<column-break/>

1. I begin with David, because this example is nearest to us. If you wish to consider David’s sin—the sin of adultery, with all its secret evils—you shall find many aggravating and terrifying circumstances; and yet, notwithstanding all this, his sins were forgiven him.

The first circumstance that aggravates David’s sin consists in the quality and nature of that sin. What sin was it? It was the sin of Adultery. Now, of all sins, adultery is one of the heaviest. There are seven circumstances to consider:

1. He who commits adultery sins against his own body.

2. He sins against the body of the woman with whom he commits that impurity.

3. It is a wrong against his own wife.

4. It is a wrong against the husband of the adulteress.

5. It is a wrong against that child who is unlawfully born in adultery, because of the shame that is continually upon him. And therefore, when David fell into this sin, it was a great sin, aggravating David's sin.

Secondly, if you consider the dignity and quality of David's person who committed this sin, he was a King.
<margin>
*The more notable the person, the more conspicuous the crime is held to be when committed through such a vice.* <note>original Latin: "Commissus vitio tanto conspectius crimen major quo peccat habetur." A common moral maxim suggesting that the status of the sinner increases the gravity of the sin</note>
</margin>
Now, the greater the person is who sins, the greater is the sin he commits (2 Samuel 12:8-9).

The third thing that enlarged his sin was this: that he began it after he had received a great measure of grace from God, as Nathan recounted to him (2 Samuel 12:8).

Fourthly, David had a wife—indeed, many wives—for himself, and therefore his sin was all the greater. For (said Nathan) there was a poor man who had no more than one single little ewe lamb that he had bought; and a rich man, who had very many sheep and cattle, killed the lamb of the poor man. His meaning was that David had committed adultery with the wife of a man who had only one, while he himself had many wives of his own.

Fifthly, this aggravates David’s sin: that he committed it while his fighting men were in the field; which was enough to bring God’s wrath not so much over the enemies as over his own army.

Sixthly, it was a great wrong to such a loyal-hearted captain of his army as Uriah was.

Seventhly, which is the most significant of all: in the commission of this sin, he committed six heavy sins, from which he could have kept himself if he had guarded against adultery.

1. He sent for Uriah, Bathsheba’s husband, a captain of his army, when it was ready for the assault; this brought danger to the entire army.

2. The text says that David made Uriah drunk, thinking that he would thereby go in to his wife.

3. He used means to make Uriah the father of his bastard child, whom he had fathered in unchastity.

4. When this would not succeed, he deliberated how he might kill Uriah.

5. David sends a letter by Uriah, in which...

It uses the detailed moral failures of King David—specifically his adultery and the subsequent betrayal of Uriah—to illustrate how God pardons great offenses.</summary>

### the forgiveness of their Sins.

...in Uriah, who unknowingly was the messenger of his own death. <note>This refers to King David sending a letter with Uriah to the battlefield, which contained the order for Uriah's own certain death.</note>

6. When Uriah was dead, the Text says <margin>2 Samuel 11:25</margin> that David said, *The sword devours one as well as another.* He laid Uriah's death solely upon God’s providence, even though he himself had written how he should perish. Oh! where was David's conscience, which, in order to commit one sin, fell into all of these? You consider it a heavy aggravation of sin when servants, in order to commit one evil, perform many wicked acts: this unrighteousness was in David; he began one sin and fell into many.

The eighth aggravation, which enlarged David’s sin, was this: that he wished to marry Uriah's wife; first killing the husband, and then marrying his wife.

The ninth and final aggravation was that David filled up the measure of his sins: he persisted in this sin, with all these enlargements, for nine months, without repentance or any stirring of his conscience. I do not say that these were his "pillows" in sin <note>The author uses "pillows" to mean excuses that allow a conscience to sleep or feel comfortable while in a state of sin.</note>; I only relate this for the sake of a troubled conscience—that although the sins are great and heavy, surrounded by many terrifying and evil circumstances, God forgives them as such. And therefore, well may David say, *The Lord forgave the iniquity of my sin*; not only the sin, but the iniquity of the sin.

2. The second Example is that of Peter. You all know the story, but perhaps not the circumstances of Peter's sin, nor how great it was. In Peter’s sin:

<margin>Matthew 26:33, 34</margin>
<margin>Luke 22:34</margin>
<margin>John 13:37, 38</margin>
First, note that Peter denied Christ, having made a confession that he would cling to Him more than the other eleven disciples. When Christ said to them, *You shall all be offended because of me this night*, Peter said, *Though they all forsake you, yet will I never do so*; yet no one but Judas and he denied Him in such a shameful manner. This was a great aggravation.

Secondly, it is remarkable that Peter denied being Peter himself, John 18:25. *And Simon Peter stood and warmed himself. They said therefore unto him, Art not thou also one of his disciples? He denied it, and said, I am not.*

Thirdly, he said that he did not know Jesus Christ. What a terrifying crime was that, that he dared to say such a thing? Luke 22:57: *But he denied him, saying, Woman, I know him not.*

Fourthly, he denied Christ not only before a servant girl, but the Text says that he did so before all the people: there was a public denial of Christ. Matthew 26:69, 70: *And Peter sat without in the palace: and a damsel came unto him, saying, Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee. But he denied before them all, saying, I know not what thou sayest.*

Fifthly, and another servant girl seeing him, said also, *You are one of them*: But Peter said, *Man, I am not, I know him not,* Luke 22:58.

Sixthly, he not only denied Him, but Matthew says, *He denied Him with an oath,* Matthew 26 verse 72. *And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man*

<column-break/>

*not.* To swear to a lie is detestable.

Seventhly, it is to be noted that for the third time, about an hour later, another came who confirmed the same about Peter, saying, *Of a truth this fellow also was with him*; and Peter spoke, *I know not the man,* Luke 22:59-60.

Eighthly, this is not all; Peter did not only speak foolishly or swear to a lie, but he cursed himself if he knew Jesus Christ: the Text says, *He began to curse and to swear,* Mark 14:71. *And he began to curse himself and to swear, I know not this man of whom ye speak.* He desired that terrifying judgments should come upon him if he knew Jesus Christ. Some interpreters believe that he cursed not only himself, but also Christ. <note>original: "Christus heeft vervloeckt"</note> So that the people would not think he cared for Him, he used certain heavy curses upon the Savior. Oh! forgiving grace can also be obtained by such a great sinner as this one was.

3. A third Example was in Paul: you shall see many aggravating circumstances that enlarge and weigh down his sin. Acts 26:9, 10, 11:
> I verily thought with myself, that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Which thing I also did in Jerusalem: and many of the saints did I shut up in prison, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death, I gave my voice against them. And I punished them oft in every synagogue, and compelled them to blaspheme; and being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them even unto strange cities.

There are no fewer than ten aggravating circumstances that enlarged Paul's sins.

1. This weighed down and enlarged his sin, if you consider the persons he wronged; they were no ordinary men, but Christ's Saints: *He shut the Saints in prison.*

2. If you consider the number whom he offended: they were *many of the Saints.*

3. If you consider the nature of the wrong: *He shut them in prison.*

4. If you consider his severity against them: *Having received authority from the Chief Priests.*

5. If you consider the place where it was: *In Jerusalem.* It was that place where Paul ought to have learned better things, because the Apostles were there, preaching the doctrine of Christ and Christianity.

6. If you consider the extent of Paul's malice; he says, *And when they were put to death, I gave my voice against them.* His voice was against the Christians to kill them.

7. Paul's rage went against their souls as well as their bodies; for (he says) *I compelled them to blaspheme.* He labored to damn their souls as well as to destroy their bodies.

8. He says, *I was exceedingly mad against them.* Always and to an extreme degree was he raging against them.

9. He pursued them from house to house: *I persecuted them even unto strange cities.*

It breaks down Peter's multiple denials and Paul's violent persecution of early Christians into specific points of guilt.</summary>

# The Saints are bound to believe

10. The last and worst thing was that he intended, by his oppression, to do honor to **Jesus Christ**: why did **Paul** do this to the Saints? He says, *I truly thought within myself, that I ought to do many things contrary to the Name of* **Jesus** *of* **Nazareth**. That was the reason why he did it; nonetheless **Paul** obtained forgiveness for all of this; for he says, even while magnifying his sin, <margin>1 Tim. 1:11, 12, 13</margin> *According to the glorious Gospel of the blessed* **God**, *which was committed to my trust. And I thank him who hath enabled me, namely* **Christ Jesus** *our Lord, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry: Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and an injurious person: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in my unbelief.* Thus I have given you an instructional indication from my teaching by way of examples; I have been more expansive here because I know that smitten consciences <note>A "smitten" or "dejected" conscience refers to a person feeling overwhelmed by the guilt of their past actions.</note> and troubled minds enlarge and weigh down their own sins; but can you weigh them down more heavily than **David**, **Peter**, or **Paul** did? Nonetheless, see—these Sinners, even these "aggravating" sinners, received forgiveness through **Jesus Christ**.

Now I come to the applications: there may be a congregation such as this one, which **God** may allow to be unclean—either before or after conversion—like **David**; to deny **Christ**, like **Peter**; to swear it off with an oath: Yes (even if we might swear falsely), to persecute the Saints like **Paul**; nonetheless we have these comforts.

1. Oh, know this for your comfort! Oh, you comfortless heart, let the sins be great, yet the mercies of **God** are much greater. A Teacher once said, *Lord, my sins are great, but your graces are even greater*; Beloved, I may say to you, though your sins be great, nonetheless the mercies of **God** are greater than your sins, and you cannot have as many circumstances that enlarge your sins as there are considerations in **God** to enlarge His own graces. Read what He says of Himself, <margin>**Isaiah** 44 verse 22</margin> *I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and, as a cloud, thy sins: return unto me; for I have redeemed thee.* Suppose your sins were not just like a small mist, but like a great cloud; **God** says, *I blot out*, not only your small sins, but also your great transgressions, even if they were like a cloud. Great sins as well as small are covered by the mercy of **God**. The Sea can just as easily cover high rocky crags as small pebbles; it flows over high mountains as well as low valleys. **God’s** grace is like an Ocean, which covers great wickednesses just as well as small stumbles. The Sun in the Heaven can make the greatest fog disappear just as well as the smallest mist: great sins as well as small are forgiven by an infinite mercy. It is worthy of your notice that **Moses** says of the Mercy Seat <note>The Mercy Seat was the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant; the author uses it as a symbol of grace covering the Law.</note>, it covered the entire Ark in which the Law was kept. Note this, says a theologian: though you were a man or woman who had broken the entire Law—not just one commandment, but all the commandments—yet

<column-break/>

the mercy seat covers all the commandments, to teach you that the graces and mercies of **God** pardon the greatest violations of the Law; therefore everything that was in the Ark, including the Law, was covered by the Mercy Seat.

2. Take this for your comfort, Oh you smitten Conscience; when you are in a corner, alone with **God** and your own Soul, enlarging your sins and thinking to yourself, *no one’s sins are heavier than mine*, Oh take this then for your comfort: that your sins are never so great but that the satisfactions <term>satisfactions<note>The theological concept that Christ's death "satisfied" or paid the legal debt of human sin to God.</note></term> and merits of **Christ** are even greater. *The blood of* **Jesus Christ** (says the Apostle) *cleanseth us from all sin*; the Red Sea swallowed up **Pharaoh** with all his horses as quickly as a single man; the Red Sea of **Christ’s** blood can just as easily cast down the strong horses and great multitudes of sins as it can small desires and failings. Though you have never shed enough tears over your sins, nonetheless **Christ** does not need to shed any more blood to blot out your sins for your redemption, for He has saved those who would go to **God** through Him. The Apostle triumphs in <margin>**Rom.** 5:15, 16, 17</margin> in this manner: that there is not as much evil in sin to condemn us as there are gifts of grace in **Christ** to save us, because sin is the debt of a Creature, and **Christ’s** satisfaction is the satisfaction of a **God**: sin is the sin of a finite Creature, but **Christ’s** suffering is the suffering of an infinite Mediator.

3. This is comforting for you who are smitten in your Conscience, who have committed great and heavy sins, that **Christ** nonetheless has also blotted out the very highest and most shameful sins committed before your conversion. Suppose you had been a publicly infamous Creature, nonetheless **Christ** has taken away all the dishonor and shame of the sin when He justified you, sanctifying your nature. It is noteworthy that **Mary Magdalene** was a public harlot before her conversion; everyone knew her as a common harlot. She was a Woman who was a great Sinner; meaning, she was an infamous and well-known harlot. What did **Christ** do when He converted this woman? <margin>**Luke** 7:47</margin> *Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much.* **Christ** washed away the dishonesty of her evil, whorish life. It is worthy to note that Women are mentioned here in the genealogy of **Christ**. What kind of Women were they? They were infamous; the best of them had fallen into great scandal—it was **Tamar**, **Rahab**, **Ruth**, and **Bathsheba**; no others are mentioned but these. To begin with **Tamar**, she committed unchastity with her Brother <note>The Dutch text says "Brother" (Broeder), though the biblical account in Genesis 38 involves her father-in-law, Judah. The author likely uses "brother" in the sense of a kinsman or is making a historical slip.</note>, an infamous Woman, as you can read in the history. <margin>**Gen.** 38:18</margin> *And he said, What pledge shall I give thee? And she said, Thy signet, and thy bracelets, and thy staff that is in thine hand. And he gave it her, and she conceived by him.* Of **Rahab**, a common harlot, you read, <margin>**Hebr.** 11 verse 31</margin> *By faith the harlot* **Rahab** *perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.* <margin>**Matthew** 1 verse 5</margin> *And* **Salmon** *begat* **Boaz** *of* **Rahab**, etc.

<summary>This page offers pastoral comfort to people overwhelmed by guilt, arguing that God's infinite mercy and Christ's sacrifice far outweigh even the most "infamous" or "aggravated" sins. The author cites the presence of women with scandalous pasts in Christ’s own genealogy as proof of God's willingness to redeem and honor the repentant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of God's grace in forgiving "heavy" or scandalous sins by examining the genealogy of Jesus, specifically focusing on the women mentioned there, before transitioning to a warning about the danger of "small" sins.</meta>

# Forgiveness of their sins.

The third woman mentioned in the **Genealogy** is **Ruth**; what was she? She was not as infamous as the others; nonetheless, she committed a great scandal. She was descended from **Moab**, whom **Lot** had fathered by his own daughter (Genesis 19:36–37). *And both the daughters of Lot were with child by their father. And the firstborn bore a son, and called his name Moab.* Regarding the person of **Ruth**, she was a good woman; but as all the theologians remark about her, she performed a deed that had the appearance of evil. What did she do? Read the history in the third chapter of **Ruth**, beginning with the fifth verse, etc. It says there that she came to **Boaz** alone in the middle of the night: an infamous deed, that a woman should come in the middle of the night to a man lying alone. Moreover, she did not just come to him, but went and lay down by him. Yet it is true that the Scripture explains something of this in the following 14th verse: *She lay at his feet until the morning; and she rose up before one could recognize another.* There was no folly or evil, yet it was a great shame for a woman to lie by a man in such a way, and it was to be feared that **Boaz** likewise would have been scandalized by this. And yet this woman is remembered in the **Genealogy of Christ**. The fourth woman is **Bathsheba**; she committed adultery with **David**. What is the mystery in this? Truly, all interpreters give this explanation: only four women are named in the **Genealogy** <note>Matthew 1:1-17 mentions Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba ("her that had been the wife of Urias"). Usually, biblical genealogies only listed men; including these specific women—some with troubled pasts—was seen as a sign of Christ's mission to sinners.</note>; some of them are more, others less, "branded" by their past. And **Christ** also came from these four, and for their benefit—to take away the infamous and shameful sins that you might have committed before your conversion. He will take away your disgrace, just as He did for these women, placing them in His own **Genealogy**.

This point having been handled—that the richness of **God's** forgiving grace is such that it wipes out the great and heavy sins in His people—now some might misuse this teaching and "suck poison from these flowers." <note>This is a traditional metaphor warning readers not to take God's mercy as an excuse to keep sinning.</note> I shall labor to frighten these presumptuous people away from their opinions and sins; therefore, my applications shall be directed to two sorts of people.

<margin>1. Observations regarding small sins.</margin>
First, this shall serve as instruction for modest and civil people who say: "Since **God** forgives great sins, burdened with shameful and heavy circumstances, as the sins of **David**, **Peter**, and **Paul** were, then I have great hope of forgiveness; my sins are but ordinary infractions. Therefore, I hope they are forgiven me, since they have never been 'crying' <note>A "crying sin" is a theological term for sins so grave they are said to cry out to heaven for vengeance, like murder or oppression.</note> or great sins."

Note first, that **God** has often shown as much displeasure against minor and small sins as against heavy and great transgressions; you have several examples of this.

First, of the sluggishness of **Moses** in circumcising his son. One might think that neglecting the circumcision of a child by a man who had so many affairs <note>The word "affairen" here refers to Moses' heavy responsibilities in leading the people and dealing with Pharaoh.</note> might provide some ex-

<column-break/>

cuse for him; nevertheless, for neglecting the same after the eighth day, the **Lord** sought to kill him (Exodus 4:24): *And it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the Lord met him, and sought to kill him.* And at another time the **Psalmist** relates to us that **Moses** spoke unadvisedly in the desert—only a hasty word—and what came of that sin? The **Lord** would not suffer **Moses** to enter into the land of **Canaan**.

Another example we have in **Uzzah**. One might think it was a small matter that **Uzzah** wanted to support the falling **Ark** with his hand; it was out of a good intention, so that the **Ark** would not fall. Nonetheless, you know how the hand of **God** struck **Uzzah** because of this.

Likewise of **David**: you will think it is surely a small matter for a **King** to count his people. Nonetheless, you know how many thousands **God** punished with the plague because of that sin. So then, Beloved, even if you have not committed any great and outstanding godlessness, you are nonetheless as guilty before **God** for small sins as for large ones; because sin, however small or great it is before **God**, displeases Him; and small sins displease Him just as much as large ones.

Secondly, although great sins bring a great blemish of shame, nonetheless small hidden sins bring a great debt from **God** upon those who commit them.

<margin>Infamies can be of greater fault even in the regenerate. <note>original Latin: "Infamiæ possunt esse majoris culpæ & renatus." Here, the author suggests that even "small" lapses in a believer are serious.</note></margin>
Beloved, the sin of the **Angels** was but a small, spiritual, and single sin—only in thought and not in deed—nonetheless you know that **God** cast the **Angels** out of **Heaven** for that sin. Truly, great sins carry a great violation of the **Name**, but small sins also carry a great guilt.

Thirdly, it is to be noted that small and minor sins can be so burdened and surrounded by such circumstances that they become great. Take two examples: in the sin of **Adam** and of **David**.

First, in **Adam’s** sin: you will consider it a small fault to eat an apple or some other fruit; nonetheless, the taking and eating of that forbidden fruit carried with it so many circumstances which made it a great and terrible sin. For:

First, if you consider **Adam's** state: he was not as we are, but he was a perfect and upright creature. And it is a greater evil for a perfect creature to sin than for us who are imperfect.

Secondly, note the place where **Adam** was: it was a **Paradise**, and yet he sinned there.

Thirdly, note the universality of his person: he did not sin only for himself, but in him we have all sinned. For a private person to sin is evil; but for a public person, representing other people, his sin is the sin of others. <note>This refers to the doctrine of Original Sin, where Adam acts as the "federal head" or representative of all humanity.</note>

Fourthly, how many enlargements and aggravations were there in **Adam's** sin: primarily six:

1. There was unbelief in his sin, doubting what **God** had said: *Surely you shall die the death.*
