### The Saints are Bound to Believe

A King of France <note>original: "Frankryk"; the text likely refers to a specific anecdote about a French monarch</note>, whenever he committed any evil against his conscience, would take up a crucifix and cry out to God for mercy for the evil he had done; many people do the same / if they can only cry out to God for mercy with common phrases / they think they have sufficiently satisfied divine justice <term>divine justice: the theological concept that sin creates a debt that must be paid to God's law</term>. And thus, I have concluded the second branch of this application / in six particular points.

The third and last branch / shall be for the comfort of a stricken conscience / terrified by the weight of its sins / and doubting its forgiveness. Five comforts I shall set down here.

First, take this for your comfort / that penance and conversion <note>original: "boete ende bekeeringe"</note> before God / erases and brings to nothing the ugliness and shame of a human being: though you may have been an openly dishonorable creature, nevertheless / conversion makes you into a **new creature** <note>original: "nieuwe Creature"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 5:17</note>.

Second, this also comforts you / that Jesus Christ reveals His love more / to those people who have fallen into great and gross sins / after their conversion / than to others in this world; this is notable in Peter. Peter sinned more than all the other Apostles / except for Judas, who was a reprobate <term>reprobate: someone rejected by God and beyond salvation</term>; afterwards / Peter humbled himself / and converted from his denial / and Christ showed more love to Peter than to all the other disciples.

1. Christ appeared to Peter after His resurrection / before He appeared to anyone else / as Paul tells us, 1 Cor. 15:5. *And that he was seen by Cephas <note>Cephas is the Aramaic name for Peter</note>, then by the twelve.* There was the love of Christ for Peter; he who had denied Him / and had wept over it / had to see Him first.

2. When Christ was risen from the dead / He sent a special message to Peter: *Go your way, tell his disciples and Peter that he is risen,* Mark 16:7. Peter was weeping and mourning / because he had denied his Lord and Master / and Christ says / *Go, and tell Peter that I am risen.*

3. Christ had more conversation with Peter after His resurrection / than with all His other disciples / John 21. And thus you see / that Christ revealed His love more / to this sinner / after he had converted / than to anyone else. It was also thus with Mary Magdalene after her conversion / what expressions of love did Christ show to her? He cast seven devils out of her / Luke 8:2. He appeared to her first / she was the first who saw Him after His resurrection / Mark 16:9. Furthermore / Christ commands that wherever the Gospel shall be preached / her praise shall be spoken of / Mark 26:13 <note>The text cites Mark 26, but the quote is from Matthew 26:13; Mark only has 16 chapters</note>. *Truly I say to you, wherever the Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also be spoken of what she has done, in memory of her.* See / what a great honor this was for Mary Magdalene? Thus it appears / that God gives those persons who have sinned most and most heavily / after they are converted / the greatest and most exceptional grounds for comfort.

Third, take this for your comfort; that it is not the greatness of your committed sin / but only the hardness /

<column-break/>

and insensitivity of your own heart / which can keep you / from obtaining forgiveness. This, as the theologians say in general / is the reason for that passage / *All sins and blasphemies shall be forgiven, but whoever shall blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come.* It is not because there are no more merits in Christ / than there is debt in the sin: but because that person cannot or will not convert from the sin; therefore the sins cannot be forgiven / because he cannot repent. Though the sin was a blasphemy / yet this does not exclude conversion. Not the greatness of the sin / but the hardness / and immovability of the heart can prevent your forgiveness. When Peter preached to the Jews / who had crucified the Son of God / he said / *Repent, and your sins shall be wiped out.* Oh, what sins could be greater / than to have a hand in the shedding of the blood of Christ? Yet only do penance, and your sins shall be done away with. It is not for a lack of God's mercy / or for a lack of Christ's merits / that many people’s sins are not forgiven: but for a lack of their own conversion.

Fourth, that no great sins / committed by a justified person / can keep the doer from forgiveness; a rule among the Scholastic teachers <term>Scholastic teachers: medieval and early modern academics who used logic to explain Christian doctrine</term>: the work of God cannot be brought to nothing by a human being; Election is a work of God / so also is Redemption / likewise Justification / which cannot be annihilated by any work of man; therefore if God has chosen, redeemed, justified, and pardoned you / the impulses toward great evils / cannot keep you from forgiveness; it is true / sins can indeed rob the doer of comfort for a time / they can indeed lay a burden on the conscience; but they cannot hold back the graces and the mercies of God. And in this you have a great and exceptional comfort.

Fifth, take this for your comfort / though you have fallen into great and heavy debt / nevertheless the goodness and mercy of God is such / that He knows how to work good out of the fall into sin: I do not recount this so that one might do evil / so that good may come of it; Oh, it is God / who allows the fall of man for His own good: there is a threefold good / which God works out / when they sin; God does not only do good to His people through their afflictions / but He also does good through their sins.

1. God sometimes lets a godly person fall into sin / to diminish the pride <note>original: "hoberdye"; an archaic Dutch term for haughtiness or pride</note> of his heart; this is seen in many people; God often allows strong lusts to come against strong gifts of grace / in order to diminish in us more and more the pride of the spirit; therefore Paul says, *I have a messenger of Satan <note>referring to the 'thorn in the flesh' in 2 Corinthians 12:7</note>, so that I should not exalt myself above measure.* God / to preserve us from pride / allows afflictions and temptations to come over us / and so He works good. Augustine says / *I am not afraid to say, that it is sometimes profitable for a good man to fall into sin.*

# The Forgiveness of their Sins

2. It prevents many other sins: It is God's mercy to let a person undergo one sorrow, in order to preserve them from many other sorrows. God sometimes allows a person to fall into sin, so that this very sin might guard them against many others.

3. Falling into sin sometimes renews the work of conversion. The Lord sometimes lets a person sleep, so that / having been awakened / he might be made all the more humble, seeing the bitterness and fruit of sin. This, then, is God’s goodness toward a sinner: that even when they fall into sin, the Lord nonetheless renews the work of conversion within them and grants greater humility to their heart.

Now / to end this matter / there are seven **cases of conscience** <term>cases of conscience: specific ethical or spiritual problems that a believer might struggle with, requiring a theological "untangling"</term> in this teaching that are necessary to resolve.

First / **Can God forgive a person's sins without that person knowing it?** *David's* sins were forgiven / and he knew it: *I acknowledged my sins, and you forgave them.* But can a person’s sins be forgiven, and yet they do not know it?

**Answer:** Yes / a person’s sins can be forgiven while they remain unaware of it. Although *David* knew of his forgiveness at this time / he did not know it at another time. *Psalm 51:14:* **Restore to me the joy of your salvation.** God broke *David’s* bones because of his adultery / and *David* shed rivers of tears / for the enjoyment of a single drop of joy. *Job 33:10:* **Behold, he finds occasions against me; He counts me as his enemy.** *Job* thought that God was his enemy. And here you have not only the confession of one individual, but the doubt of the whole Church in general. *Lamentations 3:42:* **We have transgressed and rebelled; you have not pardoned, etc.** Nonetheless, God was reconciled with them / and had forgiven them / even though they doubted it. Thus, God can pardon His chosen ones / and they may not know it, according to God’s manifold wisdom.

There are several reasons for this:

First, by keeping them in a state of doubt regarding forgiveness: it makes them more inclined toward compassion for the distress of others' minds. This was one purpose of *Christ’s* suffering / when his soul was in extreme distress / and he cried out under his **desertion** <term>desertion: a spiritual state where a believer feels completely abandoned by God’s presence</term>: *My God! my God! Why have you forsaken me?* <note>original: "Mijn Godt! mijn Godt! Waarom hebt ghy mijn verlaten?"</note> Why was this? It was so that *Christ* might have and show compassion / and "bowels of mercy" / to those who are in deep desertion. Let a scholar study many things and read in books about the storms and tempests that a sailor is subject to; nevertheless, through all his reading, he cannot be strengthened / nor truly have compassion for a person in a storm / if he has never been in one himself. Let someone read the account the Scripture makes of the pains of a woman in labor; she cannot truly have compassion for a woman in childbirth / unless she has been in that pain herself. So it is in divine things / it is **experience** that makes a person compassionate.

2. It is for this reason: then a higher estimation of forgiving grace shall rise in the heart of man. Things that are obtained with difficulty are highly valued by us. What

<column-break/>

is the reason / that birds chirp more and sing sweeter in the Spring than at any other time of the year? It is because / after having tasted a long and cold Winter / they feel a pleasant Spring. Beloved / the Lord makes his people "chirp and sing" in the feeling of forgiving grace: they rejoice all the more because it comes after the Winter of desertion. People praise the stillness when they have been long upon a wild and stormy sea. Those who have long struggled upon the waters of spiritual affliction, and have felt the raging of the tempests in their conscience / shall praise forgiving grace all the more.

3. God sometimes forgives someone’s sin / and does not let them know it / in order to rebuke them / since they have not lived in the exercise of grace. You turn your obedience away from God / and God turns His comfort away from you. This is a common reason / why God sometimes pardons a sinner / and yet gives no account of it to their own conscience. It is "done in Heaven" / and the pardon is written there; but it is not yet "done in the conscience" / or written there. This can serve as a rebuke to your own heart: "Surely I have not put the grace I received into practice, therefore God will not give me the comfort of His Spirit." When you are not active in grace / you shall have little peace / it is right for God to act so.

4. The Lord forgives sins / and does not make it known / to make the conversion more visible / and more complete to the **World** / which has been offended by their sin. The Lord wants to make it visible to the World / that if they have sinned notoriously, it shall pain them bitterly; to show the World / that conversion is no "slight work," and that it is no small matter to make peace with God.

5. To make people feel the wickedness and bitterness of sin. If a person / who is openly godless / were to daily obtain the feeling of forgiveness, he would not be willing to feel the bitterness of sin.

6. The last reason is this / to teach a doubting *Christian* that **assurance** <term>assurance: the internal certainty or feeling that one is saved and forgiven</term> does not essentially belong to forgiveness itself. Assurance can be separated from faith / and therefore also from forgiveness. A person may believe / and yet not know that he believes. The Lord does this to teach a faint-hearted *Christian* / that although they have no assurance, they nonetheless may have faith; and although they lack the feeling of forgiveness, they nonetheless possess it. There can be no fruit / unless there is a tree; yet there can be a tree / and no fruit. There can be grace in the heart / when there is no peace in the conscience. Having peace / is an "added grace." Now / the Lord / for these holy ends / sometimes grants forgiveness in Heaven / when it has not yet been applied to the conscience. Thus much for the first Case.

A second **Case of Conscience** is this / If God forgives sin, may He then still plague and punish the person for the same, after they have once been forgiven, or not?

<meta>This page continues the resolution of "cases of conscience" regarding the nature of forgiveness. It specifically addresses the timing of justification—whether it occurs before or after faith—and the spiritual state of infants who cannot consciously believe.</meta>

### The Saints are bound to believe

when he believes, then He reveals His forgiveness of sin. From this, a greater absurdity would follow; for then faith would not be an instrument of **justification** <term>justification: the legal act of God declaring a sinner righteous through Christ</term>, but only a declaration that the person is already righteous. But the Scripture says more about this faith: that it is an active instrument, laying hold of Christ for forgiveness. The grace of Christ’s love, the grace of humility, of self-denial, and of mortification—these declare a person to be pardoned just as much as faith does. This [idea] would strike at the great use of faith and make it of little or no use in justification.

Again, even more absurdity would follow if we said that a person’s sins were forgiven before their **conversion** <term>conversion: the turning of a person from sin to God</term>. It is the same as if we said: a person is pardoned before he is in Christ. This is false; for without Christ there is no forgiveness. I pass over many other absurdities that would follow if we were to deny this orthodox point.

There is a strong **Objection**, which is this:
> Does God not love man from all eternity? And does the Scripture not say that we are chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world? Now, God’s election and love for us is God’s forgiveness of us: If God loved a person before he was born, surely then God has forgiven him from eternity.

**Answer:** To argue from God’s love to the actual forgiveness of sin is a great absurdity. To argue in such a way is as if we said: Because God intended from all eternity to create the world, therefore He created the world from eternity. God decreed from all eternity to forgive; He carries out this decree when you are converted. He reveals that He has forgiven there, when He gives you the assurance of His love here. The **Antinomians** <term>Antinomians: a group who believed that because of God's grace, the moral law was no longer binding and that believers were justified even before they had faith</term> take only the decree and the revelation, and leave out the execution.

**Secondly**, observe that when we say God loves a person from eternity, you must not understand that as a love of active delight, but a love of purpose. **Theologians** <note>original: "Godt-geleerden"</note> make a good and common distinction here: that there is a two-fold love in God. There is a **love of purpose** and a **love of well-pleasing**. The love of purpose is in God toward the elect from all eternity: it is a love by which God intended to do good to souls in time. But the love of well-pleasing in God is not in God before the person is converted. Until conversion, God does not have such a love or pleasure [in the person]; for there is nothing in them that would be pleasing to God. At that time, you were "children of wrath."

**2. Counter-objection:** If God does not pardon a person before he believes, or before he is converted, what shall we say of young children who cannot actually believe or be converted? You surely would not be so cruel as to say that all young children go to Hell?

**Answer:** Far be it from me to think that

<column-break/>

all young children go to Hell. I believe that Heaven is as full of young children as any other order in the world. Furthermore, this does not serve to prove that justification happens before conversion and faith; rather, this is only spoken regarding the justification and salvation of young children without active faith.

**Thirdly**, note that there is a great distinction between the state of a young child and a person who has come of age. The Scripture tells you: *That faith comes by hearing,* **Romans 10**. That is, in adults: they must obtain faith through an ordinary means, through the hearing of the Word. But this rule does not apply to young children, because they are not capable or understanding; they lack or err in the use of reason, and God requires no more of them than He has given them. *Faith comes by hearing,* says the Scripture; but these erroneous spirits say, "Why do I need to hear? Why do I need to pray? For a person can have forgiveness without any of these." Note that although children cannot have the *exercise* of faith, they nevertheless have a **habitual faith** <term>habitual faith: a seed or disposition of faith planted in the soul by God, even if the person cannot yet express it consciously</term>, as theologians speak. They have the seed of faith, although they cannot have the workings of that grace. It is written: *You cannot know how the bones of a child are prepared in the mother’s womb.* Much more can God, through His strong and mighty arm, bring about faith within them. There is grace in the elected children; a seed of grace dwelling within them. Just as there is a sinful seed in the nature of the child—so that it is a sinner before it is capable [of conscious sin]—so also, by the same reasoning, they are capable of grace. Those who wish to deny grace in children fall into the heresy of the **Pelagians** <term>Pelagians: followers of Pelagius, who taught that human nature was not corrupted by original sin and that people could choose God without special divine grace</term>, claiming that they have no sin. But a child has a nature capable of and inclined toward sin; therefore, when it comes to its years, although it has not yet committed [outward] sin, it nevertheless desires to sin. A child cannot actually believe or convert itself—that is true—but it has that grace dwelling within it. For this reason, **Christ** took the children in His arms and blessed them. Surely, they must be His darlings. Thus I have answered the third Case of Conscience.

The fourth Case is this: **Can it be consistent with a state of pardon to frequently commit the same great sins again?** Surely these are often the thoughts of stricken minds. I shall speak of this point in two ways:
1. By way of comfort.
2. By way of warning.

->First, by way of comfort.<-

The first answer is this: It is clear through several particular examples in the Scripture that pardoned people have often fallen into one and the same sin. For,
**First**, if you apply it to spiritual sins—to evils that are committed daily, such as spiritual pride, unregulated passion, and neglect of duties—a person whose sins are forgiven often falls into such sins as these.
**Further**, the truth of this may be seen through many examples in the Scripture, such as with **Joseph**: it was a great sin...

Beloved / the falling and the relapsing into the same sin / is a dangerous and sad sign / it is a clear sign of the predominance of sin. <meta>This page continues the theological discussion on the nature of repentance and forgiveness. ### The Saints are bound to believe

When the hair had turned white in the sore; the theologians relate this to a persistence in sin even into old age; this proves that you are an unclean leper <note>The author is referencing the diagnostic laws for leprosy in Leviticus 13.</note>. Another sign was when there was raw flesh in the wound. This signified a man sinning against the feeling and stirring of his conscience. A third sign of leprosy was when, after the first healing, new scabbiness arose within it. Thus, when you are healed of your sins through promises, fasting, and prayer, through strong resolutions in Christ, and afterwards that same sore breaks out again, and the same lusts rise up once more—it is a sorrowful sign.

Fourthly, so that you should not be at ease in your sins, nor have a misunderstanding of this comfort: Consider that falling frequently into a sin hardens the heart more than anything in the world, and brings a person to the greatest godlessness. There is nothing in the world that hardens the heart more than when one and the same sin has a daily use upon the conscience and life of a person; it takes away all stirrings and feelings of the conscience. I say this on this ground: since you have examples of those who have frequently fallen into great wickednesses, you should nevertheless take heed of these four observations, so as not to wrongly claim this comforting point for yourself. But you will say, *If I frequently fell into the same sin, with what may I set my heart at ease, that I am in a pardoned state, notwithstanding all these?* I tell you, although you came to fall frequently into one and the same sin; nevertheless, if your conscience testifies to you that you have frequently done well in opposition to that sin, you may claim a portion of this comfort for yourself, and hold that you are in a pardoned state.

A fifth case of conscience follows: whether a godly person, whose sins are forgiven, may pray for the forgiveness of sin? The **Antinomians** <note>A sect believing that under the gospel of grace, the moral law is of no use or obligation.</note> consider this to be unnecessary; they hold that all praying for forgiveness is only for this purpose: namely, to make the same manifest <note>original: "openbaar te maken" - meaning to make the forgiveness known to the person’s own feelings rather than asking for the act of forgiveness itself.</note>.

Answer. First, although it may be true that God does not command man to pray for those things which have already been perfectly accomplished, to be done again—such as Election and Creation; nevertheless, God commands us to pray for those things that are still to be done, at least in part. I do not need to pray to God for the creation of the world, which is already perfectly done; nor for Election, which is so done that He does it no more. I also do not need to pray for the incarnation of Christ, for Christ has already come in the flesh; but although I do not need to pray for these things, which have already occurred so fully and perfectly, I must nonetheless pray for those things that are not yet fully accomplished, such as the forgiveness of sin, as the Apostle gives us to understand in Romans 3:24-25: *We are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past,*

<column-break/>

*through the forbearance of God.* And when the sin is forgiven and the person is converted, then he is in a pardoned state; therefore, this reasoning—that a person should cease to pray for the forgiveness of sins—is not valid; the Scripture explicitly speaks against this: *I acknowledged my transgression, and you forgave me,* Matthew 6:12. *And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.* This teaches us that brief model of all our prayers; which text, however, the **Antinomians** wish to have understood only as the manifestation of the forgiveness of sin, and not of the actual forgiveness itself in the sight of God.

The first words of that petition are to be taken as an actual forgiveness, not a forgiveness only in feeling; for note the following desire: *Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.* No reason can be shown why the first part of that petition should be understood as a felt forgiveness, and the other part not likewise so.

Secondly, note this: that you must understand sins to be forgiven in the same sense as the "non-forgiveness" of sin is used in the language of Scripture; sin is said not to be forgiven when an actual guilt lies upon a person; as the guilt that lies upon a godless person is not taken away, Matthew 12:32: *And whosoever shall speak a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him; but whosoever shall speak against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come.* Those who understand forgiveness only in feeling must understand this reasoning only as forgiveness in feeling, and not that an actual guilt lies upon the person; so that it is against the nature of forgiveness that sins are only forgiven in a man's own conscience.

The sixth Case of Conscience is: Whether a person, in requesting forgiveness, ought to make a distinction between great and small sins. The **Stoics** <note>Referring to the Stoic paradox that all crimes/sins are equal.</note> say: all sins are equal, and there is no distinction.

Answer. It is true in respect of the object; all sins are against God; nevertheless, when you come to demand pardon, according to the greatness of your sin, your desire and request must be: God can forgive great sins as well as small ones; in respect of God, or of the merits of Christ, there is no distinction; but nevertheless, in your persistence in requesting the forgiveness of sin, you must make a great distinction between the greatness and smallness of your wickednesses. For the Scripture makes a distinction between sins; therefore, we must likewise do the same; the Scripture compares some sins to beams, others to splinters <term>motes: tiny specks of wood or dust</term>, some to talents, others to pence. The Prophet **Amos** makes mention of mighty sins, Amos 5:12. **John** of greater sins, John 19:11: *Jesus answered, you would have no power against me, except it were given you from above: therefore he that delivered me unto you has the greater sin.*

# The Forgiveness of Their Sins

It is true / every sin deserves Hell / yet there is more punishment for one sinner in Hell than for another; the reason why I speak of this case / is to make known to you / that if God has tolerated some of you / having fallen into great and terrible evils / that He rebukes more from you than from other people. He rebukes more humility from you than from others: In the Law you read / that a person, touching an unclean thing / was unclean until the evening: but if a person carried any unclean thing, he had to wash his clothes; showing / that the touching of sin / rebukes humility: But the carrying of sin in one's bosom / rebukes more work / than the simple touching of the same; Peter wept bitterly for his denial / he did more for that / than for another common sin: so that you have to observe / that although / in the sight of Christ / there is no distinction between great and small sins / just as the Red Sea drowned Pharaoh and his horses as if they were a single man; nevertheless you must increase your humility according to the weight of your guilt. So much for the sixth Case of Conscience.

The Seventh Case is this: What are those great and hateful circumstances that enlarge the sin: so that I may see whether my sins are enlarged or not, which are these?

<margin>1 Kings 11:9</margin>
1. Answer. Sinning against the continuous revelation of God's love to one's soul / is greatly aggravating the sin; this aggravated Solomon’s sin / Solomon was a beloved of the Lord / yet he allowed himself to be enticed to evil / after the Lord had appeared to him twice.

<margin>James 4:17</margin>
2. To sin against the corrections and rebukes of your own Conscience / enlarges the sin / *Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.* It is sin for another person / to do that / not knowing; but to him who knows it, it is a greater sin; Christ makes this known / speaking of Judas who betrayed him / and well knew that he was the Son of God: What / my Disciple to betray me! his sin was all the greater / because he did it against his Conscience / God's steward <note>original: "steede-houder," meaning a representative or lieutenant</note> in man; it is a greater crime / to thrust a high man / rather than a low man / out of his office, because the sins are committed against the corrections / and rebukes of the Conscience / therefore it is more heavy.

3. To sin against God's judgments upon other people / is a very great wickedness: For to sin / when God gives wars and bloodshed because of other people's sin / is dangerous; this aggravated Belshazzar's sin /
<margin>Daniel 5:22, 23</margin>

Secondly / Labor to enlarge your own graces. Have you been public in sin? Why should you not be great in humility / and great in conversion?

# Christ’s Ascension into Heaven.

->John 14, Verse 3.<-

>And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself, that where I am, there you may be also.

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' inside a square frame featuring leafy and floral patterns.</image-desc>
This Chapter / from which my Text is taken / is famous among most Interpreters / because it begins with Christ’s Departure, and his last Testament, which he made when he took leave of the World: And this Last Will and Testament of Christ begins in this 14th Chapter, and lasts until the 28th <note>The author likely refers to the end of the discourse or perhaps a specific division in his source, as John’s Gospel has only 21 chapters.</note> of this Book. Christ’s objective / in this Chapter / is / to comfort his Disciples / both against the fear of their persecution in the World / and against their sorrows / upon this consideration / That his life was short in this World. And Christ here makes mention of many comforting observations, to support them against their fear that might trouble them. It was bad for them / when Christ was with them: They thought it would be even worse when he had gone away: And therefore he encourages them through these Arguments.

1. He says / I am only going to my Father’s House: And in the 28th verse, of this Chapter, he says / *You have heard that I said to you, I go away / and come again to you. If you loved me, you would*

<column-break/>

*rejoice, because I said, I go to the Father: For my Father is greater than I.*

2. He does not want them to be grieved by his departure: Because (says he) I do not go alone to the Father, but I intend to take you all with me. Although you may not go with me now, nor die with me, or now go with me to Heaven, nonetheless you shall one day be with me: *In my Father’s House are many mansions.* I do not intend to go alone to Heaven; for there is as much room for you as for me, and a place for my believers in the World. Heaven is first a dwelling, a place which signifies a permanence of the Saints in Heaven. It is not a moving place / but a fixed dwelling.

Again / There are many mansions in Heaven; there is room enough for Christ / for his eleven Apostles; and place enough for all Believers in the World. It signifies the breadth and vastness of Heaven. Hebrews 11, verse 12. *Therefore there sprang even of one, and him as good as dead, so many in multitude as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore, innumerable.* And besides these / there is an innumerable company of angels, Hebrews 12:22.

Add to this Revelation 7:9. *A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues.* Here you have the consequence of the preceding fulfilled. The word / used here / does not mean our Tent or Tabernacle <note>The author distinguishes between the temporary nature of a tent and the eternal "mansion" or "dwelling place."</note>, but our permanent dwelling.

# Christ’s Ascension into Heaven.

3. He draws his reasoning from the certainty of the matter; it is no poetic fiction; these are not "over-believing" <note>original: "boven-gelovige," meaning exaggerated or hyperbolic expressions</note> expressions, as shown just before my text: *If it were not so, I would have told you.* **Christ** does not say more than what is true; if such things did not exist, he would have plainly said so. It is as if he wished to say: I do not feed you with a false hope of a noble happiness, as the Devil deceives his own, whom he leads into a false Paradise.

4. Concerning the purpose: The Disciples might have said, "But Lord, you are going to your Father’s house, but what shall we have?" Therefore **Christ** comforts them and says: *I go to prepare a place for you;* as if he would say, I go to Heaven to prepare Heaven for you against the time you grow strong <note>likely meaning "until you are ready to enter"</note>. As **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian.</note> remarks, this expression is borrowed from a company of travelers who send a man ahead as a <term>fourier</term> <note>A military or travel term for a quartermaster or scout sent ahead to arrange lodgings and supplies.</note> to prepare the inn, make room, and provide provisions for them against their arrival; so has Jesus Christ gone to Heaven as if to clear the way for you and prepare a place there.

5. He comforts them by the promise of his return, verse 3. *And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again.*

6. Through this, he desires to receive us unto himself, Verse 3. *I will receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also.* And we shall always be with the Lord.

I shall explain this expression to you when I come to handle it according to the order of the text. This text contains within itself the most excellent substances and fundamental points of all the teachings of Christianity, such as:

First, that great doctrine of **Christ’s** physical ascension to Heaven: *And if I go.*

Secondly, the fruit or benefit of **Christ’s** going to Heaven: *I go to prepare a place for you.*

Thirdly, here is an excellent doctrine of **Christ’s** second coming, to judge the living and the dead: *I will come again.*

Fourthly, here is a doctrine of the resurrection of the body: **Christ** shall come once more, and cause all men to rise from the grave, and take the elect to himself.

Fifthly, here is a magnificent doctrine of the eternal fellowship that the Saints shall have with **Christ** in Heaven: *That where I am, there ye may be also.*

Regarding the first point, *And if I go*; there is a good note by **Calvin** <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the influential French theologian of the Reformation.</note> on these words, stating that "if" here is the same as "after"; it signifies no doubt, as if Christ were uncertain whether he would go to Heaven or not; nor is it a guess, as if he were merely speculating; but it signifies a determination of the time when **Christ** would go to Heaven. You have a similar expression in *John 12:32*: *And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.* This he spoke regarding what death he should die; though he would be "lifted up" on the Cross, he would save many through that death. The little word "if" does not signify doubt or guessing, but is an adverb of time: *When I shall be lifted up from the earth.* And so it is in my text:

<column-break/>

*And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also.* There is no difficulty in the first words, *And if I go and prepare a place for you*, from which two teachings flow: *And if I go.*

First, that **Christ’s** ascension or going to Heaven is the ground of all comfort for his people while they dwell here on the earth.

The second teaching is regarding the purpose and benefit of his ascending to Heaven: *And if I go and prepare a place for you.* That indeed the primary purpose of **Jesus Christ’s** physical going to Heaven is to prepare Heaven for all the elect.

Regarding the first teaching: *That Christ’s ascension or going to Heaven is the ground of all his comfort for his people while they dwell here on the earth.* In the handling of this point, three particular things are to be noted.

First, I shall show you from the **Scripture** that **Christ** went physically to Heaven, using these five arguments from the Word of God.

1. Through the examples that existed before the Law: **Enoch** was translated and taken up physically into Heaven, where he is now; *Genesis 5:24*. *And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.* This is confirmed by the Apostle, *Hebrews 11:5*. *By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.* And under the Law, **Elijah** was taken up in a fiery chariot; *2 Kings 2:11*. *And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.* So too is **Christ**, being a third example under the Gospel, likewise taken up into Heaven.

2. There are Prophets in the Old Testament stating that **Christ** would surely be taken up into Heaven in the Body; these prophecies are primarily three. One is in *Psalm 68*, where **David** foretells of **Christ**, verse 18 <note>the text says 19, following the Dutch numbering</note>: *Thou hast ascended on high, etc.* Now, we might not have known that this referred to **Jesus Christ’s** Ascension, had not **Paul** explained it so; *Hebrews 4:14*. *Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.* These predictions, long before **Christ’s** birth, declare that he would ascend to Heaven; and *Psalm 110:7*: *He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head.* What is that? It is spoken of **Christ**, who sits at God’s right hand; first he shall drink from the brook on the way—crying out and thirsting on the Cross, yes, dying the death of the Cross—but thereafter he shall lift up his head, rise again, and ascend to Heaven. See also *Daniel 7:13, 14*. *I saw in the night visions, and, behold...*

-># Christ’s Ascension into Heaven.<-

...there came one with the clouds of Heaven, like a Son of Man, and he came to the Ancient of Days <note>A title for God from the book of Daniel.</note>, and they brought him near before the same. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom: that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed. This cannot be spoken of Christ’s coming at the Final Judgment—at which time he shall deliver up the kingdom to his Father, 1 Cor. 15:24. But the coming of Christ here in the clouds is Christ’s Ascension into Heaven; as seen in Acts 1:9: *And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.* And thus you have this confirmed through prophecy.

3. The doctrine of Christ’s going to Heaven is confirmed to you by Christ’s own predictions; while he was on the earth, he foretold that he would go to Heaven, John 6:62: *What and if ye shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before?* And John 20 verse 17: *Jesus saith unto her, Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father: but go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.* Christ promises them that he would ascend, John 16 verse 7: *And now I go my way to him that sent me; and none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou? Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter <note>The Holy Spirit.</note> will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you.* John 16 verse 16: *A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me, because I go to the Father.* I could note many Scripture passages in which Christ promised that he would go away.

4. The doctrine of Christ’s going to Heaven is confirmed by the testimony of the Apostles, who were eyewitnesses of Christ’s ascension. Gerardus <note>Likely Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note> observes, saying: *Christ rose invisibly; no one saw him rise.* The Scripture tells us that the guards who watched him slept; yet he gathered all his eleven Apostles to be eyewitnesses of his Ascension, Acts 1:9-10: *And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. And while they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel.* And so the Apostle Peter relates, 1 Pet. 3 verse 22: *Who is gone into heaven, and is on the right hand of God; angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him.* And Paul, Eph. 4:10: *He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things.* See also Hebr. 9:24, 1 Tim. 3:16, and Mark 16 verse 19. I have taken greater pains to prove this point so that the opinions of some ancient heretics <note>Likely referring to groups like the Gnostics or Docetists who denied the physical reality of Christ's body.</note> might be overthrown by this comforting doctrine of Christ’s bodily departure to Heaven, keeping our flesh in Heaven until this present day.

<column-break/>

5. This can be confirmed by the testimony of the Angels, who were witnesses of this truth, Acts 1 verse 10: *And two men stood by them in white apparel.* These two men were Angels; the Angels give their harmonious testimony that Jesus Christ went to Heaven and would return from there. Beloved, I do not know of a single point in the entire Bible that is strengthened with as many proofs as Christ’s personal and bodily going to Heaven. And let this much be spoken to you for the confirmation of this point. I wished to lay this as a foundation so that the fruit of it might appear all the clearer to us.

Secondly, what are the reasons why Christ had to ascend to Heaven in both body and soul?

<margin>Reasons why Christ had to go to Heaven.</margin>
Firstly, Christ, according to his physical presence, had to ascend to Heaven so that his Disciples would not cling too much to his physical presence, but instead look upward for the communication of his Spirit. They asked Christ, *Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?* They expected that Christ would destroy the Roman Emperor, who was a pagan, and make himself King. Acts 1 verse 6: *When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?* It is for this reason, say the commentators, that the Disciples should not lean upon Jesus Christ or regard him as a temporal king, expecting from him a temporal kingdom; but that they might look up to that Kingdom which he truly has. To this end Paul has a passage, 2 Cor. 5:16: *Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more.* As if he wished to say: it may be that those who lived in Christ’s time knew him after the flesh as a beloved Person; but, says Paul, we know him in a Spiritual manner, looking to him in heaven, and longing for salvation with Christ.

Secondly, Christ was taken away into heaven in his Body to provide a recompense and a reward for the sufferings in his Body. Phil. 2 verses 8-9: *And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.* For this reason God exalted Christ, caused him to rise from the dead, and to ascend to heaven—because he was humbled unto the Death of the Cross and appeared in the form of a servant. Psalm 110 verse 7: *He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head.* Because you have suffered and died, therefore shall you lift up the head; therefore shall you ascend to heaven. Hebr. 2 verse 9: *But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man.* Because he suffered death

The first ground of comfort is this; Christ's bodily going to Heaven / it assures you of Christ’s full blessing and victory / obtained over all your Spiritual enemies; the Apostle draws this as a ground of consolation from Christ’s Ascension; Ephesians 4: 8. *Wherefore, he saith, when he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men.* That is / the Devil and the sins that led you captive; Christ, by his going to Heaven, has led them captive / that is / crushed your Spiritual enemies: Christ is compared to the custom of the Romans; when a Roman conquered / he extended a rod from the Capitolium <note>The main temple and citadel of ancient Rome, used here as a symbol of triumph.</note> of Rome, in rejoicing over his victory over his enemies; thus making this captivity / into a glorious chariot of victory. So has Christ also led captivity captive and triumphed / Colossians 2: 15. *And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.* So / Beloved / there is great comfort in this / that Christ, by his going to Heaven / has revealed and declared to all the World / that he has conquered the grave / Death / the Devil / and sin.

2. Christ's bodily going to Heaven / is a pledge to you / that Christ will one day bring your bodies into Heaven; he went bodily to Heaven / so that he might take you bodily into Heaven to be with him / John 14: 19. *Yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also.* As if he would say / well / I must leave you / and go into Heaven before you / but because I live in Heaven / and live bodily / so shall you likewise live with me in Heaven with your bodies; Ter-

<column-break/>

-tullian <note>original: "Tertullianus" — an early Christian author from North Africa, c. 155–220 AD.</note>, making use of this / to comfort the Christians in his days / says / Jesus Christ carried our flesh with him into Heaven, being of our flesh and bones; Now, says Tertullian, he carried our flesh into Heaven, as a pledge, that our flesh would likewise be with him in Heaven. Therefore / O flesh and blood, rejoice / that you already possess Heaven in Christ / and Christ would be incomplete in Heaven / if the bodies of the believers did not likewise come there / because just as he lives in Heaven / you shall also live there as well.

3. Hebrews 9: 24. *For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us.* Christ has gone into the true Heaven / to appear before the face of God for us. So also Hebrews 7: 26. *For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.* It was fitting for us to have such a High Priest in Heaven. Therefore take note / although it was a great benefit to the Disciples / to have Christ's bodily presence / nevertheless Christ could never have fulfilled his Priestly Office / making intercession and full atonement for all the elect / if he had not ascended bodily into Heaven. Note also this one Text / Hebrews 8: 4. *For if he were on earth, he should not be a priest, seeing that there are priests that offer gifts according to the law.* Christ had to go to Heaven / and there he is a Priest; now / if he were on earth he would not be a Priest for us / therefore we have great advantage by Christ's going to Heaven. O Beloved / look upon this then as a great comfort / that our Lord Jesus Christ is now in Heaven according to his body / with his flesh and blood / appearing before God / and performing intercession for his people; This was prefigured under the Law / Exodus 28: 9, 10, 11, 12. *And thou shalt take two onyx stones <note>original: "Sardonix-steenen"</note>, and grave on them the names of the children of Israel. Six of their names on one stone, and the other six names of the rest on the other stone, according to their birth. # Christ’s Ascension into Heaven.

...not only carried the names of all the elect upon his shoulders, but also held them in his heart, and has prayed for them there to his Father. This is the third ground of comfort arising from *Christ’s* physical Ascension.

Furthermore, the fact that *Jesus Christ* has gone into heaven comforts us because he has fully shared with us the gifts and graces of his Spirit from there—the same gifts he promised to his people while he lived on earth (*Ephesians 4:8*). Therefore he says, *When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men.* It was the custom of the triumphant Romans to scatter money among the onlookers who saw them ride by in their victory processions. So also *Jesus Christ*, having destroyed Death and the Devil through his ascension, throws his gifts among mankind and scatters his grace in great measure into the hearts of his people. This is not to say we wish to fall into the error of the *Socinians* <note>The Socinians were a 16th and 17th-century theological group that denied the pre-existence of Christ and the traditional doctrine of the Trinity.</note>, who wish to conclude from this text that before *Christ’s* Ascension there were no soul-saving gifts or Holy Spirit. They base this on another text, *John 7:38, 39*: *He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. (But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified.)* The Holy Spirit "was not yet" because *Jesus* was not yet glorified; however, this text should not be taken literally, for it would then follow that *Abraham*, *Isaac*, and *Jacob* did not have the Spirit and consequently could not be in Heaven. Rather, the meaning is that the *abundant* outpouring of the Holy Spirit had not yet occurred because *Christ* had not yet ascended. *Christ* reserved the full outpouring of the Holy Spirit for the time of his ascension, until he was glorified; therefore the Apostles received it immediately after his Ascension in a fuller measure than was ever given to the people of old. And Beloved, these are not only gifts to bring you to Heaven, but likewise *Ministerial* gifts <term>Ministerial gifts: special talents or callings given by God to individuals for the purpose of serving the church, such as preaching or leadership.</term> to prepare men for service. You must look upon this as a fruit of the Ascension (*Ephesians 4:10, 11, 12*): *He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things. And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists, and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.* So you should not only look to your Christian gifts through which God brings you to Heaven, but also see all ministerial gifts as fruits of *Christ's* Ascension.

Fifthly, *Christ’s* going to Heaven comforts us in this: that through it you can be certain, with boldness and confidence, when you come to God in prayer. When you come to God in prayer, you come to one who has *Jesus Christ* at his right hand in Heaven, constantly praying to God for you, so that you may receive a comforting answer (*Hebrews 4:14, 16*). Since we then have a great High

<column-break/>

Priest who has passed through the heavens, namely *Jesus* the Son of God, let us hold fast to this confession. Let us therefore come boldly to the Throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need. *Jesus Christ* being in Heaven drives out all fear and cowardice from us and gives us a holy boldness when we pray; for we have a High Priest who has passed into the highest Heavens, *Jesus* the Son of God. Who does not come with boldness to the Court when he knows that the King's eldest son is his friend and is assured of his love—that he will stand up for him and intercede for him before his Father? *Jesus Christ* is the King of Heaven, the eldest Son, and he is bound by his office to present all our desires and to intercede for us.

Sixthly, the fact that *Christ* physically ascended to Heaven is comforting because he thereafter maintained the same relationship to his believers that he had while he lived on earth. When he was on earth, he said, "Go, tell my brothers that I have risen"; so also, after he ascended to Heaven, he calls them his *Brothers* (*Hebrews 2:11*): *For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren.* Although *Christ* was clothed with Glory and had gone into Heaven, he was not ashamed to call his believers "Brothers." Now, in Heaven, *Christ* is their God, their Father, their Prince, their Friend, and the administrator of all comfort; so that believers, even though *Christ* is in Heaven, still have fellowship with him as if he were on earth. Because of this, *Job* could speak in a vision: *I know that my Redeemer lives*; I know that my kinsman-redeemer lives <note>original: "bloetvrient" – literally 'blood-friend,' referring to the Hebrew concept of the *Goel* or kinsman who redeems family property or persons.</note>. *Christ* called his Disciples "Brothers" when he was in the flesh, and he does so still now that he has ascended to Heaven. Suppose you were a poor woman, and your husband, who was humble and poor in the world, was taken away and attained to Royal dignity; it is nonetheless a great comfort to you that, where you were previously humble, you now have the honor of being a King’s wife. So also, no matter how humble a state they are in in this world, if they believe, they are Brothers of *Christ*.

Finally, *Christ’s* going to Heaven is comforting in this respect: because he prepares a place for us there; *I go to prepare a place for you* (*Hebrews 6:20*). Where the forerunner, *Jesus*, has entered for us, according to the order of *Melchizedek* <note>A priest and king mentioned in Genesis; the author of Hebrews uses him as a symbol of Christ's eternal priesthood.</note>, etc. *Christ* is our forerunner; he has gone to Heaven *for us*. Not only did he die for us, but he also ascended to Heaven for us (*Hebrews 10:19, 20*). *Since we then, Brothers, have boldness to enter into the Sanctuary through the blood of Jesus, by a fresh and living way which he has consecrated for us through the veil, that is to say, through his flesh.* That is, having hope to enter into Heaven through the blood of *Christ* as well as through *Christ's* flesh, when he died on the Cross. And let this much be said concerning the instructional part of this point, namely—

# Christ’s Ascension into Heaven.

...that Christ’s physical journey to Heaven is a foundation of great comfort to God’s people while they live here on earth.

Now I shall provide several instructions derived from the circumstances of Christ’s Ascension. There are five circumstances from which you may draw some instruction.

**First**, regarding the time that Christ lived in the world and at which He was carried into Heaven: if you read the Evangelists, they will tell you that it was around the 33rd year of His age when He left the world and went to Heaven. Learn from this that since Christ was willing to leave the world in the flower of His life, being a young man, this reflection must be held fast by you young men: that you should not attach your hearts too closely to this world, longing for a long life. Suppose God took you away in the flower of your days; be willing and submit yourselves to that, for God dealt likewise with Christ.

**Second**, you may also learn something here from the place from which Christ ascended. It is noteworthy that it was the **Mount of Olives**, *Acts 1:12*: *Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.* Luke says that it was outside at Bethany, *Luke 24:50, 51*: *And he led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven.* It is all one place, but there is something wonderful in it; of all the places in the world, Christ chose Bethany on the Mount of Olives to go from there to Heaven. Beloved, the reason was because Christ was there when He was betrayed by Judas and captured by the Scribes and Pharisees. From that place, where He was taken to be crucified, He chose to ascend to Heaven. **Bethany**, in the Hebrew language <note>original: "Bethanien, in de Hebreeusche sprake"</note>, signifies a **house of affliction** <note>The name Bethany is traditionally interpreted as "House of Misery" or "House of Affliction," from the Hebrew *Beth-Aniyah*.</note>; this Bethany He also makes a place of His transition into Glory. I wish to point out to you here that God sometimes makes our sufferings the steps to our Glory. So it was with Christ: from Bethany He was taken captive, and from that same place He wished to ascend into Heaven; and if you suffer with Him, you shall likewise be glorified with Him. You are sometimes brought to Heaven by the path of sharp affliction; therefore, do not be too greatly dismayed in persecution, for the Lord makes the *Bethanies*—the houses of our sorrows—doors to bring us into our Father’s dwelling.

**Third**, another circumstance in Christ’s Ascension: even as Christ traveled hence, He was busy speaking with His Disciples about the Kingdom of God, and when He had blessed them, He was taken up before their eyes. *Acts 1:9*: *And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.* While He blessed His Disciples and spoke with them of those things concerning the Kingdom of God, He was taken away. I wish to give you this observation: that when you come

<column-break/>

to the end of your departure from this world, you should follow Christ’s example. When Christ departed, He spoke of those things concerning the Kingdom of God; let your hearts likewise be full of faith and divine meditation, and of good counsel to your friends when you come to die, so that people may say of you afterward, "these are the last words of a dying friend." I may hold up this example of Christ’s departure from the world to all masters and mistresses of households <note>original: "Huys-heeren ende Huys-vrouwen"</note>, that they give good counsel to their own before their end. Let your talk not be of worldly things—let those be settled beforehand—but give good counsel and good exhortations to your children. **Jacob**, when he died, called his children to him, gave them good counsel, and blessed them. So also did **David**, *1 Chronicles 28:9*: *And thou, Solomon my son, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind: for the Lord searcheth all hearts, and understandeth all the imaginations of the thoughts: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee; but if thou forsake him, he will cast thee off for ever.* And we see this also in the example of **Isaac**, and many other servants of God, such as **Moses** and **Joshua**, when they died. I will only specifically take the example of Christ: that while you live and grow strong in this world, you should specifically have or express nothing else in your mind than those things which concern the Kingdom of God, like Christ.

**Fourth**, there is also instruction from the manner of Christ’s departure from the world. The manner was, *Acts 1:9*: *And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.* They saw Him ascend into Heaven by degrees. You must not let this pass without reflection: that a cloud took Jesus Christ away from our sight. This remains for your meditations: that when you see the clouds, you think, "these clouds that I see here above in the sky have been Christ’s **victory chariot** <term>original: "Zeegen-wagen" — a triumphal carriage used in Roman victory processions</term> which carried Him to heaven, and shall also be His seat when He comes to judge the world." Labor to have your meditations on divine things; He ascended in the clouds, therefore the clouds are called God’s victory chariots.

**Fifth**, note further the circumstance of Christ’s ascension: that He wished to call His friends around Him. It is explicitly stated that the eleven Apostles were with Him, *Acts 1*. And a certain writer believes that there were 120 with Christ when He ascended to heaven, and he proves this from *Acts 1:15*: *And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples, and said, (the number of names together were about an hundred and twenty).* Now, assuming it is accepted that one hundred and twenty witnesses saw Christ ascend, it is at least clear that the eleven Apostles were there; that He gathered these friends around Him before He departed from this world. Learn here then, that when you go away or depart from this world, you must labor to have your friends with you, to give them the testimony of a dying friend; and it is a great blessing to die...

# Christ’s Ascension into Heaven.

...die among your friends. Before Christ went to heaven and left the world, He wanted His friends to be with Him, and then He was taken away from them.

Now I come to provide even more practical applications from this point. If it is so that Christ’s physical journey to heaven is the foundation of great comfort to God’s people on Earth, then the use I shall set forth is for the rejection of four misunderstandings and errors, as well as some instructions.

**First**, this point overthrows the opinion of the <term>Seleucians and Herminians</term> <note>Followers of 4th-century heretics who taught that Christ's body was stayed in the sun</note>, who hold that Christ’s body is not in Heaven, but that it is within that glorious and shining body of the Sun. They say that this is the reason why the Sun is so glorious and gives such a clear light, more so than the Moon. Truly, this old heresy has been renewed among us. I have read this in a book called *The Divine Light*, which is in reality nothing more than darkness. But Christ is above the Sun, above all visible heavens. He sits in the third Heaven, as Paul calls it; therefore, since Christ’s body has ascended to heaven, they err greatly.

**Second**, this point also condemns those who maintain that Christ’s body, after His Ascension, is still upon the Earth. There have been some in Germany who said that they were the true Christ. Likewise, in the days of King Henry VIII, there was one who said he was the Christ; his side was pierced, and he showed the wounds of the nails in his hands, etc. Indeed, but as it is said: *If anyone says, "Look, here is Christ," or "There he is," do not believe them*; for Christ is not on the earth after His Ascension.

**Third**, the fact that Christ’s body is now in heaven overthrows the doctrine of the <term>Papists</term> <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics</note> regarding their <term>Transubstantiation</term> <note>The belief that the bread and wine literally become the physical body and blood of Christ</note>, or the essential change of Jesus Christ into the Bread. The Papists say that we physically eat Christ’s flesh and drink His blood; that He is as physically present in the Sacrament as He was hanging on the Cross. If there were no other proof to strike down this opinion than this—that the Body of Christ is now in heaven—it would be enough; and the sentiment of Transubstantiation is hereby refuted: Christ’s Body cannot be in heaven and at the same time on Earth, both at once.

**Fourth**, the Ascension of Christ casts down the opinion of the <term>Carpocratians</term> <note>An early Gnostic sect</note>, who hold that only His soul went to Heaven, and His body decayed like others. This cannot be, for the Disciples say that they *saw* Him ascend; and this must have been His body, for they could not see His Soul, since it is a Spirit. Now, you see the reason why I have been so long in giving you clear testimonies of Scripture to prove this point: because there are so many heretics who oppose the doctrine of Christ’s Ascension. Now I shall give you three practical, pressing reasons.

**First**, is Christ now physically in heaven? Then I conclude: O! you who can ascribe to yourselves and to us a good foundation, an interest in Jesus Christ: O! do not be afraid of Death, because your Christ is in

<column-break/>

heaven; and when you die, death is to you but a door through which you enter into a joyful hall where Christ is. Why should we be like children, looking at the Door as if it were a <term>bogeyman</term> <note>original: "Bulbach," a monster or scarecrow used to frighten children</note>? Look upon it instead as a passage to your Father’s House, as being a door to come to where Christ is. *Genesis 45:25, 27*: *And they went up out of Egypt... and came into the land of Canaan to their father Jacob... and when he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob their father revived.* Did Jacob rejoice so much when he saw an Egyptian wagon to carry him to his son Joseph? And shall you not rejoice much more when you see Death approaching, like a victory-chariot, to carry you to Jesus Christ, indeed, to heaven? O! therefore let your heart not be too troubled when you die, because Death is but a wagon that carries you to heaven.

**Second**, has Christ ascended? Then labor, while you live on Earth, to ascend with and to Christ in divine and holy desires and meditations. Is Christ in heaven? Why then shall our hearts not desire to be where our Head is? Why do you want to root in and upon the earth, seeing that Christ is now in heaven? It is a saying of Christ’s in *Song of Solomon 3:6*: *Who is this coming out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of the merchant?* Shall you not ascend to Christ, since you are in the desolation of the wilderness of this world? O! climb up to the Savior in holy reflections. The Apostle makes this use of it in *Colossians 3:1*: *If then you were raised with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God.* The argument is: where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, let your affections be there. So also *Philippians 3:20*: *Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also eagerly wait for the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.* Christ is in heaven, therefore our walk must be where our Head is. It is a noteworthy text, *Matthew 24:28*: *For wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered together.* That Christ is in heaven shall make your hearts soar heavenward. It is true, there are some who wrest these words and say that this "carcass" refers to the Jews, and the "eagles" to the Romans, because the Romans carried an eagle on their coat of arms and banners: for this reason (they say), wherever the Jews were, the Romans would come. Although this is true, nonetheless it is not the aim of this text, and it is generally rejected by most interpreters. But <term>Gerardus</term> <note>Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a famous Lutheran theologian</note> brings these words primarily to the Day of Judgment: *Where the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered.* That is, where Jesus Christ is in heaven, just as an eagle flies upward toward the bait, there the people of God shall be gathered around the Savior; this, I confess, is the primary aim of the Holy Spirit in this place. Yet Gerardus makes another use of it, applying it to the power and working of the Gospel...

<meta>This page continues the theological exposition of the comforts and practical applications of Christ’s Ascension. The previous page concluded by refuting errors regarding Christ's current physical location.</meta>

# Christ’s Ascension into Heaven.

...in this life; Christ is now in Heaven, he says / and the Gospel shall be so mighty upon men in this world, that they shall run as zealously after Christ in Heaven, as the eagle after the carcass. <note>original: "de Arent na het aes." A reference to Matthew 24:28, suggesting that just as eagles are drawn by instinct to food, believers are drawn by the Spirit to the ascended Christ.</note>

**Thirdly.** I conclude here / that before you dare to claim for yourself the benefits and comforts of Christ's Ascension into Heaven / that you labor to feel in your own heart the operation and power of Christ's Death and Ascension; every man applies the benefit of Christ's Death / Resurrection / and Ascension / before he finds in himself the operation of his death / and the operation of his resurrection. This is the practice of the Apostle; he says / I labor to find in me the power of his resurrection; labor you likewise / to find in yourself the power of His Death / and the power of His Ascension / before you comfort yourself with the same; this is to diminish our earthly minds / moving more toward / and having greater earnestness for the Lord Jesus Christ. The more you feel the power of the Ascension / the more heavenly of mind you become / and the less earthly you are. Oh! labor then to feel the working of this power / otherwise I may say to you / as Jacob said to his mother, Genesis 27, verse 12. *Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall be in his eyes as a deceiver: so I should bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing.* <note>Jacob feared that Isaac would discover his disguise while seeking a blessing; the author warns that God will similarly "feel" or test the heart of the believer.</note> Yes / without "perhaps" / God shall feel and test whether you are the one or not / who has a right to this blessing; whether you shall enjoy an actual privilege and benefit through Christ’s Death and Ascension. God wants to test whether you do not deceive your souls / and God Himself: If this is so / you would rather have a curse than a blessing / if you seek to claim for yourself the comfort of Christ’s Ascension / before you feel the working thereof in your own hearts.

**Question / How did Christ ascend?**
**Answer.** First / Christ ascended visibly to heaven, Acts 1. It was no passing glimmer from their eyes / but they saw him with a fixed gaze / and ascending besides.

**Secondly**, he ascended Bodily to heaven: Therefore those err / who maintain / *That he ascended only in his soul, and that his body rotted like others.*

**Thirdly**, He ascended locally to heaven. He ascended locally. There are some who maintain / *That all places where God is, is Heaven*; which is true / but Heaven is a distinct and separate place from the Earth and Hell. Christ changed from place / from the Earth to the third Heaven, therefore he says / the earth shall no longer hold me.

**Fourthly**, He was carried to Heaven full of power. Truly / others have ascended bodily to heaven / not by their own strength / but it was a borrowed power: Elijah had a fiery Chariot / with which he ascended to Heaven / but Christ had nothing / for he ascended by his own strength.

**Lastly**, Christ ascended to Heaven preeminently and specially. There are three Bodies in Heaven / there is the Body of Enoch, the Body of Elijah, the Body of Christ. All others in Heaven /

<column-break/>

are only Saints and Angels. Enoch, when he ascended / was an example of Christ's Ascension / before the Law / and Elijah under the Law / and Christ under the Gospel. The theologians say / *That this shows there was Salvation through Christ before the Law, under the Law, and in the time of the Gospel*; but there is a distinction between their ascensions to Heaven.

**First of all** / Enoch and Elijah ascended to Heaven / yet they did not die / and rise from the dead / and then ascend; but Christ died first / thereafter he rose from the grave / and then he / after forty days, ascended to heaven / there is a distinction. Again / they did not ascend to Heaven through their own strength / but through the power of God: They were carried to heaven / but we receive no good thereby / no benefit or grace do we get through their ascension; but in Christ’s Ascension is a great benefit and abundance of blessing for us / for he says / *I go to Heaven, to prepare a place for you.*

**Again** / Enoch ascended to heaven / but he could not give the Spirit / likewise Elijah; but our Lord Jesus Christ has gone Bodily into heaven / and ascended on High, and has given gifts to men.

**Lastly** / They ascended to Heaven, says <term>Polanus</term> <note>Amandus Polanus von Polansdorf (1561–1610), a noted Reformed theologian.</note>, only as Citizens of Heaven, but Christ as a Lord of Heaven, who is there in his Body and in his Person, and the others fall far short of him in Glory. And thus I have explained to you the first part of my Text.

Now I come to the second, to the benefit that the Believers obtain from Christ's Bodily going to Heaven / *I go hence to prepare a place for you.*

**The Doctrine is this** / The fruit and benefit that all the elect of God have / through Christ's Ascension to Heaven, is / that he prepares a place for them there: *I go hence to prepare a place for you.* Now / in the treatment of this Doctrine I shall do three special things.

1. I shall show you in what sense Christ / going to heaven / prepares a place for the believers.
2. I shall prove to you / how this Scripture passage stands with the truth / *Christ has ascended to Heaven, to prepare a place for us*; although in another place it is said / *That Heaven is prepared for us from the beginning of the world.*
3. Whether the Patriarchs, and truly holy Men of God, who lived before the Ascension of Christ, went into Heaven when they died; because the Church of Rome concludes from this Text / *That before Christ’s Ascension no one ascended to Heaven, but all went into a place named the <term>Limbus Patrum</term>.* <note>The "Limbo of the Fathers," a Catholic doctrine describing a place where the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ to open the gates of heaven.</note>

**First of all** / In what sense can it be said, that Christ, by his going into Heaven, has prepared a place there for the Believers? I answer / In these three respects.

<margin>Grotius.</margin>
...our nature has ascended to Heaven / as representing all the Elect. Jesus Christ has gone to heaven / representing the Persons of God's Elect on Earth. For this reason, it says in Ephesians 2:6: *And has raised us up together, and made us sit together in Heaven in Christ Jesus.* We are not in heavenly / but in earthly places / and yet we are seated in heaven / because Christ is now there: He has then ascended as a common and public Person / representing all the Elect. Hebrews 6:20: *Where the Forerunner, for us, has entered, namely Jesus, having become a High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.* He did not go there for himself / but for us. Christ stood as a public Person / representing all the Elect of God; likewise he has ascended to heaven / possessing heaven in our place. Christ preserves an inheritance for us there / says Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a prominent Dutch jurist and theologian whose works were highly influential in Reformed circles.</note>. Christ has ascended to heaven / just like a company of Travelers / when they travel / they send a Courier ahead / who orders lodging and everything for them / so that they / arriving / might find everything ready: So has our Lord Jesus Christ gone before to heaven / there preparing a place for all the Elect.

<margin>Hebr. 9: 24.</margin>
Secondly, Christ prepares a place for the Elect through Intercession, Hebrews 9:24. *For Christ is not entered into the Sanctuary made with hands, which is a figure of the True, but into Heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us.* Just as the Priests under the Law / when they went to a holy place / had the Names of all the Tribes on their Breast; so is Christ our Great High Priest, having the Names of all the Elect not only on his Breast / but in his Heart / praying to the Father / that we might come there. Jesus Christ prepares a dwelling for us in heaven / when he prepares us to be Inhabitants of heaven. Colossians 1:12, 13, 14. *Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to be partakers of the Inheritance of the Saints in light: Who has delivered us from the power of darkness, and has translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love: In whom we have redemption through his blood, namely the forgiveness of sins.* An unconverted person is not fit for heaven: Now / when Christ makes you fit for heaven / then he prepares heaven for you. 1 Peter 3: 4, 5. <note>The author likely intended 1 Peter 1:3-5, as the text following matches that passage.</note> *Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has begotten us again unto a living hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fades not away, reserved in Heaven for you, who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, which is*
