# to prepare for the Believers.

the ungodly of the world, during these thousand years, although they shall not then rule as they do now.

**Thirdly,** consider that in the Text it is said that before this new earth, the World shall burn with fire, the heavens shall melt, etc. <note>Refers to 2 Peter 3:10-12</note> Now, before the thousand years, this does not happen. The burning of the World is reserved for the day of Judgment; therefore, this future state cannot be applied to Christ’s thousand-year Reign here on the World.

**Fourthly,** it is said there that the Lord shall come as a Thief; *But the day of the Lord shall come as a Thief in the night, in which the Heavens shall pass away with a great noise,* etc. This must be applied to His coming for judgment—to His final coming—and not to any other coming. **1 Thess. 5 verse 2.** *For you yourselves know very well, that the day of the Lord shall so come, as a Thief in the night.* Furthermore, if Christ were to come and reign upon the earth, then He would come visibly and recognizably. **Matth. 24:43.** *But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what watch of the night the Thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken through. Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not, the Son of man cometh.* **Rev. 16 verse 15.** <note>The original OCR says Revelation 12, but the text "Behold, I come as a thief" is found in Revelation 16:15</note> *Behold, I come as a Thief. Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame.*

**Fifthly,** and upon this the Divines <term>Divines: An older term for theologians or scholars of the Bible</term> insist greatly: it is said there, *we look for, according to his promise, new Heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.* The "dwelling of righteousness" must not be thought to mean that such a thing will be upon the physical new earth, but the "dwelling of righteousness" is applied to the righteous people, not to the heaven or earth. The Greek word <note>The author is likely referring to the plural form or the specific usage of the verb "to dwell" (katoikei) in 2 Peter 3:13</note> explains this clearly; it is a word in the plural number. For this reason, it cannot be applied to the earth, which is only one in number; we, in whom Righteousness dwells, look forward to a new heaven and a new earth. So the dwelling of righteousness cannot be translated as the earth, but rather that righteousness shall dwell in the people; we read of no one, while being on the earth, in whom perfect righteousness has dwelt; and thus much be said of the second Scripture passage: *We look for a new Heaven, and a new Earth.*

The third Scripture passage, in which they dream that there is some strength for them, is found in **Dan. 2:44.** *But in the days of those Kings, shall the God of Heaven set up a Kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: And that Kingdom shall not be left to other people: it shall break in pieces and consume all those Kingdoms: but it itself shall stand for ever.* Now, Beloved, to give you the aim of this Text, take these Answers.

1. It is true that a Kingdom of God is given to Jesus Christ; yes, even when He was on the earth in the form of a servant, as Luke relates, **Chap. 1:32, 33.** *He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest. And God the*

<column-break/>

*Lord shall give unto him the Throne of his Father David, and he shall Reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his Kingdom there shall be no end.* So Jesus Christ has had a Kingdom, and is now King of Kings and Lord of Lords in the heavens.

2. It is said there that this Kingdom began in the days of those Kings. Now, what are the days of which this Text speaks? It speaks of Alexander’s Kingdoms <note>Refers to the successors of Alexander the Great</note>, which conquered the Medes and the Persians; which Empire was divided between Ptolemy Lagus, King of Egypt, and Seleucus, King of Syria; In that time, Jesus Christ established His Kingdom, for He was born King of the Jews.

3. It is evident that this cannot be applied to Christ’s Kingdom in this World of a thousand Years. For of that it cannot be said that it would be a Kingdom for eternity, since a Kingdom of a thousand Years is not an eternal Kingdom; but Daniel says, *the same shall stand in all eternity.*

The fourth passage is **Eph. 5:5.** *For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an Idolater, hath any inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and of God.* Gerhardus <note>Likely Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian</note> notes this text and explains it well; they say there is not only a Kingdom of God (that is, of heaven), but the Scripture mentions a Kingdom of Christ as well as of God. Upon this they build Christ’s Kingdom here upon the earth.

**Answer 1.** It is true, Christ has a Kingdom, but He says explicitly that *His Kingdom is not of this World,* **John 18:36.**

2. Although it is said there that there is a Kingdom of Christ, nevertheless it is not expressed that such shall be upon the earth for a thousand years.

3. This Kingdom of Christ, say the Interpreters, is the same as the Kingdom of God, and both are to be understood together as one and the same thing.

The fifth text that they bring forward is **Matth. 26 verse 29.** *But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the Vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s Kingdom.* They say this cannot be understood as heaven—why? Because one shall not eat or drink there. It is a promise of Jesus Christ not to come to them again until He should drink Wine with them in His Father’s Kingdom; and this cannot be unless Christ comes in Person among His People, and has a Kingdom in which to eat and drink with His People in this World. They insist greatly on this; but for an answer, this serves:

**Firstly,** this cannot be understood as a Kingdom in this world for a thousand years; my reason is this: because Christ’s personal Reign would be called the Kingdom of Christ, and not His Father’s Kingdom; He would have said "My Kingdom," and not "My Father’s."

**Secondly,** know this: that this can be applied to the time of Christ between His Resurrection and Ascension: for after Christ rose from the dead, you know that He spent forty days upon the earth.

# Christ ascends to Heaven

And the Scripture says / *Luke 24:42-43.* And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of a *honeycomb*. And he took it, and ate it before their eyes. Thus he may well have eaten and drunk afterward / although such a thing is uncertain. <note>The author is acknowledging that while the resurrected Christ ate fish to prove His physical resurrection, this does not mean physical eating is a permanent state in heaven.</note>

**Thirdly,** which is also the true purpose of that passage / *I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the Vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's Kingdom.* <note>Matthew 26:29</note> The Savior does not mean to imply here / that there shall be eating and drinking in Heaven / but when he speaks thus / he intends this / we shall have such great fellowship with one another / as if we were eating and drinking together / like holding a feast / which is the bond of fellowship and love / so shall there be a mutual love and a mutual fellowship with Christ in the Heavens; You shall drink it new, not new Wine; nor eat new Bread / but a new manner of love and fellowship with one another and with God eternally.

They say likewise that there shall be no sins in the World / and that the earth shall bring forth pure fruits / as it did before the Fall / but I shall not trouble myself with this. And thus, according to the small measure of my grace / I have labored to withdraw those Scripture passages from them / and shown from them / that Christ cannot come to reign personally upon the earth for a thousand years.

**1. Use.** <note>In 17th-century sermons, a "Use" is a practical application or lesson for the reader.</note> If this is so / that the Scripture determines no coming of Christ from Heaven other than his last / the greatest coming for Judgment? O! then labor to let Jesus Christ reign as King in your heart / through your self-mortification / that he may reign in your heart through his spirit / and kill the strong lusts that are within you.

**2. Use.** Since there is no coming of Christ into this World as King / then labor that you may have Christ to reign in his Church / through a well-ordered discipline / so that the government of Christ may be confirmed in the place where you dwell.

**3. Use.** Since there is no coming of Christ into the World as King / then do not trouble yourselves with unnecessary speculations concerning his coming upon the earth / but be diligent to be ready for his last and greatest coming.

**4. Use.** If Christ were to come to reign upon the earth / (of which the Scripture does not speak) then certainly the Saints in this time would be making a poor preparation for the reign of Christ / having a vain holy service / saying / *We are the people of God, the Church of Christ, and the Saints of Christ,* yet living in such worldliness as they now do / and committing such godlessness as they now do on the earth.

This is but a poor preparation / a meager encouragement for us / and a belittling of Jesus Christ / to come and reign among such Saints as we are / who are but a scandal to the Saints / to Religion / and to the thousand-year reign of Christ / if he were to come in such a way: but Christ desires to have better Saints than these / to reign with him.

In the treatise of Christ’s return—

<column-break/>

there is yet another question / namely / how or in what manner the coming of Christ shall be? *I shall come again.* Now / in the resolving of this question / I shall include my answer in these six things.

1. He shall **Certainly** come.
2. He shall **Personally** come.
3. He shall **Visibly** come.
4. He shall come **Glorified**.
5. He shall come **Terribly**. <note>In this context, "terribly" means "inspiring great awe or dread," rather than "poorly."</note>
6. He shall come **Unexpectedly**.

In so many ways does the Scripture describe his future coming.

**Firstly,** The Lord Jesus shall certainly come: Christ’s coming must not be counted among the Poetic fictions / or among the dreams of *Mahomet* <note>A historical reference to Muhammad; the author is contrasting Christian doctrine with what he considers the "fables" of Islam.</note> / but his certain coming / is built upon these three foundations.

1. This stands upon the unchangeability of God’s decree / *Acts 17:31.* Because he hath appointed a day, in which he will judge the world in righteousness by that Man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead. The unchangeability of God’s decree proves certainly Christ’s coming / God has appointed a day / in which he will judge the world.

2. This certainty stands upon the infallibility of Christ’s promise / *Matthew 26 verse 64.* Jesus said unto him, thou hast said it. Nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven. There is Christ’s promise / with which the other Evangelists agree.

3. The certainty of his coming is grounded on the impartiality of his Justice / where all men shall not have one single sentence / but as *Solomon* says / *A just man perisheth in his righteousness, and a wicked man prolongeth his life in his wickedness;* <note>Ecclesiastes 7:15</note> Therefore / to prove God’s impartiality / there must be a coming of the Son of man / to judge the World righteously. The Doctrine of Christ’s coming is contested by the *Atheists* / as *Peter* relates to you / *2 Peter 3:3-4.* And we read of the men of *Athens* / that they questioned this / and would not believe it / *Acts 17:32.* And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter. In olden times / in the times of Jesus Christ / or shortly thereafter / men mocked the Doctrine of the resurrection / and his coming / to judge both the living and the Dead; such types of heretics *Gerardus* <note>likely Johann Gerhard, a prominent Lutheran theologian</note> notes abundantly / such as the *Florinians*, the *Dositheans*, the *Symmachians*, and many others: Truly / there is but one Scripture passage which these Atheists misuse / to deny Christ’s coming for Judgment / *John 8:15.* Ye judge after the flesh; I judge no man.

But Beloved / this Text which they make a stronghold of their hope / to deny Christ’s return / does not help them / as appears by these two answers; when Christ says / *I judge no man;* he means / I judge no man rashly

And thus I have finished handling the third Teaching.

Now I proceed to the fourth Teaching / in these words / *I will take you to myself.*

These words contain within them that fundamental point of the Resurrection of the body / that not only shall souls go to heaven / but likewise the bodies of the Godly; Christ shall come from heaven for this purpose / to receive the bodies as well as the souls unto himself. *I will come again, I will take you to myself.*

There is some difference among the Interpreters <note>scholars or theologians who explain the Bible</note> over the sense of these words; Some say / that Christ made this promise a little before his death, and it cannot be brought to his final coming, but to his coming of forty days here on the Earth, after his Resurrection; they say / that this promise was fulfilled, when Christ after his Resurrection came to his Disciples, and ate with them of a broiled Fish, and walked forty days with them. Why? What comfort would this be to his Disciples, that Christ would return and remain forty days, and then be no more? This would cause them more sorrow, that they should see him no more. There are two or three Reasons in this Text why this cannot be. This cannot be the meaning of this place / because he promised previously / he went to his Father’s house, and there he would receive them; Now / that life on earth for forty days after his Resurrection / cannot be his Father’s house. Again / it is said there / where he went, there he prepared a place for them; now if the above-told were true / that place must actually be the earth: But the Interpreters seeing this difficulty / give Reasons that are firm / why this must be applied to Christ’s final coming / and the eternal receiving by him / after their Resurrection on the last day: as if he had wanted to say / Although I leave your bodies for a time below in this World / although they might be martyred and killed through persecution / and you for a time

<column-break/>

be without my bodily presence / nevertheless I do not go to heaven / to remain there forever / but I promise you / *I will come again, and take you to myself in heaven.* They were eager for Christ to receive them in Heaven / and that they might go with him. The Disciples, when they heard Christ speak of going to his Father’s house, they were all prepared to go with Christ into heaven: O no / says Christ / I will come again to judge the World / and then I will take your own bodies with me into heaven / just as my body is in heaven / so shall your bodies likewise be there with it.

The Teaching is this / that it is one of the primary purposes of Christ’s return / to take the bodies of the elect unto him in heaven / *I come again and shall take you to myself.* I shall not follow the common treatment of the Resurrection of the bodies / but only explain this according to the practice / showing you / what the blessedness of God’s Elect is / in their bodies / as well as their souls; first I shall handle this particular question / before I come to the Teaching itself.

The Question is this / since Jesus Christ only makes the promise, that he will receive the Believers to himself at his coming, what then of the Godly immediately after their death, before Christ’s coming for judgment? Those who hold to a sleeping of the soul <term>soul sleep: the controversial belief that the soul becomes unconscious or "sleeps" between death and the final resurrection</term> / ground it upon this Text / that there is no taking-back of one or the other, life or death, the Godless are not tormented, the Godly not glorified, immediately after their death; Therefore it is necessary / since Christ here speaks of a taking-to-himself / not [occurring] until his coming / to show what becomes of the Souls / after the death of Men / before the coming of Christ.

Before I give you the Answer / take this distinction / there is a twofold receiving.

First, there is a particular and imperfect receiving / and this happens immediately after death / that when the soul separates from the body / the soul is received by Jesus Christ into heaven / and of this see Acts 7. Stephen was received by Christ’s coming / and this is called a particular and imperfect receiving; it is only a receiving of the Spirit / and not of the body.

Secondly, there is a whole and perfect receiving / of both the body and the soul / in glory / and this is that of which this Text speaks: Although it is true / that there is no whole taking up of the Believers / until Christ comes to judge / nonetheless there is a particular receiving; I do not speak now to those who say / the soul is mortal, and shall never live after the death of the body, but to those who say / the soul shall sleep, and the soul perishes with the body until the resurrection. Now / against those who say that the souls sleep until Christ’s return, take these four things / to strengthen you.

1. There are clear Examples in the Scripture / that after the death of the Godly / their souls are received into Heaven / before Christ’s coming.

3. There are explicit passages in Scripture that confirm this.

4. There are absurd consequences that arise if this is denied.

Firstly, there are clear examples in Scripture proving that after death the soul is received into Heaven. Take three examples. First, that well-known text, *Luke 23:43.* And Jesus said to him, truly I say to you, today you shall be with me in Paradise. On the day that Christ died, he went to Heaven; therefore, on that day, the soul of the converted thief likewise went to Heaven.

Now, Beloved, there are two evasions used by those who promote the "sleep of the soul" <note>This refers to Psychopannychism, the belief that the soul "sleeps" between death and the final resurrection, rather than going immediately to heaven.</note> regarding this text and this example.

The first is by shifting the comma or period in the text; they read it as follows: *today I say to you, you shall be with me in Paradise in the day to come.* *Peter Martyr* <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), an influential Italian-born Reformed theologian.</note> gives these two answers:

1. Answer: It is not proper to change a comma or a point in the Scripture to make our own opinion stand better, as people do for their own pleasure, placing them in the headings as they please.

2. It is evident that this cannot be the meaning here; it must be related to the day and time in which Christ spoke, and not to the time when the thief would be in Heaven; for, says *Gerardus* <note>Likely Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a famous Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note>, note the thief’s prayer in verse 42. And he said to *Jesus*: Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom. Note that he prays that when Christ has come into Heaven, He would then remember him. Christ’s "today" was the answer to his "when"; otherwise, He would not have answered his prayer correctly.

3. It was unnecessary for Christ to say "today" if it only referred to the time when he spoke; he knew Christ was speaking to him and knew that he would be in Heaven with him today.

The second evasion is this: it is true, Christ promises, *You shall be with me in Paradise*; but Christ does not say, *You shall be with me in Heaven.*

Answer: Those who do not wish to understand "Paradise" as "Heaven" in this text fall, along with the *Papists* <note>A term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics.</note>, either into a Purgatory or into a "Limbo of the Fathers" <note>original: "Voor-burg der Vaderen"; a theological concept of a temporary place for the souls of the righteous who died before Christ’s redemption.</note>.

2. In other places in Scripture, when Paradise is mentioned, Heaven is understood, and so the Apostle explains it in *2 Corinthians 12:2, 4.* I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago (whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows) that such a one was caught up to the third Heaven. That he was caught up into Paradise and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. So that the Apostle understands Paradise to be Heaven; likewise in *Revelation 2:7.*

3. It cannot be any earthly Paradise, such as Adam’s Paradise was before the Fall, for this was destroyed by the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>; therefore, of necessity, when Christ says to the thief, *Today you shall be with me in Paradise*, this must be 

<column-break/>

understood as his going to Heaven on that day with *Jesus Christ*.

The second example is *Luke 16:22.* And it came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s Bosom; and the rich man also died and was buried. This is an example which clearly proves that the souls of the Elect go to Heaven after death.

There are two evasions they make regarding this text. First, they say it is a parable and not a historical account.

The answer is: although some say it is a parable, nevertheless many say it is a history. *Hieronymus* <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Bible translator and church father.</note> and many who follow him prove with many arguments that it is a history and not a parable. *Tertullian* <note>Early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note> maintains that it is a history that truly happened; and *Peter Martyr* relates that *Tertullian* recounts this history as so certain that he even names the people; the rich man was *Herod*, and the beggar was *John the Baptist*. But even assuming it is a parable and not a history, nonetheless, parables are also based on truth, and this proves that some people are in hell and some are in Heaven; that there is pain in Hell and joy in Heaven. That just as the beggar went to Heaven after death, so likewise do the godly; and just as the rich man went to Hell, so likewise do the ungodly.

The other evasion is this: that this beggar is said to be carried into Abraham’s Bosom. 1. It is evident that Abraham’s Bosom is Heaven: now, Abraham being in Heaven, all his children who are in his Bosom are there. This is the answer that *Gerardus* gives us.

Furthermore, it says they were carried by the angels into Abraham’s Bosom; therefore, Abraham’s Bosom must be in Heaven. Certainly, the good angels carry a good soul into Heaven, and the evil angels carry a damned soul into Hell.

The third example is *Matthew 22:31-32.* And as touching the Resurrection of the dead, have you not read that which was spoken to you by God, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not a God of the dead, but of the living. I conclude from that example that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob must have been living at that time, though not in their bodies; if you consider the reasoning in this text, it will not only prove the resurrection of the bodies, which the Sadducees denied, but likewise prove the immortality of the soul. The *Sadducees* denied that there were angels or spirits, *Acts 23:8.* Christ proves that there will be a resurrection of the body; likewise, He proves that souls shall not die when the body dies. A learned man makes great use of this example in *Genesis 25:8.* And Abraham gave up the ghost and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people. Abraham did not go to his forefathers or was not buried in the grave with his ancestors; how then can it be true what the Scripture says, that *Abraham was gathered to his people*? The theologians say it must refer to his soul; Abraham went to Heaven, just like his faithful forefathers; that is the meaning

from that saying / his soul was bound up in the bundle of life / and went to Heaven like his forefathers. And so much for the Examples.

The second way to prove that the souls of the Believers go straight to Heaven after Death is through explicit Scripture passages—specifically two places. **Hebrews 12:23**: *To the general assembly and the congregation of the firstborn, who are written in the Heavens, and to God the Judge over all the Spirits of the perfected righteous*; here the Apostle proves that there were Spirits of the perfected righteous there. Now, if their souls perished with their bodies, then the Apostle would say that their Spirits would perish with the body; but here they are the Spirits of the perfected righteous.

The Scripture has a general passage in which the immortality of the Soul is expressed, **Ecclesiastes 12:7**: *The dust returns again to the earth, as it was: and the Spirit returns again to God, who gave it.* Note, there are two things here:

There is the end of the Godly; the body returns again to dust, as it was, and the soul to God. Then the time when this shall be is when he goes home, when this earthly Tabernacle <note>The "earthly tabernacle" is a common biblical metaphor for the human body as a temporary dwelling for the soul.</note> shall be broken, when these supports fail him—which are the feet—and when the windows—which are the eyes—shall be darkened; when nature fades and the body decays through Death. Then the Body returns to dust, and the Spirit to God who gave it.

Thirdly, I shall prove to you from explicit Scripture passages that the souls of the Elect also went to Heaven through Christ's coming; take these four or five passages regarding this. First, **John 6:40**: *And this is the will of the Father who has sent me, that everyone who looks upon the Son, and believes in him, may have eternal life: and I will raise him up on the last day.*

There are two distinct promises: 1. A promise of eternal life. 2. A promise of the resurrection on the last day. The promise of eternal life is distinct from the other promise. The Theologians say that there is an eternal life before the resurrection; namely, that the souls shall live before the last day, when the body shall rise.

The other Text is **Luke 16:9**: *But I say to you, make for yourselves friends of the unrighteous Mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal Tabernacles.* Chemnitius <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), a highly influential Lutheran theologian known for his defense of the Reformation.</note> proves powerfully from this Text what I now intend to show: that immediately after Death, the souls of the Elect go to Heaven. Note: *make for yourselves friends of the unrighteous Mammon.* That is, from your Wealth, so-called because it is unrighteously obtained and possessed with injustice; use your Wealth well, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal Tabernacles. It is in dispute whether this can be applied to the Angels or to the Poor, who shall pray for us that we might be received into Heaven; but Chemnitius says: *Use your wealth well, so that you may be received into the eternal Tabernacles.* Upon your departure / upon

<column-break/>

your death, the Lord receives the elect into the eternal dwellings. Upon this, Chemnitius builds the argument that the souls go to Heaven immediately after death.

The third place is **Philippians 1:23**: *For I am hard-pressed between these two, having a desire to be departed, and to be with Christ. For that is by far the best.* The Apostle joins these two conclusions together: a departure from this World / or from this life, and a desire to be with Christ; he makes no mention of a middle-place where the soul would then go, nor of a Purgatory <note>original: "Vagevyer"</note>, nor of a Limbo of the Fathers <note>original: "Voorburg der Vaderen"; historically believed to be a place where the souls of the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection waited.</note>.

Likewise, you have a fourth Text, **2 Corinthians 5:6**: *Therefore we are always of good courage, and knowing that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord.* We have good courage and are willing to part from the body and to be with the Lord, toward which we labor, that whether present or absent, we may be accepted by him. Note: the Apostle strives to be out of the body and to be with the Lord, so that the soul is with God while it is away from the body.

And again, this is also proven by the prayer of Stephen, **Acts 7:59**: *Stephen said, Lord Jesus, receive my Spirit.* It would have been comfortless for him had he only come to Jesus Christ after 1600 years, and that He would only then receive his soul; but now he prays, *Lord Jesus, receive my Spirit,* which he would not have done if he had not believed that his soul would be received by Jesus Christ immediately after death.

And thus I have given you these Scripture passages which confirm this for you: that the soul does not sleep in the body, but when it departs from there, it goes immediately to Heaven.

Now, fourthly, I shall show you the absurdities that would follow in case one denies that God receives the souls of the Elect before the day of Judgment.

First, it would follow that the Godly would be in a worse state after Death than they were in life; for when they lived, they lived with Christ; Christ dwells in their hearts through faith. Now, if the soul slept with the body, or perished with the same, then Christ could not live therewith; it could not dwell there through faith. So it is unbelievable that the Believers after their death would be in a worse state than they were while they lived, since Christ then lived in them through Faith.

Secondly, it would then follow that God the Father would be crueler to his People than he wants other men to be to their servants who have done their work; note what is written in **Leviticus 19 verse 13**: *You shall not deceptively oppress your neighbor, nor rob him; the wages of a day-laborer shall not remain with you overnight until the morning.* The Master must not long keep the wages of the Workman; now, shall the great God keep something back for you—you who are his servants, who have served him here in this World with a service of faith and hope—until the last day? No, but as

Thirdly, know this: that if the souls of the Elect do not go to Heaven immediately after death, it must then follow that the souls of the godless do not go to Hell immediately after death. ### Use. <note>In 17th-century sermons, the "Use" (Gebruyk) or "Application" is the section where the minister explains how the biblical teaching should be applied to the listener's life.</note>

### 5. Doctrine.

Now I come further to the words: *I will receive you unto myself.* I shall also dwell on this for a little while. And the Doctrine is this: that the primary purpose of Christ's return is to take the resurrected bodies of the Elect unto Himself; not only to make the souls blessed after death, but also to make the bodies rise likewise. There are two questions in this Doctrine regarding the end of Christ's coming, which is the resurrection of the bodies of the Elect and their reception.

The first is: Why must Jesus Christ wake the bodies of the Elect and take them to Him, as well as the souls?

Secondly: When Christ shall take the body to Him, what gifts or presents shall it receive that it does not have now?

**Question 1.** Why must Christ take the body to Him as well as the soul?

**Answer.** There are four reasons for this.

1. Because He Himself arose in His body; Christ’s own body was raised from the dead and taken up into Heaven; and therefore the bodies of the Elect must likewise be there. Where Christ is, His members must be. Christ the head has risen from the dead and was taken up into glory. The Apostle gives this reason in **1 Corinthians 15:12**: *Now if Christ be preached that he rose from the dead, etc.* It is as if he wanted to say: Christ’s resurrection from the dead proves that your bodies must rise from the Grave, even though they lie there dead. **1 Corinthians 6:14**: *And God hath both raised up the Lord, and will also raise up us by his own power.* See also **1 Thessalonians 4:14**. So it is that because of Christ's physical resurrection from the dead and His reception into Heaven, our bodies must also rise and be taken up by Him into glory.

2. The bodies of the Elect must rise because of the indwelling of the Spirit; the Spirit sanctifies the bodies of the Elect as well as the souls. The God of peace sanctifies your purpose. And I pray God that He preserve your soul and body from the evil one at the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. **1 Corinthians 6:18, 19, 20**: *Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body. What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.* Now, the Spirit of God has His gracious working in the body as well as in the soul; therefore the body must as

# The Believers shall always

surely rise from the dead just as the soul; and the Scripture makes this an Argument for the Resurrection, Rom. 8:11: *But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you.* So that if the Spirit who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, and the graces of the Spirit, that same Spirit shall raise up your mortal bodies; therefore, the bodies of the Elect shall rise from the dead and be received into glory with the soul.

3. Because the body has a joining and a co-operation with the soul in all gracious workings; now, therefore, the body shall share with the soul, being received through Jesus Christ, because it has worked with the soul, Rom. 8 verse 13: *For if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.* And since the godly dead endure the workings of the body and the pain for Jesus Christ's sake, therefore shall the Bodies of the Elect likewise share with the souls in that which is good.

4. This comes by reason of the close union which exists between Christ and the believers; Christ is the Head, the believers are the members; now the members must rise and be received by Jesus Christ, so that his body shall be a perfect body. Thus much for the Reasons why Jesus Christ, in his second coming, shall raise up and take to himself the bodies of the Elect as well as their souls.

The second Question is this: But what benefit is this to the body, and what gifts shall the body receive through this, when Christ comes?

**Answer:** In general, I shall tell you that the body shall receive more glorious gifts than it was ever capable of receiving or enjoying here in this World; the body may have the same stature in Christ's coming, but it shall be adorned with better gifts than it is now. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> says: *Take wool, and dip the same in Scarlet or Purple Color; it changes, but the wool remains the same as it was before, yet it is now much more glorious.* The body shall be the same body, but provided with more glorious gifts than it has now.

And thus much in general; now I come to the particulars: I shall answer the question through these six things.

There are six Glorious gifts that the body shall receive from Jesus Christ at his second coming, when he shall take the bodies unto himself.

**First**, From a natural body, as it is now, it shall be made by Christ a Spiritual body; this is the first benefit. You shall set aside the old clothing of your corrupt flesh and blood and be clothed with garments of glory; there is no contradiction here when one says a Spiritual body, for the Apostle uses this manner of speaking, 1 Cor. 15 verse 44: *It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.* The meaning is: the body that lives here is a natural Body, needing natural supports; but,

<column-break/>

says the Apostle, a spiritual body is raised there; it shall no longer have need of natural food, which a natural body requires—no eating, no drinking, no sleeping, or other natural supports—but it shall be a Spiritual body that shall rise. Matt. 22:30: *For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.* The Angels have no need of food or any outward help. Rev. 7 verses 15, 16: *Therefore are they before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple: and he that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them. They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun light on them, nor any heat.* Therefore, O Believing soul, behold your blessedness of soul and body in Glory (they shall no more have need of natural things, just like the Spirits) as the Scripture says, that your bodies shall be received by Christ. The Platonic Philosophers say that the body shall change into a Spirit, into wind, or into air; but there is no reason for this, since the same substance that lived on earth shall also be in Heaven.

**Secondly**, The bodies of the Elect, when Christ shall take them to himself, shall be changed from unworthy to blessed; it may be that some of them are ugly here, yet they shall be purified and glorified by Christ. Phil. 3:21: *Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.* The body of Christ is a blessed body, having no wrinkle or spot; likewise shall our bodies be glorious. 1 Cor. 15 verse 43: *It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.* Here the body is an unworthy body; Eliphaz <note>A reference to Eliphaz the Temanite from the Book of Job.</note> calls it a hut of clay, and Job an Earthly house; It is the opinion of Gerardus <note>Likely Johann Gerhard (1582–1637), a prominent Lutheran scholastic theologian.</note>, and he gives a powerful reason for it, that if there is any defect in the body here in this World, that same shall be restored by the Resurrection; the Reasons he gives are these:

1. Because our bodies have the promise that they shall be like the body of Christ; Now, Christ’s body had no shriveled or defective members, since defect comes from sin; therefore, since our bodies are said to be like Christ’s body, they can have no defect.

2. Some members are necessarily required for the blessedness of the Elect in Heaven; suppose an Elect person was born blind, or had lost his eye by some accident; if he did not have his eye, he could never see Christ in Heaven; we shall see Christ with these very eyes of the body.

3. The third reason is because the bodies of the Elect shall be as Adam’s body was in his innocence <note>Original: "onnooselhept," referring to the state of man before the Fall.</note>; Adam’s body was created perfect by God; when Christ shall cause the body to rise,

### Thirdly,
from a mortal body it shall become an immortal body; just as it is now, it dies and rots in the grave; but it shall be made immortal through Christ; 1 Corinthians 15:52, 53. *In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.* These mortal bodies must die, but be made immortal; and these corruptible bodies must be made incorruptible, never to die or perish; This is a great blessedness of the Elect, that their bodies shall be made immortal bodies.

### Fourthly,
The bodies of the Elect shall be changed from sorrowful and suffering bodies in this world, into <term>impassible</term><note>The original Dutch 'onlijdende' refers to the theological concept of impassibility: being incapable of suffering, pain, or injury.</note> and joyful bodies; the body here is subject to illnesses, pains, destruction, and what else? The body is an Inn of illnesses, a Storehouse of all sorrows; but the Lord shall make this body free from all suffering, and he shall wash away all tears from our eyes; no sorrow nor pain shall be there: This is then also a blessedness of the body, to be freed from all suffering, not to hunger, thirst, feel pain, sorrow, or have anything similar.

### Fifthly,
from a sluggish and heavy body as it is now, it shall be made a swift and light body; the Eagle shall not fly as fast as the bodies of the Elect shall pass from one place to another; this has its ground in the Scripture, 1 Thessalonians 4:14. *For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.* Which the body could not do, if it did not lay aside its weight and sluggishness which it had here; <note>Girolamo Zanchi (1516–1590), a prominent Italian Protestant theologian.</note>Zanchius explains this by this comparison; he says, The body is like a chick in the egg, a bird in the shell and does not fly, but having been hatched and become fledged, then it flies; so also, when you have risen, you can go from one part of the World to the other in a heartbeat; so was Christ’s body after his resurrection; he was quickly taken up into Heaven, which the Astronomers say (if one may believe them) is over 40 Million Miles; Now the soul has a cloddish body that cannot follow it; therefore the body must be made conformable to the soul; the body is now a heavy pack to the soul, but then it shall not be so.

### Sixthly,
From a weak body, a strong body shall be made; 1 Corinthians 15:43. *It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.* The body of man is a weak fleshly thing. <note>Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109), an influential medieval philosopher and theologian.</note>Anselmus is of the opinion, writing on this Text, 1 Corinthians 15, That the body of man shall be so strong, as capable of carrying a Mountain as a child of carrying a catch-ball; This is a great glory which God gives to the body, that he shall make the same from a

<column-break/>

natural to a spiritual body; from a lowly to a glorious body; from mortal to immortal; from suffering to impassible; and from a heavy to a light body; from weak to strong.

### Now, before I come to the application, two objections present themselves to us:
In the Primitive times there were Sadducees who denied the resurrection: after the times of Christ, there were Hymeneus and Philetus, who said, *That the resurrection had already happened*, and with this heresy the Church of Corinth was infected: *if Christ is risen from the dead, how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?* The resurrection of the body was in those times but a poetic fiction, though it is nevertheless undoubtedly true.

#### 1. Objection.
The Scripture which they bring forward to maintain their opinion that the body shall not rise, is where the Apostle explicitly says that the body is made of flesh and blood, 1 Corinthians 15:50. *Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption.* Therefore, if flesh and blood cannot enter the Kingdom of God, how then can the body enter there?

#### 1. Answer.
It cannot be the meaning of the Apostle to deny the resurrection of the bodies, since the entire Chapter is nothing other than a proof thereof; and it is not to be thought that the Apostle would deny something on one page and confirm the same again.

#### 2. The Apostle understands
by flesh and blood, the sinful appendages of the bodies which they carry with them here in the World; the body as it is now is a sinful body, a weak and mortal body, and so it shall never enter into Heaven; this is the common explanation of most Interpreters; we shall not enter into Heaven as we are now, but we shall all be changed; *We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed*, says the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 15 verse 51. Our corruptible bodies shall not enter into Heaven as they are corruptible, but they shall be changed into incorruptible ones; that is, our mortal and weak bodies shall put on immortality and strength, so that flesh and blood, as it is now sinful and depraved, shall not enter into the glory of Heaven unless it is changed.

#### 2. Objection.
The second Text which they bring forward against the glorification of the body, and from which they conclude that it is but a fantasy, stands in Job 14:7, 8, 9, 10. *For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?* A tree, says Job, if it dies, may live again, but if a man dies, where is he? he is no more. Upon this they build that a man shall never live again.

that when Job speaks, "if a tree dies, it lives again; but a man does not," that he then

I prove this from Job’s words in the 14th verse; *So man lies down, and rises not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep;* <note>Job 14:12</note> so that Job speaks there of a resurrection / When the heavens shall be no more; when the World shall burn by fire / man shall awake; and verse 14. *If a man die, shall he live again? The reason that may seem to go against the resurrection of the Body / is this / How is it possible that the bodies of men can rise again, when they are so mingled together in the earth?

Suppose / A man was torn apart and killed by a Wolf, a Lion ate that Wolf, and that Lion happened to die, and the Birds of the air ate the Lion, and men ate these Birds: How can the Bodies of men rise again, which are so changed and confused? Suppose / A man is thrown into the Sea, and the Fish eat him, how can his substance be gathered together on the last day?

Now / in Answer: This Reason can easily be taken away; firstly / if an Artist can make a wonderfully skillful piece of glassware from ashes / why cannot the almighty God make glorified Bodies as beautiful as Christ's from dust and ashes? If from things that are mingled / those which are not mingled can be drawn / and brought to a perfect state / just as a **Refiner** <term>Refiner: a craftsman who purifies metals using heat.</term> may have before him a lump of four kinds of Metal / of Gold / Silver / Iron / and Tin / and mix them all together as one weight: Now / if the Refiner / through the use of fire and art / can separate all the Metals / and bring the Gold together / and also the Silver together / and however mingled the things are, separate them; can the almighty God not do this much more? if a man has that freedom / shall God not have that strength? although the flesh of man is mingled among a thousand worms / cannot the mighty God / through his power gather this flesh together / so that we may be glorified with this our flesh / with him in Heaven?

Again / a Gardener has various seeds in his garden / yet whenever you come to him / and ask / what seed lies in that bed / and what in that / you / because it is rotted / cannot know it / but he shall tell you distinctly / what seed is in each bed; and cannot the great God do this? he who made us knows our substance: we do not know / what man’s dust lies in the grave / but God who brought such into the grave / knows it / he knows which shall be my dust / and which shall be yours /

<column-break/>

and which is each man’s dust; therefore labor to increase your faith / in this great mystery of the resurrection and the glorification of your bodies.

Now I have to make a practical application of all this; the uses are /

1. Is it so that Jesus Christ shall raise your Bodies / and take you to himself in his second coming? let this then comfort you against all suffering in your body, suppose you must endure great suffering / fire / gallows and sword / and that for the sake of Christ; nevertheless remember / your body shall rise / and be glorified with Jesus Christ. Let it not trouble you that your body should become a crucified body / because in Christ’s coming it shall be a glorified Body.

Again / this can comfort you in natural weaknesses; suppose your Body is a sickly Body / full of sorrows / and illnesses / blind or lame / nevertheless remember that your body that is unlovely, deformed and sickly / shall be a fresh tree of Glory / and made like unto the glorified Body of Christ.

We read in the *Book of Martyrs* <note>Likely referring to John Foxe's "Acts and Monuments," a famous history of Christian martyrs.</note> of two Martyrs / who were to be burned / at Stratford-le-Bow near London, the one was named **Hugh Laborocke**, and the other **John Price**, the one was blind / and the other lame; This Price, being fearful when he felt the fire around him / so Hugh said to him / *Be not troubled, although you are blind and I am lame, nevertheless remember, that death shall deliver us, you from your blindness, and me from my lameness.* <note>Hugh Laverock and John Apprice were burned at the stake in 1556 during the Marian Persecutions.</note> Suppose you are blind / lame and crippled / Christ’s taking you up shall make you free from all those / and truly / this can comfort a person under physical infirmity / when he remembers that this Body shall rot in the grave / and shall be raised in a blessed body / free from all deformity / from all diseases and defects.

2. The second utility is for exhortation / shall Christ in his second coming raise your Bodies / and take you to himself? Learn then here to have an earnest longing of the soul for Christ’s second coming; do not strive to remain continually on the earth / but to be released and to be with Christ. Shall anyone be sad to change his old garment for a new one? This is what Death does / it renews the old skins of your flesh / into the new garment of Christ; Therefore the Apostle calls the effort of the body "to be clothed"; we must not desire to be in Heaven without clothes / but we must strive to be clothed with those Glorious gifts / which the Elect shall enjoy in glory; therefore be not unwilling to die / be not unwilling to become old and stinking carrion / a sickly / and a defective Body. Put a Bird in a cage / although a cage is made of silver or of gold / nevertheless the Bird would rather fly in the air / than sit in the cage. While you are in the body / you are in a cage / and you shall have it better / than to be here in a glorious prison.

3. Be not grieved or unwilling to die / because the Body shall be changed by death; if the Body does not turn to dust / it could never be a glorified Body; keep your corn in the house / and you shall never have a heap in the Harvest /

-> Why does Christ say that he is in Heaven, when he was nevertheless in his body on the earth? <-

1 Answer. That Christ says / **I am**, signifies the certainty of his going to Heaven / that he shall be there as surely as if he were already there. **Babylon is fallen** <note>A reference to Revelation 18:2</note> / truly the Papacy has not fallen / yet it shall be as certain / as if it had already happened.

2. The haste of the same / he ascended quickly to Heaven; there was but a day between him and his Ascension: things that happen quickly / are said to be done when they are happening.

3. Gerardus gives this Reason / Christ expresses this in the present tense / **Where I am**, although he was on the earth / to show / that he was as truly God as man / and in respect of his Divine nature / he was truly in Heaven / and according to his human nature he was on the earth. So much then for the manner of this speech / that / **where I am you shall also be**, the last part is this / that you shall be there where Christ is.

Note one thing here / that in the language of Scripture / there is a great distinction / between Christ’s being with us / and our being with Christ; when Christ is said to be with us / it signifies not a personal presence / but a presence through his Spirit /
<margin>Matt. 28: 20.</margin>
> And behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.
This was not according to his Person / for he left them / but I am with you by my blessing in my Spirit; but when the Scripture speaks of our being with Christ / then it consists of a personal presence with Christ: therefore Paul says,

Christ was with Paul, because Christ had converted him; but Paul was not with Christ / but busied himself to be dissolved and to be with him: our being with the Lord / signifies a personal presence / an enjoyment of the presence of the Lord.

The Doctrine is this; that Christ in his second coming / shall take the believers to himself in Body and Soul / so that they might always enjoy / the Personal presence of Christ in Heaven / **That you may be / where I am**. # The Believers shall always #

...present in the **State of Innocence**; <note>The "State of Innocence" refers to the theological concept of humanity’s condition before the Fall of Adam and Eve.</note> we would be exceedingly blessed in the present enjoyment of God / and have a glorious state / if it were so / as it was with Adam; but now / to be present with Christ in Heaven / is ten thousand times more glorious / than if you had lived with Adam in the State of his Innocence.

1. Adam, when he was made by God in his first state / he was only placed by God in an **Earthly Paradise** / but now that you are brought to Christ / you are placed in an eternal Kingdom.

2. Adam pleased himself / and was content in his innocence / which state / and glory he could nevertheless lose / as he / alas! did / although he was a perfect Creature / yet he could lose it; but when God shall bring you into the presence of Christ / then you shall be placed in a Kingdom / that shall not be taken from you / in a blessed state / which you shall never be able to lose.

3. When Adam was placed by God in the state of innocence / he enjoyed only the company of the beasts on the earth / and birds of the air; but when God brings you where Christ is / he brings you into a state with God the Father / God the Son / and all the Saints and Angels are your company.

**Secondly**, there is yet another part of blessedness / when you are where Christ is / that you shall enjoy the company of Jesus Christ in his **human nature**; where Christ is / there you shall be, John 17:24. 
> Father, I will that where I am, those also whom you have given me may be with me: so that they may behold my Glory. 
Beloved / this is a blessed sight / to see the Glory of Christ's Person / in his human nature / not the glory of his Divinity / but that of his humanity / which he carried about when he was on the earth; all the Elect who were long before him / lived alongside him / or have come after him / shall see him to their glory / in his human nature; it was a wish of **Augustine**, <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> a wish before his death / that he might see three things / and then he wished to die in peace; First / **Rome in its full glory**, **Paul in the Pulpit**, and **Christ in the flesh**: every believer shall see the Lord Jesus in the flesh. Job assured himself of this / long before Christ’s birth / 
> I know that my Redeemer lives, and with these eyes of mine I shall behold him. 
In this is the blessedness / being brought to the Savior / that you shall have the company of Christ in his human nature. 1 John 3:2. 
> Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be: but we know, that when he shall be revealed, we shall be like him: for we shall see him as he is. 
Now we do not fully know what Christ is / then we shall know him / and see him as he is glorified / in Heaven.

**Thirdly**, this shall increase the blessedness of the Elect / that in Christ's presence / God shall give them more honor / than they were previously capable of receiving; God gives glory / by the power of being with Christ, John 12:26. If anyone serves me, let him follow me: and where I am, there also shall

my Servant be. And if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. That is / where I am in Heaven. Beloved / now is the time to give honor and glory to God / but when you are with Christ / God shall give glory and honor to you.

**Fourthly**, this is also your blessedness / that you shall not stand under **necessary ordinances**; <note>The "ordinances" refer to the outward means of worship used on earth, such as preaching, the sacraments, and formal prayer.</note> Beloved / here a Christian stands under the ordinances / by which he must walk / like a cripple with his crutches: but when you shall have come to this perfection / that you shall be where Christ is / you then stand not under the ordinances / what need is there then for the **Candlestick** of Preaching or of Prayer / when you are present with the **Sun of Righteousness**? A **fifth privilege** / that you shall enjoy / when you are with Christ / is this / that you shall have full communion and company with Christ in his Person. Beloved / this communion here is far different from the communion which we shall have in Heaven.

1. It shall differ in respect to the **manner of enjoyment**; in this World you enjoy Christ / mediately through his ordinances / now you see him but as in a Mirror (as the Apostle says) but in Heaven you shall enjoy Christ Personally / and have company immediately with him in Heaven.

2. In respect to the **measure of your enjoyment**; here you enjoy Christ in part / a small drop of his Spirit / but then you shall enjoy a full Ocean.

3. It differs in respect to the **time and duration**: here you enjoy Christ / it is true / but sometimes and seldom / but in Heaven you shall enjoy him / always and eternally / this communion shall not decay.

4. There is also a distinction in **expectation** / in Heaven you shall have Christ in possession.

5. In respect to the **place** / there is a great distinction in the place between Christ and us / here we enjoy Christ / he is in Heaven and we are on earth: but then we shall enjoy Christ in one place / in Heaven / now you may think much of Christ / but hereafter you shall be with him in one place / see him and know him.

### I. KINGS 14.
->In the middle of the 13th verse.<-

> Because in him some good thing toward the Lord God of Israel in the house of Jeroboam is found.

<margin>1st Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry within London, March 9, 1651.</margin>
This Chapter contains within it *Ahijah’s* <note>original: "Ahia's"</note> Prophecy / recounting the sorrowful judgments / which would fall upon *Jeroboam* and his descendants; because of his Idolatry / and his falling away from the government / and the house of David. For which <margin>1 Kings 15:19.</margin> sins God struck him and his descendants: And not only the wicked / but also the good were punished for their Father’s guilt. For so it is made known in this verse / from which this Text is taken.

Here is a young Child / a Son of *Jeroboam*, who was to die for his Father’s misdeeds; and here is also a consolation regarding the punishment / that he would not die in the same manner as the others: <margin>1 Kings 14:13.</margin> he alone shall come to the grave; because in him some good thing was found. See here the goodness of God / who takes notice of a small Child / and of a little good within him. God

<column-break/>

finds, as it were, a pearl among a heap of common stones / a good young Child in *Jeroboam's* household / who had some good thing in him toward the Lord the God of Israel.

In this entire verse there are three parts:
1. A lamentation over the Death of the Son of *Jeroboam*; for it is written / all *Israel* shall mourn for him; as they also did in verse 18 / which is proof that there was yet some good in him: for if he had not been desired and praised in his life / he would not have been so lamented after his death.
2. A mitigation of his punishment / he alone of *Jeroboam’s* household shall come to the grave: the rest of his descendants / who die in the City / shall be eaten by the dogs; and those who die in the field / shall be eaten by the birds / verse 11.
3. The commendation of his life / in him some good thing is found: of which part I now intend to treat.

He is praised by the Holy Spirit / for his goodness is presented,
1. By the quality of his goodness: it was *some good thing*, not just a good word / or an intention or inclination / with which many People content themselves; but it was a good deed.
2. By the greatness of it: it was only some *small* good that was found in him: and yet God did not despise that same good.

<header>Grace, with its</header>

3. Through the sincerity of his goodness; wherein two demonstrations of this young Child's goodness are found;
1. It was before the Lord, the God of Israel.
<margin>2 Corinthians 12:19.</margin>
<margin>Galatians 1:20.</margin>
2. It was in Jeroboam's house.
1. His goodness before the Lord, the God of Israel: this was a proof of Paul's sincerity, that in his speaking, saying, and deeds he could appeal—and indeed did appeal—to God. Religion, says the
<margin>James 1:27.</margin>
Apostle, is pure and undefiled before God and the Father. Many hypocrites are good before Men, but not before God; to be rich in
<margin>Luke 12:21.</margin>
<margin>Acts 20:21.</margin>
<margin>Acts 24:16.</margin>
deed, is to be rich in God: True conversion is conversion to God: and he who is free from offense, both toward God and toward Men, he is truly irreproachable.

2. His goodness in the house of Jeroboam: a wicked Man may well seem to be good in a good place; but to be good in an evil place proves that the Man is good indeed. To be good in David's house is not as much as it was for this young Child to be good in the house of Jeroboam his Father: whom the Scripture marks for his idolatry, saying that he led all Israel into sin; yet he could not move his Son to it. This proves then that he was sincerely good: just as it was a proof of Lot's sincerity that he was righteous in Sodom; of Job, that he was pious in Chaldea; so also that there were saints in Nero's Palace. <note>Refers to Philippians 4:22, where Paul mentions "those of Caesar's household."</note> To fear God in Jeroboam's household is indeed true piety, or goodness.

There is only one difficulty in the Text, namely:
What was the "good thing" that was found in Abijah? <note>original: "Abia"</note>
It is true, the Scripture does not express in particular what that good thing was that was found in him; but Tostatus <note>Alonso Tostado (1400–1455), a prolific Spanish biblical scholar.</note> and Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), an influential Reformed theologian.</note> relate from the Hebrew Rabbis that when the Israelites of the ten Tribes wanted to go to Jerusalem at the appointed times according to God's command to worship, Jeroboam sent out soldiers to intercept and capture them on the roads; but that this Abijah hindered the soldiers from killing them, and so provided a passage for them to go to Jerusalem to worship there, also giving them courage in this, despite the cruelty of his Father, who had scorned the true worship and service of God and had set up the Calves at Dan and Bethel. <note>Jeroboam set up golden calves in these cities to prevent his subjects from traveling to the southern Kingdom of Judah to worship.</note>

Others believe that the goodness of this young Prince lay in this: that he would not agree with his Father in the rebellion against the government of the house of David: but where the Scripture has no tongue to speak, we have no ear to hear; and therefore we will not undertake to define what the Scripture has not defined.

There are many observations which I might draw from the particular circumstances of the Text; yet I shall handle only some of them. The first observation: that this pious Abijah died:
<margin>1st Observation.</margin>
Good Men, useful instruments of whom one might have great hope, can be snatched away by Death; while wicked Men live long upon the earth.

<column-break/>

The evil Jeroboam lived long; his pious Son died quickly; so true is what Solomon says: a righteous Man can perish in his righteousness, while a wicked Man prolongs his days in wickedness. Thorns and Thistles do not [wither] as quickly as Lilies and Roses; those of whom the World is not worthy can be taken away from the World; and those who are not worthy to live in the World are left behind.

<margin>1 Kings 14:16.</margin>
The second observation from the Death of the God-fearing Abijah, while the wicked Nadab, the other Son of Jeroboam, still lived, note:
<margin>2nd Observation.</margin>
That good Children can be snatched from their Parents by Death, while wicked Children live long to their Parents' shame and curse.

The third observation from the cause why this pleasant Young Man died so soon: it was because of his Father's sin, as we may read in verses 9, 10, 11, 12. Note here:
<margin>3rd Observation.</margin>
That good Children, as well as wicked ones, can be punished for the sins of their Parents.

The fourth from the mourning of all Israel over the Death of this Young Man; note:
<margin>4th Observation.</margin>
That good Men, who have been useful and might have been further useful in their lives, shall be most lamented upon their Death.
<margin>Isaiah 57:1.</margin>

The fifth from these words: "he shall come to his grave in peace"; note:
<margin>5th Observation.</margin>
That it is a great blessing to come to one's grave in peace in times of War and common sorrow.

The sixth: He was good before God; note from this:
<margin>6th Observation.</margin>
He is indeed good who is good before God as well as before Men; many are good in Man's sight who are not good in the sight of God.
<margin>Romans 8:31.</margin>

There are yet two other circumstances in which I shall engage myself a little before I come to the main point which I intend to handle; namely:

The age of the Son of Jeroboam, who is praised here for his piety: it is said, "he was a Child," verse 12.

From which we may remember:
<margin>1st Teaching.</margin>
That it is very praiseworthy to see piety in young people: it is a very excellent thing to see young Men who are also pious Men.

There were indeed more good people in that time, but none so early good as Abijah was when he was a Child: and therefore he is remembered to his praise in Scripture.

1. I shall show you that it is an excellent thing to see young Men pious: I prove this;
<margin>1 Kings 18:12.</margin>
First, because the Scripture makes a very honorable mention of it: as first of Obadiah, that "he feared the Lord from his youth." And of
<margin>2 Timothy 1:15.</margin>
Timothy, that "he knew the Holy Scriptures from childhood." Jerome writes that John
<margin>John 13.</margin>
was the most beloved Disciple because he was the youngest
<margin>Jeremiah 2:2.</margin>
of them all. God remembers the kindness of our youth: God takes more kindly notice of the kindness of our youth than of our Old Age. John rejoiced that he found Children walking in the truth.
<margin>2 John 4.</margin>

Secondly, because God loves modest and common piety in young people; of which we have an example in the Gospel, where Christ loved the Young Man for his modest piety and natural sincerity.
<margin>Matthew 19:14.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the virtue of Abijah, the young prince, exploring why piety is especially praiseworthy in youth and providing biblical examples of God favoring the younger over the elder.</meta>

# Various Degrees

<margin>2 Timothy 2:21</margin>
2. The reason why it is excellent for young people to be pious is this: because their temptations are greater, and their passions are stronger to lead them away from God. Youth has a stronger capacity and inclination toward sinning than any other stage of life; their blood rises more quickly to anger, and their strength to pleasure. Just as every station of life has its particular sins, so too does each age of a person’s life: Great Old Age is grumpy and covetous; Middle Age is proud, wicked, and inclined to revenge; young people are commonly hasty, lustful, and wanton. Therefore, Paul commanded Timothy to flee the lusts of youth. Youth is said to lie open to many kinds of temptations and evil corruptions, and therefore it is a counsel of wisdom to see young people be pious.

<margin>1st Use</margin>
You young people, then, be exhorted to become religious in your youth, and urge yourselves toward it: for observe,

<margin>Psalm 71:9 compared with verse 5</margin>
1. That if you are not pious in your youth, you can never say with the Psalmist: *Cast me not off, O Lord, in the time of old age; and forsake me not while my strength fails.* For the Prophet was heard to say, *You are my hope, O Lord, my trust from my youth up.* And who would not wish to have such a reason for comfort on their deathbed?

2. Observe that many young people are remembered in the Scriptures who were pious. And the Holy Spirit records not only their piety, but also their age in which they were pious: Solomon a young King, Obadiah a young Courtier, Daniel a young Prophet, John a young Apostle, Timothy a young Preacher, and here, Abijah a young Prince. All these were pious men; and these same ones are presented to us as examples and for encouragement, recorded by the Holy Spirit for our remembrance.

3. Also observe that God, in the distribution of His grace, often gives it to the youngest and passes by the eldest. See this in Abel, who was righteous, whereas Cain was godless; Jacob was loved, Esau hated; and likewise, the youngest son of Jesse,

<margin>1 Samuel 16:11, 12</margin>
namely David, was chosen by the Lord. God often does as Jacob did when he

<margin>Genesis 48:14</margin>
blessed the children of Joseph, stretching out his right hand and laying it upon the head of the youngest son, Ephraim. So also does God in the distributions of His grace upon the youngest; and He says, like Joseph, "Bring my Benjamin," and gives him a double portion. <note>Refers to the biblical narrative where Benjamin receives a larger share of food and favor from Joseph than his older brothers.</note>

4. The time of our youth is the best time of our lives to exercise ourselves in Religion and in the dutiful obligations of godliness. Young people who attend to their work have greater freedom and less worry than when they have come to their later years; for then they are full of the care and anxieties of the household, and their hearts are tied to that block. <note>The "block" refers to a heavy wooden clog or weight, symbolizing the heavy burdens and responsibilities of domestic and professional life.</note>

<margin>1 Corinthians 7:33</margin>
5. If you are not blessed with grace in your youth, then the sins of your youth shall trouble your conscience in your old age. Many young people, fast and windy in the heat of their youth, receive those physical breaks and blows so that they feel the pain of them until their dying day. You who give your conscience a break or a wound 

<column-break/>

in your youth may still feel it in your old age.

The sins which you do not feel now shall stir your conscience and pain your heart when you lie on your deathbed. And although God does not remember the sins of your youth for the damnation of your soul <note>For those who have repented.</note>, He will nevertheless bring them to your mind to the disturbance of your conscience. Things which are the joys of our youth shall be the bitter burdens of our old age. Beware then while you are young, so that God does not write bitter things against you when you are old, and let you inherit the sins of your youth, filling your bones with the sins of your young days.

<margin>Job 13:26</margin>
<margin>Job 20:11</margin>

Now follows a second use of reproof against two kinds of people:

First, of those who, instead of being pious while they are young, are on the contrary wicked in their youth, spending their young years in many kinds of evils. Now youth is commonly subject to these evils:

1. Puffing up <note>Pride or conceit.</note> is a sin of youth; for Paul says that a teacher must not be a novice, lest he be puffed up.

<margin>2 Timothy 3:6</margin> <note>Actually 1 Timothy 3:6.</note>

2. Thoughtlessness and indiscretion are commonly the sins of a young head. Exhort the young men (says Paul to Titus) to be sober-minded; that is, discreet and wise. How hasty and headstrong was the counsel of the young men to Rehoboam, which caused him to lose his kingdom. Years give experience.

<margin>Titus 2:6</margin>

3. Lust, which was the ground of Paul's warning to the young Timothy. If Timothy—who was such a sober young man that Paul advised him to drink a little wine with his water—still had need of the warning, how much more then those who are not so exercised in the dutiful obligations of mortification? <note>Mortification: the spiritual practice of subduing physical desires.</note> This moved Solomon to give this advice: "Remove evil from your flesh, for childhood and youth are vanity." It was a young man who followed the harlot to her house.

<margin>2 Timothy 1:22</margin> <note>Likely 2 Timothy 2:22.</note>
<margin>Ecclesiastes 11:10</margin>
<margin>Proverbs 7:7</margin>

4. Fickleness and instability of judgment; therefore, young people are more subject to the danger of errors and being led astray: children are moved like the tide and carried about with every wind of doctrine, says Paul in Ephesians 4:14. The Hebrews call young men <term>Naezad</term> <note>original: "Naezad"</note>, which corresponds with <term>Nazad</term> <note>original: "Nazad"</note>, meaning to move hither and thither, signifying that they are unstable and fickle in their judgment and resolutions. How quickly was the mind of that rich and forward young man in the Gospel changed?

<margin>Ephesians 4:14</margin>
<margin>Matthew 19:22</margin>

5. To mock and despise old age, just as the children mocked the old Prophet, and those younger in days laughed at the pious Job.

<margin>2 Kings 2:23</margin>
<margin>Job 1:4</margin> <note>Likely Job 30:1.</note>

<margin>Judges 14:10</margin>
