# Graces and their Properties

...Jehoiada stood: but when he was dead, did he <note>Referring to King Joash, who fell into sin after his mentor Jehoiada died.</note> burst out into godlessness?

<margin>Proverbs 31:1</margin> How many are there in the world who have now lost the affection and desires they once had for God in their youth! It is recounted in Scripture concerning Solomon, that when he was young, he was well-instructed by his mother; yet having become old, his wives drew his heart away from God. Likewise, David’s first days were better than his last. In the same way, we have many among us who, when they were young, loved Religion and rejoiced in the ordinances of God; but having grown old, they have abandoned them: which makes me doubt the sincerity of their piety; for he who is truly pious in his youth will also be so in his old age.

The second memorable circumstance is this: that this youth Abijah was pious in the house of Jeroboam <note>Jeroboam was the king who led the northern tribes of Israel into state-sponsored idolatry.</note>: from which you may remark,

-> That it is a great praise and honor for people to preserve their piety while living in evil places and households. <-

That this is so, we can see in the passages where the Scripture mentions those who were good in evil places. <margin>Revelation 2:12</margin> Thus God praises the Church of Pergamum: *I know your works, and where you dwell, namely, where the throne of Satan is: and you hold fast my name; and have not denied my faith; even in those days in which Antipas was my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.* Pergamum was a city more inclined to idolatry than all the cities in Asia, and yet there were some there who kept the name of Christ and did not deny his faith. <margin>Philippians 4:22</margin> To be holy in the household of Emperor Nero <note>Nero was the Roman Emperor notorious for his cruelty and first state-led persecution of Christians.</note> is very excellent. The reason for this is:

1. Because many of God’s children have lost much of their piety in evil places: just as Peter did in the hall of the High Priest; although he was fiery in good company, yet there he denied Christ. So Abraham, when he was in Gerar, and Isaac likewise, denied their wives: so Joseph learned the "oath of the Court" in Pharaoh’s Palace, to swear "by the life of Pharaoh." For this reason, God commanded the Children of Israel not to mingle with the Heathens, so they would not learn their manners and customs. Evil places are like a foul air; through the instinct to breathe and take it in, just as a sheep among thorns loses some of its wool, so the pious lose a part of their piety in evil company. Just as one scabby sheep infects an entire flock, so also can a "root of bitterness" spring up and defile many. <margin>Hebrews 12:15</margin>

2. Reason. Because it is a clear proof of the sincerity of a man’s piety to be pious in an evil place. This demonstrates your grace to be grace in deed, when your being good is opposed; and yet you remain holy: and it is a certain proof that you are sincerely good, and that your goodness is not counterfeit, nor taken up for a wrong or hypocritical purpose. It is good to be good with the good: but it is more excellent to be good among the evil; and to be the best among the worst.

<margin>Application</margin> Learn from this the power and steadfastness

<column-break/>

of saving grace. Grace keeps a man pious even in the worst of times: let a man be thrown into a prison, or into evil company (which is the worst visitation), he shall nevertheless not lose his graces. True grace is compared to oil; now, pour oil into a vessel of water, and you shall find that the oil does not mix with the water, but that it floats upon it; so also shall grace float upon the water of temptation and overcome it. All the water in the salt sea cannot make the fish salty; likewise, all the godless in the world cannot change the nature of grace: for a good person preserves his goodness in evil places, just as a fish in the sea preserves its freshness. Thus Joseph preserved his piety in the Court of the godless Pharaoh; Nehemiah in the Court of Artaxerxes; Obadiah in the Court of Ahab; Daniel in the Court of Nebuchadnezzar; the saints in Nero’s house; and Abijah in the house of the godless idol-worshiper Jeroboam.

<margin>2nd Consideration</margin> Although it is a praiseworthy thing to be good in evil places, you may and must nevertheless fear for your life in evil places: for it is your misery, though not your sin. <margin>Isaiah</margin> Thus said Isaiah: *Woe is me, for I perish; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people that is of unclean lips.* And David: *Oh woe is me! that I am a stranger in Meshech; that I dwell in the tents of Kedar:* <margin>Psalm</margin> that is, with a sinful, idolatrous, and barbaric people, the descendants of Ishmael. Thus was the righteous soul of Lot weary from day to day while he lived in Sodom and saw their immoral conduct. <margin>2 Peter</margin>

<margin>3rd Consideration</margin> Here we may learn that it is our bounden duty that the more wicked the place or house is where God has set our dwelling, the more we must strive, on the contrary, to be the better and the more blameless: for by this we shall adorn our confession; stop the mouths of our adversaries; and entice and win others to embrace Christianity. <margin>Philippians</margin> *That you may be blameless and sincere, Children of God, being without rebuke in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation: among whom you shine as lights in the world.* Just as the stars shine brightest on a dark night, and the fire burns hottest on a cold and frosty day: so also must the stars of your confession shine brightest in the dark places where you live; and the fire of your zeal burn hottest in a cold time, when the love of many grows cold.

<margin>4th Consideration</margin> It is certainly a poor defense for people to want to excuse their godlessness because they live in evil places: just as Abraham wanted to excuse his lie at Gerar. <margin>Genesis</margin> <margin>Seneca: *I am not ambitious, but the place holds me.*</margin> <note>original: "Sen. Non amb sed me sum ma ten Ser" — This refers to a passage in Seneca’s Moral Letters where he argues that we blame our surroundings for our own internal vices.</note> Seneca rebukes a man because he laid the blame for his wickedness on the place where he lived, when he said, *I am not ambitious by nature; but no one who lives in Rome can be otherwise; I am not extravagant; but I must do so because I am in Rome.* It is the wickedness of your heart, and not of the place, that makes you evil: no place, no matter how good, can make a person free from sin: the Angels sinned in Heaven, Adam in Paradise, Judas in the company of Christ: and no place, no matter how evil, can excuse a person from sin.

<summary>This page argues that true religious virtue is most evident when maintained in corrupt environments, using biblical figures like Abijah and Joseph as examples. It concludes that environment is no excuse for sin, as evil originates in the heart rather than one's surroundings.</summary>
<keywords>piety, Abijah, Jeroboam, temptation, environment, Solomon, Seneca, grace, steadfastness, Rome</keywords>

# Various Degrees.

<margin>5. Application.</margin>
If it is so laudably good to be righteous in evil places, then on the contrary, it is just as hideously evil to be wicked in good places, and to be a wild boar in a beautiful meadow. Oh, how many are evil in godly households, who despise good counsel and hate the duties of God’s service within them! If it was so evil for Peter to be wicked among the High Priest’s servants <note>Referring to Peter's denial of Christ in the courtyard of the High Priest.</note>, how much more gruesome was it for Judas to be wicked and a traitor among the Apostles—yes, even within the family of Christ Himself.

<margin>
6. Application.
A good man is easily made worse by the company of the wicked. <note>Original Latin: *Bonus malis consortio facile pejoratur*.</note>
Jude 23.
</margin>
Do not rejoice in being in evil places and companies; for if you delight in them, it is proof that you are evil yourself. We must also hate the garment spotted by the flesh. Some interpret this to mean that one must hate the opportunities to sin; but Mr. Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note> explains it well, saying that one must hate evil company. He says this refers to the ceremonial laws:
<margin>Leviticus 13:4.</margin>
If a person had a leprous garment, or a garment otherwise become unclean, their presence had to be avoided. Therefore, God commanded not to plow with an ox and a donkey together; for the donkey was an unclean animal, but the ox was one of the clean beasts; and therefore they could not be in the same yoke. This was to show (as the theologians say) that the people of God must not draw the same yoke with the worldly. Although they may eat together at convenient times, they must not go in the yoke together. One may certainly trade with the most godless person alive, for commerce is not forbidden; but our joining together with the godless is a wicked and forbidden fellowship.
<margin>Deuteronomy 22:10.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 26:4, 5.</margin>

<margin>7. Application.</margin>
Maintain conversation with the pious, and rejoice in those who are godly. It is permitted to be in evil company when it is for a righteous cause; but it is more profitable to be in good company. Solomon says, he who walks with the wise shall become wise; but he who is a companion of fools shall be destroyed. Just as a man who enters a shop of sweet-smelling spices carries the scent away with him for a while, so shall a man, by keeping company with the pious, carry something good away with him. Always labor to choose such companions from whom you can receive something good. And if God places you in a house like the house of Jeroboam, follow the pious Abijah, of whom it is said: *That in him some good thing toward the Lord God of Israel was found, even in the house of Jeroboam.*
<margin>Proverbs 13:20.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That God not only diligently takes notice of the smallest beginnings and weakest measures of grace which He works in the hearts of His people, but He also tenderly nurtures and generously rewards them.

I could bring forth a cloud of witnesses here to confirm this point. Our Savior Christ says that *He shall not break the bruised reed, and the smoking wick He shall not quench.*
<margin>Matthew 12:20.</margin>

Note: it is not said here that the strong tree shall not be broken, but the *bruised reed*; not the shining and flaming torch, but the *smoking wick* shall not be quenched. The smoking wick, which has only a little fire and much smoke of weakness—Christ will not quench it, but feed it. It is a manner of speaking called *Meiosis* in the schools <note>A rhetorical figure of speech where something is understated for emphasis; in this case, "not quenching" implies actively protecting and strengthening.</note>, where less is spoken than is meant. Instead of quenching the smoking wick, He wants to nurture it. So in another place, God is said not to despise a broken heart; that is, He shall hold it in high esteem.
<margin>Psalm 51:17.</margin>

Solomon says, *The fig tree brings forth her young figs, and the vines with their young grapes give a smell*; that is, the small measure and weak beginnings of grace in the young convert please the Lord Jesus Christ and are a sweet savor in His nostrils. Christ says, *Let us see if the vine flourishes, whether the tender grapes appear, and the pomegranates bud*; for Christ takes as much notice of the green buds as of the ripe fruits.
<margin>Song of Solomon 2:12.</margin>
<margin>Song of Solomon 7:13.</margin>

To open this Doctrine, I shall endeavor to explain these things:
1. That some of God’s people have only small measures and weak beginnings of grace.
2. That although they have only a small grace, God shall nonetheless take notice of it and reward it.

1. That some of God’s people have only a small grace, as being only beginnings of grace worked in their souls.
<margin>1. Proposition.</margin>

In this handling, three things are to be noted:
1. The truth of the proposition must be proven from Scripture.
2. I shall set forth some signs of discovery to recognize those who have only small measures of grace worked in them.
3. I shall show why God in His wisdom does not allow all His people to be of an equal strength of grace.

1. How does it appear that some of God’s people are weak in grace?
<margin>1. Question.</margin>

1. Some are called strong, others weak. 2. Some are called young children in Christ; others, fathers. 3. Some are but young goats and lambs in the flock of Christ; others are like bell-wethers leading the flock. 4. Some have a grace which flames in great fire and liveliness.

Having finished the remarks which could be gathered from the circumstances of the text, I come to the main doctrine which I intend to treat, namely:

# Grace, with its [Degrees]

<margin>1 Pet. 4:4.</margin> They have the spirit of burning, and others are like a smoking wick; that is, Christians who have much smoke of weakness and only a small flame of grace. <note>The author contrasts the "spirit of burning"—a fervent, consuming zeal—with the "smoking wick" of Isaiah 42:3, representing a fragile, flickering faith.</note>

<margin>2. Answer.</margin> 2. Through the correspondence that exists between spiritual and natural differences in age, strength, and stature in man; Holy Scripture presents all the various degrees of grace under the likeness of the different ages of men.

<margin>Gal. 4:19.</margin> 1. There is a shaping of Christ in the heart, and a spiritual conception.

<margin>1 Pet. 1:23. Song of Sol. 2:2.</margin> 2. There are those who are like newborn babes in Christ.

<margin>1 John 2:13.</margin> 3. There are those who have proceeded from their childhood to youth.

<margin>1 John 2:13.</margin> 4. There are those who have become men in Christ, fathers, and old men. All these things prove the various degrees of grace that are in Christians, some having less and some having more.

<margin>Song of Sol. 4:13, 15.</margin> In the Church of Christ, which is His orchard, there are all kinds of trees: spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh, and aloes, etc.

<margin>Brightman.</margin> Brightman <note>Thomas Brightman (1562–1607) was an influential English Puritan clergyman and biblical scholar.</note> writes concerning this passage that the various degrees of Christians are understood here. Spikenard and saffron are young, weak professors; these are the tender plants that scarcely poke their heads above the earth. Calamus and cinnamon, which were shrubs two cubits high, signify Christians of a middle state; and the other trees signify Christians of a more excellent measure and growth in grace.

<margin>2. Question.</margin> The second question is: how can a person know that he has a small measure and beginning of grace?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin> 1. If you cling too much to the "helping-duties," <note>Refers to the "means of grace," such as prayer, fasting, or attending sermons, which are meant to support faith rather than be the object of faith themselves.</note> that is a proof that you are still weak in grace. A young Christian is like a young carpenter: he makes many shavings and strikes many blows, and yet he does not produce such smooth work as an experienced carpenter, who with fewer blows and fewer shavings will make better work. So it is also with young Christians: they are very busy in the use of the helping-means, but they might also easily lean upon them. They believe that these means make them holy, and they might easily make saviors out of their helping-means. Young Christians are: 1. Very inclined toward helping-means. 2. Constant in the means. 3. They do not see their failures regarding their means, and how easily they might come to rest upon those helping-means. Just as it is a sign of an apostate professor that he lays aside his helping-means or duties, so it is also a sign of a young and weak professor that he leans too much on his means or duties themselves.

<margin>2. Answer.</margin> 2. A weak Christian has no clear observation of the spiritual failures that cling to his devotions. He sees only his gifts and pays attention to his inclinations; he does not see the vanity of his thoughts, nor the evil outcome of his purpose, nor his fleshly attachments to self-love and vainglory. But a mature Christian gradually takes notice of these things in himself; and an experienced Christian takes as much notice of the failings in his required duty as of his ability in the same. And how-

<column-break/>

ever much he sometimes notices an increase of gifts and graces in himself, he nevertheless discerns more spiritual pride, seeking the applause of the people, the showing off of gifts, and too great a pride in bringing forth his gifts—which a weak Christian seldom notices.

<margin>3. Answer. Rom. 14:1. Rom. 14:23.</margin> 3. That one has a scrupulous or troubled conscience regarding <term>indifferent matters<note>Original: "middelbare saken." These are actions neither commanded nor forbidden by God, like specific diets or holidays.</note></term> proves that one is a weak Christian. For the Apostle calls such people "weak in faith"—those who bind the conscience where Scripture has left it free. One believer thought he might well eat all kinds of food, and another doubted whether it was permissible to eat various things. Now, those who doubted, the Apostle calls "weak"; and a <margin>1 Cor. 8:7.</margin> weak conscience is quickly defiled. Not to know our liberty, and to misuse our <margin>Song of Sol. 9. <note>Original: "Cant. 9." This is likely a printer's error, as the Song of Solomon only has 8 chapters.</note></margin> liberty, is a proof that we have little grace. Young converts make more sins than God makes, for they trouble and confuse themselves solely with indifferent matters. It is true there ought to be a conscientious tenderness in all Christians, for tenderness of conscience is our required duty; but a tormenting scrupulousness is our weakness. And just as a weak Christian is better than no Christian, and a weak faith is better than a dead faith, so also is a scrupulous conscience better than a perverse conscience.

<margin>4. Answer.</margin> 4. That one binds himself so firmly to the exercises of religion that he forgets his <term>particular callings<note>Refers to one's daily work, trade, or domestic responsibilities.</note></term> is a sign of weakness in grace. It was a good proverb of that famous man of God, <margin>Dr. Sibbes.</margin> Dr. Sibbes: <note>Richard Sibbes (1577–1635), a famous Puritan theologian known as the "Sweet Dropper" for his comforting sermons.</note> *I hold that Christian in high esteem who wants to hear much and live much; who wants to pray much and work much.* In young converts, the affections are strong and impulsive; it seems to them that they can never hear enough, and they thus forget the required duties of their callings, which is a proof of their weakness and instability. An experienced, mature Christian maintains a good rule in his common and particular callings, so that the one shall not oppose or hinder the other.

<margin>5. Answer.</margin> 5. To admire the persons of men is a proof of weakness in grace. Such were the Corinthians, who wondered at the persons of men; yet the Apostle calls them young <margin>1 Cor. 3:1.</margin> children and fleshly Christians. Although they had the life of Christians, they nevertheless had little of the strength of Christians. They were fleshly; they tasted more of the flesh than of the Spirit. Ignorance is often a cause of admiration. Weak Christians, who have little knowledge, are liable to be so taken up in the admiration of persons that one cries, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollos." They thus fall into the sin that is condemned: that of having the faith of Christ with respect of persons, lifting up one teacher and putting down another. That you make an idol of one and despise the other proves that you are weak in faith. For a strong Christian loves all good teachers and can despise no one.

<margin>6. Answer.</margin> 6. To be easily led into error proves only weakness in grace. These the Apostle calls children, who are [tossed] to and fro <margin>Eph. 4:14.</margin>

<sig>G n</sig>
<meta>catchword: ge- (continuation of "ge-voerd" / carried [to and fro])</meta>

<meta>This page continues the list of characteristics distinguishing "weak" from "strong" Christians, specifically focusing on steadfastness, theological depth, emotional maturity, and the ability to receive correction. It then transitions into a new sermon (the third in a series delivered in London in 1651) based on 1 Kings 14:13, exploring why God allows different degrees of grace among His people rather than making everyone perfect at once.</meta>

# Various Degrees.

...driven and tossed about by every wind of doctrine. <margin>2 Pet. 3:17, 18.</margin> Weakness of the head <note>Meaning intellectual or doctrinal instability.</note> proves that you are not very strong in your heart. The way to avoid falling from your steadfastness is to grow in grace; for the Apostle Peter joins these two duties together. Having given a warning in verse 18 to not fall from steadfastness, he gives the counsel in verse 16 to grow in grace. Strong Christians are steadfast, whereas the weak are unsteadfast; therefore, for those professors who are driven about by various opinions, it is a proof that they have only a weak grace—as weak as anyone can have.

<margin>7. Answer.</margin> 7. Such people are those who are satisfied only with the common principles of Religion, without further searching into the depths and mysteries of Godliness. <margin>Heb. 5:12, 13.</margin> There are some professors of whom it may be said that they are young children in Christ because they still have need of milk, being ignorant in the word of Righteousness—that is, in the weightier teachings of the Gospel concerning Christ, who is our Righteousness. <margin>Luke 9:45; Mark 9:10; John 16:16, 17.</margin> Thus the Disciples and the Apostles of Christ were ignorant of the mystery of our Redemption, as well as of the Suffering of Christ, the Resurrection, and the Ascension of Christ, until the Holy Spirit came and brought these things to their remembrance, which had been taught to them by Christ.

<margin>8. Answer.</margin> 8. Weak Christians are strong in affections but not in judgment: they commonly have more heat than light. Young Christians are like young horses that have much spirit but are not yet fit for travel because they are not yet well-broken or trained. Likewise, there are many Christians who have much fire and drive, but are not yet so firm in their judgment, which proves their weakness in grace.

<margin>9. Answer.</margin> 9. A weak Christian cannot endure a rebuke. Just as raw weather reveals whether your body is weak or healthy, so also a sharp rebuke will reveal whether you are of a weak spiritual constitution. <margin>2 Sam. 12:7.</margin> When Nathan came to David and set before his eyes that he was the man who had sinned, David submitted to the Prophet's rebuke; but although Asa was a good man, he could not endure the faithful reprimand of the Prophet; <margin>2 Chron. 16:10. <note>Original: "2 Par. 16. 10." Paralipomenon is the Greek/Latin name for the books of Chronicles.</note></margin> instead, he became angry with the Seer and had him put in the prison-house.

<margin>10. Answer.</margin> 10. Also, a weak believer is one who trusts God for his Soul, but not for his body. <margin>Matt. 6:30.</margin> Jesus Christ shows that those had "little faith" who expected Heaven and blessedness from God their Father and trusted Him for their souls and eternal welfare, but not for their food and clothing. Some dare to trust God regarding Heaven, but not regarding the earth; but these are likewise of a little faith. When the Disciples lacked bread, they began to reason among themselves how they should be satisfied; but Christ, knowing that, said: "Why do you reason among yourselves, O you of little faith?" As if He would say: "Can you believe in Me for the bread of eternal life, and do you not dare to trust Me for the bread of temporal life?"

<margin>2nd Use.</margin> Therefore, do not be discouraged, you who perceive in yourselves only small beginnings of

<column-break/>

grace; but look upon your failings and imperfections in such a way that it may lead to growth in grace, and not so that you are satisfied with any current measure of it. However, do not look so much at the small beginnings of grace that you become discouraged by them. When you see a large tree in the field, you say: "This tree was once a small graft." Likewise, Christians who are now like small sprouts shall hereafter become high Cedars. Say to your soul: "Though I am currently weak, I shall yet be strong." For where there is true grace, there shall be growth; the smoking wick <note>Original: "smoockende lemmet"—a reference to Isaiah 42:3/Matthew 12:20.</note> shall become a burning and shining lamp on God's candlestick. And therefore, just as you must not be satisfied with the largest measure of grace, you must also not be discouraged by the smallest measure. For a mustard seed also grows into a great tree. <margin>Matt. 17:20.</margin>

<margin>2nd Use.</margin> Do not keep yourselves satisfied with small measures of grace: for a little of the world cannot satisfy you. A span of a foot is enough for you in your mother's womb; three feet in the cradle; and seven in the grave. But between the cradle and the grave, the whole world cannot satisfy us. Shall we then keep ourselves satisfied with a little grace? Because of the lust for riches, you are like the blood-sucker <note>Likely a leech.</note> that always cries "give, give," and the grave which never says "it is enough." And are you then satisfied with a little when it comes to grace?

# 1 KINGS 14.
<note>Original: "I. REGUM 14."</note>
->In the middle of the 13th verse.<-

## Because in him some good thing was found toward the Lord God of Israel, etc.

---

<margin>3rd Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry within London, March 16, 1651. <note>Original: "Laurence Jurii"—referring to the historic church of St. Lawrence Jewry.</note></margin> **W**e have established some Scriptural marks of those who have a small grace; now we proceed further and come to the third question, which is:

<margin>3rd Question.</margin> Why does God so arrange and ordain it that everyone among His people should not be of equal size and strength, but that some of them should have only the beginnings of grace?

<margin>Answer.</margin> Answer: It does not happen with rebirth as it did in the creation. It does not happen with the trees of Righteousness as it did with the trees in Paradise, which were all created perfect at once. It is not so in the work of grace: we are not perfectly sanctified, nor all at once; but we perfect holiness in the fear of God, and that by degrees. Now, God has given to some of His people only small beginnings and measures of grace for these reasons:

1. To establish a distinction between our state on earth and our state in Heaven. In Heaven, we shall all have an equal form of grace, although it is debated whether there shall be different degrees of glory. In Heaven, all the spirits of the righteous shall be perfect. <margin>Heb. 12:23. <note>The text says "Lib. 12. 2." which likely intended Heb. 12:23.</note></margin>

It begins a new sermon explaining that spiritual maturity is a gradual process ordained by God to distinguish earthly life from heavenly perfection.</summary>

It explores the theological reasons why God does not make all believers perfect at once, but rather leads them through stages of growth.</meta>

# Grace and Its Various Measures

<column-break/>

**Column 1:**

<margin>Ephesians 4:11</margin>
...and there we shall all come to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. All believers here are equally justified before God: for God does not excuse the strong and hold the weak guilty; rather, He justifies them all equally. However, when we reach Heaven, then our sanctification shall be as our justification is now; that is, perfect and equal to all. We shall have not only a perfection of parts, but also of degrees. <note>The author distinguishes between having all the "parts" of a Christian character (perfection of parts) and having those parts fully developed (perfection of degrees).</note>

2. To cause man to live in a constant clinging to the Divine influences and solaces through the Spirit of God. If children were born as such perfect men as Adam was created, then we would not see such a constant necessity of hanging upon our parents. We are formed in the womb, and afterwards born into the world, and then grown up through stages from greatness to greatness; so it also goes in grace. Converting grace does not make us as perfect as we shall be hereafter. In the Creation, God made all the trees fruitful and containing seed within themselves; but now it is different: for they are first kernels or seeds, then plants, and after that they become trees, depending on the influences of Heaven. Likewise, we are also first young children, then youths, and then strong men in Christ, in order to preserve our souls in clinging to or hanging upon God's grace.

3. For the greater adornment of the (mystical) hidden body of Christ. If a natural body had every limb of equal size, it would be monstrous. But a body is so proportioned in its different members that the lesser is of service to the greater; and thus they all orderly fulfill their mutual operations. Just as in music there can be no harmony if the voices are of an equal pitch; but one voice being the Bass, and the other the Higher Voice <note>original: "Superius"</note> or treble, makes the music all the more melodious. So it also goes in grace: the different degrees of grace make the body of Christ all the more harmonious. It is here as in some curious piece of needlework; if all the silk threads were of one color, it would not present the work with such luster and pleasantness as the variety of colors does.

4. To make God's people see the necessity of maintaining mutual society and fellowship for one another's edification. There would be no necessity for the discourses of Christians and holy gatherings if our weaknesses did not require them. Just as God has so placed the members of the body <margin>1 Corinthians 12:21</margin> that every limb is of service to the other, and that the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you," so it is among the people of God. Where some are weak and others are strong, there is a necessity to maintain mutual fellowship. There is an instinct in nature such that things which are weak in themselves cling to things <margin>Proverbs 30:26; Song of Solomon 2:14</margin> which are stronger than they. The rabbits <note>The Dutch "konijnen" refers to the "conies" of the Bible, often interpreted as rock hyraxes.</note> are a powerless people, yet they make their houses in the rocks; likewise among the birds, the dove, being for the most part fearful and fleeting, nevertheless hides herself in the clefts of the rocks; the vine, the weakest among the trees, braces itself against the wall; the hops among

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

the plants wind themselves around the pole. Likewise, God in His infinite wisdom has ordained that some Christians should be stronger and some weaker in grace, so that the strong should help the weak, and that every one should serve the other.

5. To exalt the glory of God in all His magnificent attributes.
1. These different measures of grace in Christians glorify the grace of God and His mild mercy, which sometimes rewards some Christians who have only small measures of grace with great measures of glory.

2. This glorifies the power of God: that when we are weak, He reveals His power in our weakness—yes, His strength is made perfect in weakness; and therefore <margin>2 Corinthians 12:9</margin> Paul boasts, *when I am weak, then I am strong*, namely in Christ. Is it not a <margin>verse 1</margin> demonstration of great power to preserve a small spark of fire so that it is not extinguished by a flood of water? Nevertheless, see: the small spark of grace in you shall not be extinguished by the flood of your corruptions. The smallest measure of grace shall be preserved by God's power. God's power is not seen so much in the preservation of the Angels as in that of weak believers; for the Angels, though changeable, are nevertheless perfect creatures; they have no weight of sins and corruptions pressing them down. But alas! we have such an inclination toward sinning that we are ready at every moment to be drawn aside from God. The power of God is seen more in the preservation of a weak believer in the state of grace than in the preservation of the Angels in the state of innocence. And just as God's power is seen in the preservation of a little grace, so it is also seen in its growth. Grace is compared to the cloud that the Prophet's servant saw, which was at first like a man's hand, <margin>1 Kings 18:44</margin> but afterwards overspread the heavens. True grace is of an expanding and growing nature: and therefore it can be compared to the vision of the holy waters, which were first to the ankles, then to the knees, then to the loins, and finally so deep that one <margin>Ezekiel 47:3-5</margin> could not pass through them.

3. Through this, God shows the glory of His wisdom. Just as God's wisdom is shown in the world through the variety of creatures, which are not all of one form and size, but some larger and some smaller; so it is in the Church of God, that some Christians have a greater and some a smaller measure of grace. Search the entire Creation, and you shall everywhere find the wisdom of God in the diversity of creatures: in the heavens, the greater and lesser lights and the stars of different sizes adorn them; in the sea, the large and small fish; in the air, the great eagle and the small sparrow; on the earth, the elephant and the dog; among the creeping animals, the snake and the ant; among the living plants, the high cedar and the hyssop on the wall. Likewise among rational creatures: the great giant and the small dwarf; the man of high stature and the child a span long. Thus God's wisdom is greatly glorified, in that just as there is a diversity of natural proportion or symmetry...

# Various Degrees.

->...in the world; so also there are various proportions of grace in His Church among His children.<-

<margin>1. Proposition.</margin>
Before I come to apply this point—which serves as a great source of comfort for the children of God—I shall recount some general propositions concerning the small measures of grace:

<margin>Jonah 4:11</margin>
Just as in a forest there are more young sprouts than old trees; in a garden, more young plants than old bushes; and in the world, more young children than old people. In Nineveh, there were 120,000 young children, but there was not so great a number of old people.
<margin>The more perfect, the fewer. <note>original: "Quo perfectiores, eo pauciores"</note></margin>
The more perfect things are, the fewer of them there are. Look among the other creatures; those that are larger are fewer in number. In the sea, there are more young and small fish than large whales;
<margin>Jeremiah 46:23</margin>
on the earth, the smallest things are countless; in the air, there are more swarms of flies than flocks of birds. Likewise, in the Church of God, there are more young and weak converts than seasoned Christians.
<margin>1 Samuel 20:36</margin>
It is with most Christians as it was with Jonathan's arrows, which he shot to warn David; two of them fell short, and only one was shot beyond the mark. In the same way, among the shots of Christians toward the mark of the prize of the high calling in Christ Jesus, many shots fall short.

<margin>2. Proposition.</margin>
There are many who possess only small measures and weak beginnings of grace, even though they have long lived under the profession of religion and the "means of grace" <note>The "means of grace" refers to things like preaching, prayer, and the sacraments which were believed to nurture faith.</note>. Such 
<margin>Hebrews 5:12</margin>
were the Hebrews, who, though they ought to have been teachers by that time, still needed to be taught the first principles of the words of God; they had become like those who need milk and not solid food.
<margin>Matthew 19:30</margin>
I can aptly apply the words of Christ here: that many who are first shall be last. There are many who set out early and took what seemed like the first step in the profession of religion, yet others who started after them have already run past them. Many who have weak beginnings of grace have been under the influence of its means for a long time; therefore, the power of grace in Christians cannot be judged by their profession, but by their progress. It is not enough to count how many years you have been a believer; what matters is the experience and judgment you have gained under God’s ordinances.

<margin>3. Proposition.</margin>
The smallest measures of grace cannot merit eternal life and glory, because even the greatest measures cannot do so.
<margin>God's mercies are our merits. <note>original: "Miserationes Dei sunt merita nostra"</note></margin>
In the matter of merit, there ought to be a proportion between the work and the reward; but between grace and glory, there is no such proportion. Our services are imperfect, but our salvation is perfect. Our services last but a moment, but our glory is eternal.
<margin>God crowns His own gifts in us, but they are His gifts. <note>original: "Deus coronat in nobis dona sua, sed dona sua"</note></margin>
There is no comparison between our light, obligatory duties and the eternal weight of glory. The Church is described in the Song of Solomon according to the various parts of her body:
<margin>Song of Solomon 2:14</margin>
for it says her voice is sweet, and her countenance is lovely, and her eyes are doves' eyes.
<margin>Song of Solomon 1:15</margin>
"Behold, you are beautiful, my love; your eyes are doves' eyes."
<margin>Song of Solomon 1:10</margin>
"Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of pearls."
<margin>Song of Solomon 4:1, 2, 3, 4, etc.</margin>
Now it is very remarkable that although

<column-break/>

Christ praises the Church for her eyes, her hair, teeth, lips and speech, the temples of her head, her breasts, and her neck, etc., He nevertheless does not praise her for her *hands*. This is to show that although she is adorned with many graces—as if with so many beautiful ornaments and lovely charms—she nevertheless earns nothing from the hands of Christ through her own doing.
<margin>Ezekiel 16:14</margin>
The Church’s beauty is made perfect through the glory of Christ.

<margin>4. Proposition.</margin>
Believers ought not to rest satisfied with the small measures of grace they have received. Although a small amount of grace can bring you to Heaven, you must not be content with that alone; if you have obtained a small grace, labor for more. To awaken you to this, note:

1. That small measures of grace are not as perceptible or evident to yourself. Small things are often not seen simply because they are small. There may be a little dust in the air, floating up and down; yet because it is so little, we do not see it.

This is the reason why Christians sometimes doubt; their grace is small, and therefore it is not easily distinguished.
<margin>Matthew 8:26 compared with Mark 4:40</margin>
Compare Matthew 8:26 with Mark 4:40. We find that in Matthew, Christ rebukes the disciples, saying, "O you of little faith!" but in Mark, He says, "How is it that you have no faith?" From the difference in these expressions, you can see that for the purpose of comfort, an unpracticed small faith is as good as no faith. Their faith was so small during their distress that it amounted to nothing. You may have a small grace, but for the purpose of consolation, that small and weak grace cannot carry you far toward a strong sense of comfort. It is true that a weak Christian is acceptable to God, and a weaker one may lie in his Father’s bosom; but the strongest measure of grace gives us the strongest comfort.

2. Note that although small measures of grace can bring you to Heaven, they are not as useful to others. A weak Christian cannot do much for the conversion of his neighbor because he lacks the advantage of experience in the ways of God. Therefore, such people should not be admitted to contentious debates.
<margin>Romans 14:1; 15:1; Galatians 6:1</margin>
Spiritually mature and strong Christians are the ones who are useful. Young converts are not fit for certain religious exercises, namely, the strengthening of others.
<margin>Luke 22:32</margin>
"When you are converted, strengthen your brothers." This should not be understood as the initial conversion, but as their progress in religion—as if Christ had said: "When you yourself are strengthened, then strengthen your brothers." There are some duties which young converts cannot perform;
<margin>Matthew 9:16, 17</margin>
for a piece of unshrunk cloth is not fit for an old garment, nor are old leather wineskins fit for new wine. Pareus <note>David Pareus (1548–1622) was a prominent German Reformed Protestant theologian.</note> and most commentators apply this passage to "cases of conscience" <term>cases of conscience: the practical application of moral and religious principles to specific life situations</term>. Why did Christ’s disciples not fast often? They were like old and weak leather wineskins, not fit for that heavy duty, which was like new wine that might burst them.
<margin>John 16:12</margin>
Christ said to His disciples that He had many things to say to them which they (given their weakness) could not yet bear.

<meta>The catchword "3. Nochtā" (3. Yet/However) indicates the next point continues on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses why the Church contains more "weak" than "strong" believers and argues that while small measures of grace are sufficient for salvation, they are insufficient for providing personal comfort or helping others. It emphasizes that spiritual maturity comes through progress over time, not merely the length of one's profession of faith.</summary>

# Of Grace, with its Various Degrees

<margin>John 15:18</margin>
3. Yet these small measures are not so glorious for God: For He is glorified when His people bear much fruit. Many means and much effort with little fruit is a shame for the Vinedresser; and therefore believers must not rest, or be satisfied, with small measures of grace.

<margin>5th Proposition</margin>
<margin>Luke 19:27</margin>
It is our bounden duty not to despise the small measures of grace which God has given us. For he who is faithful in the least shall be set over much by God.

The use of grace shall increase; and if your grace has grown, then attribute the glory to God: for it is God's pound <note>referring to the "minas" or "pounds" in the parable of the talents in Luke 19</note>, and not your effort, that has gained.

1. This application is for the comfort of weak Christians, to these young Abijahs <note>Abijah was the son of the wicked King Jeroboam; in 1 Kings 14:13, it is noted that "something good" was found in him alone of his family</note>, in whom something good is found.

And let such people know for their comfort:

<margin>Application</margin>
1. That although grace is small, it is nonetheless of great value. A pearl, though but small in substance, is nonetheless of great value: so too is small grace of great value. The heart of a godless person is of no value; he may have much knowledge and apparent grace, yet it is of no value. A shop full of empty vessels will not make a man rich; it is different when the vessels are full of useful things: spiritual gifts, even if they were as beautiful as reaching to Heaven, are but poor rags for a Christian; for it is grace that makes him rich in God.

2. Although your grace is small for the present, it shall nonetheless grow for the future into a large measure. The small mustard seed (the smallest of seeds) shall in time grow up into a tree. Grace is aptly compared to leaven, which is of a spreading nature; to the cloud which the Prophet's servant saw <note>1 Kings 18:44, a small cloud like a man's hand that brought great rain</note>; and to the Holy waters, which everything increases: a child of days shall henceforth go by steps, until he becomes like the Ancient of Days, perfect as his Heavenly Father is.
<margin>Matt. 13:31, 32</margin>
<margin>Matt. 13:33</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 18:44</margin>
<margin>Ezek. 47:3, 4</margin>

Naturalists believe that the seed of the Cypress tree is very small, and yet it becomes a very high tree: so it is also with the birth and growth of grace.

<margin>Matt. 12</margin>
3. The small measure of grace once begun in the soul shall be perfected. God shall not break the bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax, until He brings forth judgment unto victory: by "judgment" is understood there the work of Sanctification, until it overcomes corruption. Paul trusted that He who had begun the good work in them would also complete the same until the day of Jesus Christ. The Lord is faithful and will also do it. The Lord has commanded us to go forward to perfection; and He does not portray impossible things for us to do. He mocks the foolish men who do not proceed to finish what they have begun to build: Therefore God shall never begin a building of grace which He does not finish. Furthermore, He has promised to finish what His servants have begun.
<margin>Phil. 1:6</margin>
<margin>1 Thess. 5:24</margin>
<margin>Heb. 6:1</margin>
<margin>Luke 14:28, 29</margin>
<margin>Psalm 138:8</margin>

4. The weakest Christian has equal grace with others, as far as concerns the quality; although not so much as concerns the size:

<column-break/>

Although your grace is not as much in quantity, it is nonetheless as much true grace as another’s: even if it were but a conversion from yesterday; yet it is as good as that of an old pillar in religion. Faith is of equal preciousness in all believers, as far as concerns the quality; although not so much as concerns the size. Faith is equal in all believers:
<margin>2 Pet. 1</margin>

1. In respect to the Author, God:
2. The object; it looks to the same Christ:
3. The means of working are the same, namely, the Word and the Spirit. A small grace is true grace: the fire in a spark is as much fire as the flame: the filings of gold are as much gold as the whole lump: a drop of water is as much water as the entire sea. Thus a small grace is also true grace.

4. The end; it has the same salvation of the soul. 1 Pet. 1:9.
<margin>1 Pet. 1:9</margin>

5. God will not burden your weak grace beyond your power. God will contend with measure; He will restrain His hard wind in the days of the East wind. You shall not have such storm winds of trials as a stronger Christian. God will not let you be tempted beyond your power. He will take care that the Spirit shall not be melted away.
<margin>Isa. 2</margin>
<margin>1 Cor. 10 <note>The text likely meant 1 Cor. 10:13, though the OCR says 13</note></margin>
<margin>Isa. 7</margin>

6. Take this for your comfort, that the smallest measure of grace is enough to bring you to Heaven. But this is not spoken to make you lazy and idle; but only for comfort for a distressed conscience. These, because their grace is weak, think they have no grace at all.

"I have given an open door before you" (says Christ to the Church of Philadelphia); "and no one can shut it: for you have little strength; and you have kept my word; and have not denied my name."
<margin>Rev. 3:8</margin>

It is true, our comfort lies much in the greater degree; but our salvation lies in the first degree: strong grace has strong comfort: much faith shall bring you to Heaven with much comfort; yet a small faith shall still bring you safely to Heaven.

## 1 KINGS 14

->In the middle of the 13th verse.<-

### Because in him something good is found, etc.

<margin>4th Point</margin>
<margin>In the law <note>original: "in l. Iuris"</note></margin>
<margin>16. §. Concerning the defendant <note>original: "Ex de reo"</note></margin>
<margin>Needy</margin>
To come to the use of warning, I shall here pose a case of conscience; which is: Since among God's people there are found those who have only a small grace, and find only small measures in themselves; What then is the smallest measure of grace, without which a person cannot be said to be in the state of grace?

--- Page 587 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 562 regarding the "small measures" of grace. Having established that even a tiny amount of grace is valuable and sufficient for salvation, the author now begins to define the "lowest degree" of true grace to help believers recognize it within themselves, even when they feel spiritually weak.</meta>

-># **Various Degrees.**<-

...come into religion, and those who have but a small grace: nonetheless, they must confess that they have a little; and although they have no acquired strength of grace, they must nevertheless know how to acknowledge the truth of grace within themselves. For even though they fall short compared to strong believers, they are nonetheless no hypocrites: for the smallest measure of grace is better than the greatest measure of gifts <note>The author distinguishes between "grace" (saving faith) and "gifts" (natural talents or intellectual knowledge of religion).</note>.

<margin>1 Thessalonians 4:1</margin>
Secondly, the knowledge of this shall awaken the soul to dutiful reflections toward a further state, and teach her to become more and more abundant.

Now, so that we may discover what the lowest step of this true grace is, we shall show it to you in the following several particulars.

<margin>Psalm 119:15</margin>
1. It is a light in the soul to see the evil and the corrupt nature of sins, although there is no ability yet to kill them. The entrance of God's word gives light, and gives knowledge to the simple <note>The original Dutch *slechten* refers to the "simple" or unlearned, following the language of Psalm 119:130.</note>; that is the first work of the Word upon the soul, the true beginning of Conversion. Grace in the heart is the light by which you see sin and its own sinful nature. Just as in the first Creation, light was created first, so is the first work in the second Creation <note>The "second creation" refers to the spiritual rebirth or regeneration of a person.</note> to open the eyes of the blind, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God. In the work of Conversion in the soul, the first step of grace is to be enlightened with the light of the living. So that where light is lacking, there no work of grace can be.
<margin>Acts 26:18</margin>

<margin>Luke 15:17, 18</margin>
2. A firmly established purpose of the heart to leave sins and to cleave to God. Grace consists not so much in an actual killing <note>The term "killing" here refers to "mortification," the theological process of subduing sinful impulses.</note> of sins, as in a firm purpose of the heart to leave all sins. The Prodigal Son's purpose to go to his Father’s house proves some grace in him: *I shall arise and go to my Father*; that is, I shall leave my godless company and ways. And it says there: *when he was yet a great way off, his Father saw him, and was moved with inner compassion for him; and running to him, fell on his neck and kissed him*; for God worked in him a purpose to leave his sins. Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Church Father and Pope.</note> says on this passage: That the forgiveness of sins came to his heart before he made his confession before his Father. So David: *I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.* Augustine writes on this passage that David did not say that he confessed, but that he *intended* to confess his sins; his purpose was then true grace, although one of the smallest measures of grace. That holy purpose of David proves the grace in him when he said: *I have purposed that I will not transgress your Law. I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments.* It is a proof of grace when a soul cleaves to the Lord with a purpose of the heart.
<margin>Gregory</margin>
<margin>Psalm 32:5</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Psalm 17:8; Psalm 119; Ephesians 11:23</margin>

3. Another small measure of grace is this: A felt sorrow for the lack of grace. Just like the one who came to Christ and said with tears: *Lord, I believe, help thou mine unbelief.* He said

<column-break/>

<margin>Mark 9:24</margin>
not, "Lord, help my faith," but, "Lord, help my unbelief." His expression concerning his faith proves not only his deficiency, but also his sensitivity to that deficiency. This is the poverty of spirit <margin>Matthew 5:3</margin> which has the first place in blessedness: this is the lowest rung of the ladder. The Apostle tells us that the Spirit helps our <margin>Romans 8:26</margin> infirmities with sighs and groanings which cannot be uttered. Remember that it is not said here that the Spirit helps us with comforts and joys, but with sighs and groans; from which we may learn that the help of the Spirit is just as much in sighs, groans, and felt sorrows for our deficiency as it is in holy elevations. The strength of grace is seen in holy joy and the elevation of the Spirit; but the truth of grace is seen and noticed in sighs, groans, and sorrow over our deficiencies. <margin>Perkins *Cases of Conscience*, Book 2, Chapter 10: *quanto magis stupent* <note>original Latin: "the more they are amazed/confounded." Reference to William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian.</note></margin> These are said to be sighs and groanings which cannot be expressed; not in respect to their greatness, but (as Doctor Perkins well says) in respect to their weakness. God's children, at first, lack the ability to express their own thoughts. To be sensible of the lack of grace is grace, for nature cannot make a person properly sensible of the lack of grace, nor make them feelably complain about that lack.

<margin>Nehemiah 1:11 compared with 5:15</margin>
4. An earnest desire for more grace proves that there is grace in the soul, although it be small. I do not place the beginnings of grace in an ability to practice grace, but rather in an earnest desire for grace. Desire for grace is counted by God as the grace itself which we desire: for so we see that Nehemiah's desire to fear the Lord was counted as the actual fear of God. Desires are the seeds of grace, and the graces themselves are the blossoms and sweet fruits that come forth from them: the grace that is practiced is the fruit of a holy desire for grace.

That holy desire for grace is acceptable to God can be shown as follows:

1. God's people have appealed to God regarding the sincerity of their hearts, solely in their desires: so says the Church, *The desire of our soul is to thy name, and to the <margin>Isaiah 26:8, 9</margin> remembrance of thee; with my soul have I desired thee in the night.*

2. God has made many lovely promises, not only for the actuality and practice of grace, but also for the desires for <margin>Matthew 5:6</margin> grace. *Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.* *If any man thirst,* (says Christ) *let him come unto me, and drink*; <margin>John 7:37</margin> indeed, there is a general <margin>Isaiah 55:1</margin> invitation for everyone who thirsts to come to the waters: and God has promised <margin>Revelation 22:16</margin> to give to the thirsty from the Fountain of the water of life freely. The Lord has likewise <margin>Psalm 10:17; Psalm 141:19</margin> promised to fulfill the desire of those who fear him; and he shall hear the wish of the humble. So it appears from these promises that hunger and thirst, and the desires for grace, are counted and accepted by God as grace.

Now, so that people do not rest in lukewarm and sleepy desires, and thereby forget the practice of grace, I shall show you how the Scripture considers such desires for grace to be grace.

<meta>catchword: 1. It</meta>

<summary>This page identifies four indicators of the "lowest degree" of true grace: spiritual enlightenment to recognize sin, a firm purpose to repent, sorrow over one's lack of faith, and an earnest desire for more grace. The author argues that God accepts these initial stirrings as genuine faith, providing comfort to those who feel their spirituality is weak or "small."</summary>

**Grace, with its [various degrees]**

<margin>
Psalm 4:6
Numbers 23:10
The will for the end, but not the means. — Bernard of Clairvaux <note>original: "Voluntattem finis, non mediorum, Bern."</note>
</margin>
1. These are desires that are above nature. It is true that there are natural desires in the soul for that which is good; it is the voice of nature asking: *Who will show us any good?* Now, these desires arise from the movements of the natural and unsanctified will of man, and they aim for happiness, but not for holiness. Such were the desires of Balaam, who said: *Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like his.* This was merely a natural desire. But the true desires in the soul are for Heaven for the sake of holiness. Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic.</note> notes these desires of natural men very excellently, saying: "They have a desire for the end, but not for the means."

<margin>
2 Corinthians 7:11
2 Corinthians 8:12
Proverbs 1:25
Carnal men desire to attain Christ, but not to follow Him; they do not care to seek Him whom they desire to find. — Bernard <note>original: "Carnales cupiunt Christum consequi sed non sequi, non curant quaerere, quem desiderant invenire Bern."</note>
</margin>
2. Desires for grace are joined with holy efforts. Therefore, the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> joins desire and zeal together, to show that true desire is always accompanied by zealous effort. In this way, the Apostle joins a readiness of will together with the finishing of the work. God will never accept the will for the deed unless there is an effort to complete whatever we have said we are willing to do. And therefore Solomon rightly describes how shameful desires are without effort. *The desire of the Sluggard,* he says, *shall kill him; for his hands refuse to work.* Bernard describes the laziness of the body thus: "Carnal men love Christ so as to obtain Him, but not so as to follow Him; they do not wish to labor to seek Him whom they desire to find."

<margin>
Psalm 119:131 <note>The text cites 126, but the quote "my soul breaks" is closer to 119:20 or 119:131.</note>
Psalm 42:1
2 Corinthians 7:11
</margin>
3. True desires are insatiable. David speaks thus of his desires: *My soul,* he says, *breaks for the longing that it has for your judgments at all times.* Indeed, he further describes the burning and the insatiable nature of his desires by comparing them to a Hart <note>A male red deer.</note> that cries out for the water-brooks. The Hart is the thirstiest of all beasts, and its thirst increases all the more when the poor beast is hunted by dogs. So too are the true desires of souls for grace: they are fervent, burning, and intense desires.

<margin>
Psalm 42:3
Psalm 63:2
Psalm 119:20
</margin>
4. You may know true desires for grace by their objects. For desires that are more for outward things than for God are not pleasing. David says: *My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.* *My soul thirsts for you; my flesh longs for you, in a dry and weary land where no water is.* Thus his soul longed, and broke with longing for God's judgments. Now, if you wish to know whether you have any principle of grace in your soul, examine what your desires are like. Perhaps you cannot pray as you *desire* to pray; perhaps you cannot be grieved over your sins, but you keep grieving *because* you cannot be grieved. Perhaps you do not believe (as you ought), but do you *desire* to believe? Perhaps you cannot convert yourself, but do you *desire* to be converted, and do you labor to be converted? If so, then you may conclude that you have a principle of true grace in your soul.

<margin>
1 Peter 2:2
</margin>
5. We can know the truth of grace, even though it be little, by an earnest desire for the Word and the means of grace. Peter presents our desire in this way: *As newborn babes, be very desireful for the rational, unadulterated milk, so that you may grow thereby.* There is an inborn nature in children that as soon as they are born, they long for the mother's breasts. The Apostle uses this as a comparison for a spiritual person; a person spiritually born anew longs for the Word and for the means of grace <note>The "means of grace" are the tools God uses to nourish faith, such as preaching, the sacraments, and prayer.</note>, so that he may grow in grace.

<column-break/>

<margin>
1 J<unclear>ohn 3:14</unclear>
</margin>
6. A favorable love toward those who have grace. By this you know that you have passed from death into life: if you love the Brothers. The Casuists <note>Theologians who resolve "cases of conscience" or moral dilemmas.</note> regarding this text say that love for God’s children is the "first grace" and the first sign in young converts. In the conversion of the Natives in New England <note>A reference to the missionary efforts in the American colonies, likely those of John Eliot (the "Apostle to the Indians") in the mid-17th century.</note>, it is observed (for God has begun there to bring some of these poor people from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to Himself) that the first sign in them is love and respect for those who have true grace. Thus I have given you an answer to the question of what the smallest measures of grace are—without which, taken together or some of them, a person cannot be said to have grace, but where any of these are present, that person's state is secure and this small measure of grace can bring a person to Heaven. I shall now set down some Warnings here to prevent wrong applications [of this teaching], which are:

<margin>
1. W<unclear>arning.</unclear>
Hebrews <unclear>6:1</unclear>
</margin>
1. Although these small measures of grace are soul-saving, you must nonetheless not satisfy yourselves with them. Beware that what I have said to encourage the weakness of some Christians does not become a pillow for the vanity of others. Instead, let us press on toward perfection, for we must not sit still, being content with any measure of grace. And to advise you toward this, note:

1. That the things which are necessary and sufficient for the maintenance of a person’s life will not satisfy a person. What man is content, even if he has clothes enough to cover his nakedness and food enough to keep his body and soul together? He desires clothes not just for nakedness, but for adornment; and not just food for hunger and necessity, but for delight. Now, shall men be insatiable in their desires for outward things, yet sit down quietly and say they have enough of Heavenly goods?

It is the *strength* of grace that gives assurance. Small grace will indeed bring your soul to Heaven, but it is the strength of grace that will bring Heaven into your soul. *The work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and assurance forever.* A child of God seldom has peace and consolation from the mere habit of righteousness in his soul, but only from the *exercise* of righteousness. *He who lacks these things,* says Peter, *is blind, and cannot see afar off,* etc. This is not spoken of godless people who have no grace, but of those who have grace but because they do not exercise it, they do not feel the comforting

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Various Degrees" of grace, specifically addressing how believers with "small" or "weak" faith should evaluate their spiritual state without falling into despair.</meta>

# Various Degrees.

...spiritual fruits in their souls.

<margin>
Matthew 8:26 compared with Mark 4:40.
2 Peter 1:9.
</margin>
A small, unpracticed faith provides (as we have shown) as little comfort as no faith at all. Those who do not add to the stalk of grace will lack the comfort of grace. Thus, a weak Christian—whom Peter compares to a <term>steke-blindt Mensch</term> <note>literally "stone-blind person"; someone with very limited spiritual vision</note>—cannot see from afar because the sight of his faith is weak. He cannot see his name written in Heaven. He who contents himself with small measures of grace will lack the comforting testimonies of grace in his heart.

<margin>2nd Warning.</margin>
The second Warning is this: do not take as proof of the *truth* of grace those things which are only proofs of the *growth and strength* of grace. Young converts often cast themselves into a labyrinth of misery by judging themselves by these signs, which are only evidences of strong grace. You must not judge whether you are in a state of grace based on things such as elevated joys and comforts of the Holy Spirit; these are things that God gives to only a few, such as those who have been in the school of Christ for a long time. In a school, a newly-arrived scholar must not compare himself to the most learned; likewise, judge the truth of your grace by its lowest measure. The reason why hypocrites and poorly-formed Christians fail is this: Hypocrites judge that they have grace because they have <term>gaven</term> <note>spiritual gifts or intellectual talents like preaching or knowledge</note>, while weak Christians judge that they have no grace because they do not find in themselves such measures of grace as they see in others. We do not say it is not day simply because it is not noon. It is ungratefulness toward God and unkindness to ourselves to try to prove the worthlessness of grace based on its weakness. Therefore, if you cannot say, "I see my grace," it is nevertheless well if you can say, "Praised be God, I see my sins." If you cannot say that you have fully left your sin, it is still well if you can say, "I have a firm intention to do so." If you cannot cry out over the lack of grace, nevertheless comfort yourself; and do not conclude that you have no grace at all.

<margin>3rd Warning.</margin>
And do not conclude, because you have a small measure of comfort, that you have only a small measure of grace. This is the mistake of young converts; for they measure the amount of their grace by their comforts, which is a false and deceptive rule. The growth of grace must not be measured by the movement of joy. The sweet blossom of joy can fall away when the fruit of grace begins to emerge. Indeed, the Christians who have the greatest measure of grace sometimes have the smallest measure of comfort. This is to let us know in every way that—just as the essence and the practice—the comforts of our grace also proceed from free grace alone. Our Lord Jesus Christ, who was anointed above his fellows and full of grace and truth, was nevertheless without comfort in the time of his abandonment; when, because of the withholding of the favor of God his Father, he cried out, *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>original: "Mijn Godt, mijn Godt, waerom hebt ghy my verlaten?"</note> And so, sometimes Christians who have only small measures of grace can have much comfort; and this is the

<column-break/>

reason for the beams of joy which young converts experience. Yet it is God's favor toward them that they have such joy in their first conversion; and therefore their joy is more noticeable at such a time because such people commonly experience many disturbances of the mind when they pass through the pains of the "new birth." The change then brings joy and comfort; thus, they can have more feelings of joy at their first conversion, even though they may later find a growth in grace when the joy is just as real, though not as sensible. Therefore, do not judge your grace by your comfort.

<margin>4th Warning.</margin>
And do not conclude that the measure of your grace is small because you have a small measure of "gifts." Gifts are the results of time and experience, and the fruits of study, gained through the strength of natural powers or duties. A person can have a lively and ingenious ability to invent things: a deep judgment, a retentive memory, clear speech, and other such matters; and yet none of these can be proofs of grace. Rather, they are all natural endowments. Gifts can be high, while grace is low. This was the case with the church of Corinth; they were enriched in all speech and knowledge, so that they lacked no gift compared to other churches; and yet the Apostle says of these Corinthians that they had very little grace. For he rebukes them in 1 Corinthians 3:1, saying they were not spiritual but carnal, and young children in Christ; and that because of their envy, strife, and discord; and that they were carnal and walked according to the way of men. This was also the case with the Church of Laodicea, which said it was rich, and increased with goods, and had need of nothing; but it knew not that it was wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked. It is with some professors of faith as it is with a student who has read many books on geography and the descriptions of various places; he knows how to speak of them very well. But if he had to travel through those lands of which he has so often read, he would find himself very much at a loss. Likewise, gifts can carry a person far in religious discourse; but it is grace that makes a person powerful in putting religion into practice. A child of God who has only small measures of gifts can have much grace beyond them. Among all the seven churches of Asia, it is said of Philadelphia that she had but "little strength"—that is, little strength of gifts—and yet that church was very outstanding in grace. For with as much, if not more, faithfulness than the other churches, she kept Christ’s word, and had not denied his name. Therefore, do not judge your grace by your gifts; yet strive for the best gifts: for the way of true grace (even if weak) is a more excellent way.

<margin>1 Corinthians 1:5, verse 7.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 3:3.</margin>
<margin>Revelation 3:17.</margin>
<margin>Revelation 3:8.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 12:31.</margin>

Now I shall conclude this point with some further comfort to the people of God who have only small measures of grace;

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the degrees of grace, focusing on five reasons why weak faith is sustained by external strength, followed by the second and third consolations regarding the nature and durability of grace.</meta>

Grace, with its

<margin>1. Consolations.</margin>
1. Although you are weak in yourself, you nevertheless have much strength from outside of you; or rather, it is within you: Because the Spirit of Christ, who dwells in your hearts, makes you believe that even if the Devil does everything he can to make a small faith cease; nevertheless, Christ must be thanked that it does not cease. The alliances of the <margin>Luke 22.</margin> World, the flesh, and the Devil are strong against your small grace: but be of good courage, you are God's little children, says <margin>1 John 4:4.</margin> <note>Original cites John 14, 44, likely a printer's error for 1 John 4:4.</note> John, and have overcome them: for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world: and the weaker you are, the more opportunity and advantage God has to magnify the glory of his power in your <margin>2 Cor. 12:9.</margin> weakness.

1. Console yourselves then, you weak Christians: for you have a strong God. In the <margin>Ps. 26:4; Jude 24.</margin> Lord, the LORD, is an eternal Rock of ages. Your God is powerful to keep you from stumbling, and to present you blameless before his glory in <margin>1 Pet. 1:5.</margin> joy. He is powerful in his strength to preserve you through faith unto salvation. So do not fear; for you have a strong God: and his power shall be glorified in your weakness.

2. For you have a strong Savior: although your grace is weak, he is <margin>Heb. 7:25.</margin> nevertheless powerful to completely save those who go to God through him. Christ <margin>1 Cor. 1:24.</margin> <note>Original cites 1 Cor. 3:24.</note> is the wisdom and the power of God to those who are called: Yes, he is called a strong redeemer. Our redeemer is strong, the Lord of Hosts is his name. Satan is indeed the Prince of the power of the air: for so he is called in Eph. 2:2; but Jesus Christ is truly the great power of God; who is powerful because <margin>Rom. 8:37.</margin> <note>Original cites Rom 8:20.</note> he is stronger than the strong-armed warrior, to trample Satan under the feet of his saints.

3. You lie under a strong word, which is powerful to complete the work of grace that has begun in you. The word of God, although <margin>1 Cor. 1:18; Rom. 1:16; 2 Cor. 10:4-5.</margin> it is foolishness to those who are perishing; it is nevertheless a power of God to those who are being saved: yes, it is an instrument powerful through God for pulling down strongholds, casting down arguments and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, leading every thought captive to the obedience of Christ: why the Apostle Paul <margin>Acts 20:32.</margin> prays, "now brothers, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace; which is powerful to build [you] up, and to give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified." Even if faith is weak, <margin>James 1:21.</margin> nevertheless the word is strong; namely, the <margin>2 Tim. 3:16-17.</margin> implanted word which is powerful to save your souls: Yes, in a word, the word of God is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: so that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

4. You are weak, but you stand on a firm <margin>2 Tim. 2:19.</margin> foundation. 1. It is a foundation. 2. A firm foundation. 3. The foundation of God. And 4. The firm foundation of God. Now, weak believers stand by the unchangeable decree of God, which the Apostle here calls the foundation of God.

5. Weak believers are assisted by a strong Spirit. The Spirit of God is not only a Spirit of grace and of prayers: <margin>Zech. 12:10; 2 Tim. 1:7.</margin> But it is also a Spirit of power. And

<column-break/>

therefore weak believers may rejoice, even though they have only small grace, that nevertheless that small grace is protected by the great power of God unto salvation.

<margin>2. Consolations.</margin>
2. The truth and the nature of grace are not so much perceived through good deeds as through good <term>affections</term> <note>In this context, "affections" refers to the deep-seated desires, loves, and inclinations of the heart rather than just external actions.</note>. "How beautiful is your excellent love, my sister," said Christ to the Bride. God counts our beauty by our love, and our perfection by the sincerity of our affections. Natural abilities (which hypocrites and pretenders may reach) look like good deeds; but they cannot reach good affections. A painter can well paint the color of a figure; but he cannot give heat to the paintings through his art. Good deeds can give the likeness of a Christian: in that which Jehu did, he seemed to be a faithful Reformer; but good affections are a proof of life and the heat of true grace. Therefore judge your grace by your affections; and take consolation from this: even if you are small and empty in deeds, if only you are warm and active in your affections.

<margin>Third and last consolation.</margin>
The third and last consolation is this, that small grace shall be a lasting grace. Adam had perfection, but had no persevering perfection; and you (poor soul!) have imperfection of grace; but have perseverance in grace. The most violent and harmful flood of corruptions shall not <term>extinguish</term> <note>The original Dutch *upbluffchen* refers to blowing out or quenching a flame.</note> the smallest measure and least spark of true grace: the stormy gust of temptation shall not blow out the weak <term>smoldering wick</term> <note>A reference to Matthew 12:20; a "smoldering wick" represents a weak but genuine faith that God will not put out.</note>: not a drop of this Divine ointment shall be spilled like water upon the earth. Comets appear to shine for a while, but then they fall; by which it becomes clear that they are comets, and not true stars: True stars do not fall, nor can they fall. Oh! then praise God, who although he breaks the nations in his wrath like a potter's vessel with an iron scepter: nevertheless has such loving-kindness over weak believers that he shall not break the bruised reed: and although he extinguishes the lamp of the wicked, nevertheless he shall not extinguish the smoldering wick. The shining graces of hypocrites shall perish and come to nothing, while true grace shall persevere. The painted figure shall soon age, while the natural form endures. A child of God can be tossed by corruptions and temptations in a boisterous sea; but that ship shall never suffer shipwreck: because Christ is the Pilot upon it, the Scripture the compass, the Promises the rigging, Hope the anchor, Faith the cable, the Holy Spirit the wind, and the holy affections the <term>sails</term> <note>Original: *Sepelen*, likely a variation or misspelling of *zeilen* (sails).</note> which are filled with the winds of the Spirit, etc. Therefore do not fear, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the Kingdom.

### 1 KINGS 14.
