Having finished the first part of this teaching concerning the small measure of grace, I now come to the second part: which is that God diligently takes notice of, tenderly nurtures, and lovingly rewards the smallest beginnings and measures of grace in the hearts of His people.

In the pursuit of this matter, I shall proceed in this order:

1. I shall examine the truth of the same.

2. I shall also endeavor to give you an understanding of the grounds for this; and then make the Application. <note>Original: "Toe-eygeninge," a theological term for applying the sermon's lessons to the listener's life.</note>

First, that God thus nurtures and cherishes the small beginnings of grace will become evident if we consider:

1. These Scriptural sayings: Matthew 12:22 <note>Likely a reference to Matthew 12:20.</note> states *He shall not quench the smoking wick*, that is, through the figure of speech called <term>Meiosis</term> <note>Original: "Meiofis." A rhetorical understatement where one says less to imply more; here, "not quenching" implies actively fanning the flame.</note> (as I have already shown) that He shall set it alight. *He shall not break the bruised reed*, that is, He shall strengthen the same. God does not only take notice of the flames, but also of the smoke of grace; not only of the ripe fruit;

<margin>Mark 11:13</margin>

but also of the tender buds. Christ wanted green figs from the fig tree, even though the time of ripe fruit had not yet come; so some explain that passage in Mark 11:13. Christ takes not only the honey, but also the honeycombs; that is, say the interpreters, not only the outstanding services, but also the humbler services of His people. God takes notice of

<margin>
Isa. 14:15.
1 Pet. 3:6.
</margin>

the callings of our hearts; of the desires of the humble; of the innermost sighs of the soul: there is not one good word but that God takes notice of it. Yea, God not only takes notice of the smallest good that is in His people, but He also regards the "common good" which is in those who have no true grace, just as in that young man in the Gospel who came to Christ, although he had no true grace:

<margin>Mark 10:21.</margin>

yet it says there that Jesus loved him. And He also took notice of that wise

<margin>Mark 12:33.</margin>

answer of the Scribe, of which it is written in Mark: *And he said unto him, thou art not far from the kingdom of God.*

2. The truth of this point can be proven from the sweet and lovely promises. I shall give you one instead of many, which is recounted by the Prophet Isaiah: *He shall feed his*

<margin>Isa. 40:11.</margin>

*flock like a shepherd: He shall gather the lambs in his arms, and carry them in his bosom: and shall gently lead those that are with young.*

3. Through the exhortations that Christ gives us on how we ought to carry ourselves toward those

<column-break/>

who are weak, namely to bear with them with all tenderness. Now if God wants such things to be done by others, how much more shall He Himself bear with those of weak faith with tenderness?

<margin>
Rom. 15:1.
and Psa. 103:16.
</margin>

1. God wants the church to help bear the weak, yes, even their weaknesses; and that we should not please ourselves; and most gloriously then will God bear with them and endure them: See Psalm 103.

<margin>Rom. 14:1.</margin>

Rom. 14:15.
1 Cor. 8:12.
</margin>

4. We must restore a weak brother who has fallen, and set him back in the ranks with the spirit of meekness: *ye which are spiritual* (that is, strong Christians) *help up such a one* who has fallen through weakness.

<margin>Gal. 6:1.</margin>

<margin>Isa. 35:4.</margin>

<margin>
Heb. 12:12, 13.
</margin>

And make straight paths for our feet: so that what is lame may not be turned out of the way, but rather that it may be healed. We must not be like cruel beasts, which push the poor wounded beasts away from them; but must consider the healing of the wounded, and the comforting of the feebleminded, the supporting of the weak, and

<margin>1 Thess. 5:14.</margin>

patience toward all: *support the weak*; that is, put your shoulder to the task to carry those who want to stand and are yet weak. Hold them up, as a crutch does for a lame body: help him to stand who seems to fall from weakness. Let your love help hold them up, just as a beam holds up a house that would otherwise easily fall. Now if God commands us to take all these cares for those who are weak in grace, such as nurturing, supporting, and comforting them: how much more then will the God of grace and of compassion Himself be careful to nurture the smallest measures of grace in weak believers?

<margin>2. Question.</margin>

Why does God nurture the smallest measures of grace in His people?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin>

1. Because the smallest measure of grace is of a very great value: the smallest grace, and the least measure, or the lowest degree of the same, is the purchase of Christ's blood, and the merit of His heavy suffering. The smallest piece of a diamond is precious: pearls and precious stones are small in terms of size, but great in terms of quality and esteem. The lowest degree of grace is the work of God, and God will not forsake His work.

<margin>2. Answer.</margin>

2. Because small grace is of the same nature and excellence as the highest degree of grace: for just as the filings of gold are of the same nature as the gold; so the smallest measure of grace is grace. The faith of all believers is the same faith in kind, although not the same in degrees or elevations: their faith is equally precious in all; but

<margin>2 Pet. 1:1.</margin>

not of equal strength.

It exhorts stronger Christians to support the weak, mirroring God's own compassionate nature and the intrinsic value of grace bought by Christ's blood.</summary>

# Grace, and its [Degrees]
<note>The header is incomplete in the original, likely continuing from the previous page's "Grace, and its degrees."</note>

<margin>Answer 3.</margin>
3. Because God is the Author of weak grace as well as strong grace. Solomon gives a good rule as to why the rich should not be begrudging toward the poor: because God is the Author and the Maker of them both.
<margin>Prov. 22:2.</margin>
And God will no more begrudge His grace to the poor in spirit than to those who are rich in grace: for He is the Maker of both. This serves as a reason for us why we must not despise the poor: because God has made them. Therefore, it is certainly much more true that because the Lord makes poor and weak Christians, He will not despise them, etc.

<margin>Job 31:11, 15.</margin>
Job says, "I did not despise the cause of my manservant or my maidservant;" and he immediately gives the reason for it, saying, "Did not He who made me in the womb also make him, and did not one [God] fashion us in the womb?" This is then an argument why the rich must not despise the poor, nor those rich in grace despise those who are poor in grace: for God has fashioned and made them both. Now, what is a rule for us, God also chooses to make a rule for Himself: that He will not abandon that which He has made. For so it stands in the Prophet Isaiah; thus says the Lord: your Creator [O Jacob] and your Former [O Israel]: "Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine."
<margin>Isa. 43:1; Isa. 44:2.</margin>
And again: "Thus says the Lord your Maker, and your Former from the womb, who helps you: Fear not, O Jacob my Servant, and you, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen." Indeed, although Jacob is like a worm, nevertheless the God who made him will not reject him but will preserve him. See here a lovely promise made to those who have small grace, based on this foundation: that God is the Author of that small grace. "Your people,"
<margin>Isa. 60:21, 22.</margin>
"shall all be righteous; they shall inherit the land forever: they shall be a sprout of my planting, a work of my hands, that I may be glorified; the smallest shall become a thousand, and the least a mighty nation: I the Lord will hasten it in its time."

<margin>Psal. 138:8.</margin>
The Lord will perfect the work concerning His people; that is, He will stir up and complete the smallest beginnings of grace, because grace is His work in His servants. It is a very good practice in prayer to say: "O Lord, do not forsake the work of Your hands." And although God, in regard to outward things,
<margin>Job 10:8.</margin>
can bring pain to those whom His hands have made, it is otherwise in regard to grace: for God will not scatter even one measure of grace which is the work of His hands. Ownership is the ground of love, care, and tenderness: just as a man looks after a weak child because it is his child, and will repair a weak house because it is the house where he lives.

And this is the third answer regarding God’s tender care over His people: that the smallest measure of grace shall not be scattered or forsaken, because God is the Author of the same.

<margin>4th Answer.</margin>
The fourth can be drawn from the [covenant] of grace: its nature and content is to receive sincerity in place of perfection, desire instead of deeds, intentions instead of accomplishments, grains instead of pounds,

<column-break/>

and mites for millions. <note>The author uses a weight and currency metaphor: "asen" (the smallest weight unit) vs. "ponden" (pounds), and "mijten" (widow's mites) vs. "milioenen" (millions).</note> Therefore, God will accept and reward the smallest measure of grace, as long as it is in truth and sincerity. God promised Abraham, when He renewed the covenant of grace with him, that he should walk before Him and be perfect;
<margin>Gen. 15:1. <note>The text cites Genesis 15:1, but the command to "walk before me and be perfect" is famously found in Genesis 17:1.</note></margin>
that is, sincere; and God willed then to be his exceeding great reward.

<margin>1st Use.</margin>
To make some application of this truth, we may draw these consequences from it: If God nurtures and will reward the small measure of grace, it then follows that God takes notice of the smallest sins to punish them.

<margin>1st Consequence.</margin>
He who lovingly fosters the true sprouting of grace will likewise justly behold the sprouts of corruption in His people. Thus, He sought to kill Moses because he had forgotten the circumcision of his son; and the Lord killed Uzzah because he presumptuously took hold of the Ark. "Of all the
<margin>Exod. 4; 2 Sam. 6; Amos 3:2.</margin>
families of the earth, I have known you alone" (says God of His people), "therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities."

<margin>Num. 23:21.</margin>
It is true; it is said there, "The Lord does not behold iniquity in Jacob, nor see perverseness in Israel"; but this is not as the opponents of the Law <note><term>Antinomians</term>: A 17th-century theological group who argued that because of God's grace, the moral law was no longer binding and God did not "see" sin in believers.</note> explain it, as if God does not see sin in His people and as if He is not displeased by their sins. But the meaning is that God does not see the sins in His people so as to punish them eternally. Furthermore, the specific sense of that passage is this: that as Balak hired Balaam to curse the people of Israel, and as the false prophet (for the reward of unrighteousness) took every opportunity to curse them, he nevertheless at those times could not make a single curse take hold upon them because there was no "calling sin" <note>A "calling sin" or "crying sin" refers to a sin so great it demands immediate divine judgment.</note> among them. Therefore, he gave Balak the advice to tempt them to sin—to draw them to idolatry and adultery through the stumbling blocks of the Midianite women, and so cause them to fall. But God does indeed see sin in His people, yes, even the smallest sin; He sees their failings, although not to condemn them for the same, but to chasten them for them. God sees the intention to sin as well as the intention for grace. It is said of Balak that he fought against Israel.
<margin>Josh. 24:9.</margin>
Now, we do not read that Balak fought in open deed, but that he was of the intention to do so; for to that end he sent and called Balaam the son of Beor to curse them. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit reckons this godless intention as much as if he had accomplished it.

<margin>2nd Consequence.</margin>
Learn from this that in Christians of greater growth, there ought to be the same mind toward the weak that was in Christ Jesus; who, although He was higher than the highest, nevertheless looked upon the poor and lowly without disdain. And so we must also do. Heaven is the throne and the earth is the footstool
<margin>Isa. 66:1-2.</margin>
of the Lord; yet this great God will not despise the weakest saint, but He will look upon the poor and contrite in spirit, and him who trembles at His word. He will look upon the poor, weak, trembling soul—and shall we turn away from such with pride and contempt? And set them as our footstool? Shall Christ carry the Lamb on His shield, and we the Lion? Shall He be as a gentle lamb...

<summary>This page explains that God nurtures weak grace because He is its Author and because the Covenant of Grace accepts sincerity over perfection. It warns that while God fosters small grace, He also observes and chastens small sins in His people, urging mature Christians to mirror Christ's tenderness toward the weak.</summary>

# [Various] Degrees
<note>The header continues the topic of "Degrees of Grace."</note>

...be meek and tame, while you are as bold and haughty as a lion, despising all the beasts of the forest? Oh, do not be full of disdain toward weak Christians, who are despised and whose courage is taken away by certain "strong" Christians.

<margin>Matthew 9:16</margin>
1. This happens when they use such high teachings that go far beyond their strength and growth. For poor, torn, and old leather wineskins are not fit to carry new wine. Alas, poor soul! Christ Himself desired to present His teachings according to their capacity, and to lay no higher duties upon them than their ability allowed, so that He would not weaken their strength through His commands. Fasting was a hard service for the disciples; and He excused them until they had more experience in the ways of God, and until the time that the Holy Spirit would come upon them and they had received greater grace. This serves as an excellent lesson for us: that we must not discourage the beginners in the school of Christ, nor give them such writings to read which exceed their understanding.

2. When strong Christians are too harsh or too strict in their sharp rebukes against the weak for their failings and weaknesses. Young converts are like young twigs, which must be handled gently, otherwise they would be broken. Thus, the strong must bear with the weak in meekness; excuse their failings; hide their defects; urge them toward perfection; encourage their progress; resolve their doubts; help carry their burdens; and through this meekness, bring them to a love of religion, so that they do not develop a distaste for it as soon as they begin to understand it.

3. By the belittling of their gifts. Alas, how quickly is the smoking wick extinguished by too much conceit from those who consider themselves to be burning torches? How hastily is the poor spark of grace stepped upon by the foot of pride?

4. By drawing them into doubtful disputations, directly against the admonition of the Apostle: *Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.*

<margin>Romans 14:1</margin>
5. By giving them a bad example. Weak Christians can be led better by examples than by commands. Consider Peter, who was a pillar of the Church, a strong Christian who nevertheless denied the Gentiles for fear of persecution; he separated himself and acted hypocritically along with other Jews, who were in every way but weak Christians. Thus Paul teaches that they must abstain from giving offense regarding the eating of things offered to idols; *for if any man see thee (which hast knowledge—that is, who are a strong Christian) sit at meat in the idol's temple, shall not the conscience of him which is weak be emboldened to eat those things which are offered to idols?*

<margin>Galatians 2:12, 13</margin>
Therefore, you Christians, learn from God to nurture the weak beginnings of grace in God's people. *Look not upon me,* says the Church, *for I am black because the sun has shone upon me:* that is, do not look at me with a despising eye or a sour face.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, she adds to this: *my mother's children were angry with me;* that is, other congregations and peoples despised and disdained me because of my weakness. But it must not be so among Christians; rather, the strong must support the weak; for even the poorest Christians are not despised by the Angels, but are served by them.

<margin>Hebrews 1:14</margin>
<margin>3rd Consequence.</margin>
Learn from this how God, through time and stages, makes the work of grace grow in the hearts of His people toward further perfection. The Devil’s bread, or mushrooms, and all such unworthy things—as well as the wonder-tree <note>Original: "wonder-boom," referring to the gourd plant in Jonah 4:6</note> of Jonah—may spring up in a single night and perish just as hastily. But things of great weight and value do not shoot up so quickly; they are of a longer growth before they reach their perfection: like the elephant among the beasts, the tree among the shrubs, and Man among the sentient creatures. As it is in nature, so it is also in grace: it all proceeds by steps, from the smaller to the greater. The godly are called *Trees of righteousness*, and yet this happens by degrees: first there are sprouts just above the earth, then follows a larger growth, etc. verse 11. So then, young converts must not be despondent: for God’s works, both of nature and grace, are perfected by degrees.

<margin>Isaiah 61:3, verse 11</margin>
<margin>1. Use of Warning.</margin>
Although God takes notice of the smallest measure of grace, this must not make you careless about growing in grace. God said in the first Creation to the creatures: *be fruitful and multiply*; and by the power of that word, the earth brought forth fruit that same day. Likewise, the Lord expects in the new or second Creation that our grace should be fruitful and multiply.

<margin>2. Warning.</margin>
<margin>Zechariah 4:10</margin>
2. Although you have little grace, do not despise or belittle it. *Despise not the day of small things* in your soul. Do not trample the bud of the grapes, nor the new wine in the clusters, but say: there is a blessing in it. Do not despise a tiny mustard seed, for it shall grow into a tree. Likewise, do not despise a small grace which is a spark from Heaven; do not stamp it out, nor disdain the smallest measure of it—but neither be satisfied with having only the greatest.

<margin>2. Use of Consolation.</margin>
Let this comfort your soul (O weak Christians!) to whom it is a burden that you still have so much corruption and so little grace. God will overlook a great deal of sin and take notice of the smallest grace. God, in the refining of His gold and silver, will not lose a single drop of His grace, even though it lies under a heap of dross. It says in the Gospel of Christ that *He has His winnowing fan in His hand, and He will purge His threshing floor, and gather His wheat into the barn.* Now, with the winnowing fan, one generally throws out the worst and keeps the best; shaking out the chaff and keeping the wheat. Likewise, Christ—though He purges out the chaff of corruption—will nevertheless preserve and keep every grain of grace. It is quite different with the Devil's sieve. Christ told Peter that Satan desired to *sift* him. Now, the use of the sieve is exactly the opposite of the winnowing fan: for it keeps the worst, and...
<note>The text ends mid-sentence as the page concludes.</note>

<margin>Luke 22:31</margin>

# Grace, and its [Degrees]
<note>The header refers to the "Degrees of Grace," a common theological topic concerning the spiritual growth of a believer from "weak" to "strong."</note>

...let the best prevail. The Devil does all he can to stifle our grace and to make our sins increase. But God wants to, and shall, kill your corruptions and nurture your grace: and if the smallest grace is in your soul—even if mixed with much corruption—He will nevertheless not despise it.

<margin>2. Consolation.</margin>
God maintains a very tender watch over those who are weak in grace: a tender child is constantly carried in our arms; and the Good Shepherd shall carry the weakest of the flock in His bosom. Christ gave the command to Peter that he should feed His lambs.

<margin>John 21:15</margin>
1. God’s care for weak Christians is such that He will not allow them to be tempted above their ability: but He will, with the temptation, provide a way of escape. God notices that we are but dust; and that wise Physician of our souls will mercifully weigh every grain or every gift, and will not exhaust the strength of those whose strength is small.

<margin>Hosea 11:1, 3</margin>
2. God will not initially lay heavy, burdensome duties upon them: for Christ taught His disciples such teachings as their weakness could endure.

3. God will help carry their weaknesses: for He teaches His children to walk, and takes them up in His arms.

## II. TIMOTHY 2.
### VERSE 1.

->**Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.**<-

<margin>
6th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry within London, March 30, 1651.
<note>St Lawrence Jewry is a historic church in the City of London, known for its influential sermons during the 17th century.</note>
</margin>
Having previously handled the doctrine of small beginnings and of the smallest measures of true grace; and having shown you therein how God is willing to accept and reward the same, through the explanation of that passage, 1 Kings 14:13, concerning Jeroboam’s Son, in whom "some good thing" was found. But lest this doctrine should by chance (through the corruption of our deceitful hearts) produce in us a spiritual stagnation and a complacency in the weak stages of grace; I shall now continue my treatment regarding the stages of grace; and shall show you that although God takes notice of weak grace, we must nevertheless labor to obey this Apostolic command: *be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.*

In this entire verse there are three parts;
1. A friendly address, *My Son,*

<column-break/>

2. An urgent exhortation, *be strong in the grace.*
3. The reason for the same, in the connecting word, **Therefore.** <note>The Dutch "sluytwoordeken" refers to the word "therefore" which links this verse to the preceding chapter.</note>

1. Regarding the address; someone might ask how Timothy could be Paul's son: for his father was a Greek, and Paul was a Jew from the tribe of Benjamin; <margin>Philippians 3. 1 Timothy 1.</margin> to which the answer is that Timothy was not Paul’s son according to the flesh, but in the faith.

The further question is, why is he called Paul’s son? Beldunius gives this reason: because (he says) Paul had birthed him into the faith, citing 1 Corinthians 4:17 <margin>1 Corinthians 4:14, 17.</margin> compared with verse 14, where Paul calls the Corinthians, whom he had converted to the faith, his beloved sons (verse 14), and likewise Timothy in verse 17. But Timothy was not Paul’s son in such a manner: for Estius <note>Willem Hessels van Est (1542–1613), a famous Dutch commentator.</note> shows that he was converted long before <margin>2 Timothy 1:5. 2 Timothy 3:15.</margin> Paul knew him, through the godly instructions of his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice.

The true reasons why Paul called Timothy his son were:
1. Because Paul was an elderly man and Timothy was young; and it was customary for the elders to call their juniors "sons."
2. Because he strengthened him in the faith.
3. Because he loved him as a son, and Timothy in turn loved Paul as a father.
4. Because (just as a son serves his father <margin>Philippians 2:22.</margin>) he served him in the Gospel.

Before I come to the main doctrines, I will observe something in passing: from these reasons why Paul called Timothy his son, and by the address, *my son,* **Note:**

<margin>1. Observation.</margin>
1. That Ministers must use lovely approaches to the hearts of their hearers, in order to perform their customary instructions fruitfully.

Soft words turn away wrath, and hard stones are broken upon soft cushions. This was Paul's practice here and elsewhere: he first won their affections to better fashion their judgment and understanding.

<margin>2. Observation.</margin>
2. That he called him *my son* in respect to himself as a father; note therein;

That religion unites people and places them in the closest bond. For those who are glued and united together in the blood of Christ are tied together in the strongest bond. <margin>The blood of Christ binds salvation. <note>original: "Sanguis Christi glutinât Salutem"</note></margin>

Now I come to the reason for this duty, *Therefore, my son,* etc. The commentators differ as to which verse this connecting word belongs: some relate it to the 7th verse of the previous chapter, as Estius does. For "God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind": and if it is so, then note:

<margin>3. Observation.</margin>
That the receiving of the first stages of grace must be a prevailing reason to move us to grow in grace.

# Various Degrees [of Grace].

Others refer this to the example of *Paul* in verse 8, or to the example of *Onesiphorus* in verse 16, from which we may observe:

<margin>verse 16. a</margin>
<margin>3. 5.</margin>
<margin>1. 4.</margin>
<margin>5th Observation.</margin>
That the good example of the pious must be a motivating reason for us to grow in what is good.

If this belongs (as *Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD), an influential theologian and biblical commentator of the early Church.</note> suggests) to the 15th verse: *You know this, that all those in Asia have turned away from me, among whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.* Then observe:

<margin>Explanation of the Text.</margin>
**Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.**

<margin>1. 5.</margin>
<margin>3. 10.</margin>
*Timothy* can be viewed in a double capacity: either as a Minister or as a private Christian. If as a Minister, then the power of the exhortation lies in this: that he should grow in the gifts and graces of his ministry; from which one can observe:

<margin>Ephesians 3:8</margin>
<margin>6th Observation.</margin>

Ministers receive grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all nations, *Romans* 1:5. And grace is given to them so that they might proclaim to others the unsearchable riches of *Christ, Ephesians* 3:8.

<margin>7th Observation.</margin>
2. If he is viewed as a private Christian, then he is exhorted not to remain content with the grace he had received, but to labor for greater strength of grace.

**Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.**

Grace can be said to be in Christ in two ways: either

1. As in the <term>subject</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, the "subject" refers to the person or thing in which a quality (like grace) resides.</note> containing the grace, or
2. As a fountain, overflowing to His people.

<margin>John 1:16</margin>
Grace is in *Christ* in all fullness; from which His people receive grace for grace.

There are two things to observe, which I shall note from the words regarding the exhortation, without connecting them to what preceded or what follows.

<margin>1st Doctrine.</margin>
1. That believers must not be satisfied with the small measure of grace which they have already received, but must strive to obtain greater strength of grace.

<margin>2nd Doctrine.</margin>
2. That Christ is the subject in whom all grace resides, and the fountain from which believers must receive all their grace.

In explaining the first doctrine, my first task is to demonstrate that believers must not be satisfied with the small measures of grace they have already received, but that they must labor for more grace. And this I shall prove:

<column-break/>

1. Through examples. 1. That believers have advanced from weak grace to strong grace, receiving strength out of weakness, <margin>Hebrews 11:34</margin> *Hebrews* 11:34. Some commentators refer this passage to *Hezekiah's* recovery of health, 1 *Kings* 20 <note>In many older Bibles, the books of Samuel and Kings were grouped; this refers to 2 Kings 20.</note>, but it may have a more general expansion and application. The Psalmist, speaking of God's people, says, <margin>Psalm 84:8</margin> *they go from strength to strength, every one [of them] shall appear before God in Zion.* It is true the specific focus of these words is on the Jews' journey up to *Jerusalem* to worship, for they had to go up to *Jerusalem* three times a year to worship according to the law, *Exodus* 24:17. But *Ainsworth* <note>Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622), a famous English scholar and non-conformist known for his Hebrew translations and commentaries.</note> understands it as our growth in grace; just as we are said to be changed from glory to glory, that is, from small steps of grace to greater; <margin>2 Corinthians 3:18</margin> grace is but begun glory, and glory is but perfected grace. True grace is constantly panting and striving for perfection: and therefore *Paul* says, *if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead,* his meaning being that I may <margin>Philippians 3:11</margin> obtain that perfection of holiness which accompanies the state of resurrection—a substitution of the name of the subject for the attribute. He was constantly advancing and striving so that he might obtain further degrees of grace, and to that end, *Paul* forgot those things which were behind and reached forth unto those things which were before, verse 14. And although *Paul* had very great knowledge in the mystery of *Christ* (*Ephesians* 3:4), he was nonetheless always desiring to know more and more of *Christ*.

2. Through passages of Scripture where God's people have prayed for the strength of grace: <margin>Ephesians 3:14, 16</margin> *I bow my knees* (says *Paul*) *unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that He would grant you, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with might by His Spirit in the inner man.* And speaking of the <margin>Romans 15:14, 15</margin> Romans, *Romans* 15:14-15, (he says) *I myself also am persuaded of you, that ye also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge:* yet because the best and the most learned have only partial knowledge, and see through a glass in a dark <margin>1 Corinthians 13:12</margin> manner <note>Refers to "seeing through a glass darkly" or in a riddle.</note>, 1 *Corinthians* 13:12, he prays that God would fill them with all joy and peace in believing, that they might abound in <margin>Philippians 1:9</margin> hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost. So he prays that their love might abound <margin>Colossians 1:9-10</margin> more and more in knowledge and all judgment; that they might be filled with the knowledge of His will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you might walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work: and increasing in the knowledge of God. Thus has God's people prayed for a further increase in grace: *Paul* grew in greater strength after his conversion, whereby he was able to convince the Jews who lived at *Damascus*, *Acts* 9:22.

2. Through Commandments: <margin>2nd Proof.</margin> leaving the first principles of the doctrine of *Christ*, we must go on unto perfection; we must apply <margin>Hebrews 6:1</margin> diligence, and add to our faith virtue, <margin>2 Peter 1:5</margin> and to virtue knowledge: likewise we are commanded to be strong in the Lord, to stand in the <margin>Ephesians 6:10</margin> faith, to quit ourselves like men, and <margin>1 Corinthians 16:13</margin> be strong, and abound more and more; <margin>2 Thessalonians 4:1</margin>

# Grace and Its Increase

### [Page 372]

...then: many more such commandments are found throughout 
<margin>* 1 Cor. 15:58</margin> Scripture, which show us our bounden duty to apply ourselves to growing more and more in grace, and to obtaining greater measures of grace.

<margin>Prov. 4:18</margin> 3. Through promises that God's people shall do so. *The path of the righteous is like a shining light, progressing and shining until the full day.* That is, they shall grow more and more in strength. God’s gentleness shall make His people great, and make their 
<margin>Ps. 18:36, 37</margin> footsteps wide beneath them. *The weak among them shall be on that day like David,* and 
<margin>2 Sam. 18:3</margin> *the house of David like God, like the Angel of the Lord before them.* Paræus <note>David Pareus (1548–1622), a prominent German Reformed Protestant theologian and reformer.</note> in his short notes says: he who is weak in faith shall become like David—strong in faith.

<margin>**Question.**</margin> Why must believers not be satisfied with the first beginnings of grace, but instead labor to become strong Christians?

<margin>Answer.</margin> The reasons can be taken, first, especially from the necessity of it—why they must do so. And second, from the danger if they do not.

### 1. From the necessity of the same, these reasons can be given:

<margin>**1st Reason.**</margin> 1. Because the Devil always seeks to meet us with strong temptations. **Therefore** 
<margin>Eph. 6:10, 11, 12</margin> we are commanded to be strong in the Lord, and to put on the whole armor of God, so that we may stand against the cunning deceits of the Devil, for we do not have a struggle against flesh and blood: but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the world. Now, if the Devil is strong and armed, shall we keep ourselves content while being unarmed and weak Christians? Then that 
<margin>1 John 2:14</margin> which the Apostle says in 1 John 2:14—*I have written to you (young men) because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you: and you have overcome the evil one*—would be of no value to you. But when he 
<margin>verse 12</margin> writes to the children, he says in verse 12: *I write to you [little children] because your sins are forgiven for His name's sake;* indicating that although weak grace is enough to bring us the forgiveness of sins, it is nonetheless strong grace that is powerful enough to overcome the temptations of the Devil. The Devil 
<margin>1 Pet. 5:8, 9</margin> will certainly not overcome the weakest measure of grace; but the stronger our grace is, the more powerful we are to withstand that enemy of our salvation and to overcome him. The Devil is called a roaring lion, whom we must withstand, being firm in faith: and therefore, since a weak faith is not powerful enough to battle the Devil, we ought to grow into strong Christians.

<margin>**2nd Reason.**</margin> 2. If we consider the strong resistance of the world which we might encounter; so that we might have to 
<margin>1 Cor. 15:32</margin> fight, like Paul, against the beasts: we can often meet such a generation of irrational men; 
<margin>1 Cor. 16:13</margin> and therefore we are commanded to watch and stand in the faith, and to behave ourselves manfully, being strong. The reason for this is given in verse 9: there are many adversaries who meet us; and therefore it is necessary for us to pray 
<margin>Ps. 13:8, 37</margin> with the Psalmist to be strengthened and preserved by the right hand of the Lord. A weak faith is not fit to offer resistance;

<column-break/>

and therefore we must labor to grow in the grace of God.

<margin>3rd Reason.</margin> 3. We have many strong corruptions in our hearts, which a small grace is not powerful enough to kill; strong stirrings, violent lusts—how can weak grace become powerful enough to overcome them? If your graces are weak when your corruptions are strong, you shall be miserably defeated by your corruptions; therefore pray for strengthening and helping grace, through which you may be powerful, not only to withstand, but to suppress and kill the strong lusts and stirrings in your hearts. The other foundation of this teaching is taken from the danger if you do not become powerful in grace; as follows:

1. Others, who have made their profession of religion later than you in terms of time, and yet go before you in the measures and degrees of grace; as it is said: many who are first shall 
<margin>Matt. 19:30 compared with Matt. 12:16</margin> be last, and many who are last shall be first. These who were the first in the profession of the Gospel shall be the last in the degrees and measures of grace, because they did not seek to bring grace to a further increase.

<margin>Not to go forward is to go backward. <note>original Latin: *Non progred. est regredi.*</note></margin> 2. If you do not become powerful in grace, you will surely decline and become weaker: for not to go forward in grace is to go backward. Grace can in some way, or in part, be lost—as can the practice and the comfort of it—but not in its entirety, not its essence. For that is why the Apostle says, *if these things are in you and (in you) abound, they shall not leave [you] idle nor 
<margin>2 Pet. 1:8, Rev. 3:2</margin> unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.* Indicating that you shall become unfruitful if you do not add grace to grace. For if weak things are not watched over and strengthened, they must necessarily die.

3. Although you cannot lose the essence of your grace, you shall nonetheless lose the comfort of the same; and you shall be as troubled and dejected as if you had no grace at all. It is true that weak grace shall bring your soul to Heaven; but it is only strong grace which shall bring Heaven into your soul. Small grace is like some tiny thing which one cannot see because it is small or little. Small grace is in that respect as much as no grace, like that man in the Gospel who called his 
<margin>Mark 9:24</margin> faith "unbelief": *Lord (he says) help my unbelief.* The weakness of grace turns a man's assurance of God's love into presumption; his zeal into lukewarmness; his graces into [mere] gifts; and his faith, as here, into unbelief. It is strong grace that gives joy of heart 
<margin>Lam. 3:18</margin> and hope in God; therefore Jeremiah says: *my strength and my hope is perished from the Lord.* When strength in grace fails, then hope and comfort also perish. It is the Apostle’s prayer in many salutations of his letters, that grace and peace might multiply: if you then do not make your grace grow, you shall neither increase nor keep your comforts.

<margin>2 Pet. 1:9</margin> *He who lacks these things is blind (says the Apostle) and cannot see afar off;* this is not understood as a total lack of grace (as has been shown); for just as it [is mentioned] here...

<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "na" (after/to) suggesting the next page continues the explanation of the spiritual blindness mentioned in 2 Peter 1:9.</meta>

...now it is expressed / he is purified from his former sins / even though he had forgotten that very thing / having lost the sense of forgiveness because he had not added grace to grace.

4. Weak grace under heavy trials will cause a person to doubt and fall / as if he had no grace at all / small grace will preserve a person in small trials / but not in greater ones. Small grace, when a person falls into distress / is as much as no grace; and therefore when the Disciples were at Sea / and when a storm wind arose / and they were afraid / it says in <margin>Matt. 8:26 compared with Mark 4:40.</margin> Matthew, that their faith was small; and in Mark that there was no faith. I would now proceed to the second particular part / which is to give some Scriptural signs of those who have grown in grace / but let me now conclude in my Sermon / with a sharp and righteous rebuke against many professors <note>A "professor" in this 17th-century context refers to someone who "professes" or openly declares their Christian faith, rather than an academic teacher.</note> in our time / who go from one ordinance of God to the other / and yet have little progress and growth in Religion. They can aptly be compared to a group of Ants that are very busy around a molehill / running back and forth through it / but never become large: Even so we have many Christians / who run from one Church to another / from one Preacher to another / and it may be from one opinion to another; but never grow up in true grace / and knowledge of Jesus Christ. But I shall meet such people later in this treatise.

# II. TIMOTHY 2.
## VERSE 1.
### ->My Son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.<-

<margin>Sermon in St. Lawrence Church in London, March 30, 1651. Doctrine.</margin>
Having noted in the previous Sermon this Apostolic command to Timothy, to which all Christians are bound / namely / That it is the dutiful obligation of all believers, not to be satisfied with small measures of grace, but that they must strive to obtain greater strength of grace.

Having proved this both by Scriptural passages / and various reasons / I now proceed to answer this question / namely,

<column-break/>

What are the signs that Scripture gives of strong, grown-up Christians?

We must know that there are signs in Scripture of the truth of grace / as well as of the strength of grace; and these must not be confused or entangled with one another / but must be noted distinctly. Our present question concerns the growth or strength of grace.

<margin>1st Answer</margin>
I. Such / as those who have grown in grace / commonly rejoice in a firmly grounded assurance / and a confident revelation of the love of God in Christ to their <margin>1 John 4:18. <note>original: "Non ita pellitur timor quin animos nostros feliciter, sed non turbent neque impediant pacem nostram Calvin." — Fear is not driven out in such a way that it never touches our minds, but rather that it does not disturb or hinder our peace. (Calvin)</note> Eph. 3:16, 17, 18.</margin> Souls. So says John, perfect love drives out fear: The more perfect love there is / the less tormenting fear is in the Soul: for the cause of our fear and doubting is the lack of our love. We cannot comprehend the great love of God in Christ in our Souls until the time that we are strengthened by His Spirit in the inward Man: which you can see in the prayer of the Apostle for the Ephesians; that God would give them, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with might by His Spirit: that Christ might dwell in their hearts through faith, and that they might be rooted and grounded in love: and that they might be fully able to comprehend with all the Saints, what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height. And that they might know the love of Christ, etc. So that / the more strength of grace is in the Soul / the clearer the comprehension of the love of Christ is also in our Soul.

<margin>2nd Answer. 2 Cor. 1:4.</margin>
II. Strong, grown-up Christians are powerfully able to comfort others through experience, with the comfort wherewith they themselves are comforted by God; and when they are converted, they are <margin>Luke 22:32. Explanation.</margin> powerfully able to strengthen their Brothers, just as Christ said to Peter. By the "Conversion" in that place / is not meant the first work of grace wrought in the Soul; for that was already wrought in Peter before that fall: but the meaning is / Peter, when you are strengthened and restored again from your fall / when you shall have obtained strength again; then see to it that you take care to strengthen others, who might also perhaps happen to fall into the same weakness in which you had fallen. If also a Man were overtaken by any fault, (says Paul to those of Galatia) you who are spiritual restore such a one, with the Spirit of gentleness.

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
You who are spiritual / that is / you who are grown and experienced Christians / see that you diligently endeavor to set such a fallen Brother <margin>Phil. 1:9. Explanation.</margin> upright again. Paul prays for those of Philippi, that their love might abound more and more in knowledge, and all discernment; that is / that they might have knowledge with judgment and experience / so that they might use their discerning knowledge in love for the building up of others / who were weak in grace: and in the Letter to the Romans, <margin>Rom. 15:14.</margin> the same Apostle says of the strong Christians / I am persuaded of you, my Brothers; that you also yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another: From which we can note / that the more perfect a Christian is in knowledge / or any other grace, so much more fit he is to admonish others to their building up.

# Of Grace, and its Characteristics

<margin>
3. Answer.

<note>original Latin: "Aurium & Statere idem est nomen in Hebraeo: duo enim aures sunt quasi bilances, quibus ea pendantur quae audimus: mercerus in Genes. b. e. auris & Mens, ut os cibum sic Mens verba, Chrysost."</note>
"Ear" and "Scale" are the same word in Hebrew: for the two ears are like balances, in which the things we hear are weighed. Mercerus on Genesis; the ear and the Mind; as the mouth tastes food, so the Mind tastes words. Chrysostom.
</margin>

III. Strong Christians are those who understand the great and deep mysteries of Religion; they are not exactly like those who only use milk, understanding only the first principles. The Apostle calls such people *Children*, inexperienced in the word of righteousness. But they are those who can digest solid food; that is, the deep mysteries of the Gospel, which they understand to some degree: because they have exercised their senses to discern both good and evil; that is, to distinguish between good and bad teachings. Strong Christians have such an ear that it is powerful enough to test words (as it says in Job) just as the palate tastes food. It is an observation of the learned Mercerus <note>Jean Mercier (d. 1570), a famous French Hebrew scholar.</note> that the same word in Hebrew which means an Ear, in the dual number means a Scale or balance; to make known that an experienced Christian must weigh what he hears before he believes it. For just as the tongue of the balance stands as a Judge between the two scales, so must a person's heart weigh what he hears; and so will every growing and right-judging Christian do. He will not accept any truth on trust alone; but he will first examine it, and only then believe it. Nor will a mature Christian simply accept things with a small amount of knowledge; but, like a grown Scholar, he will investigate the mysteries of God.

<margin>
4. Answer.
Luke 5:33, 34, 35, etc.
</margin>

IV. A mature, experienced, and strong Christian is mostly occupied and busy in the most precise exercises of Religion which serve for <term>Mortification</term> <note>The spiritual practice of "killing off" one's sinful nature or worldly desires.</note>. Weak Christians are only for light and common exercises, such as listening and reading some good books; but the strong are more in spiritual wakefulness, special prayers, frequent fasting, self-denial, Heavenly Meditations, and such dutiful obligations that have a Heavenly influence on the killing of sin and corruption. A Child, whose gifts and strength are weak, is not busy with great and heavy undertakings as a mature Man is.

V. He believes in the fulfillment of the promises and the Prophecies of Scripture, even though God's providence seems to want to turn out to the contrary, and even though there are no outward appearances in their favor. Thus it was with Abraham, who was strong in faith; he believed in hope, against hope, and was not weakened in faith; and did not consider his own Body, which was already dead. There were several things which could have caused Abraham's faith to stumble if it had not been very strong, such as:

<margin>
Compare Genesis 15:4 with Gen. 16:16 and with Genesis 21:5.
</margin>

1. There were at least fifteen years between the promise of giving him a Son and the fulfillment of the same.
2. Abraham was about a hundred years old before he got a Son, so that it seemed nearly impossible to obtain children.
3. The mother, Sarah, was past childbearing age, and there was no common hope of procreation.
4. After the promised Son was born, God—
<meta>The catchword 'de' indicates the start of the next sentence on the next page/column: "de God tot Abraham..."</meta>

<column-break/>

—commanded Abraham to offer him as a sacrifice; yet notwithstanding all these things, he did not doubt the promises through unbelief; but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and was fully assured that whatever He had promised, He was also powerful enough to perform.

<margin>
Romans 4:21.

Matthew 23.
Job 1.
John 7.
John 19 verse 38.

</margin>

VI. A strong believer, or Christian, can suffer as well as do something for Christ's sake. Greater strength is required to suffer for the truth than to confess it: And therefore Christ asked concerning that ambitious request of the Sons of Zebedee, saying, "Are you able to drink the cup that I shall drink, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?" <note>Referring to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note> making it known that they did not well understand their own strength; and that more grace is required to suffer for the name of Christ than to believe in the name of Christ. And just as our strength of grace is, so is our courage or heart in the cause of Christ, either lesser or greater. When Nicodemus still had little grace, he came to Jesus by night: for he did not dare to appear before him openly; but thereafter, as he grew in the grace and knowledge of Christ, he also grew in boldness for Christ. As it also appeared when the cause of Christ was debated or examined in the assembly of the High Priests and Pharisees, where Nicodemus boldly pleaded for the cause of Christ: "Does our Law judge a man before it hears him first and understands what he does?" Indeed, we read thereafter of the higher resolution of this fearful Nicodemus, when Christ was crucified and at his lowest: We find that Nicodemus, who (says the text) first came to Jesus by night, brought a mixture of Myrrh and Aloes of about 100 pounds weight for the burial of Christ. We have a similar example in Joseph of Arimathea, who was a Disciple of Christ, but secretly, for fear of the Jews. But thereafter, when he had obtained more of the strength of grace, he took courage (as the Scripture tells us) and went in to Pilate, and requested the body of Christ. Boldly confessing Christ in a perilous and heavy time is a sign of a strong faith: a weak constitution of the Body dares not go out unless it is fair weather; but a strong body can well endure the autumn weather. A weak and young convert is more suited to live in the prosperity of the Gospel; but an old, experienced Christian, being like an old, tested Soldier, will not faint in the hardest trials. If you show yourself faint in the day of distress, it is because your strength is narrow.

<margin>
Proverbs 24:10.

James 3.
</margin>

VII. He is powerful enough to rule his tongue; so that, although there are impulses in his heart, he nonetheless through the strength of his grace holds them back and restrains them; so that they do not break out into open slanders, contempt, and shouting, as others do. James gives this proof of a strong Christian: "If anyone does not stumble in words, he is a perfect Man"; not according to the law, but according to the Gospel: He is a perfect Man; that is, he is strongly grown up in the grace of God.

9. This is one who works as much for unity in the Church as for purity in the Church. He shall labor with all his might so that Christ's robe may be without a seam, just as it is without a blemish. <note>A reference to the seamless garment of Christ (John 19:23), often used as a metaphor for Church unity.</note> I gather this sign from the exhortations of the Apostle: *Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded: and if in any thing ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you. Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing.* <note>Quoting Philippians 3:15-16.</note> It is a sign that you are weak when you cause a stir in the Church because of your opinions. Weak children are the most fretful; when they are sickly, nothing can distract or please them. So it is with some who are weak in the Church; their temperament is such that you do not know how to please them or satisfy them; but a full-grown, experienced Christian is temperate and wise, and very zealous to preserve the unity in the Church of Christ.

Before I proceed to speak more of the power of grace, I shall make some applications of what I have spoken concerning the marks of strong grace; and the "use" <term>Use: a standard homiletic term for the practical application of a sermon's doctrine.</term> I shall make will include some warnings regarding these previous statements; there is especially a need for a twofold warning:

<margin>

1. That you take heed not to imagine yourself to be strong in grace when you are actually weak. This is a perilous mistake.

<margin>
Proverbs 13:7.

2. Take heed that you do not think or judge yourself to be weak in grace when you are strong; for this is a comfortless mistake. *There is one* (says Solomon) *who makes himself rich, yet has nothing; and there is one who makes himself poor, yet has great riches.* Therefore, I want to warn you that you do not live above or below what you have, so that you may not proudly imagine you possess something you do not; nor be discouraged by thinking you lack what you actually possess.

<margin>
1. Use of Warning.
Hebrews 5:12.
Matthew 10:16.
Explanation.
</margin>
1. You must not measure the strength of grace by the length of your profession. <note>"Profession" here refers to the public declaration of one's faith and the time spent as a member of the church.</note> Many who have long stood in the profession of the Saints are but slow walkers in the ways and exercises of Holiness. The soul's progress in grace is not a consequence of the length of time, but the fruit of diligent grace. There were those who had been in the Church for a long time who ought to have been Teachers; but they had yet obtained little strength of grace. Those who came into the vineyard at the eleventh hour had their penny just as well as those who came early. The meaning of this parable is (as some interpreters say) to show that those who come late to the profession of the Saints can surpass many others in gifts and grace who have been in the profession long before; that is, those who made their profession long ago. How many are there among us who are eighty years old, but whose knowledge and grace are not yet eighteen years old.

<column-break/>

2. Do not measure the strength of grace by the strength of your affections toward any of the ways of God. The love of a newly-married couple may be newer and more tender at first, and only later become stronger. Women, who are "weaker vessels," are often subject to stronger passions. When the lame man was healed, we read that at first he began to run for joy; yet he did not continue doing so forever. The new change made him so inclined at first; so it is also with the young convert.

3. Do not measure the strength of grace by the abundance of the "means of grace" which gladden you. Alas: Laodicea had a glorious light shining among her. She was one of the seven candlesticks. And because she had such means of grace, she mistook herself in her greatness, saying, *I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing.* <margin>Revelation 3:17.</margin> But Christ said, *you know not that you are wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.*

4. Do not measure the strength of grace by the strength of your gifts. There is a "new disease" <note>The "English Disease" or Rickets, which was a subject of much medical discussion in the 17th century.</note> among children in which their head grows large but their limbs remain weak. This disease is spiritual in many souls among our professors; their heads grow in terms of gifts and knowledge, but they do not become strong to walk in the ways of God; they are like the Moon, increasing in light, but not in heat. In the days of the Philosophers, the gifts of men were very great, and yet the power of godliness was in those days like a low ebb; there were in those times many high contemplations, angelic visions, subtle distinctions, crafty objections, and elaborate answers to the same—solid and weighty maxims; but alas, there was only a small power of grace in the hearts of men, and in those who taught them.

<margin>
2. Warning.
</margin>
2. The second warning is to prevent the mistakes of those who judge themselves to be weak in grace, while they are in fact strong.

1. Do not conclude that you have no strength of grace because you have no perfection of grace. The truth of grace is one thing, and the strength of grace is another; the strength of grace is one thing, and the perfection of the same is another. You must wait for perfection until the time you arrive in Heaven; where alone the souls of the righteous are made perfect. It is a clever observation that someone has made: in Grammar (he says), the present tense is accompanied by the preterpluperfect tense <note>original: "voorleden over-volmaeckten tijdt" — the "past more-than-perfect" or pluperfect.</note>; just so, our present state of grace is accompanied by imperfections; but our future state shall be more than perfect.

<margin>
Hebrews 12:23.
Ecclesiastes 7:20.
Proverbs 20:9.
</margin>
There is no perfection here. *There is no man just on earth, who does good, and does not sin,* (says Solomon). *Who can say, I have purified my heart: I am clean from my sins?* *Though I wash my hands with snow-water* (says Job) *and make myself ever so clean, yet you shall plunge me into the pit,* and...

<margin>*8th Sermon in St. Lawrence Church in London, April 6, 1651.*</margin>
## 2 TIMOTHY 2:1
### Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral patterns and scrolled line work.</image-desc>
I proceed now to answer some **Cases of Conscience** <note><term>Cases of Conscience</term>: Practical problems of faith and morality where a believer's duty is unclear.</note> which can be drawn from the teaching I have presented to you.

<margin>1st Case.</margin>
I. Whether strong temptations can coexist with strong grace? This is a case of great necessity and great use, because God's people, when they are searched by the Devil, examine not only their strength but also the truth of their faith.

Before I answer this Case, I shall put forward these general propositions.

<margin>1st Proposition.</margin>
1. It is certain that where the truth of grace is, there can be strong assaults from the Devil. The Devil is like a thief who does not steal from the outhouses, for there is nothing there but manure and straw; rather, he seeks the cabinets in the locked rooms. So

<column-break/>

this great thief of the world is not so vehement in robbing and plundering the outhouses—namely, the wicked—but rather those who have the riches of grace in the cabinets of their hearts. He is like a sea-pirate who will not attack an empty vessel, but a ship richly laden with merchandise; likewise, he will set upon those to make them his prize who are laden with the rich gifts of grace.

<margin>2nd Prop.</margin>
II. Let the assaults of the Devil be as strong as possible, yet they shall not be stronger than the strength of grace which
<margin>*1 Cor.* 10:13</margin>
believers have received. *God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that you are able.* <note>Quoting 1 Corinthians 10:13.</note> He will fit the pack to the back, and the burden to the strength of the one who must carry it; if the temptations increase, our strength shall also increase, through which we shall be able to be powerful enough to fight against them.

<margin>3rd Prop.</margin>
III. It is evident that the assaults of the Devil are generally strongest after God's people have performed some extraordinary dutiful service to God, or after they have received the greatest discovery of grace from God. In both these cases, the Devil's assaults are
<margin>*Luke 22*</margin>
commonly heavy. You find that immediately after the celebration of the Lord's Supper, the Devil desired *to sift the disciples*; where you see that as soon as they had completed that extraordinary service for God, the Devil was eager to set upon them.
<margin>*Matt. 4*</margin>
Likewise, you find that after **Christ** had fasted in an extraordinary manner for forty days and forty nights, he was immediately thereafter tempted by the Devil; and also after His Baptism; for He no sooner came out of the water of Baptism than He entered the fire of temptation. The **Israel** of God can no sooner be
<margin>*Dr. Hall's observations*</margin>
out of **Egypt** than the hellish **Pharaoh** pursues them. And **Hezekiah** had no sooner kept the Feast of the Passover than **Sennacherib** marched against him. All this shows us that when we have practiced the most grace in our dutiful service, the Devil will then labor to play his "after-game" with us. If **Satan** cannot keep us from our dutiful service and the practice of it, then he will blow up our dutiful services with pride and so spoil them. Therefore, after we have received the most special revelations of God's love and favor in **Christ**, we may well expect to be stormed by the Devil. Thus **Paul**, after he had received
<margin>*2 Cor. 12*</margin>
those Heavenly revelations and the abundance thereof, was contested by the Devil with foul temptations; for there was given to him *a sharp thorn in the flesh*, namely, *a messenger of Satan*, to buffet him with fists. <note>Quoting 2 Corinthians 12:7.</note> This must not be understood as some sickness or similar defect, but as some hard temptation from the Devil. So you see also that immediately after
<margin>*Matt. 3*</margin>
that voice to **Christ**, *This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased*, the tempter came to Him. Therefore, you may well observe from the joining together of these two petitions in the Lord's Prayer—*Forgive us our debts* and *Lead us not into temptation*—that we no sooner obtain our forgiveness than we may well expect to be tempted by the Devil.

->Various Degrees.<-

<margin>IV. Proposition.</margin>

## IV. That those people who are subject to the greatest, strongest, and most fearful assaults and strongest temptations of the Devil: and this leads to the answering of this case, how the strength of grace can coexist with strong temptations?

To explain and confirm this, these two specific parts are required:

{ 1. When temptations may be said to be strong?
{ 2. How and why such strong temptations can coexist with strong grace?

<margin>1. Question.</margin>

### 1. When may temptations be said to be strong?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin>

1. Temptations may be said to be strong when the temptations of the Devil provoke the Soul to sin: when they are not weak and faint suggestions, but cruel assaults that will not be warded off until they are consented to; when the Devil so assaults a person that he will not leave them alone; then they may be said to be strong. <margin>1 Chron. 21:1</margin> It is said there, that Satan stood up against Israel; that is, he set himself to seek out David and provoked him; that is, he would not leave him untormented, but assaulted him with Hellish torments until he had numbered the People. <note>In the biblical context, David’s sin in "numbering the people" was seen as an act of pride and reliance on military strength rather than God.</note>

<margin>2.</margin>

2. When they are manifold and constant. Small temptations frequently suggested become strong. Small drops of water, by falling often, make a hollow in the hard stone; which a few large and powerful blows would not do: likewise, small temptations to sin, if they are constant and persistent, can have a greater entrance into the heart than a single powerful assault.

<margin>3.</margin>
<margin>Matt. 4:1</margin>

3. When they are directed or positioned by the Devil according to a person’s disposition or present state; just as that temptation was with which the Devil set upon Christ, after he had fasted forty days and forty nights: "Command," he said, "that these stones become bread." It was suited to his present state; food for his hunger. If you present food to a naked person, he regards it not; or clothes to a hungry person, he regards them not; because they do not suit his present need: But when the gifts which you offer match a person's necessity; clothes to him who is naked, and food to him who is hungry, then they become acceptable and pleasant. The Devil sends no temptations regardless of opportunity: he is too cunning and crafty to cry against the wind and tide: he knows well which way the stream of our inclinations and passions runs, and he follows his baits accordingly. <margin>James 1:14</margin> Every man (says the Apostle) is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own lust. It is a simile taken from a Fisherman, who has this knowledge: that he shall give the bait according to the nature of the fish; whereby he lays snares to deceive either the sight or the taste of the poor fish. The Devil is the great Fisherman of Souls; and he uses such temptations as are most useful to him for catching: he observes what sins a person’s office, calling, or the opportunities of the time make him most guilty of or subject to; and accordingly he lays his snares and spreads his nets. Although it is true that every person has a principle tending toward every sin within them: nevertheless, it is also true that every person is not equally ready or disposed toward every sin. The Devil sees what sin is most predominant in a person and thus he fits his temptations conveniently to it. He gives a wedge of gold to a greedy Achan; Cozbi, a harlot, to an adulterous Zimri; a fine promotion to an ambitious Absalom: For he knows well that a suitable object properly presented is a half-won victory. And in these three circumstances, temptations can be said to be strong.

<column-break/>

<margin>2. Question.</margin>

### 2. But how does it appear that temptations so troubling, so enduring, and so suited to a person's situation can coexist with strong grace?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin>

1. Through examples, by which it appears that the best of God's Children have mostly been tempted. Job, a holy man, yet with what strong temptations was he assaulted? The Devil made him poor in his estate, and so he wanted to attack and tempt him to mistrust God’s providence; he took the lives of all his Children to make him doubt providence: he tormented him with a grievous sickness to make him murmur against providence: and above all, he tempted him to curse God and die, through the instigations of his wife: <margin>Job 1:8</margin> And although Job was thus handled by the Devil, nevertheless he was a strong believer in grace, and the most excellent Saint in that age, and in that part of the World at that time; as God Himself testifies of him, that there was none on earth like him, so upright and godly. He was not only the greatest of all the men in the East in riches, but also the greatest on earth in holiness; yet he was thus tormented and assaulted by the Devil. Another example is David, an outstanding believer, who had this praise: that he was a Man after God’s own heart, and how fiercely was he attacked by the Devil? At one time he moves him to number the people: at another time to dishonor another man’s wife; at another time to let himself appear insane before Achish, King of Gath; at another time to judge all his holy services as vain; and at another time to doubt the faithfulness of God in His promises to make him King. He said in his haste that all men were liars; and so then also the Prophet Samuel: <margin>Matt. 16:16 &c. compared with verses 22, 23.</margin> Thus you find Peter, an excellent Apostle of Christ, after he had made such a glorious confession of his faith, and had discovered more grace than ever before in his whole life, suddenly thereafter, through an instigation of the Devil, rebuking Christ and advising Him to spare Himself: so Paul, who had such high and Heavenly inspirations, such Divine assaults of the understanding, nevertheless had a messenger of Satan to buffet him. But above all examples, you have Jesus Christ, who, although He had perfect grace, and was full of grace and truth, nevertheless this could not exempt Him from the attacks of the Devil. He was full of the Holy Spirit, yet He was tempted forty days by the Devil, and that with strong temptations: if you consider their duration and their persistence...

temptations will not be strong. God shall not test weak Christians as harshly as those who have obtained a greater measure of grace. Not every man in David’s army was appointed to break through the camp of the Philistines to fetch water from the well at Bethlehem, but only three of David’s chosen men. God will not let a young convert break through an army of temptations before they have obtained the experience and strength of grace to fight against them.

<margin>2. Use.</margin> 2. From this we may also learn that those people who have the most powerful and excellent gifts ought not to grow bold in their own strength. Look to yourself, so that you also are not tempted. <margin>Galatians 6:1</margin> You who are most spiritual, take heed that you are not defeated. Some people believe they are already above the <term>ordinances of God</term> <note>original: "Ordinantien Godts"; refers to the established religious rituals and laws intended to guide the faithful</note>; but their own experience can well teach them that they are not yet above temptations. And truly, those who are not yet above temptations have a constant need for God’s institutions; for no person in the world is, or shall be, beyond temptation. Consider Adam carefully: even he in Paradise—the best of all places—and in a state of innocence—the best of all states—was not without the temptations of the Devil, and indeed was not free from the fall. Therefore, no one must rely on their own strength.

3. Remember this for your comfort: that although the Devil tempts you, he shall nevertheless never obtain his desire against you. It is true, a godly man may fall into the specific act to which the Devil tempts him; yet the Devil shall never achieve his will in his general aim or goal—namely, the damnation of your soul. It is worth noting what our Savior said to Peter: <margin>Luke 22:31</margin> "Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat." That "Satan has desired to have you" was the Devil's general goal. Although he might obtain his will in a specific act, and you might be given over to him that far, he would never be able to drag you with him to Hell.

4. Remember for your greater comfort, you who are God’s people and armed against the Devil’s temptations: you complain that they are great by nature, long in duration, and all the more perilous because they are directed at your present state and condition. But remember that the Devil dealt with Jesus Christ in this same way; His temptations were also suited to His state, constant, and by nature very heavy—stretching even to despairing of God’s providence, to self-murder, and to blasphemy. And why was all this? <margin>Hebrews 2:17</margin> It was for your comfort. He suffered those temptations so that He might be fit to have compassion for you and to stand by you when you might come into the same state.

# II. TIMOTHY 2. Verse 1.

->My son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.<-

<margin>9th Sermon in St. Lawrence Jewry <note>original: "Laurence Jury"; a famous Anglican church in the City of London</note> in London, the same day 1651. 2nd Case.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial W with floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
We now proceed to a second case of conscience concerning the strength of grace, which is this:

Whether the strength of grace can coexist with the strength of lusts and corruptions <note>original: "verdorventheden"; refers to the innate human tendency toward sin</note> in the heart?

Regarding which, in answering, I shall speak of these particular points:

1. When can corruptions be said to be strong?

2. Why do those who have strong grace often have strong corruptions?

3. What kind of strong corruptions are those to which people strong in grace are most subject?

4. In what cases, and with what limitations, can the strength of corruptions coexist with the strength of grace?

<margin>1. Question.</margin> I. When can corruptions and lusts be said to be strong in the soul?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin> 1. When sins are allowed with a sense of pleasure. At first, sin is like a snake that is nearly dead from the cold, very weak and limp; but if it is placed in the bosom, it gathers strength. A while later, the sin receives life again and finds delight in the soul. If you do evil, are moved by sin, and then take pleasure in it, it is surely a sign that sin has great power in you. Thus God complains about His people: "What has my beloved to do in my house? When you do evil, then you rejoice." <margin>Jeremiah 11:15</margin> We can know the power and strength of the corruption within us by the activity of sin in us, and by our lightheartedness and pleasure in sin.

<margin>2. Answer.</margin> 2. Through the multitude of sins. Just as a relapse into a sickness proves the strength of that evil humor in the body, so the repeated and multiplied acts of sin prove the power and strength of those sins in our hearts. Corruption gathers strength, just as grace does, through the frequent practice and exercise of the same.

<margin>3. Answer.</margin> 3. When sin is persistent against the objections of the conscience. Just as it proves the strength of a stream when it carries away everything before it, regardless of what dike might try to hinder its course, so it also proves that there is a strong flood of corruption in your soul which pulls down all warnings, objections, and rebukes of the conscience.

<margin>2. Question.</margin> 2. Why do those who have the strongest grace often also have the strongest corruptions?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin> 1. It arises from the natural temperament and constitution of the body, which makes people more inclined toward certain sins.

2. From this we may also learn that people who have the most powerful and excellent gifts ought not to grow bold in their own strength. Look to yourself, so that you also are not tempted. <margin>Gal. 6:1.</margin> You who are most spiritual, take heed that you are not struck down. Some people think that they are already above God's <term>Ordinances<note>Established religious rites or laws, such as prayer and the sacraments.</note></term>; but their own experience can well teach them that they are not yet above temptations: and truly those who are not yet above temptations have constant need of God's institutions; now there is no person in the world who is, or shall be, above temptations: consider Adam freely, yet he in Paradise—the best of all places—and in <term>innocency<note>original: "onnoselhept," referring to the state of man before the Fall.</note></term>—the best of all states—was not without the assaults of the Devil, indeed, not free from the fall: therefore no one must rely on their own strength.

3. Remember this for your comfort: that although the Devil tempts you, he shall nonetheless never obtain his desire against you. It is true a godly man can fall into a particular act to which the Devil tempts him; nonetheless, the Devil shall never get his will regarding his general purpose or aim, namely the damnation of your soul. It is worth noting what our Savior said to Peter: <margin>Luke 22:31.</margin> **Satan has desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:** Satan has desired to have you—that was the Devil’s general aim. Although he might obtain his will in a particular act, and you might be given over to him that far; nonetheless, he would never be able to drag you with him to Hell.

4. Remember to your great comfort, you who are God’s people and armed against the Devil’s assaults; you complain that they are great because of their nature, long because of their persistence, and all the more perilous because they are directed at your present state and condition. But remember that the Devil also dealt thus with Jesus Christ; His temptations were also suited to His state, constant, and by nature very heavy, tending toward despair in God’s providence, toward suicide, and toward blasphemy: and why was this <margin>Heb. 2:17.</margin> all, if not for your comfort? He suffered those assaults so that He might be fit to have compassion for you: and to stand by you when you might come into the same state.
