## II. TIMOTHY 2.
### Verse 1.

->My Son, be strong in the<-
->grace that is in Christ Jesus.<-

<margin>9th Sermon in Laurence Pury <note>Likely referring to a church or district in London, such as St. Laurence Pountney or a similar parish.</note> within London, the same day 1651. 2nd Case.</margin>
We now proceed further to a second <term>case of conscience<note>A specific ethical or spiritual problem brought to a minister for resolution.</note></term> regarding the power of grace, which is this:

Whether the power of grace can exist alongside the power of lusts and corruptions in the heart?

Regarding which, in answering, I shall speak of these particular points:
1. When corruptions can be said to be strong?
2. Why those who have strong grace often have strong corruptions?
3. What kind of strong corruptions they are to which those who are strong in grace are most subject?
4. In what cases, and with what limitations, the power of corruptions can coexist with the power of grace?

<margin>1. Question.</margin>
1 When can corruptions and lusts be said to be strong in the soul?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin>
1. When sins are permitted with a sense of delight: sin is at first like a snake that is nearly dead from the cold, and is very weak and limp: but if it is warmed in the bosom, then it gathers strength; and a short time thereafter the sin receives life again, and finds pleasure in the soul. If you are first moved to sin, and thereafter take pleasure in it, it is truly a sign that sin has a great power in you. Thus God complains about His people: **what has my beloved to do in my house?** when <margin>Jer. 11:15</margin> **you do evil, then you rejoice.** We can know the power and strength of corruption in us by the activity of sin in us, and by our lightheartedness and pleasure in sin.

<margin>2. Answer</margin>
2. By the multitude of sins, just as a relapse into a sickness proves the strength of that "evil humor" in the body: so also repeated and multiplied acts of sin prove the power and strength of those sins in our hearts. Corruption gathers strength, just as grace does, through the frequent handling and exercise of the same.

<margin>3. Answer</margin>
3. When sin is persistent against the contradictions of the conscience. Just as it proves the strength of a stream that it carries away whatever comes before it, even whatever dike might wish to hinder its course: so it also proves that there is a strong flood of corruption in your soul, which tears down all warnings, contradictions, and rebukes of the conscience.

<margin>2. Question.</margin>
2. Why do those who have the strongest grace often also have the strongest corruptions?

<margin>1. Answer</margin>
1 It arises from the natural <term>temperament<note>In 17th-century medicine and psychology, "temperament" or "constitution" referred to the balance of bodily fluids (humors) that determined a person's character and physical health.</note></term> and disposition of the body, which makes people more inclined toward some sins

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 580 regarding the paradox of grace. # ->Various Degrees.<- #

In the past, the most pleasing sin was damnable, the smallest was abominable, and the dearest was unbearable; but it is different now through the spiritual declines and diminishments in our affections. Previously, there were many who, when they had fallen into sin, were accustomed to walk in sorrow, to sigh deeply, to weep bitterly, and to pray movingly; but now one does not do such things with such warm and active affections as before. The time has been when many Professors of Religion prepared themselves for holy services with greater care, observed them with more diligence, were engaged in them with more delight, and obtained more profit and edification through them than they do now. And that is the first sin that those who have grace—both in truth and power—are liable to fall into: namely, spiritual decline. <note>original: "geestelijcke afneminge"</note>

<margin>2. Answer.</margin>
2. Those who are strong Christians are truly subject to spiritual pride; and lean greatly upon their gifts, parts, and graces. Spiritual pride is a hidden spiritual corruption that exists in the most spiritual and lovely heart; it is an evil fruit that grows on the best root. There is nothing better than grace, and nothing more damnable than sin; and there is no sin so evil as pride; and there is no one so liable to fall into the sin of pride as those who have much grace; and there is nothing that weakens a strong Christian more than pride, and there is nothing that reveals weakness more than this boasting.

<margin>
3. Answer.
Rom. 14:1, 2, 3.
verse 13.
</margin>
3. To despise others and to carry oneself proudly toward weak Christians is a common fault of the strong. There is nowhere mentioned more frequently in Scripture than here, that we should not despise or discourage the weak; which is proof that the strong offend in this. Let us therefore no longer judge one another (verse 13); which proves that they were accustomed to do so. Spiritual pride is a root of bitterness <note>A biblical metaphor for a source of trouble or resentment</note> which bears these two bitter fruits: 1. An over-valuation of ourselves. 2. A low esteem for other men, their persons, and their gifts.

<margin>
4. Answer.
Matt. 9:14, 15.
</margin>
4. Strong Christians place too many obligatory duties and too heavy works upon the weak. The disciples of John were guilty of this toward the disciples of Christ concerning fasting. Strong Christians ought to deal tenderly with the weak; they ought to excuse their failures, hide their weaknesses, praise their accomplishments, cherish their progress, resolve their doubts, bear their burdens, and thereby make the way of Religion lovely and pleasant to them; whereas, on the contrary, by their grandeurs, the hearts of weak Christians are discouraged in their first entrance.

<margin>
5. Answer.
Luke 12:19.
</margin>
5. To be satisfied with a certain measure of grace. How liable are those who have grace to say in this sense, as someone said in another: *Soul, take your rest, be of good cheer; you have many goods laid up for many years*; and upon this many become sluggish and careless in holy duties, and do not practice the ordinances for the increase

<column-break/>

of their graces. The best of Christians can fall into this complacency, which can be nothing other than harmful to the soul. The Devil tempts those who have only a little grace to imagine that they have no grace; and those who have more grace, that they have enough. The best can fail in this, thinking that a righteous measure and a full growth of grace is to be obtained in this life. But in fact, the best practice for having much grace is to desire more, and not to be satisfied with any measure of grace until we become a perfect Man, to the measure of the great fullness of Christ; and that is not to be obtained in this life. Perfection is the target <note>original: "widt"</note> of this life, yet it is the reward of the next life. We must strive after perfection in grace; yet we shall not obtain it until the time that grace is perfected in glory.

<margin>4. Question.</margin>
4. In what cases, and with what limitations, can the power of corruptions <note>The author uses "corruptions" (verdorventheden) to refer to innate sinful tendencies or "the old self."</note> coexist with the power of grace?

The resolution of this Question is of very great utility to the soul: for that soul which is mastered by strong corruptions may not only inquire after the power of its grace, but also whether the truth of it is there. How then can I know that I have both the truth and the power of grace in me, although I am often overwhelmed by strong and conquering corruptions?

<margin>
1. Answer.
Gal. 5:17.
</margin>
1. If you maintain in yourself a strong resistance against your corruptions. The flesh desires against the Spirit; but the Spirit also desires against the flesh; although you cannot fully suppress your sins, you nonetheless seek to resist them powerfully; if so, then there is grace, and even the power of grace, which is mighty to support this opposition. A careless submission to sin proves the power of sin; but an irreconcilable opposition against sin proves the power of grace. The power of grace is not seen so much in the specific acts of suppression, and in the actual victory over it, as in that constant and settled direction of the heart in the resistance against sin.

<margin>
2. Answer.
2 Chron. 33:12, 13.
</margin>
2. Although sin is strong, nonetheless grace can also be powerful in your soul. If you have a powerful measure of humiliation, even though your sin be great; if your concern for it is great, this proves that your grace is also great. It was a great grace in Manasseh <note>A King of Judah known for extreme wickedness followed by a dramatic repentance while in captivity.</note> that he (although he had been a great sinner) humbled himself greatly.

<margin>
3. Answer.
Deut. 22:26, 27.
</margin>
3. If you have powerfully cried out to God against your sins, that is a proof of grace; when you—as your corruptions and temptations overcome—pray to the Lord with strong cries and tears, that is a proof of grace, yes, of the power of grace.

<margin>4. Answer.</margin>
4. If you have strong affections toward Christ, surely you have grace, although your strong corruptions often pull you away from Christ. Peter had more weaknesses, and corruptions, and sins than all the disciples (except Judas). He took Christ aside, gave Him fleshly counsel, and spoke concerning His suffering;

The Devil tempts those who have only a little grace to imagine they have no grace at all; and those who have more grace, he tempts to think they have enough. The best can err in this: thinking that a "just measure" and a full growth of grace is to be obtained in this life. But in fact, the best way to have much grace is to desire more, and not to be satisfied with any measure of grace until we become a *perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ*—and that is not to be attained in this life. **Perfection** is the target <note>original: "wit," meaning a target or bullseye in archery</note> of this life, yet it is the reward of the next life. We must strive after perfection in grace, yet we shall not obtain it until the time that grace is perfected in glory.

<margin>4. Question.</margin>
### 4. In what cases, and with what definitions, can the power of corruptions exist alongside the power of grace?

The resolution of this question is of very great utility to the soul: for that soul which is mastered by strong corruptions may not only inquire after the power of its grace, but also whether the truth of that grace is even there. How can I then know that I have both the truth and the power of grace in me, although I am often overwhelmed by strong and prevailing corruptions?

<margin>1. Answer.</margin>
<margin>Gal. 5:17.</margin>
1. If you maintain a strong resistance against your corruptions. *The flesh lusts against the Spirit*; but the Spirit also lusts against the flesh. Although you cannot fully suppress your sins, you nevertheless seek to powerfully oppose them; if so, then grace is there, and with it the power of grace, which is mighty enough to sustain this opposition. A careless submission to sin proves the power of sin; but an irreconcilable opposition to sin proves the power of grace. The power of grace is not seen so much in individual acts of suppression, nor in the actual victory over it, as in that steady and set resolution of the heart in resistance against sin.

<margin>2. Answer.</margin>
2. Although sin is strong, grace can nonetheless be powerful in your soul. If you have a powerful degree of humiliation, even though your sin be great; if your concern regarding it is great, this proves that your grace is also great. It was a great grace in **Manasseh** that he (although he had been a great sinner) humbled himself greatly.
<margin>2 Chron. 33:12.</margin> <note>The original margin notes "1 Cro. 33:11," but the account of King Manasseh’s repentance is found in 2 Chronicles 33.</note>

<margin>3. Answer.</margin>
3. If you have cried out powerfully to God against your sins, that is a proof of grace. When you, as your corruptions and temptations overcome you, pray to the Lord with strong cries and tears, that is a proof of grace—yes, of the power of grace.
<margin>Deut. 22:26, 27.</margin> <note>The author references the law concerning a victim who cries out for help; in this spiritual analogy, the soul's "cry" proves it does not consent to the "assault" of sin.</note>

<margin>4. Answer.</margin>
4. If you have strong affections for Christ, you certainly have grace, even though your strong corruptions often pull you away from Christ. **Peter** had more weaknesses, corruptions, and sins than all the disciples (except Judas). He took Christ aside, gave Him fleshly counsel, and said regarding His suffering:

<meta>The catchword "verre" refers to Peter's response in Matthew 16:22: "Far be it [verre weg] from Thee, Lord."</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual dangers facing "strong Christians," including spiritual pride, despising the weak, and complacency. It explains that the power of grace is evidenced not by sinless perfection, but by the soul's persistent resistance and its desperate "cries" to God when overwhelmed.</summary>

As for example, when we consider in cases of desire how David misused his neighbor’s wife, and how Abimelech would not touch another man’s wife, someone might judge David to be a heathen and Abimelech to be a believer; therefore, the power of grace or of corruption must not be judged by any particular act when some violent temptation has overcome a man.

Just as a coal glows most intensely before it goes out, or a candle burned down to the socket gives a powerful flame before it goes out: so it is when corruption is ready to depart. ## II. TIMOTHY 2.
### Verse 1.

->Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.<-

<margin>10th Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry <note>A historic church in the City of London, often used for significant lecture series in the 17th century.</note> within London, April 13, 1651.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'W' with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>We have already handled two great cases of conscience concerning the power of grace, and concerning the existence of strong temptations and strong corruptions alongside the power of grace; and we shall now proceed to a third case, which is this.
<margin>3rd Case.</margin> 3. Whether the power of grace can exist despite the lack of those strong affections <note>In this context, "affections" refers to intense religious emotions or feelings of zeal.</note> which Christians had at their first conversion?
In answering this, I shall endeavor to show three things:
{ 1. When a person can be said to lose their first affection?
{ 2. In what cases a strong Christian may lack strong affections?
{ 3. From whence it comes that those who have strong grace nevertheless lack such strong affections as they had at their first conversion?
<margin>1st Question.</margin> 1. When can a Christian be said to lose their first affections? The affections may aptly be compared to the pulse-veins of the soul, by which the state and condition of the soul can be judged; and so that we might know when these affections are weak or declining, we can judge by this:
<margin>1st Answer.</margin> 1. When we do not have such fiery desires for our required duties. It is very noteworthy that a Christian, at their first conversion, is so fiery and earnest for holy service that they will hardly allow themselves time for the necessary duties of their particular calling; indeed, how people at first bound themselves to hear so many sermons, to offer so many prayers, to read so many chapters, and to spend so many hours in holy meditation by themselves, and with other Christians in edifying conversation! But alas! afterward this heat begins to cool and cease, and people pray less and hear less; yet this comes from the multitude of their worldly occasions. In the first conversion, which commonly occurs (as theologians have noted) be-

<column-break/>

tween the eighteenth and twenty-eighth year of age (although God is not bound to any specific year), people in that age have fewer cares for the world; but afterward, when the cares, profits, and pleasures of this world steal their affections, they become more sluggish than they were in their beginnings.
<margin>2nd Answer.</margin> 2. When people do not have such uplifting joy and rejoicing as they used to have, it can be noticed that the affections have declined. How many were there not at first in the same state of heart as David: *I rejoiced in those who said to me, let us go into the house of the Lord*; but <margin>Psalm 122:1</margin> afterward the abundance of this joy decreased by degrees.
3. When the perceptible increase through the keeping of the ordinances <note>Religious rituals or established means of worship, like the Lord's Supper or baptism.</note> is diminished. A person can progress through the ordinances of God and yet be unaware of their progress. And a Christian can take firm root in the steadfastness of grace, even though it does not shoot up in blossoms of affection.
<margin>2nd Question.</margin> 2. In what cases can a strong Christian come to lack strong affections?
<margin>1st Answer.</margin> 1. Provided you have fewer sins in your required duties, even if you have fewer affections. A weak young convert often has much affection for holy duties, but also much corruption in them; they are very rash and hasty in their prayers, proud of their small measure of grace, and have a fleshly attachment to their required duties. But just as old, experienced Christians often have less affection, they also have fewer sins in their required duties. The Papists <note>A term used by Protestants in this period to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> have a great deal of affection in performing their devotions; but alas! they have the leaven of this error in their best services—that they think to earn merit thereby. But mature and sensible Christians, although they might not be as "affectioned" to the required services as the weak, nevertheless exercise themselves much more in grace than the others. And so it also goes after the required duties are completed. Weak Christians let their corruptions back in afterward, thinking they have made a payment for their sins through their merits; but a seasoned Christian, although not so "affectioned" to the duties, is afterward careful that they do not ruin all their required services through their sins.
<margin>2nd Answer.</margin> 2. A strong Christian may lack strong affections provided they have strength of understanding to compensate for the lack of their affections. Young trees are sappier, but old trees are firmer. This is why the Apostle prays for those of Philippi, that not only <margin>Phil. 1:9</margin> their love might abound, but that their knowledge might also abound. Just as a person who has come to their full age, although they do not grow in height or the prominence of parts, nevertheless grows in the firmness of the parts of the body; so also old and experienced Christians, although they do not have as much affection, nevertheless have more steadfastness, and clarity, and purity of understanding, and more deeply-searched knowledge in the

## II. TIMOTHY 2. ##
### Verse 1. ###

-> Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. <-

<margin>10th Sermon at Lawrence Jewry <note>A prominent church in the City of London where many influential Puritan sermons were delivered.</note> within London, April 13, 1651.</margin>
WE have already handled two great cases of conscience regarding the power of grace, and regarding the existence of strong temptations and strong corruptions alongside the power of grace; and shall now proceed to a third case, which is this.

<margin>3rd Case.</margin>
3. Whether the power of grace can exist alongside the absence of those strong affections <note>In 17th-century theology, "affections" referred to holy emotions or the movement of the will toward God, such as zeal, joy, or desire.</note> which the Christian had upon their first conversion?

In answering this, I shall strive to show three things.

- 1. When a person can be said to lose their first affection?
- 2. In what cases a strong Christian can lack strong affections?
- 3. From whence it comes that those who have strong grace nevertheless lack such strong affections as they had at their first conversion?

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
1. When can a Christian be said to lose their first affection? The affections can conveniently be compared to the pulse-veins <note>The pulse.</note> of the soul, by which the state and condition of the soul can be judged; and so that we might know when these affections grow slack and decrease, we can judge by this:

<margin>1st Answer.</margin>
1. When we do not have such fiery desires for the required duties. It is very remarkable that a Christian, at their first conversion, is so fiery and earnest for holy services that they will hardly allow themselves time for the required duties of their particular calling <note>One's daily job or worldly occupation, which was considered a divinely appointed duty alongside spiritual ones.</note>; indeed, how people have bound themselves at first to hear so many sermons, to say so many prayers, to read so many chapters, to spend so many hours in holy meditation by themselves, and with other Christians in edifying conversation! But alas! afterward this heat begins to cool and cease, and people pray less, and hear less; yet this often comes from the multitude of their worldly occasions. In the first conversion, which commonly falls (as the theologians have noted) be-

<column-break/>

tween the eighteenth and twenty-eighth year of age (although God is bound to no year), people in that maturity have fewer cares of the world; but afterward, when the cares and profits and pleasures of this world steal their affections, they become more sluggish than they were in their beginnings.

<margin>2nd Answer.</margin>
2. When people do not have such mounting joy and rejoicing as they used to have, it can be noticed that the affections have declined. How many were there at first in a similar state of heart as David, *I rejoiced in those who said to me: let us go into the house of the Lord*: but <margin>Psalm 122:1</margin> afterward the abundance of this joy decreased by degrees.

3. When the sensible increase through the observance of the institutions <note>The "ordinances" or means of grace, such as prayer, the Word, and sacraments.</note> is diminished. A person can advance through God's institutions and yet be insensible of their progress. And a Christian can be firmly rooted in the steadfastness of grace, even though it does not shoot up in the blossoms of affection.

<margin>2nd Question.</margin>
2. In what cases can a strong Christian come to lack strong affections?

<margin>1st Answer.</margin>
1. If you have fewer sins in your required duties, although you have fewer affections. A weak young convert often has much affection for holy duties, but also much corruption in them; they are very rash and hasty in their prayers: proud of their small measure of grace, and they have a fleshly clinging to their required duties. But just as old, experienced Christians often have less affection, so too they have fewer sins in their required duties. The Papists <note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics.</note> have very much affection in the performance of their devotion: but, alas! they have the leaven of this error in their best services, that they think to merit thereby. But mature and understanding Christians, although they may not be as "affectioned" toward the required services as the weak, yet they exercise themselves much more in grace than the others. And so it also goes after the required duties are finished. Weak Christians let their corruptions back in afterward, thinking they have made a payment for their sins through their merits; but an experienced Christian, though not so "affectioned" in the required services, is nonetheless careful afterward that they do not ruin all their required services through their sins.

<margin>2nd Answer.</margin>
2. A strong Christian may lack strong affections if they have strength of understanding to compensate for the lack of their affections. Young trees are sappier; but old trees are firmer. Therefore the Apostle prays for those of Philippi, that not only <margin>Phil. 1:9.</margin> their love might abound, but that their knowledge might also abound. Just as a person who has come to their full age, though they do not grow in height or prominence of parts, yet they grow in the firmness of the parts of the body: so also old and experienced Christians, although they do not have as much affection, nonetheless they have more steadfastness, and clarity and purity of understanding, and more researched knowledge in deep...

<margin>3rd Case.</margin>

<margin>4th Case.</margin>

Of the one who has great gifts and is proud of them, it is to be feared that he has less grace than the person who has few gifts, but with a sense of his own weakness, and low and even self-denying thoughts of himself.

<margin>5th Case.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "affections" and "gifts" of grace, expanding on how the Holy Spirit distributes different abilities among believers, just as different flowers have different scents or different organ pipes produce different tones under the same wind.</meta>

# Grace, with its

flowers; there is not the same scent, but various scents according to the variety of the flowers; yet all their scents have the same influences from above. And just as it is with musical instruments; there are various tones on the organ, but it is the same wind which causes the various tones. So it is in the Church of God: although there is the same influence from the Spirit of God, yet there is not the same measure of gifts in every member of the Church.

<margin>2. Proposition.</margin> The second Proposition is this: that the diversity of gifts must not be attributed to a man's understanding, diligence, or upbringing, but to the free pleasure and dispensation <note>The word "dispensation" here refers to God’s act of distributing or dealing out spiritual gifts.</note> or distribution of God. It is true that much can be attributed to study and diligence, which was also the foundation of the Apostle's encouragement: *Give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine, etc. and meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.* <margin>2 Tim. 4: 13, 15. <note>The author likely intended 1 Timothy 4:13, 15, which contains these specific instructions to Timothy.</note></margin> The Apostle speaks there of the advancement in ministerial gifts; which gifts are much advanced through diligence and alertness. Nevertheless, even if we were all equal in diligence and zeal, there would still be a diversity in our gifts; so that men, in obtaining these gifts, should not boast of their own diligence, and thereby exclude the goodness of God in the distribution of the same. Psalm 127:1: *Except the LORD build the house, they labor in vain that build it.* Suppose that two men (says Hildersham <note>Arthur Hildersham (1563–1632) was a prominent English Puritan minister known for his lectures.</note>) read the same book and learn the same things every day, yet one may still be a dull person and have few gifts, while the other may have excellent gifts and outstanding influences. This serves to show how we ought to look to God, whose distributions of gifts are decided in many and various ways. <margin>1 Cor. 12. 11.</margin> Therefore the Apostle tells us that all these things are worked by the one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will; so that although one man differs from another in gifts, it is nevertheless God who makes them differ.

<margin>3. Proposition.</margin> The third Proposition is this: that a man may be outstanding in one gift and yet unknown or unskilled in others; a man shall not have everything. This is very clearly observed through the testimonies you have in Scripture. The first example is of Paul and Barnabas; if you look at Paul, his gift was the gift of interpretation and eloquence, so that at Lystra he was regarded as Mercury, being the god of eloquence. <note>Reference to Acts 14:12, where the locals mistook Paul for the Roman god Mercury (Hermes in Greek).</note> And although it is said of Paul that he was "rude in speech," <margin>2 Cor. 11. 6.</margin> that is not as if it were so in fact, but rather in the opinion and understanding of the Corinthians, who, having been led astray by false teachers, listened to those who belittled Paul. Paul was a very eloquent man, and he was well endowed with the gift of interpretation; but Barnabas, in turn, surpassed him in another gift: namely, in the consolation of those who were troubled in their conscience. He was <margin>Acts 4. 36.</margin> <margin>Acts 11. 24.</margin> a "Son of Consolation," to comfort troubled consciences. Likewise also in the cases of Peter and the other Apostles; theologians note regarding Christ's command to Peter, singling him out when He says: *Peter, feed my lambs;*

<column-break/>

*Peter, do you love me?* <margin>John 21. 15.</margin> The reason some interpreters give as to why Peter was singled out is this: because Peter had an outstanding gift for preaching and for tending the lambs of Christ (that is, the weak believers). Furthermore, it is said of James and John that they were named "Sons of Thunder," as having a more powerful gift from God to terrify and awaken a sinner's conscience than Peter and the other Apostles had. <margin>Mark 3. 17. <gloss>Boanerg.</gloss> <note>Original: "Boanerges," a Hebrew/Aramaic term meaning Sons of Thunder.</note></margin> So that, although some of the Apostles had the most excellent gifts, others among them surpassed them again in certain particular gifts.

<margin>4. Proposition.</margin> The fourth Proposition is that there are cases in which men can have great gifts but weak grace. It pleases God sometimes to greatly exalt a man's gifts when his graces, by comparison, have no such exaltation; because gifts are for the good of others, for the building up of the Church of God, and not only for the good of one man. The Corinthians were lacking in no gift, and had all knowledge, and yet when the Apostle speaks of their grace, he says: <margin>1 Cor. 3. 1.</margin> <margin><gloss>metr.</gloss> <note>Likely an abbreviation for "metretice" or similar, referring to a measure or comparison.</note></margin> *I could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal.* They surpassed other churches in gifts, yet they fell short of other churches in grace. <margin>Rev. 3. 17.</margin> Such was the church of Laodicea, for she was rich in gifts and poor in grace. Now there are four Cases in which men can have great gifts and yet little grace.

<margin>1. Case.</margin> 1. When a man's knowledge is clear and strong, but his experience and affection are limp and weak; when they have more expressions than impressions. Such people are like the moon, which, although it immediately grows large again after its waning and increases to its fullness, nevertheless only increases in light and not in heat. So it is also with men when they only increase in the light of knowledge and speculation, and not in the heat of affections toward God and toward the practical part of Christianity. And it is to be feared that there are many in these times, who are considered to be of the Religion, who are of that sort; they are greater in knowledge than in movement; greater in speaking than in practicing; greater in parts or gifts than in grace.

<margin>2. Case.</margin> 2. When your gifts do not conform to your life. Note: just as it is with the sickness to which children are often subject <note>Likely referring to rickets, common in the 17th century, where the head appeared disproportionately large compared to the body.</note>: they may grow large and thick in their head, and yet waste away in the lower parts of the body. So there are also some (as has been indicated) who have such a sickness in their spiritual state; they grow in their head, becoming thick in gifts, and yet waste away in their life, wasting away in grace and the exercise of the same.

<margin>3. Case.</margin> 3. When their gifts serve to promote schisms in the Church and pride in their hearts. This was uncovered in the church of Corinth, that they lacked no gifts; but see what the Apostle says: <margin>1 Cor. 1. 11, 12.</margin> verse 11: *For it hath been declared unto me of you, my brethren, by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you.* Again, verse 12: *Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ.* They were carnal in respect to grace and walked as men, although they had great gifts. ...so proud of his outward blessings—such as clothing, wealth, and the like—as he is of his own talents. The Commentators <note>original: "Uytleggers"</note> who have written on the Prophecy of Ezekiel say that Ezekiel is called *Son of Man* <note>original: "Menschen Kint"</note> ninety-three times in the prophecy. Now, there is no other Prophet in the entire Bible more frequently addressed this way, except for one other who is called *Son of Man*; and <margin>Dan. 8:17.</margin> that is Daniel. The commentators give this reason for why he is called by this title: it is because he was a Prophet who possessed the greatest gifts and the most glorious visions of all the other Prophets. Compare this prophecy with those of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Hosea, or all the others; nevertheless, Ezekiel’s prophecy is a darker, more hidden, and deeper book. Now, because the Prophet Ezekiel was a man who possessed the greatest talents, God took care to keep his heart humble by saying, *Son of Man, Son of Man*. This teaches us that those who possess great gifts ought to spend a large portion of their time keeping their hearts humble and lowly <note>original: "leeg," literally "empty" or "void of pride"</note>, because there is a lingering disposition in our nature through which we are prone to be puffed up by our talents.

<margin>2. Application.</margin>
2. Warning. Value a small grace more highly than a large measure of gifts; for you would surely value a pearl, even if no larger than a pea, more than a great heap of stones.

There are great reasons why we must value a small grace higher than many talents.

<margin>1. Reason.</margin>
1. Grace will endure when gifts perish. A comet will fall while the star remains. A falling star is no star at all, but only a comet. Likewise, Hypocrites can have a great loftiness regarding their gifts; yet they can fall like comets that hover in the air. Grace is like a star that remains fixed in its course. There is a great difference between a painted face and a natural appearance; the painted appearance will not last forever, but a natural one will always remain. Gifts are like paint, an added ornament to the creature; but true grace, which is like the natural appearance, shall remain.

<margin>2. Reason.</margin>
2. Value a small grace above many gifts because gifts cannot bring you into heaven. Christ said to the Scribe that he was not far from the Kingdom of Heaven; but alas, with all his gifts and learning, he fell short. *Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord,* (says Christ) *and have we not prophesied in your name, and in your name cast out devils?*— <margin>Mat. 7:22. <note>The text cites 7:28, but the quote is 7:22.</note></margin> *and in your name done many wonders?* You see then that it is very remarkable: these people could claim high and great gifts, and yet God shuts the doors of Heaven tightly against those to whom He reveals the mysteries of His Kingdom. A man can be a Teacher, and the mysteries of Heaven can be revealed to him, and yet the gates of Heaven can be closed to him. A person can have the gift of casting out devils in Christ’s name—a great and wonderful gift—and yet even these people who cast out devils are themselves cast down by devils. *We have done many wonders in your name*; they who performed miracles

<column-break/>

were made into a wonder themselves: they who had so many gifts remained outside of Heaven; yes, they who could preach to others could make themselves outcasts <note>original: "verwerpelijck," referring to being a castaway or reprobate.</note>.

<margin>3. Warning.</margin>
3. Do not be deceived into thinking that the power of gifts is the power of grace. Parents will not judge their children to be healthy and strong when their heads and chests are large and thick but their feet are weak; likewise, you can grow large in your heads—in knowledge and observations, in talents—and yet be weak in the exercise of grace. Now, so that you do not mistake your position and might not be deceived, I shall show how you may know the difference between those who have great gifts and those who have strong grace. Take this as a general rule: just as art mimics nature, so do gifts mimic grace. Now, there are four differences:

<margin>1. Difference.</margin>
1. When grace strengthens, corruption weakens. It is with grace and desires as it was with the House of Saul and the House of David. As the House of David grew stronger and stronger, so the House of Saul grew weaker and weaker. When the Ark was set up, Dagon fell down; so shall the Dagon of corruption fall before the Ark of grace and the Ark of the Covenant. But gifts can strengthen, and yet corruption is no weaker for it. Indeed, gifts reveal corruption, but they are not powerful enough to suppress and kill it. Gifts reveal many corruptions but do not kill even one. Gifts take notice of many sins but never make an end of a single one. People who have gifts are compared to the Moon, and people who have grace are compared to the Sun. The Moon has an influence on the water, causing it to move in ebb and flow; the Moon gives light to all creatures, but no heat to make the creatures grow and sprout up. Likewise, a person who has gifts can have light, but no heat to make grace grow in these gifts, or to make sin weaken and wither. Graced people are like the Sun, which gives not only light but <margin>The unlearned rise and take heaven by force: while we with our learning... Aug. <note>original Latin: "Sur gung dolti: & ra piunt caelu: nos cũ doctrinas Aug." A reference to Augustine's Confessions VIII, 8.</note></margin> also heat; through its influence, things sprout and grow up out of the earth. The great gifts of a talented man often strengthen his corruptions by opportunity, but they do not weaken them. Augustine said, *the ignorant and unlearned people take heaven by storm, while the others with all their learning run toward heaven [but fail].*

<margin>2. Difference.</margin>
Where the power of grace is, there the heart is more humbled under the received measures of grace; the stronger the graces are, the more the heart is humbled. But the power of gifts in most people makes them proud and puffed up. Empty vessels make the loudest sound, and so do shallow streams. Likewise, people who have great gifts are often empty of grace. <margin>1 Cor. 8:1.</margin> They are puffed up with pride who have more gifts than grace; but by the humility of the soul, you can know whether the soul is stronger in grace than in gifts.

<margin>3. Difference.</margin>
3. He looks more toward the fulfillment of the grace that he lacks than to satisfy himself with the grace which he already has. This proves that Paul had much grace when he spoke thus: *I press on for more and more grace, if I might through...*

<meta>catchword: through</meta>

<summary>This page distinguishes between "gifts" (intellectual abilities and outward religious talents) and "grace" (internal spiritual transformation and humility). It argues that gifts alone can lead to pride and do not guarantee salvation, whereas true grace is marked by a decrease in sin and an increase in humility.</summary>

Here, the author further distinguishes between those who possess only "gifts" (talents or outward religious abilities) and those who possess true "grace" (inward spiritual transformation), urging the reader to seek the latter and to grow in it.</meta>

->various Degrees.<-

<margin>Philippians 3:3 explained. <note>The author likely intends a reference to Philippians 3:11-14 regarding the "resurrection from the dead" and pressing toward perfection.</note></margin>
...that I might by any means attain the resurrection of the dead: that is, I labor toward the perfection of grace, which those who have risen from the dead and are exalted in Heaven shall possess. But a person who has spiritual gifts is often more inclined to see what they have than what they lack.
<margin>He displays his gifts, not his wounds. <note>original: "Munera non vulnera ostendit"</note></margin>
People who possess many talents look more upon their received gifts than upon their own imperfections; they view their gifts through a magnifying glass, making them appear larger than they are, while they view their failings or mistakes through a diminishing glass, making them appear smaller.

<margin>1 Peter 3:7.</margin>
4. The more grace someone has, the more communicative they are, so that others might also partake in that same grace. When the Apostle spoke of the duties of husbands and wives, he desired that they should help one another along the way to Heaven, recognizing that they were joint heirs of the grace of God. Christ spoke similarly to Peter: "when you are converted, strengthen <margin>Luke 22:32.</margin> your brothers." By "conversion" here, it does not mean God’s first work of bringing Peter’s soul to Christ, but rather a strengthening work of grace. It is as if Christ had said: "Peter, now your grace is weak, and it shall become even weaker through your fall; but when you have recovered from your fall and from the denial of your Master, then strengthen your brothers; labor to strengthen the graces of others when your own graces are strong and you have regained your strength." This is good proof that you possess not only grace, but the *power* of grace, when you are diligent in strengthening others. But those who have only gifts, with little or no grace, are slow to share their gifts with others; they would prefer to sell their talents dearly and they grumble about sharing them. They do not want others to have such gifts as they themselves possess, lest their own honor be eclipsed. They do not have the spirit of John the Baptist, who was not troubled that he decreased while Christ increased; rather, they are more like a certain Aspendius <note>A famous ancient musician mentioned by Cicero, known for playing "within himself" or in a way that others could not learn his technique.</note>, a skillful musician who would never play in front of anyone who shared his profession, lest they should learn his art. This is a very significant discovery as to whether you have strong grace or merely strong gifts: you can know it by your willingness and readiness to share with others what God has shared with you.

## 2 TIMOTHY 2:1.
### My son, be strong in the grace that is in Jesus Christ.

You have heard the first Doctrine explained: namely, that believers must not content themselves with the weak measures of grace they have already received, but that they ought to strive to obtain greater strength of grace. Now I shall proceed to prove this point through several applications 

<column-break/>

of the same, and I shall direct this "Use" <term>Use: a standard term in 17th-century sermons for the practical application of a doctrine</term> to two kinds of Christians:
> 1. To those who are weak in faith.
> 2. To those who are strong and mature Christians.

1. To the weak believers, I shall give the following directions and comforts.
<margin>1. Application.</margin>
1. It is your wisdom to look more toward the *truth* of your grace than toward the *measure* of it. It is a mistake in many Christians, especially young converts, that they would rather bring their graces to the balance <note>to weigh the quantity</note> than to the touchstone <note>to test the quality or authenticity</note>; they weigh them when they should be testing them. When Peter was asked by Christ, <margin>John 21:19.</margin> "Simon, do you love me more than these?" he did not answer according to the *measure* of his love, but according to the *truth* of his love: "Lord, I love you, and you know that I love you." It is not the size or measure, but the nature and essence of grace that is most noteworthy. If you have grace in truth and in deed, it will grow. Only make sure that your grace is sincere; and just as the light shines more and more until the full day, and just as the nature of springtime is to make everything sprout from the clod of earth, so it is with grace—it has a sprouting and growing nature. Therefore, be diligent that if you have grace in truth and essence, even in a small measure, it may increase.

2. In discovering the truth of grace, we must not measure it so much by outward works as by the inclinations and holy dispositions of the heart. The hand, posture, and reaches of the heart are the best discoverers of grace within. When a Christian examines the entire root of the grace they possess, they will find that it consists more in desires than in outward observations; and more in the intentions and purposes to fulfill holy duties than in the fulfillment itself. The natural body can be better identified by its heat than by its color; a painter can paint the latter, but not the former. When the Lord Jesus describes the beauty of his Bride, he does not say "how beautiful is your face," but rather, <margin>Song of Solomon 4:3. <note>The author likely refers to verse 10: "How beautiful is your love!"</note></margin> "how beautiful is your love."

3. Do not lose heart, even though people who have the most glorious gifts may fall away; for the poorest Christian who has but the smallest measure of grace shall never fall away. The gifts of a Formalist <term>Formalist: someone who follows the outward forms of religion without inward life</term> can quickly wither, for they have their root in nature; but the grace of a true Christian shall never perish, for it has its root in Christ. A Christian’s life is <margin>Colossians 3:3.</margin> hidden with Christ in God—hidden in him as in the root, and as in the fountain of life. A painted image can easily fade, but a true and natural form does not. The varnish of a manufactured Hypocrite soon withers; but when true grace—like a dye in a piece of grain—has gained a firm hold in the soul, it is unchangeable. The sun would sooner lose its rays than Christ would abandon or scatter the smallest measure of true grace, which is a ray from that Sun of Righteousness.

4. Examine your small grace well, for this is the way to obtain more. "To everyone who has, more shall be given." <margin>Luke 19:26.</margin>

<summary>This page distinguishes between outward religious "gifts" and inward "grace," using metaphors like the musician Aspendius and the difference between a touchstone and a scale. It offers comfort to weak believers, emphasizing that the authenticity of one's faith is more important than its initial strength, as true grace is rooted eternally in Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the degrees of spiritual life, moving from the definition of spiritual gifts to the practical application of "grace." # Graces, with their [degrees]

That is, more shall be given. God never gave anyone a talent simply to hide it. Even the smallest measure of grace must be accounted for. Grace is recognized by these signs:

<margin>Luke 19:16.</margin>
1. When we attribute all the glory of grace to God; just as that man said, "Lord, your pound has gained ten pounds." <note>The "pound" refers to the *mina*, a unit of currency used in Jesus's parable of the talents.</note> *Your* pound—and not *my* efforts: we must do everything for the praise of the glory of God’s grace. If we give God the glory for His grace, He will give us the comfort of our grace and the increase of the same.

2. When we strengthen others in their most holy faith: doing good to others is the best way to obtain more good for ourselves. The more water is drawn from the well or pit, the more water flows in, and the better the water is; likewise, the more your grace is exercised, the more grace—and the sweeter comfort from it—you shall have.

5. To the weak Christians: Do not doubt the truth of grace in your souls simply because you cannot feel its full power within you. A poor, weak person suffering from consumption <note>The original Dutch *teeringe* refers to tuberculosis or a wasting disease.</note> cannot lift such a weight, nor carry such a pack, as a strong and healthy person can—even though he still has a body just as the strongest man in the world does. It can be day even when it is not yet noon: in regards to your spiritual state, you can have the strength of a child, even if not the strength of a man. It is not only an act of ungratefulness toward God, but also of unkindness toward a person’s own soul, to conclude that one has *no* grace simply because that grace is *weak*.

<margin>James 5:11.</margin>
6. Do not look so much at your sins, but look also at your graces, even though they are weak graces. Weak Christians look more at their sins than at their graces; nevertheless, God looks at their graces, and He overlooks their sins and weaknesses. The Holy Spirit says, "You have heard of the patience of Job." He could just as easily have said, "You have heard of the impatience of Job"; but God does not count the dross that is in His people, but rather that which is good in them. Mention is made of Rahab’s kind reception of the spies; you have heard of her lie <note>Referring to Rahab's deception of the King of Jericho's messengers to save the Israelite scouts.</note>: so that what was well done is recounted to her praise, but that in which she sinned is kept silent, or at least not held against her or recounted over her. The person who painted the portrait of Alexander <note>Likely Alexander the Great.</note> with the scar on his face, painted it with a finger over the scar. In the same way, God lays His finger over the scars of our sins. Oh, it is such a good Master to serve, who is ready to reward the good we do, and to forgive and overlook that in which we have trespassed. Therefore, you who have but a little grace, remember that God will nevertheless keep His eye upon it;

<margin>Matthew 12:20.</margin>
He will not quench the smoking wick, and He will not break the bruised reed.

7. Learn this for your comfort: that although you have only a small grace, that little bit shall not be extinguished by your strong corruption; rather, it shall at last overcome your corruptions.

<column-break/>

What was said of Esau and Jacob—that "the one shall be stronger than the other, and the elder shall serve the younger"—and how it later came to pass (in the time of Jehoshaphat) when there was no king in Edom; that can aptly be applied to the matters of the soul: "the elder shall serve the younger." Corruption in the soul is older than grace in the soul, and corruption is so set against grace that it labors to extinguish it; but this spark shall live in the midst of the sea of corruption, until the great deep is dried up; and the house of David shall have cast down the house of Saul: the Name of the Lord shall accomplish this. And therefore you, who are a weak Christian, learn to establish yourself in the Name of the Lord, until it shall be brought forth into victory.

### 2. The use of this doctrine is for strong believers, for those who have obtained a higher form and power of grace in the School of Christ.

1. Although you are strong in grace, remember nonetheless that it is not the grace of God *in* you, but the free grace of God *toward* you, or *upon* you, by which you are justified. Our inherent righteousness is not our inheritance, but the imputed righteousness of Christ which serves for our justification. Oh, consider—you who have the most grace—what would become of you were it not for free grace? Free grace is the surest and only refuge for a soul to flee to. God can find grounds for condemnation against you, not only for your worst sins, but for your best and most dutiful services. The best Christian has no reason to boast in their soul of the best thought they can conceive, nor in the best services they can perform, nor in the highest grace they ever exercised. We have an excellent example of this in Nehemiah, who had much grace and accomplished much for God, His people, His house, and His cause; yet after all these things he prays, "Spare me, according to the greatness of your loving-kindness." <note>Nehemiah 13:22.</note> Implying that God could find cause enough therein to destroy him, if God did not spare him for His loving-kindness' sake. Likewise Paul, in the work of his ministry, performed with so much sincerity that he spoke of himself thus: "I am conscious of nothing against myself; yet I am not thereby justified." <note>1 Corinthians 4:4.</note> He knew well that all grace, and his excellence, and sincerity could not justify him in the sight of God. We read of Jehoshaphat, that when he had counted up all his strength, which was very great (for he had eleven hundred thousand men in his army), he nonetheless went to God and prayed, "O God! We have no power against this great multitude; and we do not know what we should do: but our eyes are upon you." Likewise, when a Christian has counted up all the strength of his grace, and has noticed the great power of his corruptions which set themselves against him, it is best for him to go to God and say, "Lord, I have no power against these many and great corruptions; but my eyes are upon your grace, that you might help me." Just as it is with a compass: one foot stands firm within the center while the other makes the circumference; so must the soul keep itself firm in Christ...

<summary>This page addresses both "weak" and "strong" Christians, offering comfort that small grace is still true grace and will eventually overcome internal corruption. It warns strong believers that their justification comes from God's free grace alone, not their own spiritual maturity or works.</summary>

# Various Degrees.

<column-break/>

<margin>Song of Solomon 4:1 to 8.</margin>
...establish, while she exercises herself in holy duties. Although Christ (as I related before) notes many members of the Bride nonetheless with her hands; to teach us that all she did could not make her lovely in the eyes of Christ—it was not the Bride's work for Christ, but Christ's work for the Bride that made her beautiful. It is very difficult, through the power of grace, to become abundant in the work of the Lord and yet keep the heart humble; and therefore:

2. Note: those who have the most grace still have great cause to be humbled, and that in many respects:

1. Because you do not have as much grace and perfection as you once had. Once, Man was adorned with many glorious perfections before the Fall, so that it might be said of Man that he was perfect, even as his Heavenly Father was perfect: for God made Man upright, that is, perfect; nothing was lacking to make Man both a blessed and a holy creature: but alas! the image of God is now blotted out and perished within us.

<margin>Philippians 3:12, 14.</margin>
<margin>Exodus 26:10. The error of the Perfectionists <note>The "Perfectionists" were various religious groups who believed that a state of sinless perfection could be achieved during one's earthly life—a view the author here contests.</note> is very harmful.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 12:23. 1 John 3:2.</margin>
2. He who has the most grace does not have as much as he shall have in Heaven. *Not that I am already perfect, but I forget those things which are behind, and reach forward to those things which are ahead; indeed, I press* (says the Apostle) *toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.* We read in the Law of various things that were only one and a half cubits high and wide; this being an incomplete measure was to signify that no man in this life has a full perfection: the utmost that is obtainable for us in this life is but imperfection. There is in this life a *plus ultra* <note>original: "plus ultra"; meaning "further beyond."</note>; that is, something more can always be obtained in the service of God: but in Heaven, people shall be perfect. We shall become like Jesus Christ in Heaven, whom we now see only obscurely and as if in a mirror, but then we shall see Him as He is.

<margin>Matthew 20:16.</margin>
3. Those who have much grace must nonetheless be humble: for there are those who have greater grace than you, and who nevertheless have had less time and fewer advantages than you have: there are those who have surpassed you in the strength of grace, and yet came behind you in the means of grace: there are those who were the last, and are now the first, and ahead of you.

<margin>Luke 13:6, 7.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 5:12.</margin>
4. Be humble under much grace: for you do not have as much grace as you ought to have, considering the means of grace under which you have lived. How many years have you been in the schools of Christ; and how little proper progress have you nonetheless made in the knowledge of Jesus Christ? We must all blush with shame when we think what dull people we have been in the school of Christ: the trees in the garden ought to bear more fruit than the trees in the wilderness: therefore the fig tree that was unfruitful was more intolerable because it was in the garden in the vineyard. That which the Apostle to the Hebrews complains of, we may rightfully take up against ourselves, to complain about ourselves: that *whereas for the time you ought to be teachers, you have need again that one teach you which be the first principles of the oracles of God; (as) those who have need of milk, and not of strong meat.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Revelation 2:3.</margin>
5. Those who have much grace and are strong therein still have reason to be humble, because it is likely that they previously had more grace than they have now: and who is there who has not fallen away, who has not in one stage or another left his first love? Have you not had (I speak to mature and exercised Christians) more love and zeal for God, more hatred against sin, more sorrow over sin, more fear of offending God than you have now? Are there not many who have and show less desire for required duties, less zeal, less submission, and less delight in holy services than before? Alas! how many have, through pride and spiritual imprudence, through neglect of the ordinances, and through worldly-mindedness, diminished their spiritual state?

<margin>How much there is that we do not know. <note>original Latin: "Quantum est quod nescimus."</note></margin>
<margin>Romans 7:21.</margin>
6. Be humble because, although you have strong grace, you still have many corruptions in you that are stronger than much grace. Our vain thoughts are more numerous than our holy meditations: and the things of which we are ignorant are greater than the things which we know. Corruption is powerful enough to keep grace down; but in the best grace there is not enough power to completely bring down corruption. *When we want to do good, then evil is present with us* to hinder us from the good; but when we do evil, is the good exactly present to hinder that evil? We sin more than we obey. Our corruption is like Goliath, our grace like David. We practice more sins than graces. Just as in a field there are more thistles and thorns than useful trees; and in a garden more weeds than roses and lilies—so also in the souls of the best, there are entire swarms of vain, earthly, and sinful thoughts; and on the contrary, few holy and heavenly thoughts.

<margin>Romans 4:23.</margin>
<margin>Galatians 2:9.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 20:22.</margin>
<margin>James 5:11.</margin>
<margin>Job 6:9.</margin>
<margin>Numbers 12:3.</margin>
<margin>Job 33.</margin>
<margin>Numbers 11:14, 15.</margin>
7. Another reason why strong Christians must be humble is this: that although they have grace, they are nonetheless subject to falling into that sin which is most contrary to the grace in which they are most outstanding. Abraham was outstanding in faith; he is said to have been strong in faith; he is called the Father of the Faithful. *Those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham*: and yet Abraham fell into distrust of God's providence and power when he spoke an untruth and denied his wife. Likewise was Job, renowned for his patience; *you have heard of the patience of Job* (says the Apostle James), and yet we read in the history of Job's trials that his impatience broke out into many hasty words and wishes. Likewise, Moses was outstanding in meekness, so that it is said of him, *the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.* And yet it is said of him that his spirit was embittered, so that he spoke somewhat unadvisedly with his lips: and you shall find the meek Moses thus complaining of himself before God: *I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me; and if you deal thus with me, kill me, I pray you, out of hand, if I have found favor in your sight; and let me not see my wretchedness.*

It warns that even great saints like Abraham, Job, and Moses were prone to failing in the very virtues for which they were most famous.</summary>

This page addresses how the "strong" in faith should remain humble and strive for even greater growth.</meta>

# Grace, with its [own]...

8. This further observation can also humble us: that even in the highest and greatest exercise of grace, there is much mingling of sin. We can see that even those good works for which many of God’s People are mentioned with praise in the <margin>Exodus 1:17, 19.</margin> Scriptures were nonetheless tainted with some notable defects. Rahab’s faith in receiving the spies was tainted by her words, in that she lied for their sake. It was also good what the midwives did when they refused to obey the bloody decree of the King of Egypt and would not kill the infants of the Hebrews; and yet they hesitated, as some note, in their answer before the King when they excused themselves. We are prone to mixing sin with the best work we do, and so prone to <term>plowing with an ox and a donkey together<note>A reference to the prohibition in Deuteronomy 22:10, used here metaphorically to describe the mixing of holy and unholy motives.</note></term>; our corruptions are capable of revealing themselves even while we are in the exercise of our graces.

III. Let the strong labor to become stronger, <margin>Colossians 1:11.</margin> so that they might be strengthened with all power according to His glory, unto all patience and longsuffering with joy. And <margin>Romans 15:13, 14.</margin> therefore it is that the Apostle prays for the Romans, that they might be filled by the God of hope with all joy and peace in believing, and abound in hope through the power of the Holy Spirit; and yet he says to them in the next verse, "But my brothers, I myself am also certain of you, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge." And just as he prays for the Romans, so he does in the same <margin>1 Thessalonians 4:9, 10.</margin> manner for the Thessalonians, of whom he speaks thus: "Now concerning brotherly love, you have no need that I write to you, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another. For you also do the same toward all the brothers who are in all Macedonia. But we exhort you, brothers, that you abound more and more." The righteous (says Job) shall hold to his way, and he who has clean <margin>Job 17:9.</margin> hands shall grow in strength.

### To stir you up to this, consider:

1. The more grace we have on earth, the more glory we shall have in Heaven. Just as God distributes His gifts <margin>As God gives gifts in this life unequally, so He crowns them. — Bacanus <note>Original Latin: "Sicut Deus dat dona in hac vita in aequaliter communicat sic coronat Bacanus."</note></margin> unequally in this life, so He also crowns them. There are degrees of torment in Hell; the hypocritical Scribes and Pharisees, who devoured widows' houses and (did so) under the pretense of long prayers, are condemned by Christ Himself to receive a heavier judgment; and the servant who <margin>Luke 12:47.</margin> knew his Lord’s will and did not prepare (himself), nor acted according to His will, shall be beaten with many (stripes). Now, as there are distinct degrees of torment in Hell, so there are truly also different degrees of glory in Heaven, and these according to the different degrees of grace here on earth.

2. It is the very nature of grace to grow and increase; and therefore, if you have grace, it will certainly increase, whether in truth or in its strength. Grace is compared in the Scripture to a <margin>Matthew 13:32, 33.</margin> mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which afterwards sprouts so that it becomes the greatest of herbs. In the same chapter, grace is compared to leaven, which,

<column-break/>

when placed in a heap of flour, leavened the whole. Likewise, grace in the heart (as I have related before) is of a spreading nature, and it will spread itself into all the parts, powers, and strengths of the Soul and the <margin>Job 1</margin> body. Christians were previously compared to the branches of a Vine, which grow more than all other trees and bring forth the most fruit. A painting of a child will not grow, but a living child will grow.

3. Those who are strong Christians ought to increase more and more because no limit or measure has been set for spiritual growth in this world; but the <term>maximum that is possible here<note>Original Latin: "maximum quod hic."</note></term> for a Christian—the highest and greatest point he can reach—is this: he must increase in grace until his head reaches to Heaven, until grace is made perfect in glory.

<margin>If I said etc. <note>likely Peter</note></margin> 4. Shall worldly people set no bounds for their desires for wealth and land, and will you stop at small measures of grace in your religion? The common answer of ignorant people is: "What? Must we be wiser than our ancestors?" And yet these people certainly want to be richer than their ancestors were; and those who have great riches left to them by their ancestors are still not satisfied with them, unless they further increase their status. Let this shame the sluggishness and lazy negligence of many who satisfy themselves with their current measure of grace.

5. And finally, consider what value was placed on those in the Church of God who were outstanding in grace, and with what praiseworthy accounts they are remembered in the Word of God: such individuals are considered worthy of note in the Church of God. <margin>See Romans 1.</margin> See what praise the Holy Spirit gives to Job: <margin>Job 1.</margin> that there was none like him on the earth. God loves those who are especially and exceedingly good, for common goodness <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> does not please Him as much. "What do you do more than others?" says Christ. Solomon was so famous for his wisdom that it is said of him that among those many nations, there was no King like him—that is, in wisdom. Likewise, <margin>Nehemiah 1.</margin> Hezekiah was outstanding in his trust in God; he was not afraid to <margin>2 Kings [18].</margin> shatter the bronze serpent but trusted in God, so that none among all the Kings of Judah was like him. And so outstanding was the zeal of the pious Josiah for a total Reformation that he too was crowned with this praise: "And before him there was no King like him, who turned to the LORD with his whole heart, and with his whole soul, and with his whole strength." Through all these examples, it is clear what honorable esteem the outstanding and special grace of God’s servants has held in the sight of the Lord.

# Perfecter of our Grace.

### II. TIMOTHY 2:1
#### My Son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.

<margin>
34. Sermon in [St.] Lawrence Jewry <note>A historic church in the City of London, famous for its influential sermons during the 17th century.</note> within London, April 17, 1651.
</margin>
Having dealt in the last preceding sermons with grace and its power and growth, I now come to handle this added conclusion in the text: namely, *that which is in Christ Jesus*. This phrase was set down here by the Apostle so that he might let Timothy know to whom he must look regarding all the grace which he had received—namely, toward Christ Jesus.

In the tenth verse, he speaks of the **Salvation** which is in Christ Jesus, and here of the **grace** which is in Christ Jesus, to note:
1. That Jesus Christ is the **Fountain** and foundation of grace and glory. Jesus Christ gives grace, and Jesus Christ likewise gives salvation with eternal glory (verse 10).
2. That those who receive grace from Christ Jesus shall also receive salvation through him; for there is a distinct union between grace and glory.

**The grace of God which is in Christ Jesus.**
Grace can be said to be "in Christ" in several ways:
1. As a **subject** possessing the same within himself; and thus Christ is said to be full of grace and truth. He does not give the Spirit by measure; it is the Father's good pleasure that in him all fullness should dwell.
<margin>
John 1:14.
John 3:34.
</margin>

2. In Christ Jesus as a **Fountain**, overflowing and never ceasing toward his people; for from his fullness we have all received, even grace upon grace.
<margin>
Colossians 1:19.
John 1:16.
</margin>

Again, when it is said *the grace that is in Christ Jesus*, we must consider Christ:
1. As God, being of one essence with the Father; and he is the **Author** and giver of grace, and of every good and perfect gift.
2. Consider him as **Mediator**, God and Man, and so he is an obtainer and provider of grace, and of all the blessings of the New Covenant; for the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles through Christ Jesus. So, by this manner of speaking, *in Christ Jesus*, three things are understood:
<margin>Galatians 3:14.</margin>

1. That Jesus Christ is the **Author** and the **Giver** of grace; he alone is the Chief Leader <note original: "Oversten Leydt-man">A translation of the Greek "archegos," often rendered as "Author" or "Pioneer" of faith.</note> and perfecter of faith, and of every grace in his people.
<margin>Hebrews 12:2.</margin>

2. That Christ is the **obtainer** of grace; so that all the grace given to us by God is through Christ and for his sake. Grace is from Christ as from a Fountain, and by Christ as from a source.
3. That Christ is the **Preserver** of grace; all the grace that is in us is in Christ Jesus, who guards all our graces for us. Just as the rays of the Sun can be said to be in the Sun because they are preserved by their union with the Sun. Our life is hidden with Christ in God—hidden as the life of a tree is hidden in the root, and the existence of a stream is hidden in the fountain. And herein consists the comfort of 
<margin>Colossians 3:3.</margin>

<column-break/>

believers: that their state is firmer, indeed more unchangeable and more secure, than the state of Adam was in his innocence. For Adam indeed had all the perfections of a creature, but they were in his own keeping. But now, all the grace that is in a believer is in Christ Jesus, through whom and in whom grace is surely preserved, so that it shall never perish.

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
The **Doctrine** which I observe from these words is this:
**That all these measures of grace, of which believers are partakers, are received in and from Jesus Christ.**
In the handling of this, I shall proceed as follows:
1. Show you the truth of this matter.
2. Give you the reasons and foundations for it.

Now, to prove that all grace is received in and through Christ, I shall:
1. Show the truth of this through many **parables** <note>In this context, the author uses "parables" to mean biblical metaphors or analogies.</note> to which Christ is compared in the Scriptures.
2. Through many **figures** <note>Historical types or symbols in the Old Testament that foreshadow Christ.</note> of Christ in the Old Testament.
3. Through many explicit **testimonies** in the New Testament regarding this truth.

1. There are many parables in the Scripture which prove this: that all grace is from Christ Jesus.
<margin>Isaiah 11:10.</margin>
I. He is compared to a **root**. He is called the "Root of Jesse," not only because he came from the lineage of David, but because he gave grace to the Jews and Gentiles who believed; for after him the Gentiles shall seek, as follows in the next words.

<margin>
Romans 15:12.
John 15:4. <note>The original OCR incorrectly cites verse 14; the context clearly refers to the vine in verse 4.</note>
</margin>
Now, that the Prophet speaks there of Christ is clear through the Apostle’s explicit application of that prophecy to Christ, calling him the Root of Jesse in whom the Gentiles would hope. And Christ says of himself: *I am the Vine; just as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.* The life, sap, nourishment, growth, and fruitfulness of a branch are altogether from the root, with which the branches have union and communion.

<margin>Colossians 1:18.</margin>
II. Christ is called the **Head** of his People; he is called the head of the body of the Church. Now, just as feeling and movement come down from the head to the members of the body, so also has grace come down from Jesus Christ to every true believer, every living member of his body.

<margin>
Malachi 4:2.
Unless from above. <note original: "Nisi de super"></note>
</margin>
III. Christ is called the **Sun of Righteousness**, because just as heat and light are joined to the things here below by the Sun, so there is a sweet flowing-in of grace from Christ upon believers. Just as by the power of the Sun’s influence the plants and living creatures live, move, and grow; so also is the life and the growth of grace in the Soul derived from that Divine influence which Jesus Christ pours out over believers.

<margin>Zechariah 13:1.</margin>
IV. Christ is compared to a **fountain**; as a fountain opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, against sin and against impurity. So that just as water flows into the river from the fountain, so grace flows down from Jesus Christ onto believers, who is a fountain there...

It emphasizes that grace is more secure in Christ than it was in Adam, as Christ acts as both the author and the eternal guardian of a believer's spiritual life.</summary>
