<meta>This page continues the sermon on 2 Timothy 2:1, moving from the definition of grace "in Christ" to the historical and biblical proofs of this doctrine. It transitions from the theological premise (the "first proof" concluded at the top) to practical "shadows" in the Old Testament and specific testimonies in the New Testament.</meta>

Christ the cause and the <note>original: "oorsaeck en de..." – likely "source" or "fountain", completing the header from the previous page.</note>

where all fullness of grace dwells in eternity, and from where all grace is drawn and derived; and this is the first proof.

## II.

This truth can be shown through the many examples of Christ in the Old Testament, which serve as shadows <note>The 17th-century practice of "typology," where Old Testament figures are seen as "shadows" or "types" that prefigure Jesus Christ.</note> for us, showing that all grace is from Jesus Christ. I shall repeat some of them here.

<margin>Levit. 9:12</margin> 1. Aaron the high priest was meant to lay his hands upon the people and bless them. And in this, he was an example of Christ, our great and heavenly High Priest, <margin>Ephes. 1:3</margin> through whom we are blessed with all grace. God having blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heaven in Christ. Jesus <margin>Acts 3:26</margin> Christ is sent from God to bless his people, and to turn every one of them away from their wickedness. And therefore it is noted by Saint Luke that a little <margin>Luke 24:50</margin> before the Ascension of our blessed Savior, he laid his hands upon his disciples and blessed them: and so he continually blesses all true believers with the spiritual blessing of grace.

<margin>Gen. 17:3; Matt. 3:17; Col. 1:11; Gen. 37:20, 21; John 1:12; Gen. 37:28; Matt. 2:13; Gen. 39:20</margin> 2. Another example of Christ was Joseph, who in many things was a figure of Christ. Joseph was the best-beloved of his father’s children; so was Jesus Christ, the Son of his Father's love. Joseph was hated by his brothers and sold for twenty pieces of silver; so was Jesus Christ—he came unto his own, and his own received him not; he was rejected by them and sold for thirty silver coins. Joseph was led into Egypt; and so persecution drove Christ into Egypt immediately after he was born. Joseph was falsely accused and condemned; so was Christ. Joseph’s troubles ended in his exaltation; so all the <margin>Philip. 2:9</margin> troubles of Christ worked for him a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. God has therefore highly exalted him and given him a name which is above every name: for now Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father. But especially in this was Joseph <margin>Gen. 41:55, 56, 57</margin> a figure representing Jesus Christ: that during the heavy, threatening famine in Egypt, Joseph had the keeping of all the corn in the land, and the source of all the provision for bread in all the land of Egypt. So is the Lord Jesus the keeper of all that abundance of grace with which believers are endowed, which grace is given to them in time of need to help them. Jesus Christ has the key of David; he has the key to the riches of grace.

3. Another example of Jesus Christ was Joshua, who gave to Israel the entrance and the possession of the good land of Canaan, as well as all its promised blessings. Likewise <margin>Psal. 84:12; Hebr. 4:8</margin> Jesus Christ gives to his people better things than the milk and honey of Canaan. He shall give grace and honor; he will withhold no good thing from those who walk uprightly. Our Jesus gives his people a better rest than Joshua ever brought to Israel.

<margin>Exod. 25:37; Rev. 4:5</margin> 4. Another example of Christ was the lampstand of the Tabernacle, by whose seven lamps the entire Tabernacle was lit. Now, what do these seven lamps represent if not the graces of the Spirit of Christ? For it is revealed that there were seven lamps of fire burning before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God: The Holy Spirit and the

<column-break/>

graces of the same being thus described by seven Spirits in this respect, because of the variety and protection of that grace which is in the Lord Jesus, and through his <margin>Zech. 4</margin> Spirit shared with all his members <note>The author uses "members" in the sense of the "body of Christ"—the individual believers who make up the church.</note>.

## III.

The third proof of this teaching can be drawn from the consideration of the various testimonies regarding this truth in the New Testament. Saint John speaks thus of Christ: that from his fullness <margin>John 1:16 <gloss>original: "verklacr visudo reva i di va plen vasts Ple do fontis" — interpreted as: explained [as] out of the fullness of the fountain</gloss></margin> have we all received, even grace for grace. In Christ there is not only fullness but also goodness; not only an abundance of all grace, but an overflowing of grace. Christians have the fullness of a vessel, but Christ has the fullness of a fountain. Take a drop of water out of a vessel, and it is not as full as before; but draw as much water as you please from the well of the water of life, and one shall miss no water there. From Christ we receive grace for grace; that is to say, some [receive] the grace of the New Testament added to that grace which was revealed under the Old Testament; or grace for grace, as others say, a perfection of grace belonging to <margin><gloss>original: "Perfectio tium mun duum" — Perfection of the worlds.</gloss></margin> the perfection that is in Christ. Just as in a natural birth a child receives from his father limb for limb and part for part, so in this spiritual rebirth, Jesus Christ the eternal Father gives grace for grace. Or you may understand these expressions "grace for grace" to mean that Jesus Christ is not only the Author of grace, but gives grace upon grace—that is, one grace after another, grace upon grace. The essence of <margin><gloss>original: "Gratia vam-gra cumulati" — Grace upon accumulated grace.</gloss></margin> grace and the growth of grace are both from Christ. It also appears that Christ is the Author and dispenser of all graces from that ordinary prayer with which the Apostle commonly concluded his <margin>2 Cor. 1; Rom. 1; Gal. 6; Philip. 1; 1 Thess.; 1 Tim. 6</margin> Epistles: "the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all." A similar prayer we find to the Romans, to the Galatians—"Brethren, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit." So also in the conclusion of the Epistles to those of Philippi, Thessalonica, and to Timothy: "grace be with you, Amen." All this is to make known that Jesus Christ is the fountain from which, and the pipe through which, all grace is led to the believers. As in the vision that the Prophet Zechariah saw: there were two olive branches, which <margin>Zech. 4</margin> through two golden pipes emptied the golden oil out of themselves. So Jesus Christ, that true olive tree, makes grace drop upon his Church, through which she receives out of his fullness grace for grace.

->But do you not reject the honor of God the <margin>Objection.</margin> Father in giving this honor to Christ when you say that all grace is from Christ?<-

1. It is no diminishing of God the <margin>1st Answer.</margin> Father to ascribe this to Christ, because it has pleased the Father that in him all fullness should dwell.

2. And furthermore, Christ and the Father are <margin>2nd Answer. John 1; Rom. 1; 1 Cor.; Gal. 1; Eph.; Philip. 3; Col. 1:1; 1 Thess.</margin> one; in saying that all grace is from Christ, we say also that all is likewise from the Father; and in saying it is from the Father, we say also it is from Christ as well. And therefore it is a common prayer placed at the beginning of most epistles: "grace be to you from God the Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ." So that in the subscription and in the salutation of every letter, grace is ascribed to God the Son, but always in...

->Perfecter of our Grace.<-

<margin>3. Answer. John 6:38</margin>
...proceeding from God the Father / and the Son not proceeding to God the Father. <note>original: "spruytende" – referring to the theological concept of the procession of the Persons of the Trinity.</note>

3. And then again / **Jesus Christ** is commissioned and appointed by the Father / to distribute grace to His people / for so speaks **Christ** of Himself / I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will; but the will of Him who sent me. Now it is the will of God / that believers should receive from **Christ** both justifying and sanctifying grace. Our sanctification is God’s will.

<margin>1 Thess. 4:3. Heb. 10:9, 10.</margin>
And **Christ** came to fulfill that will of God: for so speaks the Apostle / Sacrifice and offering, and burnt offerings, and offering for sin you did not desire, nor did they please you; then I said, behold, I come to do your will (O God;) by which will we are sanctified, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ made once for all. Thus the will of God the Father / and the will of Jesus Christ are the same in the distribution of grace. **Jesus Christ** receives a command from God the Father / to distribute grace to His people; and if you wish to see how that command reads / you can find it in the Prophet **Isaiah**; the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me, to bring good tidings to the meek: He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, and to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound.

<margin>Isa. 61:1. John 6:27.</margin>
**Christ** had a commission under His Father's hand and seal / for God the Father has sealed Him. Joseph received power from Pharaoh, and it was no dishonor to the sovereign Pharaoh that Joseph was commissioned to distribute all the treasures of corn to the Egyptians in the time of that famine: no more is it any dishonor for the Father / that **Jesus Christ** distributes grace and leads it to the believers.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But does this not deprive the Spirit of His service, which is called the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of grace, because He works grace and holiness in the hearts of God's people?

<margin>Resolution.</margin>
What **Christ** is said to work / that the Holy Spirit also does, because Christ works through the Spirit of God. It is a good rule / that the works of the Blessed Trinity are undivided externally <note>A reference to the Latin theological maxim *opera trinitatis ad extra sunt indivisa*, meaning all three Persons of the Trinity act together in the world.</note>, all these works which are external / and belong to this / such as creating / preserving / redeeming / sanctifying / etc. These are worked equally and in common by the Persons of the Blessed Trinity, though distinguished for the sake of our human weakness.

<margin>John 5:19.</margin>
So that we may say / whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise, and these things the Holy Spirit also does; the work of sanctification is attributed equally to all the Persons.

<margin>Jude v. 1. 1 Cor. 1:30.</margin>
God the Father sanctifies His people. **God** the Son sanctifies His members / for He is their sanctification. He loved His church and gave Himself up for her, that He might sanctify and cleanse her with the washing of water by the word.

<margin>Eph. 5:25, 26. Gal. 5:22.</margin>
And yet the work of sanctification is most often attributed to the Holy Spirit; goodness, righteousness, and truth, and indeed all grace are called the fruit of the Spirit; and the Spirit is called the Spirit of grace and of longsuffering, and the Spirit of holiness and sanctification. So also is our re-

<column-break/>

birth attributed to God the Father: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to His great mercy has begotten us again to a living hope.

<margin>1 Pet. 1:3. Isa. 9:6. Isa. 8:18. Heb. 2:13.</margin>
And so we also become children of Christ through the rebirth / for in this respect **Christ** is called the Father of Eternity. Behold (says the Prophet in the name of Christ) I and the children whom you have given me; and that the Prophet speaks there of Christ is evident from the application of the same to Him in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Behold, I and the children whom God has given me: nonetheless, the Holy Spirit is not excluded from this working of grace and rebirth in us / for Christ said to Nicodemus, unless someone is born again, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, he cannot enter into the Kingdom of God: so it is said / that God the Father blessed Abraham / and yet the blessing of Abraham came upon the Gentiles through Christ, so that they might receive the promise of the Spirit. Through all these examples it appears / that although there are diversities of gifts / yet it is the same Spirit / and although there are differences of ministries / yet it is the same Lord **Jesus Christ** / the Author of all grace through the Holy Spirit.

<margin>John 3:3, 5. Gal. 3:14.</margin>
2. The reason and ground for this / why **Jesus Christ** is the Author / achiever and guide of grace to His people / is

1. Because God the Father has appointed **Jesus Christ** as mediator / to accomplish the great work of saving and sanctifying His elect.

2. Because by this, the contempt for **Christ** might be taken away / who in His life was esteemed among the greatest of evildoers / and subsequently suffered death. They were accustomed to say / can anything good come out of Nazareth? God has therefore given Him a name above all, that He should not only be anointed with oil above His fellows, by His receiving of the Spirit without measure; but that the oil which was poured out upon the head of our High Priest should descend to the hems of His garments; and that the grace which was abundant in Him / should also be so overflowing to His Church / and pour down / and spread itself over all His members.

3. To make it evident / that **Jesus Christ** was the second Adam, and came into the world to repair the breaches / which the sin of the first Adam had made. For through the Fall we have not only brought the guilt of Adam's sin upon ourselves—to take which away we have need of the imputed righteousness of Christ—but we have drawn upon ourselves the filth and possession of sin; now to take away the power of the same / only the grace / holiness, and inherent righteousness <note>original: "inklevende gerechtigheyt" – a term for "infused" or "inherent" holiness that changes a person's nature, as opposed to "imputed" righteousness which changes their legal status.</note> of Christ is powerfully brought over to us; and just as the first Adam was the author and guide of both the guilt, filth, and punishment of sin over his descendants; so **Jesus Christ** the second Adam is the source of the life of grace in His own. Just as the first Adam was the author of communicating natural life, as he was made a living soul; so the second Adam communicates the spiritual life of grace since He is made a life-giving Spirit from the first Adam.

<margin>1 Cor. 15:45.</margin>

through natural generation and procreation / received from corruption for corruption; so from the second Adam; received from grace for grace. <note>The author contrasts biological inheritance (sin from Adam) with spiritual inheritance (grace from Christ).</note>
1. The use of this teaching is for refutation.
1. Of the error of the **Socinians** / who say that all the grace in **Christ** / whether it be His active or passive righteousness / was only to make His own Person worthy / and to earn His own glory / without any regard toward us except only to be an exemplar or model. But this opinion is sufficiently refuted by this doctrine / in which it has been shown / that just as all our grace is from **Christ** / so also the abundance of grace in **Christ** is for us / just as a woman has an abundance of milk in her breasts / not for herself / but for her child; and the sun has an abundance of light / not for itself / but for the world: so is **Jesus Christ** full of grace and truth / but this fullness is in order to the filling of His members. As in the natural body / there are certain particular parts / which stand as servants for all the others. The stomach receives much food / not for itself alone / but so that it might share it with all the other members. The head has the senses fixed within itself / not for itself alone / but for the whole body / so it is also in the <term>mystical body</term> <note>The "mystical body" refers to the Church, where Christ is the head and believers are the limbs or members.</note> / of which **Christ** is the head. The abundance of grace / which is poured into **Christ** / is directed toward this / to fill every member with grace.
<margin>John 17:5.</margin> For them (says **Christ** speaking of the elect) I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. Some interpret this regarding **Christ** / being specifically appointed to the service of Mediator / that it was not for Himself / but for the service of His members; and although there be grace enough in **Christ** to make His person worthy / nevertheless there is also grace enough in Him / to justify our persons as well / and to sanctify our natures.
2. This also refutes the error / pride / and folly of the **Pelagians**, **Papists**, and **Arminians** / who take away from God / and add or attribute to themselves. These people have / like **Samson**, lost their spiritual strength / but do not acknowledge / or do not wish to acknowledge that it has been shorn from them. They are poor / and yet they are proud; and while they exalt the praise of nature, they prove themselves to be enemies of grace. <margin>original Latin: "sub laudibus naturæ latentem Dei gratiam" — Under the praises of nature, the grace of God lies hidden. Augustine.</margin> Alas / while they boast of a <term>free will</term>, they have reason to mourn a <term>enslaved will</term>, as **Luther** recounts that. <note>A reference to Martin Luther's famous work, *The Bondage of the Will* (De Servo Arbitrio).</note> It is true / man did not lose the power itself through the fall / but he has lost the governance of it. And yet proud man wants to be like the spider / spinning a thread out of himself / and thinking to climb to heaven by the threads / spun out of his own entrails / but let such people / who rejoice in this: *I owe it to myself alone, I am indebted to no one but myself* / finally test / that this hope be not cut off, and their trust become like <margin>Job 8:14.</margin> the spider's web. Alas / poor proud miserable people! who distinguishes you? **Grevinchovius** the **Arminian** gives this proud answer to the Apostle’s question / *I myself distinguish myself.* This is very similar to the

<column-break/>

poor theology of the **Heathens**. **Seneca** says / that we live; this is from God, but that we live well, that is from ourselves. And **Cicero** also has that saying / and tells us / that it is the judgment of all men / that luck and prosperity are from God, and must be sought from God; but wisdom is obtained by ourselves / which gave **Augustine** the opportunity to pass this judgment upon him; **Cicero** in trying to make men free makes them into temple-robbers. <note>Augustine's point is that by taking credit for their own virtue/wisdom, they "rob" God's temple of the glory due to Him.</note> But let us pay heed to this puffed-up leaven of the **Arminians** / and learn from this to be convinced of the emptiness and insufficiency of our nature for any supernatural good. For alas! We are not capable of thinking anything of ourselves, as from ourselves: but our capability is from God. We have no grace except that which we receive from **Christ**. And grace is by no means grace, if it be not altogether free. We have little to boast of the freedom of our will regarding anything that is spiritually good / for our will is not free / until the time that it is made free by grace. <margin>original Latin: "Voluntas libera quia liberata" — The will is free because it has been liberated. Augustine.</margin> We have no power to become children of God / until the time that it is given to us to believe in His name; and such are born not of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

### Perfecter of our Grace.

<margin>2 Cor. 10, 15, 16.</margin>
It is a great folly in a man to boast of that which another has done. And therefore the Apostle confesses that he did not behave as those false teachers had done, who had crept into the Church of Corinth. The Apostle says: we do not boast of things beyond our measure, that is, of other men’s labor, nor do we boast in another’s rule over that which has already been done for us. Now all grace is prepared for our hands, and is solely the work of Jesus Christ in us, who works all our works for us. Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman historian.</note> tells us of a certain Lampadius, a great person in Rome, who wanted to put his name on every part of the city where other people had built—not as a restorer of the work, but as the master builder. Those are guilty of such folly who wish to place their own names before God’s name regarding the work of grace in their own souls.

<margin>I and of [myself] as Mine. Rom. 3, 27. <note>original Latin: "Ego & de ut Meus"</note></margin>
O! remember, that boasting is excluded by the law of faith. Faith is that grace which empties the creature of all its imagined excellencies, and faith is that grace which shall give God the honor of the glory of all His grace. Shall the stable boy boast of his master’s horses? And the actor of his borrowed clothes? Shall the wall made of mud and slime be proud that the sun shines upon it?

<margin>2 Kings 6, 5.</margin>
We must say of all the good that is in us—just as the young man said to the Prophet concerning his iron [axe head]—"Alas, my master! For it was borrowed."

<margin>Song of Sol. 6, 10. I reflect the light I have received. <note>original Latin: "Lucem acceptam refero"</note></margin>
The Church of God is compared to the Moon. Now all the light which the Moon gives to the world, she only distributes what is lent to her; all our graces, and the shining of the same, through which our light is seen before men, is but a borrowed light from the Sun of Righteousness. David sets a striking example for us when he makes this humble

<margin>2 Chron. 29. 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16. <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Chronicles 29.</note></margin>
confession: "Blessed be thou, Lord God of our father Israel, forever and ever. Thine, O Lord, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty: for all that is in the heaven and in the earth is thine; thine is the kingdom, O Lord, and thou art exalted as head above all. Both riches and honor come of thee, and thou reignest over all; and in thine hand is power and might; and in thine hand it is to make great, and to give strength unto all. Now therefore, our God, we thank thee, and praise thy glorious name. But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? For all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee. O Lord our God, all this store that we have prepared to build thee an house for thine holy name cometh of thine hand, and is all thine own." This is an excellent example of humiliation following an increase in dutiful service. David and the people had both offered generously and willingly for the house of God; the Lord had expanded both their hearts and hands. Now, everything they did for God is here attributed to God’s grace and generosity toward them. It is an extraordinary humbling to attribute our increase in God’s service to the increase of God’s grace toward us; the way to have increasing grace is to humbly acknowledge from whence we receive every grace.

<column-break/>

2. Attribute the honor of all the grace of which you have been made a partaker to Jesus Christ.

<margin>1 Cor. 15. 10.</margin>
Thus Paul did on all occasions: "I labored more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me," and "by the grace of God I am what I am." And "I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God."

<margin>Gal. 2, 20.</margin>
<margin>Luke 19. 16.</margin>
It was well done of that good and faithful servant to say, "Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds"; he did not say, "Lord, my pounds," but "thy pound" has gained. This is when we give God the glory for His grace.

Learn, therefore, to attribute to Christ the beginning, the progressing, and the completed work of grace in your souls:

<margin>Phil. 1. 6.</margin>
Jesus Christ, who has begun a good work in you, shall perform it until His own day. Jesus Christ is the Author and the Finisher of our faith.

<margin>Hebr. 12. 2. Rev. 8. 1 Pet. 5. 10.</margin>
He is the Alpha and the Omega. And therefore the Apostle prays: "The God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you." Grace is more like the Manna that comes from Heaven than like the grain that grows out of the earth. Grace is given from Heaven. Gifts and talents are obtained through diligence and effort here on earth. What God says by way of comparison between Canaan and Egypt is very fit to apply to this proposition.

<margin>Deut. 11. 10, 12, 13.</margin>
For thus speaks the Lord to Israel: "The land, whither thou goest in to possess it, is not as the land of Egypt, from whence ye came out, where thou sowedst thy seed, and wateredst it with thy foot, as a garden of herbs <note>Referring to the manual labor of irrigation pumps or channels.</note>: But the land, whither ye go to possess it, is a land of hills and valleys, and drinketh water of the rain of heaven: A land which the Lord thy God careth for." So it is with grace and nature; nature can be, and is, obtained through diligence and effort, and is like Egypt, which can be maintained by irrigation—that is, with dug trenches and ditches, involving the labor of irrigation to let in the streams of the Nile when it annually overflows its banks:

<margin>Amos 4. 7.</margin>
but grace is like the rain from Heaven, which falls only where God sends it, which He causes to rain upon one city and not upon another; one piece of land is rained upon, but the other piece of land where it does not rain withers away.

3. Forsake all merit and even self-sufficiency; for as much as we add to our own merit, so much we subtract from the free grace and mercy of God.

<margin>Hos. 14. 9.</margin>
If God has increased His grace toward you, as with Ephraim, so that you are like a growing fig tree, nevertheless let God have the glory for all your fruitfulness, and let Him say, "your fruit is found in me."

<margin>Rom. 11. 18.</margin>
Oh, consider that you do not bear the root, but the root bears you. Say, "not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name we give the glory." A graced heart knows its own inability, its own insufficiency and imperfection—that it is not powerful enough to master the smallest sin, or to exercise the weakest grace, or to fulfill the lightest duty. And just as we have cause to confess our powerlessness, so also our sinful imperfections.

# Christ the Cause and the

**Column 1**

<margin>Heb. 1. 22. <note>The source text cites Hebrews 1:22, though Hebrews 1 only has 14 verses; this likely refers to Hebrews 12:2, which discusses looking to Jesus as the author and finisher of faith.</note></margin>
Today, if God were to enter into judgment with us, he might damn us, not only for our worst sins, but even for our best and most dutiful services.

<margin>Defining the young. <note>original Latin: "Aphorizontes l. 6. iuventes."</note></margin>
4. Keep an eye on Jesus Christ; look to him as the source and finisher of our faith. The phrase "looking to," in the original language, signifies such a looking up that we look away from those things which hinder our view of Jesus. Labor (my beloved) to look continually upon Christ as the source of grace, especially when you experience the greatest exercise, growth, or comfort of your grace. Speak when you have the greatest power of grace, <margin>2 Chron. 12. <note>The author likely intends 2 Chronicles 20:12, where Jehoshaphat prays during a crisis.</note></margin> as Jehoshaphat did when he had that great army of men, up to 500,000: *Lord, we do not know what we shall do, but our eyes are upon you.* There are three things which we must aim for in Christ’s giving of grace to us:

I. How willingly and freely Jesus Christ deals out his grace to his people; never did a mother give milk more willingly to her child—when her breast is full of juice and seems ready to burst from fullness—than Jesus Christ pours out grace upon his people. Christ does not sell his grace like a merchant, but like a King he liberally deals out everything: see the contents of the covenant of grace, <margin>Isa. 55. 1.</margin> how liberal it is: *O, all you thirsty ones, come to the waters, and you who have no money, come,* <margin>Rev. 22. 17.</margin> *buy and eat<gloss>en</gloss>, yes come, buy without money and without price, wine and milk. Let him who is thirsty come, and let him who desires take the water of life for free;* nothing is as free as grace: it is offered and distributed in the freest manner one could imagine. All that Christ <margin>Prov. 8. 31.</margin> desires is simply that we shall receive it. It is the joy of Christ to show mercy and to distribute grace over his people <margin>John 4. 34.</margin>. It is the food of Christ to do the will of God who sent him, and that is to finish his work. No man was ever more willing to eat his food when he is hungry than Jesus Christ was to do good and to pour out grace upon those who lack it. So it is also said of Christ <margin>Ps. 72. 8.</margin> in the 72nd Psalm (which is clearly a prophecy of Jesus Christ), that he would descend like rain upon the mown grass, like the droplets that moisten the earth. Now there is nothing that comes more sweetly or liberally than rain upon a dry and thirsty ground.

II. Secondly, look upon Jesus as the Author of grace, and how irresistibly he communicates his <margin>Isa. 41.</margin> grace. *I will work, and who shall turn it back?* This is true not only of God’s outward deliverances, but it is also true of God’s grace working in the hearts of his people. Who shall turn it back?

1. Satan shall not; for although he is a strong man, and armed, and has gained possession, nevertheless when Christ comes, he is <term>ischyroteros</term> <note>original Greek: "stronger"</note>, <term>h. e. fortior</term> <note>original Latin: "that is, stronger"</note>, stronger than Satan.

2. Sin shall not be powerful enough to hinder God’s work of grace. Grace shall be too hard for the most powerful opposition made against it. It is true, a man can resist and does resist the grace of God with a struggling and contradicting resistance, but not a conquering resistance.

3. Be exhorted to take your refuge in Jesus Christ for the covering of grace. Go to Jesus, and approach the throne of grace through the prayer of faith, and beg for grace, so that you may be helped by it in time of need. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Christ as the source of grace, shifting from his role as the "author" or beginner of faith to being the "finisher" or perfecter. The author provides a series of "warnings" or practical exhortations on how to properly relate to divine grace, emphasizing the necessity of spiritual union with Christ and the danger of spiritual envy.</meta>

# Finisher of our Grace.

<margin>1 Cor. 15:11.</margin>
...not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me. See how he joins God's grace and his own diligence together. You must, therefore, strive for grace as if it were to be obtained through labor, and not shown through favor; yet when you have done all you can, you must acknowledge grace to be present, as if you had not labored at all.

<margin>2. Warning.</margin>
2. Although there is an abundance of grace in Christ, nevertheless let all those who have no part in Christ take heed how they flatter themselves with a self-conceit that they shall receive grace from Christ. A right or share in the person gives a share in his grace. Just as it was in Christ’s person: he could not have had these excellencies and attributes which were in God, had not the two natures, Human and Divine, been united in him. And therefore it is 
<margin>Col. 2:9.</margin>
said, by virtue of the Personal union, that in him—that is, in his Person—all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. So, secondly, unless there is that holy, hidden union between Christ and us, we cannot be partakers, nor become strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. Union is the ground of 
<margin>John 1:12, 16.</margin>
communion; and therefore we read first of the receiving of Christ, and after that of receiving from his fullness grace for grace. Although you are near to Christ through your profession <note>The author distinguishes between "profession" (outwardly calling oneself a Christian) and "faith" (inward spiritual union).</note>, nonetheless, if you are not one with Christ through faith, you can receive no power from him. If a person applies food to any limb of his body, it will not nourish him because it is not received within, nor digested, distributed, and united with the body; only that which becomes one and the same substance with us provides nourishment. So we receive power and the growth of grace from Christ when we are united with him through faith. Take a branch and tie it to a tree; it will bring forth no fruit. But let that same branch be united with the tree through grafting; then the graft becomes fruitful. So, apart from Christ [or, 
<margin>John 15:5. Rom. 6:5. John 15:6.</margin>
as it stands in the original language] separated from Christ, you can do nothing. He who through faith has not become one plant in the likeness of Christ’s death shall never receive spiritual nourishment from him. He who does not abide in Christ is cast out like a branch; he was never a true branch, he only appeared to be one. Christ is a fountain of grace, yet it is faith that draws from this fountain. Christ is a treasure of grace, yet it is faith that unlocks this treasure. Through our communion with Christ, we receive grace for grace. We are made like Christ through love, meekness, and patience; but through faith, we are made one with Christ; and that union is the cause of communion. Therefore, graceless persons are Christ-less persons.

<margin>3. Warning.</margin>
3. If people lack grace, let them nonetheless know that the fault must be laid not upon Christ, but upon themselves. There is fullness in Christ; there is grace enough in Christ; in him is a fullness of divine sufficiency, of activity, and 

<column-break/>

of overflowing. But if a vessel be plugged up, even if you throw it into the sea, it will still receive no water; the fault is only in the vessel which is plugged, for there is no lack of water in the sea. Concerning those who receive river water or piped water in their houses: if no water comes, you must not conclude that there is no water in the river or fountain, but rather that the pipes are either clogged or broken. So it goes: if you are ever constrained <note>original: "benauwt," meaning restricted, distressed, or narrow; here referring to spiritual dryness.</note>, you are constrained in your own heart <note>original: "eygen ingewanden," literally "own bowels," a common 17th-century idiom for the seat of emotions and the inner soul.</note>, and not constrained in your God. If a house is dark, it is not because of any lack of light in the Sun, but because of the lack of windows in the house. So also, if you lack grace, it is not because of any lack of grace in Christ, but because of the lack of faith in your soul to draw and derive more grace from Christ.

<margin>4. Warning. Mat. 20:17. <note>likely referring to the parable of the laborers in the vineyard, Matt 20:1-16.</note></margin>
4. And do not envy the grace of God in others. Although Christ might show greater grace in others than in you, nonetheless your eye must not be evil because he is good. You must not have an envious eye because Christ has a generous hand. It is not only a fault in godless people to envy the grace that is in godly people—as Cain was envious of Abel because Abel’s offering was accepted and his own rejected—but godly people also easily come to envy one another. Joseph’s brothers 
<margin>John 21:20, 21.</margin>
envied their brother because he was loved by his Father; and Peter (it is recounted) envied John, the beloved disciple. But guard yourself against hatred and envy; it is a dishonor to God, and it often hinders us from receiving mercy and grace from God. To be envious over Christ’s distribution of his grace—to whom and in what measure it pleases him—is unbecoming for a Christian. Rather, to rejoice in another's blessedness is to act like the Angels of Heaven; to envy another’s good is like the Devils in hell. Will a Father take it well if his children rise up against each other over their inheritance which their Father has given to them? God is absolutely free to give one, or two, or five talents, just as it pleases him; and if another has more grace than you, nonetheless be thankful for the grace you have, and envy no one.

<margin>5. Warning.</margin>
5. Lastly, do not diminish the grace you have received. Just as no sin is small because it is an offense against the great God, so is no grace small because it comes from that great God. Ingratitude hinders this oil <note>A metaphor for grace, referencing the oil of anointing or the oil in the lamps of the wise virgins.</note> from flowing. Just as a person must not be content with even the greatest measure of grace, so he must not be ungrateful 
<margin>Ps. 138:3, 8.</margin>
for the smallest measures of grace. Take note: it is Jesus Christ who has begun the work of grace. That any small good is worked in you is the work of Christ; and he who has begun a good work will likewise finish it. He who has given grace a being in your soul will also strengthen you with power in your soul, and will finish it for you. And do not quench the wick that begins to smoke in you, nor break the reed that is bruised; but be thankful to Christ 
<margin>Mat. 12:20.</margin>
who has lit this smoking wick, and wait upon him, who shall so accomplish his work that he shall bring forth judgment unto victory.

->Funeral Sermon, being the 5th<-

### Job 30:23.

> For I know that you will bring me to death, and to the house of meeting for all the living.

<margin>A Funeral Sermon preached by Mr. Love <note>Christopher Love (1618–1651) was a prominent Presbyterian minister in London. This sermon is particularly poignant as it was his last; he was executed for treason under Oliver Cromwell's government shortly after this date.</note> over the body of Mistress B. at St. Lawrence Jewry in London, on April 29, 1651. Being the last sermon that he ever preached. verse 18.</margin>

In the handling of these words, it is necessary that I first prepare these two things:

1. To give you the objective.
2. The meaning of the words.

For the first: the objective of the words. They are introduced with a causal conjunction: **For**, which refers back to what precedes it. And so that you might distinctly notice that reference, you must look back at the 18th verse of this chapter, where Job tells you of a great sickness under which he labored: *by the great force of my disease is my garment changed: it binds me about as the collar of my coat.* It seems the sickness was so strong upon him that it constricted his breath; it was like a collar around his neck. Because of the feeling of his sickness, he breaks out into this holy reflection: **for I know that you will bring me to death, and to the house of meeting for all the living.** Now, take this observation from the objective and the context: that illness and sickness must be reminders to us regarding our dying. The sick must always think to themselves that they are dying people; and those who die daily need not fear a sudden death.

<margin>He signifies not only a known thing, but something he is persuaded of as if by a peculiar experience. <note>original: "Non solum rem notam sed quasi peculiari experientia sibi persuasam significat pinedo da Experior Junius"</note></margin>

As I come to the meaning of the words, **I know**. This must not be understood as a notional or speculative knowledge, which signifies a bare and naked science of a general truth; but such a kind of knowledge that is practical and proven. And so Junius <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a famous Huguenot theologian known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> also translates it. This searching knowledge worked in Job holy preparations for death. **I know**, and through experience I can say, I have such a kind of knowledge that contains practice and experience within itself. (**That you will bring me to death**) this proves the holiness of Job against the teachings of the Philosophers, who believe that all such events happen by luck and fortune, and not by the determined decree and counsel of the Most High. (**And to the house of meeting for all the living.**) Although he does not say here where this house is, he nonetheless does so in Job 17:13: *If I wait, the grave shall be my house: I shall spread my bed in the darkness.* Now, that which was his house must be the house of all the living, that is, the grave. Now, the grave is compared to a house for two reasons: 1. Alluding to the Egyptian burial places, which were made like a house with various triumphal arches. 2. Because we dwell therein in silence.

<margin>Job 17:13.</margin>

Thus you have the words briefly explained to you. Now I shall give you some practical expansions of the same: **for I know that you will bring me to death.** These words, being the lovely speech of Job concerning his own mortality, contain three particular parts:

1. The **reasonableness** of this saying. He introduces it with a conjunction, **For**.

<column-break/>

2. The **particularity** of the same. He draws a specific reflection of death upon "me."
3. The **piety** of the same; he acknowledges God's hand in bringing him to death. **You**, and not chance or luck.

For the first: the reasonableness of it. The godly Job does not speak of his death without cause, but because of the preceding foundation and reason: *by the great force of my sickness is my garment changed, it binds me like the collar of my coat;* and then he breaks out into this holy reflection: **for I know that you will bring me to death.** From this, notice:

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>

**That it is a very reasonable thing, in weakness, to have holy reflections regarding death.**

Job lay in a sickness which was prepared to stifle and distress him, and so he breaks out into this holy meditation: **for I know that you will bring me to death, etc.** It is remarkable, and the Ancients <note>Referring to early Church Fathers or biblical commentators.</note> observe it, that David composed Psalms when he lay on his sickbed: Psalm 6, Psalm 30, Psalm 39; and in all these Psalms are divine elevations and holy reflections regarding death. Job 17:1: *my spirit (or breath) is corrupt, my days are extinguished, the graves are ready for me.* He does not merely take a bad smell from his breath, but it was a blockage and gasping of his breath—that is, he was short of breath and distressed under a powerful sickness. It is understood that Job had that sickness which is called <term>shortness of breath</term> <note>original: "aemborstigheydt" – likely referring to asthma or a similar respiratory distress.</note>, and the observation of this sickness made him think that the grave was ready for him. So Heman, who lay in a violent sickness; Psalm 88:4-6: *For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to the grave. I am counted with those who go down into the pit: I am like a man who has no strength; set apart among the dead, like the slain who lie in the grave, whom you remember no more; and they are cut off from your hand.*

<margin>Psalm 88. Jeremiah 9.</margin>

When sickness is in the room, then death is at the window. Sicknesses are but the messengers, the <term>harbingers</term> <note>original: "fourieren" – military officers who went ahead of an army to secure lodgings; here used as a metaphor for symptoms preceding death.</note>, and forerunners of death; remember the Prophet's manner of speaking: *death has climbed into our windows.* When sicknesses are in the house, then death is on the threshold. So Job reckons: *when I lie down to sleep, then I say: when shall I arise, and the night be gone? I am full of tossings to and fro, until the dawning of the day;* and then he says, *my flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken and become loathsome.*

<margin>Job 7. 1st Use.</margin>

The first use is to condemn those who, when they lie on their sickbed, hope for life but never think on death. Their own guilt and their own wickedness of life so overwhelms them with fear and terror that the thoughts of death are troublesome and grievous to them. Just like Louis XI, King of France <note>Reigned 1461–1483; he was famously terrified of his own mortality.</note>, who, when he lay ill of a dangerous sickness, commanded his servants and ministers that they must not speak of death in his hearing. The bodies of many people are storehouses and hospitals of sicknesses, yet while they live, they never think on death, although there is but little between them and the grave.

<margin>2nd Use.</margin>

The second use is to those...

<meta>This page continues the funeral sermon of Christopher Love, moving from the physical sensation of illness to the spiritual application of mortality. Love transitions from the general fact that all men die to the personal necessity of "laying it to heart."</meta>

->The Last of Mr. Love<-

those who are healthy and strong; it is true that strengths are the nearest harbingers and precursors of death in a common way; nevertheless, you may soon die, even if you do not yet have any sickness in you. Just as the fruits of a tree perish more from uncommon winds and tempests than by remaining on the tree, so strong illnesses may quickly kill you even while there is still marrow in your bones and strength in your limbs. Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, an experienced master of medicine, boasted that if someone followed fine medical writings, he would not die by any violent death, but purely by old age; and yet that boasting man died of a fever before he was forty years old. Thus I have dealt with the first observation, namely the reasonableness of this: I am under a heavy sickness, and therefore I think of death.

Secondly, the **Particularity** of Job's reasoning must be noted. Job does not stand upon that general conclusion, *there is no man who lives, who shall not see death*, Psalm 89:48. He does not speak so generally; but *I know I must die*. Note from this point:

**That general conclusions regarding death must be impressed upon the soul through particular application.** Beloved, we must not only have general observations and mere speculation concerning death, but practiced and particular conclusions regarding our own death, such as those that can lay a sting upon the conscience.

<margin>Job 5:26, 27.</margin>
Thus in the case of the pious, says Eliphaz, *you shall come to your grave in full age, like as a shock of corn comes in in his season*; and then he adds in verse 27: *Lo this, we have searched it, so it is; hear it, and know it for your own good.* <note>original: "bemerckt ghy het voor u" — literally 'notice it for yourself'.</note> The general conclusions that all must die must be impressed upon the soul with particular application, to pull you away from the world, and to bring into you earnest thoughts regarding your future and eternal welfare. General truths do not bring that power upon the conscience unless they are brought to it through an appropriating perspective (and therefore in Psalm 73:28, the Psalmist says not only *it is good to be near God*, but *it is good for me*).

The third particular part is the **Godliness** of Job's reasoning in these words: *you will bring me to death.* Now, in this same phrase are three particular points which reveal Jesus's faith and godliness.

1. He does not attribute dying to luck and fortune, but to the providence of the Almighty. From this, note:

<margin>3rd Doctrine.</margin>
**That it is the characteristic of the godly to see God's hand in the taking away of men through death.** It was but a doting of the philosophers who did not know God to attribute occurrences to blind fortune; and it was the numbness of the Chaldeans to see the deity over the head in all fixed events; yet Job longs to see and to surrender himself to death, and to God's hand to bring death upon him. *You shall bring me to death.* Another notable thing is this: *I know that you will bring me to death.* It is not a speculative and bare knowledge of the understanding, but such a kind of knowledge that is observant and active, which works upon the affections. Note from this:

<column-break/>

<margin>4th Doctrine.</margin>
**Although all men know intellectually that they must die, yet only godly men know it actively and with observation.** To be able to know your dying according to practice, consider beforehand: how shall I emerge from the womb into the eternal depths? What shall become of me in another world when I leave this one? Is my peace made with God? Am I in the state of grace? Now Job's words have an intensity in them: *I know you will bring me to death*, that is, I know it so that I want to provide for it, and I want to prepare myself for it, and I will lay a foundation for eternal life. Solomon, speaking of the state of burial, says: *it is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting; that is the end of all men, and the living will lay it to his heart.*

<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:2.</margin>
Indeed, but all men who do not lay death to heart might perhaps speak together of death at a funeral, but the living shall lay it to the heart, or *upon* the heart, as the Hebrew text has it; *they shall lay it to the heart*, or *in, upon and their hearts*, so says Tremellius <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a prominent Jewish-Italian convert and Hebraist whose Latin translation of the Bible was highly regarded by Protestants.</note>. A wicked man has it well on his tongue, but a pious man lays this truth upon his heart. There is no one but a pious man who knows anything of dying in such a way as to know it in deed, with emotion, affection, and observation: and so as to do these three things.

<margin>"He shall give it to his heart," AR <note>Likely referring to the Aramaic/Hebrew phrasing.</note>; "to his soul," Tremellius.</margin>
1. No one other than a godly person observes in his dying that he dies according to what he deserves; he tastes the bitterness and feels the weight of sin in his sicknesses; and in the feeling of approaching death, he notices in himself that it is not the sickness that will bring him to his grave, but the sins of his life that kill him.

2. No one knows that he must die like a godly person, whose care it is to die having been prepared for it beforehand. A pious person knows he must die, and this knowledge causes him to prepare himself beforehand for the time of death, and to live every day as if it were his last day. The Prophet spoke of death in the first part of the 90th Psalm, that the days of a man are seventy years or eighty. See what follows: *so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom* [Psalm 90:12]. He understands by the numbering of our days to live as carefully as if one were to finish the number of our days, few as they are; every day as if it were the last day. And this time as the time of Christ's coming to judgment.

<margin>Psalm 90:10, 12.</margin>
3. No one but a godly person knows of his dying so as to observe that there is a necessity that sin must die in him before his body dies. Seneca, a philosopher, could say: *let your faults die before you.* There must not only be a ceasing, but a killing of sin. A godly person observes, even if each lives without reproach so that men cannot say "my eye is black" <note>An old Dutch idiom meaning someone has a "black mark" or flaw in their reputation.</note> regarding any outward practice; nevertheless, I must have my internal lusts and numbnesses killed before my physical death, and therefore those people ought to be busy with the things which tend to the killing of sin: this is to know death observantly and with emotion. On the other hand:

<margin>original: "Moriantur ante te vitia" — Latin: Let your vices die before you. Seneca.</margin>

the godless people clearly observe death; their understanding tells them that everything must die; they say all people, young and old, rich and poor must die, but this is only a matter of conversation among them, whereas the pious know it with a savory knowledge <note>original: "smaeckelijcke kennisse." This refers to a "tasting" or experiential knowledge—knowing something in the heart rather than just as a dry, intellectual fact.</note>.

Thirdly, Job’s godliness lay in this, that he presented death to himself, not in a fearful and mournful manner, but under a comforting representation; for *I know that you will bring me to death; and to the house*, etc. <note>Referencing Job 30:23: "For I know that thou wilt bring me to death, and to the house appointed for all living."</note> He represents the grave under the significance of a house, just as he also represents it elsewhere. Note this point here.

<margin>1. Doctrine.</margin> That a child of God, who has a blameless conscience before God, can and should represent death to themselves in such friendly images as can make it less terrifying and more desirable. <margin>Isaiah 57:2.</margin> Sometimes it is presented as going to bed / *they shall rest in their sleeping-places*. A godly person, when he lies on his death-bed and is weary of his life through sickness, turning to and fro until daybreak, let him think the grave will only be a resting-bed for him; so death is often reckoned as a sleep. <margin>Daniel 12:4. <note>The text cites Daniel 12:4, but the quote "those who sleep in the dust" is from Daniel 12:2.</note></margin> *And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, and others to shame (and) to eternal contempt*; death is adorned with sweet, comforting names.

<margin>6. Doctrine.</margin> <margin>John 17:13. <note>The text likely intended Job 17:13, as the following quote matches that verse.</note></margin> The grave is the house of all living to dwell in comfortably. *If I wait, the grave shall be my house, in the darkness I shall spread my bed.* The grave is the house I must go to, just as I go to bed in my house after a heavy day's labor in a dark night: so we go to our sleeping-places, as into our graves for a long night; going to bed is only for a short night, but going to the grave is for a long night; death is sometimes presented with terrifying observations, but with loveliness alongside them. There is in nature a dread of death, but it is made lovely through Jesus Christ; he lay three days in the grave to make the grave sweet to you; although your sleeping-places are cloudy and dark, nonetheless you rest in them until the day of the resurrection.

-> To open the doctrine, <-
-> I shall explain these two questions: <-

1. I shall show you why the grave is compared to a house.
2. I shall show you what kind of a house the grave is.

Concerning the first question, why is the grave compared to a house?

<margin>1. Question.</margin> 1. Some authors give this reason: because in ancient times (as has been shown) among the Egyptians, their graves and burial places were made in the manner of houses, with arches and such types of vaulting; therefore they say it is called a house.

2. Other authors give this reason: because just as a man returns after a day's labor and goes to his house to rest, so also a man after a life's labor in the world goes to his grave as to his house to rest.

<column-break/>

kind of a house is the grave? Now I shall give you these four properties of this house.
1. It is a lonely and desolate house.
2. It is a dark house.
3. It is an old house.
4. It is a silent house.
For the first; the grave is:

<margin>Job 3.</margin> 1. A lonely or desolate house. *I shall be*, says Job, *with the kings and the counselors of the earth, who build desolate places for themselves* <note>Job 3:14</note>, that is, they build tombs and monuments where they would lie, and then they shall leave all their retinue. <margin>Ezekiel 26.</margin> *When I shall make you go down with those who descend into the pit to the people of old and shall make you lie down in the lower parts of the earth in the desolate places that have been of old, with those who descend into the pit, so that you are not inhabited.* Job 17:14. *I have said to the pit, you are my Father, and to the worm, you are my Mother and my Sister*: there is all the company you shall have: the grave and the worms; friends bring you to the grave, and there they leave you.

<margin>Job 17:13.</margin> 2. Your grave is a dark house / *I have spread my bed in the darkness*, that is, in the grave. The grave is like a sleeping-place in a house, not like a place for feasting or a workshop. The place of feasting must be bright, and so also a workshop; but the sleeping-place is dark. It is only the closing of the mouth of the grave, and it is only the drawing of the curtains of the bed where you shall lie in darkness until the day of the resurrection: In the grave there is neither the light of the body, which is the eye; nor the light of the air, which is the sun: the sun shall not shine there, nor the body see there; therefore Ecclesiastes 11:9. *Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart, and in the sight of your eyes; but know, that God for all these things will bring you into judgment.* And in verse 8 he had said, *remember the days of darkness: for they shall be many.* The meaning is this: the duration in the grave, which is the house of darkness, shall be long, namely until the end of the world.

<margin>Romans 5:12.</margin> 3. The grave is an old house, as old as Adam; he made his grave with his own hands; therefore *just as through one man sin came into the world, and death through sin, and so death passed to all men in whom (or because) all have sinned.* The grave is a lasting house; a house where you must stay a long time. Ecclesiastes 12:5. *Also when they shall be afraid of heights, and there shall be terrors in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goes to his eternal house and the mourners go about the streets.* It is a long-lasting house, like a house of eternity; a long while until Christ’s coming for judgment; our long-lasting house in contrast to our present houses, which are our short-lasting houses: your houses are short-lasting houses, but the graves are your long-lasting houses.

<margin>Psalm 31:17.</margin> 4. The grave is a silent, quiet house. *Let me not be ashamed O Lord, for I have called upon you; let the wicked be ashamed, let them be silent in the grave.* The Psalmist prays here for the deliverance from

### Concerning the benefits or uses of this point.

The first use is a use of comfort to the pious / they can be comforted by this doctrine. This doctrine is a doctrine that is terrifying for godless people / their graves are to them dark prisons or dungeons / but to God's children, the grave is a house. Now you can be comforted by these four considerations.

<margin>Job 3:13, 17.</margin> 1. That although the grave is a house / nevertheless be comforted / it is a house of rest, Job 3:17. *There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary be at rest.* He speaks here of the grave / verse 13. *For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest.* There is no work to be done in this house / Eccl. 9:10. *Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.* Isaiah 57:2. *They shall rest in their beds* <note>original: "slaep-steden," literally "sleep-places."</note>.

2. That although the grave is a house / nevertheless be comforted / it is only a house of sleep / it is not a house where you shall be eternally. Beloved / although it is a house / nonetheless it is only a house of sleep / it shall not keep your bodies forever; that is the meaning of Paul's rejoicing: *O death, where is your sting?*
<margin>1 Cor. 15:55.</margin> *O grave, where is your victory?* He brings it to the resurrection; though the grave surrounds us / nevertheless it shall not overcome us.

3. Although the grave is a house / nevertheless be comforted / it is only a house of hiding / such a house that is a place of refuge for God's people. Job 14:13. *O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me!* The times can be so difficult / that there can be more safety under the earth than above the earth; those who have lain in their graves for a long time / would be happier than many
<margin>Eccles. 4:2. <note>The original text mistakenly cites "Eccles. 26. 6." but the context refers to Ecclesiastes 4:2: "Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive."</note></margin> who live / Isaiah 26:20. *Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.* Although some
<margin>Isa. 57:1.</margin> interpret this as a temporal deliverance / nevertheless others interpret it as the grave / where God shelters His children / when He takes them away from the evil to come.

4. Although the grave is a house / nevertheless be comforted / it is a fragrant house / a house made lovely and sweet-smelling by Christ's lying in the grave. All the acts that Christ did / they were for our sake. Christ died to save us through dying. Christ was buried in the grave / to make the grave into a resting place / He rose again from death / to sanctify our resurrection; and He has thereby, through His presence, made this resting place / this house, and the grave fragrant.

### The second Use is for instruction.

<column-break/>

1. Here is matter for reflection; when you are in your own houses / consider yourselves thus / "now I am here walking in my house / from room to room / but before long my room shall be in the courtyard" <note>This refers to the churchyard or burial ground.</note>. "Now I go to my resting place in a dark night / but before long God shall blow out the candle of my life / and shall lay me in the grave / as in a resting place of darkness. Now I am in my own house, but before long my house shall cast me out to my grave; and that is the house that shall take me in."

2. Let it break in you all greed and uncommon desires; you shall come from lying in the dark house of the womb to lying in the dark house of the grave. Oh, what a vast company of uncommon and gluttonous desires there are in the hearts of men. In the mother's body, a small space <note>original: "eene vocht," likely referring to the limited fluid-filled space of the womb.</note> shall suffice you / and in the cradle, three feet shall satisfy you / and in the grave, six feet; but while you live in the world / a whole world shall not satisfy you: there is such uncommon and gluttonous desire in the hearts of men / even when they have all the influx and convergence of the comforts of the creatures / now they must have their variety of houses / a country house / a summer house / a winter house / yet you must exchange your many houses for one house. The passage that you read in the Scripture / 1 Sam. 10:2: is most worthy of notice; when Samuel had anointed Saul as King / and the people had chosen him / what sign does he give him to confirm his anointing? It was to go to Rachel’s sepulcher / now the reason is this / so that he might not be overloaded with the advancement and honors / into which he was entering. The Emperors of Constantinople, in their inaugurations / on their coronation days / had a Mason / who came to them / and showed them various marble stones / and asked them to choose which of these should be made ready for their gravestones. And so we read of Joseph of Arimathea, that he had his sepulcher in his garden / to mock the pleasurability of the place <note>A reminder of death amidst a place of leisure.</note>. Now you have excess and abundance in your house. I can go to a variety of houses / but on one day you shall leave all your houses and go to one house / and there leave all your company and your friends.
<margin>Choose from these stones, Caesar, from which you would wish me to build a tomb for you, even in your lowest state. <note>Original Latin: "Eligebas his saxis, ex qui in vilissimo Caesar ipse tibi tumulum me fabricare velis."</note></margin>

But how can this be true, when the Scripture says, John 8:51. *Verily, verily, I say unto you, If a man keep my saying, he shall never see death.*
<margin>1st Objection.</margin>

To this I answer / that the Scripture does not mean there a natural and physical death / but a spiritual eternal death; and it is said / John 11:25, 26. *I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die* / that is / although he dies naturally, nevertheless he shall live eternally.
<margin>Resolution.</margin>

But you will say, Enoch was not buried, and Elijah was taken up in a chariot.
<margin>2nd Objection.</margin>

Particular examples do not nullify general rules; although they were not laid in their graves / nevertheless they underwent something equivalent to death. There was a special reason why God translated Enoch and Elijah / because they had to be examples of Christ's resurrection / and guarantees of our own.
<margin>Resolution.</margin>

2. Finally / we are bound to this decree of death / although God is not bound to it / **Romans 5:14** and **Hebrews 9:27**. ## Alongside this follow several Petitions from Mrs. LOVE, presented to Parliament regarding her Husband: as well as several Letters.

### To the Supreme Power, the Parliament of the Republic of England, the Humble Petition of Mary, the Grieving Wife of Christopher Love.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'S' <note>The Dutch original uses a 'V' for "Vertoont," but the English translation uses 'S' for "Shews."</note> featuring scrolling floral motifs and a bird perched within the vines.</image-desc>

S hews with all Respect:

That whereas the High Court of Justice a few days ago sentenced her dear and beloved Husband to death, in whose life the life of your Petitioner is bound up; in the execution of which sentence, your Poor Handmaid shall become a Wretched Widow, a miserable Mother of two young Fatherless Children, and also since the appointed time of her Childbirth is near, that she may not have sorrow upon sorrow, and be forced by unspeakable grief to bow down in labor and give up the Ghost, [and so with one blow lose both Father and Mother and Child in one day:] therefore she prays Your Honors to have mercy upon her.

And herewith the Soul of Your Honor’s Handmaid is not a little refreshed, thinking that there is hope in Israel concerning these matters, considering that her humble petition is presented this day; especially to those who make profession of Godliness, and who have abundantly tasted how gracious the Lord is, and who by God’s grace are called by God to possess a blessing and to be a blessing to the oppressed in the midst of the Land.

Therefore your humble Servant casts herself down in all humility at your feet; and

<column-break/>

prays, and beseeches you by the womb that bore you, the breasts that you sucked, by the bowels <note>In the 17th century, the word "bowels" (Dutch: "in-gewanden") was used to describe the seat of deep compassion, pity, or mercy.</note> of the Lord J. C. <note>Jesus Christ</note> that you would graciously intervene, so that this fatal and deadly blow may be prevented; which act of compassion in you shall be to your Handmaid like a resurrection from the dead, and not only shall all compassionate mothers in England, but also the unborn child rise up and call you blessed. And this shall be to you a praise and glory, and a Crown of joy for the Nation, when the blessing of him who is ready to perish shall descend upon you; And your humble Servant notes in all humility that your Compassion in this matter can bring no harm to the state, as the Friends of Your Honor’s poor Petitioner are fully ready to give all sufficient security and assurance that her Husband shall live quietly and peaceably for the future and shall never attempt anything to the detriment of this Republic and the present Government: now may the God of Heaven bow your hearts to show mercy: and your petitioner shall pray, etc.

->MARY LOVE.<-

### Another Petition.

S hews with all respect:

That whereas / Your Honor’s distressed Servant / has in all humility / in the extreme bitterness of her heart poured out her Soul / to this most serious / Honorable house / for the life of her Husband / condemned to die; which petition / as it was favorably accepted by Your Honors / so Your Honor's petitioner understands / it has been read in Parliament for which great favor / she thanks God and Your Honors. And although she has great reason / to be sensitive / of Your Honor’s displeasure against her Husband / which grieves her from the heart; yet / her trust is / that your bowels as well as hers / shall be moved in this her sorrowful state / and therefore / she resolves once more / to speak her humble supplication before Your Honors / and prays:

That if / the Husband of Your Honor's Petitioner / has so far kindled Your Honor's wrath; that he has thereby made himself Incapable / of obtaining a complete pardon; that nevertheless Your Honor’s Servant / may find so much grace in Your Honor's eyes / that you would graciously / say of Your Honor’s Petitioner’s dear Husband as Solomon once said of Abiathar: *although you are worthy of death: yet you shall not be killed at this time.* <note>1 Kings 2:26</note>

<column-break/>

Oh forgive / Your Honor’s anxious Servant / if she again beseeches and prays you / by the womb that bore you: by the breasts that sucked you: in the bowels of our Lord J. C. that you would please to postpone this sentence for a time; so that she may gather her strength / before he goes from here and shall be seen no more: so that / by a sudden blow in his execution she / her life / and the life of the tender child in her womb / might not be cut off / and poor innocent Fatherless Children be left to begin and end their days in sorrow and misery. And although he may not be deemed worthy / to draw his breath in the English air

## Another Petition.

**S**hows, etc. <note>The abbreviation "&c." here likely refers to the standard formal opening of a legal petition: "To the Honorable Parliament of the Commonwealth of England, the humble petition of Mary Love, shows..."</note>

That your poor Petitioner has great reason to say: blessed be God and blessed be Your Honors because of your favorable Act and resolution of July 15 (a day never to be forgotten), extending the life of her dear husband for one month longer; which has opened a door for her in the Valley of Achor <note>The "Valley of Achor" is a biblical reference from Hosea 2:15, symbolizing a place of trouble that becomes a "door of hope."</note>, and has gladdened and rejoiced her, although she is a woman of a sorrowful spirit;

Nevertheless, your distressed handmaid is overwhelmed with grief and anxiety of soul, and refuses to be comforted when she recalls that sorrowful day, the 15th of August, so close at hand; her soul almost dies within her, and she is like one giving up the ghost before she is delivered of the fruit of her womb. <note>Mary Love was heavily pregnant during her husband's trial and execution; she used her pregnancy as a primary argument for mercy, fearing the shock of his death would kill both her and the unborn child.</note>

Therefore, your exceedingly sorrowful handmaid again pours out her soul before you with redoubled and earnest prayers. Begging and pleading with Your Honors that you would yet take pity on her lamentable state and condition, and put on the bowels of commiseration <term>bowels of commiseration</term><note>A common 17th-century idiom based on the biblical idea that the seat of pity and deep emotion was in the internal organs.</note> and compassion toward her dear husband, condemned to death, so that she may not have to struggle with the overwhelming pains of childbirth and the unbearable thoughts of the death of her husband on the same day!

Oh! that the life of your handmaid and the life of the unborn lamb might be a ransom for the life of her condemned husband: she would much rather wish to die for him to show her affection for him, than [to die] with him out of the abundance of her sorrow.

Now may the good God incline your hearts to grant him his life as a prize <note>original: "tot een roof." This refers to Jeremiah 39:18, meaning to escape with one's life as the only thing saved from a disaster.</note>, and to banish him wherever it should please Your Honors; and your Petitioner shall ever pray, etc.

## Another Petition.

**S**hows with all humility.

That your distressed and sorrowful Petitioner, in the multitude of her anxieties and fears wherewith her soul is overwhelmed, has now made several addresses to Your Honors, and has received the sorrowful refusal of her desires, which has been heavier to her than death itself: Nevertheless, she cannot cease following Your Honors with strong cries and prayers, like the importunate Canaanite woman <note>A reference to Matthew 15, where a woman continues to beg Jesus for help despite initial refusals.</note> following the Lord Christ:

<column-break/>

and oh! that you would now at last allow yourselves to be moved by prayer, and let your innermost depths be stirred within you; so that the root and the branch might not be felled to the earth in one day. The great God hears the cry and shriek of the ravens; oh, that God would open your hearts to hear the strong cries, the heart-breaking sighs of the mother with her tender infants, who cannot keep silent as long as there is still hope!

Your desolate handmaid waits with all humility and earnest expectation (at your door), begging and pleading with Your Honors that you would not forget to show mercy to your poor petitioner and her tender infants; oh! do not make your handmaid a widow and your unborn children fatherless. But graciously prevent this terrible blow, which your petitioner trembles to think of, and she begs you most earnestly that you please change the sentence of death into a sentence of Banishment: and while you are propagating the Gospel in New England, let her dying husband (as a Prophet from the Dead) be sent away to confirm the conversion of the poor Indians <note>Mary suggests that instead of being executed, Christopher Love should be exiled to the American colonies to serve as a missionary to Native Americans.</note>, so that many souls may praise God on your behalf; and she shall receive it from Your Honors as a singular mercy.

And your Petitioner shall pray, etc.

->MARIA LOVE.<-

### Mr. Jaquel’s Letter to Mr. Love.

**M**y dear friend, and beloved in the Lord.

My heart is moved within me: I am in pain, I am in pain, even unto my soul: the Lord knows it; I lack words to express the thoughts of my heart toward you; toward you, I say, right Christian friend and true hero of Jesus Christ: I thought to have kept silent, being ashamed to send you a letter written by the hand which I thought, a few weeks ago, I had firmly set to the plow. But perceive my weakness; permit me to make my heart known to Your Honor in such sorrowful words and language as I can utter; and I pray you, accept them; and see therein my heart toward you: which at this hour is so full that I know not how to pour it out, except day and night in tears for you before the Lord; and oh! that the memory of June 7 and 21 might often come to my mind to keep my heart humble because of my sorrow, having taken counsel with my own fleshly friends and not consulting with those who were truly godly—which (as I now perceive) contributed to bringing forth that sorrowful and never-to-be-forgotten day and sentence of July 5.

Dear Friend; truly! if I could not appeal to God the Lord, who knows all things and what the intention of my heart was—thinking that I would do you more good than harm thereby, well knowing that there was one before me who had wronged you greatly, which made me testify as I did, being instructed that it would be helpful and not harmful to you, being at most but poor information—I say, were it not for the testimony of my conscience, I could not sustain my spirit, but (I fear) would sink under the burden. But
