# The Rest of the Saints

That the best of men are subject to cruel and unnatural deaths. Stephen, who was full of the Holy Spirit, was stoned to death; and John the Baptist, who was full of the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb, was beheaded; Peter was crucified, and so also was Andrew; Isaiah was sawn in two <note>According to Jewish tradition, the prophet Isaiah was martyred by being sawn in half with a wooden saw</note>, Jeremiah was stoned, and Zacharias was slain between the Temple and the Altar. But I shall pass over these.

The second part of the text is the speech which Stephen made as he fell asleep: *hoc dicto obdormivit*, <note>original: "having said this, he fell asleep"</note> that is, when he had ended his prayer, he fell asleep. Learn from this:

That it is an excellent way [of sleeping] to close our lips with prayer. **To die praying is a Christian way of dying.** They stoned Stephen while he was calling upon God. In this manner Christ died; he prayed, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit," and having said this, he gave up the ghost. This he did so that it might be an example to all Christians.

Prayer is a necessary duty at all times, but especially when we die; and that for these three reasons.

1. Because when we die, we have the greatest need of God's help; for then the Devil is most busy when we are at our weakest.

2. Because when we die, we must pray for the greatest good from God; that is, that he would be pleased to receive us into his Heavenly Kingdom. Now prayer is the primary means to obtain this grace, for it is *Porta Coeli, Clavis Paradisi*, <note>original: "The Gate of Heaven, the Key of Paradise"</note> the gate of heaven and a key to let us into Paradise. Therefore we have the highest need to die praying.

3. Because when a godly person dies, he must then take his final leave of prayer. In Heaven there is no prayer, but only thanksgiving; since there is no want in Heaven, there is no prayer in Heaven. Now, as a godly person must take his leave of prayer when he dies, it is fitting that he should die praying.

Oh, I pray you, remember this example in the text; Stephen died calling upon the Lord. Let us die praying, just as that Emperor said, *Oportent Imperatorem stantem mori*: <note>original: "An Emperor ought to die standing," a quote attributed to Vespasian</note> so I may say *Oportent Christianum mori precantem*, it befits a Christian to die praying.

**Question.** But what was the substance of Stephen's prayer?

**Answer.** He prayed for himself, and he prayed for his persecutors.

1. He prayed for himself: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit," verse 59.

2. He prayed for his persecutors: "Lord, do not hold this sin against them," verse 60.

I do not wish to enter into this part of the text, for it would consume all my time. Therefore I shall move on and come to the third part, which [with God's help] I have intended to treat: namely, what Stephen did when he had ended his prayer. When he had said that, he fell asleep—that is, he died.

See here the bravery, the godliness, and the Christian courage of Stephen; the people stoned him and gnashed their teeth at him, yet the good man died with such peace of mind as if he

<column-break/>

had died in his own bed; he fell asleep while they were stoning him. When he died, he prayed; and while he prayed, he died.

**But what made Stephen die so peacefully?** Read the 55th verse, and you shall see the reason for it: he, being full of the Holy Spirit and looking up to Heaven, saw the Glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. See [he says] I see the Heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. This made him die with such a sweet rest and quiet composure; he saw Jesus Christ standing at the right hand of God, ready to receive his soul, and this made him die with such an extraordinary peace of mind.

Death [especially the death of God's children] is often compared in the Scripture to a sleep. It is said of David that he fell asleep with his fathers; and it is said in 1 Thessalonians 4:13, "I do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who have fallen asleep"; that is, regarding those who are dead. And in 1 Corinthians 11:30, "among you many are weak and sick, and many sleep"; that is, many have died. This manner of speaking is an explanation by metaphor, and the same shall give us many rare and precious instructions regarding Death. And therefore [God's grace assisting me] I am desirous to spend the remainder of the time in the explanation of this metaphor or comparison.

**The observation is this, namely:** That when a child of God dies, although his death be ever so unnatural and violent, nonetheless it is nothing other than a sleeping; or, the death of a child of God, though stoned to death, though burned to ashes, though the same be ever so cruel and unnatural, is nothing other than a falling asleep; "when he had said this, he fell asleep."

> *Somnus est mortis imago.* <note>original: "Sleep is the image of death"</note> Sleep is a likeness of death; there are many notable comparisons between sleep and death, and I shall speak of some of them presently.

1. **Sleep is common to all men;** there is no one who can live without sleeping. A man may live a long time without eating, but no one can live long without sleeping. So it is also with death; death is common to all men; it is appointed for all men once to die. And therefore David said he would go the way of all flesh. *Statutum est omnibus semel mori, Omnibus est calcanda semel lethi via*, <note>original: "It is appointed for all once to die; the path of death must be trodden once by all"</note> all men must sleep the sleep of death, or otherwise be changed, which is a death by comparison.

2. **Just as sleep arises from the vapors** which climb from the stomach to the head and entrance the senses and hinder their workings; so death came into the world through Adam's eating of the forbidden fruit, and through the venomous vapor of sin, which brought death upon him and all his descendants. Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and so death passed to all men, for all have sinned, Romans 5:12. Had Adam never sinned, Adam would never have died; but *in illo die*, <note>original: "on that day"</note> God said, "in the day that you eat of the forbidden fruit, you shall die the death." Sin brings *omni modam mortem*, <note>original: "every kind of death"</note> all sorts of death; it brings temporal death, spiritual death, and eternal death. Now because all men are poisoned with the venom...

<meta>This page continues the funeral sermon for Christopher Love, specifically addressing the nature of the soul after death. It refutes the doctrine of "soul sleep" (mortalism), arguing that while the body "sleeps" in the grave, the soul remains active and immediately enters the presence of Christ.</meta>

# The Rest of the Saints

sleep only falls upon the body and the outward senses, but not upon the soul; the Soul of Man is often most busy when the person sleeps; and God has previously revealed the most glorious things to his children in dreams, when they were asleep; God appeared to Abraham and many others in dreams; the body sleeps, but the Soul wakes. So it is with the sleep of death; the body, that dies, but the Soul does not die. There are some people who are not ashamed to teach you that the Soul sleeps just as much as the body, and that when the body dies and falls asleep, the Soul also remains in a dull sleep-sickness <note>original: "veternoso somno correptus," meaning seized by a lethargic or drowsy sleep.</note>, subject to neither joy nor sorrow, until the resurrection. Beloved, this is a very comfortless and a very false doctrine. They seek to prove this from my Text; they say that Stephen, when he died, fell asleep; it is true in respect to his body, he fell asleep, but his Soul did not fall asleep; that which was stoned fell asleep, which was only his body; for when he was stoned, he saw Jesus Christ standing ready to receive his Soul into Heaven; *Lord Jesus,* he says, *receive my spirit.* Stephen's Soul was also not stoned, although his body was stoned. Likewise, when Jesus Christ was crucified, his Soul was not crucified; I mean when his body was killed, his soul was not killed; indeed, he suffered torments in his Soul, which made him cry out, *My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?* but nevertheless, his Soul did not die. So when Stephen died, his Soul went to Christ. It is true, when a Child of God dies, the Soul goes to sleep, but how? the Soul goes to sleep in a Scriptural sense; that is, it goes to rest in <term>Abraham’s bosom</term> <note>A biblical metaphor for the place of comfort in the afterlife where the righteous dead await the resurrection.</note> (O blessed sleep!), it goes to rest in the embraces of God, it goes into the arms of its Redeemer, it goes into the Heavenly Paradise, it goes to be always present with the Lord. But guard yourself against that godless opinion, to say that the Soul sleeps in a <term>Mortalist</term> <note>original: "Memorthische," likely referring to the doctrine of Mortalism or "soul sleep."</note> sense, that is, that it lies in a strange sort of lethargy, neither dead nor alive, subject to neither joy nor sorrow, until the resurrection. Although Stephen's body fell asleep, nevertheless his Soul did not fall asleep, but went immediately to Heaven to Jesus Christ. Thus I have given the explanation of the words.

Now give me leave to make some application of all these things to ourselves.

If the death of God's Children is nothing other than a falling asleep, let this then comfort us against the death of our Godly friends, although they die unnatural and violent deaths, although they are stoned to death, although they are burned to ashes, although they are sawn in pieces, etc. Here is a message of rich consolation, which I as a Minister of Christ this day announce to you, namely, that the death of a Child of God, let it be in whatever manner it will, is nevertheless nothing other than a falling asleep; he goes to his grave as to his bed; and therefore our burial places are called <term>Cemeteries</term> <note>original: "Koimeteria, h.e. Dormitoria." From the Greek *koimeterion* and Latin *dormitorium*, both meaning "sleeping room" or "dormitory."</note>, that is, our sleeping-houses. A Child of God, when he dies, he lies down in peace, and enters into his rest. And, just as a person, when they sleep, is free from all cares and anxieties which they have by day;

<column-break/>

so the people of God, when they are in sleep, they are free from all miseries, thorns, harms, and distresses with which they are troubled; therefore allow me to say to you, just as Christ said to the Women who followed him even to the cross, weeping and mourning for him,

> O Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children.

So I say, O do not weep over those who are dead in the Lord, who have fallen asleep in Jesus Christ; they are at rest, they know nothing of the difficulties with which we are tormented; Abraham does not think of us; they are insensible to our miseries and distresses; let us bewail ourselves, and the miseries which shall come upon us; and let us know that when God's Children die, they only lie on their beds until the morning of the resurrection, and then they shall put on the <note>original: "Stolam immortalitatis," the robe of immortality.</note> **long robe of immortality**, and their bodies shall be made like the most glorious body of Jesus Christ. And know, moreover, one thing more, which is all in all, namely, that when the body of a Child of God falls asleep, his Soul goes immediately into the arms of Christ, and there lives eternally in the embraces of Jesus Christ; although the body falls asleep, nevertheless the Soul is received into Abraham's bosom. I pray you, comfort one another with these words.

Now let the people of God pray that they may indeed look upon death, not as it is shown to us in the mirror of nature, but as it is recounted in the Scripture. Nature shows us death in a very terrifying way; and it is true, death is very terrifying for a person outside of Christ, but for you who are in Christ, the sting of death is taken away; death is nothing other than a peaceful and acceptable sleep, a laying aside of our clothes, and a going to bed until we awake in the morning of the resurrection. Death is for a Child of God nothing other than a laying aside of his earthly tabernacle, a going away from an earthly prison to a Heavenly palace, a hoisting of the sail toward Heaven, a letting out of the Soul from the prison, like a Bird from a cage, so that it may fly to Heaven, an exchange of a temporary Hell for an eternal Heaven, a going away out of Egypt into Canaan, and therefore called <note>original: "exodus, h. e. exodús." Reference to 2 Peter 1:15.</note> **departure**. It is not the <note>original: "mors hominis," death of the man.</note> **death of the man**, but the <note>original: "mors peccati," death of sin.</note> **death of his sins**. It is the <note>original: "Sepultura vitiorum," burial of vices.</note> **burial of vices**, it is the end of the Pilgrim's journey, the Sailor's harbor; an absence from the body, and a presence with the Lord. Let all the people of God look upon death with scriptural eyes, and observe it just as it is sweetly shown in my Text: remember Holy Stephen stoned to death, and yet falling asleep. And also be mindful of that excellent saying of **Augustine**: That a Child of God must die as willingly as taking off his clothes; because death to him is nothing other than a sleep, and a departure from misery to everlasting happiness.

I pray you all that you will remember this Text every night when you go to bed, and especially these four things.

# The Rest of the Saints

Think that it will not be long before you must go into your graves. And;

Thirdly / when you close your eyes to sleep, remember that before long death will come to close your eyes. And;

Fourthly / when you wake in the morning / remember that on the day of the resurrection you must all rise from the grave / and that the righteous shall rise / to eternal blessedness / but the godless to ever-enduring misery.

There is a saying of a Heathen Man <note>likely referring to Plato or Cicero, who famously wrote that "to philosophize is to learn how to die"</note>, that the entire life of a person should be nothing other than *meditation on death* <note>original: "meditatio mortis"</note>. And it is the saying of <margin>Moses, Deut. 32:29.</margin> Moses, Deut. 32:29: *O that they were wise, that they understood this, that they would consider their end.* Beloved / it is great wisdom / to remember our end every day. That person alone is a wise person / and a happy person in life and death / who always remembers their death.

But before I finish / I must answer a question / namely, whether the death of the godless is not also compared in Scripture to a sleep, just like the death of the pious;

I answer / that in the Scripture godless people are said to fall asleep when they die; it is said of the adulterous Jeroboam, that he slept with his fathers; of Baasha, and Omri, the godless Kings, that they slept with their fathers.

But then the question will be / in what way is the death of the godless compared to a sleep?

Just like a person who sleeps / sometimes finds no profit / rest / nor relief through it; when the sick person awakes / he is often sicker than he was before he went to sleep; some people become greatly disturbed in their sleep by hideous and terrifying dreams; Nebuchadnezzar when he slept / had a fearful dream / and when he woke / he was terrified by it: so it is with a godless person; death is to a godless person; a sleep, but a terrifying sleep / the Soul goes immediately to hell / where it is burned with fire which shall never be quenched / where the worm which never dies is always gnawing. The body / it truly lies in the grave and sleeps / but how? Just like a criminal / who sleeps in the prison the night before he is executed / but when he wakes / he is immediately pushed and dragged to the execution; so the godless falls asleep in death / but when he wakes, he wakes to ever-enduring damnation. But a child of God / when he sleeps the sleep of death / he sleeps in his Father’s house / and when he wakes / he wakes to ever-enduring blessedness.

And this serves for a fourth and final use / which is a use of very great consequence. And it is to pray to you all / that you would labor to live so / that when you fall asleep / you may sleep a happy sleep. There is the sleep which the godless person sleeps when he dies / and there is the sleep which the pious sleeps when he dies. Now I pray you / labor to live so / that when you fall asleep / your sleep may be a happy sleep to you / that when you wake in the morning of the resurrection / it may be a happy awakening for you.

But then the question will be / how shall I do this?

I shall give you five helpful means for this.

<column-break/>

Firstly / if you wish to sleep a happy sleep of death / then you must labor to fall asleep in Jesus Christ; it is said / 1 Cor. 15:18: *then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ*: and 1 Thess. 4:14: *If we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God [bring back] with him.* What is it to fall asleep in Jesus? To fall asleep in Jesus / is to die in the faith of Jesus Christ.

2. To fall asleep in Jesus / is to die with a rightful claim to Jesus Christ / to die as a member of Christ united with him / as our head. For you must know / that the dust of a Saint is a part of that person who is a member of Jesus Christ / and every believer when he sleeps in the dust / he sleeps in Jesus Christ / that is / he lies in the grave / and his dust is a part of Christ in a hidden way / and Christ as a head shall awaken it / It cannot be perfect without the same. Now then, if you wish to sleep a happy sleep / labor to actually obtain a right to Christ / labor to live in Christ while you live. And then / when you fall asleep / you shall be certain to fall asleep in Jesus. There are many who want Christ to receive their Souls after their death / and who say with the dying Stephen, *Lord Jesus receive my Spirit*: but if you want Christ to receive your Soul when you die / then you must certainly receive him into your Soul while you live / if you want him to receive you into Heaven / then you must receive him into your hearts. No man makes a final will without saying / *In the first place* <note>original Latin: "Imprimis," a standard legal opening for a testament</note>, *I commit my Soul to Jesus Christ my redeemer.* But how dare you think that Jesus Christ will accept this Testament / if your Soul does not have Christ’s image in it / if it is not born again and renewed / Jesus Christ will never accept it or claim it as his own; you may bequeath it to Christ in your Testament / but the Devil will claim or take it for himself / if your soul has the Devil's image in it / if it be a swinish / unclean / unbelieving / unregenerate Soul / you may give it to God / but the Devil will get the same back out of God's hands / do not take this saying poorly / it is not mine / but Saint Augustine’s. Beloved, if you ever wish to reign with Christ when you die / he must reign in you while you live: and if you ever wish to sleep a blessed sleep / you must live in Jesus so that you may sleep in Jesus.

Secondly. In the second place / if you ever wish to sleep a blessed sleep of death / then you must guard yourself against overloading yourself with worldly cares. A person who is full of care cannot sleep / therefore when people want to sleep / they lay [as the proverb says] all their worries under their pillow / they strive to put all their cares out of their thoughts: oh, beware that you do not murder your Souls through the cares of this World; beloved / a person who eats up his heart / through worldly anxiety / shall never sleep a blessed sleep; the cares of this World shall choke all the seed of the Word of God; and therefore / just as people when they sleep lay all worldly thoughts aside; so if you ever wish to sleep a blessed sleep / beware of being too much troubled and caring for the things of this World: and

<meta>This page continues the concluding points of a sermon regarding the "sleep" of death, offering practical advice on how to ensure a peaceful passing. It then transitions into a new section: a funeral sermon by Thomas Manton for the executed Presbyterian minister Christopher Love.</meta>

remember what you have heard this day; and that shall regulate and set the measure for all cares and anxieties; naked you came into the world and naked you must go out from it again; why should we worry for that which we know not who shall enjoy after us?

Thirdly, if you ever wish to sleep a blessed sleep when you die, you must guard yourself against enjoying too many pleasures of this world: a person who eats heartly in the evening shall sleep very restlessly; therefore those who wish to sleep peacefully are accustomed to eating but little in the evening; for when a person's stomach is overloaded, it takes his sweet sleep away from him; so if you ever wish to sleep a blessed sleep when you come to die, oh, guard yourself against using too many of the pleasures of this life: guard yourself against making too hearty a meal of worldly delights and the creature's comforts; these worldly pleasures shall make the sleep of death restless for you. Oh, do not let Delilah’s lap <note>A reference to the biblical story of Samson, where Delilah's lap represents dangerous worldly temptation.</note> rob you of Abraham’s bosom <note>original: "Abrahams schoot," a traditional term for paradise or the resting place of the righteous after death.</note>: remember that David, through Bathsheba’s embrace, lost the embrace of God—I mean the feeling of God’s embrace, the joy and comfort of the same.

Fourthly, if you wish to sleep a blessed sleep of death, then labor to work for Heaven while you live. Oh, how pleasant is sleep to a weary person, when the person has worked fervently the whole day, like a traveler who has journeyed the whole day, or the plowman who has worked a whole day; how peacefully, how heartily does he sleep at night? O beloved! if you ever wish to sleep a blessed sleep of death, then labor to work out your salvation with fear and trembling: and apply all diligent industry to make your calling and election sure: the more you labor for

<column-break/>

Heaven, the better and sweeter shall your sleep be when you come to die. And remember this, that just as much sleeping during the day shall be a hindrance to a person's sleep in the night, so if you waste the time of your provision for Heaven in this your day—you who sleep through the moment upon which eternity hangs—oh, you shall have a sorrowful sleep when death falls upon you. Guard yourself therefore from sleeping while you live, so that your sleep in the night of death may be comforting to you.

Fifthly and lastly, if you ever wish to sleep a blessed sleep of death when you die, guard yourself then from the sleep of sin. Sin is compared in the Scripture to a sleep: *Awake, you who sleep*, that is, you who sin. Sin is such a sleep as brings the sleep of death; sin brings the first death, and sin brings the second death <note>The "first death" refers to physical passing, while the "second death" refers to eternal separation from God.</note>: all miseries, of whatever kind they may be, are the daughters of sin. If you wish to sleep a blessed sleep, and wish to have a blessed awakening on the day of the resurrection, then guard yourself against the sleep of sin. *Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give you light,* Eph. 5:14. So also Rom. 13:11, 12, 13. With which I shall conclude, and I pray you mark it well, for it was a text which converted the Holy Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) famously converted after hearing a child’s voice say "tolle lege" (take up and read) and opening the Bible to this specific passage in Romans.</note>: *And that, knowing the time, Beloved, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we (first) believed. The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light. Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying: but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfill the lusts thereof.*

<meta>This page continues the sermon's transition into the "Triumph of the Saints," focusing on the theological victory over death. It picks up as the author analyzes the famous passage from 1 Corinthians 15 regarding death's sting.</meta>

# Triumph.

<page-num>628</page-num>

**Death, where are your plagues? Hell, where is your destruction?** <note>A paraphrase of Hosea 13:14, famously echoed by the Apostle Paul.</note> Here is Christ’s commitment and victory, to overcome death even unto hell. Christ threatens death, and the Apostle boasts and braves over it; the form of the words is changed because the enemy has now fallen, and Paul cries out the victory. Until that time, death and hell had boasted over the misery and sorrow of the human race; all the graves and ossuaries <term>bone-houses</term> of the world were like so many monuments to the victory of death.

**Golgotha**, the Place of the Skull, seems intentionally appointed for this: to defy and discourage our Savior. As many skulls and decayed remains of human fragility as were in that place, so many monuments of triumph did death bring before Christ’s eyes, as if it were said to him: *can you, or dare you, set yourself against such an enemy?* But our Lord Christ was of good courage, even as he was nailed to the Cross; he answered, as it were, those defiances of death, thus: **O death! I shall be your plague! O! Hell, I shall be your destruction.** And because Christ was faithful to his word, and in every way fulfilled his commitment, the Apostle comes as one of his followers and braves this proud enemy who had now fallen, saying: **Death, where is your sting? Hell, where is your victory?**

This explanation is clarified by addressing an objection: for someone might ask, what is this **Sting of death**? What is this **power of Hell**?

The Apostle answers: **The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the Law.** Death obtained this power through sin, and sin obtained it through the Law.

**The sting of death** signifies at once both the pricking and the anguish of death, just as there is a deadly sting, ache, and pain in the bite of a snake; and so it signifies the power of death over us. The "sting" or the weapon with which she wounds is sin. *Romans 5:12: Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin.* And the terrors of the same, which also proceed from sin; by these terrors and horrors, I understand not only the natural aversion and the fleeing of the spirits, but also the bondage, fear, and despair that lie upon the conscience, insofar as death is an evil of punishment sent by the justice of God. For guilt makes death hideous, so that the sinner is subject to bondage all his life (*Hebrews 2:14, 15*) and has a constant fear of the coming judgment. It is not always felt, but it arises suddenly, especially in times of sickness and the approach of death; when one feels its cold hands ready to snatch our souls away, then the conscience is lashed with a **scourge of six cords**: namely, **fear, terror, despair, sadness, rage, and shame.**

**The strength of sin is the Law.** How is that to be understood?

The Law gives strength to sin in three ways: *By reason of knowledge, obligation, and increase.* <note>original: "Ratione cognitionis, obligationis, & augmentationis"</note> These are the words of a German theologian [Pareus], <note>David Pareus (1548–1622) was a prominent Reformed Protestant theologian.</note> which shall give us a proper guide to open the matter.

First, the Law discovers sin, and makes it ap-

<column-break/>

pear in its own colors. The greater the light and knowledge of the Law, the greater the feeling of sin, just as one can quickly notice a speck of dust in transparent water. *Romans 7:9: I was alive once without the Law, but when the commandment came, sin revived and I died.* When, through a healthy conviction, all the masks are pulled away from the conscience, only then do we find that sin is truly sin. Paul was "alive" before—namely, in his own hope and opinion—just as many unfeeling souls hollowly reckon they shall enter Heaven until their consciences are opened; and then they find themselves in the mouth of death and Hell.

Secondly, the Law gives strength to sin in respect to its **obligation**. It binds and subjects a sinner to the curse and the wrath of God: for God has made a righteous Law which must have satisfaction, and as long as that is not satisfied, we hear of nothing else but a curse; and that makes death very hideous. There remains nothing but a fearful expectation of judgment and fiery indignation. (*Hebrews 10:27*).

Thirdly, the Law **increases** and causes sin to grow by forbidding it. Desires become more vehement and raging when they are restrained, just as a yoke makes a young ox wilder and more unruly. Now, lay all these things together and you shall understand the power of the expression: **The strength of sin is the Law.** The discovery of the Law stops the sinner’s mouth, and the curse of the Law shuts him up and preserves him for the judgment of the great day, by which restraint sin becomes more mad and frantic. All this put together makes death terrifying—not an end to misery, but a door opening into Hell.

This being the state of every human, what shall we do? And how shall we untangle our souls from such a labyrinth of endless terror? To this you have an answer in the following verse, in the thanksgiving of the Apostle, wherein he makes known to you not only grounds for hope but also for triumph: **Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.**

In this thanksgiving you may observe:
1. The **Author** and cause of grace: God through Jesus Christ.
2. The **manner** of how we come to have a right to it: He *gives* us the victory. Or rather, you may note: 1. The act of the Father in respect to Jesus Christ, that He ordained Him to obtain the victory. 2. The act of the Father in respect to us, that He applies this victory to our souls. Christ’s victory and its application are the two grounds of this thanksgiving.

First, you see **Christ’s victory** over sin, death, and the Law, for it must be extended to all those of which the preceding words spoke. They are all enemies, joined together in a firm alliance; the Law gives strength to sin, and sin gives a sting to death. As long as the Law has power, sin shall be strong; and as long as sin has strength, death shall be terrifying. But Christ has overcome death; He has slain it in His own person, as I shall presently show in full; and as for sin, He has taken away its guilt through His merits, and He shall more and...

# of the Saints.

...more destruction; the power of the Holy Spirit; when he stood before the judgment seat of God, he stood there as a surety <term>borge: a legal guarantor who takes on another's debt</term>, a surety of a better covenant, Hebrews 7 verse 22. Now he was both God's and our surety, to accomplish the work of God in us, and our work for us; he undertook to annihilate sin on God's side; he bound himself to work it out through his Spirit; on our side he has obligated us to the practice of the mortification of sins: now because Christ is a fit surety, the work is as good as done. *Knowing*, says the Apostle, *that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed; that henceforth we should not serve sin*, Romans 6 verse 6. Note: it is "crucified with him," which indicates what Christ took upon himself on the cross; "that the body of sin might be destroyed," whereby the work of God's Spirit is shown, surely obtained for us through the death of Christ on the cross; "that we should no longer serve sin," signifying the coming together of our efforts, to which we are obligated by that same surety-like act of Christ. So much has Christ done for the destruction of sin; and as far as the Law is concerned, it was a hand that could not conquer, but had to be satisfied, and so it happened through Christ, who fulfilled the whole Law and suffered its punishment, even to the very heaviest, for which it is also written that *he became a curse for us*, Galatians 3 verse 13. The sting is lost in Christ, and the honey is left for us. But this matter is appropriate for other occasions to be understood.

Secondly. The other reason for the Apostle's thanksgiving is the appropriation; he has given us the victory. To better understand this, you must know two things: first, that Christ's victory is reckoned to us as if we had obtained it in our own person: when we are truly united with him, we also possess all his merits; Christ has fought our battle, he has fought in our place; we have a mystical <term>Godt-geheyme: literally "God-secret," meaning a spiritual reality hidden from the senses</term> victory in Christ, and we are said to overcome when Christ overcame; and this is the reason why the deeds of the believers in Scripture are joined together with the deeds of Christ. *We are crucified with him, made alive, and raised up and seated with him in Heaven*, Ephesians 2 verse 6 etc. All of which words properly express the judicial union which is distinct from the moral and mystical union, as I could easily prove if it were not a matter of a different nature. Now this mystical victory has great usefulness for a believer in times of dejection of the Spirit; when the Law calls us, and Satan and conscience say, "you are a sinner and lie under the curse," then you might answer: "I am indeed a sinner, but I am crucified in Christ my surety; his payment and suffering are mine." If death or the world seeks to discourage you, then you might say: "This is a defeated enemy; I have struck him down in Christ; I have ascended in Christ," etc.

Secondly. That the benefit of Christ's victory was communicated and appropriated to us; whereby he makes us victors over sin and over death: for all the work of Christ was not finished at the cross; there is still much to be accomplished in our hearts, Romans 16 verse 20: *the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly*; not only under Christ's

<column-break/>

feet, but also under ours; just as Joshua called his companions to come and tread on the necks of the Canaanite kings: *Come near, put your feet upon the necks of these kings*, Joshua 10 verse 24. So Christ also wants to see us overcome. He who obtained the victory for us shall obtain a victory in us over sin, death, and Hell. Christ has already trodden them all underfoot when his heels were bruised <note>original: "verssenen vermorzelt," a reference to Genesis 3:15</note>; now he shall do it under your feet.

The foundation being thus laid, this is the main doctrine that I shall handle: That Christ’s victory over death serves for the comfort and benefit of believers. Death is twofold: the first and second; the temporal and the eternal. Sinners lie under the sentence of both, and both are in some way placed in the hands of Satan. *He had the power of death*, Hebrews 2 verse 14, as God’s executioner <term>Scherp-richter: literally "sharp-judge," an old term for a headsman or executioner</term>; and the one death prepares the way for the other. Death for the godless is nothing other than a removal of their persons to torment, just as scoundrels are cast into prison so that they may no longer cause any trouble; God’s patience ends with their life, and then his vengeance begins. The curse of the first covenant was eternal death. Genesis 2:15 <note>The text cites 2:15, though 2:17 is the standard reference for the decree of death.</note> *You shall die*, that is, eternally: for the curse must be proportionate to the blessing. The blessing was eternal life, and the curse was eternal death. I say, the sorrow and pain must have been continuous to correspond to the life which man would have enjoyed; therefore Christ is said to have delivered us from the wrath to come; which surely was our portion and inheritance through Adam; and without Christ there is no escape. But to come to specific things, I shall show you:

First, how Christ has delivered us from death.

Secondly, how far he has done so.

First, how has he delivered us? The Apostle answers, Hebrews 2 verse 14, that *through death he might destroy him who had the power of death*. Now Christ’s death can be considered in two ways: as a merit, or as a glorious act of battle and war; as the act of a redeemer, or as the act of a victor, which corresponds to the two-fold evil that is in death: 1. It is a natural evil. 2. It is a penal <term>straffigh: related to punishment or legal penalty</term> evil. A natural evil, in so far as it is the separation of soul and body; a penal evil, in so far as it is a curse of the covenant or the punishment for sin. First, in the voluntary death of Christ there was merit; it was a ransom for the elect, Matthew 20 verse 28, 1 Timothy 2 verse 6. He died not only for their good and benefit, but also in their place. Just as the ram was taken and sacrificed and Isaac was spared, so was Christ’s death in place of ours; God will not demand the debt twice, from us and from our surety. Job 33 verse 24: *Deliver him, that he go not down to the pit, for I have found an atonement*. One of the two had to die: the sinner or the surety; now God the Lord says, "I accept Christ’s death and suffering for this repentant person." If we fall down into the grave, it does not happen for vengeance, for through Christ’s death the merit of our sins is reconciled; justice is satisfied; God’s wrath is stilled; the Law is fulfilled; sin is forgiven; and so the bonds of death are broken. Death is in itself the sentence of the Law, the fruit of

# The Triumph

Secondly, you may behold Christ’s foot as the act of a conqueror. Christ has in His own person conquered death; after Christ had risen from the grave, death lost its retaining power. *Acts 2 v. 24.* He has loosed the pains of death; the word in the original text signifies the pains of a woman in labor <note>original: "barens-noot". The author refers to the Greek *ōdin*, which can mean both "birth pang" and "bond/snare".</note>; the grave was in labor-pains until it was relieved of this precious burden, for it was not possible that He should be held by it; and after that time the grave has been more like a mother’s womb than a dungeon and a pit of vengeance; for it does not destroy life, but renews it (*it does not snatch life, but reforms it more wisely* <note>original: "non vitam rapit, sed reformat prudentius"</note>). In nearly the same metaphorical way of speaking, Christ is called the firstborn from the dead, not because He was the first who was raised from the dead—though He was the first who rose by His own power, whereas others were raised by the power of another—but Christ rose by His own power. He is also called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, *1 Corinthians 15 v. 20.* Just as the offering of the firstfruits was a blessing for all the harvest, so Christ’s dying and rising is a ground of victory for all the elect. Christ, through His death, battled with the powers of darkness and all their subordinate instruments. Death was Satan’s last tool, but Christ defeated it in its own dungeon. The fight between Christ and death began on the Cross, and while struggling, they went to the grave; Christ, like a cautious warrior, brought the war into His enemy's land, and there He took away the sting of death; He defeated death within its own borders; He rose up and left death behind Him gasping and gaping, so that the nature of the grave is entirely changed. First it was a prison-house and Satan’s dungeon; now it is a chamber and a bed of rest, just as Christ slept in it. When the Prophet speaks of Christ’s resurrection, he says, *Isaiah 53 v. 8*, He was taken away from distress (otherwise, the prison) and from judgment; by the prison he understands the grave; but speaking of the death of the faithful, he says, *Isaiah 57 v. 2*, they shall rest on their beds. For a short time, it was a prison-house for Christ so that it might be a place of rest for us.

The other question is, how far has He delivered us from death? We see that the godly, as well as others, are subject to the changes and violent attacks of nature; how then are we delivered? I answer: it is enough that the second death <note>The "second death" refers to eternal separation from God in Hell (Revelation 20:6).</note> has no power over us, *Revelation Chapter 20 v. 6.* That it has nothing to do with us, *Romans 8 v. 6.* There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. We may die, but we shall not be condemned; though we go into the grave, we are nonetheless freed from Hell. But that is not all; the believers have an advantage in the first death; they do not die like other men; because:

Firstly, the nature of death is changed. That which was a punishment in death is now gone; it is no longer a destruction, but a deliverance. Believers have unjust, evil thoughts of death; we are delivered from death as far as it is a punishment and a curse; now it is a blessing and belongs to the inheritance which Christ has bequeathed to His Church; everything is

<column-break/>

yours, death is yours, *1 Corinthians 3 v. 21-22.* As long as death was in the Devil’s hand, it was an enemy; but in Christ, it has become a friend and a blessing; a passage from a vale of tears to the Kingdom of Glory; the end of a mortal life and the beginning of the immortal. Just like Haman against Mordecai <note>A reference to the Book of Esther, where Haman's plot to destroy Mordecai was overturned to Mordecai's honor.</note>, they intended evil, but it became a glorious privilege. For the godless, it is truly an execution, but for the godly, it is a relaxation and a releasing of their souls into the bosom of Christ, *Luke 2 v. 29:* Now, Lord, let your servant depart in peace. They send their souls away peacefully; but the soul of the godless is "taken away"; so it is expressed twice, *Luke 12 v. 20:* in this night your soul shall be required of you, or taken away. *Job 27 v. 8:* when God shall pull out his soul. They would gladly keep it longer; but God plucks it away, whether they will or not. A godly person points and sends his soul over in peace; his life cannot be "taken away," for it is only given up at the call of providence; and he dies not because he must, but because he wills to die. It may be that he dies earlier than he expected, but not earlier than he willed, for when God wills it, he submits himself. But to return to our previous point: the good which is in death consists of these three things:

**1.** The dying of a godly person is but the dying of their sins, frailties, and weaknesses. *Sin dies; misery dies; the man does not die* <note>original: "peccatum moritur; miseria moritur, homo non moritur"</note>. The man does not die, but the sin and the misery do; all other means and actions only weaken sin, but death annihilates it. When God justifies, the condemning power is taken away; when God sanctifies, the reigning power is taken away; but when He is glorified through death, the very essence of sin itself is taken away. If a house was so badly stained with leprosy that it could not be purified by scraping, it had to be torn down; we are also so defiled by sin that all other means are too weak; only death can take away that impurity. When ivy <note>original: "Aert-veyl". Literally "Earth-ivy," likely referring to common ivy roots that damage masonry.</note> has grown into a wall, it cannot be entirely pulled out unless the wall itself is thrown down. Cut off the trunk with the branches and shoots, and yet some roots will remain that will sprout again. So it is here too; original sin cannot be taken away; the believers sigh constantly: who shall deliver us from this body of death, *Romans 7 v. 24.* But now death is a hasty cure: sin brought death into the world, and as if in revenge, death destroys sin.

**2.** Through death, the way is prepared for a present and perfect union of the soul with Christ, *Philippians 1 v. 23.* I have a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. We are loosed from the body and fastened to Christ; it is better that a soul be separated from the body than absent from Christ. We have a union here, but not a presence with Christ. Judge now: what is better, to be with the body or with Christ? To have the company of the body or the company of Christ? Here the soul is locked up and, as it were, imprisoned; but there you have the free enjoyment of Christ, without the hindrance of an earthly state. The soul...

### Of the Saints ###

as soon as it separates from the body, it goes immediately to Christ. Just as when Potiphar’s wife grabbed Joseph’s cloak and Joseph escaped it, so you also leave the outer garment <note>original: "opper-kleedt"</note> in the hand of death, but the soul flees to God. The body came from Adam and passes through a fleshly channel <note>original: "vleesche goot," referring to natural generation or lineage</note>; and all that we have from Adam must for a while turn to dust, so that it may be cleansed of its clinging impurity. But the soul comes by a natural right to God, who gave it, and by a special right to Christ, who bought it and sanctified it by His Spirit.

3. The body, which seems to suffer much, has a great advantage; for a peasant’s cottage is torn down so that a better building may be erected. A natural body is sown, and a spiritual body is raised. *1 Cor. 15:44.* Here it is not capable of great delight; through sickness it is made unfit for religious duties. Again: a corruptible body is sown, an incorruptible body is raised. Here it is subject to change; there it may live unchangeably in eternity. If we love long life, there it is eternal life. It is fleshly self-love that makes one willing to remain in the flesh. If we only loved ourselves and our flesh rightly, we would not be terrified of dying; for to die is to become perfect, to have body and soul free from sin and corruption.

Secondly, the sting of death is taken away. If you are chosen and sanctified in Christ Jesus, it can do you no harm or damage. I say again: death may come to kill you, but it cannot injure you. It has no power over the best part; like the serpent, it feeds only on your dust. Indeed, regarding your body—which dies as a creature—it shall certainly live as a member of Christ. The Lord Jesus is our head even in the grave. Your bodies have within them a principle of life; the believers are raised by the Spirit of holiness. The same Spirit who now makes them fit for the duty of grace shall raise their mortal bodies; so it is written in *Rom. 8 v. 11*: He shall make your mortal bodies alive through His Spirit who dwells in you. The Holy Spirit cannot abandon His old dwelling place. How many kinds of comfort do we have against the mortality of the body? Christ is united with our body and soul, and He shall not allow a single nerve or joint to be missing from His mystical body. In the accounting that He must give to His Father, He says that He must lose *nothing*. *John 6 v. 39.* Note: He does not say "no one," but "nothing" <note>original: "niets". The author emphasizes that Christ preserves every physical part of the believer, not just the person as a whole.</note>. Christ shall not lose a single bone, or even a piece of an ear.

Again: God is in a covenant with both body and soul. When you descend into the chambers of death, you may appeal to the written promise of His own grace. God is the God of Abraham and of every believer’s dust; though it be mixed with the remains of the godless, Christ shall nevertheless separate and gather it.

Christ proves (*Matt. 22 v. 32*) the resurrection of the body with this reason: because God is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. The basis of this reasoning is that God made His covenant not only with the souls of the Patriarchs, but with their entire persons. Furthermore, Christ has bought both soul and body, as is made known in *1 Cor. 6 v. 20*: You are bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body. Christ has given a suffi-

<column-break/>

-cient price to obtain the right to both soul and body; therefore He will not lose the smallest part of what He has acquired. The Lord shall demand an accounting from the grave and say: "Where is the body of my Abraham, of my Isaac, of my Jacob?" It is written in *Rev. 20 v. 13*: The sea gave up the dead that were in it, and death and hell gave up the dead that were in them.

"Hell" <note>The author uses "Helle" here in the sense of Hades or the realm of the dead.</note> is taken there to mean the state of the deceased; for what else would be the meaning of the following words: "Death and Hell were cast into the lake of fire"? Thus, all the dead shall be cast up, just as the whale cast up Jonah; so shall the grave give up its dead. The grave is but like a chest <note>original: "kist," meaning a casket or storage chest</note> in which our bodies are safely kept until the day of Christ, and the key to this chest is not in the hands of the Devil, but of Christ. *Rev. 1 v. 18*: I have the keys of hell and of death. When the body is laid down in a cold pit, it is laid there until another day. God has special care over our dust and remains; when our friends and neighbors have abandoned them, Christ does not abandon them, but preserves them until that great and glorious day.

Thirdly, we are relieved of the terrors and anxieties of death. Death is terrifying, for it is an evil of punishment and of nature, as I distinguished before. For as much as it is a natural evil, it is the greatest evil of all: *Phoberon Phoberotaton* <note>Greek: "The most terrifying of all terrors."</note>, that is, the most terrible of all terrible things. So said the pagan Aristotle, which in Job’s manner of speaking can be translated as "the King of Terrors." *Job 18 v. 14.* We tremble when we see a snake; much more when we behold the stern face of death. In secular philosophy <note>original: "zedige Wijse-geerte"</note>, no remedy could be found for this. The pagans were either despairing, or unbelieving and ignorant, or they outwardly hid their fear.

But Christ has provided a proper remedy; He has delivered us not only from the injury of death, but also from the fear of death. *Heb. 2 v. 15*: That He might deliver all those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. He fills the soul through His Spirit with a hope of a better life. Nature may shrink back when we see the pale horse of death approaching, but we may be glad when we consider that it is the messenger who shall bring us home. Just as when the old Jacob saw the wagons coming from Egypt, how his heart leaped because he would see his son Joseph? So too is death (however ugly we may depict it) sent to carry us into Heaven, to bring us over to the Lord Jesus Christ. Now, who would shrink from becoming blessed, or from being in the arms of our dear Jesus? Let those fear death who know no better life; a Christian knows that when he dies, he shall not perish but have eternal life. *John 3 v. 16.* The world may cast you out, but you can behold heaven, beckoning to you as a friend and ready to receive you, just as Stephen saw Heaven opened. *Acts 7 v. 56.* There is an enlightenment of the understanding or a confidence of faith which is common to all saints; though everyone may not have such an ecstasy and sensible vision as Stephen had, it is nevertheless common that in the hours of their departure, their faith is so powerfully strengthened that they are freed from all fear and sorrow.

# The Triumph

### 2. 
**Insofar as death is an evil of punishment,** it is a great evil; it is sorrowful when death is sent as an executor <note>original: "uut voerster," a female officer of justice or bailiff</note> of righteousness, clothed in vengeance, and in the character of a curse. You know what was said before: the sting of death is sin. They truly die who die in their sins. For them, the day of death is a black and dark day; they drop downward (like rotten fruit) into the Lake of Fire. Now, Christ has taken away the sting—that is, the anxieties and terrors of death. He has removed death in the same way he removed sin; he did not cast out sin <note>meaning he did not yet remove the presence of sin entirely from our nature</note>, but he cast it down. He has removed the guilt and power, though not the essence, of sin. Likewise, the offense and sting of death are gone, even if death itself remains. It is like something disarmed, long without its stinger; we may lay it in our bosom without danger. Through many accusations, the Devil seeks to terrify a dying soul, making death seem fearful and full of horrors; but they overcome through the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 12:11). They overcome these doubts and fears; when sins are forgiven, the fears vanish. As Luther said: 

> Strike, Lord, strike, for my sins are forgiven. <note>original Latin: "Feri, Domine, feri, absolutus sum á peccatis meis"</note>

### Fourthly, 
finally, death shall one day be entirely abolished. We hardly know now all that the merits of Christ contain until the day of judgment comes. It says in 1 Corinthians 15:26: "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." It is now weakened and violated <note>robbed of its strength</note>, but then it shall be abolished in respect to the elect. Revelation 20:14 says: "Death and Hell shall be cast into the Lake of Fire; this is the second death." The dominion of death is reserved for Hell; it must keep company with the damned while you are with God in joy. For the present, it still endures by dispensation or permission; it performs its service for the advancement of God’s glory. But then the ungodly shall have death and hell beneath them; they shall be held in a dying life, or a living death. But all tears shall be washed from their eyes (Revelation 7:17). Death shall be no more, and you shall take the harp of God in your hands and say with a holy triumph: "O death, where is thy sting? O Hell, where is thy victory?" It is true, we may say it now in hope—yes, sing it just as some little birds sing in the winter—but only then can we truly be said to triumph or celebrate the victory.

### Now to apply this.

First, here is terror for the ungodly. It may perhaps seem strange to you that I draw terror from such comforting doctrine; but note that Jesus Christ has conquered death for no one else than those who have a right to Him. Others <insert>alas!</insert> are under the full power of death. For the present, the state of the ungodly is sorrowful; in death it shall be worse; in Hell, worst of all.

First, your state is sorrowful for the present, because a servitude lies upon your souls which, though not always felt, is soon awakened. You cannot think of death and Hell without distress. The thought of it <insert>like Belshazzar’s handwriting on the wall</insert> strikes you with trembling in the midst of your pleasure and finery. A small thing 

<column-break/>

will awaken the conscience of an ungodly person. The fingers of a man’s hand on the wall! Belshazzar <note>A biblical king of Babylon who saw a miraculous hand writing a message of doom on his palace wall during a feast (Daniel 5)</note> seemed a cheerful fellow and a fine spirit, but God quickly takes away his luster; then the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees knocked against each other from fear. If God only begins to stir the conscience once, the boldest spirits lose their courage; He needs to arm no one against you but your own thoughts. Surely, no one but a child of God can have true and steady courage against death. Without being downcast, we cannot even think of it. But David said in Psalm 23:4: "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil." It is terrifying, sorrowful, and dark to walk on the borders of death, surrounded on all sides by horror and destruction; yet even there David would not shrink but trust. It is otherwise with the ungodly: hereafter they would rather not live, and here they would rather not die.

### Secondly, 
in death it will be worse for you. The more you approach the eternal state, the more your conscience will be opened, and the more it will gnaw and terrify you. I admit, not every ungodly person dies feelingly; some are insensitive and bold. They may offer up an undaunted body with a stubborn heart, but at the last they die uncertain and doubtful, if not despondent and full of terror. Just as Pope Hadrian <note>Hadrian VI (1459–1523), the only Dutch Pope</note> said to his soul: 

> O little soul, wandering and charming, etc. Oh poor soul, where do you go now? You shall no longer play or joke. <note>original: "o Animula, vagula, blandula, & c."</note>

Or as he said: 

> I lived in anxiety, I die in doubt; alas, where do I go? <note>original: "anxius vixi dubius morior, heu quo vado!"</note>

Someone walking in the dark close to a deep pit does not know where his feet will sink; and such is the state of the ungodly. But this is not all; commonly their death is full of terror. That which is written with the juice of a lemon <note>term: "sap van een Lamoen," referring to invisible ink that appears when heated</note> is clear and readable when brought to the fire; so it is with the ungodly when they are near the fiery stench of hell—then they howl upon their beds. Few or none can look death in the face with confidence. Oh, oh, consider: when death comes, sin stares at your conscience; your conscience drives you to the Law; the Law delivers you to Hell; and Hell opens its mouth wide to receive you. What will you do in such a case? Satan attacks you; your old enticer becomes your new accuser. Yes, you then feel a great struggle within yourself; the body turns pale, the soul because of a bad government <note>meaning the poor management of one's life and soul</note>, and the soul curses the body because it was an evil tool. Oh! It is a sorrowful parting when they can expect to meet again only in flames and pains; therefore, the memory of that day when they were joined together is cursed. A godly person can take a sweet farewell of his body, saying: "Farewell flesh, go rest in hope; you shall one day awaken from the dust, and then I shall be satisfied with God’s image. I have a great longing to be reunited with you; we have lived together so long and glorified God; God will not let you see corruption," etc.

### Thirdly, 
it will be worst of all in Hell. Envy shall be as much a part of your torment as despair. Luke 16:23 states of the rich man that in Hell he lifted up his eyes and saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom, and said...

# of the Saints.

said: "I suffer pain in this flame." <note>A reference to the Rich Man in the parable of Lazarus and the Rich Man, Luke 16:24.</note> It shall increase your pain that you shall compare the eternal blessedness of the believers with your misery; they are in the presence of God and His holy Angels, but you have no company other than the Devil, death, Hell, and the damned. You are held under the power of eternal darkness; you would then wish not to live, yet you cannot die. When you have passed many thousands of years, you cannot look forward to even a moment of rest; the conscience gnaws more and more; you burn, but you are not consumed. Oh! It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31). Note that name, **living God**; we do not speak in the name of an Idol, who cannot avenge his quarrel against you, or of a god who shall die or perish, but in the name of a living God: who lives eternally to see vengeance executed upon His enemies. There is no hope of deliverance; as long as God is God, Hell shall also be Hell.

->The second utility is for the awakening of us all, to strive to have a part in this victory of Christ. Not everyone is fit to make use of Christ’s victory over death; many things are necessary to enjoy the full comfort of this; I shall name a few.<-

**First**, you must ensure that your sins are forgiven: all the power of the Devil and death hangs upon sin. Therefore, see to it that sin is buried before you are buried, or otherwise, it will not go well with you. There are two deep pits in which you can bury your sins and you shall then never hear of them again: namely, the great sea of God’s mercy and the grave of Christ. See that they are buried in the great sea of mercy; Micah 7:19 says: *You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.* There is depth enough to bury and drown them so that they never come to mind again. Then there is the grave of Christ; His merit is a deep grave, deep enough to bury all the sins of the world therein—"buried with Him through baptism," it says in Romans 6:4. Otherwise, if this is not done, you shall wish to be eternally buried and never rise again. Allow me to use another thoughtful manner of speaking, after the fashion of the Apostle’s expression in 2 Corinthians 5:3: *If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked.* It is a grave fault among Christians that when they come to die, they must then seek a shroud <note>original: "doodt kleet," literally "death-cloth"</note> and are found entirely naked. It is unseemly to see anyone in their nakedness; one must be wrapped in the winding-sheet of Christ’s righteousness—there is no other shroud like it. Come thus to the grave, and the grave shall have no power over you. But I leave this manner of speaking; Christians, this must be your primary work and concern: that you seriously consider and apply to yourself through faith the infinite grace of God, the overflowing merit of Christ, and the all-sufficiency of His righteousness for your acceptance by God.

**Secondly**, do not only put your faith to work, but also strive for the assurance of God’s love for your souls. Old Simeon said (Luke 2:29-30): *My eyes have seen your salvation, now let me depart in peace.* He held the Messiah not only in his arms but in his heart, and then he could send his soul away with comfort. "Let me now die," said Jacob when he had seen Joseph.

<column-break/>

Never can one die too early for his own comfort and benefit if he has seen Jesus; his death is not untimely or too early, by whatever blow he might be struck down. Otherwise, if you live a hundred years, you die too early if you die before you have obtained a part in Christ. A sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed; old sinners who are permitted to be consumed by their lusts are like chimneys that have long been soot-stained <note>original: "buyl," likely meaning fouled with soot or build-up</note> and finally catch fire.

**Thirdly**, kill your corruptions <note>original: "verdoemthentheden," referring to the sinful nature that leads to condemnation</note>; sin must die before we die. That man dies well whose sins are dead before he is; either sin must die or the sinner. As the Prophet says elsewhere in another case, so I say here: your life must be given for its life. You shall find that those sins are deadly to you which are not put to death <note>Theologians call this "mortification," the ongoing process of killing off sinful habits.</note>. What would an un-mortified man do with Heaven? There is no play or fleshly pleasure there; those blessed dwellings would be to him but dark, melancholy chambers. The Apostle has a particular expression in Colossians 1:12: *He has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light.* We are first made fit for Heaven before we enter it; we are weaned from the world before we leave it. If men cling to the world as long as they can, and only when they can no longer do so do they think to use God for their benefit, then the Lord God will turn them away with contempt, saying: *Go and cry to the gods you have chosen* (Judges 10:14). Let the world help and deliver you now! An un-mortified man is entirely ready to fall; he waits only for a breeze and a rustle <note>original: "wint en gepye," suggesting the slightest disturbance</note>, and he falls like a shock of grain in its time.

**Fourthly**, strive for a holy life and conduct. People live as if they never intended to die, and then they die as if they never intended to live again. The best way to die well is to live well. Those who are not ashamed to live do not fear to die. Balaam wished to die the death of the righteous, but he would not take the trouble to live godlily. Not everyone can say: "Thanks be to God who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." You cannot die in Christ unless you live in Him and, by the power of His life, hasten toward Heaven. Oh, labor then to exercise yourself in these things, to be in a constant state of preparation. In the battle of death, one goes but once; after that, it is impossible to amend what was done; we are either eternally saved or defeated. Now, if you do that which I exhort you to here, you may wait until your change comes, and when it comes, your last hour shall be your best.

->The third utility is for the comfort of God’s children, that they may use this victory of Christ for their refreshment; do not let it slip from your hands.<-

**First**, use it in respect to your friends who have died in the Lord; our weeping somewhat diminishes Christ’s victory. Why should we cry over the day of their exaltation, over their festive wedding day with Jesus Christ? In the early times, said Rivet <note>original: "Rivet, Cathol. Orthod. quaest. 40. l. I. apartis," referring to André Rivet (1572–1651), a French Huguenot theologian. The Latin title refers to his work *Catholicus Orthodoxus*.</note>, it was customary to sing Psalms of thanksgiving at burials. One ought to bring them to the grave like pious combatants, as those who have passed through the spears and finished their course, kept their faith, and [overcome] the world.

<summary>This page exhorts the reader to prepare for death by seeking forgiveness, mortifying sin, and living holily, framing Christ's victory as the only security against eternal torment. It also advises believers to view the death of loved ones as a triumphant "wedding day" with Christ rather than a cause for excessive mourning.</summary>

# The Triumph

overcome and escaped sin, death, and danger. **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful preaching.</note>, speaking in his sermons on the Letter to the Hebrews about ancient funeral customs, mentions their songs of praise, psalms, and hymns; "all these things belong to those who rejoice" <note>original: "haec omnia sunt lætantium"</note> he says, for everything signifies joy. Why would you then want to weep while simultaneously singing a psalm of praise and a song of triumph? It is true, as stated in **Acts 8 verse 2**, that some godly men carried **Stephen** <note>Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr.</note> to his grave and made great mourning over him, for it is our loss when the Church is deprived of such glorious people. There is cause for sorrow there, but there ought to be a mixing of feelings; we must not be sorrowful like others who have no hope (**1 Thessalonians 4 verse 13**). Just as Christians should not rejoice without any sorrow, so they must also be sorrowful with some mixture of joy. We must show that we hope for a resurrection, that we wait to meet our friends again in Heaven. When we weep, it should be like rain when the sun shines; there should be just as much joy in our faces as there are tears in our eyes.

Secondly, use this for yourself:

**I.** During your lifetime, so that you may be willing to die in your intentions. We are sometimes like **Lot** in **Sodom**, or like the **Israelites** in **Egypt**; we may long for **Canaan** <note>The biblical "Promised Land," here used as a metaphor for Heaven.</note>, but we leave Egypt reluctantly. This is a proof of small faith. Can we believe that there is such an excellent and glorious Heaven, and yet not want to go there? Can we hope for such an incorruptible inheritance (**1 Peter 1 verse 4**) and yet fear it? That we shall enter it too soon? What prince would want to live uncrowned? What heir would hesitate when called to receive the inheritance? What thoughts do we have of eternal life? Do we consider it a privilege, or a misery and a burden? And again, it is a proof of small love. Can we claim the love of Christ and yet shun His company and fear it? "Let him be unwilling to die, who is unwilling to go to Christ," says **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note>. It is a proof of poor judgment and observation. What, after all, is this life to be esteemed? The world is nothing but a place of banishment; here is nothing but sighing. All creatures groan together here with the heirs of the promises (**Romans 8 verse 23**). What do you see in the world or in this life that moves you to love it? Are you not weary of misery and sin? The longer you live, the more you sin; surely you have already angered God enough. It is high time to long for another state, and you have sufficiently tasted the world's misery and deceit, and the body's frailty and weakness. A longer life would only be a longer sickness. Why is it, why is it indeed, that we are so reluctant to let these present things go? If it is not a lack of faith, or a lack of love for the Lord Jesus, or a great love for the world, surely it must be the fear of death. And what kind of cowardice of spirit is it to fear an enemy who has been so often conquered by Christ and His Saints? If this is how it stands with you, then I have preached all this time in vain, and the victory of Christ, of which I have spoken, then signifies very little. And note, that the brave-hearted **Heathens** <note>A reference to classical Greek or Roman philosophers, like the Stoics, who faced death with composure.</note> can put you to shame, and so

<column-break/>

you make it so that the Gospel of Christ has less power than the natural principles of morality.

**2.** Especially use this in the time and hour of death. The great **Goliath** <note>Used here as a metaphor for death, the "giant" enemy of mankind.</note> has now fallen, and you may go out to view the dead body (**Isaiah 66 verse 24**). Death itself, which brings terror to mankind and seems to be an obstacle to a Christian’s hope, has been conquered by Christ. Therefore, at that time when it seems to overpower you, apply the victory to yourself: "Thanks be to God, who gives the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." When the heart-spasms <term>hert-vangen: acute physical pangs or contractions felt in the chest during the final moments of life</term> come, remember that these are the last attacks and assaults of death. You may well endure that; it shall trouble you no more. As **Moses** said in **Exodus 14 verse 13**: "The Egyptians whom you have seen today, you shall see them no more forever." Likewise, you shall no longer feel these things; in Heaven there are no sighing, tears, or sorrows. Be patient for only a short time, and as soon as the last gasp is given, the Soul shall be brought by the Angels to Christ, and from Christ to God. Believers are received in the same manner as Christ; He was brought into Heaven by the Angels (**Daniel 7 verse 13**). "They brought him near before the Ancient of Days." And so we are also brought by the Angels into **Abraham’s bosom** (**Luke 16 verse 22**). They have a train of Angels who accompany them to Heaven, just as their friends accompany their bodies to the grave. And just as Christ was welcomed into Heaven with acclamations, and God said to Him, "Sit at my right hand" (**Psalm 110 verse 1**) and "Ask of me, and I shall give thee" (**Psalm 2 verse 8**), so too are the believers greeted with: "Well done, good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your Lord" (**Matthew 25 verse 21**).

What remains then but that we die by faith, just as we live by faith? That we welcome death with confidence and give up our souls in triumph? When **Moses** took the serpent in his hand, it was but a staff; death, thus welcomed and received through faith, shall be at most a chastening—nay, rather a blessing of the covenant, a way and passage into glory.

One thing I had almost forgotten, namely to urge you to gratitude toward Christ. Oh, bless your Redeemer who has freed you from the fear of death! Marvel at His love and humiliation, that He thought of us from Heaven and placed Himself in our stead, taking the terrors of death upon His Soul. It says in **Matthew 20 verse 28**: "The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." Christ was a Prince by birth, an heir of all things; nonetheless, He did not come with the state and equipment of a Prince. Had He come to us thus to visit us and comfort us by word of mouth, it would have been much; but no, Christ did not come in such a manner—not in the splendor of a Prince, but in the form of a servant to serve our needs, and that in the highest way of self-sacrifice. He gave His soul as a ransom for many. Other princes do not value the blood of their subjects much; they do not care how many lay down their lives for them; many give their lives as a ransom for princes. But here it is quite different: this Prince lays down His life to redeem His subjects, and He bears the

# A true account of Man's miserable state in Nature.

-> Preached in 17 Sermons, by Mr. CHRISTOPHORUS LOVE, <-
-> *Translated by P. L.* <-

---
-> Ephesians 2:12. <-

> That at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the citizenship of Israel and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.

<margin>1st Sermon.</margin>
This Chapter from which my Text is taken is like a brief summary, containing within it a description of the <term>Little World<note>original: "de kleyne Wereldt." A common Renaissance and Reformation concept of the human being as a "microcosm" that reflects the order of the larger universe.</note></term>, Man, and that in two ways: considering Man either in the state of grace, or in the state of nature. If you consider Man in the first, in the state of grace, this Chapter gives a particular description of a Man in that state.
   1. Therein is the **efficient cause** <note>original: "werckende oorsaeck." In classical philosophy, the agent that brings something into being.</note> which brings a Man out of the state of nature into the state of grace, and that is God, verse 4.
   2. Therein is the **impulsive cause** <note>original: "aendringende oorsaecke," the internal motivation.</note> and that is the richness of God's grace, in the same verse; *but God, who is rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us, etc.*
   3. Therein is the **meritorious cause** <note>original: "verdende [verdienende] oorsaeck."</note> of the same: the suffering of Christ / verse 7. *so that He might show in the ages to come the surpassing riches of His grace; through the kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.*
   4. Therein is the **final cause** <note>original: "eyndige oorsaeck," the ultimate purpose or goal.</note> in the same verse, *that He might show in the ages to come the surpassing Riches of His grace.* And
   5. Finally, in this Chapter is the **instrumental cause** <note>original: "wercktuyginge oorsaeck," the means by which the change is effected.</note> which brings Men out of the state of nature into the state of grace, and

<column-break/>

this is faith, verse 8. *For by grace you have been saved through faith, and not of yourselves; it is the gift of God.*
   Now the other part, or the description of Man in the second capacity, in the state of nature; of that we have the two following descriptions.
   1. **Positively**, what he is.
   2. **Privatively**, what he lacks.
   First, the description of a Man in the state of nature **Positively**, what he is, and that in five specific things;
   1. Men in their natural state are described here to be *dead in their sins and trespasses*, verse 1.
   2. They *walk according to the age of this World*, as unbelievers and heathens, verse 2.
   3. *According to the prince of the power of the air*, that is, the Devil; now, the Devil is called a Prince of the air because he rules in the air, or because he has power over the winds of the air.
   4. They are called *Children of disobedience*; that is, born in the state of disobedience, walking against the commandments of God.
   5. That they follow the *lusts and desires of the flesh and of the thoughts*, and they are *by nature Children of wrath*.
   Thus far you have the Positive description of Man in the state of nature.
   Now in the second place, the Apostle describes him **Privatively**, what he lacks; and that in the words of my Text, in five specific things wherein he abundantly shows that he is the poorest Man in the World and very miserable, who lacks Jesus Christ; 1. In that time—
