->A true account of man's<-

In the treatment of this, I shall first speak in general, and thereafter in particular; first, to prove this in general. The state of an **unregenerate** <note>original: "onwedergebooren" — referring to someone who has not experienced a spiritual rebirth or conversion.</note> person, in regard to his hope of Heaven, is just like that of Paul and his ship-mates, sailing to Rome, **Acts 27:20**, when neither sun nor stars appeared, and the winds and waters went over the ship; yes, so far, that all hope that they had to be saved was gone; so it is even with you who are without Christ, if Christ does not shine upon you, neither sun nor stars enlighten you; you are like Paul and his companions in the ship, all hope of salvation is gone from you. I shall confirm the truth of this through four arguments: that a **godless** <note>original: "Godtloose" — often referring to those living without regard for divine law.</note> person is without any hope of Heaven.

**Firstly**, An unregenerate person must necessarily be without hope, because he is without Christ, who is the foundation of a Christian’s hope: Therefore remember, says the Apostle, that you were at that time without Christ, and for this reason he relates thereafter that they were without hope. **Ephesians 2:12**. For Christ is called our hope: Christ is that Person upon whom we must build all our hope of Heaven, and for this reason he is called our hope. And this is the meaning of the preceding text, *Christ in you the hope of glory*, <note>original: "Christus in u de hoope der heerlijkheyt"</note> indicating that you can hope for no glory except in and through Christ; the person who is without Christ must necessarily be without hope; this is the first argument.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin> **Secondly**, A person without Christ must necessarily be without hope, because he is without any promise of life and salvation, which alone supports a person’s hope; you shall know that this is a very vain hope, to hope that a rich man shall make you heir to all his goods, when he has never promised you a foot of land; just as vain are the hopes of godless men: But now, a word of promise is a pillar upon which the hearts of God’s people rest, **Titus 1:2**, *in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before the ages began.* The promises prove that a person has a share in Him, in the hope of eternal life, and without the promises, which are the firmness of hope, they must necessarily be without all hope of Heaven.

<margin>3rd Reason.</margin> **Thirdly**, He cannot be otherwise than without hope who is without faith, which is also the ground of hope, **Hebrews 11:1**. *Faith is the firm ground of things hoped for, and a certain proof of matters not seen:* where there is no true faith, there can be no hope; for faith is the mother, and hope is the daughter; hope is begun through faith; an unregenerate person must necessarily be without hope, because he is without Christ, the foundation of hope, the promises the pillar, and faith, the ground of hope.

<margin>4th Reason.</margin> **Fourthly**, It appears that he is without hope because, when he leaves the world, his hope also leaves him, whereas the hope of a godly man does not leave him until it has brought him into Heaven: when a godless man dies, his hope goes away and leaves him when he needed it most; had his hope been well-grounded, it would never have made him ashamed.
Thus you see that I have confirmed this point in gen-

eral. I come now to the particulars of this doctrine; Beloved, please lend me your thoughts for a little while in the investigation of these five things. Namely:

1. I shall show you the nature of that hope which unconverted people do not have.

2. I shall give you the signs of those people who are without any well-grounded hope of Heaven.

3. I shall show you the reason why (notwithstanding that the Scripture says that a godless person has no hope) he, of all people in the world, feeds and cherishes in his heart the greatest hope of Heaven.

4. I shall show wherein the difference lies between those who have only an **imagined** <note>original: "ingebeeide" — illusory or self-deluded.</note> hope of Heaven, and those who have a true and well-grounded hope of the same; and

5. **Lastly**, I shall show you the great misery of people who have nothing more than an imagined hope of Heaven.

I will begin with the first, and show you: what is the nature of the hope that unconverted people do not have?

**Answer.** Take this clear description of it: that true hope, without which the godless are, is a well-grounded and **patient expectation** <note>original: "lytzame verwachtinge" — an endurance-filled waiting.</note> of the fulfillment of those spiritual and eternal things which God has promised through faith in Jesus Christ. I call it a *well-grounded expectation* to distinguish true hope from the imagined hope that the godless have; I call it a *patient hope* to distinguish it from that hasty hope of the godless; and I say that it is a patient expectation of the fulfillment of the spiritual and eternal goods which God has promised in Christ. Because this is the ground of hope, it was called the hope of glory, the hope of eternal life, and the like; thus you have the nature of that hope which the godless do not have: when the Apostle says they were without hope, his meaning is that they were without any hope of those spiritual and eternal goods which God has promised to the believers through Christ.

**2. Question.** What are the signs of people who have no hope of Heaven, or if they have it, it is only an imagined hope by **presumption**, <note>original: "presumtie" — taking for granted without divine warrant.</note> in fact no hope? (Indeed, it would be much better to have no hope than a vain hope.)

Now, before I give these signs by way of discovery, I want to set down only four or five conclusions for the godless, so that they do not make a mistake concerning their hope of Heaven. 1. Take this conclusion: that this grace of hope can be **counterfeited** <note>original: "geconterfeyt" — faked or imitated.</note> just as well as any other grace; there is a living hope in a believer; in a godless person, there is a deceptive hope as well as a true one, an imitation as well as a good one, and therefore it says in **Job 8:13**, *The expectation of the hypocrite shall perish.* And **Proverbs 10:28**, *The expectation of the godless shall perish.*

2. Take this conclusion: that the people who have the least ground to build their hope of Heaven upon, nevertheless most of all assure themselves of the hope of Heaven in their hearts. I shall give you two primary Scripture passages to prove this: **Proverbs 14:16**, where it says that *the wise man fears and departs from evil.* A wise man is jealous over his own heart; what follows? *But the fool*, that is, a god-

### The Miserable State in Nature.

The godless is hot-tempered and careless; he runs along his godless ways and deeds without any disturbance or agitation, and yet he holds himself certain of coming to Heaven as well as the best. A wise man fears and departs from evil, but the fool is hot-tempered and careless. Those who have the least reason for hope often labor to keep the greatest hope of Heaven in their hearts. You have a similar passage in **Psalm 36:2: The transgression of the godless speaks within his heart, there is no fear of God before his eyes.** And yet it says in the following words, *he flatters himself in his own eyes, until his iniquity is found to be hateful.* The godless are very capable of having good concepts of themselves, and you shall usually find that a poor soul who walks conscientiously before God, neglects no known duty, kills all known lusts, and walks in humility before God, is fearful and jealous <note>original: "jaloers" — in this context, meaning "zealous" or "suspiciously watchful" over one's own spiritual state</note>, doubting whether all things are well between God and his soul. And yet you shall find that others, given over to sin and godlessness, doing daily the will of the flesh and of their thoughts, assure themselves more of Heaven—believing all is well with them—even as they run post-haste to Hell.

<margin>1. Question.</margin>
<margin>Answer:</margin>
3. The third conclusion is this: that a man may live and die with a strong hope of Heaven until the moment he is thrust down into Hell; he may have no thoughts other than going to Heaven, until he is suddenly cast into Hell. I shall give you some clear texts for this: **Job 21:23**, where Job speaks of a godless man, saying: *This one dies in the strength of his perfection, while he was quiet and at rest.* A theologian <note>original: "Godts-geleerde" — a scholar of divinity or a pastor</note> says regarding this passage that it is a mark of a godless man when he lies on his deathbed and, if you come to him and ask if he has any hope of Heaven, he says, "I have a very strong hope of the same." And if you ask him if any sins trouble him, and he then says, "God be thanked, I have no sins that disturb me now, nor have I committed any in my lifetime"; what shall this rest profit him? Not at all; he has no dissatisfied thoughts about himself, and therefore he cannot come to Heaven; for when a godless man dies, his expectation shall perish. Now beloved, it seems to me that this ought to move you a little, so that you do not run blindly into Hell with a quiet, restful state in the hope of Heaven, thinking nothing else even as you go to Hell.

<margin>2. Question.</margin>
5. You who have a strong hope of Heaven, let me tell you that you have no right to hope for Heaven until you have some reason or ground for your hope. Beloved, it is not natural for every man to hope for Heaven and be saved without having any ground for it, as the Apostle says in **1 Peter 3:15: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be always ready to give an answer to everyone who demands an account of the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear.** Now examine yourselves: what ground can you give for your hope of Heaven? Do you have any promise of it? Or any scriptural ground for it? Or the witness of the Spirit for it? If not, do not feed a hope of Heaven in your hearts. Now I shall handle the question itself.

What are the signs by which it may

<column-break/>

appear that you are one of those who have no hope of Heaven, or a quiet, imaginary, and ungrounded hope, which is as good as no hope?

The hearts of all the children of men are desperately godless and sorrowful above all things in the world; man is a poor creature, and yet has a high opinion of himself. For this reason, I shall give you five distinct signs by which you may know whether your hope of Heaven be true and a well-grounded hope, or not.

1. The man who feeds a great hope of Heaven in his heart, and yet at the same time cherishes and delights himself in his own lusts, has no true hope of Heaven. I shall give you a clear passage to prove this: **Deuteronomy 29:19. And it shall come to pass, when he hears the words of this curse, that he blesses himself in his heart, saying, "I shall have peace, though I walk according to the imagination of my heart, to add drunkenness to thirst." The Lord will not spare him, but then the anger of the Lord and his jealousy shall smoke against that man.** So also **Isaiah 57:10: You are wearied by your great journey <insert>of godless ways</insert> but you do not say, "It is beyond hope."** This is a very powerful passage, as if the Prophet wanted to say to them: you walk in the long ways of sin and godlessness and flatter yourselves; you will not say, "It is beyond hope"; you feed great sins and godlessness in your bosom and please yourselves in committing them; you do not doubt your hope of Heaven, and yet you walk in the ways of sin; you are content within yourselves to come to Heaven. So also in the aforementioned passage, **Psalm 36:2, 3**.

2. A man has no true, but only a vain and imaginary hope of Heaven, who is powerful in his expectation of Heaven but sluggish in his works and deeds toward holiness as his way. He who, like Balaam, can desire to die the death of the righteous, and yet takes no care to live the life of the righteous: the hope of such a person is but a vain hope, as the Psalmist says in **Psalm 119:155: Salvation is far from the godless, for they do not seek your statutes.** And if salvation or blessedness is far off, the hope of salvation is even further. But why is the salvation of the godless far off? Because they do not seek God’s statutes. People who hope that salvation is near when they are far from the observance of God’s statutes and holiness—which is the way to happiness—these people are far from salvation and from the hope of it.

A man has only a deceptive hope of Heaven if he is unwilling to have his hope tested through examination and brought to the touchstone <note>original: "Toetsteen" — a black stone used to test the purity of gold; figuratively, a standard of trial or judgment</note>; those who do not want to submit to this, as the Apostle admonishes us in **1 Peter 3:15: Be always ready to give an answer to everyone who demands an account of the hope that is in you.** Now let me ask you, what ground do you have for your hope in Heaven? Do you have the testimony of God's Spirit, or the testimony of a good conscience, which in simplicity and godly sincerity assures you of your pious walk here in this world? Do you have any promise or ground in the scriptures for your hope? If you have no ground for your hope, and are not...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "miserable state of man," focusing specifically on the difference between the false, self-reliant hope of the "godless" and the true, God-given hope of the believer. # A true account of man's...

...cannot withstand the Touchstone <note>original: "Toetsteen" — a stone used to test the purity of gold and silver; here used as a metaphor for God's judgment</note>; it is a proof that you are a counterfeit metal; that you do not have an active hope of salvation and glory in the next world.

4. The man who bases his hope of Heaven more on his own accomplishments and efforts than on God’s promises, his hope is only a deceptive hope; this is the sandy foundation that Christ speaks of in Matthew 7:26-27. To build your hope of Heaven on any of your services, or on the fulfillment of certain duties, is as much as if you built a house on a sandy foundation. Ask a godless man on what he grounds his hope of Heaven; he will tell you that he does works of charity, he gives every man his due, he lives honestly and civilly among his neighbors, he hears and reads the Word, he prays and receives the Sacraments, he performs such and such duties; and this is that upon which he holds his hope of Heaven. They believe that Christ is married to them because they take the Lord's Supper—for Christ's ordinances are His "wedding feast"—and they are ready to say with those in Luke 13:26: *We have eaten and drunk in your presence, Lord, open to us.*

I do not deny that a man must have this grace in his heart; but the greatest pillar upon which your hope must lean must be the promises of God in Christ. He who bases his hope of Heaven solely on his own duties and good works, his hope is a vain and deceptive hope. I do not deny that the graces of God's Spirit are actual proofs of God's love to the soul, just as the Apostle says in 1 John 3:14: *We know that we have passed from death into life, because we love the brothers.* And again, verse 24: *By this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.* But I say, this is not the primary pillar and ground of our hope. We must be as diligent in our duties as if we expected salvation through them; but when we have done everything we can do and laid it down at the feet of Christ, then we must conclude that our best works are but a filthy garment <note>original: "vuyl kleet" — a reference to Isaiah 64:6, implying that human righteousness is stained by sin</note>, and we have done no more than we were bound to do; we are still unprofitable servants <note>original: "on-nutte dienstknechten" — see Luke 17:10</note>. And we must lean only on the merits and mercies of Jesus Christ for our comfort and salvation.

5. The man who thinks there is no difficulty in obtaining this gracious hope, nor any work in preserving it, this man has no true hope. You who think there is no difficulty in obtaining this grace—that it is in your power to acquire and keep it—and believe it is easy to have the hope of Heaven, oh, you have never had a true hope! For it must be God who works this grace in you, as the Apostle says in Romans 15:13: *Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing.* Secondly, those who think there is no work in the preservation of this grace of hope have no true hope; for wherever true hope is, it carries these qualities with it:

<margin>1 John 3:3</margin>
1. It has a purifying power within it. *Everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure.*

2. Hope carries steadfastness with it. It is the Anchor of the Soul, both sure and steadfast; although the Devil and the world disturb and unrest you through temptations and allurements, nevertheless this grace of hope makes you quiet and peaceful; those who hope in God shall be secure and at rest.

3. Hope has a diligent <note>original: "pijnelyke" — in 17th-century Dutch, this meant "laborious" or "painstaking" rather than "painful"</note> quality with it; it is never lazy. It always finds an impossibility where hope is cut off. But what a man hopes for, toward that he will labor to obtain and enjoy it: he who plows, plows in hope. So also, the hope of Heaven will make you plow in the furrows of your heart, and make you diligent in your labor toward Heaven, so that you will take great pains and exert all your strength to obtain the same.

## We come now to the third Question, which is this:

What is the Reason (seeing the Scripture says that a godless man has no hope) that of all people in the world, the godless nourish the greatest hope of Heaven in their hearts?

**Answer:** In the resolution of this question, I shall set forth five false foundations upon which the hope of the godless stands, and at once point out the weakness and looseness of these for building any hope of Heaven.

1. The first thing upon which the godless build their hope of Heaven is this: they think they have committed only small sins in their lives, and have not broken out into great and scandalous sins like other men. Therefore they say, surely we have some ground to hope for Heaven; it is true we are sinners, but my sins are only small faults; they are not sins of a "double death." Just as the Pharisee said:
<margin>Luke 18:11</margin>
*O God, I thank you that I am not like other men—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.* Because he was not as evil as other men, he thought he had a right to Heaven; because they are not as bad as the worst, they think themselves to be as good as the best. Now I shall point out to you the weakness and the rottenness of this pillar upon which your hope of Heaven stands.

1. # A True Account of Man's [Miserable State]

Christ had been denied; he went out and wept bitterly over it. But I say, what do all these examples matter to you, who make a habit of sin and fall into great sins every day, from time to time, and yet are never mournful or sorrowful over them as David was, nor weeping bitterly like Peter? What can this then benefit you, as a ground upon which to build a hope of Heaven?

3. Know this further: that a Godly man may fall into the same sin that others fall into, as far as the *matter* <note>The physical substance or specific act of the sin.</note> is concerned, but not the *manner*. Now, it is the manner of falling into sin, and not the matter of it, which damns a man. It is true, Noah fell into the sin of drunkenness, but I shall make a distinction between Noah and any other drunkard in the world, and that in these five observations:

1. Noah was drunk, but before he knew the strength of the wine or knew that it made one drunk; and if you read the History, you shall find there was no wine before that time, for Noah set himself to be a husbandman <note>A farmer or tiller of the soil.</note> and planted a vineyard. But there is none among you who does not know the strength of wine and strong beer, and yet you will not stop drinking; there is a great difference between you and Noah.

2. Noah was drunk, but he did not boast of his drunkenness, for the Text says: *he turned into his tent and slept*; he was ashamed of what he had done. But now you shout out your sins; you swear and lie while committing your drunkenness.

3. It is true Noah was drunk, yet you do not read that he was so more than once; but you are drunk again and again, one day after the other.

4. Although he once fell into this sin, nonetheless, according to the ordinary course and practice of his life, he was an upright man in his generation; but your ordinary habit is drunkenness.

5. Noah was a tiller of the field, and in this respect he had more need of wine to revive his spirits, which is not so with the young folk; so that all these observations lessen Noah’s fault a little, although they are not entirely to be excused.

And likewise David: he began the sin of adultery; he wallowed in an unclean bed; yet nonetheless his sins may be excused in some observations.

1. When David came upon the roof of his house, he dreamed a little; he had seen there a naked woman, which was a very great temptation to him. But it may be that some of you seek out the opportunity, how you might commit such shameful sins.

2. David fell into this sin but once; you shall commonly find that the Godly have fallen into great sins only once; they keep watch after the first transgression, and seldom do they fall again into the same sin. And now, you may live in unchaste thoughts and works your whole life long; and therefore this does not serve to build up your hope.

3. Although David fell into this sin, nonetheless he did not persist long in it, for after nine months the Prophet Nathan came to David, recounted and proved the sin to him, and at the same time, the time when it was committed. But alas! some of you are adulterers

<column-break/>

of nine years; yes, there may be old adulterers among us who never have a right sorrow of heart over their sins, who never weep and mourn as David did.

And so Peter: he fell into the sin of denying his Lord and Master, but:

1. He had intended to confess Him and not to deny Him; and yet when the maidservant came to him and spoke to him, [saying] he was also one who was with Christ, Peter denied it—perhaps out of fear of death, that they would crucify him as well as Christ. Upon this (which was a great temptation to him), he denied Christ. And:

2. Although he denied Him three times, nonetheless afterward he confessed Him again as many times as he had denied Him; for when Christ asked him, *Simon Peter, do you love me?* he answered Christ three times: *Lord, you know that I love you.*

3. Peter denied Christ, but afterward he went out and wept bitterly for this; and therefore his obtained mercy can be no ground for your hope, you who are never converted from any sins you have committed. And thus you see that the falling of these three Godly men into sin may be no ground for your hope of Heaven.

Now I shall show you even more specifically that although the Godly fall into sin—even into the same sin as you do—they nonetheless differ from you in the manner: as,

1. When a Godly person falls into sin, it is unwillingly and with resistance. In Galatians 6:1 the Apostle says: *If a man be overtaken in any fault.* <note>original: "Indien ook een mensche over-vallen ware door eenighe misdaden."</note> A Godly person resists sin and temptation with all his might, yet sometimes it overcomes him against his will; but an ungodly person runs toward sin and overpowers it; he sins with a purpose of heart. Psalm 36:5: *He deviseth unrighteousness upon his bed; he setteth himself in a way that is not good.*

2. A Godly person sometimes falls into sin, but it is with resistance; the Spirit fights against the flesh; there is an opposition or resistance against the sin. They are not like the faint-hearted, but want to fight as long as they can hold the weapons in their hands; but the ungodly commit sin greedily, with delight and pleasure, without any resistance at all.

3. Every sin that a Godly person commits makes him careful and watchful for the time to come. So it was with David in Psalm 38. Compare the title with Psalm 39:1. The 38th Psalm is called *A Psalm to bring to remembrance.* The proposed subject of this Psalm was to make David remember his sins, and having kept the memory of his sins in mind, he says in the first words of the following Psalm: *I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue.* After he had brought his sins to remembrance, then he struggled with himself not to commit them anymore in future times. When a Godly person falls into a sin once, he is afraid to fall into the same again afterward.

4. A Godly person, although he sometimes falls into sins, nonetheless he seeks to gain the upper hand over sin; although for the present he often cannot overcome the sin, nonetheless he wants to at last [subdue it]...

# The Miserable State in Nature

bring. His grace calls out sin and obtains the victory over it; and thus I have shown you the second ground upon which the godless base their hope of Heaven, and that it is vain; now we come to the third.

Their third ground, if they are driven from the first and second, is the **mercy of God**; "Oh!" they say, "God is a very merciful God, and I hope that He shall save me, and that I shall go to Heaven as well as other people," and the like. Now, I do not deny that God’s mercy is the chief support of Heaven, upon which a person may build his hope of Heaven: but here I shall show you the weakness of this support, and that in four or five respects—that God’s mercies in general are not a sufficient ground to build the hope of Heaven upon, so long as you do not enjoy God’s mercy in particular; for, if you keep your hope of Heaven in general upon God’s mercy:

1. The Devils and damned spirits may then hope as well as you.

2. So long as you have no special graces from God, the general ones cannot be profitable to you. These the Godless can also have, for God is good to all, and His tender mercy is over all His works: The Devils feel the common mercy of God as well as others; but upon these common benefits of God one cannot build a hope of Heaven, until you have the saving and special benefits of God, as David prays: *Be merciful to me, O God, with the kindness of your own children*; it must be election, redemption, sanctification, and saving mercy upon which you may build your hope of heaven.

3. The common benefits of God cannot be the ground to build your hope of Heaven upon, until you have a part in Christ; For God is clothed with greatness, wrath, and terror without Christ; there is nothing to be seen in God but terror without Christ. There were two laws that God made concerning the **Mercy-Seat** <term>Mercy-Seat: In the biblical Tabernacle, this was the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant, representing the throne of God and the place where atonement was made.</term>.

1. The High Priest might not, under penalty of death, come to the Mercy-Seat until he brought incense with him; now what does this signify to us? Truly, it represented the intercession of Christ, that just as Aaron could not come to the Mercy-Seat without incense, so we cannot go to the Throne of Grace to obtain mercy from God, with any hope of being heard or accepted, until we carry incense with us, which is the Lord Jesus Christ, to speak for us.

2. Aaron had to sprinkle the Mercy-Seat with blood; which illustrates to us that we had no mercy to expect from God, unless we had a part in the blood of Jesus Christ.

4. You who build your hope of Heaven on the common mercies of God, let me tell you that God does not lavish His special mercies, or bestow them upon the whole world, but only allows them to come upon a specific number of people: *His mercy is on those who fear him* (Luke 1:50). But the godless, and those who continue in their sins—

<column-break/>

—of them the Lord Himself says: *Though He made them, yet He will show them no mercy.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 27:11.</note> The mercies of God in general are not a sufficient support to build the hope of Heaven upon.

<margin>Objection</margin> **Objection.** But it seems to me that I hear some people objecting here and saying: why do you need to pull us away from our hope of Heaven; do you want to rob us of the same and bring us into despair?

<margin>Answer</margin> 1. **Answer.** For all those who have a true ground for the hope of Heaven, I would not cause your hope to waver for the whole world; the smaller the tree, the more it shakes, and the larger it is, the firmer it stands; I want everything said this day to be understood as referring to the vain and deceptive hope of the Godless, and that it may confirm your good and lasting hope, so that it grows stronger and stronger.

2. God forbid that it should be in my heart to drive any of you to despair; O no, what I have said is not to make anyone of you fall into despair, but to keep you from idle imaginations, which is the more dangerous error of the two; for while a thousand are crushed against the stone of despair, ten thousand are crushed by idle imaginations.

3. My meaning, and what I have said, is not to rob you of all your hope of Heaven, but only of your false and poorly grounded hope; I want you to cast down all your rotten hope and build the same on a surer foundation, on Jesus Christ, being the chief Cornerstone.

4. # A True Narrative of Man’s [Condition]

...demonstrate the stability of this ground, to build the hope of Heaven upon. But I do not want you to misunderstand me, as if I were overturning good works and holy duties; for I want you to fulfill your duties as if you intended to be saved through them. But when you have done everything you can do, then lay yourself down at the feet of *Christ* <note>original: "Christi"</note> and desire everything from him as if you had done nothing. I shall show you the instability of this foundation through four points, because:

1. All fulfillment of duties does not move God the Father through *Christ* <note>original: "Christum"</note> as long as you have not been accepted through him. It would be just as possible to kneel in prayer to God for a lifetime as it would be to not kneel at all; it would be as possible for you to cry your eyes out in lamenting your sins until all the fluids in your body were dried up; it would be as possible for you to spend all your days in listening, reading, praying, and fulfilling holy duties; yet if you do not offer them to God in the name and thought of *Jesus Christ*, they are all but **ciphers** <note>In 17th-century math, a "cipher" was a zero—a placeholder that has no value on its own.</note> that make no sum, until the righteousness of *Jesus Christ* is added to them. It is *Christ’s* righteousness that makes our services acceptable to God:
> *Christ* adds his **Incense** to the prayers of all **Saints**.
Now beloved, even though you offer so many prayers, if you still have no part in the suffering of *Christ* and in his intercession to God for you, all your prayers and holy duties are worth nothing and shall never bring you to Heaven. Our persons must be in *Christ* before our services can be accepted by God; and therefore the fulfillment of duties cannot be a foundation upon which to build the hope of Heaven.

2. These things cannot be a foundation to build the hope of Heaven because the **hypocrites** <note>original: "geveynsden"</note>—whose persons and duties God hates—perform these duties just as well as you. The *Pharisees* fasted twice a week, gave alms, and performed holy duties. And likewise those of whom it is spoken in *Isaiah 58:2-3*: *They seek me daily, and delight to know my ways, as a nation that did righteousness, and did not forsake the ordinance of their God; they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in approaching to God, saying: "Why have we fasted, and you see it not?"* God did not accept anything they did. So it is also with the prayer of the **wicked**; *The prayer of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord*, says *David*; and so it is with their listening; they listen while their hearts are far away.

3. Know this: that those very duties which God accepts from the hands of his children, those same duties he will reject when they come from the hands of the **wicked**. Therefore, the fulfillment of duties cannot be a foundation of our hope of heaven; for although you might pray, hear, read, or fast longer than a godly person, nevertheless the Lord will accept his duties and not yours. I shall give you three examples of this: The first is between *Cain* and *Abel*. *Abel* offered the firstlings of his sheep and cattle, and their fat, and *Cain* offered the first fruits of his land. Now, by faith *Abel* offered a greater sacrifice than *Cain*, *Hebrews 11*. Although *Cain's* sacrifice seemed more

<column-break/>

impressive than *Abel's*, yet *Abel's* was accepted and his was not. *Abel's* sacrifice was accepted not because of its quantity or worthiness, but because he was faithful and a righteous man in God's sight; and therefore the Lord looked first at his person, and then at his sacrifice. The second example is in *1 Kings 18:25* between *Elijah* the Prophet and the prophets of *Baal*. The prophet *Elijah* took two **bulls**, and you may think that they did not take the worst one; and he prepared the other. And yet the Lord showed a sign there that he accepted the sacrifice of *Elijah*, even though it was the lesser **bull**; and he showed no acceptance of the prophets of *Baal*. The reason for this was that *Elijah* was righteous, and they were not. And so again in *Proverbs 15:8*, it is said that the sacrifice of the **wicked** is an abomination to the Lord, but the prayer of the upright is his delight. God takes pleasure in a poor little prayer coming from a pious person, whereas he will not accept the costly sacrifice of the **wicked**.

4. The fulfillment of duties cannot be a foundation to build the hope of Heaven because God does not look so much at the substance of the duty as he does at the **manner** how, and the **end** for which you fulfill it. In everything God requires and commands, God looks at the manner in which you do it. God will not accept duties if they are not done in a right manner and for a good end. *John 16:24*: *Hitherto* (says *Christ*) *you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full.* And yet they had offered many prayers in his name; but because they did not pray in the right manner, *Christ* looks upon them as if they had never prayed.

5. There is yet another false foundation upon which the **wicked** build their hope of Heaven: a misuse of the promises and grounds of hope in Scripture. And this they do in two ways: either,

1. They make these promises into foundations for their hope when they are not; or,

2. They misuse the promises which are true grounds of hope.

1. They make these into foundations of their hope when they are not. I shall give you all those passages recounted in our common church-book <note>likely referring to the Anglican Book of Common Prayer</note>: *When the wicked turns from his sins, I will bring all his sins out of my mind, says the Lord.* This **saying** has been a means to deceive a whole world of people; but it provides no ground at all to build the hope of Heaven upon.

1. Such words as these are not to be found in the entire Scripture.

2. The place where these words appear is only in the *Common Prayer Book*, which prayers are but an **offshoot** <note>original: "afvleysel," a derogatory term suggesting a scrap or derivative remnant</note> of the **Popish Mass**. For although everything that is in the *Popish Mass* is not in the *Common Prayer Book*, nevertheless everything that is in the *Common Prayer Book* is in the *Popish Mass*. It may be that you find this hard to believe, but it is nonetheless true, as you can see in the second part of the *Book of Martyrs* <note>John Foxe's "Acts and Monuments"</note>, page 667, where there is a letter from *King Edward* the Sixth sent to the *Papists* in *Cornwall*, who had risen up in arms...

# The Miserable State in [Human] Nature

...stood, concerning the translation of the Mass into the English language, which they would in no way permit; King Edward, in order to pacify them, wrote to them in this manner: "Regarding the Church-book, the translation may seem strange to you, as if it contained some new things, but they are the same words in English which they were previously in Latin; and if the Mass-book <note>original: "Misboek"</note> in Latin is good, then it is also good now, although it has been translated into the English tongue." <note>This likely refers to King Edward VI's response to the Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549, where he defended the new English liturgy against those who demanded the Latin Mass.</note>

3. You shall say: the Lord has spoken himself: "When the wicked turns from his sins, I will bring all his sins out of my thoughts." I answer that it does not say so in the entire Scripture; you shall find it otherwise, in Ezekiel 18:21. Mark the words; these are God's own: "When the wicked turns from all his sins that he has done, and keeps all my statutes, and does that which is lawful and right: he shall surely live, he shall not die." They say, "If a wicked man performs conversion <note>original: "bekeeringe"</note> from his sins": now, conversion is a work which even Judas did, yet his conversion did him no good; but here you see it is said, that when the wicked turns from *all* his sins, and does what is right and just, then he shall certainly live.

2. The other passage which the wicked take to build their hope of Heaven upon has no foundation for this, namely, that "the righteous man sins seven times a day." This is one of the greatest grounds for the wicked; they say: "Why do you recount my sins to me? The best of the righteous fall seven times a day into sin, and why should I not go to Heaven as well as they?" They misunderstand this passage and use it as a false foundation; the text stands in Proverbs 24:16: *The righteous man shall fall seven times and rise again: but the wicked shall stumble into evil.* Now, there is no mention made there of falling into *sins*, or of a *single day*; but only, *a righteous man shall fall seven times, and rise again.* Augustine interprets these words thus: "A godly man shall fall seven times, that is, often," explaining this passage alongside that in Job chapter 5:19: *In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh no evil shall touch thee.* A righteous man, says Augustine, falls seven times, not into sin, but into **affliction** <term>original: "verdrukkinge"; refers here to external trials or suffering rather than moral failure</term>, that is, he is often seized and troubled here in this world; according to the words of Job: "Out of six troubles he shall deliver thee," often and many times; and therefore this passage has no regard whatsoever for falling into sin daily.

2. Even if it were so, that the righteous man sinned seven times a day, nevertheless the text says in the following words that as often as he falls, he rises again. Now it may be that many of you who make this a ground for your hope of Heaven fall into sins every day, and never rise out of them again through repentance: you leave these words behind, "and rise again," for many of you spend your whole life in evil; you wallow and turn yourselves in sin, and therefore this can be no ground for your hope.

3. The third reason they make into a Scriptural ground—which it is not—is this: that Christ died for all and every person in the world. This agrees with the **Arminians** <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius, who argued that Christ's atonement was intended for all people, contrary to the strict Calvinist view of "Limited Atonement" for the elect only.</note>, but this sentiment is driven by others as well as by them, namely, a **General Redemption** <term>original: "Algemeen verlossinge"; the doctrine that Christ's death paid for the sins of all humanity without exception</term>. But because I have already

<column-break/>

delivered two or three sermons on this matter, I shall only say what is necessary to point out to you the vanity and weakness of this foundation.

1. Suppose Christ had died for all; those who advance this opinion still do not hold that all people are saved through Christ, but some fall away from Christ and are damned, notwithstanding that Christ died for them.

2. Take this as an answer: that they shall have no benefit through Christ's blood who have no benefit through his death.

3. To those who make this a prop for your hope of Heaven: mark that where these general expressions occur, they are difficult to understand; if you say they speak of a general redemption, as in 2 Corinthians 5:15: *For we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead. And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again.* Truly, here no one can have communion in Christ's death who does not live for Christ, who died for him; and so in Hebrews 2:9: *But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man.* But mark the restraint in the very next words: *For it became him, for whom are all things... in bringing many sons unto glory* (mark what the Apostle says) *to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings. For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one; for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren.* The Apostle limits the words here again, and therefore this can be no ground for your hope, you who are not sanctified; but let this much be said of the first branch in pointing out to you how a wicked man misuses these Scriptural passages, which can be no ground for their hope.

3. If they do not take these passages as grounds for their hopes—which they are not—they nonetheless misunderstand those passages which truly are Scriptural promises and grounds of hope, such as that Christ came to save sinners (Matthew 18:11). Now, this is a Scriptural promise, for Christ has come to seek that which was lost (Luke 19:10). But now, Beloved, people misunderstand this general ground of hope, and that in this way:

1. In the failure to consider that a person must first be *in Christ* before he has any right to the promises of Christ. They run to the promises and do not first investigate whether they have a part in Christ.

The promise is good and comforting, but it can bring no comfort to the soul until you are in Christ, no more than a pipe of water [can bring water] without a fountain: we are first made Christ's, and then we have a right to all the promises of Christ; it is through our part in Christ that we have a right to all the promises of God in Christ; if you have a right in Christ, you have all the promises as if in a small bundle together, of which you may make use as you will.

2. They object and say that the promises are in free and general terms, having no condition attached to them.

Answer: It is true, there are some promises that are absolute, having no condition going before them; yet every promise in the Gospel...

# A True Account of Man's [State]

<column-break/>

the Gospel has one condition or another attached to it; though not a condition by way of merit, but rather as a consequence. As in *Genesis 17:1*: I am God Almighty; (what follows?) walk before my face, and be upright. *2 Corinthians 6:16, 18*: I will be their God, and they shall be my people; I will be a Father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty. What follows? In the first verse of the next chapter, the Apostle says: Since we then have these promises, (a killing promise <note>The author likely refers to a promise that "kills" the old self or demands a death to sin; alternatively, it may be a critique of those who take promises without the accompanying duties.</note>) let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. So also *Hebrews 5:9*: Christ came into the world to save sinners, but the condition follows: He who sanctifies, and those who are sanctified, are all of one. There is no promise in the Gospel but that it carries a preceding or following condition with it. In *Matthew 11:28*, Christ says: Come all to me who are weary and heavy laden, I will give you rest. There is a preceding condition: we must come to Christ. I could point out other examples, but these are sufficient.

In addition to this, there are two more loose foundations. I will pass over one for now, so that it might not hinder me in my **afternoon sermon**, in showing the distinction between those who have an actual and well-grounded hope, and others who have nothing more than a false and ungrounded hope.

6. There is yet another foundation upon which the wicked build their hope of Heaven, which is: because they live a holy and righteous life among their neighbors. They give every man his due, and do no wrong to their own bodies, and the like; and therefore they conclude within themselves that their state is very good.

**Answer:** If this were a sufficient ground to hope for Heaven, more of the Heathens <note>A common 17th-century term for non-Christians, particularly the "virtuous pagans" of antiquity like Socrates or Cato.</note> would go to Heaven than you. For they walk uprightly and are righteous in their dealings. But wicked and evil people may have a "good intention" within them, as we see in *Balaam, Numbers 23:10*. He desired to die the death of the upright, and that his end might be like theirs; this was a good desire and intention in him.

2. Take this for an answer: that although an evil intention spoils a good work, nevertheless, a good intention cannot advance or make good an evil deed. Just like the Scribes and Pharisees: they did many good works in themselves, but they had their own ends and evil intentions, which wiped out all their duties. A good intention cannot justify an evil act. If the actions are wicked, a good intention cannot make them good. *Romans 8*: These say, let us do evil that good may come, their damnation is just.

3. Let your intention be ever so good, yet if you have an ignorant mind, it is of no value. *Proverbs 19:2*: The soul without knowledge is not good. A man becomes rich through means and labor; so also no one comes to Heaven solely through means without good deeds that accompany them.

But, they say, we do no man any wrong, but give each his due.

**Answer 1:** Although you give every man his due, do you give God His own? Or rather, do you not wrong God and offer Him infinite insults?

2. Although you do no man wrong,

<column-break/>

do you not nonetheless wrong your own soul? Many people are enemies to no one but themselves. So also, do you not do your own souls wrong when you harbor foul and corrupt lusts within? What will it benefit you that you do no wrong to others, when you wrong your own souls? You are no better than the Pharisees, who also gave each their due. Of this, that proud Pharisee boasted in *Luke 18:11*: He was no robber or unrighteous man. You may mean well, and give every man his due, and nonetheless be a wicked person.

-> Ephesians 2:12 <-

> That at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the citizenship of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.

We come now to the last foundation upon which the wicked build their hope of Heaven, which is this: when they are driven away from all their previous grounds—from their small sins, from the general mercies of God, from their good duties and good intentions, etc.—they say: "Have we no reason to nourish hope of Heaven? For we have been present with dying people who were as evil in their lives as we are, and yet they had a very strong hope of Heaven and strong hope in God. And you know that dying people will speak the truth; therefore, why should we not nourish a hope of Heaven in ourselves as well as they?" This is a very strong foundation upon which the wicked build their hope of Heaven. I shall show you the fragility and weakness of this in three or four particular things.

1. You must know that it is one thing to die numbly <note>original: "bottelyk" - meaning to die without spiritual sensation or awareness, like a dull blade.</note>, and another thing to die hopefully and peacefully. Truly, the worst people in the world may die unfeelingly, so that their conscience does not perform its office when they die. They may have a seared conscience and think they are going to Heaven, and never think otherwise, even as they fall down into Hell. But the godly man dies in full peace and comfort. *Psalm 37:37*: Mark the perfect man, and behold the upright, for the end of that man is peace. But, there is no peace for the wicked, says my God, *Isaiah 57 and 41*. There may be a sleepiness of the conscience and a hardness of the heart, but they cannot die in peace and in hope.

2. You who make this a ground for your hope—because you have seen a wicked person die peacefully, going out like a lamp—let me tell you this: that such a thing is the greatest judgment in the world—for a wicked person to die peacefully and fall asleep quietly, having hope of Heaven, when they are suddenly cast headlong into hell. It would be better for them if God let the sparks of hellfire fly in their face; it would be better that his conscience told him of his danger than to die in such a still quietness. *Job 21:23*: One dies in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet. No sin disturbs him, nor does any gesture make him afraid. *Psalm 73:4, 5*: They have no [bands in their death...]

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of "false foundations" of spiritual security. Having previously discussed common misconceptions about God's promises, the author now addresses the deceptive peace of mind experienced by those living in sin, contrasting their "imaginary hope" with the "well-grounded hope" of the righteous.</meta>

### The Miserable State in Nature

->**Lll 2**<-
<meta>catchword: 6. True</meta>

...have no bonds until their death, and their strength is fresh; they are not in trouble like other men. <note>This entire opening passage is a paraphrase of Psalm 73:4-5, describing how the wicked often seem to live and die without obvious suffering.</note> They have no agitation during their life, and no bonds <note>Original: "banden," referring to the "pangs" or "chains" of death.</note> until their death: now this is rather to be reckoned to them as a [false] advantage than a sign of grace.

3. If this peace and rest in the conscience of an ungodly person comes from some deep assurance or hope of Heaven, then one might view it as a blessing; but when it comes from the tranquility of his own heart, then it is nothing more than a golden door to let him into Hell; it shall be with him just as in *Isaiah 29:8*:
> When a hungry man dreams he has eaten; but when he wakes, his soul is empty.
So, an ungodly man dreams he goes to Heaven, even as he falls down into Hell.

4. A great hope of Heaven may be expressed in the words of a dying man, even when there is not so much as a spark of peace and rest in his heart. In the mouth there is laughter, but the heart is full of sorrow, says Solomon <note>A reference to Proverbs 14:13.</note>; in the mind of the ungodly is the fear of Hell.

<margin>14th Sermon</margin>
5. Although you have seen some people die with a stillness and tranquility of heart, yet other ungodly people, who had an awakened conscience, died full of horror and trembling; when their consciences recounted to them that they had lived as swearers, or liars, or drunkards, or adulterers, etc. They are filled with trembling and terror of conscience, and although they thought all the time of their life to go to Heaven, yet now they fear going down into Hell.

And thus I have handled the third Question, showing you the reasons why (notwithstanding that the Scripture says the ungodly have no hope) of all people in the world, the ungodly nourish the greatest hope in their hearts. There are only two more Questions to handle, and then I shall come to the fifth Branch of man’s Misery.

<margin>4th Question</margin>
4. The fourth Question in order is this: since the Scripture says that the ungodly man has no hope, and considers his false and imagined hope as no hope at all; how then shall we know the distinction between the well-grounded hope that the godly have, and the imagined and deceptive hopes of the ungodly?

Answer: I shall give you six clear distinctions here.

1. The hope of a godly and reborn person for Heaven is grounded upon and through the Word of God: and therefore it is called the hope of the Gospel, *Colossians 1:23*, because it is wrought through the Gospel as a means, and grounded on the Gospel as the end. So that we (says the Apostle, *Romans 15:4*):
> through patience and comfort of the Scriptures, might have hope.
A godly person has his comfort from the Scriptures, *Psalm 119:49*:
> Remember the word to your servant, upon which you have caused me to hope.
But now, as for the hope of the ungodly, they know not upon what or how it stands, nor what it is grounded upon; and this is the reason why it is called an "imaginary" hope. For it is imagination when a person believes a thing and has no suitable means or ground upon which to build his hope.

2. True and patient hope is grounded on the mercies of God and the merits of Jesus Christ: and from this, Christ is called our Hope, *1 Timothy 1:1*, because he is the foundation upon whom the believers

<column-break/>

build all their hope of heaven; and likewise they build their hope on the mercies of God, *Psalm 147:11*:
> The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his mercy.
And again, *Psalm 33:18*:
> Behold, the eye of the Lord is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his mercy.
And in *Psalm 52:10* <note>In many English translations, this is verse 8.</note>, there David says:
> I trust in the mercy of God forever and ever.
A godly person goes out from himself and from his own righteousness; his hope is placed solely on God’s mercy and on Christ’s merits. But now, the false and imaginary hopes that the ungodly have are not so much built on God’s mercy as on their own duties; and not so much on Christ’s merits—what he has done for them—as on their own duties—what they have done for themselves.

3. True hope brings comfort and lifts up the heart under all the discouragement that might happen in the world: Just as David says in *Psalm 119:81*:
> My soul faints for your salvation: but I hope in your word.
From this, we have those two wonderful expressions together, *Romans 5:2-3*:
> Rejoice in hope of the glory of God... and glory in tribulations.
These are placed together to show that when a person can rejoice in hope, he can also boast in all the tribulations that meet him in this world. But imaginary hopes are like heavy weights that make you sink under those tribulations. It is only true and saving hope that keeps your head up under torments.

4. True hope performs the works of Heaven even as it hopes for the same; but an imaginary hope hopes for Heaven as the end, yet does not practice the works of holiness as a way to Heaven. Just as true hope hopes for Heaven, it also labors to work out its salvation with fear and trembling. You have an excellent passage for this in *Psalm 119:166*, where David says:
> Lord, I hope for your salvation, and do your commandments.
Here both the hope and the working for Heaven are together; but the ungodly hope for Heaven, yet do not keep God's commandments. And so in *Psalm 37:3*:
> Trust in the Lord, and do good, says the Psalmist.
There trust and doing good are together; true hope works for Heaven as well as it hopes for it; but the false [hope] hopes much and does little. The ungodly certainly want to hope for salvation, but never work out their own salvation; to hope for Heaven, but not labor for it. This is the fourth distinction.

5. The person who has a true hope makes it a matter of conscience to keep his heart pure and to free it both from the love of sin and from the dominion of sin while he lives here in this world: *1 John 3:3*:
> Every man that has this hope in him purifies himself, even as he is pure.
He labors to keep his heart upright, pure, and free from sins. But a false hope hopes for Heaven even while it walks according to the imagination of its own heart; and of these Isaiah says:
> You have walked in the greatness of your wicked ways, yet you do not say there is no hope. <note>Original: Isaiah 57:10.</note>
Even though they had great sins, they still had great hope for Heaven. If you are of those who say:
> We shall have peace, though we walk in the imagination of our hearts, and add drunkenness to thirst, <note>Original: Deuteronomy 29:19.</note>
your hope is only an imaginary hope.

# A True Account of Man’s
### The Miserable State in Nature

6. True hope proceeds from a long and well-grounded experience; this is the reason for the Apostle's saying in *Romans 5:4*:
**Patience works experience, and experience hope.** True and well-grounded hope flows from a long experience in the ways of God, and from an experience of the grace and love of God toward the soul. It comes from the experience of His goodness, mercy, and the promises of God, and likewise from the experience of one's own heart in resisting temptations, subduing corruptions, and fulfilling holy duties. These are all the foundations of a well-grounded hope. But now, the hope of the ungodly comes only from ignorance; they have no experience of themselves, nor of the ways of God. They have the greatest hope, but their hope is only deceptive and imaginary. They go along so quietly in the state of their hope, without any actual experience of the ways of God, and this is a sign that their hope is useless. In short, it is but a **painted hope.**

And thus I have handled the doctrine contained in the fourth branch of man's misery (being without hope); we come now to the application, and the use that I shall make of this is threefold:
1. For **Consolation**;
2. For **Terror**; and
3. For **Instruction**.

<margin>1. Use.</margin>
1. This is for the consolation of God's people; for although the Scripture says that an ungodly person has no hope, yet it speaks otherwise of the people of God, saying that **your hope is laid up for you in Heaven,** *Colossians 1:5*, and that **the Lord is your Hope,** *Jeremiah 17:17, Psalm 71:5.* Although the ungodly have no hope of Heaven, yet you have a well-grounded and assured hope of the same: your hope is laid up for you in the other world. The ungodly have only their hope in this life, and when they die, their hope perishes, *Proverbs 11:7.* **When the wicked man dies, his expectation perishes,** *Job 8:13.* **The hypocrite's expectation shall perish.** But it is not so with you. For the righteous trusts even in his death. And this hope of the Godly is not as the Papists <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics, used here in a theological debate about whether a person can be "assured" of their salvation.</note> take it; for although they admit that a believer has hope, yet they deny that he has any assurance. They say that believers only live in hope of Heaven and have no assurance (a comfortless sentiment). But the Scripture says there is such a **full assurance of hope** as there is of faith; see *Hebrews 11* and *Romans 14.* Our hope makes us enjoy good things even before we die, for Christ our hope has already died and been raised again; He has made His will and Testament, and He has left us His riches. Our hopes are well-grounded hopes; not like those of other men, who must part with their hope when they need it most.

<margin>2. Use.</margin>
The second use shall be for terror, to point out to you the misery of those men who have only an imaginary hope of Heaven.
1. You are in a much worse state if you are unconverted than any other person in the world; and this is the reason why the Scripture tells us that **harlots and tax collectors shall go to Heaven before the Scribes and Pharisees,** and yet they were a strict people,

<column-break/>

walking outwardly in a holy manner. And the reason is that it is easier to convert a harlot from her sins than a proud Pharisee, who thinks himself to be as good as the best, and has lived in peace all his life.

2. Let me tell you that your hope shall desert you when you shall need it most. *Proverbs 11:7.* The place previously cited: **When the wicked man dies, his expectation perishes;** even the very strongest hope perishes. He looks toward Heaven but shall not enter it: his expectation shall be cut off and his hope like a **spider's web.** The spider weaves itself into its web and lives there securely the whole week long; but when the maid comes with a cobweb brush, she takes away both the web and the spider. Just so shall the hope of all the ungodly come to nothing, *Job 11:20.* **The eyes of the wicked shall fail, and refuge shall perish from them; and their expectation shall be the giving up of the ghost.** Just as a dying man, a little before his death, still cheers up and hopes to live longer; but when his eyes fail and the signs of death are seen in him, then his heart fails him and his expectation is taken from him. Even so it is with the ungodly: they are full of hope for Heaven until they come to die, but then their hope deserts them and all their expectation perishes.

3. Your harboring of false and imaginary hope of Heaven brings a grievous misery upon you: 1. **Deception**; 2. **Torment**; and 3. **Damnation**.
1. It deceives all your hope: When you lie on your deathbed, you hope that after death you shall go into a sea of joy and delight, but you instead shall swim in a river of sulfur which the Lord shall kindle. You hope to be carried by angels into Abraham's bosom, when you are carried by devils into the bosom of Beelzebub. You may hope that death shall be a door to Heaven for you, when it shall only be a gate to let you into Hell.
2. It shall breed torment for you; now torment comes from ruin or disparity. Truly, the ungodly shall not only find a lack of blessedness, but torment in the loss of it. And it is because of this that some theologians <note>Original: "Gods-geleerden," literally "God-learned ones."</note> give as a reason that in Hell there shall be **weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth,** saying: just as fire burns here with heat, so the fire of Hell shall burn with cold; however, these are but guesses. Our theologians say that there shall be **gnashing of teeth** in Hell, a sign of that torment of the mind which the ungodly shall have; because all their hope is suddenly in vain, they shall gnash their teeth from torment of the soul **when they shall see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets in the Kingdom of God, but themselves thrust out.** *Luke 13:28.*
3. These false grounds shall likewise lead to your damnation: An ungodly man who harbors false hope of Heaven in his heart is like a man sleeping on the mast of a ship, who dreams pleasantly while a crosswind tosses and throws him into the sea. So the ungodly man: he has a golden dream on his deathbed, hoping to go to Heaven, and he is suddenly pushed into Hell. All this shows you the miserable state of...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual hope, transitioning from its general nature to specific instructions for the reader. # The Miserable State in Nature

those who have only an imagined hope of Heaven.
We come now to the third use, which will be for instruction; and if this is so, it may teach us these two or three lessons.
1. Let us take care not to fall lightly into this peace: there are some people in the world who fall into it and say; "why may we not do this as well as others?" Therefore, guard yourselves against having false and self-made imaginations within you regarding the hope of Heaven.
2. You who are pious, take care that you do not cast yourselves out from all hope of Heaven: Do not say that your hope is cut off from you; just as the ungodly are prone to harbor unfounded hope of Heaven within themselves, so are the godly prone to cast out their well-grounded hope of Heaven; <note>The author contrasts the overconfidence of the "ungodly" with the "spiritual desertion" or doubt often felt by believers.</note> therefore do not say "there is no hope for me," for then there would be no hope for you.
3. Do not harbor in your hearts a common or ordinary satisfaction with this grace of hope, as if it were so easy to obtain; it is natural in men to think that this grace of hope is so easily gained, for they say: "if it were not for hope, the heart would break." Guard yourselves against thinking like the ungodly—that this grace is so easily acquired—and observe that there is the same certainty, the same excellence, and the same power in the grace of hope as there is in the hope of [faith]:
1. Therein is the same assurance, *Hebrews 6:11*, where it is called the **full assurance of hope.**
2. Therein is the same excellence, *Titus 1:2*, where it is called the **blessed hope.**
3. Therein is the same working as in the grace of faith. *Acts 15:9*, there it is said that **Faith purifies the heart,** and hope does likewise, *1 John 3:3.*
4. There is the same difficulty in obtaining hope as in obtaining faith; for this is obtained through the word of God, *Romans 10:17*, and likewise hope in *Colossians 1:23*; it is obtained through the preaching of the word.
5. Faith is wrought in us by the power of God, *Hebrews 12:2.* Christ is the **author and finisher of our faith,** and so likewise hope is wrought in us by the power of the Holy Spirit, *Romans 15:13.* **That you may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.** So you see here that you need not have empty thoughts of this grace of hope, as if it were easy for every person to obtain it; for there is as much certainty, excellence, and powerful working in this grace—and as much effort to obtain this grace of hope—as there is in faith. And thus I have finished the fourth branch of the misery of an unregenerate man: <note>term: "unregenerate man" (Dutch: *onwederghebooren mans*). In 17th-century theology, this refers to someone who has not yet undergone a spiritual rebirth or conversion.</note> that he is without any well-grounded hope of Heaven.

->Ephesians 2:12<-

> *That at that time you were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.*

<margin>15th Sermon.</margin>
We come now to the fifth misery of man in nature, which is this: that they are **without God in the world.** And here I shall first say something of the order of these words, and then untwist them and establish some teaching points from them.

<margin>Question:</margin>
Question: Why is being **without Christ** placed in the first part of the text, and **without God** in the last?

<margin>Answer:</margin>
Answer: Being **without Christ** stands in the first place because it was the source of all their misery; and being **without God** is in the last place because this is the end <note>The "end" here means the ultimate result or the "final blow" of human suffering.</note> of man’s misery. It is the source of man's misery to be without Christ, and it is his misery to be alienated from the citizenship of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, and to be without hope; but the conclusion of all his misery is to be **without God in the world.** And here I shall show you that there are many men and women in the world who are without God; although they serve God every day, they can nonetheless live all their days without God. But before I come to that, I must clarify two or three things in these words, such as:

<margin>Objection.</margin>
1. How can it be said here that they were **without God in the world,** since the Apostle says in another place that the ungodly cannot be without God, seeing that **the Lord is not far from every one of us, for in him we live, and move, and have our being,** *Acts 17:27, 28.* There it says that the ungodly are not far from God, and that they live in Him; how then can it be said in this text that the ungodly are **without God in the world**? To be without God and to be not far from God—how can these agree?

<margin>Answer</margin>
Answer: In one sense, there is no human or creature in the world without God; and yet in another sense, there are many people without God in the world.
1. No one is without God in terms of creation, preservation, sustenance, and the governance of God over us; everyone is "in God" through creation, etc. But now, on the other hand, there is a multitude of people without God; that is, without a special portion in Him, without reconciliation with God, without having God as a Father in Christ, without a God who shares everything with you as your own; and in this sense, there are many without God in the world.
2. The other thing I shall explain to you is this: what it is to be **without God,** and **without God in the world.**

Answer: To be **without God** contains four things in the Scripture.
1. To be without knowledge of the true God.
2. To be without the true service of the true God.
3. To be without the true obedience to God.
4. To be without a special portion and ownership in God.
1. To be **without God** is to be without knowledge of the true God; a person is said to be without God when he does not know the true God. Every person in the world holds one thing or another as his god, *Jonah 1:5, 6.* When there was a great storm on the sea and the ship Jonah was in was in danger, it is said that **every man cried unto his god,** and Jonah prayed to the Lord his God. And *Micah 4:5*: **All people will walk every one in the name of his god; but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God, forever and ever.** Every person may have some things that he serves as God,

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Ephesians 2:12, specifically identifying the marks of "practical atheism"—living as though God does not exist even while professing a faith. Miserable State in Nature. 401

<margin>Doctrine.</margin> there is no God in the world, as in Romans 1:24. <note>Original: Rom. 1. 24. This verse discusses God giving people up to uncleanness; the author likely refers to the general argument of the chapter regarding the rejection of God.</note> There the Apostle says: *The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.* I have read a strange history of a woman here in England who fell into reflections on the Godhead—whether there was a God or not. A preacher came to her to convince her and satisfy her conscience, to make her believe that there was a God. He asked her how she came to be such an atheist. The woman answered: the first thing that caused her these thoughts of not believing in God was that she saw him <note>meaning the preacher</note> live so godlessly and profanely. "For," she said, "I know you are a teacher and a learned man; you give good sermons and exhort the people well; yet my own eyes see that your life is so godless, that you swear, lie, drink, and break the Sabbath, etc. All this makes me wonder whether there is a King in Heaven or not, seeing as He lets you go on so unpunished."

3. There is yet more that makes men live as if there were no God in the world, and that is the question of the Holy Scripture. I have read of one (a great school-teacher in this kingdom) that the means by which he became an atheist were these: he began first with the question of whether the Bible was God’s word or not, because he did not know whether Moses, who first began it, was a man or a God. After that, he pondered how Moses could write those things which happened before his birth; and then whether the Papists <note>a historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> might have changed the same in translations; and many other questions, until he became an atheist by degrees and doubted whether there was a God or not. And so there are many errors now published in print which contain atheism within them. There are some who maintain that the book which is called the Bible is not God’s word; and to drive such an opinion is the same as holding that there is no God in the world. 2 Peter 3:4, the Apostle says, *There shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts* (there are the atheists; but what shall they say? note the following words) *and saying: Where is the promise of his coming? For since the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.* They say, "We have heard that all men shall be judged, that after death they must appear before the judgment seat of God to give an account of all their works; but because they do not see these things fulfilled already, they cry out: *Where is the promise of his coming?*" They do not want to believe that such a thing shall be, and their doubt of God’s truth makes them atheists.

4. Pride of heart is likewise a ground of atheism; it is very well noted by one that atheists are commonly the "greatest" men <note>meaning those of high social or political rank</note>. You shall seldom see a poor man be an atheist, but almost always the rich, like Pharaoh. Exodus 5:2. *Who is the Lord,* (he says) *that I should obey his voice to let Israel go?* Likewise Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel 3:15. *Who is that God* (he says) *that shall deliver you?* So said Alexander of himself, that he was God. Atheists are commonly the greatest, richest, and highest of the people.

<margin>Objection.</margin> But here some may object and say: "Why do you tell us here in England

<column-break/>

that we are without God in the world? You may say this against the heathens, but we hope that you will not say this against us."

<margin>Answer.</margin> For an answer, I shall give you ten discoveries of a practical atheist <note>One who acts as if there is no God, regardless of their stated belief.</note>: three from Scripture, and seven flowing from Scripture. Psalm 14:1 says: *The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.* In that same Psalm are the discoveries of an atheist.

1. A person living all his days in a profane and disorderly way, outside of God—such a one is an atheist. Verse 1: *The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.* What follows? *They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.* The person who leads a disorderly life all his time, adding drunkenness to thirst, and commits one sin upon another—that person is effectively an atheist; he lives as if there were no God in this world.

2. The person who is very sluggish in the duty of prayer. Verse 4 in the same Psalm: *They eat up my people as they eat bread, and call not upon the Lord.* Such a person is a practical atheist.

3. The person who hates and bears a grudge in his heart against those who fear the Lord—this one is an atheist. Verse 6: *Ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his refuge.*

<margin>1. Use</margin> Now give me a little leave to apply these three things to your consciences in a word. 1. Are those atheists who lead a disorderly life and walk in godlessness all their days? Are such people atheists? Oh, how many atheists are there then now in the world, who spend all their days in sin and vanity, and in the twinkling of an eye go down into the grave!

<margin>2. Use</margin> 2. Are they atheists who are sluggish in the duty of prayer? Oh then, spoken with sadness of heart: how many atheists are here in the world who perform this duty with such difficulty, both in their families and their private rooms? How many are there who can say that they never go to God on their knees in secret to obtain grace and mercy from God? And this laziness in heavenly duties is a sufficient proof that you live as if there were no God in the world, and in doing this, you are true atheists.

<margin>3. Use</margin> 3. Is the hating and despising of God's people a sign of an atheist? Then there are likewise many atheists in the world. How many are there who love a swearer, an adulterer, and an unholy person, etc.—yes, they love a dog, and yet hate a Christian? This comes from an atheistic root that is within them.
