2. Wicked men rage and are violent or powerful in the ways of ungodliness. Ungodly men are as fast as dromedaries in the paths of sin, and will you be like a sluggish donkey in the service of God? Shall a man run steadfastly in the path of sin to destroy his soul, and will you only crawl in the ways of God to save your soul? Shall a godless man run by post-haste to hell, while you only slowly creep toward Heaven? Shall a man hasten to the place of execution, and will you only sluggishly rouse yourself for a crown and a throne? Shall the ungodly not be ashamed to show their ferocity in a sinful race, and shall the pious be ashamed to be zealous in the ways of God? <margin>Jeremiah 8:6.</margin> They turn away in their course, like an unruly horse into battle (Jeremiah 9:5). They weary themselves to act perversely; will you not do as much for God as they do for Satan?

<margin>
2. With respect to the pious, Numbers 14:24.
<note>original Hebrew: מָלֵא אַחֲרָי (male acharai), meaning "He followed fully after me."</note>
He fulfilled following after me. <note>original Latin: "Implevit ire post me"</note>
He follows me with full sails. Psalm 132:4, 5. Psalm 69:10.
</margin>
2. With respect to the pious. How vehement and zealous they are toward God: Caleb and Joshua followed God fully or perseveringly (Numbers 14:24), while hypocrites follow God partially and bit by bit. (Psalm 132:4, 5) David was so zealous toward God that he would give no sleep to his eyes, nor slumber to his eyelids, until he had found a place for the Lord, and a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob. Just as, on the contrary, ungodly men (Proverbs 4:16) were so zealous in ungodliness that they could not sleep unless they had caused some to stumble. (Psalm 69:10) *The zeal of Your house has consumed me: and the reproaches of those who reproached You have fallen upon me.*

<margin>
3. With respect to Heaven itself, Luke 13:24.
To strive in the manner of boxers. <note>original Latin: "More pugilum certare"</note>
1 Corinthians 9:24, 25.
2 Timothy 2:5.
The descent to hell is easy. <note>original Latin: "Facilis descensus Averni" – a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid.</note>
Bucer, Pareus. <note>Martin Bucer and David Pareus were influential Protestant reformers and theologians.</note>
</margin>
3. With respect to Heaven itself (Luke 13:24). Strive to enter through the narrow gate; for many (I tell you) shall seek to enter, and shall not be able. Strive even to the point of agony, or just as men strive in distress for their lives; it is not enough to seek; many seekers shall never find, but there must be a striving to reach Heaven (1 Corinthians 9:24, 25). *Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but [that] one receives the prize? So run, that you may obtain [it]. And everyone who strives (for a prize) is temperate in all things. Now they do this to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.* (2 Timothy 2:5) *And if anyone also strives, he is not crowned unless he has striven lawfully.* Heaven is compared to a mountain, and hell to a pit. It will cost a man sweat and labor to climb a mountain, but it is an easy matter to descend into a pit. Heaven is as Canaan (the prototype of the same) was; although a land of promise, it was nonetheless also a land of conquests. There were many giants; the sons of Anak were in the land. Heaven is not to be obtained without great diligence (Luke 16:16). *Everyone presses into it.* The Apostle alludes to and has an eye on the soldiers who storm a city or a strong garrison with all the haste and strength they could apply. Should the soldiers go around that great work at a marching pace, they might all be cut off. And thus this much shall be enough for the second point, to show the necessity of this <term>holy violence</term>.

<column-break/>

The third matter is the discovery of this holy violence. Now it is discovered by these three following marks. A violent or zealous person is one:

1. Who is patient in his own cause, but impatient in God’s cause. This was the nature of David. That which his enemies did to David was but as a thorn in the flesh, but what they did against God was like a death blow in his bones. (Psalm 42:10) *As with a death blow in my bones, my adversaries reproach me, while they say to me all day long, Where is your God?* The reproaching of God was like death to him, as if he himself were dead through it; like a death blow in my bones. Moses was a man very meek regarding his own injuries or wrongs (Numbers 12:3). *Moses was very meek, above all the men who were on the face of the earth;* but in the cause of God (Exodus 32), he conducted himself as if he were made of all passions; he broke the stone tablets. So was Jesus Christ renowned for his meekness; he was a lamb of gentleness, and yet in the cause of his Father, he takes that zeal upon himself: *The zeal of Your house has consumed me* (John 2:17).

2. He never thinks that he begins to serve God early enough, or does enough work for Him. (Psalm 63:1) *In the dawn I will seek You,* and verse 9, *My soul clings to God.* (Acts 13:22) God gave this testimony to David, saying: *I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after My heart, who shall fulfill all My will.* (Psalm 119:6) *Then shall I not be ashamed, when I have respect unto all Your commandments.*

3. He is desirous to glorify God as much through suffering as through works; to follow the Lamb wherever He goes; to the wilderness as well as to Paradise; to a dungeon as well as to a palace. (Jeremiah 2:2) *I remember the kindness of your youth... when you followed me in a land not sown.* (Song of Solomon 8:5) *Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, leaning pleasingly upon her Beloved?*—out of the wilderness of afflictions. (Matthew 8:19) A certain scribe came to Him and said: *Master, I will follow You wherever You go.* He wanted to follow Christ in working, but not in suffering; just as cloth remains taut while being worn, but shrinks when it gets wet; for when Christ said to him: *The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head* (verse 20), his courage vanished.

4. He looks more to the required duty than to the reward, and complains more about his failings in the same than about the lack of expected rewards for it. Many people are content to follow God as long as there is some profit in doing so; they will perform their required duty, but it is in hope of reward; otherwise, it is the least of their cares or concerns. Lukewarm and faint-hearted souls follow God like a dog follows his master—until he comes by a carcass, then he leaves his master and turns aside to it. So do ungodly people follow God until they come to some "dead bait"—some stinking lust or sin, some opportunity or object of sin—but then they part from God and join themselves to it. But on the contrary...

3. The discovery of this violence.
Psalm 63:1
</margin>
...part. David followed after God and thirsted for God, even when he was in a dry and thirsty land where there was no water, *Psalm 63:1.* Had we been in David’s condition, we would have said, "O Lord, give me a drink"; had we been in a barren land, we would have said, "O Lord, give me food." But David, in a dry and thirsty land, cries out, "O Lord, give me Yourself." That is the spirit of a person who is truly zealous for the Gospel.

5. Hardships and opposition cause his zeal to awaken much sooner than to slacken; what will he not venture? What efforts will he not employ? Into what dangers will he not run for God? And just as it is with the fire in the blacksmith’s forge, which becomes hotter and more powerful when water is sprinkled upon it, or as fire burns hottest on a cold and frosty day: so also the opposition made against a zealous person only makes him more zealous through a holy <term>Antiperistasis</term> <note>A philosophical term common in the 17th century referring to the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, like heat being concentrated by surrounding cold.</note>. Thus it was in the days of Christ: the harder it was to reach His Honor, the more fiery and restless people were until they came to Him. They trampled one another, being an innumerable multitude of people, *Luke 12:1.* Some forced their passage to Christ (as we say, "hunger makes one eat through stone walls"), *Mark 2:4.* And when they could not reach Christ because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where He was, and having broken it open, they let down the bed, etc. Such was the disposition of the Syrophoenician woman, whose zeal was not extinguished by contradiction but increased, even though Christ placed Himself as an opponent against her. When Christ said, *It is not fitting to take the children's bread and give it to the little dogs,* *Mark 7:27.* Here is cold water (someone might think) enough to extinguish the zeal of many professors <note>In this context, "professors" refers to those who "profess" or declare their faith openly.</note>, but the fire of her zeal was kindled all the more by this cold speech: she answered, *even the little dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs,* *verse 28.* One might compare a zealous Christian to a burr: the more effort you make to pull it off, the more firmly it clings. So it is with a zealous Christian; the more you labor to draw him away from God, the more firmly he clings to Him. This was David’s disposition when he danced before the Lord, when Michal mocked and despised him, and treated him poorly for it: he answered, *I will be even more undignified than this, and will be humble in my own eyes, for it was before the Lord,* *2 Samuel 6:21, 22.* And thus much is said concerning the third chapter, the discovery of this holy violence: I come now to the fourth.

<margin>
4. The distinction between a servile haste and a holy violence.
</margin>
The fourth is the distinction between a headstrong and hasty zeal, and a holy and religious violence, which I shall show in ten particulars.

1. It is seen mostly in trivial matters and those of lesser weight. Such was the zeal of the Pharisees regarding the washing of their vessels and their hands before eating, but they never thought of the washing of their hearts. Likewise, the Episcopal authorities showed more heat and zeal concerning ceremonies; on the other hand, they were <term>lauto</term> <note>original Latin: "lauto," meaning "washed" or "tepid"; used here to mean lukewarm.</note>, even cold, in more substantial matters, such as the keeping of the Sabbath and the close practice of holiness, etc. They were very zealous for the linen Ephod <note>A ceremonial vestment worn by priests.</note>, even though a leprous skin might be covered beneath it; they applied great diligence to have <term>tractien</term> <note>original Dutch: "tractien," referring here to the formal arrangements or ceremonial displays surrounding the Lord's Supper.</note> around the table of the Lord's Supper, but they never took care to establish order to keep impure persons from receiving the Sacrament. But now, a pious person labors most concerning that which can be most profitable to him, which will bring him closest to heaven, which will be most useful to him for glorifying God and for preserving his soul.

<margin>
Leviticus 9:24
</margin>
2. It is kindled by passion and vain honor in the one, and by zeal and a holy unworthiness in the other. Thus many are zealous in promoting errors when they can obtain no honor by upholding the truth; then they will give themselves over to spreading errors. On the contrary, true zeal comes from a better principle and looks to a higher end. The fire on the Altar had to come from Heaven, *Leviticus 9:24.* And when Nadab and Abihu performed offerings with strange fire, it was not accepted; indeed, they were struck down in their attempt. Our zeal must be a fire from Heaven. God counts it as strange fire if we fetch it out of our own hearts.

<margin>
1 Samuel 13:13
verse 11, 12
</margin>
3. Violent, hasty zeal causes a person to go beyond the boundaries of his place and calling. Samuel rebuked Saul for his headstrong zeal, *1 Samuel 13:13,* when Saul took it upon himself to offer sacrifices. Samuel said, *You have done foolishly.* Nevertheless, Saul makes a fine excuse in *verses 11, 12.* Saul said, "Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that you did not come at the appointed time, and that the Philistines gathered themselves at Michmash, therefore I said, now the Philistines will come down to me at Gilgal, and I have not earnestly prayed before the face of the Lord. So I forced myself and offered a burnt offering."

<margin>
Matthew 26:51
Joshua 24:15
</margin>
You see, Saul had much to say; nevertheless, all this could not justify his breach into the priestly service. Such was the zeal of Peter, *Matthew 26:51.* He stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and struck the servant of the High Priest, cutting off his ear. But a holy zeal makes a person zealous at his proper time and place. A zealous Magistrate will sharply punish sin, even though other judges permit it. A zealous Minister will be faithful and zealous in rebuking sins, even though others are "dumb dogs" or flatterers who lay cushions under people's elbows. Likewise, a zealous Master of the household resolves with the good Joshua, *that he and his house will serve the Lord,* *Joshua 24:15,* regardless of what other masters and other households do. Fire in its proper place is good and useful, but out of its place, it is harmful and destructive.

### MATTHEW 11 verse 12.

And from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.

<margin>Sermon at St. Lawrence Jewry within London, April 29, 1649. <note>St. Lawrence Jewry is a historic church in the City of London, known for its influential preachers during the 17th century.</note></margin>

4. A rash zeal is more vehement at the beginning than at the final end. Philosophers make this distinction between natural and violent motions: that natural motions are slow at the start but faster when they approach their journey’s end; just as a falling stone moves very slowly when it first begins to fall, but faster as it gets closer to its center. On the contrary, violent motions are more vehement at the beginning and slower at the conclusion. Just as an arrow shot from a bow travels swiftly at first but thereafter loses its speed until it finally falls. A rash violence is like a violent motion—fast at first, then slow. But on the contrary, a holy violence is like a natural motion, which works with more vigor and power at the end than at the beginning. This was the praise of the church of Thyatira: that her last works were more than her first, <margin>Rev. 2:19</margin> **Revelation 2:19**. <note>The author uses Aristotelian physics to explain spiritual growth: true faith naturally accelerates as one gets closer to God/Heaven.</note>

5. A rash violence in religion will be discouraged by small difficulties. Such was the violence or zeal of that man mentioned previously, who was eager to come to Christ; but when Christ said to him: *The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to* <margin>Matt. 8:20</margin> *lay his head*, **Matthew 8:20**, his zeal was taken away. But a holy zeal is made alive, not diminished, by <margin>Job 32:19.</margin> opposition; **Job 32:19**. *See, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins, it is ready to burst.*

6. A rash zeal is guided more by examples than by reasons; like the zeal of the people of Ephesus for Diana, **Acts** <margin>Acts 19:32</margin> **19:32**. One cried this, another something else, and the greater part did not know for what cause they had come together. Such was the zeal of the Scribes and Pharisees, <margin>John 7:47-49.</margin> **John 7:47, 48, 49**. *Then the Pharisees answered them: Are you also deceived? Have any of the rulers or the Pharisees believed in Him? But this crowd, which does not know the Law, is accursed.* But a holy zeal is guided by the rule of Scripture and not by common examples. The Word was the rule which led Joshua to that resolution or intention: *That he and his house would serve the Lord.*

7. One who has this rash zeal is mostly busy in religion with controversies or points of dispute and circumstances or outward details. Thus Saul was zealous against the eating of the blood of the sacrifices, yet made no conscience of the blood-shedding of eighty-five Priests of the Lord. But a holy zeal keeps a person busy in those things that <margin>Titus 2:14.</margin> concern practice; **Titus 2:14**. *God's people are a people zealous for good works.* There was less power of godliness in the flourishing times of the Scholastics, <note>The "Scholastics" refers to medieval academic theologians whose complex debates were often criticized by later Reformers for being ivory-towered and impractical.</note> when the heat of men’s spirits was wasted in curious and useless speculations; while they, who

<column-break/>

should have instructed the people, became disputants, and the poor people became Atheists. It was a rash zeal between the Eastern and Western Churches concerning the time of observing Easter, when many other doctrines of religion that suffered damage were neglected, and they did not earnestly contend for many teachings of the faith which were once delivered to the Saints. Likewise, many among us waste all their time on observations and disputes, and this has brought forth a cancer to eat out the power of godliness. In the city of Megara, there was a great dispute between two persons as to which of them should stand in the shadow of a donkey on a day when the sun was shining. <note>The "Shadow of a Donkey" was a classical Greek proverb for a trivial or absurd dispute over nothing of value.</note> Such was the zeal of Paul before his conversion, <margin>Gal. 1:14.</margin> **Galatians 1:14**. He was exceedingly zealous for his ancestral traditions.

8. A rash zeal is an uneven zeal; there is no consistency in it. It is a zeal against some sins, but not all; it is for some obligatory duties, but not others; to do some good deeds, but not all. Such was the zeal of Jehu. He was very hot and zealous against the priests and the worship of <margin>2 Kings 10:28.</margin> Baal, **2 Kings 10:28**. *Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel.* But Jehu did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam, which made Israel to sin, **verse 31**. <margin>2 Kings 10:31.</margin> Such was the zeal of Saul for sacrifices, but not for obedience. But now, a holy zeal is consistent; it sets a person against every sin and toward every duty; it makes a person walk in all the commandments of God.

9. This rash zeal will cause a person to reject all human societies and civil governments and undermine all supreme powers. But a holy zeal, although a zeal for God, is nevertheless quiet and peaceful toward men; although he strives toward Heaven with violence, nevertheless he lives on earth with gentleness and tranquility. **2 Peter 2:10**. These ancient deceivers <margin>2 Pet. 2:10.</margin> were such as those *who despised authority, being bold and self-willed, and were not afraid to speak evil of dignitaries.* But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, etc. **James 3:17**. <margin>James 3:17.</margin>

10. Rash violence is accompanied by boldness of heart, both against God and men; it comes from a natural stubbornness. But a holy zeal is accompanied by humility; **Revelation 3:19**. <margin>Rev. 3:19.</margin> The church of Laodicea was commanded to be zealous and to repent. Her zeal for God had to be joined with the breaking of her own heart. So also the zeal of the Corinthians, **2 Corinthians 7:11**, was accompanied <margin>2 Cor. 7:11.</margin> with a godly sorrow, with fear, with indignation against themselves, and with vengeance. And this much will be enough for the fourth and final part of the use of instruction: namely, the distinction between a rash and a holy zeal. And so much for the third use.

The fourth use is for warning, and that in four particulars. 1. Guard yourself against pleading for, or being content with, a moderation in matters of religion. Moderation in religion is considered a virtue in these days, for which, nevertheless, Jesus Christ wants to spew us out of His mouth. If Jesus Christ recommends a holy zeal or violence in worship to us, where...

1. Mediocre things or means do not satisfy you in this world. Men rise early, and go late to bed, and eat the bread of sorrow, and are zealous and tireless in the pursuit of the things of the world: If you do not obtain as much this year, you will strive to get more the next year; no one has moderation toward the things of this world, no one is content with the state in which he is, but labors to elevate it.
<margin>Galatians 1:14.</margin>
<margin>Habakkuk 2:5.</margin>

But he gathers to himself all the Heathens, and collects to himself all nations. And is it reasonable, that you who are so immoderate in the pursuit and the desire for the things of this world, should be moderate in the things of Heaven?
<margin>2 Kings 18:28. verse 31.</margin>

2. You worked very immoderately in your desires for your lusts before your conversion, and therefore you cannot now be moderate in your desires for God and the things of God. How many times were you as if sick until you accomplished your ends in a sinful course, and will you not now be sick with love for Christ, and for heavenly things? Have you not been consumed by lusts, and do you now wish to be stone-cold in the service of God?

3. God demonstrates as great, indeed even greater, displeasure in lukewarmness in Religion, as if a person had no Religion at all. Such is the Scripture passage concerning Laodicea, *Revelation 3:15, 16.* I wish that you were cold or hot. So then, because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I shall spue you out of my mouth. Not that God wished a person should continually persist in that, or return to Heathenism or Judaism, both of which His soul abhors; but only because lukewarmness in the profession of Christianity displeases Him exceedingly.

4. In a false Religion, men have shown greater zeal and progress, *Isaiah 46:6.* They lavish gold out of their purses, and weigh silver with the scales, and hire a goldsmith, and he makes it into a God: they kneel down, they also bow themselves (before it) etc. The people were so fervent <note>original: "pherigh," an archaic spelling of *vurig* (fiery/fervent).</note> in an idolatrous religion, that they spared neither cost nor effort to fulfill the same. Likewise these false Prophets, these prophets and worshippers of Baal, *1 Kings 18:28.* They cried with a loud voice, and they cut themselves with knives and with lancets after their manner, until the blood gushed out upon them. Thus Paul, when he was a Jew and an adversary to Christianity, persecuted the church of God beyond measure, and wasted it, *Galatians 1:13.* *Jeremiah 32:35.* These idolatrous Jews built the high places of Baal, which are in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to cause their sons and their daughters to pass through (the fire) to Moloch; which I did not command them. So fer-

vent and fiery were they in their idolatrous worship and service, that they were willing to burn their children as a burnt-offering to their false God. Likewise among us, the Papists <note>A 17th-century term for Roman Catholics, often used polemically by Protestant preachers.</note> are zealous in their worship, as evidenced by their floggings and scourgings, and fasts and other penances. If men are thus fervent in false ways, how fiery ought we then to be in the true ones? But so much for the first part of the warning.

2. Take heed that you do not think that you can go to heaven without this holy zeal or violence. It was only violence that took Heaven in the days of John the Baptist. You can never go to Heaven, unless you strive to enter through the narrow gate. You must strive until you sweat; you must strive with all your might, and even then it shall be little enough. Take heed therefore that you do not think it is a light matter to go to Heaven. But take this above all: although you cannot go to Heaven without this holy violence, you shall never go to Heaven *because* of it. *James 1:25.* But he who looks into the perfect Law, which is of liberty, and continues therein, being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this one, (I say,) shall be blessed in his doing. So you see that a man shall not go to heaven because of his work, although he cannot go without it.
<margin>2nd Warning.</margin>
<margin>James 1:25.</margin>

3. When you see the Ministers of God fervent and fiery in the ways of God, see to it that you do not judge them as the world does—that you do not judge it a vain and unnecessary thing, or that you do not judge it to be a folly or a madness. When Paul was thus zealous for the spreading of the Gospel, when he came before Festus, Festus said to him, that much learning had made him mad: But Paul said, I am not mad, but speak words of truth and soberness.
<margin>3rd Warning.</margin>

4. See to it that you do not let your zeal in the service of God diminish because it may happen that you meet many reproaches and scandals from the men of the world regarding religion. David was more fervent in his dancing before the Ark, notwithstanding the scoffs of his wife. If scandals and reproaches and disturbances cause your zeal for God to diminish, you shall never be able to endure to the end. I shall never believe that a man will endure a rack for his religion, who cannot endure a scoff. He who cannot endure a sour face for the same, will never endure the fire; if you cannot suffer a reproach or a mockery for your profession of religion, much less shall you endure a half-gallows. And so much for the use of the warning.
<margin>4th Warning.</margin>

The next use is this: This Doctrine can awaken in us a powerful lamentation: If it were so, that the men in the days of John the Baptist were so holily zealous for Jesus Christ and his ordinances; how should we then, in our times, complain and weep, when we consider how diminished <note>original: "ghebeeckend'" - meaning weakened, cooled, or failing.</note> men are nowadays, and how entirely we fall short of those converts at the first planting of the Gospel.

love and affection for one another were such that they could form as good an acquaintance in half an hour as in half a year together. In those times they were so practiced in the duty of love that Saint Paul says they had no need that he should write to them regarding love, *1 Thessalonians 4:9*. In those days they were of one accord. The Heathens took notice of this and said: "See how the Christians love one another." But we have reached these times in which the love of men grows cold; we, upon whom the ends of the world have come, bite, and tear, and devour one another;

2. We fall short of them in the despising of the world. You know how much these Christians (*Hebrews 11*) held the world in contempt <note>original: *leet-feden* - to regard as loathsome or to suffer through</note>: They confessed that they were but guests and strangers on the earth, *verse 13*. They were not satisfied <note>original: *vernocht* - content or satiated</note> with the world but sought for a better Country. They came and laid their goods down at the Apostle's feet to do with them whatever pleased him. As for fine clothing, they were satisfied with sheepskins and goatskins; and instead of our costly houses, they were satisfied with holes and dens of the earth.

3. We also fall short of the first Christians in this: that they were brought away from the manner of worship in which they were born and raised, and received a new form of Religion. Against which they might have argued: "All our fathers were raised in the Law of Moses, and shall we take up a new way, a new worship?" But they did not dispute about it; they left the teachings of Moses and embraced this new way and doctrine which, as they thought, had never been taught before. But we are more accustomed to customs than to Christ <note>The original *Schristen* is likely a printer's error for *Christus* (Christ)</note>; we prefer to follow what has been, rather than to consider what it ought to be. Many have much to say and dispute concerning the old manner of worship. Many are so fixed in their old ways and paths in which they were born and raised that they do not wish to seek for a better manner and way. Heylin <note>Peter Heylyn (1600–1662) was an influential English cleric and author. His *Cosmographie* was a popular geographical and historical text.</note> in his *Geography* relates of the King of Morocco that he had said to the English Ambassador in King John's time, that he had recently read the Letters of Paul, which he so praised that, if he were to choose his worship, he would embrace Christianity; but everyone ought to die in the religion in which he was born. So it is with many among us; they believe they ought to, and resolve that they will, live and die in those customs and ways in which they were born; they do not wish to deny themselves in these small things—namely, to make Christ great—and in this also we fall short of the first Christians. And thus much for the final application. And so I have concluded the first and principal Doctrine: that in the times of the first propagation of the Gospel, greater fruit followed the Ministry, and a greater multitude gathered with more holy zeal for the commandments than before.

<column-break/>

### MATTHEW XI. verse 12.

> And from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force.

There is but one Doctrine remaining, and that is taken from the consideration of the character of those persons who expressed this holy violence; our Savior himself makes known to us who they were, *Matthew 21:31*. Jesus said to them: "Truly I say to you, that the tax collectors <note>original: *tollenaers* - those who collected tolls and taxes, often seen as corrupt agents of the Roman Empire</note> and the harlots go before you into the Kingdom of God." *verse 32*. The tax collectors and harlots believed in John. The Pharisees, who led a strict life, had a sort of righteousness according to the Law; yet they were not the people who received Jesus Christ, but the tax collectors and harlots. The Pharisees and lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, not being baptized by him. But the tax collectors justified God, being baptized with the baptism of John, *Luke 7:29, 30*. Those who used this holy violence were people who lived by robbery, deceit, extortion, and oppression; so did the tax collectors. From which this Doctrine flows:

That commonly those who have sinned the most before conversion show greater violence and fervor of affection for Jesus Christ in the Gospel after they are converted. I shall do three things in the treatment of this matter.

1. I shall show the truth of the same through Scripture passages.
2. I shall show the reasons why God looked upon such people, who were the most notorious evildoers, either mostly or principally.
3. I shall show why such people are more fervent in worship than others.

1. I shall prove the truth of the doctrine by Scripture passages. I shall give but two examples; the one in Mary Magdalene, the other in Paul. 1. Mary Magdalene: she was an unclean person, a true harlot, a great sinner; but after her conversion she thought nothing too much for Christ. 1. She anointed his feet with a pound of spikenard ointment, which was very costly, worth three hundred pence—that is, worth over ninety guilders in our money <note>The author is translating the biblical "denarii" into contemporary 17th-century Dutch currency</note>, *John 12:5*. 2. She broke through many difficulties to come to Christ. Christ was in another man's house (and he was Simon, a Pharisee), *Luke 7:36, 37*, and was seated to hold the supper. She might have made an objection and said, "I cannot come to him, and those in the house might think ill of it"; but all this could not hold her back. Further, there were more discouragements. Not only like Judas, but others were angry with her, *Mark 14:4*. There were some (not only like Judas, but others also) who took that very poorly among themselves, and said, "To what purpose was this waste made?" Yes, the disciples moreover were very displeased with her: *Matthew 26:8*. The disciples were displeased. Nevertheless, she came through all these difficulties to Christ, and she wept, *Luke 7:44*. And that so abundantly, that she washed the feet of Christ with her tears

Her eyes, which had been windows of lusts, were now floodgates of tears. <note>This likely refers to Mary Magdalene, who was traditionally identified as the woman who washed Jesus' feet with her tears.</note>

2. Another example is that of Saul. Before his conversion, he was a notorious sinner; he was complicit in the death of the holy Stephen, <term>Acts 8:1</term>. He was a man who breathed threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, <term>Acts 9:1</term>. He was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an oppressor, <term>1 Tim. 1:13</term>. He did not even know what he was doing to the people of God. Indeed, he even forced others to blaspheme, <term>Acts 26:11</term>. And being exceedingly enraged against them, he persecuted them even to foreign cities. And yet, behold! This man, who was such an extraordinary sinner before his conversion, afterward makes a recompense or restitution; he increased and became overflowing in grace. He became as outstanding in grace as he had been prominent in sin. Just as in former times he had caused people to be taken prisoner, so now he drew those same people toward Christ. He preached the faith that he once persecuted, <term>Gal. 1:23</term>. And so much for the first detail: namely, the proof of the matter through Scripture passages.

<margin>Question. Why does God call such filthy persons?</margin>
The second part is this: Why does God look most upon those who were the most famous chief offenders?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
I answer; two reasons can be given for this.

1. To turn the Pharisees away from resting on their own righteousness, so that they might see that salvation was by grace, and not by works. Had this fruit appeared in many of the Scribes and Pharisees, some would have attributed it to their own teaching, and others to their strict and holy walk and careful conduct. The people would have thought that they had earned this from God; and therefore, God passes them by and chooses other, far more unholy and unclean people, to turn them away from their own righteousness and from clinging to the same.

2. It was to glorify the riches, generosity, and greatness of God's grace, which were brought in and revealed through the Gospel. God wanted to make it understood through this that the teaching of the Gospel was a doctrine of grace (not that men might live as they pleased, for these "filthy people" were not joined to their sins, but delivered from an empty way of life). But John's work <note>referring to John the Baptist</note> was a difficult and heavy labor to cast down those who were as high as mountains in their pride, and as hard as the rocks of these mountains, to make the rough and crooked things smooth and straight. And yet, John had to do all this; John did all this to prepare the people for Christ, <term>Isa. 40:4</term>. The greater the wound is, the more the skill and care of the doctor is seen and praised. The more and greater the sins are that are forgiven, the more the grace of God is exalted.

->So much regarding the second point.<-

<margin>Why are such people the most zealous?</margin>
The third detail is this: Why are such wicked and sinful people the most zealous and fervent after their conversion?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
<margin>2 Cor. 7:11</margin>
1. Answer. This proceeds from a holy indignation against themselves, which is a fruit of conversion, as you read in <term>2 Cor. 7:11</term>. "This very thing, that you were saddened after a godly manner, what great diligence it wrought in you? Yea, clearing of yourselves, yea, indignation, yea, fear, yea, longing, yea, zeal, yea, revenge!" There arises in such persons a desire to take revenge upon themselves.

<column-break/>

<margin>Isa. 30:22</margin>
<margin>Isa. 2:20</margin>
<term>Isa. 30:22</term>. "And you shall regard as unclean the covering of your silver engraved images, and the coating of your gold cast images; you shall throw them away like a menstrual cloth, and say to each of them, 'Get out!'" <term>Isa. 2:20</term>. "In that day a man shall cast away his silver idols and his gold idols, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and the bats." Cranmer <note>Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556), Archbishop of Canterbury, who was burned at the stake. He famously held his right hand in the fire first because it had signed a recantation of his faith.</note> burned his right hand first because it had signed his recantation, and he repeated often in the flames, "Oh, this unworthy right hand!" A holy contempt made him speak thus to himself. "Should I sin more than others, and shall I now be satisfied with less grace than others? Should I be as fast as a camel in the way of sin, and shall I crawl like a snail in the way of God? Have I been zealous to commit sins, and shall I be cold in my movements toward Christ?" Such persons are ashamed of their former ways, and therefore they now labor to take away the shame through this improvement.

2. This proceeds from the feeling which is in such persons of an absolute and total necessity of obtaining Christ. You know that a person who has only cut his finger will think little of it, but he who has received a large and dangerous wound sees a necessity for healing, and knows that he is a dead man if he gets no help. Likewise, a person who lives in an ordinary way of sinning thinks his sins are of little weight, and he sees no necessity to join himself to Christ for healing. But a person who has sinned much, and is outstanding in godlessness—when God comes and opens his eyes through a powerful calling—he sees a necessity to obtain help through Jesus Christ; he sees that if he does not have Christ, he is lost and must perish eternally. And thus I have preached the doctrine; now I proceed to make the application. And this teaching is above all useful to three kinds of people. 1. To those who in former times have been very filthy and great sinners, but are now converted. 2. To purely "civil" and honest people <note>original: "burgerlijcke" — meaning people who are outwardly moral and law-abiding but lack spiritual depth.</note>. 3. To those who still remain and continue in a sinful course.

<margin>1st Use: To great sinners who are converted.</margin>
1. Labor to follow this example that is presented here in the Gospel and in this teaching. Labor to proportion your grace now that you are converted, according to the number and greatness of your sins before your conversion. Just as you were formerly zealous in sin, see that you are now just as zealous for heavenly things. So did Manasseh <note>King of Judah, known for his extreme wickedness and subsequent deep repentance.</note>; he was a great sinner, he filled Jerusalem with blood, he was a great idolater, a disturber of the calling upon God, <term>2 Chron. 33:12</term>. And therefore he humbled himself greatly before the face of the God of his fathers. <margin>2 Chron. 33:12</margin> So did Paul; because he was a greater sinner than the rest of the Apostles, therefore he labored more abundantly than them all. Therefore, if sin has been overflowing, see that grace becomes just as overflowing. Just as you formerly added unrighteousness to unrighteousness, so see now that you add grace to grace...

does. Just as you have lifted up the limbs of your bodies with much zeal as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin and uncleanness; so see to it that you use the same as instruments of righteousness unto holiness. Especially, see that you become abundant:

1. In the gift of humiliation. 2. In the gift of love. In the gift or grace of humiliation; small humility does not accord with great sins. That garment which has the most stains in it must be washed the most; that which has the most dust in it has the most need of beating out. There must be an "as" <note>original: "Sicut"</note> not only of quality <note>original: "qualitatis"</note>, but of equality <note>original: "æqualitatis"</note> or proportion, as much as is possible. There must be some equality between the power shown in the service of sin and that which you now show in the <margin>Levit. 11:24, 25.</margin> service of God. It is very remarkable in Leviticus 11:24, 25: *He who touches a dead carcass shall be unclean until evening; but he who carries a dead carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening.* <note>The author uses this Mosaic Law to distinguish between occasional sin (touching) and habitual sin (carrying).</note> Although a man is only a little defiled with sin—if he, as it were, only touches a sin or commits a small sin—he has need to be humble; but those who wallow in sinful ways and carry sin with them, they must see to being more humbled than others were.

<margin>Luke 7:47.</margin>
2. See that you proportion your love for Christ to your sins against Christ in times past. If you have been a great and base sinner before your conversion, know that a little love for Christ is not enough after your great sins. *Her sins are forgiven [her] which were many, for she loved much.* Jesus Christ expects and demands more love from such to whom he has forgiven much, than he does from those <margin>John 21:15.</margin> to whom little is forgiven. We read in John 21:15: *Jesus said to Peter, Simon [son] of Jonah, do you love me more than these?* Jesus Christ did not ask him, "Do you love me?" nor "Do you love me as these [others do]?" but, "Do you love me more than these?" You have sinned more than these; do you love more than these? Christ expected greater love from Peter than from all the [other] disciples. And so Peter loved Christ more than the rest did. And although the book of Acts is called the "Acts of the Apostles," yet more is spoken of Peter than of all the rest of the Apostles who had seen Christ in the flesh. Peter showed more love after his fall than the rest.

<margin>Acts 1:15.</margin>
1. Peter preached the first sermon after Christ's resurrection and ascension, Acts 1:15.

2. Peter was the first who entered into the grave after Christ's death and resurrection. Although Peter and John ran to the grave, and John outran Peter and arrived there first, yet Peter went first into the grave to see where Christ <margin>John 20:6.</margin> had been laid, John 20:6, 3. When Christ walked on the waters after his resurrection, Peter threw himself into the sea to go to meet Jesus; he had no patience until he <margin>John 21:7.</margin> came to him, John 21:7.

4. Peter converted more souls to Christ than all the other Apostles did—3,000 souls in one sermon.

5. Peter died for Christ's sake; he was crucified for Christ's sake; and he desired that he might be crucified with his head downwards, because he thought it was too great an honor for him to die like his Master. Thus you see that just as Peter was more treacherous to his Master than the others; so Peter also burned more in

<column-break/>

fine love for Christ than the others. And so you must all learn to see that if your sins have been more and greater than the sins of other people, so your humiliation must be the greater and your love the stronger. That is the first part of the first use.

2. This can teach you to glorify the riches and bounty of God's grace, that God would cast an eye of grace and love upon such a wretched person as you were; that God would pass by such people as the strict Pharisees and look upon you: that God would not make such an example of punishment out of you as you were an example in sin; that you should be made a monument of his mercy, who deserved to be a spectacle of wrath; that God would let his grace rest upon you, whose justice might have caused him to seize you. So much for the first use.

2. This doctrine is useful to people of a "civil" conduct <note>A "civil" conduct refers to people who are morally upright and law-abiding but perhaps lack deep spiritual conversion.</note>, of an honest and inoffensive behavior in the world, who have been raised religiously and lived sensibly, who never burst out into such coarse and wandering ways as other people have done.

->Now I want to say three things.<-

1. When you say that you lead a more repentant life than others, and so you come to persuade yourself that your state is better than others; mark this: others are more easily and sooner converted than you. The tax collectors obtain <margin>Luke 18:14.</margin> heaven before you. You read in Luke 18:14 that the tax collector went out more justified than the Pharisee. Luther has a remarkable explanation of these words: It is much easier for harlots and public sinners to be saved than for proud, supposed saints; because the former are easily brought to a feeling of their sins, but the others seem to perish in the deception of their own righteousness, unless they are converted in an extraordinary way. I say this, not that I want to discourage a "civil" course of life, or to draw you toward public godlessness: but so that you might not come to rest upon your moral works. Do not boast of your good intentions, and think that you are "sermon-proof" <note>likely meaning "hardened against the conviction of preaching"</note>, such that the Lord can hardly examine your deceptions and consciences.

<margin>Luke 7:43.</margin>
2. If God commonly converts such [moral] people, they are not so outstanding in grace as others. This is expressed in Luke 7:43, etc. The one to whom the most is forgiven loves the most and does the most service. Commonly such persons keep themselves satisfied with a smaller measure of grace than those whose transgressions have been prominent.

<margin>Jer. 5:6.</margin>
3. What your sins lack in greatness and height, you make up for in number; *your transgressions are multiplied, your backslidings have become mighty many.* Jeremiah 5:6. Your perseverance in sin makes your sins equal to greater sins; if your sins fall short of others in nature, it may be that they stand out in heaviness; it may be that you sin against greater grace, greater knowledge: it may be that you have more sins in your heart, even though another's sin breaks out more in his life.

So much for the second use.

<margin>
3rd Application to godless men in two respects.
</margin>

3. This teaching is useful to godless men, even to the most dissolute sort of people.

1. Let this be an invitation and encouragement to you to come to Christ and embrace the Gospel. Although your sins are great, yet they are not as great as the mercies of God. The mercy of God is compared to a sea; the sea, you know, is of a very great depth. A large Leviathan <note>A biblical sea monster, representing great size or power.</note> can be covered in the sea just as well as a small fish; a large rock just as well as a small pebble. You have a

<margin>
Isaiah 44:22.
</margin>

noteworthy passage in *Isaiah 44:22: I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, your transgressions, and, as a cloud, your sins; return unto me, for I have redeemed you.* The Sun can scatter both thick and thin clouds.

2. Although you have been very sinful, yet your conversion takes away all bad reputation from you. Paul was once a blasphemer, etc. <note>referring to 1 Timothy 1:13</note>, but that evil was rolled away when he found mercy through God’s grace. It is very remarkable that in the genealogy of Christ only four women are mentioned (as it is not customary to record women in genealogies), and the Scripture places a mark of infamy and dishonor upon all of them. The first is Tha-

<margin>
Matthew 1:3, 5.
Genesis 38.
Hebrews 11:31.
Genesis 19:37.
</margin>

mar, *Matthew 1:3.* She was a harlot-like woman, for she committed adultery with her father-in-law, as is recounted in *Genesis 38.* The second is Rahab, verse 5. She was a harlot, *Hebrews 11:31.* The third is Ruth, verse 5. She came from Moab, the son of Lot born through incest with his own daughter, *Genesis 19:37.* The fourth is Bathsheba, verse 6. She was guilty of adultery. This is done for the comfort and encouragement of the most shameful sinners to come to Christ.

3. If God calls you, you will perhaps be greater instruments of His glory than others. A persecuting Saul became a speaking Paul; a wanton Mary <note>likely referring to Mary Magdalene</note> became a devout Mary; she, whose harlotry had been noticed in all the places where she lived, was afterwards spoken of for her grace in all places where the Gospel was preached. So much for the first part of that application.

<margin>
2nd Application to civil men.
</margin>

2. Because many people suck poison <note>The author uses "poison" or "venom" to describe taking a good teaching and using it to justify further sin.</note> out of the teachings of comfort, and thus achieve their own destruction; therefore I shall set down a warning or two. See to it that you do not misuse this teaching.

<margin>
Luke 18:14.
<note>original: "Longe possibilius est falvari, meretrices & notorios peccatores quam superbos sanctulos: illi enim tandem cognoscunt sua peccata, hi vero in persuasione propriæ sanctitatis moriuntur, nisi mirabili modo convertuntur."</note>
It is far more possible for harlots and notorious sinners to be saved than proud "little saints": for the former finally acknowledge their sins, but the latter die in the persuasion of their own holiness, unless they are converted in a miraculous way.
</margin>

1. And do not let the conversion of a scandalous sinner become a stumbling block in your way to Heaven. It was a great stumbling block in the path of the Pharisees when they saw that Christ would eat with the tax collectors and sinners; they said He was a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Do not, therefore, have heavy thoughts of Christ, nor of the ways of Christ for this reason. Truly, if religion were any cover for sins, if it gave a happy face and encouraged people in sin, it would be worse; but it is that which makes a sinner a Saint. Conversion, though it finds us foul and evil, does not leave us so.

<margin>
Luke 7:43.
Jeremiah 5:6.
</margin>

2. See to it that you do not suck the poison out of the same: that when you hear that the worse people are before conversion, the better they will be after conversion, some perhaps will draw this conclusion: That it is best to be as foul and godless as one

<column-break/>

can be, for such a one will thereafter be the most fiery. Take heed of this. For:

1. It is a great question whether God will convert you or not; and if you are not converted, all your sins will be so many coals to drag you into hell; the weight of your sins will be additions to your torments and punishments.

2. The deeper you are in sins, the greater your humiliation must be. Would a wise man break his bone because a broken bone, well-set and bound again, will be stronger than it ever was before? Unyielding timber receives the most blows.

3. The longer you persist in sinning, the longer God will keep you in doubt, and it will be a long time before He deems you worthy of the comforts of His Spirit, so that He might fill you with wrath and fear. Although great sins cannot <note>original: "vasta gratiam"</note> lay waste to the grace of God, nevertheless they can <note>original: "vastare conscientiam"</note> lay waste to the peace of the conscience; although it may be that they will not put you into a state of total rejection <note>original: "uitwerpinge"</note>, nevertheless they shall bring you into a state of being cast down <note>original: "verwerpinge"</note>; if you are not cast away, you shall still be thrown down: and therefore take heed that you do not misuse this precious teaching.

And so much for this last application.
And thus I have handled both the teachings, and finished the text: *And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force.*

3. This Doctrine is useful to godless people—even to the most unbridled sort of men.

A great Leviathan <note>A massive sea creature mentioned in the Bible, representing something enormous.</note> can be covered in the sea just as well as a tiny fish; a great rocky crag just as well as a small pebble.

<margin>

You have a noteworthy passage in Isaiah 44:22. *I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, your transgressions, and, as a cloud, your sins: return unto me; for I have redeemed you.* The Sun can disperse both thick and thin clouds.

2. Although you have been very sinful, yet your conversion removes all ill repute from you. Paul was once a blasphemer, etc. but that evil was rolled away when he found counsel through God’s grace. It is very remarkable that in the genealogy of Christ only four women are mentioned (as it is not customary to record women in genealogies) and the Scripture places a mark of infamy and dishonor upon them all. A persecuting Saul became a preaching Paul; a wanton Mary became a devoted Mary <note>original: "scheppende Maria," likely referring to Mary Magdalene's transformation into a vessel of grace or her role in the resurrection.</note>; she whose harlotry was noticed in all places where she lived, her grace was thereafter spoken of in all places where the Gospel was also preached. 1. And do not let the conversion of a scandalous sinner become a stumbling stone in your way to heaven. can be, for such a one shall thereafter be the most fervent. Take heed of this. For:

1. It is a great question whether God will convert you or not; and if you are not converted, all your sins shall be so many cords to drag you into hell; the weight of your sins shall be additions to your torments and punishments.

2. The deeper you are in sins, the greater your humiliation must be. Shall a wise man break his leg because a broken leg, well set and bound up again, will be stronger than it was before? Knotty timber receives the most blows.

3. Although great sins cannot *lay waste to grace* <note>original: "vastare gratiam"</note>, the grace of God, nonetheless they can *lay waste to the conscience* <note>original: "vastare conscientiam"</note>, destroying the peace of the conscience; although it may be that they will not put you in a state of total expulsion, nonetheless they shall bring you into a state of rejection; if you are not cast off, nonetheless you shall be hewn down: and therefore take heed that you do not misuse this precious doctrine.

And so much for this last application.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>

The first part of the text concerned the perspective of the petitioner toward the one to whom he makes his request. The observation is this:

<margin>1st Teaching.</margin>
A person must be brought into a state of friendship or reconciliation with God before any prayer they make can be accepted.

I shall prove this teaching through three reasons and then apply it.

The reasons are three:

<margin>1st Reason. Gen. 4:4.</margin>
1. God does not accept the person for the sake of the prayers, but the prayer for the sake of the person. We read in *Gen. 4:4*: God looked upon Abel and upon his offering; first upon Abel, then upon his offering. God accepted his service because his person was in good favor with God; God is first well-pleased with the worker before He can accept the work.

<margin>Hebrews 11:5.</margin>
This is also stated in *Hebrews 11:5*: By faith Enoch was taken away, so that he should not see death—for before his taking away, he had the testimony that he pleased God. Now, without faith in Christ to justify your person, you do not come to please God. Here lies that great difference between the Papists <note>A common 17th-century term for Roman Catholics.</note> and us. The Papists say that the works justify the person; we say the person justifies the work. For make the tree good, and the fruit must necessarily be good.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>
2. Because as long as we are not brought into the state of reconciliation, we have no part in the intercession, satisfaction, and righteousness of Jesus Christ. And as long as we do not partake of these, our prayers cannot be accepted. Jacob could not receive the blessing from his father except in the clothes of his eldest brother; nor can we receive anything from God except in the clothes of Christ. No prayer can be accepted by God except in and through the advocacy of Jesus Christ. If Christ is not an intercessor in Heaven, then no prayer on earth shall be heard. In the eighth chapter of

<margin>3. Application.</margin>
3. Let this teach you not only to look at the fitness and good disposition of your hearts to pray, but also to examine who you are who prays.

It is our duty, and it is very good, to pay attention to the quality of the heart in prayer, to look at the quality of the duty; but the principal work is to pay attention to the quality of the person, and to see if you are in favor and reconciliation with God; for if the person is not in favor with God, you may be assured that the prayers will neither be heard nor accepted, but God regards them as corrupt outbursts from your sinful and depraved heart. You must therefore look to the performance of the duty, whether you come to God in prayer as to a Father. There are many who pay attention to the well-ordered state of their duty; but few pay attention to the well-ordered state of the person, to see whether they are justified or not, whether God is their friend or not. But we must look closely at this; for let the heart of man be as well-disposed as it can be (let us take it so, for truly no unreconciled man can be well-disposed, to speak properly), yet if your person is not justified, your prayer cannot be heard. God does not need the **Rhetoric** of prayers, however eloquent they may be; nor the **Arithmetic** of prayers, however many they may be; nor the **Logic** of them, however reasonable and orderly they may be; nor the **Music** of them, whatever harmony or concord and melody of words you have; but he looks at the **Godliness** of prayers, which comes from the well-ordered state of a person, of a justified person, and in a sanctified manner. It is good to examine: is my heart upright? are my thoughts well-ordered? are my affections stirred, made soaring <note>The original Dutch *vlerigh* suggests having wings or being elevated by spiritual passion.</note> in prayer? And so much for the first doctrine, and the first part of the Text: the relationship between him who prays and Him to whom the prayers are made.

I come now to the second part, which is the condition upon which the prayer was heard; and that, I say, was established in two ways.

1. In a negative, rejecting way.
2. In a positive way by form of agreement.

1. The rejecting way: *Not because he is his friend*.

The observation from this is as follows:

That a state of friendship or reconciliation with God is not enough to guarantee to a man that God will give an Answer to his prayers. Although a man must be brought into a state of friendship and favor with God before his prayers can be heard: nonetheless, it is no firm ground for a man to believe that God will give him an answer to all his prayers. He will give him, *not because he is his friend*. So that a godly man may offer many prayers, and yet God may not give a single answer to his prayers.

In the handling of this doctrine, I shall do three things:
1. Show the reasons of the Lord.
2. I shall show in what cases God may refuse to give His own people those things for which they pray.
3. I shall show how we can know when God refuses to hear our prayers, or if the refusal is in mercy.

The first particular is the reason why God can, and sometimes does, refuse to hear the prayers of His friends: and it is this. Because God has bound the Answer of the prayer not only to the Quality of the person, but also to the Quality of the duty: so that the duty might be performed not only by a fit person, but also in a right way, and in a right manner, toward a right end. God does not say: "let a godly man pray how he will, I will hear his prayers"; that would be the direct way to make him careless and faint in the performance of duties. Therefore the Lord expects the Quality of the duty as well as that of the person. God requires that the duties happen with feeling, zeal, faith, fear, and reverence: they must happen in a right manner.

There is a five-fold condition which God requires, even of His friends, as a condition of their acceptance.

1. The heart must be prepared, *Psalm 10:17*, "Lord, you have heard the desire of the humble, you will strengthen their heart, your ear will be attentive." *So Job 11:13, 14, 15*, "If you prepare your heart, then stretch out your hands toward him. If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away: and let not wickedness dwell in your tents. For then you shall lift up your face without spot, and you shall be steadfast, and shall not fear." This is the first Condition.

2. Sin must be put away. So...

<meta>Continuing the discussion on prayer, this page addresses a common theological objection: if God has already decreed the outcome of all things, why should a Christian bother to pray? The author argues that God ordains both the ends and the means (prayer), and then begins to define "holy importunity" or "shamelessness" in prayer.</meta>

# The Zealous Christian.

I am certain that I shall have these graces, let me pray how I will; and on the contrary, if God has not decided to give me such grace, then I shall not have it, no matter how well I pray, for the decree of God is effective, irresistible, and cannot be changed. All my importunity <note>Importunity: persistent, urgent, and even troublesome requesting.</note> cannot change the decree of God.

<margin>
1 Use
</margin>
<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
To answer this, I shall present three things for your consideration.

<margin>
Deut. 29:29.
</margin>
1. We must not investigate the secret will of God; we must obey the revealed will of God, and not the secret one. It does not concern us to know what God *will* do, but what God *wants us* to do. Deuteronomy 29:29: "The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children." We know nothing of the decree and counsel of God, except when it pleases Him to reveal the same. Although God can give a grace without prayer, nevertheless He has nowhere promised to give the same without prayer. Prayers are the means that God has ordained for us to use to obtain grace.

<margin>
3 Doctrine
</margin>
<margin>
2 Sam. 7:17, 28, 29.
</margin>
2. The decree of God must not make us sluggish in prayer; for God has not only decreed the end, but also the means. Just as God has decided to show you grace, so He has also decided that you should pray for the same. And therefore, where the decree or purpose of God is recounted, it is used there as an argument to awaken the people of God to prayer. "For thou, **Lord** of hosts, God of Israel, hast revealed to thy servant, saying, I will build thee a house: therefore hath thy servant found in his heart to pray this prayer unto thee. And now, O Lord God, thou art that God, and thy words be true, and thou hast promised this goodness unto thy servant. Therefore now let it please thee to bless the house of thy servant, that it may continue for ever before thee: for thou, O Lord God, hast spoken it: and with thy blessing let the house of thy servant be blessed for ever." You see here that God had intended and promised to bless the house of David, and to continue the same forever; did this make David slack in prayer? Did David argue, "Why should I pray for this grace, seeing that God is resolved to give it?" No; David holds onto this, and uses it as a good purpose in his prayer. You have another example in Isaac. God had decided and promised that the seed of Abraham should be multiplied as the stars of heaven, <margin>Genesis 15:5.</margin> and that this promise would be fulfilled in Isaac. Did this make Isaac forget prayer? No, for we read in <margin>Gen. 25:21.</margin> Genesis 25:21: "And Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren: and the Lord was entreated of him," etc. Although God had promised that in Isaac all the nations of the earth should be blessed, nevertheless Isaac gave himself to prayer to God for the fulfillment of that grace which was decreed and promised.

<margin>
1 Objection.
</margin>
<margin>
Objection.
</margin>
But you will say, "Supposing God has decided He will never give me that grace for which I pray, what profit is it then for me to pray for it?"

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>
I answer: 1. It is more than anyone knows whether God has decided that He will refuse you the grace for which you pray.

2. If it be so that God has decided not to give you

<column-break/>

the grace for which you pray, nevertheless God will give you the reward of the prayer in your own bosom, although it may be that He will not give you the specific thing which you desire. And thus I have finished the first matter, and I have answered the objections.

<margin>
Question: What is holy importunity or shamelessness?
</margin>
<margin>
Answer: Anaideia. <note>original Greek: Αναίδεια — meaning shamelessness or persistence.</note>
</margin>
The second particular is this: What is this holy importunity or shamelessness?

I answer in general: the word in the original language means "shamelessness" or "lack of shame." It is a comparison taken from beggars, who are shamelessly persistent and take no notice of a refusal; if you refuse them once, they will pray to you again and again, and never stop until they obtain what they desire. It is a gathering together of all the affections of the soul, a stirring up of them all in prayer, through which the soul becomes so earnestly desirous of the good it lacks, that it will not rest or stop from the duty until it finds a reward. # The Zealous Christian.

...I am certain that I shall have these graces, let me pray how I will; and on the contrary, if God has not decided to give me such grace, I shall not have it, let me pray ever so well, for <term>God's decree|The theological concept of predestination, where God has unchangeably ordained all that happens</term> is effective, irresistible, and cannot be changed; all my <term>importunity|Urgent, persistent, and sometimes troublesome pressing or questioning</term> cannot change God's decree.

<margin>Answer.</margin> In answer to this, I shall propose three things for your consideration.

1. We must not search into the secret will of God; we must obey the revealed will of God, and not the secret one. It does not concern us to know what God wills to *do*, but what God wills that *we* should do. <margin>Deut. 29:29.</margin> Deuteronomy 29:29: *The secret things belong unto the Lord our God, but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children.* We know nothing of the decree and counsel of God, except when it pleases Him to reveal it. Although God can give a grace without prayer, nevertheless He has nowhere promised to give it without prayer. Prayers are the means that God has ordained for us to use in order to obtain grace.

3. <note>The original text jumps from point 1 to 3; this likely indicates a printer's error or a combined point in the original manuscript.</note> The decree of God must not make us sluggish in prayer; for God has not only decreed the end, but also the means. Just as God has decreed to show you grace, so He has also decreed that you should pray for the same. And therefore, wherever the promise or purpose of God is recounted, it is used as an argument to stir up the people of God to prayer. For you, <margin>2 Sam. 7:27, 28, 29.</margin> Lord of hosts, God of Israel: *you have revealed to the ear of your servant, saying, "I will build you a house": therefore your servant has found it in his heart to pray this prayer unto you. And now, O Lord God, you are that God, and your words shall be truth: and you have spoken this goodness unto your servant. Therefore now let it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before your face: for you, O Lord God, have spoken it, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever.* You see here that God had intended and promised to bless the house of David, and to continue the same forever; yet did this make David grow weak in prayer? Does David dispute: "Why do I need to pray for this grace, seeing that God is resolved to give it?" No; David holds onto this and uses it as a good motivation in his prayer. You have another example in Isaac. God had decreed and promised that the seed of Abraham should be multiplied as the stars of heaven, <margin>Gen. 15:5.</margin> Genesis 15:5, and that this promise would be fulfilled in Isaac. Did this make Isaac forget prayer? No, <margin>Gen. 25:21.</margin> for we read in Genesis 25:21: *Isaac prayed to the Lord greatly in the presence of his wife, because she was barren, and the Lord let himself be moved by his prayer,* etc. Although God had promised that in Isaac all the nations of the earth would be blessed, nevertheless Isaac gave himself to prayer to God for the fulfillment of that grace which was decreed and promised.

<margin>Objection.</margin> But you will say, assuming God has decreed He will never give me the grace for which I pray, what profit is it then for me to pray for it?

<margin>Answer.</margin> I answer: 1. It is more than anyone knows, that God has decreed that He will refuse you the grace for which you pray.

2. If it be so that God has decreed not to give you the specific grace for which you pray, nevertheless God will give you the reward of the prayer in your own bosom, even though it may be that He does not wish to give you the particular thing which you desire. And thus I have dealt with the first matter, and I have answered the objections.

<margin>Question: What is holy importunity?</margin> The second particular is this: What is this holy importunity or "shamelessness"?

<margin>Answer. <note>original Greek: ἀναίδεια (anaideia)</note></margin> I answer in general: the word in the original language signifies "shamelessness" or a lack of shame. It is a comparison taken from beggars, who are boldly persistent and take no notice of a refusal; if you refuse them once, they will pray to you again and again, and never cease until they obtain what they desire. It is a gathering together of all the affections of the soul, a stirring up of them all in prayer, whereby the soul becomes so earnestly desirous of the good it lacks that it will not rest or cease from the duty until it finds a reward. This is meant in <margin>Rom. 12:12.</margin> Romans 12:12: *Continuing instant in prayer.* The original word <margin><note>original Greek: προσκαρτεροῦντες (proskarterountes)</note></margin> is very expressive; it signifies not only to persevere but to persevere and continue with the utmost strength, straining all of a man's power for the work. It signifies persistence and shamelessness. It is a manner of speaking borrowed from dogs, which, when they are hunting, will not stop following the wild game until they have caught it: so shall a godly person follow after God in their duty, and never cease until they obtain the grace which they pray for from Him. Thus did the godly Jacob, <margin>Gen. 32:26.</margin> Genesis 32:26; God said, *Let me go, for the day breaks*: but he said, *I will not let you go unless you bless me.* Likewise it is said of Elijah, <margin>James 5:17.</margin> James 5:17: *He prayed fervently.* In the Greek, it is "in praying, he <margin><note>original Greek: εὐχομενὴ (epuchomenē) / ἐνεργουμένη (energoumenē)</note></margin> prayed"; to show that a Christian, when he is in prayer, must still pray, must pray more earnestly, he must be as it were in agony in prayer. It is said of Augustine in his preaching, that he never ended his sermon until he found that he had done some good upon the hearts of his listeners. So you must pray, and persevere in praying, and not give it up until you find something good done upon your hearts, until you find sin weakened and grace strengthened; this is the holy shamelessness spoken of here. And so much for the second particular.

A Christian can be compared to a marigold <note>The "gouts-bloeme" or marigold was a common floral metaphor in 17th-century devotion, representing the soul opening only to the light of Christ.</note>, which, while the sun shines upon it, opens itself, but afterwards closes up. When the Sun of God’s favor shines upon Christians, then their souls are expanded, and their affections are ignited toward God; but when God hides His face, they become troubled, their hearts become narrow, and they cannot pray as they are accustomed to do. It is said of the Nightingale that when she senses someone is near her, she sings more sweetly than when she is alone in the woods. The soul, when it sees that God is near and that His favor is toward it, then sings more sweetly and prays most fervently; but when the love of God is covered, and the soul is left as if alone, then the affections and words become weak in prayer.

A holy shamelessness <note>The original Dutch *onbeschaemtheyt* refers to a bold persistence in prayer, often called "holy importunity."</note> is recognized here by this: that it makes a person more zealous for spiritual than for temporal gifts. This was the disposition of God’s people, Psalm 4:7, *There were many who said, "Who will show us any good?" Lord, lift up the light of your countenance upon us.* Notice the distinction between David’s disposition and that of the godless: their great request and desire was for someone to show them any good, any temporal good; they wanted the increase of corn and wine. But David’s heart longed for other things: for God’s favor and the light of His countenance. <margin>Psalm 143:6, 7</margin> So in Psalm 143:6, 7, 8, *I stretch forth my hands unto you; my soul thirsts after you.*

<margin>Psalm 63:2</margin> Psalm 63:2, *O God, you are my God; early will I seek you: my soul thirsts for you, my flesh longs for you in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is.* David was in a wilderness; he lacked water. One might have thought he would seek God for water; but you see that his desires ran in a different channel; he thirsted more for God than for water. He desired spiritual advancements rather than temporal enjoyments. This persistence makes a person labor more against sin than against affliction; to desire saving grace more than common gifts. But now the heart of a hypocrite is more desirous of temporal <margin>Hos. 7:14</margin> than spiritual gifts. You read in Hosea 7:14, *And they have not cried unto me with their heart, when they howled upon their beds: they assemble themselves for corn and wine, and they rebel against me.* They howled, but why? Was it for grace and spiritual blessings? No, it was for corn, wine, and oil; not for grace, nor to maintain an acquaintance with God. Another <margin>Acts 8</margin> example you have in Acts 8, where Simon the Sorcerer <note>Original: "Simon Magus"</note> offers money to obtain the Holy Spirit. What was his aim in desiring the Holy Spirit? Was it to obtain a spiritual gift? No, but it was so that he might perform miracles. And further, when Peter exhorted him to pray for a spiritual gift in verse 22—*Pray God, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you*—Simon Magus did not follow Peter’s lesson. He had no great desire for the forgiveness of sin or for any spiritual gift; but he prays that none of those things of which Peter had spoken might come upon him, verse 24. That is, that his money might not perish, nor he perish with it, and that his reputation might not fail. This was his great request and desire.

<margin>3.</margin> 3. A holy importunity of God’s people is found more in the feeling of the inner affections of the heart than in the outward <margin>Psalm 38:10</margin> expression of words; Psalm 38:10, *Lord, all my desire is before you; and my groaning is not hidden from you.* David’s heart turned over and over within him, and his strength had failed him, verse 11; yet there was not a word of expression, <margin>Rom. 8:26</margin> though his expressions were very good; Romans 8:26, *The Spirit comes to the aid of our infirmities, with groanings that cannot be uttered.* It is <margin>Rev. 5:8</margin> said in Revelation 5:8, *The four and twenty elders had golden vials full of odors, which are the prayers of saints.* They are called "odors" <note>or "incense"</note> because of their sweet-

ness, "golden" because of their excellence, and "vials," which are vessels with a wide expansion in the belly but a narrow neck. The hearts of God’s people are like vials, entirely stopped up from within when they are restricted in their words and expressions. Often the most extensive desires are in the hearts of the saints, and yet they are so "narrow-mouthed" that they are not able to speak them out. But now it is different with the hypocrites; they have more in the expression than in the deed.
