<margin>4.</margin> 4. A holy importunity makes a person more concerned for God in secret than for men in public. <margin>Song of Sol. 2:14</margin> *O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see your countenance, let me hear your voice; for sweet is your voice, and your countenance is comely.* The voice of Christ’s church is sweet, even when she is in secret, when no one but God sees her. <margin>Song of Sol. 8:13</margin> Song of Solomon 8:13, *O you that dwell in the gardens, the companions hearken to your voice: cause me to hear it.* But now a hypocrite never cares to have any private communion with God; he does not seek to pray alone; and if he is driven to it, he takes no care over his heart, he does not constrain his thoughts. All his concern is for companionship, to be praised by the common people, and for vain glory. This is like the wind in the sails of a ship, which causes their inclinations to move all the more. A hypocrite, in this respect, can be compared to a nightingale, which sings the sweetest when someone stands near her. So it is with fleshly people: when others are witnesses of their deeds, they put forth the utmost of their ability. They are of Jehu’s disposition; he was only zealous on the condition that others might see it. <note>Jehu was a king of Israel who famously said, "Come with me, and see my zeal for the LORD," though his motives were later questioned.</note>

5. This holy importunity makes a person all the more humble the more he is stirred up to pray. The reason is that he looks upon his gifts not as coming from the strength of his natural parts or abilities, but as the free gift and generous dispensation of God’s Spirit. And so he sees that he has nothing of which he may boast; and thus he appears small in his own eyes. You know a violet is one of the sweetest flowers, and it grows the lowest to the earth. The fullest ears of corn hang the lowest. The fullest vessels make the least sound. Likewise, the most graced heart is the lowliest and "vilest" in its own understanding, it is nearest to the earth—but dust and ashes. The fuller he is of divine revelations or expansion, the less he boasts in the world. A ship, the more heavily it is laden, the less it is tossed by the winds and waves; the emptier it is, the more it is lifted above the water. So a person, the emptier he is, the more he is driven to and fro by the idle wind of vain glory. Grace is like the heavy ballast of the soul to keep a person's spirit down and to make him humble in the midst of his quickness and ability. <margin>1 Pet. 4:7</margin> *Be therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.* Be sober and not puffed up, and do not boast of your...

7. Holy importunity is ignited in the heart by the motions and workings of God’s blessed Spirit, Galatians 4:6: *Because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.* In the time of the Law <note>The "time of the Law" refers to the Old Testament period.</note>, the sacrifices that were accepted were burnt with fire from Heaven, Leviticus 9:24: *There came a fire out from before the Lord, and consumed upon the altar the burnt offering.* And so in Elijah’s time, 1 Kings 18:38, when Elijah had laid his sacrifice on the altar of the Lord: *Then the fire of the Lord fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood.* Similarly, that pagan fire that was formerly kept in a certain temple by certain virgins called *Vestales Virgines* <note>original: "Vestales Virgines" - the Vestal Virgins of ancient Rome, who tended the sacred fire of Vesta.</note> was lit with the rays of the sun. True importunity is from above; it is a fire ignited by God Himself in the hearts of His people. But there is another importunity which comes from natural principles, from natural abilities: a strong memory, a deep judgment, a ready wit, a flowing speech; and these are very helpful to the duty. There is the *gift* of prayer as well as the *grace* of prayer. Some are fiery in prayer out of fleshly motives. Now this is but a counterfeit importunity. And so much for the fourth particular: the difference between a holy and a natural importunity.

Now there are three unfit times for the performance of this duty.

1. When the body is sleepy, and fit for nothing else but to take its rest. A sleepy and drowsy state is a cancer <margin>Cant. 3:1.</margin> to eat out many sweet affections, Song of Solomon 3:1: *By night on my bed I sought him, but I found him not.* Some interpreters take occasion from this to speak against late prayers.

2. That is another unfit time for prayer.

There is a proverb: *Practice makes perfection;* I am certain it is so in the duty of prayer; let a Christian pray often, and he shall come to pray well, and to pray with much brokenness of heart; but let him stop praying, and he shall find his heart exceedingly constricted. Take a key; if you use it often, it will become shiny, but if you lay it aside, it will quickly become rusty; so it will be with a man's heart: use prayer much, continue in the performance of the required duty, and it is the way to have your heart shiny. Let this key of prayer, which opens heaven, be used; it wants to be kept shiny, and your prayer shall enter into heaven; but let this key of prayer be laid aside, and if you do not use it often, it will quickly become rusty again; your prayers and performances will not be powerful enough to obtain Heaven, and you will not be powerful enough to perform the duty in that manner which God expects. If you do not watch over prayer with all diligence, you will lose your zealous and fiery affection, as well as the holy desires for God in your required duty. Just as it is with a pump: use it every day and the water will come, but if you let it stand still for two or three days, the water will come neither so easily nor so abundantly. # The Zealous Christian.

<margin>1 Pet. 3:7.</margin> notice concerning the tooth, that the side of the tooth which is not used is most subject to catarrhs <note>original: "catharren"; in older medicine, this referred to a flow of humors or "decay" resulting from stagnation.</note>. The heart which is not accustomed to prayer and holy duty is most subject to Satan’s temptations and suggestions. This is the fourth reason.

<margin>Reason.</margin> The fifth reason why this importunity <note>Importunity refers to a persistent, bold, and even troublesome level of urgency in making a request.</note> is lacking is this: because people bind themselves to prescribed forms of prayer. I do not say that it is unlawful to use set manners of prayer; we find that Jesus Christ himself used a set manner in Matthew 26:39. Christ, having gone a little further, said: *Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.* In verse 42: Going away again a second time, he prayed, saying: *My Father, if this cup cannot pass from me, thy will be done.* In verse 44: He went away again, and prayed, saying the same words. This shows that it is lawful to use set forms of prayer, but not always. You must strive for the spirit of prayer. A person who wishes to use his crutches continually will go lame all the days of his life. You live in an age in which religion is widely confessed and in which the Gospel is fully made known. Do not satisfy yourself with set forms; labor for the spirit of prayer, through which you come to go before God, and set your failings and necessities before him, and pray for those gifts which most accord with your failings and distresses. Truly, set forms will teach you to pray for the forgiveness of sins in general; but you must pray for the forgiveness of particular sins. You must not only pray for gifts in common, but you must also pray for those special gifts which you need most. And these set forms are lacking in this regard, which is nevertheless the principal work in praying. He who always binds himself to another man's manner will not become capable of praying alone, but will become soft, cold, and formal. This is the fifth reason.

6. Another foundation of this lack of importunity is a giving in to a habitual persistence in a sluggish and careless performance of one's bounden duties; this makes the affections powerless and unmakes the spirit. Whatever people become accustomed to, they form a habit of, so that they cannot do the opposite. Just like a carter’s horse, which is used to a slow pace and cannot break out of it. The neglect of actions weakens the habit. This is the last reason. And this shall be enough as an answer to the sixth question.

The fourth particularity is this: by what helpful means can a person reach this holy importunity in prayer?

In answer, I shall set forth six or seven theological helps through which a person can come to obtain this holy importunity.

<column-break/>

1. Possess your heart with an awesome fear <note>original: "ontfachelijcke vreese"; a fear rooted in profound reverence or awe.</note> for the Almighty God. Likewise, it is the counsel of the Apostle that if we wish to serve God to please him, we must do so with reverence and godly fear, Hebrews 12:28. The godly author Vitus Theodorus <note>Vitus Theodorus (1507–1549) was a German Protestant reformer and a close friend of Martin Luther.</note> writes concerning Luther: <margin>With such confidence as with a friend, with such reverence as with God. <note>original Latin: "Tanta fiducia ut cum amico tanta reverentia ut cum Deo."</note></margin> That he prayed with such confidence as if he had spoken with his friend and familiar acquaintance, and yet with such reverence as one who noticed the great distance between God and himself. Once a person reaches the point where they become fearless of God, they will soon become careless in prayer; <margin>Job 15:4.</margin> Job 15:4: *Yea, thou castest off fear, and restrainest prayer before God.* A person who casts off the fear of God soon ceases to pray to God. He who fears God the most, that person will surely pray to God the best. This is the first help!

2. Another help or means to obtain this holy <margin>2nd Help.</margin> importunity is this: to gather your thoughts through holy meditation before you come to this weighty duty of praying to God. The same word in Hebrew signifies both to meditate and to pray. <margin>שוח</margin> <note>The Hebrew word "Suach" (שוח) can mean to muse, meditate, or speak/pray.</note> You find regarding Isaac in <margin>Gen. 24:26.</margin> Genesis 24:26 <note>The text cites verse 26, though Isaac's meditation in the field is traditionally verse 63.</note> that *Isaac went out into the field to meditate*, as some read it; others translate the same *to pray*; it is all one—he did both, first meditating and then praying. Be much occupied with pondering if you wish to have your heart much improved in prayer. Ponder in whose presence you come, what a glorious God he is before whom you must appear.

2. Ponder in whose name you must come and pray, through whom you must have access to the throne of grace.

3. The meditation on these things must necessarily give a person a greater aim and awaken a person’s affections in prayer.

<meta>This page continues the practical instructions on how a Christian can achieve "holy importunity"—a state of persistent, urgent, and bold prayer—by overcoming the distractions and spiritual lethargy of the world.</meta>

# The Zealous Christian.

...he gives this as a reason, so that they might cling to the Lord without being pulled hither and thither. The concerns of the world will eat the good that is in the hearts of men; it will rob a person of that liberality and expansion of spirit which he would otherwise have in prayer. Anselm <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher.</note>, as he was walking in the field, saw a shepherd boy tying a stone to a bird's leg; and as the bird sought to fly up, the stone always made it fall down again. The spiritual meaning which he in part made, and which we make, is this: when the soul wants to climb high and become zealous in prayer, then the cares of the world come and pull it down, cooling it. And therefore you must labor to free yourself from these hindrances. You must do as Abraham did when he went to make an offering; he left his servants and his cattle at the bottom of the mountain <note>A reference to Genesis 22, where Abraham leaves his worldly company behind to go up the mountain to worship.</note>. Likewise, when you go to offer the sacrifices of prayer to God, you must overcome the obstacles and distractions of this present life. This is the third helpful means.

<margin>4th Help.</margin> Another way to obtain this holy importunity <note>Importunity in this religious context refers to a persistent, almost troublesome boldness in making requests to God.</note> is to watch over the heart in <margin>Col. 4. 2.</margin> prayer. Colossians 4:2: *Continue steadfastly in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving.* There is a watching *for* prayer, and a watching *in* prayer. A watching *for* prayer is when a person watches his heart and sees that he does not forget any duties; and there is a watching *in* prayer, of which I now speak. Now, there are four enemies against which a person must watch in prayer:

1. Watch against **sleepiness of the body**. This is a great hindrance to prayer, and we have great need to watch against it.

2. Watch against the **deadness and dullness of the spirit**, against a poor and low disposition; this is a great hindrance to importunity.

3. Watch against **Devilish suggestions**; Satan is always ready to lay snares for you; he watches to disturb you in your prayers and to cause you trouble; you have need of watching to work against him.

4. You must watch against **worldly distractions**. Against all these adversaries you must watch, and this is the way to obtain this holy importunity in your hearts.

<margin>5th Help.</margin> 5. If you want to obtain this holy importunity, you must labor to awaken all your *affections* <note>In the 17th century, "affections" meant the deep inclinations of the heart and soul, such as love, desire, or zeal.</note> when you come to pray. This you find was the practice of the holy <margin>Ps. 103, 1.</margin> David in Psalm 103:1: *Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy Name.* See how this good man musters all the powers of his soul together, how he calls up all his strength and all that he is or can do to advance the Name of God. Similarly, the Apostle Peter exhorts in his first letter, chapter 1, verse 13, those to whom he writes, <margin>1 Pet. 1. 13.</margin> to **gird up the loins of their minds**. A Christian going to heaven is compared to a man who must make a journey; now, a man who travels girds his clothes together around his loins, so that nothing may hinder him in his journey. To this the Apostle looks when he asks them to gird up their loins. <margin>Luke 17. 8.</margin> Likewise you have Luke 17:8: *Gird yourself and serve me.* It is a manner of speaking taken from a Master to his servant. God is our

<column-break/>

Master, we are his servants; we must do his work while we are in the world. To that end, let us gird up our loins, let us gather our inclinations together, so that we may be more fit for and more powerful in the work. An ungirded thought is not fit for prayer; in ancient times, in the first gatherings and church assemblies, the Deacons cried out, "let us pray, let us attend." There are many who pray and who pay no attention to the prayer; many pray *as if they did not pray*. Therefore, if we want to pray, truly, we must pay attention to it; we must awaken all that is in us to call upon the name of the Lord.

6. If you want to obtain this holy importunity, then you must fill your heart with the **fullness of the matter** when you go to prayer; it is the emptiness of the Spirit which causes the deadness of the heart.

7. If you want to obtain this holy importunity, **complain of the deadness and folly of your heart**. This was the course which the holy David took, Psalm 38:10: *Lord, all my desire is before you, and my sighing is not hidden from you.* So was it the practice of the church in Isaiah 63:17: *Lord, why do you make us wander from your ways? Why do you harden our heart, so that we do not fear you?* This was also the way which Ephraim took in Jeremiah 31:18: *I have surely heard Ephraim complaining, saying, You have chastised me, and I was chastised like an untrained calf.*

Verse 19: *Surely after I was turned, I repented; and after I was made known to myself, I struck my thigh: I was ashamed, even confounded, because I bore the reproach of my youth.* It is pleasing to God to hear his people complain and to weep over their failings and weaknesses, and this is a necessary condition required in a prayer that is pleasing to God. Weep therefore over your folly; observe that prayer without this holy importunity is like a messenger without legs, like an arrow without feathers, or an advocate without a tongue. St. Jerome <note>original: "St. Jeronimus"; an early Christian scholar known for his translation of the Bible into Latin.</note> complained greatly about his distractions and weakness in prayer, and rebuked himself thus: "What do you think? Did Jonah have this when he was in the belly of the Whale, or Daniel when he was among the Lions, or the Thief when he was on the Cross?" # The Zealous Christian.

He gives this as a reason, so that they might cling to the Lord without being pulled hither and thither. The cares of the world will eat away the good that is in the hearts of men; it will rob a person of that liberality and elevation which he would otherwise have in prayer. Anselmus <note>Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109), a Benedictine monk and philosopher known for his theological treatises.</note>, as he was walking in the field, saw a shepherd's boy tie a stone to a bird's leg, and as the bird sought to fly up, the stone always made it fall back down again. The spiritual meaning which he in part drew, and that which we draw, is this: when the soul wants to climb high in prayer and become zealous, then the anxieties of the world come and pull it down, cooling it. And therefore you must labor to free yourself from these hindrances. You must do as Abraham did when he went to make an offering; he left his servants and his cattle at the bottom of the mountain. So too, when you go to offer the sacrifices of prayer to God, you must rise above the obstacles and distractions of this present life. This is the third help.

<margin>4th Help.</margin>
<margin>Col. 4:2.</margin>
Another way to obtain this holy importunity <term>importunity: a persistent, almost demanding boldness in prayer</term> is to watch over the heart in prayer. *Colossians 4:2.* Continue steadfastly in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving. There is a watching *for* prayer and a watching *in* prayer. A watching for prayer is when a person watches his heart and sees that he does not forget any duties; and there is a watching in prayer, of which I now speak. There are four enemies here against which a person must watch in prayer.

1. Watch against sleepiness of the body. This is a great obstacle to prayer, and we have a great need to watch against it.

2. Watch against the deadness and dullness of the spirit, against a poor and low state of mind; this is a great hindrance to importunity.

3. Watch against Devilish inspirations; Satan is always ready to lay snares for you; he watches to disturb you in your prayers and cause you trouble; you have need of watching to counteract him.

4. You must watch against worldly distractions. Against all these adversaries you must watch, and this is the way to obtain this holy importunity in your hearts.

These people imagine they have this importunity <note>In a religious sense, "importunity" refers to a persistent, urgent, and almost demanding boldness in prayer, modeled after the parables of Jesus.</note> when, in truth, they do not have it:
1. Because they are fluent in their words during prayer.
2. Because they feel some stirring of the affections <note>In the 17th century, "affections" referred to deep-seated holy emotions or the orientation of the soul toward God.</note> in prayer.
3. Because God grants them the gift for which they pray.
4. Because they pray from the heart and not from a book. Now all these are false grounds, and therefore I shall strive to refute them in order!

<margin>The first false ground refuted.</margin>
The first ground of this deception is this: there are some who believe they have this importunity because they have an abundance of words and a variety of expressions in their prayer.

Now, this is no right ground for a person to conclude that he has this holy importunity, and that for four reasons:

1. In case the words come from the power of natural gifts, or abilities, and not from saving grace. A person can have a strong memory, a readiness of speech, and good natural talents, and yet all this will fall far short of this gracious importunity.

2. In case you are abundant in words but empty in affections. There are many people whose words slip away from their hearts, and their words surpass their emotions. <margin>Isaiah 29:13.</margin> So did those people in *Isaiah 29:13: Therefore this people draws near to me with their mouth, and honors me with their lips; but they have removed their heart far from me.* Some people are like boiling water when it boils hardest—it overflows violently, yet there is nothing at the bottom. All their prayers are at the surface, in their mouths, and not in their hearts and affections. Their feelings do not match their words.

3. In case your fiery words are practiced more in company than in secret. It is a sign that you do not have this holy importunity, but that it proceeds from common applause. It is not so with the people of God. Christ speaks to His people in *Song of Solomon 8:13:* <margin>Song of Solomon 8:13.</margin> *O you who dwell in the gardens, the companions listen for your voice; cause me to hear it;* to show that they should not only pray and be zealous when companions are listening to their voice in public, but also when no eye sees them, when no ear hears them, when no one is present but God alone. God expects us to pray just as well in secret as in company.

<margin><note>original: "Siccine putas orasse Ionam, sic Danielem inter Leones, sic latronem in cruce?"</note> Do you think Jonah prayed thus, or Daniel among the lions, or the thief on the cross?</margin>
4. In case your fluency of words makes you puffed up in yourself and your gifts, and causes you to despise the gifts of others; this is proof that you do not have this holy importunity or fervor of the Spirit. For the Spirit makes a person humble and empty in his own eyes. When a person comes to despise others and exalt himself above his brothers, it is a sign that your importunity or fire does not proceed from a right principle. And thus I have shown the first false ground upon which many imagine they have this importunity.

<margin>Use of warning.</margin>
<margin>Warning to those who think they have importunity on false grounds.</margin>
<margin>A second false ground refuted.</margin>
2. Another false ground on which people believe they have this importunity when they do not is this: because they find in themselves some stirrings in

<column-break/>

their affections in prayer to God; but this is no right ground for that opinion in these cases:
1. In case your inclinations are more stirred toward the prevention or removal of the affliction that is upon you, than toward the condemnation that is within you. Just as it was with the sailors in the story of Jonah: they cried out mightily to God, but why was it? Not so that they might be delivered from their sins and guilt, but so that God might save them from the tempest they were in.
2. In case your inclinations are ignited by a false principle, such as common applause or vain glory, and not by the Spirit of God.
3. In case your inclinations tend more toward forgiving grace than toward sanctifying grace. A person whose conscience is awakened can be so stirred by the fear of hell that he becomes very zealous to have his sins forgiven, yet this arises from a pure principle of self-love.
4. If these movements of the soul quickly vanish. There are many who have a flickering in their affections, but no steadfast inclinations in their hearts. They are like a man in a burning fever who, while the fit is on him, may be much stronger than he is in his ordinary course. Now, this is not the natural strength of a man, but only the power of his imbalance <note>The original uses "distemperament," referring to an imbalance of the bodily humors or a state of disease.</note> and the decline of nature. Even so, the zeal which some people have does not prove the power of grace, but rather a decline of grace. And so much for the second ground of this mistake.

<margin>A third ground refuted.</margin>
A third ground upon which many mistake is this: because God gives them the grace for which they pray. Now, they think God would not give what they ask for if He did not hear and accept their prayers. But this is also not a good ground, for these reasons:

# The Zealous Christian.

a person—to conclude that God accepts his prayers.

<margin>3.</margin>
3. If God has heard you, it may be in temporal favors, but not in spiritual graces. God gives you a temporal grace, but he refuses you spiritual graces. It may be that you desire riches, and God has granted this request to make you rich in the world; it may be that you have desired honor, and you have climbed to places of honor; but remember that you should pray for Christ, that you should pray for grace and glory; for if God does not give you these things, you shall never see the face of God. And consider, what good will all these things do you? They will only fatten you for the day of slaughter, and make you a sweet morsel for the worms and devils. Now consider what profit this will be to you, to have riches, pleasures, and worldly satisfactions, if they serve as a snare to you. Thus, it is no right ground for a person to conclude that he has prayed rightly simply because God has answered him. This is the third ground.

<margin>A fourth ground refuted.</margin>
A fourth ground for a person’s presumption regarding the goodness and acceptability of their prayers is this: they pray with their heart and not out of a book; they use no set forms, but pray *extemporaneously* <note>original: "ex tempore"; meaning to speak or pray spontaneously without preparation.</note>. But this is also a false ground, as is evident from these observations:

1. It is possible, and indeed common, for people to pray without a book and yet still pray without the heart. A person can pray in three ways: he can pray and yet pray neither with the book nor with the heart; he can pray through the power of natural gifts, just as I have told you before.

<margin>2.</margin>
2. A person can pray without a set form and yet still make only a *formal* <note>In this context, "formal" means a prayer that is a mere outward ritual or performance, lacking sincere inward devotion.</note> prayer. A formal prayer is not defined by the use of a form of words; for what did Jesus Christ do? He prayed three times, saying the same words. A person might use a form of words and yet not be formal. And on the other hand, a person can be formal and yet use no form of words; that is, he can pray and yet not have his heart and affections active in that prayer.

<margin>3.</margin>
3. Prayer is not a work of memory, invention, or expression, but a work of the heart. Prayer does not consist in changing one's manner of speaking, or varying the method and expression used in prayer, but it is a work upon the affections. God does not count that to be a prayer which does not proceed from the heart and is not accompanied by the heart; and therefore you find this expression concerning the prayers of the saints in former times: Hannah poured out her soul before the Lord; and so the Psalmist, who is said to pour out his heart; and the Israelites are said to pour out their hearts like water before the Lord. So this shows it to be a false ground. And so much for the first use of warning.

->LUKE 11, verse 8.<-

> I tell you, though he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence <note>The original Dutch uses "onbeschaemtheyt," literally "shamelessness," which in a biblical context refers to a bold, persistent importunity in prayer.</note>, he will rise and give him as much as he needs.

<margin>2.</margin>
This may serve as a warning to the godly, to prevent the mistake of those who have a true importunity but believe they do not have it. Nevertheless, they also have some seemingly plausible reasons for this. I shall name them and answer them at once.

Their first reason is this: "Others pray better than I," says a godly person. "They perform their duties with greater clarity." Now, this reason is not sound.

For 1. It may be that those whom you think pray better than you are of longer standing and greater maturity in the ways of God than you are. God does not expect more from a person than the measure of grace He gives to that person, and according to his growth and standing in grace. Paul was not at all discouraged because Epenetus was the "firstfruits of Achaia in Christ" (Romans 16:5), nor over Andronicus and Junia, who were "of note among the apostles" and were in Christ before him (verse 7). And if Paul was not discouraged, why should you be discouraged to see that other Christians surpass you? It may be that they are of much longer standing than you.

2. It may be that you judge and compare yourself with others to your own disadvantage. For first, it may be that you compare your own private praying with the public praying of others. Now, this is very disadvantageous; for in public, people have not only inward but also outward encouragements, and so at that time they are drawn out more by the "thrumming" <note>The text uses "verdoventheydt," likely referring to the collective spiritual resonance or the presence of others' hearts.</note> that is in all their hearts than they are in private.

2. It may be that you compare their words with your affection; it may be that there is more in your affections than in the abundance of their words. You must not compare your affections with the quantity of other people's words.

3. It may be that you compare yourself with others when they are at their best and highest, and you are at your worst and lowest. There is a great difference between a person and himself at different times; now you judge poorly if you compare yourself in that manner.

3. In some cases, this should not be a discouragement to you; such as: 1. If you are weaker in natural gifts. Although good affections flow from grace, good expressions often come from natural abilities.

2. In case you have not been in religion for such a long time.

3. If you have less time and opportunity to pray by reason of necessary cares and hindering duties. When Jonah had gone into the ship, there was a great storm, so that the ship was ready to sink: now when the sailors prayed, every man cried to his god...

<summary>This page refutes the idea that being answered by God or praying without a book proves one has "holy importunity," while encouraging the godly not to despair when comparing their prayers to those of more experienced or naturally gifted Christians.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's refutation of false signs of "holy importunity" in prayer, specifically addressing the misconception that worldly success or spontaneous speech are proofs of a right heart. It then transitions to encouraging the pious who feel discouraged by comparing their prayers to others.</meta>

# The Zealous Christian.

<margin>
3.
</margin>
3. If God has exalted you, it may be in temporal favors, but not in spiritual graces. God gives you a temporal grace <note>In this context, "grace" refers to a gift or favor from God, which can be either "temporal" (temporary/worldly) or "spiritual" (eternal/saving).</note>, but He refuses you spiritual graces. It may be that you desired riches and God has granted this request to make you rich in the world; it may be that you desired honor, and you have climbed to places of distinction. But remember that you must pray for Christ, for grace and glory; for if God does not give you these things, you shall never see the face of God. Consider what good all these worldly things will do you? They will only make you fat for the day of slaughter, and make you a sweet morsel for worms and devils. Now consider what profit this will be to you—to have riches, pleasures, and worldly satisfactions—if they only serve as a snare to you. Thus, it is no sound ground for a person to conclude that he has prayed rightly simply because God has answered him. This is the third ground.

<margin>
A fourth ground refuted.
</margin>
A fourth ground for man’s presumption regarding the goodness and acceptability of their prayers is this: they pray with their heart and not from a book; they use no set forms, but pray *ex tempore* <note>original: "ex tempore"; praying spontaneously without a prepared text.</note>. But this is also a false ground, as appears from these observations:

<margin>
1.
</margin>
1. It is possible, and common, for people to pray without a book and yet without having their heart in it. A person can pray in a threefold way: he can pray with a book, he can pray without a book yet without his heart, or he can pray through the power of natural gifts, as I have already told you.

<margin>
2.
</margin>
2. A person can pray without a set form and yet produce only a formal prayer. A "formal" prayer is not defined by whether one uses a form of words; for what did Jesus Christ do? He prayed three times, saying the same words. A person might use a form of words and yet not be "formal" <note>In 17th-century theology, "formal" often meant performing the outward ritual without inward sincerity.</note>. On the other hand, a person can be formal and yet use no set form of words; that is, he can pray spontaneously, and yet not have his heart and affections active within that prayer.

<margin>
3.
</margin>
3. Prayer is not a work of memory, invention, or expression, but a work of the heart. Prayer does not consist in the variation of one’s manner of speaking, or the changing of methods and expressions used in prayer, but it is a work upon the affections. God does not count that to be a prayer which does not come from the heart and is not accompanied by the heart; therefore you find this expression regarding the prayers of the saints in former times: Hannah poured out her soul before the Lord; and so too the Psalmist is said to pour out his heart; and the Israelites are said to pour out their hearts like water before the Lord. This shows that spontaneous speech is a false ground for judging one's prayer. And so much for the first use of these warnings.

<column-break/>

->LUKE 11 verse 8.<-

> I say to you, though he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity <note>original: "onbeschaemtheyt," literally "un-shame-facedness" or persistence.</note> he will rise and give him as much as he needs.

<margin>
2.
</margin>
This may serve as a warning to the godly, to prevent the mistakes of those who think they possess importunity when they do not. Yet, even the godly have certain apparent reasons for doubt. I shall name these reasons and answer them at once.

Their first reason is this: "Others pray better than I," says a Godly person. "Others perform their duties with greater devotion <note>original: "ver dinge," likely referring to spiritual attainment or fervor.</note>." Now, this reasoning is not sound.

For, 1. It may be that the one you believe prays better than you is of longer standing and greater reverence in the grace of God than you are. God does not expect more from a person than according to the measure of grace which He gives to that person, and according to their growth and standing in grace. Paul was not at all discouraged because Epaenetus was the firstfruits of Achaia in Christ (Romans 16:5), nor by Andronicus and Junia, who were of note among the Apostles and were in Christ before him (verse 7). And if Paul was not discouraged, why should you be discouraged to see that other Christians surpass you? It may simply be that they have been in the faith longer than you.

2. It may be that you judge yourself and compare yourself with others to your own disadvantage. First, it may be that you compare your own private, secret praying with the public praying of others. This is a very unfair comparison; for in public, people have not only inward but also outward encouragements, and are often carried along by the collective devotion of the congregation more than they are in secret.

2. It may be that you compare their words to your own feelings. It may be that there is more true affection in your heart than there is in the multitude of their words. You must not measure your own sincerity against the quantity of another person's speech.

3. It may be that you compare yourself with others when they are at their best and highest, while you are at your weakest and lowest. There is a great difference in a person’s own spirit at various times; you judge poorly if you compare yourself in this manner.

3. In some cases, this should not discourage you: 1. If you are naturally weaker in gifts of speech. Although holy affections flow from grace, good expressions often come from natural abilities.

2. In case you have not been a believer for a long time.

3. If you have less time and opportunity to pray because of necessary cares and hindering duties. When Jonah had entered the ship, there was a great storm, such that the ship was ready to sink; then the seamen prayed, and every one cried out to his god.

# The Zealous Christian.

but Jonah was fast asleep; now someone might have thought that Jonah had been an unfeeling person; but the reason was the greatness of his journey a little before, which caused him to be so fast asleep. It may be that a person who has less grace than you can pray better than you, because he is not troubled with these worldly obstacles, which necessarily concern you.

4. God does not distribute gifts and graces to everyone equally; God has not decreed that all people should grow equally in grace. To this reason I can add
<margin>Nehemiah 11:17</margin> the third. God does not intend for all to be equal in grace, or in gifts; God has His first, second, and third; one may fall short of another and yet all have the truth of grace, yes, all have some growth in grace. Another may pray better, and yet you pray well; another may pray more affectionately <note>In this context, "affectionately" refers to "fervor" or "emotional intensity" rather than just fondness.</note>, and yet you pray just as acceptably in the sight of God. So much for the answer to the first reason.

<margin>A second Reason refuted.</margin>
2. Many a poor soul can say, "I can remember former times when I could pray better, and with greater joy. Since I could formerly pray better than now, I have now declined, and I lack this holy opportunity." But this is not a sound reason, because:

1. It may be that you formerly had more affection, but less judgment, less experience, and less spirituality in your prayers. It may be that you are now sounder in understanding, that you are making an inward progress in holiness; that you now come to offer an inward prayer to God, and that you now have an inward communion with God. Now if this be so, then you have no cause to be discouraged. God loves a wise and understanding prayer as much as a long and affectionate one; you see that what you lack in one, you make up in the other. A young carpenter strikes more blows and makes more shavings, but an old and experienced workman does the most and best work. A young musician can play faster and more sweetly, but an old musician has more knowledge.

2. It may be that when you have more affections in prayer, you have more sin in prayer—more pride in your gifts, more clinging to your services, more condemnation of others, and many other corruptions which accompany your prayers and your fervency in them. Now although you have fewer affections, nonetheless these other corruptions are to a great extent eaten away.

3. It may be that you do not now have as many helps and opportunities to keep your heart up, and to awaken your affections in prayer, as you had in former times. It may be that you formerly lived under the teachings of a capable, godly minister. Now you have lost that opportunity. And so there are various helps which perhaps have now been taken from you.

4. Although it is true that you have declined, and that you formerly prayed better than now,

<column-break/>

nevertheless, this ought not to be a cause of discouragement to you:
1. If it does not proceed from a voluntary carelessness.
2. If it is not accompanied by hardness and insensibility.
3. If it is not persisted in with laziness and complacency. And so much for the answer to the second reason.

<margin>A third Reason refuted.</margin>
3. Another ground of doubt for God's people is this: they complain that they do not have those broad expressions in prayer which God's people are accustomed to have. For an answer, consider these things:
1. This has often been the case with God's people, that words failed them; they could find no stirring for their affections. Thus it was with Hannah; she spoke in her heart, but she was not able to speak the same aloud. So it was with holy David, Psalm 77:5: "I was troubled and did not <margin>Psalm 77:5</margin> speak." And yet in the second verse of that Psalm, he tells us that he cried to the Lord with his voice. Here was a heart full of prayers, although he lacked the utterance.
2. It is better to have affections without expressions or words, than words without affection. God looks more at the desires of the heart than at the words of the mouth. It may be that what you lack in words is made up in affections.
3. It may be that what is lacking in words is made up in life; if you are lacking in words, then you make a compensation in your conversation <note>original: "conversatie"; in the 17th century, this meant one's "manner of living" or "conduct" rather than just talking.</note>; and that is the best expression there can be. It is much better to live according to a prayer than to speak a prayer. It is good to pray for grace, but it is better to live a life of grace. It is good to pray against sin, but it is better to live against sin. And so much for the answer to the third doubt.

<margin>A fourth Reason refuted.</margin>
A fourth ground of doubt is this: many a despondent Christian is prone to say, "I am tormented with flying thoughts <note>original: "vliegende ghedachten"; a term for distracting or intrusive thoughts that "fly" into the mind during prayer.</note>; with deadness and sluggishness of heart in prayer."

I confess your case is sad, and it may be lamented, and it is a rightful cause for humiliation; nevertheless, here is also matter for comfort.
1. If you do what you can to free yourself from flying thoughts before you come to pray.
2. If you do what you can to resist the flying thoughts when you must come before God in prayer.
3. If you are afterward sensible of these flying thoughts. If you can say that you do these three things, then your flying thoughts shall never more be laid to your charge.

And thus I have finished with both these Uses of Warning. And so I have finished with the primary Doctrine, which was this: That a holy importunity <term>importunity: persistent, urgent, and bold pressing of a request</term> and zeal of spirit is a condition required in the prayers of God's people if they expect rewards for them.

There remains one other remarkable Doctrine, taken from the amplification or expansion of the granting of his prayer: he requested only three loaves, but because of his boldness <note>original: "onbeschaemtheyt"; literally "shamelessness," referring to the persistent friend in Luke 11:8.</note>, he gave him as many as he had need of.

# The Zealous Christian.

<column-break/>

<margin>
4th Doctrine.
God is better than our prayers.
</margin>
The observation to be drawn from this is: That when the heart is bold <note>The original Dutch "onbeschaemt" literally means "unashamed," implying a holy boldness or persistence in prayer.</note> to pray for grace, God generally gives more than we pray for.
In handling this Doctrine, I shall:
1. Prove the same through passages of Scripture.
2. Set forth the reason for it.
3. Answer certain objections and cases of conscience; and so I shall come to the application.
1. I shall prove the same through passages of Scripture.

<margin>
1 Sam. 1.
</margin>
<margin>
She asked for a son, she received a prophet. <note>Original Latin: "Petijt filium accepit Prophetam."</note>
</margin>
1. You have the example of Hannah in 1 Samuel 1. She prayed for a son with great importunity <note>Meaning persistent, urgent request.</note>, being a woman of a sorrowful spirit because of the lack of a son; well, God answered her. Chemnitius <note>Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586), an eminent Lutheran theologian.</note> notes that Hannah prayed for a son, and God gave her a Prophet. She asked for a son; God gave her a godly son, a son greatly beloved by God. She requested a single grace, and God gave her a double blessing.

<margin>
Gen. 17:18.
</margin>
Another example you have in Abraham, Genesis 17. Abraham prayed: "Oh, that Ishmael might live before your face." Well, what does God answer?

<margin>
verse 19.
</margin>
You find that in verse 19. "Truly Sarah, your wife, shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac, and I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him." It was Abraham's desire that Ishmael might live. Now God does not only grant that, but He gives him a better grace.

<margin>
Matt. 15.
</margin>
Another example you have in the Canaanite woman, Matthew 15, who requested Christ for the life and health of her daughter. Christ answers her thus:

<margin>
verse 28.
</margin>
"Be it unto thee even as thou wilt."
Now if you ask what is the reason why God deals thus with His people? I answer:

<margin>
1st Reason.
</margin>
<margin>
Ephes. 3:20.
</margin>
1. This proceeds from the increase and greatness of God's power, and the riches and bounty of His grace toward us; Ephesians 3:20, "Now to Him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us." One person can demand something from another and perhaps receive or obtain it, but then he must not pray again; but herein appears the power and might, the goodness and bounty of God: if we pray for something from Him once or twice, He is a God who is able to give not only according to what we pray, but *above* what we pray; and not only above what we *can* pray, but what we can pray or think.

<margin>
Exceedingly abundantly. <note>Original Greek: "ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ."</note>
</margin>
The words are so full that they cannot well be expressed; God does more than abundantly. God has not only a fullness of abundance, but of overflowing; not only of fullness, but of bounty; it is better than our prayers.

<margin>
2nd Reason.
</margin>
2. God wills to do this to come to the aid of His people, and to fill up their spiritual weaknesses. Among the weaknesses of God's people is this one: that we do not know what we need, nor what we ought to pray for as we should (Romans 8:26).

<margin>
Rom. 8:26.
</margin>
Therefore God fulfills our deficiencies not only in that which we pray for, but in that which we lack, even though we do not pray for the same nor ask for it.
So much for the Reason; I come now to answer certain objections.

<margin>
1st Objection.
</margin>
But some may say, what privilege does a pious person have more than a godless person, in having more given to him

<column-break/>

<margin>
Psalm 73.
</margin>
than he prays for, seeing that we read of godless people that they are prosperous in the world, and have more than their heart can wish (Psalm 73)? I answer:

<margin>
1st Answer.
</margin>
1. It is true that in temporal gifts God can give the godless more than the pious, and more than their heart can wish; but God does not give them spiritual gifts. Just as we can see in Balaam: God gave Balaam honors and riches, but Balaam cried out, "Oh, that I might die the death of the righteous." This God did not give. So many godless people say in general, "Lord, forgive me my sins"; God does not hear them. It may be that a child of God might pray for temporal grace from God, and God will give him spiritual graces; this is more than he desired and that much better than what He gives to the godless.
2. Although God gives the godless more than their hearts can wish, nevertheless God does not give that as a reward for prayer, but only as a fruit of general and common providence, insofar as He wishes to preserve His fine creatures.
3. God can give the godless more than their heart can wish, and this is not in grace but in wrath <note>In this theological context, "wrath" refers to God's judgment or divine displeasure, suggesting that material success can sometimes lead a person further away from salvation.</note>. They can receive favors, but not as blessings, not in grace. And there are four powerful proofs for when God hears a person in wrath.

<margin>
Angry desire and petition. <note>Original Latin: "Concupiscentia irata, & pitiu."</note>
</margin>
1. When he prays for something from God that is sinful in its own nature; as the refusal of the same is a work of grace, so the giving of it is a fruit of God's wrath. God often gives things in His wrath which He refuses when He is well pleased. God will not hear His own people according to their will, but according to His own will. It is in this case as it is with a father when a child, for lack of understanding, desires a knife from him with which he could cut his fingers; the Father will not give it to him unless he be in anger. So a person can pray for gifts from God, and it can happen that God will give them in wrath so that he may harm himself with them.

<margin>
Refusal. <note>Original Latin: "nega-" likely for "negatio".</note>
</margin>
2. If you pray for these things from God which, though they are not sinful in themselves, yet if your praying for these useful things happens for an improper end, then God will refuse these things in grace; and when He gives them, it is in wrath. For instance, if you desired temporal gifts to misuse them for drunkenness or to live in another sin and godlessness; if God gives you these gifts, it is a testimony of His anger toward you. So it was in the 78th Psalm, verse 18: "They tempted God in their heart, and desired food for their lust." That was the end of their desires; but what followed?

<margin>
Ps. 78:30, 31.
</margin>
The wrath of God: "While their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them" (verses 30, 31).

<margin>
32.
</margin>
3. If you pray for something from God and He gives it in wrath, you may know it by this: if it is a cause of sin to you, it was given to you in wrath. Thus it was with the Israelites just mentioned; the food that God gave them served as an occasion for sin (verse 32):
---
they still sinned and did not believe through His wonders. When the gifts which you receive serve as nourishment and increase for your lusts, then these gifts are accompanied by the curse and wrath of God; and this use of the gifts shall bring the weight of wrath upon you.

# The Zealous Christian.

4. Gifts are given to you in wrath <note>The author uses "wrath" here in the theological sense of a "judgment of hardening," where worldly success leads someone further away from God.</note> when the enjoyment of those very things hinders you from receiving greater gifts from God. This was the case with the Demons, in Matthew 8:31-32. They begged Christ that they might enter the herd of Swine; Christ granted them this; He let them enter the Swine so that they might not enter into people. When the granting of temporal gifts hinders you from receiving spiritual gifts, then they are given to you in wrath. There are many people to whom God gives temporal gifts—they have riches in abundance, pleasures at their whim, every thing they could desire—but these gifts take away their thoughts and affections from better things. Through obtaining these, they lose Christ, and grace, and immortality, and eternal happiness. Now in these cases, although God gives them the gifts, they are nonetheless given in wrath; and despite this objection, the Privilege of God’s people is far greater than the Privilege of the godless.

But a further objection and question may be raised: If it is true that gifts are given to the godless in wrath, and <margin>Question: When are gifts rewards for prayer?</margin> through a common providence, how can I know when gifts come to me that they are rewards for prayer?

<margin>Answer</margin> Now, I shall answer this in these particular points.

<margin>Psalm 116:2.</margin> 1. Gifts are rewards for prayer when the receiving of them becomes a means to awaken the heart to pray for other gifts from God: when the gift makes you love prayer more and use it more frequently. You find this proven by David’s experience in Psalm 116:2: *Because he has inclined his ear to me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live.* <note>Literally "in my days."</note> You see here, because God had heard David's prayer and given him the grace for which he had prayed, he makes an argument and a commitment to himself to pray for as long as he lived. So, persisting in prayer is a means to obtain more grace, and ceasing prayer once you have obtained the blessing is a means to lose what you have obtained from God. But it is not so with the godless. Gifts obtained only from a secret <note>The original "geniepne" suggests something hidden or subtle.</note> or general providence do not have such <margin>Job 21:7-8.</margin> power, as you can see in Job 21:7-8, etc. There Job tells you: *The wicked live, become old, yes, become mighty in power: their seed is established with them in their sight, and their offspring before their eyes. Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them. Their bull breeds and does not fail; their cow calves and does not miscarry.* And so he continues, describing the happy state in which the godless find themselves, and how God follows them with mercy upon mercy. Well, what was the outcome of this? Did this bind them to call upon God? Did this make them love <margin>verse 14</margin> prayer? No, it had the exact opposite effect; verse 14: *Therefore they said to God, Depart from <margin>verse 15</margin> us; for we desire not the knowledge of your ways.* And verse 15: *What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him?*

2. Gifts which are given as rewards for prayer do not only make a person notice that they are from God, but they draw the heart toward God and make the person use them in Service, to the glory of God. We find this to be the disposition of Hannah,

<column-break/>

<margin>1 Sam. 1:27-28.</margin> 1 Samuel 1:27-28. Hannah had prayed for a child; God gave her a son. Now what does she do with this gift? Note: *For this child I prayed, and the Lord has given me my petition—Therefore also I have lent him to the Lord; as long as he lives.* Since God heard my prayer and granted my request, I will therefore give this gift back to God, to be used in His <margin>1 John 3:22</margin> service. So also 1 John 3:22: *And whatsoever we ask, we receive of him, because we keep his commandments, and do those things that are pleasing in his sight.* You see, it is made a proof that what we receive is received as an answer to our prayers; because we make these gifts aids to obedience in keeping God's commandments. But now, gifts which come from a common providence do not draw the heart to God; they rather draw it toward sin, as it was with the aforementioned Israelites in Psalm 78; although God gave them their heart's desire, yet they were not estranged from their lusts.

3. Gifts come from God as rewards for prayer when they make you rejoice more in the God who hears your prayers and gives you the gift, than in the gift which you receive from God. Thus you find it in Hannah; she <margin>1 Sam. 2:1.</margin> prayed for a son and God gave her a son; yet she said in 1 Samuel 2:1: *My heart rejoices in the Lord.* God gave her a son; she was glad for that gift, but she was more glad in the God who gave it. So it was in Psalm 85:7: *Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?* We do not wish to rejoice primarily in the grace, but in You. On the contrary, those who receive gifts according to common providence rejoice more in the gifts; they rejoice more in the gifts than in the God of the gifts; they rejoice in their health and honor, in the multitude of their riches; but as far as God is concerned, they pray that He depart from them; they cannot rejoice in God.

When he thought he would die of thirst, he prayed to the Lord, and God opened a hollow place in the jawbone and gave him water. Now Samson called that place *Enhakkore*, the fountain of the one who called. He attributes it to the reward of his prayers; to that help which God gave him to pray. Likewise, Hannah attributes her gift to God, not to herself. But a godless person who receives gifts from God’s general providence says: "I worked for this; I risked my life for this; my friends left this to me; I obtained this through my foresight and wisdom." 5. That gift which is given as a reward for prayer is enjoyed with greater inward rest and contentment of mind than when it is given through general providence. When Eli told Hannah that she would have a son and that her prayer was heard, she felt such inward joy and satisfaction that it is said: *Hannah went her way; and her face was no longer sad.* The realization of this made her very joyful. The reason is that gifts given as rewards for prayer are given with a blessing, and inward tranquility, and contentment. The gifts that God gives to His own people, He gives with joy and consolation. <margin>Proverbs 10:23.</margin> Proverbs 10:22. <note>The original text cites verse 23, but the quote "The blessing of the Lord makes rich, and He adds no sorrow with it" is traditionally Proverbs 10:22.</note> *The blessing of the Lord makes rich: and He adds no sorrow to it.* <margin>1 Chronicles 4:10.</margin> You read in 1 Chronicles 4:10 <note>Original cites verse 13.</note>: *And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying: "Oh, that You would bless me indeed, and enlarge my territory, that Your hand would be with me, and that You would keep me from evil, that I may not cause pain!"* <note>Jabez’s name in Hebrew sounds like the word for "pain" or "sorrow"; he was asking God to reverse the legacy of his name through prayer.</note> Jabez knew that it was God's way, when He gave blessings as rewards for prayer, that He added no sorrow to them. Isaac prayed for a wife, and God gave her to him to be a great comfort to him. It may be that the godless have estates and are not satisfied with them, but rather have anxiety over them because they did not pray to God for them as Isaac did. They have children, but only worry over them; and an abundance of riches, yet only the burden of caring for them; and all this because they do not have these gifts as rewards for prayer. The gifts given through general providence are commonly accompanied by torment and dissatisfaction—snares and worries mixed with the gifts. <margin>Psalm 106:15.</margin> So it was in Psalm 106:15: *He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul.* Truly, God gives the godless their heart's desire; but how does it happen? With blessing and satisfaction? No, not so; they have a plague along with it. You know that Saul gave Michal to David to be a snare to him, a cross and a source of dissatisfaction. In the same way, God often gives His blessings in righteous judgment to the godless, to be snares, curses, and crosses to them.

6. The gifts which come as rewards for prayer can be recognized by this: if they are given at the very time when God draws out your heart to seek Him in holy duties. <margin>Acts 12.</margin> You have an example of this in Acts 12. While the Church was busy praying for the deliverance of Peter, the prison doors were opened; and he came and knocked at the door of the house where they were gathered. This was a clear sign that God gave Peter to them as a reward for prayer. So too in <margin>Acts 4:31.</margin> Acts 4:31: *When they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.* <margin>John 4:52, 53.</margin> You read in John 4:52–53 that the nobleman diligently inquired about the time at which the child began to recover his health; and when he understood it, he knew it was a reward for his prayer and a fruit of Christ's love. God says to His people in <margin>Isaiah 65:24.</margin> Isaiah 65:24: *Before they call, I will answer, and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.* Thus we read in the Book of Martyrs that the people 

<column-break/>

of God made it a sign of God's answer to our prayers when it pleased God to give gifts to them at the very time they were praying. Thus we read of Luther that there was a young man who had made a pact—and sealed it with his own blood—to surrender himself body and soul to the devil, simply to live in pleasure and to do and have whatever he desired. And when the time of the pact was nearly up, he being greatly troubled, came to Luther and told him what he had done and what would happen to him because of it. Whereupon Luther called the congregation together and held a solemn day of fasting on behalf of the young man. And while Luther prayed, being very zealous before God, a great noise was heard among them, and the contract was thrown into Luther’s lap in the middle of the assembly. And so the young man lived a holy and godly life from that time forward.

7. And finally, gifts are given as answers to prayers if you take care and make it a matter of conscience to fulfill the promises you made to God before you enjoyed the gift. But when we make promises to God before we have the gift, and then when we have it, we do not fulfill our promises, it is proof that we have the gifts only by a general and common providence. <margin>Job 22:27, 28.</margin> Job 22:27–28: *You shall make your prayer unto Him, and He shall hear you; and you shall pay your vows. When you decide on a matter, it shall be established for you; and light will shine upon your ways.* When you pray for a gift and say, "Lord, give me such a gift, and I will do such and such; I will walk thus and so before You; I will use it for Your honor." Now, if you pray for gifts in this way and make vows to God, then you must certainly fulfill your vows. We find this state of heart in David: <margin>Psalm 66:13, 14.</margin> Psalm 66:13–14: *I will go into Your house with burnt offerings; I will pay You my vows, which my lips have uttered and my mouth has spoken when I was in trouble.* You see, David was in distress and he prayed to God, and he made certain vows in case God would deliver him. Now, God delivered him from his distress, and he fulfilled his promises. Here was a reward for prayer. You see, David did not become careless and negligent, but he took care to pay what he had promised to God. And so you see how you can discover whether the gifts you receive from God are rewards for prayer, or whether they are merely fruits of a common and general providence. And so much for the answer to that question.

Another objection, or case of conscience, is this: *How can it be true that God gives His people more than they need, seeing that it is often the complaint of God’s people that they have prayed for gifts for a long time, and that God does not give them as much as they desire? Many say, "I pray for forgiveness of sins, and I cannot get them forgiven, nor the pardon sealed; I pray daily for strength against my corruptions, and yet I cannot get my lusts suppressed. What should I then think of my prayers?" some poor souls may say.*

Now, against this I shall set several things by way of an answer.

Sometimes, God gains honor through the denials He gives His people; indeed, He often receives more honor through a refusal than by the granting of a gift. And if the refusal of a gift to you serves to magnify God's glory, then it is better that you go without the gift while God receives His honor, than that you should have the gift and God should lose His glory. You have a magnificent example of this in <note>original: "Iob, 11." This is a clerical error in the source; the marginal note correctly identifies the passage as John 11.</note> *John 11.* There, a prayer was made by Mary and Martha for their brother *Lazarus*; they came to *Jesus* and said, "Lord, he whom You love is sick." > This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God.
When *Jesus Christ* heard that he was sick, He nevertheless remained two days in the place where He was; although He loved Martha and *Lazarus*, He stayed those two days and would not go to him. But in the 14th verse, *Christ* said clearly:
> *Lazarus* is dead: And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe.
But they said to Him, "Lord, if You had been here, he would not have died." *Christ* came and commanded them to take away the stone. Martha answered:
> Lord, by this time he smells, for he has been there four days.
This was what *Christ* intended: *Christ* knew well that it was a greater honor for Him to wake a dead man from the grave than to make him rise from a sickbed. The power of His Divinity was more clearly proven in the former than in the latter. And when Martha said to Him, "he stinks," *Jesus* answered:
> Did I not tell you that if you believe, you would see the glory of God?
That is, "you would see the power of my Divinity." This was the purpose of *Christ’s* refusal of grace, even though it was fervently desired.

5. God may refuse you the gift, not because He is not powerful enough or is unwilling to hear or deliver you, but so that He might make you more eager for it, and thus more fit for the gift. It may be that you are not yet ready for an answer. The Philosopher asked *Antigonus* <note>Antigonus was a successor to Alexander the Great; this anecdote is often used to illustrate the dignity of a king.</note> for a little money, and he gave him a Drachma <note>A small silver coin.</note>. The philosopher answered that it was not fitting for a king to give so little—a Talent <note>A very large sum of money, worth thousands of drachmas.</note> would have been a proper gift. The King replied: "Although a Talent is a fitting gift for me to give, nevertheless, you are not fit to receive it." So, although God is always fully ready and prepared to answer our prayers, we are not always ready or fit to receive those answers. God bids us to open our mouths wide, and He will fill them. God refuses us so that we might open our mouths wider and raise our desires for grace even higher. The Lord deals with His people as a father with his child; a father may seem to walk away and hide himself from his child to test the child's love for him. The child begins to cry and call out, yet the father does not come to the child. but when he hears that the child is crying out loudly, then he comes to him and takes him up in his arms. In the same way, the Lord sometimes sees His people praying, but He seems to distance Himself and hide from their prayers; He goes, as it were, out of their sight until they begin to cry out loudly and become very zealous and importunate <note>Troublesomely persistent in request.</note> in their prayers, until their desires for God are increased; and then God very bountifully rewards their desires into their lap. Now this is a very good reason why God refuses the prayers of His people. Desires which are delayed become stronger; but if the gifts 
<margin>Delayed desires grow, and quickly given ones become worthless.</margin>
are given too hastily, the desires fade and the gift is despised. When the *Manna* <note>The miraculous food provided to the Israelites in the desert.</note> came easily, they soon grew tired of it. God acts as a fisherman does: he pulls back the bait so that the fish might come for it more quickly and bite harder. God seems to pull back a gift so that we might pursue it more zealously.

8. Consider this for your comfort: that your person may be accepted and your prayer heard, and yet the thing for which you pray may not be given to you. You have an example of this in Christ; He prayed, "Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me," *Matt. 26*. Moses was a God-fearing man, and here he prays for this grace; but God was nonetheless angry with him and commanded him to pray no more for it. So, when you pray for a particular grace from God, God may refuse it here, and yet still hear your prayers and accept your person.

9. God can refuse you the grace for which you pray and give you a better one in its place; He causes your mouth to open wider so that He may give you greater gifts. Abraham prayed that Ishmael might live. Moses requested to enter the land of Canaan; it was refused him, but he was transported to a better place, into the true Canaan, the Kingdom of Heaven.

10. All of these cases I have treated before, and therefore I shall say no more of them now.

First, let me draw some Remarks or Corollaries from what we have stood upon.

1. The rewards of prayer are not given for the sake of the work, but for the sake of the person. Although the matter of your prayer may be good, yet if you are not a pious person, you shall not be accepted. God looked first upon Abel, and then upon his offering. *Ps. 34:17*: "The righteous cry, and the Lord heareth—" The person must be in a state of favor before the duty can be accepted.

2. Although prayers are not rewarded because of the work, nevertheless they are not rewarded without the work. God expects the work, and you must do the work, even though God does not want you to expect acceptance for the sake of the work.

3. Furthermore, the rewards of prayer are granted to a person considered not simply as an individual, but as a member of Christ, as one who has a share in His intercession. *John 15:7*: "If ye abide in me—ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you." *So John 16:23*: "Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you." All our prayers are but things of no value until Christ’s advocacy is added to them. 2. Another warning is this. Do not let the rewards make you puffed up and haughty because of your gifts or your graces. # The Zealous Christian. 722

<margin>Psalm 145:10.</margin>
...give thanks for what you have received. Those blessings which you have won through prayer, you must acknowledge with thankfulness, according to Psalm 145:10: *All your works praise you, O Lord, and your saints shall bless you.* All the works of God praise Him; the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament shows the work of His hands. That is to say, all these are passive or "suffering" <note>original: "lijdende"—meaning they reflect God’s glory without active intent.</note> monuments of God’s power in their creation. But the Saints are the active performers of God’s praise. Blessing is greater than mere praise: A painting praises its maker by its quality, but it does not bless or thank him. The Saints, however, thank God in a special way; their mouths are full of the praise of God. They have a principle within them to praise God; they are active agents in carrying forth His praise. Therefore, it is very profitable that you should praise and thank God.

3. See that you are very obedient: If God does much for you, see that you also do much for God. If God has a hearing ear, then you must have a doing hand. And so much for the application of warning.

<margin>3rd Use: Comfort.</margin>
### 3. I shall say something by way of comfort.

1. To such who have neither this importunity <term>Importunity: persistent, urgent, and even bold pressing in prayer.</term> nor these rewards of prayer.

2. To such who do have rewards of prayer.

1. Here is a word of comfort to those who lack this holy importunity, and that in three respects:

1. You can pray with sincerity even if you do not pray with boldness or fire. The Lord, says David, is near to all who call upon Him; but how? Not only to those who call upon Him with fire and power, but near to all those who call upon Him in truth, and with a sincere heart, so God shall be near to you.

2. It is the office of Christ in heaven to pray for you, when you do not pray on earth. It is the work of Jesus Christ to make intercession for you with His Father. Although you find no importunity in yourself, consider nonetheless, O believing soul, that Christ in heaven is earnestly praying to the Father for you.

3. A feeling and a lamenting of the lack of this holy importunity is counted by God to be a degree of the same. If you never complained about the lack of the Spirit, it is a sign that you never had the Spirit; but now that you complain about the lack of it, it is a sign that you have it.

<margin>2nd Part.</margin>
2. Here is also a word of comfort to those who have received rewards of prayer; and that in four respects:

<margin>Psalm 91:15.</margin>
1. Your gifts are double gifts: It is a grace to have grace, but to have it in such a manner is a double grace. Psalm 91:15: *They shall call upon me, and I will hear them; and I will be with them in trouble, etc.* It is grace to have deliverance out of trouble; but to have it through prayer, or as a deliverance by means of prayer, is a double grace.

2. These blessings are sanctified benefits; gifts, as you are God’s creatures, are good in themselves; but as rewards of prayer they are sanctified: and blessed gifts are much better to the soul which enjoys them.

<column-break/>

3. The gifts which you have as rewards of prayer are precious gifts. The gifts which come through ordinary providence are like a "good bargain" <note>original: "goede koop"—meaning something obtained easily or cheaply.</note>, but the gifts which come through prayer are costly; they cost the price of Christ’s blood to obtain them, and they cost you many a prayer and tear to obtain them.

4. These gifts are sealing gifts <note>A "sealing" gift is one that serves as a confirmation or spiritual guarantee of God's favor.</note>, and that in three particulars:

1. They are seals to you that you have the Spirit of God; for Christ hears no prayers, and no spirit, except His own. God is as well pleased with the barking of a dog as with the prayers of a Christless person.

2. It is a seal to you that you have a share in Christ’s intercession. If your prayers are rewarded, it is a sign that they are accepted. Now, no prayers are accepted except through the power of the mediation of Jesus Christ.

3. These rewards are a seal of greater gifts; a sign that you shall obtain greater gifts from God. A gift which is given through prayer is a pledge of another gift; and your gift in this life is a pledge to you that you shall have eternal happiness in heaven for all eternity.

### 1 THESSALONIANS 5: verse 9.

> For God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>Romans 9:22, 23.</margin>
This text encompasses within itself the unchangeable decree and the unchangeable counsel of God regarding the human race; although all men are made by the same hand, nonetheless they are not all appointed to obtain the same end by that God who made them. Some are made to be vessels of honor, and others to be vessels of wrath: some are appointed to be vessels of honor, fit for the use of Jesus Christ, and others to be vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, Romans 9:22, 23. Some, as my text says, are appointed to wrath, and others to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ; so that the entire human race is included under these two parts: there are only sheep and goats, people of the right hand and people of the left hand; there are only some elect and others rejected, some appointed to wrath and others to obtain salvation.

And since there are only these two ways for all flesh, we must observe what the counsel of God concerning us may be: whether we are appointed to wrath, or to obtain salvation.

I shall not detain you longer at the entrance of the text; some are appointed to wrath. "Wrath" is here an expressive word, and includes within itself all the torments of the damned; and if you ask me why the torments of the damned are here called "wrath," the reason is because it is the wrath of God that makes hell into a hell. If the favor of God could be in hell, hell would not be hell; and if the wrath of God could be in heaven, heaven would not be heaven. The loss of God’s favor is the greatest punishment which...
