# Wrath and Grace. 723

...which can regenerate a person; the terrors of hell are called "wrath" to make known to us that the greatest agony a creature can suffer is to lie under the wrath of God. Missing the favor <margin>2 Thess. 1:10.</margin> of God shall be the full agony of the damned; all the torments of the ungodly are called by this general expression: the coming wrath.

Beloved, these words are not hard; I shall handle them under a double consideration: First, under a relative consideration; and second, under an absolute consideration.

First, under a relative consideration, for God has not appointed us to wrath; for this word ("for") refers back to something that precedes it in the previous verse: *But let us who are of the day be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and as a helmet the hope of salvation, for God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation.* It is as if the Apostle wanted to say: you must not conclude from this that if God has decreed for me to be saved, I may live as I please, for I shall be saved regardless; or if God has decreed that I shall be damned, I may do what I can against it or not, I shall still be damned! Because I cannot change the decree of God. You must not make such a conclusion, he says, but let us who are of the day be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, etc., for we are not appointed to wrath. God’s decree should not be a discouragement to you to live as you please, but a spur to awaken you to live in the daily exercise of grace; from which I must note this Doctrine.

**Doctrine 1.** That the Lord's decree of election and rejection—or the ordaining of some people to glory in Heaven and others to be vessels of wrath in hell—is, or ought to be, a particular inducement and spur to awaken people to live in the exercise of grace.

<margin>1st Doctrine.</margin> This is what is set forth here by the Apostle; and the use which I shall make of it will be to condemn those improper conclusions which fleshly hearts draw from this Doctrine of Predestination <term>Predestination: the theological concept that God has foreordained all that will happen, especially regarding the salvation of some and the rejection of others.</term>. Thus the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who emphasized human free will over divine grace—a view often opposed by Reformed theologians.</note> conclude from God's decree, saying: "If God has ordained some to be saved and others to be damned, then we may live as we please; for let us do all we can, we cannot change God’s decree." And again, others say: "If God has ordained some for Heaven and others for hell, and God’s decree is unchangeable, why then should anyone fast or pray or perform any holy duty? For if he is to be saved, he will be saved, or if he is to be damned, he will be damned." *Faustus Rhegiensis* <note>Faustus of Riez, a 5th-century bishop associated with Semi-Pelagianism.</note>, one of the sect of the Semi-Pelagians, says: *Let no one watch, let no one fast, let no one resist his lusts, etc.* <note>original: "Nemo vigilet, nemo jejunet, libidini contradicat, &c."</note> In this way, they spit venom out of this sweet doctrine of God’s decree, whereas it ought to be a motive and an ignition for our required duty; for in the same decree wherein God decides the final state of a person, He decides the means to that end just as well as the end itself. If God decrees to make such a person saved, in that same decree He also decides that this

<column-break/>

person shall have grace, and shall use these means, and shall fulfill these duties which are required in a person who shall be saved. The elect of God are ordained by God to be conformed to the image of His Son. <margin>Rom. 8:29.</margin> Rom. 8:29. God has ordained beforehand that we should walk in good works. <margin>Eph. 2:10.</margin> Eph. 2:10.

And just as God has decreed that such a number of people shall be damned, He has likewise also decreed to allow these people to walk forward according to the vain imaginations of their own hearts, and to do what is right in their own eyes, so that their deserved end may be their destruction.

It is a piece of folly to use the decree of the end as an argument for the rejection or neglect of the means.

I know there is no one among you who would not consider it a very absurd and unreasonable conclusion if a person were to reason thus: "God has unchangeably fixed in His decree how long I shall live; my days are numbered; I shall live that long and no longer: and therefore I will use no means to prolong my life, or to regain my health; I shall neither eat, nor drink, nor use the Doctor, etc." This would be an obvious absurdity and madness; for just as God has decided how long you shall live, so He has also decided that you shall use those means which He has ordained to bring your life to that length.

It was just as in that great, violent storm when Paul and the other men were in the ship sailing to Rome, *Acts 27:24*. The Angel of God said to Paul that none of them should perish, but only the ship; nevertheless, Paul says in the 31st verse to them that unless they stay in the ship, they could not be saved. God decrees the means which must be used as well as the end. So it was with Hezekiah in *2 Kings 20:6*, when the Lord, at his prayer, added fifteen years to his days; now notice, would it have been reasonable in him if he had concluded from this: "The Lord has promised, I shall live so many years longer; and therefore, I shall neither eat nor drink, nor sleep and such like to prolong my life"? No, certainly: for when God decreed that he should live fifteen years longer, He also decreed that he should use the means to regain his health and to prolong his life, in the 7th verse.

But I shall stay no longer on this point, but come now to handle the words in an absolute consideration: *we are not appointed to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.* In these words, something is first implied: "we are not appointed to wrath," which makes it known that there is a certain number of people appointed by God to wrath. Secondly, something is expressed here: namely, that there is a certain number of people who are not appointed to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation. And thirdly, it is expressed here that Jesus Christ is the means ordained by God the Father, in and through whom people should obtain salvation.

These are the three main points upon which I shall stand; I shall begin with that which is implied, and in the afternoon come to that which is expressed. First—

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>

    That there is a certain number of people appointed by God to be the objects of his eternal **Wrath**. <margin>Deut. 29:4.</margin>

former is a work of God’s supreme power; the latter a work of his justice. One considers a human as a rational creature and changeable; the other as fallen into sin.

    **Question:** How can this consist with the mercy of God, to ordain any of his creatures to wrath?
    I answer: It can very well accord with God’s mercy to set his creatures for wrath.
    1. God has an **absolute sovereignty**, or supreme power and freedom over all his creatures, to do with them as he pleases: *May I not do what I will with my own?* (Romans 9:21). And who are you, O man, who talks back to God?

He was capable of doing both the will of God and also of persevering in that state in which God had placed him, and so to be eternally blessed. It is true, had God infused any evil qualities into man, it would be another matter; but God’s hand is free from such a thing. *God made man upright at the first, but since then they have sought out many schemes* (Ecclesiastes 7:29). Adam was in a state of perfection, but only under a possibility of falling if he willed it; and God, foreseeing that man would fall, had great reason why every man should be condemned, because every one fell. So with the Angels; they were first created perfect, yet changeable, and because they fell away, the Lord condemned every one of them, and...

and he did not save any [of them]; but he does not deal with us in this way; he spared none of the fallen angels; yet nevertheless he saves some of us; and therefore he has shown greater mercy to you who are the sinful sons and daughters of Adam than he did to the fallen angels. Take this for an answer: that the Lord shows greater mercy in saving and ordaining a person to life and salvation than he would have shown strictness of justice if he had condemned every person in the world. I shall prove it to you in this way, because God was not bound to save anyone; and therefore if he does so, it is a proof of grace and mercy. Give me leave to explain this to you by this parable: imagine a company of evildoers who were all condemned to die. Now, if a Prince were to come to them and single out one of them, he would show greater mercy in saving that one than he would have exercised strictness of punishment if he had hanged them all, because every one of them had deserved it.

This is how it stands with us: We have all transgressed and violated God’s Law, and therefore we lie under the guilt of damnation. Now, all being condemned persons, it is greater grace in God to save even one of us than it would be strictness if he had saved no one. And let this much serve as an answer to the first question.

<margin>Question.</margin>
The next matter of which I shall speak to you is to show you what these "black marks" <note>The "black marks" refer to spiritual signs or evidence that a person might be a "reprobate"—someone not chosen by God for salvation.</note> are, which the Scripture sets forth regarding such persons who are ordained by God to be the objects of his eternal wrath?

<margin>The marks of a reprobate revealed.</margin>
(Beloved) we can judge no one for the present: we may say that a person who continues in such a sinful way of life is not yet called; but we cannot say he is not elect. But if he perseveres, living and dying in such a course of sin, this clearly proves that such a person is an object of wrath.

<margin>The sin against the Holy Spirit described.</margin>
1. A person who has committed the sin against the Holy Spirit <note>Historically, this was considered the "unpardonable sin," involving a willful and malicious rejection of known spiritual truth.</note> is without doubt ordained by God to damnation. This is beyond dispute, because it shall not be forgiven him in this life, nor in the life to come (Matthew 12:32). There are several "ingredients" that come together to make up this sin—the sin against the Holy Spirit—namely:
1. A person must be a professor <note>A "professor" in this context is someone who openly declares or "professes" their religious faith.</note> of the Religion.
2. He must have knowledge alongside his profession.
3. He must have some appearance of holiness.
4. He must fall away from all these things.
5. He must persecute the same, and
6. He must do all this willfully, against his own conscience. All these things are present together in the sin against the Holy Spirit. And when a person reaches this point, the Lord has no intention of saving him.

Now the other marks which I shall give you are not as clear and indisputable as these; but nevertheless they are likely symptoms and accompanying things which the Scripture points out regarding

<column-break/>

such people who are appointed to wrath.

<margin>2nd Mark of Reprobation.</margin>
<margin>Acts 13:48.</margin>
2. A person of whom you can give a bad sign of possibly being appointed to wrath is one who, all his life, persists in rebellion and contempt against the Ministry of God’s Word (Acts 13:48). *As many as were ordained to eternal life believed*; but the others, who were not ordained for it, rejected it and put the Word of God far from them. Thus did Amaziah (2 Chronicles 25:16) when the Prophet rebuked him for seeking help from the gods of the Heathen, who could not deliver themselves. The King answered him and said, "Have they made you the King’s Counselor? Stop, why should they strike you?" Then the Prophet stopped and said, "I perceive that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel." A person may guess that God has determined to condemn such a person who is under the Ministry of God’s Word and yet spends his whole life resisting and despising it.

<margin>3rd Mark.</margin>
<margin>Romans 2:5.</margin>
<margin>Romans 11:7.</margin>
3. That person who is given over by God to a judicial hardening of the heart and to a final impenitence: you may fear that such a person is ordained to wrath (Romans 2:5): *but after your hardened and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath against the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.* So too in Romans 11:7, the Apostle speaks there of a remnant according to the election of grace, but the rest were hardened. When God shall give a person over to a condemnatory hardening of the heart—when he shall harden his heart by a righteous judgment and give him over to final impenitence—it is a sign that such a person is appointed to wrath.

<margin>4th Mark.</margin>
4. In the event that God, all your life long, has withdrawn the power of his Spirit from his ordinances <note>The "ordinances" refer to the standard practices of the church, such as preaching, prayer, and the sacraments.</note> which you have enjoyed: when you notice that the person sitting with you in the pew in God’s house becomes better and better through every ordinance and means of service, and you become worse and worse; his heart more humble, and yours more proud; his heart softer and more tender and sensitive to the least sin, and yours harder and unyielding; his conscience more awakened and noticing the danger of sin, and yours more dull and insensitive—when he binds the word of God to himself as "marrow and fatness" (the delight and testimony of his heart), but you find no sweetness or delight in it at all.

You people who have these sorrowful signs upon you are in a very grievous state; and therefore, consider earnestly what shall become of it on another day. If you continue in this state of unfruitfulness under the means of grace, and God withdraws from you the power of his Spirit from his ordinances under which you live, this is a bad sign that you are a person appointed to wrath.

When God shall say, as in Isaiah 9:10 <note>This citation is actually Isaiah 6:9-10, though the text lists it as 9:10.</note>: *That hearing you hear, but do not understand; and seeing you see, but do not perceive; make your heart fat, and your ears heavy, and shut your eyes, lest you see with your eyes, nor hear with your ears, nor understand with your heart, and be converted and healed*; this is a sorrowful sign of your rejection.

5. When a person makes the grace and mercy of God a means to keep him in the ways of sin and rebellion—

<margin>Jude v. 4.</margin>
"Shall we sin (says the Apostle) because grace abounds? God forbid!" He speaks of this with loathing and horror—when people grow bold because of God's grace, and because He is so good and merciful, they desire to be all the more godless and sinful. This is a dismal thing. In the Epistle of Jude, verse 4, the Apostle speaks of certain godless men who "turn the grace of our God into lewdness." Why, and who are these? He says they are those "who were marked out long ago for this condemnation." The Apostle sets it down as a sign of people who are ordained to wrath, who change the grace of God into wantonness and sin because grace is abundant.

6. Apostasy <note>Renouncing one's faith.</note> unto the end is a sign that indicates a person is ordained by God to be an object of His wrath.

Now, therefore, examine yourselves, whether any of you are written on this "black page," and if you live and die under any of these sorrowful signs, you have reason to fear that you are people ordained to wrath, and that you perhaps cannot obtain salvation through Jesus Christ.

And thus I have finished the doctrinal part of this point. I could now, in the application, touch upon the disputes between the Papists <note>A term used by Protestants for Roman Catholics.</note> and our theologians, and between the Arminians <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius who disagreed with strict Calvinist views on predestination.</note> and the Orthodox <note>The "Rechtsinnige," or those holding the traditional Reformed/Calvinist view.</note> regarding this doctrine; but these disputes are better suited for the Schools <note>Universities or academic debates.</note> than for the Pulpit, and better for a scholar than for a common listener. Therefore, I shall only make a clear and practical use of the same, and thus be done.

<margin>1st Use.</margin>
Use. It is so, then, that there is a certain number of people ordained by God to be objects of His eternal wrath. Oh, then! What cause do you and I have to thank God and Jesus Christ that He has not appointed us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation? That we are delivered from the coming wrath through Jesus Christ, as in 1 Thessalonians 1:10 <note>The text says 1 Tim. 1:10, but the context and citation "the last" verse suggests 1 Thess. 1:10 is intended.</note>. You praise and thank the name of your God that His thoughts toward you from eternity have been of mercy and grace, of forgiveness and reconciliation, of peace and loving friendship. Oh, praise God and thank Jesus Christ, who has stilled that wrath of His Father which otherwise, like a consuming fire, would have burned your soul like stubble. And when you would not have been able to stand before this everlasting burning, Jesus Christ came to be, as it were, a

<column-break/>

partition between His Father's wrath and you. Oh, thank Jesus Christ that He placed Himself between the two, so that you might obtain salvation through Him.

The second use. If God has ordained a certain number of people to wrath, this can be a matter of instruction, by which the people of God may know that they are not appointed to wrath, but to salvation; and this is clear in the Text. The Apostle says, *we are not appointed to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation.* This is a great comfort to you: that you do not merely have a "guessing" faith, but a firm and certain faith. You have the testimony of the Spirit and the zeal of the Spirit for that very thing; you can reach a full assurance that you are not appointed to wrath.

Through the revealed will of God, you come to know His elective will—that He has had thoughts of grace, mercy, forgiveness, and glory over you from all eternity. For how else could the Apostle here say so confidently, *we are not appointed to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation?* So 
<margin>2 Cor. 13. 6. 7.</margin> 
2 Corinthians 13:5-7 says the Apostle: *I hope you will understand that we are not reprobates,* although we are accounted as such by the people of the world. Although you may be reprobate in your own eyes, nevertheless, have confidence that we are not so in the sight of God. So God’s people can certainly know in themselves that they are not reprobates—or what amounts to the same thing—that they are elect, and will certainly obtain salvation through Jesus Christ.

<margin>3rd Use</margin>
The third use: I draw this from it—that Christians should not hastily conclude of themselves that they are ordained to wrath simply because they do not perceive that they are in a state of grace. Although it is true that a person cannot be "effectually called" <note>A theological term for the moment God draws a person to faith.</note> without having grace, nevertheless, he can be elect and yet for the present still be without grace. For all of God's elect persist for a time in a state of unregeneration <note>The state before being "born again."</note>. Therefore, be as evil as you wish to be, or as evil as you can be; it is true, you may say for the present, "I am not called," but you cannot say, "I am not elect."

Christians must not conclude that because they do not feel themselves to be in a state of grace, they are therefore not elect but appointed to wrath. It is true that whomever God has predestined to eternal life, He will effectually call that person before they die; nevertheless, a person can remain a long while in a state of unregeneration before they are called. Therefore, beware of this hasty conclusion against yourself: from your present sinfulness, you can only judge "no calling," but you cannot conclude "no election." For election happened before all ages, but calling happens in time.

<margin>4th Use</margin>
The fourth use: seeing as it is so, that God has appointed some people to wrath, what then? What comfort can this be to all of you who are among God's elect, and are not of that number appointed to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation? It may be that your state here in this life is dismal and miserable, but this can lighten your heart: that you are not appointed to an everlasting mi-

<meta>This page continues the sermon on 1 Thessalonians 5:9. The previous page discussed the "signs" of being rejected by God; this page moves to the nature of "Salvation" and the doctrine of Predestination (the idea that God has chosen a specific group of people for heaven).</meta>

# ## ### ->Wrath and Grace.<- 728

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
I shall at present only speak of the two first particulars: that which a Christian is not ordained for, and that which he is ordained for. We are not appointed to wrath, but to the obtaining of Salvation, from which we can learn this observation:

That there is a certain number, which is ordained by God, not to wrath, but to the obtaining of Salvation. It is not necessary to bring forth many Scripture passages to prove this, since the Lord speaks so clearly in these words. In following this point, I shall do three things:

1. I shall show you what this Salvation is, to which a certain number of people are ordained.
2. I shall examine whether this Doctrine of Predestination <note>The theological belief that God has determined beforehand who will be saved.</note> and God's ordaining of a certain number of people to Salvation is a doctrine which would make people lazy and careless.
3. I shall show you whether God, in ordaining some people to Salvation, looks upon their foreseen faith or good works. First, then:

<margin>* Question.</margin>
1. What is meant here by the "Salvation" to which some people are ordained?

<margin>Answer. A description of what salvation is.</margin>
I answer: there are two things included in this word "Salvation." You must know in general that it is that happy and glorious state which the glorified persons in Heaven shall have and enjoy. This state contains within itself two things: there is in this state something **Privative** <note>Meaning something that is absent or removed.</note> which you shall be free from, and something **Positive** <note>Meaning something that is actually present and possessed.</note> which you shall actively enjoy.

<margin>Ephesians 5:27.</margin>
1. There is something **Privative** that you shall lack: you shall be delivered from sin, and from the causes of sin, and from the punishments of sin. But here [on earth] you are not so; the best of God's children are not delivered from sin here, but it is a stain even in the most beautiful form. But then you shall be revealed—as it says in Ephesians 5:27—without spot or wrinkle or any such thing; yes, you shall be holy and blameless.

2. You shall also be free from the causes of sin, which are two: either from within, such as a sinful, corrupt, and defiled nature; or from without, such as the temptations and suggestions of Satan. Then you shall be delivered from the cause of sin within, from the corrupt and tainted nature, which shall then be changed into a very glorious and purified nature—a nature which will not have in itself the slightest pull or inclination toward wickedness. And thirdly:

3. You shall be delivered from the temptations of the Devil. He shall then no longer be powerful enough to disturb you or trouble you, or to entice you toward sin.

<margin>1 Kings 6:32</margin>
3. You shall be delivered from the punishments of sin, whether they be outward—such as troubles, anxieties, disgraces, persecutions, and death—or inward, such as terror, fear, and trembling of the conscience, and the like. When you come into Heaven, you shall be delivered from all these things. But before you get there, one cannot have any of these [freedoms]; you shall be delivered neither from sin, nor from its causes, nor from its punishments. In 1 Kings 6:32, it is said: That in the entrance to the Holy of Holies, palm trees were carved upon the doors. Now, a palm tree is an *emblem* <note>A symbolic image.</note> or a sign of victory and triumph; and these were placed there to signify that as long as we

<column-break/>

live in this world, we are soldiers called to fight; but we are not victors until we come into the Holy of Holies—until we come into Heaven. It was the rule under the Law that if an unclean thing fell into an earthen vessel, the vessel was unclean until it was broken. So it is with us: there is uncleanness in our bodies, and we shall not be pure until our earthly tabernacles <note>A biblical metaphor for the human body.</note> are laid down in the dust.

But secondly: In this Salvation, there is not only something **Privative** (that which one lacks or is free from), but also something **Positive**, or that which is actually present and truly enjoyed. First, we shall clearly know God and see Him as He is. Here we only know what He is *not*; and we behold Him by what He is not. We know that He is not unrighteous, nor unjust, nor unwise, nor unmerciful, and the like. But we do not know [fully] what that wisdom is, and that holiness, and omniscience, and omnipotence, etc., which are in God. But in Heaven we shall know Him as He is. We shall know God fully, and love Him perfectly and without hypocrisy, and serve Him tirelessly, and praise Him continually, and enjoy Him eternally and inseparably. <note>original: "Deum sine fine videbimus, sine fastidio amabimus, sine defatigatione laudabimus, sec. Bernardus" — We shall see God without end, we shall love Him without distaste, we shall praise Him without weariness, according to Saint Bernard.</note> It is true, the people of God have an enjoyment of God here in this life, but this is very different from that which they shall have in Heaven. 

1. It differs in **Mode** (*in the manner of enjoyment*): here they enjoy God mediately <note>Indirectly, through other things.</note> and in and through His Ordinances <note>Religious practices like prayer or the sacraments.</note>; but then we shall enjoy Him immediately, without ordinances and established helping-means. Here we see Him only as if in a dark mirror, but then we shall see Him face to face. 

2. In **Measure**: here we enjoy Him only in a small, weak measure; but there we shall enjoy Him in a greater and fuller measure. 

3. In **Duration**: here we enjoy Him only for a time, now and then; but in Heaven we shall enjoy Him always and for all eternity, without separation. 

4. In **Certainty**: here we have the enjoyment of God only in hope and expectation; but there in the actual enjoyment, being continually blessed in the full act—there is the soul-saving vision.

But so much for the first matter: what this Salvation is to which God has appointed us.

**Question 2.** The next matter to be handled is this: whether God's ordaining of some people to be objects of His wrath and others to obtain Salvation—whether this decree of God gives people any righteous plea or excuse to embolden themselves to continue sinning against God? Can a person conclude thus: "If God has ordained and decided from all eternity that I should be a vessel of wrath, and His decrees are unchangeable, then let me do what I will—even if I hear many sermons or fulfill many good duties—it is nonetheless impossible for me to be preserved or saved"? And on the other hand: "If God has not ordained me to wrath but to the obtaining of salvation, I may then live as I please; I have no need to hear, or to read, or to pray, or to perform any holy service..."

<summary>This page defines the Christian concept of "Salvation" as the removal of sin and suffering (Privative) and the direct, eternal enjoyment of God's presence (Positive). It also introduces a defense of the doctrine of predestination against the claim that it encourages immoral or lazy behavior.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the doctrine of predestination from page 728. It addresses the common objection that if God has already decided who is saved, then human effort and morality do not matter.</meta>

### ->Wrath and Grace.<- 729

...accomplish, for I am certain that I shall be saved. Beloved, although the teaching of God's irrevocable and unchangeable decree <note>A theological term for God's eternal plan or decision regarding the fate of humanity.</note> is in itself very good, nevertheless a great many wicked people put it to a bad use; they are very quick to adopt such corrupt reasoning as this. But now let us examine for a moment whether this teaching of God’s decree brings about any such consequences as these: "if I am ordained to wrath, let me do what I might, it is impossible for me to be saved; and if I am appointed to salvation, I may live as I please, for I am certain I shall never be condemned."

Now, here I shall show you in four or five specific observations that this teaching of God's decree—in ordaining some men to be vessels of wrath <note>A biblical metaphor for those destined for judgment.</note> and others to the obtaining of salvation—does not at all drive men to such conclusions. For first, in this very passage, the Apostle makes a directly opposite use of it: in the verse preceding my text he says, *let us who are of the day be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.* Why? *For God has not appointed us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.* And the Apostle makes the same use of it in <margin>2 Peter 1:5, 10.</margin> *Be diligent to make your calling and election sure... add to your faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge temperance,* etc. The assurance of your election <note>The belief that God has chosen a person for salvation.</note> should be a motive for you to add grace to grace, and not sin to sin. So, this is the first answer: the Scripture makes a different use of the assurance of our election—namely, to be a motive to awaken us to add grace to grace and holiness to holiness.

2. Know this as an answer: that when God in His eternal decree ordained some men to the obtaining of salvation, in that same decree He also decreed the means which must be used in order for them to reach their salvation, just as much as He decreed the salvation itself. Truly, if God had said, "I have determined such and such people to be objects of grace, and therefore they may do what they want, they will be certain to be saved," that would be one thing; but there is no such promise as this in the Book of God. Rather, just as He has destined some for salvation, so He has also ordained them to use the means that lead to that end, as you can see in Ephesians 1:4. There the Apostle says, *He has chosen us in him before the foundation of the world.* But what follows? To what end? *That we should be holy and blameless before him in love.* Where God decrees an end, He also ordains the means which must be used to obtain that end.

<margin>Question.</margin>
3. Consider this: you would think it a very ridiculous conclusion if someone brought forth this logic in natural things; and therefore it is also vain and foolish to conclude this way in spiritual things. For God has determined how long you and I, and every one of us, shall live, and when and by what death we shall die; and all the world cannot change this decree of His. Now, because these 

<column-break/>

things are decided by God, and His decrees are unchangeable, should we conclude for ourselves that we will not eat, drink, or sleep, but instead put ourselves in danger and run into ruin? You would surely consider this nothing but highly unreasonable in natural things, and therefore it is much more so in spiritual things. 

I have read of a man who was a great promoter of this opinion which I am now contradicting. When he fell into a great sickness, he sent for a doctor to come to him. When the doctor arrived, the man desired him to prescribe something for the recovery of his health and to take away his illness. The doctor, knowing that he was a man of that opinion, said to him, "Sir, everyone's time is determined, and God has decreed how long you shall live, and His decree is unchangeable; therefore, why do you need to take a doctor or use any means? For if He has decreed that you shall recover from this sickness, then you shall recover." He answered, "That is true"; but he nevertheless did not want to be advised to neglect the means, but desired the doctor to prescribe something for him. The doctor did so, and through God's blessing upon it, he restored him to his former health, whereby he was afterwards always convinced of the error of his previous opinion. You must therefore note that just as God has ordained the end, so He has also ordained the means, which stretch toward and work together for that end.

4. Note further that even if a person knows what God’s decree concerning him is, this must not be a hindrance to holiness, or a spur or awakening to godlessness. Even if God had not ordained you to life at all, you would still owe Him service simply because He is your Creator. Even if you could know (which you cannot) that God has appointed you to wrath, this could still be no excuse for you to break out in rebellion against God. For since He is your Creator and Maker, and you are the work of His hands, He may demand from you service and submission as His rightful due; you owe this to Him because He is your Creator.

But if you know (of which a person can certainly be assured) that you are not appointed to be a vessel of wrath, but an object of grace, then much greater and stronger obligations are laid upon you to serve Him with cheerfulness and to be constant in the exercises of holiness. And thus I have finished the second particular point.

<margin>
3rd Question: Whether foreseen faith or good works are the moving cause which moves God to ordain someone to salvation.
</margin>
3. We come now to the third question in order, and it is this: whether God, in ordaining someone to life and salvation, looks upon their foreseen faith or good works; or whether the foresight of faith or good works is the moving cause which moves God to ordain someone to salvation. 

In answering this question, I shall present these three conclusions to you.

<margin>
Answer.
1st Conclusion.
Romans 8:29-30.
</margin>
1. It is entirely true and certain that those whom God has ordained to salvation shall have grace and holiness in their hearts before they obtain salvation; this is true, for those whom God foreordained, them He also called.

The author uses a story about a sick man and a clever doctor to illustrate that we must still use "means" (like medicine or prayer) even if the outcome is known to God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding predestination, specifically refuting the idea that God chooses people based on "foreseen" merits. It maintains the distinction between God's grace and human effort.</meta>

### ->Wrath and Grace.<- 730

2. It is also true that those whom God has ordained to salvation, He foresaw that they would be holy; and that all those whom He has ordained to life would be sanctified. But—

3. Although God foresaw that such people would be holy, nevertheless His foresight of the same was not the moving cause <note>The "moving cause" refers to the primary motivation or reason that prompts an action—in this case, God's decision to save someone.</note> why they were ordained to life and salvation. God foresaw that every person whom He previously ordained would be called; but nevertheless, God’s foresight of the good works that these people would do was not the moving cause which moved God to ordain them to eternal life. This I shall proceed to prove to you from the Scriptures, such as in Romans 11:5, 6. There is, says the Apostle, a remnant according to the election; but of which election? Indeed, the election <margin>Romans 9:5, 6, 7.</margin> of grace. If this election had occurred because of the foresight of good works, then it must be called the "election of good works," that being the moving cause of the same according to some people's opinion; but here you see that it is called an "election of grace." <margin>2 Timothy 1:9.</margin> *Who has saved us, and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages began.* <margin>Ephesians 1:5.</margin> So again in Ephesians 1:5, the Apostle says, *Who has predestined us to the adoption of children, through Jesus Christ in Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will,* not because of their foreseen faith or good works. And so again in the ninth verse: *Having made known to us the mystery of His will, according to His good pleasure which He purposed in Himself.* And again in the eleventh verse: *We who were predestined according to the purpose of Him who works all things after the counsel of His own will.*

It is purely the good will and the pleasure of God which is the moving cause or motive why He ordains some people to the obtaining of salvation.

<margin>Reasons why God has by no means chosen anyone to salvation based on the foresight of his works.</margin> But now I shall prove this to you and make the same clear and evident through reasons: that God has by no means chosen anyone to be a vessel of glory and for the obtaining of salvation based on the foresight of his good works; and that first:

<margin>1st Reason. Romans 5:24.</margin> 1. Because God justifies no man for his possession of good works, and therefore God chooses no one based on the foresight of his good works. God does not justify men because of the having and the performing of good works; rather, we are justified freely by His grace. And if we seek to be justified by works, we have fallen from grace; much less can a person be chosen out of the rest to salvation because of God’s foresight of his good works.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin> 2. Good works in us are the fruits and effects of our election; and therefore they cannot be the cause of the same. The same thing cannot be both the cause and the fruit of <margin>Ephesians 1:4.</margin> another thing. Now, good works are the consequence of our election; for those whom God has chosen, He has chosen to this end: that they might be holy and <margin>Acts 22:14.</margin> blameless before Him in love. As was said to Paul: *The God of our fathers has chosen you beforehand, that you should know His will, and see the Just One, and hear the voice from His mouth.*

<column-break/>

3. If this were so <note>That is, if salvation were based on our own merits.</note>, then men would have something about which they might boast against God; for if God had chosen them because He foresaw that they would be holy and righteous and upright, or the like, then they might boast and say, "Lord, I am not so much beholden to You, looking at myself, that I am saved." But God does not want any flesh to boast in His presence. And He chose us for salvation, not because there was more beauty or loveliness in us than in others—there was nothing in us that His love could desire or deserve—but solely out of His grace and mercy. He sets His love upon us because He wishes to show His mercy to those to whom He will be merciful; and this obliges us all the more to show all thankfulness and obedience to God, and to wonder at and glorify His rich grace and mercy toward us.

4. All these good works which you could possibly perform can have no equality or proportion to the salvation for which God has chosen you. Our salvation is perfect and complete, but the best of our services is not so; rather, they are full of imperfections and defects. There is no proportion between them, and therefore they cannot be a moving cause why God would choose anyone to life and salvation based on the foresight of the same.

5. If election depended on foreseen faith or good works, then little children dying as such could not be chosen, because they have neither faith nor good works; but many children are chosen.

6. We are not chosen for Christ's sake; therefore, not for our own sake. Christ, indeed, is the cause of our salvation, but not the cause of our election. Christ Himself was predestined <margin>2 Peter 1:10.</margin>, and therefore He could not be the cause of our predestination. It is true, we are said to be chosen in Christ <margin>Ephesians 1:4.</margin>. We are chosen in Christ as a public person <note>A "public person" in 17th-century theology refers to a legal representative, like a King or a head of a family, who acts on behalf of others.</note>; He was the first person chosen among us, and we in Him. Suppose a new kingdom were to be established and a new King chosen: all his successors are chosen in him. God has established a kingdom of glory and has chosen Christ as King of the same, and us in Him, whom He has made kings and priests before the Most High God.

And thus I have finished the doctrinal part; we come now to the application and the use which I shall make of the same. It shall only be to draw three or four practical consequences from this, and so conclude.

1. Is it so, that God has ordained a certain number of people to the obtaining of salvation, and not to be objects of His wrath? Oh, I pray you then, in the fear of God—all you who are in the election of grace—that you will take heed that you do not value your souls too cheaply, and make them too common for base and dishonest services or uses, which God has appointed for glory. Shall your soul, which is a vessel of glory, be used in the slavery of the Devil, and in sinning against God, and in the dishonoring of God? Just as it is unbecoming for a vessel of gold to be put to a bad use...

<margin>Reason.</margin> Just as it is unbecoming to use a fine vessel for common or filthy purposes, so it is also unseemly for you—who are vessels of honor <note>A biblical metaphor from Romans 9:21, referring to those chosen by God for a noble purpose.</note>—to have your souls defiled with the muck and heap of sin and godlessness. Therefore, take heed not to spend your souls on sinful and slavish services.

<margin>2nd Consequence.</margin> 2. If this is so, then it refutes the Lord of the Sadducees <note>The Sadducees were a Jewish sect during the time of Jesus who denied the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits or the afterlife.</note>, who believed that there was no resurrection of the flesh, no immortality of the soul, no salvation for the saints, and no damnation for the sinners. How could they have held this opinion if they had believed this doctrine: that God from all eternity chose some for salvation and rejected others for damnation? God’s decrees would have to be false if their opinions were true. Take heed that you do not live in the world as if there were neither salvation for the saints nor damnation for the sinners.

<margin>Reason.</margin>
<margin>3rd Use</margin> 3. Let this teach you to undergo, with patience and contentment, all the troubles and distresses that you encounter here in this life. Seeing that God has destined you for a crown, why should you not be patient under a cross? Seeing that God has appointed you to obtain salvation hereafter, why should you not be content to endure some distress here? What does it matter if God has appointed you to imprisonment, or persecution, or misery in this life, so long as He has not ordained you for the hellish fire hereafter? This light distress, which is but for a moment, works for you a far-reaching and eternal weight of glory; therefore, let your hearts be comforted.

<margin>4th Use</margin> 4. Since this is so—that there is a certain number of people ordained by God to obtain salvation—oh, do not rest contentedly; give no rest to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, until you find some pledges and seals in your hearts that you are among those who are not appointed for wrath, but for the obtaining of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.

# THIRD SERMON.

<margin>Doctrinal conclusions concerning Predestination.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a stylized landscape or floral pattern in a square frame.</image-desc> I shall now, in order to continue this great doctrine of Predestination, present to you seven doctrinal conclusions concerning the same. First:

<margin>1.</margin> 1. That a person who is ordained and appointed by God from all eternity to obtain salvation can know that he is so ordained and appointed. Not only does the Lord know those who are His, but man can also know for certain that he is ordained by God to obtain salvation. However, the Papists <note>A historical term, often polemical, referring to Roman Catholics. The author is referencing the Counter-Reformation debate over whether a believer can be certain of their salvation.</note> are of a different opinion; they view this truth as a very harmful and arrogant doctrine—that a person could be firmly assured of his salvation. They believe that he can only have a conjectural faith, but not an assured faith. But this is an obvious untruth. For why would <margin>Luke 10:20.</margin> our Savior in Luke 10:20 command His disciples, saying: *Nevertheless do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rather rejoice because your names are written in*

<column-break/>

*heaven*? How could they rejoice in this privilege if they were ignorant of it, or could not know that their names were written in the book of life? So in <margin>Eph. 1:5.</margin> Ephesians 1:5, the Apostle says, *having predestined us to adoption as sons*; they were assured of their adoption. So in Revelation <margin>Rev. 2:17.</margin> 2:17: *To him who overcomes I will give some of the hidden manna to eat. And I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written which no one knows except him who receives it.* The "new name" signifies here the rebirth, and the "white stone" <note>In ancient courts, a white stone was given to signify acquittal or a "yes" vote. In this context, it represents God's "vote" or verdict of innocence and acceptance of the believer.</note> is the reassurance of pardon. They have a white stone given to them—that is, the Lord shall give them a seal and pledge in their hearts that their sins are forgiven and that they are brought into a state of grace and salvation; and he who has this white stone will know that he has it.

->But I shall further prove and explain this to you by demonstration, that a man can be assured of his salvation, and that firstly,<-

<margin>2 Pet. 1:10.</margin> 1. Because God commands and binds people to labor to make their calling and election sure, as in 2 Peter 1:10. *Therefore, brothers,* says the Apostle, *be even more diligent to make your call and election sure.* This does not mean making it sure on God’s side, but sure with respect to your own knowledge of it. And if it were not an attainable thing, the Apostle would by no means have commanded us to do the same. Therefore, it is not an impossible thing, but one which can be obtained, and has been obtained by many of God’s worthy servants.

<margin>1 Thess. 1:4.</margin> 2. Other people can have a conjectural knowledge of our salvation, as in 1 Thessalonians 1:4: *Knowing, beloved brethren, your election by God.* Paul gave a strong indication that the Thessalonians were chosen by God. What then? Now, if another person can judge so rightly of us, then we ourselves can be much more assured of the same. So again in Philippians 4:3, <margin>Phil. 4:3.</margin> Paul, speaking of some of his fellow laborers, says *whose names are in the book of life.* If others can know that our names are in the book of life, how much more can we ourselves? We can be certain of our calling; and if so, then we can also be certain of our election, for an effectual calling is an infallible sign of our election. Romans 8:30. And that we <margin>Rom. 8:30.</margin> can be assured of our calling is frequently recounted in Scripture. This is the first doctrinal conclusion: that those who are chosen by God and appointed to obtain salvation can know and be fully assured that they are so ordained.

<margin>2nd Conclusion.</margin> 2. Note this conclusion: that no one can know for certain that he is chosen by God and appointed to obtain salvation by "climbing up" and searching into God’s decrees and hidden mysteries. For *who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?* Rather, we must investigate and find the same by the power of God’s decrees upon our hearts. If we find these fruits and effects of election in our hearts—which accompany those who are chosen—then we can conclude that we are chosen. In 2 Peter <margin>2 Pet. 1:10.</margin> 1:10, the Apostle says, *be diligent to make your calling and election sure.* Election was before calling; but here calling is placed before election: to know—

# ->Wrath and Grace.<-

...to give [reason] that although election precedes calling, a man cannot know his election except by his calling: and therefore, if you have a seal in your heart of your powerful calling, from that you can conclude your election without doubt. Romans 8:30 <note>original: "Rom. 8.30"</note>, *for whom he predestined, them he also called*; we can know our election as it is active and powerful in our hearts, bringing forth in us all new obedience. We must first demonstrate our calling, and then, through it, our election. If you do not test or examine your election, and do not demonstrate it through sanctification <note>The process of being made holy or being set apart for God's service</note>, it is but wild and loose guesses, foolish delusions, spirited deceptions, and bold imaginings of a deceived heart.

<margin>3rd Conclusion.</margin>
3. Take this as a final conclusion: that although a man can know, and ought to know, that he is chosen and appointed by God to obtain salvation, he nevertheless ought not to know—indeed, he cannot know—that he is appointed for wrath. A man can make his election sure, but he cannot make his rejection and damnation sure. We find in the Scripture those who were assured of their election, but no one who was assured of their damnation. A man who continues in godless and sinful ways can say that he is not [yet] called; but he cannot say that he is not chosen. No, not even the most godless man in the world (unless he has committed the sin against the Holy Spirit); for although he may run for a long time in sinful and harmful ways, yet God can call him to Himself at the last.

<margin>4th Conclusion.</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 2:19.</margin>
4. That God's decrees and ordinances regarding man's future state and condition are irrevocable and unchangeable. In 2 Timothy 2:19, it says: *The firm foundation of God stands*, that is, the decree and the purpose of God regarding man's salvation is unchangeable, it stands firm. If the laws of the Medes and Persians were so absolute that they could not be changed, much less can the decrees of God be changed. No one who is not chosen can [later] be chosen, and no one who is chosen can be damned. John 6:39 <note>original: "Ioh. 6.39"</note>, Christ says, *this is the will of the Father, who has sent me, that of all he has given me, I should lose nothing*: not one of those given to Christ in God’s decree shall be lost. Romans 11:2 <note>The text cites Rom 11:22, but the quote corresponds to Rom 11:2</note>, *God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew*; those whom God first intended to bring to eternal life, He rejects none of them.

<margin>John 6:39</margin>
<margin>Romans 11:22.</margin>
<margin>Objection.</margin>
But now the Papists <note>A historical, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> and others strongly oppose this teaching, viewing God's decrees as changeable; and in these days, this opinion prevails among many who hold that God's decrees are changeable. They bring forward three passages from Scripture to prove this. The first is John 6:70, where Christ says to his disciples, *Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?* From this they conclude that all those who are chosen by God might not obtain salvation through Him.

<margin>John 6:70</margin>
<margin>Answer.</margin>
There is a twofold election: an outward and an inward election, and you must make a distinction between these. When Christ

<column-break/>

says, *Have I not chosen you twelve?*, He speaks there of an outward election to the office of Apostleship. Judas was not chosen in God’s decree of election unto salvation; for he was a son of perdition <note>A biblical term for one destined for destruction</note>, and Hell was his place: but he was only outwardly chosen to be an Apostle.

Another Scripture passage which they bring against the unchangeability of God's decree is in Exodus 32:32, 33. There Moses prays that if God would not forgive the sins of His people, He should blot his name out of His Book. And the Lord said to him: *Whoever has sinned against me, him I will blot out of my book.* Now they say, if the names of those written in God's Book of Life can be blotted out, then the decrees of God are changeable. So also in Revelation 22:19, it is said, *if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part from the book of life.*

Answer: I shall answer this objection very briefly. Theologians note that three kinds of books are attributed to God in the Scripture.

1. A Book of Providence, in Psalm 139:16: *all these things were written in your book*, that is, the book of God’s providence.

2. There is a Book of God’s Judgments in Revelation 20:12: *And I saw the dead, small and great, standing before God: and the books were opened, and the dead were judged according to those things written in the books.* When Christ comes to judgment, then a great ledger <note>original: "kieken-boeck"</note> will be opened, in which everything done here on earth is remembered.

3. There is a Book of Life, in which a person's name, once written, can never be blotted out again. But the "Book of Life" mentioned in the Scripture has a double meaning: sometimes by the Book of Life is meant the eternal decree and purpose of God regarding those who shall be saved by Him, and in this sense it must be understood in Philippians 4:3, *Whose names are in the Book of Life*, and likewise in Luke 10:20 <note>The text cites Luke 19:20, but the quote is from Luke 10:20</note>, *Rejoice, because your names are written in the book of life.* Throughout the New Testament, the Book of Life must be understood as the eternal decree and purpose of God regarding those who shall be saved.

2. There is also in Scripture a Book of Life which must be understood not as the eternal decree of God, but as the providence of God and His special care and protection over His Church—the preservation of His people under the wings of His providence. This is called the Book of Life, as in Exodus 32:33: *Whoever has sinned against me, him I will blot out of my book*, that is: that man who stubbornly, obstinately, and pridefully continues in sin, I shall blot his name out of my book; meaning, I shall cast him out from my protection and providence; he shall be a man excluded from the community. And in this sense it is used by Moses when he asked God to blot his name out of His Book.

So God says in Ezekiel 13:9: *And my hand shall be against the prophets who see vanity and divine lies, they shall not be in the assembly of my people, nor shall they be written in the record of the house of Israel*, which is even...

# ->Wrath and Grace.<-

<margin>Objection. Exod. 32:32, 33. <note>original: "Exod. 32. 2, 33." The text likely refers to Moses asking to be blotted out of God's book.</note></margin>
...is as much as if he had said, they shall not be written in the book of life; not to be written in the book of life in this sense is to be excommunicated or excluded from the Congregation.

I shall further confirm this Doctrine to you by demonstrating that God's decrees are unchangeable and irrevocable; for were it otherwise:
1. God would necessarily have to be a changeable God, which is directly contrary to what the Scripture assures us of him, namely, *that in him is no variableness, neither shadow of turning*, James 1:17.
<margin>James 1:17.</margin>

<margin>John 10:28.</margin>
<margin>Rev. 22:9. <note>The OCR likely misread 20:12 or 22:19.</note></margin>
<margin>Answer.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 139:6.</margin>
2. Jesus Christ (if I may speak with reverence) would be a liar, and his words false, if this were not so; for he says in John 10:28: *And I give unto my sheep eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.* Christ would not be as good as his word if any of those who were given to him by his Father should be lost; or if any of those appointed for salvation should come to miss it.

<margin>Rev. 20:2.</margin>
3. If God’s decrees were changeable, then Paul’s "Golden Chain" in Romans 8:30 would be broken: *Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.* We now come to a fifth concluding reason.

<margin>5th Concluding Reason.</margin>
5. That God's decree regarding salvation concerns only the smallest number of the human race in the world. God's decree regarding the ordaining of men to life extends only to a very small remnant: the world of unbelievers is like herds of goats, very easy to count; on the other hand, the elect of God are only like sheep scattered here and there upon the mountains. The godless are like weeds which grow everywhere; but the pious are like "Trees of Righteousness" of Christ's own planting, yet planted very sparsely in the world. Christ’s flock is but a small, very small flock in comparison to the world; there is but a remnant according to the election of grace, a very small remnant which shall obtain salvation; the rest are hardened.

6. Although God’s decrees regarding man’s salvation extend to so very few, nevertheless this is absolutely no ground for us to have heavy thoughts of God, or to look upon him as cruel and unmerciful: the reasons for this have been partly presented here previously.

1. Because God is not obligated to make anyone blessed, and therefore it is no cruelty or injustice in him that he preserves so few.

2. God has sovereignty and supreme power over all his creatures, and can do with them what pleases him, and no one may say to him, "What are you doing?"

3. The Lord would have shown even greater mercy if he had made only one person in the world blessed, than the severity of justice he would have exercised had he damned them all; because they had all sinned, and therefore deserved damnation, and God is not obligated to preserve any of them.
<margin>Zech. 13:9</margin>

<column-break/>

4. God has dealt better with us than he did with the Angels who sinned; for you know that all the Angels in Heaven who sinned by wanting to become like the Most High were cast down and damned, and not one of them is preserved, but they are all kept in chains of darkness until the great day of judgment. Nevertheless, despite the fact that the entire human race had sinned and so fell short of the glory of God, they were not all damned; and that is because Jesus Christ did not take on the nature of Angels, but the nature of man. Therefore, although all the Angels who sinned perished, we, although we have all sinned, do not all perish; but there is a remnant, delivered from death and damnation, and ordained to the obtaining of salvation.

<margin>Mark 13:20.</margin>
<margin>Isa. 1:9.</margin>
<margin>Isa. 65:8.</margin>
5. The world fares better because of these persons who are set apart in God’s decree for the obtaining of salvation; for were it not for God's decree of election—that such a number of men should be saved—the world would not have stood until this day; and it shall stand no longer than until the number of the elect is fulfilled, and then the elements shall melt with fervent heat, and the earth with everything that is in it shall be burned up. God still gives deliverance, and safety, and preservation to the world for the sake of the elect. We must look at God's decrees in respect to the elect, that the world still stands to this day. Worldly men fare better in terms of the comforts of this life for the sake of God’s elect. The days of affliction which came over Jerusalem and all of Judea were shortened for the elect's sake, Mark 13:20. It was for their sake that Israel was not made like Sodom and Gomorrah; that a remnant was left, Isaiah 1:9. So it went in Isaiah 65:8: *Thus saith the Lord, As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one saith, Destroy it not; for a blessing is in it: so will I do for my servants' sakes, that I may not destroy them all.* And Job testifies that an island is delivered by the pureness of hands, Job 22:30.

Finally, consider this conclusion: that although you are bound to pray for the forgiveness of your sins and for the sanctification of your nature, you are nonetheless not bound to pray to God for your election. Why? Because this work is already perfectly done. Just as we do not need to pray for the Creation of the world because that work is complete, so we do not need to pray for our election because that work is fully finished. We must not pray for works already completed; but we must pray for the consequences and fruits of predestination and election, such as calling, sanctification, forgiveness, rebirth, and the like; but not for the election itself.

### FOURTH SERMON.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' within a square frame featuring floral or architectural motifs.</image-desc>

I shall now speak to you with joyful confidence, so that there may not be one poor, lowly, smitten soul among you who fears that they are rejected by God, and not in the number of those who are ordained to Salvation.

1. Let me now say this for your comfort: when I present to you the fruits and effects of election, it must not be understood that these must be in you as soon as you are born; for Paul, although he was chosen, was nevertheless a man of a very godless life and conduct for thirty years. Therefore, do not say that you are rejected by God because you are so godless; for a person can live in sin for a long time and yet be chosen by God for Salvation, as seen in *Titus 3:3*.
<margin>
Titus 3:3.
</margin>
There the Apostle says: *For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another; but* (he says) *after that the kindness and love of God our Savior toward man appeared*; indicating that an elect person can be a slave to his lusts for a long time and live in sins, when nevertheless the purpose of God is to bring him to glory.

2. When I express these things as signs of your election, I do not mean the having of them in actual practice [at all times], but in the "habit" <note>term: habit / habitual grace; this refers to an internal state or quality of the soul given by God, which exists even when a person is sleeping or not actively performing a religious act.</note> of the heart; although for a time it may be without use or exercise. For in children, although they have no actual conviction through the Word, they can nevertheless have the graces habitually within them, which is enough; there must be in everyone who goes to Heaven either a habitual or an actual grace.

3. Although you do not feelingly find or experience these consequences and fruits of election in yourself, yet if they are there in essence, it is enough to bring you to glory. I do not mean the having of these things by degrees [of perfection], but in sincerity; an elect person may lack many degrees of grace, but if he has the same in sincerity,

<column-break/>

even if in the smallest measure, it is a sufficient proof of his election.

We come now to the last part of the Text: *but to the obtaining of Salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.* In these words, beloved, are placed the glorious titles which are given to the Son of God: he is a Lord, a Jesus, and a Christ; and he is *our* Lord Jesus Christ.

Before I come to touch upon the "Lord" in these words, it will be necessary to do these four things: 1. To explain these titles to you. 2. To note something regarding the placement of the words. 3. Regarding the joining together of the words. And lastly, regarding the appropriation of the titles.

1. For the explanation: *through our Lord Jesus Christ*; the first title is **Lord**, and this is a name of dominion and power, and signifies a capacity and strength in Christ to carry out the work of our Salvation. Were Christ a "Jesus" and not a "Lord," he could not save us; and if he were a "Lord" and not a "Jesus," he would not save us.

2. He is **The Lord Jesus**; just as "Lord" is a title of dominion, so is "Jesus" a title of mercy and goodness, and signifies a Savior <note>original: "Saligheydt" / Salvation; the name Jesus (Yeshua) literally means 'The Lord is Salvation'.</note>; he is not only a Lord, and so has the power to do us good; but he is also a Jesus, and so he has the will to do us good. The manner of speaking in the Old Testament is "the Lord our God," but never "the Lord Jesus," until the New Testament.

3. He is the **Lord Jesus Christ**, (that is) he is God’s Anointed <note>original: "Ghesalfde"; the title 'Christ' comes from the Greek 'Christos', meaning 'Anointed One'.</note>; he was set apart and appointed by God to carry out the great work of man's Salvation; "Christ" is a name of Office and ministry.

2. I further observe in the placement of these words, that "Lord" is placed before "Jesus": 1. To let us know that we can never look upon Christ as a Jesus, a Savior, if we do not accept him and appropriate him as our Lord, to rule over us and to have dominion in us. Christ can never perform the work of a Savior and Redeemer for us unless you let your will be ruled and steered by him, and be obedient and subject to him. 2. To give us to know that Christ could in no way be a person powerful enough to complete the work of our Salvation if he were not Lord; and therefore his Divine nature is placed in the first position, to assure us that he is powerful enough to carry out the work of our Salvation.

3. I further observe in the composition of the words, that it is not said "through our Lord Christ Jesus," but "through our Lord Jesus Christ": the Divine and human natures of Christ being united in one person, the "Lord" and "Jesus" together by these two titles in one person is an indubitable power and strength to carry out the Salvation of the children of men. Many people may have a will and desire to help those who are in need, and to do good to others; but they lack the power and ability to do the same: and others may have the power, and yet the will is lacking in them to do the same. Power without will would only be...

...an unpolished ability; and will without power would be only a powerless kindness: If Christ had not been **Lord**, He would not have been able to save us; if He had not been **Jesus**, He would not have wanted to save us.

But **Jesus Christ** has both the power and the will to do us good; He lacks no power, because He is a **Lord**; nor does He lack the will, because He is a **Jesus**; and therefore the Apostle joins these together: *we obtain Salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.*

4. Regarding the appropriation <note>The theological act of claiming a general truth as a personal reality.</note> of these Titles; he did not say through *a* Lord Jesus Christ; or through *the* Lord Jesus Christ; but through **our Lord Jesus Christ**; you shall never obtain Salvation through Christ if you do not have a particular part in Him; (Beloved) it will not benefit you that there is a Christ, and a Jesus, and a Lord, if you cannot cry out this appropriating word, to say that He is **yours**: we obtain Salvation, not through a Lord, the Lord Jesus Christ; but through **our Lord Jesus Christ**. And thus I have spent a little time in detaining you with that which is remarkable regarding the explanation, position, joining together, and appropriation of these words; the Doctrine <term>Leere: a formal teaching or point of dogma.</term> here, upon which I intend to stand, is this.

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That the Lord Jesus Christ is the person ordained by God the Father, through whom all the elect of God shall obtain Salvation: *We are not appointed to wrath, but to the obtaining of Salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.*

In the handling of this matter, I shall send forth three warnings; and then answer and explain some questions.

<margin>Warning.</margin>
1. Take this warning: although Jesus Christ is the person through whom we must obtain Salvation, nevertheless all the world shall not be saved through Him: there are but few people in the world who shall obtain Salvation through Jesus Christ.

2. That no more are saved through Jesus Christ—who is the person ordained by God through whom men should obtain Salvation—the fault of that is not in Christ, but in ourselves; for there is virtue and power enough in Christ to save as many worlds as there are people in the world, but the fault lies in us: *We will not come to Christ, that we might have life.* <margin>John 5:40.</margin>

3. Note this warning: although Jesus Christ is the person ordained by God to bring about man's Salvation; this nevertheless brings no one to negligence or carelessness in the working out of their own Salvation; for although Christ must save you meritoriously <note>By the legal and spiritual merit of His sacrifice.</note>, nonetheless you must be diligent in working out your own Salvation, by applying the merits and righteousness of Christ to yourself. <margin>Phil. 2:12.</margin> The common saying of Augustine is true: although God made man without his help, nonetheless He will not save him without his help; by way of dutiful service a man must use the means which God has prescribed in His word, in order to the working out of his own salvation. We

<column-break/>

now come to the handling of the Questions, which I promised to explain; which are these two.

1. Question: What kind of salvation is it which we obtain through Christ?
And secondly: How can it be said that Christ is the person whom God has ordained so that we should obtain salvation through Him?

1. Question: What kind of salvation is it which we obtain through Christ?

1. Answer: It is a perfect or complete salvation; secondly, a salvation uniquely obtained; and thirdly, an everlasting salvation. There are these three surpassing properties in Christ, who is the Savior of the Elect; He saves them perfectly; He alone saves them; and He saves them eternally.

1. Christ is said to save the Elect perfectly, <margin>Heb. 7:25.</margin> *He is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through Him*; but although Christ saves perfectly, nonetheless we must first come to Him. Christ saves perfectly: He saves your body; and He saves your soul; He delivers you from sin, and from the punishment of sin; He delivers you from the filthiness of sin, and delivers you from the guilt of sin. Christ has obtained a perfect Victory over all our enemies; and He is no Savior who does His work by halves; but He saves perfectly.

2. Christ saves His elect alone; He has no co-worker <note>Dutch: "Medewercker," a partner in labor.</note> in the execution of the work of their salvation, <margin>Acts 4:12.</margin> *Neither is salvation in any other: for there is no other Name under Heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.* There is no other person, nor way, nor means in the world to save men thereby, but only through Jesus Christ. I may apply this passage here: He trod the winepress of His Father's wrath alone, and there was no one who helped Him; He alone accomplished the work; and therefore the Church of Rome does very poorly, in that they join together good works and the intercession of the Saints as being partakers with Christ in the work of Redemption; for Christ did the work alone, and therefore the Psalmist tells us, <margin>Ps. 49:8, 9.</margin> *No man can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him: For the redemption of their soul is precious.*

3. Christ saves eternally; He does not save as men here below are saved: here a man can be delivered from one peril, and yet fall into another; be delivered from one villain, and yet be killed by another; but now Jesus Christ delivers us eternally, <margin>Heb. 5:9.</margin> *He is become the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey Him.* And so much for the kind of salvation: Christ delivers or saves perfectly, uniquely, and eternally.
