# ->Wrath and Grace.<-

I shall show you in four main points what it is that Christ has done, to which the Scripture attributes the obtaining of our salvation.
Namely: 1. The Scripture attributes our salvation to the suffering and death of Christ. 2. To the resurrection of Christ. 3. To the Ascension. And finally, 4. To the intercession <term>Voorsprake: the act of Christ acting as a legal advocate or mediator, speaking on behalf of believers before God the Father.</term> of Christ.

<margin>Rom. 5:9. Rev. 5:9. Heb. 10:19. Heb. 5:8, 9.</margin>
1. The salvation of mankind is attributed in Scripture to the suffering and the bitter death of Christ; this was the price paid by Christ; and it is from this that you so often encounter these and similar ways of speaking: that we are made saved through his blood, and through faith in his blood (Romans 5:9, Hebrews 10:19), and likewise in Hebrews 5:8, 9: *Having been made perfect through suffering, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him.* So you can see here the great grace and infinite love of Jesus Christ in suffering for us: that he would rather lose his own life than that we should lose our souls. Oh, look and wonder at the priceless love of the Son of God; your sins are the price of blood, and your letters of forgiveness and acquittal are written with letters of blood. Through Christ’s death we live, and by his stripes we are healed. If Christ had not died, we would have had to die; but he came into the world in the form of a servant and gave his life for us willingly, so that through his death we might live eternally. Our salvation is then attributed to the suffering and death of Christ as the meritorious cause <note>The "meritorious cause" is a theological term meaning the actual work or payment that earns a reward—in this case, Christ's death earning humanity's salvation.</note> of the same.

2. So too it is attributed to the resurrection of Christ, through which he makes manifest to the world that he was a perfect Savior. It is attributed to the same in a clarifying way; for if Christ had died and not risen again, everyone would have thought it a great sign of weakness; that he, who could not even rise from death himself, should nevertheless deliver others from death. Therefore the Apostle says in 1 Peter 1:3, 4:
<margin>1 Pet. 1:3, 4.</margin>
*Praise be to the God who has birthed us again unto a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fades not away, reserved in heaven for us.* Not only through his death, but also through his resurrection, we have a living hope; for we see that Christ has conquered death, and the grave, and all the powers of darkness: and that he is therefore a perfect Savior of all God's elect. So also in
<margin>1 Pet. 3:21.</margin>
1 Peter 3:21: *we are saved through baptism, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ,* namely, as a sign to the world that Jesus Christ was a perfect Savior and a conqueror over death and the grave. It is said in
<margin>Rom. 1:4.</margin>
Romans 1:4: *Christ was powerfully proven to be the Son of God by his resurrection from the dead.*
<margin>Rom. 5:10.</margin>
Romans 5:10: *For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life.*

3. The Scripture also attributes our salvation to the ascension of Christ; it is attributed to the same in a preparatory way. After he had been with his Disciples for 40 days, he was taken up and ascended to Heaven: but before he departed, he said to his Disciples (see
<margin>John 14:2.</margin>
John 14:2): *Behold, I go before you, but the same is to work out your salvation for you.*

<column-break/>

*I go away,* says Christ; *but I go to prepare a place for you, and if it were not so, I would have told you: and if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and take you to myself, so that you also may be where I am.* Christ has gone before to Heaven to prepare a place for us; but he also had to prepare Heaven for us: we enter into the Holy of Holies through Jesus Christ.

4. And finally, it is attributed to the intercession <note>original: "voorsprake"</note> of Christ, and that in an appropriating sense. The Apostle expresses this in Hebrews 7:25: *Wherefore he is also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him, since he always lives to pray for them.* So in Romans 8:34: *Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died, yes, what is more, who is also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also prays for us.* Christ did not only suffer much for us, but he rose again from the dead and ascended to Heaven, and there he prays for us at the right hand of his Father, and all this to work out the work of our salvation. We have the benefit of his suffering, resurrection, ascension, and intercession together in order for our salvation.

I shall now make some applications <note>original: "toeeygeninge," literally "appropriations," referring to the personal application of a sermon's teaching.</note>; but one objection must first be refuted.

Now I think I hear a loose Libertine <note>A "Libertine" in this context refers to someone who believes that because grace is free, they are "liberated" from the need to follow moral laws or obey God's commands.</note> speaking thus within himself: "If it is so that I must expect salvation through Christ, and he has done and suffered so much to obtain it, why then should I not hope that I am a blessed person in Christ, and in a very good state?"

Answer: What I said can be true, and yet you could still be in no better a state: for Christ is not appointed by God to bring you salvation unless these four things have been worked into your heart before you can receive any benefit or comfort from him. 1. He who wishes to obtain profit through Christ must look upon him and receive him as much for his **Lord** as for his **Jesus**: not only holding him as a Jesus to obtain grace and salvation through him, but also looking upon him as his Lord, fulfilling all obedience and showing him all submission. God has exalted Christ to be a Prince and a Savior, through whom people would receive the forgiveness of sins. You must not only seek to be saved by his blood, but also to be justified by his commandments. I can apply here what Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note> said of his two friends: he said, "Hephaestion loves me as much as I am Alexander, but Craterus loves me as much as I am King Alexander." The one for his person, the other for the benefits which he received from him. So some love Christ as much as he is a Lord and a judge of justice and judgment; but others love him for the benefits and advancements they receive through him, because he delivers them from the coming wrath—otherwise they would not look for a Messiah at all.

2. If Jesus Christ is the person ordained by God to work out our salvation, then know this: that the Gospel <note>original: "Euangelium"</note>, whether sooner or later, shall come upon your heart with an irresistible power (Romans 1:16), for the Gospel is a power of God unto salvation to every...

<margin>1 Cor. 1:18</margin> who believes. So in 1 Cor. 1:18: *For the message of the cross is to those who are being saved the power of God.*

3. If Christ is your Savior, he will not only free you from the condemnation of sin, but also from the dominion and power of sin. Christ will not only be a Savior to free you from hell, but also from sin itself. And therefore Christ is called a Savior because he shall save his people from their sins <margin>Matt. 1:21.</margin> (Matthew 1:21); that is, from the reigning and ruling power of sin. And therefore, beloved, you who call upon Jesus as a Savior for the forgiveness of all your sins, and yet cannot say that God has killed and brought down any sin within you, you are greatly deceived; for Jesus Christ frees his own from sin just as well as from hell.
<margin>Heb. 7:25.</margin>
<margin>Rom. 8:34.</margin>

4. Know this much: that if Christ is your Savior, he will prepare your heart for an Evangelical obedience to his will. In <margin>Heb. 5:9.</margin> Hebrews 5:9, *Christ became the cause of eternal Salvation,* but for whom? To what end? *To all those who are obedient to him.* And therefore, you <margin>Dedication.</margin> who persist in rebellion and opposition of the heart against God, running along in sinful ways and refusing to bring your neck under the yoke of Christ, you deceive yourself; you call in vain to Christ and for the Salvation and blessedness found through him.

<margin>Application.</margin> If it is indeed so that Christ is the person through whom all the elect shall obtain Salvation, then do not attribute your Salvation to any other thing, but only to Jesus Christ. Do not attribute it to Saints, or Angels, or men; nor to the intercessions of the Virgin Mary; not to anything within you or outside of you; but only to Jesus Christ, who perfectly saves all those who go to God through him.

2. Be convinced of your own inability and incapacity to save yourself. Everyone is born with "merit" in his heart <note>The author suggests that humans naturally believe they can earn their way to heaven through their own worthiness.</note> and by nature thinks himself capable of being his own Savior; one clings to his religious duties and services, another to his spiritual gifts, and so on. But you must labor to be stripped of all imagination of your own strength, righteousness, and power, so that you may cling entirely to Christ <margin>Acts 5:31.</margin> who is the person ordained by God to work out your Salvation.

<column-break/>

3. Do not think that you do too much, that you suffer too much, or that you pay too high a price for these things; for this Christ considered nothing too much to do, or too heavy to suffer, so that he might thus accomplish the work of your salvation. Since Christ left Heaven for you, do you not think it too much to lose the earth for him? Since he came from the bosom of his Father for you, are you then unwilling to leave Father, or Mother, or hands, or anything else for his sake? Since he endured such suffering, contempt, distress, persecutions—yes, death itself—for your sake, why should you be grieved or impatient under any trouble or misery which you meet here in the world for his sake? We must simply consider this: if Christ is the person ordained by God to work out our Salvation, and he could not do so except through suffering and enduring the punishments that were deserved by our sins—through his Resurrection, Ascension, and Intercession <note>The original Dutch text says "Door biddinge," which likely means "Voorbiddinge" or intercession.</note>—we must count nothing too much to do or suffer for him.

4. Let this teach you to glorify and thank the Name of Christ, to praise him, to love him, and to cling to him all our days. Will you not praise and love him who has done so much for you?

It is remembered—I have read a story of an Elephant which, having fallen, was unable to help himself or stand up again because of the inflexibility of his bones <note>A common historical misconception was that elephants had no joints in their legs and could not get up if they fell; here it serves as a metaphor for human helplessness in sin.</note>. A hunter coming upon him helped him up, whereby the Elephant, through a natural instinct, was so moved that he followed this man, desired to do service for him, and never left him until his dying day. Now, if such love is shown by "dumb beasts" toward those who have done something good for them, should we not much more love and praise Christ, who has done so much for us? For we were fallen and could not raise ourselves up again, and Christ has helped us up; he has redeemed us with his blood when we were lost and corrupted. Oh, how this must stir us up to cling to Christ, to love him, to obey him, and to show him submission all our days.

### Vindication, to all Lovers of Peace and Truth, and those who love the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:1, 10:1</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' within a rectangular frame featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>If a man’s name is better than precious ointment, there will be no lack of dead flies to corrupt the same; although I deserve no name among the children of men from the great God, nonetheless I do not wish to lose the place of worthiness which some have for me in their hearts, nor to become a reproach to them. It is true, this Sermon which I preached unexpectedly has brought upon me the envy of the wicked, the jealousy of the good, indeed the scandalous contempt of all. Were I to remain silent now, I would strengthen these rebukes and validate the unjust rumors that rise up against me.

<margin>28 Years.</margin>
I confess the smallness of my graces, and the fewness of my years (being no more than days) <note>Love is highlighting his youth—he was about 27 or 28 at the time—as a reason for his supposed lack of standing.</note> which is a great hindrance to my spirit in coming into public view; to hold forth a small light for the Wanderer, now in the Sunshine; to bring in my poor Mite when men in these days have abundance before them from God’s Treasury. Had I not been pressed under the press of reproach, I would never have brought my Sermon to the press; when I preached it, I considered it no more than an untimely bird that would never see the sun. The reason why I now bring it into the light is not a high opinion that I have of it, but a false opinion which many have, both of the Sermon and of myself who preached it. I am currently suspected by the world as an enemy of Covenants or peace; but I may appeal to Heaven, where my witness is, that from the depths of my soul I have unceasingly called to God for a good progression of this Truce, so that peace and truth might flourish in our days. Only have I preached and prayed against an unfounded and unstable peace. I am not one of those who say in their hearts, <margin>Cicero.</margin> *I prefer the most unjust peace to the most just war* <note>original: "Iniquissimam pacem iustissimo bello antefero." A quote attributed to Cicero expressing a desire for peace at any cost.</note>: I do not hold a godless peace above a righteous 

<column-break/>

war; through a righteous war, we have only men as enemies, but God as our own friend; through a godless peace, we shall have God as our enemy, and men as only our fair-weather friends. Let us not flatter our enemies, nor ourselves; so long as they are possessed of pleasant dispositions, they want no treaty with us, but treaties with themselves: they never negotiate with us, but compel us with wickedness. I may say of them what the Prophet Micah says of a godless Government: *They bite with their teeth, and cry peace; but against him who puts nothing in their mouths, they prepare a holy war.* <note>Referencing Micah 3:5.</note> Mark this: they bit with their teeth, and yet they cried for peace; an unfounded peace has destroyed some nations more than a long war. I can but adapt the final words of the Poet and say: 
->*No more by the sword than by a treacherous peace.*<-
<note>original: "Non plurus gladio quam perfere pace."</note>

History is filled with sad massacres which followed upon a feigned day of peace and deceitful peace. The Trojan Horse was brought into the City of Troy, presenting nothing but peace, amusement, or renown, when the Murderers were hidden within it, who in one night murdered the inhabitants and took possession of the City for themselves, building their City on a heap of overturned stones, which they could not do in a ten-year siege. The Politician does more through deceit than through power; under the guise of peace, than through open persecutions of war. I may recount the Massacre of Paris in the year 1571 <note>Love likely refers to the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, which actually began in August 1572. The Dutch text says 1571.</note>, which followed the peace with the Executor, St. Charles the Ninth; the King of France made many strong Covenants with the French Protestants, that they should enjoy the free exercise of their religion, and swore publicly that he would keep this for them, for their good. Indeed, so that the Protestants would not be jealous of his intentions, he let his daughter marry the young King of Navarre, a Protestant Prince. And he invited the French Protestant Nobles to the Wedding; soon thereafter he had them cut down and most treacherously murdered—around 10,000 Protestants in the Church of Paris, besides many thousands in other parts of France. O you English Noblemen! Do not forget the Parisian massacre. I can bring it even closer to home for you...

# Vindication.

Go to Ireland and see what a wicked cessation of arms <note>original: "stil-stant van wapenen." This refers to the "Cessation of Arms" treaty in 1643 between King Charles I and the Irish Catholic rebels, which outraged English Protestants.</note> (which the King made with the Rebels, against the Act of Parliament) has done there; it has encouraged and strengthened the Rebels (who at that time had little supply, money, or weapons) to harm and destroy the Protestant party, so that they likewise did more through an unjust war. Should I bring you to the Scriptures, you would see the treachery of Princes; read Daniel 8:23, 25, concerning Antiochus, King of the fourth vision, that he would destroy the holy people. But what was the instrument that he used? Read verse 25: *Through his craft, he shall cause deceit to prosper in his hand... and by peace he shall destroy many.* Read likewise Daniel 11:23: *And after the league made with him, he shall work deceitfully.* So we also read of King Saul, what a feigned friendship and agreement there was between him and David; he gave him his daughter Michal as a wife, 1 Samuel 18:25. Who would think that the King plotted against David? Nevertheless, he did it; he gave his daughter, and yet he was David’s enemy all his days, verse 29. He commanded Jonathan and his servants that they should kill him, 1 Samuel 20. In John 2:24, Jesus himself did not commit himself to them, because he knew them all. Oh, that we knew some men a little more; we would trust them less; neither fearing their threats, nor trusting their promises. The Italians fear men more when they are insulted than when they are done harm: Joab killed Amasa under the appearance of friendship, while he showed compliments and asked him, 2 Samuel 20:9, *Is it well with thee, my brother?* and Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him, and killed him.

<margin>We know that Saul often promised everything smoothly, indeed flattered David, so that he might lure him into his snares; and there is no doubt that the courtiers followed the same craftiness. Calvin on Psalm 55:21. <note>original Latin: "Scimus Saulem sæpe blandus..."</note></margin>
The Prophet David describes such spirits in Psalm 55:21, 22: *He hath put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him: he hath broken his covenant. The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.* Calvin, speaking on this passage, says that David here looks upon the feigned friendship of King Saul, who broke his covenant (it is no new thing for Kings to break their covenants now) and came to him with a beautiful appearance and desired peace; he had butter in his mouth, but in his heart was war. All that I shall say is this: put not your trust in Princes, nor rely too much on covenants. Should I say what an Old Writer says, I would be rebuked (though I do not rebuke him, nor am I favorable hereunto): "It concerns [says that writer] without doubt a small trust, to believe that we would be secure through a covenant with the Papist party; the covenant may be kept by us with them, though they do not keep it with us." It is the sword (along with disputes or negotiations) that must end these matters; therefore, change your plowshares into swords, and your spades into bows, to fight the battle of the Lord, to avenge the blood of the Saints which they have shed; it must be drawn, either it kills us or we it. Let me but use the words of the Prophet Jeremiah 48:10: *Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord deceitfully;* Yea, *cursed be he that keepeth back his sword from blood.* The killing of the Moabites is called a work of the Lord; the children of Moab are among us; may the Lord give us

<margin>R. Franc.</margin>

<column-break/>

wisdom to see our ways and works; this is enough; to many it will already be too much. Now, before the entrance of this work (like the city of Mundus) becomes longer than the sermon itself, I shall withdraw my thoughts. I have only two things in true humility to bring to your consideration. First, the calling I had to preach on that day at Uxbridge. Second, the matter which I handled. Concerning the first, namely, the calling I had to preach, I shall relate it briefly. On Wednesday night, January 29 [being the monthly Day of Prayer/Fast Day], I was told that the Commanders had come to Uxbridge, and that Mr. Martiall <note>Stephen Marshall (1594–1655), a prominent Presbyterian clergyman and influential preacher to the Long Parliament.</note> or some other Teacher would preach in the hearing of such Honorable Commissioners on the following Thursday (which was the first day of the truce). Hearing this, I rode from Windsor Castle to Uxbridge on Thursday morning; I intended to ask Mr. Martiall if he would preach; he said no, but nonetheless that there was a sermon. As soon as I turned to the church to be a listener, I met the Governor of the Tower <note>A reference to the Lieutenant of the Tower of London, likely Isaac Penington or a deputy acting as an escort for the commissioners.</note> in passing, who told me that he with some others had been waiting in the assembly for the sermon, but the Minister who was expected had not come; whereupon he desired of me that I would preach, otherwise the assembly would be fruitless. To which I answered, having no thoughts of preaching but to be a listener, nonetheless rather than the assembly should be fruitless, I would be occupied for a half or a whole hour to speak a word of exhortation, which I afterwards did. Now whether this was not a hand from Heaven that laid this work upon me, let my accusers themselves be my judge. I am content to write the manner of how I came to preach, to wipe away those scandals that have been cast upon me.

<margin>As Captain Voyce, Ensign Ford, Mr. Alkington, with several others.</margin>
Some say that I thrust myself into that work, but others can witness how earnestly Captain Hampton, the Governor of the Tower, urged me, telling me that the assembly would otherwise be fruitless. Some are so shameless as to say that I pushed Mr. Martiall from the pulpit, when it is well known Mr. Martiall was never there that day; Beloved, had he been there to preach, I am very far from such un-Christian works as to disturb an assembly from the labor of one whose books I am not fit to carry; Yea (if I may say so) whose shoe-latchets I am not worthy to unloose. Others say that a certain Mr. Kem <note>Samuel Kem (1604–1670), a naval chaplain and preacher.</note> was supposed to preach there; others a neighboring Teacher (whose turn it was to perform the service there that day); either one or the other, I know not who; only this I know, that it was already eleven o’clock when they begged me to preach; the Governor and some others of the people came out of the assembly, thinking they were deceived; yea, I took it upon myself to give the Clerk a long Psalm, so that if the Teacher came who was appointed to preach, more time would pass and he could take the place.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Whatever your calling was to preach that day, nonetheless the matter of your sermon was out of time in that place, for those listeners, and at such a time.

# Vindication.

but an evening gathering; none of the commanders from that side were there.

2. Had they been there, I spoke not a word concerning them or their side; I spoke only for our own. 3. If anything had been out of place <note>original: "buyten propooste," meaning irrelevant or inappropriate to the occasion</note>, it must have been this: I urged the listeners not to rest or rely too much on treaties of peace. How untimely was this? I surely hope that a Minister <term>Leeraer: literally "Teacher," a common term for a Reformed minister</term> may address the people, telling them not to rely too much on ordinances and duties; yet this does not diminish the Authority of God, who enjoys both. One may exhort another not to lean too much on wife and children, and yet this exhortation is not to the dishonor of the Minister <note>The Dutch text uses "pmiant," likely an abbreviation for "Predicant" or Minister</note>. In like manner, may not a Minister exhort a gathering not to lean too much on these Truces <term>Treves: specifically referring to the ongoing peace negotiations at Uxbridge</term>, and yet this exhortation be in no way harmful to the Makers of the Truce themselves? I say further: that while our enemies continue in their Godless way, and we preserve our Principles, it is as easy to unite fire and water, and (I had almost said) to reconcile Heaven and Hell, as to reconcile their Spirits and ours—unless they become better and we become worse—before it is possible for us to agree. In what way is this out of place? Show me, and I will fall at your feet with a confession of guilt.

<margin>2. Objection.</margin>
--- Why did you not write this clearing of your name sooner? If there had been no guilt in you, you would not have remained silent so long, and allowed so many slanders to be so widely spread.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
To which I briefly answered: 1. The knowledge and feeling I had regarding these poor fruits of my study (for I had no intention of letting my Sermon be printed, had not the urging of various friends—Godly and wise men—persuaded me), and observing these scandals thrown not only upon me, but upon other Ministers who are also for the advancement of Parliament, as if they were of the same spirit (which I, indignant, present to the world as being so); had these considerations not spurred me on, I would never have brought my Sermon to public view. But I waited in silence, humility, and the patience of my God, with a sigh, knowing for certain the innocence and uprightness of my heart and the purity of this matter. I thank God that the uprightness of my spirit (being conscious of nothing wrong within myself regarding this subject) has been a strong bulwark against all those scandals brought against me here, and none of them has been able to take away the satisfaction of my spirit. I remember the words of the Poet:

<margin>Horace.</margin>
> --- Let this be a wall of brass: <note>original Latin: "Hic murus aheneus esto / Nil conscire sibi, nulla pallascere culpâ." From Horace's Epistles.</note>
> To be conscious of no wrong, to turn pale at no fault.

2. It was fitting that I remained silent so long until I had the response of Parliament (before whom some accusers had appeared against me). I would have cleared myself through the Law, and what not; have I not waited for their pronouncement? They have (by order of the House of Commons, on the fifth day of this month of March) declared me clear regarding this matter.

3. They required I should rest until the cessation <note>of hostilities</note> was over, so that it might not stir up the spirits of our enemies, and suggest that there was not a peaceable nature in me, which truly might be overturned, and

<column-break/>

said before their own doors; although their words are softer than butter, yet war is in their hearts, and peace is in their mouths. <note>A reference to Psalm 55:21.</note>

4. I judged it better to wait a while to hear more of the slanders against me, so that I might clear myself more easily. Some rebuke me, saying that I left Uxbridge as soon as I had preached, as if ashamed of what was done there; but others know that I went openly into and out of the City, and remained in the same for four hours after the Sermon. Others say that I made away with myself <note>i.e., went into hiding</note> when I sensed I would have to appear before Parliament; yet various witnesses can come forward to show I went openly up and down in the City. Indeed, so far was I from hiding myself from any court of light, that I used means to be heard and to answer those accusations that were against me. The ill-intentioned (who wished it to be so) said that I was whipped out of Uxbridge, or shut up within Uxbridge by our Commissioners; brought prisoner to London, and by order of Parliament imprisoned in Newport; with many other things they pointed out to me. But it is well known to everyone that I never appeared before Parliament or the Commissioners regarding these delusions; not because of anything brought against me, for I was discharged by them. I have but one more word to say regarding the second part of the subject of my Sermon and its publication. I never polished it with intellect, using the thirty souls <note>possibly a mistranslation or typo in the Dutch for "rules" or "tools"</note> of Rhetoric; you shall see it in that draft as it was preached. This Sermon (I confess) was preached in the Castle at Windsor the day before (being a Monthly Fast Day <term>Maendeljke Bededagh: A day set aside by Parliament for fasting and prayer for the success of the war</term>), and being so hastily called to preach <note>at Uxbridge</note>, having no more time to think it over than while the Psalm was being sung, I was necessitated to preach the same Sermon in Uxbridge that I had delivered in Windsor. I must confess (since it was so late before I began at Uxbridge, that I could not repeat everything I had previously studied and preached) that I added a little to this Sermon; nevertheless, I have had no significant passages removed, to my knowledge, from the Sermon at Uxbridge. I place myself and my Sermon under your favorable eye. The Sermon has little in it; it stands on its own. The writer has nothing in it of which he should boast; what Tertullian writes at the end of his letter, I may place in mine: I judge myself the least of the least Ministers of the Gospel, yet I profess to be:

<margin>The least.</margin>

<header>England’s Sickness.</header>

# ENGLAND’S SICKNESS.

->Based on Jeremiah 33 verse 6.<-

> Behold, I will bring health and healing to them, and I will heal them: and I will reveal to them an abundance of peace and truth.

<margin>
Even if that law-giver [Josiah] was a worshiper of God, things were then in a very bad state, for the law of God had perished. <note>original: "Etsi lex ille facerus erat Dei cultor..."</note> Calvin’s commentary on the first chapter of Jeremiah.
</margin>
This Prophet was extraordinarily gifted by God and arose in a time of great confusion and concealment in Israel. Although he began his prophecy under the reign of the pious King Josiah, nevertheless at that time religion was neglected and the Law of God could not even be found until the 18th year of Josiah's reign, as seen in 2 Chronicles 34:18. For a full 18 years under Josiah's reign they were without the Book of the Law; in this we should note that God preserves the best people for the worst times.

Regarding this Prophet, I shall speak only of two things: 1. The duration of his prophecy. 2. The subject matter of his prophecy. Regarding the first—how long he prophesied—you must know when he began, which was in the 13th year of King Josiah. He prophesied under four kings besides Josiah, from which we can easily determine the span of his ministry. Specifically: under Josiah, 19 years (2 Kings 22:1 compared with Jeremiah 1:2); under Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, three months (2 Kings 23:31); under Jehoiakim, the brother of Jehoahaz and son of Josiah, 11 years (2 Kings 23:36); under Jehoiachin, three months (2 Kings 24:8); and under Zedekiah, 11 years (2 Kings 25:2 compared with Jeremiah 1:3). Add all these together and the time of his prophecy will be over 42 years, during which he prophesied within Jerusalem amidst great danger and hardship until Israel was carried away. Later, he prophesied in Egypt for 4 years, and in that exile he was stoned to death.

<margin>
Amidst the greatest difficulties he most diligently performed his duty. <note>original: "Inter summas difficultates..."</note> Pappo, in the preface to Jeremiah.
</margin>
<margin>
Tertullian in *Scorpiace*, Chapter 8.
</margin>
Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from the 2nd century</note> mentions this and believes Jeremiah to be one of those referred to in Hebrews 11:37 who were stoned. This concludes the timing of his prophecy. Now for the second point, namely, the subject of his prophecy; I shall say but a word. He prophesied primarily of the Jewish Captivity and their misery in Babylon for 70 years, and of their restoration from Nebuchadnezzar's yoke when that time would be fulfilled. He speaks of this in many chapters of his book, particularly in Chapter 32 where he speaks of their restoration, and in Chapter 33 (from which my text is taken) of their great and glorious restoration. He foretold that although they would be carried away as captives, the time of their refreshment would be certain, and the days of their servitude would not last forever. Though they were in prison, they would be delivered; though sick and unwell, they would be healed; though they were rolled in blood, they would have peace; and though surrounded by heresies and errors, they would have the truth. These are the great blessings promised in this chapter following their restoration. Concerning the prophecy of their—

<margin>
God showed that He appeared to be in this prison. <note>original: "Quod Deus paruit esse carcere hoc"</note>
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
In this way He showed that this one man was of more value than all the Jews; He did not speak in the Temple at that time, nor in the whole city; therefore the prison was the Sanctuary of God. How great an honor it was that God deigned to enter freely when He had deserted His own Temple. Calvin on this passage.
</margin>
—deliverance, there are four things to note in this chapter.

1. There is the time when this comforting prophecy was given to Jeremiah, namely, when he was shut up in the court of the prison (Chapter 33:1). From this, note: That God's servants in a state of suffering usually receive more comforting revelations of God's will than otherwise. The time of imprisonment is best for divine contemplation and meditation on God.

2. There are the conditions which God requires to be fulfilled before their restoration (Verse 3): "Call to me, and I will answer you, and show you great and mighty things, which you do not know." Although God had determined the year and the day to deliver them from their captivity, they still had to pray for this fulfillment. From this we can note: That we must pray for those graces of God which He has already certainly determined in His counsel to give.

3. There are the means which God uses for the healing of their land and their restoration to former health: namely, peace and truth (Verse 6).

4. There are recounted the great benefits and blessings which shall follow the deliverance, from verse 7 to the end of the chapter.

My text belongs to the third part, namely, the means which God wishes to use to heal the land. The text also has a metaphorical sense: the Jews are described as being unwell or sick. The great God is the <term>Heelmeester: Physician or Master-Healer</term>; peace and truth are the plasters and salve which God, the wise Physician of kingdoms and peoples, prescribes for the healing of a sick land.

In these words, three things are to be noted:

1. There is the sick Patient, indicated by the pronoun *them*—the land of Israel. 2. The Physician who undertakes to heal this patient: "behold, I will bring health and healing to them." Who is this? It can be no one other than the great God, who wounds and heals, brings to the grave, and leads out again. 3. Here are the medicines with which God heals a sick land. In these, there are again three things: (1) The qualities of these medicines, namely, peace and truth. (2) Their quantity: an abundance of both. (3) The mixture of these two together—not just peace or truth, but peace *and* truth, and an abundance of both. From these three parts, I shall take only two points, and learn from the first two that:

When Kingdoms and Churches are in a sickly state, the Lord, the Physician of nations, undertakes to heal and cure them.

From the third part—namely, the quantity and quality of the medicines God uses to heal a land—learn: That an abundance of peace and truth are the customary medicines by which God heals a weak and sick Kingdom.

<margin>
1. Doctrine
</margin>
1. Doctrine: When Kingdoms and Churches are in a state of sickness, the Lord, the Physician of nations, undertakes to heal and cure them.

In the handling of this point I shall follow this order: 1. What it is that makes a land sick; 2. When a land is sick; 3. How God is the Physician of nations; 4. What the reason is, or how it happens, that our land is not yet healed; 5. What clear evidence...

<header>England’s Sickness.</header>

...are there signs that God is now healing our powerless hand? <note>original: "hont," likely an archaic spelling or error for "handt" (hand), though it could also mean "dog" as a term of self-humiliation.</note>

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
— What is it that causes the sickness of a Land?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
I shall proceed somewhat metaphorically. Whatever brings sickness to a natural body also causes illness in the body of the Government; such as:

1. Bad and poisonous food causes diseases of the body; likewise, evil and deceptive <note>original: "verassige," likely implying something as hollow or burnt-out as ashes</note> heresies and opinions bring great unrest and sickness into the body of the Church or Kingdom. My soul is troubled by the consideration of those harmful and venomous errors which are spoken and preached throughout our entire Land. What harmful Teachings were preached during the rise of our state (though now fallen) by the Clergy; who would keep silent under the highest penalty (the means by which they declared their status) asserting that Kings might do whatever they wished, and that life, liberty, and estate stood at the King’s pleasure, according to his own will? Indeed, did they not impose upon the people the idea that if the King demanded the life of some or all of his Subjects, they must lay their necks upon the block, and must in no way defend themselves with weapons? These harmful opinions have taken hold of the minds of most of our Nation, leading to great slavery, which is evident in this: that the Parliament has so many secret and open enemies. If we look at the venomous errors which have crept into the Church, we shall soon find what has so unsettled us. Oh! What damnable heresies have been in the body of this Nation concerning Free Will, Falling from Grace <note>the idea that a believer can lose their salvation</note>, General Redemption <note>the belief that Christ died for everyone equally, rather than just the elect</note>, the nullification of the Moral Law, and much else; oh, this has brought our Land into a grievous sickness on this very day!

2. Excess, beyond a healthy measure, brings sickness to the body just as much as poison does. Oh, what an excess of the Gospel this Nation has! They are surrounded with Sermons, Days of Delight, and Fasting Days; yet what a loathing of the Spirit there is in man, for they have no taste for the Word. There are souls who are weary of this Manna, even though it be new and good; this brings about their sickness. May the Lord heal us so that we do not die of our wounds.

3. Living in foul air brings sickness to the natural body. This "inflamed air" is a corrupt, scandalous, and superstitious Church service, which is the stench <note>original: "hoochne," likely meaning a foul odor or height of offense</note> of the Land. And oh! What ailments, sores, blindness, superstition, and offense has this not brought among the people of our Land.

4. The fourth cause that brings sickness to a natural body is heat and cold; whether through excessive heat of the blood, which brings fever, or through the grip of cold, which brings pain and lameness to the body—this is how sickness comes. The heat of human Spirits in some things, and their coldness in others, has brought grievous illnesses to our Land. How hot and violent were our puffed-up Prelates <note>high-ranking church officials like bishops</note> in their ungodly conduct, in the promotion and defense of the superstitious fictions of their own brains; yet they were cold and careless in those things which concern God in His Glory or the building up of the Churches. How fiery they were in the decoration of Churches, wanting the walls and windows to be magnificent, yet they never cared for the conduct—

<column-break/>

—of the people, to ensure it was holy. How forceful they were to have all Ministers in their consecrated garments, guarding the white Surplices <note>the white robes worn by clergy</note> (images of their purity, as they say), yet they never looked to the life of the Clergy; through which they have gained such Sons of Belial <note>original: "Zonen Belials," a biblical term for wicked or lawless men</note>, who like the sons of Eli <note>priests in the Bible known for corruption</note>, draw the people away from the Lord. With what heat and bitterness of Spirit have they driven away and persecuted the most godly and conscientious people of the Land, passing and enforcing a law against those who differed from them only in minor circumstances? Yet how cool they were in the persecution of the Papists <note>Catholics</note>, who differ from us in fundamental principles; they were sooner cherished and excused from the penalty of the law than punished by it. How fiery they were in their antique gestures, consecrations, singing, and in all their outward works of service; yet never beholding the inward and Spiritual part of Divine service. All they look for is an extravagant service, following the dregs <note>original: "spoog," literally spit or vomit</note> of their vain fictions, and they thrust them upon the people under the title of "Decency." Yes, they stood so firmly on their outward and ornate manner of Worship, that I may boldly say they would rather have rolled their garments in blood than suffer a spot or blemish on their Surplices. Indeed, holes would sooner be made in our bodies than a tear in their golden caps, and all our houses would sooner be cast down and turned into heaps of stone than that any Popish relic should be taken from the walls of their Church. Oh Beloved, the heat and power of their Spirits in these things, and their lukewarmness and coldness in the things which concern God, has brought it about that all these sicknesses are among us.

### When is a Land sick?

There are five signs by which you can judge if the body is out of order, which will also teach you to recognize a sick Kingdom.

First, when the head, or any other part, is divided from the body or from one another. A sin (says Hippocrates) is nothing other than *discontinuatio partium* <note>original Latin: "separation of parts"</note>. When one part is divided from another, even if it be the smallest part of the body, the whole body is unsettled and sick; how much greater is our misery, as this sign is clearly seen in our Land this day. Is not our King, the head, divided from his Parliament, representing the body of this Realm? And is not one Member divided from the other? If you look at the public affairs of state, oh, what divisions are there! Is it not Protestant against Protestant? Nobleman against Nobleman? Citizen against Citizen? Neighbor against Neighbor? Is it not with us as Christ foretold in Luke 12:51, 53? That He did not come to give peace on earth, but division: the Father shall be divided against the Son, and the Son against the Father: the Mother against the Daughter, and the Daughter against the Mother. If we observe Spiritual things, oh, what divisions of opinions! What conflicts of judgment! What casting out and opposing of the Spirit is there among the Professors of Godliness? This is the first sign that we are sick.

Secondly, a sign of sickness of the body is when good and proper food does not become nourishment for us, but remains raw in the stomach; this shows and brings about...

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "det" (the), indicating the start of the next page.</meta>

He identifies the division between the King and Parliament as a primary symptom of a failing national body.</summary>

...that these sicknesses are present or taking hold in the body.
Likewise, a People is sick when the people cannot endure or digest the Gospel; when the ordinances do not turn into spiritual nourishment or cause our gifts to grow—to the strengthening of our graces, the killing of our lusts, and the improvement of our lives. This is a second high-sign <note>original: "boog-teken," likely meaning a prominent symptom or omen</note>.

Thirdly, by the beating of the pulse, you can know whether a body is sick or not. If the pulse beats with a violent motion, it is proof of a fever; if it is faint and weak, it is proof that the living spirits are departing and the person is failing. Let us look to ourselves; God—let me speak thus—feels the pulse of this Kingdom; that is, He looks into the hearts and dispositions of the people to see how they are situated. I think I hear the Lord asking the inhabitants of this Land: "What, do you want the Bishops back in their state and place? Do you want your Common Prayer Book back in use? Do you want your spiritual (or rather carnal) conduct back in your power, and to be scot-free in your impurity and fornication—a great band <note>original: "gebende," likely referring to a group or fetter</note> for your discharge?" Oh, how violently this people aches and longs for the flesh-pots, leeks, and vinegar of Egypt! <note>A biblical reference to the Israelites longing for the comforts of their slavery in Egypt rather than the hardships of the wilderness.</note> On the other hand, the Lord asks the people of this Land: "Do you want the Gospel in your power? A Reformation for purification? To restore your assembly? To have the reign of my Son within you? Do you want to judge my cause, and fight my fight, and overcome those who have insulted my great name? Do you want to lay down your life for me? Do you want to come to my Parliament in truth and full purpose of heart?" Oh, how faint the pulses of the people are here, as if they were already dead! Some are inclined toward malice, others toward neutrality; most toward formality and insensitivity. Thus, by the beating of a Kingdom's pulse, you may see that this poor Land is sick in these days.

<margin>Question Answer.</margin>
Fourthly, when someone sends for the Healer or Physician, one concludes that some are sick or wounded in that family. That God has sent us healers and physicians shows that we have many sick among us. These Physicians are our Worthies of Parliament, the healers of our breaches, who pour oil into our wounds; and were it not for them (the Lord knows), we would have bled to death in our wounds by this time. The healers are our soldiers, the <term>guards of our flesh</term> <note>original: "Pantien," likely referring to protectors or defenders</note>, and they let our blood; this shows that there is much corrupt blood in our veins and many sinful humors gathered in the body of our Nation. God sees that there are worldly noblemen, corrupt citizens, and many malicious humors among the commonality; otherwise, so much blood would not have been shed, nor so many veins opened.

Fifthly, a person's body is disordered when the advice of the Physician is not accepted, or received as if it were not good; it proves the strength and danger of the sickness. Beloved, our State-Physicians commanded us to take up arms in defense of our laws, God’s service, and liberties; to do more for the cause of God, to renounce neutrality in this common cause, and to make good on our covenant. Oh, alas! Their counsel is not followed; people want to have their own will and go their own ways, etc.

<column-break/>

### What does it mean to heal a sick Land?

<margin>
3rd Question.
Answer.
</margin>
A sick Land is healed: 1. When God comforts a People during their suffering (Isaiah 57:18): *I will heal them and restore comforts to them.* The wound is half-healed when God supports the spirits of a People with patience and comfort in their afflictions.

2. God heals when He delivers a People from their suffering and sorrows (Jeremiah 30:17): *I will cause healing to rise for you, and heal you of your plagues;* but how? See verse 18: *Behold, I will turn back the captivity of Jacob’s tents, and have mercy on his dwellings.*

3. God heals a Land when He pours privileges and mercies into its wounds, which they immediately enjoy (Jeremiah 30:17, 18): *I will cause health to rise for them, etc. The city shall be rebuilt on her own hill, and the palace shall remain according to its style.* That is, they would enjoy those privileges and mercies which they had before.

### If God is the Physician of Kingdoms and Nations: what is the reason, or how does it happen, that the Land is not healed?

<margin>
4th Question.
Answer.
Know, Reader, that I did not handle this fourth Question in Uxbridge, but only preached it in my own place at Windsor.
</margin>
Answer: The fault must not be laid upon God; He never lacks the understanding or power to perform the healing; but the fault must be in the patient who is sick, or in the remedies that God might use for the healing of the Nation.

The faults in the patient why he is not healed may be reduced to these five:

1. If the Patient lets the sickness root within him too long and does not look for a Physician or Healer, it can become so deep-rooted that he is never healed by anyone. Oh, Beloved! We have let the sores and pests in this Kingdom dwell so long that God knows if we shall ever be healed; we only have to note those two plague-like evils concerning the Bishops and the Common Prayer Book, which have been eye-sores to the most godly people of this Land. For how many years have we been like Issachar’s Donkey <note>A reference to Genesis 49:14, describing one who is strong but bows to a heavy burden</note>, willingly bearing the burdens which were laid upon our shoulders, subjected to their tyrannical yoke, so that they have now wound themselves into the laws like ivy on a wall? Thus we, being the walls of the Kingdom, are shaken and plucked up by the roots. We have reason for humiliation, as we have let our sores root so long and did not protest or go against them sooner. And regarding the second sore, we have great cause for complaint that we did not go against them as far as against others. It was the primary goal of the Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials, usually bishops</note> to remove many godly ministers from their places; it has been a church-robbery and a robbing of the souls of the people of their teachers who prayed for them, even though it stiffened the spirit of prayer in those who used it. Some who had accustomed themselves to these crutches later remained lame and unhealed. This has brought an ignorance and superstition upon us, and an assurance for the Papists in their hope of our coming to their religion, saying that the difference only between their Mass-book and our Common Prayer Book is in these two things: 1. They say theirs is Latin, and ours is English. 2. Everything that is in the Mass-book is not in the Common Prayer Book, although all or most of what is in our Common Prayer Book is also included in the Mass-book. It is worthy of your notice what Doctor Featly says...

He argues that the nation remains unhealed because of spiritual compromise and the self-interest of those in power.</meta>

<header>England’s Sickness.</header>

<margin>In his notes on *Veritamnus Romanus* <note>Likely referring to a polemical work against Roman Catholic influence.</note></margin>
it is said regarding the Common Prayer Book (though whether he is of the same opinion, I cannot assure you): The Common Prayer Book was not adopted to oppose the Papists' confession, absolution, collects, etc., being either the same as the Papists themselves use, or at least such as do not displease them. This person who wishes to carry such a snake in his bosom—it is dangerous; he shall be bitten by it.

2. It is a fault in a Patient that he will not suffer his wound to be touched with sharpness <note>In 17th-century medicine, "sharpness" refers to caustic treatments or the scalpel used to clean a wound.</note>; if so, his wound shall rot, stink, and never be perfectly healed. Oh, that this had no place in England’s healing and curing! Are there not many among us who cannot endure being touched harshly for the sake of healing? I take this "sharpness" to mean King James and Prince Henry his son, taken by an untimely death; whether it was they themselves, yes or no, some of the Parliament did not live long when there was but a murmur; they had a part in their deaths. Was it not "sharpness" at Rochelle and for all the Protestants? Were they not betrayed into the hands of their enemies, and by whom? <note>Referring to the Siege of La Rochelle (1627–1628), where English support for French Protestants was seen by many as a failure or betrayal.</note> If I go to find the "sharpness" of the Irish Rebels, was it not helped, promoted, prepared, and brought into England, and by whom? The latter is partly why this Truce <note>original: "Treves," likely referring to the "Cessation of Arms" in Ireland in 1643.</note> was made. I wish that it may not hinder the healing of this poor Nation.

3. Being unwilling to bear the costs of the healing; Oh, poor souls! Such shall die in their wounds. Oh, what sluggishness there is in most men to spend any costs, to use any money or any of their estates to reduce this blood-shedding; this is the reason why we are not healed.

4. A fourth reason why a wound is not healed is because one keeps his wound open and quiet for a long time, just as many cunning beggars keep their wounds open for a long time, notably for their profit and advantage; there are many such beggarly spirits among our military men, who have no calling other than War to live by, who do not care how long they have wars, and how long this unnatural war has lasted. Had we not had evil and self-interested spirits among our Poor <note>original: "Armen," here likely meaning the rank-and-file or the disadvantaged in the conflict.</note>, so much Protestant blood would not have been shed, so many fair opportunities would not have been lost thereby, and England’s miseries would not have been so many.

5. Cutting into a sore before the dead and corrupt flesh is out keeps the wound from a perfect healing—or applying a healing plaster when a drawing plaster is required. The public, profane worldlings, and incurable ill-wishers want to cut into the sore, or think that our disputes can soon be laid to rest in peace, never looking toward a true Reformation: let Religion perish and fade, it shall never move them. Augustine describes excellently the behavior of the Ill-willed in their desire for an untimely and shallow peace:

<margin>Augustine on Psalm 85, verse 10, regarding these words: "that Justice and Peace should kiss each other."</margin>
> Saying: <note>original Latin: "Pax & Iustitia duæ sunt amicæ..."</note> Peace and Justice are two friends, but perhaps you want one and do not want the other; there is no one who does not want peace, but not everyone wants to work for Justice. Ask all men: do you want peace? With one voice the whole human race answers you: I desire it, I long for it, I want it, I love it. Therefore, love justice, because they are two friends; if you do not love the friend of peace, peace itself will not love you, nor will it come to you. For what great thing is it to desire peace? Any evil man may desire peace.

I shall translate Augustine's words into Dutch <note>The translator has rendered them into English here for the reader.</note>, since they

<column-break/>

belong so well to the condition of men in this time in which we live. Peace and truth, he says, are two friends, but of them you would like to have the one, but not the other; there is no one who does not desire peace, yet not all want to do justice [or have truth]. Ask all men: do you want to have peace? All the children of men shall answer as if from one mouth: I wish for it, I desire it, I want to have it, I love the same. If you love peace, then love truth, because they are two friends; if you do not want to love the friend of peace, peace will not love you, nor will it come into you. What a great matter is it to desire peace? Every ill-willed person desires and loves peace. Just so do the ill-willed in our times, as the ill-affected did in the time of Augustine. Thus much for the faults in the Patients.

Likewise, there may be reasons in the instruments <note>The "instruments" are the leaders or means God uses.</note> which God uses for the healing of this land as to why we are not healed. There are three evils or faults in the Physicians <note>original: "Medicijn-meesters"</note> why a sick person does not regain his health. First, greedy desire. Secondly, too much mercy. Thirdly, division among themselves; when one Physician is contrary to the other in judgment. Now, if these three things are found in our State Physicians, it shall greatly hinder the healing of our Nation. Regarding the first: are there not many among us who, like greedy Physicians, keep their Patients back from healing so that they might fill their bags the more? Who strive, as much as is in them, to withhold the healing of the Kingdom. As for our honors of Parliament, no one shows himself less, fears his advancement less than they, or keeps themselves content with their steady dwellings and satisfied with a dark chamber, and thus think to do service to the Kingdom in that place and with that work to which they are called. They, I say, of all men deserve the least suspicion of guilt in this generation; but nevertheless, let the great Commanders and old soldiers in our military heaps remember this, who now have offices full of profit (during these troubles), whether they are not found guilty of the lengthening of our troubles.

The second evil (if I may call it so) in a Physician which prevents the healing of a sick person is too much mercy; when he cuts or uses a sharp plaster, though it be service-able for the wound, yet he has a wrong-headed pity for the sick. I have sometimes failed, and suffered in all ways, that yet too much mercy and pity in our State Physicians might not prevent the healing of this Land. People who abandoned their loyalty, who falsified their covenants—how quickly are they received back into favor and enjoy their State again as if they had never been enemies. Oh, how the Neutralists and the ill-willed are spared! And the heaviest burdens laid on the shoulders of those who meant well, who have done ten times more in willingness in the Parliament's righteous war than the ill-willed (who have ten times more property) have done through compulsion. The ill-willed preserved their estates when the well-affected of this Nation have lost the greater part. It is pity; for the sake of their purses they were enemies of the war, whose hearts are enemies; if you handle a kettle softly, it will sting you...

but if you are stern, she <note>The "ill-willed" or "wickedness" personified.</note> shall not harm you. The more gently the ill-willed are handled, the worse they become; but the more sternly you confront them, the less evil is to be expected from them. I have often thought: the more mercy shown toward the ill-willed, the more criminals there are. Mercy does not cancel out justice; in God they are both equal, why should it not be so in man? Compassion for the wicked has produced cruelty toward the good; the sparing of evildoers has made many worse, and few or none better. Let those who have shown no mercy be laid hold of, for they are without mercy; debt must be paid. How much innocent blood have they shed, which must be avenged either upon us, or through us.

The third fault in the Physicians—namely, division in their advice among one another regarding the sick—proves the danger to the afflicted party. The experienced and diligent Healers whom God has called together to preserve the life (if it be possible) of this powerless Land are the Lords and Commons assembled in Parliament, whom I call the State-physicians. Should there also be division among them? A diverse and contradictory judgment concerning the sickness of this Nation; how dangerous would that be! It was a terrible judgment that God threatened over the land of Israel in <margin>Amos 6:11</margin>: *Behold, the Lord shall strike the great house with breaches, and the little house with clefts.* By the great house and the little house, Calvin and others understand the Nobles and the Commons in Israel; if I may speak thus, both Houses of Parliament in Israel; and that there would be schisms and discord between them. May the Lord deliver England’s two houses—the House of Lords and the House of Commons—from such schisms and from the Spirit of division, so that this sick Nation might encounter no more danger, but might be healed.

<margin>¶ Question.</margin>
When does the Lord undertake to heal a sick people?

<margin>Answer.</margin>
1st Answer: When a people feels its sickness heavily and cries out to God for healing. <margin>2 Chron. 7:14.</margin> *If my people, upon whom my name is called, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then will I hear from Heaven, and will forgive their sins, and will heal their land.* Also, if the Spirit of sensitivity and of supplication were in the spirits of our inhabitants, how quickly our land would be healed! If we follow the Almighty in the footsteps of His providence, we shall find that the Lord restores His miserable churches when their spirits are released to cry out to Him in prayer. Read an excellent text to this purpose in <margin>Isaiah 32:14, 15.</margin> *The palace shall be forsaken, the bustle of the city shall cease, Ophel and the watchtowers shall be as dens forever, a joy for wild donkeys, a pasture for flocks. Until the Spirit be poured upon us from on high.* And in <margin>Hosea 5:14, 15.</margin> *I, even I, will tear and go away; I will take away, and none shall rescue him. I will go and return to my place, until they acknowledge their offense and seek my face.*

2. Then is the Lord healing a Land when our enemies—yes, even we ourselves—look upon ourselves as incurable. <margin>Jer. 30:17, 18.</margin> *I will cause health*

<column-break/>

*to rise for you, and heal you of your plagues, says the Lord: because they called you an outcast, saying, This is Zion, whom no man seeks after.* Note: when the enemies said Zion is an outcast and no one cares for her, then was the time of Zion’s healing. Let us bring this home to ourselves: did not the Enemies, the Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials, specifically bishops, whom the Puritans opposed.</note> and their associates, have such thoughts of us? Did they not say we were as outcasts, and no one looked after us? Did they not think this when they deposed so many godly Teachers, and with their shackles <note>original: *Spanje*; likely referring to the restrictive measures or "yokes" of the ecclesiastical courts.</note> displaced so many zealous believers? When they stopped the King’s ear against so many righteous complaints of grievances; when they stopped all ways of appeal to the Common Law; when they banished many godly Teachers and Christians of this Nation; when they laid so many snares to trap conscientious Teachers, such as idle and undisciplined church customs, that frivolous Book <note>The *Book of Sports* (1617/1633), which permitted Sunday recreations that Puritans considered a desecration of the Sabbath.</note> allowing the desecration of the Sabbath, and much more besides. In their last assembly, did they not make everything certain? Did they not judge us to be incurable? Did they imagine that the imprisoned, banished, insulted, and abducted servants of God would ever be delivered, and they themselves be removed in their place? Did they think that such a fire which they had kindled would burn their own wings and not even singe the hair <note>original: *Hoostpappen*; likely a metaphor for the heads or finest parts of those persecuted.</note> of those whom they had thrown into the furnace of oppression? They fixed their feet as if by Divine Right <note>original: *Iure Divino*</note> (which is now found rather to be by Devilish Right <note>original: *Iure Diabolico*</note>), thinking us thus cast down upon the dunghill and ruined before all the people. Have they not brought those who had titles of honor into disgrace, and brought contempt from all the people upon those Teachers who taught this Nation rightly and warned against the carnal? This gives us certainty that the time of the Lord’s healing has come. Again, then is the time that God heals, when not only our Enemies, but we ourselves look upon our sickness as incurable. <margin>Jer. 30:15.</margin> *Why do you cry over your affliction, that your pain is deadly?* No, look at what follows in verse 17: *I will cause health to rise for you, and heal you of your plagues.* When Zion said her pain was deadly, then God undertook to heal her. And was it not so with us? Did we not say our wound is incurable? Who among us, seven years ago <note>Circa 1640, the start of the Long Parliament and the dismantling of the Episcopacy.</note>, could imagine that this Land would be healed of those two heavy wounds of this Land—namely, the Common Prayer Book and the Episcopal state <note>The office and power of Bishops.</note>; of the lesser ministries like Deans, Prebendaries, Chancellors, Archdeacons, Singers, Promoters, and so many others, together with their spiritual conduct and all their superstitious ceremonies? We thought we would never be healed of these sores, and that these monsters would never be excluded; or have not thousands left the Land of their birth and given up England as incurable? Has this not caused many Teachers and Christians to turn to New England, leaving many tears and sighs behind them, thinking what might befall this poor Land? They saw bloody clouds hanging over our heads, which drew them away to another Land; yes, have they and we not given it all up in vain? Imagining that the sons of Zeruiah <note>A biblical reference to 2 Samuel 3:39; used to describe powerful political or military factions that the ruler cannot control.</note> were too hard for us.

now God has a hand in our healing; the skill of the Physician is now evident, and the cure is more likely under these sorrowful oppressions.

**3.** The Lord heals a Land when a people reject and cast away all those Ornaments of Idolatry and superstition, with a Spirit of judgment; read *Isaiah 30, 22.* compared with verse 26. *You shall also defile the covering of your graven images of silver, and the ornament of your molten images of gold: you shall cast them away as a menstruous cloth... In the day that the Lord binds up the breach of his people, and heals the stroke of their wound.* All the Ornaments must be cast away: the Crosses, Crucifixes, Images, Paintings, etc. <note>The author refers to the "iconoclasm" or removal of Catholic-style religious imagery common during the English Reformation and the Puritan era.</note> and this shall be an infallible proof that God begins to heal us; if we still permit those Superstitions and oppose the true service of God, we shall become worse. It was a wholesome counsel which the Priests of the Philistines gave to the Philistines, who had taken away the Ark and thus corrupted the Jewish service of God, *1 Samuel 6, 3.* *If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, send it not empty; but in any wise return him a guilt offering: then you shall be healed.* So may I say: Send the Ark back, let the service of the Lord have its free passage and not be insulted; yet send it not empty, but return Him a full Guilt-offering—I mean a confession of your sins; show your former wickednesses, satisfy God for the wrong done to Him, and you shall be healed.

**4.** God undertakes the healing of a people when He gathers together an entire company of Physicians; when the Physicians come together, a great cure is at hand. See, this is what the Lord has wrought: He has brought the Physicians together: I mean the Nobles and Commons assembled in Parliament, who have investigated the causes of our sicknesses, proposed remedies, and have (thanks be to God) made such good progress in our cure. I have now only one word of application, and then I shall leave this point and come to the second Doctrine.

<margin>1. Application.</margin>
**1.** Is God the Physician who undertakes the healing of our Land? Oh, then bring no Ill-willed Spirit against your healing! Do not be like those rebellious ones of whom we read in *Hosea 7, 1.* *When I would have healed Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim was discovered, and the wickedness of Samaria.* Ephraim contains the ten Tribes, and Samaria was the seat of the Kings of Israel after their rebellion from the house of David; from which you may note that Court and city, Prince and people, together produce many who are unwilling to be healed. Oh, that such a Spirit were not in our days: are there not many against a Reformation? Slow to establish the Government of the Church to the liking of our Lord Jesus? Unwilling that the ordinances of Christ might shine again in their old strength? In a word, what ill-will has there been in the discovery of Episcopacy <note>The system of church government by bishops, which the Puritans sought to abolish.</note>, with the abuse of the church service, the restoration of a new Government in the Church, the cleansing of the Sons of Levi <note>A biblical term for the clergy or ministers.</note>, and the casting down of the Sons of Belial <note>A biblical term for wicked or lawless men.</note> from their places and Offices; oh, what ill-willed outbursts have come from the mouths of many people while

<column-break/>

these things were in motion. Oh, my beloved, let such a Spirit not be found in any of you who hear me this day, or God shall say: you shall surely die, and your wound shall never be healed.

**2.** Since God undertakes the healing of our Land, oh then, do not despair of your recovery. The Lord will not suffer such a disparagement to happen to Him, that He should begin the healing and not finish it; if He once undertakes our healing, we shall undoubtedly be healed. *Jeremiah 17, 14.* *Heal me, O Lord* (says the Church), *and I shall be healed.* And the Lord even gives the reason to His people in *Isaiah 66, 9.* *Shall I bring to the birth, and not cause to bring forth? says the Lord.* This is as much as if He had said: should I give a beginning of deliverance and not work out a fulfillment? Far be that from my thoughts.

**3.** Look through all instruments to God, *2 Chronicles 16, 12.* *Asa was diseased in his feet... yet in his disease he sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians.* And for this reason he was never healed. Whatever instrument God uses for your healing, give God the praise and Glory for it. Although Cyrus was an instrument of God to deliver Israel from her bondage in Babylon, nevertheless they looked to God and gave Him the honor for that great deliverance, *Jeremiah 17, 14.* *Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise.*

**4.** Since God undertakes the healing of Kingdoms, oh, that all these State-physicians would make God their Patron in the healing of this Land. **1.** God heals through the plaster of peace and truth; oh, that these both might also be mixed together among them; Peace alone is not powerful enough to work our healing. **2.** God heals through cleansing. *Isaiah 4, 4, 5.* *When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof... and upon all the glory shall be a defense.* O, there are many Ill-willed humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to control health and temperament.</note> to be cleansed from many Nobles and Citizens in this Kingdom before it can be healed; I wish that men would follow God in this. **3.** The Lord heals a land by the cutting off of those evil and corrupt members who hinder the healing of a land; it was the Lord who troubled Achan *Joshua 7, 25.* and cut him off because he troubled Israel. Oh, that our State Surgeons would follow God in this, to cut off those from the Land who have caused this Sickness. <note>original: "Melius est ut pereat unus quam unitas."</note> *It is better that one perish than the unity.* It is a well-known saying of the Poet.
