# England’s Sickness.

The healing of a sick Kingdom. In the handling of this point, I shall maintain this order: First, to show you the nature of these two Medicines. Secondly, to show you what their effects are, and how they come to heal a Nation so powerfully. Thirdly, I shall give you some instructions on how to use these means well. And then I shall conclude everything with a word of exhortation.

Regarding the first, to show you the nature of these Medicines, I shall begin with the first Medicine: **Peace**, which is an all-encompassing word; generally taken, it is a calling-forth of all outward blessings. Yet, to make you understand its nature more distinctly and particularly, know that there is a threefold Peace.

<margin>2 Use.</margin>
1. There is a **Divine Peace** with God, *Rom. 5:1.*

2. In contrast to the state of enmity, an **Ecclesiastical Peace**, in contrast to Church disputes and divisions; which consists in an agreement of the members of the Church among one another, walking together in love and the fellowship of the Gospel.

<margin>3 Use.</margin>
3. A **Civil or Political Peace**, in contrast to wars or unrest in a Nation; which consists in a regulated order, or the government of a state according to the Law, when it is not disturbed by internal rebels or external attacks. My Text refers to this last one: that although the Jews would be captive in Babylon for seventy years, slaves in their persons, insulted in their freedoms, cast out from their opportunities, and in danger of their lives all around from their enemies, nonetheless they would have Peace and Truth together. Flaccius Illyricus <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575) was a Lutheran reformer and scholar known for his work on biblical interpretation.</note> notes that when Peace and Truth are joined together, it signifies a certain, firm, and infallible Peace, not a poor or hypocritical one.

<margin>4 Use.</margin>
The second Medicine I must speak of is **Truth**. It was a good question which Pilate put to Christ, *John 18:38:* *What is Truth?* His haste caused him to lose the answer, which makes it more important for us to know its nature. There is a fourfold Truth. 1. **Metaphysical**, that is, for contemplation. 2. **Logical**, that is, for disputation. 3. **Ethical**, that is, but a spring-source of speech. 4. **Theological**, and this is twofold: 1. **Subjective**, as written within us, which we obtain from the Word. It encompasses Truth in our judgments, when we are guided by the essence of things; Truth in our will and affections, when we obediently come into agreement; Truth in our walk, when we are upright according to the Word. 

<margin>Ovid.</margin>
2. **Objective**, as it lies in the Scriptures, both in its principles and the conclusions proceeding from them. I prefer to understand it in this latter sense; yet to speak more clearly, Truth is taken in three ways in the Scriptures:

<margin>5 Use.</margin>
1. For **sincerity**, in contrast to hypocrisy, *John 4:24.* *God is a Spirit, and those who worship him must worship him in Spirit and in truth*, that is, in sincerity of heart.

2. For **impartiality** in the courts of justice, in contrast to injustice, *Isaiah 59:14.* *Therefore justice is turned back, and righteousness stands afar off: for truth is fallen in the street, and equity cannot enter.* Here Truth is to be taken for justice in the Courts of the Judges.

<margin>2 Doctrine.</margin>

<column-break/>

3. For **truth in our words**, in contrast to lies, *Psalm 15:2.*

4. For the **entire truth of God** in His Word, contained in all that matter of doctrine or discipline which agrees with the will of God, *John 17:17.* *Sanctify them in your truth: your Word is the truth.* *Proverbs 23:23.*

<margin>Cornelius à Lapide.</margin>
Now, the question is, which of these is understood here in my Text. Truly, Cornelius à Lapide <note>A prominent Jesuit priest and biblical exegete (1567–1637) whose commentaries were widely read across denominations.</note> understands Truth as the diligence of God in the fulfillment of His promises regarding the deliverance of His Churches. Others understand Truth as justice; yet I understand it here as neither one nor the other, but prefer to take Truth in the fourth sense: for the entire truth of God, in the matter and doctrine of Religion, in which sense it is commonly taken when it is joined together with peace, as in *Zech. 8:19*, *2 Kings 20:19*, and *Isaiah 39:8*.

I proceed now to the second particular: namely, to show what the effects are, or wherein the power of these Medicines lies. The first remedy, **Peace**, is a sovereign Medicine against all the calamities of war. War destroys and ruins Kingdoms, overturns the dwellings of men, turns sturdy buildings into heaps of stone. But peace compensates for these damages, fills the desolate places with inhabitants, and builds up again that which has fallen. War makes blood flow through a Land; but peace makes it overflow with honey and milk. War brings scarcity, but peace the fullness of all blessings. War creates irrational creatures, having a lust for bloodshed (having deviated from the end for which they were first made). The horse is prepared for battle, the trumpet blows the march, and the outcome stands on the point of a pike or the mouth of a cannon. But peace preserves these poor creatures from this heavy bondage, and restores them shortly to their first privileges. This is the effect of the first Medicine. The effect of the second, **Truth**, follows now to be explained. Truth is a sovereign remedy, both preserving and expelling. It is preserving; it preserves the minds of men from being inflamed with evil opinions and abominable errors. And it is expelling or driving out, as well as preserving; it purges out heretical and false opinions that lurk in the inner parts of the Church, whether in Doctrine or in Discipline. These two Medicines, well-tempered and applied, are of sufficient effect (through God’s blessing) to accomplish the healing of this Nation.

The third particular, upon which I must dwell a little, is to give some instructions which you must observe regarding the use of these Medicines, namely:

<margin>1 Instruction.</margin>
Be certain that these Remedies are not counterfeit. If **Bezoar** <note>A "bezoar" was a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of certain animals, highly prized in the 17th century as a universal antidote to poison and a cure for various ailments.</note> or any other thing is falsified, though it bears the name, it nonetheless lacks the nature or effect of the genuine article; the Patient will not get better even though he takes it. So, Beloved, should these Medicines, peace and truth, be counterfeit, the Land cannot be healed. First, peace is deceptive if it is not made on good terms, or otherwise not with appropriate persons. It stands on bad ground if it leads to the wounding of the...

<meta>This page continues the sermon or treatise "England’s Sickness," expanding on the metaphorical medical treatment required for the nation's spiritual and political turmoil. # England’s Sickness.

The Mark of the Beast is this: that they are Lords over the conscience; that in time they shall be as wicked as the Bishops, and that they are introducing Presbyterianism <note>The author is likely an "Independent" or "Sectary" who feared that the Presbyterian system of church government would be just as oppressive as the Anglican Bishops they had just overthrown.</note>: these men are pregnant with these and similar jealousies. Oh, that men would allow such things to arise from their own spirits.

<margin>
3. Instruction.
</margin>
Do not take one of these medicines without the other. Many wish to have peace and never look toward the truth. Augustine (as I have recounted before) proves such people wrong: *Peace and Justice are two friends, but perhaps you see one and do not want the other*, etc. *what great thing is it to desire peace? Any evil person desires peace* <note>original Latin: "Pax et Justitia duae sunt amicae sed tu forte unam vides alteram non vis... quid magnum est desiderare pacem quilibet malus desiderat pacem"</note>. Peace and truth are two friends, but you want one of them and not the other; there is no one who does not desire peace, yet not all wish to do justice. What a great matter is it to desire peace? Every ill-willed person desires and loves peace. To seek peace without truth proves a rebellious spirit; to seek both without truth shows a spirit of ill-will; to seek peace without truth proves the highest wickedness; to seek both without truth is a spirit that runs among our profane soldiers; and to seek peace without truth proves un-Christianity, and cannot keep us in peace or preserve us from errors—all of which are enough to make us miserable. Therefore, seek both.

Take a large quantity of both these medicines; a grain <note>original: "aes," a tiny unit of weight</note> or a scruple <term>scruple: an apothecary’s weight equal to about 1.3 grams, used here to mean a tiny amount</term> is not enough. See in my text: there must be an abundance of peace and truth. A small prayer or a little truth does not have enough strength to drive out those old and stinking humors <note>In 17th-century medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to cause disease if unbalanced.</note> which we have nourished for so long in the body of our nation. As the plaster <note>A medicated bandage or poultice.</note> must match the wound, you must necessarily have a large quantity of both.

<margin>
4. Instruction.
</margin>
Seek truth rather than peace; truth is the primary medicine. Promises are the guides and allies of a Christian’s desire: Now when God wishes to pour out a great blessing upon His Church, He promises peace and truth; indeed, more truth than peace, *Isaiah* 48:18. Oh, that you had listened to my commandments! Then your peace would have been as a river, and your righteousness as the waves of the sea. Note: truth is promised as the waves of the sea, but peace only as a river. This was the greatness of their blessing: they had more truth than peace, and they had such a peace that flows high from the truth, as the river flows from the sea. It will never go well with us until our spirits exalt the truth of God above outward peace, and desire such a peace as proceeds from the truth. It is told of the Sybarites <note>Ancient inhabitants of Sybaris, famous for their luxury and excess.</note>, a people overflowing with outward blessings, that they sent to the Oracle of Apollo to know how long their peace and prosperity would last; the Oracle gave them this answer: "As long as you value your Gods above your prosperity and peace, these shall remain; but when you regard these things above your Gods, you shall be cut off." I may truly say, as long as you hold the truth of God dearer than peace or anything you enjoy, so long shall your peace and prosperity last; but if you value these above the truth of God, they shall depart from you.

<margin>
5. Instruction.
</margin>
Lay these medicines upon your heart. The sickness lies before the heart, just as when the stomach is overloaded

<column-break/>

with food; oh, let peace and truth be laid closest to the heart: love peace with your heart, and be not like King Saul and his followers, *Psalm* 55:21 <note>In the original text cited as 55:22</note>. His mouth was smoother than butter, but his heart was war. And likewise love and obey the truth from the heart, without hypocrisy. Thus I have finished the instructions: now one more word of application and then I shall end.

1. Is the abundance of peace and truth that which God uses to heal a sick kingdom? Oh, then be willing to bear some costs for these medicines; take some risks, put aside difficulties, undergo the malice of others, and take part with those who may be as a plaster to you, and who strive for the preservation of our nation.

2. Do not diminish even a scruple of these medicines; there are some statesmen who think that peace does no harm to some soldiers, and that the truth will choke the ill-willed, and that one should therefore moderate somewhat between both parties: for this reason, they think a small portion of truth is enough, as much as the ill-willed can bear. Oh no; this cannot be crumpled to fit every man’s humor; this would be as great a folly as if we made shoes for our feet, and they being too small, we wanted to cut off our toes to make the shoes fit. They are little wiser who wish to bend the truth of God to their corrupt humors. It was a heroic resolution of Luther: *Let justice be done, though the heavens fall* <note>original Latin: "Fiat Iustitia, ruat Coelum"</note>, let the truth have its place; let this medicine be applied, and nothing else, even if it does not accord with our conditions.

<margin>
3. Application.
</margin>
Are peace and truth the remedies which must heal us? Oh, then do not hold too much to this Truce <note>Likely referring to the ongoing negotiations between the King and Parliament.</note> or peace (which begins this day), as if without danger this Truce would heal our sickness, settle all disputes, and fulfill all our hopes. Dearly Beloved! There is a great chasm between our enemies and us: there are people who cannot bear such stinging corrosives and suppurating medicines as God prescribes in my text—people who love neither peace nor truth. First, they are no lovers of peace, but have bloodshed and revenge in their hearts against us, making the well-affected of this nation the target of all their malice; those who hate not only our bodies but also our souls, who drink toasts to our destruction; is it even possible to have peace with such people as these? While they persist in this, we could as soon mix fire and water together, yes (I had almost said) reconcile Heaven and hell, as reconcile their spirits and ours—either they must become better or we must become worse before we can agree. Secondly, they do not love the truth: Would the bloodthirsty rebels of Ireland? The idolatrous Papists <note>A derogatory term for Catholics.</note> of England? The proud Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials, like Bishops.</note>? The rest of the corrupt clergy and that profane household among this nation who have bowed hand in hand; would these (I say) be patrons of truth? Do not deceive yourselves, there is little likelihood of peace with such: what I have said before, I say again, either they must become better or we must become worse before we come to an agreement. Although I do not discourage you from standing upon this Truce; nonetheless

### Edifying
# MEDITATIONS
### and Godly
## RESOLUTIONS.

->By<-

->Mr. CHRISTOPHER LOVE.<- <note>Christopher Love (1618–1651) was a prominent Welsh Presbyterian minister in London. He was eventually executed by the government of Oliver Cromwell for his involvement in a plot to restore Charles II to the throne.</note>

->Translated by J. P., lawyer.<- <note>The initials "j.c." in the original stand for *juris consultus*, indicating a legal scholar or lawyer.</note>

---

1. Many men's all-too-great and strange Ambition is whether they may be considered men of honor, even though they are not so at all; if they cannot make things as well as they might wish, they will not do as well as they could. I shall do my utmost best to make things better, and that which I lack in my own power, I shall fulfill through my wishes; so that as long as I pay in part, I shall not be indebted for the whole; he is most in debt who pays nothing at all.
2. Pride is the greatest Enemy of Peace, and modesty most contradicts pride; for while prudence ensures that art is a sign of Nature, pride brings it about that nature is a sign of art. A wise Man cuts his coat according to the proportions of his body; the Proud man cuts his body to fit his clothes <note>A metaphor for someone who forces their natural self to fit into social fashions or artificial roles.</note>. Thus it is no wonder that he does not know himself, being today not the same man he was yesterday; nor is it any less wonderful if an honest Man does not wish to recognize him, since he comes to forget both himself and everything that is good. I shall be as I am, so that God, when he comes to judge me, does not find me changed; and finding me not as He had made me, does not reject me as not being of His making. Whatever the day may be, I shall set aside the old reason for my clothing <note>Refers to the biblical "garments of skin" or the necessity of clothing due to the Fall.</note>, but I shall not be draped and dressed in new clothes according to the fashion every day. I see there is great reason that I should be ashamed of my pride, but I see no reason to be proud of my shame.
3. The reason why many do not come to enjoy what they wish is that what they wish is devoid of reason; he can do what he wants, who wants to do nothing but what he can.
4. I would marvel to see how a greedy man can always be poor,

<column-break/>

since a rich man is always greedy; were it not that I see a poor man knows how to be content, and only a contented man is rich. The one has lack in his abundance, while the other abounds in his lack. I see then that we are neither rich nor poor by what we possess, but by what we desire; for he is not rich who has much, but he who has enough; nor is he poor who has but little, but he who has a lack of more. If God then makes me rich through Abundance, I shall not impoverish myself through greed; but if He makes me poor through lack, I shall enrich myself through contentment.
5. Hypocrisy <note>original: "gewepnthept" (feigning/hypocrisy)</note> wishes to seem good, rather than to actually be so; simplicity wishes to be good, rather than to seem so. Worldly people gain reputation by selling their merit; wise people buy merit at the hazard of their reputation. I would do very much to hear good of myself, but more to be worthy of that good; and I would rather lose my reputation than my merit. It shall be more joy to me that I know myself for what I am, than it will be troublesome to hear what others say I am. I would rather deserve good without praise, than do evil while being praised.
6. A timid man on a Battlefield is like a wise Man's fool: his heart lies in his mouth, and he does not know what profession <note>In this sense, "profession" means his public declaration of faith or duty.</note> he makes. But a timid man in the faith is like a fool in his wisdom: his mouth lies in his heart, and he would not dare to make a profession of what he knows. I would rather not know the good that I must do, than not do the good that I know; it is better to be beaten with few stripes than with many.
7. Every true Christian is a true Traveler: his life is his walk, Christ his way, and Heaven his home. His walk is difficult, his way perfect, and his home delightful. I shall not gaze idly upon the way, for fear of falling short; I shall not step aside, for fear of staying on the side; but I shall be content to travel cheerfully, as I am assured of being on the right way. Thus my certain way shall border upon my Fatherland, and my difficult walk shall make me find my land much more pleasant.
8. What a wound is to the body, a sinful body is to the soul: the body is in peril as long as the wound is not healed; the soul is not healthy as long as the sin of the body is not cured. And the wound of either cannot heal without being bound, nor can it be bound without pain. Now, just as the pain of the wound repeats itself through the healing of the body, so the pain of the body is softened by the healing of the soul. Let my wound bring me pain through the application of remedies, rather than let my body die; let my body be weary through chastisement, rather than let my soul be lost.
9. It is a sort of goodness not to become worse; it is the quality of wickedness not to become better. I shall take narrow care not to blow out the sparks, and shall exert myself to light a fire. If I have the goodness which I ought to have, that itself is not too much—why then should I diminish it? If I have the good-

### Edifying Meditations.

10. Health can be possessed; sickness must be endured; one and the same body is the object of both the one and the other. The same God is the Author of both. If God gives me health, I shall use it with thanksgiving, and shall not believe it to be too good <note>Meaning: "I will not take it for granted or grow proud in it."</note>, since it is His grace that shares it with me. If He sends me any sickness, I shall endure it with patience, and shall not believe it to be too great, since it is my sin that has deserved it. If I live in health, glorifying Him, I shall do my best to remain in it; if He places me in sickness, I shall do my best to ward it off through prayer. He shall be my God in sickness and in health, and my expectation shall be upon Him in health and in sickness. In doing so, I have nothing to fear from sickness in health, nor to despair of health in sickness.

11. The ordinary excuse of the poor is to slander their misfortune; but the subject of their complaint comes from their own actions. I shall ensure either that my fortune is good, or satisfy myself that it is no worse. If it is not as good as I might wish, it is nonetheless not as bad as I know it could have been. What does it matter if I am not as lucky as I wished? It is enough for me that I am not as miserable as I deserve.

12. There is no profit to be made from the love of the World; no loss (save for her love) through her hatred. Why then should I strive to court that love which can bring me no profit? Or should I fear that malice which cannot wound me? If I came to love her because she loves me, God would hate me for that love. If I have an abhorrence for her because she hates me, she cannot wound me. Let her hate me then, and I shall forgive her; but if she loves me, I shall not do the same for her, for since her love is harmful and her hatred is without harm, I shall despise her hatred and hate her Love.

13. Just as there is a folly in knowledge, so there is a wisdom in ignorance. I would not gladly be ignorant of necessary knowledge, nor be wise above wisdom itself. If I know enough, then I am wise enough; if I seek more, then I am a fool.

14. It is no wonder that Man has lost his Dominion over the Creatures <note>This refers to the "Dominion of Man" over animals and nature described in Genesis, which theologians argued was corrupted after the Fall of Man.</note>, since he did not wish to submit himself to the will of his Creator. Why should they fear man, since man did not wish to obey God? I would very gladly wish that no creature had the power to harm me; I am well pleased that those creatures are ordained to help me. If God shows me enough to serve me therein, I shall not expect that they must all be mine.

15. No afflictions (for the time being) seem joyful; all temporal affliction seems grievous. I shall compare my miseries here on Earth with my joys in Heaven, and the

<column-break/>

length of my torments with the eternity of my joys; in doing so, my journey shall seem short and my burden light to me.

16. There is nothing more certain than death, and nothing more uncertain than its hour. I shall then prepare myself at every hour, because it can overcome me at any hour, and I must undergo it at one time or another. I shall not hasten my death because I am always ready, but rather sweeten it; I shall not die any sooner for it, but indeed die better.

17. The praise of an evil thing is its short duration; of a good thing, its endurance. It would be a happiness for the damned if their torment knew an end; it is a greater happiness for the Saints that their joy is eternal. If Man, born of a woman, is full of miseries, it is a happiness for him that he has but a little time to live. If his life is a journey of affliction, it is a blessing to him that his days are but a hand's breadth long <note>A common biblical metaphor for the shortness of life, from Psalm 39:5.</note>. Happy miseries that end in joy; happy end, that dissolves into an eternity.

18. If I were to place no more faith in the truth of my Savior than in the traditions of Men, poverty could make my faith waver, and carry my thoughts to a despairing Purgatory <note>original: "Vage-vier"</note>. How are the poor happy if release is obtained only through money? Or how is it difficult for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven if money can buy off the most dangerous debts—the present, the future, his own, those of his deceased children, and his descendants after him? If Heaven is thus sold, what advantage does my poverty have through the price already paid? I find no happiness or salvation in the Roman Teaching <note>original: "Roomsehe Leere". Love is critiquing the Catholic sale of indulgences and the concept of Purgatory.</note>; it is a happiness to me that I have the Lord of Heaven.

19. There is no condition of life here on earth so happy that it could give a Christian man perfect contentment; and yet, there is no condition of life here on earth with which a Christian man should not be content. Although I can have nothing here on earth that could give me full contentment, I shall nonetheless learn to be truly content with what I possess here below. What does it matter to me if I do not have much? I have as much as I wish, if I have as much as I need; I have as much as the greatest multitude, if I have as much as I wish.

20. The greatest sin is that one always gives birth to more sin; for where the habit of sinning increases, there the conscience or the certainty against sin decreases. It is easier to extinguish a small spark than a whole fire. I would rather break the eggs of the Basilisk <note>A mythical serpent-like creature said to kill with its gaze. Love uses it here as a metaphor for small sins that grow into deadly habits.</note> than have to kill the Serpent. O daughter of Babylon <note>A reference to Psalm 137:9: "Happy is the one who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks," used allegorically to mean destroying sins while they are small.</note>, happy shall he be who takes your little children and dashes them against the stones.

21. Nature commands me to love myself and to hate all those who do me evil; Reason commands me to love my friends and to hate those who begrudge me; Religion commands me to love all men and to hate no one. Nature shows care; Reason, understanding; Religion, love. Nature can advise me; Reason...

### Edifying Meditations.

21. Nature may persuade me toward a certain likeness, but **Religion** shall govern me; I shall lend my ears to nature in many things, to **reason** in more, and to **Religion** in all things. Nature shall make me careful over myself, but hateful toward no one; reason shall make me wise for myself, but good toward everyone; **Religion** shall make me amiable toward everyone, but not negligent of myself. I might listen to the first, but I shall not lend my ears except to the last. I subject myself in some things to nature, in many things to reason, and in all things to **Religion**.

22. Abundance is a disturbance, necessity a misery, honor a burden, lowliness a contempt, advancement dangerous, and disfavor hateful. There is no good like a middle-state <note>The "Golden Mean" or *via media*, a popular 17th-century ideal of avoiding extremes.</note>, which gives a quiet contentment. I shall not climb high, for fear of falling, nor shall I lie down upon the Earth, for fear of being trodden underfoot. I am in greater safety when my own legs bear me; a moderate warmth is the healthiest for my body—I would not wish to freeze, nor yet to burn.

23. A great promise without effect is like a fire set to a great Cannon, which, touching nothing but the priming-powder, discharges a great expectation through a foul noise or a mere flash. I shall consider beforehand what I wish to promise, so that I do not promise what I do not intend to keep. In so doing (so long as my words are guided by my thoughts and followed by my works), I shall be careful in my promises and righteous in fulfilling them. I would rather keep my word and not promise, than promise and not keep it.

24. An honest man has two tongues <note>Meaning he speaks to both God and man with the same intent.</note>; a **Hypocrite** has a double tongue. An honest man’s heart speaks without his tongue; the tongue of a **Hypocrite** speaks without his heart. An honest man often has God in his heart when he does not speak with his mouth; the **Hypocrite** has God in his mouth, even as the fool says in his heart: *there is no God*. I can understand the tongue more easily, but the heart more surely; the tongue speaks louder, but the heart more truly.

25. The speech of the tongue is better known to Men; God understands better the speech of the heart. The heart without the tongue can pierce the ears of Heaven; the tongue without the heart speaks an unknown language. It is no wonder, then, if the desires of the Poor are heard, while the prayers of the High are despised. I would rather say three words in a language that God understands, than pray for three hours in a language He does not understand.

26. **Meditation** or Reflection is the **Womb** of our actions; the action is the **Midwife** of our **Meditation** or Reflections. If a good and perfect conception lacks the power to be brought forth, it perishes in the womb of the understanding; and if it can be said to be born at all, one must say it is a miscarriage. If an evil and imperfect conception has the luck to be born, then the mind is only delivered of a burden of imperfections, in the perfection of deformity, which might limp before the door of the Church or perish through its own flaws. If I reflect upon what

<column-break/>

is good to do, and do not the good that I have reflected upon, then I lose my labor and make my knowledge wither. If I do a thing that is good, but have no intention toward the good that I do, then it is a good deed, but not well done. Others may receive some benefit, but I deserve no praise. A resolution without a deed is an empty folly; a deed without resolution is a reckless folly. Know first what is good to do; thereafter, do that good which you know. If foresight is not better than labor, then labor is not good without foresight. I would not want my actions to happen without knowledge, nor yet against the same.

27. It is the folly of affection not to rebuke my **Friend** when he happens to fail, for fear of making him angry; it is a deadly folly to be angry with my **Friend** because he rebukes me when I happen to fail. I would be no friend if, seeing my friend wander from the path, I did not warn him; I would be unworthy to have a friend if, when he makes my error known to me, I grew angry with him. Let me rather have the hatred of my friend than deserve it; let the righteous rather strike me kindly with the rod of rebuke than wound my head with the sweetness of the oil of flattery or connivance <note>original: "pluimpstrijckerije ofte oogh-luyckinge"—literally "feather-stroking or eye-closing."</note>. It is folly to flee from disfavor when one gives righteous cause for hatred. I consider him to be the best friend who is worthy of my friendship, rather than he who merely desires it.

28. When children encounter **Flowers**, or **Nuts**, or **Apples** on their path, I often see that these same things delight them and draw them away from their errands, so that they are certain to feel the anger of their Fathers and Mothers, and often find the door of their house closed by waiting too long. Meanwhile, those who encounter constant danger hasten on their journey, and their diligence makes them welcome with praise at their home. Nature has sent me into the World, and I travel daily toward my home. If I encounter many miseries on the way, prudence shall teach me to make a godly end to my journey; and if I encounter pleasures, they shall only give me pleasure in that they remind me of the delights of my home, which shall make me despise these worldly things as mere trifles. I shall never consider a miserable life to be a curse, but rather a blessing; a pleasant journey is bought very dearly if it is at the loss of one's **Fatherland** <note>In this context, "Fatherland" refers to the Heavenly home/Kingdom of God.</note>.

...Fisher of Men is / so it is good that one first looks before one leaps / one can eat the Honey / if one only watches out for the Hook / I shall honorably avail myself of my pleasures / but shall not buy the same with peril.

30. I notice / that / whenever I have a short journey to do / I have soon returned again to my house / soon out of the difficulty of my journey / soon in the possession of my rest / if my life is but a walk / and Heaven is my home / why should I wish for a long journey? knowing for a truth that my home is so delightful / I would not be weary of a long walk / but nonetheless the shorter my journey is / so much closer is my rest.

31. There come into my thoughts the Pharisee / and the Tax Collector <note>original: "Tollenaer"; a reference to the parable in Luke 18:9-14</note>: the one casts his eyes upward while his actions tend toward the depths of Hell: the other stands with a downcast countenance / while his hands and his heart lift themselves Heaven-ward; it is no shameful thing to let one's Profession be seen / if you only prophesy that which we let be seen; but of those two / I would rather be good / and not seem so / than to seem good / and in deed not be so / the Tax Collector returned to his house more justified than the Pharisee.

32. When I think upon the Eagle that takes up the Tortoise into the air only to crush him by his fall <note>This refers to a common fable used in emblems to warn that those raised high by flatterers are often dropped to their ruin.</note>. 33. When I see the leaves falling from the trees in the beginning of Autumn / such is / as I believe / the friendship of the World / so long as the sap of my wealth lasts / I have friends in abundance / but in the Winter of my need they leave me entirely naked / he is very happy who has a friend in need: but he is in truth much happier who has no need of a friend.

34. 35. 36. ### Edifying Meditations.

[...as a] Fisher of Men is <note>likely a reference to the apostolic calling in Matthew 4:19</note>; so it is good that one looks around before one leaps up; one can eat the **Honey**, if one only guards oneself against the **Sting**; I shall honorably make use of my pleasures, but shall not buy them with peril.

30. I notice that whenever I have a short journey to make, I have quickly returned to my house, quickly out of the hardship of my travel, and quickly in the possession of my rest. If my life is but a walk and **Heaven** is my home, why should I wish for a long journey? Knowing through the truth that my home is so delightful, I would not be weary of a long walk; nevertheless, the shorter my journey is, the nearer is my rest.

31. There come to my mind the *Pharisee* and the *Publican* <note>original: "Pharizeeus" and "Tollenaer"; referencing the parable in Luke 18:9-14</note>: the one casts his eyes upward while his actions tend toward the depths of Hell; the other stands with a downcast countenance while his actions and his heart exalt themselves toward Heaven. It is no shameful thing to make one's Profession known, if only we prophesy that which we allow to be seen; but of these two, I would rather be good and not appear so, than to appear good and not be so in deed; the *Publican* returned to his house more justified than the *Pharisee*.

32. When I think upon the *Eagle* that takes the *Tortoise* up into the air only to crush him by his fall, that same thing reminds me of the lovely and precious politeness of the **Devil**, who, through the generosity and liberality of his subtlety and cunning, always stands ready to destroy us. Thus he dealt more than once with my Savior; he had no sooner brought him to the Pinnacle of the Temple than there immediately followed: *Cast yourself down from here*; and having placed him on a high Mountain, that he might fall down, and he would be richly rewarded from his own. If advancement is so dangerous, I shall take great care not to be ambitious; whatever state or condition it be, the same shall satisfy me; I am high enough if I can stand upright.

33. When I see the leaves falling from the trees in the beginning of **Autumn**, such is, I believe, the friendship of the **World**; as long as the sap of my wealth lasts, I have friends in abundance; but in the **Winter** of my necessity, they leave me entirely bare. He is very happy who has a friend in need; but he is in truth much happier who has no need of a friend.

34. I would wonder that the insatiable desires of ambition could find even the slightest degree of contentment, if I did not see that they seek a perfect honor here on Earth, where the fullness of glory is not found except in **Heaven**. The honors of the World are full of steps, but no step reaches to perfection; whereas the glories of Heaven allow for steps <note>This refers to the theological concept of "degrees of glory," where inhabitants of heaven experience different levels of bliss according to their capacity, yet all are perfectly satisfied.</note>, but every step possesses its fullness. Here, one may be in honor beneath another, and yet the most highly exalted always lacks one step or another; there, even though one Star differs in glory from another, they nevertheless shine together in the fullness of glory like Stars. Here, the very greatest can lack something; there, the least have enough. Here, the whole Earth cannot

<column-break/>

be enough for one Man; there, one **Heaven** is enough for all men. Lord, let me rather be the least there, without honor here, than the greatest here, without honor there; I would rather be a **Gatekeeper** <note>original: "Poortier"; a reference to Psalm 84:10: "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness."</note> in that House, than a **Ruler** here in these tents.

35. When I behold the *Sun* buried under the Earth toward the Evening, and which in the Morning finds again a resurrection to its Glory: Why (I come to think to myself) cannot the **Children of Heaven**, buried under the Earth in the Evening of their days, expect the Morning of their Glorious resurrection? Every night is nothing else but the burial of the passed day, and the Morning its resurrection; why then should our mortal sleep be anything other than our nightly sleep? Why should we not just as well awake to our resurrection as we awake in the Morning? I see that the night is rather an intermission or pause of the day than a taking away, and that death much rather borrows our sleep from us than robs us of the same. Since, then, the Glory of the *Sun* finds a resurrection, why not the children of Glory? Since a dead Man can live again, I shall not look so much at the end of my life as toward the coming of my change.

36. I see that a *candle* gives me but a small light during the day, which does me great service at night; and I know that the cause is not that the brightness of the *candle* is less by day, but because the brightness of the day is less in the evening. Just as the friendship of my *Friend* toward me, so also mine toward my *Friend* can be the same at all times; yet we find it better when we have the most need of it. Even if it is fine that I receive some kindness according to my want, I shall nevertheless estimate a kindness according to its worth. That my fortune has no need of the kindness of my *Friend* is my luck; but if my luck should come to despise his kindness, that itself would be a folly for me.

37. I see that the *candle* by day has no great shine, which by night gives a Glorious luster; not that the *candle* then at that time has greater brightness, but because the air at that time is dark. How much greater a disadvantage then is that ambition which makes me appear less than I am, by presuming to make myself greater than I am. Those sparks in the midst of the stalks lose their brightness if one compares them to the children of Glory. I shall not set myself higher than my step, for fear of suffering the shame of being humbled; but if I set myself lower than my place, then I might be advanced to that honor: *Friend, sit up higher* <note>Reference to the parable of the wedding feast in Luke 14:10.</note>. I would rather be exalted through my humility than lowered by my exaltation.

38. I see that the *candle*, which is like a *Sun* in the darkness, is nothing but darkness in the *Sun*; the *candle* no more illuminating the darkness of the night than the *Sun* obscures the light of the *candle*. I shall then take great care not to contend especially with the great; just as something can be all too strong for the weaker, so must I be all too weak for the stronger, and cannot...

# Edifying Meditations.

39. I see / that when I follow my shadow / it flees from me / and when I flee it, it follows me / I know that pleasures are nothing other than shadows / which come to last no longer than the glinting Sun of my fortune / for fear then that my pleasures shall leave me / I shall leave them / pleasures flee me most / when I flee them most.

40. To speak evil of all those whom we know to be evil / is not a complete thing / much less to judge someone as evil / who might be good / to speak evil through knowledge / shows a lack of love / to speak evil through suspicion / shows a lack of goodness / I shall not say as much evil of many as I well know: I shall say nothing worse of anyone than what I do not know / to know another's evil and not to speak of it / is sometimes courtesy / to speak evil of someone / and not to know it is always pride / he himself can often be evil / who through knowledge of another speaks good / but he himself cannot be good / who speaks evil of someone through suspicion.

41. A crowd of the great / is a great crowd <note>The author uses a play on words: "hoopen grooten" (a heap of great ones) vs "grooten hoopen" (a great heap)</note> / for the greatness of the wicked makes his wickedness even greater / it is the unfortunate Privilege of authority / not so much to commit evil as to teach the same / and through a second crime to ensure that the sin of the offender / is no longer his alone but another's: Every fault in a Shepherd <note>original: "Herdes-man"; here used as a metaphor for a leader or minister</note> / is not so much a crime / as it is a rule to cause others to sin / and though their crimes are not great / at the very least they are examples to do evil / to sin by command is as common as it is damnable / and men run in post-haste / when they go through the Devil with authority / and power / if then the crimes of those / who govern others / are the high rules of another's crimes / it must be that the crimes of all the great / are the greatest of all crimes / let me then be great in goodness / or otherwise it would be better for me to be without greatness / my own crimes are already too heavy a pack for me / why then should I burden myself with another's crimes?

42. To say everything / that is the truth / is the characteristic of fools: to say more than the truth / is the folly of far too many People: he who spends all that he has / is a useless waster or Producer: He who spends more than he has / is a useless Deceiver / I can sometimes know far / that which I do not wish to reveal / I must never reveal things that I do not know / I would be sorrowful if my tongue were as hot as my heart / I would curse it if my heart were less than my tongue / for if the saying / of everything that I know / shows all too great a foolishness / to say more than I do not know / shows all too little sincerity.

<column-break/>

43. The ambitious folly of far too many People is / to follow greatness much sooner than goodness / they shall much sooner come to follow the example of their Lord <note>original: "Heere"; referring to a worldly master</note> / than the commandments of their God / I shall always honor greatness / but I shall only follow that which is good: and shall much sooner do good without an example / than evil / through imitation / it is better to be saved without an example / than damned by resemblance.

44. There is no safety in bad company / where often the good find themselves / and the evil do not better themselves / for the perverse industry of wickedness / is / to have companions <note>original: "hanteerd-gesellen"</note> / it is likely that those / who commonly troop together / and seek one and the same Shore / wish to be birds of a feather / for commonly conversation or conduct <term>conversation: in this period, "conversatie" referred to one's entire social conduct and manner of living with others</term> makes us such as those are with whom we associate / I cannot be certain that I shall meet no bad company / but I shall be careful not to bind myself to them / I shall willingly companion myself with those / who either teach godliness <note>original: "Godtvruchtigheyt"</note> or learn the same themselves / and if my <unclear>companion</unclear> does not better me / nor I can make him good / then I would rather leave him evil / so that he does not make me worse.

45. To teach Godliness / is the greatest praise / to learn Godliness is the greatest profit / though it is beautiful that he who teaches is the wisest / nonetheless he who learns is even wiser / I shall then not teach with a haughty manner / nor learn with shame / I could not be so ignorant / that I could not teach something / nor so wise that I could learn nothing more / I shall then teach / that which I know / and learn that which I do not know / although it is greater praise to teach / than to learn / nonetheless it is less shame to learn / than to remain ignorant.

46. Just as in lack / there is misery / so is there danger in excess / I shall then wish / neither more nor less / than only that which I have need of / I can die just as well from excess as from hunger.

47. It is a cunning nature and characteristic of many / to follow / examples much sooner than commandments: but it would be the safest to learn / much sooner through commandments / than through examples / for one finds many good theologians / who cannot learn that which they themselves teach / it is easier to say do this / than to do the same / when I see a good doctrine / with an evil life / I shall weep for the one from my heart / but shall not practice anything but the other / good teachings are everyone's own / evil deeds belong only to the Author.

48. Two things are necessary for a Traveler / to bring him to the end of his way: the knowledge of his way / and the perseverance to travel / if he wanders from the right way / the hastier he goes / the further he steps away from his house / if he sits down / and does not move from the place / even if he is on the right way / he shall never know his country / but shall never arrive there / he who takes his resting places at the proper time / makes much better progress in his journey / I shall then first of all know my way / before I set out on a journey / the knowledge of the same is a great part of my journey / he / whose heart fails in the completion / loses the honor of the deed / I shall then not only know my way / but shall also follow the same / I would rather that my journey had no beginning / than to come to a hasty end / if then heaven is my country / and I know Christ as my way / before I undertake the journey / he who on a way

[one who] he does not know / runs hastily / can very quickly come into a land / that he does not love / so if Christ is my way / and Heaven is my house / I shall much rather endure my troublesome journey / than not have my perfect rest / I value my country <note>Meaning his true homeland, Heaven</note> more than my journey / my goal shall be guided by knowledge / my knowledge followed by my doing / ignorance is a bad mother to devotion / and idleness a bad housekeeper for knowledge.

49. I cannot wonder enough at the foolishness of faint hearts / who plague themselves / yes, even kill themselves because of the apprehension of death <note>original: "door," likely a transcription error for "dood" (death)</note> / making it so that the tidings / and harbingers / of a following misfortune / bring about or cause an even worse misfortune for them / than that / of which they had the tidings / whereas the foresight of an impending misfortune / is no small benefit / for if it is / that it cannot teach us to prevent the same through foresight / it can teach us / how one shall endure the same through patience / I could grieve / over the difficulty of an evil / as soon as I shall feel it / but shall not grieve over the difficulty of an evil / as soon as I shall hear talk of it / my evil / when it shall come / can make my pain great enough / why then should my tormenting / before it comes / make my evil even greater?

50. Herein I find / that it goes with the Soul / just as with the Body / those are often the most sensitively sick / who feel their evil the least / whereas on the contrary those / who consider every small wound to be deadly / come to seek healing in time / and are healed / I shall not consider it a fortune to have many sores / but if I have them / I shall be glad that they cause me pain / I know that the healing is not dangerous / because my wounds are more perilous / I would be much sicker / if I complained less.

51. This is not one of the least evils / that one does not shun the appearance of evil / which is often the cause that the innocent is justly punished / and that through an undeserved suspicion / I would indeed wish that people thought me to be good / but would rather actually be so in deed / it is no small fortune to be beyond suspicion / but it is a much greater fortune / to feel oneself to be beyond a crime / I would very much wish to be neither evil / nor held to be evil / but of the two / I would rather be thought evil / without deserving it / than to deserve the evil / without being thought so.

52. I know but one way to Heaven / I have but one Mediator in Heaven / namely a single Christ / and yet I hear talk of many Ways / and of many Mediators / are there then many Christs? Are the ways of the Lord like unto your ways? That we must go to the King of Heaven / just as to a King of the Earth? If I am exalted only in the name of her Son / why should I make use of the name of his

<column-break/>

Servants? Would it be a lack of politeness / or disobedience / to come when I am invited? Is another better than I am / or am I myself too good to do my own errand / to the Almighty? There are still always unrighteous Vinedressers <note>An allusion to the parable in Matthew 21, referring here to corrupt clergy</note> in the Vineyard of the Lord / who not only treat the Servants badly / but who rob him of his own Inheritance. 53. 54. 55. But oh alas! those merchandises here / are worth less than nothing / in Heaven / I would very much wish to be at rest with the world / but even rather to have peace with my conscience / the friendship of men

# Edifying Meditations.

56. Just as faith / is the clarity / of things that one does not see / so / those things that one sees / are the perfection of faith / I believe that a Tree shall turn green / when I see the same in Winter without leaves / I know that it is green when I see it standing in bloom in the summer / it was a fault in St. Thomas <note>The Apostle Thomas, who famously doubted the Resurrection until he could see and touch Jesus' wounds</note> not to believe before he saw / it would have been a madness in him / not to believe after he had seen / faith can sometimes exceed reason / but not suppress it / and faith is often above the understanding / without being contradictory / and so also / while faith / assures me that I come to eat Christ effectively <note>A reference to the spiritual reality of the Eucharist or Holy Supper</note> / the understanding must assure me that I taste it reasonably / for though it is true that I often do not see those things that I believe / yet I must always believe those things that I see.

57. 58. 59. 60. # THE TRUE DOCTRINE OF MORTIFICATION <term>Mortification: The spiritual practice of "putting to death" the sinful nature or "the flesh" through discipline and the power of the Spirit.</term> AND SINCERITY.

### Together with the nature of ingratitude, and the duty of the hearers.

->By<-
->**Christopher Love**, in his lifetime a faithful servant of *Jesus Christ*<-
->at *St. Lawrence Jewry* <note>original: "Lauwrence Jurij"; a historic church in the City of London</note> within *London*.<-

->Translated from English by **P. D. L.**<-

---

->Life in sin is the death of the soul.<-

->ROM. viii. verse 13.<-

>For if you live after the flesh, you shall die: but if you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.

---

<margin>1st Sermon.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' containing a seated figure, likely a prophet or scholar, holding a book or scroll.</image-desc>
That which Moses said to Israel in *Deuteronomy* 30:19, ["I set before you today life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both you and your seed may live,"] is the sum and objective of this matter which I shall now treat, to whose attention and observation I not only invite you, but also humbly pray you; for these are matters of great importance, of life and death: For if you live after the flesh, you shall die; but if you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.

<margin>The connection of the words.</margin>
This Chapter, from which my Text is taken, contains a broad description of a Christian, and holds within it many privileges of believers; and yet among these, there are cast here and there some sorrowful doctrines and threats: among all these, this in my Text is one: *If you live after the flesh, you shall die.*

<margin>The Text opened.</margin>
If you live after the flesh] All men who live, live *in* the flesh, but no one [saved] shall live *after* the flesh; If you live after the flesh (that is) after the sinful inclina-
<meta>catchword: tions</meta>

<column-break/>

tions and sinful suggestions of nature; To live after the flesh contains these three things:

<margin>What is here understood by living after the flesh.</margin>
1. *Continuity* and *constancy* in sin; it does not say, *if you act after the flesh, you shall die*; for even the best of God's children do this; but nevertheless they do this without living after the flesh; to live after the flesh signifies a continual working of sin.

2. It signifies not only a constancy and continuity, but likewise a pleasure and delight in sin; men are accustomed to rejoice in life, and so to live after the flesh, having a delight and pleasure in sin.

3. It signifies a great diligence and labor in sinful ways: it is one thing when sin follows you, and another thing when you follow sin; *Galatians* 6:1. There the Apostle says, *Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in the spirit of meekness*: A Godly person [is one whom] sin runs after, and the same overtakes him; but a Godless person runs after sin, and overtakes it: it is one thing that your corruption follows you, another thing that you run and race after sin, and have a fleshly desire in your mind to accomplish it: To live after the flesh signifies persistence, pleasure, and diligence in the ways of sin.

The corrupt incitements and movements of the body are called "flesh" for these reasons:

<margin>1st Reason.</margin>
1. Because sin is in the flesh as well as the Spirit; the habits of the body are as corrupt as the soul. *James 4:1.*

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>
2. Because sin is so natural to a man—

<summary>This page serves as the title and introduction to a sermon series by Christopher Love on the doctrine of "mortification," specifically analyzing Romans 8:13. Love defines "living after the flesh" as a state of persistent, pleasurable, and diligent pursuit of sin, distinguishing it from the occasional stumbles of the godly.</summary>
<keywords>Christopher Love, Mortification, Romans 8:13, the Flesh, Sin, St. Lawrence Jewry, Sermon, Theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the first sermon of Christopher Love on Romans 8:13. The text is completing a list of reasons why the "flesh" (the sinful nature) is so persistent and dangerous, and why its "death" is necessary for the soul's life.</meta>

<header>The true Doctrine of</header>

<margin>3rd Reason.</margin> man as his own flesh / and it is from this that it is compared to the Right Eye and Right Hand, etc. Matt. 5, 29, 30. Rom. 6, 13.

3. Because sin is rooted out through the flesh / and that / being the instrument of sin / is expressed by its own name. Sin was in us as soon as we were clothed with flesh / and shall remain in us as long as we are in the flesh; as David says Psalm 5, 5. <note>likely a reference to Psalm 51:3; original: "Ick kenne myne overtredingen, en myne sonde is steeds voor my."</note> *I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me.* And verse 7. Sin desires to remain in us / as long as we remain here in the world.

**If you live after the flesh you shall die,** ] This is a great thing / it would be good for a man / who takes pleasure and delight in sin / that he might die like a beast / and that there might be an end of him : but this must not be so understood / as if the soul should eternally die and be dead / but you shall die, that is / you shall go and be cast into damnation if you live after the flesh.

<margin>Objection.</margin> **Obj.** But here some might ask / how the Apostle could say / that those who live after the flesh shall die / since nonetheless the corrupt in hell shall live eternally in those Torments / Mark. 9, 44.

<margin>Answer.</margin> **Ans.** Although the Godless shall live in hell / nevertheless their damnation is called a death for two reasons: 1. Because the Scripture / which does not ascribe the name of life / to that which enjoys no comfort with the same (1 Tim. 5, 6.) and the Scripture expresses a sorrowful and wretched state through the name of death. 2. It is called a death / because they are separated and divided from God who is life.

**If you live after the flesh, then you shall die : but if you through the Spirit, do mortify the deeds of the body, then you shall live.** If you [through the Spirit;] sin through your own weakness / even so you cannot kill sin except through the Spirit.

**If you kill the deeds of the body**] that is / subduing the power and dominion of sin / if you kill the deeds of the body; that is / those sins / which are shown in and through the body / then you shall live, not only here / but hereafter eternally in Heaven / you shall be blessed; This is the proper condition upon which God allows salvation to follow / **If you through the Spirit kill the deeds of the body, then you shall live.**

And now having thus opened the words / I need say no more to you than Moses said to Israel. *See, I set before you today life and death, blessing and curse; therefore choose what you will.* I have set life before you / **If you through the Spirit kill the deeds of the body, then you shall live.** Now I have set death before you / **if you live after the flesh you shall die.** Therefore choose now what you will / either salvation / or damnation, whether you will live or die.

The primary objective of the Apostle in this Chapter is to awaken and exhort the believers / to walk worthily of their Justification <term>Justification: The theological concept of being declared righteous before God through faith.</term>; although Christ does everything for us in Justification, nevertheless we must add to it <note>In this context, the author means that justification must be followed by the active pursuit of holiness, or sanctification.</note>; although Christ justifies us from the guilt of sin / nevertheless we must likewise labor / to be freed from the filthiness of the same; And the Apostle expresses this exhortation / through various Arguments / Rom. 8, 12, 13. **Brothers (he says)**

<column-break/>

**we are debtors not to the flesh, to live after the flesh. No, we are debtors to the Spirit, to live after the Spirit;** We are debtors to God to kill our sins and corruptions / and it is our duty to pray for that.

2. He impresses this upon them / by the sorrowful consequence / of their not walking worthily of their Justification / **If you live after the flesh you shall die :** And

3. He impresses it upon them / by the great blessing and benefit / which follows those / who fulfill this duty / **if you through the Spirit, do mortify the deeds of the body, then you shall live.**

Before I shall come to the distinct handling of these words / and stand upon the main point / I shall only set forth seven or eight instructive resolutions or observations / so that you may see the power of this Text / briefly / only naming them.

1. From the observation of the persons / who they were / to whom Paul says / **If you live after the flesh, you shall die.** They were not only the Godless / such as were in the state of Heathenism / unbelievers, but these were in a converted state / true Believers, and to those Paul makes this threat from which I wish to teach.

> **That threats and sorrowful discourses, may also be applied to the converted, as well as to unconverted men.**

It is truly to be noted / that the word of the Lord is not only compared to milk, <margin>1 Cor. 3, 2. 1 Pet. 2, 2.</margin> Which is of a pleasant taste / but likewise also to Salt, <margin>Mat. 5, 13. Col. 4, 6.</margin> For the Godly have many rottenesses and corruptions / which must be eaten out by the salt of the word / to the end / that they may be preserved pure and without blemish.

2. The Apostle preaches not only comfort to the believers / Justification to them / that there is no damnation for those / who are in Christ Jesus / but likewise he also preaches threats to them / from which we learn.

> **That terrifying teachings, may as well be used upon the believers, as teachings of comfort and consolation.**

And therefore they preach but half the will of God / who only handle / teachings of comfort / and neglect the duties / or the exhortation of men to the practice of Godliness <term>Godliness: The outward practice of a holy life and devotion to God.</term>.

3. The Apostle does not only preach / terror and damnation, but he joins together these threats, with the teachings of comfort : from which we further observe.

> **That when the preachers preach teachings of Wrath and terror, they must mingle them, with teachings of comfort and consolation.**

And therefore just as they are to be blamed / who always preach teachings of comfort / so are they likewise worthy of blame who never preach comfort; variety of teaching / sets out the ministry with a greater luster / honor / and impressions upon the hearts of the listeners.

4. From the order that the Apostle uses here / he preaches terror first / thereafter comfort / **If you live after the flesh, then you shall die; but if you through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the flesh, then you shall live.** Then where we observe this Doctrine.

> **That when Christians perceptibly grow**

# Mortification and Sincerity.

<margin>5th Observation.</margin>
5. Regarding the addition of these words in the Text: [*through the Spirit*]. "If you through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the body," this was not said in the first part of the verse: "If you [through the power of the Devil] live after the flesh, you shall die." [But here these words are added: "If you through the Spirit"] of which note this:

<margin>3rd Doctrine.</margin>
That a man may commit sin through his own strength, yet he cannot mortify it except through the help of the Spirit.

You, who are but a single man, might as soon hope to defeat a whole army of men with your own hand as to bring down a single sin through your own power. A man may wound himself, but he cannot heal himself; you might commit the sin, but you cannot purge it away; a man can easily run down a mountain, but it is difficult to climb back up it; so also, a man can easily commit sin, but he cannot kill it except through the strength of the Spirit.

<margin>6th Observation. 6th Doctrine.</margin>
6. "If you through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the flesh," *teaches*:
That in every regenerate <note>original: "wedergebooren"; referring to one who has been "born again" or spiritually renewed.</note> person, there remain some remnants of sin and corruption as long as they live.

<margin>7th Observation. 7th Doctrine.</margin>
And from this we may further learn:
That Christians stand as necessarily in a state of mortification <note>The term "mortification" (doodinge) refers to the subduing of physical or worldly desires through self-denial.</note> as other men, seeing that they have some irregular movements, or untamed affections, or impure lusts, which must necessarily be tamed in them, just as in other men.

Godly people must restrain, bind, and kill their corruptions just as much as the worst people in the world.

<margin>8th Observation. 8th Doctrine.</margin>
Finally, we may also learn from these words:
That men have a better condition to expect in the other world than here; or rather, as they live here, so shall they fare hereafter.

Are you a man who gives yourself over to sinful desires and the corrupt movements of your own heart? I say this: as surely as you live this way in this time, if you persist in that course, you shall die and be damned forever: *If you live after the flesh, you shall die*.

But if you labor to bridle and keep yourself from impure lusts, and seek to restrain your affections so that grace may obtain the blessing over your corruptions, and sin does not come to reign in your mortal bodies, you are already on the way to obtaining eternal life. Therefore, I pray you, my Brothers, do not think or reason thus with yourselves: "If I shall be saved, I shall be saved, even if I live ever so unholy; if I shall be damned, I shall be damned, let me do what I will to the contrary." Do not argue so, for here you see that the Scripture expressly tells you that *if you live after the flesh, you shall die; but if you through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.*

And thus I have given you these eight instructive conclusions regarding the general scope of these words; I shall now extract three more doctrines from them, upon which I intend to dwell a bit longer.

<column-break/>

"If you live after the flesh, you shall die," from which we learn in the first place:

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That to live in the world according to the sinful movements and corrupt dictates of nature, without laboring to kill and subdue them, is that which brings men to death and damnation.

I include this reason in the doctrine—"without mortification of them"—because "living after the flesh" stands in opposition to the "mortification of the flesh." If you live after the flesh without diligence to kill and subdue its movements, that shall bring you to death and damnation; *Galatians 6:8, says the Apostle: "He who sows in his flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh; but he who sows in the Spirit shall reap eternal life from the Spirit."* In "sowing in the flesh," it is meant following the desires of the flesh, and those who do so shall thereby reap damnation; you who have your seed-time in sin shall have your harvest in Hell; you shall gather in damnation and the hellish fire forever: *If you sow in the flesh, you shall reap corruption from the flesh.*

I shall handle this doctrine in this first sermon, because my thoughts are primarily focused on the other part of this text: *if you through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.* Therefore, I shall only answer one question and then give you some practical applications, and so be finished.

**Question.** Some may say: if it is so, that those who live after the flesh must die, how may I then know and be assured in my conscience that I am a man who lives after the flesh, and that sin is not subdued or killed in my soul?

**Answer.** I shall give you two general discoveries by which you may know whether sin is unmortified in you or not, by your disposition both before and after the commission of any sin.

<margin>The first discovery of an unmortified man.</margin>
1. In your disposition *before* the commission of any sin: when there is a craving and eager longing in the soul to do the sin, and a deliberation on how it is to be carried out. By this, the Scripture describes an unmortified man: *Psalm 36:4 <note>The text says 36:5, matching many older Dutch bibles.</note>: "He devises mischief upon his bed; he sets himself in a way that is not good."* When a man deliberates and plots how he shall carry out some sins, and that secretly, it is a proof (when upon such deliberation and plotting a man sets himself in a way that is not good) that he has an unmortified heart. Therefore, if it is thus with you, that you busy yourself and deliberate how you shall commit sin, it is a powerful proof that the power of sin in you is not subdued or killed.

<margin>2nd Discovery.</margin>
2. A corruption is unmortified in the soul when a man is more vehement to commit the sin to which he is inclined than to resist it; when a man is hot as fire in fulfilling his lusts to satisfy his promptings, so that he casts away all thoughts of resisting them; this proves that such a man has an unmortified heart. A godly man who has the power of mortifying grace upon his heart may fall into the same sins as you; nevertheless, he deliberates more on how he might flee and resist them than how to commit them. But now (it may be) all your thoughts are taken up with how you shall satisfy your lusts and do the sins in secret, but not at all how to resist them—

# The True Doctrine of

<margin>3rd Discovery.</margin>
3. When you never apply your strength in prayer against those <term>corruptions</term> <note>original: "verdorbentheden"; the inherent sinful inclinations of human nature.</note> to which you are most prone; when men attack one sin one day, and other desires on another day, and yet never go to God in prayer to obtain the power of **mortifying grace** to resist those corruptions; this is a sign of an unmortified heart. <term>Psalm 51:15.</term> <note>The Dutch text cites verse 17, following a different numbering common in older translations; in modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 51:15.</note> David says, *O Lord, open my lips*: Note here, that as long as David lay under the guilt of his sin, his lips were closed all that time; he could not pray to God; and therefore it is after he had confessed his sins that he desires the Lord would open his lips, so that his mouth might declare His praise. As long as your mouth is closed, so that you cannot pray against your corruptions, it is a sign that sin in you is not yet mortified.

<margin>4th Discovery.</margin>
4. When corruptions and temptations toward such and such sins most of all disturb and unsettle you during **holy duties**; <note>"Holy duties" (heylige plichten) refer to religious activities like prayer, reading scripture, or attending church.</note> when a person, during some <term>ordinance</term>, <note>original: "ordinantie"; a religious rite or service, such as a sermon or the Lord's Supper.</note> is overcome in his heart by the assault of godlessness—when that sin and corruption are so fixed upon your heart that you do not know what the preacher says for a whole hour—this proves that you have an unmortified heart. <term>Jeremiah 23:11.</term> There God says, *even in my house I find their wickedness.* If you give place to sinful thoughts and pleasurable imaginings even in God’s house, in the midst of holy duties, this reveals not only an unmortified state but a very wicked heart, flourishing even in the presence of God. When many a young man comes to the Church, he looks for a beautiful and adorned woman, to cherish his lusts by the sight of her; guard yourself against this, for it is proof that you live according to the flesh, when you give place to such sinful allurements during holy duties, when you ought to be attentive to God in His ordinances.

<margin>5th Discovery.</margin>
It is proof that sin is unmortified in your heart when the mind rises up again toward the same sins that it has committed before, and does not humble itself, but longs in its heart to commit that wickedness again, which it has done once or many times. It may be that in former times you were a drunkard, and now you ponder how you might commit that sin again with pleasure; or an old whoremonger or adulterer, and now you deliberate within yourself how you might commit that sin again. This is a sure sign of an unmortified heart: <term>Ezekiel 23:19, 21.</term> *She multiplied her harlotries, remembering the days of her youth, when she had played the harlot in the land of Egypt.* You have brought back the shameful deed of your youth. The children of Israel thought of their adulteries in Egypt and fell back into their sinful pleasures.

<margin>6th Discovery.</margin>
When an invitation to sin is very hastily consented to; when you commit a great sin upon a small provocation; when your heart is like gunpowder, quickly ignited by sin—just like the young man with the harlot in <term>Proverbs 7:22.</term> *He went after her straightway.* This is proof of an **unmortified heart**.

<margin>3 Marks regarding the committing of sin.</margin>
And thus I have given you six marks (before the committing of sin) of an unmortified heart: now there are three more marks (which I shall give of an unmortified heart) after the committing of some sin. As:

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin>
1. If you find more joy in the places of sin after committing it than sorrow over having committed the sin; if you have more delight in the sweetness of the sin than grief in considering the evil of it. And

<margin>2</margin>
2. When you cannot endure a **rebuke** <note>original: "bestraffinge"; a formal or sharp correction for a fault.</note> for some sin you have committed, this is proof of an unmortified heart; when people are like nettles, which sting you if you touch them even slightly. So also, when you cannot endure the rebuke for your drunkenness or uncleanness, or something similar, this is proof that you are asleep or dead in sin. To be unable to endure a rebuke is proof that you love sin well, as you cannot bear for it to be spoken against. The Apostle says, <term>James 1:19, 21.</term> *Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.* When the word of God rebukes you for your sin, you must be slow to wrath—not struggling against every rebuke, but *receive with meekness the word implanted in you, which is able to save your souls*, verse 21. An unmortified heart is very ready to resist, to mutter, and to grumble when he is rebuked.

<margin>3</margin>
3. When, after committing sin, you seek more to hide yourself from the sight of men than to repent and be humble before God’s presence; when you labor more to hide yourself than to turn away from the sin. This comes from the dominion of sin and corruption in your heart.

And thus I have given you nine discoveries of an unmortified heart; may the Lord give you all earnest grace to examine your own souls, whether you are mortified men or women, or not.

The **application** I shall make of this will be for rebuke: if it be so, that those who live after the flesh shall die, oh, how worthy of rebuke are all those who run into this grievous judgment of death—those who would rather kill their souls than their sins! It is said of the <term>Basilisk</term>, <note>original: "Basilicus"; a mythical serpent-like creature said to kill with its breath or gaze.</note> that if you do not kill it, it will kill you: and so it is here; if you do not kill your sins, your sins will be the death of your soul. And therefore, how blameworthy are you, who would rather endure that sin kills your soul than undergo some pains to kill and subdue your sins?

I have read of a man who still loved a fox dearly, despite the fact that it had torn the entrails out of his own child, and yet he would not put it away. And so, I fear there are many among you who harbor such unclean lusts and corruptions in your hearts, which will destroy your souls, yet you do not abandon them, but endure them and let them reign in you—never going to God through prayer, nor having any **mortifying grace** to bring sin under subjection. And thus I have finished the first part of the text: *If you live after the flesh, you shall die.*
