<meta>This page continues the exposition of Romans 8:13, transitioning from the previous discussion on the signs of an unmortified heart to a more formal "Second Sermon" on the nature of true mortification—the spiritual practice of "putting to death" sinful desires.</meta>

->Mortification and Sincerity.<-

# True mortification is the only way to salvation.

> ROMANS 8:13.
> .... But if you through the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live.

<margin>2nd Sermon.</margin>
I come now to the second part of these words: "but if you through the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live."

The <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "doodinge"; the theological practice of subduing one's sinful earthly passions.</note> of the deeds of this body cannot be understood as referring to the religious members of the body, for those are to be nurtured; nor to the natural functions of the body such as eating and drinking; but it is to be understood as the sinful <note>The original Dutch reads "sandige," likely a transcription error for "zondige" (sinful).</note> actions performed through the body, arising from the enticements and "injections" of Satan, or the corrupt impulses of our own sinful nature. "If you put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live." You see here (Beloved) that the Lord walks in ways that seem contrary to the judgment of flesh and blood; He invites us with sorrow and tears to receive joy and gladness; He invites us to death, and declares that this is the very way to life. No way could be more opposed to our human nature, and yet there is no other way to life than this. We must first put to death sin and the world in order to live a life of <term>grace</term>; and we must die a natural death before we come to live a life of glory.

<margin>Marks to note.</margin>
There are two Teachings to be noted from this last part of the Text.

<margin>1st Doctrine.</margin>
1. That the mortification of <term>corruption</term> <note>original: "verdorventheydt"; the inherent sinful state of humanity.</note> is a necessary quality required in every person who shall obtain salvation: "If you put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live." And;

<margin>2nd Doctrine.</margin>
2. Regarding the source of this work (through the Spirit): "If you through the Spirit put to death..." Learn from this /

<margin>application.</margin>
That although a person can commit sin through their own strength, they cannot, however, put sin to death except through the power of the Spirit. These are the two points I shall handle from this last part of the Text. With God's help, I shall speak of the first point in several sermons; but for now, I will only present some things by way of introduction to this necessary Teaching on mortification. Then I will deal with the specifics of this Doctrine: I will give you its nature and its identifying marks, and the false delusions that might occur here, as well as the "holy jealousy" of the godly, which often leads them to think they are not mortified when they actually are, etc. For the present, I shall only speak of some things as an introduction and to clarify the handling of this point: that the mortification of corruption is a necessary quality required in every person who shall obtain salvation.

<margin>9 Rules for those who are unmortified.</margin>
I shall first give eight or nine rules concerning those who are unmortified, and then as many in contrast concerning those who are truly mortified; I shall begin with the first.

<column-break/>

<margin>1st Rule.</margin>
1. Do not mistake the restraint of sin—preventing it from becoming an outward act—for an actual "putting to death" of sin. Restraint is not mortification. As in Genesis 20:6, where God says to <term>Abimelech</term> <note>A king of Gerar who intended to take Abraham's wife, Sarah, but was stopped by God.</note>, "I also kept you from sinning against me: therefore I did not allow you to touch her." He had restrained the sin but had not removed the inclination. Just as a lion sitting behind bars is still a lion, even though he cannot go out to his prey, so also, although people restrain themselves from acting out the sins to which they are naturally inclined, the restraint of the sin is not the death of it. A person may for a time put a bridle and bit on their lusts so that they do not break out into deeds and sins, yet this is not the power of mortifying grace. A person may avoid a certain lust for many years, and yet the lust remains unbridled in the heart; therefore I say, do not count the restraint of sin as the mortification of sin.

<margin>2nd Rule.</margin>
2. Another Rule is this: that a lack of pleasure in a certain kind of sin is no infallible proof that such a sin is mortified. Do not take a present unwillingness to commit certain sins as a sufficient putting to death of them. This is a great misunderstanding into which many people fall: because they have no desire to commit certain sins—either because they cannot or are ashamed to fulfill them—they think they have a work of Mortification and <term>sanctification</term> <note>The process of becoming holy or being set apart for God.</note> wrought in them. However, there are various external causes that make a person unfit for certain sins, such as illness, old age, the disturbance of the conscience, one's upbringing, or even a person's natural temperament.

<margin>Some reasons why some people do not commit certain sins.</margin>
<margin>1st Cause.</margin>
1. A person may have some unwillingness toward certain sins arising from an illness they contracted in the past; perhaps having been a drunkard or an adulterer, but because they became sick through it and are barely recovered, they now have no appetite or desire for these sins. Or, even if they have renewed desires for these sins, they perhaps lack the physical strength to carry them out. Such a distaste for sin comes from the sick-bed, and not from mortifying grace. Or,

<margin>2nd Cause.</margin>
2. The inability to sin may come from old age, whereby a person's strength weakens and declines, and so they are not fit for the sins of adultery, drunkenness, etc., which they previously committed with pleasure. And,

<margin>3rd Cause.</margin>
3. it may come from a good upbringing and principles of modesty in a person, which hold them back from many great and scandalous sins.

<margin>4th Cause.</margin>
4. It may likewise come from the stirring and disturbance of the **Conscience**, when it seizes a person so that God throws the sparks of hellfire in their face. This may keep them from sin for a time while this dread lies upon them. Just as a terrible thunderstorm spoils the beer in our cellar, likewise when God thunders upon the Conscience, it will sour and embitter a person's sin so that they have no desire for it. But nevertheless, this is not mortifying grace in the heart, but the terror of the Conscience that grips and gnaws at them, making them fearful of sin during such a time.

<meta>This page continues the "Second Sermon" on Romans 8:13, specifically detailing the "rules" and "causes" for true mortification—the spiritual practice of killing off sinful desires. The previous page introduced the concept that mortification is the only path to life.</meta>

<header>The True Doctrine of</header>

<margin>5th Cause.</margin>
5. This is also an outward cause of a person’s lack of desire for certain sins: their natural temperament. For although every person has the seed of sin within them, there are certain sins to which one is more naturally inclined than others, depending on one's circumstances and disposition. For example, a person with a **choleric temperament** <note>In historical medicine, a "choleric" person was thought to have an excess of yellow bile, making them prone to anger.</note> is more inclined to wrath; if they are **full of blood** <note>A "sanguine" temperament, associated with being lively but also potentially prone to lust.</note>, then they are most inclined to unchastity, and so on with the others. Thus, there are many sins for which human nature has an aversion. As **Luther** <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German priest who catalyzed the Protestant Reformation.</note> confessed of himself, he was never in all his life tempted by greed. Now, this did not come from **mortifying grace**, but from the natural disposition of his body; it was a gift of nature given to him by God, and not a gift of grace. And therefore (Beloved), you should not attribute this to mortifying grace; it comes more from a severe illness, old age, a terrified **conscience**, or a person’s natural circumstances. Allow me the freedom to explain this to you a little through this common Comparison: Suppose you had a sheep and a dog, and you threw meat to the sheep and grass to the dog; neither would eat anything. The sheep does not desire to eat the meat, nor the dog the grass, which comes from the nature of the creatures. Truly, so it is here: the natures of men are inclined toward some sins and not others, which therefore must not be attributed to the power of mortifying grace.

<margin>3rd Rule.</margin>
The third preventive Reason concerning this Doctrine of mortification is this: Let mortification be extended to internal and hidden sins, as well as to outward and scandalous sins. Not only the lusts of the flesh, but of the mind must be killed; not only the parts of the body, but the thoughts of the heart and the secrets of the inner man must be subdued. You must extend mortification to the binding of evil inclinations as well as evil works. **Colossians 3:5**, says the Apostle, *put to death your members which are on the earth: namely, fornication, uncleanness, etc.* You might think these two are likely one and the same; no, **fornication** is the sin in the deed or action, **uncleanness** <note>original: "onreynigheydt"</note> is the sin in the affections and in the thoughts. Now, the Apostle prays for them to kill fornication, which is the work of uncleanness; yet he does not stop there, but further relates that they must subdue their sinful affections and evil inclinations toward those sins. You must kill the first stirrings and hidden intentions of any sins in your hearts.

<margin>4th Rule.</margin>
4. Let mortification be specifically directed toward breaking those sins which would be masters, those that reign in your heart, those sins against which you have prayed most and which are the hardest to resist; those sins which attack you most strongly and can most easily overcome you. So did **David** do in **Psalm 18:24** when he says, *I kept myself from my iniquity*, that is, from my particular sins, my inclined sins, my **bosom iniquities**. I may give you here the same reasoning and command that the King of Syria gave to his captains in **1 Kings 22:31**: *Fight neither with small nor great, but only with the king of Israel.* So I may speak to you: do not fight against just any sin, but against your beloved and cherished sins, which easily beset and overtake you.

<margin>5th Rule.</margin>
5. Do not think to embrace or encompass this

<column-break/>

great work of mortification through a general view of sin, until you come to a distinct and particular understanding of it. If you take all your sins and corruptions together in one heap, you will never be able to break or kill them. Just as when a bundle of rods is tied together, the strongest man in the world is not powerful enough to break them, yet each one taken alone can easily be broken; so it is here. If you take sin piecemeal and labor to have a distinct knowledge and sight of it, this is the way to overcome and kill sin. If you shoot at random, you will never hit the mark; likewise, if you look at sin in general, you will never be able to kill it. Just as if a man must fetch a large tree far from his house, he will not take the entire trunk of the tree at once—that would be impossible—but he must chop it into pieces, and then he carries it easily. So many people act in subduing their sins; they think to do it all at once, but this is not the way. You must strive to have a particular knowledge of them, and then to break and overpower them one by one, and then you shall also overcome the strongest.

6. Let your mortification be extended not only to particular acts of sin, but to the whole lump and the **body of sin**. This is a great defect among many Christians: that if they are troubled by impulses, they kill them; or with unclean and sinful thoughts, they subdue them; but nonetheless, they live most of the time with the whole body of sin unkilled. So then, do not just deal with some particular lusts, but labor to mourn over the whole body of sin and to pull out the root of it. Whenever someone wants to stop a tree's growth, they must not only break off the branches but especially pluck out the root of the tree. Likewise, you can indeed cut off some branches of sin, but if you do not pull out the sin by the root, it will grow all the more, not only in that same sin but also in other sins worse than the root itself. When David went to mourn the sin of his adultery, he likewise mourned the sin of his nature in **Psalm 51:5** <note>The text cites 51:7, following different verse numbering found in some older Bibles.</note>: *Behold, I was born in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.* Showing that when we go to kill any particular sin, we must likewise mourn and labor to subdue the whole body of sin.

7. When you wish to accomplish the work of mortification, do it in **Christ’s strength** and not in your own. I have told you before that you can commit sins through your own strength, but you cannot kill them through your own strength. *If you through the Spirit put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live.* It is an arrow shot from Christ's quiver which alone can kill lusts. Therefore, do not depend here on your own reason, understanding, or knowledge in the accomplishment of this work of grace—mortification—and the subduing of sin. For although you can discover your sin and its danger through reason, nonetheless, through your own strength, you are not capable of subduing it. *We are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation* (**1 Peter 1:5**). You cannot act against sin by your own strength, for you are but as a feather before a strong wind; you have no power of yourself to resist even weak temptations...

In 1 Samuel 17:45 he says: *You come to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to you in the name of the Lord of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel.* Now, if you go against sin in the power and might of God, this is the only way to bring it under and keep it from unregulated desires.

<margin>8th Rule.</margin>
8. Beware of letting sin remain long in your heart without rebuke; but labor to kill it in its first movements. When nature first begins to agree with sin, labor then to pull it out by the root; for it is easier at first than when it has taken root to drive the sins out of our hearts. Sin is like a **Serpent**, which if it once gets its head into a place, it will soon wriggle its whole body in; so also when we allow these movements within us, they will soon become master over us. Sin is like the flooding of a mighty River; when the water has 
<margin>5th Rule.</margin> <note>Though the margin says "5th Rule," the text continues the 8th Rule regarding the river analogy; this may be a printer's error in the original manuscript.</note>
made a small hole in a dike, if it is not immediately stopped, it will soon overflow the entire Land; so also, if the first movements of sin are allowed, they will soon overcome the whole man.

<margin>9th Rule.</margin>
9. When you kill a sin through the strength of Christ and withstand a temptation, do not think your work is now finished, but keep a firm footing for another battle; your corruption will follow after you again, the Devil will shoot his arrows at you once more, and send one temptation after another to strike you down if he can; and God allows this in His wisdom to test us, and to humble us, and to make us see that we have constant cause to stand on our guard and take care of our hearts; and as long as we live, we shall stand in need of **mortifying grace**. <note>The term "mortifying grace" (doodende genade) refers to the divine help needed to "kill off" or suppress sinful impulses.</note> Just like the branches of a tree: no matter how often you chop them off, they want to sprout again. So also, when you have killed one corruption, another comes forward again; although you cut off one lust today, yet tomorrow another will easily bring forth another. If you have killed Pride one day, Passion comes the next morning, or Greed one or another sin the following morning,

So that we have constant reason to stand on our tiptoes on our watch, and to notice the deceitfulness of our hearts, and always to keep **mortifying grace** beneath our corruptions.

And thus I have finished nine Rules, by way of precaution, concerning the **Doctrine of Mortification**, all of which must be used very carefully in the handling of these points which are now further to be discussed. And because, in what I have already said, (it may be) I have touched the hearts of many and spoken to souls for their refreshment, there may be a poor humbled soul, or someone else among you, who has the power of mortifying grace in his heart, and yet he is truly grieved because he finds his corruptions so strong within him that he is not able to master them. Therefore, if you will follow me a little in your thoughts, I want to give you seven comforting observations; the first is this.

<margin>
7 Comforting observations for mortified hearts.
1st Observation.
</margin>
1. That the stirrings and fermentations of cor-

<column-break/>

ruptions in the heart can nonetheless exist alongside true **mortification**; that every lust which is killed may still make a great and grievous uprising in the soul. And this observation will give great comfort to many poor souls, if they only compare themselves in this, as in Romans 7:9 Paul says: *When the commandment came, sin revived.* And yet Paul was a mortified and holy Man. In this regard, it is with the Godly as it is with a sick or lightheaded person; although he may be near death, yet the strength is so violent in him that it makes him tumble and turn, so that two or three men are not enough to keep him resting in bed; yet this does not come from his own strength, but from his sickness which makes him thus. And so it may be in many poor souls: sins may be near their death, and yet stir and rage more and more; but this does not come from the weakness of the person to resist sin, but from the strength of **Satan's temptations**. Just as it goes with many birds: after their heads are pulled off, they fly more strongly than before; so you can give a deadly wound to sin, and yet when the "head" of the sin is gone, it will rage violently in the soul.

<margin>
2 Cases in which some corruptions in a person's heart do no harm in a mortified heart.
</margin>
But here (Beloved), because I know that many evil uses can be made of this comforting observation, therefore let me only say this in two cases; the rising of corruptions and the noticing of the same in the soul do no harm to a mortified heart.

<margin>1st Case.</margin>
1. When corruptions rise in you, if there are intentions and strivings against these sins, and humility regarding that rebellion within you; when the enticements of Satan and the promptings of sin increase, then pray to God heartily, and take up a resolution against this sin to diminish it; if you cannot rest because of the sin, nor the sin rest in you—in this case, the rising of corruption is no proof of an unmortified heart, but rather that the sin is already being put to death.

<margin>2nd Case.</margin>
2. The rising of corruptions in your heart, though very strong, is nevertheless no proof that your heart is unmortified, provided that after such stirring uprisings of sin in your heart, these corruptions become weaker and weaker. It is with sin in a believer as it is with a person in a head-fever, whose brain is violently disturbed; it will so deprive and steal his courage that everyone must wonder how such a sick person is still so strong; but now, when it is properly over, and the power of this sickness has passed, the poor man, because of his previous strong movement, is very limp and weak. Now, if it is so with you that after the strength of sin comes a weakness of the same; that having wrestled against it, you have overcome it and find its strength weakened—this is a powerful proof that **mortifying grace** is in your heart.

<margin>2nd Observation.</margin>
2. The second observation is by way of comfort, and it is that the mortification of sin does not extend so far in a reborn person as to the uttermost removal and pulling out of sin from the soul. Never expect that it will go that far; it is with sin in the soul as it was with the **Leprosy** in some cases, as said in Leviticus 14:44-45: *If the plague is spread in the house, one shall break down that house, its stones and its timber, as well as all the...*

# The True Doctrine of...

the clay of that same house: and it shall be carried outside the city to an unclean place. <note>The author is referencing the laws in Leviticus 14 regarding a house infected with "leprosy" (likely mold or fungus), which had to be dismantled if the infection persisted.</note> In this way, the <term>Leprosy</term> <note>original: "Melaetsheyt"</note> of sin is not cleansed as long as you live in the world, until the body of sin is entirely cut down. I may compare the sins in the soul to the tree of which you read in <margin>Dan. 4:14, 15.</margin> whose branches and leaves were cut off, but the root remained. You may prune the branches of sin, but you will never entirely pull up its root. Do what you can, sin will plague and disturb you as long as you live in this world. And therefore I say, do not expect that the killing of sin will go so far that it will be completely finished in this life.

<margin>3rd Consideration.</margin>
3. Take this for your comfort: although God does not will that this killing should entirely do away with sin, He nevertheless intends to work it so far that it takes away the **Dominion** of sin. Although it does not take away the *essence* of sin, it nevertheless takes away the dominion and reigning power of sin. It shall be in your souls just as it was with those beasts spoken of in <margin>Dan. 7:12.</margin> Their dominion was taken away, but a lengthening of life was given to them for a time and a season. So God will allow sin to live in you for a short time, but not to reign in you. <margin>Rom. 6:14.</margin> For sin shall not have dominion over you: for you are not under the law, but under grace. You are not under the law, and therefore sin shall not reign over you, but under grace. You are not under sin as a Law, but under the command and the law of grace; for the law is taken from the law of sin, <margin>Rom. 7:23.</margin> as the Apostle speaks, saying: *I see another Law in my members, warring against the Law of my mind,* etc. Sin shall not have the dominion over you, although it lives in you for a little time.

<margin>4th Consideration.</margin>
4. Take this for your comfort: that a rising desire, or a sincere striving in the soul to drive out and kill sin, is accepted by God as an actual killing. The Lord looks upon the struggle against lusts, and the resistance against sins, and all the primary beginnings of resistance, as if it were a perfect resistance. It is a remarkable passage that we read in <margin>Lev. 11:33, 36.</margin> It was part of the ceremonial law that every earthen vessel into which any unclean thing fell was unclean; both the water and the vessel were unclean. Yet, a fountain of water shall be clean. The interpreters give this reason: because if any unclean thing fell into a water vessel that had no power of cleansing itself, it must necessarily be unclean; but if any unclean thing fell into a fountain or a stream, it would not be contaminating because, through its constant motion, it purifies itself of all uncleanness. And so it is here: if you let sin rest in you without resistance, not pulling out its root, you are unclean; but if sin falls into you, and you have a stiff and resisting blood against it—from the principle of grace within you—laboring to be clean, purified, and free from sin, then you are not unclean but cleansed. Oh, what an unspeakable comfort this brings to each of you: that you resist sin and seek to overcome it with God's help! God looks upon this as a total subduing of the same.

<margin>5th Consideration.</margin>
5. Another comforting consideration is this: that you have God's promise and Christ's power to 

<column-break/>

help you in the completion of this great work of killing sin. Beloved, there is no child of man belonging to Christ who fights and struggles with the Devil alone, or carries his own burdens alone. There is none among you who has any part in Christ but that he has God's promise and Christ's power helping and supporting him in the killing of every sin. And therefore it is very remarkable that when God commands the killing of sins in some places—such as <margin>Col. 3:5.</margin> *Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness,* etc.—He promises in other places to do the same for us: <margin>Mic. 7:19.</margin> *He will subdue our iniquities.* When God commands His children to obey Him, He gives power and ability along with it to do what He commands. God commands them to kill sin; "Alas!" says a poor soul, "I am not able to fight with my corruptions or to keep myself amidst them." What then? God says, "I will help you, teach you, and kill your sins." Oh, under what a gracious and benevolent <term>Commander</term> <note>original: "Hooftman"</note> do we fight! He does the work for us, and yet He gives us the honor for it; He fights our battle for us, and yet He gives us the glory of victory! Oh, what a comfort that is, that we have such a gracious God who fights for us and brings down our iniquities for us.

<margin>6th Consideration.</margin>
6. There is yet another consideration: that sin and corruption often thrive and stir more after a person's conversion than they did before their conversion. So it was with Paul: <margin>Rom. 7:9.</margin> *I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.* "Before my conversion I lived, no sin disturbed me, I considered myself in a good and happy state, that I was a blameless man who had killed sin; but when the commandment came, sin became alive again." By the commandment of God, he means the Ten Commandments, which govern our thoughts—that none of them may be sinful or evil—and that if we have them, this sin alone is enough to damn us, even if we were innocent of all the other Commandments. When this commandment came, sin became alive again, *but I died*; that is, I saw myself in a completely miserable state without a Savior. Now, this rising up of sin after conversion is no proof that there are more sins in the soul than before conversion, or that the person is worse, or that he sees himself as sinful in every way; you simply did not have an eye as capable of seeing sin before as you do now. I may explain this to you with this parable: Suppose you bump your finger against a chair or bench or some other thing; and shortly thereafter, by chance, the same finger is cut. Truly, the bump to your finger after it has been cut will pain you more. So also, you might have bumped yourself once or more before and yet never felt it; but now every thing you touch disturbs and upsets you. It is the same here with a person after his conversion. The poor man cries out, "Lord, what is the reason for these sins, and why does every one of them disturb me so? I was not used to this before!" Truly, the reason is because your conscience was not as sensitive before conversion as it is after; you did not know the small sins then as well as you do now, when the Lord Christ shines in you with His burning flame and brings light...

<margin>3rd Sermon.</margin>
As:
1. I shall show you the Nature of mortification. And
2. the necessity of the same in respect of salvation.
3. The discoveries by which you may know whether God has brought you into the state of mortification or not. And
4. I shall show you the great misunderstandings into which many people fall concerning this Doctrine of mortification: some think they are mortified and are not; others the contrary.
5. I shall show you the difficulty of this duty and other necessary things concerning this Doctrine. First I shall resolve three questions and dwell somewhat longer on the last.

<margin>1st Question.</margin>
Quest. What is the nature of mortification?
<margin>Answer.</margin>
Ans. I shall give you this clear description of it: it is a holy disposition in a reborn person <note>original: "wedergheboren mensche," a common term for a "born-again" believer.</note> proceeding from the operation and power of the death of Christ, by which the strength of sin becomes weak, and the dominion is taken away, being outwardly able to have a commanding power or Rule over the person and more.

I call it a disposition in a reborn person because an unregenerate person is an unmortified person, and that it comes from the power and operation of the death of Christ because the death of Christ not only takes away the guilt of sin in respect of its own damning power, but it also likewise takes away the Dominion and power of sin, so that sin in us no longer reigns. Not that I say a total bringing to naught of sin, but only a bringing under and weakening of our corruptions; although there are still some remnants of sin, nonetheless the reigning power of sin is gone.

<margin>2nd Question.</margin>
2. Question. The next matter now to show you is the necessity of this great work of mortification, which lies in these three things.

<column-break/>

<margin>Answer.</margin>
Ans. It is a very necessary point to know whether you belong to Christ or not; there is nothing in the world of greater importance than whether you have a part in God or if the Lord has brought you into the state of mortification: you can have no part in the living God so long as your lusts and corruptions are still living in you. I may here relate a story which I have made known to you several times, of an Island located between Scotland and Ireland; <note>The author refers to a legendary test of land ownership based on the belief that venomous creatures could not survive in Ireland due to the blessing of St. Patrick.</note> and there being a dispute between both those Nations as to which of the two the Island belonged, the matter was settled thus: they would take a great multitude of toads, snakes, and unclean animals and bring them to the Island; if these unclean and harmful beasts lived there, then the Island would belong to Scotland, but if they died, then it must belong to Ireland, because no vermin lives there. I may apply this so: there is a great dispute between God and the Devil to whom the soul of the person belongs; now therefore, if poisonous lusts and unclean corruptions live in your heart and reign there, this is a proof that it belongs to Satan; but if they do not live or reign there, it is an undeniable proof that the same belongs to God.

2. The necessity of mortification consists in this, because grace cannot live in the soul until sin and corruptions are killed therein; before there can be the life of grace, there must be the death of sin; Rom. 6:11. You must consider yourselves to be dead to sin, but alive to God. Says the Apostle, if corruption lives, grace cannot live in your heart: Just as it is told of Doves, that they cannot live in smoky and filthy places, so also the Spirit of God will not live in the soul that is full of sins and corruptions.

3. The necessity of mortification appears in this, because the soul cannot live in glory until sin dies in the heart: just as grace cannot live in the heart before sin is brought under, so the soul cannot be glorified before the death and dying away of sin: as a <unclear>star</unclear> <note>original: "steer," possibly a name like Peter Sterry or the Dutch word for "star" (ster).</note> well says, if sin does not die, the sinner must die. Indeed, if God does not kill the sin, the sin will kill the soul. 1 Cor. 15:36, the Apostle says, You fool, that which you sow is not made alive, unless it has died. Just as the seed must rot and die before it sprouts up again, so also the soul cannot come up again or live with God in glory before the corruptions are rotted, died, and stifled in the soul. And this much is enough concerning the necessity of mortification.

<margin>3rd Question.</margin>
3. Question. I shall now be a bit longer in the following question, which is to give you clear discoveries by which you can know whether the Lord has brought you into the State of mortification or not. Of which some among you are very desirous to be satisfied. I shall give you six marks and go over them briefly.
<margin>Marks of mortification.</margin>

<margin>1st Mark of mortification.</margin>
1. Ans. Do you want to know whether God has brought you into the State of mortification or not? You may know it by this mark: if you are now more careful to avoid the occasions of sin than before, this is a proof that you are a mortifying person. An unmortified heart is strong and powerful and will long for the occasions of sin, whereas a mortified heart is careful to shun all occasions for evil. One compares a mortified person...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "marks" or "signs" of mortification—the spiritual practice of "killing" sinful impulses—following the introductory sermon on Romans 8:13 from the previous page.</meta>

# The True Doctrine of... <note>The header is incomplete in the original; it likely refers to "The True Doctrine of Mortification."</note>

...resembles a dove or a partridge; these not only feel dread and fear toward the hawk, but even hate and shun its feathers. So too, a person dead to sin does not only fear the sin itself but shuns those things that might lead them toward it. Now, if this holy fear, or displeasure at the thought of offending God, is found in you, I may surely judge of you that you are a person dead to sin. You are in such a gracious state and spiritual disposition as those we read of in Jude verse 23: *Hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.* This corresponds with those who, under the Law, were defiled with leprosy (Leviticus 13:45). The children of Israel feared not only such a person but also the clothes in which that plague resided; likewise, we must hate the garment covered with flesh—that is, all things that might ignite or give opportunity to sin.

<margin>2nd Sign.</margin>
2. When a "good" opportunity to sin presents itself to a person, and all circumstances invite him to sin, yet he nevertheless resists and refuses to commit it, this is a sign of a truly deadened heart. And if God has brought you into such a state, He has truly put your corruptions to death. Beloved, an unmortified person may keep himself from sins when there is no lure or opportunity to commit them; but it is proof of a deadened heart when, even though all opportunities for sin surround him, he nonetheless keeps himself from them. You have two examples of those who proved their mortification in this way. The first is Joseph in Genesis 39:9. He had a prime opportunity to commit the sin of adultery, for he and his mistress were alone; he was urged toward it; she enticed him day after day; and he could have done it in secret, for the text says the doors were closed and no one was in the house but the two of them. Furthermore, great advantages were offered to him—she wanted to make him master over her house. See how all these circumstances invited Joseph to the sin of unchastity, and yet he rejected them all, saying: *How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?* There you see that the power of sin was deadened in Joseph's heart. Now, test your hearts by this: when all opportunities tempt you to commit a sin, can you say "no" to your lusts?

Another example is David in 1 Samuel 24:4. Saul came into the same sheepfold where David and his men were. The text says that while Saul was in the sheepfold, David arose and secretly cut off a corner of Saul's robe. Now, David could have easily cut off Saul's head if he had wished; and although Saul persecuted David and sought his life, nevertheless, when David had this opportunity to kill Saul, he would not. This showed that the sin of retaliation <note>original: "vergeldinge," meaning vengeance or repayment</note> was deadened in David's heart. Now, I pray you, examine your hearts in these two things, and see how the matter stands between God and your soul.

<margin>3rd Sign.</margin>
3. If there is in your heart a tender sensitivity and a greater resistance against the Devil’s assaults to sin than before, it is proof that the Lord has brought you into the state of mortification. It may be that your nature was previously like gunpowder, flying up in a flame at any provocation; but now it is like green herbs, which lie upon the fire for a while

<column-break/>

before they burn. So it can also go with your temptations; and this is a true proof that you are progressing in the work of mortification.

<margin>4</margin>
4. If there is a beautiful correspondence between the death of sin and the life of grace in your soul, then you are a person dead to sin. Beloved, the Lord’s work is no halfway work; He does not merely kill the corruptions in your heart and nothing more. If the Lord has brought down sin in your soul, He will work a contrary work of grace in you, which shall live and act in your soul. Mortification—the death of sin—must be matched by the life of grace. Thus, if sin is dead, grace shall live in your soul. Therefore the Apostle joined both together in Romans 6:11: *You are indeed dead to sin, but alive to God.* And Peter says: *He who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin,* so that he no longer lives the rest of his time in the flesh but according to the will of God (1 Peter 4:1-2). Here the Apostle makes known to us not only that we should not spend our time in the sinful lusts of the flesh, but likewise live unto God. Therefore, beloved, it is merely a "pause" and not a "killing" of corruption when there is only a leaving behind of our lusts but no further pursuit of good.

<margin>5</margin>
5. Mortification is discovered by this sign: whether the guarding against corruption is mixed with humility. That "killing" of sin which has never been preceded by true humility is more of a standstill of sin than its death. Sin has never been truly killed if the heart has not been humbled. Many people deal with sin as stage-fencers do on a platform: they may poke at one another, but they deal no deadly wound. Many want to play and fence with sin, but not kill it. A true Christian is like a soldier: he kills and destroys sin; he wants to kill his sin so that it does not kill him. Now examine yourself in this: are you merely a fencer, fencing with your lusts, or a soldier who fights tirelessly against them? Have you given sin only a scratch, or a death-wound?

<margin>6</margin>
6. Mortification does not consist in the suppression of a few particular sins, but in the uprooting of the core and the whole "body" of sin. Therefore the Apostle admonishes us to *mortify the earthly members: impurity, evil desire, etc.* (Colossians 3:5), to crucify the flesh with its passions and lusts, and to put off the entire body of sin. It is with the mortification of sin as it is with the death of the body: death does not strike only an arm or a leg—one or two members—but all the members of the body must die. So also, this mortification is not the cutting off of one "limb" of sin, but something that strikes the whole body of corruption. Abstaining from some specific sins is no proof of mortification until you have dealt a deadly wound to the entire corrupt body.

And so I have finished the instructional part of these three questions. Now I shall touch upon some things by way of application <note>original: "toe eygninge," meaning the personal application of the doctrine to the listener's life</note>. I will proceed and dwell on these a little longer, but for the present, I will only use some points for the sake of comfort.

This doctrine might dismay many sad hearts and cause the godly to pass a heavy sentence upon their own hearts, thinking sin lives in their soul and grace is dead. Therefore, I shall set down some comforts; the first is this:

# Mortification and Sincerity.

<margin>1st Application.</margin>
1. There is a "killing" <note>original: "doodinge," a theological term for mortification or subduing the power of sin</note> of corruption in the heart even when there is a strong surging of that same corruption. The Devil can cause corruption to flare up in the heart, and yet you may still be in a state of mortification. I shall have occasion to speak more broadly of this in the future; I will only add this passage here, *Romans* 7:9, where Paul says: *Apart from the Law I once lived, but when the commandment came, sin became alive again, and I died.* Previously, Paul thought himself to be alive and sin to be dead; in his own understanding, he was innocent according to the Law of God. But when the Lord gave Paul a spiritual insight into his heart, he then saw himself as dead and sin as alive. Thus, there can be a strong rising of sin in the heart, and yet those same sins have already received their death-wounds.

<margin>2nd Application.</margin>
2. Take this for your comfort: that the re-committing of the same sin is not necessarily proof of an unmortified heart. I mention this to you only so that you may clearly distinguish whether a person has truly put a corruption to death, despite often falling into that same sin.

<margin>3rd Application.</margin>
<margin>Notice-</margin>
3. The mortification of corruption is not regarded by God as a total uprooting or annihilation of sin; rather, if the *rule* or dominion of sin is taken away, the Lord looks upon it as a complete killing. Sin (as I have told you) is like the tree spoken of in Daniel <note>See Daniel 4:10-15</note>, whose branches were chopped off, but the root remained. So too, if the sovereignty and power of sin are taken away, you are in a sufficiently good state.

<margin>Notice-</margin>
The reverend Mr. Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian</note> uses a very clear analogy to explain this great work of mortification. He says: just as a farmer cleans his grain ever so purely before he sows it, yet despite this, when it grows up again, it does not come up pure; rather, much chaff, stalks, leaves, and other things accompany the corn that were not seen there before. So it is with you: you may wash your heart ever so clean of sin, yet corruptions will repeatedly surge up again from the heart. God removes the filth of sin for the state of "glory" <note>meaning in Heaven</note>, but not for this earthly state of mortification.

<margin>4th Application.</margin>
4. You who believe your corruptions are unmortified, take this for your comfort: that God will not allow a greater power of temptation toward sin to come upon you than you are able to bear and eventually overcome. Be certain that He will not lay more upon you than you can endure. How could the temptations to sin be so strong if God gives you sufficient Grace and strength to withstand and conquer them? It is a very good observation that some make on *Genesis* 26:2 compared with *Genesis* 46:3, where we read that there were two great famines in the land where Isaac and Jacob lived. Now, in the first famine, in the days of Isaac, he asked the Lord if he should travel to Egypt for grain; the Lord said no. He forbade Isaac to go there. But later, when there was a famine in the days of Jacob, he likewise asked the Lord about going there, and the Lord commanded him to go. Now, why did the Lord refuse Isaac and allow Jacob to go into Egypt? They give this good reason: God would not let Isaac go because he

<column-break/>

was only a weak believer. God says, "You are but a weak Christian, not fit to endure temptation, much less the occasions and inducements to sin that are most prevalent in Egypt; therefore, you shall not go." But now, Jacob was a strong believer, fit to endure the trials, and therefore God commands him to go. Here you see that the Lord lays no more upon His children than they can endure. Oh, what a comfort this is for us, that we have such a good God who serves us with "tenderly-feeling bowels" <note>a period idiom for deep, visceral compassion</note> toward all His children. If you are weak and newly converted, the Lord will add His power and strength to yours so that you can endure the temptation, laying no more on you than you are capable of bearing.

<margin>5th Application.</margin>
5. Take this for your comfort: that in some cases, strong temptations to sin are not sin in the person being tempted, but in the one doing the tempting. A believer may think that if the Devil seeks to lead him to godlessness from day to day, place to place, and time to time, the Lord will charge it to him as his own guilt. But temptation to sin is not always evidence of sin in the person tempted, but in the tempter. For if the temptation to sin were always sin in the person tempted, then Christ Himself would have had sin in His nature (which would be blasphemy to say), for He was tempted by the Devil toward two great sins: Murder and Idolatry. Yet these were not sins in Him, but in the one who tempted Him. So now, when any allurements come before you, labor to withstand and ward them off; as long as they do not come from your own nature and internal corruptions, but are the Devil’s suggestions and sins, he shall bear the burden of them.

<margin>6th Application.</margin>
6. A principle of opposition and an intentional setting of oneself against every corruption is regarded by God as a mortification. For mortification on our part is but a struggle and a conflict with sin. I will only bring here that passage mentioned before, *Hebrews* 11:33, 36 <note>The author likely intends Leviticus 11:33-36, which discusses ritual purity laws</note>, where the Lord makes this law: that if any unclean thing were thrown into a vessel of water, the water would be unclean; but if it fell into the stream, it would be clean. And the reason is that the vessel of water has no cleansing power, but the river or running water purifies the uncleanness of the things thrown into it. So, although corruptions are in your heart, nonetheless, if you are like a running river, you will drive away the uncleannesses of the sins, and the Lord will look upon you as a person who has mortified them.

<margin>7th Application.</margin>
7. Take this for your comfort: that in the mortification of every sin, you have Christ's strength to help your own. Therefore, just as He commands us in some places to kill sin, He promises in another to do the same for us. Oh, what a good Master we serve, who does the work for us and yet credits it to us; who commands us our duties and fulfills them all for us! Though we do nothing, He nevertheless counts it as if we had done everything of ourselves.

ROM. <note>This likely stands for 'Romanus,' potentially a printer's mark or a reference to the Epistle to the Romans</note>

It uses biblical examples like Isaac and Jacob and theological analogies from William Perkins to show that God values the struggle against sin and provides the strength to overcome it.</summary>

### ROMANS 8:13

> ... But if you through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.

<margin>
4th Sermon.
4th Question.
</margin>

So I come to the fourth question, which is this:
**Question:** What are the misunderstandings into which many people fall regarding this great doctrine of mortification? <note>Mortification: the traditional Christian practice of "killing" or subduing one’s sinful nature through the power of the Holy Spirit.</note>

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>

**Answer:** There is a double misunderstanding into which people fall.
1. A misunderstanding on the right hand, into which Christians fall through doubt and perplexity, when they think their corruptions are not mortified when they truly are.
2. There is a misunderstanding on the left hand, into which sinners run, thinking their corruptions are mortified when they are not. At this time, we speak only of the first, which is the current state in the hearts of God’s people: thinking their hearts are [still] unmortified.

<margin>
1st Objection.
</margin>

"Oh," says a poor soul, "this makes me think that my heart is not yet mortified, because I still feel such a strong stirring of sins within it."

<margin>
Answer.
</margin>

To take away this mistake, I have only these seven points to say to you—you who make it a ground for your sadness that your corruptions are not mortified because you feel the stirrings of sin within you. You have

<margin>
1st Misunderstanding of a mortified heart.
</margin>

1. To notice whether these stirrings of sin come from the Devil, or from your own heart. If these stirrings and allurements to sin truly come from the Devil—from his hatred and malice against your soul—then you have no cause to fear. For these uprisings and stirrings toward sin in your soul are a proof that they are mortified, because Christ himself had great stirrings and allurements to sin; not toward small sins, but even toward murder—to break his own neck <note>This refers to the temptation of Jesus to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the Temple (Matthew 4:5-7).</note>—and to the sin of covetousness, when the Devil showed him all the glories of the world. Therefore, although you are often advised by the Devil to follow him, and feel those stirrings in you, if you can truly say and know that these come from Satan and not from your own heart, I want to assure you that they are the Devil's sins and not yours. The Lord will charge them to him and not to you. In some cases, the allurements of sin belong not to the one who feels them, but to the one who works them.

<margin>
2nd Misunderstanding.
</margin>

2. Suppose it is true that these stirrings and disturbances in your heart did not come from Satan’s injection, but from your own heart, which is like a sea that casts up nothing but mud and slime. Suppose your heart was like a cage for an unclean bird, and a cave for every unclean beast to live in; suppose your heart was like the stirring of an anthill <note>original: "nyshoop," likely a variant of "mierhoop" (anthill) or "mishoop" (manure pile); the author compares the agitation of sin to the busy movement of an anthill and its resulting "stench."</note> that gives off a foul and evil stench. Nonetheless, if these stirrings are not accompanied by a voluntary consent, but are resisted and opposed, these sins shall never condemn you. If the heart does not perform them with pleasure, it is no proof that you are unmortified, but rather proof of the opposite. God will never condemn you for that which makes you complain, be humble, and resist sin. You might die from

<column-break/>

running away from him, or from not fighting with the Devil, but you shall never die while fighting him.

3. Take this for an answer: that the oppositions and workings of corruption in your heart are not always proof that the corruptions have more strength and life in you than before, but rather that you shall soon receive more light and discovery than previously. When Paul’s commandment came (he says), then sin became alive again. Then he saw sin to have a greater power in his heart—not that he now had *more* sin than before, but because he now *saw through* it, which he did not do before. A godly person in whom a work of conversion has newly been wrought, because he has a spiritual insight into his own heart, nonetheless sees in the beginning great and terrible evils. For this is the proof of a true Christian: that he notices inward and secret wickednesses and small sins. Many people, long after their conversion, see more workings of sin in their hearts than they discovered before their first conversion. Now, such people do not have an *increase* of sin, but a *revelation* and *lighting*. Just as on a dark day, although the air may be very full of dust and small fibers <note>original: "veeseltjens," referring to dust motes visible in light.</note>, yet they can hardly be distinguished; but if the sun shines, then you can see them clearly. They were there even when the sun did not shine, although you could not recognize them. This is a third answer: the stirrings and uprisings of sins in the heart come not only from the increase and strength of life in sin, but from the rising light that God gives in the soul.

4. The stirrings of sins in the heart are not always proof that corruptions are unmortified, but rather that the conscience has become more sensitive. Suppose one of you had a cut finger; anything touching it disturbs you. But before it was cut, you could strike your finger against something without concern; it would never hurt or disturb you. Now, this is no proof that your finger was worse before the injury than now, even though you feel the pain; it is just that you are more sensitive to the touch. So it is in this case: your conscience being now enlightened, you have a greater understanding and feeling regarding the burden of sin than before.

5. You are not to consider yourself unmortified because of the stirrings of corruptions now and then, caused by unusual and powerful temptations in your soul. Although a corruption sometimes falls upon you and you resist it, you are not to judge yourself by this regarding the state of mortification. Instead, you are to judge by the constant and habitual deceitfulness of your heart. Is it ordinary with your heart to be like a cage of an unclean bird, or like a sea constantly throwing up mud and slime? While it is so, you have cause to fear that sin in you is still unmortified. Just as you can only judge the depth of a river by its ordinary flow, and not by a flood, you cannot judge the mortification of your corruptions by some unusual stirring of sin in your soul after powerful attacks, but by the ordinary disposition of your heart.

6. Take this for your comfort, that...

# Mortification and Sincerity.

<margin>3rd Misunderstanding.</margin>
...internal movements and workings of sin in your soul, in some cases, are more a proof of departing from sin than that you are departing from mortification. And I will show this in three cases, if you will follow along with your thoughts for a moment.

<margin>1st Case.</margin>
1. In case the working of sin makes you more watchful against all occasions of sin, and against the first movements of it in your heart: just as a lustful eye might be caught in the glow of desire, so a watchful eye is a powerful proof of a mortified heart.

<margin>2nd Case.</margin>
2. In case the rising up toward sin moves you to humility, and to holy resolutions against those sins, and to strong petitioning to God that He would subdue them within you. Such a state of heart is more a proof of strong grace than of the strength of sin.

<margin>3rd Case.</margin>
3. In case that, after such powerful movements and uprisings of sin in the soul, the corruptions <note>verdorventheden: a theological term for the innate sinful tendencies of human nature</note> daily grow weaker and weaker. It may be a movement toward lusts or pride, or passion, very great and unreasonable in your heart, against which you pray strongly and yet cannot seem to protect yourself; but if you root them out and kill them a bit at a time, taking away their power and making them daily weaker and softer, you have nothing to fear that your sins are unmortified. I have told you before that the movement of sins in some people is like a dying person thrashing about; when he is in the heaviest and strongest attack of sickness, he will stir and move so much that two or three strong men are barely able to hold him in his bed. Now, this does not come from the strength of the man, but from his sickness; for as soon as this is over, the man is so faint that there seems to be no life left in him, and he is unable to move himself. So it is also when sin in your soul is like a fever in a person, such that no warnings, rebukes, or teachings could keep him from sin and from running after the fulfillment of his lusts and desires of the heart; yet if you find that this powerful movement toward sin has ultimately made your corruptions soft and weak, you have cause to thank God that He has begun the work of mortification in you, and has only allowed Satan to make a noise.

<margin>7th Misunderstanding.</margin>
7. Take this for your comfort: that the movements of sin in your heart may be used by God as means to complete the mortification of sins in you. If sins did not move but were still and quiet, you would grow careless in them and take no knowledge of the sinfulness of your heart; but now that their stinking vapors and evil movements rise up in your heart, this will be a powerful means to kill and subdue them and to pull out the root of this corrupt tree. And thus I have finished with these seven particular points of comfort for those who complain in their hearts that they are unmortified because of the uprisings and movements of sins they feel.

<margin>4th Misunderstanding.</margin>
Now I move on to the second misunderstanding, which makes a godly soul fear that his heart is unmortified, and it is this:

<margin>5th Misunderstanding.</margin>
<margin>8th Misunderstanding.</margin>
<margin>2nd Misunderstanding.</margin>
<margin>6th Misunderstanding.</margin>
2. "Oh," say the pious, "I have not only the movements of sin in my heart (may the Lord show mercy to my soul), but I am in a thousand times worse state than before; for I find that I have prayed, again and again, against all my particular

<column-break/>

corruptions, and yet, notwithstanding all my prayers, desires, and supplications, every sin has gained the upper hand in me, rules over me, and all my sins remain unmortified." I think I hear such accounts coming from a godly soul. "Oh, woe is me! I have offered many prayers, and renewed many good resolutions of my heart, seeking to keep it from sin, and yet I cannot; sin overcomes me, I am not powerful enough to get above it; and therefore this makes me fear whether I have the power of mortifying grace or not."

<margin>Answer</margin>
**Answer:** Beloved, your state is sorrowful, yet I have words to say to you here.

First: You who make this complaint, it may be that regarding the evils you complain of, you cannot keep yourself from them; it may be that they are great and heavy wickednesses, but they are internal and accompanied by sorrow; if so, then you have little reason for jealousy <note>original: "jaloesie," here meaning suspicion or anxious doubt regarding one's spiritual state</note> that your corruptions are unmortified. However, if the sins you bewail are great and "crying" sins <note>crying sins: a reference to sins like those of Sodom or the blood of Abel that "cry out" to God for justice; here used for blatant, outward sins</note>, you have cause to fear. But if they are only internal and weak corruptions—such as idle thoughts, unsettled emotions, spiritual pride, vainglory, and the like—you may offer a thousand prayers against such things and yet not root out the root entirely.

Second: Granted that the corruptions are great, against which you intended to pray, and you cannot subdue them; nevertheless, turn this to your comfort: that this is as much as God requires of you—that you set yourself against them and labor to resist them. And if you do this duty, even though you are overcome, God will not hold you guilty. In this case, it is just as it was in the Law, where God made a rule concerning a <margin>Answer</margin> betrothed young woman found in a field, where a man forced her and lay with her; in that case, only the man who lay with her shall die, etc. <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 22:25-27, where the woman is considered innocent because she cried out for help and no one was there to save her</note>. Beloved, it is likewise in this case; the Devil may commit a spiritual violation upon you, and you may give yourself over to him during an assault; but nevertheless, if before and after committing the sin, you bewail and hate it, and set yourself against it, the Lord will lay the sin on Satan’s shoulder, and demand it of him and not of you.

Third: You who complain that your corruptions are unmortified, having often prayed against them and yet they are not subdued: take this for your comfort—that the praying and rising up against sin is an infallible proof that they are dying, even though they are not yet entirely dead. Were the corruptions alive and healthy, the heart would not weaken your prayers; rather, the sins would make your prayers grow faint. You who constantly pray against sin—it is an infallible proof they are dying, even though they are not yet dead. Just like some birds, which seem to show more strength after their head is cut off than they did before—which is nonetheless a powerful proof that they are dying, though not yet dead—so also, when you find such violent movements and stirrings of sins in you despite so many prayers against them, you may be certain that your corruptions are dying, even though they are not yet entirely mortified.

Fourth: Note this for your comfort, that...

It is a rule among the theologians <note>Godt geleerden: literally "God-learned," referring to scholars of divinity or pastors</note> that all

3. There is yet another misunderstanding into which a

<margin>Answer.</margin>
Answer: For you who make this complaint, I have only
three or four words of comfort to say.
1. You must know that the entire work of
grace and sanctification <note>heylighmakinge: the lifelong process of becoming more holy</note> is not done all at
once. Truly, you are justified once and
chosen once, but you are not made holy all at once.
You must not expect that the
work of sanctification will be completed
in a moment; but just as children reach their
manly years not at once,
but by degrees: so the work of sanctification happens periodically and by degrees.

2. Take this for your comfort: that there may
be a fainting and weakening of common
gifts, and yet the living operation and the
true saving faith remain in the soul. Common
gifts and graces can die while
true grace is still powerful in the soul. It
may be that you have little skill
in your tongue to speak, and yet a strong
memory, etc., better in your old than in your young days. These things may die and perish even while you live and grow powerfully in grace in
your soul.

Just as a theologian observes that a
Music Master can play better on instruments
in his youth and sing much more agreeably,
with more delight, than when he
has grown old; yet he has more understanding and judgment in his art than before. So
it can be that you lose the "loose flowers of
grace" <note>This likely refers to the outward, emotional, or performative aspects of early faith</note> and yet grow more in understanding,
judgment, and experience, etc. Now then, to build upon that.

3. You who complain and fear that your corruptions are not killed because grace
is not so living and active in you: know this

<column-break/>

for your comfort: that God usually gives more
at a person’s first conversion than
afterward, because He wants to
lead the person to religion and draw them up into the exercise of godliness. The transition of a person from the state of nature
to the state of grace is a remarkable change;
the change within a godly person is only
step-by-step, and therefore less perceptible. New
conditions and new things move us more,
just as it is with a married couple:
a greater bond grows between them by degrees,
but they nonetheless love each other continually. We
read in Acts 3:8 that when the lame man was first healed,
he leaped up praising God; yet
he did not do so afterward. So in our first
conversion we are more powerful and more sensible in
our movements, and yet afterward we are stronger (like
the lame man in his walking) in grace.

### ROMANS VIII, 13.

-> ... But if you through the Spirit <-
-> kill the deeds of the body, you shall <-

I shall now deal with the misunderstandings
on the other hand: those
who think that their corruptions are killed when they are not. The heart
of man is deceitful above
all things, a bundle of deceit, and man himself is a proud creature, capable
of holding a high opinion of himself. And the
grounds of this misunderstanding are three among the godless, who falsely imagine that their corruptions are killed. Namely:

1. Because they find an opposition against
sin, they therefore conclude that sin is
killed in them.

2. Because they find within themselves the power of
rational grace. And

3. Because they leave and forsake some sins: it may be that he was an adulterer in
former times and now is not, or a swearer
or a drunkard, etc., in times past, but now
none of these. I shall spend two hours on this answer
and show the groundless looseness
of these foundations and the strength of the killing work in their hearts; to begin with
the first.

1. Because they find in themselves some opposition against certain sins, they therefore conclude they have the killing work in their hearts. I Answer: A resistance to sin
may arise from the light in a natural
conscience, which makes a person feel
what sin is or is not. The godless have a law within them by which they
oppose some sins, such as impurity and drunkenness,
etc., and their consciences may accuse them
when they do evil and excuse them when they do well;
but this is only in general. I shall
speak a bit more specifically, and I pray you lend
me your thoughts for a moment, for I do
not think that there is any man or woman among us so wicked or godless that they have not
sometimes resisted some corruptions and sinful movements in their hearts. Now
I shall show you eight specific cases wherein
you can resist corruptions and yet remain unmortified; as one may resist through:
1. Jesting. 2. Parsimony. 3. Partisanship.
4. Hypocrisy. 5. Slavishness. 6. Compelled...

-># Mortification and Sincerity.<-

<margin>5th Sermon.</margin>
<margin>1. Jesting.</margin>
1. One may oppose the corruption of **Jesting**. <note>original: "Jockinge" — here meaning to spar or play-fight without intent to kill</note> He may act like **Fencers**; to hit one, they threaten another, yet they soon deliver a deadly wound. Though they may seem to hack and hew at another, they hardly draw blood, for what they do is only in jest. So, although a godless person opposes sin, nonetheless he does not wish to be wounded or to hurt his sins. But a mortified person <note>gedoot mensche: literally a "deadened person," one who has "killed" their sinful nature through grace</note> opposes sin and wishes to bring it under subjection, not like a fencer, but as a soldier against his deadly enemy, knowing he must either kill or be killed. Thus a godly person stands against sin, the deadly enemy of his soul; he knows that he now contends for his salvation. Truly, mark this: I believe there is no one among us who does not now and then oppose sin; but if you do it only in **Jesting**, this opposition is worth nothing.

<margin>2. Sparingly.</margin>
2. In a similar case, you do it **Sparingly**. It may be that some of you resist corruptions because you see sin to be sin, and then labor against it; but you do it **Sparingly**; you do not wish to root out the sin entirely. You deal with it as **David** dealt with **Absalom** (he said), *deal gently with the young man Absalom*; so you deal gently with your sins and oppose them sparingly. But now, a mortified person fights his lusts with a holy violence and wishes to show no mercy to sin, nor give any quarter to his lusts; his sins will not spare him, and therefore he will not spare them either.

<margin>Three grounds of misunderstanding in an unmortified heart.</margin>
<margin>3. Partiality.</margin>
3. You have an unmortified heart if you oppose sin with **Partiality**, resisting some sins while sparing others. You love your desires; it may be that you are an enemy of **Drunkenness**, and yet take pleasure in other sins, such as **false weights and measures**, or secret deception in your shop and trade. It may be that you resist adultery and impurity, and yet feed other lusts in your bosom. But mortification is like the death of the body, which seizes all the living parts of the body. So, if you do not oppose all sins, you are a stranger to mortification. You deal with your sins as **Saul** did with the **Amalekites**; although he killed them, he nonetheless spared **Agag** their King, and the best of the Sheep and Cattle, whereas he should have destroyed them all. So you, though you oppose some sins, nonetheless let others lodge in your hearts; and just as Saul lost his Kingdom through this partiality, so shall you—through the pleasure you take in certain sins—lose your souls and, consequently, the Kingdom of Heaven.

<margin>1st Ground of misunderstanding.</margin>
<margin>4. Hypocritically.</margin>
4. If you oppose sin **Hypocritically**, or upon false reasons and grounds. This is when a person opposes sins not because they hinder him *in* what is good, but because they hinder him *from* what is good. <note>The author distinguishes between hating sin because it ruins the soul's purity ("in" the good) versus hating it only because it stops one from getting rewards ("from" the good).</note> He never opposes sin because this or that lust prevents him in prayer or prevents him in holy duties—such as hearing and reading God's word, etc.—but because it prevents him from the good, because it keeps him from Heaven, Blessedness, and glory; it prevents him from hoping for or expecting these goods. He does not oppose sin because it strives against the glory of God, but because it blocks and

<column-break/>

hinders his expectations; so that a person may oppose sin with these feelings and yet not be dead to sin.

<margin>5. Slavishness.</margin>
5. If you oppose sin **Slavishly**, fearing hell and the coming wrath more [than God]. You would not oppose sins if you did not know that hell and eternal punishment would follow afterward. A person opposes his sins **Slavishly** when he more fears the punishments of God, hating them because sin has a *damning* power, and not because it has a *defiling* power—because sin is against a local, avenging justice of God, not because it is against the holiness and purity of God. He opposes it because there is a hell *for* sin, but not because there is a hell *in* sin. But a godly person hates sin even if there were no Devil in hell, nor any punishment for it; he sees a hell in the sin itself, worse than hell itself.

<margin>6. Constrained.</margin>
5. <note>The original text repeats "5" here, though the margin correctly identifies this as the 6th point.</note> If you oppose sin **Constrainedly**; people oppose the corruptions of their hearts, but it is because they have a terrifying and gnawing conscience within them. They have such light in their natural conscience that they cannot give themselves over to sin without some resistance; they seek to overwhelm their gnawing conscience and lull it to sleep so much that it does not perform its work, so that they might commit sins with pleasure. Such resistance is no proof of mortification at all.

<margin>7. Sluggishly.</margin>
7. If you oppose corruptions **Sluggishly** and faintly. It may be that you have a purpose to resist corruptions at first, but afterward grow sluggish and weak. Previously you could not endure drunkenness and impurity, but now you are more inclined to those sins. These people are in the struggle against sin like the **French** in battle, of whom it is told that no people in the world are so bold in the attack; but if they are strongly parried by their enemies, then their courage fails, and they retreat very fearfully. So it may be that some among you have a great resolution against sin at first, but when the Devil comes upon you with a violent fury, then you are weak and soft in battling sin—just as **Balaam** did in Numbers 22:13, 18. When **Balak** sent for **Balaam** to curse Israel, he first refused to go (verse 13). He said to the princes of Balak, "Go to your land; for the Lord refuses to let me go with you." And again in the 18th verse he says, "If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the word of the Lord my God, to do less or more." Truly, you would think then that Balaam was a very good man; but nonetheless, when the King sent for him a third time, then he wanted to go. But you will say, God commanded him to go, and therefore he is to be excused (verse 20): "God came to Balaam at night, and said to him, 'If the men come to call you, rise up, and go with them.'" And yet, when Balaam rode away in the morning, God wanted to kill him because he went. Now, how can this be? Can God punish a man for doing what He commands?

I Answer 1. God commanded him to go on the condition: "If the men come to call you, rise up, go with them," but we never read that the men called him; and
