### 2.
God commanded him to go—just as you might command a child to do something, even though the child still has and intends to follow their own desire—saying, "Do as you wish, follow your own mind, and see what comes of it." So God said to **Balaam**, <note>A biblical prophet who was tempted by gold to curse Israel; see Numbers 22.</note> if you certainly wish to go, and love the lure of money, and wish to walk the paths of unrighteousness, see what will come of it.

### 3.
God commanded him to go, not to curse, but to bless Israel. Now the text says that God’s anger was kindled because he went. God commanded him to bless Israel, but he went with the intention to curse them, and that was the reason why God was angry with him.

So it may be that some of you, like **Balaam**, refuse to satisfy your lusts once or twice; yet if you follow them the third time—even though you resisted the sin at first, but eventually carried it out—it is a sign that your heart is not yet deadened to sin.

<margin>8. Civically.</margin>
**8.** If you oppose sins **Civically**. My meaning is this: a person may oppose sin in two ways.

1. Because of the outward punishment that follows the sin, rather than because of the spiritual and final judgment.

So did **Abimelech** in Genesis 20, when he was in danger of misusing **Sarah**, **Abraham’s** wife; yet when he knew she was Abraham’s wife, he let her go and said to Abraham: "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought a great sin upon me and my kingdom?" A godless person can oppose sin because it brings evil upon his body, his house, or his kingdom, but not because the sin is a dishonor to God. A person opposes sin **civically** when he does it mostly out of fleshly considerations.

2. When a person opposes one sin only to allow another sin to harbor within him with less suspicion. It may be that he takes no pleasure in **Drunkenness**, only to cover another sin with that outward restraint. In this way, you seek to please the "Civic Government" <note>This refers to social standards or legal behavior.</note> while still damning your own soul. And so I have dealt with these eight particular things; but if you go no further in resisting your lusts, you cannot conclude that the work of mortification is in your hearts.

And this is enough regarding the basis of the first misunderstanding that the godless have in resisting their corruptions.

<margin>2. Basis of misunderstanding.</margin>
**2.** But others say, "Oh! I do not only oppose my corruptions, but (thanks be to God) I keep myself from them so that they do not break out into action in my life and conduct; therefore, I hope my heart is deadened to sin, and all is well with me, since I have the power and ability to withstand my corruptions."

<margin>Answer.</margin>
**Answer.** I must confess that this is a good step on the path to Heaven, when a person resists his lusts and does not come to the act. But nonetheless, I have three things to say to you, so that you may not take up a misunderstanding here.

1. A person can resist sins out of the principles and drives of nature; the power of nature can keep him from committing certain sins. We read of **Socrates** <note>The famous Greek philosopher, often cited in this era as an example of "natural virtue" without Christian grace.</note> that he boasted of being naturally hot-tempered, and yet he never committed any foul desire with his eye or body, despite being only a heathen.

<column-break/>

**Cato** <note>likely Cato the Younger, a Roman statesman known for his strict morality.</note> was so averse to **Drunkenness** that he never drank more than his custom; they did this because of their nature. Truly, such people surpass many Christians.

2. Lusts and desires can be resisted through the strength of a religious upbringing and good examples; we read in 2 Kings 12:2 of **Joash**: "And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the Lord all his days, in which **Jehoiada** the priest instructed him." While Jehoiada lived, Joash did what was right in the sight of the Lord; but when the priest was dead, Joash became godless. He resisted sin as long as he lived under the oversight of this good man, but afterward, the sins broke out. So it may be that while you are under masters and overseers who keep a sharp eye on you, you resist sin while you serve; but when you become your own master, go where you wish, and do what pleases you, then you run out into many sins which you now resist through upbringing, but not through mortification.

3. A person can resist his lusts and keep himself from some sins because of his troubled and terrified **conscience**. His conscience tells him there is a Hell prepared for him if he takes such a course or commits such and such sins; he feels the flickers of the hellish fire in his face, so that he does not dare commit such sins.

It is like a dog that has a bone before him and his master’s stick over him; if he takes up that bone, his master’s stick makes him lay it down. The dog fears his master’s punishment; otherwise, he would take it. So it is with the godless; were there not a gnawing and terror in his conscience that makes him troubled and afraid, he would make no effort to stop any sin or godlessness. Such a resistance as this in no way proves that your sins are deadened. And here I will further show you that there can be a resistance to sin in these particular cases, and yet the sins will not be killed thereby.

1. If you resist sin as a pack upon you, not willingly, but as a burden against your will. It may be that through sickness or weakness of the body, you cannot commit certain sins, and this is a burden to you. If it be so, you truly have an unmortified heart.

But a godly person resists sin out of willingness; he considers it his happiness and a great grace to have resisted his sins. Therefore, examine your own heart: if it is a burden to your soul that you cannot follow sin—in drunkenness, satisfying your lusts, and running out into them in all ways—believe me when I say you have no mortifying grace in your heart.

2. In the event that you resist sin only to fall into it more earnestly later, and to commit it more than before. It may be that through your weakness you resist fornication, drunkenness, or Sabbath-breaking, etc., because you are sick or unable to do them; but now, in this case, if you later run to the same sin, it is a sign that your heart is unmortified, and that you are near the door of damnation and rejection.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "misunderstandings" regarding the mortification of sin. The previous page discussed opposing sin "civically" (for social reasons or fear of punishment); this page focuses on the limitations of "natural light" or reason and the false security of simply ceasing a sinful action without a change of heart.</meta>

# Mortification and Sincerity.

As I have told you before: you may resist some great sins and guard yourself against them through the **light of nature** <note>The "light of nature" refers to human reason and innate conscience, which even those without Christian faith possess.</note> within you, such as **Socrates** and **Cato**, who were heathens; and therefore, as long as you do not resist inward and "bosom" sins <note>Personal, cherished, or secret sins.</note> as much as public wickednesses, you cannot conclude that you have the power of **mortification** <term>mortification: the spiritual practice of "killing off" or subduing sinful desires through the Holy Spirit</term> in your heart. The light of nature teaches and convinces a person that he must not lie, steal, or swear, nor be a drunkard, an unclean person, or the like; but although a godless man guards himself from "crying sins" <note>Sins so blatant they "cry out" for judgment.</note>, he cannot refrain from small ones, because he does not consider them to be sins. They think that inward evils are no evils at all. And therefore we read of **Aristotle**, that he calls many things virtues which the Scripture says are faults. The Heathens considered **jesting** to be a virtue, which nevertheless **Paul** places among sins: *let jesting not even be named among you.* <note>See Ephesians 5:4. Original: "Jockerije."</note>

So **Aristotle** regards the **magnanimity** <note>Aristotle’s "great-souled man" (megalopsychos) was one who rightly believed himself worthy of great things; the author argues this contradicts Christian humility.</note> of a man as an honor, whereby he deems himself worthy of the greatest and most honorable places in the world; but **Paul** calls this **pride of heart**, when a person imagines himself to be high and noble in himself. I relate these things to you only in passing, so that you may see that the light of nature is but a partial covering for many sins, especially when they are small and inward; you may refrain from public and known sins and yet not have the power of grace in your hearts; mortification looks primarily at the inward and secret sins, which a person goes against as much as against great wickednesses.

And thus I have finished handling the first two grounds of misunderstanding in the godless, whereby they think their corruptions are mortified when in fact they are not.

### ROM. VIII. 13.

> .... But if you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live. <note>original: "Maer indien ghy door den Geeft de werckingen des lichaems doodet, soo sult ghy leven."</note>

<margin>
6th Sermon.
3rd Ground of misunderstanding.
</margin>
Now I come to the **third premise** and ground of misunderstanding, which deceitfully makes people think their sins are mortified when they are not, and it is this: "I set myself" (says he) "not only against corruptions, and oppose the outward actions of sin, but I am at rest and have left my sins. I was a person" (it is true) "in former times very unchaste, but now I am pure. I have previously been a drunkard, but now I am sober, etc. And therefore I hope that my corruptions are mortified within me."

<margin>Answer.</margin>
**Answer:** I confess it is a very good conclusion that you make; and I may say to you what **Christ** said to the Lawyer: *You are not far from the Kingdom of Heaven;* but nevertheless let me tell you, if you go no further and do no more, you shall never come to that place; and therefore, so that you may not deceive yourself, I shall show you in some particular things that a person may leave some sins and yet be a stranger to mortification. Note these three cases.

<margin>1st Case.</margin>
**1.** If you leave the sin you were inclined toward from an **untrue principle**, and these are fourfold.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
**First.** Many people forsake sin because the strength and ability to carry out the sin has forsaken them; this is from an evil principle. For example, when a man has spent his previous time in impurity and pleasurable lusts with women, but now, when he has become old and sickly, he stops; truly this is no mortifying grace, but he forsakes the sin because his body is unfit and the strength of his spirits has departed, so that he can no longer commit certain sins.

And it may be that another person, who was strongly inclined to drunkenness in former times, now—now that his means are exhausted and his money falls short—lacks the ability to follow his previous walk, and therefore stops doing so. Let it be whatever sin it will, if you leave it from such principles, you are a stranger to mortification.

**2.** If you leave the sin because you perceive no opportunity for the committed sins; you have neither the occasion, nor the certainty, nor the fitness to commit such sins; you cannot do what you want to do; you cannot walk in those ways in which you have a desire to walk. This is another wrong principle for ceasing sin.

**3.** In the event you leave the sin because the movements and enticements toward such sins leave you. Beloved, the **Devil** does not always take the same paths to attack a person; one day he seeks to lead you away to evil lusts, and tomorrow to drunkenness; the Devil does not always play upon one and the same string to entice you. Now, it may be that you have left some sins, but it may be that the enticements of the Devil toward these have ceased, and then it is not thanks-worthy; for you can leave sin on this principle and yet be a stranger to mortification. Some people have given themselves to unchastity and impurity in their youth, and afterwards, in their middle age, the Devil suspended his temptations for a while; they then also have a loathing for the same sin; they cannot endure an evil sight or any unchaste action; and yet afterwards, through the renewed temptation of **Satan**, they run back into the same sin with more pleasure than before. The Devil may leave you, and you may leave the working of sin for a time, and yet afterwards, upon the seduction of the flesh, fall back into the same sin.

**Fourthly.** A person may leave sin on this ground: because he knows that if he does not, the disturbances of **conscience** will never leave him. He knows that if he quietly continues in his swearing, lying, cheating, and evils in his shop; **Sabbath-breaking**—writing a sermon he hears one day in his book, and writing the same in the **Devil's book** <note>The "Devil's book" is a metaphorical ledger of sins or hypocritical behavior throughout the week.</note> the whole week thereafter—if he quietly follows the fulfillment of his lusts, he knows that his conscience will accuse him and more and more terrify him; and therefore he wants to resist and bridle his corruptions for a while, until his conscience is muzzled and satisfied. And therefore it is very remarkable that the Scripture compares a "mortified" man <note>Meaning one who only appears mortified but is not truly changed.</note> to a **dog that returns to its vomit.** 2 Pet. 2, 20, 22. The Apostle, speaking of some who had gone so far in the way of Christianity that they *escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord Jesus*...

# The True Doctrine of Mortification

...in Christ, and being entangled in them again, they are overcome by them. As the **Scripture** <note>original: "de Text" - likely referring to 2 Peter 2:22.</note> says, it has happened to them according to the true proverb: *the dog has returned to his own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire.* What is the meaning of this? There is much of the Divine in this passage. A person who has once left his sinful course, yet later follows it again, is here compared to a dog returning to its vomit and a sow wallowing in the mud. Now, you know that a dog, when he has a painful or bad stomach (to which he is often subject), spits and vomits; so a godless person, when his conscience disturbs and accuses him, leaves and forsakes his sin. But as the dog is delivered from his pain, he returns to his vomit; so a godless person, when his conscience is quiet and the terror is over, returns to his old sins and commits them with greater delight and pleasure than ever before.

And thus you have seen in four particular things how you can leave sin on bad grounds and principles, and yet still be strangers to **mortification** <term>mortification: from the Latin 'mortificatio', meaning the spiritual practice of "killing off" or subduing sinful desires through the power of the Holy Spirit.</term>.

<margin>2nd Case.</margin> 2. If you leave your corruptions in a wrong manner (which happens in 6 ways), you are strangers to mortification:

1. You leave sin in a wrong way when you forsake one sin and follow another. I have read of one who was very prone to **drunkenness**, and yet through reading **Plato's** <note>Plato (c. 427–347 BC). His moral philosophy was often admired by early modern Christians but considered insufficient for true salvation.</note> lessons—which speak much against this sin—he was held back from drink; but nevertheless, he fell into other sins worse than that. So if you forsake one sin and commit another, this is no mortification; because, as I have told you before, such is a complete destruction of the **body of sin** <note>A biblical concept (Romans 6:6) describing the entire system of human fallen nature as a single "body" that must be destroyed.</note>.

A person may give himself to the sin of **unchastity** in his youth, and when he has become old, to the sin of **worldliness**; again, at times he may be wasteful, at another time miserly and greedy. Sometimes guilty of hypocrisy, then falling into apostasy and open godlessness. The **Naturalists** <note>Writers of natural history or emblem books who used animal behavior to illustrate moral points.</note> tell us that a serpent sheds its skin every year, but nonetheless, although it has no other in its place, it remains a serpent. So it may be that some of you shake off old sins, but only so that you make room for others; this is merely "exchanging" sin and not "killing" it. The exchange of a sin is not its subduing. The sin to which you were previously very inclined may now sleep while others live and work powerfully in your heart. This changing of your sins falls far short of mortification.

2. A person may be said to leave his sin in a wrong manner when he only desists from the great *acts* of sin, but does not leave the inward longing and desire of his soul for that sin. **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). In his *Confessions*, he famously describes his long struggle with lust before his conversion.</note> at one time left the sin of fornication, but nevertheless he confessed that he had a longing in his soul for that same sin. If you do not drive out the desire of your soul for sin, you never truly leave it; for example, a man may leave the outward act of uncleanness, and yet harbor within himself adulterous thoughts, lecherous eyes and words, and unchaste gestures; his heart can be like the **Devil's anvil**, upon which he forges false and wicked thoughts of god-

<column-break/>

-lessness; and therefore this is no mortification. For this [true mortification] makes you leave not only the outward working of sin, but likewise the hidden delight and pleasure in that sin; and this is a wrong way of leaving sin.

3. Then a man leaves sin wrongly when he only leaves public, outward, and "crying" <note>Sins so blatant they were said to "cry out" to heaven for justice.</note> sins, and yet entangles himself in some inward and secret evils. This is only leaving sin halfway. We read of many **Heathens** who kept themselves from great crimes—such as **Socrates**, **Cato**, and **Aristotle**, as we have related before—while they, through the **light of nature** <note>Innate human reason and conscience, as opposed to divine revelation.</note>, shunned great sins as evil; yet they did not regard the small and secret ones.

4. A person leaves his sins in a wrong way when he does so **unwillingly**, as when he leaves sin like sailors leave their goods in a time of storm; the Captain says that if they want to keep their lives, they must leave their goods, and therefore they throw them away, loving their lives more than their goods. So also when the godless see the fire of hell and the trembling pit before them into which they must go, then they forsake and leave their sins—though unwillingly.

5. Then a man leaves his sins in a wrong way when he does it with a reservation and a keeping of the mind to commit the sin again at another time. It may be that he reasons with himself thus: "I have great pleasure in drunkenness and wasting goods, but now I am sick and weak and not fit to do such things; but if I become well again, I will follow my old course and go to my good companions." And others may think to themselves: "I have now left the sin of unchastity through the sickness of my body, being unfit to practice it; but if I recover, I want that pleasure again." Now, when a person leaves his sins in this manner, his sins will break out again in his soul like powerful water, with more power and strength than in times past.

6. A person forsakes his sins in a wrong way when he leaves them without any **humility or sorrow**. There is an observation made by **Mr. Bolton** <note>Robert Bolton (1572–1631), a famous English Puritan scholar and preacher known for his works on the "comfort of afflicted consciences."</note>, who had been with someone who (as he thought) lay on his deathbed, very inclined to wine and women, a great drunkard, and a very unchaste person. Mr. Bolton asked him, as he lay on the bed, whether he had any hope of Heaven or not. "I confess it," he said, "it is true, I have been a drunkard, but not now; also an adulterer, but not now." But Mr. Bolton, noticing no humility or sorrow in him over his past sins, asked him again: if God gave him health again, would he not be the same man he was before? He answered, "No, not for all the world." It pleased God to heal this man shortly after, and a few months later he returned to his old sins and was worse than ever before.

It may be that many of you leave off swearing and lying; but have you done so with humility? Have you wept quietly over them and...

<meta>This page continues the author's examination of "mortification"—the spiritual practice of killing off sinful desires. Having previously discussed leaving sin due to the "light of nature" or temporary fear, the author now addresses the "wrong ends" or motivations for forsaking sin, contrasting them with the sincere motivations of a true believer.</meta>

# Mortification and Sincerity

<margin>3rd Case.</margin>
...mourning? If it is not so with you, you have no assurance in your heart that you are a mortified man or woman.

And thus I have finished with the second particular instance: when you leave sin from a wrong principle and in a wrong manner.

3. The leaving of sin is no proof of mortifying grace in your heart if you leave sin in a wrong way; and herein I must probe your bosoms a bit more closely. There are 6 wrong ends <note>Here, "ends" means goals or motivations.</note> why a person may leave their sins and yet remain a stranger to mortifying grace.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
1. A person may leave their sins so that the peace of their conscience will not leave them. He knows that as long as he lives in sin, the peace of conscience will depart; therefore, in order not to break his own peace, he wishes to leave his sins, even though he breaks God’s heart (if I may speak so) through his sins. When a person forsakes his sins only so that the peace of his conscience remains, this is a wrong end.

2. When a person leaves sin only to escape temporal punishment, not because God hates the sin, but because he hates the punishment itself. This is when sin is forsaken not because it has a defiling power, but because it is painful; not because it is hateful, but because it is harmful. Just as some people refrain from outward deeds, not because they conflict with the law, but because of the resulting punishment. So they do not leave sin because God hates it, but because He punishes it; this is another wrong end for the leaving of sin.

3. When a person leaves sin because it stains his honor and reputation among men, and not because he dishonors God thereby; because he brings mockery and blame upon his name and credit, and not because he violates the honor and glory of God.

4. When a person leaves sin so that the torments of hell should not follow him; he knows, if he continues in his godlessness, that after sin the torments of hell will come upon him. A godless person leaves sin because there is a hell that follows sin, and not because it draws after it the vengeance of God; not because it is committed against the holiness and purity of God, and not because God has commanded him to leave it, but because there are punishments ordained by God in the world against it. Now, this is a very false and slavish end, for in this way a person merely forces himself to leave sin.

5. When a person leaves sin on this ground: so that he may harbor other sins within himself with less suspicion; as I have related this to you before.

6. When a person leaves and resists sin so that he may be considered a holy and religious person in the world. I have read of one who left his evil course, to which he was very inclined, so that one of his friends—whose heir he hoped to be—might have a good opinion of him. A person may leave great sins so that he may be considered a new person and a holy man among his neighbors, which is a shallow and self-serving end for leaving evil—seeking only that others may have good thoughts of him.

And thus in these two Sermons, I have dealt with the misunderstandings into which many people fall regarding this great duty of **mortification** <term>mortification: the spiritual process of subduing the "flesh" or sinful nature.</term>.

<column-break/>

Now I have only a word of comfort; it may be that those particular things which I have related have been very hard on many godly and conscientious hearts, who think: "Perhaps my corruptions are not yet mortified; I have left sin from some wrong principles, or in a wrong manner, or for some false ends, even when such matters were not present." And therefore for your comfort, O you who are Sons and Daughters of God, lift up your heads with joy and gladness, if your hearts have this testimony: that you have left your sins from other grounds, and in another way—deriving from true mortification of the heart—and for other ends than the godless do.

You who can say that you have forsaken sin, not for lack of means, but through the power of sanctifying grace in your hearts, like **Joseph** <note>Referring to Genesis 39:9, where Joseph refuses temptation by asking, "How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?"</note>: You who can say, "I have forsaken my sins, not because my conscience revolts like a dog, or because the sparks of hellfire fly in my face, but for the love of Christ toward me, because Christ shed His blood and paid a precious price for my sins." I have left my sins in a right way; I have not left one just to live in another; but I want, if I can, to leave all my sins. I do not want to leave them by force or violence, for the Lord knows that never did a slave come so willingly from the **galley** <term>galley: a ship where prisoners were forced to row in miserable conditions.</term> as I came out of sin. There was never a prisoner so glad to be released from his bonds as I have been to leave my sins; there was never a beggar who so gladly shook off his filthy clothes and put on precious ones, as I have the filthy rags and tatters of sin, to be clothed with that long white robe of **Christ’s Righteousness** <note>The theological concept that a believer is justified by being "covered" by the perfect life and sacrifice of Jesus.</note>.

O you poor soul whose heart has this testimony, that it stands so with you, you are in a blessed state. And if you can say, "My heart testifies to me that I have left sin for a right end"—not because there is a curse against your lusts, but a commandment against them; if you leave them not so much because they conflict with the Justice of God, but against the holiness and purity of God; not because there is a hell *against* sin, but because there is a hell *in* sin; not so much because it defiles, but because it destroys nature—if it stands so with you, you may lift up your head with joy and walk in a sea of consolation, in the assurance that God has brought you into the state of mortification.

<margin>Use for comfort.</margin>

And thus I have shown you in these six Sermons many weighty things regarding this great doctrine of mortification. In the next place, I shall give you some general means and instructions on how you may obtain this duty of mortification—not specifically how you shall kill every sin (for that would be too tedious a work), but only in general how you may kill any lusts; and then I shall treat some other cases of conscience, such as whether a person may fall into sin after he is mortified or not, and several others.

# The True Doctrine of

<margin>
7th Sermon.
</margin>

<margin>
The petition of doubting Christians.
</margin>

->ROMANS 8:13<-

> ... But if you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.

I shall now explain only one question concerning this doctrine of mortification <note>In 17th-century theology, 'mortification' refers to the spiritual practice of "killing off" or subduing sinful desires through the power of the Holy Spirit.</note>, namely: I think I hear a poor, dejected soul saying (having heard all these sermons preached on this text), "I confess that everything you have said or spoken regarding this duty of mortification is but a looking-glass <note>A mirror.</note> to make me see into my own heart, by which I know that my heart is not yet dead to sin, and that I have many great lusts and corruptions <note>Innate sinful tendencies or flaws.</note> not yet brought under subjection within me; and therefore, I would dearly like to know how I might kill my sins, guard myself against them, and overcome these corruptions."

<margin>
8 General helps to kill sin.
</margin>

This, then, shall be what we treat here: namely, to point out the helps by which you may promote the mortification and subjection of your corruptions. I shall treat this not in particular, but in general, and give you seven or eight helps to guard you from sin, of whatever kind it may be.

<margin>
1st Help.
</margin>

1. The first means you shall use is this: be very diligent to shun and flee all opportunities for sin to which you are most inclined. When a man is sick, even though he has a desire and pleasure in eating, the doctor will forbid him from eating much. For if he does not resist that which feeds and increases his sickness, he can expect no healing. So it is here: you must shun all those things that might arise and give opportunity to your lusts. You must take heed of the wandering of your eyes as much as you would avoid bloodshed; if you do not wish to fall, you must shun all inducements to evil, as the Apostle says in the letter of Jude, verse 23: *Hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.*

There is a remarkable passage to this purpose in Numbers 6:3–4, where the Lord makes a law that the Nazirites <note>A group of Israelites consecrated to God who took special vows of abstinence.</note> must drink no wine or strong drink. The Lord forbids them even from eating the seeds: they were not only forbidden from drinking wine or strong drink, but even from eating the seeds or the skins. This was so they might have no opportunity to come near the grapevines; they had to avoid all opportunities for sin. In the same way, the people of God must not only be careful not to commit sin, but also to shun all opportunities and enticements toward it.

I know that it was Pharaoh’s instigation against Moses (when he and the children of Israel were to leave Egypt) that he should leave the children and servants there; but when Moses was resolved to go and take them with him, Pharaoh wanted him to leave the sheep and the cattle there. But Moses said to him, *Not a hoof shall be left behind.* For he knew that if he had left anything there, it would have been an enticement for the children of Israel to long for Egypt again. The way to the mortification of sin is to avoid all opportunities to commit the sin toward which you are being pushed.

<margin>
2nd Help.
</margin>

2. Another general means for mortification is this: the resisting of a lust or corruption at its first pressing action in

<column-break/>

the heart. If you pave the way for sin, the more power it will have over you, and the more difficulty you will have in bringing it under subjection. Therefore, smother the crocodile in its shell. It is easier to keep a man out at the gate than to drive him out once he has entered into you. You must guard your soul like a garrison and give no way to sin, but resist it at its first movement.

3. The greatest strength of your heart consists in powerful prayers to God against the corruptions that assault you, just as Paul did in 2 Corinthians 12:8. When he had a sharp thorn in his flesh, namely, a messenger <note>original: "Engel," literally angel or messenger.</note> of Satan, he says: *Concerning this thing I pleaded with the Lord three times, that it might depart from me.* And in Psalm 56:9 <note>The Dutch text cites verse 10, following a different numbering system.</note>, David says: *When I cry out, then my enemies will turn back.* Thus, when we cry and call out to God, it is a means by which our lusts are turned back. There was never a mortified person who was not a praying person; the actual subjection of any lust cannot be obtained without prayer, for prayer is the Sword of the Spirit <note>Usually, the Word of God is called the Sword of the Spirit (Eph 6:17); the author here links the two in the practice of spiritual warfare.</note> through which alone we can overcome our corruptions. Until such time as you truly and sincerely pray, you will be met with unmortified lusts and corruptions. In Isaiah 64:6–7, the church complains: *We are all like an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are like a discarded garment; and there is no one who calls upon Your name.* They say: *We all fade as a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.* But why? Because *there is no one who calls upon Your name.* It is a rule given by an author of our time: either sin will make you stop praying, or prayer will make you stop sinning. If you continually pray against sin, prayer will in time kill your sins and corruptions. This is the third means.

4. If you wish to guard yourself from failings, keep within you certain maxims from Scripture which most clearly suppress and destroy the strength of sin. This is an excellent way to resist the corruptions of your heart. So did David in Psalm 119:11, where he says: *Your word I have hidden in my heart, that I might not sin against You.* That is: "I have specifically kept Your word in my heart against my beloved and darling sins, so that whenever I am tempted to commit them, I might bring forth the commandment against the sin."

And so when our Savior was tempted by the Devil, He said to him: *It is written thus and so* (Matthew 4:7), *You shall not tempt the Lord your God.* He overcame sin through the Scriptures. Now, if you keep in your thoughts certain expressed passages of Scripture against those sins to which you are most inclined, it will greatly help you in subduing those sins. Therefore, look through the whole Bible and choose those passages that make you most sorrowful for your sins. If you are inclined toward impurity <note>original: "onkuysheyt," often referring to sexual immorality or lust.</note>, consider that passage in Proverbs 2:19: *None who go to her return, nor do they regain the paths of life.* And *fornicators and adulterers God will judge* (Hebrews 13:4; 1 Corinthians 6:9; Ecclesiastes 7:26). Gather such passages as stand against your sins.

5. Observe yourself in weaning yourself from that sin to which you are most inclined. In 1 Corinthians 9:25 and 27, the Apostle says that everyone who strives for the

## Mortification and Sincerity.

<column-break/>

<margin>3rd Help.</margin>
...the one who competes for a prize abstains from everything. I fight in this way, not as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection <note>The author is paraphrasing 1 Corinthians 9:25-27, where Paul uses the imagery of an athlete to describe spiritual discipline.</note>. The law for taming a disordered heart is fasting and prayer. These duties are of great use in subduing corruptions; fasting and prayer are the slaughterhouse of sin. I may say of sin what Christ said of the Devil in *Matthew 17:21*: Not all kinds of demons are the same; this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting. Likewise, some sins will not leave us by ordinary means, but only through fasting and prayer.

<margin>6th Help.</margin>
6. If all these means do not help to subdue your lusts, then use this: enter into a solemn covenant with God, so that you (through the strength of Christ) may prevent those sins which would otherwise reign in you. I say, enter into the strength of Christ; for all your covenants and promises must be made within God's covenant and promise. There is no one who makes a covenant or promise with God (in the strength of Christ) to subdue his lusts, who shall not succeed. And if you make a promise to God, it must be done in the right manner:
1. It must be a lawful matter, or against some sin.
2. It must be in a weighty matter, and not in trivial things.

Secondly, it must be done at appropriate times, when all other means have been used and have not helped.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
**Objection:** But if we break this promise, and we are not able to fulfill it, it will be a double sin.

<margin>Answer.</margin>
**Answer:** If you are weak and unable to fulfill this duty, you are unable to fulfill any other duty required of you. But...

<margin>4th Help.</margin>
2. If God helps you and stands by you in this work with His strength, then you can do it; and a promise is God's ordinance <note>original: "ordinantie"</note> (*Numbers 29:39*). And if you do it in the strength of Christ, He will assist you in fulfilling it.

<margin>7th Help.</margin>
7. If you are busy in this work of mortification <term>mortification|the spiritual practice of "putting to death" sinful desires</term>, do not use your strength against only some particular sins, but set your whole strength against the entire "body of sin" <note>A biblical term referring to the totality of one's fallen nature.</note>. Taking away a tree’s growth does not happen by chopping off a few branches, but by pulling up the entire root. And so, if you truly wish to kill your lusts, you must pull out the entire body of sin, laboring to restrain and subdue it. Therefore, David in *Psalm 51*, when he humbled his soul before God for the sin of adultery, did not say, "Lord, forgive me only that sin," but he complained about the entire body of sin that was in him: *O Lord,* he says, *I was born in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me,* etc.

<margin>8th Help.</margin>
8. Do you wish to kill sin and guard your heart? Meditate on the death of Christ and on your own death; these are suitable means to preserve you from sin.

<margin>1st Contemplation.</margin>
1. Meditate on the death of Christ, and say to yourself: "Shall I live in those sins from which the Lord Christ has redeemed me through His death? Shall I harbor those lusts in my heart, for which the heart-blood of my Savior was poured out? Shall I not kill those sins that killed Christ?" The blood of those lusts shed the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Such observations will keep a

<margin>5th Help.</margin>

<column-break/>

person away from sin and subdue it. The contemplation of Christ's death is the most powerful means to crucify and kill our lusts. And then—

<margin>2nd Contemplation.</margin>
2. Meditate on your own death; this will greatly advance your mortification. Say: "I shall not live here forever; I must die sooner or later, and after death comes the Judgment, where I must give an account of everything I have done in the body, whether it be good or evil." And those sins that are now sweet and pleasant to me shall, when I come to die, be like gall and wormwood to me, and like a gnawing worm in my skin. This will certainly bring about improvement in your end; and if you earnestly consider our death, it will be a powerful means to keep us from sins.

---

And thus I have briefly run through these eight special instructions on how you may kill sin. Now there remains a use for comfort.

<margin>Use for comfort.</margin>
It may be that there are many conscientious souls listening today whose conscience testifies that they have not been enemies to this part of their souls, but have diligently labored to kill their lusts, but who nevertheless find the workings of corruptions strong in their hearts. For such as these, I have five words of comfort.

<margin>1st Use.</margin>
1. Take this for your use: that however much you strive to kill sin, you nevertheless cannot subdue the entire presence of sin in your heart. Sin wants to be in your soul just like that Beast in *Daniel 7:14* <note>The author likely refers to the beasts whose "dominion was taken away, yet their lives were prolonged for a season."</note>, as I have recounted. Although its reigning power is taken away. An Apostle (*2 Corinthians 4:7*) compares our earthly bodies to vessels <note>original: "vaten"</note>, and the contaminating impurity in us cannot be entirely washed away unless the vessels are broken in pieces and our bodies laid down in the dust—unless we have shed this fleshy body and are set free from this body of sin. Therefore, it is a great comfort to you that God does not expect the entire pulling up of the root of sin, but only the safeguard that sin does not reign in you.

<margin>2nd Use.</margin>
2. This is your comfort: that if you use all reasonable means to restrain your lusts, you can be assured that you shall at last obtain the victory over sin. Sin may be a fighter, but it shall never be a conqueror. Grace is compared in the Scriptures to oil (*Matthew 25:3*) and corruptions to water. And just as oil floats on top—do what you will, you shall not keep it under the water—so grace shall at some time gain the victory over corruptions. And Christ will not break the bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax (*Matthew 12:20*). By the "bruised reed" and "smoking flax," we understand weak Christians. Christ does not wish to discourage such people, even though their graces do not burst into a flame. Yet, if they but smoke, He will not quench them until they have won the victory in Judgment; that is, until those weak and small beginnings of grace in them burst into a flame and obtain the victory over their corruptions. A reed is weak in itself, and a bruised one even weaker; but nevertheless, it shall not be broken until the work of grace is accomplished in the soul and has obtained victory over all the assaults and temptations of Satan.

<margin>3rd Use.</margin>
3. Remember this for your comfort: that if you walk diligently in the fulfillment of these me—

# The True Doctrine of...

means / that the Lord will sanctify you in the work of <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "doodinghe"; the theological process of "killing off" sinful desires</note> / despite your sins appearing to overcome you; in this case the Lord will hold you innocent. I may use here that same passage concerning the Law of God regarding a violated daughter in Deuteronomy 22:25, 26, 27, previously mentioned. <note>In Mosaic law, if a woman was attacked and cried out for help, she was considered innocent of the sin. The author applies this to a soul crying out to God against the "assault" of sin.</note> Whenever the Devil seeks to spiritually violate you, if your soul has this testimony—that it has called to God for help, fought with all its might against corruptions, and sought to keep itself, yet without achieving victory—know this for your comfort: that God will consider you innocent.

<margin>4th Use.</margin>
4. God will not damn you for those sins which you sought to resist and subdue by all means during your life. You may plead thus with God when you die: "O Lord, will you damn me and cast me into hell for those sins against which I have labored my whole life, seeking to root them out of my heart?" The <term>Naturalists</term> <note>Ancient and medieval writers on natural history, such as Pliny the Elder.</note> recount of the Crocodile that if a man is afraid of him and flees, he gains strength and pursues the man; but if a man sets himself against him and fights with the Crocodile, the creature becomes afraid, runs away, and is easily killed. So it is here: if you resist sin and corruptions, they shall be killed; but if you flee before them, they will kill you. Pour out all your tears, all your prayers, and direct all your strength against sin; though you do not then entirely overcome it, the Lord will hold you innocent.

<margin>5th Use.</margin>
5. Take this for your comfort / that the trembling and agitation of your heart is much more a proof that sin is being killed than that it is not. When sin fights against you, and you go against it with holy resolutions, that inner upheaval is more proof that sin is being killed than that it lives, reigns in you, or has the upper hand.
And so much time have I spent in the treatment of the first doctrine / namely / that the mortification of corruption is a necessary quality required in all those who wish to be saved.

### ROMANS VIII. 13.

> ... But if you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.

<margin>
8th Sermon.
2nd Doctrine.
</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'N' containing a figure in a landscape environment.</image-desc>Now I proceed further to the second doctrine / *If you through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live.* From which I observe / that the mortification of corruptions is wrought in us through the strength of Christ's Spirit, not through our own.
Before I come to treat the <term>cases of conscience</term> <note>Specific moral or spiritual dilemmas brought to a pastor for resolution.</note> necessarily belonging to this point / I shall first prove the same through two reasons: "if you through the Spirit mortify," that the killing of corruption is wrought in us by the Spirit of God. And that /

<margin>1st Proof-reason.</margin>
1. Because the <term>Sanctification</term> <note>The process of being made holy.</note> of a person's nature is a proper and special work / or office of the Spirit of God, called the Holy Spirit because His proper office is to make a person holy.
Now / mortification is but one part of sanctification, for sanctification consists of these two parts: mortification (the dying away of sin) and <term>vivification</term> <note>original: "levendighmakinge"; being made alive to God.</note> (living unto God). And therefore / if sanctification in general

<column-break/>

is a work of God's Spirit / then mortification must likewise be a work of the Spirit.
You find this often in the Scripture / that the Spirit of God is called / the Spirit of Sanctification. 1 Peter 1:2: *To the elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit.* And 1 Corinthians 6:11: *And such were some of you, but now you are washed, but now you are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.*
Since mortification is a part of sanctification, and the Spirit of God works sanctification, He must necessarily perform the primary part, which is mortification.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>
2. This is evident because only the Spirit of God can preserve and enlighten the mind of man and overcome his judgment to see the evil of sin; a person will never go about killing sin until he be convinced of the evil and danger of the same. And therefore you read / John 16:8 <note>OCR says 16:18, but the text describes 16:8.</note>: *Therefore God has sent His Spirit into the world that He should convince it of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment.* A person will not look for healing until he feels his sickness; so also he will not drive out sin until he feels the danger and the guilt of sin / and you shall never be convinced of this evil until the Spirit of God enlightens you. So that this work of mortification is mostly wrought by the Spirit because He alone can convince us of the evil of sin, making us hate it and shrink back from it.
Here, various cases of conscience regarding this point must necessarily be addressed. Such as:

1. Seeing as the text says here / "if you through the Spirit": the words seem to imply another means of mortification not wrought by the Spirit, but through the power of man's good nature or upbringing. And therefore I shall show you the distinction between corruptions killed by the power of the Spirit and corruptions resisted by the power of nature. Secondly, I shall show you how you may reassure your conscience that you have truly killed your corruptions. Thirdly, I shall show you / whether falling often into the same sin can coexist with mortification.

<margin>1st Answer</margin>
1. Wherein lies the distinction between corruptions killed by the power of nature and a true mortification performed by the Spirit of God?
In these eight specific things:
1. A corruption resisted by the power of nature only makes the sin cease for the present / but does not bring into the heart a hateful disposition against the sin: just as it is with a thief in prison / he resists the evil because he cannot do it / but nonetheless he loves the sin just as much as before. So a person for the present time resists the sin / and yet he has no inward hatred in his heart against it. Thus <term>Balaam</term> <note>original: "Biliam"; the prophet in Numbers 22-24.</note> gave two refusing answers / that he would not go to curse Israel / and yet at the last he went / because he loved the reward of unrighteousness (2 Peter 2:15).
But where there is an actual mortification / wrought by the power of the Spirit of God / there is a contrary and hating disposition of the heart against the sin / so as not to do it. So that you do not only leave the sin, but also loathe it: there is not only a withholding from sins, but a striving against them.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "8 general helps" for the mortification of sin, specifically contrasting natural human effort with the internal work of the Holy Spirit. The previous page established the comfort believers can take when they struggle against sin; this page provides specific "proofs" to help a reader determine if their resistance to sin is truly spiritual.</meta>

# Mortification and Sincerity.

<margin>
Proofs.
</margin>
2. Resisting sin through the power of nature allows one to only stop committing large and obvious sins, but not small sins or "bosom lusts" <note>private, deeply-held desires</note>. In contrast, **mortifying grace** <note>original: "doodende genade"</note>, wrought by the Spirit, brings a fear of committing both inward and outward sins. **Colossians 3:5** says the Apostle: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth, namely fornication, uncleanness, etc." Not only the act of fornication, but also unclean thoughts, desires, and evil stirrings. Mortification through the Spirit crucifies the entire inward man; therefore, examine yourself in this. **2 Samuel 24:10** tells us that David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. Theologians find it difficult to say exactly what David's sin was in counting the people; nevertheless, there was pride and fleshly confidence involved, and yet his heart struck him. Tender consciences are troubled over small sins; likewise, his heart struck him when he had cut a corner from Saul's robe, **1 Samuel 24:4**, which was essentially no sin at all, yet he was troubled by it. But a godless person is never troubled over small sins; those sins that break the hearts of the godly never rob the godless of their sleep. Small sins disturb the very members of the godly, but they do not even touch the "clothes" of the godless.

3. Resisting corruptions through the power of nature is a violent act that the person does unwillingly. **Genesis 20:6** says God to Abimelech: "I have kept you from sinning against me." This indicates there was a strong inclination toward that sin, but God prevented him from doing it. A natural heart, even if it does not commit the sin, lets it go unwillingly; but when sin is mortified through the strength of the Spirit, then he gives up his lusts willingly. A godless person leaves sin like a child leaves its parent—unwillingly and with tears in the eyes; but a godly person leaves his sin like a poor prisoner leaves his stinking dungeon, or a poor beggar his torn clothes, or a galley slave the galley. God's people shall be a willing people, **Psalm 110:3**. They shall say to their inward idols: "Get out!"

4. When a person resists sin only by the power of nature, then after that resistance, he often runs back to greater and greater sins than before. **Hosea 7:6** says the godless are like an oven; now you know that the fire in an oven, the more tightly it is enclosed, the more powerfully it burns. So it is with a godless person: the more he burns in his heart, the more he hunts after his lusts. Just like a stream that is dammed up; when the dam is broken, it flows out with greater power and strength. **2 Chronicles 24:2** shows that Joash did what was right in the eyes of the Lord all the days of the priest Jehoiada; but when he was dead, his lusts broke out, and he ran mightily into all sins and godlessness. So too with Balaam: although he resisted his sins for a time, he afterwards committed more evil than ever before.

But a **mortified** person, who has the power of mortifying grace wrought in him by the Spirit of God, finds his sins are continually being killed; and although not yet entirely dead, their strength shall never act as fully as before, nor lay formally upon his heart.

5. A person who resists sin only through the power of nature does so mostly out of fleshly considerations.

But Joseph, when he was tempted to sin, looked higher and said: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?"

2. Because sin brings temporal punishments upon him. For this reason, Abimelech avoided the sin in **Genesis 20:9**. For knowing that Sarah was Abraham's wife, he said to Abraham: "What have you done to us? And in what have I offended you, that you have brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin?" This is what kept him from sin—not that God would have been offended by it—but he who kills sin through the Spirit of God resists it based on spiritual considerations: because it dishonors God, is a blemish upon the Gospel and one's profession of faith, and the like.

6. A person who resists sin through the power of nature does so more because of the eternal punishments that follow sin than because of the inward evil that is *in* the sin itself. He keeps himself from sin not because there is a holy God, but because He is a righteous God; not because God hates sin, but because He punishes it; not because there is a hell *in* the sin, but because there is a hell *before* or *after* the sin.

But a truly mortified person shuns sin more for its inward evil than for the outward punishments that follow it; as one says: if hell stood on one side and sin on the other, upon consulting with his soul, he would rather run into hell than into sin.
<margin>
Anselm.
</margin> <note>Referring to St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), who famously wrote that he would rather be pure from sin in hell than spotted with sin in heaven.</note>

7. A person who has resisted his corruptions through the power of nature finds it only lasts for a time; following temptations and opportunities, he is compelled to commit them again and goes along easily to fulfill them. As in **Proverbs 7:22**, you read of a young man who walked through the streets in the twilight, and there came a woman who was a harlot who enticed him, and he went with her without any reasonable resistance or consideration that God saw it, or whether God would punish him for that sin or not; he simply followed her.

On the contrary, a person who has mortified his corruptions through the power of God's Spirit resists the sin and will not commit it except against his will; sin may sometimes overtake him by surprise, but he flees from it as far as he can.

8. A person who resists sin through the power of nature does so with pain and grief, as **Proverbs 13:19** says: "It is an abomination to fools to depart from evil." And on the other hand, he has delight and is glad if he may later commit the sin again, **Jeremiah 11:15**: "When you do evil, then you rejoice," and **Habakkuk 3:14**: "Their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly."

But the godly rejoice and thank God that they are kept from committing sin. So did David in **1 Samuel 25:32**. When Abigail came to David and kept him from shedding innocent blood, David blessed the Lord because He had sent Abigail to meet him and had kept him from shedding innocent blood. A godly person is joyful when he resists sin, and if he falls into any sin, it troubles him; he is sorrowful and weeps. It is like the fish from which the pearls of the East are taken; these pearls are painful to the fish from which they are taken, but when a man has them, they serve him as an ornament. So the sins that the godless rejoice in are pain and sorrow to the Godly.

And therefore examine your own minds, and see if you can distinguish yourselves from those people who resist their corruptions through the power of nature, and do not kill them through the Spirit of God.

And so I have finished the first case of conscience, showing you the distinction of eight particular things that exist between a person who resists his sins only through the power of nature, and him who truly kills them through the power of the Spirit of God.

I come now to the second case of conscience, which is this:

<margin>2nd Case.</margin>
2. "Oh," a poor soul may say, "how shall I be satisfied in my own conscience that my sins are truly killed and my corruptions brought under subjection by the strength of the Spirit?"

<margin>Answer.</margin>
**Answer.** I shall give you two clear and infallible proofs of a person who has killed <note>Theologians use the term "mortified" to describe the process of sin being put to death in the believer's life.</note> their sin.

1. If it be so, that the corruptions which were previously very strong and powerful in you are now weak and feeble through resistance: this is a certain proof that these sins are killed in you. Previously, nature was like tinder and sparks—not to be touched <note>meaning it would ignite into sin at the slightest provocation</note>—but now that you have the opposition to and the upper hand over committed sins, this is an infallible proof that the sin is killed. This proof declared that Joseph’s sins were killed because he shunned all the attacks of his mistress <note>Potiphar's wife</note>; there was no one in the house but he and the woman; he had hopes of great advantages, yet he could not bring himself to sin against God.

I hope that there are many among you who hear this today, who have had just as many invitations to sin as Joseph did—even though no eye could see you—and yet for the whole world you would not commit that sin. Truly, this proves that the work of the Spirit is within you; without which you could never go so far.

2. Another proof: when you make a matter of conscience and are troubled by inward and hidden sins just as much as by public and great transgressions. When there is in your heart a conflict and true sorrow over small and hidden sins as well as over public scandals, this is an indubitable proof that God has wrought in you a work of killing [sin] through His Spirit. When sins as small as molehills lie as heavy on your heart as mountains, and when your conscience can testify to you that no hidden lusts creep into your soul without you laboring to resist them.

3. Whether a person whose lusts and corruptions are truly killed by the Spirit of God may afterwards commit and fall into those same sins that were killed.

4. What marks can be given of "bosom" or beloved sins <note>Sins that an individual is most naturally inclined toward or finds hardest to give up.</note> that are mostly unkilled in a person.

particular corruptions which continually trouble a person.

I shall begin with the third: whether a person who has truly killed his sins can often fall back into those same sins that were killed.

I shall give you these six things by way of answer:

1. We have some examples in the Scripture of people who did not fall again into the same sins that were previously killed in them. First, **Genesis 38:26**, where it says of Judah that after committing his sin in the violation of Tamar, his sister <note>Tamar was actually Judah's daughter-in-law; the text refers to her as "Suster" (sister), likely a broader use of kinship terms or a scribal error.</note>, he acknowledged her, and he "knew her no more" from then on. After he saw his sin, he confessed it and never fell into that same sin again. You have another example in the good Jehoshaphat, **2 Chronicles 20:37**. When the prophet Eliezer <note>The OCR reads "Elizeus" (Elisha), but the biblical account in 2 Chronicles 20:37 identifies the prophet as Eliezer.</note> came to him and recounted his sin—that he had made a covenant with Ahaziah, for which the Lord was angry with him—after he was called back, he would not bring the guilt of that sin upon himself again, as you can see in **1 Kings 22:49**. When Ahaziah spoke to Jehoshaphat, asking that his servants might go with Jehoshaphat’s servants in the ship, it says Jehoshaphat would not.

2. However, it serves as an answer that we have no explicit example in the entire Bible of a person who, having truly killed a sin and humbled himself for it, afterwards fell back into that same sin which had been brought under and killed.

This is not only my observation, but also the judgment of Perkins <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), an influential English Puritan theologian whose works on "cases of conscience" were foundational in the Dutch Second Reformation.</note>, that in all the examples of the Old and New Testament, he can find none with certainty where a person killed a sin and later fell back into it. And therefore, if your sins are killed and yet you often fall back into that same sin, you are a person without any [biblical] example.

3. And although there is no example in the whole Scripture of a person falling back into the same *great* sins which he had previously killed, nonetheless there are various examples of such godly people who often fell into the same sin before they knew it to be sin—before they were sensitive to it, truly humbled, and sorrowful for it—and before the earnest consideration between God and their own souls regarding what evil they had done. So Solomon fell twice into godlessness before the Lord; and Peter three times into the sin of denying his Master. And the children of Israel fell ten times into the same sin of murmuring against the Lord (**Numbers 14:22**).

Where a person is killed <note>meaning the sin is killed/mortified</note> and truly humbled for the sin, does he often fall into the same sin?

4. Although there is no example of it in the whole Scripture, nonetheless according to Reason and experience, it can be the truth that a person who has killed his sin can fall again into the same sin of which he repents and for which he has been humble. And the teacher Mr. Perkins gives this answer, saying: *There is no reason or experience that can assure you who kills corruptions—especially if they are inward and hidden sins—that you would not break forth and fall into that sin of which you have repented.* Take, for example, the sin of passion <note>often referring to a quick or violent temper.</note>; although you resist it, pray against it every day, and God wants to preserve you from it through His Spirit, nonetheless that does not

<margin>1st Caution.</margin> 1. Observe first that falling often into the same sin expresses the obstinacy and hardness of your heart; and therefore I say, if you fall again and again into the same sin, you lie under a state of hardness before the Lord; you do not have a broken heart within you.

There is no less danger (in falling often into the same sin) in respect to spiritual healing.

<margin>Signs of beloved sins.</margin>

<margin>1st Sign.</margin> 1. That sin is a "bosom" or master sin which you most often perform, and which you fall into most in your life.

**N**ow I shall give you some specific remedies against certain specific corruptions: On the last Lord's Day, I spoke in general, but now I shall go specifically against three corruptions, namely: how to kill impurity, spiritual pride, and evil or reigning passions; I cannot think of any other corruptions that overcome the mind of man more than these three. Of the one I shall be a bit longer than the others; five or six remedies are necessary to kill impure lusts.

1. A special help to kill impure lusts is to live in a constant observation of God's all-seeing eye upon you: thus it is a general remedy against all sin, but nonetheless, the Scripture applies it to this sin, Job 31:1, 4. There Job says: "I have made a covenant with my eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" And in verse 4 he says: "Does he not see my ways, and count all my steps?" There is nothing that will rebuke your lusts more than the observation of God's all-seeing eye, that he sees and takes knowledge of all our ways. I have heard a story of a young woman who was diligently sought after by a young man for unchastity, and she said to him: if he would bring her to a place where no eye might see her, she would grant his desire; the young man led her from one place to another, and finally, when he thought they were in the most secret place, he wanted his desire from the young woman: "Oh," she said, "the eye of God is upon us everywhere, he sees us, and takes knowledge of our deeds." And by this observation, she lived chastely thereafter all her days.

2. Keep a special watch over all your outward senses: The Apostle speaks of some in 2 Peter 2:14, "Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin." Therefore you must set a watch over your eyes and guard yourself against a harmful sight. It is a window through which the lusts of the world come into your heart. In Hebrews 14:9 <note>The author likely intended Leviticus 14:9, which details the cleansing of a leper.</note> the Lord makes a law that the lepers, who were unclean, had to have the hair of their head and their eyebrows shaved off. Thus there is no way so powerful to call out the impurity of your fleshly lusts as to set a watch on the same, so that they do not look upon vanity.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "mortification" of sin—the spiritual practice of subduing sinful desires. Having previously discussed how to identify a "master sin," the author now provides practical remedies against two specific types of sin: physical impurity (lust) and spiritual pride.</meta>

# Mortification and Sincerity.

Just as Job says, "I have made a covenant with my eyes"; you must guard your eyes from wandering if you wish to protect yourself from fleshly lusts. This is why you read of Abimelech in Genesis 20:16. When he sought to move Sarah, Abraham's wife, he said to her, "Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver; behold, he is to you a covering of the eyes, to all who are with you: yes, before everyone." <note>This refers to the biblical account where Abimelech returns Sarah to Abraham; the "covering of the eyes" is often interpreted as a sign of her status as a married woman, protecting her from the gaze of others.</note> This means that a woman must not cast her eyes upon anyone in sinful ways except her husband; he must be a covering for her eyes, and for all who are with her.

<margin>3rd Remedy.</margin>
3. Use a proper measure in eating and drinking. There are certain types of food—and excesses in the consumption of them—that stir up your lusts. 2 Peter 2:13 says, "While they are at their feasts, they have eyes full of adultery." And this is the reason Paul expresses in 1 Corinthians 9:26, 27: "I therefore run thus: not with uncertainty. Thus I fight: not as one who beats the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified."

<margin>4th Remedy.</margin>
4. If you wish to guard yourself against fleshly lusts, then turn your thoughts away when the lusts first begin to rise. If a person allows meditative thoughts to dwell with pleasure in their heart, it is a thousand to one that they will not break through into the act itself. It is a great preparation for impurity when a person nourishes speculative and wavering thoughts regarding some evil objects within themselves. Ezekiel 23:19 says, "She multiplied her harlotries, calling to remembrance the days of her youth, when she had played the harlot in the land of Egypt." The resistance and turning away of our thoughts is a great help in keeping us from sin. "I have made a covenant with my eyes," says Job; he does not say, "Why should I look upon a maiden?" but rather, "How then could I gaze upon a maiden?" <note>The author distinguishes between a passing glance and a focused, intentional gaze.</note>

<margin>5th Remedy.</margin>
5. If you wish to mortify and subdue your lusts, use this for your help: that there is more actual evil than apparent good in the sin of impurity. When a harlot wants to invite and move a young man to commit impurity with her, she says in Proverbs 7:13, 15, 17: "I have come out to meet you, diligently to seek your face, and I have found you. I have spread my bed with tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen from Egypt. I have perfumed my bed with Myrrh, Aloes, and Cinnamon." Mark here, says a writer, how she joins two bitter things and one sweet together. "I have perfumed my bed with Myrrh, Aloes, and Cinnamon." Cinnamon alone is sweet, and the other two are very bitter herbs, which signifies to us that there is more misery and evil in the sin of impurity than there is joy and pleasure.

<margin>6th Remedy.</margin>
6. Seriously consider the evil companions that accompany the sin of impurity. First, there is theft in that sin; you steal a body that is not your own. John 8:4 states, "This woman was caught in the very act, committing adultery." In the original language, it can also be read as "she was caught in theft," <note>original: "op diefte ghegrepen"</note> indicating that adultery is no better than theft. Proverbs 9:17, 18 calls the committing of adultery with a woman "stolen waters": "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."

<column-break/>

(This is clearly spoken of a harlot, for there follows:) "But he does not know that the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell."

2. That sin brings dishonor and contempt upon a person. Proverbs 6:33: "Whoever commits adultery... wounds and dishonor shall he find, and his reproach shall not be wiped away."

3. It causes poverty in a person's estate, and he is brought thereby to the beggar's sack. Proverbs 29:3: "He who keeps company with harlots wastes his substance." And chapter 6, verse 26: "By means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread."

4. It will consume flesh and bones; it corrupts the blood and the entire person. Proverbs 5:8, 11: "Remove your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house; lest you mourn at last, when your flesh and your body are consumed."

5. It makes a person a warehouse of all defects.

6. It brings dullness to the heart of a person; an impure person is a dull sinner and an unwise one. Hosea 4:11: "Harlotry, wine, and new wine take away the heart." And thus I have finished the remedies against the first sin of impure lusts.

Answer: I shall give you four remedies against this sin.

<margin>
4 Remedies against spiritual pride.
1st Remedy.
</margin>
1. If you wish to guard yourself against spiritual pride, notice that most of you have more reason to be humble than to be proud. The best of you has more sin than grace within; just as there are more stones than diamonds, and more thorns than roses in the field, so is there more sin than grace in your hearts. Over what, then, shall you become proud? Thinking you have many good gifts in you, while you are nevertheless of an evil and sinful nature.

<margin>2nd Remedy.</margin>
2. Read with constant and serious consideration that all those gifts and talents for which you are proud are merely presents and gifts from God. Now, if all those gifts you have were given to you by God, why then should you be proud? Shall a beggar be proud of the clothes that another has given him? It is even so with you; all that you have are alms, gifts, graces, and mercies given to you by God. As the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 4:7: "What do you have that you did not receive?" <note>The text incorrectly cites 1 Cor 7, but the quote is from 1 Cor 4:7.</note> And therefore, this must humble us.

<margin>3rd Remedy.</margin>
3. If you wish to guard yourself against spiritual pride, notice that of all things in the world, this will keep you back and rob you of grace. James 4:6: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." He fights against him like a soldier in battle; He gives grace to a humble heart, but not to a proud one. Therefore, beware of exalting your spirit; and if you are there, this must move you to humility: that pride will make your soul barren of grace. The low valleys are usually the most fertile, while the high mountains are dry; so the humblest Christians are the most fertile in grace. Furthermore, the philosophers give a clear reason for the evil of this sin above any other: because other defects only set themselves against their [opposites]...
