<meta>This page continues the author's practical guide on the "mortification" of sin—the spiritual process of subduing sinful impulses. After discussing physical lust on the previous page, the author now concludes the section on spiritual pride and moves to the third "master sin": reigning anger or passion.</meta>

# The True Doctrine of, etc.

<margin>4th Remedy.</margin>
4. A major means for the mortification <note>In this context, "mortification" refers to the spiritual practice of "killing" or deadening sinful desires.</note> and guarding of your heart against pride is to earnestly observe the great difference there is between God and you; between yourself and others; and between yourself and yourself.

1. How great a difference is there between God and you? He is like the bright Sun; you are like a filthy garment; He is the righteous Judge of Heaven and earth, you are a poor sinner, dust and ashes, etc.

2. Observe also the difference between you and others; it may be that others have fewer means of grace than you, and yet have greater advantages in the School of Christ <note>A common 17th-century metaphor for the process of Christian learning and spiritual growth.</note> than you; and this must guard you from pride.

3. Note that great difference between yourself and yourself; you are proud of the gifts you have now, but oh, note what you were in Adam <note>Refers to the state of humanity before the Fall, which theologians argued was a state of perfection.</note>. I am certain you fall far short in the gifts and adornments of the Spirit that you had in him. And look further at the difference there is between you now and what you were at your first conversion; then you were light toward grace, constant in prayers, full of affection for God, and fiery for Him, etc. But now you are cold and negligent in holy duties; now you lack the greater part of that grace in which you previously shone. You are like that people of whom I have read, who in the first year offered Gold to their Gods, the next year Silver, and the third year nothing at all. So were you at first fruitful in grace, and afterwards you became weaker, and now you are worse than ever, and yet prouder than ever before. It seems to me that these observations ought to guard your hearts very well. And so I have finished with the second sin: Spiritual Pride.

I come now to the third: Reigning Anger, commonly called passion.

But oh, says another, neither of those two previously mentioned sins troubles me so much as my hasty temper and passion; and therefore I am eager to know how I might kill it and bring this sin into subjection.

<margin>
6 Remedies to restrain and kill passion.
1st Remedy.
</margin>
Answer: I shall give you six Rules for instruction, by which you may restrain your passions when you might be offended by some wrong or the like.

1. Observe that you have given God more reason to be angry with you than you have ever had with any man. Should the Lord strictly punish what you do to Him, and seek out the iniquity you commit against Him, you would long ago have been cast into hell; and therefore let this keep you back and guard you from passion.

<margin>2nd Remedy.</margin>
2. Observe that all those wrongs that come upon you, and which cause your passions to rise, come upon you through the providence of God. And this was what restrained David's passion when Shimei cursed him; "let him curse," says David, "for God has bidden him." <note>original: "Godt heeft het hem geheeten." See 2 Samuel 16:10-11.</note>

<margin>3rd Remedy.</margin>
3. When any occasion for anger is given, labor to check it and 

<column-break/>

resist the urge for revenge; let there be some sober reflections before you flare up in anger and passion. Solomon says in Proverbs 12:16, "A fool's wrath is known at once, but a prudent man covers shame." <note>original: "Spreuck. 12. 16."</note> A fool cannot hide his anger, but it breaks out immediately; yet a wise person considers the shame. It is a shame to be angry, therefore a wise person conceals his passion.

4. Another great remedy to kill passion is this: withdraw from the company of those who are ready for anger, or else you will partake in their anger. The way to subdue passion is to depart from the company of those who wrong you. You learn this (and it is very noteworthy) in 1 Samuel 20:24: when Saul was angry with Jonathan, it says "Jonathan rose from the table," from the presence of his Father. So also Abraham and Lot, so that they might not fall out against one another, separated from each other. So says Solomon in Proverbs 22:24-25: "Make no friendship with an angry man, and with a furious man do not go, lest you learn his ways and set a snare for your soul." <note>original: "Spreuck. 22. 24."</note> If you are near a hot-tempered person, he sets a snare for you, and you for him; this is the way to let passion increase.

5. If you wish to guard your passion when any wrong occurs that might make you angry, then labor to quiet that occasion and that wrong; do not use a multitude of words, for here words are wind, and just as wind blows up the fire, so words feed revenge. Proverbs 26:21: "As charcoal is to burning coals, and wood to fire, so is a contentious man to kindle strife." <note>original: "Spreuck. 26. 21."</note> Many words will awaken the passions, and therefore if you wish to guard yourself from anger, do not use many words, nor rebuke after rebuke, for this is the way to make anger grow.

6. To keep yourself from passion, note that it is a sin that includes many other sins within itself: you can commit other sins alone, but you cannot be angry without committing many other sins. Proverbs 29:22: "An angry man stirs up strife, and a furious man abounds in transgression." <note>original: "Spreuck. 29. 22."</note> Robbery and murder sometimes follow anger. Genesis 49:6: "Simeon and Levi... in their anger they slew a man." <note>original: "Genef. 49. 6."</note> There is an abundance of sins in the bosom of an angry person, which if you observe them, will guard you from it.

And so I have dealt with three kinds of modest remedies against those particular sins, which I hope, if they are earnestly considered, will further the work of mortification in you.

Now I have only a word or two left for instruction, and with that I shall conclude this Text.

1. When you have subdued and killed one sin, be sure to expect another from the root of it. Beloved, a Christian's life is a forced struggle; he must fight with spiritual wickednesses in the air. The Devil will never leave him alone, but if he has repelled one attack, another immediately comes alongside him; when one lust or corruption is killed, another rises from the root. Therefore you must constantly stand on guard; this is the first point by way of advice.

2. Do not be satisfied with a small beginning of mortification; many people are satisfied because they have a pause in their lusts and think they are killed; and many are satisfied...

### The True Israelite.

->John 1 verse 48.<-

> Behold truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile.

<margin>1st Sermon.</margin>
These words are a living portrait of the sincerity of Nathanael, in which Christ reveals his heart to us, knowing from within what might be in him. Julius Drusius <note>The author likely refers to the Roman statesman Marcus Livius Drusus, though he names him Julius. Drusus famously asked his architect to build his house so that his entire life was visible to his fellow citizens.</note>, a Roman Counselor, was so open in his own integrity that he wished his house to be so transparent that all people might see how he lived. Another wished that his breast were a window of Crystal, so that every man might look into his heart. Such a man was Nathanael: Christ looked into his inward parts and gave him this glorious testimony: that in him there was no guile.

I shall spend no time in a preface to these words, but go immediately to the words themselves, first explaining them, and then setting forth some instructive points of assistance from them.

In the explanation, two things are to be done:
1. I shall show you who this man was of whom Christ speaks here. And
2. What it is that Christ commands here concerning him: *Behold truly an Israelite, in whom there is no guile.*

Firstly, who was this man? Answer: His name was Nathanael, a Hebrew name <note>original: "een Hebreeuwsche name"</note>, and it signifies as much as "a gift of God" <note>Nathanael is derived from the Hebrew "Netan'el," meaning "God has given."</note>;

<column-break/>

but so that you may know in particular who this man was—although there is much variation among the Commentators on this point—nonetheless, I shall set before you the clearest proofs of this from the Scripture. I find that this Nathanael was Bartholomew, one of the Apostles. And of this, I shall give you these three reasons from the Scripture:

1. Because you see in the verses preceding my Text that this Nathanael was converted through Philip (verse 46): *Philip found Nathanael and said to him, we have found him of whom Moses in the Law wrote, and the Prophets: namely, Jesus the son of Joseph, of Nazareth.* Now this proves that Nathanael was Bartholomew because, wherever Bartholomew is named, Philip is placed with him, as in Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, and Luke 6:14. In all these places, Bartholomew and Philip are joined together; this is one reason.

2. The other reason is taken from the promise which Christ makes to Nathanael in John 1:51–52. *Jesus answered and said to him, because I said to you, I saw you under the Fig tree, you believe; you shall see greater things than these. And said to him, Verily, verily I say unto you, from now on you shall see Heaven opened, and the Angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.* Now, if this Nathanael were not Bartholomew, this promise could not be made good to him, for only the twelve Apostles saw Christ ascend to Heaven; and if Nathanael had not been an Apostle, this promise could not have happened to him.

3. Yet another proof that Nathanael was Bartholomew is taken from John 21:2. There were together (when Christ showed himself to his Disciples) Simon Peter, and Thomas, called Didymus, and Nathanael. Here Nathanael is named among the Apostles, and this is the third proof. And although Salmeron <note>Alphonso Salmeron (1515–1585) was a Spanish Jesuit theologian and one of the founding members of the Society of Jesus.</note> says these are "grave arguments," this is a powerful argument because no one was there but the Apostles.

<margin>Objections.</margin>
Objection: But some will say, if Nathanael was Bartholomew, one of the Apostles, how does it happen that he is not remembered or named in the register of the twelve Apostles?

Answer 1. Most of the Apostles carried two names in the Scripture, and they are not called by both those names at the same time; Peter was also called Simon, and Thomas was surnamed Didymus, etc. Now, if other Apostles had two names, why not likewise Bartholomew, being called Nathanael and Bartholomew—Nathanael being his proper name, and Bartholomew his surname <note>Bartholomew is a patronymic, meaning "Son of Talmai."</note>.

Secondly, what is it that Christ says of this man, or commends? Namely, that he was *Truly an Israelite*, a man in whom there was no guilt. I shall first explain the word "behold," which signifies three things in the Scripture:

1. This word "behold," when it precedes any matter concerning God, is a sign of wonder; as in 1 John 3:1: *Behold what great love the Father has given us, namely, that we should be called children of God.* That is, a matter of wonder.

2. When it stands before any things concerning the godless, then it is a derision <note>original: "versottinghe," meaning to make a fool of or to mock.</note>, as in Psalm 52:9 <note>In many English Bibles, this is Psalm 52:7.</note>: *Behold the man, who did not make God...*

3. Whenever a text stands before any matter concerning the **Godly**, it is a sign of imitation; and so it must be taken here in our Text: *Behold truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.* <note>original: "Siet waerlijck een Israëlijt in welcken geen bedrogh en is." This refers to John 1:47. In many English Bibles, "bedrogh" is translated as "guile."</note> That is to say: follow him and imitate him.
Alas! many Israelites were children of deceit and wickedness, in whom much guilt was found; some were Jews outwardly, but not inwardly; they had the circumcision of the flesh, but not of the heart; their praise was from men, but not from God, **Romans 2:28, 29.** The Rich Man <note>A reference to the parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16.</note> called Abraham "Father," and yet he was a son of perdition. Many were Israelites by natural descent who were not so by a spiritual birth; but Nathanael was not one of these.
*Behold an Israelite*, that is, not only one descended from Jacob by nature; but *truly an Israelite*, that is, so by rebirth and in truth, as well as in name; for they are not all Israel who are of Israel; nor are the children of the flesh the children of God. **Romans 9:6, 8.** Nathanael was not only an Israelite by natural birth, but likewise by spiritual rebirth.
*Behold truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit:* He does not say, "in whom there is no sin," but "in whom there is no deceit." Now, although it is true that it is said here of Nathanael that he was a man without deceit, and the same is said of Christ in **1 Peter 2:22**: *He knew no sin, neither was any deceit found in his mouth*; yet you must know (though the phrases are the same) that there is a great difference between Christ’s and Nathanael's state of being without guilt or deceit. Of Christ, it is said that no sin was in him, nor was any deceit found in his mouth; but this is not said of Nathanael, for he was sinful. Indeed, Christ was without sin; his nature was like crystal and pure water. Although the glass might sometimes be soiled on the outside, nonetheless he was not stained with sin. But our natures are like a glass splashed with muddy water; if you merely move the glass, the mud will immediately show itself.
**Question**, *What does it mean to be a man without deceit?*
**Answer.** A man without deceit is one who is a sincere professor of the Gospel, and can assure himself before God in his heart that he seeks to fulfill all those duties which the Lord requires of him—doing so from a right principle, in a right manner, and toward a right end—and labors to be better before God than he appears to be before men. *Truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit:* These words are in agreement with the testimony given to Jacob, who was named Israel, in **Genesis 25:27.** There it says that Jacob was a plain <note>The Dutch "oprecht" implies uprightness or integrity; the Hebrew original in Genesis describes him as "tam," often translated as "plain," "quiet," or "perfect."</note> man, dwelling in tents. An upright or perfect man—that is, a man without guilt, a man in whom there was no deceit: **Psalm 32:2.** *Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.*
I have been a bit too long in opening these words: It is my custom at the first entrance into the Text to take a little speed in the explanation before I

<column-break/>

establish any doctrines from the same: And yet before I do that, I want you to take note of these four things.
1. Christ does not say here, "behold an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit," but "behold *truly* an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit"; for they are not all Israel who are of Israel. A man can be an Israelite by natural birth and yet be full of flaws, a hypocrite, and full of deceit; therefore Christ does not say, "behold an Israelite," but "truly one."
2. He does not say, "behold an Israelite in words, or in appearance, or in profession alone," but one in deed and truth. There are many people who are so in words or profession, but in their deeds and actions they are far removed from it. Not words or profession, but practice and works are the evidentiary arguments of true conversion.
3. Christ does not say, "Behold truly an Israelite, *with* whom there is no deceit": Hypocrisy may be *with* us, but it cannot be *in* us; hypocrisy was not *in* Nathanael. There is a certain distinction between doing a thing *in* hypocrisy and *with* hypocrisy. The Godly often do their duties *with* hypocrisy, but not *in* hypocrisy. A man does something *in* hypocrisy when he involves himself in devious ways and performs duties for an evil end; for instance, if a man follows the ordinances so that he may be esteemed among good people or that he may exalt himself, this man's act is hypocrisy. However, doing something *with* hypocrisy is when it makes a storming and powerful intrusion upon a person, like flies landing on him even though he tries to drive them away.
4. Although Nathanael was not a deceitful man, he could still be a sinful man; and therefore Christ does not say that he was without sin, but without deceit.
Now I shall establish some doctrines from these words, taking a twofold consideration of this Text.
1. From a relative consideration of the same—that is, relatively, what is said or found in Nathanael.
2. From the absolute consideration—as the words are in themselves.
1. Regarding the words as they relate to Nathanael: This Nathanael was a very ignorant man; for when Philip told him that they had found the Christ, he said, "Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?" He could not conceive that anything good could come from Nazareth. And then again (for the second time), he doubted Christ's omniscience, saying to Christ, "How do you know me?" He was ignorant both of Christ's Divinity and omniscience; and yet of this Nathanael, who was so ignorant, Christ says that he was a man without deceit. From which we learn:
> That a Godly person can have much ignorance in his mind, and yet in God's estimation be without deceit in his heart.
And then, taking the words in their own meaning, you may learn this:
1. That it is a good testimony for a person who makes a profession of Religion to be such a one in whom there is no deceit.
**1.** We shall begin with the first: that a Godly person can be without deceit in his heart, and yet be very ignorant in his

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Nathanael's character, specifically addressing how spiritual sincerity ("lack of guile") can coexist with intellectual ignorance or human weakness. # The True Israelite 787

must. Weakness of grace exists alongside sincerity of grace: the children of God are sometimes compared to doves; now, a dove is not only harmless and innocent, but likewise a small and ignorant creature; so a person can be a harmless person without deceit, and yet be an ignorant person.

The Disciples of Christ themselves were ignorant of many things: as in **Matthew 15:16, 17, 18**, where Christ speaks of that great doctrine of original sin—that those things which come out of the mouth come from the heart and defile the man; and that from the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witnesses, blasphemies, etc. These are the things that defile a man. There it is said that the Disciples did not understand these things; although they were clear and well-known truths, yet they did not understand them. Likewise in **Matthew 16:6**, where Christ asks them to take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. And they reasoned among themselves, saying, "It is because we have taken no bread." And so again, when Christ rose from the dead, they would not believe it; they were ignorant of the doctrine of his resurrection, **Luke 24:45, 46, 47** and **Acts 19:2**. When the Disciples were asked about receiving the Holy Spirit, they answered, "We have not so much as heard whether there is a Holy Spirit." And yet all these men were Disciples of Christ and men without deceit. From this, you clearly see this truth: that Godly people may be very ignorant in their minds, and yet in the estimation of God, have no deceit in their hearts.

<margin>† Use.</margin>
The use I shall make of this will first be by way of caution. If it be so that people may be very ignorant in their minds and yet have no deceit in their hearts, then beware on this ground of allowing yourselves to remain in any ignorance while still thinking yourselves to be sincere; for although in some cases people may be ignorant in their minds and yet without deceit in their hearts, it is not so in all cases. Solomon says in **Proverbs 19:2**, "The soul without knowledge is not good." Just as I shall show you in these three particular things. Namely:

1. If you are ignorant and do not seek or labor for knowledge, this cannot coexist with sincerity: if you are like those spoken of in **Job 21:14, 15**, who say to God, "Depart from us, for we desire not the knowledge of your ways." Such ignorance cannot exist in a sincere heart. These are willingly ignorant, **2 Peter 3:5**. They were ignorant and desired to remain ignorant; they did not sigh for it, nor labor for the knowledge of the truth.

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
2. To be ignorant and yet stubbornly remain ignorant—this likewise cannot coexist with sincerity, when you are like those written of in **Psalm 82:5**: "They know not, neither will they understand." Godly people may not know, or they may struggle to understand; but only the wicked know nothing and *refuse* to understand.

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
3. To be ignorant and yet to hate knowledge—to strive further into ignorance and resist knowledge—that cannot coexist with sincerity; of this sort Solomon speaks in **Proverbs 1:29**: "They

<column-break/>

hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the Lord." And therefore, although this doctrine is true, it should not encourage or feed you in a state of ignorance.

Secondly, do not think to conclude for yourself that all knowledge in the mind is an infallible proof of the truth of grace in the heart; for there is a shadow of knowledge just as there is a form of godliness; therefore, do not conclude that an abundance of knowledge is a sufficient proof of sincerity. There are many people who have heads full of knowledge but hearts full of deceit. Such as:

First, when they only know things through teaching in their minds, and not through experience in the heart. **Psalm 51:8**, David says, "In the hidden part (the innermost) you shall make me to know wisdom." When knowledge exists only in the brain, it can be no proof of sincerity.

Secondly, to know with self-satisfaction; when a person is satisfied and content with himself and thinks he knows much; this is no proof of sincerity, as in **Habakkuk 2:4**: "His soul which is lifted up is not upright in him." Just as boils or swellings in the flesh are a sign of rot and corruption, so also, when knowledge makes one proud, it is a mark of an unhealthy heart.

Thirdly, to know things theoretically but not practically; to know and not to do; to recognize and not to practice; this is likewise no proof of sincerity in your heart.

3. Take this caution: you who are sincere Nathanaels, do not conclude against yourselves—because you have some ignorance—that you therefore have no truth or sincerity in you. Christ, you see here, speaks of Nathanael, who was a man of great ignorance regarding both Christ's Divinity and omniscience <note>Christ's all-knowing nature</note>, and yet He says of him that he was a man without deceit: and therefore I pray you that you do not pass hard judgments upon your souls; do not say, "We have no truth in our hearts," because you have little knowledge in your brains.

4. Take this caution: that sincerity of heart exists not only alongside ignorance of the mind, but likewise with many weaknesses in practice. David is said to have been a man after God's own heart, **1 Samuel 13:14**, and that he was a perfect man, except for the matter of Uriah; and yet he had many other stumbles and weaknesses; he was guilty of the hasty fury against Nabal, he committed injustice against poor Mephibosheth, he erred in the numbering of the people, and was guilty of many other faults. Likewise Jehoshaphat: he is said to have been a perfect man and to have done what was right in the eyes of the Lord, and yet his sins were very great; he joined himself in battle with Ahab at Ramoth-Gilead, **2 Chronicles 20:32**, although he was warned not to go, he went anyway: and he gave his son as an offering to an idol, and yet the Scripture says he was a sincere man before God all his days.

So much has been said of the first use,

### The Use of Caution.

# The True Israelite 788

where much ignorance can exist in the human mind, and yet no deceit in the heart. Let this then be a test for you, whether you—on Scriptural grounds, each one for yourselves, your consciences testifying to it—are people without deceit.

And to better assist you in this, I shall set out for you certain identifying marks, divided into three general main parts, and shall reveal to you an "Israelite indeed" <note>This refers to John 1:47, where Jesus describes Nathanael as "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile."</note>, a person without deceit.

1. In regard to his sinning against God.
2. In regard to his performing of duties toward God.
3. In regard to his walk and conduct among men.

These are the three general main points, and under these, I wish to note about twenty particular things as so many revelations of a person without deceit.

### First, a person without deceit may be
### discovered in regard to his sinning against
### God; and under this main part, I shall give you eight
### discoveries of him.

<margin>Psalm 119:1, 3</margin>
1. **Such a person** is one who does not give himself over to or allow himself the practice of the smallest sin; "Blessed are the upright in the way, who do no unrighteousness: but walk in His ways." That is, they do not allow themselves to indulge in injustice. "The evil that I do, I do not want to do," says the Apostle; a person who does not allow himself to do such things does not truly do them. <margin>Proverbs 16:17</margin> The highway of the upright is to depart from evil (that is), it is his ordinary habit and course. Likewise <margin>Isaiah 56:2</margin> An upright person keeps his hand from doing any evil. That is, he does not do evil willfully. And this is why the Apostle says of himself in <margin>2 Corinthians 1:12</margin>, "We have conducted ourselves in the world in simplicity and godly sincerity." And again he says in <margin>1 Corinthians 4:4</margin>, "I am conscious of nothing against myself; yet I am not justified by this." <note>original: "Ick en ben my selven geens dings bewußt"</note> There were some who accused Paul and condemned him for various things; but he says, "I thank God, I am conscious of nothing against myself"; That is, I do not practice sin knowingly, nor with a delight in order to obtain Heaven thereby; yet I am not justified by this. Such a one is an upright man and worthy of Heaven, who does not give himself over to the practice of known sin. So did David in <margin>Psalm 139:23, 24</margin>: "Search me, O God," he says, "and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts. And see if there be any wicked way in me: and lead me in the way everlasting." **This is the first mark.**

<margin>Psalm 19:13, 14</margin>
2. A person without deceit makes it a matter of conscience to resist small and hidden sins just as much as great and public transgressions; David says, "Cleanse me from secret faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me; then I shall be upright." A godly person keeps the Law as the apple of his eye; <margin>Proverbs 7:2</margin>. A tiny speck of dust damages the eye as much as a large splinter; just as hidden wickednesses and a little dust of sin disturb you as much as great mountains of transgressions. When you do your best against a Gnat <note>A reference to Matthew 23:24, "straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel."</note> as well as against sins as large as a Camel, that is a sign of an upright heart. An upright Nathanael, upon the conviction of a committed sin, is troubled in his

<column-break/>

conscience over the commission of small and hidden sins, just as much as for great and scandalous sins. Thus David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people; <note>2 Samuel 24; David's "numbering" of the people was seen as a sin of prideful self-reliance.</note> undoubtedly this sin was committed in the pride of his heart. Likewise, his heart struck him after he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe. It is a sign of an upright heart when a person melts over the breaking of the least jot or tittle of God's commands.

<margin>Daniel 1:8</margin>
3. He stands not only against all kinds of sins, but likewise makes it a matter of conscience to resist all occasions or inducements to sin that might lead him there. Daniel was an upright person in this regard. It is said of Daniel, who was a rising young man, that he would have no part in the King’s portion, but had purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portions of the King’s meat, nor with the wine which he drank. And what was the reason why he would not eat of it? The Interpreters differ here; some say he would not eat of it because it was forbidden under the Law as unclean; but most are of the opinion that he would not eat of the King's portions, nor drink of his wine, because if Daniel had lived at such a full table and indulged in the King’s delicacies, he might thereby have forgotten himself and fallen into insensitivity, and so have grown sluggish in his duties and services to God, and forgotten the calling of the Church. It would have led him to sin against God, and therefore he preferred to keep himself content with water and peas rather than involve himself in eating from the King's portion. This is proof of an upright heart; he hates the garment spotted by the flesh. <margin>Jude 23</margin>. He alludes to the garments of the Lepers under the Law; he who wished to flee from Leprosy had to flee from all those things which could cause it. Now, all you whose hearts can give you witness that you make it a matter of conscience to flee all inducements to sin, you are those people who are without deceit.

<margin>Psalm 19:13, 14</margin>
4. A person without deceit prays powerfully and forcefully against sin, more because it is such a great evil than because of the punishment for it. I shall give you a clear text for this: "Cleanse me from secret faults," says David. But why does he make this prayer to God? "So," (he says) "I shall be innocent from great transgression." He does not say, "cleanse me from secret faults so that I may be delivered from hell," but "so I shall be innocent from great transgression." He does not say, "so shall I be free from great correction," but "from great transgression." Thus, when you pray to be delivered from sin, you do so because you do not want to sin, much less set yourself against God. If you come to appeal to Heaven, praying against sin more because it is evil than because it carries punishment in its wake, then you pray sincerely, and this is a sign of a pious heart.

I can explain this discovery a bit more closely through a common parable: Beloved, suppose a child and a man are both placed near a house; now neither of them wants to touch a coal from the house, yet they differ in their reasons. The child does not want to touch the coal because it is hot and would burn him, but the man because it would soil <note>original: "befoetelen", meaning to dirty or smudge.</note> his fingers.

<meta>This page continues the list of identifying marks of a sincere person (a "True Israelite") started on page 788. It concludes the first section regarding a person's relationship to sin and begins the second section regarding their performance of religious duties.</meta>

# The True Israelite.

Thus, the ungodly sometimes leave off their sin and do not wish to commit it because there is a "sting" in the sin; they think they shall die and be damned for it, and therefore they will not commit it. But a godly person does not want to sin because—even if it did not damn their soul—it nevertheless stains and defiles it; God is dishonored by it, and it causes them to fall into disharmony with Him, etc. A sincere person hates sin more because it defiles them than because of the punishment it brings.

5. A person without deceit reveals their sincerity regarding sin in this: that they make a matter of conscience to direct their greatest strength and exert all their power against their "common" sins—the sins of their profession, or those to which they are most naturally inclined. This is proof of a sincere person, as you may see in that passage which I have often repeated: <margin>Psalm 18:24</margin> "I was upright before him, and I kept myself from my iniquity." Why? Were not all of David’s sins his sins? Yes; but he kept himself especially from that sin to which he was most inclined. A sincere person guards himself from his own wickednesses—that is, those evils to which he is most prone and suited. It is a remark I have from an old writer still living <note>Likely referring to a contemporary Puritan author the preacher admires.</note>, speaking on this subject: he gives proof of the sincerity of Job in the 31st chapter of that book, saying that merely turning away from sin is not sincerity, for many people's natures are naturally averse to certain sins. But this is sincerity: to withstand and fight against that sin which agrees with a person's nature and disposition. And so did Job; he stood against the sin of his eyes, which suited his disposition and nature; <margin>Job 31:1</margin> he says, "I have made a covenant with my eyes; why then should I look upon a young woman?" In this, he bridled the sin of his youth. Secondly, he says: "While I sat in the gate, I never oppressed the poor or the needy." That was the sin of his profession <note>Job was a magistrate or judge, "sitting in the gate" refers to his official capacity.</note>, which he resisted. Thirdly, he says: "I have never eaten my morsel alone, so that the fatherless would not have eaten of it." That was the sin of his circumstances; he was a rich man, yet he resisted his own greed. The person who resists the strongest of those sins to which their nature, profession, and circumstances are most inclined—this is truly a person in whose spirit there is no deceit.

6. In regard to sin, a person reveals their sincerity if they are more distressed by sin because it conflicts with the grace in their heart than because it conflicts with the glory of their soul; more because it makes them unfit for any good than because it robs them of good. There are many who can grumble against sin because it hinders them from what is beneficial, but not because it makes them unfit for doing good. Yet Paul murmured against sin because he could not do the good that he wanted to do: <margin>Romans 7:19</margin>. A sincere person resists sin because it makes them unfit and prevents them from doing the good they wish to do. And therefore, you who can appeal to Heaven that you murmur and are grieved over sin because it hinders you in your duties—in prayer, in reading and hearing God’s Word, etc.—you are truly sincere people.

<column-break/>

7. A sincere person can weep over the sin of their nature as well as over the sin of their life. This is a sincere person indeed: one who can complain as much about the "body of sin" <note>A term for original sin or innate human depravity.</note> which they carry with them, as about the outward sins of their body. On this point, Hildersham <note>Arthur Hildersham (1563–1612), a prominent English Puritan clergyman and author.</note> remarks and calls all people in the world to a text wherewith he proves that no hypocrite has ever truly mourned the sin of his nature—that is, the desire, lust, and inclination toward wickedness and ungodliness that is naturally in his heart. And therefore, you who carry around evil and impure natures which defile you and all your services, and yet can never complain or shed a tear over them—this is a sign that you are not good and sincere people. But when you look upon the body of sin that you carry with you as the primary burden and pack of your soul—as a block that hinders you in your duties and service to God—this is proof of a sincere heart.

8. A person without deceit maintains a suspicion and jealousy over their own heart. <margin>Matthew 26:21, 22</margin> When Christ foretold to His disciples that one of them would betray Him, those who were most free from that deed were the first to have a suspicion in their own hearts and cried out, "Master, is it I?" There are no people more jealous over themselves than the godly; no one prays more against hypocrisy: <margin>Psalm 51:12</margin> "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." O you whose souls can bear witness that you are fearful of sin and jealous over your false hearts—lest they betray you—and that you constantly pray against hypocrisy: know that these are certain proofs that you are true Nathanaels, people in whom there is no deceit. <note>Referring to John 1:47: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!"</note>

And thus I have concluded the first eight discoveries of a sincere person in regard to sin.

Secondly, a person reveals their sincerity in regard to their duties toward God in these three general ways:
1. A sincere person performs the duties of God from a right principle.
2. In a right manner.
3. To a right end.

First, he performs the duties of God from a right principle, and that in two ways:
1. A principle of Faith, and
2. A principle of Love.

1. From a principle of faith: and of this is spoken "the obedience of faith," <margin>Romans 16:26</margin> because all obedience, if it be sincere, must flow from faith.

2. From a principle of love; he performs all his duties out of love for God and His service. When Christ wanted to find out the sincerity of Peter’s heart, He asked him: "Simon Peter, do you love me?" <margin>John 21</margin>. He did not ask him, "Simon Peter, do you preach eloquently? Do you labor in the conversion of souls? Will you follow me?" but "Do you love me?" Do you preach in love, do you pray in love, do you do everything in love?

And if you do this: 1. Love is generous and does not think about how long you have been busy in the service of God; if you show love to God, you are liberal in your duties toward Him.

2. Love makes a person see as much delight in the performance of the duties themselves as in the answer and return of your prayers upon your head.

# The True Israelite.

3. The love which you bear toward God, and toward the duties you perform for Him, shall banish the love of sin and every unclean lust; just as David says in <margin>Psalm 119:163.</margin> 
> I love Your Law, but I hate falsehood and find it an abomination.

Now then, perform your duties from a true principle of faith in God and love for God.

2. A person without deceit <note>The Dutch "sonder bedrogh" refers to a person of absolute sincerity and integrity, often called "guileless" in older translations.</note> strives to perform their duties in a right manner, specifically in these four particular ways:

First, a sincere person makes as much a matter of conscience of the *manner* in which they perform their duties as they do of the *matter* or substance of the work itself.

Second, he strives that both the inward and outward man might be engaged in the performance of duties; <margin>Romans 1:9.</margin> "God whom I serve in my spirit." Likewise, David says in <margin>Psalm 103:1.</margin> 
> Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, praise His holy name. 

And of Ezekiel it was said that he served the Lord with his whole heart. You shall strive to apply both your inward and your outward man to the service of God.

Third, he sensitively mourns the sinfulness of his duties <note>This refers to the "impurity" or distractions that creep into even religious acts.</note> just as much as he returns from his prayers with heartfelt joy.

Fourth, he makes as much a matter of conscience to be attentive in secret duties before God as in public duties before men. In <margin>Song of Solomon 2:14.</margin> Christ speaks to His Church: 
> O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely. 

Some believe that Christ speaks here of His Church being in a sorrowful state; but others understand these words—"my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places"—to refer to the prayers of God’s people in secret. Therefore God says: "let me hear your voice, show me your countenance, for your voice is sweet and your countenance is lovely." Truly, such a person who makes it a matter of conscience to pour out his heart to God in secret—even if it be in a corner where no eye sees him nor ear hears him—is indeed a sincere person.

3. He reveals his sincerity in performing duties for a good end <note>The "end" here means the ultimate goal or motivation.</note> in these ways:

1. Seeking to obtain inward and saving grace through his duties rather than outward and common favors. Hypocrites perform duties, but it is for their outward advancement; however, a sincere person does them to obtain inward and saving grace and comfort through them. As David says in <margin>Psalm 4:7-8.</margin> 
> There be many that say, "Who will show us any good?" Lord, lift Thou up the light of Thy countenance upon us. Thou hast put gladness in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their wine increased. 

The godless assemble themselves for corn and wine, <margin>Hosea 7:14.</margin> not for inward grace, but for outward blessings.

2. The goal of a godly man’s prayer during any affliction is more to turn away sin than to turn away the punishment. Here you have a design of a godly man's heart.

<column-break/>

<margin>Hosea 14:3.</margin> 
> Shall I say, "Lord, deliver us from the prison," or "rescue us from the sword"? No; but say unto Him, "take away all iniquity." 

What was Pharaoh's prayer? <margin>Exodus 8:8.</margin> 
> Entreat the Lord, that He may take away the frogs from me and from my people. 

But a person without deceit prays: 
> O Lord, turn away from me my sins and corruptions.

3. A sincere person performs duties more to express his submission and obedience to the authority of a commandment than to relieve the pressure of a self-accusing conscience.

4. He performs duties more to have fellowship with God than to have a distribution <note>Or "handout."</note> from God. And thus I have concluded the second part, having given two "discoveries" of a sincere person: first, regarding his sins (in eight parts); second, regarding his duties to God (in three general branches: performing duties from a good principle, in a right manner, and for a right end).

3. I now proceed to the third discovery of a person without deceit, which shall be regarding his walk and conduct among men; wherein he shows his sincerity in several ways:

First, he is the same man in all company. He is not like cinnamon <note>The author uses "Kaneel" (cinnamon) as a metaphor for someone who is inconsistent or perhaps someone whose only value is on the "outside" (the bark). A sincere person does not change their character to suit the room.</note>, unable to please all sorts of people. If he is in bad company, he wishes to show a displeasure with their ways and strives to improve them; if in good company, he wishes to be taught by them. You cannot pull godly, sincere people from their course; they remain the same, wherever you find them, whenever you find them, and in whatever company you find them. He is like Aristides <note>Aristides "the Just" was an Athenian statesman renowned for his integrity.</note>; of whom it was said that you could as easily stop the Sun in its course as stop him from the administration of justice.

Second, it is a delight and a matter of joy for him to associate with the pious; and it is a sorrow to his heart to be among the godless or to have any fellowship with them. You find this mark in <margin>Psalm 15:2, 4.</margin> 
> He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart; 

you may know him by this: 
> In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the Lord. 

It is the joy of the godly to be among the pious, and his sorrow to be among godless men. So says David, "My delight is with the saints, and with those who excel in virtue." And again: 
> Woe is me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar! 

The inhabitants of Meshech were a rough and unmannerly people, as you may see in <margin>Genesis 10.</margin> And David, dwelling among these godless people and in the tents of Kedar—a wicked generation (Kedar was Ishmael's son)—he mourned his sorrowful state therein. So we read of Jacob, the forefather of the Israelites, from whom they all had their name, that he did not wish to be buried among a godless people, to show his separation from them. <margin>Genesis 49:29.</margin>

Third, a person without deceit reveals his sincerity in his dealings among men by this: that he so orders his walk as to give no offense to those among whom he lives, neither to Jews nor Gentiles, nor yet to the Church of God. You have an out-

# The True Israelite.

<margin>
Discoveries of a sincere man from his conduct among people.
</margin>
An excellent passage regarding this is Philippians 1:10. The Apostle prays that they might be sincere and without offense, which indicates that those who are sincere walk in their daily interactions without giving offense. The fact that Paul makes his sincerity evident in the course of his ministry may likewise be a proof of our sincerity in our Christian walk: 2 Corinthians 6:3. Paul gave no offense in anything, so that his ministry would not be slandered. Likewise, if you walk without giving offense in your Christian course, it will be a proof of your sincerity.

And thus I have finished these three general discoveries of a man without deceit, in respect of his sins, his duties, and his conduct.

<margin>Application.</margin>
We come now to the application <note>original: "toe-eygeninghe" — the process of applying a spiritual truth to one’s own soul</note>: and the use I shall make of this will be for the comfort of all you who have the testimony of a good conscience, that these marks of a sincere Nathanael <note>Nathanael is the biblical figure Christ calls "an Israelite in whom there is no deceit" in the Gospel of John.</note> are found in you. Know, to your comfort, all you sincere Nathanaels and people without deceit, that the Lord looks upon you as perfect men and women. If you have sincerity within you, the Lord values you as if you were perfect.

## John 1 verse 48.

> . . . Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.

<margin>2nd Sermon.</margin>
We come now to consider these words as a pure and sincere presentation; and then the Lord Himself shall be the subject.

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That it is a wonderful and great excellence in a Christian to be a person without deceit. In the handling of this doctrine, I shall first show you the excellence of this condition—being without deceit—and then come to the application.

I have set my thoughts on ten particular things in which the excellence of this quality is revealed.

First, sincerity, or being without deceit, has this excellence in itself: that if a person has a sincere heart, his sincerity shall cover a great multitude of sins and iniquities in him. Just as a hypocrite may do as many duties as he wishes, yet in terms of Divine acceptance, they are as if they were never done; so sincerity makes many committed sins and iniquities as if they were never committed in terms of Divine regard and disregard. The sincerity of a man’s heart without deceit covers all his sins. Just as you may see in David; there were many sins in him, such as his numbering of the people, his feigning himself to be mad <note>referring to David’s actions before King Achish in 1 Samuel 21</note>, his hasty swearing to the death of Nabal, his unjust distribution with Mephiboseth, etc. Yet his sincerity covered all his sins, so that God looked upon him as a sincere man, except only in the matter of Uriah. And so with Jehoshaphat; he had many great stumblings, such as:

1. He made a covenant with Ahab, a godless king, which was against God's command.

2. He undertook a battle with Ahab against Ramoth in Gilead, 2 Chronicles 18:27, 28.

<column-break/>

3. Although he was rebuked because of the covenant with Ahab, he nevertheless made a covenant with Ahab’s son a second time: 2 Chronicles 19:2. Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, "Should you help the godless and love those who hate the Lord? Therefore, great wrath is upon you from before the face of the Lord." And yet it says in 2 Chronicles 20:35, "After this, Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted very wickedly."

4. He gave his son in marriage to Ahab’s godless daughter, 2 Chronicles 21:6. And yet, notwithstanding all these iniquities, it is said of him that he walked in all the way of his father Asa; he did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the eyes of the Lord. 1 Kings 22:43.

I will give you but one more example, and that is in Asa, a pious man, and yet he had many failings: 2 Chronicles 16:10, 11, 12.

1. He was agitated and hateful toward the good prophet of the Lord, who recounted his sins and his danger to him.

2. He was so vengeful that he shut him up in prison.

3. He did wrong not only to the prophet but likewise to the people of the land.

4. When he was afflicted in his feet, he did not go to the Lord, but to the physicians.

5. The high places in the reign of Asa were not torn down, 1 Kings 15:14. And yet, notwithstanding all these, it is said, "The heart of Asa was perfect with the Lord all his days." 1 Kings 15:14. His sincerity was like a mantle or covering for all his iniquities. A person without deceit has the piety of his heart as a mantle to cover iniquity. But on the other hand, if sincerity is lacking, all the good that a person does is not acceptable and worth nothing; as was the case with Jehu. He had been zealous for the Lord his God, had destroyed the idol worship and the honors of Baal, etc. Yet because his heart was not sincere, God rejected him, notwithstanding all his service.

Secondly, this is also an excellence of a sincere heart: if our hearts are sincere and without deceit, then the sincerity of the heart shall fill up the lack in the measure of our grace. The lack of our grace is made up in the Divine estimation by the truth of our hearts. And therefore the Hebrews note <note>original: "mercken de Hebreen aen" — likely referring to the Hebrew word *Tam* or *Tamim*, which translators often render as both "sincere/upright" and "perfect/complete."</note> that the same word in the Hebrew language that means sincerity also means perfection, which indicates that he who is without deceit is also, in God's estimation, as if he were perfect and without sin. 1 Chronicles 12:33. Those coming out of Zebulun into the army, equipped for battle, are said to be men not of a double heart, or of a perfect heart; indicating that those who are of a sincere heart are of a perfect heart.

And it is from this that you often read in the Scriptures that perfection and sincerity are joined together: "Job was a man perfect and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil." Job 1:1. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the "True Israelite" and the excellence of sincerity (uprightness of heart), following the introduction to the second sermon on this topic. It specifically addresses how sincerity compensates for weaknesses and provides comfort in trials.</meta>

# The True Israelite.

"O Lord, remember now how I have walked before your face in truth and with a perfect heart." All these passages clearly and nakedly reveal to us that the truth and sincerity of the heart in God’s estimation compensates for the lack of the <term>measure of grace</term> <note>A theological concept referring to the varying degrees of spiritual gifts or strength a believer might possess; the author argues that being "sincere" is more important than being "highly advanced" in spiritual status.</note>.

And therefore, it is worthy of your observation (in what I am presenting to you) the question which *Christ* posed to *Peter* in John 21:15: *Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?* You have sinned against me more than these, and do you now have greater love than these? But *Peter* does not answer Him regarding the quantity, but rather the quality of his love: "I love you," though not more than these. Regarding this, one observer notes that although we may not love, fear, and honor God more than others, yet if we fear, serve, and love Him in truth, the sincerity of our hearts will fulfill and make good the lack of our grace. *Christ* asked about the measure of *Peter's* love; *Peter* answered according to the truth of it; and yet *Christ* accepted this as an answer to His question.

Thirdly, to be without deceit has this excellence in itself: it is a comforting reinforcement against the fear of death. Oh, what comfort this will be to a person—to have within them the approval of their conscience, that they have lived without deceit in this world—when you come to depart from this world. We read in Isaiah 38:1, 3: When the sentence of death came upon *Hezekiah*, saying: *Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.* Then *Hezekiah* prayed to the Lord and said, "O Lord, remember now how I have walked before your face in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes." This observation comforted him against the sentence of death pronounced against him. I have read of one who, lying on his deathbed and being asked if death were terrifying to him, answered, *No*; for he had the testimony of a good conscience, that he had walked in simplicity and godly sincerity in this world; and therefore he said, "My heart tells me that I need not fear death at all." Another, being asked the same question, answered: "I thank God that I have not lived in such a way that I need to fear death."

The fourth excellence of sincerity is this: it shall refresh the heart against all scandalous slanders that are cast upon a person by the wicked. It may be that the wicked reproach you for going to a sermon, or for carrying a Bible under your arm to church, as if you did it like the hypocrites. Now, the testimony of your own conscience shall be as a strong bulwark against all their rebukes. As in 1 Corinthians 4:3, 4, where *Paul* says: *But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by a human court... for I know nothing against myself* <note>original: "ick en ben my selven geens dings bewußt" — an older way of saying 'my conscience is clear regarding these charges'</note>; as if he would say, "My conscience does not accuse me of that which you charge and reproach me with, and therefore I do not worry about it; it is a very small thing to me to be judged by you, since I am not conscious of anything in myself." So said *Job* in Chapter 31, verses 35, 36, 37: *Oh, that I had one to hear me! Behold, my desire is that the Almighty would answer me, and that my adversary had written a book! Surely I would carry it on my shoulder; I*

<column-break/>

*would bind it on me like a crown. I would declare to him the number of my steps; like a prince I would approach him:* (that is) I want to go toward him with an unbowed heart. The sincerity of *Job's* heart allowed him to speak this freely against all the rebukes cast upon him by his friends. Likewise in Job 27:5, 6, he says: *Far be it from me that I should justify you; till I die, I will not put away my integrity from me.* Herein lies the excellence of a heart without deceit; such a person can unburden themselves before God, notwithstanding all the slanders and contempt which the wicked cast upon them. *Politianus* <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), an Italian Renaissance humanist and poet.</note> (though he was not known for sincerity) could say: "Some flatter me, others slander me; but I hold myself no better for the one, nor worse for the other; just as I do not consider myself taller in the morning because my shadow is long then, nor shorter at noon because my shadow is short then." How much more then may a sincere Christian say so!

Fifthly, sincerity comforts and encourages a person under suffering for *Christ's* sake: it will make a person willing to suffer from the hands as well as from the tongues of men. It will make them like a steel wall against all oppressions. 2 Corinthians 1:12: there *Paul* says that although they had the sentence of death in themselves, nevertheless, it was their joy and gladness to have the testimony of their conscience, that they had conducted themselves in the world in simplicity and godly sincerity. And in 2 Timothy 1:7, the Apostle says: *For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind.* The spirit of fear is there contrasted with a sound mind and power—that is, the power to endure oppressions and persecutions.

Now, hypocrites are like stubble or fabric that gets wet: they are troubled and tremble in the time of oppression. Isaiah 33:14: *The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness has seized the hypocrites: Who among us can dwell with the devouring fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?* But herein lies the excellence of sincerity: that it makes a person full of courage even in the time of oppression and persecution.

Sixthly, a sincere person also wants their heart to be known; just as *David* said in Psalm 139:23, 24: *Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my thoughts. And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.* Thus *Job* was not concerned with what people said against him, because he knew his own sincerity; "I will show him my steps, I will challenge him with my whole life; let us see what he will accomplish; I am so pure in my own conscience that I would approach him like a prince." I want to come to Him, not mournfully like a slave, but boldly like a prince. A sincere person wishes their <term>bosom to be made of crystal</term> <note>A common 17th-century metaphor for total transparency and honesty, where one's inner thoughts are visible to all.</note>, so that everyone might see into their heart.

Seventhly, yet another excellence is this: as hypocrisy fights against all grace, so sincerity fights against all sins. Sincerity is not like other particular graces; for those only fight against their specific impulses, just as humility fights against pri-

<meta>This page continues the sermon on "The True Israelite," specifically detailing the final points (eight through ten) of why sincerity or "uprightness of heart" is a superior spiritual virtue. It transitions from the previous discussion on sincerity as a shield against death to its role in spiritual growth and divine favor.</meta>

# The True Israelite.

pride and lust against passion; zeal against sloth; and the fear of God against the fear of men, etc. But sincerity fights against the whole <term>body of sin</term><note>A theological term referring to the total corrupt nature of humanity rather than individual bad acts.</note>, just as much as against any particular sin of the body. Sincerity causes a person to cut down all his lusts, so that no hidden things shall rise up against him any longer, but he desires to extinguish them all together with the assistance of God. The first special weapon of which you read in Ephesians 6:14 is "the belt of truth." Now, sincerity is that which binds the truth together within you and makes you strong against all sins and hidden evils that might try to force their way into you.

¶ Eighthly, a sincere heart has a greater capacity to have an increase of grace and to make greater progress in the <term>divine ordinances</term><note>The established means of worship and spiritual growth, such as prayer, reading scripture, and the sacraments.</note> than anyone else in the world. <margin>Psalm 92:12</margin>Psalm 92:12: *The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.* There the righteous shall grow. Among all the types of soil into which <margin>Luke 8:8</margin>the seed was cast in Luke 8:8, there was only one ground in which the seed fully rose up, which was the good earth: the good and sincere heart of a man. And therefore it is well <margin>1 Peter 2:1</margin>noted by Peter in 1 Peter 2:1, where the Apostle drives him and all believers toward growth under the ordinances; first he prays them to lay aside all malice, and all deceit, and all hypocrisy, and then, as newborn babes, to desire the rational, pure milk, so that they may grow thereby. Sincerity is the way to obtain an increase of grace and to grow through the ordinances. The seed of God’s word will not grow to any perfection in rotten, hypocritical hearts; whereas a sincere heart is of such a quality that it constantly increases in grace.

¶ Ninthly, sincerity brings a glorious luster and appearance to all the gifts and graces in a person; you cannot say your gifts are <term>saving graces</term><note>Gifts that lead to eternal salvation, as opposed to "common graces" or natural talents which even non-believers might possess.</note> until your heart is sincere; but sincerity is of such a nature that it causes your gifts to be true graces. What is faith but a fantasy if it is not <margin>1 Timothy 1:5</margin>unfeigned? 1 Timothy 1:5. What is love but flattery if it is not without <margin>Romans 12:9</margin>hypocrisy? Romans 12:9. What is wisdom but a <term>Machiavellian</term><note>Refers to the political philosophy of Niccolò Machiavelli, associated here with cunning, deceit, and worldly pragmatism rather than godly wisdom.</note> and <term>Ahithophel-like</term><note>Ahithophel was King David’s counselor who betrayed him; his name became synonymous with a treacherous and wicked advisor.</note> policy if it <margin>James 3:17</margin>is not without hypocrisy? James 3:17. What are all your good works but "shining sins" <note>original: "schijn sonden" — a reference to the Augustinian idea that the seemingly good deeds of the unregenerate are actually sins because they lack the right motive of faith.</note> until sincerity is in your heart? Good deeds in an unregenerate heart are like a precious ring in the snout of a swine, or a pearl on a dung-heap; but on the contrary, sincerity brings a glorious luster and appearance even to small and common gifts.

¶ Tenthly, the excellence of a sincere heart is evident in this: because the promises of God run most and foremost toward the sincerity of our hearts, rather than toward the <term>measure of our graces</term><note>The quantity or strength of one's faith or spiritual abilities.</note>. God does not say, "I will do this or that for you if you are strong or have such a measure of grace"; but they primarily concern the sincerity of the heart. <margin>Psalm 145:18</margin>Psalm 145:18: *The Lord is near to all who call upon him: to all who call upon him in truth.* <margin>Psalm 18:24</margin>Psalm 18:24: *The Lord rewarded me according to my righteousness [sincerity].* <margin>Proverbs 14:11</margin>Proverbs 14:11: *The tent of the upright shall flourish.* <margin>Psalm 84:11</margin>Psalm 84:11: *The Lord God is a sun and shield; the Lord will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from those who walk in sincerity.* <margin>Psalm 125:4</margin>Psalm 125:4: *The Lord does good to the good, and to those who are upright in their hearts.* <margin>Psalm 112:2</margin>And Psalm 112:2: *The generation of the upright shall be blessed.*

These promises of God generally flow in this channel—not because of the measure of grace, but because of the truth of it; and therefore this is a wonderful excellence in sincerity; this gives you instruction in all the promises of God.

I may add to this: a person of a sincere heart is in such a state wherein the Lord desires to reveal His counsel and will to him more than to anyone else in the world who has an impure heart. I shall explain this to you by this parable: suppose you had two servants in your house. One of them was light-fingered and sought to steal from you whatever he could get in secret. Now, for such a person you lock your doors, keep a sharp eye on him, and trust him no more than you absolutely must. But your other servant, whom you know to be faithful, you give your own eyes to, and trust him with your cash box; you involve him in your business, reveal your counsel to him, and tell him the secrets of your trade—and that because you have found him to be a faithful servant.

Truly, so does the Lord deal with His people. The hypocrites are like flighty servants, and therefore the Lord looks at the divine truth in them. But where God sees sincerity in the heart, so that He can say, "I have experience with this man or woman, that they are old and faithful servants," He can trust them with His treasures and graces; and therefore He will reveal Himself to them and open His whole heart to them. If God has found you faithful before Him, He will deal with you as you deal with faithful servants: He will reveal His secrets and counsels to you.

And thus I have finished the instructional part of this point: that there is a communicative benefit and excellence in being a person without deceit; which I drew from the very consideration of these words. We come now to the application, in which I shall be brief for the present, as I have spoken of it at other times.

<margin>The Use.</margin>The use that I shall now make of this will be for comfort to all of you who can rightfully claim this wonderful excellence of sincerity for yourselves—you who are true Nathanaels, people in whom there is no deceit. Let other people boast in other things; nonetheless, you have a greater cause for joy than any person in the whole world. Let the Church of Rome boast that their church is the true Church because it is universal, unique, great, or old; nonetheless, if you only have sincerity, you undoubtedly have the assurance of eternal life. The <term>School-men</term><note>The Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages and early modern period, known for their complex logical arguments and academic rigor.</note> may boast that they have found sound judgment, subtle writing, strength of memory, and the like; nonetheless, although you lack all these things, you can boast above all these that you have a sincere heart. And when you have that, you have more than all the gifts of the philosophers—yes, more than all the people in the world have who are without grace. You may thank God that, although you have nothing in this world, you are nonetheless happy—yes, eternally happy—if you only find a truly sincere heart within you. He who has a diamond or a pearl of great value has more than he who has many heaps of stone...

2. **By way of lamentation:** If it is true that being without guile is such a wonderful excellence, then may this teaching give us cause for lamentation / considering how many hypocrites there are in the world / and how few Nathanaels <note>A reference to Nathanael in John 1:47, whom Jesus called a "true Israelite" in whom there was no guile.</note>: The Lord may rightfully say against us,

<margin>3rd Use.</margin>
3. **By way of instruction:** Is it such a wonderful excellence in a Christian / to be without guile? Then I may take from this these three instructions: Namely /

**First** / through this you can see the shamefulness and villainy in the nature of a hypocritical heart; if it is such a great excellence / for a person to be without guile / what a hateful thing it is then for a person to have a guilty and a hypocritical heart? I shall show you the hatefulness of this in these specific things.

1. Deceit and hypocrisy in the heart / corrupts all the duties and services that you come to perform for God; herein lies the hatefulness of the same / that it makes all your duties disregarded by God. So it was with Jehu, although he did many good things / nonetheless / because he did not walk in the ways of God / with an upright heart / the Lord sees and accuses Jehu as a murderer / his deeds only being good in their outward substance; Hosea 1:4. God says / I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu. Hypocrisy or deceit in the heart is like a Fly in the box of ointment / spoiling all your duties; or like poison in the pot / that poisons everything: So hypocrisy poisons all duties that you perform for God. Just as it is told of a precious stone / of wonderful power / that if the same is placed in a dead man’s mouth / it loses all its power: So also / Prayer and other duties coming from a hypocritical and deceitful heart / lose all their power and operation.

2. The hatefulness of this sin appears in this / that / deceit in the heart shall rob the person of those common gifts / which God has given him. Counterfeit graces soon fade and die away. Just as Christ speaks of it / Luke 8:18. Whosoever hath, to him shall be given; and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have. That which the hypocrites have in appearance / shall be taken from them; not only the gifts but also the graces wither and die; as you may see in the example of the bloody Bonner <note>Edmund Bonner (c. 1500–1569), Bishop of London, notorious for his role in the persecution of Protestants during the reign of Mary I; he was often used in later sermons as an example of a fallen or false leader.</note>, who / at first was an excellent Preacher; but having hypocrisy in his heart / he soon brought to nothing all gifts and graces / and he confessed that he had lost the gift of preaching. A painted child, though ever so costly and excellent / loses more and more of its luster and beauty / and becomes worse and worse; but a living child grows and waxes from one day to the next. Painted graces may shine for a time / but before long their luster perishes and becomes vain.

3. Hypocrisy and deceit / so hardens a person's heart / that he cannot convert himself from that hypocrisy / which is in his heart 

<column-break/>

is. 1 Timothy 4:2. The Apostle speaking there of some says / that through the hypocrisy of liars they have their own conscience seared as with a hot iron. A deceitful heart / is a hard and seared heart; it makes conversion a heavier work than it otherwise would be.

4. A heart full of deceit is hateful / in the respect that it brings a person to all errors and heresies. A person who has an unhealthy heart / will hardly have a healthy head / and a pure judgment. As you read in 1 Timothy 1:19 <note>Original text cites 1:18, but the quote is from verse 19.</note>. That those who have put away a good conscience, concerning faith have made shipwreck. Those people who put away a good conscience / shall not long preserve a pure judgment. Hypocrisy will speak evil just as well as godlessness will act: it leaves a person open and plunges him into error. If the heart wishes to fall into evil practices / the mouth and the mind will easily carry damaging reasons and feelings. A pure faith cannot well be preserved in an impure conscience. Acts 20:29. ... Grievous wolves shall enter in among you, not sparing the flock: He refers / not only to open Tyrants / but hypocritical deceivers / Wolves in Sheep’s clothing / who have an appearance of Holiness and Godliness (but not the substance itself); these lie and cry out like gentle people / luring the Sheep to them / and so they fall upon the flock.

5. The hatefulness of the same appears in this / because God has more displeasure and heavier punishment for hypocrisy and the hypocrite / than for anyone else in the world; and therefore when God wants to punish known sinners / he says / his portion shall be with the hypocrites, Matthew 24:51.

Plutarch tells of a certain Thespesius <note>Thespesius is the protagonist of a myth in Plutarch's "On the Delays of the Divine Vengeance," who supposedly died and returned to life, describing the punishments of the afterlife.</note>, that he saw Hell in a vision / and seeing therein those who had mimicked the service of the true God and served him deceitfully / with a hypocritical heart / he saw that they, among all others, enjoyed the greatest torments among the damned. To this purpose serves / that of Ezekiel 14:7-8. Where God says: 

> Every man of the house of Israel, or of the stranger that sojourneth in Israel, which separateth himself from me, and setteth up his idols in his heart, and putteth the stumblingblock of his iniquity before his face, and cometh to a prophet to inquire of him concerning me; I the Lord will answer him by myself: And I will set my face against that man, and will make him a sign and a proverb, and I will cut him off from the midst of my people. 

A person who thinks to be godly / and nonetheless has deceit in his heart / I will strip him away from me, says God; as if no one could punish a hypocrite enough until God himself did it.

This is then the first instruction / that since there is such excellence in a person without guile / that you then notice the harmfulness of a deceitful and evil heart.

**Secondly** / if this be so / then shall this doctrine be an encouragement for you / to drive out all hypocrisy and to purify your hearts / and to gird your loins with the belt of sincerity and truth. We have a proverb among us [Girded is blessed] <note>The Dutch original "omgort, omzeegent" refers to the idea that being prepared or "girded" (as in the armor of God) leads to being protected or blessed.</note> although I do not say that this is the absolute truth / nonetheless know this from me / that if you are girded with this belt of truth / you are blessed / O therefore purify this deceit out of your hearts.

<margin>4th Mark.</margin>

All you who are upright Nathanaels <note>Refers to the "True Israelite" in whom is no guile, from John 1:47.</note> have here these comforting remarks as supports for your spirits.

1. You must make a distinction / between having hypocrisy / and letting hypocrisy reign in your hearts : everyone can have hypocrisy / even though he labors ever so much against it : but where hypocrisy reigns / there is deformity / all evil / and no laboring against it.

2. Notice that you distinguish / the doing of things with hypocrisy / and in hypocrisy. 3. Notice that you must have an assuring witness in your own heart / that you are no hypocrite / if you have these three properties in you / which are such / that no true child of God can be without the same : and for a hypocrite it is not possible / that he has these things.

1. You are not hypocritical / if you seriously bewail your own hypocrisy and the sin of your nature. It is Hildersham's observation <note>Arthur Hildersham (1563–1632), a prominent Puritan theologian.</note> / in order to banish hypocrisy / to bewail the sin of nature; there is never a godless person who bewails his own hypocrisy / or mourns over the sinfulness of his own nature. And that is why Paul was never sensitive / or troubled over the sins and sorrows / which were in his heart / before his conversion / but afterwards he cried out / O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of death. *Romans 7:24.* And therefore / you who bewail your hypocrisy / and murmur against the sin of your nature / that body of death that you carry about with you / this is an infallible proof / that you are born again.

2. If you are experienced in the mortification <term>mortification: the spiritual practice of subduing one's sinful desires and passions</term> of your inclined lusts; hypocrisy may have some struggle against sin / but a godly person strives and fights in all seriousness against all sins. Now / if you can appeal to Heaven / that all your sins grieve you / and that you hate them / even your sweet and beloved sins / it is a proof that you are free of hypocrisy.
