# The Misfortune of Ingratitude.

<margin>
*Lesson.*
</margin>
[Hezekiah] <note>Though not named, the text refers to King Hezekiah of Judah, who became ill after the miraculous defeat of the Assyrians.</note> did not praise God enough for that glorious blessing against Sennacherib and his Army; therefore the Lord sent him a deadly sickness, because he had not glorified God for that great benefit of deliverance.

<margin>
*Practical Use.*
</margin>
Beloved, the Lord knows whether our ingratitude—amidst present benefits, or peace, or being spared from the devastation of the sword—might move the Lord to send heavy Judgments upon us.

Fifthly, it shall stop the stream of future blessings, so that they do not flow upon us; Ingratitude not only holds back God's present benefits, but likewise corrupts and prevents other blessings from coming upon us in the future.

Thus, I have finished these two lessons regarding the number of these persons.

### 3. Concerning the comparison between the number of those who returned and praised Christ, and those who did not do so; there were nine who did not return, and one was grateful; Where are the nine? From this, note:

<margin>
*Lesson.*
</margin>
That among a multitude of people who receive benefits from Christ, commonly the greatest part of them do not return with joy to thank Him for the same. I shall make only a brief use of this: to make you marvel at the greatness of God's Benefits, that He shows them to such people whom He knows will not thank Him for them. Oh, praiseworthy generosity of God, who shows us mercy when we do not wish to glorify Him for it: <term>Luke 6:35</term> <note>A verse emphasizing that God is kind even to the ungrateful and the wicked.</note>. The Lord is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. He bestows His graces upon those who do not wish to run to Him for them.

<margin>
*Objection.*
</margin>
Objection: But some will say, does not the greatest number of people who have received benefits from God return to glorify Him? Although it is true that then, nine out of ten did not do so, nonetheless, I hope that it is not so now?

<margin>
*Answer.*
</margin>
Answer: I wish that it were so; and so that you do not deceive yourself, I shall give three signs by which you may be certain whether you are one of these ungrateful ones who does not return to glorify God for benefits received, or not.

<margin>
*Three signs by which we may know if we are ungrateful for received benefits or not.*
</margin>
1. If the feeling of one affliction under which you live swallows up the comfort of a thousand benefits which you enjoy, then you are an ungrateful person. And this revealed the ingratitude of the Israelites toward God in <term>Exodus 17:3</term> <note>Where the Israelites complained about a lack of water shortly after being delivered from Egypt.</note>. Because they lacked water, the people murmured against Moses and said: *Why have you brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?* One affliction in the wilderness made them forget the great benefits and works that God had shown them in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness; all those received benefits were swallowed up by one pressure. If you are grateful, you will say with Job (under every affliction or loss), *The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.*

<margin>
*1st Sign.*
</margin>
2. An ungrateful person makes a wicked interpretation of the forthcoming acts of God's providence, just as those did in <term>Deuteronomy 1:27</term>. *They murmured in their tents and said: Because the Lord hates us, He has brought us out of the land of Egypt to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to destroy us.*

<column-break/>

Because God hates us (they say), He has brought us out of the land of Egypt. Yet God nonetheless promised to guard their feet, that He would bless them and make them into a great nation.

You, who because of one affliction can grumble against God and make wicked conclusions about His sharing and the reaching out of His providence, you are the ungrateful one.

<margin>
*3rd Sign.*
</margin>
3. This is an ungrateful person: one who shows no more good works even as they receive more benefits; for he is not grateful who only praises God with the mouth, but he who loves Him at the same time. True gratitude consists in obedience and work for God’s sake. When God places mercies upon our heads, we should labor to work grace and obedience into our hearts and lives. Actual grace consists in a ready obedience to God. You must not judge your gratitude by what you say of God, but by what you do for Him. When you add grace to grace, and duties to duties, just as God adds mercy to mercy; then you are truly grateful. Otherwise, you shall be reckoned among the number of these nine ungrateful lepers. *And were not the ten cleansed? Where are the nine?* So much for the third Lesson.

### 4. From the consideration of the different dispositions in these nine lepers: before they were cleansed, they cried with a loud voice, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us"; but after they were healed, they had no thoughts of Christ. They were praying for their healing, but not praising after they were healed. Lesson from this:

<margin>
*Lesson.*
</margin>
That it is very natural for man to desire grace when they lack it, and yet to be negligent in thanking God for His benefits once they have enjoyed them.

The reason for this is man's own self-love which reigns in him, which looks more to his own good than to the glory of God; and looks more toward obtaining benefits when he lacks them than returning to praise God when he has enjoyed them. Many people (says <term>Bernard</term> <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential French abbot and mystic.</note>) are earnest in desiring benefits and impatient until they receive them, yet ungrateful once they have obtained them.

<margin>
*Many receive importunately until they have received restlessly, and when they have received, they are ungrateful. Bernard, On Consideration.* <note>Original Latin: "Plerique accipiunt importuni donec acceperint inquieti, ubi acceperint ingrati." The OCR "Plenisque" is a likely error for "Plerique."</note>
</margin>
Let us look at ourselves in this mirror, whether we are of this sort or not. And let us be humble, acknowledging with gratitude the grace we have obtained through prayer, and let it not be that our praise bears no comparison to our prayers.

<margin>
*1st Practical Use.*
</margin>
Many people are like that Sailor of whom we read in Turkish History, who was in fear of shipwreck at sea; a great rising storm brought the ship into danger of soon being in pieces. In this gesture, he makes a covenant that if he were delivered, he would offer as a sign of gratitude a wax candle to the Virgin Mary as thick as the Mast of his ship. But when he reached the shore (and his promise came to mind), he then resolved to light a candle of half a pound.

So it is with many of us: when we are in need, then we make covenants and promises of better obedience; but when we receive those benefits we desire, then we turn our backs on our expression <note>Literal: "turn with the bottom to our expression," a colloquialism for reneging on a vow.</note> and forget to thank Him for it. We have reason to be humble because we often—

# The Misfortune of Ingratitude.

...since they have enjoyed benefits, and yet having received them, are ungrateful for them; someone has made a good observation regarding Jonah (he says) that the sailors with whom Jonah was in the Ship, being in danger of Shipwreck, all turned themselves to prayer, each to his own God, for mercy and deliverance; but there was no mention made that any of those returned to thank God for His mercy after they were delivered. Many people under heavy oppressions make covenants and promises of a better life, to walk more humbly and holily before Him; and yet afterwards they return again to their old sins.

<margin>
2. Practical Application.
</margin>
2. For exhortation; be encouraged in the fear of God, that those benefits which you obtain through prayer, you would use with gratitude; never receive anything without honoring Him; pay those promises that you made to God before you received anything from Him: when you promise to God that if He gives you such a thing, you shall praise, serve, and love Him, fulfill those when you have received the benefit from Him, just as David says in Psalm 66:13. *I will pay my vows to you, which my lips have uttered, and my mouth has spoken when I was in distress.* Now that I have my benefit, God shall have His praise. It is our nature, when we are sick, to promise something; "Oh, if God would restore and heal me, I would become a new person, and live a holy life, and never do as I did before," etc. And yet, when God restores us, we forget our promises, and return like <term>the dog to his own vomit, and like the washed sow to her wallowing in the mire</term> <note>A reference to 2 Peter 2:22 and Proverbs 26:11, describing a return to sinful habits.</note>.

And thus I have finished the first part of the Text: the complaining or rebuking question of Christ; *Were not the ten cleansed? but where are the nine?*

### LUKE 17, verses 17, 18.

> And Jesus answering said, Were not the ten cleansed? but where are the nine? Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?

<margin>
Sermon.
</margin>
Now I come to the second part of my Text: *Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?*

Before I actually handle the words, I shall give you this caution: to beware that you do not twist this History into a wrong sense; and say that these nine lepers were an example of the <term>rejection of the Jews</term> and the calling of the Gentiles, as some would have it. Such as Gorrandus and Gualterus <note>Nicolaus de Gorran (13th c.) and Rudolf Gualther (16th c.) were prominent biblical commentators.</note>: But this is a true Historical account of what happened, and not a symbol of some future matter. Beloved, why do we need to bring this History to that purpose, while there are sufficient explicit Scripture passages that prove such a thing? My text is only a Historical account of ten lepers, healed by Christ.

And regarding this one leper who (after he was healed by Christ) returned to give glory to God, I shall briefly note these things for you.

This one leper of whom Christ speaks, as you see from the circumstances of the Text,

<column-break/>

you shall find that he was a man worthy of praise, and willing to obey His commands; This you shall see, if you consider the great obstacles that might have hindered him from coming to give Christ glory.

1. He might have said: there are nine of my companions healed as well as I, and they have as much cause to honor God as I; am I wiser than all those who are healed? If they want to go with me, I will go too; otherwise, if I return alone, I shall stand out above them, and consider myself wiser than the rest, and such like. Beloved, had any of us been in his state, this objection would have taken more place in a thousand of us than in him alone. This poor leper overcomes all these difficulties, and though he can obtain no company, nevertheless he determines to go to Heaven alone; from which I wish to note this:

->That it is more profitable to do good alone, than<-
->to do evil with the multitude.<-

Had this man taken an example from others, he would have been ungrateful like the rest; but he thought it better to do good alone than to do evil with company. Joshua also took this path in Joshua 24:15. *Choose you this day whom you will serve, whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.*

To do well alone is a good and pleasing distinction, but to do evil with a multitude is a shameful conspiracy against God. When you walk in lonely ways you have God for your company, while you follow good things, 2 Timothy 4:16, 17. *At my first answer no man stood with me, but the Lord stood by me.* Such a person may say, as Christ did in John 16:32. *You shall leave me alone, and yet I am not alone.* And as the Philosopher spoke; *Never less alone, than when alone* <note>original Latin: "Nunquam minus solus, quam cum solus." A famous quote attributed to Scipio Africanus.</note>. He was never less alone than when he was most alone. I shall note two or three things from this, and then proceed.

1. If a Godly person will not do as a Godless person does, nor run with others in the same outpouring of unholiness, he does not look upon this as a peculiar whim, but he simply does not want to sin as they do.

2. Beware of making examples the rules of your conduct; but let the Scripture be your Rule, according to which you set your deeds; had this man taken examples as his Rule, he would never have come to Christ. Exodus 23:2. *You shall not follow a multitude to do evil; nor incline after a multitude to pervert justice.* If you live like the multitude, you live like the worst. Ephesians 2:2. Elijah made the Scripture his Rule, following God, although he was nearly alone, 1 Kings 19:14. It is better to go to Heaven alone without a predecessor than to go to hell with a great company, or to be damned by following examples. Loneliness is in some cases not only lawful, but also praiseworthy. Sometimes we must not take an example, but give an example to others.

3. Be certain that if you differ from other people in the world, you shall separate yourself from them; do not stand out in peculiar fantasies, but in peculiar holiness and gratitude.

I know that there is a fantastical and peculiar...

# The Misfortune of Ingratitude.

of their imagination / which consists in the vanity of the mind / this is an evil isolation / and so that you may be better instructed in this / I shall give you these identifying signs of it.

First. A fleshly isolation / causes a person to separate themselves from the greatest, holiest, and best of people; when a person lives as the worst, and yet specifically walks apart from the best of the people among whom they live. Now, a holy solitude does not separate a person from the pious but from the wicked and evil; and the most ungodly part of humanity; that is the language of the Apostle, he does not wish to run with others to the same outpouring of wickedness.

Second. You can recognize an evil separation by this; such a person wants to be separated from others, even though he is divided from the Church of God.

When a person, for small and trivial things, walks against the godly, thereby creating disturbance in God’s Church and offending their weak brothers; this is an evil separation. When people separate themselves from others and gather churches outside of the Church, not when there are faults, but when there is restoration, and there is no necessity to do so.

Third. An evil separation / consists only in trials and circumstances, and not in the essence itself.

This is a separation we must guard against / harmful and vain when it stands alone; but true solitude is as good alone as it is in company. Of these things, I speak only in passing.

The second ambush / which might have hindered this <term>leper</term> <note>original: "Melaetsche"; a person suffering from leprosy, often socially ostracized in biblical times</note> from coming to Christ is this: Christ commanded all the lepers to go and show themselves to the Priest; now the Text says they all went away after they were healed. Therefore, this leper might have thought: if I return to give honor to Christ and obey Him, I shall be disobedient, for He has commanded me to show myself to the Priest. He might have reasoned within himself: if I go to the Priest, it may be that I will not find Christ afterward to give Him honor; or if I go to Christ first, He might ask, why do you not follow my command and go to the Priest? But finally, he considers that going to the Priest was only a ceremony of the Law, but returning to give honor to Christ was a moral duty; therefore, he judges the latter to be better than the former. From which we can observe:

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That it is wisdom in a person to maintain that order in their Christian course, making less of small duties than of great ones.

When two duties come together in comparison / to leave the small aside and fulfill the great. Thus God says: *I desire mercy and not sacrifice*; that is, when both of these appear, I want mercy rather than sacrifice.

<margin>Application.</margin>
The use I shall make of this is for rebuke and correction / of those who make a great deal of small and trivial duties, and yet are very lazy and negligent in great and weighty services. Of these, it is spoken in *Matthew 8:21*. Christ called a Scribe to follow Him, and he says: *Lord, let me first go and bury my Father.* This was only a

<column-break/>

ceremony / and a natural duty to his dead Father, which made him slow in the moral duty of following Christ.

Some people are of such a nature that they are drawn away from weighty matters by small opportunities. Had this leper been so, he would never have come to give Christ honor, and he would never have been such a man whose name shall be remembered as long as the world stands—the one who glorified God above the nine others.

This Doctrine likewise rebukes those who are very scrupulous about small and minor matters, but negligent and careless in greater services, like the Pharisees in *Matthew 23:23*. They were careful in <term>tithing mint, dill, and cumin</term> <note>A reference to the Pharisees meticulously giving a tenth of even their small garden herbs while ignoring justice</note>, simple and minor things, and yet negligent in great matters, omitting the weightiest parts of the Law: judgment, mercy, and faith. Likewise Saul; he was afraid to eat the blood of beasts and yet he made no conscience of shedding human blood. *1 Samuel 22:17*.

So too were the Jews afraid to stain their clothes with blood, yet they made no conscience of having the shedding of innocent blood upon their hearts. Beloved, this is nothing better than gross and great hypocrisy. And thus much for the two obstacles that might have hindered this leper from coming to Christ to honor Him.

Now we come to the second part of the Text / *were there none found who returned to give glory to God except this stranger?* Here it is to be noted that Christ does not say, "to give me honor," but "to give God honor." From this place, we can refute the doctrine of the <term>Arians</term> <note>A theological group that denied the full divinity of Christ, arguing he was a created being</note>, who deny the divinity of Christ; for the Text clearly proves that Christ is God, because the leper gives honor to Christ, and the Scripture counts that as honor given to God. But I shall not dwell on this, and instead explain a bit more what it means to give God honor. You must know that one does not give God honor by doing something "worthy" for His nature, for God is infinite and incomparably glorious, so that nothing can be added to Him; rather, giving God honor is nothing other than acknowledging the greatness, excellence, and glory of God which is in Him.

And there are specifically two things in which the Scripture explains giving honor to God consists. Such as:

1. In the confession of our sins against God / *Joshua 7:19*. Joshua says to Achan: *My son, give the Lord, the God of Israel, the glory, and make confession to him.*

2. An acknowledgment that all the benefits we receive come from God / *Psalm 50:23*. *Whoever offers thanksgiving, honors me.* And so in my Text: this leper gave honor to Christ through the knowledge he had received regarding the benefit and healing from Him.

*And were there none who returned to give God honor except this stranger?* Nine forgot the benefit of healing; only one stranger remembered it. Now here are three points of instruction / I will speak only of the last two and then I shall end.

Regarding the character of this leper who returned to give Christ honor, the Text says / *he was a stranger,* and in the verse before my Text, it says that he was a Samaritan. Now the Samaritans were idolaters; their religious service was composed of...

# The Misfortune of Ingratitude.

Heathens and Jews / they served the God of Israel and the idols of the land; yet this one <term>Samaritan</term> <note>Samaritans were an ethnic and religious group often despised by the Jews of the time; his gratitude is highlighted as an example of unexpected faith.</note> gave God glory / while the other nine Jews / did not return to do the same / even though they had even more reason to do so. Learn here:

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That God sometimes makes lowly persons from unknown places in the world into great instruments of His praise.

David from a shepherd became King / in place of a shepherd’s staff / he received a Royal Scepter / and from living in a shepherd’s hut / he came to sit upon a Throne. And so / Bethlehem of Judea was the place / in which Christ was born / the least among thousands in Israel / no place so poor / despised, and lowly as this; I could bring forth more examples but let us move forward.

<margin>1st Reason.</margin>
->The reasons / why I state these / are /<-

First / To preserve your hearts from burden and discontent; suppose you live in a dark and isolated place / and you can find no apparent means of deliverance or protection for yourself / nevertheless remember that the Lord can work deliverance even from dark places / and caves / and the Lord can rescue people from such to be instruments of His glory / and for the good of His people.

<margin>2nd Reason.</margin>
Secondly / You are exhorted (you whom God has made into Instruments of His glory / held in regard among men / and in that place where you live) to thank Him and to make the name of God great; It may be that God has brought some of you / out of lowly places into this pleasant <term>Country</term> <note>original: "Contreye"; likely referring to the Dutch Republic, which was seen by many 17th-century inhabitants as a land of divine blessing and prosperity.</note> / and has given you here great estates / riches / and made you people of standing and faith / therefore labor to give God glory / and return to praise Him for His benefits and blessings.

Again / from the observation of the varying effects / regarding one and the same benefit received / by these ten lepers / I pray you take note; There were ten lepers all sharing in the same benefit / cleansed of their leprosy / at the same time / and yet notwithstanding / the same benefit / at the same time / produced such a different effect upon them; For nine of these are ungrateful / and only one returns / to give God glory; From this, learn:

<margin>Doctrine.</margin>
That the same benefit, the same deliverance, and the same blessings of God, do not have the same effects upon the hearts of men.

It may be that God gives another person as many benefits as you / and yet his riches make him thankful / humble, and generous / while the same things make you ungrateful / proud, and unmerciful. The same Sun makes the Wax soft / and the clay hard / gives a pleasant scent to the pleasure gardens / and a great stench to the stagnant pools; So also the same grace of God has various effects upon the hearts of men.

<margin>1st Application.</margin>
The application of this is; Do not conclude that God gives you His benefits / in His grace / until they produce those effects upon your heart / for which God sent them. If another grows more in holiness / humility / and thankfulness through grace / and is fruitful in good works; and you grow more in wickedness / godlessness / and a shameful life / it is a sign that these were not given to you in grace. The nine lepers / had the same benefit / as the other / but they did not have that same benefit / bestowed upon them in grace.

<column-break/>

The same good does not have the same effect on our hearts; as in the services of God / the same sermon / makes one person humble / so that he thanks God for the word which he has heard / and the same sermon makes another hardened as stone / so as not to accept the word.

We are accustomed to saying / that food which is good for one person / is poisonous to another. So also the same benefit is useful to one person and venom to the other. It is a cord that binds some people to Christ / and separates others from Him.

Oh! therefore you who enjoy the same benefits with the children of God / labor to use them so / that they may have the same effects on your hearts as on theirs.

I have but one more observation / and this is taken from the number / of those who gave Christ no glory / and the one who returned to praise Him.

That there are only a few found among many, who give Christ Jesus glory for all His benefits.

Beloved / one would think / that it would have been right / for all ten of them to have given God glory; and yet only one acknowledges the benefits of Christ. I shall give you only four proofs for this point.

1. It appears that only a few are found among many / who thank God for benefits received / if you consider the portion of Heathendom in the world / and those who live therein / for they give God no glory; as the Apostle says / <margin>Rom. 1, 21.</margin> The <term>Heathens</term> <note>original: "Heydenen"; referring to the non-Christian world.</note> who know God, have not glorified or thanked Him as God. The Heathens, being unconverted, gave God no glory.

2. The Jews / who were the church of God / many of them did not thank God as was proper. <margin>Psal. 106, 21.</margin> They forgot God their savior, who had done great things in Egypt, Jer. 2, 6. They did not say; where is the Lord, who brought us up out of the land of Egypt? who led us in the Wilderness. — <margin>Hos. 13, 6.</margin> After that, according to their pasture, they became fat; when they became fat, their heart was exalted; therefore they have forgotten me.

3. It is so / because such is the wickedness of the last times and ages of the world / that those who make a profession / to give God glory in many duties / shall be found wanting. <margin>2 Tim. 3, 1, 2.</margin> In the last days perilous times shall arise. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, &c. It is a good explanation which a theologian / has regarding this passage / he says / just as old age brings bad humors / so in the last of days there shall be corruption in morals.

4. God’s own people are often very negligent in this duty. <margin>2 Chron. 32, 25.</margin> <term>Hezekiah</term> <note>original: "Jehizkia"; the King of Judah who, despite being healed, initially failed to show proper gratitude to God.</note> did not render again according to the benefit done unto him. Now if the people of God are negligent in this / and do not return / to thank God for His benefits / what can you expect from the godless and the children of wrath?

The use of this is for correction / to awaken you to the fear of God / to have no part with these nine Lepers / but with this one / that you, as His people, thank God / and give Him glory / for all His benefits. And to this end, I shall give you eight motivations /

# The Misfortune of Ingratitude.

...here by way of observation / and here by way of comparison.

To encourage you through these observations / listen:

<margin>2nd Application</margin>
1. Observe / that thanks for a benefit received / is the way to receive more; he who is thankful for a benefit he has received / shall receive more and greater graces: **Psalm 40:10-11.** <note>Original: "Psal. 40, 11, 12." The numbering in 17th-century Bibles often differs slightly from modern ones.</note> David says, *I have not hidden your righteousness within my heart; I have spoken of your faithfulness and your salvation: I have not concealed your lovingkindness and your truth from the great congregation. Do not withhold your tender mercies from me, O Lord: let your lovingkindness and your truth continually preserve me.* The best way to receive more blessings / is to thank God for those which we already have.

2. Observe / that the glory of God is the true purpose / of His giving. God's gifts are not meant to exalt us in the world / but so that His Name might be glorified.

<margin>Teaching</margin>
3. Observe / that you have no glory to expect from God when you die / if you have not been an instrument to give God glory / while you lived. This is a sound argument that Christ used in **John 17:4.** *Father,* He says / *I have glorified you on earth; and now, O Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was.* If you can truly say this and appeal to God / when you die / "O Lord / I have glorified you on earth / glorify me now with you in Heaven"; this is a very powerful evidence for being with Him above / otherwise how could you pray or expect / that God will glorify you in Heaven / when you were never careful to glorify Him on earth.

4. Observe / that if God receives no glory from you / He will nevertheless be glorified in one way or another. Although you do not wish to give glory to Him / nonetheless He can take it for Himself / in your destruction and damnation / He can be glorified in His justice and power / when He destroys you. As God demonstrated His power in His judgments upon Pharaoh / so He can display His glory in your destruction / just as well as in your salvation: God will have glory from you / if He is not glorified through you.

So much for the observations / now I only have comparisons left here / which shall greatly urge you to fulfill this duty.

1. Compare your graces <note>In this context, "graces" refers to God's favors, blessings, or mercies.</note> and afflictions together.

2. Compare your graces / and your gratitude together.

3. Compare your graces / and your sins together.

4. Compare your graces / and the graces of other people together. And if all these do not move you to glorify God / you will never do it.

<margin>Application for Reproof.</margin>
First / compare your graces and afflictions together / graces flow upon you like a stream / but afflictions fall upon you like drops / for every one affliction you have a hundred benefits. It may be that you have had a month of sickness / but for the most part of your life you have been healthy. A person in the worst state / enjoys more mercies / than afflictions / because his entire life is a greater mercy / than any affliction that comes upon him / be it a cross or a disturbance: For, *skin for skin, and all that a man*

<column-break/>

*has, he will give for his life.* <note>A reference to Job 2:4, emphasizing that life itself is the greatest earthly blessing.</note> And therefore the Church says / **Lamentations 3:39.** *Why then does a living man complain?* If he is a living man, he has more reason to thank God for His mercy / than to complain about any affliction. **Ecclesiastes 7:14.** *In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider; for God also has set the one over against the other.* The meaning of this is / that God weighs the afflictions against the graces. If you are prosperous / thank God for it / just as you must endure the affliction; the Lord sets prosperity against adversity / and so must you also do / set your benefits against your sufferings / and see if the number of the former shall not be greater / and more than your afflictions: the greatest support for our ingratitude / is because we look at our miseries through a magnifying glass, but our blessings through a diminishing glass. When David wept over the death of his son / *O Absalom my son, my son, would to God I had died for you!* Had David set a good Solomon against a wicked Absalom, it would have moderated his sorrow. If you set your blessings against your afflictions / and weigh the one with the other / you shall find that your blessings / far outweigh your sufferings. I remember what I have read of an old man / who (in the last two years of his life) was visited by God with a heavy sickness / and those who were around him wondered / how he could be so patient / under such great affliction / and endure it with such a meek spirit. He answered them, "I have been healthy for many years, and have only lain in great affliction these two years; therefore I have more cause to thank God for many years of health, than to complain to Him about two years of sickness."

2. Compare your graces and your gratitude together; Alas, poor and weak creature / you are scarce in thanking / and abundant in receiving benefits. And although you decrease in gratitude / nonetheless your graces increase in abundance. Shall God cause graces in us / and we show no gratitude? What reason then have we to complain? God performs many and great benefits for us / we offer little and small gratitude to Him / shall this not move us to magnify His Name?

3. Compare your graces and your sins / and this will move you to thank God. Notwithstanding that you have committed great sins / nonetheless see how many graces and benefits you enjoy. Oh, that we could lift up our hearts to thank God for all those blessings / observe that we have committed great sins in the place where we live / and yet we enjoy glorious benefits in that same place / God mingles His blessings / why should our households / not be households of affliction just as much as they are households of sin? O thanked and praised be the name of God who does not deal with us according to our sins / nor reward us according to our iniquities.

4. Compare your grace / with that of other people / and then you shall have cause to thank God because He has set you far above many of your brothers in the world; You eat the good and drink the sweet / while many of God's children eat the bread of affliction / and drink the waters of adversity. The Lord gives you the sweet to drink / while others drink tears in their own blood. Compare...

# Instructions to listen profitably.

## L U K E  V I I I. verse 18.
The beginning of the verse.
*Take heed, then, how you hear, etc.*

<margin>Preached at Aldersgate <note>Likely referring to a parish in London where "Morning Exercises"—a series of Puritan sermons—were frequently held.</note> during a morning exercise held there for a month.</margin>
Beloved, I intend to spend this hour only in delivering this sermon as a preparation for a morning exercise, which shall be held in this place for a month.

It shall be my care and earnest consideration to exhort such godly people to these morning exercises who are fit for it; and I hope you will take care to prove this not only with your ears, but especially with your works. I shall take care of *what* you hear; it is your task to see *how* you hear.

*Take heed, then, how you hear.* We must not only see *what* we hear and *whom* we hear, but likewise *how* we hear. In these words are two parts:
1. An earnest warning that Christ gives: *take heed, then, how you hear.*
2. A reason for this warning, expressed in the word *then*: *Take heed then how you hear.*

Why?
Answer: Because there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed: just as He looks upon your faces, so Christ sees your hearts, and He notices your innermost thoughts and ways, and how you serve Him in His duties; *take heed, then, how you hear.*

<margin>1st Observation.</margin>
From this warning that Christ gives here, we can observe that Christians must not only see the person *whom* they hear and the matter *what* they hear, but likewise also the manner *how* they hear God’s word.

<margin>2nd Observation.</margin>
From the reason for this warning, note further that the consideration of God’s all-seeing eye—which sees and takes knowledge of your behavior as you approach Him—ought to move you to take heed in what manner you hear God’s word. The all-seeing eye of God shall be a motive for us to restrain our hidden sins. As Job says: *I have made a covenant with my eyes; why then should I think upon a young woman? For does the Lord not see my ways and count all my steps?* <note>Job 31:1, 4.</note>

But I shall not dwell on these things, but I shall only speak some practical things from these words to you. And the Lesson on which I shall stand shall be the very words of my 

<column-break/>

Text; and therefore it shall be unnecessary to bring up many more passages to provide proof for it.

->Doctrine: Christians must necessarily take heed how and in what manner they hear God’s word.<-

The reasons for the confirmation of this Doctrine shall be these, being taken from within this Parable. For this seed, given here by Christ, is but a concluding reason of the preceding parable of the four kinds of hearers; our Savior winds it all up in this warning when He says that we must take heed how we hear. The reasons, then, are:

1. Because most hearers in the world hear poorly; and therefore you must see how you hear. There is only one of the four kinds of soil <note>Referring to the Parable of the Sower earlier in Luke 8.</note> that hears God’s word rightly; indeed, most people are idle hearers of the word, therefore let us take heed.

2. The second reason in this parable is this: because the Devil seeks to hinder you in a great part of your hearing. Therefore you must take heed how you hear; in the 12th verse of this chapter, when the seed was sown, *Then comes the Devil and takes the word away from their heart, so that they should not believe and be saved.* Now, if the Devil is so diligent to prevent the actual workings of the Word upon your heart, should there not be care to hear with attention and without distraction when you come into God’s presence? The Devil deals with us in the hearing of God’s word just as he did with the children of Job: it says that when they came together before the Lord, Satan came in the midst of them. So also, when we come into God’s presence to hear His word, the Devil stands at our right hand to pull our thoughts away from paying attention to it. In Genesis 15:11, it is said that when Abraham made an offering to God, the birds of prey came down to peck at it; which signifies (says Diodati <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a Protestant theologian famous for his Bible translations and commentaries.</note>) the constant attack and destruction that the people of God face from Satan to pull them away and hinder them in the performance of the holy duties they are about. Therefore, *Take heed then how you hear.*

3. You must see how you hear, because if you do not, the word shall not only be ineffective for you, but also very harmful. You find this in the 16th verse: *No one* (says Christ) *when he has lit a candle, covers it with a vessel or puts it under a bed, etc.* This text must not be applied to the Preachers of the Word, for it is not to be understood of *their* light; rather, this must be applied to the *hearers* of the Word. Now, says Christ, the light that they have must not be hidden under a vessel or under a bed. Regarding this, one writer well observes: that if a candle is placed under a bed, not only is the room not lit, but the bed and the man on it are in danger of being burned. So that person who lies under the means of grace and under the communication of the Word, but does not take heed how he hears, is like a man who has a candle under his bed; he is in great danger of the fires of hell, just as the other is in danger of being burned by physical fire.

4. Take heed how you hear, because God’s great all-seeing and fearful eye takes knowledge of the conduct of your heart and the endurance of your spirit while you hear. Thus the Apostle makes this an argument...

# Instruction on how to hear profitably.

<margin>
Teaching.

Because of the angels. <note>original Greek: διά τὰς ἀγγέλους</note>

(1 Corinthians 11:10) why the Corinthian women had to have a covering on their heads as a sign of their subjection to their husbands, "because of the angels." He says: *For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.* Therefore, we must take much more care how we hear, not only because the angels of Heaven are present there in the assembly of the saints when they come to Divine Service, but because the God of the angels takes knowledge of the forming of your hearts and of the condition of your spirit when you are before Him. This reason is grounded in the 17th verse of this chapter: *For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.*

<margin>
3. Reason.

Reason.
</margin>
5. The last reason is because God withholds His blessings until we express a conscientious care in the hearing of His Word; and this we have in the words of our text: *Take heed then how you hear, for whosoever hath, to him shall be given: and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have.* Thus, that person who hears God's word out of a mere habit—even that which he thinks he has shall be taken from him. And therefore, *take heed how you hear.*

Now I shall set down some practical things by way of application regarding what has already been said, and then conclude. And so that I might urge upon you this advice which our Savior gives us here, I shall present to you these seven instructions.

First, *take heed how you hear*, being prepared for the Word of God. Just as the preacher must take care to find out suitable words, so must the people labor to bring suitable affections <note>In this period, "affections" refers to the holy desires, emotions, and orientation of the heart.</note> to the Word. In the Holy Place <note>The inner chamber of the Tabernacle.</note> there was on one side a Table or tablet, signifying the tribes of Israel, and a Candlestick on the other side, signifying the Service of God, and the incense-burning in the middle, which is prayer; this was a sign that when we come to the service of God, we must hear with attention and pray with affection.

<margin>
Reason.

They attended with one accord. <note>original Greek: Πρισείχον ὁμοθυμαδὸν</note>

All the people hung [on Him]. <note>original Greek: ὁ λαὸς ἅπας ἐξεκρέματο. Latin: *pendebat*, i.e., *inhiabat*, meaning they hung upon his words or gaped with eagerness.</note>
</margin>
Secondly, hear the Word not only readily, but also attentively, like those mentioned in Acts 8:6: *And the people with one accord gave heed unto those things which Philip spake.* Likewise in Nehemiah 8:5, 6: When Ezra opened the Book of the Law and read it in the presence of all the people, they all stood up; and when he pronounced the blessing of the great God, all the people answered, *Amen, amen,* with the lifting up of their hands. Likewise in Luke 11:48 <note>Likely a citation error for Luke 19:48.</note> it is said that all the people hung upon Him and heard Him. And therefore, those who hear the Word with wandering eyes, wandering thoughts, and sleepy bodies, they cannot hear it attentively, but rather to their own destruction. And let them remember that while they hear the Word so sluggishly and sleepily, the Devil is neither sluggish nor sleepy. Let such hearers read the history of Eutychus <note>Eutychus was a young man who fell asleep during a long sermon by the Apostle Paul and fell from a third-story window (Acts 20).</note> in Acts 20:9 and meditate upon it. And so are those to be rejected who hear the Word of God with an unsettled countenance, wandering from place to place; for it is said in Nehemiah 8:6 that when Ezra read the book of the law, all the people stood up.

<margin>
Reason.
</margin>
Thirdly, hear the Word of God retentively. Labor to keep that in your memory which you hear to be useful to you

<column-break/>

in the practice of your life: for hearing is not only for the sake of knowing, but for doing. Those who hear must be like the Ark was; that was the storage place for the vessel of Manna, so must this Manna of the Word of God be locked up in your heart. A good hearer (Luke 8:15) hears the Word of God with an honest and good heart and seeks to keep it. In Isaiah 42:23 the Prophet says, *Who among you will give ear to this? who will hearken and hear for the time to come?* Who will lock up the Word for the time [ahead], so that it may afterwards have a lasting impression on your heart?

Fourthly, hear the Word of God with understanding. Christ exhorts the multitude that they should hear and understand. Just as the palate tastes food, so must the ear distinguish doctrines; as Job says in Chapter 12:11, *Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat for itself?* And in Hebrews 5:14 the Apostle says, *Those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.* Those who know that the Word is a sound and practical preaching; one must not be like a sponge during the sermon, taking in everything without distinction, but with understanding searching the Scriptures to see if these things truly agree with one another. Mercerus <note>original: "Merner," likely referring to Jean Mercier (Mercerus), a 16th-century Hebraist.</note> on Job makes a good observation: that the original word for "ear" signifies a scale or balance; showing that we hearers must also be weighers, not only using a touchstone to see if it be true or false, but likewise a balance to see if it has weight or not. If one were to weigh all the doctrines of our time in the balance of the Sanctuary, how many would be found too light!

Fifthly, hear the Word of God with appropriation. Even if a patient is given excellent advice or a healthy medicine is prescribed, if he does not apply it to himself, it will help him no more than if he had never known it. And Beloved, there is not one among us who should not apply to himself that which he hears in the preaching of the Word: such as in the rebuking of the soul over the greatest sins, of which I may be or might be guilty; for even if the guilt were such as if I had already committed it, yet if God brings me to myself, I may be guilty of it. Therefore, hear the Word by appropriating it, and say with David: *I will hear what the Lord says to me.*

Sixthly, hear the Word of God with Reverence. Because our God is a consuming fire, not only the godless but also the people of God shall look upon God with this understanding. Some people come from God with such a familiar knowledge that they afterwards end up with a contempt for God, which we thought they would not do. But rather notice that our God is a consuming fire, and let us therefore serve Him with reverence and godly fear. It is very true that through Christ we may go to God with a holy concern and assurance, as to a Father; but moreover, we must go out of ourselves and come into His presence with a humble reverence.

Seventhly, you must hear the Word of God obediently, coming with a hear-

<meta>This page continues the practical application of the sermon on Luke 8:18. The preacher is transitioning from the theological reasons for attentive hearing into specific instructions on how the congregation should prepare their hearts before and during a sermon.</meta>

[...an] obedient heart, ready and prepared to submit yourself to all the instructions, admonitions, and rebukes of the Word of God; just as those of whom it is spoken in *Acts 10:33*: *We are all here now present before God, to hear all the things that are commanded of you by God.* Such a formed and ordered heart you ought always to bring to the hearing of God's Word; be willing to submit yourself to it, and even if you had a thousand necks, bow them all under the obedience of the Word (as a German theologian <note>Likely a reference to a Protestant reformer such as Martin Luther</note> says). Hear the word with fear. We read of an "un-hearing ear"; why? The ear is for hearing, but the meaning is: hear obediently.

Is this what we must do: see how we hear?

1. Then by way of admonition, see to it that you do not come unprepared; beware of coming into God’s presence with unclean and un-humbled hearts.

2. See that you do not come to the hearing of the Word with a malicious spirit; there are many in these times who come to the hearing only to interpret it poorly and to catch the Preacher <note>original: "Predicant"</note> out if they can; they forget all the good material of the sermon, but if there is any thing not well or appropriately <note>original: "pertinentelyck"</note> put (according to their understanding), that they hold onto in order to criticize, while letting all the rest go.

3. Do not hear the Word "attachment-wise"; do not hang too much upon the hearing, or the prayer, or any other service. You must make your duties your paths, but not your Christ. Many times the Lord preserves and withholds the working of His word from the hearing, because you rely too much on the act of hearing the word or on the Preacher. When the Israelites fought with the Philistines and suffered defeat, they attributed their loss to the absence of the Ark; but when they had the Ark with them, they fared worse than before. And a theologian <note>original: "Godtsgeleerde"</note> gives this reason for it: because they committed idolatry with the Ark and leaned too heavily upon it.

And therefore, in the hearing of the Word, lean

<column-break/>

not so much on your own strength, or on the Man, or on the matter that he preaches; for although the matter is good, nevertheless this is the way to make this benefit vain for you. Just as in Prayer: we should prepare ourselves for this duty as if we had no spirit in Heaven to help and strengthen us, but when we have fulfilled that duty, we must look upon ourselves as if we had not said a word of our own, but that Christ had prayed in us and done all in all for us. And so when we have heard a sermon <note>original: "predicatie"</note>, we must look to Christ and desire His blessing upon the same, that it may not remain only a voice, but be joined together with the work for which it was sent, and be powerful to note the good of our souls.

5. See how you hear, and be brought in the Lord to the practice of this rule on this ground: because the Lord, according to the measure of His blessings upon the word, answers your care in the hearing of the same.

The Lord requires in us an equal care in the use of the means for the growth of these graces in us, for which He has established these means. *With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again.* Sometimes this is applied to works of righteousness; just as you judge others, so also will God do to you. And sometimes to works of Mercy; give a full over-measure, for with what measure you mete, you shall be measured again; God will repay the love you have shown to others.

But another Evangelist <note>The author refers to Mark 4:24, where the "measure for measure" proverb is linked directly to hearing the word</note> brings this proverb to the hearing of the Word: *see how you hear, for with what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again.* That is: just as you "measure" the word in your preparation <note>original: "voorbereydinghe"</note> for it before you come to the hearing, so will God in turn "measure out" profit to you—blessings after you have heard it, and powerfully work the profit of the word upon your hearts, as a reward for your preparation and care in receiving it. See then, how you hear.

### Mr. CHRISTOPHER LOVE.

### Of Prayer in general.

<margin>Question.</margin> What is a Prayer?
<margin>Answer.</margin> It is an uplifting of the heart to God / in the Name of Christ / through the assistance of the Spirit / for the obtaining of that which we need for both Soul and body.

<margin>Question.</margin> Why do you call upon God in prayer, and not the Saints and Angels?
<margin>Answer.</margin> Because God alone is all-knowing / so as to know all our deficiencies / and also almighty / to give us all that we desire / insofar as it may serve for His Glory and our own good.

<margin>Question.</margin> What does it mean to say that you call upon God in the Name of Christ?
<margin>Answer.</margin> By the Name of Christ is understood the worthiness of Christ / so that when I call upon God in Christ's name / this is my meaning / that God the Lord would hear me for the sake of the merits / and worthiness of Christ.

<margin>Question.</margin> Why do you call upon God through the assistance of the Holy Spirit?
<margin>Answer.</margin> Because I do not know what I should pray for as is fitting, but the Holy Spirit comes to the aid of my weakness. Romans 8 verse 29. <note>The text cites Romans 8:29, though the reference to the Spirit helping our infirmities in prayer is found in Romans 8:26.</note>

<margin>Question.</margin> How might someone know whether they pray through the assistance of God’s Spirit, or through the power and strength of natural gifts?
<margin>Answer 1.</margin> Whoever prays through the Spirit / has both a feeling and strong workings of his affections as well as a full expression of words; but whoever prays only through the strength of natural gifts / has only an extension of words but seldom or never warm and active affections.
<margin>Answer 2.</margin> He who prays by the assistance of the Spirit / sees his own weakness / in performing any duty; and therefore he is most highly humble / after he has performed his duties to the very best / because he knows / that it was Christ’s strength / and not his own / by which he was helped. But he who only prays through the power of natural gifts / is puffed up / and becomes proud / after he has outwardly performed the required duties.
<margin>Answer 3.</margin> Whoever prays through the help of the Spirit / strives constantly and without ceasing for those things / for which he prays / but the other sits still and idle / and he does not strive with all the

<column-break/>

powers of his soul to put into practice and to obtain / that for which he prays.
<margin>Answer 4.</margin> Whoever prays through the Spirit / pours out his Soul just as fully / when he is in private before God alone / indeed he then often has a sweeter communion with God / than he had with others in public. But he who only prays through the power of natural gifts / can only do so when he is in the public assemblies of the saints / but he has no secret enjoyment of God alone: but when he is in his private chamber / then he is vain / empty / dead / and distracted.

<margin>Question.</margin> How must one pray, if one is to pray well?
<margin>Answer 1.</margin> With an actual realization of God’s Majesty.
<margin>Answer 2.</margin> With a deep sense of our own misery.
<margin>Answer 3.</margin> With fervency of the Spirit.
<margin>Answer 4.</margin> With faith in His promises.

---

### An explanation of the Lord’s Prayer.

<margin>Question.</margin> How many things are to be noted in the Lord's Prayer?
<margin>Answer.</margin> Three things. 1. The preface. 2. The petitions. 3. The conclusion.

<margin>Question.</margin> Why is it called the Lord's Prayer?
<margin>Answer.</margin> Because the Lord Jesus Himself made it and gave it to His Disciples / as a prescription for Prayer.

<margin>Question.</margin> Are you bound in Conscience <note>term: "Conscience" (Conscientie) - the inner sense of right and wrong, often viewed in this period as a court where one is accountable to God.</note> always to use the Lord's Prayer, whenever you pray?
<margin>Answer.</margin> No / this prayer was only given as an example and a rule of prayer / to know from it / how and what I must desire from God: Christ’s intent was not to bind me to certain words in every prayer. I read throughout the Gospel / that Christ often prayed other prayers with other words / and so also did His Apostles and Disciples: If they then were not bound to it at that time / so I cannot be bound to it now.

<margin>Question.</margin> Which is the Preface of the Lord’s Prayer?
<margin>Answer.</margin> Our Father, who art in Heaven.

<margin>Question.</margin> What do you learn from this, that in praying you call God your father?

### The Marrow of the

Answer. I learn three things from this; namely:
1. That whenever I wish to pray / I must then come to God with the obedient heart of a child, Malachi 1:6. **If I be a Father, where is my honor?** 
2. That I must then have a firm trust of the heart / that I come to a Father / who will not refuse me / for we have received this comfort and encouragement from Christ, Matthew 7:11. **If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?**
3. That I must strive to obtain a heart / which submits itself to God’s will / since God is my Father: now fathers know well / what is best for their children / even better than the children themselves.

Question. In how many ways is God a Father?
Answer. In three ways / namely:
1. Through Creation / and so He is a Father of the whole World / being the work of His hands.
2. Through Generation / and thus He is a Father of Christ / who is born of Him. <note>In traditional theology, "Generation" refers to the eternal relationship where the Son is "begotten" of the Father.</note>
3. Through regeneration or rebirth / so He is a Father of all true believers. Romans 8:15, 16. **For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.** <note>Abba is an Aramaic word for "Father," used here to show an intimate relationship with God.</note> Galatians 4:4, 5.

Question. Why do you say in the Lord’s prayer, *Our Father*, and not, *my Father*.
Answer. To show / that I am as much obliged to pray for others as for myself.

Question. How do you say that Heaven is the place where God is, since God is everywhere?
Answer. Because God reveals and shows His glory in / and from Heaven in a most excellent way.

Question. What do you learn from that, when you say that God is in the Heavens?
Answer. 1. That I must come to prayer with reverence and fear / since I do not call upon a great Prince of this earth / but God who is in the Heavens.
2. That my Enemies shall not hinder the hearing of my prayers: for God who hears the prayer / is in Heaven / where the godless are not / and never shall be.
3. That although God is everywhere / nonetheless His Glory shows itself most of all in Heaven.

Question. Why do you say in the Lord’s prayer, *Our Father*? And when you recite the Creed, you say, *I believe in God*.
Answer. Because every person must believe for themselves: another’s faith cannot save me / but their prayers can do me good.

Question. Which is the first Petition in the Lord’s prayer?
Answer. *Hallowed be Thy Name.*

Question. What is understood by the Name of God?
Answer. The Name of God is taken in the scriptures for the works of God / for the attributes of God / and for God Himself.

Question. What is understood by hallowing God’s name?
Answer. To honor and glorify God in His attributes.

Question. What do you pray of God in this petition?

<column-break/>

Answer. I desire / that the great God may be honored and glorified by me and by all people in His name / nature / and glorious attributes of His power, justice / wisdom, and goodness.

Question. How do you hallow or glorify the Name of God?
Answer. 1. When my aim and His end in everything is the honor and the glorification of God.
2. When I praise God with a thankful heart because of His mercies. Psalm 50 verse 23. **Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me.**
3. When I am steadfast in an irreproachable conduct <term>conduct: "ommegangh," referring to one's social dealings and moral behavior</term> with the people of this World. Matthew 5:16. **Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.**
4. Through an unyielding and unashamed confession of God’s Name. Psalm 119:46. **I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.**

Question. Why is this the first petition in order?
Answer. Because it is most fitting and most proper / that we desire the honor of God first and above all.

Question. Which is the second petition?
Answer. *Thy Kingdom come.*

Question. How manifold is the Kingdom of God?
Answer. Threefold.
1. There is an outward kingdom / or the means / which is the time of the preaching of the Gospel. Matthew 3:2. **Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.** Matthew 23:13.
2. An inward kingdom / or through the means / which is the work of God’s Spirit wrought through the Gospel in the hearts of men. Luke 17 verse 21. **Behold, the kingdom of God is within you.** This is called the Kingdom of grace.
3. An eternal Kingdom / or after the means / which is the Kingdom of Glory.

Question. For which Kingdom do you pray here that it may come?
Answer. I must exclude none of them / although primarily the last two Kingdoms are understood.

Question. What do you pray then in this petition, saying, *Thy Kingdom come*?
Answer. That the Kingdom of the Gospel may flourish through the whole world / and that the work of grace through the Gospel may be wrought in my heart / and finally that God may bring me to the eternal Kingdom of Glory.

Question. Which is the third petition?
Answer. *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.*

Question. Why is this petition placed after the second, namely / *Thy Kingdom come*?
Answer. To show that every natural man is useless and unfit to do God’s will; therefore it is necessary / that we first pray / that the Kingdom of His grace be established in our hearts / so that we may thus fulfill God’s will.

Question. How many things are to be noted in this petition?
Answer. Two things / 1. The matter for which is prayed. 2. The measure thereof; namely that it be done on earth / as in Heaven.

# 809
## Practical Theology.
<note>The original title "Werckige Godtgeleertheydt" refers to theology that is lived out through actions rather than just studied as theory—frequently called "Practical" or "Applied" Divinity.</note>

Question. In how many ways is God’s will distinguished?
Answer. In two ways / a hidden and a revealed will.
Question. What is the hidden will of God?
Answer. It is God’s eternal purpose and counsel regarding the outcomes of all things.
Question. What is the revealed will of God?
Answer. It is that part of God’s will / which is revealed to us in the Books of the Old and New Testaments.
Question. For which will do you pray that it may be done?
Answer. For the revealed will.
Question. Is it not a needless prayer to ask that God’s will be done, which no one can ever resist?
Answer. It is indeed true / that no one can resist the hidden will of God; for He can do whatever He pleases. But the revealed will of God is often resisted by men. Now, I do not pray that God should work out what He desires / but that I may bring about what He requires of me.
Question. What does it mean to do God’s will?
Answer. It is to show willing obedience to God’s commands with all our power. Exodus 24:7. <note>The source text cites Exodus 27:7, but the quote "All that the Lord has spoken, we will do and be obedient" is actually found in Exodus 24:7.</note> **All that the Lord hath spoken, will we do, and be obedient.**
Question. What do you ask of God in this petition?
Answer. That God would give me strength / to obediently follow His blessed will here on earth in everything / and to do so with faithfulness / cheerful willingness, and perseverance / just as the Angels do in Heaven.
Question. How do the Angels and the Saints do the will of God in Heaven?
Answer. Willingly / faithfully / swiftly / tirelessly, and perseveringly. Hebrews 1:14. **Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?** Psalm 103:20.
Question. Is this not an unnecessary prayer, since you seem to pray for impossible things when you ask that God’s will be done on earth as it is in Heaven?
Answer. No / for by this I show / that I must always strive for perfection in grace; so that my aim and end must be to live here on earth / as the Saints and the Angels in Heaven do: This is my desire. It is indeed true that while I am here on earth I cannot fulfill God’s will as perfectly as they do, but nevertheless my efforts can be of the same nature and essence / though not to such a high degree.
Question. Why does our Lord Christ say that we must do God’s will here on earth as it is done in Heaven? And not as it is done on earth by the holiest men among us?
Answer. Because there is no perfect example of obedience on earth; for even the best of men have many imperfections mixed in with their obedience.
Question. What do you learn from this, that you pray for God’s will to be done on earth as it is in Heaven?
Answer. 1. That I must be humble; since my works differ greatly from my prayer.
2. That I am imperfect in my obedience / as long as I live here on earth.

<column-break/>

3. That I must not be satisfied with small beginnings of grace / but that I must strive for more perfection / in order to live like the Saints.
Question. What is required of you to do the will of God?
Answer. 1. I must have a clear knowledge of His will / to know what He demands of me.
2. I must have a heart-felt acknowledgment / that His will in itself is good and righteous.
3. I must be fully convinced / that whatever God wills concerning me / that same thing is best for me / even if it seems ever so contrary or unpleasant to me.
Question. How many types of people do not fulfill God’s will?
Answer. 1. The ignorant do it not / for they do not know God’s will.
2. Worldly people will not do it / even though they know it.
3. The civilly-honest people do it not / for they do everything for their own profit and pleasure. <note>The "civilly-honest" (borgerlijck-eerlijcke) refers to those who are well-behaved by society's standards but lack true spiritual motivation.</note>
Question. Which evils conflict with this petition?
Answer. 1. Self-will <note>The Dutch "Eygensinnigheyt" implies stubbornness or following one's own mind instead of God's.</note>.
2. Attributing anything to the fickleness of fortune; so that one does not attribute all outcomes to God's will.
3. All kinds of grumbling and impatience under the pressing hand of God.
4. Willful obedience to the Devil’s will. John 8:44. **Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do.**
Question. How must you do God’s will?
Answer. 1. Wholly / and His entire will.
2. Faithfully / and nothing other than His will.
3. Willingly / without compulsion.
4. Patiently.
5. Continually.
Question. What is the fourth petition?
Answer. **Give us this day our daily bread.**
Question. What do you understand by "bread" here?
Answer. All that is necessary for the refreshment and maintenance of my natural body.
Question. What do you learn from the fact that you express all your outward needs through this word, "bread"?
Answer. 1. That bread is the primary means / to maintain natural life.
2. That if I had only bread / I must be satisfied with it.
Question. What do you learn from the first word of this petition, "give"?
Answer. 1. That every outward blessing I enjoy / is a free gift from God. James 1:17. **Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights.**
2. That I have no right in myself to what I possess / except only in Christ. Romans 8:32. **He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?** Hebrews 1:2.
Question. What do you learn from this, that you pray that God give "us" "our" bread?
Answer. By this is indicated: 1. That others have just as much right to my bread as I do myself. Therefore I do not say *my* bread / but *our* bread. 2. That I may not beg for another man’s bread. <note>This implies one should not covet or take what belongs to others, but work for their own while being willing to share.</note>
Question. What do you learn from this, that you pray for your "daily" bread?

# 810 The Marrow of...
<note>original: "Het Mergh van de..." This likely refers to "The Marrow of Divinity," a famous theological work by Edward Fisher that was popular in the 17th century.</note>

<margin>1 Thess. 5 verse 17. Pray without ceasing.</margin>
Answer 1. That I am obligated to pray every day.

2. That I must cast out from my heart all distrustful and anxious care for the time to come / and must only seek necessities for the present day / letting tomorrow care for itself.

Question. Why is this petition placed before the following one, since the first asks for temporal things, and the other for the forgiveness of sins, which is one of the chief blessings?

Answer 1. To show / that without proper provision for these outward needs, I am unfit for spiritual services / and therefore before God calls me to any service / He first makes me fit for it.

2. It points out to me / that my highest end / in praying for these internal graces / is that I might be made better fit for spiritual services.

Question. What distinction ought there to be between the seeking of temporal and spiritual things?

Answer. I must seek temporal things less primarily and with conditions / but spiritual things I must desire primarily / absolutely, and without ceasing.

Question. What then do you pray for from God in this petition?

Answer. That God will grant me all outward necessities / which are needed for this present life / and that it may please Him to continue with His gracious care for all outward things / which promote our life and godliness.

Question. Which is the fifth petition?

Answer. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

Question. How many things are to be noted in this fifth petition?

Answer. Two things / 1. The Grace / for which I pray / which is the forgiveness of sins. 2. The condition / upon which I pray for it / namely that I shall forgive others.

Question. Who forgives sin?

<margin>Micah 7 verse 18.</margin>
Answer. No Saints / nor Angels / nor the Pope / nor anyone else but God alone. > *Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage?* <note>original: "Wie is een Godt gelijck ghy..."</note>

Question. What is the forgiveness of sin?

<margin>Isaiah 43 verse 25.</margin>
Answer. It is a gracious act of God whereby He takes away the guilt and punishment of every sin from a justified person / not laying them to his charge unto damnation. > *I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.*
<margin>Psalm 51: verse 3. Psalm 32 verse 2.</margin>

Question. How does it happen that someone’s sins are forgiven?

<margin>Col. 1 verse 19, 20.</margin>
Answer. Not through any merits or worthiness / that are in man / but through the freeness of God’s love and grace / and through the fullness of Christ’s merits and satisfaction. > *For it pleased the Father that in him should all fullness dwell, and, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself.*
<margin>Eph. 1 v. 7.</margin>
> *In whom we have redemption through his blood, namely the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.*

Question. What do you desire from God in this petition?

<column-break/>

<margin>Psalm 51 v. 3.</margin>
Answer. That God would look down upon me in His Son Christ / and for His infinite worthiness and satisfaction forgive my sin / and not reckon it toward damnation. > *Be gracious unto me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: blot out my transgressions according to the multitude of thy tender mercies.*

Question. How could someone know whether their sins are forgiven or not?

<margin>Luke 7 verse 47.</margin>
Answer 1. In one whose sins are forgiven / there arises in his heart an'inflamed love for the Lord Jesus. > *Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.*

<margin>Psalm 32 verse 1, 2.</margin>
2. God gives him a spirit without guile: so the Lord God Himself describes a sinner / whose sins are forgiven. > *Blessed is the man whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered, and in whose spirit there is no guile.*
If you are upright in all your ends and aims, it is a sign / that your sins are forgiven.

3. He whose sins are forgiven / also feels even the smallest sin as a burden upon his soul / he would as willingly part with his hidden / pleasurable, and profitable evil / as a prisoner would wish to leave his heavy chains.

Question. What is the happiness of a person whose sin is forgiven?

Answer. 1. The natural enmity is taken away. God and the sinners who were once the greatest enemies / have become the dearest friends / once sin is forgiven.

2. They may take comfort in the midst of afflictions.

3. They are freed from the shackles and the condemning power of the Law.

Question. Which is the sixth petition?

Answer. Lead us not into temptation: but deliver us from evil.

Question. What is understood by the word temptation?

<margin>1 Thess. 3 v. 5. James 1 v. 14.</margin>
Answer. An evil movement suggested by Satan or our own heart / to move us toward sin.

Question. Since God tempts no one, is it not a needless prayer that God lead us not into temptation?

<margin>Deut. 8 v. 2.</margin>
Answer. It is true / God tempts no one / by advising or urging him to sin; nevertheless, God can be said to tempt us through testing / when He brings affliction upon us. > *And thou shalt remember all the way which the Lord thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.*
I pray then / that / when His pressing hand is upon me / or when He allows Satan to tempt me / He does not let me be overcome by the temptation.

Question. What do you require of God in this petition?

Answer. This I pray of the Lord God / that / when I am tempted / He does not let me struggle through my own strength / but that He grants me His assistance / to escape the temptations with which I shall be surrounded.

Question. What moves God to give people over to themselves, and so let them be overcome by the temptations of Satan?

Answer. 1. Our readiness / to accept the temptation / as soon as it is offered to us.
