# Practical Theology.

**Question. Has anyone besides Christ ever held these three offices?**
**Answer.** No; some were indeed Prophets and Kings, like David; others were Prophets and Priests, like Abraham; indeed, one was even King and Priest, namely Melchizedek <note>A mysterious figure from the Old Testament (Genesis 14) who serves as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ</note>, but never has anyone besides Christ been King, Priest, and Prophet all at once.
**Question. Why is Christ a Priest?**
**Answer.** To offer sacrifices and prayers for his people.
**Question. Which Sacrifice did Christ offer?**
**Answer.** Himself / that is / his human nature.
**Question. Every Sacrifice had to be offered by a Priest; who then was the Priest?**
**Answer.** Christ himself.
**Question. Every Sacrifice was offered upon the Altar; what then was the Altar upon which this Sacrifice took place?**
**Answer.** Christ, in respect to his Divinity, bore the humanity as the Altar; the Divine nature supported the human nature / to be a sacrifice for man's sin; so that you see from this / that Christ is the Altar / the Priest / and the sacrifice all at once.
**Question. What do you learn from the Priestly office of Christ?**
**Answer.** 1. That although there is no worthiness in my usual service to God / nevertheless Christ offers the same to his Father / and so I hope to be acceptable through his worthiness.
2. That I must never come to God / in my own name or worthiness.
3. That Christ is sensibly touched by all the weaknesses of his children. *Hebrews 4:15*. We do not have a high Priest who cannot have compassion for our weaknesses, but who in all things, just as we are, has been tempted, yet without sin.
4. That Christ makes reconciliation between God and my soul / *Hebrews 4:17*. He had to become like his Brothers in all things so that he might be a merciful and faithful high Priest, in the things that were to be done before God, to reconcile the sins of the people.
**Question. Why did Christ have to be a Prophet?**
**Answer.** So that he might teach his people.
**Question. Christ is indeed in Heaven, and his children are on earth; how then does he teach them?**
**Answer.** Christ teaches his children / 1. Through his Spirit. 2. Through his word.
**Question. How does the Spirit teach us?**
**Answer.** 1. By enlightening our understanding to His knowledge.
2. By inclining the hearts to His love.
3. By bending our will to His obedience.
**Question. What do you learn from this, that Christ is a Prophet?**
**Answer.** 1. That I must go to Christ to obtain knowledge / for he is the great Prophet.
2. That those who die in ignorance / have no right to Christ / for he teaches all his children from the least to the greatest.
**Question. What is Christ's Kingly office?**
**Answer.** It is that supreme power / which Jesus has over all creatures / through which he governs his Church by Laws according to his own will / and subdues his enemies / who do not want / him to rule over them.

<column-break/>

**Question. What do you learn from this, that Christ has this Kingly office?**
**Answer.** 1. That I must be led by all those laws / which Christ our King gives us. *Isaiah 33:22*.
2. That Christ is willing and powerful / to protect his entire Church.
3. That Christ shall trample all his enemies under his feet. *Revelation 19:15, 16*.
**Question. What must move people to seek the knowledge of Christ?**
**Answer.** 1. Because the knowledge of Christ is a most glorious knowledge: *Philippians 3:7, 8*. What was gain to me / that I have counted loss for Christ's sake / yes certainly / I also count all things to be loss / for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord; for whose sake I have counted all things as loss / and count them to be dung / so that I might win Christ.
2. Because eternal glory is joined to the knowledge of Jesus Christ. *John 17:3*. This is eternal life; that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.

Question. What must one do to remove this obstacle?

Answer. These three things. 1. One must consider that God is as just as He is merciful. 2. That His mercy in salvation is only promised to those who have repentance. Nahum 1:2, 3, 4. 3. There is no motive so strong in the world to persuade a man to conversion than this: that God is a merciful God. David made this use of God’s mercy: "With you is forgiveness, that you may be feared." Psalm 130:4.

Question. What is the second obstacle to Conversion?

Answer. An unfounded concern that the work of conversion will bring people into a sad, melancholy, and inconsolable way of life; that it will rob a person of their joy and pleasure.

Question. What must one do to take away this hindrance?

Answer. These five things. 1. Consider that conversion does indeed work a sorrow, but one that is godly, and of which you will never repent, as the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 7:9. 2. Conversion will indeed bring forth sorrow in you, but it will preserve you from sorrow in hell. 3. This sorrow, flowing from conversion, is the seed of joy. Matthew 5:4. "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." Psalm 126:6. <note>The original text cites Psalm 36:6, but the context of "sowing in tears" refers to Psalm 126:6.</note> 4. A repentant sinner, being sorrowful over his sins, has more inward, spiritual, and firm joy in his heart—even at the very time he weeps over his sin against God—than all the godless companions of the world have in their delights and lusts. 5. Conversion will not cut off your delight and pleasure, but it will guide and govern you in the use of them, so that they do not exceed their proper measure.

Question. What is the third obstacle to conversion?

Answer. The hope for a long life, thinking that they will certainly convert later on: this often withholds people from the necessary work of conversion.

Question. What must one do to take away this obstacle?

Answer. These things: 1. Consider that you are not assured of living as long as you hope.

2. Even if you lived that long, God might perhaps not give you the <term>means of grace</term> <note>External tools like preaching, scripture, and sacraments used by God to work in the heart.</note> to work conversion in your heart.

3. Even if God gave you the means of grace, God might perhaps give you over to hardness and an unconvertible state of heart; therefore you must convert today, so that God does not harden your heart tomorrow.

Question. What is the fourth obstacle to conversion?

Answer. A thought that conversion is unnecessary, or if it is not unnecessary, that it is very easy—that one can convert whenever one wishes.

Question. What must one do to take away this hindrance?

Answer. 1. Consider that if it is unnecessary to convert, it is also unnecessary to be saved, for without conversion you cannot be preserved. 2. That Christ commands it, Matthew 3:2. Now, Christ does not command unnecessary

<column-break/>

things. 3. That it is also not easy, since to convert oneself one must leave behind those sins which are as dear as the members of one's own body.

Question. What reasons are there to move people toward conversion?

Answer. 1. Eternal life is bound together with conversion.

2. Sinners have wronged God, who has never wronged them; therefore there is good reason to convert.

3. There is enough evil in sin to move people toward conversion, such as: 1. It is a filthy work. 2. It is a fruitless work. 4. It is a shameful work. Romans chapter 6, verse 21. It is a damning work.

Question. What motives are there to move people to conversion immediately?

Answer. 1. Consider the uncertainty of human life; one begins to die as soon as one begins to live.

2. God the Lord calls people to convert themselves immediately. Joel 2:12. "Turn now to me with your whole heart, and that with fasting and weeping."

3. If you do not convert immediately, you might provoke God to harden your heart, so that He would never give you the grace of conversion.

4. The faster you convert, the less unrest you shall have.

Question. Why should people convert in their youth, and not postpone conversion until old age?

Answer. Firstly, the motives can be taken from the youthful time of life, such as:

1. It is the most fit time for conversion.

2. They have the most reason to take the work of conversion in hand, as those who are subject to so many sins of youth which the elderly are not.

Answer. Secondly, the motives can be taken from old age, such as:

1. Consider that old age is an unfit time; are they not unfit for the work of conversion who are not fit to perform the work of their daily calling?

2. It is a very inconsolable time, for what comfort can an old person create when he has done the works of the Devil?

3. It is an ungrateful time—that one lets the Devil enjoy our strength and exhaust us, and then gives God the dried bones of old age.

4. It is a very dangerous time; it is a thousand to one that an old person converts: he has been used to sinning for so long that it becomes too difficult for him to leave it. Jeremiah 13:23.

Question. What means must I use to obtain a repentant heart?

Answer. 1. Go about searching and testing your heart and ways, to see in what you anger God and in what you have brought your souls. Lamentations 3:40. "Let us search and examine our ways, and let us return to the Lord." Jeremiah 8:6.

2. Earnestly ponder within yourself the evil nature of sin. Job 15:16. It makes you filthy before God the Lord, and it defiles all your <term>religious services</term>. <note>Original: "Godts-diensten." This refers to acts of worship, prayers, and church attendance.</note> Isaiah 1:13, 14. Titus 1:15.

3. Ponder in what a damnable state you are because of sin, and that conversion is highly necessary if you are to be saved.

<meta>This page continues the instructional dialogue on spiritual life, moving from the obstacles to conversion into a detailed examination of the nature, types, and signs of saving faith.</meta>

<page-num>824</page-num>
<header>The Marrow of the <note>original: "Het Mergh van de..." likely referring to "The Marrow of Modern Divinity" or a similar compendium of theology.</note></header>

Question. What are the signs of conversion?
Answer. 1. He who converts for the sake of salvation is more grieved by sin because it dishonors God than because it might bring him to hell.
2. He is deeply humbled by the sins he has committed and is carefully watchful to prevent sin in the future.
3. He sets himself against the most hidden, the smallest, and the most pleasurable and profitable sins.

->*Of Faith.*<-

Question. How is the word "faith" used in the Scriptures?
Answer. 1. Sometimes the word is used for the doctrine of faith; that is, for the Word which produces faith. Jude verse 3.
2. It is also used for that common work of faith which can also be found in the ungodly—namely, generally agreeing to the truth of the Scriptures. James 2:17, 18, 19.
3. It is used for 그 saving work of God in the hearts of the elect, whom God wishes to bring to eternal life and salvation; and so it is used here.
Question. Do all people have faith?
Answer. No; there are but few believers in the world. Isaiah 53:1; 2 Thessalonians 3:2; Romans 10:16. <note>The original cites 1 Thess. 3:2, but 2 Thess. 3:2 is the standard reference for "all men have not faith."</note>
Question. How many types of faith are there?
Answer. Four types. 1. A historical faith, by which someone generally agrees with and knows the history and truth of the Scripture.
2. A faith of miracles, by which people performed miracles, such as healing the sick if they only saw or touched the afflicted part, or casting out devils, etc.; this faith has now ceased.
3. A temporary faith, which is the common work of God’s Spirit, by which people make a superficial profession of love and agreement with the truth; but because they are not grounded in Christ through saving faith, they fall away when persecutions come. Matthew 13:20, 21.
4. A saving faith, which will be spoken of here.
Question. Of how many kinds is saving faith?
Answer. Twofold: 1. A special adhering faith, and 2. a special applied faith of assurance <note>original: "baerblijcklijckhept," meaning a manifest or evidentiary certainty</note>, which is the same as being fully assured.
Question. What distinction is there between these two kinds of faith?
Answer. 1. Every one of God’s elect has this adhering faith, but not all have the faith of assurance.
2. He who has the faith of assurance also knows that he believes; but he who has only the faith of adherence may not clearly know that he himself is a believer, and may thereby be comfortless and sorrowful.
Question. What is this faith of adherence?
Answer. It is a special grace of God’s Spirit, commonly wrought in the souls of the elect through the hearing of the preached word, whereby a sinner—seeing and feeling his sin and misery—is willing to receive Jesus Christ on those conditions upon which He is offered, expecting life and salvation through Him.
Question. On what conditions is a believer willing to receive Christ?

<column-break/>

Answer. 1. That he shall forsake sweet and pleasant sins for Christ’s sake.
2. That he shall serve Christ precisely.
3. That he shall endure heavy suffering for Christ’s sake. Now, an unbeliever cannot receive the Lord Jesus on such conditions.
Question. Who is the principal worker of this gift of grace?
Answer. God, through His Spirit. Ephesians 1:19, 20.
Question. What is the instrumental or mechanical cause of faith?
Answer. The preaching of the Gospel. Romans 10:16, 17.
Question. What gracious effects does believing have on the souls of those who possess it?
Answer. 1. Their souls are made firm in the midst of perils and difficulties. 2 Chronicles 20:20; Psalm 52:3 <note>The author likely intended a different Psalm or verse, as Psalm 52:3 discusses evil; however, the cross-reference to Psalm 108:1 points to a "fixed heart."</note> compared with Psalm 108:1; Isaiah 7:9.
2. Faith has a peace-making power upon the heart. Romans 15:13.
3. It has a soul-purifying power. Acts 15:9.
4. It has the power to overcome the world, 1 John 5:4, such as the pleasures, profits, and honors of this world. Hebrews 11:24.
Question. Are there no qualities and preparations that must precede faith?
Answer. If we take those preparations to be any kind of saving work, then there are none before faith, for faith is the "Mother grace." <note>A theological term implying that faith is the source from which all other Christian virtues (like love or hope) spring.</note> Now, just as no child can exist before its mother, so no grace can exist without or before faith. Nevertheless, there are common workings of God’s Spirit that God usually works in people before they believe, such as:
1. God gives them a sight of sin.
2. He gives them a feeling of sin and of the misery resulting from sin.
3. God convinces them that there is in them an utter inability to deliver themselves from this misery.
4. God convinces them that Christ alone can do it. Now, these are not saving workings, but can also be found in a reprobate; however, God is accustomed to bring people to Christ along this path. To insist upon 1. the absolute necessity of these preparations, 2. the exact degree of them, or 3. the length of time they remain in the soul, is not useful.
Question. What are the marks of saving faith?
Answer. 1. He who has this faith is willing to receive the Lord Jesus on the aforementioned conditions. John 1:12.
2. The more faith someone has, the more it makes them holy, and the more the fruits of faith will shine in their conduct.
3. True faith causes the hearts of men to be inflamed with love for God and for His people. Galatians 5:6.
4. He who has this faith overcomes the world. 1 John 5:4.
Question. What obstacles keep people from believing?
Answer. 1. Ignorance of their own worthlessness and misery, and of Christ’s glory and excellence.
2. Because they do not have the preaching of the Gospel in power, which is the usual means to work faith in men. Romans 10:16.

<meta>catchword: 3. Thinking,</meta>

<summary>This page defines the nature of saving faith, distinguishing it from historical or temporary belief, and outlines the "conditions" of following Christ. It also explains the "common workings" of the Spirit that prepare a soul for faith without being the cause of salvation itself.</summary>
<keywords>saving faith, conversion, assurance, elect, preaching of the Gospel, Mother grace, obstacles to faith, historical faith</keywords>

--- Page 849 ---
<meta>This page continues a series of questions and answers regarding the nature of faith, specifically focusing on how true saving faith is obtained, how it differs from false faith, and the nature of spiritual assurance. It concludes by introducing the doctrine of Election.</meta>

<page-num>824</page-num>
<header>Practical Theology <note>original: "Werkige Godtgeleertheyt." This refers to "practical divinity," the branch of theology focused on how one lives out their faith and experiences God’s grace in daily life.</note></header>

3. Thinking that it is a light matter to believe; for alas, the very same power that God used to raise Christ from the dead must be used to work faith in the hearts of men. Ephesians 1:19.

**Question.** What means must one use to obtain faith?

**Answer.** 1. Seek to be convinced of the *possibility* of faith—that you *may* believe—and of the *necessity* of faith—that you *must* believe.

2. Seek to be convinced of your damnable state in yourself, and that you cannot be your own Savior; then let your souls reach out to the Lord Jesus, that He may do for you what you cannot do for yourself.

3. Diligently use the established means of worship which God has ordained to work faith in your heart through them. Romans 10:17.

**Question.** By what marks does one recognize a false faith?

**Answer.** 1. It is a false faith that is obtained without effort. 2. Which is kept without care. 3. Which endures without temptations. 4. Which remains firm without holiness. 5. Which is not mixed with <term>godly jealousy</term> <note>A holy concern or protective watchfulness over one's spiritual state.</note> and humility.

**Question.** What is the faith of manifestation, or this assurance?

**Answer.** It is a gracious work of God’s Spirit, through which a believer knows on certain and infallible grounds that he believes, and that he may apply the merits of Jesus Christ to his soul for his salvation.

**Question.** What are the acts of Faith?

**Answer.** 1. There is an act of faith that goes straight out, through which one beholds Christ alone for salvation. <note>Often called the "direct act" of faith, focusing entirely on the object—Christ.</note>

2. There is a reflective act of faith, through which one not only beholds Christ as a Savior of mankind, but also looks back upon oneself, and knows and believes that Christ is *his* Savior.

**Question.** Do believers always have this assurance?

**Answer.** No; Job sometimes did not have it. Job 13:24. So also David in Psalm 42:6, 12. Furthermore, if believers always had this assurance, it would follow that whoever doubted his salvation would be lost; thus we would disadvantage the righteous and make them despondent.

**Question.** What distinction is there between this saving assurance in the heart of a godly person, and the delusive imagination in the hearts of hypocrites?

**Answer.** 1. Someone who has this assurance bases his comfort on clear Scriptural texts, but a deluded person builds his comfort on the deceits of his own heart.

2. He who has assurance is in great fear of losing it, and he takes great pains to preserve it, but a delusive imagination is never mixed with jealousy and concern.

3. He who has assurance often searches and tests his heart to know if it is upright and if his signs are good, but a deluded person cannot bring himself to look through his heart or test his ways.

<column-break/>

4. He who has assurance is often tempted and tormented by Satan, but a deluded sinner is left alone by the devil and rocked to sleep; he lets him go on with a firm imagination of Heaven until he is cast down into hell.

**Question.** What particular effects flow from assurance?

**Answer.** 1. It fills a person’s spirit with an unspeakable joy. 1 Peter 1:8; Romans 15:13.

2. It causes people to perform all their worship with cheerfulness, willingness, and fervor.

3. It fills people with gratitude and rejoicing in the grace and goodness of God.

**Question.** What obstacles keep a believer from assurance?

**Answer.** 1. A thought that one must not be assured until he is as deeply humbled, for as long a time, and in as great a measure as he thinks he must be before reaching such a step of grace. Such spiritual mistakes as these keep a person from assurance.

2. Neglect of proper examination: for if so many people would look into their hearts, they would read clear marks therein, and infallibly conclude their eternal well-being from them.

3. Living according to present feelings; because they do not feel that warmth of affections, that brokenness of spirit, and outpouring of the heart, they therefore do not dare to be assured.

4. Allowing some hidden sin to dwell in the soul with consent and pleasure. Oh! Sin is like wind in the bowels of the earth which causes an earthquake; so also sin, when it is fostered in the soul, causes a "heart-quake"—it makes a man’s faith waver, it erases his marks, and breaks his peace.

**Question.** What means are there to obtain assurance?

**Answer.** 1. You must search your heart impartially.

2. You must prize the evidences of faith above your present feelings.

3. Keep your conscience free from fondling or maintaining any sin.

---

->*Of Election.*<-

**Question.** What is election?

**Answer.** It is a decree or purpose of God, through which He has chosen certain people, men and women, out of the human race for salvation.

**Question.** What are the properties of Election?

**Answer.** 1. It is a voluntary and singular act of God’s grace.

2. It is from eternity, before the foundation of the world. Ephesians 1:4.

3. It is unchangeable; none of the elect can be lost, and no one can be saved who is not elected.

**Question.** Does God elect anyone because of the foreseen good that will be wrought in them?

**Answer.** No: but solely according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the glory of His grace. Ephesians 1 verses 4, 5.

<meta>This page continues the "Practical Theology" instruction from the previous page, transitioning from the nature of faith into the specific doctrines of Election and Justification. <page-num>826</page-num>
<header>The Pith of the <note>original: "Het Mergh van de." This likely refers to the "Marrow of Divinity," a popular way of describing the essential core of Christian doctrine.</note></header>

**Question.** Can anyone in this life be certain of their election?
**Answer.** Yes. 1 Thess. 1:4; Eph. 1:3, 4, 5; 2 Pet. 1:10.
**Question.** Can someone truly be chosen and then later be lost?
**Answer.** No. 2 Tim. 2:19; John 6:37, 39; 2 Thess. 3:3; Rom. 11:1.
**Question.** But does it not say of Judas in John 6:70, *Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?* It seems then that someone can be one of God's chosen and yet ultimately be damned?
**Answer.** There are two kinds of election: one to a temporal office, and another to eternal glory. In the first sense, Judas is said to be chosen for a temporal office, but he was not chosen for eternal life.
**Question.** What are the likely signs of people who are *not* Elect?
**Answer.** 1. Such are not chosen who fall away from the confession of religion without ever returning. Heb. 10:38, 39.
2. Such who are given over to impenitence and hardness of heart until the end. Matt. 13:14, 15; John 12:40.
3. Such who live and die in opposition to God’s word. 2 Chron. 25:16; Acts 13:46, 48, 49.
4. Such who commit the sin against the Holy Spirit. Matt. 12:23; 1 John 5:16.
**Question.** Does the doctrine of election not make people negligent and careless in their lives, causing them to cry out: "If I am to be saved, I shall be saved, even if I live as I please, for God's election will stand firm"?
**Answer.** When God has chosen someone for such an end, He has also simultaneously decreed the use of the means serving that end. If God has chosen someone for eternal life, He has also decreed that they shall walk holily in order to reach that end. Now, just as God’s decree does not make people careless or negligent regarding the use of means in temporal matters, so it is also in spiritual matters. Although God has decreed how long I shall live, I do not therefore neglect to feed myself when I am hungry, nor do I fail to use medicine when I am sick to preserve my life. So it is also in spiritual things.

->Of Justification.<-

**Question.** What is Justification?
**Answer.** It is an act of God by which He freely remits the guilt and punishment of sin for the sinner and accepts him as perfect in His Son.
**Question.** By whom are we justified?
**Answer.** By Jesus Christ.
**Question.** Through what are we justified?
**Answer.** Through faith.
**Question.** Why are we justified?
**Answer.** Because of His free Grace.
**Question.** To what end?
**Answer.** To show the prize of His grace.
**Question.** Which is the working <term>Efficient</term> Cause?
**Answer.** God.
**Question.** Which is the <term>Instrumental</term> Cause? <note>The original text repeats "Werckende Oorsaeck" (Working/Efficient Cause) twice, but in systematic theology, the second refers to the instrument through which grace is received.</note>
**Answer.** Faith.
**Question.** Which is the <term>Meritorious</term> Cause?
**Answer.** The merits of Jesus Christ.
**Question.** Which is the <term>Material</term> Cause? <note>The "matter" or basis upon which the justification rests.</note>
**Answer.** Christ’s righteousness imputed to us.

<column-break/>

**Question.** Which is the <term>Formal</term> Cause of justification? <note>The "form" or essence that makes the justification what it is.</note>
**Answer.** The forgiveness of sins.
**Question.** Which is the <term>Final</term> Cause? <note>The ultimate purpose or goal.</note>
**Answer.** The glorification of God.
**Question.** What is the difference between Justification and Sanctification?
**Answer.** 1. Sanctification is a work of God *inside* the soul, but justification is a work of God *outside* the soul. <note>Justification is viewed as a legal or "forensic" declaration by God, while sanctification is the internal moral change.</note>
2. All are equally justified, but not all are equally sanctified.
3. Justification takes away the guilt of sin, but sanctification takes away the filth of sin.
**Question.** How would you reconcile those places in Scripture where one says we are justified by Christ’s blood, another by faith, and a third by good works?
**Answer.** We are justified by the blood of Christ before God’s face; by faith in respect to our souls; and by good works to demonstrate before men that we are justified.
**Question.** Are we not justified by works, since you say we are justified by faith? Is faith not a good work?
**Answer.** We are not justified by faith insofar as it is a good work, but insofar as it is an *instrument* through which Christ justifies us.
**Question.** But does the Scripture not say that we are justified by good works? For it says in Luke 7:47, *Her sins, which were many, are forgiven; for she loved much.* Are good works then not a cause of justification?
**Answer.** The word "for" <note>original: "want." The author is discussing the Greek word *hoti*, which can mean "because" (causal) or "since/evidenced by" (demonstrative).</note> is taken in two ways: either as a cause (2 Tim. 3:2) or as a sign of something. So it is here: as a sign of her justification. Because she loved much, her love was a sign of her justification. Thus, when you read "for" after a sin, it is taken as the cause of that thing; but when you read it after something good, it is taken as a sign of a thing.
**Question.** The godless are damned for their evil works; why then are we not saved for good works?
**Answer.** They are damned for those evil works insofar as they are their own; but I cannot be saved by good works, insofar as they are not mine but Christ’s. And also, there are enough "merits" in evil works to damn them, but no merits of my own are sufficient to make me saved.
**Question.** What is required in a work to make it meritorious?
**Answer.** 1. It must not be a mandatory duty; therefore, good works cannot merit anything because one cannot even do all that one is already bound to do.
2. The work must be perfect, but our good works are altogether imperfect.
3. It must be your own; therefore, good works cannot merit anything because our virtues are not our own, but the gift of God.
**Question.** Can anyone who is once justified ever fall away from their righteousness?
**Answer.** No: For God is unchangeable.

<summary>This page uses a question-and-answer format to define the doctrines of Election and Justification, emphasizing that salvation is a fixed decree of God and that good works are the evidence (sign) of salvation rather than the cause of it.</summary>
<keywords>election, justification, sanctification, Judas Iscariot, free grace, merits of Christ, instrumental cause, perseverance of the saints</keywords>

<page-num>827</page-num>
<header>Practical Theology.</header>

### Of the Sacraments.

**Question.** What is a Sacrament?
**Answer.** It is a holy sign, instituted by Christ, to show us a holy seal; to confirm to us a holy instrument <note>original: "werck-tuyg," meaning a tool or means through which God works</note>; to bring Christ with all his merits and graces to us who believe in him.
**Question.** How many Sacraments are there?
**Answer.** Two: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
**Question.** Why do you receive the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper many times, and yet you are baptized only once?
**Answer.** The Sacrament of Baptism is but an invitation and an ingrafting into Christ, but the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper is for our strengthening and growth in Christ. Now, I am born only once, but I am fed every day.
**Question.** What difference is there between a Sacrament and a Sacrifice?
**Answer.** In a Sacrifice, something is offered to God, but in a Sacrament, everything is given to us.
**Question.** What does this word *Sacrament* mean?
**Answer.** An oath or vow, such as soldiers make when going into war to their commanders, that they will serve them alone and no other; so we also swear in every Sacrament to the Lord Jesus that we will serve him, and him alone. <note>The author is referencing the Latin word *sacramentum*, which originally referred to a Roman soldier's oath of allegiance.</note>
**Question.** Why is it called the Lord's Supper?
**Answer.** 1. Because the Lord Jesus instituted it just after the Passover Supper.

<column-break/>

2. Because this Sacrament has some resemblance to a Supper: just as here is the Lord of the Feast, that is, Jesus Christ; here is food and refreshment, that is, the body and blood of Christ; here is a hand and mouth to receive that food, that is, faith. Here are also the guests, that is, the believers; and here is the effect of this food, namely, growth.
**Question.** Why must you receive this Supper many times?
<margin>Luke 22:19</margin>
**Answer.** 1. Because Christ has commanded me to do so, Luke 22.
2. Because this is the way of doing things for true Christians.
3. Because I daily feel many failings and weaknesses in myself, therefore I must necessarily come to this Sacrament many times.
**Question.** What benefits and purposes are there for this Sacrament?
**Answer.** 1. It is a renewal of my covenant; just as we take him to be ours, so we bind ourselves to be his.
2. It is a confirmation of our faith: Christ places himself into our hands in every Sacrament, so that we should believe in him.
3. It also occurs to set the death of Christ before our eyes; Christ is there, as it were, hanging on the cross and lying in his blood, and then I must think of my cursed sins, which caused him this death.
4. To draw us up to gratitude because of his great love toward us.
5. To get strength against my strong corruptions.
6. To strengthen those graces that are weak.
